# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 68

**Complete Course of Patrology**, or universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all monuments of Catholic tradition produced during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and most carefully corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual biblical texts and in what places of their works. A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form, are taken into consideration.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin for 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 548

## Saint Leo, Bishop of Sens

[Col. 0009]

## Notice (from Gallandius)

[Col. 0009A] I. Very little is known from written records about Saint Leo, bishop of Sens. There exists a letter of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, addressed to three bishops—Heraclius, Leo, and Theodosius—concerning a certain priest named Claudius, in whose case he complains that he had been disregarded by them. After Sirmondus [Note: [Col. 0009D] Sirmondus, *Gallican Councils*, vol. I, p. 204.] and Cointius [Note: [Col. 0009D] Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, under the year 512, § 2.], we arranged for it to be printed elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0009D] *Library of the Fathers*, vol. X, p. 805.]. Of those three bishops, Cointius [Note: [Col. 0009D] Cointius, cited work, p. 293.] does not doubt that two held episcopal office in the province of Fourth Lyons: Heraclius at Paris and Theodosius at Auxerre. They were present at the First Council of Orléans, convened in the year of our Lord 511; consequently, the third appears to have been our Leo of Sens, metropolitan of the same province.

Remigius wrote this letter after the death of King Clovis, who, he says, was “not only a preacher of the Catholic faith, but also its defender.” Clovis died toward the end of 511, shortly after the dissolution of the aforementioned First Council of Orléans, as Adrian Valesius [Note: [Col. 0009D] Adrian Valesius, *Frankish History*, book VI, vol. I, pp. 313 ff.] and Cointius [Note: [Col. 0009D] Cointius, cited work, under the year 511, § 52.] report from ancient records. Thus Remigius’s letter was written, at the very latest, in 512, and not in 510, as Papebrochius says [Note: [Col. 0009D] Papebrochius, *Acts of the Saints*, April, vol. III, p. 31, no. 2.].

II. From what has been said, we understand that Leo already occupied the see of Sens in that year, 512. What distinguished him thereafter in the governance of his diocese is preserved in only one account: namely, that he won for Christ the people of Melun, who had not yet been fully converted, through Saint Aspasius, bishop of Auxerre. This is read in the Sens breviary on 22 April, from which the oft-cited Cointius copied it [Note: [Col. 0009D] Cointius, cited work, under the year 538, § 71.].

Moreover, through the priest Orbat, Leo took part in the Second Council of Orléans. That it was held in the twenty-second year of King Childebert—namely, in the year of Christ 533—is confirmed by the subscription of Honoratus, metropolitan bishop of Bourges. This is shown, after Valesius [Note: [Col. 0010D] Adrian Valesius, cited work, p. 379.], by Cointius [Note: [Col. 0010D] Cointius, cited work, under the year 533, § 35.], Pagius [Note: [Col. 0010D] Pagius, under the year 536, § 17.] and the authors of the *Literary History of France* [Note: [Col. 0010D] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 244.].

On this point there are two errors in Papebrochius [Note: [Col. 0010D] Papebrochius, cited work.]: first, that Optatus is named instead of Orbat; second, that the council is said to have been held in the year of Christ 531. Since Clovis died in 511, as we have seen above, the twenty-second year of Childebert, his successor, brings us to 533.

III. Leo, who attended the Second Council of Orléans through his representative, attended the Third in person. This council was convened, according to the subscription of Lupus, metropolitan bishop of the province of First Lyons, on the Nones of the third month—that is, on 7 May—in the twenty-seventh year of King Childebert, namely in the year of Christ 538, as the writers cited above, Valesius [Note: [Col. 0010D] Adrian Valesius, cited work, p. 478.], Cointius [Note: [Col. 0010D] Cointius, cited work, under the year 538, §§ 60, 61, 66.] and Pagius [Note: [Col. 0010D] Pagius, under the year 540, § 6.] report. Papebrochius must again be corrected, since he assigns this synod to the year 536.

Yet the holy bishop did not take part in the Fourth Council of Orléans, held three years after the Third, as is clear from its canon 27, where we read: “If anyone, after the council of Orléans established three years before this...” The council was therefore held in the thirtieth year of King Childebert, and in the year of Christ 541.

Cointius discusses this matter more fully [Note: [Col. 0010D] Cointius, cited work, under the year 541, § 2 ff.] and also gives the reason [Note: [Col. 0010D] The same author, ibid., § 71.] why our bishop of Sens was absent from that council: namely, the disagreement between him and King Childebert, because he was vigorously defending the rights of his Church. The matter is made clear by his letter to the same king, which we have published.

From it we understand that the metropolitan city of Sens was under the dominion of King Theudebert, whereas Melun, although subject to that metropolitan see, obeyed not Theudebert himself but his uncle Childebert. When, therefore, Childebert attempted to establish an episcopal see at Melun, Leo of Sens, the metropolitan, resisted, since that stronghold still belonged to the diocese of Sens. Consequently, King Childebert, having found Leo to be a most determined defender of his rights, would permit neither the bishop himself nor a visitor in his name to come to Melun. [Col. 0011A] Hence Leo’s letter, in which he begs the king not to create a new bishop at Melun—that is, in a parish of his diocese—where there had never previously been one.

IV. In what year the letter was written is not entirely known. Since Leo says in it that he is old and infirm, he does not appear to have survived long after 541. Certainly Leo’s successor, Constitutus, from the province of Fourth Lyons, took part in the Fifth Council of Orléans. From the subscription of Sacerdos, bishop of the province of First Lyons, it is clear that the council was held on 28 October in the thirty-eighth year of the reign of King Childebert, that is, in the year of Christ 549 [Note: [Col. 0011A] Cointius, cited work, under the year 549, §§ 21, 47.]. Adrian Valesius agrees [Note: [Col. 0011A] Adrian Valesius, cited work, p. 478.].

Accordingly, Papebrochius’s date must once again be rejected, since he assigns this council to the year 547 [Note: [Col. 0012A] Papebrochius, cited work, no. 4.]. The memory of Saint Leo of Sens is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 22 April. In the breviary of the Church of Sens, however, as the often-mentioned Cointius reports [Note: [Col. 0012A] Cointius, cited work, under the year 541, § 71.], the following is read on the same day:

> Having worthily fulfilled the episcopal office and obtained eternal rewards, he was buried in the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius in the suburb of Sens. At his invocation God worked many cures of the sick and many miracles. Thus it came about that, when that church became a parish church, it was thereafter called by the name of Saint Leo himself.

## Letter of Saint Leo of Sens to Childebert, King of the Franks (C)

[Col. 0011]

[Col. 0011B] To the illustrious lord and son in Christ, King Childebert: Leo, bishop.

I declare that I have received the letter of Your Highness with the honor that is due to it. In it Your Highness deigns to hope that, for the ordination of a bishop at Melun, our presence or our consent ought to be given. Let Your Glory know that we have been greatly astonished that, without the command of our most glorious lord and prince, your son King Theudebert, under whose royal administration we are subject, you enjoin that what was not done in former times should now be begun with our presence or consent.

Above all, we could never have suspected or believed that you would wish to inflict upon our order, or even upon your own times, such an injury as to allow our diocese, entrusted to us by God and until now, by God’s favor, guarded in episcopal order, to pass into another’s power as though we were negligent and sluggish, or to transfer its administration through an unreasonable decision. Therefore, greeting you with the worthy and dutiful affection of charity in God, we beg and solemnly urge you not to allow any bishop to act against the decrees of the Fathers, lest he be convicted in synodal judgment and condemned for unlawful presumption.

Nevertheless, by God’s inspiration, those things ought to be accomplished in your time that can preserve peace among the priests and prevent the people from being torn away from the care of their own shepherd through a new and illicit ordination. Please observe the decrees of the Fathers, and, bound by the strictness of the canons, do not allow, as you write, another bishop to be ordained at the request of that people while their own priest is still alive. For if they ask for what it is impious to believe they desire, they should be judged deserters rather than faithful. The prayers of those whose petitions would produce scandals rather than preserve the peace beloved by God ought not easily to be heard by a ruler. For just as blessed are the feet of those who bring peace, so woe is pronounced upon those through whom scandal comes.

If perhaps they ask to have another bishop appointed for themselves because, with the roads closed, we can neither send them a visitor nor go to them, that fault does not concern us. For if the route from your side had not been closed for so long, as you know very well, then, even though old or infirm, we could have visited the people entrusted to us by ecclesiastical discipline, or at least sent a visitor, as the canons prescribe.

Your Glory ought both to believe and to know very clearly that, if any bishop should wish to ordain a bishop at Melun contrary to the decrees of the canons and without our consent, then, until the matter reaches the knowledge of the pope or a synodal hearing, both those who ordain and the one who is ordained will be separated from our communion.

Leo, servant of Christ, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0011C] From Cointius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. I, p. 604, and also from the appendix to the works of Saint Gregory, bishop of Tours, edited by Ruinart, p. 1328.]

# In the Year of Our Lord 550

## Junilius, African Bishop

[Col. 0011]

## Notice (from Gallandius)

[Col. 0011C] I. Junilius is commonly regarded by recent writers as bishop of an unidentified city in Africa, although, so far as I know, no mention of his episcopal dignity exists among ancient authors. Indeed, if one follows Fabricius [Note: [Col. 0013D] Fabricius, *Medieval Library*, vol. IV, p. 600.], some assert that he was bishop of Utica, others that he was bishop of Hadrumetum. Here I certainly miss Fabricius’s customary diligence: with Labbeus before his eyes, he took from what Labbeus wrote about Primasius [Note: [Col. 0013D] Labbeus, *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 663.]—of whom I shall shortly speak—and applied it himself to Junilius.

The reason I still hesitate over whether Junilius was ever a bishop is Junilius himself. In the preface to his work, addressing Primasius, he calls him twice “venerable Father” and also mentions his “most reverend fellow bishops.” Someone might therefore conclude that Junilius would hardly have used this manner of speaking if he himself had been honored with the same dignity.

Moreover, our author is nowhere said to have attended the African synods, although several were convened during that period. “But suppose,” you will say, “that at the time when he wrote and dedicated his little work to Primasius he was not a bishop. What prevents his being raised to that dignity afterward? What if he called Primasius ‘Father’ because of his venerable gray hair, while he himself was younger both in age and in the acquisition of his see? What if Junilius’s name is not found among the signatures of certain African councils because illness or some other serious impediment detained him?”

To this may be added the authority of the manuscripts, in which it is reasonable to believe that the title “bishop” was prefixed to the work of our Junilius. I would not oppose these arguments if the common opinion rested on more reliable evidence. However the matter may stand, I do not begrudge Junilius the honor of the episcopate.

II. Junilius is said by Sixtus of Siena [Note: [Col. 0013D] Sixtus of Siena, *Holy Library*, book IV, vol. I, p. 429, new edition, Naples.] to have been educated in the liberal arts in the world and highly skilled in the Holy Scriptures, concise in expression and penetrating in thought. Cassiodorus lists him among the introductory writers on Scripture [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cassiodorus, *On the Institution of Divine Letters*, chapter 10.].

For this author wrote two books *On the Parts of the Divine Law*, in which he gives rules of great usefulness for learning and understanding the sacred writings. He testifies that he received these rules [Note: [Col. 0013D] Junilius, preface, below, col. 15.] from a certain Paul, a Persian by origin, who had been taught in the school of the Syrians in the city of Nisibis.

Senator mentions this school [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cassiodorus, cited work, at the beginning of the preface.] and states that it was diligently cultivated by the Hebrews. To illuminate that passage of Senator, Garetius, the distinguished editor of his works, cites the testimony of Junilius that we have just mentioned.

Brasichellus warned that certain passages in this work of Junilius should be read cautiously [Note: [Col. 0013D] Brasichellus, *Index of Purged Books*, vol. I, p. 57.]. Simonius attacks the author of this little book more sharply [Note: [Col. 0013D] Simonius, *Critique of the Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. I, p. 229, and vol. III, p. 32.], though later treating him more mildly and judging that his little work had been corrupted.

For, he says, it is not permissible to suppose that an African bishop placed not only certain deuterocanonical books but even protocanonical books outside the canon of Sacred Scripture [Note: [Col. 0013D] Junilius, below, col. 15.], and thus was ignorant both of what the African councils had decreed on this matter—the Council of Hippo, held in 393, canon 38, and the Third Council of Carthage, held in 397, canon 47—and especially of what Saint Augustine taught according to the judgment of the Church, presenting in condensed form the decrees of the preceding councils [Note: [Col. 0014D] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 8.].

Martianaeus likewise does not spare Junilius in his learned *Historical Treatise on the Canon of the Books of Sacred Scripture*, published in French at Paris in 1704 [Note: [Col. 0014D] Martianaeus, *Historical Treatise on the Canon of the Books of Holy Scripture*, pp. 204 ff.], a work certainly worthy of careful reading.

III. This African bishop found an eager student—Greek: **σπουδαστήν**, “student” or “devotee”—in the Englishman Leonard Twells. While preparing his *Vindication of the Divine Authority of the Apocalypse* against the anonymous author of a *Historical and Critical Dissertation on the Apocalypse*, who had claimed Junilius for his own position, Twells wrote:

> The author of the dissertation ought to have known that Junilius, in his book, presents not his own opinions but those of a certain Paul the Persian, whose rules of Christian instruction he translated and set forth in the form of a dialogue.... Junilius could therefore favor the Council of Carthage, even though that Paul the Persian had doubted the canonicity of certain books.

Twells’s *Vindication*, published in English at London in 1732, was considered worthy by Wolfius of being included in his *Philological and Critical Observations* [Note: [Col. 0014D] Wolfius, *Philological and Critical Observations*, vol. V, p. 427.].

Had Humphrey Hody published his work *On the Original Texts of the Bible* after the *Vindication* of his fellow countryman Twells—or, rather, had he not neglected to read either the censures of Simonius or those of Martianaeus written against Junilius’s little book—perhaps he would have ceased forcing this African bishop upon us as one of the Latin Church’s writers who compiled catalogues of the sacred books [Note: [Col. 0014D] Humphrey Hody, *On the Original Texts of the Bible*, p. 652.].

IV. Junilius dedicated his little work to Primasius, bishop of Hadrumetum, or Justinianopolis, who in 555 subscribed to the Constitutum of Pope Vigilius concerning the Three Chapters.

I am certainly surprised that Labbeus hesitated over the see of Primasius, whom, he says, some consider to have been bishop of Utica and others bishop of Hadrumetum. Fabricius, however, wrongly calls the same bishop “Justinianopolitan in Africa” more than once [Note: [Col. 0014D] Fabricius, *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, chapter 5, p. 255, § 16, and *Medieval Latin Library*, vol. IV, p. 600.]. For what has Justinianopolis to do with Africa?

Both writers must therefore be corrected from the subscription of the bishop himself, which is given in the acts of the councils as follows [Note: [Col. 0014D] *Councils*, vol. V, p. 1358, first Venetian edition of Labbeus]:

> I, Primasius, by the grace of God bishop of the city of Hadrumetum, which is also called Justinianopolis, of the Council of Byzacena, consenting to this Constitutum which the blessed Pope Vigilius issued concerning the Three Chapters, have subscribed.

Junilius’s work was first published at Basel in 1546 under the care of Johann Gastius and was subsequently printed many times. Fabricius, cited above, lists its various editions after Cave [Note: [Col. 0014D] Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, p. 526.].

We have preferred the edition printed in the Paris Library of the Fathers in 1644 [Note: [Col. 0015A] *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, vol. I, p. 1.], which is more accurate than the others, and we have also illustrated it in places with notes. To these, if you please, add Fabricius’s correction [Col. 0016A] of book II, chapter 29 [Note: [Col. 0015A] Junilius, below, col. 42.], where he judges that *testificatio* should be read instead of *rectificatio* [Note: [Col. 0016A] Fabricius, cited works.].

# Two Books of Junilius *On the Parts of the Divine Law* (C, S)

[Col. 0015]

[Col. 0015B] To the holy and most blessed Bishop Primasius, Junilius sends greetings.

You yourself know, venerable Father Primasius, that, being conscious of my life and purpose, just as I do not deny that I devote myself to the study of the divine law, so I do not presume to call myself a teacher. I fear the prophetic saying:

> But to the sinner God said: “Why do you recount my justifications and take up my covenant upon your lips?” (Psalm 49:16).

Yet when the usefulness of a foreign province had compelled you to travel as far as Constantinople with your other most reverend fellow bishops, we came, through our affection for the city, to know one another and to converse. In your customary manner, however, you first asked whether there was among the Greeks anyone who burned with zeal for the study and understanding of the divine books.

I replied that I had seen a certain man named Paul, a Persian by origin, who had been taught in the school of the Syrians in the city of Nisibis, where the divine law is taught by public teachers in an orderly and regular manner, just as grammar and rhetoric are taught among us in secular studies.

When you had long pressed me to say whether I possessed anything from his teachings, I said that I had read certain rules by which he used to imbue the minds of his pupils, who had been instructed in the surface of the divine Scriptures, before he disclosed the depths of their interpretation. In this way they might meanwhile learn the purpose and order of the matters treated in the divine law, so that they would learn each thing systematically rather than in a scattered and confused manner.

You, Father, judged these matters necessary for all Christians who wished to be educated, by some means unknown to me, and compelled me for a long time—even to the point of shameless self-defense—to undertake the task. Consequently, I collected these regular principles into two very brief books, adding, as far as I could, a useful form of presentation, so that each point might be stated briefly and transparently, as though pupils were asking questions and a teacher were answering.

And so that no confusion might arise through the negligence of copyists, as commonly happens, I placed the Greek letter **Μ** before the Teacher and **Δ** before the Pupils, so that all error might be completely removed by these foreign characters, which Latin writing does not use [Note: [Col. 0015C] We have used Latin characters. EDITOR.].

There are other notable works by that man. I also heard him expound the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Romans more subtly, as I believe. I took it down from his lips so that it would not slip from my memory, but the thorns of cares and affairs prevent us from producing any fruit in the Lord’s field.

This single act of presumption is enough: from acknowledged poverty, I dare to cast these two little coins into the divine treasury. There are those who heap up talents from which they may distribute to the needy; they can offer to the divine shrines gems of virtue, gold of life, and silver of knowledge.

I possess nothing beyond these two little coins [Luke 21:2], and even these were lent to me by another. Yet I promise myself much from the Gospel’s examiner: although others can give precious things from their riches and more from their abundance, I, because I have given everything, have offered more.

Farewell.

# Book One

## Chapter One

[Col. 0015D]

**P.** Into how many primary parts is knowledge of the divine law divided?

**T.** Into two. One concerns the actual surface of the wording; the other concerns the matters which Scripture itself teaches us.

## Chapter II. What Concerns the Surface of the Scriptures

**P.** How many things belong properly to the surface of the wording?

**T.** Five: the kind of expression, authority, author, manner, and order.

**P.** How many kinds of expression are there?

**T.** Four. For it is either historical, prophetic, proverbial, or simply instructional.

## Chapter III. On History

**P.** What is history?

**T.** An account of past or present things.

**P.** In how many books is divine history contained?

**T.** In seventeen: Genesis, one book; Exodus, one; Leviticus, one; Numbers, one; Deuteronomy, one; Joshua, one; Judges, one; Ruth, one; the Books of Kings, four according to us and two according to the Hebrews; the four Gospels—according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John—and the Acts of the Apostles, one book.

**P.** Do no other books belong to divine history?

**T.** Many add these: two books of Chronicles, one of Job, two of Ezra, one of Judith, one of Esther, and two of Maccabees.

**P.** Why are these books not included among the canonical Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0017D] Read cautiously, for he improperly removes certain books from the canon of the Sacred Scriptures. Brasichellus, *Index of Purged Books*, vol. I, p. 57.]?

**T.** Because among the Hebrews also they were received as belonging to a different category, as Jerome and others testify.

**P.** Is no other kind of expression found in these books?

**T.** The other kinds occur, but not principally. For although the persons by whom the words were first spoken used the other kinds of expression, nevertheless, as narrated by the one who wrote the book, they are related as history.

Thus the blessings of the patriarch Jacob were indeed spoken by the prophet himself, but Moses, who reports them, narrates them in historical order. And when Moses himself says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), he speaks by the prophetic Spirit, but narrates it in historical form.

Similarly, history sometimes has a proverbial sound, as in: “The trees went forth to anoint a king over themselves” (Judges 9:8). At other times it teaches simply, as in: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Nevertheless, as I have said, everything is woven together in historical form.

**P.** What does the historical form possess that the other forms do not?

**T.** The other forms depend upon it; it depends upon none.

**P.** What does it have in common with the others?

**T.** It has this in common with simple instruction: both appear clear on the surface, although they are generally difficult in meaning. The others are the reverse.

## Chapter IV. On Prophecy

**P.** What is prophecy?

**T.** The disclosure, by divine inspiration, of hidden things—whether past, present, or future.

**P.** Give an example of prophecy concerning the past.

**T.** “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm 33:6). And: “For he spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 148:5). And: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1).

**P.** Give an example concerning the present.

**T.** The prophet Elisha saw in the present the knowledge of Gehazi’s future action (2 Kings 5:26); and the Apostle Peter saw that of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:3).

**P.** Give an example concerning the future.

**T.** “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isaiah 7:14), and so forth.

**P.** Why was the word “hidden” included in the definition?

**T.** Because if someone speaks of things already known, even if they are future things, he is not a prophet. Thus, when we preach the resurrection, we are not prophets. But if someone discloses hidden things belonging to any time, then he is a prophet, as we have already shown.

[Col. 0017D] **P.** Prove this.

**T.** By the testimony of the Apostle in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says:

> If the whole Church comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and outsiders enter, will they not say that you are insane? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all and examined by all; the secrets of his heart are also made manifest. Then, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you (1 Corinthians 14:23–25).

Behold, the Apostle indicated the power of prophecy in the manifestation of hidden things. The following passages in the same Epistle and elsewhere contain many examples of this kind.

**P.** Why did we add the words “by divine inspiration”?

**T.** Because those who disclose hidden things either by the impulse of demons or by other means may indeed be called prophets, but they are not counted among the authors of the divine Scriptures.

**P.** In how many books is prophecy found?

**T.** In seventeen: the one hundred and fifty Psalms, one book; Hosea, one; Isaiah, one; Joel, one; Amos, one; Obadiah, one; Jonah, one; Micah, one; Nahum, one; Zephaniah, one; Habakkuk, one; Jeremiah, one; Ezekiel, one; Daniel, one; Haggai, one; Zechariah, one; Malachi, one.

As for the Apocalypse of John, it is very much disputed among the Easterners [Note: [Col. 0018D] The matter is now entirely beyond doubt: the book of the Apocalypse is both canonical and prophetic. The same author, cited work.].

**P.** Is no other kind of expression found in these books?

**T.** The others occur, but not principally, except as proof of prophecy. Thus, in Isaiah chapters 7, 31, and 37, a kind of history is related concerning the kings Ahaz and Hezekiah; but the purpose is prophetic—not to weave together a record of events, but to confirm the outcome of the things foretold.

When Jeremiah says, “Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord” (Jeremiah 22:29), he calls the earth, proverbially, the people who inhabit it. And when Isaiah says, “I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord, but loose every bond of wickedness” (Isaiah 58:6), and so forth, he appears to teach simply, but he proclaims these things because he has been commanded to do so by the prophetic Spirit.

**P.** What does prophecy have in common with the others?

**T.** It has this in common with Proverbs: both are difficult on the surface, but most are not difficult in meaning.

## Chapter V. On Proverbs

**P.** What is the proverbial form?

**T.** A figurative expression that sounds one thing, means another, and gives admonition in the present time.

**P.** In which books is this form found?

**T.** In two: one book of Solomon’s Proverbs and one book of Jesus son of Sirach.

**P.** Is no other book subject to this form?

**T.** Some add the book called Wisdom and the Song of Songs.

**P.** Do other forms occur in these books?

**T.** Only simple instruction occurs, and not principally, except for the explanation or commendation of Proverbs, as in: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 1:7; 9:10).

D. What do Proverbs have in common with the others?  
M. They have this in common with prophecy: they appear difficult on the surface, although for the most part they are not difficult to understand.

D. What distinctive feature does the proverbial genre possess?  
M. [Col. 0018D] It is not intermingled with either history or prophecy; and it alone is understood in such a way that, in a certain sense, the surface of the words is removed.

D. Why is it permitted in this case alone for us to consider not the text of Scripture itself but its meaning, whereas in the other three genres we admit mystical allegories in such a way that it is necessary to preserve the credibility of the narrative?  
M. Because if we were to accept the proverbial genre everywhere as allegory in such a way that the truth of the narrative were weakened, we would give enemies an opportunity to interpret the divine books as they wished.

D. In how many ways is allegory recognized in divine law?  
M. [Col. 0019A] In four ways. Either according to transference or metaphor, as in: “The Lord was angry, and he descended” (Exod. IV, 14), and similar passages, where causes drawn from human behavior are transferred to God in order to suggest them; or according to imagination or *hypotyposis*—that is, vivid representation—as in the Gospel: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke X, 30); and again, the parable of the vineyard and the cultivators (Matt. XX, XXI). For the sequence of the things performed by Christ is reported as though it had been fulfilled in the image of another person and matter.

Or according to comparison or likeness, as it says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed” (Luke XIII, 19), and so forth. For the narrative is not woven together as in the preceding example; rather, only the outcomes of the causes are compared.

Or according to the proverbial manner, as in: [Col. 0019B] “Drink water from your own vessels, and from your own cistern, and from your own wells” (Prov. V, 15), when Scripture wishes to indicate that carnal desire should be restrained within the permitted bounds of marriage.

## CHAPTER VI. On Simple Doctrine

D. What is simple doctrine?  
M. It is that by which we are taught plainly, in the present age, about faith or morals.

D. Why did it receive this name?  
M. Because all Scripture does indeed teach something, but under the other genres we mentioned above, within which something else is also being accomplished. This genre, however, neither constructs a history, nor prophesies, nor speaks proverbially; [Col. 0019C] it simply teaches.

D. Which books belong to simple doctrine?  
M. Sixteen canonical books: Ecclesiastes, one book; and the Epistles of the Apostle Paul: one to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; one to the Galatians; one to the Ephesians; one to the Philippians; one to the Colossians; two to the Thessalonians; two to Timothy; one to Titus; one to Philemon; one to the Hebrews; one of the blessed Peter to the Gentiles; and the First Epistle of the blessed John.

D. Do no other books belong to simple doctrine?  
M. Many add five others, which are called the Canonical Epistles of the Apostles: namely, one of James, the Second of Peter, one of Jude, and two of John.

D. Is no other genre found in these books?  
M. The other genres occur as well, but not principally, except for the proof of the doctrine. For when the Apostle says, “When I had come to Troas, a door was opened for me in the Gospel of Christ” [Col. 0019D] (II Cor. II, 12), he appears to be constructing a history. Again, when he says, “Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (I Cor. XV, 51), he takes up the work of a prophet. When he says, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” (Titus I, 12), he uses proverbial words. Nevertheless, all these things are inserted, as we said, for the proof of the doctrine.

D. What does simple doctrine have in common with the other genres?  
M. It has this in common with history: both appear easy on the surface, although on examination or in understanding they are for the most part difficult.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Authority of the Scriptures

[Col. 0020A]

D. How is the authority of the divine books considered?  
M. Because some possess complete authority, some intermediate authority, and some no authority at all.

D. Which possess complete authority?  
M. Those that we have enumerated absolutely as canonical within each genre.

D. Which possess intermediate authority?  
M. Those which, as we said, are added by many.

D. Which possess no authority?  
M. All the rest.

D. Are these distinctions found in every genre?  
M. In history and simple doctrine. For among prophecy, all the books of intermediate authority are found, with the exception of Revelation; nor in the proverbial genre is there any at all—

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Writers of the Divine Books

[Col. 0020B]

D. By what means do we know the writers of the divine books?  
M. In three ways. Either from titles and prefaces, as with the prophetic books and the Epistles of the Apostles; or from titles alone, as with the Evangelists; or from the tradition of the ancients. Thus Moses is believed to have written the first five books of history, although the title does not say this, nor does Moses himself report it by saying, “The Lord said to me,” but rather, as though speaking about another person, “The Lord said to Moses.”

Likewise, the book of Joshua is traditionally said to have been written by the person after whom it is named. And Samuel is reported to have written the First Book of Kings. It should further be known that the authors of certain books are entirely unknown, such as Judges, Ruth, the Third Book of Kings, the last book, and other similar works. This is to be believed to have been divinely arranged, so that other divine books also might be understood to have attained the summit of authority not through the merit of their authors, but solely through the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0020C]

## CHAPTER IX. On the Forms of the Scriptures

D. How many forms does divine Scripture have?  
M. Two. For they are either composed in Hebrew meters in their own language, or in straightforward prose.

D. Which are composed in meter?  
M. The Psalms, the book of Job, Ecclesiastes, and certain passages among the Prophets.

D. Which are composed in straightforward prose?  
M. All the rest.

D. Why are those composed in meter not composed in the same meters among us?  
M. Because no diction preserves its meter in another language if it does not alter the force and order of the words.

## CHAPTER X. On the Order of the Scriptures

[Col. 0020D]

D. What is the order of the divine volumes?  
M. Some belong to the Old Testament and some to the New.

D. Which belong to the New Testament?  
M. The four Gospels, as stated above; the Apostolic Epistles; and Acts.

D. Which belong to the Old Testament?  
M. All the rest.

D. What is distinctive of the Old and New Testaments?  
M. The purpose of the Old is to point out the New through figures and announcements; the purpose of the New is to kindle human minds toward the glory of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Things That Holy Scripture Teaches Us

[Col. 0021A]

D. Since enough has been said about those matters that properly concern the surface of Scripture itself, I now ask what it is that Scripture itself teaches us.  
M. Three things: for it speaks either about God, or about the present age, or about the future.

## CHAPTER XII. In How Many Meanings Scripture Speaks About God

D. In how many meanings does Scripture speak about God?  
M. In four. Either it signifies his essence, which in Latin we call *substance*, as in: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14); or the persons, or, in Greek, the *subsistences*, as in: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, [Col. 0021B] and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19); or his operation, as it is written: “According to the operation of the power of his might, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and making him sit at his right hand” (Eph. I, 19–20); or his relation to creatures, as in: “To the King of the ages, incorruptible [Note: [Col. 0021D] According to the Greek, ἀφθάρτῳ (*aphthártō*), ‘incorruptible.’ Some manuscripts and several Fathers, however, read ἀθανάτῳ (*athanátō*), ‘immortal,’ as the Vulgate has it], invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever” (I Tim. I, 17).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Meanings of the Divine Essence

D. In how many ways is the divine essence signified?  
M. In two ways: principally and consequently.

D. By which words is it signified principally?  
M. By eight. For it is called either God, or Lord, or, together, Lord God; or Adonai; or Sabaoth; or Heli; or Eloi; or “He Is.”

D. Do these words signify nothing other than God?  
M. Two of them are sometimes also used improperly of others: God and Lord, as Paul testifies: “For there are many gods and many lords” (I Cor. VIII, 5); and: “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Isa. IX, 6). The other six, however, are never used except of God.

D. What do these words signify about God?  
M. Not what he is, but that he is. For what God is cannot be comprehended.

D. In what ways is God signified consequently?  
M. When Scripture explains his persons, his operation, or his relation to creatures. For when it names the Father, although at first hearing it signifies one who begets, consequently we understand God; likewise when it names the Son or the Holy Spirit.

And when it says “almighty,” although the first statement announces his operation, consequently we understand God. And when it says “invisible,” although it principally indicates one who cannot be seen by mortals, and by comparison with us assigns to him what we are not, consequently we understand God.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Meanings of the Trinity

D. In how many ways does Scripture signify the persons—or [Note: [Col. 0022D] Read: “subsistences”—or substances of the divinity [Col. 0022A]?  
M. Likewise in two ways: principally and consequently.

Principally, when it says Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Consequently, through those things by which essence, operation, or relation to creatures is signified. For when I say “God,” I speak of what pertains to essence; when I say “almighty,” of what pertains to operation; and when I say “unchangeable,” of what is said in relation to creatures. Although the first hearing may convey something else, I nevertheless consequently understand the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, either together or individually, as God.

## CHAPTER XV. In How Many Ways the Father Is Signified

D. In how many ways is the Father signified?  
M. By the name “Father” you understand one person, but not in only one way: it is said properly in relation to the Son, and generally in relation to a creature—there by the truth of nature, here by the goodness of grace. [Col. 0022B]

D. Is the Father signified in this one way only?  
M. This is the principal way. For he is also understood consequently through all the things that signify, in whatever manner, the essence of the divinity, its operation, or its relation to creatures. Moreover, the Father is understood consequently from the name of the Son; and in the name of the Holy Spirit, the Father himself—namely, the one whose Spirit he is—is implied.

D. In the Trinity itself, is the title “Father” assigned to no other person?  
M. It is written of the Son: “Father of the age to come” (Ps. LXXXI, 6). But this is said according to the flesh, and not properly or signally, so that he might be shown to be the cause and begetter of our blessedness. Through the resurrection of the flesh, human nature thereby begins both to hope for and to receive the life to come. [Col. 0022C]

## CHAPTER XVI. In How Many Ways the Son Is Signified

D. In how many ways does Scripture speak about the Son?  
M. In five ways. Sometimes his divinity alone is signified, as it were, and the assumption of flesh is understood consequently, as in: “The only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father” (John I, 18).

At other times only the man assumed by him is signified, with the divinity understood consequently, as in: “In these last days he has spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. I, 1–2).

At other times both are signified together, as in: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Col. 0022D] (Phil. II, 5–7).

At times statements that concern the body appear to be made of him, although they must principally be referred to the divinity, as in: “The Son of Man [Note: [Col. 0022D] Read, perhaps: “who is.”] is indeed in heaven” (John III, 13).

Again, statements that properly refer to the flesh sometimes appear to be attributed to the divinity, as in: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8).

D. Why does Scripture speak about the Son in these five ways?  
M. It speaks distinctly according to the natures in order to show their properties without confusion; it speaks jointly in order to assert their unity. It alternates human things with divine and divine things with human, so that both may be shown to belong to one undivided Person.

D. In how many ways is the person of the Son usually signified?  
M. In two ways. He himself is signified principally when “Christ” is said absolutely. When others are called christs, they are called someone else’s, as in “the Lord’s Christ” (I Kings XXIV, 7, 11), or “my Christ” (Ps. CIV, 15). But only Christ, the Son of God by nature, is called “Christ” absolutely. Thus it is declared that this designation properly belongs to him alone.

Consequently, the person of the Son is understood from those three things by which the Father is also understood, from the name of the Father itself, and from the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit is said to be the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

## CHAPTER XVII. In How Many Ways the Person of the Holy Spirit Is Signified

[Col. 0023B]

D. In how many ways is the person of the Holy Spirit signified?  
M. Principally in one way, as it is written: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). And again: “You are the temple of the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. VI, 19).

Consequently, the grace that he himself bestows is also called the Holy Spirit, as in: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke I, 35); and: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22).

Likewise, he is signified consequently through those things by which the divine essence, operation, or relation to creatures is signified, just as we said concerning the Son. Moreover, the persons of the Father and the Son consequently signify the Holy Spirit, because whatever of these things we mention, we consequently understand the person of the Holy Spirit either as co-working or as consubstantial.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What the Persons of the Trinity Have in Common and What Is Proper to Them

[Col. 0023C]

D. What is proper to each individual person of the Trinity?  
M. The Father is never called the Son, nor, in a combined expression, the Holy Spirit, although separately he can be called both “Spirit” and “holy.” Nor can the Son properly be called the Father, or, in a combined expression, the Holy Spirit. Nor, again, is the name of the Father or of the Son assigned to the Holy Spirit.

D. What do these persons have in common?  
M. Everything recognized as pertaining to the signification of essence, operation, or relation to creatures. Hence it is established that the Trinity is of one substance.

D. What is signified in these persons by the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?  
M. Only that they are. For what they are—as we said above concerning God—speech cannot explain. [Col. 0023D]

## CHAPTER XIX. Through How Many Classes the Operation of the Divinity Is Designated

D. Through how many classes is the efficacy or operation of the divinity designated, which the Greeks call ἐνέργεια (*energeia*)?  
M. Four: either by creation, or by providence concerning creatures, or by preparation of future things concerning them, or by the outcome or realization of what has been prepared.

D. Give examples pertaining to operation.  
M. Such as when God is called Good, chiefly because he made and makes those things that did not exist; Wise, because we see all things ordered by him with such wondrous wisdom; and Strong, because he was able to bring to completion what he so well and wisely willed. [Col. 0024A]

D. In God, are these things essences or acts of will?  
M. God is simple, and in him essence is not something other than will. Hence, although all the names of his operation differ in definition from one another, in God himself no difference or diversity is found. Thus essence or nature acts, because nothing accidental belongs to him; yet he also acts by will, because he accomplishes nothing by necessity or under compulsion.

For God does not operate as fire burns by natural necessity, or bees construct honeycombs by natural necessity, or spiders weave webs by natural necessity. God is therefore said to act by nature or essence so that will may not appear in him as something quasi-other; and he is said to act by will because he is compelled to perform no operation. Rather, he wills essentially, [Col. 0024B] and subsists by will.

D. Give examples pertaining specifically to creation.  
M. Such as when he is called Maker, Craftsman, Creator, and similar names, although “to make” is also said in the sense of “to arrange,” as in: “He made salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXXIII, 12). In that case it is said according to the class of providence.

D. Give examples pertaining specifically to providence.  
M. Such as when he is called Helper, Foreknower, Almighty, and similar names.

D. Give examples pertaining to the preparation of future things.  
M. Such as when he is called Way, Hope, Refuge, and similar names.

D. Give examples pertaining to the outcome of what has been prepared.  
M. Such as when he is called Exultation, Joy, and other similar names.

All things pertaining to operation are recognized not only in names but also in words and similar revelations. [Note: [Col. 0023D] “To things” seems necessary as an addition, judging from the context.]

D. Is divine operation declared only in these ways? [Col. 0024C]  
M. There is another figurative way, when divine operation is signified through human things.

D. In how many ways does this occur?  
M. In two ways. Either those things that pertain to our mind are spoken figuratively of God, such as fury, anger, and repentance; or those things that concern the body—namely, feet, hands, and fingers.

Sometimes human actions are also transferred to God, as when it says: “Take hold of weapons and shield” (Ps. XXXIV, 2). All these things, however, must be joined to the four classes of operation mentioned above according to the character of the statements.

## CHAPTER XX. In What Ways God Is Signified by Relation to Creatures

D. In how many ways is God signified by relation to creatures?  
M. In two ways: by affirmation and by negation. [Col. 0024D]

By affirmation, when things are said of God that, in the same manner, apply to no creature, such as Simple, Ancient of Days, Before All Things, and Spirit—that is, unbounded—and First and Last, and similar terms. All these things are said of God because, by comparison with him, they apply to no creature.

Relation by negation occurs when, by means of a privative prefix, things that exist in a creature are denied of God, such as Unbegotten, Incorporeal, Uncreated, Incorruptible, Immortal, Impassible, and similar terms.

D. What then? Are these words never said of a creature?  
M. They are indeed said of a creature, but not according to the same sense. For when a human being is called simple, this is not because he is uncompounded—for only God is essentially simple—but a human being is called simple because he does not possess duplicity of deceit.

Likewise, when something is called invisible, this is not because it cannot be seen by anyone insofar as it exists—for that belongs to God alone—but because it is hidden from certain people. The other terms are used similarly. [Col. 0025A]

D. Which relational terms are said of God in such a way that they cannot be said of a creature?  
M. Those that are supreme and unique in him, such as Unbegotten, Everlasting, Without Beginning, and similar terms.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0025]

## CHAPTER I. What Scripture Signifies About the Present Age

[Col. 0025A]

D. Since enough has been said about the ways in which Scripture speaks about God, I now ask what Scripture signifies when it speaks about the present age.  
M. Five things: either its generation—that is, creation—or its governance; or properties accidental to natures; or things that occur according to wills; or things that follow upon the outcome of the will.

## CHAPTER II. The Modes and Distinctions Scripture Has Established in the Operation of Creatures

D. In how many ways has Scripture signified the generation of the world?  
M. In three ways. Either something is written to have been made by the will of God alone, as in: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1); or by will together with speech, whether command, as in: “Let there be light” (ibid., 3), and: “Let there be a firmament” (ibid., 6), or deliberation, as in: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (ibid., 26); or by will, speech, and decree, as in: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (ibid., 28).

And again: “Let the earth bring forth grass producing seed according to its kind, and a fruit-bearing tree producing fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its kind upon the earth” (ibid., 11), together with the other things that, after the seventh day and until the end of the age, he brings about in stages. For they proceed from that decree.

D. Is there any difference among these three?  
M. There is. Those things that were made by will alone, or also by speech, were newly made; but those made by decree are already similar to the things that, as we said, were newly made. Again, the former came into being during the first six days, whereas the latter continue until the age endures.

D. Give the order of the things made during the six days.  
M. At the very beginning of creation, heaven, earth, angels, air, and water were made.

D. Prove that the angels, waters, and air were made.  
M. That they were made is shown by these passages of Scripture: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. CIII, 4); and: “Praise him, all his angels” (Ps. CXLVIII, 2); and: “Let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke, and they were made” (ibid., 4–5).

Air is indicated in Scripture by the name “heaven,” as in: “The birds of heaven” (Ps. VII, 9), since it is certain that birds fly in the air. We have already shown that heaven was made.

That these things preceded the other creatures is demonstrated by Scripture in the case of the angels, since they are placed before the other creatures in praises and blessings; and reason requires this, for it was fitting that a heavenly creature should precede earthly creatures. Concerning the waters, Scripture itself says that “the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. I, 2). [Col. 0026A]

D. Continue with the order of generation.  
M. In the beginning, on the first day, light was made; on the second day, the firmament; on the third, the sea and the things growing from the earth; on the fourth, the lights of heaven; on the fifth, the swimming creatures and flying creatures; on the sixth, the remaining animals and the human being.

D. What distinction exists in the operation of the creatures themselves?  
M. Some were made from nothing, such as heaven, earth, and the other things that we said were made up to the completion of the first day; others, however, were made from things already made on the first day.

D. Give proofs of these things.  
M. Whenever Scripture wishes to show that things were made from something else, it either indicates this openly, as in: “Let the earth bring forth” (ibid., 11), and: “Let the waters bring forth” (ibid., 20), and similar passages; or it indicates it through the subtle meaning of the words.

Thus, when it says: “Let there be a firmament” (ibid., 6), it plainly signifies that something fluid and liquid—namely, the waters—already existed. Since these were shown to have been solidified, the thing that was being made was called the firmament.

Again, it called the lights made on the fourth day derivative, in order to show that they were made from the light produced on the first day. But among the things made on the first day, Scripture declares neither openly nor through any subtle word that one thing was made from another.

D. Therefore, is nothing shown to have been made from things that did not exist after the first day?  
M. Only the human soul. This too serves to show that, whereas other things were made either from nothing or from things already made, the human being alone is composed from both.

D. What other distinctions do we assign to creatures?  
M. Those things made during the first six days did not arise naturally or through reproduction from similar things; but the remaining things that are made naturally arise from the divine decree, except, of course, for miracles.

D. Give a third distinction.  
M. Some creatures—namely, rational creatures—were made for their own sake, such as angels and human beings. The rest are known to have been made not for their own sake, but for the sake of the angels or human beings mentioned above. The human being, however, is to be understood as having been made principally for his own sake according to the soul. [Note: [Col. 0025D] That is, not for the sake of other creatures; otherwise it is established that human beings and angels were created not for their own sake but for God’s sake.] According to the body, this is consequent. [Note: [Col. 0026D] I would prefer: “intelligible.”]

D. What then? Apart from human beings and angels, did other creatures not need one another?  
M. They did need one another, though not for utility, but for adornment. For they are useful not to themselves, but to the angels or human beings for whose sake they are also known to have been made.

They also provide adornment to one another. Heaven, for instance, was unadorned without the heavenly lights; and the lights themselves, lest they should have been made superfluously, needed the eyes of those who see. The sea was unadorned until it either occupied its proper place or was filled with animals; the earth was unformed apart from the use of those dwelling or growing upon it; irrational animals were inept without human governance; and grasses were superfluous in the absence of animals’ use.

Thus all things need one another, either those made during the six days or those made each day. But, as we have already said, it is made clear that one thing is unformed, another usefully unformed, and another in itself useful to another.

D. Is there any distinction within adornment itself?  
M. There is. Some things were adorned during the six days, such as heaven with its lights, earth with grasses, and the sea with fish. Some are adorned as long as the world exists, such as the sea with ships, the earth with buildings and other things constructed by human skill, and the human being himself with knowledge.

Others will receive their beauty in the future: the body, incorruption; mortal beings, immortality; and the heavenly kingdom, the dwelling of the saints.

It should be noted concerning adornments that, among those things produced either by skill or by the arts, the cause lies in human beings; but in the rest, it lies in God. [Col. 0027B]

D. Give a fourth distinction.  
M. Some things emerged as though created all at once and suddenly, such as those we said were made during the first days: grasses, lights, swimming creatures and flying creatures, as well as terrestrial animals and quadrupeds.

Others were not made all at once, but as though with a certain delay, such as the sea, the earth, and the human being. For the human being too is written to have been made gradually, just like the others.

D. Give a fifth distinction among creatures.  
M. Some rule over the others by reason, such as rational creatures; some are used for service, such as the heavenly lights; and some obey by the necessity of nature, such as birds, quadrupeds, and similar creatures.

D. Give a sixth distinction.  
M. Those that rule over the others—that is, rational creatures—are moved by will and reason; but those that obey for the sake of use and by necessity are moved by nature.

D. How many materials did those things that were made from something else have?  
M. Six: earth, waters, air, fire, light, and the rib.

D. Give the origins of each.  
M. From earth came growing things, plants, and animals; from the waters, the firmament, the sea, swimming creatures, and flying creatures; jointly from earth, waters, fire, and air, all things that are renewed through successive generations; from light, the lights; and from the rib, Eve.

D. How is it proved that fire was made, or from what, or when?  
M. That it was made can be demonstrated from the general testimony of Scripture, when it says of God: “Who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Ps. CXLV, 6), since fire is certainly also among them.

It can also be demonstrated from a specific declaration: “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, and stormy wind” (Ps. CXLVIII, 7–8), concerning which he had said earlier: “For he spoke, and they were made” (ibid., 5).

And again: “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord” (Dan. III, 57); and he added: “Bless the Lord, fire and heat” (ibid., 66).

Whether it was made from nothing, like the other things, or from something else, is uncertain. For many wish it to be a portion of the heavenly lights, since we often see human beings drawing fire from the rays of the sun in a particular manner. If this is so, it was made on the first day. But Scripture more wisely called this element “light” rather than “fire,” so that it might receive its name from its more excellent use.

D. Give a seventh distinction among creatures.  
M. All things that were made from something else, or from which other things were made, are corporeal. Incorporeal things, however, were made neither from something else nor were other things made from them.

These incorporeal things must be understood not in the same way that God is called incorporeal. For in comparison with him nothing is incorporeal, just as nothing is immortal or invisible. There is one sense in which these words apply only to the divinity, and another in which Scripture speaks of creatures, such as souls or angels.

D. How is God said to have worked for six days and rested on the seventh, if he neither labors when he makes anything, so that rest would be necessary for him, nor ever ceases, since the Lord says in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17)?  
M. God is said to have rested on the seventh day not from creating, since every creature is daily renewed and maintained through his dispensation and providence; rather, this was signified: after those six days he created no substantial form unknown to the world, nor any new and untested nature. [Col. 0028B]

D. Can we ask how God made the world?  
M. This question is asked more rashly than cautiously. For it is not permitted to a human being to know the manner in which any divine creature was made. If anyone knew how certain things were made from nothing, he would in fact be equal to the Creator in knowledge and power.

## CHAPTER III. On the Things Pertaining to the Governance of the World

D. Since the creation of the world has been adequately discussed, it remains for us to ask in how many ways its governance is signified.  
M. In two ways. For it is either general or special.

D. What is general governance?  
M. It is that by which the things that have been made remain according to the manner in which they were made. This is signified when it is said: “God saw that it was good” (Gen. I, 4 and following); and: “That they were very good, and he blessed them” (ibid., 31).

The blessed David also demonstrates this when he says: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them forever and for ages of ages; he gave a command, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5–6).

D. What is special governance?  
M. It is that by which individual creatures, and especially rational creatures, are governed by God, as in the command concerning the tree in paradise (Gen. II, 9). For just as divine power sustains all creatures so that they may remain, so it also instructs rational creatures through various circumstances so that they may advance.

## CHAPTER IV. In How Many Classes General Governance Is Divided

D. Into how many classes is general governance divided?  
M. Into two. For it consists either in succession or in stability.

In succession, as with human beings, beasts of burden, and other things that perish through death or corruption and are renewed through the likeness of those born again.

In stability, as with those things that are not subject to these processes but obey the movements of the world, such as heaven, the sun, the stars, and the rest.

D. What further distinction exists among them?  
M. Those things that are dissolved through renewal also need certain remedies, such as food and rains, and sometimes the ministries of angels and other similar things.

But those that subsist without succession are governed by God without any such mediation. [Note: [Col. 0027D] We have emended *meditatione* to *mediatione*. Editor.]

Whether anything is also accomplished in these through the ministry of angels is a secret and difficult question. [Col. 0029A]

## CHAPTER V. In What Ways Special Governance Is Carried Out

D. In how many ways is special governance carried out?  
M. In three ways. It is carried out either by God, for the sake of angels and human beings; by angels, for their own sake and for the sake of human beings; or by human beings, for their own sake.

D. How is it carried out by God for the sake of angels and human beings?  
M. Through legislation.

## CHAPTER VI. On Legislation and Its Distinctions

D. Into how many parts is legislation divided?  
M. Into two: natural discernment and a law established externally. [Col. 0029B]

D. Prove that natural discernment is called law.  
M. The Apostle says: “When the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law, these, though they do not have the law, are a law for themselves” (Rom. II, 14). According to this law, Cain too was guilty of killing his brother.

D. Into how many parts is the law established externally divided?  
M. Into two: works—that is, the retribution of actions—and words.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Law Through Works

D. In how many ways does the law operate through works?  
M. In four ways: either through a general present retribution, such as the yield of fruits and other things; or through a special present retribution, such as Abraham being enriched during his wandering, or Noah being saved in the Flood; or through a general visible punishment, such as general famine or drought; or through a special punishment, such as the punishment of Cain or Saul.

All these things instruct angels and human beings in the manner of a law. Indeed, the fall of the devil both terrified and strengthened the angels, although it must be believed that angels are instructed in one way and human beings in another.

D. What is the purpose of all legislation, and in what does it consist?  
M. In the discernment of good and evil, which are recognized either in teaching—that is, faith—or in actions.

D. Why did we call the punishments and retributions present?  
M. Because they themselves instruct in place of a law. Future and eternal things will benefit neither those who suffer them nor those who see them, since by then there will no longer be time for repentance.

D. Through which ministers is this governance recorded in Scripture as having been carried out?  
M. Sometimes by God himself, as when he commanded Adam not to touch the tree; sometimes through angels, as the Apostle testifies: “If the word spoken through angels was made firm” (Heb. II, 2). And again, the firstborn of Egypt are said to have been killed by the hand of an angel (Exod. XII, 29).

Or it is carried out through human beings, as through the prophets; or through beasts, as through the serpents in the wilderness (Num. XXI, 6), and similar instruments. Through these as well, as through a kind of substantial and material law, they prohibit evils because of which such things are inflicted, and urge people toward goods for whose retribution prayer is offered.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Law Through Words

[Col. 0030A]

D. Into how many parts is the law established in words divided?

M. Into two: for either something immutable is commanded, or something temporary.

D. How many kinds of immutable things are there?

M. Two: love of God and love of neighbor.

D. Into how many parts are temporary commandments divided?

M. Into two: for either they were observed for a long time, as circumcision, or for a short time, as the receiving of manna.

D. What other difference is there among laws?

M. Some either command something, as: “Honor your father” (Exod. XX, 12), or forbid something, as: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (ibid., 13–14).

D. Give a third difference.

M. Some things are useful in themselves, while others are necessary on account of those things.

D. What things are useful in themselves?

M. Love of God and of one’s neighbor.

D. What things are necessary on account of others?

M. For example: “You shall not kill”; for by murder the love of one’s brother is driven out. Likewise, the observance of the Sabbath: in its observance there is a commemoration of God’s rest from the work of creating the creatures; and in that solemn observance love of God as Creator was signified.

D. Give a fourth difference.

M. Certain commandments were, as it were, bodily or external, such as those concerning clean and unclean animals, leprosy, and similar matters. Others were spiritual, such as: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart” (Lev. XIX, 17).

D. Give a fifth difference.

M. Some commandments belong specifically to the Old Testament, such as the command concerning the jubilee; some specifically to the New Testament, such as: “You shall pray in this way: Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9); and some are common to both, such as: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Matt. XXII, 37; Mark XII, 30; Luke X, 27).

D. Give a sixth difference.

M. Some commandments are understood according to the sound of the words, as: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX, 14). Others sound one way, while their meaning is another, as: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3).

D. Give a seventh difference.

M. The transgression of some commandments is punished by a penalty, as: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Lev. XLV, 20). For some there is no penalty, as: “He ate the priestly bread, although he was not a priest” (1 Kings XXI, 6; Matt. XII, 4). In the case of others, transgression is even praiseworthy, as: “If I repaid those who did me evil” (Ps. VII, 5).

For at that time the law commanded that evil be repaid with evil.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Treat this law cautiously: for the law did not command private individuals to repay evil with evil, but required it juridically, by public authority; [Col. 0030D] nor is its transgression good. BRASICHELL. *Index of Expurgated Books*, vol. I, p. 57.]

Thus contempt of the law is found to be praiseworthy.

D. Give an eighth difference.

M. Some commandments pertain to faith, others to conduct; and the subdivision of these is recognized as exceedingly extensive.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning angelic governance

D. How is the governance of angels, both for their own sake and for the sake of human beings, carried out?

M. It is not plainly stated in Scripture; nevertheless, since Scripture says that there are degrees and orders of angels, and that they move about on account of human life—as in the case of Tobias, Daniel, and others—it undoubtedly signifies that they govern the affairs in the world entrusted to them. By obeying the Creator, they provide for themselves; and by overseeing the administration entrusted to them, they provide for human beings.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning human governance through human beings

D. In how many ways is the governance of human beings for their own sake carried out?

M. In three. Someone either labors for the commonwealth, as a king; or for his household, as a head of a family; or for himself, as any monk or poor person.

D. Does governance belong to no other creatures?

M. It certainly belongs to all of them; for the Creator has enclosed in each according to its nature something resembling a certain prudence, as it is written: “I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks” (Matt. XXIII, 37), and in similar passages.

But Scripture’s purpose is not to teach subtle matters concerning irrational creatures, nor is it the desire of those who are making progress in it to wear away their time in investigating such things.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the accidents of nature

D. Since enough has been said about the governance of the world, what things are accidental to natures?

M. Nothing happens accidentally to the divine nature. Since it is incomprehensible and always remains in the same condition, it does not admit the diversity of accidents.

D. What things certainly occur accidentally to creatures?

M. Standing, as with the earth, according to Scripture; moving, as with the heaven, fire, waters, and the other things that grow or arise. Then there are time, place, and number. For all things began at some time, exist somewhere, and are either one or many.

Likewise, generation, corruption, health, illness, form, position, and the capacity for arts and disciplines occur accidentally. So too growth, nourishment, sensation, life, death, difference among one another, and opposition. In addition, order, succession, coherence, and things similar and contrary to these—though not all of them belong to each individual thing, but to the whole.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the accidents of the will

D. Since enough has been said about the accidents of natures, we must now speak about the accidents of the will. What is the will?

M. It is an inviolate, or spontaneous, power of the soul, according to which diverse and contrary thoughts and actions are produced. The natural distinction between good and evil is common to us; but the spontaneous movement concerns those things that have already been distinguished and are to be pursued. The law itself instructs it; grace prepares, assists, strengthens, and crowns it.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning what follows the outcome of the will

D. What things follow the outcome of the will?

M. Four things. For in this life some things happen either as good things to the good and evil things to the evil, as Abraham’s prosperity (Gen. XIII, 6) and Cain’s punishment (Gen. IV, 11); or, conversely, as good things to the evil and evil things to the good, as the rich man who is described in the Gospel as happy until death (Luke XVI, 19), while Lazarus, on the other hand, is tormented by sores and poverty.

Or else neither for the former nor for the latter is either kind of recompense given, as in the case of Joseph, who was sold (Gen. L, 18), when no vengeance was inflicted upon his brothers. Nor was Moses’ father-in-law, who gave counsel concerning the governance of the people (Exod. XVIII, 17), although praised, granted any reward by God.

D. What causes do we assign for this diversity?

M. To some people appropriate things are repaid here, lest the world be thought to be governed by chance rather than by divine providence, and also so that an abundance of good things may console the good and the punishment of similar things may deter the evil.

But happiness is permitted to the evil so that the good may be tested and learn to despise those things which they see to be shared with themselves by the unworthy. Evil things likewise befall the good.

Or no image of recompense is granted here to either class, so that elsewhere we may most certainly recognize both judgment and full recompense for their actions.

D. Give the fourth mode.

M. When people have done neither anything evil nor anything good in themselves, they share in good things or in evil things, as infants do; or perhaps in neither, as with those who are aborted. Concerning both their condition and their merit, the matter is subtle and the discussion uncertain.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the things that pertain to the age to come

D. Since we have completed all the parts of the rules concerning the present age, what things do we believe pertain to the age to come?

M. Four, certainly. For there is either acceptance or calling, or a type, or a prediction, or the effect or outcome of the things predicted.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning acceptances

D. What do we call acceptance, or calling?

M. That by which God deigns to reconcile certain people or peoples to himself through the benefit of a special grace, and shows toward them more than toward other human beings the indulgence of divine favor and, as it were, the kindness shown to members of his household.

D. How many acceptances are there?

M. Ten.

D. Give the order of the acceptances.

M. The first is that of blessed Abraham; the second, Isaac; the third, Jacob and the twelve patriarchs born from him; the fourth, the tribe of Judah; the fifth, the whole people in Egypt; the sixth, holy David; the seventh, David’s own house, and through it the whole tribe of Judah; the eighth, the people’s return from captivity; the ninth, that of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh—whom the Son of God, joining to himself from David’s stock, and through David from Abraham and Adam, made provision for the salvation and remission of all of us; the tenth, that of all the nations through the dispensation of the incarnation of our God and Savior himself.

D. What, then? Were there no just people pleasing to God before Abraham?

M. There certainly were. For those who had been begotten from Seth were called sons of God (Gen. VI, 2); Enoch was translated; Noah became the renewer of the perishing world; and Melchizedek was an example of the supreme priest.

But in these people divine acceptance—that is, that special familiarity and favor—is not displayed; rather, their righteousness is declared.

In the case of Abraham, however, God’s frequent speech with him and, as it were, companionship, together with the administration of each matter, the promised rewards of testing, and the remembrance of him among his descendants, display the extraordinary force of divine acceptance.

Likewise, in the case of the others mentioned above, a certain special favor of divinity and a governance openly administered, as it were, through each individual act of life declares the exceptional assistance of grace.

D. Why do we say that these things pertain to the age to come, since they happened in the present?

M. Because each thing is understood from its outcome, and the cause of an action is the same as the intention of the one who performs it.

D. Prove that the causes of these acceptances look toward the future.

M. The faith of the nations follows the Christian religion in hope of eternal life. For Christ the Lord himself, through the whole remedy of his teaching and the miracles of his actions, as well as through his resurrection and ascension, taught, promised, approved, and granted future life.

Now who is unaware that the remaining acceptances were effected for the sake of the Lord and the sacraments?
