He himself is promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as one who will bestow salvation upon the nations. On account of him, Abraham’s seed is separated from the other nations; and on account of him, the tribe of Judah both excels in blessing, is led into captivity last, and is saved first, because the Lord deigned to take flesh from it, so that the Jews were even named from it.

He is promised to David, to his house, and to his tribe as the one who will reign forever from his seed.

Therefore, if the faith of the nations was for the sake of future life, and Christ’s incarnation was for the sake of the faith of the nations, it follows from the very intention that the whole series of acceptances pertains to the age to come.

All these things are also easily confirmed by the testimonies of both the New and the Old Testament, since they are scattered everywhere.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning types

D. What is a type?

M. What we call a figure or form, as the Apostle says: “For all these things happened to them as a figure” (1 Cor. X, 11). And again: “Adam, who is the form of the one to come” (Rom. V, 14). For it is not without reason that one thing is signified by many terms.

D. What, then, is a type, or figure?

M. It is the manifestation, through works—according to what they are as works—of unknown present, past, or future things.

D. Give examples of types of past things.

M. The humility of catechumens is one. For they bear the type of Adam, excluded from paradise and, from awareness of his offenses, fearing the divine gaze; for this reason they also walk in public with their heads covered.

D. Give examples concerning the present.

M. Aaron’s vestment, in which he carried the names of the twelve tribes set into stones, showing that in a certain way he was making supplication for the whole people.

D. Give examples of future things.

M. There is no difficulty in these matters. Nevertheless, by way of excess, the two sons of Isaac showed the two Testaments (Gal. XIV, 4).

D. Since we have given an almost similar definition of prophecy, what is the difference?

M. In prophecy, future things are signified by words, according to what words are; in types, things are declared through things themselves.

Nevertheless, these two may be combined on the basis of their objects and expressed in this definition: prophecy is a type in words, according to what words are; and conversely, a type is prophecy concerning things, insofar as they are recognized to be things.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the differences among types

D. How many kinds of types or figures are there?

M. Principally, four. For either pleasant things are signified by pleasant things, or sorrowful things by sorrowful things; or pleasant things by sorrowful things, or sorrowful things by pleasant things.

D. Give examples of each kind.

M. Pleasant things are signified by pleasant things in the resurrection of the Lord according to the flesh and his dwelling in heaven: these are forms of our resurrection and an indication of the future dwelling of the righteous in heaven, as the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Coloss. III, 3).

Sorrowful things, however, are prefigured by sorrowful things. Thus the casting down of the devil and his angels, and the promise of future punishment, are a figure of those who, because of the similarity of their deeds, will be thrust into similar punishments. Blessed Peter also uses the same form to frighten sinners, saying concerning God: “For he did not spare the angels when they sinned, but handed them over to prisons of darkness” (1 Pet. II, 4).

The third mode occurs when pleasant things are signified by sorrowful things. Thus Adam’s transgression was a type of the righteousness of our Savior, as the blessed Apostle teaches: “For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one man the many will be made righteous. For death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the form of the one to come” (Rom. V, 19, 14)—that is, a type.

In Greek, the word *typos* is specifically used. Therefore Adam’s transgression was, by way of contrast, a figure or type of the grace of the second Adam, that is, Christ.

The fourth mode occurs when sorrowful things are figured by pleasant things, as in baptism. For baptism is a figure of the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, as the Apostle says: “All who were baptized were baptized into the death of Jesus Christ” (Rom. VI, 3).

For what is more pleasant than baptism, in which we are cleansed from sin and by which we become children of God? Or what is more sorrowful than death, toward which even he who was voluntarily going to undergo it nevertheless approached in sorrow?

D. What other things occur in types?

M. A difference of times. Some belong before the Law, such as Abel, killed by his brother, who prefigured Christ’s passion (Gen. IV, 8), and Noah’s ark, which prefigured the Church (Gen. VII, 7), along with other similar examples.

Others belong under the Law, such as Moses’ own death and the glory of Joshua.

Others belong under Grace, such as the garments of the baptized, the vestments of priests, participation in the Lord’s body, and each of the other things. To display all these as types belongs not to the teaching of the rules but to the exposition of the text.

D. In what way do we say that figures or types pertain to the age to come?

M. Because the figures of the Old Testament look toward the New according to their intention; and the figures of the New promise the blessedness of life. Thus everything proceeds toward hope in the age to come according to its very intention.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning predictions

D. Since we have discussed the rule of types, let us consider prediction. What is prediction?

M. It is the manifestation, by words—according to what words are—of future and uncertain things.

D. What characteristics belong to predictions?

M. Principally three: some occurred before the Law, some under the Law, and some under Grace.

## CHAPTER XIX. In how many ways were predictions made before the Law?

D. In how many ways were predictions made before the Law?

M. Five.

They were made concerning the human race in general, as: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Matt. XIX, 5). And again: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (Gen. III, 17). For this is understood to have been predicted, through one person, for the whole human race.

Or they were made in part or in the middle, as: “I will multiply your sorrows” (ibid., 16). And: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (ibid.). For this was said not to the whole human race, but only to all women.

Or they were made individually, as: “And Adam called his wife’s name Eve, because she is the mother of all living” (ibid., 20).

Or they were made with reference to the beginning of the Old Testament, as: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Gen. IX, 25).

Or they were made principally with reference to the New Testament. For when it says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26), and: “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages” (Gen. XI, 27), the plural number is the judgment of the Trinity, which is proclaimed more openly in the New Testament.

And when it says: “The blood of your brother cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV, 10), the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is predicted, as the Apostle testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebr. XII, 24): for the sprinkling of Christ’s blood had greater power to cry out to the Lord on our behalf than Abel’s blood had cried out against his brother.

## CHAPTER XX. In how many ways were predictions made under the Law?

D. In how many ways were predictions made under the Law?

M. In two: either concerning those things that were done under the Law, or concerning those that were to be done under Grace.

## CHAPTER XXI. How many predictions concern things done under the Law?

D. How many kinds of predictions do we find concerning things that were done under the Law?

M. Nearly twenty-two.

Sometimes the increase of the people is predicted, as in the promise to Abraham: “You shall become a great and numerous nation” (Gen. XII, 2).

Sometimes the promise of an inheritance, as: “To your seed I will give this land” (ibid., 7).

Sometimes the separation of the unworthy, as: “Cast out this slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gal. IV, 30).

Sometimes vengeance against the people’s adversaries and reward for their friends, as: “I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you” (Gen. XII, 3).

Sometimes the people’s deliverance from enemies, as: “Your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own, and they will go out from there with great preparation” (Gen. XV, 3), and so forth.

Sometimes the births and names of certain people, as Isaac and Samson.

Sometimes the greatness of descendants, as: “Kings shall come forth from you” (Gen. XVII, 6).

Sometimes the manner of departure, as: “But you shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age” (Gen. XV, 15).

Sometimes the distinction between peoples, as: “One people shall precede another people, and the greater shall serve the lesser” (Gen. XXV, 23).

Sometimes abundance, as: “May God give you the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, an abundance of grain and wine” (Gen. XXVII, 28).

Sometimes divine assistance, as: “Behold, I am with you, guarding you on every road” (Gen. XXVIII, 15).

Sometimes the choice of priesthood or teaching, as: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. XLIX, 7).

Sometimes strength and the immutability of the inheritance, as: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the root of my son you have risen; lying down, you have slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub—who will rouse him?” (ibid., 9).

[Note: [Col. 0035D] The Vulgate has *fili mi*, “my son,” rather than *filii mei*, “of my son.” And shortly afterward it has *habitabit*, “he will dwell,” rather than *inhabitavit*, “he dwelt.”]

Sometimes the purpose of life, as: “Zebulun dwelt as a stranger, and he himself was a haven of ships, and knew rest, because it is good” (ibid., 13), and so forth.

Sometimes transgression, as it says: “For I know that at the end of my passing you will act wickedly and turn aside from the way that I commanded you” (Deut. XXXI, 29).

Sometimes punishment, as: “Because evils will meet you at the end of days” (ibid.).

Sometimes general expulsion, as it says: “For they have been jealous of me with foreign gods and have provoked me with their idols; so I will make them jealous with a non-nation, and I will provoke them with a foolish nation” (Deut. XXXII, 21).

Sometimes the effect and reward of virtue, as: “Who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain? He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness” (Ps. XIV, 1–2), and so forth.

Sometimes the form of punishment, as: “Gad came to David and announced to him, saying: Choose for yourself either three years of famine upon the land, or three months of fleeing from the face of your enemies while they pursue you, or three days of pestilence in your land” (2 Kings XXIV, 11–13).

Sometimes signs, as: “And this shall be a sign to you, that God has anointed you king over his inheritance” (1 Kings X, 1), and the rest.

Sometimes the choice of prophecy, as: “And you, child, shall be called prophet of the Most High” (Luke I, 76).

D. Give predictions concerning the nations for the sake of the people.

M. For example: “His hand shall be against all, and the hand of all shall be against him” (Gen. XVI, 12). And: “Rise and go out from this place, because the Lord will destroy the city” (Gen. XIX, 14).

The visions of Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh, as well as those spoken by the prophets concerning other kings or nations, refer to general causes; nevertheless, their intention concerns the people, for whose vengeance each of these things came to pass.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning predictions under the Law about Christ

D. How many kinds of predictions are there concerning Christ?

M. Nearly twenty-six.

Some concern his marvelous conception and name, as: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14).

Some concern the place of his birth, as: “And you, Bethlehem, city of Judah, are in no way the least among the cities of Judah; for from you shall go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Mic. V, 2).

Some concern the things he did in his early life, as: “Before the child knows how to recognize evil and choose good” (Isa. VII, 16).

Some concern his righteousness and judgment, as: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

Some concern his divinity, as: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8).

Some concern the visitation involved in his assumption of humanity, as: “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” (Ps. VIII, 5).

Some concern the unity of deity and flesh, as: “A child is born for us” (Isa. IX, 6); and afterward it adds: “Mighty God.”

Some concern his power and kingdom, as: “But I have been established by him as king over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. XI, 6).

Some concern the breaking of his enemies, as: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. VIII, 8).

Some concern his teaching, as: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3).

Some concern the benefit of his teaching, as: “Because of truth, meekness, and righteousness” (ibid., 5).

Some concern miracles, as: “And your right hand shall lead you wondrously” (ibid.).

Some concern the glorification that he rightly received from the faithful, as: “Therefore the peoples shall confess you forever and ever” (ibid., 18).

Some concern the confirmation of his preaching, as: “Lord, our Lord, how marvelous is your name” (Ps. VIII, 2)!

Some concern his priesthood, as: “You are a priest forever” (Ps. CIX, 3).

Some concern his judgment and righteousness, as: “Among the splendors of the holy ones” (ibid., 4). And again: “He will judge, fill the ruins, and crush the heads in the land of many” (ibid., 6).

Some concern the labors of his life, as: “He will drink from the torrent on the way” (ibid., 9).

Scripture signifies the mystery of the incarnation as pleasing to the Father, as: “Behold, my servant, my beloved, in whom my soul was well pleased” (Matt. I, 18).

Some concern the infusion of the Holy Spirit, which the man assumed by him certainly merited, whether at the beginning of his incarnation, during his growth, at his baptism, in his miracles, in his teaching, or in his resurrection, as: “I will place my Spirit upon him” (Isa. XLII, 1); and: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me” (Luke IV, 18), and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] Read this cautiously, for it does not agree with the positions of theology, which teach that Christ merited neither his own incarnation nor the grace or glory of his soul, but only the glory of his body and the exaltation of his name. St. Thomas, Part III, question 19, article 3. BRASICHELL. *Index of Expurgated Books*, vol. I, p. 57.]

Some concern his care for the disciples, as: “He will not speak, nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Matt. XII, 19).

Some concern his sitting upon a beast, as: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes, sitting upon a donkey’s colt” (Zech. IX, 9).

Some concern his sufferings, burial, and the causes of these, as it is said: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty, but an dishonorable appearance, lower than all human beings.”

And again: “A man in wounds and knowing how to bear humiliation, because his face was adverse and disfigured, and he was regarded as nothing: he himself bears our sins and suffers for us; and we thought that he was in pain, in a wound, and in misery. But he was wounded because of our iniquities, and he was weakened because of our sins” (Isa. LIII, 2–5).

[Note: [Col. 0038D] The Septuagint has *μαλακίαν* (*malakian*), “weakness”; the Vulgate has *infirmitatem*, “infirmity.”]

Some concern the division of his garments, as: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Ps. XXI, 19).

Some concern the Lord’s resurrection, as: “You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10).

Some concern the calling of the Son according to the humility he assumed, as: “From Egypt I called my son” (Hos. XI, 1).

Some concern the generation of his divinity before the beginning, as: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3).

Some concern his second coming, as: “Behold, upon the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man” (Dan. VII, 13).

D. Are all these predictions understood of the Savior alone?

[Note: [Col. 0038D] Perhaps read: “Are they understood?”]

M. We customarily receive these in two ways. Some things were predicted in such a way with reference to his person that they cannot apply to anyone else, as it is written: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes to whom the things laid up belong” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

But some things are spoken under the occasion of another person, although in their meaning they look toward Christ, as: “In you and in your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18).

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning predictions under the Law that pertain to the calling of the nations

D. Since we have proved that the predictions spoken about Christ are contained in the ancient Law, give those that have been set forth concerning the calling of the nations.

M. We understand that the predictions concerning the calling of the nations are set forth in nearly seventeen ways.

Sometimes they signify their acceptance, when it is said: “I will make them jealous with a non-nation; I will provoke them with a foolish nation” (Deut. XXXII, 21).

Sometimes their infirmities, the expulsion of sins, and the teaching of better things, when it is said: “He sent me to announce good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives, and sight to the blind” (Isa. LXI, 1).

Sometimes the grace they had received, whether the grace of adoption or of miracles, when it is said: “The daughters of kings stood in your honor; the queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. XLIV, 10).

Sometimes admonition, as in what follows: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people” (ibid., 11).

Sometimes the glorification that we owe to Christ, when it is said: “For he is the Lord your God; you shall worship him” (ibid., 12).

Sometimes the blessedness and virtue that the faithful person merits, when it is said: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after him” (ibid., 15).

Sometimes the joy in which they live as they see their own progress, when it is said: “They shall be brought with joy and exultation” (ibid., 16).

Sometimes priesthood and ecclesiastical custom, when it is said: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (ibid., 17).

Sometimes the spiritual edification of the Church, when it is said: “From ivory steps, from which they delighted you” (ibid., 9).

Sometimes ecclesiastical authority, when it is said: “You shall appoint them rulers over the whole earth” (Ps. XLIV, 17).

Sometimes the fullness of believers, when it is said: “The whole earth shall be filled with his glory; let it be, let it be” (Ps. LXXI, 19).

Sometimes the endurance of either temptations or persecutions, when it is said: “Until he brings judgment to victory, and in his name the nations shall hope” (Isa. XLII, 4).

Sometimes the destruction of enemies, when it is said: “And his enemies shall lick the earth” (Ps. LXXI, 9).

Sometimes the peace in which the Church rejoices after persecutions, when it is said: “In his days righteousness shall arise and an abundance of peace, until the moon is established” (ibid., 7).

[Note: [Col. 0039D] Hebrew, literally: “until the moon is absent.” The Septuagint has *ἕως οὗ ἀνταναιρεθῇ ἡ σελήνη* (*heōs hou antanairethē hē selēnē*), “until the moon is removed.” The Vulgate has *donec auferatur luna*, “until the moon is taken away.”]

Sometimes the errors of heretics and the presence of Elijah, when it is said: “Behold, I send you Elijah the Tishbite, and he will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” (Mal. IV, 5–6).

Sometimes the hope of the faithful and the Savior’s second coming, when it is said: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

Sometimes the baptism of John, when it is said: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. III, 1).

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the kinds of predictions made under Grace
D. Since we have discussed the kinds of predictions found in the Law, give those which are read as having been uttered in Grace.

M. Twenty-three kinds of predictions made in Grace are found. Either the generation and life of John the Baptist are foretold to his father Zechariah, as in that entire speech delivered through the angel and in Zechariah’s own prophecy (Luke 1:13–17, 68–79); or the miraculous conception and birth of the Savior, as in the prediction spoken by the angel to holy Mary (ibid., 28–37); or the revelation to the Magi, or the unbelief and conversion of the Jews (Matthew 2:1 ff.), as it is said: “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:34); or the reward of the heavenly kingdom, as in: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2), and what follows; or the calling of the nations, as it is said: “Many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11); or the exclusion of the Hebrews, as in what follows: “But the children of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness” (ibid., 12); or salvation through the preaching of the apostles, as when it is said: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19); or the splendor of miracles, as it is said: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14:12); or the temptation and persecution of the righteous, as it is said: “They will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will flog you” (Matthew 10:17), and so forth; or the endurance of the faithful amid adversity, as when it is said of the Church: “The gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). And again: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12); or the contemplation of the heavenly kingdom and of the second coming, which the souls of the saints also enjoy in this life, as in: “For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his works. Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matthew 16:27–28); or the recompense of good or evil, as when it is said: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46); or the presence of the Holy Spirit given to the apostles, as in: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17); or ecclesiastical authority foretold, as it is said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven” (Matthew 16:19); or the death, passion, and resurrection of the Savior, as it is said: “From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests, and be killed, and rise again on the third day” (Luke 9:22); or the general resurrection, as the Apostle says: “As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22); or the resurrection of Christ and of us together, as it is said: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32); or the betrayal by Judas, as Christ says: “Did I not choose you twelve? Yet one of you is a devil” (John 6:71); or the manner of the temptation and death of certain disciples, as the Lord foretold to Peter both his future denial and the form of his passion, saying: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26:34); and: “When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18); or the presence of Christ’s captors, when he says: “Rise, let us go; behold, the one who betrays me has drawn near” (Matthew 26:46); or the dispersion of the apostles, as in: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (ibid., 31); or the finding of the colt of the she-ass, which the Lord foretold in the Gospel that the disciples would bring (Matthew 21:2–3); or the presence of Antichrist, when it is said: “Let no one deceive you in any way; for unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition who opposes, is revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:3); or the presence of Elijah, when it is said: “Elijah will come first” (Matthew 17:11); or the consciousness of the elect, as concerning Paul: “This man is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9:15); or the prediction that some will not be changed but will taste death, as the Apostle says: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51); or a future pestilence, as in the prophecy of Agabus (Acts 11:28); or the opposition of heresies, as it is said: “But understand this: in the last days difficult times will arise” (2 Timothy 3:1). And again: “They will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will accumulate teachers for themselves” (2 Timothy 4:3); or the grace of baptism, as in: “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3:11); or the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish temple, as in: “Pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the sabbath” (Matthew 24:20); and: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38); or the preaching of the Gospel, as it is said: “The Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14); or the evils of the end together with the end itself, as when it is said: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened” (ibid., 29).

D. How do we say that these predictions pertain to the future age?

M. As we said concerning the applications: the things predicted before the Law were directed toward the times of the Law or of Grace; again, the things predicted in the Law foreshadowed Grace; and the things predicted in Grace had as their cause and reward the heavenly kingdom. Thus the entire purpose of the predictions is gathered as referring to the goods of the future age.

[Note: We have restored this from chapter 15 above and chapter 25 of this book. The editions read: “we speak of applications.”]

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Effects of Predictions

D. Since we have now shown three parts of the things that we said pertain to the future age—namely, applications, figures, and predictions—there remains a fourth part, that we discuss effects. What, then, are effects?

M. Effects are the realities toward which the intention of the applications looked, which the likeness of the types represented, or which the knowledge conveyed by the words foretold.

D. How many periods are there for effects?

M. Three. For either the things that were predicted were brought about in the time of the Law, or they are now taking place under Grace, or they are to be completed in the time of the future ages.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What Was the Reason for Making the Present Age

D. If everything that took place in the present age looked toward the future, why was it necessary for God to make the present age?

M. Because it was fitting that rational creatures should first learn, so that they might be roused amid uncertainties and afterward enjoy eternal things; that what was given might rightly appear to have been bestowed upon those who had been tested; that past struggles might become more pleasing when remembered; and that they might glorify more greatly the giver, who helps the godly in this age—so that they might conquer and he might grant eternal rewards to the victors.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Instruction of Rational Beings in This Age

D. In how many ways is the instruction of rational beings carried out in this age?

M. In two. Either through understanding created things, as the Apostle says: “His invisible attributes are clearly perceived from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20). For whoever considers the world and everything placed within it, distinguished by its modes and orders, must understand that there is a God who both made and governs these things. Or through the divine Scriptures, which, as we have said, are divided into four kinds: historical, prophetic, proverbial, and simply instructional.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What Must Be Observed in Understanding the Scriptures

D. What are the things that we must preserve in understanding the divine Scriptures?

M. That the things said be appropriate to the speaker; that they not depart from the causes for which they were said; and that they agree with the times, places, sequence, and intention.

D. What do we say is the intention of divine teaching?

M. The Lord himself said: “That we should love the Lord with all our heart and with all our soul, and our neighbors as ourselves” (Deuteronomy 6:1). The corruption and opposite of teaching is not to love God or one’s neighbor.

D. What is the cause of this opposition?

M. The cause of evils lies in those who are evil; for, while rational creatures use free will—which was well granted to them—in a disorderly way, they become the cause of evil and punishment for themselves.

## CHAPTER XXIX. From Where the Books of the Catholic Religion Are Asserted to Come

D. From what do we prove that the books of our religion were written by divine inspiration?

M. From many things. First is the truth of Scripture itself; then the order of events, the harmony of its precepts, its manner of speech without affectation, and the purity of its words. To these are added the character of those who composed and preached them: that human beings should have handed down divine things, lowly persons exalted things, and the ineloquent subtle things, having been filled only with the divine Spirit. Then there is the power of the preaching, which, while it was being preached, gained authority, although by a few despised people. To these are added the correction of contrary teachings, such as those of the Sibyls and philosophers; the expulsion of adversaries; the usefulness of what followed; the fulfillment of the things foretold through applications, figures, and predictions; and finally the miracles continually performed until Scripture itself was received by the nations. Of this, for the present, the following is a sufficient miracle: it is known to have been received by everyone.

## CHAPTER XXX. Where Faith Is Necessary to Religion

D. If the proofs of the divine Scriptures are sufficient, why is faith necessary to religion?

M. Our faith is indeed above reason; nevertheless, it is not adopted rashly or irrationally. For faith understands what reason teaches, and where reason fails, faith goes ahead. We do not believe whatever happens to be heard, but those things which reason does not disapprove. What cannot be fully attained, however, we confess with faithful prudence.

**In the Year of Our Lord 550**

**MAPPINIUS, BISHOP OF RHEIMS**

[Col. 0043]

# TWO LETTERS OF MAPPINIUS (C)

[Col. 0043]

## FIRST LETTER. TO SAINT NICETIUS

[Note: Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier.]

[Col. 0043A]

**For the Council of Toul, held in the year 549**

To his holy and most blessed brother in Christ, Nicetius the pope,

[Note: In the earliest centuries of the Church, the word *pope* was given indiscriminately to all bishops, although the Roman pontiff, as head of the universal Church and prince of pastors and the faithful, was always so regarded.]

Mappinius, bishop.

The teaching of the Gospel reading bears witness that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand (Matthew 12). If this is rightly and deservedly believed concerning lovers of the world and those who remain in earthly desire, it is certainly still more rightly thought concerning the persons of priests, if they are found to be divided among themselves by discordant wishes and interests. And with what confidence shall we offer prayers to our Creator, who commanded us to live in the unity of the structure that is the body of his divinity, if we in turn separate ourselves from mutual charity?

As the divine word teaches in one place, we ought to strive that brother may support brother, so that, like a fortified and strong city, he may stand upon an unshaken foundation: namely, that we all share with equal-minded compassion in one brother’s sorrow and lift one another up through mutual labors.

For this reason, most devout and dearly beloved lord and brother, we inform you that we received a letter from our son, the lord King Theudebald, stating that I ought to be present in the city of Toul on the first day of June, without declaring any reason for the summons. In a replying letter we indicated that we ought not to go there, since we were evidently ignorant of the cause and circumstances.

In repeated letters he informed your Blessedness that, while, from zeal prompted by the fear of God, reproving certain Franks and removing them from ecclesiastical communion because of incestuous unions, you were enduring scandals or anxieties of many kinds. Concerning this matter we deeply grieve that you did not inform us through your report whether they are condemned on the basis of canonical judgment, or whether, out of pastoral diligence, they are being corrected for lesser offenses.

Although we know that you could discover nothing new concerning these matters that the ancient diligence of the Fathers had not already discovered, it nevertheless seems absurd that those should be received by us who, according to the sequence of the canons, are rejected by you with ecclesiastical severity. For we know that, if we do this knowingly, we become involved in the crimes of others; if unknowingly, we are not subjected to guilt.

Therefore, while greeting you with the charity that is due, we also advise you to endeavor to make us participants in everything, both in the difficulties of your tribulations and in the advantages of your prosperity. For, through our head, who is Christ, no adversity tears us away from concern for you, and no hardship divides us from your charity.

If, nevertheless, we are not presumptuous, we dare to say this. It would have been fitting for your consolation concerning such circumstances, rather than a royal summons, to have brought us together, because, if something similar—which we think might happen in the future—had occurred to us, we would immediately have sent a letter to your brotherhood, so that, appearing face to face at a suitable time or place, we might see one another.

Although it is both fitting and pleasing for us to obey royal commands in good matters, we are no less ready to obey your letters, if they are directed by the zeal of charity and not by the arrogance of contempt; for your bitterness cannot become our sweetness, nor can your rejection stand without our humiliation, and the veneration due to you, though bestowed by us, cannot be recognized from afar.

And would that, as we have said, persuaded by charity and through a flowing letter, you had decided to disclose to us the distress of your heart! We would have learned whether we sympathized with your troubles or rejoiced in them; for, when you remain silent—as you yourselves know—humanity can understand divine things only when a man speaks.

Let your Perfection know this more fully: if the repeated letters of the lord king had reached us five or six days before the first of June, you would have had our humble presence in the appointed place on the stated day.

[Note: Labbe, *Councils*, vol. V, col. 404; Dom Marlot, *History of the Metropolitan Church of Rheims*, vol. I, p. 212.]

## SECOND LETTER. TO VILLICUS, BISHOP OF METZ

[Col. 0044C]

To his lord Villicus the pope, Mappinius, bishop.

All of us unanimously proclaim you happy and blessed, most blessed father, for heavenly piety has granted you such understanding and such an inclination toward kindness that you are shown to live with singular perfection. Although we read that the Lord said this to Saint Peter—“Feed my sheep”—the present sentence applies to all who perform the priestly office. But you, surpassing all others through your singular sweetness, are seen not only to feed the sheep entrusted to you, but never cease to nourish the priests of other sheep with honeyed perfection and an abundance of delights.

[Col. 0045A] He who searches the reins and the heart is witness that this is written for us not as flattery but as a truthful assertion. And if our Creator and Redeemer advances you, as we pray, to the age of sixty, you will be foremost among all and preferred to the other priests; and all who profit from the instruction of your life will grieve at your absence and lament that they must live after you.

Therefore, greeting you with the love that is due and earnestly praying with love, do not cease, with assiduous entreaty and with thanksgiving and praise, to implore for us the mercy of the merciful Lord. We therefore ask that your Charity deign to inform us how many solidi we should send to those regions to purchase pigs,

[Note: See Saint Remigius’s Testament, volume 65 of our *Patrologia*, at the end. **Editor.**]

because it is clear to us that the gift bestowed by you in place of a present will be found to be a benefit, if this favor has been arranged by your direction.

[Note: Dom Marlot, *History of the Metropolitan Church of Rheims*, vol. I, p. 214.]

**In the Year of Our Lord 551**

**ARATOR, SUBDEACON OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH**

[Col. 0045]

# PROLEGOMENA. HENRIK JOHANN ARNTSENIUS TO THE READER

It is nearly ten years since I published Sedulius, illuminated by my own observations and those of highly learned men. Even then I had resolved to purge and edit Arator as well; for in most editions he was added as a companion to Sedulius, and the editors seemed to have followed their own judgment more than the authority of the manuscripts.

I publicly bound myself long ago to this task,

[Note: In the *Miscellanies*, p. 39.]

but the reasons that prevented me from carrying out my plan were sufficiently serious. Not to mention the duties of public office, I counted among them, with good reason, the hope held out by variant readings from the Leiden manuscripts. Having obtained these, I took up again the web whose completion I had temporarily laid aside, and now hand the poet over to you, if it is permissible to hope for such a thing, more carefully corrected by these labors and modeled upon the best manuscripts.

And if things that appear rarer are more welcome, I may conjecture that there will be some who gladly approve this undertaking, whatever it may be, since editions of Arator have not been known everywhere, and although this poem is indeed found in the older editions of Christian poets, it has not been polished by the work of more recent scholars.

Prudentius found Cellarius and Heinsius as his restorers; Juvencus, Omeis and Reusch; Sedulius, Cellarius and Gruner. But I know no one among more recent scholars who has illustrated Arator with notes. Why, however, do I mention more recent scholars, when learned men in general have contributed nothing to him by way of notes,

[Col. 0046B] except for Arrius Barbosa, the Portuguese, whose commentaries on this poet were published in folio at Salamanca in 1516,

[Note: See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, I, p. 346. The same author calls him “Arrius Mendosus” in *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. III, p. 307, and Funccius does so in *On the Decline of the Latin Language in Its Old Age*, p. 247.]

but which I have not been able to see.

Others, indeed, seem to have attempted similar things, but only attempted them. That Christian Daumius had thought about illustrating Christian poets, and consequently Arator as well, and that, if patrons had been available, he had wished to complete the work, is apparent from his letter to Heinsius.

[Note: Burmann’s *Collection of Letters*, vol. V, pp. 214, 216, 222.]

Andreas Rivinus, professor of humanities at Leipzig, must also be mentioned here; Daumius refers to his little works on Christian poets,

[Note: Burmann’s *Collection*, vol. V, p. 225.]

as does Nicolaus Heinsius,

[Note: *Collection*, at the place cited, p. 218.]

and writes that Rivinus published them after explaining them publicly, illuminating them with observations, and purging them from manuscripts. This is stated by Johann Georg Graevius.

[Note: In the preface to the *Syntagma of Dissertations*.]

Daumius testifies that, in correcting them, Rivinus indulged himself considerably.

[Note: Burmann’s *Collection*, vol. V, p. 226.]

Certainly the editions of Dracontius and Drepanius Florus prepared by Rivinus are known. But whether he also thought of publishing Arator I cannot determine.

Francis Juretus, moreover, stopped at the attempt itself. Because of his plan to publish Christian poets, although he achieved no success, he was praised by Johann Albert Fabricius.

[Note: *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. I, p. 721.]

When I mention him, I truly regret Arator’s fate, since less favorable circumstances denied him that Fabricius as a restorer. For Fabricius, equipped with the Cambridge manuscript, which Eric Benzelius, bishop of Linköping and prefect of the Uppsala library, had collated, promised that he would publish Arator,

[Col. 0047A]

[Note: *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. I, p. 706.]

and had decided to preface it with the Acts of the Apostles, reproduced in Greek and Latin from the Laud manuscript, and to add Florus’s *Sparsion* on the Acts and Grotius’s commentaries.

[Note: *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, I, p. 347.]

If anyone considers all these plans, together with the learning of that excellent man, he will be all the more sorry that this Ajax has fallen upon the sponge, since without doubt he would have contributed outstanding materials. Whether he had already drawn the first lines of these works, and whether they later came into Reimarus’s hands, I utterly do not know. I nevertheless doubt it, since Reimarus mentions nothing of them among Fabricius’s posthumous manuscripts, especially in the place where a suitable opportunity would have arisen, when he was discussing Fabricius’s specimen of the Acts of the Apostles and his plan to reproduce them in Greek capital letters from the Laud manuscript.

[Note: See Reimarus’s *Life of Fabricius*, p. 206.]

I have sometimes suspected that Fabricius set Arator aside after abandoning his plan to publish the sacred poets, once he entrusted Juvencus to Omeis and Reusch for illustration. That is what a testimony of Reimarus in the *Life of Fabricius* seemed to indicate.

[Note: p. 208, where he discusses Commodian’s *Instructions*.]

But I later discovered facts that oppose this suspicion, namely what Fabricius himself promised elsewhere.

[Note: *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. I, p. 703.]

From all this it is clear that men distinguished for learning judged these writers not unworthy of their care, especially since they seemed to be unknown even to the more learned. This was so true that Georg Fabricius, to whom we owe a collection of the ancient ecclesiastical poets—however rare it may be in this age—did not blush to admit in his preface to Prince Alexander

[Note: p. 8.]

that, apart from Prudentius, he knew none of these poets.

Since they seemed commendable on no ground other than that of religious writing, few were willing to peruse them, judging these poems light and worthless. Christian Daumius complained of his age,

[Note: *On the Causes of the Loss of the Roots of the Latin Language*, chapter 21, toward the end.]

saying that few cared about Christian poets or had any understanding of their elegance. Who, then, would be surprised that scarcely anyone spent effort correcting them or time reading them?

Thus Franciscus Floridus Sabinus says:

> Sincerus surpasses Prudentius to such an extent that, without doubt, a single epigram by the former to the supreme pontiff is worth more than countless myriads of Prudentiuses, Arators, and Juvencuses—not to mention oxen.

[Note: *Supplementary Readings*, book III, chapter 6, vol. I of Gruter’s *Facsimiles*, p. 1204.]

Although this judgment is too harsh and bitter, and although Daumius rightly resisted it, believing that much good could be drawn from these poets,

[Note: *On the Causes of the Loss of the Roots of the Latin Language*, chapter 21.]

it must nevertheless be admitted that these poets carried with them the faults of their age, both in their words and in their presentation of subjects. Yet for that very reason they should be considered no less worthy of the care of learned men than the prose writers of that age, who deserve to be censured for still more blemishes and for superstitious judgment. But this is not the place to discuss it.

One further point should be added: the reasons for Arator’s neglect, and for his being almost unknown, lie in the very method of writing that he employed. He is certainly excessive in accumulating allegories, whether one prefers to call them types, forms, or figures.

[Note: See the remarks on book I, verse 139. Compare J. G. Vossius, *Institutes of Oratory* IV.11, at the beginning.]

But even in this he readily deserves excuse because of the practice of that age, which tested the sharpness of its intellect through such devices. It is well known how greatly this kind of exposition pleased Origen, and how eagerly, after the third century, writers ignorant of the Hebrew and Greek languages seized upon it. Since, lacking knowledge of letters, they could not bring light to the expressions of the sacred text, they attempted to add it through such elegant interpretations.

A pious purpose was also joined to this: they believed that historical matters, set down plainly, served little for the proper formation of morals and life unless, as though a veil had been removed, the truth they believed to be hidden was exposed for the advancement of piety. I would neither wholly condemn nor praise this purpose.

Here there is error in these matters, both outside the walls and within. I would value most highly their attempt to advance piety, according to the merit it has in these writers; but they should have taken care not to fall into inflated speech, bombast, and words a foot and a half long—and, what is more, into mere nonsense.

Who, I ask, can tolerate a moral, allegorical, and anagogical interpretation of the sacred text arising from a historical narrative? On this subject, Georg Fabricius has an observation worth reading.

[Note: Below, on book II, verse 891.]

But why should we not tolerate these things in the writers of that period, when enthusiasm for the humane disciplines had long since cooled? Even the age that, by the favor of the supreme God, enjoys greater light of learning and letters sometimes approves such things and listens to them willingly.

[Note: Compare Johann Franz Buddeus, *Introduction*, vol. II, pp. 1740 and 1786.]

But I return to Arator, so that I may pass the same judgment on his allegories as Christian Adolph Klotz somewhere gives on Manuel Phila:

[Note: *Literary Acts*, vol. V, part I, p. 41.]

> Everywhere he hunts for clever conceits, and while he wishes to express ideas in a novel manner, he provokes laughter—unfortunate in constructing figures and comparisons.

To continue with the matter itself, the name Arator is not entirely unknown in the monuments of antiquity. Ammianus Marcellinus mentions a commander named Arator,

[Note: Book XXVIII, chapter 2.]

whom Valentinian ordered, through the notary Syagrius, to build a fortification beyond the Rhine on Mount Pirus. I do not deny, however, that the reading in Ammianus is uncertain, since Valesius testifies that *Orator* is read in the Regius manuscript, the Colbertine manuscript, and also in the Augsburg edition.

There is also an Arator on an ancient Narbonese stone, whose sister’s son was Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne. Stephanus Baluzius brought the stone forward in his notes on book VII of *On the Government of God*.

[Note: p. 348.]

The nearest parallel is Arator, the father of our Arator, whom I suspect lived in Liguria and who was celebrated for eloquence and learning. Athalaricus bears witness to this in writing to our author:

[Note: In Cassiodorus, *Variae* VIII.12.]

> You are also assisted by the eloquence and character of your father, whose speech could instruct you even if you had not had leisure for the books of the ancients. For, as we know, he was exceptionally learned in letters.

And afterward:

> Therefore you should be thought to have extended your talent by your father’s example.

Our poet was born of such a father toward the end of the fifth century. The date of his birth will be more certain if Hoogstraten wrote correctly that Laurentius, bishop of Milan, with whom Arator was raised after his father’s death, died in the year 504.

[Note: In the lexicon, under “Arator.”]

Moreover, he had already held various offices before the year 544, when he presented his poem to Vigilius—offices such as one would scarcely believe entrusted to younger men. Hence those who affirm that he was born in the year 490 do not seem to me to be wrong.

[Note: Luiscius, in the lexicon.]

At least I would establish this with greater justification than the other claim, maintained by some, that Ravenna was his birthplace.

[Note: Hoogstraten, in the lexicon.]

That he was at Ravenna with Parthenius is evident from a letter written to the same man:

[Note: Verse 35.]

> Since we were being held by these household gods in the city of Ravenna,  
> I stood before you as an eager guest, night and day.

But that he was born there is not yet clear to me; indeed, it is altogether unlikely, since Ravenna is farther removed from Liguria, where I suspected that his father had lived and where I think the poet was born. Georgius Fabricius [Note: In *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, p. 11.] writes that it has not yet been discovered what Arator’s fatherland was, although others suppose him to have been Italian. But, unless I am mistaken, Athalaric assigns Liguria to him as his homeland, writing thus to Arator in Cassiodorus [Note: *Variarum* VIII, 12.] [Col. 0049C]:

> You did not, then, discover Roman eloquence in its native regions; and there the reading of Tully made you eloquent where the Gallic language once resounded.—Liguria, too, sends forth its own Tullies.

John Albert Fabricius [Note: *Bibliotheca medii et infimi aevi*, vol. I, p. 346, in the notes.] also used the same argument. But perhaps someone might conjecture that these words refer more to the place where he learned eloquence than to his native soil. Yet Athalaric seems to me to have indicated two things: that Arator possessed such a fortunate natural ability that he excelled in eloquence although he had not been trained as an orator at Rome; and that it was therefore possible for men of the highest eloquence to arise even from Liguria. The very word “sends forth” seems to contain an indication of native soil.

The words of the Latin Pacatus opportunely come to mind [Note: *Panegyric*, chapter 4, § 5.]:

> This land—Spain—produces the toughest soldiers, the most experienced generals, the most eloquent orators, and the most distinguished poets; this is the mother of judges and of princes; this land sent forth that Trajan, and afterward Hadrian, to imperial power.

It is therefore sufficiently clear, unless I am mistaken, that he was born in Liguria; and Hoogstraten, in his lexicon, perhaps not improperly assigned Milan as his homeland. Saxius suspected the same [Note: *Prodromus de studiis Mediolanensibus*, chapter 5; I owe the passage to Georg Christoph Hamberger, *Nachrichten von den vornehmsten Schriftstellern*, part III, p. 405.], and his suspicion becomes more plausible if Milan is reckoned as belonging to Liguria, since it is sometimes called its metropolis.

Ennodius, who was Arator’s intimate friend, celebrated Arator’s childhood. Three epigrams of his survive, *On the Scourging of the Child Arator* [Note: Book II of the poems, epigrams 114, 115, and 116.], and one on Arator’s birthday [Note: Book II, epigram 105.]. At this age—certainly in earliest childhood—he seems to have been deprived of an excellent father. I infer this with plausible probability from the fact that, in Ennodius [Note: *Diction*, or suasoria 9.], where he discusses the father’s death, Arator is said to have been taken in by Laurentius, archbishop of Milan. He was therefore brought up by Laurentius as by a guardian; for that is the sense of *suscipere* (“to take up” or “take under one’s care”) [Note: Cortius, on Pliny’s *Letters* II, 4, 2.]. This would not have been necessary if, by reason of his age, he had been able to protect and defend himself.

Someone might perhaps conjecture from these words of Athalaric [Note: In Cassiodorus, *Variarum* VIII, 12.] that Arator’s father was still alive when Arator devoted himself to literary studies:

> You are aided, moreover, by the eloquence and character of your father, whose speech could have instructed you even if you had not had leisure for the books of the ancients. For, as we know, he was exceptionally learned in letters.

But these words more probably refer to the example to be drawn from the character and eloquence of his father after the latter’s death—an example that Arator diligently imitated. Certainly, as regards the acquisition of eloquence, it will appear from what follows that he did not make use of his father’s instruction.

But since the strong are begotten by the strong and the good by the good, Arator likewise wished to reproduce the model of the man whom nature had intended him to resemble, just as Pliny wrote of his own Genialis [Note: Book VIII of the *Letters*, letter 13.]. Stimulated by praise of his father’s learning, he devoted himself entirely to literary studies, under the instruction of Deuterius, a grammarian of Milan. When he entered Deuterius’s school, Ennodius—who seems to have taken particular care of his own Arator [Note: That he was his intimate friend is clear from Book VIII, letters 4 and 11, and Book IX, letter 1.]—delivered a preface that still survives as the ninth of his *Dictions* [Note: Add also *Dictions* 12, 17, and 18.]. John Nicholas Funccius reports that at that time Arator was also trained in the art of speaking through the efforts of Ennodius [Note: *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 243.].

Using such teachers, he made such great progress that Athalaric denies that he had an equal in literary studies [Note: In Cassiodorus, *Variarum* VIII, 12.]. There will be another occasion to discuss his ability to compose poetry. His eloquence was especially celebrated; he was able to display its power all the more widely because he had pleaded cases in the forum, suffused with the torrent of his eloquence. Athalaric writes to him:

> The field of advocacy trained you; the summit of our judgment chose you.

[Col. 0050D] “For such a broad profession of every kind of learning existed within you”—I think **quar­umvis**, “of every kind,” should be read instead of **quamvis**, “although”—“that we would not allow your talent to grow old there. You entered service, although you could have acted as a legal representative (*cognitor*).” [Note: By “military service” he means civil service, or, as he soon says, “armed eloquence.” Jurists commonly use *milites* in this sense. See Book 14 of the *Code*, *On Advocates of Different Courts*: “He is so strong who renders distinguished service to his clients.” See Graevius on Cicero, *For Quintius* 2.]

And although eloquence drew you toward speaking in defense, justice nevertheless urged you to state what ought to be judged. It was proved what usefulness eloquence armed with character possesses. The safety of the state therefore commanded that a man so highly adorned with learning and natural gifts should be advanced to the highest honors.

Athalaric testifies that he had reached these honors at an early age [Note: Cassiodorus, *Variarum* VIII, 12.]. Hoogstraten, and after him Luiscius, writes that he served Athalaric as secretary [Note: Both in their lexicons, under “Arator”]; but I confess that I do not know on what authority this is asserted. It is more certain that he undertook an embassy on behalf of the Dalmatians to King Theoderic. Funccius assigns this to the year 526 [Note: *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 243.], whereas Hamberger assigns it to 527 [Note: *Nachrichten von den vornehmsten Schriftstellern*, part III, p. 405.]. Both, in my judgment, rely on conjecture, and not on sufficiently firm evidence.

Funccius’s opinion is more probable if the event is referred to the beginning of the year 526; Hamberger’s is entirely impossible, since Theoderic had already died in 526, in August or at the beginning of September [Note: Compare Johann Peter Ludewig, *Life of Justinian*, chapter 8, p. 401, and the notes.], leaving the empire to his grandson Athalaric, under the guardianship of Amalasuntha, Theoderic’s daughter.

The extent of the praise for his eloquence that he earned from this embassy cannot be set forth more clearly than in Athalaric’s own words:

> But, he says, so that we may assert your merits by means of commendable examples, it is worthwhile to recall the splendid embassy that you completed not with ordinary speech but with a torrent of eloquence. Sent from the region of Dalmatia to our lord and grandfather, you pleaded the needs of the provincials and the public interests in such a way that, before him—deeply concerned and extremely cautious—you were both abundant and free from offensiveness. Words flowed forth in profusion, together with the most delightful wit; and when you had finished, you seemed still to wish to speak. By moving and delighting, you filled out the effort of a true orator all the more, since you had already abandoned the role of an advocate.

Others also report—although this is not yet certain to me—that Arator was the leader of the embassy sent by Athalaric to Justinian, which Hoogstraten and Luiscius assign to the year 527.

It is more certain that Arator subsequently prepared his own way, through his learning, for the honors he was to hold at the royal court. Athalaric appointed him *comes domesticorum*. John Nicholas Funccius seems not to report this with sufficient accuracy when he assigns it to 526 [Note: *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 243.], given the king’s youth and the guardianship of his mother Amalasuntha—unless one supposes that the letters bearing Athalaric’s name should rather be attributed to his mother, who, because of Athalaric’s extremely poor judgment, was acting in his place. This is Ludewig’s opinion [Note: *Life of Justinian*, chapter 8, p. 413, in the notes.].

Nevertheless, in this matter I prefer to follow Johann Friedrich Buddeus [Note: *Isagoge*, vol. II, p. 1629.], who dates the event to approximately 534, although Hamberger also assigns it to that year [Note: In the work cited, p. 405.]. If this is correct, it must be said that it occurred not long before Athalaric’s death. Athalaric died of wasting disease in that same year, at only eighteen years of age [Note: Ludewig, *Life of Justinian*, chapter 8, p. 412.].

A letter of Athalaric—or, if one prefers, of Amalasuntha—on this matter survives in Cassiodorus [Note: *Variarum* VIII, 12]. Among other things it says:

> Hence it is that we adorn you, distinguished by the honor of *comes domesticorum*, so that you may expect much greater things from our judgments, since we believe that still better qualities are to be found in you. You see that a great responsibility has been entrusted to you.

The subsequent words are clarified by what Jacobus Gutherius [Note: *On the Offices of the Imperial Household* III, 28.] and Valesius [Note: On Ammianus Marcellinus XIV, 10.] discuss concerning this office. On the *domestici*, see also Bunemann on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 22, no. 3.

I have quoted the actual words so that it may be clear that Funccius and John Albert Fabricius did not proceed with sufficient accuracy: Funccius [Note: *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 243.] when he asserts that Arator was appointed *comes domesticorum et privatorum* by this letter; Fabricius [Note: *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*, vol. I, p. 346, in the notes.] when he declares that he was appointed only *comes privatarum*. For he became *comes privatarum* only later—an office that was especially honorable [Note: Gutherius, *On the Offices of the Imperial Household* III, 25; Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XXIX, 1]—perhaps after Athalaric’s death.

Although no reliable writer confirms that he held this office, the memory of the fact has nevertheless been conveniently preserved by the Rheims manuscript of Arator belonging to the monks of Saint Remigius. At its beginning, Jacobus Sirmondus [Note: On Ennodius IX, letter 1.] and Aubert Miraeus [Note: Scholium on Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 38. Add Funccius, in the work cited, p. 245.] testify that the following words can be read:

> With the blessed lord Peter assisting, this codex was presented by the illustrious Arator, former *comes domesticorum*, former *comes privatarum*, a religious man, and so forth.

At last, weary of the affairs and troubles that the court continually supplies, Arator turned to another way of life. Georgius Fabricius writes that he first became a monk [Note: In the commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 11.]. Certainly, as he enlisted his head in the sacred militia, he offered it to be tonsured according to solemn custom [Note: See the letter to Parthenius, verse 70; and concerning this custom Sirmond on Sidonius IV, letter 24]. Thus he became a subdeacon of the Roman Church. Funccius assigns this to the year 541 [Note: *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 244.], when Totila was in control of affairs in Italy, and he connects it with what Arator himself records in the elegy to Vigilius. I have discussed this in the notes and additions.

In the chronicle of an uncertain author preserved by Canisius, however, he is already given the title of subdeacon for the year 538, unless one supposes that this was done by anticipation. Alfonso Ciaconius [Note: In the *Bibliotheca*, p. 239.] and Johann Hildebrand Withofius [Note: *Specimen of Gunther*, pp. 37, 92, 157.] do not proceed with sufficient accuracy when they call our man a deacon. The manuscripts consistently support the other designation, as do the testimony of Hermannus Contractus [Note: *Thesaurus Canisianus*, vol. III, part I, p. 225.] and that of the anonymous author of the chronicle [Note: In Canisius, *Thesaurus*, vol. III, part II, p. 240.]. This must be maintained all the more because the functions of deacons and subdeacons were sharply distinguished [Note: See what I noted, p. 2.].

With still less justification Aldus [Note: In the *Life of Arator* prefixed to his edition.], Ciaconius [Note: In the *Bibliotheca*, p. 239.], Gyraldus [Note: *History of the Poets*, dialogue 5, p. 297.], and certain editors called him a cardinal deacon. I have discussed this matter in the letter to Florianus [Note: Below, pp. 2 and 3.]

From these facts it is perfectly clear that our Arator flourished especially under Justin the Thracian and Justinian, and that his childhood must be assigned to the reign of Anastasius [Note: See Vossius, *Ars Grammatica* II, 39, and what I said in the *Miscellany*, chapter 4.]. Taubmannus [Note: On Virgil’s *Culex*, verse 78, and the authors cited by Funccius, *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 246.] and others, however, extend the period of his flourishing life too far, down to the year 560.

Considering the span of human life, I readily grant Ciaconius’s claim [Note: In the *Bibliotheca*, p. 239.] that Arator could have lived that long, since he would then scarcely have been more than seventy. But it is one thing to speak of the time when someone chiefly became famous through his deeds or writings, and another to speak of the end of life to which he may have survived.

I therefore do not know why Gyraldus contradicted Aldus, who remembered Arator as flourishing in 544, following Paul the Deacon and Palmerius, who refer him to 560 [Note: Gyraldus, *History of the Poets*, dialogue 5, p. 298.]. I prefer what Gyraldus adds, unless perhaps we are to understand him as saying that Arator wrote this at that time—namely, in 544—and died in the other year, 560.

Although it is not established with complete clarity when he died [Note: See Funccius, *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 246.], his life may plausibly be extended to that year or one close to it. I wish Georg Christoph Hamberger had supplied the authority by which he asserted that Arator died in 555 [Note: *Nachrichten von den vornehmsten Schriftstellern*, part III, p. 405.].

[Col. 0053C] These, then, are the matters concerning Arator’s life that I have been able to gather from monuments of antiquity and the commentaries of the most learned men. I now proceed to an understanding of his poetry and to the poem itself, for whose sake this entire preface has been prepared.

Just as I showed above that Arator had been entrusted to and imbued with the liberal disciplines, so in cultivating those disciplines he had Parthenius as his guide. While staying with him at Ravenna, he first read Caesar’s histories, or *Ephemerides* [Note: Letter to Parthenius, verse 39.]. Parthenius then drew various materials from the treasury of his own learning, by which Arator might become more learned; and since Parthenius himself was seized by an extraordinary love of reading poets, he stimulated our author toward poetry by his own example.

Arator had devoted himself to composing poems from earliest youth, especially poems in which he seemed to reproduce the myths of the ancients [Note: Letter to Parthenius, verse 51.]. At Parthenius’ encouragement he turned to sacred poetry, and the matters mentioned in the letter to Vigilius [Note: Verse 16; compare the notes.] must be explained in this connection. He therefore resolved to expound either David’s Psalms or Genesis in verse [Note: Letter to Parthenius, verse 73.].

Nor is it surprising that Parthenius was his instigator in this undertaking, since Parthenius excelled among his contemporaries in the ability to compose poetry. Later scholars also judged him worthy of this praise. Daniel Heinsius thought that he had been made for poetry by nature, except insofar as he drew many things from his own age [Note: *Sacred Aristarchus*, p. 329.]. John Louis de La Cerda calls him a poet of no mean rank [Note: On Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 39.]; Maderus, a poet of not unsuccessful talent [Note: On Panvinius, *On the Triumph*, chapter 7, at the end.]; Barthius, a poet of great talent and one of the foremost among Christian poets [Note: On Statius, *Thebaid* II, 706; on Claudian III, *Consulship of Honorius*, preface, verse 1.].

Changing his plan, however, Arator applied himself instead to the celebrated *Acts of the Apostles*, following Luke as his guide, and finally produced this poem, *On the Acts of the Apostles*. I shall show below that this was more properly the title of the work than *Apostolic History*, as some thought [Note: Page 32.].

Aldus writes in the *Life of Our Author*, prefixed to his edition, that Arator imitated the examples of Juvencus and Sedulius in this matter. The work was completed in the year of Christ 544, as Labbe correctly pointed out from the Vatican manuscript [Note: *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, vol. I, p. 688. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. I, p. 705; *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*, vol. I, p. 346. Hermannus Contractus also assigns it to the same year in *Thesaurus Canisianus*, vol. III, part I, p. 225.], as will soon become clearer.

Aldus is therefore not sufficiently accurate in the *Life of Arator*:

> While he was composing these books, the city of Rome was besieged by the Goths and Vandals, and there was considerable dispute in the city over the election of a pope. At last, when the city had been freed from its enemies by divine mercy and Vigilius had been created pope, peace was restored to the Church in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 507.

Unless there is a printer’s error in the numbers, this is a very serious error on Aldus’s part. According to the more common chronological records, Vigilius became pope in 537 or the following year, at which time those disputes also occurred, especially on account of Silverius, who had been expelled from the papal see [Note: See Platina, *Lives of the Popes*, p. 75.].

Arator first presented the completed poem to the abbot Florianus and afterward to Pope Vigilius. He commended it to both with an appended letter, which, following others, I have judged should be placed before the work. It was presented to Vigilius on the eighth day before the Ides of April, and it pleased him greatly, so that it was not only read publicly but also honored with everyone’s praise.

To make the fortunes of this poem better known, I shall append what had been written at the end of the second Vossian manuscript, adding various readings from Vossian manuscript 3 and from the Vatican manuscript [Note: What had been written in the same manuscript appears in the *Library of the Fathers of Lyon*, vol. X, p. 125.]

[Col. 0055A] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [the Vatican manuscript does not have these opening words]:

> With the blessed lord Peter assisting [the latter word is absent from the Vatican manuscript], this codex was presented by Arator, subdeacon [the Vatican adds: “of the holy Roman Church and”], to the holy and apostolic man Pope Vigilius. [Note: In the Rheims manuscript of the monks of Saint Remigius, cited by Sirmond on Ennodius IX, letter 1, it reads: “by the illustrious Arator, former *comes domesticorum*, former *comes privatarum*, a religious man, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Apostolic See, holy and apostolic, and so forth.”] It was received by him on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the presbytery before the confession of Saint Peter [the Vatican manuscript: “blessed Peter”], while many bishops [the Vatican adds: “presbyters”], deacons, and most of the clergy were present there together. After he had caused part of it to be read there immediately, he gave it to Surgentius, a venerable man, first secretary of the school of notaries in the archive [the Vatican has: “Surgentius, a venerable man, first secretary,” and Aldus has the same in the *Life of Our Author], to be properly deposited [read from the Vatican and Vossian manuscript 3: “in the Church”].

All the learned men, the most learned of them [read from the Vatican: “and the most learned”], immediately begged his Blessedness to order that it be read publicly. When he had commanded this to be done in the church of blessed Peter called *Ad Vincula*, a crowd gathered consisting of religious men, noble laymen, and also various people from the populace [the preceding nine words are absent from the Vatican manuscript]. With the same Arator, the subdeacon [absent from the Vatican manuscript], reciting it, both books were heard four times on separate days [the Vatican manuscript: “seven times,” but incorrectly, as is clear from what follows]. On any one day only a small portion of a book was read [the Vatican manuscript has: “when only half of one book was read,” which I prefer], because of the repeated requests for further readings, which they demanded with great enthusiasm.

The same reading was therefore held on these days: first, on the Ides of April; second, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [Col. 0055C] [Aldus in the *Life of Our Author*: the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May]; third, on the eighth day before the Ides of May [Note: The Vatican manuscript omits this eighth day before the Ides of May. It mentions three readings and places the third on the third day before the Kalends of June. But this is a copyist’s error: he omitted the middle occurrence because of the repetition of the word “third,” so that he joined the third reading immediately to what follows, namely, the third day before the Kalends of June.]; and fourth, on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the third year [the Vatican adds: “of the year”] after the consulship of Basil, a man of consular rank, in the seventh indiction.

These later details sufficiently indicate the year 544, as I noted above. Relandus may be consulted in his *Chronological Tables*. The editors of the *Library of the Fathers* [Note: Vol. X, p. 125.] refer these events insufficiently accurately to the fifth year of Vigilius and the nineteenth of Justinian.

Once this work on the *Acts of the Apostles* had been praised and deposited in the Church archives, Arator sent it to Gaul to Parthenius, his intimate friend and the son of Ennodius’s sister. Sirmondus discusses him more fully [Note: On Ennodius, letter 6, p. 1494.]. Funccius shows that he had been Arator’s fellow soldier [Note: *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 246.].

Parthenius, distinguished by an illustrious name, master of offices and patrician [Note: See the heading of the letter to Parthenius.], could by his authority have added considerable distinction to the poem. Arator therefore commended it to him in a remarkable letter. From this letter, just as most of Parthenius’s qualities and distinguished merits can be learned, so the learned world owes the letter itself to the careful diligence of Jacobus Sirmondus, who first published it from the Rheims manuscript of the monks of Saint Remigius in his notes on Ennodius [Note: Book IX, letter 1.]. The editors of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers* subsequently reproduced it [Note: Vol. X, p. 141.], and I have followed the same procedure, although the letter is not found in our manuscripts.

Barthius, indeed, judged the letter unworthy of Arator [Note: *Adversaria* XXIX, 2.], but his arguments are not important enough to require a laborious refutation; this will also appear from what has been noted concerning the letter.

I have not become acquainted with any other writings of Arator. From Thomasini’s *Paduan Library*, however, Fabricius mentions letters of Arator in manuscript [Note: *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*, vol. I, p. 348.]. Since I have no opportunity to inspect the books, I would not dare determine whether these are the letters addressed to Florianus, Vigilius, and Parthenius.

As for the poem itself, just as it pleased Vigilius, so it was celebrated no less by others for its eloquence. Thus Venantius Fortunatus [Note: *Life of Martin*, at the beginning.] writes:

> The deeds and Acts called those of the apostolic succession  
> the poet Arator ploughed with eloquent speech.

And Eberhard of Béthune [Note: In Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*, vol. II, p. 225.] writes:

> Arator’s meter does not lie fallow in its sequence, but flourishes.  
> Learned, he fittingly plows the apostolic deeds.

Later scholars also bestowed the same praise upon him. Alexander della Torre calls Arator “most eloquent” in his highly polished poem [Note: *On the Shining Ray of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, part I, book IV, p. 223.]. Caspar Barthius considers him a writer of acute intelligence [Note: On Statius, *Silvae* III, 2, 58.], well learned and even more fluent amid all those difficulties than the entanglements of that age generally allowed [Note: On Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 19.], very learned [Note: On Statius, *Thebaid* VI, 550.], learned [Note: On Claudian, *Praise of Stilicho* III, 122.], and by no means contemptible [Note: *Adversaria* VIII, 12.]. He also calls the poem itself noble [Note: On Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 19.], so much so that many centuries could not admire it sufficiently. And indeed it contains much elegance, especially because Arator followed the best guides. Withofius has already touched upon this [Note: *Specimen of Gunther*, p. 108.]; among the ancients he followed Lucan in particular, as I have shown with several examples in the *Observations* [Note: See the note on Book I, verse 49, and other passages.]. Hence Bede praised, in one place, the very pleasing concatenation of the verses [Note: *On Meters*, p. 2367, among the grammarians of Putsch.], and Barthius rightly wrote that, in describing Paul’s departure, Arator surpassed the Latinity of his age by the sharpness of his talent [Note: On Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 25.].

Nevertheless, I do not deny that he was sometimes carried away by an excessive zeal for allegories and that he thereby left not a few blemishes upon his otherwise highly elegant poem—especially in passages where he interpreted Hebrew words badly and derived from them allusions that were usually weak. Daniel Heinsius correctly thought that in such matters these writers often engaged in trifles [Note: *Sacred Aristarchus*, p. 329.], and Johann August Ernesti, a man of consular rank, was also right. For, he says [Note: *Philological and Critical Essays*, p. 213.]:

> When the Christian religion was propagated among the Greeks, most of the teachers of the Church who occupied themselves with explaining the divine writings were ignorant of the Hebrew language and used only Greek in interpretation. Hence many interpretations of the sacred books arose and were introduced into the Church and approved as true, although they did not conflict with the central doctrine of Christianity—although there were also interpretations of this kind that were false and far from accurate, together with many further matters on this subject that are entirely worthy of reading.

[Col. 0057B] For this reason Barthius calls Arator a writer of disordered language [Note: On Statius, *Silvae* III, 2, 58.], a poet of more difficult expression [Note: On Statius, *Thebaid* II, 706.], a writer of little effectiveness in moving the emotions [Note: The same work, on *Thebaid* IV, 19.], and a more intricate writer [Note: The same work, on *Thebaid* VI, 550.]. Yet he is not entirely consistent in these judgments, for they do not sufficiently agree with what I quoted above from the same author. Others, however, have attached the same criticism to certain of Barthius’s testimonies.

Funccius’s judgment is more precise [Note: *On the Extreme Old Age of Latin Literature*, p. 246.]:
