> It is enough that the work is pious, even if it is not sufficiently learned; nor, as the age demanded, did the poetic spirit fail the writer in composing it, although he sometimes committed errors—perhaps unknowingly—against the strict laws of meter.

I have frequently cited examples of the latter kind in the notes, collected in the index under “Prosody.” But Arator shares this with the other Christian poets because of their pious purpose, a matter touched upon by Cornelius Valerius Vonckius [Note: *Latin Readings*, book II, chapter 2.].

Since I am now about to investigate the merits of this poem, I should not omit that Arator did indeed propose to compose the apostolic Acts in verse, but generally touched upon the events only with his fingertips and, adding material of his own, wandered more freely than Juvencus and the others. This is the true judgment of Richard Simon [Note: *Critical History of the New Testament Commentary*, chapter 23, p. 335. I owe the passage to Buddeus, *Isagoge*, vol. II, p. 1629.]. Hence I do not know whether anyone has rightly called this poem, with the distinguished John Albert Fabricius, a “poetic paraphrase of the Acts” [Note: On the *Glossary of the New Testament*, p. 78.].

Thus I seem to have completed what concerns the poet himself and the poem, except that I should add this: it seems to me that he composed the poem in a continuous sequence, in the manner in which Fabricius published it, and did not divide it into chapters, as can be seen in the Antwerp edition, where the beginning of Book II is made chapter 25.

I have therefore rejected the chapters, which by the editors’ judgment are now longer and now shorter, although the manuscripts also contain them. Nevertheless, as I discovered in Sedulius, they are due to the copyists, especially those who added ornaments to the titles of books and to the beginnings of chapters—men who were **καλλιγράφοι** (“beautiful writers”) or **χρυσογράφοι** (“writers in gold”). Adapting themselves to the spaces that the earlier copyist had left vacant for such ornaments, they would either contract or extend such headings [Note: See Christian Gottlieb Schwarz, *Scholia philologica on the preface to the Institutes*, p. 23.].

To show, however, how much liberty the editors have taken in these matters, I shall here add what Nicolaus Heinsius excerpted from the codex of Balthasar Moretus, supplying the verses to which the entries refer.

That these entries are due to the copyists is clear from the fact that they are read much more fully in the Vossian manuscripts, more elegantly, however, in the first manuscript, differently again in Aldus’s edition, and differently yet in the Tornesian manuscripts and similar witnesses.

And this is all. It remains for me to explain the aids that I used in preparing the poet. First of all, three Vossian manuscripts must be mentioned, written on parchment and preserved in the extraordinarily rich library of the University of Leiden. When Ludovicus Casparus Valckenaer, a most distinguished man, was informed by the illustrious Burmann the Younger of my plan concerning Arator, he kindly gave me the opportunity to inspect them; for this favor I acknowledge that I owe him the greatest thanks I can offer. No less did Everwinus Wassenbergius place me in his debt, for, having stayed at Leiden for the sake of his studies, he voluntarily offered to collate these manuscripts and carried out the work with the greatest accuracy. Just as, moved by his proven devotion, he performed this service for me, once his former teacher, so, when an honorable position was soon afterward offered to him in the Deventer school, he fulfilled everyone’s expectations and became the distinguished ornament and glory of our Muses whom I had long foretold he would become.

The first manuscript, so called because it seemed superior to the others, is in octavo; the remaining two are in quarto. The second contains the whole of Arator, except for the letter to Florianus; the first begins only at Book I, verse 427, while the third begins at Book II, verse 704. The latter is the most corrupt of all, so much so that one would say its scribe scarcely knew Latin; this is why I silently passed over most of its variants, since they are trivial and rather the ravings of a dreaming scribe. In the second manuscript several interlinear glosses could be seen, although for the most part they disappear in Book II. I consulted them in obscure passages and frequently gave them a place in the notes.

Apart from these, I must celebrate and gratefully commemorate above all the remarkable kindness and goodwill toward me of the distinguished Petrus Burmann the Younger. In addition to so many other proofs of his friendship toward me, he contributed so much to the Arator that almost everything now added to the poet’s presentation is owed to him alone. From this most distinguished man I received collations of three manuscripts: the Cambridge manuscript, the University manuscript, and the Balthasar Moretus manuscript.

The first two had been collated with Fabricius’s edition by Gottlieb Cortius; Burmann had acquired the same copies from the Mencke library, which had been sold at Leipzig. Nicolaus Heinsius had collated the Moretus manuscript and recorded its variant readings on a slip of paper. Cortius had identified the Cambridge manuscript as a very ancient and beautifully written parchment manuscript of Trinity College, Cambridge, written in uncial letters. I believe it is the same manuscript that Johann Albert Fabricius had received from the collation made by Ericus Benzelius [Note: See *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. I, p. 706; *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 346.].

The other manuscript was somewhat more recent but, according to Cortius, written more accurately, and it was preserved in the University library. Since Cortius did not say which university it belonged to, I have called it simply the University Manuscript. I suspect, however, that it is the parchment manuscript which Christ. Daumius mentions in a letter to Heinsius as being preserved in the Leipzig Paulinum library [Note: *Sylloge Burmanni*, vol. V, p. 255.].

Heinsius calls the Moretus manuscript the oldest, but he collated no farther than verse 204 of Book I, and thus we are painfully deprived of the remainder. Perhaps he inspected the same manuscript during his travels, when, returning from the Spa springs, which he had visited for the sake of his health, and traveling through Brabant, he visited Moretus at Antwerp, the foremost printer of his age [Note: See Burmann the Younger, *Commentary on the Life of Nicolaus Heinsius*, p. 5.].

It should also be added that, besides the variants from the Cambridge and University manuscripts, Cortius attributed certain readings marked with the letter P. I suspect that these were taken from the papers of Pulmannus, who seems to have copied them from manuscripts, since some readings are plainly contrary to the meter—for example, to give only one instance, *vetus* in Book I, verse 149. Certainly Christ. Daumius testifies in a letter to Heinsius that Pulmannus’s hand is present in the Arator [Note: *Sylloge Burmanni*, vol. V, p. 254.], and Georg Fabricius reports that he consulted three manuscripts: one Bruges manuscript and two from Liège [Note: In his *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, p. 11.]. This makes me suspect it all the more, because, likewise through Burmann’s kindness, I obtained another copy of Fabricius’s edition, formerly belonging to Carolus Andreas Duker, in which several readings from Pulmannus’s papers concerning Arator were recorded, although they were of lesser importance.

Led by this suspicion, I inserted Cortius’s readings among the other variants under the heading “Pulmannus’s Papers.” I wish that I had also had access to the variants of the parchment manuscript in quarto which Zacharias Conrad Uffenbach saw preserved in the Westminster Library in London [Note: *Itinerary*, vol. II, p. 515.], as well as those of the Suollanus and Deventer manuscripts mentioned by Georg Fabricius [Note: *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, p. 11.]. As for the latter, I do not know where it went; at least, the distinguished Rhoerius wrote to inform me that it is not preserved in the public library of that city.

[Col. 0061B]

The editions of Arator are as various as they are numerous. Through the kindness of the distinguished Burmann the Younger, I chiefly examined the Aldine, Antwerp, Basel, and Tornaesian editions. Two other editions of Tornaesius were in my possession; in distinguishing them I sometimes used the numbers I mentioned in the preface to Sedulius.

Not counting the quarto edition without date or place of publication mentioned by Fabricius [Note: *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 346; *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. III, p. 307], the first of all those listed is the Milan edition of 1469, in octavo [Note: See Beuchem, *Incunabula Typographica*, p. 16.]. It may perhaps be the same edition that Hamberger, following Mattair, assigns to the following year [Note: *News concerning the Principal Writers*, part III, p. 406.]. Fabricius testifies that Juvencus and Sedulius were added to it; from this it is clear with what justification the Sedulius edition printed at Deventer in 1519 is called the first edition in the catalogue of the Gochenian Library.

Aldus Manutius followed. At Venice, in 1511, he published Arator together with other Christian poets, in quarto. This edition is excellent and more carefully corrected.

Arator was published alone at Strasbourg in 1507, in octavo.

Together with Sedulius and Juvencus at Leipzig in 1515, in quarto.

At Salamanca, together with the commentaries of Arrio Barbosa, in a larger format, in 1516.

At Antwerp, from the press of Joannes Grapheus, in 1535. Its readings agree with those which I appeared to have taken from Pulmannus’s papers, so that it reproduces even the most defective readings.

Next come the Basel editions attributed to Pulmannus. Fabricius mentions one without a date, preceded by a preface of Reinhard Hadamarius and containing variant readings, in octavo [Note: *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. III, p. 304.]. He also states that it was reprinted at Cagliari by Vincentius Sembenius in 1573, although Ciaconius dates it to 1571.

There is also a Basel edition of 1537, printed by Bartholomeus Westhemerus and Nicolaus Brylingerus. Through Burmann’s kindness I consulted it, and it agrees so closely with the Aldine edition that it too omits the verses omitted by Aldus. Perhaps the remaining Basel editions derived from it, those assigned to the years 1541, 1551, and 1562 [Note: Funccius mentions the first and the last, *On the Decline of the Latin Language*, p. 247.].

There are three Tornaesian editions, from 1553, 1566, and 1588. The first is the best of all and seems to have been modeled on the Aldine.

Fabricius also published Arator in the *Corpus of Ecclesiastical Poets* in 1564, although he claimed less for himself in Arator than in Sedulius and the others. This matter has been discussed sufficiently near the end of the preface to Sedulius.

Arator also appears in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, whose editions Fabricius lists [Note: *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. III, p. 305.]. I have taken the variant readings from the Lyons edition published by the Anissons in 1677. I have never seen the Cologne edition of 1573, in a smaller format, with some material from the earlier editions; Fabricius and Funccius mention it.

From the manuscripts and editions listed above that I examined, I reported the variant readings with the greatest possible accuracy, including readings that are plainly corrupt, except in the case of Vossianus 3. In this I followed the principle of Johann August Ernesti [Note: *Philological and Critical Opuscula*, p. 330.]: “Today the needs of others and the convenience of posterity are better served by adopting almost this rule: when manuscripts are examined, nothing, however slight or corrupt, is to be neglected. By this means all further necessity of collation is removed.”

I added excerpts from the observations of Caspar Barthius’s *Adversaria*. I wish, however, that he had brought forward more material from his manuscripts for the correction of the poet, especially since he seems to have possessed excellent manuscripts of Arator. He himself claims to possess an Arator parchment manuscript scarcely still legible because of its age [Note: *Adversaria* XIII, 20], extremely ancient and accurate parchments [Note: *Adversaria* on Statius, *Silvae* III, 2, 58], the oldest and most trustworthy Cologne manuscripts [Note: *Adversaria* XIII, 20], good and very ancient manuscripts which he had bought from the spoils of the Carthusians near Strasbourg [Note: *Adversaria* XXXIII, 3], and four complete, distinct parchment manuscripts, in addition to those assembled by Pulmannus [Note: *Adversaria* XIII, 20.].

Besides these, I excerpted from Georg Fabricius’s commentary whatever seemed to pertain to Arator, especially since Fabricius’s *Corpus* is in the hands of very few.

There is nothing more to add concerning my own work. If a fair-minded judge does not deny me the praise of diligence in collation and the desire to serve literature well, I shall consider my labor adequately rewarded. The conjectures of the distinguished Wassenbergius that you see inserted among these notes were communicated to me in letters by my excellent friend. I regret, however, that most of them had to be placed in the Addenda because the printing of the work overtook them. I have added sufficiently accurate indexes, especially the first, by which anyone may more easily compare Arator with the Acts.

In the Addenda I passed over the printer’s lesser errors and noted only the more serious ones. I mention this so that no one may attribute the omission of the rest to negligence or carelessness. These, learned reader, are the matters I wished to discuss with you. Farewell, and favor this undertaking to serve Arator well.

[Col. 0063]

## LETTER OF ARATOR THE SUBDEACON TO FLORIANUS (C)

[Col. 0063]

[Note: **Arator.** The name Arator itself was also used by others. For Ammianus mentions a commander named Arator, Book XXVIII. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, chapter 20.

The passage in Ammianus is chapter 2. But Valesius notes that in other manuscripts *Orator* is read there. The great scholar hastened, in his larger commentary on Phaedrus IV, 1, 8, to call him *Aratus*. Vossius does the same at the end of *De analogia* III, 30.

**Subdeacon.** In the ancient Church subdeacons were not merely deacons, but the lowest of the ministers, although the Acts of the Apostles do not mention the lower orders; they were “deacons of the deacons,” that is, subdeacons. Arator held such an office in Rome, and his little work is entitled *ARATOR THE SUBDEACON*. In the ancient parchment manuscripts in my possession it is prefaced as follows: “To the holy and venerable lord Florianus, spiritually instructed in the grace of Christ, Florianus the abbot, Arator the subdeacon.” A similar designation occurs in Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 3: “Soon afterward our priest Etherius enters, with Callipius the deacon and Amator the subdeacon.”

Theodor Pulmannus should not have removed this from Arator’s title; his manuscripts were bought by us in Belgium. Below, perhaps at a more suitable place, I shall explain who Calliopius was. For now I think the masculine name should be restored in Sulpicius Severus. The parchment manuscripts collated by Pulmannus and returned to us read *Calipiane*, *Calypione*, and otherwise, which confirms that *Calliopius* should be restored. Barthius, *Adversaria* II, chapter 2.

The Greek word διάκονος (*diakonos*) means “attendant” in Aristophanes, *Birds* 73; “minister of sacred rites” in Antoninus Liberalis, *Metamorphoses* chapter 29; and generally designates a servant who pours wine at banquets. So too in Anacreon, ode 4, verse 6, where Barnesius printed the Ionic form διηκονείτω, against Baxter and Tollius in the margin of the edition I possess. On the word itself see Eisner on Luke 17:8; Cerda, commenting on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 181, compared it with the Latin *ministrare* in this sense. Segaar, *Observations on Luke*, p. 167; from this the meaning “to serve” must be derived.

Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food* I, §9, reads ἐξ ἀρχῆς τῶν τὰ πλήθη διακονησάντων, “from the beginning of those who served the multitudes,” if the reading is sound. Reiskius and Rhoerius altered it to διακομησάντων; I would prefer διαπονησάντων, “those who labored,” which is less harsh, if I see correctly.

Among Christians the word then passed to those entrusted with the care of the poor and assigned a ministry at sacred banquets. Cave explained this in his *Life of Stephen*, p. 41, and Martinus in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. X, p. 237. Hence also *deaconesses*, concerning whom I have offered some material in *Miscellanea*, p. 34. In particular see Gothofredus on Book XXVII of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Bishops and Clergy*; Van Hoven, *Evangelical Antiquities*, p. 67. Hence *diaconium* itself means the office of deacons.

Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Martin*, chapter 5: “The same Hilary attempted, by imposing upon him the office of the diaconate, to bind him more closely to himself and to tie him to the divine ministry.” Thus read the passage on the basis of both Utrecht manuscripts. Those manuscripts that give *vincire* there were deceived by the scribes, who omitted the pronoun and thereby caused the difficulty. I have shown that the same thing happened elsewhere, in Book II of *On Being Summoned to Court*, chapter 8.

The Greeks call a companion of the deacons a συνδιάκονος (*syndiakonos*). Johann Heinrich Maius asserted this from Clement of Alexandria, *Sacred Observations* IV, p. 207; the term is also found in Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, Works, vol. I, pp. 783 and 850.

The minister of the deacons was the ὑποδιάκονος (*hypodiakonos*), or subdeacon. So Ignatius says in a letter, if it is genuinely his, p. 88 of Vossius’s edition. These men were appointed to guard the doors; they also served at the altar. Gothofredus on Book XLIV of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Bishops*, and Tribbechovius, *Continuation of the Exercises on Baronius*, p. 165.

A subdeacon of this kind is mentioned by Reinesius, *Inscriptions*, class XX, no. 57. I shall quote Isidore, *Etymologies* VII, 11, in order to correct it: “The hypodeacons, in Greek, whom we call subdeacons, are so called because they are subject to the commands and offices of the Levites. For they themselves receive the offerings of the faithful in the temple of God and carry them to the Levites to be placed upon the altars.” This passage must be read in this form from the very ancient Groningen manuscript. I have removed what appears in the intermediate edition of Gothofredus.

The verb ὑποδιακονέω, a word overlooked by most lexicons, occurs in the inscription on the column of Diana; the inscription was corrected by the distinguished Paciaudius, *Monuments of the Peloponnese*, vol. I, p. 8.

Moreover, in some printed editions I found *subdeacon, cardinal of the Roman Church*. I removed these words, which were added at the editors’ discretion and supported by no manuscript authority. Nor do they seem appropriate to Arator’s age. Otherwise, the cardinal deacons were those specially attached to the Roman Church, and hence they are called deacons of the Holy Apostolic See. See Gothofredus on Book VII of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Receivers*, and Du Fresne, *Glossary*, s.v. CARDINALIS.

The passage of Sulpicius Severus cited by Barthius is not read in the same way in the manuscripts. The Utrecht manuscript has *Calipione*. In his unpublished commentary Wopkensius favors *Callipione*, on the basis of Giselinus’s better books; he adds that Ausonius mourned an uncle of the same name in *Parentalia* 7.

**Lord.** The Antwerp edition has: “Prologue of Arator the subdeacon of the city of Rome.” The Basel edition has: “Preface of Arator the subdeacon, Christian poet, to Florianus the abbot, on the most holy Acts of the Apostles.” Most editions more simply have: “Arator the subdeacon to Florianus the abbot.” On this manner of addressing a work, see my father-in-law’s dissertation *On the Date of Avianus*, chapter 5. I have adduced these examples to show how much each editor indulged his own judgment in this ἐπιγραφή (*epigraphē*, title or heading).

In the manuscripts I found: “To the holy and venerable lord, spiritually instructed in the grace of Christ, Florianus the abbot, Arator the subdeacon.” The Moretus manuscript has “endowed” instead of “instructed”; it also adds “greetings.” After arranging these matters, I prefixed the form that seemed more faithful to the usage of that age. The three Vossian manuscripts, however, do not contain this letter.

**Spiritually.** *Spiritalis* instead of *spiritualis* … Prudentius, *Stephanos*:

“And with spiritual milk you refresh the breast.”

In the hymn:

“And spiritual anointing.”

Fabricius, in his commentary, p. 125. Only the Moretus manuscript has *spiritualiter*. Which form one should prefer I scarcely care. Both were used by sacred writers. See Noltenius, *Anti-Barbarus*, p. 732; Vorstius on Sulpicius Severus, Letter 2, §13, and *Dialogue* 2, chapter 10, where the Utrecht manuscript has “seasoned spiritually with salt.” In the Groningen manuscript of Isidore, a manuscript of the highest value, I found in Book VI, chapter 2, *spiritual kingdoms*, and afterward *struggles of spiritual warfare*, where Gothofredus incorrectly printed *specialis*; Book VI, final chapter, *spiritual effect*; VII, 3, *spiritual seal*; VII, 8, *he saw spiritually*. The same manuscript should correct XI, 1: “But the spirit either according to spiritual nature,” where Gothofredus likewise has the erroneous *speciali*.

**Florianus.** Several men of this name are mentioned in the *Prosopography of the Theodosian Code*, vol. VII, part II, p. 56. Add the rescript of Antoninus to Florianus in Book II, title *On Inheritances or Sales*, and Florianus, prefect of the praetorium, in the inscription of Book IV, title *On Petitions to the Imperial Officials*. The Moretus glosses correctly note that this man lived under Justinian. I would not venture to determine whether he is the same person about whom various accounts are given in the *Historical Collection* III, 13, in Canisius, *Ecclesiastical Treasury*, vol. II, p. 193. Florianus is also mentioned in the heading of a letter in Cassiodorus, *Variae* I, 5.]

1 To the holy and venerable lord, 2 spiritually instructed in the grace of Christ, 3 Florianus the abbot, Arator the subdeacon, greetings.

[Col. 0065A]

[Note: **1. Flower.** He plainly alludes to the name Florianus, which was familiar to the poets of this age and no less so to Arator. See Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 24. In the same way, in the elegy to Parthenius, he sought elegance—if the gods permit—in his own name:

“And since you bear the name by which we call you, Arator,

Let the harvest-field not be hidden but open to you.”

Venantius Fortunatus plowed the same field of elegance at the beginning of his *Life of Martin*. Jerome cleverly altered Vigilantius’s name, which he was playing upon, into *Dormitantium* in his letter to Parthenius. See Sagittarius, *On the Birthdays of the Martyrs*, chapter 3, §6. Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria* 43: “I now come to that golden name, Chrysogonus.” On the name Hosius, from ὅσιος (*hosios*, holy), see Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, Works, vol. I, p. 703.

A similar form may be found in Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 9. On the conjecture of Gale and Graevius: “Then at last he began to rage and to despise the name. Diocles—for that was his name before the empire.” They print “to despise everything,” from which I myself had conjectured *omina*. I now follow Heumann, who restores “to despise everything,” because there is no allusion to the name Diocletian, since the words concerning Galerius continue only as far as *Diocles*.

Burmann the Younger rightly judged that such allusions were unworthy of poets in his commentary on Lotichius V, elegy 13, 17. Because of the allusion in the name Acontius, he there correctly denies that Ovid wrote the letter of Cydippe. Stephanus made the same judgment in *Various Observations on Horace*, dissertation 4, as did Valckenaer on Euripides, *Phoenician Women* 639, although Valckenaer thinks that certain allusions possess charm.

Without doubt Arator followed the ancients in this allusion, since they used *flower* of any outstanding person. Strato, epigram 39: “Antiochus, the flower among radiant young men.” This seems to have been correctly emended by Herelius in Klotz’s *Literary Acts*, vol. II, p. 360. Agathias, *On the Reign of Justinian* II, p. 65, calls Damascus and others ἄκρον ἄωτον (*akron aōton*, “the very choicest”), adding, as he says, κατὰ τὴν ποίησιν (*kata tēn poiēsin*, “in poetic terms”). On Latin examples see Drakenborch on Livy XXVIII, 35, 7.

**Mouth.** The reading *nominis orbe*—“by the circle” or “scope of the name”—from the parchment manuscript, scarcely still legible because of its age, is many thousands of times better. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 20. Yet I do not approve that reading, although *orbe* for *ore* also appears in some editions below, at I, 93, and scribes frequently confuse the two. See Drakenborch on Silius III, 654; the notes on Valerius Flaccus II, 57.

Arator seems to have been excessively fond of this word for us to remove it. To me “the mouth of the name” seems to designate agreement or correspondence with the thing itself, in the same way that Pitiscus, in Suetonius, *Caesar* 88, explained *ore decernentium* by “with the agreement of those voting.” Oudendorpius disagrees, but I follow him more readily. The expression is nevertheless harsh, and I have found nothing in my manuscripts that could support Barthius.

**2. Florianus.** Here he improperly shortens the first syllable, although shortly afterward he lengthens it in *florem*. The poets of this age often do such things. The name itself is appropriate, as are *Anthus*, found in Gorius, *Florentine Inscriptions*, part I, p. 44, and likewise *Anthusa* and *Chrysanthe*, ibid., p. 209.

Althelmus seeks a similar elegance to Arator’s in *On the Praise of Virginity*, p. 729 of the first volume of Canisius’s *Treasury*:

“There was once a bishop named Narcissus, perhaps,

Fragrant with the merits of his virtues, flowering in his name;”

and on p. 732:

“I do not delay to recall the renowned praises of Chrysanthus,

Whom the world rightly celebrates with famous praise.

Thus I think his father regarded him as flowering in due season.”

I would prefer *in the first time* there. Gronovius conjectures *tempore proto*, *Observations on Ecclesiasticus*, chapter 20.

**3. Youthful.** Poets frequently praise a young man for possessing mature, manly, or even old age in his character. See the notes on Sedulius II, 137; Martinus, *Various Readings* III, 6; Cerda on Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, 234 and 310; Menagius on Diogenes Laertius I, section 91; Burmann on Lotichius IV, elegy 3, 104.

Add also the inscription cited by Montfaucon, *Antiquity Explained*, vol. V, plate 61: “To a daughter endowed with prudence beyond the capacity of her sex and her age.” If Withof’s conjecture in *Specimen Guntheri*, p. 13, is correct, Venantius Fortunatus, *Life of Martin* I, p. 288, should be referred here:

“Then the old man flies forward, youthful in his aged years.”

I nevertheless retain *armis* there. Ambrose, *Duties* II, 20: “For in the Gospel we read of John as a young man and, in his own words, though in merits and wisdom he was second to none of the elders. For he possessed the venerable old age of character and gray prudence.” In my manuscript I would rather delete *et sua voce* there.

Paulinus of Périgueux should be corrected from this, *On the Life of Martin* III, 417:

“Humble in heart, outstanding in death.”

Write instead: “outstanding in mind.” I prefer this to *merito excellens*, which Wopkensius ordered to be restored in *New Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. VII, p. 880.

**4. Prepared a way.** The same parchment manuscripts have *pararetur*. Others have *pareret itum*. We regard this reading as legitimate because of the less familiar word, especially to monastic ears. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 20.

I do not understand what *pareret* is supposed to mean in Barthius’s observation. It must certainly come from *pareo*, whose first syllable is long. Deriving it from *pario* is prevented by the meter, although in that sense *parere* and *parare* differ in nothing. See the notes on Florus I, 12, 6. Perhaps the printer intended to print *pararet*. “He prepared a way” could easily be defended. See Klockius on Livy VII, 36, 5.

Ammianus Marcellinus XXVII, 10, p. 544: “through regions extended by a long journey.” Freinshemius, commenting on Florus I, 16, 12, conjectures that *situ* should be read there. Isidore, *Etymologies* XV, 16: “*Iter* or *itus* is a road along which a person may go in any direction.”

In Phaedrus III, 6, 6, Wopkensius emended:

“He moderates my journey with a slow whip.”

This comes closest to Burmann’s conjecture, “journey or course.” I restore *itionem* in this sense in Book 37, §1 of the Digest, *On Religious and Funeral Matters*, where I think we should read “in the surrounding porticoes, passages,” contrary to Raevardus, *Various Readings* III, 7; followed by Gutherius, *Roman Law* II, 30; and differently by Marckartus, *Probabilities*, part II, p. 1.

In this passage of Arator, however, I retain *iter*, both because the manuscripts make no change and because poetic ears scarcely tolerate *itum* here. The meaning is that Florianus gave such instruction that the manner of life wisely established by him might prepare a road to heaven. Cortius explained *vita* as “manner of living” in Pliny VII, Letter 9, 13, and IX, 19, 6. On this word in detail see Nicolaus Loensis, *Miscellanea* VI, 3; on the use of the preposition, see Drakenborch on Livy IV, 47, 1.

Theophrastus, *Ethical Characters*, Preface: παρατεθεαμένος ἐξ ἀκριβείας πολλῆς, “having set forth from very careful observation.” In a manuscript whose variants a learned hand recorded in the margin of my edition, the reading is παρατεθραμμένος; this, however, agrees poorly with what follows.]

4 You possess the flower of merit, sprung from mature judgment,

Already, Florianus, in the mouth of your name;

5 For, though still youthful, you have given instruction to the aged,

From which life might prepare a road to heaven.

[5]

[Col. 0067A]

[Note: **5. Converge.** Barthius referred this to Florianus alone in *Adversaria* XLV, 24. There he also showed that such words, which by their grammatical composition apply to several persons, may nevertheless be used of one person. Thus Oudendorpius explained *conferre in aerarium*, “to contribute to the treasury,” of one person in Suetonius, *Augustus* 29.

Isidore, *Etymologies* V, 1: “Lycurgus first devised laws for the Lacedaemonians on the authority of Apollo.” I think *legum* should be deleted before *auctoritate* on the basis of the Groningen manuscript.

Yet I would not refer *concurre* here to Florianus alone, but also to Vigilius, whom he makes the support of his poem in the following letter. Parthenius could also be included here, as is clear from what he mentions in the letter to him.

**6. Extend.** “Offer assistance.” The expression is derived from those who join hands in a crowd in order to penetrate farther. Barthius discussed the expression at length in *Adversaria* XV, 13.

“Because of your favor” means “because you favor me.” See Manutius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VI, 10; and Noodtius on Ulpian, Digest 37, *On Malicious Fraud*, p. 461, where he explains *propter dolum* as “because of fraud.”

Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 6: “So too the sea’s appearance is unreliable, since, as the winds likewise change, it is fair in calm, moderate in rough water, and suddenly becomes turbulent in great waves.” Cerda explains this passage in his notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 522.

**7. Meager.** Humble, empty, and thin. See the distinguished Ernesti, *Ciceronian Key*. There are parallels to this in Sedulius’s prologue, where verse 4 similarly says:

“Nor should you seek here the work of a craftsman’s book.”

Some think *codicis* has been corrupted there. If so, Martinus, bishop of Dume, also encountered a corrupt manuscript and imitated the passage as follows:

“Nor should sumptuous dishes be sought through the many recesses,

With the counting-board gleaming, by the art of a book.”

Sirmondus gives the whole poem in his notes on Sidonius, poem 19.

**7. Rich.** Magnificent: things from which not merely the greatest usefulness is obtained, but which are also so great that, given the dignity of the subject, they can scarcely be properly explained. Thus, below, in Book I, verse 572, *the richness of the divine word*, and in the elegy to Parthenius, *the richness of speech*, which Barthius thought had been modeled on this passage, *Adversaria* XXIX, 3.

Since the following line says “a drop flows beneath the weight of the sea,” I thought Arator had taken the metaphor from waters flowing in immense abundance. In this sense a spring is called “richer” for irrigation in Hegesippus, *Destruction of Jerusalem* IV, 17.

The word had another usage among the best authors, for whom *rich speech* means harsh and unpleasant speech. See the distinguished Ernesti in his *Ciceronian Key*. Elsner correctly compared the Greek παχύς (*pachys*, “thick, dense”) in his notes on Matthew 13:14.

Here, however, *quidem* is omitted, although it is frequent later. See Drakenborch on Livy VIII, 12, 8; add Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, beginning. Conversely, *quidem* is used while *tamen* is omitted. See the learned writer in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. III, part III, p. 389.

**8. And.** “For example,” as Cortius correctly explained in the margin of his edition. Add Menckenius, *Observations on the Latin Language*, p. 7.

**10. And shorter.** The Cambridge manuscript has *haec*, “these.” The source of the interchange must be sought in the aspiration which scribes sometimes added and sometimes omitted where it was unnecessary. See Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, pp. 596, 610, and elsewhere.

I think *et* should be retained, since here it has adversative force. In Martial VII, epigram 19, I think the following should be restored from the excellent Thuane manuscript:

“The ages have conquered, and although it has yielded to the years.”

The common reading *sed* is due to a scribe with little sense of elegance. The same is true shortly afterward in the letter to Vigilius, verse 8. The Moretus manuscript has *et mihi*.

Among the Greeks, καί (*kai*, “and”) is similarly adversative. See *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. X, part III, p. 353, and Mollius on Longus, *Pastoral*, p. 50.

**11. The diverse one which.** “Which [the author] made of things.” Four manuscripts have *variam quam condidit auctor*, “the diverse [world] which the author fashioned.” This is extremely suitable to the meaning. Consider what follows.

In the following verse I also think *gignit*, “begets,” is preferable to *genuit*, “begot,” since the same books supply it. It is not surprising that these manuscripts differ so greatly from the common editions, since, whenever individual verses were copied by unlearned scribes in the Middle Ages, they almost always reached us wounded. If we can heal wounds that are unpleasant to look at but minor, why should we allow them to fester? Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 20.

My manuscripts consistently have *quam rerum condidit auctor*, “which the author of things fashioned.” Cortius added nothing from the manuscripts, so it seems certain that they too read this way. Nevertheless I restored the reading given by Barthius from four manuscripts; the meaning itself requires it, and it is more elegant if one considers what follows.

**11. Author.** It is written with *c*, not otherwise did the ancients write it. Rodolphus Agricola writes *autor* and derives it from *aveo*, so that *autor* would be one who desires something. Others write *author* with an aspiration, deriving it from the Greek αὐθέντης (*authentēs*). I therefore prefer Rudolph’s view, while following the orthography of the ancients. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 13.

The University manuscript has *actor*, “doer,” which is wrong but arises from a frequent error. See the Father on Victor; Caesar 20, 3; Drakenborch on Livy I, 26, 5.

*Author* designates the creator. Wopkensius on Sedulius III, 114, and V, 191. Corippus II, 180 said “begetter of things”:

“And the begetter of things, which he himself created,

Imposed upon him the cares of governing.”

Perhaps the punctuation should more correctly be: “He imposed them—the begetter of things which he himself created.” Priscian used “begetter of Nature” in *On the Position of the World*, verse 1.

*Author* is correctly written in the best form. The more corrupt spelling is followed by the editions at this and other passages. Besides Dausquius, Vossius, and Cellarius, see Sigonius on Livy I, 3.

**12. Let them agree.** The Cambridge manuscript has *conveniant*, “let them come together,” apparently from a gloss.

**12. Or the lowest.** Victor of Utica, Book I: “He had already completed the books, except for the countless bishops, or the exposition of the entire Psalter and the Gospels.” Venantius Fortunatus, Book I *On Martin*:

“For the Father and the Begotten and the equal gracious Spirit.”

Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards* II, 3: “He was most distinguished in grammar, rhetoric, and also in meter.” Latin writers truly use the expression in this way.

Censorinus, chapter 4: “So that in Colchis or in Boeotia offspring armed with teeth may be born”; for the stories place them in both regions. Barthius, *Adversaria* XVII, 1.

Compare the same author *Adversaria* XIII, 17, and the repetition of the same discussion in his notes on Rutilius I, 40. This usage delighted him because, as he admits on Rutilius I, 218, “good things come twice and three times.” Add his notes on Claudian, pp. 759 and 1314; the notes on Sedulius V, 428; Anna Fabri on Eutropius VIII, 23; Salmasius on Tertullian’s *Pallium*, p. 403; Wopkensius in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. X, part I, p. 19.

*Pervigilium Veneris*, verse 23:

“Here the girls of the countryside will be, or the girls of the mountains.”

Weitzius comments there: “In the same way, *sive*.” In the Middle Ages the same usage is found, as my father-in-law showed in *On Postumus*, chapter 16, and in his letter to the most illustrious Count Lynden, p. 16.

**13. Begot.** Barthius above, at verse 12, preferred *gignit* on the basis of his manuscripts. Our manuscripts make no change, and the common reading is very pleasing because of what follows.]

6 Join your aid to my poem, and to my faltering feet

Often extend your hand from tranquil favor.

7 In meager speech, indeed, but with rich deeds,

We have written, and a drop flows beneath the weight of the sea.

[Col. 0068A]

8 Among grandiloquent books extending through a thousand volumes,

Though you possess the greatest works, yet read the shorter ones.

And, in the manner of Nature, which the Creator made diverse,

Let high and low things accord with your studies.

9 The earth that begot tigers and nourishes lions,

[Col. 0069A]

[Note: **15. Let him dispense.** The Moretus manuscript has *dispensat*, “he dispenses”; the former reading is more correct. On the word itself see Gronovius on Justin VII, 6, 4; Schultingius on Seneca, p. 62.

**16. Talent.** Natural ability, cleverness. Aldhelmus:

“You who breathe into the brutish breast with a life-giving breath,

Who adorn hearts with talents and lips with speech.”

That is, with sharpness of understanding, for which the heart itself is often used. Sidonius, *In Burgo*:

“And the Cyclops, deprived of light by Ithacus’s cleverness.”

Paulinus, *On the Death of Celsus*:

“Nor should a wise man rejoice in great talent.”

Barthius, *Adversaria* XLVI, 10. The same author has more on this in his notes on Claudian, *Rape of Proserpina* I, 143.

I scarcely think this differs from what Florus attributes to elephants, namely a perception of captivity, I, 18, at the end; see the notes there. The phrase *the law of the wise* also belongs here, meaning the law which nature taught all animals; I discussed this to some extent in *Miscellanea*, chapter 15, p. 166.

*Meruere* means “they attained,” “they acquired.” I discussed this meaning in my notes on Sedulius I, 331. Add Burmann on Claudian, *Epithalamium of Honorius* IV, 24.]

[Column 0069B] 17. **Unbroken strength.** The Cambridge manuscript has *virtute*, an obvious error. *Virtus* denotes those who are endowed with strength and who, amid the harsh labors of war, occasionally insert lighter activities so that they may be able to endure any labor more readily. Thus an abstract noun is used here for a concrete one, as *occursus* (“meeting”) for those who meet. Schulting on Quintilian, *Declamations* 6, p. 177: *mortes* (“deaths”) for dead men. Burmann in the same place, p. 250: *redemptio* (“redemption”) for the redeemer. Venantius Fortunatus, *On the Virgin’s Parturition* I, p. 699. Correct Isidore accordingly from the Groningen manuscript, book X, p. 1070: “A bachelor, without marriage, such as are the names of those in heaven who are without spouses.” The printed editions wrongly have “which are without spouses.” The copyist altered the text because he did not perceive this construction, which is frequent in Latin, as I shall show below. On the abstract noun, see further Muncker on Fulgentius, p. 623; in the notes on Sedulius I, 218 and 237; Wopkens in the same place, II, 220; *Miscellaneous Observations* II, volume I, p. 93. Thus *industria societas* should be understood as “an industrious companion,” in *Digest* 17.2, *Pro Socio*, as I demonstrated in *Miscellanies* chapter 15. Maius has produced similar examples from Greek, *Sacred Observations* I, p. 44. Conversely, *artifex* may mean “artifice,” and similar cases are given by Salmasius on Tertullian’s *Pallium*, p. 265.

By “unbroken strength,” however, are understood those whom no art can conquer or subdue. Taubmann writes that *infractus* belongs among the words admitting contrary meanings, so that it may mean both “unbroken” and “thoroughly broken,” in his notes on Virgil, *Georgics* IV, 145, and Plautus, *Captives* III, 1, 26; I would not make this a general rule. It does admit a contrary meaning in several compounds, as I showed in *Specimen of Observations* chapter 6, and the distinguished van Hoven defended in *Literary Leisure*, fascicle I, p. 67, where he supports *Digest* 17.2, §52, *Pro Socio*—though Marckart had long before done so on the same grounds, *Probabilia* II, p. 89. Wasseus on Sallust, p. 26, and others agree. Thus *implorare* should also be explained in Juvencus II, 373, and Sedulius III, 298, as “to weep intensely,” though Wopkens preferred to understand the verb itself as implied.

Although this meaning of the preposition accords with analogy, I do not think it should be admitted everywhere; one must rely exclusively on the evidence. To students of Roman elegance, *infractus* means “broken”: Heinsius on Claudian, *The Gothic War* 214; Verheyk on Eutropius II, 22; or “very much broken”: Oudendorp on Frontinus II, 6, 5; never, however, “strong” or “unbroken.” This latter meaning began to be admitted in the declining period of Latin, which Cellarius derived from Symmachus and Jerome, *Later Curiosities*, p. 246, and *Antibarbarus*, p. 182. How greatly, therefore, those interpreters of Virgil who explained *infractos Latinos* in *Aeneid* XII, 1, as “unbroken Latins” went astray, Vorstius demonstrated at length in *On the Suspicion of Latin Errors*, chapter 4, and Reitzius in *Ambiguities*, p. 304.

Nor does the authority of Servius move me. Since he had said something different above, I do not think that the material he subsequently transmitted is Servius’ own. That the grammarian has been interpolated is shown by Emmenessius on *Eclogue* I, 12; Justus, *Specimen of Critical Observations*, chapter 11, p. 33; and Burmann the Younger in his preface to Virgil. See also the note on Sedulius I, 11, although I know that the ancient grammarians claimed for themselves the liberty of condemning or approving whatever was at hand according to their own judgment. Schrader demonstrated this with respect to Servius himself in his notes on Musaeus, *Animadversions*, chapter 2.

I am therefore surprised that Barthius, in his notes on Claudian, p. 406, assigns this meaning to Virgil, and also explains the following passage from Statius, *Thebaid* X, 199—

“While affairs are unbroken, and driven back we retreat toward the rear”—

as “while affairs are not broken.” The poet’s own meaning requires us to understand “broken affairs.” I do not deny that in Arator’s period *infractus* may have been understood as “strong”; Jerome’s testimony alone perhaps proves this. Nevertheless, if the manuscripts supported it, I would prefer *virtus invicta*, “unconquered strength.” On this expression see Withof, *Specimen on Gunther*, p. 37.

He correctly adds *laborem*, a word proper to brave soldiers and warriors. Curtius III, 10, 6. Justinus said *laborem militiae*, “the labor of military service,” III, 2, 10. Isidore, *Etymologies* V, 7: “A proper division according to the qualities and labors of persons” [the Groningen manuscript has *laboris*, “of labor,” and this is not wrong]. The word should likewise be understood in Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 435, as Cortius correctly explains in his notes on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VII, 17. Justinian said *bellicos sudores*, “warlike sweat,” in the preface to the *Institutes*, §1. Florus joins “labors and dangers” in this sense in his preface.

[Column 0070C] 20. **Naked.** This word may be explained in two ways. If one considers the origin of the preceding word, *Gymnasium*, it may refer to a soldier laying aside his clothing and weapons, so that the reference is to wrestlers and a similar class of men. A learned man confirmed this very familiar meaning of the word from Virgil, *Eclogue* I, 61, where “naked fish” means fish without clothing. I wish he had not done so! He later changed his view in his commentary on Exodus, p. 147, where he interprets Virgil’s *nudus* as “unarmed.” Nor does that please me.

Better is Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* V, final verse, and Idsinga, *Various Legal Matters*, chapter 20. In this passage of Arator, however, I would rather explain *nudus* as “unarmed,” so that a soldier clad in armor is contrasted with one who has laid down his weapons. Cicero, *On Ends*, book VII, joins *inermem et nudum*, “unarmed and naked”; so also Tacitus, *Histories* IV, 64, and Isidore, *Etymologies* XV, 2. See Burmann on Ovid, *Amores* I, elegy 2, 20. I explain Curtius VI, 1, 15 in the same way, where the “naked breast” is one from which the shield had been somewhat removed—the shield with which Agis protected his body in order to blunt the force of the weapons.

Justinus wrote *nudatum*, “stripped,” III, 1, at the end. I strongly prefer *nudantem*, “while stripping,” which I found in another Franeker manuscript, because of *exuentem*, “while removing,” which precedes, and because Artaxerxes does not seem to have killed Artabanus after he had removed his cuirass, but while he was in the act of unfastening it.

In Valerius Maximus II, 10, 2, Wopkens, in the manuscript adversaria in my possession, emended the text to *proinde se securum nudis*, that is, “therefore safe among the unarmed,” drawing on Curtius V, 4, and Sallust, *Jugurtha* 107. The Greek γυμνός (*gymnos*) has the same meaning. Cuperus cited a passage from Aelian, *Observations* II, 7; Perizonius explains another from 2 Maccabees 11:12 in his *Historical Notes*, p. 238. I add Homer, *Iliad* XVI, 815, where Patroclus is γυμνός, “unarmed.” Herodian mentions γυμνούς πρὸς ὡπλισμένους, “the unarmed in comparison with the armed,” *History* II, 13, 8. Conversely, *indutus*, “clothed,” may mean “armed,” as Cerda explained it in his notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, 83.

The following passage accords with Arator’s meaning, from Sedulius’ letter to Macedonius, p. 9: “Often the warrior delights in fighting and playing with the weapons to which he is accustomed.” See the notes there. The following verses of the very elegant poet Sidronius Hosschius certainly deserve to be quoted, book VI, elegy 7:

“Your own soldier does not always remain in arms.

Often he bares his head of its helmet and his hands of his sword.

You too release the shield from your anxious arm,

and let your head be free of the helmet and your hand of the sword.

With his helmet laid aside, Achilles handled the lyre,

moving the soft plectrum with the hand that previously held his weapons.”

[End of note.]

“She herself offered her bosom to ants and bees.

[15] And if you consider that the ruler distributes everything,

the mild have earned intelligence, the fierce strength.

10 And unbroken strength itself, accustomed to continuous labor,

[Column 0070A] abandons it and seeks to have varied changes.

11 The soldier accustomed to place a cuirass upon his limbs,

20 rejoices to approach the place of the Gymnasium.”

[Column 0071A] 21. **And who.** Moreti’s manuscript has *At qui*, “but he who.” The reading transmitted in the editions is better suited to joining the sentences. I do not repeat what I brought together concerning this passage in *Miscellanies*, chapter 4, p. 44.

[Column 0071B] 23. **Therefore.** He shortens the final syllable contrary to the practice of the best poets, for whom it is long, since the word derives from ἔργῳ (*ergō*). This is indeed the practice of poets who wrote in the age of Augustus; later poets proceeded arbitrarily. See Burmann on Lotichius I, elegy 2, 32, and II, elegy 4, 76; in *Antiklotz*, p. 97; and on the *Anthology*, p. 357. Following the grammarians, Isidore distinguishes the word in this way, *Etymologies* I, 17: “Or for the purpose of distinguishing an ambiguity, as in *ergo*. For when the *go* is lengthened [the Groningen manuscript has *ergo*], it signifies a cause; when shortened, it is a conjunction.”

[Column 0071B] 24. **Yield a day.** “Grant time,” so that, having set aside concern for ancient volumes, you may devote even a brief period to reading this work. *Cedere* in the sense of “to grant” occurs in *Digest* 8.6.20, §1, *On Urban and Rural Servitudes*, and elsewhere, as Schroder explained, *Legal Observations* III, 4, p. 215. Ambrose, *Duties* I, 24: “He thought that his food ought to be ceded to his brother.” In Sallust, *Jugurtha* 47, 3, Wopkens found in the manuscript he received from d’Orville: *omnia Metello cedere*, “everything yielded to Metellus”; the common editions have *dedere*, “gave.” Hegesippus III, 22: “Wishing to grant pardon for the offense, he yielded.” Nor should Wasseus be followed in his note on Sallust, *Catiline* 55, where he emended the reading to *fecit*. Likewise below, book I, verse 301, *cedit* has wrongly been changed to *fecit*, and *cessa* should be read in book I, verse 490. Isidore, *Etymologies* V, 25: “Cession properly means the granting of a thing, as in the expression, ‘I yield by right of kinship.’ For we say *cedere*, as though *concedere*, ‘to grant.’”

“To yield” is properly said of one who agrees with another against the truth. The following words I have reproduced from the Groningen manuscript and the old edition; that this is the true reading is confirmed by Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 704.

[Column 0072B] 24. **May it benefit.** I restored this reading from the Cambridge manuscript. The old editions had *juvat*, “it benefits,” but the other reading is more elegant. The present subjunctive is often used for the future indicative. Perizonius discussed the matter in his notes on Sanctius I, 13. Bosius supplied Greek examples in his note 14 on Matthew XI, §3, where he shows that this usage is especially frequent in interrogative forms. Hence Sedulius, hymn 1, 86, has been correctly emended to *Quid faciant?*, “What will they do?” And in his letter to Macedonius, p. 2, *expurgem*, “may I cleanse,” is preferable; there is no need to explain it as *perage expurgem*, “finish cleansing,” with some, or to adopt *exponam* or *expromam*, “I shall explain” or “I shall bring forth,” with others.

12 “And those who overcome iron-clad battle lines and ranks

strike the unwarlike beasts with their weapons.

[Column 0072A] 13 Therefore, while retaining your step and abandoning the ancient volumes,

yield a day to the work which a pious cause may assist.”

[Column 0071]

## Arator’s Letter to Vigilius (C)

[Column 0071]

**Apostolic.** In several manuscripts the title here reads: “To his apostolic lord, the most blessed Pope Vigilius, from Arator, humble subdeacon of the Holy Church.” The circumstances of the period require me to regard this as the true reading: they granted little to foreign power but much to the divine reason and authority of holy bishops, whom Hilary calls “apostolic men” in the preface to his *Historical Books*. Gildas calls the episcopate “apostolic dignity” in his vigorous invective against the clergy of Britain. Germanus calls the future bishops of Paris “apostolic men” in the privilege preserved by Aimoins, book III, chapter 2, which was written in the year 569. Thus Ivo of Chartres simply calls the Roman pontiff “apostolic” in letters 134 and 140.

Claudius of Turin says elegantly: “His fifth objection against me is that the apostolic lord was indignant at me.” You said this of Paschal, bishop of the Roman Church, who had already died. *Apostolicus* means, as it were, “guardian of the apostle” or “one performing the apostle’s office.” Certainly one should not be called apostolic merely because he sits in the apostle’s chair, but because he fulfills the apostolic office.

Adalbold, in the *Life of Henry I*: “He also obtained this from the apostolic lord by humility and devotion, that he might enter Alemannia.” Eccerhard, *Life of Notker*, chapter 9: “Vitalian the bishop, whose chant some still customarily perform when the apostolic celebrates.” That bishops were accustomed, according to solemn usage, to receive the title “apostolic” is shown by Eufrasius’ letter to Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, bearing this address: “To the holy lord, most blessed in merits, the pope, worthy of veneration in the dignity of his office, and apostolic father, Lord Ruricius the bishop, from Eufrasius.”

Another letter of Faustus to the same man is addressed: “To the most blessed lord, worthy of veneration in dutiful devotion, and most worthy brother of the apostolic see, Ruricius the bishop, from Faustus.” Two other letters of Sedatus to the same man openly ascribe apostolic reverence to him. If the name Aenius is preserved, Ruricius himself gives him the same title in book II, letter 8: “To the holy and apostolic lord, Pope Aenius, from Ruricius.” The same Aenius is called “holy and apostolic” in book II, letter 15, and Sedatus in letter 33, as Caesareus is in the preceding passage. Desiderius of Cahors calls Victorinus “apostolic father” in letter 39. The same Desiderius is said by Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, to be worthy of veneration “as one seated on an apostolic see”; Aviulf calls him “apostolic father,” as does Eligius—without doubt the very Eligius whose sermons of no small merit have reached us. Rauricius calls him “apostolic bishop,” though he is wrongly confused with the Limoges bishop of that name.

Nor did Sigebert, the most ancient king of the Franks, address this same Desiderius with any lesser honor. Abbo likewise calls him “apostolic pope.” Constantius and Gallus, distinguished bishops of the same period, call him “apostolic father.” Venantius Fortunatus addresses Pope Gregory in comparable words in his books on the life of Saint Martin. Leo of Marsicanus simply calls Victor III “apostolic” in book III of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*; Bruno does the same in book IV, chapter 33, of that work, as does Peter the Deacon. Innumerable other examples could be collected if anyone devoted himself to the matter.

These examples suffice to defend Arator’s genuine reading, if we add that the principal temples of cities were once called “apostolic,” not because of their name but because of apostolic authority. Thus Corippus calls that magnificent church of Holy Wisdom—which Benjamin of Tudela affirms, after so many centuries, to have remained incomparable even in its own age—the following in book III of his poem on Justinian’s death:

“Until, entering the halls of the apostolic temple,

they laid the famous limbs in a consecrated tomb.”

As for Arator’s addition of *miser*, “wretched,” in reference to himself, he drew it from the common usage of his age. Paulinus very often describes himself as a sinner in his letters. Evantius the abbot used the same word of himself in his letter on the use of flesh and blood: “Since the opportunity presented itself at a suitable time, therefore, my misery took care to send this little page of my poverty [this should be the reading] before your eyes.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, chapter 20. The same Barthius collected many similar examples in *Adversaria* XLIII, 8, though they are too long to quote here.

That bishops were once generally called apostolic is well known. See Athanasius, *Works* I, p. 832C, and Baluzius on Salvian, p. 368. In the earlier period, therefore, this title distinguished neither bishops nor the pope; later it did, especially after *apostolicus* and *apostolica sedes* began to be applied specifically to the Roman bishop and the city of Rome. See Casaubon on Baronius’ *Annals*, p. 280, and Basnage’s preface to Canisius’ *Thesaurus*, p. 37. Arator undoubtedly adds, for purposes of distinction, “first of all priests in the whole world.”

For the rest, nearly every editor appended an inscription altered according to his own judgment. Most printed: “Arator the subdeacon sends greetings to Vigilius the pontiff.” The manuscripts differ from these editorial inventions as widely as possible. Moreti’s manuscript has: “To the lord, sacred and most blessed apostolic, and first of all priests in the whole world, Pope Vigilius, from Arator the subdeacon.” The Antwerp edition is nearly the same. In the University manuscript it reads: “To the illustrious and lordly Florianus, abbot. To the holy and most blessed, apostolic lord, and first of all priests in the whole world, Pope Vigilius, from Arator the subdeacon, greetings.”

Ev. Wassenbergius, formerly a pupil of our discipline and now a notable ornament of the Deventer school, informed me that in Vossianus II the color of the ink made him think the inscription had been added by a later hand. In that manuscript the inscription was: “To the most sacred and holy, most blessed, and first of all priests in the whole world, Pope Vigilius, from Arator the subdeacon.” I think the title *sancti*, “holy,” should be preferred to *sacrosancti*, “most sacred.” *Sanctissimus*, “most holy,” is proper to bishops. See the elegant discussion in Justus, *Specimen of Critical Observations*, chapter 3. Once these materials are combined, scarcely anyone, I believe, will doubt that the inscription I placed above is genuine.

**Pope.** The word is undoubtedly derived from the Greek πάπας (*papas*), by which a father was designated. See Suidas under Πάππα and Hesychius. Just as *father*, so *pope* was once generally applied to bishops as a mark of honor and reverence. Casaubon against Baronius, p. 280; Sirmond on Ennodius, letter 4, 1.

Gothofredus writes in his note on *Codex Theodosianus* 2, *On Bishops*, that this usage and authority made the word proper, before all others, to the bishop. Its authority should be traced to the decree of Gregory VII. He became famous in history for various innovations, for taking episcopal election and confirmation away from princes, and later for launching his thunderbolt against Henry IV. See Bruno, *On the Saxon War*, p. 123, volume I of Freher’s *German Affairs*. He was unsuccessfully defended against Guibert by Anselm, bishop of Lucca; that defense appears in Canisius’ *Thesaurus* III, part I, p. 372.

To Gregory’s arrogance refer the decree by which he claimed exclusively for the Roman bishop the title “pope,” previously common to bishops. See Archibald Bower, *History of the Popes* V, p. 429, Belgian edition. Vossius dates this decree to 1073 in his *Etymology*, under *PAPA*. I would place it in the following years. In the year given by Vossius, Gregory was first created pontiff, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. See Platina, *Lives of the Pontiffs*, p. 146. In the following year and thereafter, once councils had been convened, he began above all to display his arrogant spirit toward everyone.

15 To the holy and most blessed 16 apostolic lord, and 17 first of all priests in the whole world,

Pope Vigilius, Arator the subdeacon, sends greetings.

[Column 0074A] 1. **Undosis.** Heinsius had entered *undosis* or *undisonis* from Moreti’s manuscript. The later form appears in the Antwerp editions of Fabricius and in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*. The earlier form is preserved by the Cambridge, University, Vossianus II, and London manuscripts, from which Uffenbachius cited it in his *Journey* II, p. 315; such exchanges are frequent in manuscripts. See the notes in *Miscellaneous Observations* II, volume I, p. 74. I prefer the later form. *Undosa moenia*, “wave-like walls,” means walls full of soldiers; poets commonly use *unda*, “wave,” of a multitude. Barthius on Claudian, p. 758; Valerius Flaccus I, 539:

“It surges with horses and blooms with men.”

Especially relevant is Silius Italicus IV, 159:

“And thick waves of Boians

rush in a mass through the crowded weapons.”

See Drakenborch there. Salvian, *On the Government of God* VI, p. 120: “Barbarian peoples flooded Gaul”; see Weitzius and Rittershusius there, and add Heinsius on Claudian, *Against Eutropius* II, 271. Pacatus, *Panegyric* 37, §4, has “streets overflowing with curtains”; learned men rightly restored *undantes*, “overflowing,” there in place of *tardantes*, “delaying,” and Trekell rightly approved this in his notes on Brissonius’ minor works, p. 325. Nevertheless, I do not accept the reading “old men giving thanks to the years.” Restore: “old women giving thanks, old men”; Schwartzius has already found this in a manuscript, and it is confirmed by the Vatican manuscript and by Vossius’ excerpts in my possession.

*Undisonis* would be more appropriate to the noise of weapons, with a meaning taken from the sea, as Musaeus said πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης, “of the loudly roaring sea,” in *Hero and Leander* 234. Aristophanes has the equivalent ὠκεανὸς βαρυαχής, “the heavily roaring ocean,” a phrase which the distinguished scholar judged should be rendered in Oppian, *Halieutica* 4, 569. See *Miscellaneous Observations* IV, volume II, p. 216.

The meaning of Arator is made especially clear by the scholia in the Cambridge manuscript, which read as follows: “When Rome was besieged by Iliricus, king of the Goths; likewise, at the time when the Goths besieged Rome and devastated the whole region, there arose m. [perhaps *modo*, ‘just now,’ or *mox*, ‘soon’] a great dispute over the election of the apostolic. When Pope Vigilius had indeed [v., *vero*] been elected, the enemies withdrew, and Arator is speaking of this.”

In that passage replace “Iliricus” with “Ildericus,” who succeeded his father Thrasymund, although he cannot in fact be said to have besieged Rome. The reference to Alaric would be more accurate, but he is too far removed from this period. The following words, “likewise at the time when the Goths besieged Rome,” may refer either to the siege conducted by Vitiges and repelled by Belisarius, or to Totila, who, while Belisarius was campaigning against Chosroes, took advantage of his absence and captured Rome. Belisarius recovered it, but when Chosroes renewed the war, Totila regained possession of the city; he was later defeated by Narses.

If anyone wishes to refer the passage to Totila, the siege of the city would have to be assigned to the year A.D. 543, since Arator’s poem was publicly read the following year. This is indeed Pagi’s view. Ludewigius, however, in his *Life of Justinian*, chapter 8, p. 453, does not refer Arator’s words to Totila’s actual siege, but rather to a display of arms and troops made from a distance, because Totila’s true siege did not take place until 546. But what if the poem was indeed recited in the year I mentioned, while this letter to Vigilius was not written until later? If that is rejected, the words may conveniently be referred solely to Vitiges; concerning his siege, see Ludewigius in the cited passage, §96.

1. **Incendia.** He may perhaps have drawn this from Lucan, whom he sometimes imitates, *Pharsalia* II, 390:

“... the headlong course of the blazing war

that held everything in its grasp.”

See Gebhard on Livy XXIX, 31, 5. Cicero said *scintillam belli*, “the spark of war,” in *Letters to Friends* X, 14. Compare here δαΐφρων, “war-minded,” in Homer, *Iliad* II, 23, which the scholia there explain as πολεμικὸν φρόνημα ἔχων, “possessing a warlike disposition.” The similar expression *incendia Carthaginis*, “the fires of Carthage,” in Horace, book IV, ode 8, 17, is discussed by the distinguished de Rhoer in *Daventer Festivals*, p. 129.

18 Seeing the fires of war around the wave-like walls,

[Column 0074A] I was then part of the people fearing the weapons.

[Column 0075A] 3. **Libertas.** He calls Vigilius this because of the benefits he had conferred upon his country and because he had successfully settled the disturbances arising from Silverius’ exile. Consult Victor of Tunnuna in his *Chronicle*, p. 330, and Basnage there. In the same way Claudian calls Stilicho “the confidence of war and the counsel of peace,” *On the Praises of Stilicho* III, 122; Barthius should be consulted there. Compare Demeas’ address to Timon in Lucian, *Timon*, p. 151, Amsterdam edition: “Hail, O Timon, the great benefit of your race, the support of the Athenians, the defense of Greece.” Similarly Oppian calls Antoninus “the glorious support of the land,” *Cynegetica* I, verse 1, where Rittershusius appropriately compared Lucian’s passage.

[Column 0075B] 3. **Vigili.** Moreti’s manuscript and Vossianus II transpose the words: “most holy pope Vigilius.” The Antwerp edition and others followed them. But the quantity of the middle syllable in *Vigili* scarcely permits this.

4. **Advenis.** The second-person singular of the fourth conjugation is shortened contrary to normal usage in Arator:

“You do not know how to love God”;

and:

“You hunger for crime”;

and:

“That which you guard, panting.”

Likewise in Sedulius IV:

“You reach Christ.”

Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 102.

Thus all the ancient manuscripts agree. The error in the syllable is the author’s, and later copyists should by no means have corrected it according to their own judgment. Examples from Christian poets everywhere present themselves. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, 20.

My manuscripts and the better editions likewise preserve *advenis*. Waltramus of Naumburg also cites it in book II, chapter 22 of his *Apology against Hildebrand*, as Barthius testifies in his notes on Claudian, *On the Praises of Stilicho* III, 122. Cellarius proved the same from ancient and recent books in his notes on Sedulius V, 280, although he observes that in the Leipzig manuscript the words are transposed, with *adveniens*, “coming,” enclosed. Many editions changed the word to *advenit*, “he came,” but this is unnecessary, since these poets frequently shorten the final syllable. Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 31; Burmann on the *Latin Anthology* III, p. 697.

4. **Solvere.** In the Greek manner, meaning *ad solvendum*, “in order to release,” a usage familiar to Arator, as in *venis sumere*, “you come to take,” below, book I, 679, and *veniens avertere*, “coming to turn away,” in the same book, verse 189. Similar examples include ὅσα κόνις, “as much as dust.” See Vechner, *Hellenics* I, 38; Drakenborch on Silius IV, 795; Emmenessius on Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 527; Burmann on Valerius Flaccus VI, 647; and *Miscellaneous Observations* VIII, p. 370. Emend Seneca, *Hercules Furens* 1137, on this basis:

“Go, visit the angry kings.”

Two Utrecht manuscripts have *visere*, “to visit,” which I prefer.

6. **Inque.** Moreti’s manuscript has *linque*, “leave.” But carrying someone on the shoulders signifies the highest affection. I think this expression should be restored to the anonymous author of the *Panegyric of Constantine* 19, §5: “Wherever you went, he eagerly desired to carry you on his shoulders and in his eyes.” This is the reading of Vossius’ excerpts; the inferior editions omit *et humeris*, “on his shoulders.” There is then a proper contrast between Cicero, whom he mentions, carried back to his homeland on the shoulders of Italy, and Constantine, carried on shoulders and in eyes.

Arator continues the metaphor of the flock and shepherds, who place wandering sheep upon their shoulders in order to return them to the flock. He may perhaps have taken the expression from Luke’s Gospel, chapter XV, §5. Cerda rightly explained this passage in his notes on Virgil, *Eclogue* I, verse 13. Pricaeus had already noted Tibullus I, 1, 11, in his notes on Luke:

“And may it not be a burden to bring home

the lamb or the kid, abandoned and forgetful of its mother.”

Since these same shepherds also call back the straying animals by their voice, Arator rightly adds *revocante*, “calling back,” below, I, 1000:

“Those sheep whom he was seeking, these indeed he was preparing,

those whom he now properly calls ...”

Book II, 778:

“He calls back the scattered lambs

with his voice.”

See also verse 259. The speech of the Savior in John X, 16 and 27 likewise corresponds: τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούει, “my sheep hears my voice.” Similarly Longus, *Pastoral* p. 8: “For some one must use the shepherd’s crook, for others only the voice.” Pricaeus cited another passage of Longus in his note on John’s Gospel X, §3.

8. **At mihi.** Moreti’s manuscript has *Et mihi*, “and to me,” a common scribal alteration. See Cortius on Sallust, *Catiline* III, 2. It could also be retained on the basis of what I brought forward concerning the letter to Florianus, verse 10.

*Plus* means “more” or “rather.” Barthius on Claudian, p. 823; Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XV, 21.

9. **Ecclesiam.** It means “the assembly and company of the Christian people,” or “the holy house,” as in Prudentius. Sedulius, Arator, Fortunatus, and Drepanius shorten the antepenultimate syllable by systole (τῇ συστολῇ), more by authority than by correctness, but according to a certain common usage. They also shorten the first syllable by paraleipsis (τῇ παρελλείψει), though nowhere else except in Tertullian, as in book III:

“To be the head is Christ, whose members are the Church”;

and in book II:

“Clearly, seeing that your glory is in Christ, O Church.”

The same occurs in several other passages. Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 47.

The irregularity in *Ecclesia* belongs to the license of the Christian age. Modoinus, in his poem to Theodulf:

“Add also that, while still inexperienced, the ecclesiastical order,

unformed and sluggish, lacked its law.”

Arator, book I:

“... and he caused a slight savor

of the Law to grow hot in the books of the Church.”

Sedulius, book IV:

“Christ joined the Church to himself in beautiful honor.”

Venantius, book II:

“... he restored the stable Church,

himself hanging upon the cross.”

Drepanius Florus:

“What shall I say of Solomon, swollen with his splendid buskin,

who sings of Christ’s bridal chambers and of the Church?”

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXI, 17.

Arator also shortens the penultimate syllable below, I, 121, and elsewhere. So too does the anonymous author of *The Deeds of Charlemagne*, book V, verse 518, and Ermoldus Nigellus, preserved among Mencken’s *German Writers*, even in passages where he could have avoided it by transposing the words. Perhaps, however, some poets made the word trisyllabic. See what will shortly be noted on verse 24.

The first syllable is not short only in Tertullian, as Fabricius thought, but also in Paulinus of Périgueux, *Life of Martin* II, 326, where *Eclesia* is printed. Nor does Tertullian’s final passage in Fabricius seem sufficient to establish the shortening of the first syllable. Contract *tuum* into one syllable—for this is apparently what these poets, especially Tertullian, allowed themselves to do; see Fabricius’ commentary, p. 129—and the meter will be correct. See similar cases in the notes on Sedulius V, 8 and 431.

9. **Naufragus.** This word is commonly used of those who have suffered serious loss. Cicero called a man “shipwrecked in property” in *For Sulla* 14. Christian writers apply the term to those overwhelmed by the burden of affairs of another kind, so that they can scarcely attend to matters suitable for the care of salvation; or to those who entirely neglect and renounce such matters. Paul calls this περὶ τὴν πίστιν ναυαγῆσαι, “to suffer shipwreck with regard to the faith,” in 1 Timothy 1:19; the expression was illustrated by the distinguished de Rhoer in *Daventer Festivals* II, 7. Hence Athanasius calls human nature χειμαζομένην, “storm-tossed,” *Works* I, p. 98.

Sedulius, letter to Macedonius, p. 2: “You will rejoice that, with God as pilot, I have suffered no shipwreck.” Salvian, *On the Government of God* III, p. 41: “For we have not been shipwrecked only three times, since nearly our whole life is a shipwreck.”

Arator declares himself shipwrecked in this sense, since he had been assigned to civil and public affairs at court. Gifted in eloquence, he first conducted cases in the forum; then he served as an ambassador for the Dalmatians to King Theoderic; afterward Athalaric made him *comes domesticorum*, “count of the household troops,” concerning which Athalaric’s letter in Cassiodorus, *Variae* VIII, 2, is well worth reading. He next became *comes privatarum*, “count of the private estates,” and finally was given to the Church as a subdeacon.

I affirm that he was *comes privatarum* on the authority of a manuscript from the monks of Saint Remigius at Rheims, in which he is called *excomes domesticorum* and *excomes privatarum*, “former count of the household troops” and “former count of the private estates.” See Sirmond on Ennodius, letter 9, 1. These were the names given to those who had held such offices; see Joseph Castalio, *Various Readings*, chapter 5.

Thus Tribonian is called *exquaestor*, “former quaestor,” in the preface to the *Institutes*, §3. I am surprised that Schwartzius, in his scholia on that passage, understood it with Aldobrandinus as “chief quaestor”; Ritter saw the matter more accurately in his notes on Heineccius’ *History of Law* I, §388, as did Bachius, *History of Jurisprudence*, p. 625.

In the same manner Turcius Rufus is called *exconsul*, “former consul,” in a manuscript. I discussed this in the notes on Sedulius, p. 20, and in *Specimen of Observations*, p. 69, where I produced a similar example from Gruter’s inscriptions, p. CXLIII, 2. From this the reading in Eutropius, *Breviary* VI, “Publius Servilius, former consul,” can easily be defended. Verheyk writes that the expression is nowhere found in the author. Nevertheless, the distinguished Oudendorp restored *exconsulibus*, “former consuls,” to Vegetius from the best manuscripts in *Miscellaneous Observations* VII, volume III, p. 359. Add Salmasius on the *Augustan Historians*, pp. 117, 137, and 209.

Isidore, *Etymologies* IX, 3: “They are called former consuls because they have already left or departed from the consulship after completing their year of office.” Through a printer’s error, Gothofredus’ edition there has *pacto*, “having made,” instead of the correct reading. The same author, book XV, chapter 13: “A barren field is so called as if *excolidus*, because it has already left cultivation, just as a former consul has departed from the consulship.” Hence the expression *exconsul* in Eutropius is, I think, sufficiently confirmed.

19 Public freedom, most holy Pope Vigilius,

you come to release the bonds of the enclosed flock.

[5] 20 The sheep are snatched from swords, with the shepherd assisting,

[Column 0076A] and we are carried upon pious shoulders, as you call us back.

21 It is enough for the bodily danger to have been escaped in this way,

but from it a greater salvation for my soul is born.

22 I enter the Church, having left the court as one shipwrecked;

[10]

[Column 0077D] 10. **Desero.** He shortens the final syllable contrary to the practice of the ancients; more recent poets were extremely careless in this matter. See Burmann the Younger in *Antiklotz*, p. 93; on Lotichius I, 1, 51, and IV, 4, 194, where he nevertheless shows that Tibullus shortened the final syllable in *desino*. See also book V, elegy 12, verse 71, in the same work. The same occurs shortly afterward in *defero*, verse 27; *solvo*, verse 28; and *disco*, verse 29. This one warning will suffice, since Arator contains many similar examples.

13. **Littoris.** He indicates the tranquility he enjoyed, removed from the bustle of the court and civil affairs. Virgil also joins *stationem et sinum*, “anchorage and bay,” *Aeneid* II, 23. Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV, 8: “An anchorage is where ships remain for a time; a harbor is where they spend the winter. An inhospitable place is one in which there is no refuge, as though there were no harbor. A harbor, however, ...” I have entered these words from the Groningen manuscript and the better editions; Gothofredus shamefully omitted them. A bay often indicates tranquility. Pliny, *Panegyric* 6, 3: “The shaken Republic took refuge in your bay,” or “your safe bay,” as the Guelpherbytan manuscript has; I prefer the latter. The same applies to the harbor in Cicero, *For Milo*, chapter 33.

Ermoldus Nigellus has a similar passage in volume I of Mencken’s *German Writers*, p. 884:

“Your right hand, which raises faithful Peter

above the surging wave lest he perish, also places him upon the ship;

may it, in compassion, preserve me as I plunge through the waves,

and bring me, excellent Caesar, to your harbor.”

14. **Sicca.** This passage confirms the reading of the Cambridge manuscript in Sedulius III, 227, concerning Peter:

“And the fields of the vast sea pressed upon him, and dry streams

surrounded and lapped his sacred feet.”

See the notes there and the additions, p. 227. Ermoldus Nigellus, p. 910, volume I of Mencken’s *German Historical Writers*:

“He who traveled across the sea on dry feet.”

15. **Potero.** This is a notable periphrasis meaning “I shall be liable” or “I shall be guilty.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III, 297:

“... for neither can he not have wished for these things,

nor can that man not have sworn”;

that is, “the one certainly wished for them, and the other certainly swore.” Arator below, book I, verse 529:

“Whenever he himself commands in turn,

that what is unaccustomed may be possible”;

book II, 695:

“If they cannot, through the ages,

be without an end, O God.”
