The Greek **δύνασθαι** (“to be able”) was likewise defended by Pricaeus in his commentary on Luke 16 §2, and by Maius, *Sacred Observations*, part I, p. 52. On Latin usages, see Cortius at Pliny, *Letters* X, 94, 1; Wopkensis, *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. VII, part II, p. 238; at Sedulius III, 321; Burmann at Ovid, *Heroides* XVII, 209; and Drakenborch at Livy XXXII, 13, 4.

Restore the same expression in Mamertinus, *Gratiarum actio*, chapter 7, beginning: “It certainly could have sufficed for the expedition.” Thus the Wolfenbüttel manuscript and the excerpts of Vossius; the printed editions have *suceret*. The same reading also occurs in the Groningen manuscript at Isidore, *Etymologies* I, 38: “Terentianus usually calls these verses elegiac, so that such a clausula may, as they say, be more suitable for mournful measures.” The printed editions differ slightly from this; but, in my judgment, the passage should be arranged as follows:

“Terentianus: ‘They called these elegies.’ He usually says that such a clausula is more suitable for mournful measures, as they relate.”

This is a testimony concerning Terentianus Maurus, whose verse this is, *On Metres*, p. 2422 in Putsch’s edition.

As for what Arator immediately says—“to render thanks,” whereas others say “to offer” or “to return” thanks—Ausonius has, in the opening of his *Gratiarum actio*: “I give you thanks, Emperor Augustus; if I could, I would also return them.” The old edition there reads *esse referrem* (“I would return them to be”), whence Vossius conjectured in the margin *si possit esse, referrem* (“if it could be, I would return them”). I would retain *possem* (“if I could”). Cicero, *Letters to Friends* X, 11: “I cannot affirm that I shall return it”; XI, 13: “I give you thanks, for to whom could I scarcely return the favor?” Some have considered *grates reddere* (“to render thanks”) poetic; prose writers, however, also use it. See Drakenborch at Livy XXI, 12, 7.

### 16. Nine

The passage is sufficiently obscure. It seems to me to mean that, having withdrawn from the tumult of the court and devoted himself to sacred service, he abandoned secular studies and the foolish notions of worldly wisdom, as Sedulius says in the preface to *Macedonius*, p. 3. By “nine,” therefore, I think the nine Muses are to be understood, and consequently, in general, the compositions of the ancient poets.

From earliest boyhood he had devoted himself to poetry and had composed the stories of the ancients in verse. But after Parthenius advised him to sing sacred subjects instead, he changed his plan and intended to compose the Davidic psalms or Genesis in verse. At last the Acts of the Apostles pleased him more. Arator himself gives a fuller account in his letter to Parthenius, which should be consulted.

Here, then, he declares that those ancient stories had displeased him because of the service of one person—that is, Peter, whom he had just mentioned—or, what I much prefer, because of Parthenius. Explain *officio* (“service”) as “benefit.” See the notes on Cato, *Distichs* I, 15, and IV, 42.

> I abandon the treacherous sails of the worldly sea.
>
> 23 I am transferred to Peter’s snowy folds, without storm,
>
> and now I enjoy the anchorage of the desired shore.
>
> 24 He prepared that inlet of the shore for our sails,
>
> amid the waves, where there was a dry path.
>
> [15] If I cease to render thanks, I shall be liable.
>
> The Nine Muses displeased me through the benefit of One.
>
> 25 An ardor is in my mind to celebrate the labours of these men,
>
> by whose voice faith makes its way through the world.

[Note: **19. *Ergo*.** The Basel edition has *ipse canam* (“I myself shall sing”), which is indeed more correct if one attends to quantity. But since the manuscripts make no alteration, let us defend the received reading on the basis of what has been noted in the letter to Florianus, at the penultimate verse. I discussed the matter itself in *Miscellanea*, p. 47.

**19. *Rettulit*.** I do not know whether this indicates that Luke wrote down what he himself had seen. Others, on the contrary, have supposed that he learned his information from Peter. Wandalinus, in his *Diatribe*, chapter 2, p. 249; Graevius’s *Syntagma*; and the distinguished Segaar in his observations on Luke, pp. 2 and 16, have discussed the matter. On Luke himself—whether called *Lucas*, *Lucanus*, or *Lucius*—see Heumann, *Poecile*, vol. II, p. 519.

**20. *Carmina*.** Perhaps *carmine* (“in verse”) could be read; below, I, 802:

> “We sing of Joppa in verse.”

And “to relate triumphs in verse” occurs in Corippus, *Panegyric in Praise of Anastasius*, 51. In the same way Vonckius correctly emends *talia carmine pando* (“I disclose such things in verse”) to *talia carmine pando* in the poem of Antonius, *Against the Nations*, in his *Critical Specimen*, p. 1.

Nevertheless, *carmina* (“poems”) is genuine: they are poems composed without the fault of fiction, as Asterius says in the epigram to Macedonius, verse 2. In the preceding verse others have likewise printed *veracia dicta poetae* (“the poet’s truthful words”); but only *veracis* (“of the truthful poet”) is correct there.

**21. *Reserabo*.** The final syllable is shortened, a practice from which the leading poets of the better age abstained. See Burmann at Lotichius III, elegy 10, 29. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* IV, 20, beginning, is relevant here: “He disclosed the letters of Holy Scripture, that is, the hidden things of the prophets.” Arator indicates that he will expound the history of the events in alternating modes or turns, and whatever hidden meanings he discovers in it.

I could wish that he had more often neglected this rule that he imposed upon himself; for through his allegories he is obscure everywhere, not to say something more serious. In such matters, to be overly inquisitive is generally foolish and barbarous, according to Fabricius in his commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 49.

**21. *Littera*.** The sacred books; compare *littera vetus* (“the ancient letter”) below, II, 362.

**22. *Mystica*.** Greek **μυστικόν** (*mystikon*), “something to be concealed.” Hilary, *Hymn*:

> “Yet they confess the true God,
>
> by bearing the mystical gift.”

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 90.

Rather, the word means “hidden” or “secret things” that lay concealed in the historical events and were to be referred to that meaning. Such is properly the force of adjectives ending in **-ικός** (*-ikos*), as Cattierus correctly explains in his *Method*, p. 33. Thus, below, I, 385, the manuscripts speak of “the mystical things of doctrine”; *mystical Adam*, verse 1038; “mystical gifts,” II, 89; “mystical power,” Sedulius I, 59. Compare what I said in *Miscellanea*, p. 48.

**23. *Metrica*.** The biblical books written in verse are listed by Arator in the preface to Vigilius: “The metrical power,” and likewise by Drepanus in his letter to Moduinus:

> “Job first unfolded his wars in heroic verse;
>
> David himself sounds forth divine things on the lyre.
>
> What should I say of swollen Solomon in his splendid buskin,
>
> who sings of Christ’s bridal chambers and of the Church?”

Saint Jerome, in his preface to Eusebius, says:

“What is more melodious than the Psalter? In the manner of our Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, it now runs in iambics, now resounds in Alcaics, now swells in Sapphics, now proceeds in half-feet. What is more beautiful than the song of Deuteronomy or Isaiah? What is weightier than Solomon? What more perfect than Job? All these works, as Josephus and Origen write, proceed among their own people composed in hexameter and pentameter verses.”

The same author says in his preface to the book of Job:

“Hexameter verses,” he says, “run in dactyls and spondees and, because of the nature of the language, frequently admit other feet—not of the same syllables, but of the same temporal quantities. Sometimes the rhythm itself is carried along sweetly and sonorously in loosened metrical numbers, something that those versed in metre understand better than the ordinary reader.

“If this seems incredible to anyone—that among the Hebrews there are metres, and that, in the manner of our Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, Alcaeus, and Sappho, either the Psalter, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, or nearly all the songs of Scripture are composed—let him read Philo, Josephus, Origen, and Eusebius of Caesarea; their testimony will prove that I speak the truth.”

Thus Saint Jerome. Those not mentioned here I listed above in the preface to Alexander, Duke of Saxony. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 79.

In the first edition of Tornaesius the reading is *metri vis* (“the power of metre”).

**24. *Psalterium*.** **Ψαλτήριον** (*psaltērion*) is both a musical instrument and the book itself, the Psalms. Arator shortens the antepenultimate syllable contrary to ordinary practice:

> “The lyric feet composed the Psalter,”

where the reference is to the book of Psalms. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 110.

The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornaesius editions read *Nam Psalmos lyrici* (“For the lyric feet composed the Psalms”). This is unnecessary. The syllable may be shortened in the same way as in *crepida*, from Greek **κρηπίς** (*krēpis*), and *medeor*, from **μήδω** (*mēdō*), and in similar forms cited by Vossius under *haeres* in his *Etymology*. Schottus offers other examples at Valerius Flaccus I, 331; and Christian poets do not observe such matters with complete consistency.

Thus Greek **η** is likewise shortened in *Ecclesia*; see above at verse 9. In Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 370, we find *eremus*; in Symmachus II, 52, *poesis*, according to Heinsius’s manuscripts. Conversely, **ε** is sometimes lengthened, as in *thema* and other words cited by Fabricius in his *Commentary*, pp. 134, 135, and 143. **ω** is changed into short **ο** by these and other poets. Drakenborch notes *Leucosia* and similar forms at Silius IV, 778; Oudendorp notes *Sophene*, with the first syllable short, at Lucan II, 593.

*Idolum*, with the middle syllable short, occurs below, I, 264. Some have nevertheless changed it there to *idolaque*, as also in Sedulius V, 146. See that passage, as well as Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIV, 4, and Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 34, who in chapter 33 also noted a fault in Arator’s use of *Psalterii*.

But what prevents us from reducing the word to three syllables through **συνίζησις** (*synizēsis*, contraction)? The same happens in *ariete*, *pariete*, *vindemiator*, and other forms; see Burmann at Lucan IX, 790, and Ausonius, epigram 44.

For *omnia mercatus* (“having purchased everything”) I found in the old edition *hoc die mercatus* (“having purchased on this day”), which confirms Lucius Scoppa’s conjecture there, though Vinetus says that the metre does not hold. But contract *die* into one syllable, and the metre, unless I am mistaken, will hold. I defended this conjecture in *Miscellanea*, p. 49; Boltius later added his agreement in *Critical Silva*, p. 13.

Nor was this method of contraction unknown to Arator: below, I, 116, he reduced *duodenarius* to five syllables. Compare Daumius at Cato IV, 4, and Vonckius, *Latin Readings* II, p. 142.

On the metre of the Psalms, Isidore, *Etymologies* VI, 2, says:

“It is established that all the Psalms among the Hebrews were composed in metrical verse. For, in the manner of the Roman Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, some now run in iambics, now resound in elegiacs, now shine in Sapphics, proceeding in trimeter or tetrameter feet.”

The old Paris edition there reads: *Psalmi—constant esse compositi* (“The Psalms are established to have been composed”). This has been sketched from Jerome’s passage cited by Fabricius. The comparison with Pindar was developed by the distinguished Ruckersfelder, *Collection of Commentaries*, fascicle I, chapters 1 and following. Klotz disagrees with him in *Literary Acts* I, part II, p. 119, and II, part II, p. 151.]

> Therefore I shall sing in verse the deeds that Luke related,
>
> [20] and, following the history, I shall speak true poems.
>
> 26 In alternating modes I shall disclose what the letter reveals,
>
> and whatever mystical matter is granted to me in my heart.
>
> 27 The metrical power is not unknown to sacred books;
>
> the lyric feet composed the Psalter.

[Note: **25. *Sonis*.** I restored this reading from the Moretus, Cambridge, and University manuscripts and from the Aldine and Basel editions. The others printed *modis* (“in modes”), but the meaning of that word already seems to be present in *hexametris*. Cortius, in the margin of his edition, explained *sonis* as “verses” or “feet.” I prefer the former. Menckenius, *Observations on the Latin Language*, pp. 919 and 921, vindicated *sonus* for “song” and *sonare* for “to sing,” both of which Faber had neglected.

**26. *Cantica*.** Isidore, *Etymologies* VI, 2, speaking of the *Song*, says: “The poems of these three books are said to have been composed among their own people in hexameter and pentameter verses, as Josephus and Jerome write.” The whole subject of Hebrew metres, which is sufficiently intricate, was explained by Robert Lowth in his *Academic Lectures*.

**26. *Hieremiae*.** I restored this reading from the Moretus, Cambridge, and University manuscripts and from the Aldine, Basel, and first Tornaesius editions. The others have *Hieremiam* or *Jeremiam*, as does the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*. Long ago, in *Miscellanea*, p. 50, I preferred the manuscript reading, but at that time I thought *Hieremiae* should be referred to the *Cantica* (“Songs”). I now think otherwise, after considering the matter more carefully and recognizing that Arator is speaking of three books: the *Songs*, as he also calls them below, I, 697; the sayings of Jeremiah; and those of Job.

By “the sayings of Jeremiah” he means the *Lamentations*, as Cortius correctly explained in the margin. I would not therefore likewise explain “the sayings of Job” by “lamentations”; for a single word often bears a double meaning, depending on the word to which it is referred, as I showed in *Specimen of Observations*, chapter 2, p. 17, and in the additions.

Concerning the book of Jeremiah, Isidore, *Etymologies* I, 38, says:

“Jeremiah was the first to compose in verse the *Threni*, which in Latin we call a lament, over the city of Jerusalem and the people when they were led into captivity.”

And in book VI, chapter 2:

“Jeremiah likewise published his book together with his *Threni*—the Groningen manuscript reads ‘his’—which we call laments because they are used in sorrowful circumstances and at funerals. In them he composed an alphabet in four sections with different metres. The first two are written as if in Sapphic metre, because three lines joined together and beginning with one letter conclude a heroic *comma*. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and each group of three verses begins with three letters. The fourth alphabet is similar to the first and second.”

I have altered several readings here on the basis of the Groningen manuscript. On the same subject, see Huet, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition 4, p. 262.

**26. *Job*.** Isidore, *Etymologies* I, 38, says:

“Job too, who was contemporary with Moses, proceeds in hexameter verse, in dactyls and spondees.”

And in book VI, chapter 2:

“The beginning and end of the book of Job among the Hebrews are woven in prose. Its middle section, from the passage where he says, ‘Perish the day on which I was born,’ to the passage, ‘Therefore I condemn myself and repent,’ proceeds entirely in heroic metre.”

I conjecture that *decurrunt* should be written; the remaining words, which differ from Gothofredus, I have reproduced from the Groningen manuscript. Bede, *On Metres*, p. 2366, testifies that it was composed in simple hexameters. Cassiodorus, *Divine Readings*, chapter 6, says: “It begins in prose, flows in verse, and ends in pedestrian speech.” But everything concerning the metre of this book—which some attribute not to Job but to another author—remains sufficiently uncertain along with the other matters. See Huet, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition 4, p. 222; Friedrich Spanheim, *Works*, vol. II, book I; Schultens, the leading scholar of his age, in his commentary; and Samuel Wesley, dissertations 3 and 4 on the book of Job.

**29. *Magistro*.** From this word Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, concluded that Arator had been a disciple of Vigilius. This is not clear to me. Until more certain authority is produced, I explain the word as referring to someone distinguished by greater dignity than other men, such as Vigilius the pope. In this sense *magister auctionis* (“master of the auction”) is explained by Graevius at Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XII, 30, and by Pricaeus at Apuleius, p. 389. *Magister pecoris* (“master of the herd”) occurs in Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 717. I am all the more inclined to apply it here because above, at verse 4, he compares Vigilius to a shepherd. Pricaeus, in the place cited, p. 62, explained *magisterium* as “authority”; Christian writers apply this word especially to the apostles. See Paulinus, *Poems* XXII, 178; XXXIII, 353 and 373. For additional matters relevant here, consult our preface.

**30. *Ab*.** “Because of.” See Cortius at Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XIII, 10. What he intends by *ore* (“mouth” or “speech”) is rather obscure. I had conjectured *ab arte* (“from skill”), but I determine nothing. I seem to have discovered that Arator was especially fond of this word. Below, II, 3, he uses it for the proclamation of divine matters; above, in the letter to Florianus, verse 2, for suitability or harmony.

Perhaps here he attempted through the word to express elegance and verbal charm—but it was only an attempt, unless, because of the preceding “gift of love,” he is imitating Prudentius, *Peristephanon* XIII, 3: “Our [life is] with love and speech.” In manuscript scholia that I once saw, the words of Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, verse 1310, “I hold the light soul first in my mouth,” were explained thus: “In the first word of your mouth: if you say that you will live, I shall live; if you say that you will die, I shall immediately die.” Farnabius offers a better interpretation there.

In the Moretus and Vossianus 2 manuscripts is added: “The prologue ends.”]

> 28 They say that the Songs, the sayings of Jeremiah, and Job too
>
> consist of hexameter rhythms in the language of their origin.
>
> 29 This gift of love I bring to you, great Father:
>
> regard it as the payment I owe for your merits.
>
> 30 Under your guidance I am chosen as a novice; with you as teacher I learn doctrines.
>
> If anything pleases through my speech, the praise will belong to my instructor.

**ARATOR THE SUBDEACON, ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES (C, S)**

**BOOK ONE**

[Note: **On *Actibus*.** The *Acts of the Apostles* bears this title, just as among the gentiles public records were once called *Acta publica*, in which the account and trustworthiness of imperial affairs and the administration of the state were recorded. Scarcely any book of our religion explains the doctrine of truth so clearly through irrefutable examples and the reliable history that followed from it. Certainly, apart from the apostles’ letters, which combine these two elements, there is no other such book.

The Romans had commentaries of this kind called *Acta Urbis* (“Records of the City”), by which later generations were instructed concerning what had been done, as though the trustworthiness of their ancestors had been publicly deposited there. Lampridius, in his life of Commodus, says:

“Furthermore, he had the practice of ordering everything that he did shamefully, impurely, cruelly, or in gladiatorial fashion to be entered in the *Acta Urbis*, as Marius Maximus testifies.”

While the republic still existed, individual leaders composed such brief accounts of the deeds they had performed. The *Acta* of Pompey the Great are mentioned by Pliny.

It is also permissible to interpret *actus* as “matters worthy of remembrance.” Capitolinus, in his lives of Maximus and Balbinus, says:

“But before I speak of their deeds, I think it appropriate to say something about their character and origin—or about their life itself.”

Venantius Fortunatus, book VIII, poem 4, on virgins:

> “Whatever she, watchful, shall meditate upon her deeds,
>
> she will here be admitted to share in an honored rank.”

Add the notes at Claudian I, *Against Rufinus*, verse 283. Barthius, *Adversaria* III, chapter 13.

The title of the work in the Cambridge and University manuscripts is: “Here begins book I of the *History of the Apostles* by Arator, subdeacon of the Roman Church.” In Vossianus 2: “Here begins the first book of the *Apostolic History*.” The Aldine and other editions differ little from these.

I have departed from them because they seemed to have arisen from the ingenuity of copyists, just as other editors indulged themselves in inventing the title. I preferred *On the Acts of the Apostles*, not because Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I, 1, 3; Cassiodorus, *Divine Readings*, chapter 9; and others mention *Actus apostolorum*, but because many considerations persuaded me that Arator himself placed this title before his work.

Fabricius, *Latin Bibliography* III, p. 307, reports that it appears in an undated edition, which ends with: “The second book of Arator the subdeacon, on the distinguished Acts of the Apostles, ends.” Uffenbach examined a manuscript in the Westminster Library in London and, from it, reports in his *Journey* II, p. 515, the title: “The versified Acts of the Apostles by Arator the subdeacon, addressed to Pope Vigilius.”

Nor are arguments lacking from elsewhere. Arator himself, in his letter to Vigilius, verse 19:

> “Therefore I shall sing in verse the deeds that Luke related.”

In the elegy to Parthenius, verse 77:

> “That book came before me which the rule calls the ‘Actus,’
>
> a book filled throughout with the harvest of the apostles.”

Venantius Fortunatus, *Life of Saint Martin*, beginning:

> “The deeds and Acts of the apostolic calling
>
> Arator, the poet, ploughed with fertile eloquence.”

Hermannus Contractus, *Chronicle*, p. 225, vol. III, part I, of the *Thesaurus Canisianus*:

“Arator, a Roman subdeacon, published his book on the Acts of the Apostles in heroic metre.”

Following these authorities, I preferred *Actus* to *Acta*, which the Westminster manuscript has. Vossius, *Art of Grammar* III, 36; Drakenborch at Silius X, 136; and Burmann at Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI, 58, defended the masculine form in Latin.

There are many such forms of the second and fourth declensions. See Gronovius at Seneca’s *Controversies*, p. 306; Burmann at Valerius Flaccus II, 207; Drakenborch at Livy VI, 9; and what I noted on Asterius’s epigram, verse 7, where I showed that *fastos* and *fastus* are similarly used. The latter is more common among poets. I am therefore surprised that Bunemann, at Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VI, 5 §21, orders the following passage in Orientius, *Commonitorium*, p. 77, to be emended at his own risk:

> “Come, imagine that your name is inscribed in the lasting records,”

for *fastus*. I would prefer the transmitted reading, because of *mansuri* (“lasting”) and because it has sufficient authority to defend it.

In Isidore—I use Gothofredus’s edition—I found in the very ancient Groningen manuscript: book I, chapter 21, *contractu omnium* (“by the contraction of all”); book VIII, chapter 9, *eventa praedicare conantur* (“they try to proclaim events”), and immediately afterward *diverso fatu* (“with a different expression”); book IX, chapter 3, *gravissimo dictu corripuit* (“he rebuked him with a most serious saying”); book XIV, chapter 8, *montem rupit acetu* (“he broke the mountain with vinegar”), a verse from Juvenal, satire X, 133; and book XIX, chapter 4, *tormenta autem a torto dicta* (“torments are so called from twisting”).

Statius and Passeratius, at Tibullus IV, 1, 4, explained the word itself as referring to accomplished deeds and matters most worthy of remembrance. Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, 10, used *acta gesta* (“deeds accomplished”). The Greeks say **πράξεις** (*praxeis*), which Cicero translates by *facta* (“deeds”). See Victorius at Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX, 14. More recent Greeks use **ἄκτα** (*akta*), as in **Ἄκτα Πιλάτου** (*Acta Pilati*, “Acts of Pilate”), though these are of dubious reliability. Du Cange, *Glossary*, under the word; Van Dalen, *On Oracles*, p. 608.

These are records in the manner of daily proceedings, part of which Dodwell published from the Vossian manuscript, though the material is spurious. Compare Oudendorp and others at Suetonius, *Julius Caesar* 20.

Novatianus also used *actus* for life and one’s manner of living, chapter 18, p. 140.

In some manuscripts, chapter headings are inserted, into which the poem is divided; the first concerns the Lord’s Ascension. But these headings differ so greatly in the manuscripts and printed editions that it is easy to see that they are not Arator’s. I therefore removed them and, following Fabricius, arranged everything in continuous order. I formerly approved the same procedure in Sedulius.

**1. *Sceleris*.** The first word is shown to be corrupt by the oldest and most trustworthy Cologne parchment manuscripts, in which, instead of *sceleris*, there is the remarkable word *pareti*. I do not understand it. The common reading contributes nothing to the excellent sense and distinctive sharpness that beginnings generally possess. Certainly a word such as *Salvatoris* (“of the Savior”), or something of that kind, is required.

For the present I do not intend to examine the reading I found in the manuscript, especially since the letters differ so greatly. **παρέδρου** (*paredrou*) is plainly insufficient, and perhaps some ordinary corruption lies beneath it. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, chapter 20.

I cannot understand what the remarkable reading of the Cologne manuscripts means; it is a source of astonishment to me. The nearest possibility would be *Pararii*, from *Pararius*, which the glosses explain as **μεσίτης** (*mesitēs*, “mediator”). See Cerda at Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, 14, and Vossius, *Etymology*, under this word. But the quantity is against it.

The passage seems sound to me, and the manuscripts agree on it. It undoubtedly refers to the imprecation of the Jews recorded by Matthew in the Gospel, chapter XXVII, verse 25. Among others, the distinguished de Rhoer has illuminated it in *Daventer Feasts* I, 20. These are the vows of blood that he mentions below at verse 191.

Nevertheless, I do not think *sceleris* depends on *cruore* (“blood”). This seems to have misled Barthius. There is no obstacle to referring it to *opus* (“work”), and for this reason I have placed a punctuation mark after *sui*. The meaning is that Judea, polluted by the blood of the Savior and having dared an abomination, completed the work of its crime—that is, its criminal work.

Sedulius expressed the same idea by *cruentum opus* (“bloody work”), V, 305; Paulinus of Pella by *exitiabile scelus* (“destructive crime”), *On the Life of Saint Martin* V, 111. Wopkensis illustrated the latter passage in *New Miscellaneous Observations* VII, p. 900, and supplied similar examples of the expression used here, *opus sceleris*, on p. 830. Thus *fides annalium* (“the credibility of the annals”) occurs in Florus I, 12, at the end. Add Vonckius, *Latin Readings* II, 10. Staveren discussed the Greek parallels at Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, p. 614; V. D. at Quintilian, *Declamations*, p. 25; and the passages I presented at Sedulius V, 126, and in *Miscellanea*, chapter 6, p. 62.

This also vindicates a passage of Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* III, 12, 18: “Nor can anything arise for anyone without the virtue of knowledge—that is, without knowledge of God and justice.” Davies had emended it at Cicero, *On Divination* I, 15, to *scientia et virtute* (“by knowledge and virtue”). There is no need: *scientiae virtus* means “virtue endowed with knowledge,” or with knowledge of God. In the same manner *doctrina superstitionis* (“the doctrine of superstition”) is sufficiently defensible in the *Collation of Mosaic and Roman Laws*, title 15 §3, where my teacher Roverus likewise attempted to emend the phrase to *doctrinae et superstitionis* in his *Juridical Specimen*, chapter 12. Cannegieter gives a different account at *Fragments of Ancient Jurisprudence*, p. 319.

**3. *Sine crimine*.** The Moretus and Cambridge manuscripts and the Aldine and Basel editions have *sine semine* (“without seed”). Corippus similarly has, II, 54:

> “And remaining a virgin, without the seed of a father.”

Claudian, *Phoenix* 23: “nor does it arise from seed.” The word is corrupt in Martianus Capella VI, p. 224. Grotius’s edition reads *eum Jovis semine procreatum* (“begotten from the seed of Jupiter”). It should be read *femine* (“from a woman”), on the basis of the excellent Vossian manuscript, whose variants are at hand. Oudendorp likewise restored this reading from two very ancient manuscripts at Suetonius, *Vespasian* 5.

Formerly, in *Miscellanea*, p. 172, I preferred *semine* (“seed”) here; but after considering the matter more carefully, I now change my opinion. *Crimine* (“crime”) is more forceful, because it heightens the point: the Savior, free from crime, underwent death for those who were liable to every crime.

Sedulius expressed this in II, 159:

> “He himself possessed nothing that could be lost.”

Unless, with the distinguished Schrader, *Observations* I, 4, you prefer *tergat malis* (“he wipes away evils”) there from the prose version. The verb *sumere* (“to take”) is used in the same way below, verse 335:

> “Which I pray took human flesh
>
> for this reason.”

Arnobius, *Against the Nations* I, p. 37, says *assumpsit formam hominis* (“he assumed the form of a man”); see Elmenhorst there and my notes at Sedulius I, 337.]

> 31 Thus Judea, polluted by the blood of its crime,
>
> having dared an abomination, completed the work; and the Creator of things
>
> 32 gave for the human race this which he had taken from human limbs,
>
> deeming it worthy to touch the lowest depths of hell,

[Note: **6. *Solvit*.** The remaining parts of this sentence too are corrupt. For *dignatus* (“deigning”) requires another word, so that the phrase does not become offensive in itself. Perhaps the passage should be read:

> “Deigning to touch the lowest depths
>
> of hell, while not abandoning the heights of heaven,
>
> to free those condemned from eternal night;
>
> day entered among the shades.”

This is certainly a more polished reading, and consideration of what follows seems to demand it. The phrase is interrupted in *ad manes ingressa dies* (“day having entered among the shades”), where *est* (“is”) is understood. Thus immediately afterward:

> “The third light rises,
>
> majesty returns with flesh.”

Understand: “where the third light rises.”

Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, chapter 20.

I see no reason to alter the text. *Dignatus* is sufficiently supported by Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* XI, 32:

> “And he himself, having long deigned
>
> to visit the sinful world.”

Fortunatus, *On the Birth of the Virgin* I, p. 699:

> “Through whom the world’s redemption deigned to be born.”

If *solvere* (“to free”) is accepted, the construction will be Greek; compare the letter to Vigilius, verse 4. But the meaning then seems less straightforward. Moreover, the manuscripts make no alteration, quite apart from the fact that *ingressa dies* is not an interrupted expression.

The meaning is that, after the Creator of things had given for the human race what he had taken from human limbs, he freed the condemned darkness from eternal night. There is no need here for an interrupted expression; compare Cortius at Sallust, *Catiline* 34, at the end. I would add Florus I, 1, 10: “The affair was of one age: a people of men.” But I would not admit an interruption there either; I would rather, rejecting the punctuation mark, read everything in a single breath.

Here *tenebrae* (“darkness”) means those who dwell in darkness; the word is a frequent designation for the underworld. See Barthius at Claudian, *Against Eutropius* I, 459. One who is condemned is handed over to night or darkness. Lactantius, *On Anger*, chapter 23 §22: “The human soul, enslaved to the body, is condemned to eternal death.” Claudian, *Consulship of Olybrius* 43:

> “Nor did he condemn riches to darkness.”

Especially relevant is Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, 6: “He says that a great star descended from heaven for their salvation, to bring the aid of light to suffering mortals condemned to long darkness.”

**9. *Natura*.** See the note at Sedulius V, 237, and what I said in *Miscellanea*, p. 172. Add below, verse 320.

**10. *Se vincente*.** That is, “with death itself conquering”: death perishes through its own victory. Wopkensis correctly explained it thus at Sedulius IV, 8. This is a form of oxymoron; see the note at verse 149.

Arator himself sufficiently explains this passage in what he says at verse 181:

> “Then hell fears to exist, and no punishment
>
> restraining anyone returns upon itself;
>
> the torturer grows weak for new inactivity.”

And at verse 318:

> “When the Lord approached to destroy hell,
>
> he carried away from it his own flesh,
>
> once the burial place had been despoiled.”

Book II, verse 117:

> “Death at last was conquered,
>
> having passed beyond the limit of conquering.
>
> Touched by the judge, it was ordered to leave the guilty;
>
> stripped of its ancient spoils,
>
> it falls through its own wars.”

Athanasius, *On the Passion of the Lord*, works, vol. I, p. 1016, concerning the devil:

> **Καὶ νομίσας κρατεῖν τὸν Χριστὸν ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ, αὐτὸς μᾶλλον ἐδείχθη νεκρός.**
>
> “And thinking that he held Christ in death, he himself was shown rather to be dead.”

**12. *Ligans*.** “Restoring to life.” Arnobius, *Against the Nations* II, p. 76: “For what are human beings except souls bound to bodies?” Below, *stringere* is used in this sense at verse 786:

> “Long loosened for death, the limbs are bound to salvation.”

Conversely, the dead are said to be “loosened,” below at verse 758:

> “And the soul, released from its bonds,
>
> the burden having been loosened.”

Book II, verse 127:

> “Death cannot be loosened.”

So too *solvi* (“to be released”). See Barthius at Claudian, epigram I, verse 101; Cortius at Sallust, *Jugurtha* 17, 6. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 3: “May a swift hour dissolve the human being”; and prose 7: “The body released by its final death.” Add Burmann at the *Greek Anthology* III, p. 465, and Barthius, *Adversaria* XII, 15; XIV, 2.

The Greeks likewise attribute **λύειν** (*lyein*, “to loosen”) to death. Cerda at Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 418, on **ἀναλύειν** (*analuein*, “to dissolve”); Perizonius at Aelian IV, 23, on **ἀπολύειν** (*apolyein*, “to release”); Elsner at Philippians I, note 23. **Λύσις** (*lysis*, “loosening”) is used for death; see Duker at Florus IV, 11, 11. Homberg observes that the ancients spoke thus because they considered the body the soul’s bond and prison, *Sacred Miscellanies*, p. 123.

**13. *Monumenta*.** Greek **μνημεῖα** (*mnēmeia*), things that remind us of something, such as tombs. Juvencus:

> “Then the monuments of ancient men were opened,
>
> once the barriers had been removed.”

Servius says that *monumenta* are connected with memory, while *monimenta* are connected with the mind; whoever wishes may agree with him. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 89.

Marckart taught the jurists that a *sepulcrum* (“tomb”) and a *monumentum* (“monument”) are distinct, *Probabilities*, part II, p. 4. But writers did not observe the distinction and used this word for a tomb, as I showed at Sedulius V, 390. Add Trotz, *Memorial Propagation*, p. 13.

Orosius, *History* VII, 7, has *ad monumentorum bustorumque diversoria* (“to the resting places of tombs and funeral pyres”). Read *ad monumentorum mansiones* (“to the abodes of monuments”), for this is how John of Salisbury quoted the words of Orosius, VIII, 18.

Isidore V, 24, reads: “because it is not valid except after the testator’s monument.” But the Groningen manuscript has *mortuos* (“the dead”); I therefore think it should be read: “after the testators are dead,” as he immediately adds: “it is not valid except after the testators’ death.”

**Μνημεῖον** (*mnēmeion*) is used in this way by later Greeks, more rarely by the ancients. See Segaar at Luke, p. 323. Athanasius, *Against the Arians*, oration 4, works, vol. I, p. 507:

> **Καὶ τὰ μὲν μνημεῖα, ὡς προεῖπον, ἠνοίγετο.**
>
> “And the tombs, as I said, were opened.”

The translator wrongly omitted this sentence.

It is sufficiently clear that Arator is referring here to Matthew’s testimony, Gospel chapter XXVII, verse 53. There, however, I approve the opinion of those who place a punctuation mark after **μνημείων** (“tombs”) and join **τὴν ἔγερσιν** (“the rising”) with **εἰσῆλθον** (“they entered”). The other interpretations conflict both with the laws of nature and with the rules of interpretation.]

> 33 He should touch the depths of hell, while not abandoning heaven’s heights;
>
> he freed the shadows condemned to eternal night.
>
> 34 Day entered among the shades: the fleeing stars abandoned the heavens,
>
> accompanying God; terrified by Christ’s cross,
>
> 35 nature likewise wished to suffer, and death’s power,
>
> victorious over itself, perished, submerged beneath the weight of triumph,
>
> 36 seizing more than it had any right to seize. And divine power,
>
> binding the limbs again, moved the corpses back to life.
>
> The tombs opened toward life, and the ashes of the righteous
>
> renewed their birth after burial. The third light rises.

[Note: **15. *Speciemque*.** “Splendor” or “beauty.” See the note at Sedulius II, 60; from this passage Wasseus rightly defends the passage of Juvencus at Sallust, *Catiline* 57.

Understand especially the splendor and pomp that strikes the eyes and by which someone is recognized as a god, as Burmann explains the word at Claudian, *Fourth Consulship of Honorius* 83. Add Elmenhorst at Arnobius, *Against the Nations* IV, p. 146.

At Corippus II, 48, I remember that Vonckius once emended the passage:

> “The bravest prince stood upon that shield,
>
> possessing the appearance of the sun.”

The common reading there is *specimen* (“model” or “image”), which Virgil’s authority could nevertheless support, *Aeneid* XII, 164:

> “Twelve golden rays surround the shining image
>
> of the ancestral sun.”

For this is how any distinguished thing is described by which someone is to be seen and esteemed. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 4: “the image of ancestral talent shines forth.” Schulting, at Seneca’s *Controversies*, p. 60, has *specimen aurei saeculi* (“an image of the golden age”); Gronovius restored it not unsuccessfully in Donatus’s *Life of Virgil* at the end. Add Drakenborch at Livy XXXVIII, 17, 20.

**“Exiled from the clay.”** He indicates that Christ rose in order to prepare for human beings access to the heavenly homeland and blessed life, an access closed by the sins into which humanity had plunged headlong. He explains the thought himself in book II, verse 556:

> “We too, rejected through guilt from our first place,
>
> are cast into the world’s exile;
>
> at last the way is restored
>
> by which we may return along the road to our homeland.”

*Limus* (“clay”) designates the human being. See Elmenhorst at Arnobius, *Against the Nations* II, p. 93; below, verse 374:

> “We are earthly material,
>
> and by naming clay as its parent
>
> the human being discloses it.”

Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*, chapter 16:

> “Who could have fashioned a human being from joyful clay?”

I do not understand what *laeto limo* (“joyful clay”) means there. I think it should be emended to *lento* (“sluggish” or “sticky”). Thus Alcimus Avitus, *On the Origin of the World*, book I, p. 368:

> “And he meditates the organs within the sticky mud.”]

The earth is said to become viscid in Virgil, *Georgics* II, 250; hence Servius, commenting on the same passage, explains *lentum virus* as “viscous slime.” Add also *Georgics* IV, 41. These expressions, however, are frequently interchanged. See Brouckhusius on Tibullus I, 11, 58; Burmann on Nemesianus, *Eclogue* 4, line 128; on Ovid, *Tristia* II, 514; Drakenborch on Livy III, 26, 12, and V, 5, 7.

**17. *Interclusa*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *interclausa*. So too the Aldine and Basel editions, but in these and similar cases the forms belonging to the ancient verb *cludo* have been restored; hence *clusit* occurs for *clausit* in older parchment manuscripts. See the notes on Silius VI, 451; Schottus on Seneca’s *Suasoriae*, p. 350; Stewechius on Arnobius V, p. 113. Cortius found *clusa* for *clausa* in the Wolfenbüttel manuscript when commenting on Sallust, *Jugurtha* 12, 5. See also Duker on Florus III, 20, 13; Bynkershoek, *Jurisprudentiae Observationes* VIII, 5.

**20. *Semine*.** The genuine reading in four books is *spermate*. Clearly, in the manner of such writers, he first sought erudition in the Greek word, and then a play upon the letters in *spermate* and *germine*. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIII, chapter 20.

In my manuscripts there is no alteration. These writers indeed commonly seek learned effect in Greek words, as Stewechius observes concerning Arnobius’s Greek vocabulary in his notes on *Against the Nations* VII, p. 150, and Salmasius concerning Tertullian in his notes on *Pallium*, p. 290. I am less certain that this applies to Arator. Soon afterward, in line 32, he uses *chrisma*; but this word was already established in baptism, and he therefore seems to have written it from ordinary usage rather than from a desire to display Greek. Sometimes, too, a Greek word cannot conveniently be rendered in Latin and must therefore be retained, although that is unnecessary here. Thus, in Novel 105, chapter 1, where Gothofredus most incorrectly printed *quem adorna vocant*, Taffinus, in *De Anno Saeculari*, chapter 9, rightly restored *porna*, from the Greek *πόρνας* (“prostitutes”); Hombergius followed him, though without mentioning Taffinus.

**20. *Florigero*.** He means Paradise, which Sedulius calls a “flower-bearing abode” (*florigeram sedem*) in II, 2. It is not inelegant to render the foreign word in this way, rather than derive it, as Mollius does in his notes on Longus’s *Pastoral*, p. 48, rather absurdly from *παρὰ* and *δεύσω*.

Sedulius writes elegantly in V, 222:

> And with him he rejoices to lead them  
> Into your fields, O Paradise, where the meadow, with its everlasting flower,  
> Delights in its grassy softness, and the pleasure of the groves  
> Is nourished by unfailing waters; and among gardens,  
> Conspicuous and kindly, whose fruits never fail,  
> The serpent groans that its ancient colonist dwells there.

There, following Wopkensius, *decipientibus* must certainly be restored. Concerning Paradise Isidore writes in XIV, 3: “For it is planted with every kind of tree and fruit-bearing tree, and it also has the tree of life. There is neither cold nor summer heat there, but an everlasting moderation of the air.” Thus the editions I have seen read. From the Groningen manuscript, however, restore *non aestus* (“not heat,” rather than *non aestas*, “not summer”).

Dracontius likewise writes of Paradise in the *Hexaemeron*, p. 353:

> Its fruits are not scorched  
> By the panting rays, nor is it shaken by any blasts;  
> No whirlwind rages there with storms conspiring together;  
> No hardened ice subdues it, nor does a blow of hail  
> Beat it, nor do the meadows grow white with icy frosts.

The sense requires “a blow of hail.” Alcimus Avitus writes in I, p. 371:

> Here winter never succeeds to alternating time,  
> Nor do summer suns return after the cold.

The description of Alcinous’ gardens in Homer, *Odyssey* η, line 118, is not very different; Justin Martyr believed that the poet was describing Paradise. See Brassicanus on Salvianus, p. 263. In this manner temperate regions are generally described. Justin, II, 17, says that Egypt had always been so temperate that neither winter cold nor the heat of the summer sun oppressed its inhabitants.

**22. *It is*.** This refers to the eleven apostles: Judas had already been removed, while Thomas was present, although previously absent. Paul does indeed mention “the twelve” in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XV, verse 5; but the complete number is sometimes used although one or another is missing. See Perizonius on Aelian, *Various History* III, 17, who also interprets Paul’s passage as referring to the eleven apostles. This works in Arator; but in Paul’s passage more than ten cannot be understood, since it concerns the appearance made on the very day of the resurrection, when Thomas was absent. Gerdesius, *Sacred Studies*, p. 80.

**23. *Usque sub*.** The Lyon library has *usque ad*, plainly an error. Compare the notes on Florus, book I, preface; Burmann on Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 289.

**23. *Extremum*.** “To the end of the earth” (*ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς*) occurs in Acts I, verse 8. Tennulius compared it with the Latin construction in Frontinus I, 3, 10. Add the distinguished Segaar on Luke, p. 318.

He uses *mundum extremum* for “the farthest part of the world,” just as *extremus annus* occurs in Livy II, 64, and *summa rota* in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 107. In Sedulius I, 212, I formerly altered the manuscript reading to:

> He brought forth the waters of the rock from below.

I now incline more strongly to restore *saxo imo* (“from the lowest rock”), on the evidence noted in my comments on the same author III, 123, and by Heinsius on Ovid, *Heroides* XX, 41. The distinguished de Rhoer, in *Deventer Miscellanies* I, p. 43, elegantly emends Seneca, *Hippolytus* 956:

> And call the swollen waves from the lowest Ocean.

The manuscript mentioned by Gruterus seems to support this; it has *omni*.

*Diffusus limes* means “a space extended farther.” Drakenborch, in his notes on Silius IV, 105 and XVI, 338, and Burmann, on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 901, have shown that *limes* is used for any space or road. Hence scribes frequently confuse it with *trames*. See Burmann on Valerius Flaccus IV, 614.

**37**

> Majesty returns with flesh and brings back a radiant form  
> From the seat of shadows, so that from the exiled clay,  
> Long shut away, the origin of the homeland may be recovered.  
> The Almighty himself prepares the roads and commands bodies,  
> After the tombs, to reign with him; when the seed of poison  
> Had died, he restored his own shoots to the flower-bearing garden.  
>   
> And now, for forty days, the Lord had confirmed his faith  
> By signs witnessed by them,  
> Even to the farthest world, along the extended boundary.

**26. *Mandere*.** To show that Christ truly lived, he asked for food, as Luke records in the Gospel XXIV, 41; hence this passage should be explained in connection with Acts of the Apostles X, 41. On this subject see also Ericus Phaletranus, *On the Removal of the Jewish Scepter*, p. 425, in Graevius’s *Syntagma of Dissertations*.

**27. *Petiturus*.** The penultimate syllable is short. Fabricius, in his commentary, p. 102. Fabricius plainly intended to write “the antepenultimate syllable.”

**28. *Quia*.** I restored this reading from the manuscripts of Moretus, Cambridge, and the University, and from the Aldine and Basel editions; the others have *qua*. The distinguished Wassenberg added his agreement.

Since he speaks of a “place of light,” he alludes to oil, customarily poured into lamps, which Ovid called *infusam Pallada* (“Pallas poured in”) in *Tristia* IV, 5, 4. Thus *lumen* is used of a lamp in the same author’s *Fasti* II, 743; Burmann rightly explains it in his notes on *Metamorphoses* X, 691.

He calls it a “place of peace,” whose sign was the olive. Hence below, line 656:

> And the modest beak  
> Was a pledge of the olive; love, always upon the lips,  
> Bears the fruit of peace.

For this reason it is called “peaceful” in Ovid, *Ex Ponto* I, 1, 31. Add Drakenborch on Silius XIII, 68; Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI, 279.

Polybius speaks of the barbarians in *Histories* III, p. 285:

> They met him carrying branches and wreaths. For this is almost universally a token of friendship among the barbarians.

There *θαλλός* signifies an olive branch. See Perizonius on Aelian, *Various History* VI, 6, at the end; Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI, 81.

Prudentius, or—according to others—Amoenus, has something similar in the *Enchiridion of Epigrams* 44, entitled “The Mount of Olives”:

> From the summit of the olive-bearing mountain Christ went upward  
> To the Father, marking the traces of peace.  
> A rich fluid melts from the eternal leaves,  
> Proving the gift poured upon the earth from the chrism.

On this passage also compare Bochart, *On the Animals of Scripture* II, book II, chapter 6.

**30. *Signata*.** Those baptized were anointed with oil, and their foreheads were marked with a cross. Rittershusius first demonstrated this in his notes on Salvianus, *On the Government of God*, p. 27. Arator refers to it below, line 626:

> Seeking the region near Samaria, he marked  
> The sheep washed clean in the waters of baptism.

Prudentius writes in the *Cathemerinon*, hymn 6, line 125:

> Worshiper of God, remember  
> That you have entered beneath the sacred dew  
> Of the fountain and the bath,  
> That you have been renewed with chrism.

Other manuscripts there have *innotatum* (“marked upon”); this is not displeasing, since it refers to the sign of the cross placed upon the forehead. Prudentius shows that this was done in the *Psychomachia* 360:

> After the marks inscribed in oil upon the forehead, through which  
> The royal ointment was given, and everlasting chrism.

From this Sedulius may be interpreted, line 327:

> And beauty was fixed upon the forehead.

Add Fabricius in his commentary, p. 39. From this Gothofredus derives the reason for Constantine’s prohibition against branding the forehead with a mark: the forehead, previously adorned with the sign of the cross, was not to be disfigured by a more dishonorable mark. See his commentary and book II of the *Theodosian Code*, under “On Punishment.”

**32. *Chrisma*.** *Χρίσμα* means any anointing. An uncertain author writes in *Bebianus*:

> Both pouring a sacred imperial offering and fragrant with chrism.

Elsewhere it is the anointing by which Christians who had been baptized were marked. Prudentius writes in the *Cathemerinon*:

> That you have entered beneath the sacred dew,  
> That you have been renewed with chrism.

And in the *Apotheosis*:

> Is there any disciple  
> Of chrism whose temples he would mark  
> With an inscribed sign?

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 33.

The Aldine and Basel editions have *ablivit* for *abluit*. These words seem to refer to the Christian belief that sins were abolished through baptism, which consequently was sometimes postponed until the end of life. See Baluzius on Salvianus, *On the Government of God* VI, p. 345.

Optatus, *On the Donatist Schism* VII, p. 103, Du Pin’s edition, writes: “For ordinary oil is simple and has one proper name; once prepared, it is called chrism, in which there is a sweetness that softens the skin of the conscience, hardness of sins having been excluded.” The change was therefore undoubtedly believed to take place through baptism.

I tentatively wonder whether Hesychius should be brought into connection here: *Ἄλλαγμα, ὁ βαπτιζόμενος* (“a change; the one being baptized”). Alberti conjectures *Βασταζόμενος* (“the one being carried”) and supposes that a Chaldean-Syriac word lies concealed there; the learned man says this in *Miscellaneous Observations* X, volume I, p. 67. I think the matter should be investigated further.

**34. *Pompa*.** Ovid, *Ex Ponto* II, 1, 19:

> Through which, displayed amid the enclosed Getae,  
> The triumphal procession is mine;

and III, 4, 95:

> Why do you delay preparing the chariot and procession for triumphs?

Pacatus mentions a procession of bearers of dishes in the *Panegyric* 47, 3.

**35. *Arva*.** “Land,” below, line 322:

> The lands tremble, shaken in their places;

line 375:

> His force bent and drove the lands;

line 509: *arva Sidonia* (“Sidonian fields”) in Sedulius III, 242.

In the same way poets use the word for a kingdom. In this sense Burmann restored it in Rutilius, *Itinerary* I, 83:

> What could be comparable? It fell to the Assyrians  
> To join their lands with the Medes, once they had subdued their neighbors.

Crusius’s conjecture there, *comprendere* or *contendere*, in *Critical Probabilities*, p. 57, is inferior. Vonckius proposed two emendations in *Latin Readings* I, 2, at the end; I would prefer the latter.

Soon afterward the Lyon *Library of the Fathers* has *petit*.

> He commands them to be his witnesses. The wonders of events  
> Could not conceal God; the resurrected one gave  
> Such certain proofs—what better proof could the risen one give than to eat? By this  
> Human bodies prove that they have life. About to seek heaven,  
> He proceeds to survey the olive grove, because it is a place  
> Of light and peace through its sacred shoot. He wishes to return from there,  
> From which divine fragrance commends the creature, gleaming with its forehead marked;  
> when chrism, in Christ’s name, washes the anointed inwardly from above,  
> the victor is raised to return to the star-bearing heaven,  
> And carries with him what he took up: a new triumphal procession!  
> God sought the fields, the man the stars; what is granted to him?

Here *homo* means “the man,” not humanity.

**36. *Parte*.** Fabricius printed *patre* (“father”), yet did not alter *aetherea* (“heavenly”), which makes me suspect a printer’s error. The common reading is supported by Salvianus, *On the Government of God* I, p. 18: “the dreadful crash of the whole air on every side,” and by the passages noted by Heinsius on Claudian, *Gigantomachia* 74. Otherwise, *aetherio de patre* (“from the heavenly Father”) would also possess considerable elegance.

Burmann, in his notes on Valerius Flaccus I, 72, and Drakenborch on Livy IV, 60, 3, long ago showed that scribes confused such forms. *Pater meus* (“my father”) occurs in Victor, *Caesars* 3, 8; the interchange was especially easy because scribes frequently transposed letters.

I shall give a notable example from Isidore, *Etymologies* IX, 2: *Vascones, quasi Vaccones—quod genus Pompeius edomita Hispania* (“The Vascones, as though Vaccones—that people whom Pompey subdued after Spain had been conquered”). So Gothofredus printed it; write, from the Groningen manuscript, *quos Gnaeus* (“whom Gnaeus [Pompey subdued]”). The same reading already occurs in the edition of 1509, as I later discovered.

**38. *Evehit*.** He uses this verb correctly, for it applies to those who, after an achievement, have attained greatness. See Burmann on Velleius II, 41, 1.

*Excelsis* could be understood as *in excelsis* (“in the heights”), since a verb compounded with a preposition sometimes takes another preposition: for example *subire in latebras* (“to enter into hiding”) in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, 600. Add Perizonius on Mela in *Miscellaneous Observations* VII, volume III, p. 460; Drakenborch on Livy III, 21 and XXII, 3.

Here *in excelsis* would stand for “into the heights.” Grammarians scarcely observe the distinction in this preposition. See the notes on Cicero, *For Quintus*, 5 and 11; Muncker on Fulgentius, pp. 624, 626; Schultingius on Seneca’s *Controversiae*, p. 170; Struchtmeyer, *Annotations*, p. 120; and the notes on Sedulius IV, 107.

Nevertheless, I would rather take *excelsis* here as a dative, as in Virgil’s *it clamor caelo* (“the shouting goes to heaven”) and Silius’s *ire castris* (“to go to the camp”) X, 622. See the notes there and on XV, 326. Add Wopkensius in *Miscellaneous Observations* VII, volume II, p. 247; Oudendorp on Lucan II, 685; Paternas on Victor, *Origin of the Roman People* 14, 3.

Pricaeus, on the Epistle to Titus, chapter I, §5, relates the same dative to the meaning of a place in which something happens, as when Scribonius, *Compositiones* 169, writes *nascitur Siciliae* for *in Sicilia* (“is born in Sicily”). That is correct; but I would utterly deny that it is a dative, and I am surprised that Pricaeus thought so. It is a genitive, like *Aegypti*, *Cypri*, and similar forms, a construction explained by Vossius, *Art of Grammar* VII, 25.

**39. *Tropaeo*.** Barthius, on Statius, *Thebaid* II, 706, rightly explains this of Christ’s body carried into heaven, for it truly is a trophy conspicuous of victory over death. Athanasius, *Works* I, p. 75, writes:

> For this was the trophy against death, to display it thus.

The cross is likewise called *νίκη* (“victory”) in the same author I, p. 79, and the resurrection is called *τρόπαιον* (“trophy”) on pp. 83, 85, and 100.

Ambrose writes in the hymns on the advent of Christ, p. 792 of Fabricius’s *Corpus*:

> Equal to the eternal Father,  
> Gird yourself with the trophy of flesh.

Christ’s flesh is called a royal chariot, in an expression taken from triumphal language, by Paulinus to Cytherius, p. 849. Add Maderus on Panvinius, *On Triumph*, chapter 7, at the end.

**40. *Atri*.** Poets commonly use this word of the underworld and death. See Barthius on Claudian, *Rape of Proserpina* I, 2; on Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 440; and Burmann on Ovid, in the same passage, line 80.

Boltius, in *Critical Silvas*, p. 14, rightly saw that Juvencus should read *artis corporis vinculis* (“by the bonds of the body’s limbs”) rather than *atris*. It already appears thus in the more accurate editions.

**41. *Arce*.** Poets frequently use the word in this way. See Barthius on Claudian, *Rape of Proserpina* I, 213. This shows how carelessly the Aldine and Basel editions print *arte*.

**42. *Qua pietate*.** I adopted the verse from the Cambridge manuscript in Moretus’s codex. The Aldine and Basel editions also read *qua pietate*, but in the following passage they have *propter quem*. In all the others the verse is printed:

> Whom he receives through compassion, for whom he had come, he went.

I approve only the Cambridge manuscript’s reading. The meaning is: “With the compassion by which Christ was moved to come for sinners, with that same compassion—and for which he had come—he went into heaven, so that by interceding with the Father he might wipe away the sins of his own.”

The distinguished Wassenberg also approves the reading of the Aldine edition, which he used, and explains it thus: “Christ lived on earth for humanity’s sake, and for humanity’s sake also returned to his own heaven. The compassion that prompted his coming was also the reason for his return.” Nothing in the distinguished man’s explanation, whose agreement I gladly acknowledge, is more correct.

The interlinear glosses in Vossianus 2 explain *propter quem* as “the man” or “for what reason.” The omission of the pronoun has caused much confusion here, and has often provided an opening for corrupting passages. See the notes on Florus I, 1, 12, and what I said in my dissertation on book II of the *Digest*, *On Summoning to Court*, chapter 8, where I defended, against the emendations of others, a passage of Pliny, *Letters* VIII, 27, 11, corrupted in the same way. I later discovered that the same thought had occurred to Gronovius in his notes on Seneca’s *Letters* 22; I gladly credit him with the discovery.

Explain *pietatem* as “clemency.” See Martinus in *Miscellaneous Observations* X, volume II, p. 243; Cellarius on Sedulius IV, 196.

**43. *Altus*.** “Grave,” and something that penetrated their minds most deeply and seemed, as it were, to sit upon them. Ammianus Marcellinus XXX, 2: “with anxiety thereafter growing more deeply oppressive”; XXXI, 10: “carried away by a deep desire to fight.” Petronius, *Satyricon* 128:

> And deep fear possesses the mind.

Tacitus, *Annals* IV, 41: “but fearing more deeply”; see Freinshemius there. *Altius moveri* (“to be moved more deeply”) occurs in Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 14.

Seneca, *Letters* 3, has *altior tamen illa voluptas est* (“yet that pleasure is deeper”); Heumannus emends it thus in *Poecilographia* II, p. 31, although I would retain the transmitted reading there.

Arnobius, *Against the Nations* V, p. 155: “Do we believe that they are bound by sleep and plunged into forgetfulness of the deepest slumber?” Write there *victos somno* (“overcome by sleep”), as on p. 158: “by an extraordinary circumstance, he is overcome by sleep and sunk into the deepest [slumber].” Virgil uses the same expression in *Aeneid* IX, 337, although Heinsius found *vinctus* (“bound”) both there and in some manuscripts.

On *altus* see also Burmann on Valerius Flaccus VII, 88. Pacatus, *Panegyric* 41, 4, says *stuporem attonitum* (“astonished stupor”) for “deep stupor.” I nevertheless agree rather with Schwarzius, who conjectures *attonitis* (“the astonished”), a reading which I later found confirmed in Vossius’s excerpts.

The Greeks have the same idiom. Lucian, *Amores*, p. 898, has *βαθεῖαν ἐπιτεθειμένη λήθην* (“deep forgetfulness imposed upon [them]”). See Mollius on Longus’s *Pastoral*, p. 18; Alberti, in his notes on Hesychius under *Βάθος*, proves that this word contains the meaning of depth.

In general, the Greeks express what is great in this way. Aelian, *Various History* III, 18, p. 220, has *πλούτῳ βαθεῖ* (“deeply rich”). See Perizonius on the same work VI, 6. In book II, chapter 11, the distinguished scholar attempts to restore *βαθύτατα πλουτοῦντας* or *βαθυτάτους* (“being exceedingly rich” or “exceedingly rich”) in *Miscellaneous Observations* II, volume II, p. 249.

**43. *Ore*.** It may be referred to *dixere* (“they said”), an expression very common among poets, especially Virgil. Thus *ore locutum* (“spoken with the mouth”) occurs below, I, 694.

I would rather refer it to *perspicui* (“radiant”), indicating a face shining like lightning, to which *coruscus* (“flashing”) belongs; Fulgentius has *vultus coruscamen* (“the flashing of the face”) in *Mythologies* I, p. 618.

In the Vulgate version of Matthew XXVIII, 3, the appearance of the angels at Christ’s tomb is said to have been like lightning. Alcimus Avitus expressed it thus in his book to his sister, p. 431:

> A shining garment gleamed upon his snow-white body,  
> And a fiery radiance had sprinkled his face everywhere.

Sedulius called it *flammeum aspectu* (“flaming in appearance”) in V, 328. Tertullian generally describes angels in *On the Judgment of the Lord*, p. 289:

> Their vigor is fiery, their bodies radiant; the divine power of heaven flashes.

In Luke these men are said to have been *ἐν ἐσθῆτι λευκῇ* (“in white clothing”), a garment commonly attributed to angels. See Elsner on John XX, 12.

Burmann, on Valerius Flaccus V, 349, rightly explains the expression as “clothed in a white garment”; for through its whiteness it drew all eyes toward itself. This meaning derives from *λεύω* or *λεύσσω*, which Hesychius explains by *ὁρᾷν* (“to see”).

Because of the words *ore corusco* (“with flashing face”), *ἐσθὴς λαμπρά* (“brilliant clothing”) seems to have been more present to Arator’s mind, although it must be completely distinguished from *λευκῇ* (“white”), despite Thomas Magister’s confusion of them on p. 566, rightly corrected by Trillerus and others.

Hence the Greeks call a purple garment *ὀξὺ* and *λαμπρόν* (“sharp” and “brilliant”). Salmasius on Tertullian’s *Pallium*, p. 182; the Latins likewise attribute light to it. See Vonckius, *Critical Specimen*, p. 23.

**43**

> A crash from the heavenly region? And how loudly the celestial choirs  
> Resound in praise, when the ruler of Olympus  
> Raises to the heights whatever he took up from below?  
> And entering heaven, with the trophy of flesh accompanying him,  
> He places in the citadel of light the spoils snatched  
> From the black jaws of the abyss, and raises up earthly limbs.  
> With the compassion by which he receives them, for which he had come, he went.  
> Deep astonishment seizes the disciples; to them the shining men spoke with flashing countenance:  
> things which, once known to us, sound wondrous. Now let us, rejoicing, contemplate them  
> and prove the measure of his dominion by the laws subject to it.  
> Born from a virgin mother, rising after trampling death,  
> Seeking the scepters of heaven, he announces these deeds to his servants.

**46. *Jura*.** Vossianus 2 has *jure* (“by right”).

**47. *Calcata*.** “Conquered,” an expression taken from victors who placed their feet upon enemies whom they had defeated. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* I, meter 5:

> And the guilty trample  
> Sacred necks in unjust reversal.

See the notes on Pacatus, *Panegyric* 36, 3 and 45, 4; Burmann on Valerius Flaccus IV, 312. Hence *calcare* and *conculcare* mean “to despise insolently.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XVIII, 2; Weitz on Salvianus, p. 174; the distinguished scholar in *Miscellaneous Observations* VIII, p. 9. Thus below, line 408:

> And they teach that gold must be trampled,  
> Which they place beneath their feet.

Stephanus compared the Greek *λὰξ πατεῖν* (“to tread with the heel”) in his notes on Aeschylus, *Eumenides*, line 544. Add Heinsius on Silius III, 85. Hesychius therefore explains it under *Πατέουσι* by *καταφρονεῖν* (“to despise”).

**48. *His nuntiat*.** The Antwerp edition and Fabricius have *bis* (“twice”). Cortius had written *nuntia tacta* in the margin, adding the letter P. I believe this indicates Pulmannus, who corrected a few passages in Arator. This became especially clear to me from the corrections written by a learned hand in Fabricius’s edition, now in the possession of the distinguished Burmann. A comparison will show that the Antwerp edition frequently agrees with Pulmannus.

**49. *Nec cessant*.** Vossianus 2 has *ne*.

**49. *Tonanti*.** He imitates Lucan I, 35:

> And heaven serve its Thunderer.

Oudendorp noted the same in his additions. Thus below, line 160, some manuscripts have:

> But first Peter, whose step is served by the sea.

Pricaeus on Matthew IX, 26, and Oudendorp on Lucan V, 602, explain the passage. Add the notes on Sedulius III, 68.

Mamertinus, *Panegyric to Maximian Hercules* 12: “What prosperous results will follow you in maritime affairs, when the very weather already obeys you so favorably?” Read *cui jam* (“which now”) from the excellent Wolfenbüttel manuscript, formerly belonging to Gudianus. Cortius likewise saw this in Pliny VII, 10, 4.

Eumenius, *Panegyric to Constantine* 13: “Certainly, Constantine the Great, nature itself serves your divine power.” The same manuscript deletes *Constantine* but has *ipsarum rerum* (“of things themselves”).

**50. *Praegressa*.** The Aldine, Basel, Antwerp, Pulmannian, and Fabrician editions have *progressa*. Heinsius had written both readings in the margin of Moretus’s manuscript. Such forms are frequently interchanged. See Drakenborch on Livy IX, 10, 7; these prepositions are written almost alike in manuscripts. Muncker on Fulgentius, p. 681, Staver’s edition; Reitzius in *Miscellaneous Observations* X, p. 376.

In the Salisbury manuscript III, 19, p. 644, one should read *manus praeferebant* (“they held out their hands”), from Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 19. Here I prefer *praegressa*.

Sedulius called it the “guiding star” in hymn 2, 34. Juvencus I, 245:

> Behold, midway along the road they see the star  
> Running ahead, furrowing the air with flames.

[Editorial note: *iteris* stands for *itineris*, by syncope, to preserve the metre.]

Weitzius on Valerius Flaccus I, 568, and Burmann on Lucan V, 562, elegantly explain *sulcare* (“to furrow”). Arator and other poets therefore state that the star went before the Magi on their journey, whether this is understood of the entire journey or of the road leading to Bethlehem. Heumann denies both interpretations in *Poecilographia* II, p. 131, a view that is particularly attractive.

**50. *Magos*.** The Magi were Persian philosophers, skilled interpreters of nature, as Prudentius paraphrases them. Juvencus writes in I:

> There is a people born in the East, close to the kingdom  
> Of Phoebus, skilled in observing the risings and settings  
> Of the stars. Its leading men bore the name of Magi.

The Magi held a rank next to that of kings, and at one time seized power through the brothers Patizithes and Smerdis, from whom an astute and courageous nobility later took it away again. Hence the Persians kept the day of the *μαγοφονία* (“slaughter of the Magi”) as a solemn festival, on which no Magus dared go out in public.

Many believe that the Magi who honored Christ with gifts belonged to the school left behind by Daniel. Among the Persians the Magi corresponded to the gymnosophists among the Indians, the Chaldaeans among the Assyrians, and the Etruscan haruspices among the Romans, as Strabo says in book XVI; he adds: “Moses and his successors were of the same kind.” There was also a distinct nation of Magi in Media, according to Herodotus, and in Bactria, according to Pliny. Fabricius, commentary, p. 83.

The University manuscript and Vossianus 2, in a second hand, have *Magis*. But the accusative can be supplied after *praeire*, *praecedere*, and *praecurrere* (“to go before,” “precede,” “run ahead”). See Bangius, *Philological Observations*, p. 1015.

**50. *Honori*.** Pulmannus and the Antwerp edition have *honore* (“with honor”). He seems to have expressed Claudian’s famous line:

> For whom the heavens serve.

**51. *Euntis*.** Earlier, in *Miscellanies* chapter 16, p. 174, I conjectured *eunti* (“for the one going”), as below, II, 153:

> That we may serve him.

Sedulius I, 224: “His work serves the Creator.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II, 5, 6: “Although they see these things obeying the divine laws, they serve with perpetual necessity the advantages and uses of human beings.” See Bunemannus there.

But *euntis* is now not displeasing, both because of the preceding *venientis* (“of the one coming”) and because *obsequio euntis* (“in the service of the one going”) may be explained as *in euntem*, “the service rendered to the one going.” Compare *reverentia fratris* (“respect for a brother”) in Eutropius VIII, 10, and *injuria raptarum* (“wrong done to the abducted women”) in the same author I, 2. Verheykius rightly restored this against Havercampus, and before him the learned men of Leiden had already done so in the *Acts* of 1729, p. 492.

In the same way, *odium consulis* (“hatred of the consul”) occurs in Livy II, 43; see Raphelius on Mark II, verse 22, concerning *fides patriae* (“faith toward the fatherland”). Lucian has *ἔρως τῆς γυναικὸς* (“love of the woman”) in *Dialogues of the Dead*, p. 309, and *εὐεργεσία τῶν φίλων* (“benefaction toward friends”) in *Timon*, p. 65.

**46**

> And now, rejoicing, let us contemplate the wondrous sounds  
> And prove the measure of his empire through the laws subjected to him.  
> Born from a virgin mother, rising after trampling death,  
> Seeking heaven’s scepters, he announces these deeds to his servants.  
> Nor do the elements cease to serve their Thunderer;  
> The star, having gone before as companion to the Magi,  
> Serves the honor of the one who comes: the cloud obeys the one who goes.  
> Therefore, after she had spoken with angelic utterances,  
> She left the venerable heights of the olive-bearing mountain.

**54. *Qui*.** The manuscript originally had *manus praecesserat* (“the hand had gone before”), but writers commonly use the construction in this way. Below, line 305:

> Lest they violate those whom the crowd cherishes, for whom I close my eyes.

Add Wopkensius in *Miscellaneous Observations* VII, p. 402. Isidore uses the same construction in book X, p. 1070. From the Groningen manuscript I would prefer: “There are names in heaven that are without marriages.” Writers sometimes attend more to the sense than to the words.

Festus uses the Greek manner of writing in *Solitaurilia*, book L, 236, §1, of the *Digest*, *On the Meaning of Words*: “Following the example of the Greek language, among whom …” Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII, 7: “It was taken from the Hebrew language; among them …”

Calventius wrongly attempted to emend the passage of Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 24: “Thus Roman superstition was born, whose rites …” He preferred *Romanorum* (“of the Romans”), as with *Germanorum* (“of the Germans”) in Suetonius, *Caligula* 51, rightly rejected by Burmann.

I am surprised that jurists so often debate Ulpian’s words in the *Digest*, *On Covenants* I, 1: “For what is so consistent with human good faith as to preserve what they have agreed among themselves?” Justinian supports Ulpian in VI, 1, 1: “According to the character of human beings, who, the more they possess, desire the more extensive things.” Add Marckartus, *Interpretation of Received Readings* II, 6, §1. Hence the words in book IV, §10, *On the Determination of Boundaries*, are also sound. See what I said on Arnaldius, *Lives of the Scaevolae*, p. 66.

**55. *Mille*.** Eucherius, book I of the *Instructions*: “What does that passage indicate which we read, ‘having a Sabbath-day’s journey’? That is, one thousand paces. On the Sabbath, the Jews were permitted to go as far as the Mount of Olives; or at least, wherever they happened to be, they assumed permission to walk that distance.”

Arator, book I: “The walls …” These two thousand units are derived by the Jews from the promises of Barachiah, Simeon, and Hillel, as Agobardus writes from their teachings to Louis the Pious, p. 75. Hillel and Simeon were leaders of the Pharisaic sect and flourished a century and a half before the Lord’s birth, as Joseph Scaliger observes; see him in *Elenchus of the Threefold Heresy*, chapter 12.

I think Eucherius should read *tanto spatio redambulandi* (“permission to walk back the same distance”). For he says that they went and returned one thousand paces. In this way what the Jews and others write about two thousand being only one Sabbath-day’s journey can be reconciled. Our learned friend J. Drusius, deeply versed in rabbinic books, did not notice this in book V of his *Miscellanies*. Barthius, *Adversaria* III, 13.

Am-Ende, in *The Christeid*, p. 7, reckons six stadia for a Sabbath-day’s journey and derives the seven reported by the Syriac translator from the fact that some measured from the mountain itself and others from its outer foothills. The distinguished Alberti, *Philological Observations*, p. 203, suspects that Luke’s words *σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδόν* (“having a Sabbath-day’s journey”) should be understood of the mountain’s size.

**57. *Porta*.** I suspected that this word required an emendating hand in *Miscellanies*, p. 174. I now restrain myself, having learned that for these writers it is a name of Mary, because Christ was born from her.

Venantius Fortunatus, *On the Virgin’s Birth*, p. 687:

> This is the closed gate into which no man enters, nor goes out,  
> Except the Lord alone, for whom even closed things are open.

A hymn of Gregory, p. 802 of Fabricius’s edition, concerning Mary:

> You are the gate of the high King  
> And the shining gate of light.

Cyprian, in his *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, quoted by Weitzius on Prudentius, p. 645: “The prophet Ezekiel had previously represented the marvelous manner of her childbirth, figuratively calling Mary the Lord’s gate, through which the Lord entered the world.” Arator plays upon the same word below, line 533:

> It is wondrous if, in the body, he approaches such a gate,  
> Whom a virgin gives birth to.

The Greeks call Mary *πύλη* (“gate”). See Nansius, *Additions to Nonnus’s Paraphrase*, p. 16; Bynaeus, *On the Birth of Jesus* I, 3, p. 43, and II, 3, p. 505.

Arator expressed this from Luke’s words I, 14, *σὺν γυναιξὶ καὶ Μαρίᾳ* (“with the women and Mary”), where a more distinguished species is added to the genus. On this elegance see Putmannus, *Interpretations*, chapter 7, no. 3.

**57. *Maria*.** The middle syllable is long, in accordance with the customary practice of these poets, though not approved. See the note on Sedulius II, 30.

After *Dei* (“of God”), the Aldine edition has a full stop. I preferred the lighter mark of punctuation, neglected by the other editors. For *Dei* should be referred to *portam* (“gate”).

**57. *Intacta*.** Sedulius II, 36:

> The angel sang of the hastened birth of untouched Mary.

The ancient writers likewise use the word. Horace, *Odes* I, 7, 5, and Ovid, *Heroides* XVII, 31, speak of untouched Pallas. See Goes on Petronius 43; Titius on Calpurnius, *Eclogue* II, at the beginning.

Conversely, *tangere* (“to touch”) occurs in Ovid, *Heroides* XX, 147, and *Amores* III, 7, 39. The Greek *ἅπτεσθαι* is used in this way by Epictetus, *Enchiridion* 47; *προσάπτεσθαι* by Lucian, *Timon*, p. 92; *ἀφάσσειν* by Musaeus, *Hero and Leander*, 82.

**58. *A nato*.** “Adorned by her offspring.” There is certainly nothing astonishing in this, nor does the commentator dwell upon the miracle. But write: “springing from her offspring.” In our manuscript it is *a nato formata suo* (“formed from her offspring”), and since I found this reading in three other manuscripts, I consider it preferable to the conjecture. Barthius, *Adversaria* X, 5.

*A natoque ornata* (“adorned by her offspring”) is found in the Antwerp edition and the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, and was printed by Fabricius. Barthius rightly defends *a nato formata* from the manuscripts; our manuscripts have the same, except that the Cambridge manuscript omits the preposition.

On the matter itself see Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXVI, 16. Sedulius II, 39:

> The unwedded virgin is astonished at her swollen womb  
> And rejoices that she is about to give birth to her own parent.

Bishop Damasus writes of Christ, p. 774 of Fabricius’s edition:

> The virgin womb swelled, and the unmarried mother,  
> Astonished, felt her inward organs filled by a hidden birth,  
> About to give birth to her own creator.

Fabricius attributes this most elegant poem to Damasus; others to Claudian. Following Heinsius, I would rather ascribe it to Lactantius. See the notes on Claudian’s epigram 45.

**59. *Sexus*.** That is, the female sex. Silius III:

> If we are seen only according to sex, and you abandon sex …

Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 15, concerning alum: “It is highly beneficial for the ears, whether poured in or applied, and for ulcers of the mouth if saliva is held with it. It is also suitably included in medicines for the eyes and for the sexual organs.” Barthius, *Adversaria* X, 5.

See Heinsius on Silius III, 14; Stewechius on Arnobius II, p. 70; Elmenhorst in Apuleius’s index under the word; the notes on Sallust, fragment II, p. 53, Havercampus’s edition; Scaliger on Festus, p. 173; the distinguished scholar on Livy XXVI, 47, 1. Hence it is also clear that the word is sometimes added for purposes of distinction.

**60. *Tulit*.** “Took away.” See Barthius on Claudian, *Laudation of Stilicho* III, 164; Cortius on Pliny VIII, letter 6, 12; Burmann on Valerius Flaccus II, 577; and the notes on Sedulius I, 205.

Thus *ἐβάστασεν* (“he carried away”) should be understood in the Gospel of John, chapter XII, 6.
