Beza translates it as “carried around,” and the common translator and Tremellius as “carried”; both are wrong. It means “took away,” so that the reason why Judas was a thief becomes evident. Menagius rightly explains it this way in his notes on Diogenes Laertius IV, section 59; Elsnerus followed him.

Sedulius agrees on the matter itself in II, 30:

> Mary, coming from the sacred stock of Eve,  
> The pious new virgin atoned for the crime of the ancient virgin.

There “new virgin” corresponds to “second virgin” here.

> The band chosen beforehand for the harvest seeks the familiar walls by a swift path,  
> Where it is permitted to travel a thousand paces on the Sabbath,  
> where at that station abode the Gate, Mary,  
> the untouched mother of her creating God,  
> formed by her own offspring. The second Virgin dispels  
> the evils of Eve’s sin; there is no violation of her sex.  
> She restored what the first had taken away. She does not utter complaints in words—
61. *Fatiget*] The Cambridge manuscript has *fatigat*.

[Col. 0097B] 63. *Mercede*] That is, if the fruit should result from it, as Burney explains on Phaedrus IV, 1, 8. It is an imitation of Lucan I, 37:

> Now, O heavenly powers, we complain of nothing more: the crimes themselves, and the wickedness,  
> Are pleasing at this price.

Oudendorp had already noticed this in his *Omissions on Lucan*, as had Burmann.

[Col. 0097B] 66. *Tumuit*] An elegant expression for a pregnant woman. See Sedulius I, 94, with the notes, and the notes on book II, 39. In Ambrose’s hymn, p. 792, ed. Fabricius, *onus*, *pondus*, and *sarcina* frequently occur in this sense. See Elmenhorst on Arnobius III, p. 113, and the notes on Sedulius I, 96. From this Segaar derived *βαστάζειν* (*bastazein*, “to carry”) in his notes on Luke, p. 315.

[Col. 0097B] 67. *Mediator*] Greek *Μεσίτης* (*Mesitēs*, “mediator”). Prudentius, *Apotheosis*:

> The Son is Mediator both of us and of the Almighty.

Fabricius, commentary on *Christian Poets*, p. 86. Below, II, 301:

> And the Mediator completes man in all things.

Nevertheless, this word is used only by Christian writers. See Cellarius, *Curæ posteriores*, p. 274, and *Antibarbarus*, p. 71. Among more elegant writers the expression is “the agent of peace.” See Heinsius on Ovid, *Fasti* I, 287; Drakenborch on Silius VI, 347; and Perrenonius, *Annotations* I, 15, on the word *sequester*. Some also call him *medium* (“the middleman”). See Cannegieter on Avianus, fable 22, line 5, whom Duker praises in his notes on Florus IV, 2, 55. Coelius Secundus, in his notes on Cicero, *Philippics* XII, 1, thinks that *pacificator* (“peacemaker”) should be used. Sterkius explains the word *μεσίτης* from the ancient making of wills among the Romans, so that the *familiae emptor* (“purchaser of the estate”) was the *μεσίτης τῆς διαθήκης* (“mediator of the testament”). See *Historical-Theological Library*, class VII, fascicle 4, p. 585. Yet this opinion is not without points that may be urged against it.

[Col. 0097C] 71. *Squamea*] Others read *squamigerum pecus* (“scaly livestock”). See Giphanius, *Collectanea on Lucretius*, under *PECUDES*, and Taubmann on Virgil, *Georgics* IV, 168. *Turba*, *gens*, and *populus* are used of the multitude or abundance of animals, as are the Greek *δῆμος* (“people”) and *ἔθνος* (“nation”). See Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI, 22; on Phaedrus, longer commentary I, 11, at the end; and on Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 282. Vossius, *Institutes of Oratory* IV, 6, 8; Lennepius, *Annotations on Coluthus* II, 6; notes on Sedulius IV, 118. From the passage itself Peter is called *ἐργατίνης πόντοιο* (“worker of the sea”) by Nonnus in his *Paraphrase of John* I, 43. Heinsius discusses this passage more fully in *Aristarchus*, chapter 17; for fishermen are said to “work the sea,” *θάλασσαν ἐργάζεσθαι*. See Wesseling, *Observations* I, 15.

[Col. 0097D] 74. *Humanum*] Sedulius II, 220:

> Therefore at once he fitted men, from fishermen,  
> To fish for human souls.

Below, line 992:

> From whose whirlpool Peter,  
> Drawing his dripping nets, filled the boats  
> With a greater catch, his word serving as the bait.

Book II, 565:

> Peter, catching fish, catches men.

Althelmus, *On the Praise of the Virgin*, p. 723, volume I, in Thomas Canisius:

> Whom Peter, renowned fisherman of Christ throughout the world—

Thus also *σαγηνεύειν* (“to net”) and *ζωγρεῖν* (“to catch alive”) are used of human beings. See Segaar on Luke, p. 173. Otherwise, the Moretus manuscript has *laxat* in the preceding line.

[Col. 0098B] 75. *Clavem*] The Universal manuscript has *clavum*. The copyist evidently restored that reading out of sympathy with papal domination and ecclesiastical government, since Cicero said *clavum tenere* (“to hold the rudder”) in *Letters to Friends* IX, 15, and *For Sextus* 20. Add Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXV, 19. Here Arator himself defends the ordinary reading, below, line 825:

> Soon he flies above the stars, because he enters with his own keys.

Peter is likewise called *claviger* (“key-bearer”) at line 899, and in the epitaph of Trophimus, in Menckenius, *Writers of German Affairs*, volume I, p. 119; and *claviger polorum* (“key-bearer of the heavens”) in Ermoldus Nigellus, *On the Deeds of Louis the Pious*, book IV, p. 954, in the same volume. The Antwerp edition has *clavim*, which Fabricius follows, as do the editors of the Lyon Library of the Fathers; they also omit the word that follows.

[Col. 0098C] 76. *Vertere*] I conjecture that *verrere* should be read. See Nonius Marcellus, *On Proper Usage*, chapter 4, no. 491. Thus *verrere examina* (“to sweep together swarms”) occurs in Ausonius, *Mosella* 244, and *everrere piscem* (“to sweep out a fish”) in Apuleius; these examples I owe to Bentley on Horace, *Satires* II, 3, 235. Add Drakenborch on Silius III, 321. Hence *everriculum*, a kind of net, about which I spoke in *Miscellanies*, chapter 15; and Lotichius on Petronius, p. 257. Others say *verrere aequor retibus* (“to sweep the sea with nets”), as Silius XIV, 262; yet in the old Lyon edition I also find *vertere*, which supports our conjecture, especially since the two forms are very often confused. See Oudendorp on Lucan III, 542, and VI, 585; Burmann on the same author VII, 616; on Sammonicus, line 258; and on Claudian, *Rape of Proserpina* II, 295. Burmann the Younger on *Anthology* III, epigram 106, line 24. Hence van Hoven, *Probability*, fascicle IV, p. 48, and *Introduction to Historical Readings*, p. 16. Sulpicius Severus elegantly corrects *post gesta converrere* (“after the deeds, to sweep together”) in *Sacred History* I, 1; I am surprised that Wopkens, in his unpublished *Adversaria* in my possession, mocked it as inept. Oudendorp very properly restored *verratur* for *versatur* in Avienus, *Description of the World*, line 818, in *Miscellaneous Observations*, volume V, p. 70. Compare what Burmann learnedly brought forward on *Anthology* III, p. 563.

[Col. 0098D] 77. *Ratem*] The Moretus manuscript has *ratim*. Compare Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 12.

[Col. 0098D] 78. *Levat*] Below, line 162:

> So that the rejoicing fisherman may lift these shoals from the spring.

[Col. 0098D] 79. *Latices*] The Moretus manuscript has *laticem*; and shortly afterward *lucra querens* (“seeking profits”), certainly instead of *quaerens*, is metrically impossible and derives from a gloss. *Sequi lucra* means “to seek profits,” “to pursue eagerly.” *Sequi dona* occurs below, II, 942; *sequi documenta justitiae* (“to pursue proofs of justice”), in the same book, line 1034. See the notes on Pliny VIII, letter 18, 8. Nor does the word indicate anything else than *tendere*, “to stretch toward,” or “to direct one’s course eagerly toward something.” See Burmann on Valerius Flaccus I, 3, and the notes on Sedulius V, 230.]

52. Let grief awaken, or by lament fatigue the sorrowing hearts,

> In place of the ancient law; the crimes themselves and the wickedness  
> Please at this rather price, and, once the world has been redeemed,  
> A better lot comes forth from disaster; the person,  
> Not nature, brought about the ruin; then the pregnant woman was a danger,  
> Now she swelled, about to bear God, giving birth to a mortal  
> And bearing what is divine. Through her the Mediator  
> Came forth into the world and carried true flesh to heaven.  
> Peter was the first, summoned from a little boat to the apostolic  
> Band; by him the scaly multitude was accustomed  
> To be caught. Suddenly seen from the shore,  
> While he was dragging, he himself deserved to be dragged; Christ’s fishing  
> Deigned to seize the disciple who would loosen his nets  
> To capture the human race. The hand that had held the hook  
> Was transferred to the key; and he who burned to drag  
> The dripping prey of the deep sea toward the shores,  
> And to fill the boat with spoils, now, on better waters,  
> Lifts up other things from another side, nor abandons his craft,  
> Pursuing his profits through the waters, to whom the Lamb entrusted  
> The sheep whom he saved through his suffering, and throughout the whole world  
> Enlarges the flock under this shepherd, by whose service the supreme—

[Col. 0099A] [Note: [Col. 0099A]]

83. *Quia*] I restored this reading from the Moretus, Cambridge, and Universal manuscripts, and from the Aldine, Basel, and first Tornaesian editions; in the others it is *quod*. The latter is more usual among these writers. Isidore, *Etymologies* I, 38: “Unless because Ennius among us used it earlier”; there too the Groningen manuscript has corrupted it to *quod*. Consentius, *Art*, p. 2021: “We must observe that we may use *quia*—.” Bondamius likewise noted this passage in *Various Readings* II, p. 218. Add Vopkens on Sedulius II, 165. So too the Greeks say, in the Epistle to the Romans II, 2, *οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι* (“but we know that”). See Gronovius on Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander* II, p. 89; yet there Kusterus shows in his *Critical Discussion against Gronovius*, p. 55, that he misunderstood this construction in Xenophon.

[Col. 0099B] 84. *Taedia*] The distinguished Wassenbergius conjectured *solvit, qui taedia* (“he paid, who [felt] disgust”), but this is wrong. In some editions the passage is punctuated incorrectly; I have restored the better arrangement.

[Col. 0099B] 85. *Vocem*] Fabricius has *nocens* (“guilty”), contrary to the meter; nevertheless the editors of the Lyon Library of the Fathers follow him. It is clear from this that Arator understood the famous expression *ἀπάγχεσθαι* (“to be strangled”) as referring to hanging, not to death from mental anguish. Cerda collected similar expressions for hanging in his notes on Virgil XII, 603.

[Col. 0099B] 86. *Cessante*] Without precedent, as in *gemitu cessante* (“with the lament ceasing”) below, line 357, and *reditu cessante* (“with the return ceasing”), line 661. He seems to have imitated Lucan IX, 169:

> Lacking an example and unknown to every age.

The scholiast in Vossianus 2 explains it thus: no betrayer of his master had previously killed himself by hanging. But that is stated too generally. Arator’s words should rather be referred to the fact that before Judas there had been no example of anyone betraying his Lord and God, as the distinguished Wassenbergius warned that the passage should be understood.

[Col. 0099C] 88. *Judicio*] In *Miscellanies*, chapter 16, p. 177, I preferred *indicio*, as below at line 102; and so do the Aldine and Basel editions. The interchange is frequent; see the learned notes on Pliny, *Panegyric* 5, 2; Burmann on *Anthology* I, p. 48; Drakenborch on Livy VII, 39; and the notes on Sedulius II, 232. Mamertinus, *Thanksgiving to Julian*, chapter 21, 1: “The more ready he was for slavery, the more unworthy of honor he would be called.” The Wolfenbüttel manuscript there has *indicabitur* (“will be declared”), but the excerpts of Vossius preserve *judicabitur* (“will be judged”). In Arator, however, let us retain the received reading; Judas was, as it were, his own judge.

[Col. 0099C] 88. *Permisit*] Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* II, chapter 11, §5: “Giving thanks that he had not been abandoned to his error.”

[Col. 0099D] 89. *In medio*] Other editions have *aeris*, so that he might place it in the common air.

[Col. 0099D] 90. *Coelo*] The Antwerp edition has *coeli terraeque* (“of heaven and earth”), and so Fabricius in his edition and in his commentary on *Christian Poets*, p. 102; the Lyon Library follows him. The two Tornaesian editions have *coelum terramque* (“heaven and earth”), which Cellarius has now rejected in his notes on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* III, 41, though he follows Fabricius more closely. I, following the Moretus, Cambridge, Universal, and Vossianus 2 manuscripts, restored *coelo*. For here an active sense does not seem to be required; rather, Judas is said to have perished hated by God and by human beings, just as someone is called *perosus Deo* (“hated by God”) in Commodian, *Instructions* XXX, 13. On this passive usage see Falster, *Supplement to the Latin Language*, p. 123; Heinsius on Claudian, *War against the Getae*, 513; and Cannegieter on Avianus, fable II, 13. Jacob Gronovius used these words of Arator in *Dissertation on Judas*, p. 184, and *Defense*, p. 53; but I doubt whether he inspected the passage itself, for he joins certain verses read below at line 443 to these as though they formed one continuous series. The sense is legitimate, but the procedure is not exact.

[Col. 0100A] 92. *Viscera*] Casaubon against Baronius, p. 527; Perizonius, *On the Death of Judas*.

[Col. 0100A] 93. *Ab ore*] The Aldine, Antwerp, and Fabrician editions have *ab orbe* (“from the world”), an interchange that is not uncommon. See Burmann on Ovid, *Ibis* 74. Hence, in *Miscellanies*, chapter 16, p. 177, I formerly conjectured *ab ore canis* (“from the dog's mouth”). Dogs are called those who betray someone and crush him with false accusations. See Burmann on Petronius 74; Hommel, *Illustrated Numismatic Jurisprudence*, p. 39; and it will be clear at line 102 that the names of animals were often applied to human beings. The word *cinis* (“ash”) is admittedly not very satisfactory. The scholiast in Vossianus 2 explains it as “through a dusty life,” and Wassenbergius had noted that it seemed to him to be understood in the same way as “the body’s ashes” below, line 537. It may perhaps be a faulty imitation of Sedulius, who writes of Judas, V, 55:

> Or, badly poured upon the ground, he would at once lose  
> The gifts of light, like dust which the mighty wind  
> Casts from the face of the earth.

The wording differs little from Ovid, *Tristia* I, 5, 11:

> And the spirit, first thinned out into empty breezes,  
> Will go.

Others use *exspuere animam* (“to spit out the soul”) and similar expressions; see the notes on Valerius Flaccus III, 107.

[Col. 0100C] 93. *Judae*] It could also be punctuated as follows: “This vengeance is not empty, which denies Judas his final [honor].”

[Col. 0100C] 94. *Vindictaque*] Vossianus 2 has *vindicta mercis iniqua* (“the vengeance of an unjust reward”). By *suprema* (“final things”) he means burial, which is also called the final honor. See Gutherius, *On the Law of the Manes* II, 17; Elmenhorst, index to Apuleius, under *FERALIA OFFICIA*; and the notes on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III, 137. Cicero, *For Milo* 32, speaks of “the celebration of the final day.” On the denial of burial to Judas, compare Gronovius, *Dissertation on Judas*, p. 185. I would not have some scholars referred here to the *τόπον ἴδιον* (“his own place”) into which Luke records that he went, interpreting the expression as referring to a grave. Thus Vindingius explains *ἴδιος* by *αὑτοῦ* (“his own”) in his notes on Dictys Cretensis, p. 42, as in Virgil’s account of Misenus, *Aeneid* VI, 152:

> Restore him to his own dwelling and lay him in the grave.

Livy VI, 36, 11: “The family estate would be open to him for a necessary roof or a place of burial.” I rather understand Luke’s words as referring to a suitable and worthy place; in this sense *δίκαιον* (“fitting,” “just”) occurs in the Alexandrian manuscript. See Price, and Heinsius on Silius III, 95, concerning the meaning of that word. Knatchbull’s opinion about Luke’s passage seems hardly credible.

[Col. 0100D] 95. *Parasset*] Explain it as “would have provided the occasion,” so that it might be prepared. For he himself did not prepare it; the chief priests did. In the same way, in Acts I, 18, *ἐκτήσατο* (“he acquired”) rightly means “he gave the occasion for the field to be acquired,” as Le Moine translates it in his notes on Polycarp’s epistle, p. 515. Thus philosophers are called *ῥέοντες* (“flowing”), because they are the cause of everything being believed to flow. See Menagius on Diogenes Laertius IX, section 8, and Kusterus, *Critical Discussion against Gronovius*, p. 52. The learned writer in *Miscellaneous Observations*, volume II, p. 233, explained *πίπτειν* (“to fall”) as “to make fall,” and *νοσεῖν* (“to be ill”) as “to make ill.” The gods are said to “migrate kingdoms” (*migrare regna*) for “to cause kingdoms to migrate.” Drakenborch on Silius VII, 431; *damnare* (“to condemn”) for “to cause someone to be condemned,” Drakenborch on Livy VII, 16, 9. My father, on Victor, *Illustrations* 63, 1, and similar examples at the end of chapter 6; *resonare* (“to resound”) for “to cause to resound,” Burmann on Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 12. Compare the same author, *Jove Fulgerator*, p. 251. Florus IV, 3, at the end: *mota sidera tonent* (“the moved stars thunder”), that is, “they cause thunder to arise.”]

> He rises and, introducing the divine matters, says reverently before them:  
> “You know that the deranged betrayer paid the price of his crime  
> 55 To himself; he himself shuddered at the disgust of his guilt,  
> Strangling the guilty voice in his throat in an unprecedented act,  
> He deserved to be killed in the part in which the fault lay;  
> And, reviewing his crime, he gave his limbs over  
> To the fury of such a judgment, so that due punishment might assign a place in the common air  
> 56 To the enemy of all.  
> Hated by heaven and earth, he perished between the two;  
> His ruptured entrails fell, not to be consigned to any tomb,  
> And, escaping into thin air, his ash fled from his mouth.  
> This vengeance is not idle,  
> 57 Which denies Judas final rites; the vengeance for his unjust reward  
> Comes in this way, destined to please. For when he had just provided  
> The fields—

[Col. 0101A] [Note: [Col. 0101A]]

96. *Pretio*] Luke says *ἐκ τοῦ μισθοῦ τῆς ἀδικίας* (“from the reward of unrighteousness”), “the price from the betrayal,” with *ἀντί* or *ἐκ* suppressed. See Alberti, *Critical Exercises*, p. 49.

[Col. 0101A] 97. *Favillas*] It was intended for the burial of strangers; but the passage refers to the custom of burning corpses, customary among the Romans, about which I spoke in *Miscellanies*, p. 136. Just as here he transfers words indicating cremation to burial, so others transfer words of burial to cremation. See Wopkens, *New Miscellaneous Observations*, volume II, p. 22. Hemsterhusius explains the Greek *πυρὶ θάπτεσθαι* (“to be buried by fire”) in his notes on Xenophon of Ephesus, in *Miscellaneous Observations*, volume V, p. 21.

[Col. 0101B] 98. *Fecundet*] Horace, *Odes* II, 1, 29:

> What field is not richer in Latin blood?

Ovid, *Heroides* I, 54:

> The rich earth luxuriates in Phrygian blood.

Emmenessius rightly compared Virgil, *Georgics* I, 91:

> Twice by our blood  
> Emathia and the broad fields of Haemus grow rich.

[Col. 0101B] 100. *Ferunt*] Heinsius had written in the margin of the Moretus manuscript *ferunt* (“they bear”) or *serunt* (“they sow”). The latter occurs in the Cambridge and Universal manuscripts, and the two forms are frequently confused. See Drakenborch on Silius V, 235.

[Col. 0101C] 101. *Signifer*] I do not object whether this is taken literally, of Judas giving the signal, which is attributed to him in Matthew XXVI, 48. See the notes on Sedulius V, 62. Or it may mean “instigator” and “torchbearer of all.” Eumenius, *Panegyric of Constantine* 15, 5: “the standard-bearer of the wicked faction.” Cicero, *For Plancius* 30: “the leaders and, as it were, standard-bearers of our cause”; *Letters to Atticus* II, 1: “you as standard-bearer and leader.” Florus III, 23, 6: “the leaders and standard-bearers of Sulla’s domination.”

[Col. 0101C] 101. *Fingens*] Most printed editions have *figens* (“fixing”), as in the author of *Consolation to Livy* 95:

> But the pitiable mother did not fix the final kisses.

Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III, 24:

> And she fixed kisses  
> Upon the foreign earth.

Lucan II, 114:

> To have fixed trembling kisses upon the polluted right hand.

Meursius shows in *Philological Authorities*, chapter 18, that poets use this expression of equals, when they are said to “sip” kisses. But I have taken *fingens* from Vossianus 2, Pulmann’s notes, and the Antwerp and first Tornaesian editions; the sense itself recommends it. Judas was feigning peace and friendship by this kiss. Sedulius V, 64:

> You press mouth to mouth, and insert poison with honey,  
> And betray the Lord beneath a flattering appearance.  
> Why do you pretend to be his companion and greet him with friendly deceit?

Nevertheless, the two readings are frequently confused. See Drakenborch on Livy VII, 39, 3. Thus Burmann the Younger restored *figere* for *fingere* in Virgil in his notes on *Anthology* II, p. 375. In Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* I, prose 4, I found in the manuscript and old edition *aliquod crimen affigitur* (“some crime is fastened upon him”), not *affingitur* (“is fashioned”), which Sitzmann restored. Ammianus Marcellinus confirms this, XIV, 1: “They fastened accusations of forbidden arts upon innocent men,” where Gronovius—

[Col. 0101D] 102. *Lupus*] Below, line 710, of Paul:

[Col. 0102A]

> Toward whom the wolf hastens to rage.

And line 717:

> He tames that ravening wolf.

Velleius II, 27, 2: “There will never be a lack of wolves who prey upon Italian liberty.” Similarly, of Judas, Sedulius V, 68:

[Col. 0102B]

> Or the savage wolf offers kisses to the pious lamb.

Hence this passage seems to have been modeled on that one. In general, wicked people are commonly designated by the names of beasts. See Alberti on the Second Epistle to Timothy IV, 17. Hence some explain *ἐθηριομάχησα* (“I fought with beasts”), which Paul uses in First Corinthians XV, 32, as a struggle with enemies of the truth. Compare Maius, *Sacred Observations*, part I, p. 79, and Baschius, *On the Interpretation of the New Testament from the Fathers*, §9, in the notes; these people are indeed sometimes called beasts. Arius is called *θηρίον* (“beast”) by Athanasius, works, volume I, p. 113. Add Gerdesius, *Sacred Studies*, p. 318.

I have already noted at line 93 the use of *canis* (“dog”) for a false accuser; the same word is interpreted of false teachers in Paul’s passage at Philippians III, 2. See Gataker, *Posthumous Adversaria*, chapter 38, and Price on Matthew’s Gospel, p. 51—unless one prefers to understand the Cynic philosophers there, since Lucian calls Menippus *κύων* (“dog”) in *Dialogues of the Dead*, p. 265, and often elsewhere. Thus *gallinae* (“hens”) and *lupae* (“she-wolves”) are used of prostitutes, whence *lupanaria* (“brothels”); see Pareus, *Selected Plautine Readings*, p. 19. *Feles* (“cats”) is used of pimps, ibid., p. 33. *Juvenca* (“heifer”) is used of a lustful girl, Horace, *Odes* II, 5, 6, and Ovid, *Heroides* V, 117. *Sus* (“pig”) is used of a man devoted to gluttony; Martinus, *Various Readings* II, 3. *Serpentes* and *viperae* (“snakes” and “vipers”) are used of those who injure their benefactors; Segaar, *Observations on Luke*, p. 138. For *asinus*, *hircus*, *capra* (“ass,” “he-goat,” “she-goat”), and similar expressions, see Justus, *Specimen of Observations*, chapter 15. More generally, Boethius offers an excellent passage in *Consolation of Philosophy* IV, prose 2; Vossius, *Institutes of Oratory* IV, 6, 2, and Barthius, *Adversaria* VIII, 14, should also be consulted.

[Col. 0102C] 103. *Clamant*] On Psalms LXIX, 26, and CIX, 8, Usserius compared the latter passage with Acts in *On the Origin of Bishops*, p. 3. Where the Lyon Library of the Fathers reads *Clamant*, “they testify,” I explain *proclamare* as “to testify openly,” as in Aurelius Victor, *Origin of the Roman People* 23, 7. But this conflicts with our received reading, *proclamans historia Liviana* (“Livian history proclaiming”), where the meaning of the word *memoria* (“memory”) misled interpreters, who either emended the passage or explained it. Klotzius, *Critical Miscellanies*, p. 34, conjectures *nostram memoriam proclamans*: “proclaiming our memory,” that is, narrating or disseminating the deeds. I retain the received reading, and understand *memoriam* as the narrative and report of that event itself. *Proclamans nostrae memoriae* means “adding open testimony to our narrative,” which differs from that of Egnatius, whom Victor had mentioned earlier.

[Col. 0102D] 104. *Summa precantes*] The manuscripts offer no variant here, yet I do not see what *summa precari* (“to pray for the highest things”) is intended to mean. *Summa petere* (“to seek the highest things”), which Livy uses XXXV, 42, 14, is different; likewise *summa sequi* and *summa capere*, discussed by Wopkens, *Miscellaneous Observations*, volume VIII, p. 63. The scholiast in Vossianus 2 took the expression to mean “praying to the supreme God,” but that scarcely satisfies. I think Arator wrote *summa petentes* (“seeking the upper room”). He thus expressed Luke’s words in Acts I, 13: *ἀνέβησαν εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον* (“they went up into the upper room”). Arator himself below, line 824, supports the conjecture:

> Then, seeking higher things, his prayer poured forth to the Thunderer.

And line 878:

> Peter advances to enter the lofty upper rooms.

For those upper rooms were in the higher part of the house. See Barthius, *Adversaria* III, 13, and XXXII, 22. Hence the Greek word *ὑπερῷον* (“upper room”), as Rittershusius already noted on Oppian, *Halieutica* II, 135—not, as Mollius foolishly says on Longus, p. 9, from *ὦον*, but from *ὑπέρ*, in the same form as *πατρῷος* from *πατήρ*. For this the Ionic poets use *πατρῷϊος*, a form which the learned interpreter of the Greek Venuses, and one deserving a longer life, Pierson, aptly compared in his notes on Moeris, p. 295; and Koenius on Gregory, p. 75. Bosius elegantly shows in his notes on Acts I, 13, that *οἴκημα* (“dwelling”) is suppressed in this expression. In Latin it is sometimes *pergula* (“upper gallery”). See Salmasius on Spartianus, p. 155 of the larger edition. Add Pfeiffer, dissertation on the care of Virgil, p. 7. Our conjecture is further supported by the custom according to which people would go to this part of the house in order to pray. Prideaux gives examples in *History of the Jews*, book VI, p. 589, Belgian edition.]

> For when the turf, bought at the price of death and named for blood,  
> 58 Lays graves among foreign ashes  
> And makes the ground fertile from its tombs, the impious man lacks  
> The fertility of his own field and is alone excluded from the lands  
> 100 Which bear memorials of him whose savage trumpet  
> First sounded the bloody crime: he, the signal-giver, feigning kisses  
> 59 Of peace, as a wolf brought war upon the lamb at the signal.  
> Now, as the prophetic words proclaim, prayers must seek one  
> 60 Whom it is permitted to appoint as successor. Then, praying to the Highest,  
> They appointed two, Joseph surnamed Justus—

[Col. 0103A] [Note: [Col. 0103B]]

106. *Dei parvum*] This is a new invention. For the name Matthias is usually explained as “gift of God.” Hesychius: *Ματθαῖος, δεδωρημένος* (“Matthew, having been given”), and *Ματθίας δὲ δόμα Θεοῦ* (“Matthias, a gift of God”). Compare Alberti on *Glossary of the New Testament*, p. 16. The Greek *Θεόδωρος* (“God-given”) and *Dositheus* correspond to it; Smith compared the latter with both the names Matthew and Mattathias in his notes on the Palmyrene Inscription, p. 51. Hence Isidore, *Etymologies* VII, 9, says: “Matthias, who alone among the apostles is found without a surname, is interpreted as ‘Given,’ with Judas understood.” For he was chosen by the apostles in Judas’s place, when the lot was cast for the two men. Arator undoubtedly followed others in this, as the words themselves seem to indicate. Perhaps, being entirely ignorant of Hebrew, he added this explanation. I have already noted in the preface to Sedulius how ignorant writers of this period were of Hebrew, as well as of Greek. A friend suspected that Arator may have sought the meaning of this word in such a subject, following whatever authorities he used, because it designated “to incline” or “to tend,” a meaning that could be drawn from Deuteronomy XXVIII, 43; Psalm XVII, 11; and other passages.

[Col. 0103C] 107. *Hebraeo*] Fabricius and others have *Ebraeo*. I retained the aspirate, following usage and the examples of others, not etymology. See Cellarius, *Orthography*, p. 42, and Dausquius, part II, p. 151.

[Col. 0103C] 109. *Transcenditur*] “He is surpassed by the merits of little Matthias.” Others have expressed the same idea with *transire* (“to pass beyond”). See Oudendorp on Lucan VI, 336, and *transgredi* (“to step beyond”), Argolius on Panvinus, *On the Circensian Games* I, p. 175, volume IX of Graevius’s *Thesaurus*. It seems to me that Arator had in mind the lot cast into the urn. For when a vote was taken, the lot was said to “go out” from it; similarly the Septuagint uses *ἐξῆλθεν* (“went out”) in First Chronicles XXV, 9. Thus Tremellius translates *ἔπεσεν* (“fell”), in this passage of Acts, chapter I at the end, as “rose.”

[Col. 0103D] 111. *Jaculatur*] Vossianus 2 has *juculantur*; this does not displease me. If the other reading is genuine, he used it in a passive sense, an example of which Barthius produced from Victor of Utica in *Adversaria* XXV, 7. This could either arise from the fact that deponent verbs are often used passively, or from the active *jaculo*, which the dictionaries cite from Claudian. It could certainly also have been said in the same way as *comito*, *populo*, and other verbs noted by Vossius, *Art of Grammar* V, 7. See Ciofanus on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, 259, and Heusinger on Mallius Theodorus, *On Meters*, p. 41. Although Vossius judges that the passive *jaculor* is not readily found except in the participle, I found in Isidore, *Etymologies* I, 20, in the excellent Groningen manuscript: *ut quasi sagitta jaculet supervacua* (“so that, like an arrow, it may shoot forth what is superfluous”). I would not doubt that this reading is superior to *jugulet* (“may slaughter”), which Gothofredus has there, or *indulget* (“indulges”), which the old edition gives. The reading of the Vossian manuscript pleases me all the more because Arator wished to express the idea that the twelve apostles, like the twelve signs of the heavens, provided a path by which, like the sun, they might illuminate the whole world. He drew this from Sedulius I, 345:

> Thus too the apostolic honor, always twelvefold,  
> Shines forth in its summit, imitating the months and hours in number,  
> So that the entire year may serve you in all things.

[Col. 0104B] 112. *Praeferat*] “May bear before him and display.” Below, line 903, *praefertur imago* (“the image is displayed”), where Vossianus I has *profertur* (“is brought forth”). Add Schulting on Seneca’s *Controversiae*, p. 86, and Bunemann on Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VI, 18, 1.

[Col. 0104B] 113. *Quatuor*] I printed this form, following Fabricius; most manuscripts have *quattuor*. Those who determined that the first syllable was short doubled the consonant; among them is Barthius, *Adversaria* XXVIII, 16. Vossius correctly explained his arguments from Ennius and Ausonius differently in *Art of Grammar* II, 17. I approve the judgment of the learned author of Fabri’s dictionary, also expressed by Noltenius, *Antibarbarus*, p. 147, especially since he follows Burmann the Younger, the best judge in these matters, in his notes on Lotichius, *Elegies* V, 18, 69. Indeed, the first syllable must certainly be long if one accepts Cerda’s derivation in his notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 207, that *quatuor* arose from *χᾄτερον* for *καὶ ἕτερον* (“and another”).

[Col. 0104C] 113. *Discretus*] The Lyon Library of the Fathers has *discretis*.

[Col. 0104C] 115. *Computat*] Heinsius had written in the margin *vel comparat* (“or compares”); I have not found this elsewhere.

[Col. 0104D] 116. *Duodenarius*] Daumius notes that the penultimate syllable is shortened here in his notes on Cato IV, maxim 4. The same occurs in Sedulius II, 275, and others have already observed it in *denarius* as well. But perhaps Arator reduced the word here to five syllables; I discussed this in the note on the letter to Vigilantius, 24. I believe this more strongly because he produced the form below at line 866.

[Col. 0104C] 117. *Quibus*] “I command you,” with the dative. *Πρυλέεσσι κελεύων* (“commanding the Pylians”). Juvencus III:

> Then he orders his disciples to board the ship.

Prudentius, *Apotheosis*:

> Who could command the savage north winds? Go, come.

Victorinus II:

> He gave the will and ability to his servant, whatever he commanded.

Arator I:

> He commanded me to show this open way  
> To the nations.

Fabricius, commentary on *Christian Poets*, p. 74. Barthius says that *jubeo tibi* (“I command you”) is scarcely Latin, but it is so far from being un-Latin that he thought it modeled on Cicero, book XXXVI of his *Adversaria*, 16. Those who judge that the best writers used this construction very rarely are more correct; it is more frequent among writers approaching the declining period of Latin. See Drakenborch on Silius XII, 607. For whatever other examples are brought into this category may rightly be explained by ellipsis. Nor do the two passages of Livy cited by Drakenborch on the same author XXVII, 24, 3, seem to pose an objection. Fabricius and Vossius, *Art of Grammar* VII, 36, rightly compared this construction with the Greek, although among them the dative and accusative are sometimes attached to the verb *κελεύειν* (“to command”). Compare Pierson on Herodian, *Philetaerus*, p. 433.

[Col. 0104D] 118. *Remeare*] I printed this form from the Cambridge, Universal, Moretus, and Vossianus 2 manuscripts. The printed editions have *recreare* (“to restore”), which arose from a gloss, as the scholiast in Vossianus added *restaurare, recreare* (“to restore, renew”). *Remeare* (“to return”) is used for *redire*, as *salus remeare* (“salvation return”) below, line 298; *dies remeare* (“the day return”), line 861; and *remeare ad officium* (“to return to duty”) in book 9 of the *Code*, *On Advocates of Divine Judgments*. Claudian, *Consulship of Stilicho* I, 331:

> We acknowledge that the laws of Romulus have returned.

There the Moretus manuscript has *remeasse*; the others have *rediisse*, which I attribute to a gloss. Compare the notes. On the construction *dedit remeare* (“he gave [him] to return”), consult the notes on Sedulius I, 65; Wopkens on the same author IV, 282; Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XII, 202; and below, line 365:

> Give, through your gifts,  
> The seeds of the word to be cultivated.

] 61. And Matthias, whose name, they say, means “little one of God,”

> Sounds so in the Hebrew tongue, and confirms it by calling him humble.  
> O how far human judgments differ from those above!  
> That man who was just in human esteem is deservedly surpassed by the little one. The twelve  
> Signs of the choir shine forth, and Olympus hurls its radiance upon the earth.  
> 62 I shall continue to explain what this light of the work also displays.  
> The world is divided into four parts by its four sides;  
> The triune faith calls it by the name in which it is washed in the font.  
> Therefore, repeating four three times together, it counts the whole figure  
> 63 Which the twelvefold order carried around.  
> And to the holy disciples, for whom this baptism is commanded,  
> For a mystical reason it gave the number to return to its former state.

[Col. 0105A] [Note: [Col. 0105B]]

119. *Aula*] Below, line 1055:

> Whom God appoints guardian of the heavenly hall.

Sedulius II, 61:

> The hall of heaven cannot contain him.

Add the notes on the same author I, 15. Lactantius, *On the Passion of the Lord*, at the end:

> In the pleasant hall of eternal peace  
> He will reign happily with me forever.

[Col. 0105C] I especially compared these passages because Muratorius calls *aula* (“hall”) an unusual word in this sense in his *Treasury of Inscriptions*, p. 1767, 18; Justus rightly criticized him in *Specimen of Observations*, chapter 17.

[Col. 0105C] 121. *Magistro*] For they had been instructed by the Holy Spirit as their teacher. In a similar form he calls punishment a teacher below, line 729; and *ore magistro* (“with the mouth as teacher”) should be read from the manuscripts at II, 136, just as *errore magistro* (“with error as teacher”) occurs at II, 448. Thus *ars magistra* (“art as teacher”) is illustrated by Burmann on *Catalecta* I, p. 127, and Withovius, dissertation 2 on Cato, p. 562. I would therefore prefer the received reading to the form found in the Moretus manuscript, *ministro* (“servant” or “minister”), although Elmenhorst likewise asserted *manus ministras* (“ministering hands”) in his notes on Arnobius II, p. 73, and the confusion is frequent. See the notes on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 49, 8. Heumann gave a novel explanation of Luke’s words in *Poecile* II, p. 333.

[Col. 0105C] 122. *Ora*] Vossianus 2 has *hora* (“hour”).

[Col. 0105C] 123. *Populosa*] This word was unknown to the earlier writers. Bentley tried to establish it in Manilius, *Astronomica* II, 224; but see Burmann on Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 708, and de Rhoer, *David’s Festivals* II, p. 183. It indicates the multitude of different languages, which *populus* (“people”) denotes. See the notes on Sedulius IV, 109. Isidore discusses their number in *Etymologies* IX, 2; this passage was treated by Joan Cannegieterus, the excellent relative, in *Observations*, chapter 18.

[Col. 0105D] 124. *Ore*] Vossianus 2, the Antwerp and Fabrician editions, and the Lyon Library of the Fathers have *ab aure* (“from the ear”). I suspect the same reading existed in the Cambridge and Universal manuscripts, because Cortius appended no variant to Fabricius’s edition. The glosses in Vossianus 2 explain this as: “They did not hear from a teacher.” The result is the same, but *ore* (“from the mouth”) seems to be supported by Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 79:

> And again she hangs upon the mouth of the speaker.

Cerda discusses this; and Meursius rightly restored the same wording in Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* I, chapter 1, §4, in *Critical Exercises*, part II, p. 146, where it had been printed incorrectly as *amore tuo pendens* (“hanging upon your love”).

He derived the verb *stillare* (“to drip”) from Job XXIX, §22, where the Vulgate reads: “My speech dripped upon them.” He elegantly took the metaphor from water; thus *dictis fluentibus* (“with flowing words”) occurs at line 122, and below, line 493, he uses *aridum rivulum* (“a dry stream”) of his power of speech. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX, 18, similarly says that the power of speech has dried up. *Εὔροια λόγων* (“a flowing stream of words”) occurs in Aelian, *Various History* VIII, 12. See Cortius on Pliny IX, letter 26, 9. “A river of talent” occurs in Cicero, *For Marcellus* 2, where Abram comments. The manuscript, whose variants I have in my possession, wrongly has *fulmen* (“thunderbolt”) there. I would rather restore this word in the same Cicero, *On the Orator* II, 45: “There is such a river of the weightiest and finest words … that you seem not merely to inflame the judge, but yourself to be burning.” The latter words absolutely require *fulmen*; so too *fulmen ferventis ingenii* (“the thunderbolt of fervent genius”) occurs in Sidonius Apollinaris V, letter 8.

[Col. 0106B] 125. *Signavit*] Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I, 36, 5: “Sacred history signified,” that is, “indicated” or “taught.” Thus *signare fidem* (“to confirm faith”) should be restored from the manuscripts in Pacatus, *Panegyric* 32, 2. He therefore indicates that these languages were not learned from books, alluding to the custom of the ancients, who coated tablets with wax. Ovid, *Amores* I, 12, 8:

> And you, wax filled with letters that will deny.

And *Metamorphoses* IX, 521:

> His right hand holds the sword, his left holds empty wax.

A learned writer noted that this passage was drawn from Euripides in *Miscellaneous Observations*, volume II, p. 37. Ulpian mentions wooden tablets and wax tablets, *Fragments*, title 20, §9; Cannegieter discusses the expression there. Learned scholars have offered more examples, but Isidore XV, 2 seems closest: *ex tabulis lignisque* (“from tablets and pieces of wood”), as the Groningen manuscript and old edition read. Add Pareus, *Selected Plautine Readings*, p. 372, and Granger on Juvenal I, 63.

[Col. 0106C] 127. *Datum*] Thus the ordinary translator renders *δόσις* (“giving”), for “gift” and “endowment.” See Rittershusius on Salvian, *Government of God*, p. 132, and Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI, 106. After *origo* (“origin”) there is a full stop in Vossianus 2, incorrectly. What follows is more involved. I conjecture that the poet’s meaning is that the heavenly gift—the new origin of speech—alone sufficiently supplied eloquence to the learned speakers. I would take *loqui* (“to speak”) as a gerund; *unus* (“alone”) is defended in the notes on Sedulius II, 197.

[Col. 0106C] 130. *Superasset*] The Cambridge manuscript has *properasset* (“had hastened”).

[Col. 0106C] 133. **Affectus**] Vossianus 2 has *effectus*: thus these words are confused below, II, 154. The former reading is preferable, so that a special effort toward completing the undertaking is indicated, while the beginning of the work itself has not yet been brought to completion; for *afficere* is thus used in the sense of “to begin.” See the learned Lipsians in *Acta*, A, 1761, p. 156. Savaronius shows that *affectus* and *effectus* are opposed in his notes on Sidonius, *Epistles* III, 14, and VII, 1.

[Col. 0106D] 134. **Consimili**] I have printed this form from the Moretian manuscript and the Aldine, Basel, and Antwerp editions, as below, verse 410:

> He is tossed upon similar earth.

The other copies have *in simili*, “on similar [earth].” This preposition is sometimes corrupted in compounds. From the Groningen manuscript, in Isidore XVI, 13, restore *concolor Pyropo*, “of the same color as pyrope.” The printed editions have *cui color*, “whose color,” and consequently in what follows one should read *et ei qualitas ut ignis*, “and its quality is like fire.”

[Col. 0106D] 135. **Quoniam**] Pulmannus’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *quondam*, “once.”

[Col. 0106D] 137. **Fecunda**] Vossianus 2 and the Antwerp edition have *facunda*, “eloquent.” The same interchange occurs below, verse 818. Thus he would rather elegantly contrast that ancient confusion, in which people could not understand one another, with the apostles speaking eloquently. So below, verse 224:

> The eloquent fire brought unfamiliar words to men.

But since above, verse 123, he mentions the populous harvest of languages, and at verse 128 the numerous origin of speech, *fecunda* can easily be referred to this, especially since the better manuscripts make no alteration.]

## 64

The holy Spirit, descending from his heavenly court,

[120] irradiates with radiance the place where the blessed foundation  
of the newborn Church was established. There, with fire as teacher,  
he warmed their mouths, and from their flowing words there emerged  
a populous harvest of languages. No letter performed  
its service; no vein of eloquence trickled from the mouth of genius,

[125] 65 nor did wax record their noble utterances.  
Faith alone was their instruction, and the rich substance of the word,  
a heavenly gift, a new origin of speech,

[Col. 0106A] 66 which came in many forms and alone sufficed  
for eloquent speakers from the whole world to speak. Long ago,  
when the ancient ark of the sea had overcome the waters,  
the wicked desired to raise their tower

[130] to heaven. Their impious hearts followed the several modes of speech,  
and purpose perished together with the voice among their proud companions.  
Then there was confusion of language among a similar people; now one language  
belongs to many, because it rejoices in the image of the coming Church,

[135] which will possess harmonious sounds; and, restored in peace  
to the humble, it becomes fruitful and gathers up its scattered order,

[Col. 0107A] [Note: [Col. 0107A]

138. **Tumidi**] Nothing is more common among Christian poets than to describe pride indirectly by the name of swelling; the usage is Greek in origin. Euripides, *Hecuba*:

> Thus we have come to nothing, from the spirit  
> that was formerly firm; and then, indeed, we swell with arrogance.

Horace elegantly:

> Inflate the swelling bladder with boastful words.

Prudentius:

> Lictor, tribunal, and three hundred insignia,  
> by which you swell, and soon afterward subside.

Marius Victor, book III, on Genesis:

> Now let us descend, and with proud agreement  
> let us disturb hearts swollen with arrogance  
> by the varied sounds of our mouths.

The same author:

> Swollen with proud arrogance,  
> he despised the Lord.

Alcimus Avitus, book VI:

> Lest swollen pride parade before us  
> the name of vanity.

[Col. 0107C] Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII, 19.—Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 8: “swelling with wisdom.” In a similar way, “inflated.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIII, 7. Savaro on Sidonius, *Epistles*, p. 448. Adami explained the Greek ὄγκος, “swelling,” in his *Observations*, p. 392. Add the notes on Ovid, *Art* I, 715, and *Metamorphoses* II, 86.

[Col. 0107C] 140. **In flamma**] He is referring to Acts of the Apostles, chapter II, § 3; on this passage see Majus, *Observations* IV, p. 170. There Segaar, in his *Observations on Luke*, p. 110, connects αὐτοῖς, “to them,” with ὤφθησαν, “they appeared.” But Stephanus’s manuscript there has ἐκάθισαν, “they sat,” and Athanasius likewise presents this reading, *Works* I, p. 233. But see Alberti on the New Testament, p. 418.

[Col. 0107C] 140. **Jordanis**] Correctly with a long medial vowel; others shorten it. See Burmann on Lotichius IV, *Elegies* 6, 35. Immediately afterward the Moretian manuscript has *in amne*, “in the river.” Since he understands baptism in the Jordan, I think *ab* must be taken in the sense of “after”; on this usage see Scultingius on Seneca, *Controversiae* III, p. 215. The meaning of the passage is clear from the glosses in Vossianus 2: “He speaks of that for which the Holy Spirit appeared to the disciples in fire and to the Lord in the form of a dove.”

[Col. 0107C] 141. **Tunc**] The second hand of the Moretian manuscript has *nunc*, “now”; this is also my Wassenberg’s conjecture.

[Col. 0107D] 143. **Simplicitas**] Both other birds and the sacred Scriptures teach that the dove is without gall. The Lord Jesus says in Matthew 10: “Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Γένεσθε οὖν φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις, καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί).

Sedulius, book II:

> At once the heavens opened, and the holy Spirit,  
> in the form of a dove, clothed Christ with honor;  
> through the bird without gall he teaches him  
> to be gentle and to walk in great meekness.

Aldhelmus expressed Sedulius in his riddle on the dove:

> Therefore I always carry a gentle heart within me,  
> and, a happy bird, I shall remain without black gall.

Marius Victor calls it human-minded for the same reason, book III:

> And the chaste turtle-dove, joined to the human dove.

Alcimus Avitus, book IV, calls the dove sent out from Noah’s ark a simple messenger:

> Thus the simple messenger confirmed the covenant  
> by sound judgment, and in piety found the world pure.

[Col. 0108A] Juvencus, book II:

> Yet in simplicity to surpass the pure doves.

So that it may be proverbial: “simple as a dove.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII, 19.—Add below, verse 662; the note on Sedulius II, 170; and Bochart, *Hierozicon*, part II, book I, chapter 4.

[Col. 0108B] 144. **Ne**] The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *nec*, “nor.”

[Col. 0108B] 145. **Ibi**] The Universitarian manuscript has *ubi*, “where”; incorrectly, for the reference is to the Jordan mentioned above.

[Col. 0108B] 146. **Unanimes**] Pulmannus’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *unanimos*. I retain the form found in the manuscripts, which it is best to follow in such matters, since both forms are in use. On such words ending in *-us* and *-is*, see Colvius on Apuleius I, p. 9; Heinsius on Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 8, and VII, 335; Burmann on Valerius Flaccus III, 571; Burmann the Younger on *Catalogues* III, p. 525; Oudendorp on Lucan III, 746; Drakenborch on Livy VII, 21, 5. Thus *magnanimes* is found in the better manuscripts below, verse 951, and *unanimem panem* in some copies of Sedulius IV, 219. *Corpus exanime* occurs in the Utrecht manuscript of Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* II, chapter 4, § 6; *imbecillus* in Salvianus, *On the Government of God* III, p. 45. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* X, p. 210:

> while easily suppressing the slight ardor,  
> his strength still being weak,

as correctly emended by Lennepius in his *Annotations on Coluthus* III, 4. In Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* I, meter 2, I found in the 1511 edition:

> and bearing a face bowed down by weight.

And in a manuscript, in the same author III, prose 2:

> weak and without strength.

[Col. 0108C] 147. **Amor**] This refers, in the customary allegory, to the dove; sincere love is especially attributed to doves.

[Col. 0108C] 148. **Hos**] Pulmannus’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *Nos*, “we”; these letters are frequently interchanged. See the note on Sedulius III, 302. On the matter itself compare Barthius, *Adversaria* V, 3. On the word *typicus*, see the notes on Sedulius I, 102.

[Col. 0108C] 149. **Verus**] This is the reading of the manuscripts. Fabricius and others printed *priscus*, “ancient”; Pulmannus’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *vetus*, “old,” which is the source of the error. When they saw that this conflicted with the meter, they substituted *priscus*, although it had arisen from the corrupted *verus*. Arator’s wording is *error verus*, “true error,” and he thus joins opposites in an oxymoron. So above, verse 72:

> While he drags, he himself deserved to be dragged.

And below, verse 393:

> and to pursue gain through losses.

Many similar examples occur in Arator. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 1:

> steadfastness in the very mutability of himself.

Thus Heraldus emends *spem insperatam*, “unexpected hope,” in Plautus, *Mercator* III, 4, 13, in his notes on Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, p. 5. Compare Cerda on Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 295, and VIII, 350; Barthius on Claudian, *Panegyric on Stilicho*, p. 266; Martinus, *Various Readings* III, 9; Burmann on Rutilius, *Itinerary* I, 398; on Ovid II, 627; on Claudian, *Consulship of Manlius*, 90; Burmann the Younger on *Catalogues* I, p. 45, and III, p. 465; Oudendorp on Lucan I, 98. See the notes on Sedulius III, 89, and Barnes on Anacreon, ode 64, p. 224.

[Col. 0108D] 149. **Fonte**] A kind of sober drunkenness is described in the sacred Scriptures, beginning with the obscure saying of Jacob, when he blessed Judah: “His eyes are redder than wine,” in the penultimate chapter of Genesis. Of this drunkenness I have read only two examples in the sacred Scriptures. One is in the Old Testament, in the First Book of Samuel, when Eli the priest charged Hannah, the mother of Samuel, with drunkenness after she had poured out her soul before God in sighs and prayers. The other is in the New Testament, in the Acts of the Apostles, when certain mockers accused the apostles of drunkenness after they had received the Holy Spirit and were speaking of God’s mighty works in various languages. Gregory, hymn I:

> Let us joyfully drink the Spirit’s  
> sober drunkenness.

Paulinus of Cythera:

> Let him be made drunk by the sobering cup  
> from the fountain of the Holy Spirit.

This drunkenness, then, is not of wine or strong drink but of the Holy Spirit: it occurs when afflicted or rejoicing minds are so kindled and carried away that they do and speak not their own things but God’s; and by a certain heavenly inspiration and agitation they are borne along as those drunk with wine are accustomed to be. Of this, unpracticed people understand nothing—namely, those who have never prayed earnestly while placed in distress of heart, or, stirred by divine benefits, have never leapt up from the heart. Fabricius, *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, p. 46.—Heinsius had written in the margin *corde* or *fonte*, “heart” or “fountain.”]

What the swollen men scattered. A great matter compels me

67 not to keep silent long about why the nourishing Spirit is

[140] given to these in flame, while at the Jordan, from the river, he appears as a dove;  
this I shall properly sing then, and fulfill the promised obligations,  
if he brings his gifts. These are two signs of a figure:

[Col. 0108A] let there be the simplicity that the fitting bird loves,

68 so that it may not, sluggish, carry tepidness without the fire of doctrine;

[145] let faith likewise be kindled. There he appoints the like-minded  
to the waters; here he commands the teachers to burn in speech.  
Love presses upon their minds; ardor seethes in their words.

69 True error says that these men too are moved by new wine in a figurative sense,

made drunk by a fresh fountain,

[150] [Col. 0109A] [Col. 0109C]

151. **Acerbo**] The scholiast in Vossianus 2 says: “perhaps through wine,” and “read *de aspero liquore*, ‘of a harsh liquid.’”

[Col. 0109C] 152. **Lacus**] See the note on Sedulius III, 8; the glosses in Vossianus 2 explain it as “through the moistened jars of the Jews.”

[Col. 0109C] 153. **Verbis**] The Moretian manuscript has *mensis*, “tables.” The glosses in Vossianus 2 explain *convivia*, “banquets,” by “drinking parties.” By *convivia verbis data*, “banquets supplied by words,” I think he indicates eloquence.

[Col. 0109C] 154. **Aquas**] I restored this reading at the command of the manuscripts. The printed text had *aquae*, “waters”; but it failed to recognize the elegance explained by Drakenborch on Livy XXXI, 44, 2. Thus Scaliger emended Virgil, *Georgics* II, 22, in the preface to Manilius, p. 8:

> There are other ways that use itself has found for itself.

Vossius had written in the margin of his edition *quas ipse viae*, “which it itself [has found] ways”; but Burmann defends the transmitted reading, and the nephew does not differ from his uncle in the note on the *Anthology* III, p. 527.

[Col. 0109C] 155. **Legis**] By excellence, this means the law of Moses; below, verse 792:

> having attained the measure of the Law.

Book II, 926; Isidore, *Etymologies* VI, 2, “which are in the Law or in the books of the Kings.” Gothofredus incorrectly printed *legum*, “of laws,” there. Perizonius likewise explained Isidore’s passage IX, 5, in his dissertation *Trias*, p. 9, although I disagreed with him in *Miscellanies*, p. 20. Later some wrote that the Twelve Tables were indicated there; but I do not yet see on what grounds. What is contained in them differs entirely from Isidore’s meaning. Who at Rome would have doubted that a posthumous child, if legitimately born, was called by his father’s name? He was certainly his son under Roman law; therefore there was no need for a law on that point.

[Col. 0109D] 157. **Simplex**] See the note on Sedulius I, 282. Arator often uses this manner of expression. See verses 451, 857, and 918; II, 900. He did so especially on account of the doctrine of Arius.

[Col. 0109D] 159. **Instrumenta**] He means the methods of investigating things that lie hidden, as it were, in such matters. They usually call these “allegories,” though not according to the customary usage of rhetoricians, who understood by them rather a continued sequence of modified expressions. See Vossius, *Institutiones oratoriae* IV, 11. He uses *documenta* in a similar sense below, verse 491, “documents full of figures,” verse 725, “documents of a figure,” and *figura* at verses 690, 771, 858, and 982; *species* at verse 751; *forma* at verses 210, 905, and 1029. There Vossianus 1 changes the text to the insecure *male firma*. Prudentius, *Diptychon* 15, “into the form of disciples.” Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I, 24, “although these things had been presented beforehand in the form of a type of the Church.” He did not consider the usage of the word among these authors who, in *Veris and Veros.*, p. 80, emended *femina*, “woman,” as Vonckius reports in *Latin Readings* I, p. 10; perhaps Vonckius himself preferred it. I use Vonckius’s testimony because I have never examined *Verisimilia*, rather than because I would have ventured to state any opinion under the author’s name—a thing I would not wish to have escaped the author of the Campen edition, p. 109.

[Col. 0110B] 159. **Hoc**] The Antwerp edition has *haec*, “these things.” The three persons and the time of the third hour show how widely the “instruments” extend.

[Col. 0110C] 160. **Primus**] Matthew calls him Πρῶτος, “first,” in the Gospel, chapter 10, § 2. On this see the distinguished Van Hoven in his letter to Rhoerius, p. 18. Hence *senior*, “elder,” could be defended in Sedulius V, 104. Salvianus calls him *princeps*, “chief,” in *On the Government of God*, p. 169; see Rittershusius there, and an inscription of comparatively recent date in Montfaucon, *Italian Diary*, p. 4.

[Col. 0110C] 160. **Qui figit**] The Moretian manuscript, Pulmannus’s papers, and the Aldine, Basel, Antwerp, and first Tornesian editions have *cui servit*, “which serves him”; the Lyon *Library of the Fathers* has *quod figit*, “which fixes.” *Servire* could here be understood in the sense mentioned above at verse 49. But I do not know whether then one should not rather say that the surface serves his steps.

[Col. 0110C] 162. **Piscator**] The Cambridge manuscript has *piscatur*, “he fishes.” Fabricius also printed that form, but the other is preferable.

[Col. 0110C] 164. **Carnaliter**] Cellarius safely established this word in ecclesiastical Latin, *Later Observations*, p. 259, since its force cannot be adequately expressed in the pure speech of the Romans; Noltenius therefore thinks it should be retained, *Antibarbarus Lexicon*, p. 454. Christian writers generally use it with the meaning given there by Noltenius, but this passage is different: *carnaliter editus* means “made man,” as the learned scholar correctly interprets it in Fabricius’s *Thesaurus*, under the word.

[Col. 0110D] 170. **Erectos**] I restored the reading of the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, and the first hand of the Moretian manuscript; Fabricius and the Lyon *Library of the Fathers* also printed it. The other editions have *ereptos*, “snatched away,” incorrectly. For he indicates the sick raised from the beds on which they were lying, a usage for which this word is ordinarily employed. See Burmann on Valerius Flaccus VIII, 20; below, verse 468:

> and removed from doubtful death  
> they raised their heads;

and verse 833:

> and joyfully offers him raised up to the rejoicing crowds.

Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* IV, prose 2: “as physicians are accustomed to hope, it is a sign of a nature already upright and resisting.” Similarly, *levare*, “to raise,” is used for “to heal” below, verses 485 and 836; II, 114, 215, 820, and 1208. How easily *erectus* could be changed into *ereptus* is clear from Drakenborch on Livy III, 5, 7.]

## 70

The teaching of heaven filled them; new vessels received

the new liquid, nor are they spoiled by the harshness

with which the ancient jars were moistened, drinking from the vine

that, with Christ as its cultivator, supplied banquets through words.

From it they redden—the waters that he turned—and he made the thin taste

[155] of the Law grow fervent in the books of the Church.

The third hour shone forth with heavenly speech.

## 71

This number belongs to the one God, whose simple substance

is distinguished by three persons; countless instruments

are revealed to us, and the times likewise display this.

[160] [Col. 0110A] But first there is Peter, who fixes his steps upon the sea,

already longing to cast nets for the salvation of men,

so that, rejoicing as a fisherman, he may raise these crowds from the fountain;

before the wondering people he brought back triumphs from heaven.

## 72

God, made flesh, came to the western shores,

[165] under human law. He, free from time, received a beginning from his mother,

and did not regard it as base, though powerful in majesty,

to assume the form of an earthly body,

to become, as the maker of men, a part of his own creation,

and to restore us to himself at his price, after granting salvation,

[170] and after raising so many sick people by driving away their ailments,

[Col. 0111A] [Note: [Col. 0111B]

171. **Perfunctaque**] *Functus* is used in the same way. See the note on Sedulius III, 164; Oudendorp on Lucan VII, 130, although Burmann, in his note on Ovid, *Elegy to Livy*, 393, does not allow this meaning for *defunctus* in the best manuscripts. Solinus, *Polyhistor*, p. 7: “among bodies that have died.” In my edition a learned hand had written in the margin, apparently from a manuscript, *defunctorum corpora*, “the bodies of the dead.” I do not know whether Curtius IV, 4, at the end, should be understood in this way, where Tyre is said to have “died through many disasters” and to have been reborn after its destruction. Pitiscus explains it as “freed”; but because of *renata*, “reborn,” I prefer to understand it in the other sense, since cities are often said to die. See Faber, *Semestria* I, 9; and Burmann on *Catalogues* II, p. 261.

[Col. 0111B] 172. **Superas**] Poets sometimes oppose this expression to death. Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 91:

> He departed from the regions above.

Paulinus of Nola, *Panegyric*, p. 828, in Fabricius’s collection:

> whom he had despised when begging among the realms above.

Dresigius therefore rightly claimed this usage for Latin in *Acta Lipsiensia*, A, 1740, p. 192. Likewise ἄνω, “above,” in Lucian, *Dialogue of the Dead*, p. 265, and frequently elsewhere.

[Col. 0111C] 173. **Fusus**] This is the reading of the manuscripts and the Aldine and Basel editions; the others have *fusae*, “poured,” which was restored through ignorance of the construction. Cortius has already defended the same construction here in his note on Pliny, *Letters* X, 26, 1, and explained this enallage at greater length in his note on Sallust, *Jugurtha* 33, 2. *Fusus*, “poured forth,” is used for “born.” Elmenhorst on Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* I, p. 33; Heraldus on the same author III, p. 149; Burmann on Claudian, *Fourth Consulship of Honorius* 73; notes on Sedulius V, 55. Virgil had this passage in mind, *Aeneid* II, 328:

> Standing tall amid the walls, the horse pours forth  
> armed men.

Thus those heroes would seem to have been born from the horse; I now see that Burmann has already observed the same thing.

[Col. 0111C] 175. **Maluit**] This expression indicates an inclination of will, as Wopkens notes in *New Miscellaneous Observations*, part X, p. 127. Below, II, 108: “Lest you perish, he himself desires to die.” De Rhoer, *Daventer Festivals*, p. 51, indicates that to be able to die is a great thing and worthy of a hero.

[Col. 0111D] 177. **Et ligni**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *fit ligni*, “becomes of wood,” transferring that phrase here from the following verse.

[Col. 0111D] 177. **Vacuatur**] This verb is used for “to empty.” Below, verse 447: “He dies emptied of his entrails.” Daumius established this verb in Latin, *Roots of the Latin Language*, p. 513, in Graevius’s *Syntagma*. The scholiast in Vossianus 2 explains it thus: “The devil’s sin, which through wood brought death into the world, is again overcome through wood and healed by the medicine of God.”

[Col. 0111D] 178. **Fit**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *et*, “and,” through the same error noted at the preceding verse. Athanasius calls the cross of Christ θεραπεία τῆς κτίσεως, “the healing of creation,” *Works* I, p. 2.

[Col. 0111D] 179. **Pallida**] See Barthius on Claudian, *Rape of Proserpine* I, 40.

[Col. 0111D] 180. **Chaos**] Among poets this designates the underworld, not merely that ancient shapeless and undigested mass. Arator, book I of the *History of the Apostles*: “for the fearful … Chaos,” where he also uses it to designate night. Ambrose, in his hymns:

> You who command that the day joined to evening  
> be called one day,  
> dark Chaos pours in;  
> hear our prayers with our tears.

But sacred poets also call the world *chaos*, as it was when first created. Hilary of Arles, *On the Maccabees*:

> You who, mingling confused Chaos in blind darkness,  
> divide it into parts and give night and day.

Paulinus, or Mamertus, to Collea:

> Describe by your word the beginnings of created things,  
> Chaos before day, and the first twilight of light.

Sometimes *chaos* designates the deep abyss of the sea. Alcimus Avitus, book IV:

> Meanwhile, as the sea moved with its great mass,  
> abandoning the world, it returned to ancient Chaos.

All these meanings, less commonly known, are nevertheless pleasant to learn. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXII, chapter 22.—The same author shows at length in his note on Claudian, *Against Rufinus* II, 215, that this word is used of the underworld. Thus the common translator also used it in Luke’s Gospel, chapter XVI, § 26, where the Greek has χάσμα, “chasm”; Burmann defends the translator in his note on Valerius Flaccus II, 86. Arator certainly referred to Luke’s words in Acts of the Apostles, chapter II, § 27, εἰς ᾅδου, “into Hades.” This word is sometimes understood as the matter from which they believed all things had been made and into which they believed all things would return; poets call this *chaos*. See Casaubon, *Exercise against Baronius* I, p. 78. Hence it is used of the underworld and the grave, as noted on Sedulius I, 204. In Luke, moreover, the Cambridge manuscript has εἰς ᾅδην, “into Hades,” and the Greek interpreters have the same in Psalm XV, § 10. The Alexandrian manuscript there nevertheless has ᾅδου, “of Hades,” as in Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, pp. 86 and 155. Note the ellipsis, on which see Rittershusius on Oppian, *Halieutica* IV, 107, and Bossius, *Ellipses*, p. 58; the Latins imitated it. See Vechnerus, *Hellenics*, p. 124.

[Col. 0112C] 180. **Dolores**] He rendered ὠδῖνας, “birth pangs,” from the Greek; this word properly concerns women in labor. Bos, *Philological Exercises*, p. 69; Lucian, *Dialogue of the Gods*, p. 200; Aelian, *Various History* IV, 1; and ὠδίνω, “to suffer birth pangs,” in the same author I, 14. From this it is also used of every severe pain. Staverius on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, p. 624: there Vossius, in the margin of his Lyon edition, conjectured for the corrupted *ido dinin* εἶδος ὀδυνῶν, “a form of pains,” understanding ὀδύνη, “pain,” as anxiety. In Musaeus, *Hero and Leander* 11, συνοδυνάομαι, “to suffer pain together,” a form overlooked by Stephanus, was established by Majus, *Observations* IV, p. 224.

[Col. 0112D] 181. **Infernus**] Vossianus 2 has *infernum*. It was perhaps changed because they thought the word could not be used substantively for the realm of the dead; but see Cellarius, *Later Observations*, p. 268, and *Antibarbarus*, p. 55. Noltenius, *Antibarbarus Lexicon*, p. 1001, admits that it often has adjectival force, denoting what belongs to the underworld, but concedes to Barthius, *Adversaria* XXII, 10, that it rarely designates the place itself. Nevertheless, I cannot agree with Barthius when he emends *inferus* in certain passages. What if *locus*, “place,” is understood? Sedulius says *infernas vias*, “underworld ways,” V, 266; add Wopkens, *New Miscellaneous Observations*, part VII, p. 885.—For *esse timet*, “fears to be,” Wassenbergius conjectures *ipse timet*, “he himself fears,” and this is not displeasing. Athanasius, *Works* I, p. 150: ὁ ᾅδης ἔπτηξε, “Hades was terrified.”

[Col. 0112D] 182. **Poena**] Christ’s death brought it about that death itself was conquered and itself, as it were, underwent punishment. Comparable passages may be read above in the note on verse 10.]

When he also restored to the light bodies that had been mourned

and had completed their course,

## 73

and again granted them the upper air;

he himself, permitting himself to be poured forth from his mother’s womb,

to undergo the laws of flesh lest the world perish,

[175] preferred to die himself. But that which is born from the pregnant virgin
dies; the innocent one is hung upon wood,

and the burden of wood is emptied. Thus the wound of the wicked

[Col. 0112A] becomes God’s medicine. He shone upon the frightened shades,

## 74

seeking the pale kingdoms; Chaos could not darken him,

[180] radiant with his own light; the pains fled.

## 75

Then the underworld fears to exist, and, restraining no one,

the punishment returns upon itself; the torturer languishes into new idleness.

The gloomy Tartarus groans because all its chains are at rest.

[Col. 0113A] [Note: [Col. 0113B]

184. **Portitor**] Pius thought the word originated in the age of Sidonius. But see the notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 298; Heinsius on Ovid, *Fasti* IV, 715; Barthius on Claudian, epigram 47, and *Adversaria* LIII, 8; Savaro on Sidonius V, epistle 4. In Symmachus I, epistle 90, I found in a manuscript *levia rerum portator festivus exornet*, “may the cheerful bearer adorn the light things of affairs,” instead of *portitor*, which appears in the printed edition.

[Col. 0113B] 186. **Jesum**] In some editions a point is added so that the word depends on *levat*, “raises.” I removed it, and, if I am not mistaken, rightly.

[Col. 0113B] 188. **Funesta**] Pulmannus’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *et funesta*, “and deadly.” They seem to have referred the expiatory rites to the Jews themselves. I would rather understand it of a crime deserving expiation, and of the guilt on account of which the deadly punishment of death follows. Salvianus says *addici piaculis aeternis*, “to be consigned to eternal expiations,” *On the Government of God* II, p. 32. Add Reitius, *Ambiguities*, p. 435. He also uses the disputed passage of Florus I, 1: “whether he should inaugurate and govern, they employed expiatory rites.” Scholars read from Jordanes: “they decided to employ the gods.” I think one should read *adhibuere prodigia*, “they employed portents.” A copyist changed that word into *pericula*, “dangers,” from which it passed into *piacula*, “expiatory rites.” Similarly in Florus I, 10, 3, the reading was formerly *tunc illa R. pericula*, “then those dangers of Rome.” It is now printed *prodigia*, “portents,” which Boxhornius says he first restored there in his letter to Pontanus, p. 100. The later *Sylloge of Matthias* followed Boxhornius’s emendation, although I am surprised that Duker mentions it nowhere.

[Col. 0113C] 190. **Vulnera**] “Vices, sins.” Wopkens on Sedulius IV, 77; in the same way Boltius defends *saucia mens*, “a wounded mind,” in Ausonius, *Critical Silvas*, p. 34.

[Col. 0113C] 191. **Cur**] Pulmannus’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *cui*, “to whom”; Fabricius likewise cites it in his commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 98. In Arator, however, he printed *cur*.—Arator’s meaning closely corresponds to these lines of Ovid, *Heroides* XI, 107:

> What did the boy do wrong, born only a few hours ago?  
> By what deed did he offend, scarcely born,  
> that he should be thought to have deserved his grandfather’s death?  
> Ah, wretched boy, he is punished for my crime!

[Col. 0113D] 192. **Parricida**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *cur paricida*, “why, murderer.” —Soon afterward, *quod Christi*, “which belonged to Christ,” is found in the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*.

[Col. 0113D] 195. **Serior**] Heinsius had written *serior vel saevior*, “later or more savage.” With the latter, the elegance seems to disappear.

[Col. 0113D] 196. **Alit**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *habet*, “has”; the other reading is preferable, though these words are frequently confused. See the note on Sedulius II, 81.

[Col. 0113D] 199. **Crementa**] *Crementum* means “increase.” The glosses give *crementa*, “increases,” as αὐξήσεις. Otherwise *crementum* is γόνη, “offspring,” if Isidore is to be trusted, *Etymologies* IX, 5, and XI, 1. Our Strabo writes:

> Once entrusted  
> without hope of increase, he enclosed it beneath the sluggish sod.

The same author, chapter 7:

> It receives splendid increases.

Juvencus, book II:

> As soon as he has received  
> the increases of righteous strength.

Arator, book I; and the same author, book II:

> and will demand back the increases  
> of its measure from the servants.

Barthius, *Adversaria* IV, chapter 24.

[Col. 0114B] 200. **Reparate**] Heinsius had written from the Moretian manuscript *reparate vel reparare*, “restore or to restore”; the latter is found in the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*. The Universitarian manuscript has *repetite*, “repeat,” and the Cambridge manuscript *reperate*. The meaning demands *reparate*. He is urging the Jews that, if they wish to free themselves from their growing evils as from chains, they should restore their extinguished race; thus *reparare afflictum*, “to restore the afflicted,” in Hegesippus I, 33, at the end.

[Col. 0114C] 200. **Remitti**] Heinsius had written *remitte vel remitti*, “forgive or to be forgiven”; the Aldine and Basel editions have *remittit*, “he forgives.” I would change nothing. The meaning is: the one hope is that the deserved punishment may be remitted, if one wishes to be reborn after one’s crimes. Sallustius similarly says *remittere injuriam*, “to forgive an injury,” in the *Fragments*, p. 52 of Wasse’s edition. Cellarius referred *remittere peccata*, “to forgive sins,” to ecclesiastical Latin, *Later Observations*, p. 281, and *Antibarbarus*, p. 218. Noltenius, in the *Antibarbarus*, p. 1721, maintains that *permittere* can be used in the same sense; but Gronovius judges the passages he cites corrupt in his letter to Salmasius, volume II of Burmann’s *Sylloge*, p. 612. Add the notes on Aurelius Victor, *Origin of the Gentile Nations*, chapter 9, § 4.

[Col. 0114C] 202. **Tria**] In Acts of the Apostles II, § 41, ὡσεὶ, “about,” is added, indicating that the number is not complete. Arator seems to have used the full number in order to obtain his allegory.

[Col. 0114C] 203. **Diluit**] The Moretian manuscript has *deluit*, “washed away.” Claudian, *Against Eutropius* II, 23:

> What age will wash away so great a crime?

There Barthius notes that *diluit* has been substituted for *deluit*.

[Col. 0114D] 204. **Primum**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *primus*, “first”; this is not displeasing.

[Col. 0114D] 204. **Jussa**] Heinsius had written *jussa vel jura*, “commands or laws.” I approve the former; it refers to Christ’s command in Matthew’s Gospel, chapter XVIII, § 19. The latter is objectionable because of the following *jura*, “laws.” —Up to this point Heinsius had collated the Moretian manuscript.

[Col. 0114D] 211. **Sensus**] Vossianus 2 has *census*, “wealth,” and the distinguished Wassenbergius conjectured that this should be read. Soon afterward, verse 214:

> Wealth binds hearts without limit.

Add Drakenborch on Silius VII, 167, and the note on Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius, p. 11. Thus Tornesianus 1 has *sensus* for *census* at verse 214, and the Lyon *Library* at verse 417. These words are likewise confused in Martial, *Epigrams* IV, 74; add Burmann on *Catalogues* III, p. 554. I think that by *omnes sensus*, “all perceptions” or “all minds,” Arator indicates the common opinion of all and expresses Luke’s words ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, “together,” in Acts of the Apostles II, § 44. They usually disagree about the meaning of those words; I would prefer to translate them simply: “all who believed were in agreement.” That is the force of the expression, as Struchtmeyer correctly explained in *Critical Observations* I, 4, and Bascius in *Interpretation of the New Testament from the Fathers*, p. 16, where he shows that Clement and Ignatius used the expression in the same sense.]

What could death do there, where the bearer of life was going?

[185] The almighty God, upon whom no limit ever presses,

raises him after the sacred tomb; we saw Jesus radiant in body,

and beheld him returned among his own stars.

But flee, unhappy ones, the deadly expiatory guilt of the people,

## 76

which, when God came, turned aside their former offences,

[190] while added wounds increased their sacrilegious guilt.

Why, Judaea, do you, murderer, drag your children

through vows of blood? Why, after Christ’s blood was shed,

do you, condemned, press these men down with yourself,

hasten to bring forth those not yet created as guilty,

and with a murderous tongue strike the path of nature?

[195] For the later birth nourishes a distinction from the crime,

and the offspring of the crime perishes from its birth,

which, wounded by the voice of its parents,

[Col. 0114A] comes into the light already punished. If it is your concern

to dissolve the increases of fruitful evil,

[200] 77 restore the extinguished race; the one hope is that the punishment owed

may be remitted, if one wishes to be reborn after crimes.

Now the shepherd multiplies the sheep; that day no fewer than three thousand

of the people were washed in the river of the Lamb.

Here, after God’s commands, the use of baptism first arises,

[205] 78 confirming the laws that were given; for threefold power

gathers this offspring, dividing the number equally.

The number denoted by a thousand is complete; thus, when we speak of the world’s times, we assign ages to its centuries.

[Col. 0114B] What is complete once is joined three times, and

[210] the mystical power of the number makes a multitude. It is a sacred figure of the new flock.

Meanwhile grace is poured through all minds,

[Col. 0115A] [Col. 0115C]

214. **Limite**] The Universitarian manuscript has *limine*, “threshold,” as these forms are sometimes confused. See Burmann on Valerius Flaccus IV, 614, and Lucan I, 354. The meaning itself demands *limite*, “limit”: he indicates that no boundary had been imposed upon their wealth, but that they possessed everything in common. Hence Arnobius calls Christians *familiaris communicatores rei*, “intimate sharers of property,” *Against the Pagans* IV, p. 152. Nevertheless, Moshemius did not attempt to demonstrate that everything among them was held in common, *Reflections on Selected New Testament Passages* I, chapter 6, p. 114.

[Col. 0115C] 214. **Census**] The first Tornesian edition has *sensus*, “mind” or “perception.”

[Col. 0115C] 216. **Ubere**] From Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 95, and Valerius Flaccus VI, 711:

> and land fertile in waters and in rich soil.
