Heinsius conjectures *agris*, “fields”; Palladius’s passage cited by Burmann opposes this, as does another passage of Homer, which the learned scholar compared with Valerius in *Miscellaneous Observations* IV, p. 185.

[Col. 0115C] 219. **Proprium**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *quod proprium*, “which was private”; Vossianus 2 has *qui primum*, “who first.” I conjecture that Arator wrote *qui privum*. The reading *proprium* seems to have arisen from a gloss. Nonius Marcellus I, no. 152: “*Privum* means the property of each individual, whence also *res privata*, private property.” Burmann has restored this word with great success in several passages of Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, 20, and *Fasti* I, 113 and 137. In Justin XII, 8, 3, my Cannegieter, in his note on Nonius, p. 16, agrees with this, although Wopkens follows Scheffer in *New Miscellaneous Observations*, part X, p. 130. Restore it also in Cicero, *On the Laws* III, 19, *in privos homines*, “against private individuals”; and Triller seems not to have restored it badly in Varro, *On Agriculture* I, 41, *privis generibus*, “to private kinds,” *Critical Observations*, p. 466. My conjecture in Arator is the more probable because *primus*, *privus*, and *proprius* are frequently confused. See my father on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 83, 1.

[Col. 0115D] 219. **Nihil**] The Cambridge manuscript has *nil*, “nothing.” So too the Antwerp edition, the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, and Fabricius. The Aldine and Basel editions reject *nihil esse*, “that nothing exists,” which is plainly erroneous. It agrees with Sidonius Apollinaris VIII, epistle 4: “whatever you scatter among the churches, you gather for yourself.”

[Col. 0115D] 221. **Hinc**] This is Virgilian, from *Georgics* I, 5.

[Col. 0116B] 222. **Spiratus**] This is the reading of the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, the Antwerp edition, Fabricius, and the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*. The others have *spiratur*, “is breathed.”

[Col. 0116B] 224. **Nescia**] “Unknown,” things that they themselves had not previously learned. Barthius discusses the passive use of this word in his note on Statius, *Thebaid* III, 30. Thus I understand the word in Hyginus, *Fabulae* 88, *se in compressione nocturna nescio cui eduxisse*, “that he had brought forth a child in a nocturnal union with someone unknown”; for the things Staverenus adduces concerning the expression *nescio quis*, “I know not who,” seem unrelated to that passage. So *ignarus*, “ignorant,” can mean “unknown.” See Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 134; Manutius on Sallust, *Jugurtha* 98; Abram on Cicero, *For Caelius* 2; Heusinger on Vechnerus, *Hellenics*, p. 420. Arator’s words refer to the fact that the apostles were considered ἀγράμματοι and ἰδιῶται, “unlettered” and “ordinary men,” according to Luke in Acts IV, § 14—that is, common people and inexperienced in affairs, which is the force of the latter word, as the distinguished scholar observes in *Miscellaneous Observations* X, p. 9. Add Savaro on Sidonius VII, epistle 14; hence Christians were subsequently regarded as untrained in learning and unskilled in the arts. Elmenhorst on Minucius Felix, p. 9; on Arnobius I, p. 52, and II, p. 62.

[Col. 0116C] 230. **Ferventi**] Cortius inserted after this word a sign of weaker punctuation, so that it would refer to *mente*, “mind.” But it undoubtedly belongs with *amore*, “love.”

[Col. 0116C] 231. **Charus**] The Lyon *Library of the Fathers* transposes the words: “may he also be dear to you.” Noltenius rightly attributes *proximus*, “neighbor,” in this sense to ecclesiastical writers, *Antibarbarus Lexicon*, p. 1129.

[Col. 0116C] 232. **Omne**] Whatever others may think about the principle of natural law, I would judge that the mutual “relationships,” as they are called, and duties arising from the love of God derive from it as from their first source. If one considers God the Creator, one owes everything to him, and likewise to the other human beings formed by that same God. For to them must be attributed whatever can assist the Creator’s purpose in forming them. But this is not the place to discuss these matters at greater length. I therefore think that James called it the “royal law” (*νόμον βασιλικόν*) in his Epistle, chapter II, § 8, not because the law was promulgated by God, the great King, as Raphelius believes, but because it is the most excellent and greatest of all laws, containing in general everything that ought to be done. Thus *king* is one who excels. See Fabricius on Anacreon, p. 169; and in this sense the Latin word is *regius*. Vriemoet, *Dictionary of Classical Terms*, vol. II, p. 107.

[Col. 0116D] 234. **Misit**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana edition I reads *missus*; the manuscripts have the other reading, and the preceding *dedit* supports it.

[Col. 0116D] 236. **Amat**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana edition I reads *amet*.

[Col. 0116D] 236. **Secunda est**] I restored *est* from the Cambridge and Universitas manuscripts and the Aldine and Basel editions.

[Col. 0116D] 238. **Secundam**] The Universitas manuscript has *secunda*.

A will rich in love reaps riches.

And so that the devout may join in covenant with one another, with a sure pledge,

they loosen their goods and bind their hearts, without limit of wealth,

[215] 79 though their affection is shared; new laws have flowed to the blessed

from a bountiful hand, by which, in joyful abundance,

divided riches are doubled, and what they make common for themselves

grows for all and is wholly embraced by those

who wish that nothing be private property. From what source has flowed

[220] this uprightness, and what was the origin of that goodness?

From here I shall begin to sing: the gracious Spirit had twice

been granted to the holy disciples: once, breathed into them

by Christ when he rose; afterward, sent from heaven,

eloquent fire brought unfamiliar words to the men.

[225] [Col. 0115B] 80 Lest we vainly attempt anything untried in zeal,

come, gracious Spirit! Without you, you are never spoken of;

[Col. 0116A] grant gifts to the tongue—you who grant tongues as a gift.

These repeated gifts, I think, strengthen the righteous,

so that they may observe the two commandments inscribed on the two tablets:

[230] Love God with your mind, full of ardent love.

Again he says: Let your neighbor too be dear to you, as yourself.

This compact contains the whole law, which the gracious Spirit,

81 coming twice, creates in hearts: once the Creator gave him

on earth, that humanity might be loved; afterward he sent him from heaven,

[235] that human beings might burn for God. The first love

is that which ardently loves the Lord; the second is that

which joins mortal humankind. Yet what is latter in number begins first,

and is attended by the second, which is prior; thus the form teaches: “Unless you love,” it says,

[240] [Col. 0117A] [Note: [Col. 0117B]

240. **Potis es**] Vossius 2 has *potis est*. The sense itself rejects this. *Potis es* is used for *potes* (“you are able”); on this see Stewechius on Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* II, p. 81; Elmenhorst on the same work I, p. 28; Stephanus on Saxo Grammaticus, *Danish History* XV, p. 248; Falsterus, *Supplement to the Latin Language*, p. 272; Vossius, *Art of Grammar* IV, 21; Oudendorpius in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. III, p. 133.

[Col. 0117B] 240. **Non es**] I restored this from the Cambridge manuscript and the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana I editions, so that *potis* may be repeated. In the others appears *non est*, which they understood in the sense of *licet* (“it is permitted”); Heinsius explained this usage in his notes on Ovid, *Art of Love* II, 28; *Metamorphoses* II, 189; Drakenborch on Silius IX, 451; Joannes Cannegieter, *Observations*, chapter 1, p. 370. The Greeks use the construction likewise. Cebes, *Tablet*, p. 221, ed. Schrod., has ἐστὶν ἰδεῖν (“it is possible to see”), and p. 229, θεωρεῖν ἐστίν (“it is possible to contemplate”); Aelian, *Varied History* II, 34, νοεῖν ἔσται (“it will be possible to understand”). See Perizonius on the same author IX, 7; Schultingius on Seneca, *Suasoriae*, p. 29.

[Col. 0117B] 241. **Nescis**] See the note on the Epistle to Vigilius, line 4, and Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 31.

[Col. 0117B] 242. **Dominumque**] Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition have *Dominum votoque* (“and the Lord by a vow”). The Antwerp manuscript also has *in pectora* (“into the breasts”).

[Col. 0117C] 243. **Sit**] Vossius 2 has *sint*. My very dear Wassenbergius likewise conjectured this, with the following sense: “May the twin causes—the love of God and of one’s neighbor—be one substance in themselves, so that you cannot separate either from the other.” I am almost persuaded. Nevertheless, I did not dare alter the text because of the agreement of the remaining manuscripts, provided that *causae* is taken in the third case [dative]. The two causes subsist and stand firm in relation to one another.

[Col. 0117C] 245. **Coaevo**] Some wrongly attribute this word to Cicero in *Against Vatinius* 13; it belongs to declining Latin. See Noltenius, *Antibarbarian Lexicon*, p. 463. Vossius assigns *coaequalis* to the same period, although Vorstius on Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I, 26, 6, shows that it was used by earlier writers; see also Noltenius, *Lexicon*, p. 860.

[Col. 0117C] 246. **Gerens**] Some have condemned this expression, but Burmann defended it as Latin in his notes on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 497. See also Wopkens on Sedulius II, 141, and on Justin in *Miscellaneous Observations*, New Series, vol. X, p. 45.

[Col. 0117D] 247. **Avarum**] For he hoped for some gift from Peter, so much so that he was intent upon it. Luke writes Ἐπεῖχεν (“he fixed [his attention]”) in Acts III, § 5; Heinsius correctly supplies the sense “with his eyes” (*per oculos*) in his notes on Valerius Flaccus VII, 114, although Elsnerus prefers τοῦν.

[Col. 0117D] 248. **Cumque**] The distinguished Wassenbergius elegantly conjectures *quique negat* (“and he who denies”), since otherwise the passage is obstructed; he recommends comparing line 284:

Who, driving away what is harmful,

Avoids the burden of gold.

[Col. 0117D] 251. **Gaudebit**] I restored this from the Cambridge and Universitas manuscripts and the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana I editions. The others have *gaudebat*; what follows requires the other reading. He uses *meruisse* immediately in the sense of “to attain.” See the note on the Epistle to Florianus, § 16.

[Col. 0117D] 253. **Sibi**] Sedulius III, 303:

“Give back to me, or give it back to himself.”

In the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum* the reading is *ipse: sibi*, with a punctuation mark inserted for no reason and contrary to the elegant usage by which *ipse* is ordinarily distinguished by its case from the other pronoun. See Rivius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VII, 1. Graevius writes that the ancients spoke no differently in the same passage, book III, letter 4. Several passages, however, stand against Graevius; if his view of ancient usage were correct, all of them would have to be emended. Dukerus discussed the matter elegantly in his notes on Florus III, 18, 7; add the remarks on Sedulius II, 203. The learned men of Leipzig seem, in my view, not to have distinguished badly in the *Acta* of 1761, p. 26, whether the opposition is made to another thing or not. They require the nominative when one thing is not opposed to another, but a different case when it is. Thus in Cicero, *For Marcellus* 5, one should read *memet mihi—reliquos amplissimos viros et sibi ipsis et patriae reddidit* (“he restored me to myself, and the other most distinguished men both to themselves and to their country”), not *ipsos*, which Graevius printed and which appears in the manuscript; its variants are at hand.

[Col. 0118B] 254. **Respondit**] Peter, naturally. See Acts of the Apostles III, § 6.

[Col. 0118B] 254. **Aegro**] In the Cambridge manuscript the scholiast had written: “He calls the rich *aegros* [the sick], because they are always in need; they are λῆροι [fools].” Cortius takes *aegro* as a dative, so that Peter, having declared that he possessed neither gold nor silver, might appear poor to the lame man, although he was actually richer. This is not a bad interpretation: let each choose what pleases him, for it makes no difference.

[Col. 0118C] 255. **Abi**] I adopted this from the manuscripts, the Antwerp editions, Fabricius, and others. In some copies, with the sentence joined together, one reads *progressus ubi*, referring to a word of command; the sense is good, though not especially elegant. The letters *a* and *u* were easily confused, especially in Lombardic script. See Salmasius on Florus I, 3, 5. In Isidore, *Etymologies* X, p. 1071, *cupidus* is said to derive from *cupiendo*, “from desiring,” that is, “from receiving.” Read *capiendo* (“from taking”) from the Groningen manuscript; or the following word itself requires this reading.

[Col. 0118C] 256. **Exsiliit**] This is supported by ἐξαλλόμενος and ἀλλόμενος, both of which occur in Acts of the Apostles III, § 8. The Aldine and Basel editions have *exuit*; perhaps the manuscript read *exivit*, as the Vulgate translator has it in Luke VI, § 19: “because power went out from him and healed them all.”

[Col. 0118D] 256. **Hospite**] He seems to have taken it for “stranger,” or someone who was not his own; he calls the footprints “foreign” in line 311. *Hospes* is an honorable word in Claudian, *Sixth Consulship of Honorius* 651. I nevertheless conjecture that one should read *a sospite gressu cum vixere pedes* (“with a sound step, when the feet lived again”), or *ac sospite gressu convixere pedes* (“and with a sound step the feet lived together again”). Drakenborch shows that *sospes* and *hospes* were confused in his notes on Livy V, 28, 4; and *sospita* and *hospita* in his notes on book XXII, chapter 1, § 17. He explains *gressu* by βάσεις (“steps”), which occurs in Luke, Acts III, § 7; Elsnerus likewise suspected that this is how the word should be understood. Compare Duportus on Theophrastus, *Characters*, p. 226.

[Col. 0118D] 257. **Convixere**] Vossius 2 has *convinxere*; the Aldine and Basel editions have *cum vixere* (“when they lived together”).

[Col. 0118D] 260. **Edidit**] Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition have *addidit* (“added”). The Cambridge manuscript, Fabricius, and the Lyon *Bibliotheca* have the manifestly corrupt *edidit ortas*.

[Col. 0118D] 263. **Israel**] With the middle syllable lengthened, in Theodulf’s epigram:

“Israel, you king, illustrious offspring of David.”

Alcimus V:

“Israel, carrying on his battles with his sight alone.”

With the middle syllable shortened by contraction (*κατὰ κρᾶσιν*), so that the word is disyllabic, in Arator:

“The lame

Israel they are accustomed to carry, and strive to attach to the gates.”

And:

“Whom afterward, in his mother’s wound,

The lame Israel possesses.”

The same occurs repeatedly elsewhere in this author. FABRICIUS, commentary on *Christian Poets*, p. 74.]

You cannot love God, whom you are unable to see, if you do not love

the brother whom you are able to see. Therefore let harmony, bound together,

grow warm in equal devotion, and let love of one’s brother enshrine the Lord

in the heart; let the two causes be one substance in themselves.

82 He was lame, to whom the first day gave the beginnings of life

[215] amid the ruin of his limbs, bearing eight lustres

with an illness of equal duration. Peter, accompanied by John, said to him,

“Look!” Hope had mocked his covetous expectation;

but, when Peter denies it, he prepares something better. How often are those burdened

by despair helped by what they had despaired of, and prosperity born

[250] from an adverse origin, concealing happy ends in sorrowful

beginnings, comes to their desires! The needy man will rejoice

[Col. 0118A] that he has gained more with an empty hand, for he who sought gifts

has himself been given back to himself. “There is no vein of metal here for me,”

83 he replied, “to pour out wealth; I, though poor, shall be richer than the sick man.

[255] Go forth—walk!” At the word of command,

powerful healing leapt forth, and with an unfamiliar step

84 his feet lived again. Leaving behind his long infancy,

the old man trod the earth, and his ancient frame began to move on new soles,

and in swift course produced a gait which birth had not produced.

[260] The manifest proof of the deed stands; but another matter also

reveals what the cause signifies: the nation called Israel bears the name

of one who had left the contest afflicted,

[Col. 0119A] [Note: [Col. 0119B]

264. **Deo**] Verbs of fighting with the dative, in the Greek manner. Prudentius, *Psychomachia*:

“They fight against vices and preserve themselves for their rewards.”

Arator, book II:

“But mortal beings cannot

Fight against God their Creator.”

The same author in the same place, p. 111; below II, 939:

“I would dare to fight against him.”

Silius Italicus X, 57:

“He dared to fight against the Thunderer.”

See Drakenborch and Vossius, *Art of Grammar* VII, 37; Vechnerus, *Hellenics* I.ii.25; Boltius, *Critical Miscellany*, p. 54.

[Col. 0119C] 265. **Mentis**] Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition have *matris* (“of the mother”): incorrectly. He is establishing a comparison between Jacob, who was lame, and the Jews, dull and lame in spirit; this expression occurs in the author’s *On the Ordering of the Republic*, epistle 1, chapter 7, § 2.

[Col. 0119C] 266. **Claudus**] The Cambridge manuscript and the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana I editions have *clodus*, and so throughout in what follows. Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII, 5, says that the ancients used *clodus* for *claudus*. See above, line 17.

[Col. 0119D] 267. **Fluit**] That they stained their minds with vices more deeply than they pursued the luxurious pleasures of the body. *To flow in the mind* is attributed to one corrupted by vices, especially luxury. See Douza, *Emendations on Tibullus*, chapter 7; Drakenborch on Livy VII, 29, 5.

[Col. 0119D] 267. **Spatiisque**] Understand the journey of the Israelites through the desert. *Spatium* denotes the place through which we pass. See Menchenius, *Observations on the Latin Language*, p. 926.

[Col. 0119D] 269. **Idola**] *Εἴδωλον* always has the middle syllable shortened among ecclesiastical writers, perhaps because they yielded to popular usage, lest there be disagreement in the temples between the educated and the multitude. Aldus, Nebrissensis, Clichtoveus, Wimphelingus, and Sichardus sometimes altered the passages in ways that were possible, but contrary to the authority of the ancient reading. Prudentius, *Psychomachia*:

“Whom neither raging anger nor images in war

Had compelled to yield.”

The same author, *Against Symmachus* I:

“Calling the blue souls and the black images.”

Sedulius V:

“She always loved the groves;

She loved the images.”

Arator II:

“The images gathered from all Rome, the world having been subdued.”

Tertullian I:

“To follow empty images, imagining a crowd of gods for oneself.”

The first maker of images was Syrophanes for the Egyptians, Prometheus for the Greeks; the Jews, by divine command, and the Persians, by ancestral custom, did not admit them. FABRICIUS, commentary on *Christian Poets*, p. 71. Similar examples were given by Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIV, 4, and Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 34. Add the notes on Sedulius V, 146; above, on the Epistle to Vigilius, line 24; and Aldhelm, *On the Praise of the Virgin*, p. 720, vol. I of Canisius’s *Thesaurus*:

“They prayed to the king’s images.”

A first syllable shortened is also read in Alcuin, *Life of Saint Willebrord*, vol. II of Canisius’s *Thesaurus*; see Basnage in the preface. Nansius, in his notes on Nonnus’s *Paraphrase*, p. 57, and Falsterus, *Supplement to the Latin Language*, p. 149, think that these poets observed the accent in shortening the middle syllable; this is not yet clear to me. As for what Fabricius writes about Aldus, it is evident from Aldus’s own edition, in which, as also in the Basel edition, the reading is *idolaque*. I nevertheless marvel that Fabricius charged Aldus and others with this alteration, since he himself indulged excessively in similar matters and was ingenious in the works of others, as Joannes Albertus Fabricius writes in his *Latin Bibliography*, vol. III, p. 709. I discussed this matter at greater length in the preface to Sedulius.

[Col. 0120C] 270. **Speciosam**] Compare Alberti, *Observations on the New Testament*, p. 225.

[Col. 0120D] 272. **Qui sunt**] I adopted this from the Cambridge and Universitas manuscripts and the Aldine and Basel editions. The others have *nam sunt* (“for they are”).

[Col. 0120D] 275. **Isaias**] Other poets have *Eseias* or *Esaias*. See Heinsius on Prudentius, *Additions*, p. 158. He refers to Luke’s words in Acts of the Apostles III, § 24, where Alberti, in his *Observations on the New Testament*, p. 462, correctly translates καί as “moreover.” Immediately afterward, the reading *uno ore* (“with one mouth”) appears in Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition; but the other reading is better suited to Luke.

[Col. 0120D] 276. **Obscuris**] Vossius 2, in the first hand, has *obscuri*; I conjectured *obscuro*, so that it may refer to *ore*. The distinguished Wassenbergius interprets the received text as meaning that Christ made manifest by his coming the sayings of the prophets, which had formerly been obscure. On the meaning of *canere* as “to prophesy,” see the note on Sedulius II, 35. Isidore, *Etymologies* VII, 8, has “what they had foretold in their future deeds and sayings.” Thus the Groningen manuscript is correct, not *praenuntiassent*.

[Col. 0120D] 277. **Et portae**] This verse is missing from the Aldine and Basel editions.]

He had ventured to fight against God; he himself bore beforehand the likeness

[265] of a grievously afflicted body, which afterward, in the wound of the mind,

85 lame Israel possesses. Stumbling through his crimes,

he is more depraved in heart than in flesh, and in those very stretches,

for forty years, kept away from Egypt’s border,

he limps, desiring Egypt and seeking idols.

[270] 86 A cripple is placed at the Beautiful Gate; the wretched man

cannot go farther or touch the gate’s threshold;

guilt has denied him the way. Who are they who are wont to carry

[Col. 0119B] Israel, lame in heart, and strive to bring him to the gate

[Col. 0120A] which, by the beauty of its own name, reveals Jesus?

[275] Isaiah, Daniel, and all prophets like them in utterance

proclaim Christ’s manifest miracles in obscure sayings.

And he himself, who bears the name of Gate, thus warns:

“I am the gate for you; whoever refuses to enter through me

will be a guilty thief.” The prophets can carry him

[280] to the gate, speaking of things to be seen rather than merely viewed;

they cannot carry him into the temple. This gate was entrusted to Peter,

who, having confessed Christ, shows forth what has been made known;

he does not proclaim things to come. O old man, you will lie without end,

87 unless you now, lame man, ask Peter, who drives away what is harmful

[285] [Col. 0120B] and avoids the burden of gold, whom the Maker of all things decreed

[Col. 0121A] [Note: [Col. 0121B]

286. **Non**] Vossius 2, the Antwerp edition, Fabricius, and the Lyon *Bibliotheca* have *nec* (“nor”).

[Col. 0121B] 289. **Porticus**] Zeibichius discussed the matters relevant here at length in *Leipzig Miscellanies*, vol. III, p. 576. Immediately afterward, with the punctuation removed, *regnante fide* (“while faith reigns”) is connected with *ad pacificus* in the Aldine and Basel editions.

[Col. 0121B] 290. **Quis**] Vossius 2 in the first hand and the Aldine and Basel editions have *qui*. This is not objectionable, since Dukerus on Florus I, 18, 20, and Drakenborch on Livy V, 40, 7, have shown that it can be used in a question. An *s* could easily have been added from the following word. Some marginal notes on line 324 are relevant here; hence passages are often to be cleansed where adjacent syllables or letters have become attached, for such places are especially corrupt. I recall the much-discussed passage of Victor, *On the Caesars*, chapter 5, § 10: “For when vices have invaded the mind, shamefulness is by no means given a more humane association with external things, but the habit of sinning is made more savage.” Besides the conjectures mentioned in the notes, add those of Klotzius, *Critical Miscellanies*, p. 38, and Joannes Cannegieter, *Disquisition on the Notes*, p. 324. I think what has coalesced should be divided and altered thus: “For when vices have invaded the mind, external shame is by no means satisfied, but the habit of sinning is made more savage for it.”

[Col. 0121C] 292. **Praesule**] Through his agency, with his help. See Wopkens on Sedulius I, 60.

[Col. 0121C] 299. **Solidumque**] One might read *solitumque* (“and the accustomed one”), namely the one he had previously been, as the confusion described by Drakenborch on Livy V, 4, 7 shows. Yet *solidum* can be explained as “whole” or “complete.” Thus in Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, 427, Cerda explains *in solido* as “in entirety.” See Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* V, 20. Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV, 4, has: “The strong and solid region, enclosed by two sufficiently swift rivers …” This is how Gothofredus prints it; but the Groningen manuscript and the old edition more correctly have *et solo laeta* (“and joyful in its soil”).

[Col. 0121D] 300. **Quam**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana I editions have *qua*.

[Col. 0121D] 300. **Novant**] “They renew and restore.” See Drakenborch on Silius VII, 141, where he refers to Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 260:

“Aeneas building citadels and renewing roofs.”

Thus Burmann ordered it to be printed, although Daniel Heinsius gave *tela novantem* (“renewing weapons”), which is not found in the manuscript. That reading is nevertheless not objectionable, since *tela novare* could be used for “to alter something from its former form,” indicating that Aeneas changed the Trojan arms for the Tyrians. For this reason Mercury was sent by Jupiter to warn him how greatly, in founding Carthage and changing his arms, he was neglecting what fate had ordained. Virgil afterward assigns him a sword shining with jasper and a cloak of Tyrian purple, so that one may recognize that his arms and clothing had been changed.

[Col. 0121D] 300. **Hic**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana I editions have *huic*.

[Col. 0122B] 301. **Restituit**] The Aldine and Basel editions omit this verse. The syllable here is lengthened before aspiration, although the Antwerp and Tornesiana I editions avoided this by restoring *qui mortua*. It will be clear from the notes on Sedulius I, 19 that there is no need for this.

[Col. 0122D] 301. **Cedit**] I restored this from the manuscripts and Tornesiana I. Cortius correctly explained it in the margin as “grants” or “permits.” The printed editions have *fecit*, but that is a gloss, as appears from Vossius 2, where the scholiast had written it above. Arator is not otherwise unfamiliar with this construction: *fecit fervescere* (“made [it] grow hot”), line 155; *fecit habere* (“made [him] have”), line 377; *facis debere* (“you make [him] owe”), line 403; *facit ire* (“makes [him] go”), line 322; *facit esse* (“makes [him] be”), lines 624 and 727; *fecit procedere* (“made [him] proceed”), line 628. Add Ciofanus on Ovid, *Heroides* XVII, 174; Wopkens on Sedulius IV, 90. Likewise ποιῆσαι νηστεύειν (“to make [someone] fast”) occurs in Luke’s Gospel V, § 34. Relevant here is Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* I, p. 30: “By a single command he drove the demons from their bodies, and restored their senses to the lifeless; while they writhed beneath these torments, they were restored by no other command to health and steadfastness.” The word *casibus* there has caused interpreters much difficulty. I approve the learned man’s conjecture in the margin of my edition: *cassibus* (“nets”), for they were as though entangled in the bonds of demons.

[Col. 0122C] 303. **Neces**] Below, line 589:

“Blessed in the deaths they will possess.”

Book II, line 127:

“Deaths that cannot be loosened.”

He seems to use this number to indicate the greatest dangers and every kind of death. Burmann explained *mortes* in this way in his notes on Quintilian, *Declamations* X, beginning, and on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI, 538. Pacatus, *Panegyric* 29, § 1: “I speak of the deaths of men.” Solinus, *Polyhistor*, p. 4: “the accused deaths of sons.” My own collation confirms this reading: in the Venetian edition of 1498 I found “the granddaughter accused of disgrace; the deaths of sons.” Vonckius correctly restored the same word in Sulpicius Severus, letter 3, § 10, from both Utrecht manuscripts. Athanasius used Θανάτους (“deaths”) in his works, vol. I, p. 678. Add Barthius, *Adversaria* LIV, 6; the notes on Valerius Flaccus VIII, 332; Oudendorpius on Lucan VII, 100; and Drakenborch on Livy, *Epitome* XXXI.

[Col. 0122D] 306. **Levant**] He expressed ἀινοῦντα (“praising”), which occurs in Acts of the Apostles III, § 9, or ἐδόξαζον (“they glorified”), there IV, § 21. In this sense the Vulgate translator has *levemus* (“let us lift”) in Lamentations of Jeremiah III, § 41: “Let us lift up our hearts.”

[Col. 0122D] 309. **Vernula**] Compare Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastes*, chapter 4, p. 49.]

not to carry a purse for himself. Seek the gifts of salvation;

do not pursue fragile riches, which one who will be rich with the Lord

must despise. Beyond the temple threshold

Solomon’s portico contains him—Solomon is rightly called

[290] “Peaceful.” While faith reigns, who in all the world will always be

peaceful except Christ? He protects everyone

who pleases him with Peter as guide, under whose leadership he rises.

Already the summit of the Church was growing in a snow-white throng

of five thousand men; Judaea labours

[295] to prevent him from being worshipped, though from his gift flowed

what power accomplished. Yet Peter’s love cannot abandon Christ:

[Col. 0121B] “We shall not be silent about him,” he says,

“by whose beneficence salvation returns, who by the Creator’s right

[Col. 0122A] made up what was unfinished in the work. The part which the commands renew restores

[300] 88 its whole beauty: here the Redeemer restores

wounded limbs; here he grants that the dead may rise.

89 They have the will to commit wickedness and to inflict

sacrilegious deaths upon the holy and venerable. O ever unjust men!

They see the gifts and stir up wars, but abandon their undertaking,

[305] lest they violate those whom the crowd cherishes, for whom the lame man, as witness,

was proof of their merit; and by this they exalted their hearts.

For his gait furnished the people with no small miracle—

he whom his native earth had brought forth, both an infant and an old man,

[Col. 0122B] now free of every constraint of age, and with whom nature herself marvels to move,

[310] nature which had long lain inert and had only lately been strengthened,

[Col. 0123A] [Note: [Col. 0123B]

311. **Proprio**] Thus the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana I editions. The Cambridge manuscript supports it, reading *proprio novo vestigia* (“with his own new footprints”); the Universitas manuscript has *propiore novo* (“with a nearer new [step]”). In Vossius 2 the entire verse is missing. This reading was especially pleasing because of what follows, *quae fuerant aliena sibi* (“which had been foreign to him”), so that “his own” and “foreign” are opposed. The other editions have *properata novo vestigia* (“hastened footprints with a new [step]”), which has this in its favor: that it indicates the lame man setting down his footprints with a faster step, although then *aliena* seems somewhat weakened.

[Col. 0123B] 312. **Fuerant**] The Cambridge manuscript has *fuerint*.

[Col. 0123B] 314. **Cadis**] Vossius 2 has *vecors* (“foolish”).

[Col. 0123B] 315. **Emis**] In Vossius 2 the entire passage is punctuated as follows:

“The resurrection of Christ

You purchase so that it may be concealed as theft. But, madman,

You seek empty evidence from sleep. Through the fading

Envy that you feel, and so on.”

[Col. 0123B] 317. **Vis**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesiana I editions have *jus*, a frequent interchange, as below in line 375. Add Stewechius on Arnobius, p. 84; “my father,” in Pliny’s *Panegyric* 77, 4; and in Martianus Capella I, p. 9. Vossius’s manuscript has *consilium jus ferre meum* (“my counsel to bring the law”), which I rejected in *Miscellanies*, p. 204. Isidore, *Etymologies* X, p. 1071, has *a viris peritis capite diminutus* (“diminished in status by learned men”), from which learned men should write *capite juris peritis* according to the Groningen manuscript. Cicero, *For Marcellus* 4, also remains to be corrected: “For although, by the condition of victory itself, we had all rightly been put to death as the conquered, we were preserved by your judgment of mercy. Therefore you alone are truly unconquered, since even the condition and force of victory itself have been defeated by you.” The preceding words require *conditio jusque*, or *et jus* (“both the condition and the law”); for the Leiden manuscript, whose collation I possess, has *et vis* (“and force”). Nor is it an obstacle that *jus* requires *devictum*; Drakenborch sufficiently defends this construction in his notes on Livy IX, 35, 5, and XXVI, 34, 12, and Burmann on Lucan I, 176.

[Col. 0123C] 320. **Crucis**] Refer this to the standards. For Christians, the soldiers of Christ, are assigned a standard bearing the sign of the cross. Sedulius I, 321:

“Behold, the consecrated standards of the cross flash with their sign.”

Soldiers used to have the initial letters of their name inscribed on standards or shields—for example, Λ on the shields of the Lacedaemonians and II on those of the Peloponnesians. Thus, from Χριστός, the standard of Christians receives X, or the mark of the cross. Cerda elegantly observed this in his notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 396. The names of commanders, too, were inscribed on standards, as Harenbergius proves in *Historical-Theological Bibliography*, class VIII, fascicle 3, p. 396. Elmenhorst, in his notes on Minucius Felix, p. 76, discusses the worship of the cross among Christians in various ways.

[Col. 0123D] 321. **Sol**] Sedulius V, 234:

“The sun, concealing its flashing rays

Beneath a cloud and veiled in a dreadful covering,

Lay hidden and stained the sorrowful world with grief.”

In some editions these three verses are added there:

[Col. 0124B] “Because Delia had a brother set opposite to her,

When one was beneath the earth and the other upon heaven’s upper height,

The impious ages feared perpetual night.”

Cellarius denies that these verses came from Sedulius; the first two are clearly by another hand, and their meaning is obscure, while their style is unworthy of Sedulius. I think, however, that the last should be included among the Sedulian verses, borrowed from Virgil, *Georgics* I, 468, in that poet’s customary manner; Cerda accordingly attributes it to Sedulius, as does Freinshemius on Curtius X, 9, 3. Soon afterward Vossius 2 has *tenebris* (“in darkness”).

[Col. 0124B] 322. **Arva**] See the note on line 35. *Tremere* (“to tremble”) is often used in this sense. See Cerda on Virgil, *Georgics* I, 475. Through this earthquake the centurion is said to have recognized Christ as the Son of God, Matthew XXVII, § 54. Those who attribute this to the opinion of the ancients—that through an earthquake they recognized the presence of the deity—do not seem to have judged badly. The centurion was certainly a Roman. Compare the notes on Silius IV, 444.

[Col. 0124B] 327. **Sociare**] An imperative construction. The expressions are taken from the grafting of trees, which Columella, *On Trees*, chapter 26, will illuminate. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, 630:

“Having just split the bark,

He inserts the branch and supplies foreign nourishment to the fosterling.”

This passage supports the reading in Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII, 6: “Grafting is so called when, after the trunk has been split, a shoot of a fruitful tree is inserted into a sterile one.” The Groningen manuscript has *inciso trunco* (“with the trunk cut”), which is preferable. The later words in Isidore shed light on Arator, when, after the bark has been cut, a shoot is inserted into the wood of another tree.

[Col. 0124C] 328. **Viduata**] “Deprived,” as in Sedulius IV, 50:

“Immediately the fig tree, deprived of its own juices.”

Thus in Greek ὄρφανος (“orphaned”) and ὀρφανίζειν (“to deprive”). See Martinus, *Various Readings* I, 26; and the learned author in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. VIII, p. 196.

[Col. 0124C] 328. **Cibis**] The Cambridge manuscript has *sucis* (“juices”). The quantity is opposed to it, although the spelling is correct, as I showed in the notes on Sedulius I, 36, and Heinius, *Observations on Tibullus* IV, 2, 16; Ovid also uses the same expression in grafting, *Metamorphoses* XIV, 630. Columella, *On Trees* 26, at the end, has: “so that there may be nothing by which the juice can be drawn out.” The Cambridge reading derives from a gloss, as in Varro, *On Agriculture* I, 23, 2, where once it was read, “which are the greater juices.” It has now been more correctly emended to *cibi* (“food”); Ursinus shows that this word is used of the nourishment of trees and plants. Add the *Rural Lexicon*, under the word **PABULUM**.

[Col. 0124D] 329. **Quia**] Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition have *quoque* (“also”); Tornesiana I has *quae* (“which”). In the word *tempore* he refers to καιρὸς σύκων (“the season of figs”) in Mark II, § 13, although Heinsius there prefers the reading οὗ γὰρ ἦν καιρὸς σύκων (“for it was not the season of figs”), supported by Colomesius, *Sacred Observations*, p. 15. Abreschius offered a new interpretation in his notes on Aristaenetus I, p. 16.

[Col. 0124D] 331. **Insertus**] Following Virgil and others, he uses the masculine. Some think that Cicero preferred the feminine in *Against Verres* III, 23; but the reading there is doubtful, and Graevius printed *quodam*. See also Vossius, *On Analogy* I, 13. Arator reproduces Paul’s passage in Romans II, § 17; he uses ἐγκεντρίζειν (“to graft in”), which occurs there, in the same way as Athanasius in his works, vol. I, p. 551. Theognis used Ἐνθεῖναι (“to insert”) metaphorically, *Sentences* 430.]

he now marks new footprints with his own step,

90 though they had been foreign to him. Yet the wicked offspring

still rages and forbids him to speak what his joy proclaims.

Why do you fall so often, Judaea? You purchase Christ’s resurrection

[315] so that it may be concealed as a theft; but, madwoman,

you seek empty proofs from sleep in your fading envy:

what you see accomplished by power, you seek to deny by fraud.

When the Lord went to destroy hell,

he brought back his own flesh, death despoiled.

Victorious from the height of the cross, he supplies radiant standards.

[321] 91 The sun rushes into darkness; but you rebel, black in heart.

[Col. 0124A] The fields tremble, shaken in their places; but you cling more firmly.

The rocks crack, but you remain hard. Now the rending of the veil

has exposed the mysteries of the temple, which had long lain hidden.

[325] Your light has come upon us; with you alone night remains.

Endless death presses upon one for whom life never rises again.

Old plant, be joined to new shoots and plant yourself in their bark,

92 lest, deprived of nourishment, without whose gift

you will be a dry fig tree, because at no season do you wish

[330] to bear fruit for Christ’s hand; nor do you see how greatly

the wild olive, once unrecognizable, has flourished in producing olives,

[Col. 0125A] [Note: [Col. 0125A]

332. **Per gentes**] He refers to the Gospel announced to the Gentiles and transferred from the Jews because of their stubbornness. Otherwise I had conjectured *per sentes* (“through the thorns”), so that the metaphor might continue from thorns. Thus Sedulius III, 249:

“And compelled the nation, sprung from the thorns,

To feed on the grass of the Hebrew field.”

Likewise in Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 31. Vonckius substituted *de vestris sentibus* (“from your thorns”) in *Latin Readings* I, p. 59. Other editions disturb the passage still more by giving *pergentes* as one word. Rather, this should be restored in Aldhelm, *Praise of the Virgin*, p. 728, vol. I of Canisius’s *Thesaurus*:

“Together they receive [him] on Christ’s advancing path.”

Hanck has *per gentes* there; but the two words should be joined, and the sense will be easy.

[Col. 0125B] 333. **Exhaustis**] “Dried up.” Vegetius, *Veterinary Art* III, 1, § 11, used *exhaustum animal* (“a drained animal”) for “emaciated.” Unless, however, someone thinks *exustis* (“burned”) should be read; it is evident from the notes on Phaedrus I, fable 6, line 7, that the two were confused. It means “destined to be burned,” as in Sedulius IV, 52:

“For everyone who nourishes nothing fruitful for God,

Like a sterile trunk, will be made equal to burned logs.”

Wopkens explains this as “destined for fire”; Voorda teaches in his *Interpretation*, chapter 32, that words ending in *-tus* can signify future time.

[Col. 0125C] 334. **Succisa**] The Cambridge manuscript has *succissa*. Perhaps the scribe intended to write *subscissa*, but dictionaries do not recognize the word. The Vulgate translator uses *excidere* (“to cut down”) in this matter in Matthew III, § 10; my father noted that this is proper to trees in his notes on Victor, *Illustrations* 31, 6. *Succisa* is sufficiently supported here by Columella, *On Agriculture* XI, 2, § 11.

[Col. 0125C] 334. **Translata**] Columella III, 5, § 2, and Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* III, prose 11, use this word in a similar sense.

[Col. 0125C] 335. **In**] I restored this from the Cambridge and Vossius 2 manuscripts and the editions of Fabricius and Antwerp. The others have *de* (“from”).

[Col. 0125C] 337. **His**] Pulmann’s manuscript notes have *bis* (“twice”).

[Col. 0125C] 338. **Deus**] It may be understood according to Attic usage, on which see Bosius on Luke’s Gospel XVIII, § 13. Add Gregory, *On Dialect*, p. 47; among Latin authors, Burmann on Ovid, *Heroides* XVII, 100, and Burmann the Younger on the *Catalecta* III, 74, line 2. Writers of inferior style use *Dee*. See Vossius, *On Analogy* II, 5. Or it may be referred to the form discussed above in the note on line 154.

[Col. 0125D] 339. **Artifici**] Vossius 2, in a second hand, has *artificis* (“of the craftsman”): incorrectly. See the note on Sedulius, Prologue, line 4, in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. V, p. 17; Arator regularly uses it in this way, as I shall show below.

[Col. 0125D] 340. **Creas**] I adopted this from the Cambridge manuscript and the Basel and Tornesiana I editions; the others have *creans* (“creating”). Vossius 2 has *per omnia* (“through all things”), but another hand subsequently corrected it. This agrees with Sedulius III, 21:

“In God’s manner, who, before anything was born, by seeing

Perceives the past—whatever he wills to be future.”

[Col. 0125D] 342. **Imperium**] Sedulius I, 224:

“Every work serves him and follows the command

Of the one ordering it, wherever his purpose draws it by a sign.”

[Col. 0126A] Athanasius used Κτίσιν ὑποτεταγμένην (“creation subjected”) in his works, vol. I, p. 976.

[Col. 0126A] 342. **Spiritus**] From Psalm XXXIII, 6. Sedulius II, 211, agrees:

“He bent the greatest

Limbs of the highest heaven.”

[Col. 0126B] 344. **Operis**] The Cambridge manuscript has *operi* (“to the work”). This is not objectionable. See Drakenborch on Livy XXI, 53, 2; but it is difficult to determine what the poet wrote, since either case can be used in this way. See Dukerus on Florus II, 6, 48, and my father on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 54, 1. The following letter *s* makes the matter still more uncertain, since it could either have adhered to the preceding word or been absorbed by it. See the notes on Sedulius II, 214, and V, 153; similarly in Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 174. In the Clermont manuscript my father found:

“And first Achates struck a spark from the flint.”

The printed text has *silici* (“from the flint”); see Heinsius. In a collation of the manuscript I possess, Solinus, *Polyhistor*, p. 5, has *enitentis spiritum retinere* (“to retain the spirit of the striving one”), not *enitenti*. In Martial VIII, epigram 21, the excellent Thuane manuscript reads:

“Now, Caesar, you come even by night; the stars hold sway, if it is permitted.”

Hence a learned hand represented it not inelegantly: “Come, [Col. 0126C] let the stars stand.” In Isidore, *Etymologies* XVI, 14, the Groningen manuscript has *marmori similis non marmoris* (“like marble, not of marble”); and although the same letter does not follow, the spelling may nevertheless be equally doubtful in similar cases. Let the better manuscripts resolve such uncertainties by their authority. Thus in Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Martin* 11 § 1, from two Utrecht manuscripts, I would prefer *proximus monasterio locus* (“a place near the monastery”), not *monasterii* (“of the monastery”), which is printed in Isidore, *Etymologies* IX, 2; from the Groningen manuscript and the old edition, *proxima mari loca occupavere* (“they occupied places nearest the sea”); in the same author, X, p. 1072, from the same witnesses I prefer *navis cui eminentia vi tempestatis adimuntur* (“a ship whose projections are removed by the violence of the storm”), not *cujus* (“whose”); Book XI, chapter 2, from the Groningen manuscript, *libidini frangit impetus* (“it breaks the force of lust”), not *libidinis* (“of lust”); Book XIII, chapter 21, *Exordium Argivae gentis primus dedit* (“he was the first to give the beginning of the Argive race”). Yet perhaps *genti* (“to the race”) is preferable there, since the old edition also has it, Book XV, 7. In the Groningen manuscript and the old edition, *quod domui lucem ministrat* (“which supplies light to the house”), not *domus* (“the house”). In Cicero, *On the Orator* II, 23, the Utrecht manuscript has *sororis filium fuisse Demosthenis* (“that he was Demosthenes’ sister’s son”). The printed text has *Demostheni* (“to Demosthenes”). Add similar examples in Rulinken, [Col. 0126D] *V. C.*, on Rutilius Lupus II, p. 83. Because of the preceding letter, it is likewise uncertain whether Tertullian wrote in *On Patience* 14, *Lapidatur Stephanus, et veniam hostibus suis postulat* (“Stephen is stoned, and he asks pardon for his enemies”), or *sed veniam* (“but he asks pardon”), which I found in a manuscript; nevertheless the former seems preferable in view of what is said concerning the letter to Florianus. Many more examples could be accumulated, but “nothing in excess” (*μηδὲν ἄγαν*). —Furthermore, *materiamque*; Vossianus 2, Library of Leiden.

[Col. 0126D] **345. *Imago***] A gloss in Vossianus 2: “Lest man, made in the image of God, should have a shameful sin.”

[Col. 0126D] **347. *Furores***] Vossianus 2, by a second hand, has *furoris* (“of fury”). The copyist took *coepta furoris* (“the beginnings of fury”) for *furibundis* (“raging”), about which the customary expression was discussed at verse 1. He thus rendered *ἐφρύαξαν* (“they raged”), which Luke uses in Acts IV § 25. Thomas Magister and Ammonius both apply it to horses, using *φριμάττεσθαι* (“to neigh or snort”); hence it refers to any kind of movement, and Hesychius explains it by *ἐπεγείρεται* (“is stirred up”).]

And throughout the nations the grape springs forth from thorns.

93 Anger hangs over the exhausted roots, ready to cut,

so that, once cut down, you may fall—unless, already transplanted, you grow green again.

[335] After wondrous salvation, born in an aged body,

became known to the disciples by report, and the proud nation’s

threats were recognized, they celebrate a hymn in these words:

You, God, who make all things, giving them life in their proper forms,

who by the artificer’s word make what has been brought forth,

[340] [Col. 0126A] 94 and, seeing them beforehand, create the forms of things by names.

When they were made, the voice was their seed; nor did nature,

following the command, delay their arising. Then the breath of his mouth

arched the sky, knit together the lands, poured forth the seas,

and his will alone supplied the material of creation.

[345] 95 Lest the likeness should bear an unbecoming yoke,

the ruler of Olympus hid beneath a servant’s covering,

so that the nations might fulfill the fury of their own undertakings.

[Col. 0127A] [Note: [Col. 0127B]

**348. *Moveret***] Other manuscripts have *moveres* (“you might move”).

[Col. 0127B] **352. *Cujus tulit***] Vossianus 2, by a more recent hand, has *cui abstulit* (“from whom he took away”). That reading was doubtless added as a gloss.

[Col. 0127B] **353. *Quem***] I restored this reading, as all the manuscripts require it, as do the Antwerp and Basel editions. The others have *quod* (“which”). The agreement of the manuscripts prevails; nevertheless, there is something harsh in the reading unless one refers it to the form of synthesis discussed by Cortius on Sallust, V, 8. Arator seems to have had another word in mind to which the pronoun could refer. In the Cambridge manuscript the following was written:

“He therefore said *quem* because among the Greeks it is masculine, whereas among us such forms become neuter in *-um*. Whoever has found the *aevum*, that is, the age of this life, recognizes the course of life, that is, sin. But these lost the *aevum* before they knew how to sin; before they knew and understood how to live, they lost life.”

[Col. 0127C] **356. *Posse***] See Withof, *Specimen Guntherianum*, p. 77.

[Col. 0127C] **356. *Quis***] Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 6:

“Who, in telling such things,

could restrain his tears—the soldier of the Myrmidons,

the Dolopes, or of savage Ulysses?”

And at verse 361:

“Who, in telling of deaths,

could unfold the sufferings, or equal them with tears?”

Cerda supplied similar examples there.

[Col. 0127C] **357. *Pilati***] The first syllable is shortened. So below, II, 101:

“He seeks this man from Pilate’s jurisdiction.”

The uncertain author of *On the Passion of the Lord*, verse 34:

“And the unspeakable deeds of blind Pilate.”

[Col. 0127C] **359. *Periclis***] The distinguished Wassenbergius conjectures *piaclis* (“expiations”), as at verse 188, “the fatal expiations of the nation.”

[Col. 0127C] **360. *Et ferus***] The Tornesian edition 1 has *efferus* (“savage”).

[Col. 0127D] **363. *Ultra***] Used absolutely for “beyond that extent.” See Duker on Florus, preface § 1. Sedulius II, 12:

“To behold nine hundred years and more, happily.”

[Col. 0127D] **364. *Damnatio***] Cortius had written in the margin: Valesius on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, 10, p. 166.

[Col. 0127D] **365. *Da***] Vossianus 2 has *das*; the following letter became attached to it. Compare also above, verse 118.

[Col. 0127D] **366. *Segnisque***] I printed this reading from the Cambridge manuscript; nor do I suspect that Vossianus 2 disagrees, where *senesque* occurs, with the letter *g* written above the *n*. In all the others there is *signisque novalibus*. What that expression means I do not explain. By the “sluggish hand” he indicates people devoted to sins and unproductive in cultivating true piety; nevertheless, once the tares of vices have been cut away, they will bear the richest fruits of piety, like a field. For by *novalia* he understands a newly ploughed field. He then proceeds with an excellent metaphor: a field is called *segnis* when it is unproductive. Servius explains *carduum segnem* as “useless, unproductive” in his note on Virgil, *Georgics* I, 151, and *terras segnes* in II, 37. In a similar way the copyists corrupted Aurelius Victor, *Epitome* chapter 12 § 6, reading *signisque* absurdly; it is now correctly printed *segnisque*. —Sedulius I, 349 does not depart far from our author’s words:

“And by sowing tears

I shall reap lasting joys. For we who mourn in Adam,

scattering seeds, shall soon all rejoice,

bearing our sheaves when Christ comes.”

[Col. 0128B] **370. *Qua sancti***] The Aldine and Basel editions have *quam sancti* (“which the holy feet”). —Instead of *fulsere*, contrary to the meter, Vossianus 2 has *stetere*, with the gloss *fulsere* written beside it.

[Col. 0128C] **370. *Concurrere***] I do not know what this is intended to mean. The subject is an earthquake; Luke has *τόπος ἐσαλεύθη* (“the place was shaken”). A similar verb seems required; hence immediately afterward, “One place leaps forth and is shaken.” I think we should read *consurgere* (“to rise up”), which agrees extremely well with the verb *σαλεύειν* (“to shake”), since it is also used of the movement of waves. Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 530:

“Then from the deepest bottom it rises toward heaven.”

Seneca likewise uses *fluctuare* (“to surge”) of an earthquake in *Natural Questions* VI, 1. How easily copyists could have exchanged these two words will be clear from Burmann on Lucan I, 579.

[Col. 0128C] **372. *Obortis***] The Cambridge and Basel manuscripts have *ab ortis* (“from those having arisen”). The Aldine and Tornesian edition 1 have the single word *abortis*.

[Col. 0128C] **374. *Parentem***] Vossianus 2 has *parentum* (“of parents”). See above, verse 16. Isidore XI, 1: “God created man from the mud of the earth.” There the Groningen manuscript has *de humo* (“from soil”).

[Col. 0128C] **375. *Vis***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *jus* (“right”). See above, verse 317. —For *flexit* (“bent”), the Cambridge manuscript, by a second hand, has *fluxit* (“flowed”).

[Col. 0128D] **377. *Magis***] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian edition 1 have: “But why does one place leap forth more?” The punctuation is faulty. The meaning is: “Why does that one place leap forth rather?” He immediately supplies the reason. That *magis* is used for *potius* (“rather”) is clear from the notes on Sedulius’s preface, verse 7.

[Col. 0128D] **378. *Cecinit***] In the Cambridge manuscript, by a second hand, one reads:

“And the place is shaken—you would marvel—seek out what lies hidden.”

But these words are not Arator’s. He had in mind the prophecy of Nahum I, 15. So thought the distinguished Wassenbergius. One may also add Isaiah LII, 7.

[Col. 0128D] **381. *Pii***] Vossianus 2, the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian edition 1 have *piis* (“pious”). But these writers frequently attribute *pietas* (“piety”) to Christ. Thus the sower is called *pius* (“pious”) in Sedulius II, 20, and with good reason I restored the same word there in Book III, verse 44.

[Col. 0128D] **383. *Cor***] The syllable in *cor* is ambiguous among the Latins: sometimes short and sometimes long, and even the greatest poets place it with either quantity. Because a copyist did not know this, he introduced a hiatus into Lucilius’s verse in Book XX of the *Satires*:

“And thus they think all these things are fabricated;

they believe that a heart is present in bronze images.”

There is no difficulty if one rewrites it:

“They believe that a heart is in bronze images.”

Ovid lengthened the word in the *Letter of Sappho*:

“My tender heart is penetrable by light weapons.”

Ausonius shortened it:

“Here, where it is written *eo*, to read *cor*, if he had a heart.”

An old poet on Bellerophon, I think:

“Eating his own heart, avoiding the tracks of men.”

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXVII, chapter 3. In Ovid’s passage, *Heroides* XV, 79, the more accurate editions have *levibusque* (“and by light [weapons]”). See Heinsius. Certainly *cor* is lengthened here contrary to the practice of the other poets. Compare Vossius, *On the Art of Grammar* II, 30. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts consistently preserve the reading I printed. But Barthius, on Claudian, *Against Rufinus* I, 105, and *Adversaria* XXX, 20, cites *cor inesse catervis* (“that a heart is present in the throngs”). I do not know whether this was conjectural; it does not appear in the editions I have seen, though I would not object to it if the manuscripts supported it.]

“What trick of Herod’s was this, when he stirred up mournful wars,

ordering infants to be put to death? Those torn from the breast

[350] receive wounds wandering across their tiny limbs,

scarcely finding room, and under the command of the savage tyrant

birth became punishment. The force of that punishment carried away his lifetime,

which he did not know how to live, the man who lost it. O strange

96 condition of death—to undergo life with death as its sole end,

[355] and, when the first and final day are simultaneously one,

to be able to die rather than to know how! Who, with dry eyes

or with groaning stilled, could recount the crime of Pilate,

which the elements mourn? Under whose judgment did Christ

choose to subject his limbs to dangers for the world,

[360] so that flesh might undo the evil of the flesh, and the savage enemy,

from whose ingenuity weapons of poison flowed,

[Col. 0127B] might lose the tearful expiations of the ancient war,

the equal material having prevailed, so that the burden of guilt

might no longer issue forth through offspring? The condemnation of the just

[365] has become freedom for the guilty: grant that the seeds of the word

[Col. 0128A] 97 may be cultivated through your gifts, and let the sluggish hand,

using the newly ploughed fields, gather sheaves,

while you make them fruitful, from which you yourself may fill

the granaries of your heaven and crown the wheat-like faith,

while the darnel perishes.

[370] Where the holy feet shone, the earth seemed to come together,

oppressed by a heavy weight; and soon the nourishing Spirit

shone upon them, and eloquence grew upon their tongues.

Their prayers, once heard, prevailed. The human race

98 is earthly material; man reveals his parent, the soil,

[375] by his name. The power of the apostolic voice bent and drove

the fields, and made those created from the earth possess faith.

But why does one place leap forth and shake? Scripture sang

that beautiful feet bring peace; therefore beneath the steps

[380] of these men the joyful earth is moved, to whom by the word of the Master

[Col. 0128B] peace was entrusted by the pious one, and which, carried through them,

went forth to all lands as a swift gift.

Behold how many outstanding groups become one heart.”

[Col. 0129A] [Note: [Col. 0129C]

**384. *Incipit***] Barthius, on Claudian, *Against Rufinus* I, 105, gives this verse differently:

“You see how the people acquire one soul.”

I cannot determine where he obtained it; I have found nothing similar either in the manuscripts or in the printed editions. —Ouzelius discussed the matter itself—that one mind can exist in many people, a sure sign of friendship and agreement—in several places, though he borrowed the material from others with insufficient candor, in his note on Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, p. 5. Add the notes on Sallust, *Catiline* 20, on Silius Italicus IX, 406, and Elmenhorst on Minucius Felix, p. 4. [Col. 0129D] Mamertinus, *Panegyric on Maximian*, chapter 11: “For you govern the state with one mind, and such a great diversity of places does not prevent you from governing it, as though with unconquered right hands.” It should rather be read “with joined right hands”; others have already seen this, and Spanheim approves it in his note on Julian, *Oration* I, p. 59. Mamertinus confirms this in *Maximian’s Birthday Speech*, chapter 11 § 4: “Do you see Diocletian? Do you see Maximian? They are both there, they are there together; how closely they sit!” In some editions, however, one also finds *invicti sedent* (“the unconquered sit”). Compare Schwarz.

[Col. 0129D] **384. *Populus***] See above, on verse 123.

[Col. 0129D] **385. *Mysteria***] The Cambridge manuscript has *per mystica* (“through mystical things”). This reading pleased me in the *Miscellanies*, p. 180, and I have retained the reading already accepted. Cicero, *Against Verres* II, 22: “which had absolutely no cause for doubt.” Ovid, *Tristia* II, 331:

“Perhaps I might even doubt this.”

See Burmann there.

[Col. 0129D] **386. *Cum***] The Cambridge manuscript has *cui* (“to whom”), which is not displeasing because of the elegant use of the dative.

[Col. 0130B] **388. *Quae***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *quam* (“which”). —In the preceding verse the Tornesian edition 1 has *numenque frequentis* (“and the divinity of the multitude”).

[Col. 0130B] **390. *Habitura***] “About to possess,” as in the Greek *ἔχειν* (“to have”). Muncker on Fulgentius, p. 664; Elsner on Luke XVIII § 24.

[Col. 0130B] **391. *Parte***] The Basel and Tornesian edition 1 have *patre* (“father”). See verse 36.

[Col. 0130B] **392. *Caducorum***] Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* III, 12: “Virtue therefore despises riches and wealth because they are fragile.”

[Col. 0130B] **392. *Pensare***] Velleius II, 115 § 1: “with which he might balance the loss of the dead soldier.” Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* I, prose 5: “unequal rewards are weighed according to merits”; there, Wasseus correctly ascribes to the translator what he found in a manuscript as *reddi* (“to be rendered”), in his index to Sallust under the word *PENSANTUR*. Add Barthius, *Adversaria* VI, 17, and Vonck, *Critical Specimens*, p. 16. —[Col. 0130C] Barthius correctly explained *manentia per aeterna* (“things remaining through eternity”) in his note on Statius, *Silvae* IV, 2, 5; for it refers to the *ὕπαρξιν μένουσαν* (“abiding existence”) mentioned in the Epistle to the Hebrews X § 34.

[Col. 0130C] **394. *Jura***] This is the reading of all the manuscripts. I suspect Arator wrote *rura* (“fields”). Hence above, verse 390, *sprevit agros* (“he despised the fields”); and shortly afterward, verse 396, *spargere rura* (“to scatter the fields”). Similarly, *ruris* was emended to *juris* in Aurelius Victor, *Caesars* 39, 26; and it is clear that these forms were confused in Tibullus I, 1, 49, and Lucan IX, 249.

[Col. 0130C] **401. *Quo***] Fabricius, the Antwerp edition, and the Library of Leiden have *quae* (“which”). Sedulius IV, 19 is almost identical:

“For he manages his own riches well, and wishes his treasures

to be stored in heaven, where whatever is possessed

is devoured neither by biting rust nor furrowed by moths.”

[Col. 0130C] **401. *Non***] The Cambridge manuscript has *nec* (“nor”).

[Col. 0130C] **403. *Quod***] The Cambridge manuscript, Fabricius, the Antwerp edition, and the Library of Leiden have *quae* (“which”).

[Col. 0130C] **404. *Sagaci***] Withof notes that Gunther expressed this in *Ligurinus* II, 421, in his *Critical Specimens of Gunther*, p. 45.

[Col. 0130D] **405. *Volve***] Vossianus 2 has *Volve. Quid* (“Consider. What?”), and this is not inappropriate.

[Col. 0130D] **405. *Quod***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *quoque* (“also”); the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian edition 1 have *quia* (“because”). If the manuscripts supported it, I would not reject it. See verse 83. In Luke’s Acts of the Apostles IV § 37, *χρῆμα* (“money, property”) is used for the pomp of wealth. For that word, in the singular, is sometimes used for resources and money, although *χρήματα* occurs more frequently. Thus the distinguished scholar explained the passage in Luke as referring to money, that is, money obtained from the sale, in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. X, p. 352. Pollux attributes this usage to the Ionians. See Koenius on Gregory of Corinth, *On Dialects*, p. 79. Compare also the elegant discussion by Pierson on Moeris, p. 411.

[Col. 0130D] **406. *Non debita***] Fabricius, with some others, printed *non sacris* (“not for sacred things”). The Aldine and Basel editions have *non tradita* (“not handed over”); the Antwerp edition, *non dedita* (“not given”).

[Col. 0130D] **407. *Destitui***] “To be despised and abandoned.” See the notes on Livy XXIII, 10 § 5. Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition therefore have *restitui* (“to be restored”) without justification.]

99 “He begins, and the people acquire one soul.”

[385] Who could doubt that the mysteries of the doctrine teach that the one God

is three persons? When thousands of common people

come together with one mind, and the minds of a great multitude

are like one man—this crowd, which will bear the enduring cross,

100 and, following the faithful Lord,

[390] has despised the fields, destined to possess the heavens: surely this power

is stronger—to seek the whole from a portion,

to weigh enduring things against the causes of things transitory,

and to pursue gain through losses. It is not you, seller of possessions,

who extravagantly squander them, but the man who desires ambitiously

to retain your rights,

[395] [Col. 0130A] and in a brief span abandon what you always wish to be yours.

Thus, to scatter the fields was to be unwilling to lose them.

For what benefit is property that perishes when preserved?

He who gives it up possesses it more advantageously,

when it is placed in the citadel of the stars. Ask from there, creditor,

[400] the help of greater interest, and store away your treasures,

where no misfortune can affect them; no accident destroys

101 your perpetual riches there. You will hold without end

what you make the Lord your debtor. Now consider the pious party,

learned reader, and with a discerning mind reflect on what you think it means

[405] that the display of shining metal is placed before the feet,

not owed to sacred hands; they prove that it ought to be abandoned,

because they avoid touching it,

[Col. 0131A] [Note: [Col. 0131B]

**408. *Calcandumque***] See verse 47.

[Col. 0131B] **410. *Avare***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *avara* (“greedy”), thus adding two adjectives to the noun *mens* (“mind”), which Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 392, indeed says is faulty. Nevertheless, Schrader, in his *Observations on Musaeus* chapter 12, and Burmann on Lotichius V, elegy 11, 37, and elegy 18, 47, show that this is not unusual, especially among poets. Boltius, *Critical Miscellanies*, p. 57, apparently did not condemn *δεσμοῖς ἀλύτοις ἀγρίοις* (“with savage, unbreakable bonds”) in Aeschylus; nor did Henri Estienne in his notes on *Prometheus Bound*, verse 154. Cicero, *For Milo* 2: “many noble merits”; Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* III, meter 8:

“Alas! by what misguided path the wretched wander.”

But from the manuscript and old edition I read *tramite devio* (“by a misguided path”). In the former passage, however, *heu, heu* (“alas, alas”) should be restored from the same witnesses, as will be clear from Burmann’s notes on Lotichius II, p. 467, and on Virgil, *Eclogues* 2, 58. Nor is the distinguished Burmann’s conjecture displeasing, which he proposed on Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 2, removing the two adjectives, in *Catalecta*, vol. I, p. 196.

[Col. 0131C] **414. *Tunc***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *te* (“you”).

[Col. 0131C] **415. *Parant***] The distinguished Wassenbergius emends this to *parat* (“prepares”), so that it refers to gold, which is also shortly afterward said to be “carrying gifts.”

[Col. 0131C] **417. *Decidit***] I printed this reading from the Cambridge manuscript and the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian edition 1. The others have *occidit* (“dies”). Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *cecidit* (“fell”). But *decidere* (“to fall away”) often occurs in the sense “to die,” and is frequently hidden under copyist corruptions. Burmann correctly restored it in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, 10; and in some manuscripts *deciderat* occurs in XIV, 805.

[Col. 0131C] **418. *Census***] The Library of Leiden has *sensus* (“sense”). See verse 211.

[Col. 0131C] **421. *Consensus***] Vossianus 2, the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian edition 1 have *consensum* (“agreement”).

[Col. 0131C] **421. *Nam***] The Antwerp edition has *non* (“not”). It undoubtedly arose from *nonne* (“is it not?”), so that the force of the sentence would be increased as a question. I supplied examples in *Specimen of Miscellaneous Observations* chapter 3, and from Greek authors in Majus, *Sacred Observations*, part I, p. 9.

[Col. 0131C] **422. *Sententia***] “Punishment.” See Wopkens on Sedulius V, 204.

[Col. 0131C] **423. *Amor***] “The accursed hunger for gold” occurs in Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 57; “the guilty love of possessing” in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 131. These passages support Drakenborch’s conjecture, who emended the reading in Priscian, *Periegesis* 704, to *dirum lucrum* (“dreadful gain”). It appears in the distinguished scholar’s notes on Silius XIV, 126. Claudian, *Against Rufinus* I, 188:

“Thus by waves of gold

that fever cannot be filled.”

Add Barthius, *Adversaria* LX, p. 2961.

[Col. 0131D] **424. *Capitur***] The ancients had already said that everything is subject to the same power. Martial I, epigram 77:

“What do you seek from Phoebus? The money chest holds coins:

this knows; this alone governs all the gods.”

Marckland emended the passage in his note on Statius, *Silvae* III, 3, 105; but Bauldri, on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, p. 133, defends the common reading. Add Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastic Authors*, p. 11.

[Col. 0131D] **425. *Radice***] This was said by Paul, First Epistle to Timothy VI § 10. Relevant here is Cassiodorus, *Variæ* IV, 39: “And divine reading also testifies that avarice is the root of all evils, and that it was punished in such a way that, although it seizes much, it is always in want.” Phocylides expressed the same thought in his *Sentences*, p. 101:

“The love of money is the mother of every wickedness.”

It is also called “the citadel of evil” (*ἀκρόπολις τῆς κακίας*). See Rhoer on Porphyry, *On Abstinence* I § 33. Add Barthius, *Adversaria* LIV, 4; on Claudian II, *Laudation of Stilicho*, 112; and Granger on Juvenal XIV, 173. Lycurgus abolished the use of gold and silver as the material, so to speak, of all crimes, according to Justin III, 2 § 12.

[Col. 0132B] **425. *Violentior***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *violentiaque* (“and violence”); the Cambridge, Aldine, and Tornesian edition 1 have *violentius* (“more violently”). But adjectives placed in the position of adverbs are sometimes corrupted in this way. Bondamius successfully restored several passages to their elegance in *Miscellaneous Readings* II, 13 note 9. I add one from Boethius, in whose *Consolation of Philosophy* I, prose 2, I emend from a manuscript: “which, unless you had previously cast away.”

[Col. 0132B] **427. *Famem***] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian edition 1 have *fame* (“by hunger”). The final syllable is sometimes read long, since the word was once of the fifth declension. See Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 25. Here *famem* (“hunger”) seems more strongly required by the sense, and is supported by the agreement of the manuscripts. Pacatus uses the word in a similar sense, *Panegyric* 25 § 6: “The hunger for possession grew daily, and what had been acquired stimulated the frenzy for obtaining.” I would prefer *praedandi rabiem* (“the frenzy for plundering”) there, from the Guelferbytanus manuscript; I also found the same reading in Vossius’s excerpts. Horace, III, ode 16, 18, has “the hunger of our ancestors.” Sedulius II, 264 has “the hunger for learning.” Our author below, verse 568, has “the hunger for virtue,” and II, 367, “the hunger for learning.” Likewise Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, meter 2, has “the thirst for possessing,” which he calls “the love of possessing” in meter 5. “To greedily yearn for things with thirst,” in Salvianus, *On the Government of God* IV, p. 76; and frequently in Weitz on the same author, p. 202. Thus *sitire* (“to thirst”) means “to desire intensely” below, II, 510 and 1063. Add Savaron on Sidonius, poem 9, 295; Barthius on Claudian, *Against Rufinus* I, 103; Elmenhorst on Arnobius, *Against the Nations* I, p. 18; and Heraldus, p. 24. Alberti compared the Greek *πεινᾷν* (“to hunger”) and *διψᾷν* (“to thirst”) with the Latin forms in his notes on the New Testament, p. 29; and Vriemoet did so in his notes on Matthew, p. 96. Aelian, *Various History* III, 7, has *ἀγορεύειν διψῶντας* (“to speak while thirsting”); and Athanasius, *Works*, vol. I, p. 306, is not without this elegance either.

[Col. 0132D] **428. *Cautio***] The scholia in Vossianus 2 explain it as “a confirmation, definition, or promise through the will itself, whatever that will may have been.” My good friend Wassenbergius correctly observes that *cautio* here is the same as *sponsio* (“pledge”) at verse 432. Sedulius II, 270:

“For the guarantee of one’s own word

holds those who make promises openly.”

There *cautio verbi* (“the guarantee of the word”) differs in no way from *cautio voti* (“the guarantee of the vow”).

[Col. 0132D] **429. *Prius***] The earlier vow, by which the promised thing was pledged, is to be violated and taken away by the later vow concerning the preservation of the thing.

[Col. 0132D] **430. *Proprium***] In the Cambridge manuscript the following was written: “A gloss of Remigius says: ‘It is more lawful to remove one’s own right than to retain it’; that is, it is better to divide than to preserve.” I fear this is not quite right. I think the meaning is: “It is more lawful to retain one’s right—that is, not to promise by a vow something that belongs to one’s own ownership—than to remove it, that is, to break the vow and the faith given by it.” This is the sense of Luke V § 4. The order of Arator’s words is more confused; arrange it as follows: “But it is more lawful to retain one’s own right than to remove it, because a changed will bears the guilt of falsehood, and because it is proper to stand firm and not wish to violate an earlier vow by a later one, when there is a guarantee of the vow.” Vossianus 2 punctuates it badly: “right; to retain what is one’s own.”]

They teach that the gold beneath their feet must be trampled;

from it earthly cares come to the heart; it is tossed about

[410] in like soil. Greedy man, learn at what point

your mind should stop; what you guard while panting,

what you press down in your station, what you burn to see more often,

102 into whose embrace you return through all your dreams—

the pious shudder to handle, nor do they carry it even then,

[415] when they prepare good works. How greatly they contemplate

the crime standing in that object! And gold, carrying gifts, is despised.

Unhappy Ananias falls, wounded by the blow of guilt,

a thief of his wealth under false pretenses; his impious wife falls,

[Col. 0132A] struck by an equal punishment, because from one crime

[420] a common evil is made whenever agreement makes

a previously committed crime one’s own. For that verdict

was the avenger of the greedy mind. In the end, when does

the love of gold cease? It burns the hearts continually,

103 by which the mortal race is ensnared, from which every evil

[425] grows, whose ambition burns more violently

as it increases, and the profits added to the plunder imitate hunger.

But since a changed will bears the guilt of falsehood,

104 and when there is already a guarantee of the vow

it is proper to stand firm, and not wish to violate the earlier vow by the later,

[430] it is more lawful to retain one’s own right than to remove it.”

[Col. 0133A] [Note: [Col. 0133B]

**431. *Sanxit***] “Confirmed, established.” Barthius on Claudian, *Laudation of Stilicho* IV, 573; on Statius, *Thebaid* V, 106. Justin III, 2 § 8: “He established nothing by any law concerning others”; two manuscripts of D’Orville, collated by Wopkens, have *in aliis* (“in other matters”).

[Col. 0133B] **432. *Sponsio***] If things have already been promised, they cannot be offered again as gifts, for by the promise they are already owed. Athanasius speaks excellently about this same matter, *Works*, vol. I, p. 993: “For one must know, and not be ignorant, that what we promise to God is no longer ours, but belongs to God; and if we withdraw it from these things, we are not taking it as though it were ours, but committing sacrilege against what belongs to God.” [ [Col. 0133D] Supply the article and read *ὡς τὰ ἡμῶν* (“as though they were ours”). EDITOR.]

[Col. 0133B] **433. *Fides***] The Library of the Fathers at Leiden has *vides* (“you see”). Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 316:

“Do not doubt; for you see the truth.”

But the other reading is defended by the notes of Heinsius there.

[Col. 0133C] **434. *Beato***] I printed this reading from the Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus 2. The Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian edition 1 have *beati* (“of the blessed”); most others have *dogmata* (“doctrines”).

[Col. 0133C] **435. *Probans***] “By proving, he decided that you should deceive.” Other editions punctuate: “Who persuaded you to deceive?” and then conclude: “proving human beings.”

[Col. 0133C] **435. *Homines***] Vossianus 1 has *hominem* (“a human being”). Luke has *ἀνθρώποις* (“human beings,” dative plural).

[Col. 0133C] **436. *Mentire***] This is the reading of Vossianus 2; Fabricius also printed it, and it is likewise found in the Antwerp edition. The others have *mentite*. The former better agrees with Luke’s words in Acts V § 4: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (*οὐκ ἐψεύσω ἀνθρώποις, ἀλλὰ τῷ Θεῷ*), where it is unnecessary, with some interpreters, to supply *μόνον* (“only”). See Duker on Thucydides IV, 92, p. 202. —The dative is added to the Greek verb in Greek fashion, as in the Vulgate, Ezekiel XIII § 19, and Hosea IX § 2. —Pagan writers likewise detested lying. Plutarch, *On the Education of Children* II, 16, at the end, judged it slavish and deserving of the hatred of all people, and thought that even ordinary slaves should not be pardoned for it. Aeschylus, however, in the *Fragments of the Ancient Pythagoreans*, in Thomas Gale’s *Mythological Treatises*, p. 720, says:

“God does not stand apart from righteous deception,

and there is an occasion for lies whenever God honors it.”

The latter seems to refer to what they call a “useful lie”; yet Cicero, *On Duties* III, 20, asks: “Does it befit a good man to lie for his own advantage, accuse, seize, or deceive? Surely nothing could be less fitting.”

[Col. 0133D] **436. *Quae***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *qui* (“who”).

[Col. 0133D] **439. *Tendimus***] The Aldine and Tornesian edition 1 have *tenditis* (“you go”). Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *tendimus ulti* (“we go, having taken vengeance”).

[Col. 0134B] **442. *Forma***] The scholia in Vossianus 2 add that Peter is called “the form of the Church.” Compare below, verse 667.

[Col. 0134B] **442. *Amare***] Perhaps *avare* (“greedily”).

[Col. 0134B] **444. *Fusa***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *fuso* (the masculine form agreeing with *alvus*, “belly”). For *alvus*, this gender was preferred by the older writers, Calvus and Cinna; others preferred the feminine form. See Oudendorp on Suetonius, *Vespasian* 24; Burmann the Younger on *Catalecta* III, p. 621. Vossius, *On Analogy* I, 31, prefers the latter. —On this death of Arius, compare Athanasius, *Works*, vol. I, pp. 301 and 844; Sedulius I, 287, and the notes there. —Jacobus Gronovius used these words of Arator in his *Exercise on Judas*, p. 184.
