I doubt whether he examined the passage, since he mixes everything according to his own judgment, joining to it what is read above at verse 90.

[Col. 0134B] **447. *Sequestrat***] “Separates, divides.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XIX, 12; on Statius, *Thebaid* II, 425; Sitzmann on Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 5. The same author, III, prose 1, has *sequestrari nequit* (“it cannot be separated”). Nevertheless, I would not deny to Falster, *Supplement to Faber’s Lexicon*, p. 317, that this may be of a later character.

[Col. 0134C] **448. *Par***] Livy speaks of a “partnership in guilt” in VI, 24 § 8.

[Col. 0134C] **449. *Diremit***] Arius had declared Christ to be different from the nature of the Father, and not *ὁμοούσιον* (“of the same substance”).

[Col. 0134C] **450. *Arbiter***] For poets, *arbiter* means the same as “king.” Seneca, *Hercules Furens*:

“At last, he says, the ruler of night: we conquer.”

Horace:

“Than whom no ruler of the Adriatic

is greater, whether he wishes to raise or lower the waves.”

Claudian:

“The greatest ruler

of night.”

Alcimus Avitus, Book II:

“Offended by such things, the judge and ruler of the world.”

Victorinus of Pettau:

“To you, greatest ruler

of the world, the sea makes its plea.”

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXV, 10. —Add his note on Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpine* I, 55; Sedulius II, 78:

“The savage ruler of the court

burns in the Hebrew palace.”

Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII, 6: “They affirm God to be creator, ruler, and judge”; thus the Groningen manuscript. Gothofredus incorrectly has “guardian.”

[Col. 0134D] **452. *His***] Vossianus 1 has *hic* (“this man”). But I see no one to whom *abstulit* (“he took away”) can be referred. The sentence is difficult, and I frankly confess that I do not sufficiently understand it.

[Col. 0134D] **454. *Fecerit***] The Cambridge manuscript has *fecerat* (“had made”).

[Col. 0134D] **457. *Suis***] Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition have *solo* (“alone”), and shortly afterward *orbis*. —He mentions beds, corresponding to Luke in Acts V § 15: “on beds and pallets” (*ἐπὶ κλινῶν, καὶ κραββάτων*). [Col. 0135B] By the two words he may have indicated that both the more powerful and the poorer were brought; for *grabatus* (“pallet”) was more appropriate to the latter, and *lectus* (“bed”) to the former. Compare Cicero’s passage in Bartholinus, *On Paralytics in the New Testament*, p. 387, vol. V of the *Philological Essays*. Add also p. 325 there. *Σκίμπους* (“couch”) differs in usage from *grabatus*; see Thomas Magister under that word.]

The punishment of the two established an example for all,

105 so that no one might call gifts what a pledged obligation demands.

Look to the true faith, clear in blessed doctrine,

and seek Peter’s words: “Who, then, persuaded you to deceive,

[435] and, by proving it, decided that you should deceive? You do not deceive

human beings by speaking such things—you lie to God.” What condemns

the wicked builds up the pious through instruction.

106 That the nourishing Spirit is God is fully demonstrated

in many books. And yet faith takes up weapons from this point:

where do we go beyond it? Who could doubt what Peter says?

Those who rightly come to the waters, stand in this place;

[440] it is sufficient to oppose the enemies that the form of the Church resounds:

divider, bitterly fear judgment concerning the end!

You are the author of crime

[Col. 0134A] and of your own error. Arius falls, his belly emptied,

[445] unhappy, falling still farther in mind, and, killed by death,

bore a common destruction with Judas, who, hanging by his throat,

dies emptied of his entrails; nor does punishment separate

those whom equal guilt binds, who prepare a wound against the honor

of majesty from their mouths. One betrayed; the other severed [him]

[450] by sacrilegious speech. God, ruler of the world,

107 exists in three persons, in whom there is simultaneously one power.

He took away from them the forms of works, created in goodness—

those who did not behold the beauty of the Maker,

and, going astray, think that the one who made everything was himself made.

[455] Rumor summons the peoples to hasten from every place

to the mysterious signs of salvation, and to carry the sick,

afflicted by diseases, on their own beds,

to that part of the city where Peter keeps the sacred footprints.”

[Col. 0135A] [Note: [Col. 0135B]

**460. *Daret***] The Cambridge manuscript has *darent* (“they might give”), certainly because of the two nouns; Cortius discussed this usage on Sallust, *Catiline* 47, at the end. —The poets’ similar idea is well known. Alcimus Avitus III, p. 391 of Fabricius’s corpus:

“Scarcely could anyone have even a hundred tongues, or a voice of iron.”

The uncertain author of *On the Praise of the Lord*, p. 767 of Fabricius’s corpus:

“Would that I had an iron voice and a thousand tongues

to sing.”

Add Savaron on Sidonius, poem 23, 459; the notes on Sedulius I, 83; especially Cerda on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 625, who thinks that ancient writers used the number one hundred because they believed a definite number was exposed to envy and the evil eye. Compare Taffin, *On the Secular Year*, chapter 1; and especially the well-known passage at the beginning of Persius’s fifth satire:

“This is the custom of prophets: to ask for a hundred voices,

a hundred mouths, and to wish for a hundred tongues for their poems.”

[Col. 0135C] **462. *Figuris***] See above, on verse 158.

[Col. 0135C] **463. *Grandia***] Horace, III, ode 3, at the end:

“Stop, stubborn one,

from recounting the words of the gods,”

and:

“To diminish great things by small measures.”

[Col. 0135C] **471. *Furtivaque***] “What they did not know,” that is, “unknown things.” See Barthius on Claudian, *The Nuptials of Honor and Genius*, p. 778; and on *Against Eutropius* I, 88, where *furtum* means something done secretly. Thus Popma, in his note on Velleius II, 63 § 1, explains “a pontiff created secretly.” Casaubon similarly explained *κλέπτειν* (“to steal”) in his *Observations on Athenaeus* I, 15.

[Col. 0135D] **473. *Rapit***] “Carries away.” Salvianus, *On the Government of God* III, p. 43: “unless, insofar as we can, if circumstances permit, we seize everything from them.” This verb seems especially to have been used to indicate speed, for that meaning is inherent in it. Barthius on Claudian, *Against Eutropius* I, 375.

[Col. 0135D] **475. *Splendoris***] The glosses in Vossianus 2 say that this is the same as the “shadow of light” above.

[Col. 0135D] **477. *Donis***] Here too the meaning is not entirely clear. The glosses in Vossianus 2 explain: “It consists in miracles.” He seems to indicate that the power of the deed consisted in the gift itself, or in the miracle, although it was not apparent in what manner this occurred.

[Col. 0135D] **478. *Toros***] The Cambridge manuscript has *toris* (“on couches”). Since the healed left their beds as witnesses to their restored health, the common reading is preferable.

[Col. 0135D] **478. *A sensibus***] Vossianus 1 has *et sensibus* (“and from the senses”). By “enemies” and “dark things to the senses” one could understand those whom the devil had driven astray. See above, verse 40. The conjunction *que* is often used in this way, followed by *et*, to join two things. Copyists nevertheless frequently corrupted this elegance. Thus my father correctly conjectures in Aurelius Victor, *Caesars* 20, 5, *tenuique et indocto* (“by the slight and unlearned man”). Compare also his notes on the *Epitome* 1 § 13 and 8 § 3; Drakenborch on Livy X, 30 § 2 and XXIX, 12 § 5. Nevertheless, I have retained *a sensibus* here, and the sense requires it.

[Col. 0136B] **479. *Larvalibus***] *Larvae* are disturbances such as occur in the imagination in darkness; hence *larvalis* (“ghostly”). Fabricius, commentary, p. 77. —The Cambridge manuscript has *larvaribus*. Agesilaus Mariscottus, *Syntagma on Persons*, vol. IX of Graevius’s *Thesaurus*, p. 1110, teaches that *larva* denotes an empty terror. [Col. 0136C] Hence *nebulae larvales* (“ghostly mists”) could mean “frightful,” like *species larvalis* (“a ghostly appearance”), discussed by Swartius, *Analecta* III, 11. Add Elmenhorst’s index to Apuleius; or it may specifically refer to the demon, which darkens the human mind as though with mists so that it cannot discern the truth. Thus Augustine called the expulsion of the evil spirit “ghostly purification” in Letter 2, p. 3.

[Col. 0136C] **480. *Frequentans***] The scholia in Vossianus 2 explain it as “going around in motion.”

[Col. 0136C] **482. *Adde***] He imitates Lucan IV, 759:

“Nor now do they add a step, either compelled by whips and goads,

or, though ordered, by however frequent spurs.”

He explained the expression at greater length, with no forgetfulness of our author, Heinsius on Virgil, *Georgics* I, 513.

[Col. 0136C] **482. “Joys” (*Gaudia*)**] Vossianus 1 has *grandia*, “great things.”

[Col. 0136C] **486. “Silent” (*Tacens*)**] I preferred this reading from the Cambridge manuscript and the Aldine, Basel, and Tornesian editions. All the others, both manuscripts and printed editions, have *jacens*, “lying down.” Since the subject concerns sick people, that reading is not inappropriate, as I showed in my notes on Sedulius III, 97; and Elsner explained *κατακεῖσθαι* (“to lie down”) in his notes on the Gospel of Mark I, 30. It is also clear from the notes on Sedulius II, 227, and IV, 88, that these readings were often confused. Here, however, *tacens* seems preferable. The crowd had received health solely from Peter’s shadow, without using any prayers for that purpose. Luke also indicates this in Acts V, § 25, saying that the sick were brought only on beds, “so that the shadow might overshadow some one of them” (*ἵνα σκιὰ ἐπισκιάσῃ τινὶ αὐτῶν*). On this expression see the learned Segaar on Luke’s Gospel, p. 44. He therefore contrasts this silent crowd with the man who had obtained health through prayers; I believe the latter is the man described in Acts chapter III. The crowd is called silent all the more appropriately because it was unaware of the prayer.

*Sumere* here is used for *accipere*, “to receive.” Sedulius III, 165:

> You have received freely; bestow on all freely.

Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II, 41, § 4, has “the desire to receive what you ask for.” In his unpublished notes Wopkens adds passages from Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, 3; Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 2; and the Vulgate translator on James III, § 1.

>

[Col. 0137A] **[Note: [Col. 0137B]**

**487. “For all” (*Omnibus*)**] This verse is absent from the Cambridge manuscript and from the Aldine and Basel editions. Vossianus 2 has it written at the bottom of the page. I do not think it belongs to Arator, nor does it properly cohere with what precedes; I have therefore enclosed it in brackets. Who is that one who asks? Surely it is not the man mentioned in Acts chapter III, for he was not the cause of salvation for everyone.

In any case, the use of *venibat* for *veniebat* is sufficiently supported by the evidence cited by Vossius, *Ars grammatica* V, 34; Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, p. 609; and Burmann on Ovid, *Heroides* XVI, 36.

[Col. 0137B] **489. “Typical” (*Typicum*)**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *typii*; perhaps the printers intended to set *typici*. See the note on Sedulius I, 102.

[Col. 0137B] **490. “Has been granted” (*Cessa est*)**] I printed this form from the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1 and 2, and the Antwerp edition. The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *soli est concessa*, “has been granted to Peter alone”; the others have *soli concessa haec*, “this has been granted to Peter alone.” That the genuine text of Arator has been restored will be clear from the notes on the final verse of Florianus and above on verse 301.

[Col. 0137C] **491. “May remain hidden” (*Lateant*)**] The Cambridge, Antwerp, and Fabrician editions have *latitant*, “may lurk.”

[Col. 0137C] **493. “Arid” (*Aridus*)**] “So that I, myself hardly endowed with eloquence, may recount a great matter.” *Aridus* refers to thin and meager diction. Gronovius explained “arid declaimers” in his notes on Seneca, *Controversies* V, p. 393. Thus Heinsius emended a passage in Petronius, *Satyricon* 2: “the body of the speech would be weakened and grow arid.” Add Ernesti, *Clavis Ciceroniana*, under the word; he also cited Gronovius. I noted the same metaphor on verse 124.

[Col. 0137C] **496. “What is perceived” (*Sensa*)**] Cortius explains it in the margin as “that which is perceived.”

[Col. 0137C] **496. “And follows” (*Sequiturque*)**] The Cambridge manuscript and the Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *sequiturque a*. Vossianus 2 has *sequitur quae a corpore*. Nearly all editions have this reading. Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *sequitur quam corpore*. My text comes from Vossianus 1 and was certainly corrupted by scribes who could not tolerate *que* before *et*. I discussed this above on verse 478.

[Col. 0137D] **499. “On earth” (*Terris*)**] Withovius, *Specimen* of Gunther, p. 157, emends this to *in terris*. The change is less necessary because prepositions are frequently omitted. The learned Schrader has already defended the soundness of the transmitted text in his *Observations on Musaeus*, chapter 16, p. 277. Arator himself uses the same construction above, verse 140: “the dove from the river Jordan.” The same defense may be offered for Paul’s *Sentences* V, title 28, § 3: “one man defends his life, another his honor, by a public crime.” On this passage see my Cannegieter on Ulpian’s *Fragments* I, § 18. If one thinks an emendation necessary, replace it with *in publico*, “in public.” The words were explained by the learned Vryhovius in *Observations on Law*, chapter 21. In *potuit* the first letter may have concealed an *m*, which also caused Withovius to tamper with Arator’s passage. It will be clear from the notes on Sedulius II, 169 and 235, that this error occurred frequently. Thus the Trajectine manuscript has *speciem intueri* in Cicero, *On the Orator* II, 52, where the common text has *tueri*. In Martial, *Spectacles*, epigram 27, Farnabius printed:

> Now there would have been no need of monsters in the world.

Other copies have *in monstris*. The learned van Hoven recognized the same origin of the error in his *Propempticon to Anton de Roy*, p. 9. But I cannot determine what he means when he adds that Martial would otherwise have written *orbi*. If I may reach the truth by conjecture, Martial did not write it that way so as to avoid violating the metrical quantity.

[Col. 0138B] **499. “To none” (*Nulli*)**] Vossianus 1 and 2 have *nullis*, as do several printed editions. The Cambridge manuscript has *nullum*. The result is the same.

[Col. 0138B] **500. “Aetherial” (*Aetheream*)**] Fabricius too, and all the editions I have seen, have this form. Correct it by dividing the words into a single, slightly emended line:

> We worship on earth the Church, which none may betray;
>
> and it is permissible to have doubted the true one, but truer is that  
> which, remaining above the stars, is called heavenly and lofty.

If the author himself did not confirm this emendation in the words immediately following, with greater clarity than sunlight, we could say more. Withof, *Specimen* of Gunther, p. 157.

This conjecture is especially attractive, unless one thinks that *on earth* and *aetherial* are set in opposition, as shortly afterward in verse 517:

> This, which we see cultivated in the fields,
>
> is therefore a figure: firm is what the clouds bear.

Nothing, however, varies in the manuscripts. There is only uncertainty in Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition. The alternative is more customary among poets, as in verse 540:

> Which it would have been wrong to have doubted.

[Col. 0138C] **503. “Life” (*Vitam*)**] Thus in the Cambridge manuscript; in Vossianus 1 the text is *ad vitae datur esse via*, “a way is given for life to exist.” The editions have *ad vitae datur esse viam*. Compare verse 118 above. Meanwhile, Wassenberg’s conjecture, certainly ingenious, appeals to me greatly:

> Through this, which is seen in passing across the doubtful world,
>
> a way is given to have gone toward life.

The ease of this emendation will be clear from Brouckhusius on Tibullus I, 10, 36; the notes on Sedulius V, 2; and Cannegieter on Ulpian’s *Fragments*, title 1, § 8.

[Col. 0138D] **503. “That” (*Isto*)**] Vossianus 1 has *ipso*, “that very.”

[Col. 0138D] **504. “Eternal” (*Aeternae*)**] Vossianus 2, in a second hand, has *aeternis*, “eternal” in the plural.

[Col. 0138D] **506. “Led” (*Ductis*)**] Absent from Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition. Some editions have *sortis*, incorrectly.

[Col. 0138D] **508. “Thus” (*Sic*)**] Vossianus 1 has *seu*, “or.”

[Col. 0138D] **509. “Cultivated” (*Culta*)**] The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *cuncta*, “all things.” I formerly thought a word was required to stand in opposition to *firma*, “firm,” in the following line. But Arator himself seems to defend his wording in verse 499:

> We worship the Church on earth.

I think he means that the Church cultivated on earth is a figure of the one that is in heaven.

[Col. 0138D] **510. “Would be” (*Foret*)**] Vossianus 1 has *fuit*, “was.”

[Col. 0138D] **510. “Which” (*Quam*)**] The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *qua*, “by which.”]

[Col. 0139A] **[Note: [Col. 0139C]**

**511. “Both” (*Utramque*)**] The Aldine, Basel, and other editions have *utrumque*, “both” in the neuter.

[Col. 0139C] **512. “Will have loosed” (*Resolverit*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *resolveret*, “would loose.”

[Col. 0139C] **513. “May be led” (*Ducantur*)**] The Cambridge manuscript, Fabricius, and the Lyon Bible have: “and whom … the innocent are led.”

[Col. 0139C] **517. “With the heart” (*Corde*)**] The learned Wassenberg’s conjecture, *quo corda metant*, “with which they may reap hearts,” is elegant. Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition support it, having *quod corda*, “which [the] hearts.” Thus he soon mentions hoes, and the passages read immediately above at verse 365 closely correspond.

[Col. 0139C] **518. “Hoes” (*Sarcula*)**] The Basel and first Tornesian editions have *surcula*, “shoots.”

[Col. 0139C] **520. “Caves” (*Antra*)**] Vossianus 1 and 2 and the Antwerp edition have *astra*, “stars.” I would change nothing because of verse 523; and in Vossianus 2 the scribe himself seems to have read *antra*, since he interpreted it as “the dark places of the prison.”

[Col. 0139C] **521. “At an unfamiliar time” (*Alieno*)**] Virgil likewise said *alienos menses*, “foreign months,” in *Georgics* II, 149, where Cerda remarks that Arator seems to have supposed that they went out to the temple while it was still night. Luke records that this happened “at dawn” (*ὑπὸ τὸν ὄρθρον*). Among the ancient Greeks, *ὄρθρος* certainly denotes the time near sunrise, when it is not yet daylight. But Luke, following the later meaning, seems rather to have understood the time when morning was already clearly present. Salmasius explained it in precisely this way, *Hellenistic Studies*, p. 102.

[Col. 0139D] **524. “Battlement” (*Crepidine*)**] This meaning of the word is rare. It seems to designate the bonds mentioned in verse 1050. The metaphor may have been taken from a sea-wall, by which the violence of the sea is broken, just as such prison bonds withstand every assault. On *crepido* see Bertius, *On Embankments and Bridges*, chapter 10.

[Col. 0139D] **528. “Denies” (*Negat*)**] Sedulius IV, 8:

> And whatever nature denies.

Add Barthus, *Adversaria* XVII, 9.

[Col. 0139D] **530. “To be able” (*Posse*)**] This periphrasis was discussed at length above in the note on the letter to Florianus, verse 15. Here it is enough to add Luke’s passage, Gospel XVI, § 2: *οὐ γὰρ δυνήσῃ ἔτι οἰκονομεῖν*, which should be translated, “you will no longer dispense or administer.” I now see that Pricaeus also approved this translation; I entirely agree with him in the more difficult passage in Mark VI, § 5: *οὐκ ἐδύνατο ἐκεῖ οὐδεμίαν δύναμιν ποιεῖν*, which he translates, “he did not perform.” Matthew’s parallel passage sufficiently confirms this point.

[Col. 0140C] **531. “Still” (*Adhuc*)**] Vossianus 1 has *ad hoc*, “for this.”

[Col. 0140C] **535. “Which” (*Quae*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *quem*, “whom.”

[Col. 0140C] **536. “May raise up” (*Suscitet*)**] Vossianus 1 has *suscitat*, “raises up.”

[Col. 0140C] **539. “You learn” (*Discis*)**] Vossianus 1 has *disce*, “learn.” This also seems to have originally stood in Vossianus 2, but a later hand altered it.

[Col. 0140C] **541. “For us” (*Nobis*)**] The Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, Fabricius’s editions, the Antwerp edition, and the Lyon Bible have *vobis*, “for you.”

[Col. 0140C] **543. “Darkness” (*Tenebras*)**] The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *latebras*, “hiding places.” But *tenebrae*, “darkness,” is used for a dark place. The Vulgate translator of Matthew XXII, § 13, has “cast him into the darkness.” See Vossius, *Institutions of Oratory* IV, 7, § 10.

[Col. 0140C] **546. “From the house” (*Domo*)**] Vossianus 1 and 2, in the first hand, have *domu*, an ancient case form. It is also found in manuscripts of Livy I, 1, § 4, and VII, 31, § 3. See Vossius, *Ars grammatica* IV, 20, and Joan Cannegieter on Ulpian’s *Fragments*, p. 41.

[Col. 0140C] **546. “Holds back” (*Retentat*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *retentet*, “may hold back.” It is used for *retinere*, “to hold back,” as in Virgil, *Aeneid* V, 278:

> The crippled part holds back because of the wound.

Burmann remarks: “Thus Barthus explains Claudian, *Consulate of Manlius* 293, mindful of Maro.”

[Col. 0140D] **547. “Whom” (*Quos*)**] Vossianus 1 has *quos lumen ipsa lux*, “whom the light itself, the light.”

[Col. 0140D] **550. “Darkness” (*Tenebras*)**] Vossianus 1 presents the passage not inelegantly in this form:

> Concerning whom, when errors had been driven into darkness, the world
>
> conquered and deserved to know the eternal light.

I would almost attribute this to Arator.

[Col. 0140D] **552. “Rights” (*Jura*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *cura*, “care.” In these verses Bede notes a very pleasing concatenation, *On Metres*, p. 2326, in Putsch’s grammarians.

[Col. 0140D] **552. “Ministry” (*Ministerii*)**] Pignorius shows that the term was derived from *ministerium mensae*, “service of the table,” in *On Slaves*, p. 103. Add the remarks on the beginning of the letter to Florianus. For *ministrare* means to attend upon a diner and carry out his orders; Barthus discusses this at length in *Adversaria* II, 16. I would preserve this reading in Isidore VII, 11, where, concerning Stephen, the text says: “because he was first in ministry, as an example to the faithful.” The Groningen manuscript has *in martyrio*, “in martyrdom.”

[Col. 0140D] **552. “Suitable” (*Apti*)**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *aptis*, “suitable” in the plural.]

> so that those whom here he has freed from harmful sins and faults

[Col. 0141A] **[Note: [Col. 0141B]**

**553. “They divided” (*Secuere*)**] Pulmann’s papers, the Antwerp, Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *statuere*, “they appointed”; the later edition additionally has *viris*, “for men.”

[Col. 0141B] **553. “From everywhere” (*Undique*)**] He seems to have understood that they had been chosen from different Jews, whether Alexandrians or those born in Judea. The Greek names recorded by Luke led some people to the same opinion.

[Col. 0141B] **554. “Levites” (*Levitas*)**] A Levite, or *Levites*, is a minister of the high priest, a *flamen* among the Romans, and a deacon among the Greeks; the name derives from Levi, the third son of the patriarch Jacob. Arator I:

> The rights of ministry suited to the sacred altars,
>
> he divided among seven men, whom, chosen from everywhere,
>
> it is pleasing to call Levites.

We have cleansed this passage, which had generally been corrupted, from Bede. Prudentius, *Stephen*:

> Here is the first of the seven men
>
> who stand nearest the altar,
>
> the exalted Levite.

The same author:

> Vincentius, a Levite of the sacred tribe,
>
> minister of God’s altar,
>
> one of the seven from the milk-white columns.

Drepanius, hymn 1:

> Born from the sacred blood of Levites.

Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 79.

Isidore, *Etymologies* VII, 12: “Levites are called from the name of their founder. For from Levi the Levites arose, through whom the mysteries of the mystical sacrament were fulfilled in God’s temple.” Gothofredus has this form, but I would rather emend it from the Groningen manuscript to “the ministries of the sacrament.” See the note on verse 552. These two words were frequently corrupted. Demster rightly corrected a passage of Cassiodorus in his notes on Rosinus V, 5. Add also my father’s note on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 49, § 8. Salmasius aptly restored *ministerium*, “ministry,” for *mysterium*, “mystery,” in his notes on Solinus, *Polyhistor*, p. 8; this is confirmed by the comparison of a manuscript in my possession. Conversely, the same manuscript, together with others, correctly has *mysterium* for *ministerium* in the same author, p. 11.

[Col. 0141D] **554. “Splendid” (*Splendida*)**] The Cambridge manuscript has *splendide*, “splendidly.”

[Col. 0141D] **555. “Which” (*Quae*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *qui*, “who.”

[Col. 0141D] **557. “For this” (*Huic*)**] The Aldine, Basel, Antwerp, and first Tornesian editions have *hoc*, “this.”

[Col. 0141D] **558. “Which” (*Quae*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *quem*, “whom,” referring it to *honor*, “honor.” It rather belongs to *sacramenta*, that is, “mysteries,” which Arator was exceedingly eager to investigate, though here, being concerned with brevity, he omits them. I wish he had omitted them more often. Prudentius uses *sacramentum* in the same sense, *Peristephanon* X, 588:

> I know that you are incapable of the sacrament, impious man,
>
> and cannot take in our mystery with blind senses.

In Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius, p. 11, *sacramentum evangelicae doctrinae*, “the sacrament of evangelical teaching,” is explained by a gloss in the Almeloveen manuscript as *mysterium*, “mystery.” What Paul calls *μυστήριον* in his Letter to the Ephesians I, § 9, the Vulgate translator renders *sacramentum*. See also chapter III, § 3. In general, Vorstius notes on Sulpicius Severus II, *Sacred History* 39, § 5, that this word refers to the weightier doctrines of the Christian religion.

[Col. 0142B] **558. “Now” (*Nunc*)**] The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *me*, “me.”

[Col. 0142B] **559. “Of the way” (*Viae*)**] See the note on Sedulius I, 266.

[Col. 0142B] **559. “Having spoken” (*Locutus*)**] Gunther, *Ligurinus* I, 273:

> I fear that by saying much
>
> I may be found to have said too little;

an imitation of Arator, as Withof notes in *Specimen* of Gunther, p. 37. Compare Sallust, *Jugurthine War* 19, § 2: “I think it better to be silent about Carthage than to speak inadequately, since time urges us to hasten elsewhere.” Compare Cortius’s note there.

[Col. 0142C] **560. “May be” (*Sit*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *si*, “if.”

[Col. 0142C] **561. “To weigh” (*Librare*)**] *Librare consilia*, “to weigh deliberations,” occurs in Ammianus Marcellinus XVIII, 2, at the end. Barthus notes on Claudian, *Panegyric on Stilicho* I, 75, and on Statius, *Thebaid* VIII, 288, that the word is used for “to assess” and, more precisely, “to weigh carefully.”

[Col. 0142C] **562. “This” (*Hunc*)**] The Cambridge manuscript has *nunc*, “now,” through the frequent interchange of letters discussed in the note on Sedulius III, 302, and verse 321. Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *hunc decet hinc*, “this one is fitting from here”; the Basel edition has *hunc doceat*, “may teach this one.”

[Col. 0142C] **563. “Heavenly things” (*Coelestia*)**] Vossianus 2 has *Ecclesiae*, “of the Church.” The scholiast explains it as “spiritual things.”

[Col. 0142C] **565. “Is pleasing” (*Convenit*)**] This correctly translates *ἀρεστόν*, which Luke has in chapter 6, § 2.

[Col. 0142C] **571. “May be for the people” (*Populo sint*)**] The Basel, Aldine, and first Tornesian editions incorrectly transpose this as *sint populo*, “may the people have.”

[Col. 0142C] **572. “And widely” (*Lateque*)**] I printed this from Vossianus 1 and 2 and the Antwerp edition; all the others have *lauteque*, “and sumptuously.” *Lautus* is indeed attributed to lavish banquets; see the notes on Petronius, *Satyricon* 26; Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VII, 14; and Heinsius on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, 762. But *late*, “widely,” belongs no less well here. Horace, *Satires* II, 2, 113:

> I have known no one to use his intact resources more generously.

Bentley there notes the contrasting expression *anguste uti*, “to use narrowly.” Cicero metaphorically called a meager mind “narrow” in *Philippics* 14, 6. Heinsius tried to free Florus III, 9, § 5, from a similar error by reading *lautius aerarium*, “a richer treasury.” Learned men nevertheless rightly defend *latius*, “more broadly.”

[Col. 0142D] **573. “Fatness” (*Pinguedo*)**] Others call it *pinguitudo*, a more Latin form, and that word has been restored in the better texts of the authors. Compare Duker on the *Opusculum concerning the Latinity of the Jurists*, p. 370. Vossius nevertheless defends *pinguedo* in *On the Purity of Speech* VII, p. 364. Noltenius discusses the passage of Pliny used in this connection in his *Antibarbarus Lexicon*, p. 664.

[Col. 0142D] **578. “Lest” (*Ne*)**] The Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions have *ut*, “so that.”]

> They divided them among seven men, chosen from everywhere,
>
> whom it is pleasing to call Levites. How splendidly
>
> [555] **117** the hand of the Church began to shine! It mixes the cups of life
>
> and offers the liquid together with the blood of the Lamb.
>
> The honor conferred upon this number carries with it sublime
>
> mysteries, through which the measure of the road now prevents me
>
> from going farther, lest, speaking too much,
>
> [560] **118** I be found to have said too little. Let the ministers take care
>
> to weigh their office, so that this choir may shine
>
> in the garment of praise that suits it, a choir consecrated

>
> I shall keep the promised limit. The venerable assembly says to the world:

>
> of the apostolic mouth! Never to allow the people

> money entrusted to a tongue displeased him when it stood alone.

>

>
> and that the fatness of heavenly speech nourishes the learned mind

>
> **119** For what benefit are bodily foods,
>

>

>

>

[Col. 0143A] **[Note: [Col. 0143A]**

**579. “He should abandon” (*Deserat*)**] He would be forced to abandon them.

[Col. 0143A] **579. “Whoever” (*Quisquis*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *quibus et*, “and by which.”

[Col. 0143A] **580. “Let food bring” (*Ferat*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *nam fecerat esca*, “for food had made”; this is contrary to the meter.

[Col. 0143B] **584. “Having been left” (*Relicta*)**] By the twelve apostles, who had left that ministry to the seven deacons to administer.

[Col. 0143B] **585. “The superior number” (*Supernum*)**] You could scarcely discover by conjecture what he intended. I believe that by *supernum numerum*, “the superior number,” he understood the twelve apostles: the precious cause, that is, the preaching of the Gospel, was more valuable than service at the table, and the apostles surpassed the deacons even in number. I would explain *tenere* as “to possess” or “to obtain”; see Drakenborch on Livy XXIII, 20, § 10.

[Col. 0143B] **586. “Contest” (*Agone*)**] *Ἀγών* has three meanings. First, the contest that each person sustains in his own office. Arator II:

> Here I shall be given the chance to contend
>
> in the struggle of varied contests.

Then the contest of martyrs in enduring tortures and punishment. The same author I:

> From here Stephen leaps forth, who first in the contest
>
> has the crown, an heir of this man.

Prudentius, *Stephen*:

> That force, exercised through the deaths
>
> of so many guilty men,
>
> accomplishes nothing in this contest.

Finally, it means the struggle of the spirit at the final moment, when a person is already giving up his soul. Juvencus IV:

> A messenger arriving tells us that, at the point of death,
>
> the young man beloved by Christ lies dying.

Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 3.

The Aldine, Basel, Antwerp, and first Tornesian editions have *primus qui in agone*, “the first who in the contest.” In the word *coronam*, “crown,” he alludes to Stephen’s name; thus *coronare* and *στεφανοῦν* may be used of any honor. See De Rhoer on Porphyry, *On Abstinence* II, § 24; add the note on Sedulius II, 253.

[Col. 0143C] **587. “Of the name” (*Nominis*)**] I restored this from the manuscripts and better printed editions. Others read *haeres hujus*, “heir of this man.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV, 819:

> And his own son, heir of his name,

and *Fasti* I, 615:

> With the gods as sponsors, heir of so great a surname.

See the note on Sedulius I, 162.

[Col. 0143D] **588. “Battles” (*Praelia*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *praemia*, “rewards.” But expressions such as *serere praelia*, “to wage battles,” and *serere bella*, “to wage wars,” occur frequently. See the notes on Silius I, 394, and Burmann on the *Catalecta* I, p. 175.

[Col. 0143D] **589. “Punishment” (*Poena*)**] *Est*, “is,” is added in the Aldine, Basel, and first Tornesian editions.

[Col. 0143D] **590. “Origin” (*Ortus*)**] Vossianus 1 has *palma*, “palm,” apparently from a gloss.

[Col. 0143D] **590. “With openings” (*Patentibus*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *parantibus*, “preparing”; the Aldine, first Tornesian, and Lyon Bible have *parentibus*, “parents.” The common reading is supported by Ovid, *Heroides* VIII, 53:

> And Aegisthus with his throat exposed;

and *Metamorphoses* XIII, 693:

> This breast, not womanly, to strike with exposed throat.

Lucan VI, 555:

> Let him burst forth first with exposed throat.

Arator seems generally to have taken the expression for violent slaughter; for Stephen cannot be said to have been “throat-cut.”

[Col. 0144B] **592. “The beginning of life” (*Vitae principium*)**] This verse is absent from the manuscripts, except that in Vossianus 1 it has been pushed down to verse 595, perhaps written at the bottom of the page. I do not think it belongs to Arator, and therefore enclosed it in brackets. The following verse coheres properly with the preceding one, indicating that the rewards were of eternal life, so that he deserved to die in this way.

[Col. 0144B] **594. “You seize” (*Rapis*)**] This passage might support Marckland’s emendation of Lysias, *Oration* IX, p. 554. In Acts VII, § 58, he conjectures that one should read *ἐλιθολόγουν* or *ἐλιθοφόρουν*, “they were collecting stones” or “they were carrying stones.” He ingeniously suspects a corruption in *ἐλιθοβόλουν*, “they were throwing stones,” because the same verb is repeated shortly afterward in § 59; Luke would otherwise seem to have said the same thing twice. Yet the first *ἐλιθοβόλουν* could be understood of intention, the second of result, a possibility that did not escape Marckland.

I would certainly prefer to translate Luke’s words: “and, driving him outside the city, they wanted, or intended, to stone him.” The use of the imperfect in this sense is elegant in both Greek and Latin. See Wesseling on Herodotus I, p. 34, and Wopkens, *Miscellaneous Observations* V, p. 305. Thus someone is often said to have done something when he merely attempted it. Accordingly, *ἐνέδραν ποιοῦντες* in Acts XXV, § 3, is correctly translated by Marckland in his notes on Lysias, p. 550, as “intending to lay an ambush.” Add Schulting on Seneca, *Controversies*, p. 115, and Duker on Florus I, 18, § 12.

It should be added that the later *ἐλιθοβόλουν* refers to the witnesses, and that the words should be translated “who stoned Stephen.” For the witnesses threw the first stones at the accused, and *καὶ* often has the same force as *ὅς*, “who.” Thus in Acts VI, § 6, *καὶ προσευξάμενοι* should be translated “who had prayed,” referring it to the apostles. The learned Schacht correctly explains this in *Bremen Biblical Miscellany*, new series, class 2, fascicle 3, p. 482, as does Segaar on Luke, p. 166. I now see that Duker has cited him in his notes on Thucydides VIII, p. 548; he should certainly be consulted.

[Col. 0144C] **595. “Stony” (*Saxea*)**] John of Salisbury calls the Jews a hardened people, harder than any stone, in II, 7, at the end; and the expression is conventional for harsh people whom one cannot easily move. The Greeks call such people *λιθίνοι*, “stony.” Duport brought together several relevant passages in his notes on Theophrastus, *Characters*, p. 464. Add *Miscellaneous Observations* V, p. 61. Thus *λίθοι*, “stones,” is understood by some in Luke’s Gospel XIX, § 40, where Pricaeus comments; although in that passage I especially approve the opinion of the very learned man who explains it as referring to stones and the ruins of the temple destroyed by the Romans.

Pareus, *Selected Notes on Plautus*, p. 354; Heraldus on Arnobius II, p. 76; Savaro on Sidonius IV, letter 23, and V, letter 7, likewise show that people are called stones. Hence a heart of stone is attributed to them. Vriemoet, *Classical Dictionary* II, p. 273. Poets say that such people were born from rocks or have flints in their breasts. Ciofanus collected the passages on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII, 32. They are also called *rupices*, “rock-like”: Rittershusius on Salvian, p. 13; Elmenhorst, *Index to Apuleius*, under *RUPICONES*. Festus shows that they are also called *petrones*, “rock-men.” Sedulius uses a similar metaphor when he calls a man “wooden” in I, 252; Wopkens there did not neglect Arator.]

> Let him not abandon the blessed couches, withdrawn from them,
>
> whoever comes to that table deformed, with filthy speech.
>
> [580] Let food bring salvation as it advances from the bread of heaven;
>
> let the throat of the heart surround it, and let the inner man
>
> hasten to taste it with the full palate of the soul. Let it not be
>
> thought that the cause left to illustrious ministers was therefore
>
> of lesser worth to be handled;
>
> [585] it is entrusted, and the precious cause held the higher number.
>
> From here Stephen leaps forth, who first in the contest possesses
>
> the crown, heir of the name, concerning whom a voice foretold
>
> the palm of victory and gave the cause: “Wage battles, martyr,
>
> battles that will bring blessed deaths, where glory is punishment,
>
> [590] and falling is origin; with exposed throats life is born,
>
> embracing the gifts of eternal life—
>
> [The beginning of blessed life was without end—]
>
> thus he deserved to die.” O rebellious Judea, in a frenzy
>
> you seize stones and hurl them at Stephen; because of your hard crime
>
> you will always be stony. Finally Christ adopts him,

[Col. 0145A] **[Note: [Col. 0145B]**

**597. “And desiring” (*Cupiensque*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition delete *que*, “and.” The omission of this particle has often caused textual disturbances. In Justin XII, 6, § 8, “having first burst into tears, he proceeded to embrace the dead man … turned the weapon he had seized against himself,” Boltius thinks, in *Critical Sylvae*, p. 108, that *deinde*, “then,” has fallen out before *arreptum*, “having seized.” It should rather be written *arreptumque*, “and having seized,” which I found in two manuscripts of the Franeker library and three of D’Orville’s, collated for me by Wopkens.

Ambrose, *Duties* I, 39, has likewise been corrupted: “he repels anger as though with certain weapons, which removes prudence, and avoids it as though it were a sickness.” Write it entirely according to my manuscript: “may he repel it with rams and weapons, and remove abuse as though it were a sickness,” and so forth.

[Col. 0145B] **597. “For rewards” (*In praemia*)**] Florus II, 6, § 23, has *in sacramentum militiae liberata servitia*, “freed slaves for the military oath.” For the elegant use of this preposition, see Duker on the same author II, 15, § 10, and IV, 7, § 13; Burmann on the *Catalecta* II, p. 271. Thus Oudendorp explained *facere in usus*, “to make for uses,” in his notes on Suetonius, *Domitian* 7. Likewise, in law 31 of the *Codex* concerning the Julian Law on Adultery, *nubit in feminam* means “she marries a woman,” that is, “so that she may be a woman and perform her part.” Ruhnkenius, the very distinguished scholar, appears to hold the same opinion about this passage in his notes on Rutilius Lupus II, p. 96.

To strengthen the point I add a passage of Orosius concerning Nero, book VII, chapter 7: “he took a man as his wife.” Likewise, in *Fragment of the Ancient Jurist* § 17, I explain *in censum manumittere* as “to manumit into the census.” Compare the notes on Cicero, *For Flaccus*, chapter 37. There is therefore no need to emend *in censu* there; Joan Cannegieter takes it differently in his notes on Ulpian’s *Fragments*, title I, § 8.

[Col. 0145C] **598. “Snowy” (*Nivei*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *nivei et*, “snowy and.” On the snowy path, compare Barthus, *Adversaria* LV, 2. Expressions such as *emensus iter*, “having measured out a journey,” are explained in *Miscellaneous Observations* I, p. 203.

[Col. 0145C] **600. “Of the rock” (*Petrae*)**] Stephen, the first martyr, was buried under stones after Christ’s ascent into heaven:

> And through so many stones he is joined to one Rock,

as Arator sings in book I. Concerning the same man, Fortunatus I:

> Founded upon God’s strength, triumphing over death,
>
> he received the stones, for Christ was his rock.

Bembus on Stephen:

> He went rejoicing in spirit and lightened his losses with his hope.

I have heard this verse especially praised by Philip Melanchthon. Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 126. Melchior Adamus adapted Bembus’s verse to Sebaldus Munsterus at his death, *Lives of German Jurists*, p. 72.

[Col. 0145D] **602. “Not willing for the devout” (*Nolle pio*)**] Pulmann’s papers and the Antwerp edition have *nulli impio*, “for no impious man.” Arator seems to attribute this act of the Jews to frenzy rather than to their usual judgment. Wagenseilius takes the contrary view in *Fasciculus of Works Relating to History* V, p. 242.

[Col. 0145D] **604. “Hail” (*Grando*)**] It refers to the multitude of stones. Thus *imber*, “rain,” *nimbus*, “storm-cloud,” and similar words are often used. Silius XIV, 430:

> … dreadful with a hail of stones.

See the note on the same author XII, 53; Duker on Florus III, 8, § 4; and expressions such as “a cloud, a storm-cloud of weapons,” in Burmann on Valerius Flaccus II, 521, and Drakenborch on Silius XVI, 566. Lucan IV, 774:

> He is overwhelmed at close quarters by slanting spears, and from afar by straight ones,
>
> not only by wounds and blood,
>
> but by a storm-cloud of weapons destined to destroy him.

Cerda, in his notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 522, emends this to:

> At a distance by slanting spears, and at close quarters by straight ones;

but I do not approve the change. Vossius, *Institutions of Oratory* IV, 6, § 5; Sitzmann on Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* III, meter 11; Nansius, additions to Nonnus’s *Paraphrase*, p. 4; Bos on the Letter to the Hebrews XII, § 1; the notes on Pacatus, *Panegyric* 35, § 1; and De Rhoer on Porphyry, *On Abstinence* I, § 25, have discussed this usage and the Greek *νέφος*, “cloud,” at length.

[Col. 0146B] **604. “Unspeakable” (*Nefanda*)**] Barthus notes on Statius, *Thebaid* I, at the beginning, that the repeated letter *a* in this verse indicates harshness suited to the subject. Vossius, however, *Institutions of Oratory* IV, 2, § 2, thinks that this letter, when lengthened, indicates gravity, and when shortened, sweetness. I could scarcely affirm that Arator repeated the letter with the intention Barthus proposes. Poets of this kind are generally strangers to such refinements. Still, I should not conceal that elsewhere he pleasantly accumulated dactyls to indicate speed, verse 831:

> Rise, Tabitha. Called, she returns, restored to the light.

Emmeness derives the same effect from other passages in his notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 250. Such devices certainly add to a poem an elegance exceedingly well suited to expressing the subject. Virgil excellently marks the labor and fatigue of ants through the slowness of spondees, *Aeneid* IV, 405:

> Along the narrow path they carry their loads; some push great things.

See Cerda and Taubmann on *Aeneid* I, 3; and again Cerda on *Aeneid* XII, 718. The “canine letter” wonderfully expresses horror in this fragment of Ennius, p. 129:

> Africa, a dreadful land, trembles with terrible tumult.

The sound of the sea striking the shores with its waves is understood in this passage of Homer, *Iliad* ρ, 265:

> The shores roar as the sea bellows outward.

This verse deterred Plato from competing with Homer. Compare Tollius on Longinus, *On the Sublime*, section XIII, § 7. On the imitated sound of whispering water and flying birds, add Barthus, *Adversaria* XIII, 3.

[Col. 0146D] **604. “Amice”**] In all editions the reading is *amicae*, except in the Fabrician edition, which I have followed. Cortius had written nothing in its margin; hence I suspect that this reading was also found in the Cambridge and University manuscripts. The authority of the distinguished Wassenberg moreover lends weight to it, since he conjectured that it should be read in this way.

[Col. 0146D] **607. “Fine”**] The scholia in Vossianus 2 explain it as “death.” See Barthius on Statius, *Thebaid* IX, 661; his note on Cato, *Disticha* I, 24; Schulting on Seneca, *Suasoriae*, p. 43. Thus *τέλος* in Aelian, *Various History* III, 25; *τελευτὴ βιότοιο*, “the end of life,” in Homer, *Iliad* π, 787; *τελευτᾶν*, “to die,” in Raphel on Matthew 2, § 19.

[Col. 0146D] **608. “Surgat”**] Tornaesianus 1 has *surgit*, “he rises.”

[Col. 0146D] **610. “Coelos”**] Some have condemned this reading; see Nolten, *Antibarbarus*, p. 860.

[Col. 0146D] **612. “Videt”**] The Cambridge manuscript has *vidit*, “he saw.”

[Col. 0146D] **613. “Juncta”**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesianus 1 have *vincta*, “bound.” These words are frequently confused. See my note on Sedulius V, 358; Heinsius on Claudian, *Nuptials of Honorius* 267 and *Epigrams* VII, 3; my father on Pliny, *Panegyric* 17, 2; Heinsius on Tibullus, *Observations* I, 6, 64.

] To whom the exultant soldier, summoned through sacred wounds,

122 Made his path with blood, and, desiring to hasten by this road

Toward the victor’s rewards, measured the honor of the snowy

Path and proceeded to the heights of the lofty king,

[600] And through so many stones the rock is joined into one.

123 What new madness is this, second to none in savagery:

Not to spare the righteous? With your arms brandishing, you hurl

Rocks; he prepares his prayers, nor looks from where

The unspeakable hail may fall—he who, at the hour of death,

[605] [Col. 0146A] 124 Prays for the sinning people. Though you carry with you every

Weapon, and heavy flints and massive weights, the man

Whom you kill will live; he who, with the husbandman dead,

Sows an example from which Christ’s vine may rise,

And crown the Lord’s banquets with the cup.

[610] Having the eyes of his heart, he saw the heavens opened.

So that what Christ does may not be hidden, he rises for the martyr,

Whom he sees then standing, though our confession is more accustomed

To celebrate him seated—the flesh joined to the Thunderer.

[Col. 0147A] [Note: [Col. 0147B]

**616. “Testis”**] The base text has genitive *testis*, “of the witness,” while Vossianus 2 and the Aldine, Basel, Antwerp, and Tornaesian editions have dative *testi*, “for the witness.” The scholiast in the Vossian manuscript explains the latter as “for the martyr Stephen.” I do not object; nevertheless, I preferred to follow the larger number of manuscripts. I do not know whether the poet may rather have written:

*Corpus in arce Dei patuit pro munere. Testes*

“The body lay exposed in God’s citadel as a service. Witnesses”

[Col. 0147C] *Ad Sauli*, etc.

“At Saul’s [feet],” etc.

For Luke likewise says in Acts VII, § 58: **καὶ οἱ μάρτυρες ἀπέθεντο τὰ ἱμάτια αὑτῶν παρὰ τοὺς πόδας**, “and the witnesses laid their garments at the feet.”

[Col. 0147C] **618. “Infernum”**] Let those more learned than I determine what this means. For my part, I have been unable to extricate myself from these difficulties.

[Col. 0147C] **618. “Jam”**] The Cambridge manuscript has *nam*, “for.” These words too are confused below, at verses 924, 988, and 1018. Add Duker on Florus, preface § 2; Drakenborch on Livy V, 51, 6; my father on Pliny, *Panegyric* 36, 4; Burman on the *Catalecta* II, p. 221; Cannegieter, *Dissertation on Abbreviations*, p. 359. Here *jam* is defended by the usage touched upon by Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VII, 18. — I would immediately prefer *utrosque*, “both.” Burman on the *Catalecta* III, p. 471, shows that this word was used of two persons. In John of Salisbury VIII, 19, p. 644, the reading is *utrisque non amplius esset*, “there would no longer be for either”; but *utrique* occurs in the same words in Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 19. Isidore XI, 1, has *quibus se utraeque clausae contingunt*, “with which both closed [things] touch themselves”; but the Groningen manuscript reads *utraque clausa*, “each closed [thing].”

[Col. 0147C] **620. “Inferna”**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesianus 1 have *infirma*, “weak”; but *inferna*, “the lower regions,” is opposed to the preceding *sidera*, “stars.” Thus, later, the martyrs dying for Christ are represented as believing that they were passing into life. See Justus, *Specimen of Observations*, chapter 14, though I do not agree with him concerning the passage in Minucius Felix.

[Col. 0147D] **623. “Patescant”**] Pulmann’s manuscript notes have *patescunt*, “are opened.”

[Col. 0147D] **624. “Facit”**] The Cambridge manuscript has *fecit*, “made.”

[Col. 0147D] **625. “Virgo”**] He may perhaps have had in mind a passage of Jerome, who calls John a virgin disciple. I owe this reference to the diligence of the learned man in Faber’s lexicon.

[Col. 0147D] **626. “Samariae”**] Concerning this, Isidore says in *Etymologies* XV, 1: “Samaria, from which the whole region around it received its name, was built by Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, and he called it Samaria, that is, ‘watch,’ because, when he transferred Israel to the Medes, he stationed guards there.” I have copied the passage from the Groningen manuscript, which is in extremely poor condition in Gothofredus but more accurately represented in the Venetian edition.

[Col. 0147D] **629. “Fonte”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition place the following verse before this one.

[Col. 0148B] **630. “Simon”**] The Basel edition has *Simo ille*, “that Simon”; it was certainly changed in this way because the first syllable is long in Sedulius IV, 112 and 118. Yet Arator shortens it again at verse 663, and there the Aldine and Basel editions alter it. Christian poets paid little attention to quantity in this name. Thus in the middle syllable of *Simonis* the vowel is sometimes lengthened and sometimes shortened. Fabricius indicates the passages in his commentary on the Christian poets, p. 123. — Concerning this Simon, see Mosheim in his dissertation on ecclesiastical history, p. 226. It is well known that some believed that divine honor had been paid to him by the Romans, on account of a passage in Justin Martyr’s *Apology for the Christians* 2, p. 69. Wonna, *On Spirits*, chapter 3, § 6, maintains that Justin was led into this error by Semo Sancus, a Roman god mentioned in inscriptions. Many, however, understand Hercules by that name. See Thulemarius, *Miscellaneous Observations* on Einhard, p. 228. The whole matter is examined at length by Theodorus Cruger, *On the Custom of Devoting Oneself*, p. 34, who understands by Semo that notorious Antinous of Hadrian.

[Col. 0148C] **632. “Numisque”**] Fabricius and the Lyon Library (*Bibl. Lugd.*) read *numinisque*, “and of divine power.”

[Col. 0148C] **636. “Auro”**] Vossianus 1 has *aurum*, “gold.” I would rather refer this to what grace bestows, which is grasped not by money but solely by the mind’s thought and judgment. On the word, compare Barthius on Claudian, *Consulship of Manlius* 160.

[Col. 0148C] **639. “Quies”**] The distinguished Wassenberg scarcely doubted that *fides*, “faith,” should be written, since the words of Luke VIII, § 22, are expressed: **οὐκ ἔστι σοι μερὶς οὐδὲ κλῆρος ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ**, “you have neither part nor share in this matter.”

[Col. 0148C] **640. “Dolis”**] I restored this reading from the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1 and 2, the Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesian editions, and Pulmann’s manuscripts. In the others it is *pollute potes donis*, “polluted, you can [with] gifts.” In support of the reading I have printed, I have the authority of the distinguished Wassenberg, who agrees with me.

[Col. 0148D] **641. “Felle”**] Thus Arator also understood *εἰς* in place of *ἐν* in Luke’s words, Acts VIII, § 23. I would nevertheless prefer to follow the judgment of the distinguished Alberti on the New Testament, p. 236.

[Col. 0148D] **643. “Lux”**] The Cambridge manuscript has *lex*, “law.” It could be understood as “manner” or “condition,” as in Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* IV, 2. But since he is speaking of a figure, that is, an allegory, as I explained above at verse 158, and since it is often obscure and mystical, *lux*, “light,” seems more suitable here: a figure whose entire meaning becomes apparent, as at verse 690:

*Non parva figurae*

*Causa sub obscurae regionis imagine lucet.*

“Not a small cause of the figure shines beneath the image of an obscure region.”

[Col. 0148D] **648. “Columbam”**] I adopted this reading from the Aldine, Antwerp, Basel, and Lyon editions; Fabricius likewise has it. Cortius had written nothing from the Cambridge and University manuscripts; I suspect that these too favored this reading. The others have *columba*, “the dove.”]

125 In Stephen the matter itself supports him; the foreseeing leader arms

[615] Those whom he summons to the gifts, lest anyone here fight uncertainly.

The witness’s body lay exposed in God’s citadel for his service.

At savage Saul’s feet they laid the garments.

*Infernum quod Hebraeus ait*—literally, “the underworld, which the Hebrew says”—

[Translation note: The printed syntax at verses 617–618 is damaged, and the editor expressly says that he could not resolve it; the Latin is therefore retained here with a literal gloss.]

Now it is clear that each side experiences its own desert: the martyr

Seeks the stars, [620] while the executioners seek the lower regions. The first lot reveals

And establishes the example: for one who wages such wars,

This flows from the same source, so that Tartarus immediately follows

Those who kill, while the stars open to those who die.

Peter often makes John his companion,

[625] 126 Because the virgin pleases the Church; when at last joined with him,

[Col. 0147B] He went toward neighboring Samaria and marked with the waters

Of baptism the washed sheep, whom the nourishing

Spirit attended and made various tongues come forth.

Washed indeed in the spring, but not clean in heart,

[630] This was that magician Simon, whom the punishment that followed

[Col. 0148A] Exposed to the world as ignorant of faith. By contracts involving gold

He wishes to equal the gifts of God and to ascribe to divinity

What a merchant may buy for a price. When Peter saw him

Attempting such things, he said: “What madness, doomed man,

[635] Moved you to this? That which the grace of the Lord gives,

So that you regard it as merchandise, is not acquired with gold,

But by this understanding. Nor is it permitted that heaven be sought

With corrupted money, which the investigator of earth loves.

Certainly no rest remains for you in this portion, nor will you be able

[640] To come to these things, polluted by deceit, swollen with the gall

Of a bitter heart, seeking what belongs to others; for the Spirit

Enters those chambers of the mind that shine with simplicity.

From this saying, the light of the sacred figure is manifest.

The structure once presented the likeness of the Church,

[645] [Col. 0148B] Built in the time of Noah, which alone received

Every kind, and, carrying them within closed spaces as a likeness of baptism,

Turned the waters to life while the wandering multitude

Suffered deadly storms. At the same time it washed the dove

[Col. 0149A] [Note: [Col. 0149B]

**649. “Diluit”**] The Cambridge manuscript and the Aldine and Basel editions have *deluit*, “washed away.” See above at verse 203.

[Col. 0149B] **651. “Funere”**] “To feed on a corpse.” Barthius on Claudian, *Praise of Stilicho* I, 101. Concerning the raven, Sedulius I, 155:

*A bird devoted to plunder*

*And filling its hollow throat with its greedy beak.*

Florus I, 1, 7, says that these birds are accustomed to blood and prey. Aelian, *On Animals* IV, 43, testifies that the raven is so voracious that it even devours a parent worn out by old age. Add Demster on Rosinus V, 39.

[Col. 0149B] **652. “A es”**] The Cambridge manuscript has *alis*, “with wings.”

[Col. 0149B] **654. “Nutriri”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts, the Antwerp edition, and the Lyon Bible have *nutrici*, “for the nurturer.”

[Col. 0149B] **657. “Fuit”**] Vossianus 1 has *dedit*, “gave.” Bochart discusses the matter itself in *Hierozicon* II, p. 31. Join with it what was said above at verse 28.

[Col. 0149B] **660. “Purgati”**] Vossianus 2 and the Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesian editions have *purganti*, “purifying.”

[Col. 0149C] **661. “Cessante”**] Sedulius I, Arator I, and Victor II write that Noah sent the raven out from the ark. Nebrissensis noted that this was an error arising from ignorance of the language, and that in his time Sedulius possessed an uncorrected manuscript; for the reading should be *egrediebatur et revertebatur*, “it went out and returned,” evidently because it had nowhere to settle. Nebrissensis’s diligence is praiseworthy: he understood the language. Yet he did not examine the phrase. The meaning is, as a man thoroughly versed in the language explained it, that the raven, flying back and forth, delayed its return until the waters had dried up from the earth, as though the poet said that it never returned to Noah. Allegorically, he refers the raven to the Jews: Alcimus, book IV; Arator I refers it to apostates. For both Jews and apostates, though raised up and preserved in the Church, have fallen away from it and, wandering about and causing tumult, never return to its peaceful fellowship. Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 39. On the word *cessante*, “with its return delayed,” see above at verse 86.

[Col. 0149C] **662. “Felle”**] Sedulius, letter to Macedonius, p. 11, says that “the dove should not lose its guileless spirit”; likewise II, 171:

*Through the bird that is free from gall.*

There are notes there. Althelmus, *Praise of the Virgin*, p. 721 in volume I of Canisius’s *Thesaurus*:

*Since she alone is free from the cruel gall of poison.*

Athanasius, works I, p. 471, mentions **τῆς περιστερᾶς τὸ πρᾷον**, “the gentleness of the dove.”

[Col. 0149D] **663. “Simon”**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *Simo*. See the note on verse 630.

[Col. 0149D] **669. “Sublimat”**] *Sublimare* means “to raise on high.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis*:

*Or raises the swelling hum through a copious blast.*

Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 127.

[Col. 0149D] **671. “Dignatus”**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesianus 1 have *dignatur*, “he deigns.”

[Col. 0149D] **673. “Celebrare”**] I restored this from the Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus 1 and 2. The remaining editions have *celerare*, “to hasten,” which Barthius approves in his note on Statius, *Thebaid* X, 618. But I think the subject is not so much speed as the journey itself. Nor should it be explained by *per frequenter obire*, “to visit frequently,” as *celebrare atria*, “to frequent the halls,” in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 172. Add Cortius on Pliny VI, letter 30, 1; Bunemann on Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VI, 5, § 7. I take it simply as “to complete a journey,” since this verb is ordinarily used not only of repeated activity but of the activity itself. Drakenborch demonstrates this in his note on Livy I, 4, 9. How often copyists corrupted this word is clear from Burman on Valerius Flaccus III, 251, and on Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 641. In Lucan VI, 183, *celerem* and *celebrem* were interchanged in the Thuaneus manuscript; see the notes on Suetonius, *Vespasian* 7, for *celebriter* and *celeriter*. Burman made several excellent corrections on this basis in his note on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, 304. Add Isidore, *Etymologies* I, 22, where the spelling *celebris* is made shorter. The Groningen manuscript correctly has *celeris*, from which *celeris breviorque* could be restored; the distinguished Gisb. Koenius, a man worthy of a longer life, saw this brilliantly, and in his *Juridical Dissertation*, p. 24, reproduced both the Groningen manuscript’s reading and that of the old edition. Cannegieter added his agreement in his *Dissertation on Abbreviations*, p. 299.

[Col. 0150C] **673. “Qua”**] Vossianus 2 has *quam*, “which.” I would not reject it. Terence, *Hecyra* I, 2, 119, has: “I shall continue by the path on which I began”; unless one prefers to refer it there to the following word. In Sallust, *Jugurtha* 47, 1, Cortius found in the Welferbytanus manuscript *ab eo itinere quod Metellus pergebat*, “from the road along which Metellus proceeded”; ibid. 79, 5, *maturavere iter pergere*, “they hastened to continue the journey.” The learned ornament of his Friesland, Johannes Schraderus, produced many similar examples in his *Annotations on Musaeus*, chapter 17. Add Drakenborch on Livy III, 6, 7; Duker on Florus III, 4, 5. Barthius explained *iter gradire* as “to walk a journey.” Thus *currere pelagus*, “to run across the sea,” in Sedulius, letter to Macedonius, p. 2, and Heinsius, *Addenda to Prudentius*, p. 155; *vecti maria*, “carried across the seas,” in Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 524.

[Col. 0150C] **673. “Spado”**] The first syllable is long, though it is short in Juvenal, as Vossius notes in *Grammar* II, 39. Stephanus derives the word itself from Spado, a Persian district; Barthius has already used his passage in his note on Claudian I, *Against Eutropius*, 345, as has Brissonius, *On the Persian Kingdom* II, § 164. [Col. 0150D] Vossius gives other material in his *Etymology*, under the word.

[Col. 0150D] **673. “Jugatis”**] Trebellius Pollio, *Gallienus* 8, has *cornibus auro jugatis*, “with horns yoked with gold.” This passage has been variously emended. Triller explains the opinions of Casaubon and Salmasius in his *Critical Observations* II, 8; he himself prefers *fucatis*, “painted.” I defend *jugatis* from this passage of Arator, but think that *cornibus auro* should be understood as “from gold,” or “golden,” just as *puppes abiete*, “ships from firwood,” in Virgil, and *damnum injuria*, “loss through injury,” among the jurists; Cannegieter produced other such examples in his *Fragments of Ancient Jurisprudence*, p. 60.

[Col. 0150D] **674. “Fidus”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *sidus*, “star”—certainly an elegant word for a person who adds ornament to anything whatsoever. See Barthius on Claudian, *Sixth Consulship of Honorius* 23. But the other reading is more appropriate. Eunuchs were placed in charge of various matters, and were more valued in proportion to their fidelity. Compare Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 372.]

and it also washed the raven; but harmony of mind

[650] 128 Did not make the two equal. A throat full of plunder drew the raven

Away from its course; desiring to feed on a corpse,

It could follow nothing living. The friendly bird returns

With fruits and, though shipwrecked, succumbs to no waters,

Fearing to be nourished by death; through zeal for its labor

[655] It gives proofs of the devotion by which faith,

More dedicated to its work, is bound. The olive was the pledge

Of its modest beak: love always bears the fruit of peace in its mouth.

Both birds fly amid the waves from one holy bosom,

Purified in the belly of their preserver while the sea surrounds them;

[660] Yet one is exiled and, with its return suspended, perishes.

[Translation note: The compact syntax of *servantis in alvo / purgati vallante freto* is difficult; the translation preserves *purgati* with “both” and takes *servantis* as “of their preserver.”]

Therefore washing water is not sufficient for salvation unless the one

[Col. 0150A] 129 Born from the waters is a dove without gall.

This Simon had touched the water of baptism,

[665] But was a raven seeking his own gains,

Which never merited God, who is accustomed to drive sellers

From the threshold of the temple. Let us pursue better things!

Peter calls us to them, he who by the mouth of God

Is said to be the dove’s son and, rightly born of this mother,

[670] Raises high the work of the Church. From the gift of her offspring

The mother receives the name which the nourishing Spirit chooses,

Deigning to appear in the image of the innocent bird.

The angel addresses Philip, full of virtue:

130 To travel the southern road, along which the eunuch, faithful in the queen’s court,

Proceeded with the Ethiopians’ harnessed horses.

[Col. 0151A] [Note: [Col. 0151B]

**677. “Rotas”**] He seems to have had in mind the words of Ecclesiastes, chapter XXXIII, § 5.

[Col. 0151B] **680. “Fructu”**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesianus 1 have *fructum*, “fruit.” The following letter has been joined to it.

[Col. 0151B] **681. “Lampadis”**] **Φίλιππος**, “Philip,” [is interpreted as] “lover of horses,” that is, of military service. Arator gives a Hebrew etymology: “Impose Philippum,” etc. As I said above, Arator is allegorical; therefore he sometimes twists meanings and sometimes words. Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 104. — Here the Cambridge and Vossianus 2 manuscripts differ remarkably: *Cor oris quod Hebraeus ait*, “the heart of the mouth, as the Hebrew says.” Vossianus 1, Pulmann’s manuscripts, and the Antwerp edition have *Oris cor quod Hebraeus*, “the mouth’s heart, as the Hebrew says.” The scholiast in Vossianus 1 had added: “Philip is interpreted as ‘heart of the mouth,’ because whatever he had in his heart he revealed with his mouth; and ‘mouth of the lamp,’ because with his mouth he illuminated everyone.” All of this is nonsense. Barthius, in *Adversaria* II, 21, more correctly assigns a Greek source to the word. I attribute *lampadis os*, “mouth of the lamp,” to Arator; the other is a scribal invention. Thus Isidore too has, *Etymologies* VII, 9, “Philip, mouth of lamps,” or “mouth of hands.”

[Col. 0151C] **683. “Quia”**] I printed this reading from the Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus 1 and 2. In addition, Vossianus 1 had *discipulis*, “to the disciples”; the Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesianus 1 have *qui jura*, “who teaches laws”; the Antwerp edition has *quae jure*, “which rightly”; all the others have *qui jure*, “who rightly.”

[Col. 0151C] **683. “Dabit”**] “He will say,” or “explain,” what the words of the prophet Isaiah should be understood to mean; compare Luke, Acts VIII, § 31 and following. On this passage of Isaiah itself, see Colomesius, *Observations*, p. 125. Luke reports some words from the Greek interpreters, and Amende therefore thinks that they had been read from a Greek manuscript in the *Christeid*, p. 80. — *Dare*, “to give,” has the same sense in Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 85:

*Give me my own house, Thymbraean Apollo.*

Servius, approved by Burman, explains it by “say.” Thus I understand *dare sortem*, “to give an oracle,” in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 381, as **χρησμοῦ δοθέντος**, “an oracle having been given,” in Apollodorus, *Bibliotheca* II, 6, § 3. Ambrose, *On Duties* I, 14, says that they wish “to give him knowledge of hidden things.” My manuscript is corrupt there, reading *dicere*, “to say”; and in Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII, 7, I prefer *quaerentibus responsa dare*, “to give answers to those who ask,” although the Groningen manuscript has *praecanere*, “to foretell.” Similar examples are given by Barthius, *Adversaria* LV, 11; the distinguished scholar on Valerius Flaccus V, 219; Burman on Ovid, *Fasti* VI, 334, and on Claudian, *Rape of Proserpine* III, 337; and Heinsius in his notes on Tibullus I, 6, 13.

[Col. 0151D] **684. “Sonant”**] The Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, and Fabricius have *sonent*, “may sound.” Arator’s words are the same as Luke’s in Acts VIII, § 32: **περιοχὴ τῆς γραφῆς**, “the passage of Scripture,” which others call *τόπον*, “place,” *χωρία*, “sections,” *ῥήσεις*, “utterances,” or something similar; Valckenarius explains these terms learnedly in his note on Herodotus II, p. 157.

[Col. 0151D] **684. “Cumque”**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *quique*; the others have *cum qui*. Vossianus 1 then has *fecerat*, “had made.” He indicates Christ as the author of things, and as subsequently born from Mary.

[Col. 0151D] **687. “Properanter”**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *properatur*, “it is hastened.”

[Col. 0151D] **688. “Gurgite”**] Vossianus 1 has *in gurgite*, “in the torrent.”

[Col. 0151D] **692. “Omnipotens”**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *Heptaticus*. This name designates the first part of the Old Testament, containing the books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges. Vossius, *On the Purity of Speech* III, 14, thinks that *Omnipotens* is found here because of the more recent books; he alone approves *Heptaticus* and cites Juretus, who agrees with him, in his note on Ivo’s letter 83. I have found nothing similar in my manuscripts, and therefore I dare agree with Vossius even less, since *omnipotens* is a familiar word to Arator. See only verses 185 and 529, among other passages. Cassiodorus mentions the *Octateuch* at the beginning of his *Divine Institutes*.

[Col. 0152B] **692. “Mosem”**] Moses, found in the papyrus of the Nile, received his name from the fact that he was drawn out of the waters. The same form is written with respect to orthography by Juvenal, Pliny, and Justin, who mention him; from it Juvencus forms the unusual accusative in IV:

*Mosea, who was able to command the precepts of the laws.*

He also formed the possessive in book II:

*He was lifted up with the hands of Moses in the highest honor.*

And Fortunatus, book V:

*Rebels against the law of Moses.*

Christian poets sometimes write *Moyses*, shortening the first syllable and lengthening the penultimate. Prudentius, *The Martyrdom of Saint Stephen*:

*He himself loosens*

*The sandals of his feet, as Moses did.*

The same poet, *Hamartigenia*:

*As Moses himself,*

*The historian of the world’s beginning, testifies.*

Sedulius III:

*They saw Elijah and Moses, illustrious in virtue,*

*Unknown to the eyes, but with the light of the heart.*

Prudentius calls him the “Genealogist” because he describes the origin of the world and traces the families from which Christ’s ancestry descends to Adam. The same most learned writer calls him “the prophet” in *Apotheosis*, and in *Hamartigenia*, *Against the Poets*:

*Moses, venerable under the ancient name of lawgiver.*

Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 89. — What Fabricius says about the derivation of the word rests on the testimony of those who compose it from **μῶ**, “water,” and **ὕσης**, “saved.” Triller indicates the testimonies in his *Critical Observations*, p. 437. But Bochart long ago rejected these fancies in *Phaleg* I, 15. Here too, as so often elsewhere, the manuscripts—both handwritten and printed—differ in the spelling of the word. Basel, Antwerp, Tornaesianus 1, and the Lyon Bible have *Mosen*. The Cambridge manuscript has *Moysen*. But if what Fabricius notes is correct, and Vossius, *Grammar* I, 9, is right that the first syllable of *Moyses* is short and the middle one long, the verse will not scan. Certainly Grunerus, in his note on Sedulius III, 208, judges that the laws of meter at the end of the poem do not permit this spelling. Nevertheless, the manuscripts have it there as well, at IV, 169. If *Moyses* could be made disyllabic, the Cambridge manuscript’s reading could be defended. I do not approve it, however. In Victorinus Afer, *On the Maccabees*, verse 252, some editions read:

*The ruler of the world handed over Moses, who sought it;*

and at verse 327:

*They asked Moses to give waters to the thirsty.*

But Fabricius printed *Mosesque* and *Mosen* there, undoubtedly following better manuscripts.

[Col. 0152D] **693. “Aethiopam”**] *Aethiopam* is used for *Aethiopissam*, “an Ethiopian woman.” Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 3. — The two Tornaesian editions have *Aethiopem*, “an Ethiopian”; more correctly they would have written *Aethiopin*, which Vossius, *On the Purity of Speech* I, 16, prefers to *Aethiopissa*. Arator seems to have derived *Aethiopam* from the Greek accusative, which is the source of similar words in Latin. Thus Vorstius lengthened *Marathona*, the accusative, in his note on Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II, 9, 7. Vossius collected *cratera*, “bowl,” *crepida*, “sandal,” *lampada*, “lamp,” and other examples in *On the Purity of Speech* III, 15. Salmasius restored *Iliadam* in Solinus, *Polyhistor*, p. 7, and the *Collatio* in my possession approves it. Later Greeks likewise formed new words in this way, such as **σιαγόνα**, the accusative, from **σιαγών**, “jaw.” See Meursius on Psellus, *Commentary on the Song of Songs*, p. 183.]

[675] He guarded the queen’s riches; he flies on a swift axle,

Seeking fixed joys, and by the chariot itself he will deserve

To cast away the wheels of Error. O how many seeds

Of good things you will receive! You come to take such precious gifts

Of the washing and store them in a barren body,

[680] So that you may reap them with better fruit. Take Philip as your guide,

Whom the Hebrew calls “the mouth of the lamp,” and who, as his name

Testifies, confirms the dignity of the mind. He delights to hear this teacher,

Because he rightly teaches the disciple; he himself will explain from which prophet

[Col. 0152B] 132 The words resound, and how he who formerly made all things

[685] Has now been begotten. If you hear in faith,

He will also be born for you, and you will be reborn from him.

At the sight of the waters the eunuch’s fruitful faith

At once began to burn; immersed in the flood,

He laid aside the serpent’s burden and sped onward in the chariot,

[690] Contemplating Elijah’s journey. No small basis for the figure

Shines beneath the image of the dark region.

The Almighty confirms through the marriage covenant of the torches that Moses

133 Joined an Ethiopian woman to himself, whom the teachings reveal

[Col. 0153A] [Note: [Col. 0153C]

**696. “Cum juncta”**] The Aldine, Basel, and Tornaesianus 1 have *conjuncta*, “joined.”

[Col. 0153C] **697. “Celant”**] Basel, Tornaesianus 1, and Fabricius have *coelant*, “they engrave”; Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *cedant*, “they yield.”

[Col. 0153C] **699. “Solomonis”**] Thus the other manuscripts also have it; see Heinsius in the *Addenda to Prudentius*, pp. 145 and 158. The Aldine, Antwerp, Tornaesianus 1, and Lyon Bible, however, have *Salomonis*; so too above at verse 289. The former seems to have stood in the Vossian manuscripts, the latter in the Cambridge and University manuscripts.

[Col. 0153C] **704. “Potior”**] Vossianus 2 has *potius*, “rather.”

[Col. 0153C] **704. “Ditius”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *dicitur*, “is said.”

[Col. 0153C] **706. “Quo”**] The Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus 2 have *qua*, “by which.” Cortius refers this in the margin to *ecclesiam*, “the Church,” but that word is too remote; rather, if one accepts this, repeat *fides*, “faith.”

[Col. 0153C] **708. “Acerba”**] Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 398:

*He stood there, savage and roaring.*

Valerius Flaccus III, 229:

*He rages, savage and roaring.*

[Col. 0153D] Weitzius comments: “Thus neuter adjectives are commonly used.” Burman on the same author II, 126; Oudendorp, *Miscellaneous Observations* II, p. 306. In these words Arator expressed Luke’s phrase in Acts IX, § 1: **ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου**, “breathing threats and slaughter.” Rhoerius discussed the latter phrase in *David’s Feriae* II, 3. Alberti indicated the ellipsis of the preposition **ἕνεκα**, “on account of.” Besides Elsner, Heinsius on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, 348, and Drakenborch on Silius XVII, 536, compare it with the Latin *spirare*, “to breathe.” — Vossianus 2 has *acerva*, showing how frequently *b* and *v* are interchanged. On this account a corrupt passage occurs in Isidore, *Etymologies* II, 30: “What is a *thesis*? Let it be answered: ‘to whom the *vis* is absent, so that it may be an art.’” Thus Gothofredus. But this is a monstrosity of a reading, long since so corrupted that I suspect these words were omitted in the old edition for that reason. It should be written from the Groningen manuscript: “What is a *tressis*? Let it be answered: ‘to whom a *bes* is [rather, is lacking], so that it may be an *assis*.’” In Martial V, 20:

*I give you useful advice, which you do not want.*

Write instead: “useful to us.” The excellent Thuaneus manuscript has this reading, and Rutgersius adopted it by conjecture in his *Various Readings* VI, p. 580, with Scriverius’s approval; Heinsius likewise found it in manuscripts in *Adversaria* I, 2, and III, 16. The same Martial VIII, 6:

*The son of Aeacus drinks the unmixed wine more generously himself.*

Scriverius correctly printed *vividiusque merum*, “and the unmixed wine more vigorously”; the Thuaneus manuscript confirms it. This *vividius merum* recalls to me a passage in Aurelius Victor, *On the Illustrious Men* 76, § 8: “because he drank the poison more slowly.” I conjecture *viveret*, “he might live,” for this verb could be used of poison whose force penetrates and affects the whole body, no less than wine. *Videret*, “he might see,” was preferred there by Crusius, *Critical Probabilities*, p. 257.

[Col. 0154C] **709. “Judaica”**] The Jews derive their name from Judah, the fourth son of Jacob. *Judaea* and *Judaica* are used with the same meaning, “Jewish,” in Alcimus. But in this author the antepenultimate syllable is sometimes long, as in book V:

*When the Jewish people, fleeing the hardened king,*

*escaped;*

and sometimes short, as in Sedulius II:

*Recently, among the Jewish peoples, from the eastern horizon,*

*they saw a leader born shine forth;*

and in Arator. Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 74. — Tornaesianus 1 has *Judaea*. Compare *Miscellaneous Observations*, new series, part V, p. 434. From the character of the people, *Judaicus* is often used for “savage.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XI, 4.
