[Col. 0154D] **710. “Ruinae”**] This is the reading of the manuscripts and of the Antwerp and Lyon editions, as well as Fabricius; the others add *est*, “is.”

[Col. 0154D] **711. “Qui”**] Thus Vossianus 1 and 2. The Cambridge manuscript has *didicitque e corpore*, “and learned from the fallen body”; Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *didicitque*; all the others have *didicit de*, “learned from.”

[Col. 0154D] **717. “Excutit”**] I approve the very elegant conjecture of the distinguished Wassenberg, *excutis*, “you shake off,” so that *Anania* is a vocative; for *Ananias* is more correctly written above at verse 415. Nevertheless, all manuscripts consistently have *excutit*, “he shakes off.”

[Col. 0154D] **721. “Calens”**] The Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus 2 have *canens*, “singing.”

[Col. 0154D] **722. “Plena”**] The Cambridge manuscript has *plenum*, “full”; but the other reading is more suitable for Arator, who very often joins such things through oxymoron.

[Col. 0154D] **725. “Tectumque”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *rectumque*, “and straight.”

[Col. 0154D] **726. “Tempora”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *tempore*, “in the time.”

[Col. 0154D] **727. “Triduana”**] Vossius notes that here the first syllable is shortened contrary to customary usage, in *Grammar* II, 39.]

134 Afterwards he spoke more closely, mouth to mouth, with the Lord.

[695] What wonder if love of the law then began to grow

When she was joined to the Church? For the everlasting bride

Comes especially from this people, nor do the songs conceal her

Whom they call dark and beautiful. She proceeds from the South,

Which scorches the Ethiopians’ land, to praise in Solomon’s mouth

[700] Her own “Peaceful One,” by which name what Christ possesses

Was long ago signified. Now she sends the guardian of her riches

Ahead into the world, as a pledge by which she will begin

To bring forth her treasures. What treasure in her is more precious

Than the honor of the font? What gold is richer,

[705] What faith beneath the heart more abundant? How fittingly, finally,

[Col. 0153B] Is the eunuch her forerunner? As he advances, lust

Is driven away, and the chaste take possession of the heavenly kingdoms.

Saul, raging savagely, prepares to wage war at Damascus

135 With Jewish ferocity; but the lamb will be loved,

[Col. 0154A] 136 Against whom the wolf hastens to rage. Happy is the fall

In which guilt falls away: he whose body had fallen

Learned now to stand upon the level of the mind. When he closes

His eyes, he then opens his heart, and heaven’s creator is recognized

As day departs. How much the darkness earned!

[715] Beyond his eyes he sees greater things; nurturing faith

Gave the ages a wondrous example. Ananias shakes off

His fury—O new victory! He tames the ravening wolf,

Whom the Hebrew called a sheep. Through this herald, God will be proclaimed

To the world; freed from the shadow of the law

[720] Beneath which he was blind, Saul will shine through every land,

Warmed by the everlasting sun. Do not cease, Saul,

To celebrate this day; this night, full of many a light,

Is given to you, and here you bear your clouds

[Col. 0154B] So that you may cleanse the world. Now I shall pursue teachings

[725] That are inwardly full of figures, and undertake to bring forth

The radiance veiled in hidden places. The three-day span that Saul

Spends in darkness makes the measure of its own example trustworthy,

And at last, compelled—

[Translation note: The supplied source breaks off here in mid-sentence after *coactum* (“compelled”); only the subsequent apparatus is present in this chunk.]

[Col. 0155A] [Note: [Col. 0155A]

**729. “Dominum”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts have *laesum*, “injured.” The Antwerp edition has *Jesum*, “Jesus.”

[Col. 0155A] **731. “Orbibus”**] “With eyes.” Below, book II, 225:

*And exiled day illuminates the eyes;*

and at verse 932:

*And darkening shadows*

*Press upon the eyes.*

Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* III, p. 107, has “the mobile little circles of the eyes.” Elmenhorst and Heraldus comment there. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 670:

*He turned the burning circles of his eyes toward the walls.*

See Burman on Valerius Flaccus III, 178 and 739; Weitzius on the same author IV, 235; Savaron on Sidonius II, letter 1. Poets ordinarily use the plural rather than the singular, and Burman rightly corrected Barthius’s error on Claudian, *Battle of the Giants*, 259. Arator seems to have used this word especially when speaking of the serpent, to which Virgil attributes *orbes*, “circles,” in *Aeneid* II, 204; the Greek equivalent is **κύκλοι**, as Spanh. explains on Callimachus, *Hymn to Delos* 93. He adds that the scales peculiar to snakes are called **φολίδες** in Greek, whereas those of fish are **λεπίδες**. See Rhoerius on Porphyry, *On Abstinence* IV, § 14. Similarly, below, book II, 1185, of Saul:

*When the scaly horror fell from his eyes,*

*Which the ancient serpent had given.*

[Col. 0155B] **733. “Ratione”**] Pulmann’s manuscripts have *ratioque*, “and the account”; the Antwerp edition has the same reading without *que*, “and,” which is inferior.

[Col. 0155C] **734. “Aspide”**] The asp is regarded as one of the most poisonous beasts, and thus the serpent became proverbial as a kind of archetype. Arator, book I: “the poison of Judea …” Venantius Fortunatus:

*The basilisk and asp yield; before them all poisons retreat.*

Arator called it cruel because of its deafness: one who is deaf to the voices of mourners cannot be moved to compassion. For the same reason, Mahomet, the lawgiver of the Turks, placed deaf evil spirits among the dead, so that they could in no way be softened by the wailings of condemned men. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXII, 22.

[Col. 0155C] **736. “Salvator”**] **Σωτήρ**, “one who gives salvation.” Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I:

*I pray, savior of the Romulean race.*

The more Latin form is *servator*, “preserver,” as in Propertius, “Augustus Caesar, preserver of the world.” In old copies of Juvencus one finds sometimes *servator*, sometimes *salvator*. They differ in Latinity and usage. Fabricius, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 118. — What Fabricius says about usage seems to concern the fact that some deny that Christ should correctly be called *Servator*, distinguishing between *servare*, “to preserve,” and *salvare*, “to save.” They refer the former to one who spares those whom he could have killed, while they attribute the latter to one who not only grants life but also adds a better and happier condition. Therefore they call Christ rather *Salvator*, considering that one should not examine what is more Latin but what more fully expresses the importance of the matter. Thus Daumius judges in *On the Causes of the Loss of the Latin Language*, chapter 26. Add Borrichius, *Reflections on the Latin Language*, p. 229; Nolten, *Antibarbarus*, p. 1158; and those cited by Burman the Younger on Lotichius IV, 6, beginning. The verb *salvare*, “to save,” occurs also below at verse 833 and above at verse 80; Reinesius, *Various Readings* II, p. 194, does not reject its use for the care provided by medicines. In general, *servator* is the more Latin form, as I showed in my note on Sedulius II, 156. Hence Mamertinus, *Panegyric on Julian* 21, beginning, has correctly been emended in the better printed editions to *ac libertatem suam salvator vilis imminuat*, “and may the base savior diminish his own liberty.” The inferior editions have this reading; but in the Vatican and Welferbytanus manuscripts, whose excerpts are at hand, the reading is *salutator*, “one who greets,” which Juretus approves in his note on Symmachus VIII, letter 41, and which had already been adopted. Vossius had conjectured in the margin of his edition that this should be restored, or perhaps *adulator*, “flatterer.” Whether *Servator* sufficiently expresses Christ, I have not determined. Certainly in Cicero’s time the poverty of the Latin language was not sufficient to translate the word **σωτήρ**; thus in *Against Verres* 2, 63: “And so I saw him inscribed at Syracuse not only as the patron of that island but also as *soter*. What does this amount to? So great is it that it cannot be expressed by a single Latin word. He is plainly a *soter*, one who has given salvation.”

[Col. 0156B] **736. “Angues”**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *anguem*, “the serpent,” undoubtedly so that the devil may be understood. But **ἐπάνω ὄφεων**, “over serpents,” occurs in Luke, Gospel X, § 19, and he is referring to that passage.

[Col. 0156B] **739. “Iniquos”**] The Aldine and Basel editions have *iniquas*, “wicked,” feminine; they certainly refer it to *insidias*, “ambushes.”

[Col. 0156B] **740. “Clausis”**] Vossianus 1 and 2 change the word order. Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *portis evadere clausis*, “to escape through closed gates.” — In place of *portis*, the Aldine and Basel editions have *sportis*, “baskets”; but Luke mentions **πύλας**, “gates.”

[Col. 0156B] **741. *Solens*.** Vossius I, Basilian, Aldine, and Tornesian edition 1 have *solet*. Thus Luke, *Acts* IX.25: “they let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.” Sallustius, *Historical Fragments* II, p. 53, ed. Havercamp, differs little: “They lowered dogs [more correctly, according to others, citizens] from the walls in baskets.” Vossius derives *sporta* in his *Etymologicon* from the accusative Greek *σπυρίδα*; others derive it from *spartum*, and Arator seems to hold the same view when he adds “woven with rushes.” Objects of this kind were commonly made from *spartum*; hence Turnebus, *Adversaria* XXVIII.5, and Mattheus, *De Criminibus*, p. 585, report that the executioner’s sack (*culeus*) was made from it. Both followed a passage of Isidore in the glossary; Casaubon, however, criticizes Isidore in his note on Suetonius, *Augustus* 33. Prudentius, *Peristephanon* V.457, seems nevertheless to support a *culeus sparteus*, which he also calls a little basket (*fiscella*) in the same work, line 492. I generally grant Casaubon’s view that it was made of oxhide; Dositheus III.16 calls it *μολγός*. Goldastus notes that Hesychius explains this word by *βόειον ἀσκόν* (“an ox-hide vessel”). The legal glosses likewise record the word *πομπνίους*. “Oxhide” (*δέρμα βόειον*) occurs in Cedrenus, *Compendium of History*, p. 161, whom I owe to Demster’s note on Rosinus VIII.31, p. 654. Some think that Plutarch, in *Gracchus*, p. 834, calls it a vessel (*ἀγγεῖον*); more correctly, however, the translator renders the word as “chest.” It could also refer to some kind of container, as in Homer, *Iliad* II.471. Casaubon refers Isidore’s gloss to a tunic smeared with pitch, in which those condemned to be burned were clothed. I once suspected that Juvenal’s scholiast on *Satires* VIII.234 should be emended from this passage of Isidore: “A garment made of paper, smeared with pitch, in which those condemned to punishment by fire customarily burn”—so that we should read “made of *spartum*.” A rush tunic (*tunica spartea*) is certainly more suitable to this purpose than one made of paper. But let this remain a conjecture; I will not conceal that the same scholiast mentions papyrus in this connection in his note on *Satires* I.155, and Schwarzius likewise asserts this in his note on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 73, p. 125. But I return to Arator; let the more cultivated reader not resent the digression.

[Col. 0156D] **742. *Saulo*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *Paulo*; but in this matter *Σαῦλος* (“Saul”) is the form used in *Acts* IX.24. Nor does Luke call him Paul even once before he records his arrival in Cyprus from the mainland of Asia, chapter XIII.9. I approve the opinion of my excellent father-in-law, Henricus Cannegieter, in *De Mutata Nominum Ratione*, chapter 6: Paul wished henceforth to be called by his Roman name only after he had left the mainland of Asia, while among his own people—and on his return to his homeland—he used the name Saul. Add Barthius, *Adversaria* VII.4.

> Punishment, as teacher, instructs him not to reject the Lord any longer  
> [730] after the third day to have overcome chaos, when he himself began  
> [137] thus to restore his own, because from the dark orbits  
> the heavy scales fell away, which is what the serpent’s nature  
> customarily bears; reason is vigorous: Judaea always vomits  
> poison from its mouth, more savage than the deaf asp.  
> [735] The serpent of the Synagogue hisses from the cavern of treachery.  
>   
> [Col. 0156A] The Savior says to the disciples: “You shall tread upon serpents,”  
> [138] so that the course of obedience may be purer toward heavenly things.  
> He casts the viper before the outrage, and soon the teacher  
> wages better battles; when he had overcome the wicked,  
> [740] he earned the means of escaping ambushes through closed gates.  
> [139] A basket, accustomed to be woven in turn from rushes and palms,  
> gives coverings to Saul, retaining in honor the figure  
> [Col. 0157A] [of the Church].

[Col. 0157A] **Note: [Col. 0157B]**

**742. *Honore*.** The Basilian, Aldine, and Tornesian edition 1 have *ore* (“mouth”).

[Col. 0157B] **743. *Coronis*.** Thus Vossius 1 and 2, Pulmann’s sheets, the Antwerp edition, the Aldine, Basilian, and Tornesian edition 1. Other manuscripts and editions have *coronae* (“crowns”).

[Col. 0157C] **746. *Nutriti*.** The Lyon Bible has *nutrici* (“nurse”). Immediately afterward Pulmann’s sheets have *sibi* (“for itself”).

[Col. 0157C] **753. *Doctor*.** By far the greater number of editions have *ductor* (“leader”). Yet he himself calls himself “teacher of the nations” (*διδάσκαλον ἐθνῶν*), *First Epistle to Timothy* II.7. *Ductor* and *doctor*, *ducere* and *docere*, and similar forms are often interchanged. See Drakenborch on Livy XXI.27.4. Immediately afterward Vossius 2 has *cui* (“to whom”).

[Col. 0157C] **756. *Lyddae*.** The Aldine, Basilian, and Tornesian edition 1 have *Lydiae*, incorrectly, as is clear from *Acts* X.32. The scholiast in Vossius 1 had added: “Lydda, a city of Palestine situated on the shore of the Great Sea, which is now called Diospolis.” It does not seem certain when it subsequently received this name. See Cellarius, *Geographia* III, p. 322. It must be distinguished from the Diospolis mentioned by Pliny, *Natural History* V.20, outside Palestine; see Wesseling on the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, p. 150. For *arva* (“fields”), Tornesian edition 1 has *ora* (“shore”).

[Col. 0157C] **756. *Ubi*.** Vossius 1 has *sub*, transferred back from the preceding letter. Yet the expression is not without parallel. Aurelius Victor, *Origin of the Roman People* 14.2: “to have established the camp below Lavinium.”

[Col. 0157D] **758. *Anima*.** Vossius 2 has *animam*. On the following expression, see above at line 12.

[Col. 0157D] **759. *Paralytice*.** *Παραλυτικός* means “loosed throughout the body,” as in Sedulius, *Acrostichis*; or “relaxed through all the limbs,” as Celsus paraphrases it. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 98.

[Col. 0157D] **760. *Vectorem*.** Sedulius III.102:

> “And he brought back his bearer with grateful payment.”

Wopkensius compared this passage of Arator with it. From these passages Boltius, *Silvae Criticae*, p. 91, proposed restoring in Claudian’s preface to book II of *Against Eutropius* 73:

> “You will call the dolphin your bearer in vain as you die.”

[Col. 0157D] **760. *Nec*.** The Aldine and Tornesian edition 1 have *ne credere* (“do not believe”).

[Col. 0157D] **761. *Portate*.** I have printed this form on the authority of the Cambridge manuscript and Vossius 1 and 2. All the others have *portare* (“to carry”), if I am not mistaken, through a Greek construction; but why then *diu* (“for a long time”)?

[Col. 0157D] **762. *Solidum*.** So that the man might be whole and complete. See Burman on Ovid, at the cited passage, line 573.

[Col. 0158B] **763. *Cadaver*.** Sedulius III.89:

> “Behold, they were already present, carrying the living man who had now become a corpse.”

Wopkensius compared similar passages. Add the note above at line 149.

[Col. 0158B] **764. *Exstinctos*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *exstinctus* (“extinguished,” singular).

[Col. 0158B] **767. *Stare*.** Vossius 2 has *ire* (“to go”); the glosses had added *credendo* (“by believing”).

[Col. 0158C] **770. *Lavans*.** Vossius 2 has *levans* (“raising”), which could be defended by the annotation at line 170. The Greeks use *κουφίζειν* in this sense, although Thomas Magister wrongly rejected it as insufficiently Attic under the word *ῥαίσας*. See Trillerus. Here I prefer the other reading. Above, line 114:

> “By whose name he is washed in the fountain.”

[Col. 0158C] **770. *Firmas*.** The Basilian, Aldine, and Tornesian edition 1 have *firmat* (“he strengthens”).

[Col. 0158C] **771. *Hinc*.** Thus the Cambridge manuscript, Vossius 1, the Aldine, Basilian, and Tornesian edition 1. The others have *hic* (“here”). On the word *figura* (“figure”), see the note at line 158.

[Col. 0158C] **772. *Corda*.** Pulmann’s sheets and the Antwerp edition have *verba* (“words”). The transmitted reading is preferable. Among older poets, *movere* is frequently used of frenzy and divine inspiration. Brouckhusius on Tibullus I.7.51. Thus Burman, not inelegantly, conjectured in *Catalecta* I, epigram 89.9:

> “And savage Mars moves the heart.”

This is instead of *fovet* (“cherishes”), which Oudendorp preferred.

[Col. 0158C] **779. *Liquidis*.** The epithet is not idle, as Burman showed in his note on Lotichius I, elegy 8.27. Martial, *Spectacles*, epigram 28:

> “He shuddered to walk in the liquid waters.”

Thus the Thuanus manuscript; others have *abnuit* (“refused”) and *pedester* (“on foot”). Sedulius I.61:

> “He would show that monsters can be renewed through liquid waves.”

Silius VII.501:

> “The bait draws the fish from its liquid chambers.”

Calpurnius, *Eclogues* II.88:

> “Whenever I behold myself in liquid fountains,  
> I marvel at myself each time.”

Titius explains the word as “pure and transparent.” Modius, however, correctly prefers *ipse* (“myself”) from the manuscripts in *Novantiae Lectiones*, letter 43; others followed him. Cassiodorus, *Variae* I.35: “amid liquid waves.” Burman shows in his note on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.66, that such expressions as “mute silences,” “fearful fear,” and the like are likewise not idle epithets.

[Col. 0158D] **779. *Solidavit*.** Rutilius, *Itinerary* I.120:

> “May despised grief strengthen closed wounds.”

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II.130:

> “Until he strengthened his powers with ordained strength,”

and line 960:

> “May he strengthen the marrow conceived in tender milk.”

> [140] of the Church, for rush is always present in waters and palm in crowns.  
> The Church is refreshed by the water of baptism  
> [745] and by the blood of martyrdom. Long ago, while the crowd was feeding,  
> the foods nourished beneath its teeth; the seven  
> folds of the baskets began to expand: Scripture plainly sings  
> that there are so many Churches throughout the world, because the Spirit  
> is present there in this way and divine power marks their names,  
> [750] although we celebrate one renowned Church in them all.  
> Thus the appearance protects the man, in whom the vessel itself  
> remains within a vessel and serves him; safe under this guide from the enemy,  
> he goes forth—the teacher who conquers all things by his weapons.  
> [Col. 0157B] Peter, ever watchful over the sentinels of the entrusted sheepfold,  
> [755] after seeing everything and inspecting the saints in order,  
> crossed the fields of Lydda, where, standing beside the walls,  
> he sees Aeneas living with limbs that had been dead,  
> [141] and in his soul, its bonds loosened and its burden released,  
> to die without dying. “Rise,” he said, “paralytic;  
> [760] [Col. 0158A] put your bearer in order, and do not delay to repay  
> its service, after being carried for so long.” By this office of speech  
> he who had previously flowed away in his sinews is bound together whole.  
> Then the man was formed anew, and the corpse of long  
> [765] time, its extinguished limbs, raises itself again to life.  
> Raising himself, he leaves behind the traces of his empty bed,  
> which had been part of death for the wretched man. Along that way  
> the whole populace began to stand, and a great salvation  
> came upon many through the illness of one man; and, when touched by the water,  
> [770] washing souls in the fountain, he strengthened them by another’s power.  
> [142] From this point I shall explain what the sacred figure signifies,  
> if he whose voice restores bodies moves my heart.  
> [Col. 0158B] The age of eight years, which is disclosed as the duration  
> of his illness, shows that under the ancient law his limbs  
> failed during this period, deprived of strength,  
> [775] lying beneath the old law; for they always inflict deadly wounds,  
> by which an infant is wounded when the eighth day comes. From that  
> point he healed the man long afflicted and torn by the peril of the flesh,  
> and in liquid waters made him whole, so that the eighth  
> [780] [Col. 0159A] [Note: [Col. 0159B]

**781. *Numero*.** Pulmann’s sheets and the Antwerp edition have *munere* (“service”): plainly an error that could have been avoided by transposition.

[Col. 0159B] **783. *Hinc*.** Vossius 2 has *hic* (“here”).

[Col. 0159B] **784. *Ruunt*.** “They come to an end; they collapse.” The Cambridge manuscript prefixes the following line to this one.

[Col. 0159B] **785. *Hinc*.** The Antwerp edition and the Lyon Bible have *hic* (“here”).

[Col. 0159B] **785. *Priore*.** The Aldine, Basilian, and Tornesian edition 1 have *priora* (“former things,” neuter plural).

[Col. 0159B] **786. *Neci*.** Of natural death caused by illness. Below, II.127:

> “Deaths that cannot be loosened.”

[Col. 0159C] See Freinshemius on Florus III.23.7.

[Col. 0159C] **788. *Siloa*.** It was a lake or pool, or, as the evangelist John calls it, a *κολυμβήθρα* (“pool”), in which people swam and washed themselves when afflicted with various diseases. Christ commands the man blind from birth to go there in John IX; and beside it, according to the same evangelist, the paralytic had lain helpless for thirty-eight years, chapter V. Isaiah, chapter VIII, testifies that the waters of Siloam were shallow and tranquil. John relates that they were stirred at a fixed time. There were also many other health-giving and medicinal waters in various places in Judaea. In the same evangelist the pool is called *προβατικὴ κολυμβήθρα*, chapter V, as Theophylact quotes it, almost as though one said “the cattle-trough.” Drepanus, letter 1:

> “If we seek the life-giving water of a tranquil fountain,  
> behold, the healing spring of Siloam is here for us.”

Porticoes had been built beside it, where the sick could lie without exposure to the weather. Hence Arator:

> “A pool enclosed  
> by porticoes.”

In this name the syllable has three possible quantities. Sedulius III:

> “He had come to the water of Siloam,  
> and, through the healing remedy of kindred mud,  
> he had bathed his eyes in pure water.”

Arator I:

> “For whom nearby Siloam was stirred.”

Sedulius, *Enchiridion*:

> “They call it Siloam, where the blind,  
> with spittle applied, recover their eyes.”

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 123.

[Col. 0159D] **790. *Judaea*.** The Lyon Bible has *Judaee*.

[Col. 0159D] **791. *Mosi*.** The Cambridge manuscript and Vossius 1 and 2 have *Moysi*; the Aldine, Basilian, and Tornesian editions have *Mosae*. I have not dared to follow the Cambridge and Vossian manuscripts. Repeat the reasoning given above at line 692. I retained *Mosi* from *Μωσεύς*, just as *Achilli* comes from *Ἀχιλλεύς*. Vossius, *De Analogia* II.9; Vorstius on Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I.17.3; Gronovius on Ecclesiastes X; Burman on Ovid, *Heroides* VIII.9; Arator I.743; Heinsius on Virgil, *Eclogues* VIII.70 and *Aeneid* I.30, 120; II.7, 436; XI.243; Burman the Younger on the *Anthology*, vol. I, pp. 85 and 191; Wopkensius, *Miscellaneous New Observations*, vol. II, pp. 25 and 62, provide numerous examples. To these I add Marius Victorinus on Genesis, p. 311 of Fabricius’s *Corpus*:

> “Now disclose the famous archives of Moses, the lawgiver.”

John of Salisbury, *Policraticus* I.10: “to confess the finger of God in the signs of Moses.” Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ* 6, who rejects “the God of Moses.” In the margin Scaliger preferred *Moysei*.

[Col. 0160B] **792. *Adepta*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *adempta* (“taken away”).

[Col. 0160B] **794. *Hinc*.** The Lyon Bible has *huic* (“to this one”). The Antwerp edition likewise has *cui veniens* (“to whom, when he came”) immediately afterward.

[Col. 0160C] **796. *Gerit*.** Vossius 1 has *regit* (“guides”). The error occurs frequently. See my father on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 4.4 and Drakenborch on Livy XXVII.40.2.

[Col. 0160C] **800. *Fide*.** The Basilian and Tornesian edition 1 have *fides* (“faith,” nominative).

[Col. 0160C] **800. *Projicit*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *projicit*. Older books frequently use this form in compounds of *jacio*. See Duker on Florus I.10.5. The Groningen manuscript has in Isidore, *Etymologies* XIX.25: “because half of it is thrown backward.” I greatly prefer this to *ejicitur* (“is cast out”), which appears in the editions.

[Col. 0160C] **803. *Fundebat*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *fundabat* (“founded”). The other reading should be retained, as Sedulius’s letter to Macedonius, p. 11, confirms: “By distributing everything to the needy, he lost nothing through the outpouring of so great a fortune.” This passage so closely resembles the present one that one might almost say that the latter was copied from it. Tacitus, *Annals* XIV.31: “They poured out all their fortunes.” Orosius, *History* IV.16: “Private wealth was poured back into the impoverished treasury.” Add Ruhnken on Aquila Romanus, *On Figures of Speech*, p. 177. The error in the Cambridge manuscript arose from the frequent interchange of *a* and *e*; traces of this corruption survive elsewhere. Isidore, *Etymologies* XII.1: “They shake out the arrows they have received.” Read, from the Groningen manuscript, “the arrows they have caught.” A more disgraceful error occurs in the same work XIV.2: “From the south, Armenia”—the passage concerns Persia; who would place Armenia south of it? The Groningen manuscript admirably has “Carmania.” Book XVII.5: “unfit through fruit and affected by sterility.” Write *effeti* (“made barren”). From the same manuscript, John of Salisbury, *Policraticus* V.3: “The shields and the Palladium testify to this, certain sacred pledges of empire.” I read *secreta quaedam* (“certain secret things”) from Florus I.2.3. *Secreta* first became *sacrata* and then *sacra*. Florus I.7.3: “so that he might greet the man as king.” It must certainly be written *salutarat* (“had saluted”): the sense and the testimony of others require it. This is the fortunate conjecture of Anna on Aurelius Victor, *Illustrious Men* 7.19, and on Eutropius I.7; I am surprised that Duker remembered none of this.

[Col. 0160D] **805. *Feretro*.** The bodies that were carried to the pyre or burial among the ancients were placed upon a bier, which Latin, imitating the Greek word, called a *feretrum*. Isidore XX.11: “A *feretrum* is so called because the dead are carried in it. It is a Greek name, for *φέρετρον* is derived from *φέρειν* (‘to carry’). In Latin it is called *capulus*.” Sedulius III:

> “He brought life-giving help and, touching the bier,  
> said, ‘Rise.’”

Venantius likewise suggests this in book I of *The Life of Martin*:

> “That burden is added; they lower the corpse from their shoulders,  
> and now they can no longer bear it, but death grows heavier in the weight.”

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII.19. Luke has *ἡ σορός*, the little bed on which the dead person is carried out. Virgil has *torus* (“bed”), Plautus *capulum* (“bier”), Martial *sandapila* (“funeral bier”), Horace *libitina* (“funeral apparatus”); the Gospel translator renders it *loculus*, which properly means a jar or urn in which ashes are stored. Sedulius III:

> “He brought life-giving help and, touching the bier,  
> said, ‘Rise, young man.’”

At funerals there was a *libitinarius*, who arranged everything pertaining to the funeral; a *pollinctor*, who washed and anointed the corpse; a *designator*, who prescribed the order of the funeral; and *sandapilarii*, who carried out the dead. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 103.

Luke says nothing about a bier. He merely records that they washed the corpse, which is also what Arator’s words refer to: “washed more by tears.” This custom was common among various peoples. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.218:

> “Some prepare warm water and bronze vessels boiling over the flames,  
> and wash and anoint the cold body.”

See Servius and Ouzelius on Minucius Felix, p. 63. Luke adds that the corpse had been placed in an upper room, which Buxtorf explained in *The Jewish Synagogue*, chapter 49, p. 700; there Peter restored her to life. See *Acts* IX.39. I would therefore understand *feretrum* here rather as the bed on which the corpse had been placed in the upper room. Among certain peoples, the washed and anointed body was placed on a bed in a particular part of the house, usually in the vestibule. An excellent representation of this form appears on a monument published by the learned men of Leipzig from the *Literary Observations* in the *Acts* for 1740, p. 20. The Greeks call this practice *προτίθεσθαι* and *πρόθεσις*; Kuhnius showed this in his note on Aelian, *Various History* I.10. A learned man, however, rejected Kuhnius’s view of that passage in *New Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. III, p. 84. Duportus collected some material on this bed in his note on Theophrastus, *Characters*, p. 470, and Kirchmann, *On Funerals* I.12; but he wrongly applies to it the passage of Lysias, *Against Eratosthenes*, p. 197, ed. Taylor: *ἀλλὰ κλίσιον μισθωσάμενοι, προὔθεντο αὐτόν* is correctly translated “having rented a little hut, they exposed him there,” not “having rented a little bed.” A learned man has already noted Kirchmann’s error in his *Annotations on Hesychius*, *New Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. I, p. 80.]

> [143] May the year release the body extinguished by wounds;  
> when the day arrives according to that number, Christ, rising again  
> in solemn fashion, consecrated the work. Time remains in force,  
> but returns with a better ordinance: hence wounds creep forth,  
> hence what was taken away collapses. There the rule subjects men to  
> [785] punishments; here medicine purifies in the waters,  
> and, after the former interval, the limbs long relaxed in death  
> are bound again to salvation.  
>   
> The paralytic too, marked by the number of years,  
> had lain helpless; for him nearby Siloam, once stirred,  
> alas, provided no waters. The pool, enclosed  
> [790] [144] by porticoes, was Judaea; for it holds five courts  
> within its five enclosures, having acquired the pattern of the Law  
> through the five books of Moses. Enclosed in its circuit,  
> [Col. 0159B] infirm Judaea had forever beheld Jesus without receiving his gift,  
> [Col. 0160A] sick in her own books. From her he rescues one,  
> [795] he who, coming, bore away sins; a figure rightly  
> borne throughout the world. After he drove him to the fountain,  
> releasing the sabbaths, grace overcame the law.  
> Peter restores to the Church the teachings of the Master,  
> by whose hand the one paralytic leaps up throughout the world;  
> [800] and, as faith advances, the world casts off its bonds.  
>   
> [145] You too, Joppa, famous for heavenly signs and powerful  
> in praise, we sing in our poems—the place where Tabitha  
> poured out enduring wealth and was always a mother  
> to the needy, who, when the term of her life had closed,  
> [805] was laid in the midst, washed more by tears, upon a bier,  
> [Col. 0160B] [146] destined to live after her own funeral. Confidence summons Peter;  
> [Col. 0161A] [Note: [Col. 0161D]

**808. *Vacet*.** Sedulius V.71:

> “So that the pious man might not be lacking in piety.”

Wopkensius compared this passage.

[Col. 0161D] **809. *Praestaturus*.** Justinus XI.12.14: “that he would provide these things for Darius”; in one manuscript of Franeque this is *praesentaturum* (“that he would present”). Add Drakenborch on Livy XXXVII.25.2.

[Col. 0162A] **809. *Lugentia*.** Pulmann’s sheets and the Antwerp edition have *ingentia* (“huge”), incorrectly. Sedulius III.129:

> “They had come to the mournful heights of the grieving house  
> and to the house in mourning.”

That is, “weeping,” as Wopkensius explains in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. II, p. 53. Similarly “trembling walls,” “terrified roofs,” and other examples were collected by the learned commentators on Silius I.129. Incerus, *Panegyric on Constantine* 22.6, has “mournful and grieving houses”; from Vossius’s excerpts I emend it to “funereal houses,” since *mournful* and *grieving* seem inelegantly joined.

[Col. 0162B] **811. *Exuviis*.** Thus the Cambridge manuscript, Vossius 1 and 2, the Basilian and Tornesian editions. The others have *exuviisque*. Understand “garments.” See the note on Sedulius V.200.

[Col. 0162B] **811. *Dorcadis*.** A Greek name, *δόρκων*, “doe” or “young deer.” See Mollius on Longus, *Pastoral*, p. 16. Gifanius, *Collections on Lucretius*, p. 54, shows that it was a feminine name. In Hebrew she was called Tabitha. Sacred writings often give one person two names taken from different languages. See Vorstius, *Academic Exercises* V.13. Thus Thomas was Syriac, while Didymus was Greek. Sedulius, forgetting this, later took one of these names as a surname, V.379. Perhaps Nonnus does so as well in his *Paraphrase*; see Nansius’s notes, p. 129.

[Col. 0162C] **811. *Ipsis*.** The Aldine, Basilian, and Tornesian edition 1 have *ipsae* (“they themselves,” feminine). Luke has *μετ’ αὐτῶν* (“with them”), IX.39. Arator perhaps embraced the preposition in his thought more than he expressed it, a phenomenon for which traces may be found elsewhere. See Vossius on Velleius Paterculus II.65.3 and Drakenborch on Livy I.14.7. If anyone prefers to understand the word as a dative, because of the following *dederant* (“had given”), I do not object.

[Col. 0162C] **812. *Texuerant*.** Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* I, prose 1: “which she herself had woven with her own hands”; and prose 3: “the garment which I had woven with my own hands.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.263, is close:

> “The rich gifts which Dido  
> had made, and had embroidered the fabrics with fine gold.”

It is well known that women, even those of the highest rank, devoted themselves among the ancients to spinning and weaving wool at home. Hence the titles *lanifica* (“wool-worker”) and *domiseda* (“home-sitter”) were considered no small honor on inscriptions. See Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 252, no. 3.

[Col. 0162D] **815. *Quidquid*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *quisque et*; Vossius 1 and 2 have *qui quod*; the Antwerp edition has *quisque*. Immediately afterward Pulmann’s sheets, the Aldine, Basilian, and Tornesian editions have *bona facta* (“good deeds”).

[Col. 0162D] **818. *Facunda*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *fecunda* (“fruitful”), as in book I.137.

[Col. 0162D] **819. *Nimiumque*.** Pulmann’s sheets and the Antwerp edition have *nonnunquam* (“sometimes”). The word *sonorus* (“sonorous”), condemned by some, is granted to poets; they consider *canorus* (“melodious”) preferable, at least in prose. See Vossius, *On the Purity of Latin Speech* VII, p. 367. Hence, from the Groningen manuscript and an old edition of Isidore III.18, I prefer “melodious through striking.” Gothofredus printed *sonorum*.

[Col. 0162D] **821. *Pulsante*.** Vossius 1 has *pensante* (“weighing”). The transmitted reading is more pleasing and appropriate to sound. Rutilius, *Itinerary* I.203:

> “When struck, the familiar voices are returned by the air.”

See Heinsius on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.123, and Bonda, *Various Readings* I.8. The meaning is that the matter itself seemed to cry out—the matter of which they were silent—and that this was heard by everyone, because faith signified it with such clarity.]

> Confidence calls him forth; bearing the pledge of divine love,  
> so that he may never fail in the piety that vows require,  
> [147] he is present to render what is sought. As he approaches the grieving house,  
> [810] poor flocks and bands of widows stand there and display their arms,  
> burdened with the garments which Tabitha’s own hands  
> had woven and given them. O what remedies burning grief  
> implores! They do not display the feeling of compassion  
> [148] with mournful murmuring, nor frequently bring to their lips  
> [815] [Col. 0162A] the instruments of prayer; whatever good deeds deserve,  
> they wished to express through services, and chose to reject  
> the speech of their own voice, lest the wounds of their hearts  
> lie hidden—wounds that have made a path through tears.  
> For the mourner, to have said nothing is eloquent matter; and the cause,  
> [820] much more sonorous, asks for what the tongue is silent about,  
> nor does it cease striking the ear with clamorous faith.  
> By this faith they approach Peter, who is accustomed  
> to hear minds, and orders everyone to go outside,  
> [Col. 0163A] [Note: [Col. 0163C]

**823. *Flexoque*.** See Sedulius, *Hymn* II.54. They sometimes say *ponere genu* (“to place the knee”), as Luke does in *Acts* IX.40, *θεὶς τὰ γόνατα* (“having bent the knees”). Some have judged this expression insufficiently Greek; Burman corrected their error in his note on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.340.

[Col. 0163C] **823. *Arvis*.** Vossius 1 has *artus* (“limbs”). The more familiar Greek construction could defend this. Juvenal, *Satires* VIII.4:

> “and the shoulders smaller than those of Corvinus.”

In a manuscript I saw *nasumque minorem Corvini* (“and the nose smaller than Corvinus’s”). Add Vossius, *Ars Grammatica* VII.41. Yet *arvis* seems more suitable to Arator. See above at line 35.

[Col. 0163C] **825. *Propriisque a*.** I printed this form from both Vossian manuscripts. All the others have *propriis quia*. The copyists corrupted it because they did not recognize *a* as used for *propter* (“because of”); see Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XIII.10.

[Col. 0163C] **826. *Dic*.** Sedulius I.204:

> “Tell me, Nature, where your laws are after such things.”

Here there are notes. The Tornesian edition 1 has *legis* (“of the law”). If preferred, *mundana* may be a neuter plural, just as *caerula ponti* (“the blue things of the sea”) and similar expressions, which I discussed in my note on Sedulius I.120.

[Col. 0163D] **829. *Sensit*.** The Basilian and Tornesian editions have *sentit* (“he senses,” present tense).

[Col. 0163D] **830. *Defleta*.** Both Vossian manuscripts have *deflecta* (“turned aside”); in the first, however, a deletion mark had been added over the superfluous letter. *Defleta* means the same as *fleta* (“wept over”). Above, line 171:

> “Even when the bodies had been mourned and their course completed.”

Add Wopkensius, *New Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. II, p. 53.

[Col. 0163D] **836. *Itura*.** The elegant and highly probable conjecture of my very dear friend Wassenberg is *iterata* (“repeated”). Below, II.84:

> “Teaching these things to be repeated,”

and II.605:

> “He does not repeat discordant things.”

Above, line 228:

> “I think these things were repeated.”

Add Gronovius, *Dissertation on Statius*, chapter 34, and Burman on Ovid, *Heroides* XVIII.135. From the Groningen manuscript I believe the same reading should be restored to Isidore I.16: “Palimbachius was so called because he was drawn from Bacchus.” Thus the old edition and Gothofredus. Write: “because he was repeated.”

[Col. 0163D] **837. *Hanc*.** Pulmann’s sheets and the Antwerp edition have *huic* (“to this one”). Several others, apart from the Aldine and Basilian, have *hinc* (“from here”). The passage indicates that Peter’s hand came upon Tabitha, through which life was given to the poor by her generosity.

[Col. 0164C] **847. *Gentili*.** Christians called all those *gentiles* who were devoted to the superstitious religion of the ancients. Vorstius explained the reason for the name in his note on Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II.11.4. Compare Sedulius I.1:

> “While pagan poets devote themselves to their own fictions.”

Justus, *Specimen of Observations*, p. 71, prefers “they devoted themselves to the poets’ inventions,” because this is how it is read in the anonymous *Life of Adalbero*. But the argument is not sufficiently strong. Against that reading I set the anonymous *Life of St. Tillo* by Paul, in Bollandus under 7 January, where we find: “Therefore, while pagan poets strive to embellish their own fictions with lengthy styles.” This is plainly taken from Sedulius; the passage was supplied by Vossius’s diligence in *On the Purity of Latin Speech* IV.17.

[Col. 0164C] **851. *In*.** Both Vossian manuscripts and the Antwerp edition delete this word.

[Col. 0164C] **852. *Quae*.** Vossius 2 has *quae et* (“and which”).

[Col. 0164D] **855. *Fixit*.** Vossius 1 has *fudit* (“poured out”).

[Col. 0164D] **856. *Magis*.** The Aldine and Basilian editions, placing the punctuation afterward, join the word with *hora* (“hour”). It is better to refer it to *rectius* (“more rightly”); a comparative is often accompanied by this word. Fabricius also recognized this in his commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 37. Thus Heraldus aptly defends *potius magis* (“rather more”) in Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* II, p. 81. Add Vossius, *Ars Grammatica* VII.16; Barthius, *Adversaria* XXI.3; Taubmann on Virgil, *Culex* 48; Duker on Florus IV.2.47; and the note on Sedulius V.347. The Greeks use *μᾶλλον* in this way. See Nansius on Nonnus’s *Paraphrase*, p. 41; Heupel on Mark VII.36; Davis on Maximus of Tyre, p. 531; Valckenaer on Herodotus II, p. 171; Rhoer on Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, p. 76. Likewise *valde*, *maxime*, and *admodum* (“very,” “especially,” “exceedingly”) are added to superlatives. Wopkensius, *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. VIII, p. 38; and the Greek *μάλιστα*, as in Aelian, *Various History* II.4. Thus *ὄχ’ ἄριστος* (“by far the best”) in Homer, *Iliad* I.69.

[Col. 0164D] **862. *Nata*.** The Cambridge manuscript, Fabricius’s edition, and the Lyon Bible have *orta* (“arisen”). It seems to have arisen from a gloss and been fashioned from the preceding *ortum*. Yet *nasci* (“to be born”) is elegantly used for “to arise.” Lucan III.231:

> “To open the gates opposed to the rising Phoebus.”

See Burman on the same work II.106. Compare *mori* (“to die”). Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 12: “The day dies into night.”]

> they go outside; and, bending his knee, he bows more lowly toward the ground.  
> [149] Then, opening more fully, his prayer rises on high to the Thunderer  
> [825] and soon flies beyond the stars, entering because of its own keys.  
> “Tell me, worldly wisdom, where are your laws?  
> By what power do you deny that things corrupted within themselves  
> return, when you see life come from death?” When Peter perceived  
> that God’s gifts were present, by which she was to be restored to salvation,  
> [830] he turned toward her and spoke: “Rise, Tabitha.” Called, she returns,  
> restored to the light; she was astonished to survive herself. Immediately  
> he took her hand, raised her, and presented her to the rejoicing crowd.  
> She deserved to touch Peter’s right hand,  
> [835] the hand that had been generous to the poor, by which, as life returned,  
> [Col. 0163B] the rest of her limbs were lifted, and life, about to pass through  
> [150] her whole body, entered her—life that had been the cause.  
> If we are rightly moved, the restored day of the soul is revealed,  
> suited to the figures: the shadow of ancient danger  
> [840] had pressed it down too deeply. At Peter’s voice it turned,  
> and the head, previously weighed down in the bosom of the obscure law,  
> rose as another Church appeared, repelling the darkness,  
> with the light of works accompanying faith. Salvation had not been promised  
> [Col. 0164A] from the mouth of the law, because grace, through the fountain of rebirth,  
> [845] began to grant the gifts of everlasting life.  
> Cornelius was revered in the city of Caesarea,  
> born from a gentile stock. His life, devoted to pious causes,  
> consecrated him to the waters; by performing what faith customarily  
> provides for those washed in baptism, he began to believe—  
> [850] he who performed those things. For an angel sent from the stars  
> approached him and said: “In the sight of the Most High Lord  
> stand the things you scatter, and the words for which you pray.  
> [151] So that rewards may not be lacking for your virtues, receive  
> a certain path, with Peter coming here.” Thus, flashing with speech,  
> [855] the messenger established the commands for eternal washings.  
> [Col. 0164B] It was then the ninth hour, at which faith, more rightly  
> proceeding, would emerge threefold; for the simple third  
> teaches this again three times, and each single element makes  
> a sacred figure threefold, and the threefold repetition of three confesses it.  
> [860] This is the powerful ninth hour that restored eyes to the world  
> when day returned after darkness, when light arising  
> from the rays of the cross brought forth the dawn  
> and filled all things with this radiance without end. For the world is certainly a place burdened  
> with Gentiles, who, once washed in baptism,  
> [Col. 0165A] [Note: [Col. 0165B]

**865. *Plena*.** Pulmann’s sheets and the Antwerp edition have *plenave purgato* (“or, once purified, full”).

[Col. 0165B] **868. *Sinit*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *sint ut*; Pulmann’s sheets and the Antwerp edition have *sunt ut*.

[Col. 0165C] **868. *Praecedant*.** Vossius 1 has *praecellant* (“excel”). There is no substantial difference. The variant spelling arose from the proximity of the letters D and L, which were confused, as Scioppius shows in *Verisimilia* III.8. I add Isidore, *Etymologies* II.30, as a witness: “The letter A is an indication, when something is said with the indication of its own name.” The Groningen manuscript correctly has “something is extracted from the indication of its own name.” The same work IX.1: “from which Naevius … and from the orators Gracchus, Cato, Cicero, and the others shone forth,” not “flowed forth.” I established the passage from the Groningen manuscript; Gothofredus treated it badly, and the old edition corrupted it. Benzo’s *Panegyric on Henry III*, in vol. I of Mencken’s *Writers of German History*, p. 960, should likewise be corrected: “The Mantuan poet Maro, Lucan and Statius, Pindar or Homer, and our Horace, Grillius, Quintilian, the comic Terence.” Who is Grillius? I think *Ovidius* should be read, unless someone would prefer to think of Gellius, which does not seem very probable to me.

[Col. 0165C] **868. *Tardos*.** “Those called later.” He does not permit those called earlier to precede those called later in payment, that is, to receive a larger share of money than those called later. The entire meaning of this passage depends on Christ’s narrative recorded at the beginning of Matthew XX.

[Col. 0165D] **876. *Venit*.** Thus the Cambridge manuscript and both Vossian manuscripts. All the others have *veniet* (“will come”). He uses the perfect tense, referring to Cornelius’s actual action.

[Col. 0165D] **877. *Orbis*.** The Cambridge manuscript, Vossius 2, and Tornesian edition 1 have *oris* (“of the mouths”), having altered the text because they did not consider that *orbis* could refer to its individual parts. Barthius on Claudian, *The Gothic War* 3. Hence it is also used for “region.” Burman on Gratius, *Cynegeticon* 150. This verse is absent from the Basilian edition.

[Col. 0165D] **878. *Coenacula*.** See the note above at line 104, and Demster on Rosinus V.48. This passage also shows that writers of this period did not understand Luke’s word *δῶμα* in *Acts* X.9 as meaning a roof, as Bartholinus in *The Paralytic of the New Testament*, p. 366, and Alberti in *Philological Observations*, p. 139, maintain, but as an upper room, as the common translator renders it—“into the upper parts”—a usage approved by Pricæus and Vitringa, *The Ancient Synagogue*, part I, book I, chapter 6. Stephanus shows in *Miscellaneous Notes* III.28 that *δωμάτιον* occurs in Lysias for an interior part of a house which was at the same time an upper room.

[Col. 0166B] **885. *Hac tandem*.** Vossius 1 has *hac veniens aetate Redemptor eadem* (“the Redeemer coming at this same age”); Vossius 2 has *haec eadem veniens*. The Aldine, Basilian, Antwerp, and Tornesian edition 1 have *hac ipsa* (“at this very age”). The latter is not displeasing.

[Col. 0166C] **893. *Laetabitur*.** Vossius 2 has *jactabitur* (“will boast”), which the glosses explain by *laetabitur* (“will rejoice”). Gorallus, on Severus’s *Aetna* 23, cites from ancient glosses: *jactari*, *καυχᾶσθαι* (“to boast”). He says, however, that he has no other example.

[Col. 0166C] **894. *Pinguior*.** Barthius, in his note on Sedulius’s *Prologue*, line 7, cites *ditior* (“richer”). The other reading is defended by the arguments given in the note on the letter to Florianus 7.

[Col. 0166C] **895. *Deliciosa*.** See Barthius on Sedulius’s *Prologue*, line 7. Rutilius, *Itinerary*, 378:

> “Pleasant pools enclosed by a shallow ford are pleasing.”

The learned man’s attempt to read *desidiosa* (“sluggish”) there, in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. III, p. 366, is futile.

[Col. 0166C] **895. *Relinquit*.** Vossius 2, and the Basilian and Tornesian editions, have *reliquit* (“left”). It could be explained by enallage. Ruhnken has noted that different tenses are joined together countless times in his note on Rutilius Lupus I, p. 45.

[Col. 0166C] **901. *Vasis*.** Luke has *σκεῦος*, a word used generally for utensils; in view of what follows, it seems to refer to a covering such as a sheet or similar cloth.

[Col. 0166D] **901. *Visio*.** The Cambridge manuscript has *viso* (“having seen”). Below, line 931:

> “When called, Peter discovered what his vision meant.”

[Col. 0166D] **902. *Quidquid*.** The Aldine and Basilian editions have *quidquam* (“anything”). Immediately afterward Vossius 1 has *subdit* (“he adds”), which should be printed.

[Col. 0166D] **903. *Praefertur*.** Vossius 1 has *profertur* (“is brought forth”). The transmitted reading is preferable. Above, line 112:

> “What this light of the work displays.”

See there. “To prefer savagery” occurs in Isidore X, p. 1086; but from the Groningen manuscript I would rather establish the passage as follows: “For he endures the savagery, neither having taken revenge nor being moved by any pain of disgrace.” Orosius VI, 15: “And when Pompey’s head had been brought to him and seen.” I think that *praelatoque* should be read from the Utrecht manuscript; I am not greatly surprised that Havercamp neglected the manuscript’s reading, since learned men have long observed that he was rather careless in excerpting variants. The interchange of the prepositions *pro* and *prae* is, moreover, common. See Drakenborch on Livy VI, 40, 1. Add what was said above on verse 50.

The lights shone fully upon the cleansed world.

The number ten is usually wont to follow this, bestowing all things,

152 which the judge offers to those who observe the ten commandments,

and does not allow the slow to precede their elders in bronze,

the aid of this age, which the pioneer approached

[870] by the sacred font—would that the action of our life seek it,

and that mortal birth set before itself this purpose,

so that the love of the believer might contemplate the honor of things

and bear an example in its merits, he who offered it to the waters!

And now Cornelius, receptive of faith, by a votive indication,

[875] orders three men to go to Peter. The threefold confession

thus comes to the water that generates, and through it the number

of Europe, Asia, and Libya will be held together.

[Col. 0165B] 153 Peter advances to enter the lofty upper rooms,

now at midday; the elevated place instructs

[880] and, looking down upon the earth, [instructs] Peter always

to follow heavenly things, not earthly ones. The circle of the sixth hour

also reveals the era in which Christ came into the world

to bestow the saving aid; and the number of days

put forward the example by which he had previously founded the world,

[885] [Col. 0166A] which the Redeemer, finally coming in this age,

forbids to be oppressed by the dominion of sin. Thus, finally, the sixth

is said also to have brought that event about: the master, wearied from the road,

when, sitting above the mouth of the well,

through the girl’s vessels he seeks cups of water,

[890] intending everywhere to give rest to his Church from its own spring.

At that hour Peter is hungry; he is thirsty, that pious master

who always loves to add to his gifts, for whom he increased

the honor of the name and likewise grants nourishment to faith. The world will rejoice,

when this hunger is satisfied, which flows more richly than every gift,

[895] 154 delightful, and leaves no one empty,

bearing perpetual banquets. You who know how to loose,

shake off, Peter, the sluggish restraints of my speech,

and extend your tongue to me, exhausted by your feasts.

The heavenly key-bearer saw heaven opened,

[900] exercising his own honor; from there a likeness

of a vessel is lowered, so that on earth the vision may be

that everything can be contained in Peter’s body;

whatever he takes as food,

he makes into food for the Church. The image is preferred,

[Col. 0167A] [Note: [Col. 0167C]

904. *Ordinibus.* I confess that I do not know what meaning Arator gave this word. The manuscripts alter nothing, and there is no room for conjecture. He intended to express *ἀρχαῖς* (*archais*), which occurs in Acts X, § 11. The Vulgate translates it as “beginnings,” and not with sufficient accuracy. The Greeks use the word for the extremities of anything. Valckenaer’s observation on the meaning of the word, in his note on Herodotus IV, p. 308, deserves the closest examination.

[Col. 0167C] 905. *Ecclesiae.* Vossianus 1, Fabricius, Antwerp, and the Lyon Bible transpose the words: “The form is of the Church.” Consult the note on the Letter to Vigilantius, verse 9.

[Col. 0167C] 911. *Quod.* The Cambridge manuscript has *quot*; the Basel edition has *quae*. The received reading is preferable in this sense: “Take away from them what they are,” and, once that has been removed, “make them like yourself.”

[Col. 0167D] 914. *Sanctae.* Fabricius, Antwerp, and the Lyon Bible have *sancto*, so that it refers to Peter.

[Col. 0167D] 916. *Sonuit.* Vossianus 2 has *sonavit*.

[Col. 0167D] 919. *Sabellius.* The first syllable is long, although Sedulius shortens it in I, 317:

“And we must confess that we are Sabellius.”

Vossius already noted this in Arator, *Ars grammatica* II, 39.

[Col. 0167D] 922. *Trino.* Vossianus 1 has *in uno*, contrary to Arator’s intention.

[Col. 0167D] 923. *Relinquit.* Aldine and Basel have *reliquit*, as above at 895.

[Col. 0167D] 924. *Nam.* Vossianus 1 has *jam*. See above at 618, and the very friendly van Dorp in *Observationes*, chapter 11.

[Col. 0167D] 924. *Monentis.* Antwerp has *moventis*; the same confusion occurs below at 1044.

[Col. 0167D] 926. *Quo.* Cambridge has *qui*.

[Col. 0168C] 928. *Lateris.* Aldine, Basel, and Tornæsius 1 punctuate: “your side, who...”

[Col. 0168C] 929. *Oberrat.* Some editions have *oberret*, and shortly afterward *gemat*, so that a definite matter is designated; the other reading is preferable.

[Col. 0168C] 931. *Quae.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *quam*.

[Col. 0168C] 934. *Patescit.* Thus the manuscripts, but Aldine, Basel, and Tornæsius 1 have *patescat*. The sense indicates that Christ was manifested through Peter’s recognition; *cognoscere* is used for *agnoscere*. See the note on Sedulius V, 11.

[Col. 0168C] 938. *Cognorat.* Cambridge has *cognovit*. Basel shortly afterward has *aquas*. The former reading is more correct, because it specifically understands the waters of baptism.

[Col. 0168D] 942. *Cornelii.* Fabricius notes in his index that the second syllable is shortened here, although it is lengthened at verses 846 and 874. I do not see this: Arator contracted the final syllables, as shortly afterward in the same words.

[Col. 0168D] 943. *Quem.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *quae*. On the bent knee, see the note on Sedulius, Hymn II, 54. Noltenius correctly asserts the ecclesiastical Latin use of *sanctificare*, *Lexicon Antibarbarum*, p. 718. Add the note on Sedulius II, 244.

[Col. 0168D] 945. *Erigis.* Thus I wrote from Cambridge and Vossianus 1. All the others have *erigit*. The following lines condemn that reading. Vossianus 1 has *caput huic*. The learned Wassenbergius also preferred *arcet honoris opes*, because of the preceding *gratis*.

[Col. 0168D] 947. *Natalemque.* Vossianus 1 has: “The font has just restored a birthday to you.”

[Col. 0168D] 951. *Magnanimes.* Thus Vossianus 1 and 2, Aldine, Basel, Antwerp, and Tornæsius 1. The others have *magnanimi*. See the note on verse 146.

[Col. 0168D] 952. *Quid.* Vossianus 1 has *quam*.]

Four orders submitting themselves; one

[905] 155 form of the Church rises above the four

parts of the world and opens as many mouths for heralds,

retaining every kind alike of birds, cattle, wild beasts,

and reptiles. These are joined to mortals

according to their merits and vices. Therefore it is clear what the author

[910] commanded: that the nations be poured into the Church’s inward parts.

“Kill and eat,” while he commands; “take away what they are,

and make them like yourself.” He who is transformed is regarded as another.

Finally Saul dies, because Paul has begun to live.

“Far be it,” Peter says; “how great is the reverence due to the holy

[915] [Col. 0167B] Law!” And, hungry, he rejects the foods offered.

Three times the Lord’s voice sounded, a voice prescribed for salvation:

this the Father, the Son together, and the Holy Spirit accomplished.

Against this faith the combative Arius falls, denying

that three Persons are one; Sabellius, however, asserts one [Person],

[920] but, confessing the Father, says that he is afterward called

the Son and the Holy Spirit in turn,

and that he is wholly the Father himself; what one summit contains

in threefold order, the former divides and the latter leaves undivided.

156 Both, defeated, lie prostrate, for the threefold command of the one who admonishes

[925] indicates through the Persons one number in their powers,

by which command he calls the nations. This must be believed,

if we wish to complete the faith: you do all things, Christ,

cleanse them with your blood, which flowed from the wound in your side,

joined to the separated water. The spotted serpent wanders

[930] and groans that its poison has been extinguished by the water.

When summoned, Peter learned what his vision was,

he who bears the name from its meaning—for “Peter” in the Hebrew

language means “recognizing” (*agnoscens*). As a gift Christ granted

him to be so called, so that, through the one who recognizes, it might become clear

[935] that he descended to see those whom he had sent there.

Peter, who had been a seeker of the waters, is said to descend,

coming to the people and the new nation,

which had not yet known the water. That portion, plainly, is submerged

without the sacred font, whose path leads those who go onward

[940] [Col. 0168B] to the aid of a better homeland; whoever ceases to proceed

does not enter where life calls. Accompanied by these same men,

he hastens to give the heavenly kingdoms to Cornelius,

to sanctify his house—yet he does not allow him to fall

on his knees, with bent knee. Accustomed to give gifts freely,

[945] he forbids the work of honor. From this point the new world raises its head,

which had been struck by the tooth of its ancient parent,

and the font has restored a birthday to you: born again,

do not bow your neck, free from your own sins, beneath the sins of another.

As soon as Peter began to speak sublime doctrines

[950] and to disclose the mysteries of eternal Christ,

the great-hearted men were astonished, and, following his voice,

found the way. What does unquestioning faith not offer

to believers? Its gifts are never delayed,

nor do divine things cause delay. Soon the gracious Spirit,

[955] bestowing various tongues in an abundant gift,

[Col. 0169A] [Note: [Col. 0169C]

958. *Locus.* Vossianus 2 has *lacus*. That may perhaps be preferable because of the following *aquas*. Isidore XIII, 21, should certainly be emended thus: “A *gurges* properly means a deep place in a river. A well is a place dug out.” From the Groningen manuscript write *lucus* in both passages. Through the same confusion of the letters *a* and *o*, Martial IV, 22, should be emended. Write, from the excellent Thuane manuscript, whose variants are at hand, *candida*:

“Thus the lilies enclosed in clear glass are counted.”

The comparison itself with Cleopatra’s body, shining through the water, requires this reading.

[Col. 0169C] 958. *Quo.* Some editions have *quos*. The following letter has adhered to it, as often happens.

[Col. 0169C] 959. *Sanxit.* Vossianus 2 has *sancit*.

[Col. 0169C] 959. *Qui talia.* Thus Cambridge, Vossianus 1, Aldine, Basel, the Lyon Bible, and Fabricius. The others have *vitalia*.

[Col. 0169C] 963. *Quod.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *quae*, as though it referred to *meritis*. Arator rather thinks that no one should suppose that this—that is, those gifts of the Spirit—comes from merits, since the Spirit freely prepares these gifts, whether as flame, as among the apostles, or as water, as in others. See Acts of the Apostles XI, § 16. *Variare* means “to alternate.” See Wopkens on Justinus, in *Miscellanea Observationum Nova*, vol. X, p. 237.

[Col. 0169D] 967. *Crucis.* Below, II, 257:

“He stretches toward the places of the city,

whose monuments shine with the cross,”

and at 845:

“I go to see the city revered by the nations for the cross.”

[Col. 0169D] 969. *Nunquam.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *nusquam*. He reproduced Peter’s words in Acts XI, § 17: “But who was I, that I could hinder God?” (*Ἐγὼ δὲ τίς ἤμην δυνατὸς κωλῦσαι τὸν Θεόν*). There Sopingius preferred *ἥμην*, rightly censured by Alberti in *Observationes Philologicae*, p. 427, and *Periculum Criticum*, p. 24.

[Col. 0169D] 970. *Veniunt.* Cambridge has *veniani*. Vossianus 2 has *pietate Dei*, not without merit. See the note on Sedulius I, 196.

[Col. 0169D] 973. *Fores.* He refers to Peter the key-bearer, discussed above at verse 75.

[Col. 0169D] 974. *Teris.* “You diminish.” See Withof, *Specimen Guntherianum*, p. 92. In this sense they take *deterere* in Sedulius, Letter to Macedonius, p. 15: “Whom you are accustomed to cherish, you maliciously wear down.” Thus Barthius produced it from a manuscript, and Bondam approved it in *Otium ad Isalam*, fascicle 2, p. 59. But *deterreas*, which I printed after following others, is entirely correct. For Macedonius seemed to deter Sedulius from dedicating his book to anyone else. Compare what Sedulius himself records about him on p. 10.

[Col. 0170C] 975. *Tot vicibus.* Aldine and Basel have *persaepe assignata prius*.

[Col. 0170C] 976. *Huic.* The Cambridge manuscript does not contain this verse.

[Col. 0170C] 977. *Naves.* A gloss in Cambridge had written *barcas*. On these see Fabricius in his commentary, p. 20, and Vossius, *De Vitiis Sermonis*, p. 268.

[Col. 0170C] 987. *Quae crevit.* Vossianus 2 incorrectly places the following verse before this one.

[Col. 0170C] 988. *Nam.* Thus I printed from Cambridge, Vossianus 1 and 2, Aldine, Basel, and Tornæsius 1. The others have *jam*. On this interchange see the notes on verses 618 and 924. Arator contrasts the catch made at night with that made by day: at night they caught nothing, whereas in the daytime there seemed to be a great abundance of fish. Those who did not consider that *nam* can sometimes be adversative, meaning “but,” therefore restored *jam*. See Duker on Florus, preface, § 2. I interpret the passages discussed by Cannegieter, *Disquisitio de Notis*, p. 359, in this way. It is also used in objections, unless one should prefer to posit an ellipsis there. See Ernesti, *Clavis Ciceroniana*, under *nam*.

[Col. 0170D] 989. *Quia.* Aldine, Basel, and Tornæsius 1 have *qui*; Antwerp has *quae*.

[Col. 0170D] 989. *Salsa.* See the note on Sedulius III, 53.

[Col. 0170D] 993. *Lina.* From Virgil, *Georgics* I, 142:

“And another drags the wet nets through the sea.”

There see Cerda. Silius VII, 503:

“Dragging the captive toward the shores with a curved net.”

I also found *ducens hamato* in the old Lyon edition of 1514.

[Col. 0170D] 993. *Carinas.* Aldine and Basel have *carinam*; but at verse 978 he mentions two ships, with which in the following verse he compares the two peoples.

[Col. 0170D] 994. *Turba.* Vossianus 1 has *iterata*.]

He filled the household in an unprecedented way; Peter repeatedly administers baptism,

so that he might cleanse in the waters those washed by flames.

This passage has no parallel: here the gracious Spirit

158 anticipates the waters he sanctified, and is always accustomed

[960] to add such gifts and to hasten his hand upon those reborn from the font alone.

He acts in turn, so that no one may think the gift his own

or suppose that it comes from merits—he who freely prepares

what varies. For the gracious Spirit, knowing no measure,

bestows rewards and, giving more

[965] than the hope of the one who asks, goes before the prayer.

[Col. 0169B] From there, departing, Peter reached the lofty city,

which bears the standards of the cross. All the people ask

whence salvation comes to the nations; to them the teacher opens all things,

and, adding an admonition, declares that it is never lawful to deny

[970] what comes from the goodness of God. The statement,

worthy of the voice of the devout guardian, openly displays his love,

so that he wishes the heavenly kingdoms to lie open to all

who holds these gates without end. Why, crowd, by your complaints

[Col. 0170A] 159 do you wear down our joys? The gifts are not new for Peter,

previously marked out so many times, when Christ grants this man

to enjoy the praise of the gracious name, whom he appointed by law

to carry his own Church. When, looking out from the shore, he sees two ships

standing there, he gives his commands and wishes to ride

[980] in Peter’s boat. The Synagogue indeed remained dry upon the ground

after the teacher’s doctrine gave the Church leave to follow lofty things;

the faithless one stands upon the earth,

while faith runs across the sea, for its own figure

clung to both boats. Joseph called him born of Judea,

to whom Peter says: “You, Christ, are proved to be

[985] the Son of God.” This part is fixed in the fields,

[Col. 0170B] the part that fell while following earthly things; that part rose on high,

which grew while speaking of divine things. When there was a catch

without a single fish in the darkness, then, at the time of light,

because Christ is present as light, he strips the salty waters of the dragon,

[990] so that the sacred nets of the font may drive all toward the shore,

and they may be snatched from the mouth of the blue deep.

For the sea was the world, from whose abyss Peter,

drawing the wet nets and fishing with his word, filled the ships

with a greater inward capacity, because the crowd was to come from two

[995] [Col. 0171A] [Note: [Col. 0171C]

997. *Recondit.* Pulmann’s notes have *recondat*; Antwerp has *recondet*.

[Col. 0171C] 1004. *Quia.* The reading *quam*, found in Vossianus 2 and Tornæsius 1, is by no means displeasing. Barthius shows that the apostles were called hunters, *Adversaria* XLIII, 8.

[Col. 0171C] 1006. *Cinxit.* He refers to hunters encircling forests. Ausonius, Letter IV:

“Or, with your brother, while you surround wandering deer

through pathless thickets, with spotted nets and a great line of pursuit.”

The hunt was conducted by a line marked with red feathers, called a “scare.” See Casaubon on Apuleius, *Apologia*, p. 182, and Dempster on Rosinus I, 7, p. 119. Duker on Florus III, 6, 11, and Drakenborch on Livy VII, 37, 14, show that this pursuit-line was called an *indago*.

[Col. 0171D] 1012. *Regit.* Perhaps *tegit* should be read; these two words are often confused. See Drakenborch on Livy XXXVII, 11, 3, and Burman on *Catalecta* III, epigram 260. My father emended the passage in Aurelius Victor, *Caesares* 61, 3, in the same way: “He protected the enemies while their honor and fortunes remained.” The Lipsian scholars, however, in the *Acta* of 1734, p. 3, defend *texit* there, in the sense “received into his protection.”

[Col. 0171D] 1014. *Portat.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *porta*.

[Col. 0171D] 1015. *Ruinam.* Aldine and Basel have *ruinas*. Although Schrader has demonstrated that the plural is extremely common among poets, since he understands universal ruin I prefer the singular, for the same reason that Burman defends *cinerem* in Ovid, *Heroides* I, 24.

[Col. 0171D] 1018. *Quos.* Vossianus 2 has *quo*. The following letter has adhered to it. [Col. 0172C] “Now the earlier concern” is found in Aldine, Basel, Antwerp, and Tornæsius 1.

[Col. 0172C] 1018. *Jam.* Cambridge has *nam*. See the note on verse 988.

[Col. 0172C] 1019. *Astra.* “Bringing light with him.”

[Col. 0172C] 1029. *Et quae.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *aeque*. “It remains firm” is found in Vossianus 1; but see the note on verse 159.

[Col. 0172C] 1030. *Apertae.* Vossianus 1 and 2 have *aperte*.

[Col. 0172C] 1034. *Clausis.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *clausus*. Fabricius does not distinguish accurately enough: “Noah: with the animals shut in” is the source of this.

[Col. 0172C] 1038. *Adam.* The first syllable is long, although others shorten it. Examples of both quantities can be gathered sufficiently abundantly from Fabricius’ index to the Christian poets.

[Col. 0172D] 1044. *Calceamenta.* The antepenultimate syllable is short. Prudentius, *The Martyrdom of Saint Romanus*:

“He alone, bent forward, tried to remove

the sandals from his loosened feet.”

Victor I:

“To whom I am not worthy

to touch the sandals of his feet.”

FABRICIUS, commentary on the Christian poets, p. 25. The later testimony in Fabricius is not by Victorinus, but by Our Poet below, II, 79. I am surprised that Falster, in *Supplement to the Latin Lexicon*, p. 47, asserts that *calcimentum* was used instead of *calceamentum*. He cites Columella, *On Agriculture* XII, 3, 1; but *calceamenta* is read there. Arator took this from Acts of the Apostles XII, § 8, “put on your sandals” (*ὑπόδησαι τὰ σανδάλια*). The Vulgate translator renders it: “and put on your sandals”—the same wording found in John Cassian, *Institutes of the Coenobia* I, 2. I would not have wished Vonckius to emend it in *Latin Readings* II, 7. Yet the translator is not sufficiently precise: he ought rather to have translated *sandalia*, as Dilherr shows in *Sacred Rites* II, 16; nor did Arator use the word *calceamentum* correctly. Luke would rather have written *ὑποδήματα* if he meant footwear enclosing the entire foot, whereas sandals protected only the soles; hence they are also called “bindings,” as Cerda teaches in his note on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 458, although the word is sometimes used for ordinary footwear. Compare Perizonius on Aelian, *Various History* I, 18. This distinction deserves all the more attention because otherwise the passages in Matthew’s Gospel X, § 10, and Mark VI, § 9, seem to conflict. Salmasius reconciled them admirably in his note on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 388; he is followed by Sagittarius, *On Ancient Nudity*, chapter 1, § 19, and Segaar, *Observations on Luke*, p. 244. Segaar discusses the matter at length and also shows that in ancient times sandals belonged to wealthy women, although they were sometimes assigned to men as well. Those who are cited by Burman on *Catalecta* II, p. 262, show that sandals were attributed to heroes and heroines; and Graevius, in his note on Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices* 21, shows that Roman women used slippers or sandals. In the angel’s words here I seem to find an indication that Peter need not act with the utmost speed, but should take the proper time to fasten his sandals; for there was no fear that the guards would be awakened. Sandals had to be fitted to the feet by those who were not under such pressure to hurry. The opposite is found in the story of Alcmena, who awakened her husband Amphitryon because the bedroom was filled with light at midnight, in Theocritus, *Idyll* XXIV, 36:

“Rise, and do not put sandals beneath your feet.”

Martin explained this passage in *Various Readings* I, 4. Salmasius on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 72, teaches that Luke’s word *περίζωσαι* refers to a tunic girded up.]

from peoples, and then, with the sea in service, he lifted the nations; in the full ship he recognizes

the Church, whose calm station stores

what it receives from the Lord’s word, who had said earlier

The places will not lack their own fame. Peter, who grasps everything,

was born in the city of Bethsaida, which in the Hebrew language

[Col. 0171B] Caught in a dark prison, but not without light, Peter

is confined, and the darkness cannot conceal from the Church

the day in its yellow gloom. That fear makes a common

punishment for all: Peter’s confinement was a public penalty;

[1010] but the shepherd rules his own flock, with its guardian preserved,

and enriches him with the honor of having confessed the Lord

three times. Bearing the name Peter from the name of the Rock,

he carries an eternal designation,

bearing foundations that will never suffer ruin.

[1015] Awaited by your own, dear at every moment,

come now also to us, Peter! Come forth together for all

[Col. 0171C] whom original nature goads! Now, in the deep night,

the angel, carrying the stars and bright with the constellations,

enters the prison; day accompanies him.

[1020] [Col. 0172A] With the heavenly minister approaching,

162 the shadow of the prison flees; the beaten darkness perishes,

when the new Morning Star shines. The black color departs,

and, transformed, the nocturnal twilight sees the sun.

While the hand of the guards surrounds him, Peter’s body

[1025] was in sleep among the chains, but faith—which does not know how to sleep—

was awake within him. The Songs proclaim this:

“I sleep in my heart, yet I keep watch.” Learn the joyful

lessons of the figure, you who have deserved to be reborn

in the clear font, and with devout heart behold

The angel himself teaches the way of this manifest virtue:

touching his side, he struck the part in which the head
