deigned to give his limbs to the cross and to be pressed down

[1040] in death, through which life returns. Through the path of his side

he consecrated new gifts of liquid. Now the angel calls Peter

[Col. 0172C] at that part, so that every mind may believe

that the glory of the Church stands in him

and may hold faith in the heavenly guarantor, by whom, when he admonishes

[1045] [Col. 0173A] [Note: [Col. 0173D]

1044. *Monente.* Cortius correctly explains in the margin as “encouraging.” This word is used especially of those who announce something by divine command. See Heinsius’ note on Tibullus I, 6, 49. Some editions therefore wrongly have *movente*, as above at verse 924, where the words have been confused.

[Col. 0173D] 1046. *Gradientibus.* Cambridge has *gradentibus*.

[Col. 0174B] 1050. *Postes.* At one time, when I conjectured *pontes*, this was my interpretation: the doors of prisons, arched like bridges, were so called. See Meursius, *On Roman Luxury*, in the *Mantissa*, chapter 12. But there is now no need to change the reading. The passage agrees with Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 699:

“It is said that the doors opened of their own accord,

and that the chains slipped from the arms of their own accord,

with no one loosening them.”

Statius, *Thebaid* VII, 64:

“And the doors, closed with everlasting adamant,

burst apart.”

[Col. 0174B] 1051. *Abscidens.* I restored this from Vossianus 1 and 2 and the Antwerp edition. The others have *abscindens*. Since here he speaks of the sharp point of savagery, as of a severed limb, I preferred the former according to the distinction I discussed in the note on Sedulius V, 272. Thus in Althelmus, *On the Praise of the Virgin*, p. 721 of volume I of Canisius’ *Thesaurus*, I think one should read:

“While they carry the severed head of the people to the banquets,”

not *abscissum*.

[Col. 0174C] 1054. *Si cedunt.* Cambridge has *sic edunt*, with the letter transposed. *Sic cedunt* is found in Fabricius and the Lyon Bible. Alexander a Turre cites *si cedant* in *On Fulgentius’ Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* I, IV, p. 223. *Hostia* is found in Aldine, Basel, and Tornæsius 1. It is surprising that three editions, and the better ones at that, could have joined in this same error.

[Col. 0174C] 1055. *Deputat.* “Designates, assigns.” This meaning belongs to later writers; the earlier ones used the word to mean “estimate” or “judge.” See Vorstius on Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I, 53, 4, and Noltenius, *Lexicon*, p. 498.

[Col. 0174C] 1057. *Jubet.* A question mark was added in Vossianus 1.

[Col. 0174C] 1058. *Puella.* Rhode, a name derived from “rose,” just as other women’s names are noted by Mollius in his note on Longus’ *Pastoral* as derived from flowers and herbs, p. 116.

[Col. 0174C] 1059. *Cui.* Thus Cambridge. Vossianus 1 has *quia gratia*, and so do all the editions except Tornæsius 1, which has *quia sanguine*.

[Col. 0174D] 1062. *Hinc.* The Lyon Bible has *huic*.

[Col. 0174D] 1063. *Suum.* Vossianus 1 has *suam*.

[Col. 0174D] 1063. *Portet.* Cambridge has *portat*.

[Col. 0174D] 1065. *Aut.* Vossianus 1 has *ut*. The same confusion occurs in Virgil, *Eclogues* 6, 74. Learned men note that these forms are often confused; nevertheless a learned hand had written *at Scyllam* in the margin of my edition. Add Drakenborch’s note on Livy IV, 12, 8. Arator himself supports *aut* above, at verse 357:

“Who could recount it in dry light

or when the groaning has ceased?”

Add the passages cited there.

[Col. 0174D] 1069. *Quod.* Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *quam*.

[Col. 0174D] 1072. *Praestent.* Aldine, Basel, and Tornæsius 1 have *praestant*, wrongly. See the note on the Letter to Florianus, at the end. In Juvenal, *Satires* I, 139, restore from the manuscript whose variants are at hand:

“But who could endure those

filthy stains of luxury?”

From the same manuscript one may read *probo* in *Satires* II, 5. Virgil VII, 145:

“Where they may establish the walls owed there.”

In Clermontius’ manuscript my father found *condent*. In Sedulius V, 401, from Almeloveen’s manuscript and my own, I now prefer:

“Who could doubt that there is one,”

rather than *non ambiget*. Compare Heinsius’ *Observations* on Tibullus I, 4, 79.]

163 These feet deserved it, which the master’s right hand touched,

which he wholly cleansed with water. For those proceeding, the closed doors

Now the iron gate is open in its bolts;

[1050] the rigid doorposts loosen their chains.

Cutting away the edge of harshness from the nations,

he subdues everything rough, lest the fixed door impede

the journey of the world, along which its course will run. Tell me, glory of all things:

what wonder is it if the iron doors yield to Peter,

[1055] whom God appoints guardian of the heavenly palace,

165 and makes him retain the summit of his Church,

[Col. 0173B] commanding him to overcome the underworld? Soon, free from the enemy,

he celebrated the divine work, which the first girl

proves by returning from darkness; to her Christ’s grace

gave a like experience. He himself, appearing after resurrection,

[1060] approaches the women and speaks. The glory of returning flesh

is addressed to the sex that has a mother; from this point also

it is clear that the prophet understood his own Church,

which should bear joys spread throughout the entire flock.

Who could explain such things in speech

[1065] or raise the weight of these events in words?

That greatest fear, which had gripped their chilled limbs,

became the measure of joy. The summit of this pledge remains

through all ages and, like a star, occupies the place

that Peter consecrated with his body and the angel with his voice.

[1070] With these things faith has been made firm; with these chains,

Rome, salvation has been made perpetual for you.

Surrounded by their bond, you will always be free.

For what could the chains not accomplish,

166 which were touched by him who can absolve all things? These walls, unconquered

by his hand or made holy by triumph,

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0175A] [Note: [Col. 0175B]

3. *Oris.* See the note on the Letter to Vigilantius, at the end. Verburgius explains *os* by “lofty and grandiloquent words” in his note on Ovid, *Tristia* I, 1, 13:

“Either avoid these men, or, if you have sufficient boldness of speech,

make them speak of Oedipuses and Telegonuses,”

but in my judgment this is wrong. Ovid rather designated the audacity with which they might make an attack for the sake of reproach. Graevius discusses this meaning in his note on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* V, 10, and Cortius in his note on the same work IX, 8.

[Col. 0175C] 5. *Cyprum.* Delrio, in his note on Seneca, *Oedipus* 539, declares this word corrupt, since one who leaves Cyprus cannot be said to have gone to Paphos, which was itself in Cyprus. Cellarius demonstrated that the new Paphos is intended, *Ancient Geography* III, 7, p. 166. The manuscripts offer no help, so completely do they all agree. Luke’s own words also seem to have caused Arator to write *Cyprum* without qualification. Perhaps someone might posit a hendiadys, so that Salamis, which is in Cyprus, is understood. I have also sometimes wondered whether this belongs to the manner of speech in which a region and a city situated within it are occasionally distinguished. See Perizonius on Aelian I, 31, and, following him, Elsner on the Gospel of John IV, § 34. I would rather understand “Cyprus” here as the interior regions of Cyprus. After leaving Salamis, he traversed the whole island, and hence in Acts XIII, § 6, Valckenaer, in his note on Herodotus V, p. 432, regards the manuscript reading *ὅλην τὴν νῆσον* (“the whole island”) as not without merit. Thus, traversing the inland island, he continued his journey to Paphos. A similar passage occurs at the beginning of Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* V, 43: “When he had spent sufficient time around Alexandria, he set out for Egypt” (*Ἱκανῶς δὲ ἔχων περὶ τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρειαν, ἐστέλλετο ἐς Αἴγυπτον*), that is, toward the interior of Egypt and away from the sea, as Olearius correctly explains. The great Hemsterhuis used the same passage in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. VI, p. 340, to elucidate a similar passage in Xenophon of Ephesus.

[Col. 0175D] 6. *Amoribus.* Sacred to Venus, who was therefore called Paphian. See Cuperus, *Observations* II, 4, p. 166, and “Cyprian” in Arnobius, *Against the Nations* V, p. 169. Some also call her *Cypris*, though not on the authority of the better poets. See Burman on *Catalecta* III, pp. 484 and 615. Others think she was called Cytherea from the Cypriot city Cythera. Cellarius refutes them, *Ancient Geography* III, p. 169.

[Col. 0176B] 8. *Aligerosque.* “Loves,” the attendants of Venus, as Fabricius explains in his commentary, p. 6. He certainly means doves, sacred to Venus, about which see Maius, *Observations* II, p. 134; hence a dove appears on coins of the Erycinians. See Perizonius on Aelian I, 15. Henninius found the same interpretation elsewhere; see his note on Tollius’ *Travel Letter* II, at the beginning.

[Col. 0176C] 9. *Procedit.* Cambridge has *procedet*.

[Col. 0176C] 11. *Laudum.* Cambridge, in its first hand, Vossianus 2, Pulmann’s notes, and Antwerp have *dudum*, contrary to Arator’s intention. The error arose from the frequent interchange of *d* and *l*, discussed in the note on Book I, 868.

[Col. 0176C] 13. *Luxus.* Vossianus 1 has “they will be in the luxury of the region.” Florus III, 9, at the beginning, calls Cyprus an island abounding in ancient wealth and therefore sacred to Venus; there Lipsius’ conjecture *deliciis* is by no means displeasing. Alberti, in his note on the New Testament, p. 98, seems nevertheless to defend the other reading with others.

[Col. 0176C] 14. *Nescia.* “Unknown”; see the note on I, 224. The meaning is that it would be difficult for her to follow honesty, since, according to Paul’s teaching, she had first arisen from a licentious place. I placed a question mark after *loco*, and it is also found in Antwerp.

[Col. 0176D] 20. *Monstrat.* Aldine has *monstrant*.

[Col. 0176D] 23. *Ad usque.* I separated these words, which were incorrectly joined in the editions, following the authority of Burman on Lotichius, *Elegies* II, p. 171.

[Col. 0176D] 25. *Vinxere.* Thus Cambridge. Vossianus 1 has *fecere*; Vossianus 2 has *fixere noctis*. Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *cervicis notis fixere*; all the printed editions have *fixere*. I preferred *vincire*, because blindness had oppressed the eyes like sleep. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI, 238:

“As you lay bound by sleep.”

[Col. 0176D] 27. *Eat.* Fabricius and the Lyon Bible have *erat*.]

The Spirit, forbidding the lamp kindled by the radiant word

to shine beneath a bushel, said: “Set Saul apart for the work

of speech.” Soon Peter consecrated him as he went

by laying on his hand—Peter, to whom the Master’s speech

[5] granted power over all things. Leaving Cyprus and Salamis,

168 he proceeds to Paphos, once said to have been devoted to love

and to have remained a cave of sacrilegious lust,

and to have cultivated the wandering winged Loves with wanton zeal.

From this point the summit of his works advances, because greater grace

[10] came to sins: that guilt could be forgiven this man,

Paul was already an example. What a splendid

subject for praise has been added to the man! He sows chaste beginnings

in a region of luxury, and the lascivious field multiplies

modest fruits. For whom after this would it be unknown

[15] and difficult, when honesty seems to have begun from such a disgraceful place?

Yet, so that no part might remain barren of merits,

the wicked Magus attempts to contend in speech;

things contrary to virtue always made a path for it. The Church’s warrior, deflecting

the darts hurled at him, says:

[20] “Deceit shows from what parent you were born. The boundaries of death

will be yours; you will suffer them in your own darkness,

and you will not be granted time to see the sun

and attend to the forms of things whose creator

you deny. Then clouds bound your face

[25] with blue marks, and color came upon the face of your dark breast.

Now, with the path denied, he seeks by what guide

he may go safely, whose footsteps he may follow,

[Col. 0177A] [Note: [Col. 0177B]

29. *Proconsule.* According to the ancient usage, about which see Oudendorp on Suetonius, *Caesar* 54. Ignorant of this, the scribe in Vossianus 1 gave *Paulo*; Vossianus 2 has *Paulus*, which is indeed correct. This reading is confirmed by the authority of Capitoline inscriptions and coins. See Duker on Florus II, 6, 17, and V. D. on Livy X, 3, 3. I have not changed Arator’s text, however, because writers of this period seem generally to have followed the Greek spelling. Sergius Paulus is intended; concerning the name, compare Ryckius on Tacitus, *Annals* IV, 17 and *Histories* II, 18, and V. D. on Victor, *Caesares* 6. Some have been perplexed by the way in which that Paulus is called proconsul, since Cyprus was a province of Caesar. They therefore decide that he ought rather to be called propraetor. Grotius, that oracle of Batavia, suspects that the honorific title was given to Sergius through flattery. Schultingius, in his note on the *Digest*, p. 146, judges that the title *proconsul* extended broadly enough to include propraetors. But Alberti, most effectively, in his *Philological Observations on Acts* chapter XIII, shows from Dio Cassius that Cyprus, previously a province of Caesar, was restored by Augustus to the Roman People, and that from that time proconsuls were sent there. Wesselingius added support to this view in his note on Hierocles, p. 706, where he gives similar examples of proconsuls of Cyprus. Rhoerius added one example from Gruter in *Daventer Festivals*, p. 152. If I may add anything, I add *PRO. COS. DESIG. PROV. CYPRI.* from Gudius, *Inscriptions*, p. 125, no. 4. Compare with it the inscription in Reinesius, *Inscriptiones*, class VI, no. 136.]

### [Col. 0177C] 32. “From darkness”

Thus Vossianus 1, and formerly also read in Vossianus 2; but there it was subsequently changed to *in obsequio tenebris*, which is also found in Tornaesianus 1. *E tenebris* appears in the Aldine edition, which I formerly approved in the *Miscellanea*, p. 184; now I prefer to follow the manuscripts. Some printed editions have *obsequia tenebris*; Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp manuscript have *obsequia et lucem tenebris*; Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca Lugdunensis*, has *obsequia et tenebris lucem*. Nothing was written in the Cambridge and University manuscripts; they therefore seem to have reproduced Fabricius’s reading. *Obsequia salutis* is to be understood in the same way as *obsequia officii* in Symmachus, Book X, Letter 83, and *obsequia pietatis* in Hegesippus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem* I, p. 6.

In Tornaesianus 1 the punctuation is as follows:

> Paul, these are not new things: you know  
> That through salvation’s service light rises well from darkness;  
> All things reveal the hidden form, etc.

### [Col. 0177D] 33. *Reserant*

Vossianus 1 has *referant*. I like that less because of *secretam*. — *Si liberat* in Vossianus 1.

### [Col. 0177D] 34. *Pulsare*

Similarly below, verse 142:

> To strike the credibility of history;

He seems to have given this word the meaning “to summon,” and consequently “to disclose” or “reveal.” Barthius discusses it extensively in *Adversaria* XXVII, 8, in his notes on Claudian, *Bellum Gildonicum* 170, and Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 477.

### [Col. 0177D] 38. *Tenebrisque*

Both Vossian manuscripts delete *-que*. — [Col. 0178B] *Patentibus* is found in Vossianus 1. I prefer the other reading on the basis of what Wopkens notes in his commentary on Pacatus, chapter 21. It plainly means “to show” or “declare.” See Schulting in his notes on Seneca’s *Controversiae*, pp. 153 and 260, and Martial, Book I, Epigram 82:

> You know that you were born from a slave, and readily admit it,  
> When you call your master, Sosibianus, your father;

This couplet is extremely difficult, and Scriverius’s explanation does not satisfy me. Perhaps the meaning is: “You know that you were born from a slave, and readily admit that your father is a slave when you call him your master,” or “when you are subject to another’s dominion.” Since everyone knew that he had not been reduced to that master’s power by the procedures of civil or international law, yet he called him his master, it was plainly evident that he was a house-born slave, and therefore born from a slave.

### [Col. 0178B] 40. *Visitat*

The learned Wassenbergius conjectures *visit ad*.

### [Col. 0178B] 41. *Dare verba*

“To speak.” Otherwise, this expression is more commonly used to mean “to deceive.” Likewise below, verse 1032:

> He uttered ineffectual words.

Avianus, *Fables* 24.10:

> And he uttered words from his enraged heart.

Add Barthius, *Adversaria* IX, 9, and LI, 7; Vonck, *Specimen criticum*, p. 138; and Withof, *Guntherus*, p. 96. *Officium sermonis dandi* occurs in Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* I, p. 31. Drakenborch explained *dare dicta* in his note on Livy VII, 33, 1. Wherever *dare* is used for “to say,” I think an ellipsis of a similar noun should be admitted in several passages. I discussed this expression in my note on Book I, verse 683.

For *extemplo*, Vossianus 2 and the Lugdunensis write *exemplo*; the Cambridge manuscript has *extimplo*. Ruhnkenius noted a similar variation in Rutilius Lupus, Book II, p. 125.

### [Col. 0178C] 42. *Dextraque*

By the extension of the right hand with which speakers secured the silence and favorable attention of their audiences. See Erhard in his note on Petronius, *Satyricon* 17; Schott in his note on Seneca’s *Controversiae*, p. 641; and Barthius in his note on Claudian, *Bellum Gildonicum* 135. This was indeed done with the right hand, whose use in speeches was especially important. Cuperus explained the matter from Aristophanes in *Observationes* III, 2.

### [Col. 0178D] 46. *Vices*

Sedulius uses the same expression in Book I, verse 125:

> Nature changed its course.

### [Col. 0178D] 47. *Terga*

Cassiodorus, *Variae* I, 35: “A ship standing upon the back of the sea.” Greek νῶτα θαλάσσης, “the back of the sea,” in Homer, *Iliad* II, 159; Coluthus imitates him in *The Rape of Helen* 200. Add Elmenhorst in his notes on Arnobius, p. 45, from whom Ouzelius borrowed by disgraceful plagiarism in his notes on Minucius Felix, p. 20; Barthius on Claudian, *Epigrams* IX, 36; Cerda on Virgil, *Georgics* III, 361; my father on Pliny’s *Panegyricus* XII, 3; and Segaar on Luke, p. 164.

### [Col. 0178D] 49. *Est*

Vossianus 1 omits this word.

### [Col. 0178D] 53. *Percussa*

See Weitz in his notes on Salvian, *On the Government of God*, p. 190.

> Who, pitying, might grant aid, and through the empty air

> You know that through salvation’s service light rises well from darkness.  
> All things reveal the hidden form.

> [35] 171 Paul rightly began to establish miracles,

> Who, though blind, deserved to see without end.

> “I am not he; after me will come one whose sandals

> [95] And miracles owed to the wood appear in the ford.

> Recalled these things in order: after Christ,  
> Clothed in the covering of flesh, had everywhere given  
> The signs of God, making it clear to the world that salvation itself

> [Col. 0181A] Since vows could not bring everything to the one who desired them,  
> The gifts of Christ the bringer of salvation yielded willingly,  
> [105] He who came from the stars as the price of your freedom,

> It thinks that an immortal being can be held by mortal law

### [Col. 0179C] 57. *Ferens*

Thus the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesianus 1. But *gerens* is found in Vossianus 1 and the remaining editions. This interchange is almost continuous. See my notes on Sedulius II, 150; III, 134 and 325.

### 57. *Quam*

The Cambridge manuscript has *quia*. This is not displeasing, just as it was not formerly displeasing in the *Miscellanea*, p. 185.

### 58. *Semine monstrat*

I restored *semine* from both Vossian manuscripts; the others have *semina*. It may also have been found in the Cambridge and University manuscripts, since Cortius added nothing in the margin. Next, Vossianus 1 and the Lugdunensis have *monstrant*; Vossianus 2 has *monstrans*. I think *monstrat*, found in the other witnesses, is correct. Refer it to the eternal law, which shows that things separated in their origin can nevertheless be given—namely, food from dew and water from the rock. Below, verse 1012:

> Food flowed from dew, and in turn the dry rock poured forth water.

Sedulius I, 136 also belongs here, though its confused punctuation should be restored in the manner I proposed in *Miscellanea*, chapter 17, p. 185.

### [Col. 0179D] 60. *Fluerent*

Vossianus 2 has *pluerent*. Heinius discussed this confusion in his *Observations on Tibullus* I, 10, 68.

### 66. *Sic gratia*

Vossianus 2 has *si gratia*.

### 68. *Amoeni*

Vossianus 1 has *amoenus*.

### 70. *Davidica*

Vossianus 1 and 2 have *Davitica*. The same variation occurs in Sedulius I, 7. The second syllable is shortened here, as also below, verse 115. Likewise in Peter Apollonius, *On David’s Duel*, at the beginning:

> The battles of prophetic David and savage Goliath.

See Heumann there. Others lengthen the syllable.

### 71. *Tota*

“Everything,” as Wopkens explains in his note on Sedulius III, 159.

### 73. *Virgineos*

Vossianus 1 reads:

> And virgin folds. Unfold whatever [is contained] in this matter.

### 74. *Vestra*

Vossianus 1, in its first hand, has *nostra*.

### 75. *Sacri*

The Lugdunensis has *sacris*.

### 78. *Potens*

An epithet repeatedly applied to John. See Wopkens in his note on Sedulius II, 143.

### 79. *Veniet*

The Cambridge manuscript has *venit*.

### [Col. 0180C] 80. *Summam*

Fabricius, the Antwerp manuscript, and the Lugdunensis have *summa*. Wassenbergius thinks that a gloss lies behind *calceamenta* and that Arator wrote *indumenta*, as he mentions *instrumenta pudoris* at verse 345. Prudentius, *Peristephanon* VI, 85:

> He himself loosens  
> The coverings of the feet.

Yet he also suspects that Arator may have erred against the meter here, as elsewhere.

### 81. *Qua*

I adopted this from the Cambridge manuscript. All others have *quae*.

### 81. *Corrigia*

It is the strap of a shoe, or a sandal—Greek ὁ ἱμὰς τῶν ὑποδημάτων, “the strap of the footwear”—as all the Evangelists have it except Matthew, who merely names ὑποδήματα, “shoes.” Juvencus I:

> Whose bonds of the feet I am not worthy to touch.

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 39. See also Bynaeus, *On Hebrew Shoes* I, 7.

### 83. *Epistola*

He refers to the passage of Paul in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter X, at the beginning.

### [Col. 0180D] 85. *Mosi*

Vossianus 1 has *Moysi*. See above, verses 692 and 791. The Aldine has *Mosae*.

### 87. *Dura*

Fabricius, the Aldine edition, and the Lugdunensis have *surda*. He himself seems to support the other reading below, verse 246:

> Hard-hearted people, why do you summon  
> Iron and stones any further?

Thus he called this people stony at I, 595; see the note there. *Surda* might perhaps be attractive because of the following *sonat* and *susurrant*, verse 89; but the manuscripts prefer the other reading.

### 88. *Ne*

The Cambridge manuscript has *nec*. The following letter has become attached. Perhaps Isidore, *Origines* III, 10, should be corrected in this way: “For, stirred by zeal, they thus began.” The Groningen edition rightly prints *studiosi coeperunt*, “the zealous began.”

### 90. *Jesus*

The Cambridge manuscript has *Ihesu*; the Antwerp manuscript, *Iesus*.

### 95. *Vado*

The Aldine edition and Tornaesianus 1 have *in vado*, “in the shallow water.”

### 96. *Saepius*

The Antwerp manuscript is confused here: before this verse it inserts what follows from verse 156 through verse 241.

### 97. *Rursus*

Vossianus 1 and 2 have *rursum*.

### 101. *A jure*

Vossianus 2, the Antwerp manuscript, Fabricius, and the Lugdunensis have *ab jure*.

### [Col. 0181B] 103. *Possent*

Vossianus 1, in its first hand, has *possint*. Tornaesianus 1 has *possunt*.

### 106. *Perdita*

This is a half-line of Sedulius V, 251.

### 110. *Geminum*

By “the twofold crime” he means the savage deed of the Jews by which they crucified Christ. *Tristis*, “sad,” is used for *saevus*, “savage.” See Barthius on Claudian III, *Consulate of Honorius*, 30. They added another crime to this one, by which they attempted to preserve the corpse with guards; hence Sedulius V, 297 says that they “increased their guilt,” where Wopkens also compared Arator.

### [Col. 0181C] 111. *Surgenti*

I wrote this on the basis of the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesianus 1. The others have *surgendi*. Participles are often corrupted by copyists into gerunds. Ruhnkenius restored Velleius Paterculus brilliantly on this basis in his note on Rutilius Lupus I, p. 4. Add Isidore, *Origines* II, 21: “Continuous speech creates fatigue and disgust in both speaking and hearing.” Write, following the Groningen edition, *tam dicenti quam audienti*, “both for the speaker and for the hearer.” In the same way, *d* and *t* are often confused because of their similar sound. See Cannegieter on Ulpian, title XXII, § 32; Brouckhus on Propertius I, 13, 36; Heinsius on Ovid, *Heroides* XIII, 208.

On this occasion I shall correct part of the Constitution of Leo and Anthemius, which has been corrupted in the same way. It is found in the *Codex Theodosianus*, volume VI, latter part, p. 161, Ritter’s edition:

> Or may a more heedless man, embracing in a woman a lineage plainly distinguished by the splendor of such freeborn liberty, diminish it nakedly [reading uncertain].

Several scholars have offered conjectures, as has Cannegieter, *Disquisitio de Notis*, p. 313. I think we should read:

> Or with the radiance of such ingenuous liberty glowing.

Thus Ambrose said *irrutilari splendore nobilitatis*, “to glow with the splendor of nobility,” in *Hexaemeron* III, 11.

### 111. *Damnare*

“To obstruct.” See Wopkens on Sedulius III, 125.

### 111. *Pro*

Thus the Aldine edition and Tornaesianus 1; most others have *proh*, a worse spelling. See Drakenborch on Livy IX, 24, 9; Burman on Lotichius, *Poems* II, 15, 25; and on the *Catalecta* II, p. 204.

### [Col. 0182B] 115. *Davidicae*

The Aldine edition and Tornaesianus 1 have *Daviticae*. See above, verse 70. He refers here to Psalm XVI, § 10.

### 116. *In*

Absent from Pulmann’s manuscripts and from the Antwerp manuscript.

### 123. *Mori*

A half-line of Sedulius IV, 139.

### 124. *Fuit*

He inserted it: a Graecism. See Vechner, *Hellenismus* II, 9. The meaning of the passage itself is apparent from what is noted on Book I, verse 11.

### [Col. 0182C] 128. *Sociamur*

The Cambridge manuscript has *potiamur*, “we may enjoy.” Wopkens explained *herilis*, “belonging to a master,” in his note on Sedulius IV, 106.

### 131. *Dant*

In Vossianus 1 the passage appears as follows:

> The illustrious men of the Church forbade  
> The pious words to be uttered further.

This is not displeasing, except that Arator seems to have expressed two things: that certain men of the Church were added to Paul’s words, and that they forbade the Jews to speak further. See Acts of the Apostles XIII, §§ 43 and 45.

### 133. *Semina*

Vossianus 2 has *semine*. The Cambridge manuscript has *vetas*. The quantity of the syllable rules that out.

### 134. *Magistro*

I wrote this from Vossianus 1 and 2, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesianus 1. The remaining editions have *magistri*. The other reading is more suited to Arator’s style. See my note on Book I, verse 121. Thus Drakenborch correctly defends *jussis magistris* against Dausqueius in his note on Silius III, 387. *Artes magistrae*, “arts as teachers,” occurs in Ovid, *Heroides* XV, 83, where it is noted; *artifex doctor*, “an instructor skilled in his art,” was explained by Savaron in his note on Sidonius IV, Letter 1; see also the note on Sedulius, p. 25, and *Miscellaneous Observations* V, p. 17. *Leges servae*, “enslaved laws,” in Heinsius on Ovid, *Amores* I, 6, 74. *Urbs domina*, “the city as mistress,” in the same author’s note on *Remedies for Love*, 291; and he brilliantly restored *flammis maritis*, “husbandly flames,” in Martial IV, Epigram 75. See his notes on Claudian, *Bellum Gildonicum* 407: *membra ministra*, “serving limbs,” and *manus ministrae*, “serving hands.” Add Bunemann on Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God* 16, § 5.

### [Col. 0182D] 137. *Posui*

Fabricius and the Lugdunensis have *posuit*. The following letter has become attached. He refers to Isaiah XLII, § 6.

### 142. *Pulsare*

See above, verse 34.

### 146. *In*

The Cambridge manuscript has *ab*. He refers to Paul’s words in the Epistle to the Romans IX, § 12.

### [Col. 0183B] 152. *Erit*

Tornaesianus 1 has *erat*. — Vossianus 2 has *quae jam*.

### 153. *Famulemur*

The Cambridge manuscript has *famulentur*.

### 154. *Affectu*

Vossianus 1 and the Antwerp manuscript have *effectu*. See my note on Book I, verse 133.

### 157. *Lystram*

The Aldine edition and Tornaesianus 1 have *Lystram*. In Greek it is ἡ Λύστρα and τὰ Λύστρα. See Perizonius on Sanctius, *Minerva* I, 9, 4, and Wesseling on Hierocles, p. 675.

### 159. *Membris*

I adopted this from the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1 and 2, Fabricius’s editions, the Antwerp manuscript, and the Lugdunensis, except that Vossianus 1 has *aegris*. The remaining editions have *membri*. I think *aegri membris*, “sick in respect of his limbs,” is expressed in the same way as *aeger animo*, “sick in mind,” in Cicero, *For Caelius* 8.

### [Col. 0183C] 160. *Nascente*

“Born,” or “when he was being born,” as Wopkens explains in his note on Sedulius IV, 8.

### 163. *Sensu*

Correctly so in the Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus 1 and 2. The Aldine edition, Tornaesianus 1, and the others have *mente*, “in mind.” Rittershusius on Salvian, *On the Government of God*, p. 137, will show that the other reading is preferable.

### 164. *Humo*

Vossianus 2 and Tornaesianus 1 have *homo*. One might understand *homo plenus et perfectus*, “a complete and perfect man.” But the preceding *aethera* demands the opposite, *humo*, “earth.” The learned Wassenbergius prefers *necatis*, “killed,” to *negatis*, “denied,” as above, verse 159:

> A part of his sick limbs had begun  
> To die as he was being born.

Likewise Book I, 757:

> He looks upon Aeneas living with limbs that had died;

And verse 764:

> And he raises the limbs long dead  
> Through time back to life;

And verse 780:

> When the eighth year was to release the sick man  
> From the wounds of his dead body;

Especially verse 786:

> His limbs, formerly loosened for death,  
> Are now bound to salvation.

The learned man himself had added these passages, in letters sent to me, to support the conjecture. Nor does he think verse 26 an obstacle:

> He now seeks, along a forbidden path,  
> By what guide he may go safely.

There the subject is a blind man who could not walk without a guide; here, however, the subject is a lame man.

### [Col. 0183D] 165. *Imo*

Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp manuscript have *uno*. The same interchange occurs below, verse 234. Isidore, *Origines* I, 19, says: “And a point is placed down to a single letter.” Write, following the Groningen edition, *imam*, “the lowest” or “the very bottom,” so that in the following passage also *ad imam litteram* means “to the very last letter,” not *ad unam litteram*, “to a single letter.” From the same interchange of *un-* and *im-*, restore the same author in XVII, 7: *Coquimella, quam Latini ob colorem primum vocant* (“Coquimella, which the Latins call *primum* on account of its colour”). Read *prunum* following the Groningen edition.

### 166. *Cuperet*

The Aldine edition and Tornaesianus 1 have *caperet*. See my note on Book I, verse 255.

### [Col. 0184B] 166. *Claudique*

Vossianus 2 omits *-que*. It had appeared there earlier, but a careless copyist corrupted it, as also shortly afterward *verba dedit*, verse 167, and *novella*, verse 169.

### 167. *Infit*

Fabricius, the Antwerp manuscript, and the Lugdunensis have *inquit*. In the Cambridge manuscript I suspect that this was also the reading, because Cortius had added nothing to Fabricius’s edition.

### 170. *Persona*

*Persona* sometimes denotes someone who presides over another and under whose authority someone protects himself. Paulinus, in the *Panegyricus of Celsus*:

> Christ became the refuge and representative of the needy;

Otherwise *persona* designates the body. Tertullian, *Poem IV Against Marcion*, in a very corrupt poem:

> Here a truly proper person is bound, not a shadow,

And elsewhere he uses it for the man himself. Arator, in Book II on the healed lame man, says: “He proceeds.” Sidonius, Book II, Letter 8:

> To whom the lesser person at home and abroad owed obedience,  
> The greater person duty, and the equal person affection;

There it denotes rank or dignity. But lest anyone condemn these examples, a more authoritative witness must be brought forward. Seneca, *Apocolocyntosis*:

> Therefore, lest I seem to be pronouncing judgment against a person rather than against the matter, I propose that from this day onward none of those who eat the fruit of the plowed earth (ἀρούρης καρπὸν ἔδουσιν) become a god.

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXV, 10. Barthius correctly saw that the word here designates the man himself. Nor do some deny this meaning to later writers; they deny it only to the more elegant authors. Perizonius nevertheless assigned it to the latter as well, and not without reason. Noltenius repeated his arguments in the *Lexicon Antibarbarum*, p. 1094. Cicero, *For Milo* XII, may also be added:

> Let that Cassian question—“for whose benefit?”—apply in these cases.

### 171. *Perque*

The Antwerp manuscript has *per quae*.

### 172. *Quod*

The Cambridge manuscript has *qui*. This is not displeasing, just as it was not formerly displeasing in *Miscellanea*, chapter 17.

### [Col. 0184D] 174. *Divumque*

Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp manuscript have *Dominumque*. That title is indeed applied to gods; but *divus*, “divine,” is more forceful here. For in Acts XIV, § 11, the word is not κύριος, “Lord,” which would require *Dominum*, as Bunemann restored it in Lactantius, *Institutes* IV, 13, 10. Rather, those who brought aid to human beings are called θεοί, “gods”; Burman shows that this is indicated by κατέβησαν, “they came down,” in *Jovianus Fulgens*, chapter 1.

### 175. *Ut*

I supplied this, and *procedat*, from the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1 and 2, and the Aldine edition. The others have *et procedit*. These garlands were supplied so that the victim might be adorned and slain. He refers to Luke’s words in Acts IV, § 13: ταύρους καὶ στέμματα, “bulls and garlands.” I am uncertain whether Arator recognized a hendiadys there, as Mollius noted in his commentary on Longus’s *Pastoral*, p. 60; Cellarius in his note on Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 37; Alberti, *Philological Observations*, p. 15; and as I discussed in *Miscellanea*, chapter 3, p. 20.

In *στέμματα* I think gilded horns are also to be understood. On this adornment of victims, see Bulaeus on Valerius Flaccus III, 431, and Cerda on Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, 627. I am especially led to this view because Luke mentions bulls—namely, larger sacrificial victims—in which, as Brouckhus shows in his note on Tibullus IV, 1, 15, this practice was customary.

### [Col. 0185B] 175. *Tauri*

For the bull was sacrificed to Jupiter, with whom they compared Barnabas. Athanasius also testifies to a bull sacrificed to Jupiter, *Works*, volume I, p. 26. On this matter, however, see Rhoerius’s discussion in *Daventria’s Festivals* II, 6. Hovenius suspects in his *Leisure beside the Isala*, part I, p. 59, that the same honor was paid to Paul, whom they compared with Mercury, because this was a common kind of sacrifice.

### [Col. 0185C] 176. *Rumpit*

Because of the divine honor which they were attempting to confer. For this was customary among the Jews when God’s majesty had been violated. See Barthius on Statius, *Thebaid* IX, 354. The same scholar wrongly refers this passage of Arator, in his notes on Book I of the *Thebaid*, 593, and IX, 354, to the mourning for which he taught that Jews and other peoples tore their garments, in his note on Book II of Statius’s *Silvae*, I, 171. Here the explanation must be derived solely from the majesty of God, just as in the action of Caiaphas; for this reason he more correctly attributes it to indignation in his note on Claudian, *Against Rufinus* I, 33.

### 177. *Prohibens*

The learned Wassenbergius conjectures *prodens*, with this meaning: “Paul, by tearing his tunic, openly showed that he and Barnabas were men—that is, human beings—not gods.” The conjecture gains weight from the preceding *festinus*, “hastening,” as though he quickly tore his clothing and revealed the man by baring his breast; hence verse 178:

> Whom it is clear to be weighed down  
> By the earthly law in a fragile body.

### [Col. 0185D] 181. *Sui*

The Antwerp manuscript has *suis*. Athanasius discussed this matter excellently in his *Oration Against the Pagans*, *Works*, volume I, p. 15.

### 182. *Abscissis*

Tornaesianus 1 and the Antwerp manuscript have *abscisis*, incorrectly. See my note on Book I, verse 1051.

### 182. *Deis*

The Cambridge manuscript has *diis*, incorrectly, since in that spelling the first syllable is lengthened. See Burman in *Antiklotz*, p. 98.

### 182. *Libebat*

The Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1 and 2, and the Aldine and Tornaesian editions have *licebat*, “it was permitted,” as this confusion also occurs below, verse 509, and in Lucan II, 306, and V, 177. Here *libebat*, “it was pleasing,” seems to be supported by the repetition at verse 185, *nunc libeat*, “now let it be pleasing.” And since that impious honor is called such at verse 179, I do not see how, according to Paul’s meaning, he could assert that it was permitted.

### 184. *Vocem*

The responses of the gods, from which the priest sought to learn their will. Silius I, 120:

> The victim is slain for the goddess, and the priest quickly opens  
> The breathing entrails, seeking responses.

Virgil, *Georgics* III, 491:

> Nor can the consulted prophet give a response.

Lactantius also used this passage for the same matter in *Divine Institutes* IV, 27, 3; compare his text. Likewise Sulpicius Severus spoke of sacred utterances concerning God’s will in *Sacred History* II, 33, 3. Otherwise I had conjectured *atque omen*, “and an omen.” But *vocem* has support from Arator’s style, by which he can defend himself. On the matter itself, see Bulenger, *On Lots* I, 6. Statius, *Thebaid* II, 246:

> These men sacrifice with entrails and with life.

I am surprised that Cellarius, in his note on Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* III, 8, 8, explains *animam* there as *animal*, “an animal” or “beast.” Statius is referring to a double practice: either they examined the entrails, or, if they did not perform an examination, they sacrificed only the life, which was called the victim’s *animal*. See Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 231, and IV, 56.

### [Col. 0186C] 185. *Cessantibus*

Altars were entirely unknown among Christians in the earliest period, as Georgius Remus correctly saw in his letter to Kirchmann, which is found in *Letters of Illustrious Men*, p. 212. Later their use became prevalent. Athanasius mentions a τράπεζα, “table,” in *Works*, volume I, p. 122; Tertullian mentions altars and sacrificial altars in the passages cited by Rigaltius in his notes on Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter 32.

### [Col. 0186D] 190. *Evocat*

This is found only in the Cambridge manuscript. The remaining manuscripts and printed editions have *educat*. Thus Ovid, *Ex Ponto* I, 3, 51:

> Here the field produces neither fruit nor sweet grapes;

And Seneca, Epigram 2:

> Autumn does not produce fruits, nor summer crops.

I preferred *evocare*, because it is elegant in this context. Pliny, *Natural History* XVII, 22: “A vine, before it completes its seventh year from the shoot, having been summoned to fruitfulness.” I owe this passage to the *Rural Lexicon*, where similar examples are also produced from Columella.

### 192. *Quae*

Pulmann’s manuscripts have *quam*. It agrees with Horace IV, Ode 7, 9.

### 203. *Collata*

Vossianus 1 has *collecta*.

### 204. *Astat*

The Cambridge manuscript has *exstat*.

### 205. *Gerens*

Thus the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1 and 2, and the Aldine edition. The others have *regens*. The same words were confused above, Book I, verse 796.

### 209. *Cui*

I wrote this from the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesianus 1. Supply *genti*, “to the people.” Vossianus 1 and the remaining printed editions have *qui*; this was also found in Vossianus 2 in a second hand.

### [Col. 0187C] 217. *Secundum*

Thus some others also placed Peter before Paul; others made them equal. Barthius discussed the matter in *Adversaria* XLIII, 8. Lactantius, *Institutes* V, 2, 17, violently attacked both Paul and Peter. In other copies there is *Petrum Paulumque*, “Peter and Paul.”

### 219. *Ut*

The Cambridge manuscript has *at*.

### 220. *Hi*

Vossianus 2 has *hic*. — The Cambridge manuscript has *turmis*, “crowds” or “companies.”

### 224. *Semper amica*

See Wopkens on Sedulius III, 81.

### 229. *Cum*

Thus the manuscripts, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesianus 1. The others have *tunc*, “then.” Tornaesianus 1 has *tempore*, probably through a typographical error.

### 232. *Sentire*

The Lugdunensis has *servire*, “to serve.”

### 233. *Maxima*

The Cambridge manuscript has *maxime*.

### 234. *Splendor*

Pulmann’s manuscript has *rerum est splendor*; the Antwerp manuscript has *rerum splendor*.

### 234. *Ima*

Pulmann’s manuscripts and the Antwerp manuscript have *una*. See above, verse 165.

### [Col. 0187D] 235. *Aggere*

“Roadway” or “embankment.” Below, verse 553:

> He built strong dwellings on a movable embankment.

Heinsius collected several similar examples from Christian poets in his note on Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, 375.

### 236. *Quoniam*

Thus Vossianus 1 and 2, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesianus 1. The others have *quomodo*, “how.” In *vestigiis speciosis*, “beautiful footprints,” he refers to the lame man about whom he treated in Book I, 270, as placed at the Beautiful Gate; and *huc portant*, “they carry here,” seems to belong to this same matter, with the same elegance, if I may say so, that he used there at verse 279.

### [Col. 0188C] 242. *Rabidas*

The Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus 1 have *rapidas*. Heinsius noted that this term is used of wild beasts for “ravenous” in his note on Ovid, *Heroides* X, 96. But the anger of the Jews can be called neither ravenous nor swift. I preferred the other reading, so that a savage anger, such as is attributed to wolves, might be indicated. See Heinsius on Ovid, *Art of Love* III, 8. This interchange of words is extremely common; thus the manuscripts vary below, verse 1084. Add the notes on Sedulius I, 58; Oudendorp on Lucan VI, 66 and 337; and Drakenborch on Silius IX, 312, and X, 127. In his note on Book VIII, 640, Drakenborch corrected Priscian’s *Periegesis* 709 to:

> *Victorem barrique canem rabidique leonis* (“the conqueror, and the dog of the barbarian and of the raging lion” [syntax uncertain]),

not *rapidi*, “swift.” This conjecture is confirmed by the manuscript of St. Gall in the *Proceedings of the Jena Society*, and by two of the oldest editions.

### [Col. 0188C] 243. *Velificante*

“Proceeding favorably,” or “increasing,” as found later in the scholia of Vossianus 2. The translation is taken from ships making good use of their sails and advancing on their intended course; the verb has this meaning in Florus III, 7, 3.

### 244. *Judaica*

Tornaesianus 1 has *Judaea*. See Book I, verse 709.

### [Col. 0188D] 247. *Haec*

Vossianus 2 and several printed editions have *hoc*. Fabricius and the Lugdunensis shortly afterward have *mensura*, “measure.”

### 253. *Deflexaque*

I think *reflexaque* should be read. Thus Prudentius said *reflexas semitas*, “paths turned back,” in the preface to the *Apotheosis* II, 6. I am especially persuaded by the added *retro*, “back,” which is elegantly redundant in a similar construction. For this reason I restored *retro rejicitur* in Isidore above, Book I, 800. Ovid said *retro redire*, “to go back,” in *Metamorphoses* XV, 249:

> Even to draw back the bound hands.

See Prudentius, *Peristephanon* VI, 103, and *Miscellaneous Observations* III, p. 178. The Greeks use the same construction. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter VI, § 6, has παραπεσόντας, πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν, “those who have fallen away, to renew them again.” Rhoerius, in *Daventria’s Festivals*, p. 103, thinks the punctuation there should be changed so that πάλιν is construed with παραπεσόντας. There is no need: πάλιν is added to a verb compounded with ἀνά with the same elegance.

From his holy mouth he began to bring before untaught crowds  
the traces of a steadfast mind, and to heal the people  
whom the ancient voice of God had escaped. Thus, when each of the two lame men hastens,

[215] 184 he raises up all mankind and, in his person, signified the course of a people's salvation,  
which the glory of events bestowed, so that the order might make Paul follow Peter,  
who remains the architect upon those foundations.

Yet, to recall the author’s praises in every respect,  
[220] these two are the blind men who, with crowds pressing in from every side,  
said together to the Lord: “Best Son of David,  
grant that we may escape these heavy shadows; grant that we may see the light,  
which we still do not know!” Then that hand, ever friendly to healing,  
[225] suddenly brought in its radiance, and night left their eyes;  
day, now an exile, illuminates their orbs,  
and their restored sight was startled by the unfamiliar twilight.

It is clear that these are two peoples whom the harmful vein  
of their own nature had blinded. When Jesus, in his mercy,  
[230] undertook the journey, when he willed to possess the times of the flesh,  
he renews them from the light and purifies the form  
that sins had given them; soon the image shone forth whole,  
which had deserved to perceive God. The greater part, joined to the brain,  
[Col. 0187C] [Col. 0188A] consists of the eyes: Christ creates these as a gift,  
who is the head and splendor of all things. The lowest part for all  
[235] 185 is at the end the feet; these he heals by the ministry  
of the apostolic voice, since those footprints are called beautiful  
which carry peace throughout all the lands.

Light has arisen from darkness through the gifts of the teacher.  
These establish the steps to which the lot of the word has been entrusted,  
[240] so that the healing that follows may flourish through the goodness of what came before,  
and salvation may gradually pass throughout the whole world.

Paul had already overcome the savage anger of men.  
[Col. 0188B] As faith set sail, sudden storms vomited forth  
from a Jewish cloud of deceit, claiming that ablutions could not first be given to anyone  
[245] before circumcision of the flesh had been added according to God’s law:  
“Hard-hearted people, why do you summon iron against stones any longer? This shadow  
was a figure, not a lasting reality; leave behind the representation  
that you now see to be certain. Life enduring has proceeded from Christ’s mouth,  
[250] and commands all who come to be born again from the font. Why should they cut their limbs  
and sever a part, when they can save the whole? Do not seek  
to have the aid of novelty pressed down by ancient custom, and, having turned back—”

[Col. 0188C] [Note: [Col. 0189C]

255. “Cut down”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “heavens.”

256. “Of the city”: Vossianus 1 reads “the city.”

257. “Monuments”: The manuscripts and Aldine edition have *monimenta*. I discussed this at Sedulius I, 5. I noted parallels to this passage at Book I, 967.

259. “May be”: The Aldine edition and the Lyon Bible read “are.”

264. “Purchaser”: Above, verse 93:

“So the creator washes everyone clean,  
so he purchases them”;

and the following phrase belongs to that price.

265. “To distinguish”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “to depart.”

266. “Open”: Vossianus 1 reads “open things.” There is nothing to which that reading can be referred.

267. “Why”: The Lyon Bible reads “which.” Vossianus 1’s *tardarive* is not displeasing.

268. “Grey”: This is found in Vossianus 1 and 2 and the Antwerp edition; all the others read “is useful.” The repetition from the preceding passage, *juvat* (“is useful”), is possible but unnecessary. Contrasts suit Arator’s style especially well, and thus he opposes “grey riddles,” that is, ancient ones, to the new light; I noted that these are synonyms at Sedulius I, 75. Above, verse 83:

“Blending ancient things with new.”

272. “Each”: Used for *quisquis* (“whoever”), a usage familiar to Prudentius and Juvencus, as in:

“Happy indeed is whoever stretches out his right hand,”

and:

“Whoever consecrated Hercules as a god  
by a sign or shrine will feel Juno’s anger.”

There are many other passages of the same kind. Juvencus, Book I:

“Whoever will dedicate both ears and deeds to my admonitions.”

The same author, Book III:

“Whoever longs to climb to heaven’s lofty seat.”

Similarly Helpidius, *On Christ*:

“Nor should anyone refuse  
to endure willingly for the Lord.”

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 113. Arator, *Elegy to Parthenius*, verse 10:

“For each person is given to you, and honor soon grows for him.”

Add my father’s remarks on Aurelius Victor, *Caesars* 33.29, on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 68.3, and on the frequent occurrence of this usage in writers of a later age, as Burman notes on *Catalecta* II, p. 356.

274. “Ministers”: Thus the manuscripts, the Aldine edition, and Tornaes 1; all the others read “ministers” in the dative or ablative.

279. “More savage”: The Cambridge manuscript reads “lest fornication again.” These are a copyist’s words, although the term *fornicatio* was not unworthy of Arator’s age. See Vorstius on Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* II, chapter 10, section 4.

283. “Abraham”: The Aldine edition has *Abraam*. Prosper likewise lengthens the medial syllable in *Sentences* 66:

“Abraham believes himself the father of the world.”

Tertullian shortens the first two syllables in *Against Marcion* III, p. 269 of Fabricius’s edition:

“This is Abraham, whose offspring  
you deny yourselves to be.”

286. “Circumcise”: On this custom and its origin, see Vonckius, *Miscellaneous Observations* I.

287. “Let us scrutinize”: Vossianus 2 reads “we scrutinize.”

288. “Which”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “who.” Perhaps he wrote “whoever.”

291. “From the fountain”: Vossianus 1 reads “perhaps.”

292. “By which”: Vossianus 2 reads “who.”

293. “And of vice”: The Lyon Bible reads “and by vices.”

296. “What”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “which.” Wassenbergius later conjectures *onus* (“burden”): extremely elegantly. I scarcely see what that work could mean. To confirm the conjecture I add Sedulius II, 38, concerning Mary:

“And soon the heavenly burden  
fills the girl’s womb.”

Add the note there, and above I, 96.]

Do not seek for the aid of newness to be oppressed by ancient custom, or for lights turned backward to be established after the straighter path  
[255] directs everyone and illumines the world with paths cut through by the cutting of thorns.  
Amid uncertain dispute Paul makes his way toward the city  
whose monuments of the cross shine forth, and revisits the holy leaders  
of apostolic law, to whom he reports everything that has occurred. Peter, whose greatest concern is  
[260] to increase the flocks entrusted to him, calling everyone to the joyful pastures  
under his leadership, unfolds these words from his mouth:

“You see that what the prophets, remembered through the ages,  
sang with obedient lips to the people, God has fulfilled in us—  
he who preferred to be the purchaser of salvation for all,  
[265] [Col. 0189B] 187 allowing no one to be excluded.  
At the price by which life returns, he commanded me  
to show this open way to the nations. Why delay the prayers?  
Why delay? Or why mingle these ancient riddles  
with the new light? Those whom grace purifies,  
[270] no law forbids to come. Hasty faith is the material  
of heavenly love; Christ adopts it,  
makes it his own, and grants each person the right to use it.  
The circumcised man is present and rightly is reborn in the waters.

“Since they have decided to follow the shepherd, it is therefore pleasing for ministers  
[275] [Col. 0189C] to go together and release the nations through holy writings.  
[Col. 0190A] Yet they must be warned that this yoke does not remain upon them:  
188 they must not worship images, whose libations would always be accursed;  
they must not eat what has been polluted by strangled blood;  
and lust, more savage than the enemy, must not oppress  
[280] those whom the light cleanses through baptism.”

So that the meaning of this figure may become clearer,  
and why the image that advanced earlier now departs,  
it is useful to recall the beginning. God says to Abraham:

“Now establish my everlasting covenant  
with you and your offspring in the flesh;  
[285] gladly circumcise the foreskin with iron, and bind the heavenly covenants.”

Let us scrutinize the hidden aid; let us see in this wound  
the covenants of God, what testaments the foreknowing one concealed,  
so that he might join the fellowship of heaven to the earth—  
what the boy learned to swear, who first discovered the Church  
[290] running toward the water in the fountain of Rebecca.

That bodily place where Abram is circumcised  
contains wantonness in its licentiousness, and lies under the law  
of nature as the servant of vice. The father himself, destined to be  
the source of the seed from which the world’s salvation springs to life,  
[295] empties what guilt weighs down. Desire, cut off, promises virgin work;  
for this offspring conceived the divine path. Hence holy Mary  
was born for a new birth, who, without a husband,  
[Col. 0190C] has the mother within her, and the Son of God flashes forth from the Virgin’s womb,  
and, as mediator in all things, fills the human being,  
lifting earthly things here and bestowing heavenly things there.

Therefore, with Christ’s birth, the old figure passes away.  
This form renews every right; with the knife driven away,  
[305] the Spirit, burning, circumcises the heart in the waters  
of those who are healed by the waters, so that they may not fasten wounds upon their limbs.

Meanwhile Paul, unaware of how to relax rest through cares,  
teaches throughout the world; with the mattocks of the word he cultivates everyone  
and compels the harvest of faith to grow golden,  
[310] while the frost of errors flees. The gracious Spirit forbids him  
to bring these things into Asia, nor could Mysia, rich in fields,  
[Col. 0191B] then bear the seeds of this salvation in its fertile yet barren soil.  
For a Macedonian man appeared to him in a dream and said:

“Have mercy, we beg you! Deign to enter the Illyrian shores!”

[315] O how much unexpected grace prepares! Suddenly those  
who already have the appointed time blaze with love. Thus, when night was driven away,  
the eloquent teacher changed his course, and hungry Macedonia  
fed upon the fruit of his speech; through the gifts of sleep  
[320] it deserved to comprehend the language that brings salvation.

A frequent question is heard: if the Almighty preaches  
when he is full of abundant grace—“I have not come to destroy the world,  
but rather to save it”—what reason could cause this to be denied to some  
and given to others, when Jesus’ lavish  
[325] mercy wishes to come to the aid of all in common?

There is an abundant supply of examples, and Scripture  
teaches us a many-sided figure in this matter. I shall sing of a few,  
as Luke relates them.

A certain man from the people asked to go with Christ.  
[330] Christ forbids him to go forth with him, and afterward calls one who is silent of his own accord.  
The cleansing teacher knows what hearts already receive the word,  
and whom inwardly obstructs still-unrighteous error,  
so that doctrine may perform its office only when it comes safely.  
“See,” he says, “lest holy things begin to be violated by dogs,  
[335] and lest pigs, weighed down with filth, turn them into pearls.”

[Col. 0193A] [Col. 0193C] [Note:

336. “Turn”: Vossianus 1 reads “to turn contagions.”

337. “Hard”: The word is such that the laws of meter scarcely allow it to be expressed; the rule of the foot and the nature of the noun stand in the way, as Ovid writes in *Ex Ponto* IV, 12.5.

343. “Segmented”: Latin writers call something *segmentatum* when it is compressed and compacted from various pieces or fragments of different colors or materials. Juvenal, *Satires* VI:

“Although, amid great wealth and her father’s down,  
the little girl had slept in segmented cradles,”

that is, cradles laboriously put together and variegated by a Daedalian workmanship. Ovid uses the word in the same way in his *Elegies*. Arator likewise, in Book I of the *History of the Apostles*:

“He stands, segmented, amid the altars,”

that is, in a multicolored garment adorned as though with golden tesserae. Aldhelm, *On Virginity*:

“And the woman gleamed in a segmented garment.”

Symmachus, Book IV, letter 42:

“White coverings clothe the faith of an unsegmented robe.”

Juvenal, *Satires* II:

“She puts on segments, long garments, and a flame-colored dress.”

For *segmenta* are small fragments that fall from a saw. Prudentius:

“Did he throw the severed fragments  
of a body after the saw  
to wild beasts or give them to the waters?”

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXII, 22. Tornaes 1 reads “who is segmented”; Vossianus 2, “who is increased.” In the Cambridge manuscript a gloss had been added: “that is, clothed in a tunic.” *Segmenta* is a long, ankle-length tunic. In the long garment, enduring conduct is understood through the *segmata* or *segmenta*. Juretus, in his note on Symmachus III, letter 12, explains the word here in the same way as Barthius. Savaro, on Sidonius VIII, letter 6, shows that *segmenta* are bands and borders woven with gold. Hence “segmented cradles,” about which see Barthius on Claudian III, *Consulate of Honorius* 16.

343. “Stands”: The Aldine edition reads “may stand.”

345. “Of modesty”: Thus the Cambridge and Aldine editions. The others read “to modesty.” It is difficult to say what the poet wrote. See Book I, 344.

347. “Bound”: Vossianus 1 and 2 read “blocked,” that is, closed or concealed, as *obstruere gladium* (“to conceal a sword”) in Ambrose, *On the Death of Theodosius*, p. 52. I retained “bound,” because of the following *devincta* (“tied”), although I lack the authority of another writer for this word. The Aldine, Antwerp, and Tornaes 1 editions incorrectly read “with bound loins.”

350. “To offer”: The Lyon Bible reads “to free,” which yields no meaning. Nor do I approve *litare*, found in Vossianus 1. That word was used more elegantly in Latin of appeasing and propitiating the gods; see the note on Livy VIII, 9.1, and Bunemann on Lactantius IV, 27.3 and 7. Yet *litare Deo* (“to offer sacrifice to God”) is not sufficiently appropriate here and conflicts with the quantity of the syllables.

352. “And barren”: The Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, Fabricius, the Antwerp edition, and the Lyon Bible read “and sterile.”

357. “Of begetting”: Vossianus 1 reads “for begetting.”

360. “May approve”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “approves.” The former is more elegant. See the note at the end of Book I.

361. “Success”: The Aldine edition reads “successor,” apparently using it for “succession.” Its proper meaning concerns the act of advancing, from which the sense “prosperous outcome” developed, as Menckenius notes, *Observations on the Latin Language*, p. 946. The passage could refer to that original meaning, but “succession” is more usual here.

362. “Remains”: Vossianus 1 reads “stands”; some editions read “will remain.” The “old letter” means the Old Testament. See the note on the letter to Vigilantius, verse 21.

365. “To beget”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “to have begotten”; Vossianus 2, “general.”

366. “Presses on”: The Cambridge manuscript reads “may press on, let him know the ardor.”

374. “Cleansed”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “commanded.”]

192 Lest pigs turn their defilements into pearls.

Another matter also remains in the poem, a difficult one;  
but for those to whom everything was made clear from the ancient source,  
it is easy to recognize the drops given by a subtle mouth.

That book, Exodus, recalls the coverings of the sacred  
high priest, by which he might shine in his garment  
and arrange the dress of his office with brilliant adornment—  
he who stands, segmented, amid the altars,  
[Col. 0193B] 193 among these adornments are counted, in matching attire,  
the coverings for the thigh, by which the priest, as he proceeds to the temples,  
may put on the garments of modesty and strive  
with his loins bound to approach the mysteries chastely.

[Col. 0193B] What the ancient law established more strictly, and commanded those bound members  
to be covered, which black desire possesses,  
[350] when he hastens to offer sacrifice to God—leaving them loosened  
for marriage after the sacred rites, nevertheless, lest the more sparing use  
should impede the work of offspring, and the love of marriage  
grow cold for a barren husband, when a definite progeny,  
bearing this solemn office, would never admit men from an outside stock—  
[355] where, under the ancient name, honor persists from the sanctuaries  
[Col. 0194A] and the offspring returns, to be sanctified throughout the ages:

Now the nourishing faith of the Church, to be replenished without end through successive spiritual begettings,  
commands its priests to be chaste,  
and carefully seeks in every tribe those whom it may rightly approve. Nor will this succession  
[360] be one of blood, but of merit. Yet that figure,  
without which no ancient letter remains,  
survives more fully in this new form and varies, recurring  
in alternating order, its turns—lest perhaps the priest  
[365] should then wish to beget when he sees that the flocks are not yet capable in mind,  
[Col. 0194B] and when noble ardor and hunger for learning press upon him,  
so that he may open their mouths more fully and lest anyone go away hungry.  
For Paul too often says that offspring can be given through the seed of the word,  
calling them “my little children.” Therefore it is useful for a little while  
[370] to restrain generative speech and to distribute the teacher’s zeal  
according to its proper measure, relaxing the powers of his intellect for the time  
and bearing them constrained, lest, once poured out, they be trampled  
by the profane; reserving holy things for the cleansed.

[Col. 0195A] [Col. 0195B] [Note:

375. “May impute”: Tornaes 2 reads “imputes.”

378. “To give”: To release, pardon. See the note on Sedulius II, 26.

380. “Disposition”: Vossianus 2 reads “by disposition.”

383. “Of the Macedonian”: This is a hemistich from Lucan, whom Arator also sometimes imitated, Book V, verse 2. Some editions have the inferior reading *Macedum*, which Scaliger did not correctly pronounce as either Greek or Latin. See Weitzius on Valerius Flaccus I, 96. It derives from *Maceta*, from Greek Μακέτης (*Makétēs*). See Cellarius on Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II, 546; add Barthius on Rutilius, *Journey* I, 85; Drakenborch on Silius XIV, 5 and XVII, 633; Heinsius on Claudian, *Against Rufinus* II, 279; Oudendorp on Lucan II, 647.

*Maceta* derives from *Macetia*, an ancient name of Macedonia, concerning which see Bochart, *Phaleg* III, 5, and Eustathius on Dionysius Periegetes, verse 427. There an unpublished scholiast, whom Bochart brought from the Swedish library and whom I preserve in a copy made by Palmerius Grentemesnilius, says:

“Macedonia was first called Emathia, after Emathion, son of Zeus and Electra; later Macedonia, after Macedon, son of Aeacus.”

Palmerius changes the latter name to Aeolus; I would rather think that *Thyias* has fallen out. For Macedon was the son of Zeus and Thyia, as Salmasius teaches, *Exercises on Pliny*, p. 110.

383. “Famous”: The Lyon Bible reads “new.” I think he called the city “famous” because in Acts XVI, section 12, it is called “the first city of the district of Macedonia” (πρώτη τῆς μερίδος τῆς Μακεδονίας πόλις). I discussed this at length in *Miscellanies*, chapter 17, and do not repeat it here. Add only Burman on Virgil, *Georgics* I, 490.

385. “Of Python”: Vossianus 1 reads “of Phiton,” incorrectly. Saxo Grammaticus, *Danish History* I, p. 9, speaks of possessing the Pythonic art. See Stephanius there, and Pignorius on magical boys, p. 355.

391. “Demon”: Christians frequently use this word of an evil spirit. See Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* I, 7.9. Among the older Greeks it denotes fortune, or a genius or hero; hence *daimones* are demigods. Duportus, *Lectures on Theophrastus*, chapter 16, p. 451. Thus Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 11, inserts a *daimōn* between a god and “some divine man” (θεὸν and θεῖόν τινα ἄνθρωπον). Cuperus nevertheless distinguishes it from heroes, *Observations* III, 16. In Theognis, *Sentences*, p. 13 of Sylburg’s edition:

“Wealth a demon gives even to a thoroughly wicked man.”

The translator renders this badly as “a demon”; he should more correctly have rendered it “fortune,” set in opposition to virtue. For in the plural it is said of gods, but in the singular of fortune and fate. Spanheim on Aristophanes, *Plutus* 81.

392. “Divine”: The Lyon Bible reads “wealth.”

392. “This”: Thus the manuscripts, but the Aldine edition and Tornaes 1 read “that.” It could be explained as: “Beware of attacking and troubling that any further,” concerning which meaning see Oudendorp on Suetonius, *Claudius* 17.

394. “Possessor”: Tornaes 1 reads “professor,” not badly, if one considers verse 386:

“True profession  
sounds from a lying witness.”

Nevertheless, Christian poets often describe such spirits as unjust possessors of another’s house. Sedulius III, 307:

“Then the raging robber and harmful enemy,  
whose long possession of another’s lawful house  
compelled him, when it had been invaded, to depart.”

396. “Begun”: Vossianus 2 reads “seized.”

398. “Profit”: See Acts of the Apostles XVI, section 19.

400. “Opposed”: Contrary. See Duker on Florus III, 14.4; Burman on *Catalecta* III, p. 504. *Obviare* (“to resist”) occurs below, verse 516, and in John of Salisbury VIII, 19, p. 646: “These things are in no way opposed to one another.” See Vossius, *On the Nature of Language*, p. 376; Barthius, *Adversaria* XLVI, 5; Wasseus on Sallust, *Jugurthine War* 5. Its proper meaning is “to go to meet,” as in Cassiodorus, *Variae* V, 16; copyists badly forced it upon Livy IX, chapter 23, section 4. On the verb *viare*, see Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 139, and Daumius, *Roots of the Latin Language*, p. 485.

402. “Gods”: This was the origin of the hatred directed against Christians, whom the Romans consequently called atheists. I would not attribute the punishments inflicted on Christians to mere savagery, but to the fact that they considered them guilty of treason against majesty, as Bynkershoek rightly suspected in *On the Religion of Foreigners*. Whatever was announced about Christ’s kingdom was judged contrary to the peace of the state. Moreover, the old law forbade the public practice of rites not officially accepted. Anyone who refused to fulfill vows to the emperors and to pay them divine honors was undoubtedly guilty of treason against majesty, and Christian religion forbade this. Grunerus examined these matters more fully in his *Exercise on the Hatred of the Human Race Formerly Charged against Christians by the Romans*.

402. “Hurriedly”: Vossianus 1 reads “of the common people.” But it is not sufficiently clear how these magistrates could have afflicted Paul with blows. They are called στρατηγοί (*strategoi*), civil and urban magistrates in municipalities and colonies. See Casaubon on Athenaeus, *Annotations* V, 14, and Burman on Petronius, *Satyricon* 65. These men possessed only the right of arrest and imprisonment; punishment had to be left to the governor. Either, then, they did this by usurpation, out of fear of sedition, or greater authority was also granted in larger cities. Schulting suspects as much in his note on the Digest, *On Jurisdiction*, section 35.]

Right forbids complaint on that account; let the punishment of his own stock be imputed to Adam's sins. For what can offspring rightly claim for itself  
from the guilty source of its parents, unless that kindly begetter should wish  
to pardon whatever reckless error brought forth in corrupted birth?

[380] The only path of salvation will be the disposition of one who spares;  
compassion is always without condition. Christ, bestowing what is undeserved,  
hastens kindly to these, while, being just, he delays his gifts to those.

In the land of the Macedonians, when the famous walls of Philippi  
celebrated the teacher’s journey, a girl, frenzied  
[385] [Col. 0195B] under the goad of Python, said: “Know that Paul is the servant  
of the eternal God.” True profession sounds from a lying witness;  
a faithless source has a faithful voice. Yet the honor is not transferred  
to what fear compels her to say, nor does fear stand united in her mind,  
[390] [Col. 0196A] naked of love.

Paul, pitying the hearts oppressed by the dark  
demon, and unwilling to allow a profane spirit  
196 to disclose divine paths, said: “Flee, and beware of attempting  
this further!” The enemy delayed none of the commands; he departed,  
and the unjust possessor abandoned the empty house.  
[395] The woman, saved from danger, fell silent about the man’s praise;  
she completed what had been begun and, by keeping silent, shows this to have been still more so.  
She had been making profit for her masters from the service of the crowd,  
whom the turbulent frenzy that she lacked filled,  
and in the ear of the brazen people they raged with sedition:

[400] “Roman rites are opposed to the giving of rites,  
new customs are going out throughout the world,  
and the old gods have fallen.”

Then hurried crowds, with countless clubs,  
197 having crushed Paul’s body—

[Col. 0197A] [Col. 0197C] [Note:

406. “Wood”: On this restraint, see Le Moine on Polycarp’s letter, p. 500; Markland on Lysias, p. 556; Wesseling on Herodotus IX, p. 710; Elsner on Acts XVI, section 24. This wood is also called ποδοκάκη (*podokakē*). See Harpocration under the word. “Submerged” may perhaps derive from feet compressed in the wood, as in Prudentius, *Peristephanon* V, 243; Cellarius explains *mersi* as “confined in the narrowness of the stocks.” Otherwise I had conjectured “inserted.”

411. “There is a rush”: The Aldine edition and Tornaes 1 read “is shaken.”

412. “May fasten”: Savaro discusses the custom of fastening a kiss to sacred thresholds, especially those of the Apostles, in his note on Sidonius I, letter 5.

413. “Cylinder”: Greek κύλινδρος (*kylindros*), a rounded column. Fabricius, commentary, p. 42. The Cambridge manuscript has *chelindri*; the Aldine, Tornaes 1, and Antwerp editions have *chylindri*. Savaro interprets the word as rounded half-columns in his note on Sidonius II, letter 2.

414. “Nocturnal”: Ovid, *Heroides* I, 42:

“To touch the Thracian camp by nocturnal deceit,”

that is, by night. Horace, *Satires* II, 6, 100: “to creep up upon the walls of the nocturnal man.” Cicero, *For Milo* 13: “a nocturnal dog.” Isidore XIV, 3: “which exhales fire through nocturnal heats.” Thus the Groningen manuscript and the old edition; Gothofredus reads “nocturnal things.” The uncertain author of the *Panegyric on Constantine* 16.5 has: “Driven by terrible Furies and beaten by nocturnal Avenging Spirits.” I wrote “Furies” from the Vatican manuscript and excerpts from Vossius in my possession; all editions print “omens” or “all things.” Thus Orestes is “driven by Furies” in Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 331. On this use of the adjective, add Nansius on Nonnus’ *Paraphrase*, p. 90, and Burman on Phaedrus I, 23.3.

415. “Leapt up”: Thus the manuscript and Fabricius, together with the Antwerp edition and the Lyon Bible; Drakenborch defends this reading in his notes on Silius VII, 46, and Livy II, 10.11. The other editions have “leaped.”

415. “Threatening”: Both Vossian manuscripts, Pulmann’s notes, the Aldine, Antwerp, and Tornaes 1 editions read “imitating,” that is, “as though it were falling”; it merely presented the appearance of a collapse.

418. “Becomes clear”: The Aldine, Antwerp, and Lyon Bible editions read “you become clear.”

423. “Sword”: Greek μάχαιρα (*machaira*) occurs in Luke, Acts XVII, 27. He correctly understands the word as a sword; for others it is a large knife. Consult Alberti, *Philological Observations*, p. 157.

424. “Throat”: Pulmann’s notes and the Antwerp edition read “watchtower.” Did they have *vigilum* (“of the watch”) in mind? But Luke in Acts XVII, 27 stands against this, for he explicitly says that the man intended to lay violent hands upon himself.

427. “Ministers”: Vossianus 2 reads “minister.” On the custom of washing blows and wounds, see Mollius on Longus, *Pastoral*, pp. 17 and 53.

429. “About to receive”: Thus the manuscripts; the Aldine and Tornaes 1 editions read “about to touch.”

429. “Hearts”: Vossianus 2, the Aldine, and Tornaes 1 read “heart”; but then he would have written “salvation.”

431. “To whom”: Thus the manuscripts and better editions; others read “who.” I freely admit that these lines are rather obscure.

436. “Spoil”: Both Vossian manuscripts and the Antwerp edition read “robber,” incorrectly; he indicates that the wicked one carried away spoil, or victory, from Eve.

438. “Lifting”: The Lyon Bible reads “washing.” I do not sufficiently understand this passage; it is so confused and obscure that there is no secure place for conjecture.

440. “Let us fear”: The Cambridge manuscript reads “let us fear.” Vossianus 2 and all the others have “and all.”

441. “To dare”: Some editions read “to hear.” Above, I, 2:

“Having dared an impious deed,  
she completed the work.”

442. “Honey”: I once conjectured *felle* (“gall”). But because the common reading is supported by *amari* (“bitter”), I prefer it, since he often joins similar opposites. He means enticements that are pleasant at first and bitter afterward. Thus certain editions of Lactantius, *Institutes* V, 1.10, have: “these are honeys concealing poison.” Bunemann nevertheless ordered this passage to be removed as spurious.]

They came to the prison, which confined them  
[405] in its lowest cells; with Silas accompanying, their feet,  
sunk into hollow wood, were held in blessed chains.

O happy place arising from calamity! Its bright lights shine  
in place of darkness; there ancient night gave perpetual day,  
and, transferred into the snowy hall of the Church,  
[410] it now bears gifts of salvation to all.

How well it was a prison! The whole city rushes together:  
whoever might first reach the new structure, or whoever might fasten kisses  
to the doorposts, and consecrate the part of the cylinder that had been touched.

198 By now nocturnal rest had begun to creep through their weary bodies.  
[415] The earth leapt up, threatening collapse, shaken in its own entrails;  
as it relaxed the bolts, the ground moved and wandered,  
and the storm, serving the ground, obeyed the singers' hymn.

O how great a faith becomes visible, incapable of being overcome by anyone!  
When danger approaches, punishment flees, and dangers grow through twofold fear,  
[420] so that torments may lose their place. Terrified,  
shaking his limbs from his high bed, when the guard saw  
the chambers of death lying open, he drew the naked sword  
and wished to strike his throat, but he was not permitted,  
[425] 199 with Paul as witness, to die. Through Paul’s consolation  
he recovered life and deserved to be released from his own prison.

Descending into his house, he ministers remedies to the sacred wounds,  
and prepares a clear stream for himself, about to receive heavenly water.  
For Paul, desiring to fix hearts upon salvation,  
[430] washes them all together in the flowing heavenly stream; to him, for whom the grace of light had previously opened a way not to perish,  
he escaped death, and afterward his life grew through rebirth.

In former times Eve was captured by flattering words,  
about to deceive the man. Now the wicked demon acts through the girl's mouth,  
returning to his crimes the sex from which he had gained spoil,  
and, by foretelling many things to come, was the begetter of sin. But the Apostle, an Adam  
now better, raising in the image a heavenly sign—  
he who had been an earthly man and had received no sure sign—  
says: “Since what comes from the enemy deceives, let us fear,  
[440] lest we all dare this impious deed, nor be corrupted by the bitter  
honey of deceit, if he who supplies falsehood should sing truly.”

[Col. 0199A] [Col. 0199B] [Note:

445. “In eloquence”: Thus both Vossian manuscripts and the Aldine, Antwerp, and Tornaes 1 editions. The others read “of eloquence.” The reading I adopted is more suited to Arator’s style. See the notes on verses 134 and 1100. I discussed the metaphor itself in Book I, 124.

447. “Flows”: Thus I wrote from both Vossian manuscripts and the Aldine, Antwerp, and Tornaes 1 editions. The others read “comes.” *Fluit* (“flows”) seems to have pleased Arator, so that the elegance of the speech might be expressed. See the note on Book I, 124. Greek πολλῷ ῥέοντι (“flowing abundantly”) occurs in Pliny IX, letter 26.9; its gloss there is εὐλαλεῖν (“to speak well”), which is added in the Vossian manuscript; Cortius aptly noticed this.

447. “Sower”: Greek σπερμολόγος (*spermologos*), troublesome in loquacity. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 138. Arator followed those who derive σπερμολόγος from σπείρειν τοὺς λόγους, “to scatter words.” So also in Acts XVII, section 18. The Vulgate translates it as “sower of words,” in which sense *sator verborum* (“sower of words”) means an eloquent man in Cassiodorus, *Variae* II, 3. But according to the laws of composition it should then be σπειρόλογος or λογοσπόρος. I rather agree with those who derive it from σπέρμα (“seed”). The word properly refers to birds gathering grains. It is then transferred to worthless people who collect all sorts of things in order to sustain their poverty, after the manner of birds; hence it denotes a chatterer or trifler, the sense Duportus assigns to the passage in Luke, in his note on Theophrastus, p. 303. Alberti prefers “jester,” which nevertheless differs little from it, in his *Greek Glossary*, p. 76.
