449. “Eloquent”: Pulmann’s manuscript notes and the Antwerp edition read “fertile,” just as these words are confused in Book I, 137. It is not displeasing, especially since the metaphor concerning seed continues from above, verse 188:

“From the dying grain the crop rises  
with full ears, and the vine-branch cut by a wound  
calls forth more fertilely the grapes it has conceived.”]

[Col. 0199C] **449. Orbe]** Vossianus 1 has *urbe*, “city.” It could be understood of Athens: those women were called, by way of distinction, ἄστυ (“city”), just as Alexandria was called πόλις (“city”) by Antoninus Liberalis, *Metamorphoses* 15: εἰς ἄστυ κατιόντες, “going down into the city.” See Barlaeus on Lucian’s *Timon*, p. 73. I nevertheless understand *orbis* generally as the world. On these confused words, see the note on verse 308.

[Col. 0199D] **453. Manus]** Pulmann’s Antwerp Schedae have *munus*, “gift.”

[Col. 0199D] **454. Hunc]** Thus both Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine edition, the Antwerp edition, and Tornaesius 1. The remaining witnesses have *huc*, “here.”

[Col. 0199D] **455. Cecropidae]** See the note on Sedulius I, 26.

[Col. 0199D] **456. Vernare]** “To bloom”—a familiar metaphor, by which a crown is also said to bloom in Lactantius, *On Easter* 111.

[Col. 0199D] **457. Sacrilegae]** He seems to be referring to those whom Luke calls δεισιδαιμονεστέρους in Acts XVII, § 22—properly translated “religious”; the Vulgate has “superstitious.” Compare Duportus on Theophrastus, p. 448, and Heumann at length, *Poecile*, vol. II, p. 587.—*Novitatis* refers to Luke XVII, § 21: εὐκαίρουν ἢ λέγειν τι καὶ ἀκούειν καινότερον, “they had time for nothing but saying or hearing something newer,” as in Theophrastus, *Characters* 8: ἔχεις περὶ τοῦδε εἰπεῖν καινόν, καὶ ἐπιβαλὼν ἐρωτᾷν, μὴ λέγεταιί τι καινότερον, “can you say something new about this, and, interrupting, ask whether anything newer is being said?” I shall also cite Duportus, p. 243. In the Vossian manuscript, the reading there is κενόν, “empty.”

[Col. 0200B] **358. Ignoto]** Elmenhorst, on Minucius Felix, p. 14, shows that there were several such altars. Le Moine, in his dissertation on Jeremiah, chapter XXIII, § 6, p. 290, maintains that the inscription was in the dative case. He thinks that it read ἀγνώστο Θεῷ, “to an unknown god.” Montfaucon, *Greek Paleography* II, p. 131, explains at length the use of Ο for ου. I would not deny that this case was used in altar inscriptions; the same thing occurred in temples. But examples of the other case are also not lacking, even in inscriptions; hence the learned man has now rejected this opinion in his notes on *Schedius, On the German Gods* 12, p. 219. On this altar see Berthaldus, *On the Altar* 10, § 4; Reinesius, *Inscriptions*, class 1, no. 1; and Wonna in his dissertation, whose arguments, however, Heumann refuted in his notes on Jerome’s letter to Magnus, § 5.—I understand *posuisse* as referring to the consecration of the altar; I discussed this meaning in *Miscellanea* 2, p. 23.

[Col. 0200C] **459. Parentem]** Paul, in Luke, Acts XVIII, 28, has ἐν αὐτῷ ζῶμεν, “in him we live,” that is, “through him we live; we owe our life to him,” as Rhoerius explains, *Daventry Festivities*, p. 153. Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 32: “We not only act under him, but also with him, or, to speak precisely, live.” Marius Victorinus, *On Genesis*, preface, p. 309, Fabricius’s edition A:

“Through whom we exist and move.”

[Col. 0200C] **461. Imago]** Oppian, *Halieutica* V, 7, calls mankind ἀντωπὸν μακάρεσσι γένος, “a race resembling the blessed ones.”

[Col. 0200C] **461. Poetae]** The Cambridge manuscript has *prophetae*, “prophets,” incorrectly. Luke has Τίνες τῶν ποιητῶν, “some of your poets,” in Acts XVII, § 28. Wonna, *On the Genii*, Exercise II, chapter 1, § 5, and Bochart, *Phaleg* I, 42, understand Aratus. I would suppose that Paul understood both Aratus and Cleanthes. It seems too harsh to refer the expression to only one. Cleanthes, moreover, used the same half-line in his hymn to Jupiter, verse 4. See Ursinus, *Nine Fragments of Women*, p. 272. Add Harenberg, *Bremen Library*, new series, class 2, fascicle 3, p. 444. Yet I would not attribute everything he presents there to fragments of ancient poets, especially since verses have so often slipped into writers’ prose; on this subject I spoke in *Miscellanea*, p. 189. I would scarcely doubt that these poets were known to Paul and had been read by him. The distinguished Ernesti, however, *Philological Works*, p. 201, denies this and thinks that these verses provide no stronger evidence that Paul had read those poets than would someone’s quoting a familiar line of Virgil. That may be true of the line from Menander used in the First Epistle to the Corinthians XV, § 33; but here Paul points specifically to those poets, just as he does to Epimenides in the Epistle to Titus I, § 12. If he had quoted this as a saying familiar to everyone, mention of the poets themselves would apparently have been unnecessary, as it is in the passage from Menander. The same may be inferred from Paul’s words in the First Epistle to the Corinthians XIV, § 11: ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος, “I shall be a barbarian to the speaker,” etc. Duportus was wrong to suspect that Paul had read Ovid’s *Tristia*, where, in Book V, Elegy 10, line 37, we read:

“Here I am a barbarian.”

For that line is taken from the middle of a speech, as Burmannus already observed there.]

**200** Paul, renowned for genius and eloquence, enters Athens,

and overwhelms the swollen city with fierce contests

[445] of his torrential speech. The crowd, amazed at his learned

modes of utterance, says: “From what shores does this sower

of words flow?” The ignorant populace calls Paul

a bearer of seeds and enjoys its error as its teacher,

while he speaks the truth; for this eloquent traveler

[450] **201** walks through the world and cultivates the field whose labor

presses upon all, so that the divine land may grow

and the purified human mind may bear fruit,

and not be fouled by the weeds of darnel,

which it is fitting that the crops should bear. An eager hand compels

him to go also to the leaders, before whom, standing, he declares:

[455] “Sons of Cecrops, whom fame celebrates in eloquent speech

as blooming in your gymnasia, where the lofty

love of sacrilegious novelty presides: we see that you have set up

an altar to an unknown God, who founded the stars,

who gave the sea and the lands, whom life has

[460] as its parent, so that through him we may move,

whose fire gives us breath, whose image we are,

of whom the poets have sung that the human race

is constituted. Him I proclaim, who by his word

established all things. Why do you call these divine things,

[Col. 0201A] [Note: [Col. 0201C]

**466. Latet]** Both Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine and Antwerp editions, and Tornaesius 1 have *jacet*, “lies.” Thus these words are confused in Lucan II, 162. Add Burmannus on the same author IV, 364.

[Col. 0201C] **467. Opem]** Fabricius, *Lyon Library*, has *opus*, “work”; but Arator frequently uses *opem* in the same way.

[Col. 0201C] **468. Timoris]** Vossianus 2 has *timori est*, “is for fear.”

[Col. 0201C] **469. Fusum]** Vossianus 2 has *fassum*. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I, 325:

“That true God, than whom no material substance is greater.”

[Col. 0201C] **473. Luetis]** Vossianus 1 has *luentes*, “paying.”

[Col. 0201C] **477. Cruciet]** Vossianus 2 has *cruciat*, “torments.”

[Col. 0201C] **477. Devoret]** Thus both Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine, and Tornaesius 1. The others have *devorat*, “devours.”

[Col. 0201C] **478. Juncta]** Vossianus 2 has *vincta*, “bound,” as above, I, 613.—The Cambridge manuscript soon after has *artus*, “limbs.”

[Col. 0201C] **479. Ultor]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *author*, “author.”

[Col. 0201C] **483. Loci]** The Aldine and Tornaesius 1 have *soli*, “of the sun.” By the first phrase, *in arce*, he understands the Areopagite. The Areopagus was on the citadel at Athens. Perhaps he looked to the hill of Mars, which some think is the origin of this word. A citadel is often used for a mountain or ridge. See Drakenborch on Silius XV, 305; and thus Heinsius correctly rendered Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 357.

[Col. 0201D] **487. Quod]** Vossianus 2 has *quem*, “whom.”

[Col. 0201D] **487. Graia]** Vossianus 1 has *Graeca*, “Greek”; Vossianus 2 and Pulmann’s Schedae have *grata*, “pleasing.”

[Col. 0201D] **488. In dogmate]** Thus the manuscripts and Tornaesius 1; I preferred to follow them. The printed editions have *doctrina*, “teaching,” which seems to have arisen from a gloss. For *dogma* is likewise used above, verse 130:

“Then those doctrines give certain men

to the Church.”

And verse 160:

“Having learned Paul’s doctrine.”

And below, verse 515:

“They flourished in the works of study and in the doctrine of the law.”

Thus they were unconquered in doctrine, yet conquered by Paul. Cicero writes that reason and a well-ordered way of life were born and raised there, *Letters to Friends* VI, 1; Justinus gives this city exceptional praise, II, 6, 6. [Col. 0202C] Hence Athens is said to fashion the breast in Martial, *Epigrams* VI, 64; there the best manuscript of Thuaneus also confirms that *finxerunt* should be read. Add Barthius on Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina* II, 19; and Savaro on Sidonius VIII, letter 6.

[Col. 0202C] **492. Corpore]** He refers to pleasure and luxury, in which Epicurus was thought to have placed the supreme good. Compare Gataker in the preface to Marcus Aurelius, *On His Own Affairs, or To Himself*, as Heumann, *Poecile* II, p. 10, prefers to translate the title; others, not without reason, free Epicurus from this blemish. They maintain that he understood pleasure not as the refinements of life but as freedom from pain and disturbance, and that after his death those who joined the Epicurean sect shamefully interpreted this pleasure. Staverenus discussed this matter excellently in his notes on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* II, p. 665.

[Col. 0202C] **493. Animi]** Vossianus 1 has *animae*, “of the soul.”

[Col. 0202C] **494. Vitam]** Thus the manuscripts, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesius 1; the others have *vitae*, “of life.”

[Col. 0202D] **494. Themate]** Τὸ θέμα, “the subject” or “proposition,” here means a proposition or first product brought forth contrary to nature. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 134.—See above, note on the letter to Vigilantius, 24. Vossianus 2 has *schemate*, “form”; Vossianus 1 has *vincto*, “bound.” See above I, 613; II, 478.

[Col. 0202D] **496. Animae]** The Cambridge manuscript has *animi*, “of the mind.” Vossianus 1 has *commissis*, “entrusted.”

[Col. 0202D] **498. Neuter]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *venter*, “belly.” They therefore refer the expression only to the Epicureans; for *belly* signifies lust and gluttony, in which the Epicureans placed the supreme good. On the word compare Barthius on Claudian II, *Against Eutropius*, 328. But Arator is speaking of a complete human being, that is, one endowed with body and soul. He asserts that Stoics and Epicureans, pursuing different paths, are not fully human: the latter, caring only for the body, destroy it, while the former destroy the soul through false teachings. *Neuter* could have become *venter* through transposition of letters, which has deceived scribes and often corrupted good authors. Martial, certainly, *Epigrams* XI, 100:

“How often, when you rise from your chair, I have already noticed

that the wretched tunics proclaim you, Lesbia.”

The manuscript of Thuaneus has this excellent reading: *saepe ima*, “often the lower parts.”]

“Why do you call divine what you make, and, in empty fear, regard as heavenly help that which the earth produces? The nature of metal

lies hidden in the deepest recesses of the soil; once dug out,

it receives the aid of the craftsman’s ingenuity, whether from this

the gods come to temples or vessels to hearths. Art has fashioned

gods for itself as the cause of fear. No one can enclose

[470] the Lord, diffused above all things, or confine him in small figures;

what is contained is smaller than the space of that which contains it.

In gold there is material; the maker of things does not submit to the use which those whom he himself creates fashion for him.

How harshly you will pay for your crimes! How foolishly your wisdom

[Col. 0201B] [475] will judge itself on the day of judgment! When Christ commands

all bodies to rise, and punishments will have no end,

he preserves them so that fire may torment the guilty and consume them.

Thus the flesh, joined to God, expiates fleshly acts,

and the avenger examines before it the deeds entrusted to it—the flesh

[480] which he chose to suffer in dying, and which, untouched by burial,

[Col. 0202A] he restored to the stars, wishing to give it life after Tartarus.”

These words summon many to the gifts. Dionysius himself,

**204** first in the citadel of the place, joins new rewards to honor,

and, embracing the faith, thus begins to be a sophist.

[485] “O ravenous wolf, Paul! The blessing of Jacob

has granted you this name. What now will remain in the world

that you will not draw forth with your mouth, after Greek ingenuity

has yielded and you conquer Athens, unconquered in doctrine?

Why do Epicurean and Stoic stir up impious

[490] wars upon the soil? We must disclose under what name

the many gathered flocks of sects have come together:

both have chosen to pursue a happy life;

[Col. 0202B] one loves it in the body,

**205** the other cultivates it through the virtue of the mind.

Paul’s action also gives precepts for a holy life. Thus, with the subject joined,

[495] they have opened their mouths more fully in alternating speech:

a complete human being emerges, composed of the parts

of body and soul. But now, pursuing different studies,

both desire what neither possesses. A vessel full of light

[Col. 0203A] [Note: [Col. 0203B]

**498. Vas]** Paul; he is so called in Acts of the Apostles IX, § 15. Vorstius explains this in *On Hebraisms*, chapter II, p. 26.

[Col. 0203B] **499. Clamans]** He alludes to the passage in the Epistle to the Galatians V, § 17.

[Col. 0203B] **507. Bimarisque]** Between the Ionian and Aegean seas. Ovid, *Heroides* XII, 27:

“Here is two-sea Corinth.”

Florus II, 16, 1: “where Sidonius Apollinaris notes,” *Poems* II, 476:

“And Corinth, a kingdom blessed by two seas.”

See Savaro there.

[Col. 0203C] **508. Reperit]** The Antwerp manuscript has *reppetit*. All editions have *repperit*. I have removed the second consonant, since *re-* in compounds is anceps. See Drakenborch on Silius I, 300; Burmannus on *Catalecta* I, p. 67; and the note on Sedulius, *Hymn* II, 48.

[Col. 0203C] **509. Licet]** Vossianus 2 has *libet*, “although it pleases,” as above, verse 182.—Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *undam*, “wave.”

[Col. 0203C] **510. Ibi]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *ubi*, “where.” On the verb *sitire*, “to thirst,” see above I, 427.

[Col. 0203C] **511. Aquila]** A host at Corinth and Paul the apostle’s fellow craftsman, ὁμότεχνος. He placed the first syllable long, perhaps to distinguish the word. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 10.—Born in Pontus, he had lived in Rome and from there withdrew to Corinth because of Claudius’ edict. That the house of Aquila and Priscilla was still being shown at Rome to superstitious visitors is clear from Montfaucon, *Italian Journal*, p. 164.

[Col. 0203D] **513. Hospitio]** “To hospitality,” or “to a lodging.” Rufinus uses the same construction in *Ecclesiastical History* VI, 3: “applying himself more closely to the word of God.”

[Col. 0203D] **514. Scenifactor]** “Maker of a stage,” modeled on the Greek word σκηνοποιός, “one who weaves curtains.” Arator II has *Nam scenae factor*, “for he was a maker of a stage.” This was Paul’s craft, by which he earned his livelihood among the Corinthians. In theaters, the floor was spread with curtains, as Arruntius states. Arator soon translates “who made tents” with *σκηνοποιόν*, “tent-maker,” and describes what tents are:

“Going farther away, the traveler everywhere

raises these and with their hides wards off winters and suns.”

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 121.—I restored this reading from both Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesius 1. Fabricius approves *scenae factor*, and almost all editions have it. The Cambridge manuscript has *schenefactor*; evidently the scribe thought of *schoenefactor*, from σχοῖνος, “rush,” as though it meant a maker of ropes. Du Cange indeed testifies that he found *scoenaefactor* elsewhere under *SCENOFACERE* in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, and he too refers it to σχοῖνος, although one might question whether *scoenae* is not corruptly written for *scenae*. I know what some have decided about Paul as a weaver of curtains, but I follow Reinesius, *On the Punic Language*, chapter 13, who understands σκηνοποιός as referring to tents and tabernacles made of hides. The Vulgate likewise translates it *scenofactoriae artis*, “of the tent-making craft”; Beza and Tremellius understand it no differently. Indeed, no other word can be preferred in Arator, since he clearly indicates that he means tents at verse 552.

[Col. 0204C] **518. Firmo]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *firma*, “firm.”

[Col. 0204C] **519. Monent]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *movent*, “move”; the same confusion occurs above.—Vossianus 1 has *trado*, “I hand over.”

[Col. 0204C] **522. Nomine]** See Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXV, 10.

[Col. 0204C] **527. Honore est]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *honorem*, “honor.”

[Col. 0204C] **530. Senio]** I would note that the early Christian poets write remarkable things about the eagle as a mystical and divine bird—things which, if one searches for them in the commentaries of others, one may scarcely find illustrated or confirmed. The story Arator relates is certainly marvelous.—There are two variant readings in the written tradition: *declinatis senio* is read, and *quae fervidus incutit aestus* in good and very old parchments that we purchased from the spoils of the Carthusians near Strasbourg. I do not recall having read this story or fable about the eagle anywhere else except in Aldhelm’s *Book of Riddles*, edited by Martin Antonius Delrio. His words under “The Eagle” are:

“While weary old age corrupts its bodies,

it bathes its sinking limbs in clear fountains.

Afterward I am restored by Phoebus’ splendid light.”

But he unquestionably imitated Arator, although he reverses the order. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII, 3.—I adopted *senio* from the Cambridge manuscript, in a second hand, Vossianus 1, the Aldine edition, Tornaesius 1, and Barthius’ manuscripts. The others have *senior*, “older.” Barthius makes the same observation about this story of the eagle in his notes on Claudian, *Third Consulship of Honorius*, preface, verse 1. There, however, he also adds Jerome’s testimony in his letter to Praesidius: “The eagle, when it grows old, finds its feathers and eyes weighed down; it seeks a spring, raises its wings, and gathers itself into the heat, and thus its eyes are healed; it plunges itself three times into the spring, and so returns to youth.” Barthius emends the passage to *ipsi os, pennae et oculi*; this is unnecessary. Eustathius supports it in his *Commentary on the Hexaemeron*, p. 27: Τὸν ἀετὸν ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ὄψεις, καὶ βαρεῖσθαι αὐτοῦ τὰς πτέρυγας, “that the eagle’s eyes become dim and its wings grow heavy.” I owe the reference to Bochart, *Hierozicon*, second part, book II, chapter 1, where there is more on this subject.]

“He places both under God. ‘I see,’ he cries, ‘how unjust

[500] the flesh is toward my mind,’ and again he begins healthfully:

‘What grace grants is not accomplished from its own portion.’

**206** Let us celebrate this journey, since Christ is life,

and he himself calls himself the way; let us walk through him toward him.

And so that the holy lamp may not cease beneath our feet,

[505] the herald appointed for faith supplies the world with its traces.

Leaving Attica, Paul had already abandoned the Athenian bands,

conquered by pious eloquence; seeking the walls of two-sea Corinth,

he found a populous city which, although it touched

the waves of alternating seas, thirsted for perpetual waters.

[510] There the man from Pontus, Aquila,

[Col. 0203B] was then a teacher, a man bearing many instruments of praise.

Paul entrusted himself to his friendship and, judging it worthy,

entered the house of his companion in love of their shared craft;

for each was a maker of the stage.

[515] **207** They flourished in the labors of study and in the doctrine of the law.

[Col. 0204A] Christ says: ‘Now teach, Paul; no one opposes you

while I accompany you. You see what crowd is mine

within these walls; persist in speaking. I strengthen hearts.’

These things warn us that no one can ever complain

[520] of a delayed gift, since Christ’s mercy gives freely.

So that the meaning concealed beneath an ambiguous figure

may not lie hidden, I shall explain the reason in which it is given.

The pious Scriptures have sung that arguments are often drawn

from a name and that the greatest proofs arise from it. Therefore it is pleasing

[525] to seek more deeply why the companion dear to Paul is joined

to him, made his partner in the craft, beneath whose image

the matter was so named, and with what honorable distinction

he is adorned, pleasing also in this respect. The faithful nature

of the eagle spontaneously bears what its form contains; for the bird,

[Col. 0204B] **208** weakened by age,

[530] with its sight already dimmed by old age,

lies beneath the fire-emitting sun, and opens its eyes,

[Col. 0205A] [Note: [Col. 0205B]

**532. Ejus]** Below, at verse 773, there is *ejus velle aditum*, “his wishing access.” But Bentley, in his notes on Horace III, *Odes* 11, 18, declares that this word is contrary to the dignity of the poem—a judgment based more on his own taste than on the authority of the ancients. On the matter see Burmannus on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII, 16; *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. II, p. 33; and Burmannus, *Antiklotz*, p. 90.

[Col. 0205C] **533. Ingerit]** Vossianus 1 has *inserit*, “inserts.”

[Col. 0205C] **537. Incutit]** Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIII, 3, and in his notes on Claudian, p. 470, cites *ingerit*, “thrusts in,” but I have found this in no manuscript or printed edition. Barthius himself produces *incuit* from his parchments; I think this is a printer’s error for *incutit*.

[Col. 0205C] **538. Mundanda]** I adopted this from Vossianus 1. All the others have *purganda*, “to be cleansed,” which I attribute to a gloss. Above, verse 331:

“The teacher who cleanses the inner things knows.”

In Sedulius III, 29, following the authority of the manuscripts, I restored:

“You can cleanse me from stains,”

instead of *purgare*, “to purify.” See my *Specimen of Observations*, chapter 9.

[Col. 0205C] **538. Mergitur]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *mergit in*, “plunges into”; this is not at all bad if one supplies *se*, “itself,” as Bunemann correctly saw in his notes on Lactantius, *On the Pentad*, 68, § 28. I am therefore surprised that, in his notes on the *Poem on Easter*, verse 57, he takes this as an active verb used in place of a passive. I have shown that the pronoun is frequently omitted in this construction in my notes on Sedulius IV, 80. Learned men have sometimes failed to notice this in their emendations, at least not Latin Latinius, who altered *si se pudicam sciret* in Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men* 46, 2; see *Observations*, vol. II, p. 53. Isidore XIV, 6: “The Fortunate Islands, by their name, signify that they bear everything good.” This should be read from the Groningen manuscript and the old edition, not *fere*, “almost.” Supply *se ferre*, “that they bear themselves.” Add Cannegieter on Ulpian, title II, § 6.

[Col. 0205D] **539. Decoris]** Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII, 3, and in his notes on Claudian, p. 470, cites *vigoris*, “of strength”; I have found this in no manuscript. The other reading refers more appropriately to the brightness of the feathers. Phaedrus I, fable 13, verse 7:

“How much beauty you bear in body and face.”

[Col. 0205D] **540. Apertior]** Vossianus 2 has *apertius*, “more openly.” I have already shown above that adjectives are elegantly used for adverbs, book I, 425.

[Col. 0205D] **543. Accendente]** Vossianus 2 reads this elegantly, and I followed it. Others have *accedente*, “approaching.” The comparison with burning rays, verse 533, and with the light of the sun, verse 541, clearly supports the former; Christians commonly speak in this way. Below, verse 628:

“with which burning faith was present,

so that that vapor might fall.”

Verse 1204:

“Faith has been kindled.”

Sedulius I, 189:

“The flame of the burning faith of the furnace has been extinguished.”

IV, 36:

“which feels faith blazing.”

The manuscripts frequently vary in these expressions. See Burmannus on Valerius Flaccus II, 238, and Drakenborch on Livy XXIII, 46, 2. In Cicero, *For Archias* 6, read from the Erfurt manuscript: “he might kindle the light of letters.” In Isidore X, p. 1077, the Groningen manuscript has *quod incendat*, “which sets on fire”; but I would prefer *incedat*, “which advances.”

[Col. 0206C] **545. Seni]** The Aldine edition has *saevi*, “fierce.”

[Col. 0206C] **545. Manantibus]** The Cambridge manuscript has *geminoque manentibus*, “and remaining in a double [source].” Vossianus 2 has *geminoque manantibus*, “and flowing from a double [source].” Vossianus 1 has *geminoque venientibus*, “and coming from a double [source].” Pulmann’s Schedae and the Antwerp edition have *gemino venientibus*, “coming from a double [source].” But that is a gloss: thus Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* V, 30, mentions an origin flowing from God, that is, proceeding from him.

[Col. 0206C] **547. Exempli]** Vossianus 1 adds *est*, “is.”

[Col. 0206C] **547. Opimam]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *opima*, “rich.” He refers to Psalm 102, § 5.

[Col. 0206D] **548. Renovaberis]** Vossianus 2 has *renovaveris*, “you will renew,” arising from the frequent interchange of letters discussed in book I, 708.

[Col. 0206D] **553. Tectis]** Thus the manuscripts and Tornaesius 1. Du Cange likewise cites it under *SCENOFACERE* in his Latin Glossary. Pulmann’s Schedae have *testis*, “witnesses.” Almost all editions have *textis*, “woven,” as Heinsius shows that these words were confused in his notes on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, 446. I followed the manuscripts because tents may equally be called “coverings,” just as Virgil calls forests “the coverings of wild beasts,” *Aeneid* VI, 8; and Arator himself soon calls them *habitacula*, “dwellings.”

[Col. 0206D] **555. Pellibus]** Tents were made from hides. See Barthius on Claudian, *Panegyric on Stilicho* I, 122; Lipsius, *On Roman Military Matters* V, dialogue 1; and the note on Florus I, 12, 8.

[Col. 0206D] **556. Prima]** Vossianus 2 has *primam*, “the first,” namely Adam’s guilt.

[Col. 0206D] **557. Est]** Both Vossian manuscripts, the Antwerp editions, and the Lyon Library edition omit this word.

[Col. 0206D] **559. Sunt]** The Aldine edition has *sint*, “may be.”]

“He warms its feathers in the fire, and exposes its night-darkened,

sick eyes to the burning rays,”

**209** destined to return to its former day. Thus the bird,

[535] weak, receives gifts of heat from the source,

and repairs the losses of its ancient age.

So that the gifts which the fervent heat bestows might not be its only possessions,

it is to be cleansed in the channel of waters;

it plunges three times into the waves,

lays aside its old age in the waters, and lifts from the spring

[540] an image of youthful beauty. What act could be more openly

religious? When we are touched by the light of the true Sun,

we release the contagions of the ancient age,

as faith kindles; soon, reborn through the mother-water,

[Col. 0205B] **210** we are seen as inexperienced in our newness:

[545] infancy returns to old age; with a double-flowing origin,

this better birth comes, well aware of the example

[Col. 0206A] of this bird, whom the Spirit moved to ply

his rich hand upon the lyre: ‘You will be renewed,’ he says,

‘like the eagle.’ By this law the approved learn to perceive

[550] that the praise of the type is pleasing, as the songs of the righteous confirm.

Nor is Paul’s craft idle, celebrated under that very companion:

by the power of a hidden good, he made strong tents

on a mound, with coverings that could be moved.

Going farther away, the traveler everywhere

[555] **211** raises these and with their hides wards off winters and suns.

We too, driven from our first place because of guilt,

are cast into the world’s exile; at last the way is restored

by which we may retrace our journey to our homeland.

In your camp, Paul, we have defenses, so that the rains

[Col. 0207A] [Note: [Col. 0207C]

**560. Mundana]** Vossianus 1 has *mundata*, “cleansed.”

[Col. 0207C] **563. Feri]** Vossianus 1 has *feris*, “of wild beasts”; the following letter has attached itself to the word.

[Col. 0207C] **564. Artis]** The Aldine edition and Tornaesius 1 have *arteis*. The praise of the craft seems to be used for “praised crafts.”

[Col. 0207C] **568. Verbo]** The Aldine edition has *verbis*, “with words.”

[Col. 0207C] **572. Venerit]** The question is whether they had received the Spirit. In Acts of the Apostles XIX, § 2, the Cambridge manuscript has εἰ Πνεῦμα ἅγιον λαμβάνουσί τινες, “whether some receive the Holy Spirit.” But Marckland already noted, in his notes on Lysias, *Oration* X, p. 555, that this is the work of an interpolator ignorant of the idiom.

[Col. 0207C] **573. Maduisse]** Vossianus 2 has *maluisse*, “to have preferred.”

[Col. 0207C] **579. Tu nunc]** The Cambridge manuscript has *nunc tu*, “you now.”

[Col. 0207C] **580. Tibi]** A rarer construction. Bondam, *Various Readings* I, 5, did not think that a dative could be joined to this word; here, however, you will not resolve the difficulty unless you prefer to emend the text to *te*. Such usages may be admitted in these authors but rightly condemned in others.

[Col. 0207D] **581. Semita]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *semina*, “seeds.”

[Col. 0207D] **583. Quod]** Thus the manuscripts, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesius 1; the others have *quae*, “which.”

[Col. 0207D] **583. Donique]** Tornaesius 1 has *doni quoque suscipis*, “you also receive as a gift.” All agree, however, on *resuscipis*, “you receive back,” and the dictionaries defend it only on Arator’s authority. Yet because of *reddamus*, “we may return,” a similar compound seems necessary.

[Col. 0207D] **587. Potestas]** Cortius had cited Hincmarus, *On the Non-Trinitarian Deity*, vol. I, p. 500.

[Col. 0207D] **591. Ulterius]** Vossianus 2 has *alterius*, “of another.”

[Col. 0207D] **592. Diluit]** The Cambridge and Aldine manuscripts have *deluit*, “washed.”

[Col. 0207D] **594. Hoc cessit]** Vossianus 1 has *concessit*, “granted,” incorrectly. See the note on the letter to Florentius, at the end, and I, 301.

[Col. 0208C] **594. Dogmata]** The Aldine and Tornaesius 1 have *dogmate*, “with doctrine”; so does Vossianus 2 in a second hand.

[Col. 0208C] **596. Deo]** Thus the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1, and several editions, incorrectly. Vossianus 2, the Aldine, Tornaesius 1, and the Antwerp edition have *veniente Dei praenuntius*, “when God was coming, the herald.” There is nothing to which *veniente* can then refer.—*Ex quo* means “after,” or “since.” With the help of the Thuaneus manuscript, remove the gloss from Martial VI, 50:

“After he began to preserve obscene catamites.”

The manuscript has *obscoenos* from *co*; hence *ex quo* should be restored.

[Col. 0208C] **597. Prius]** The Cambridge manuscript has *pius*, “pious”; thus these words are confused in Sedulius III, 44. This could be referred to Jesus, but that is not necessary.

[Col. 0208C] **597. Fecit]** I followed the manuscripts. The Aldine and Tornaesius 1, however, transpose the words: *quo tempore fecit Jesus*, “at which time Jesus did [it].” The Antwerp edition also reduces the final word to three syllables.

[Col. 0208D] **599. Cur solitum]** Thus the manuscripts and the Aldine edition, except that the Cambridge manuscript has *cum*, “when”; all the others have *insolitum*, “unusual.” But John’s baptism was customary, Christ’s unusual. He also contrasts his own baptism with Christ’s. Compare Acts of the Apostles XIX, § 4.

[Col. 0208D] **602. Insinuans]** Vossianus 2 has *insignans*, “marking.” Du Cange’s Latin Glossary shows that *insignare* means “to indicate and show by a sign.” Arator himself uses the other word above, I, 82:

“And indicating divine matters.”

Yet refer *digito* to *prodidit*, “he revealed with his finger”; since the scribe in Vossianus did not perceive this, he seems to have altered the word.

[Col. 0208D] **605. Iterant]** Thus the Cambridge manuscript, both Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesius 1. The others have *iterat*, “repeats.” The Lyon Library edition has the worse reading *inerat*, “was present.”]

“the world’s storm may bear the clouds of crime,

and the fiery tempter drive on its vapors. Under such a covering,

safe salvation receives no blow of danger,

nor does the fallen enemy yield to the fierce powers.

Mystical signs send their leaders ahead with praises of the craft.

[565] Peter, acting as a fisherman, catches men; the guest of the sea

persists in the sacred waters. While Paul raises earthly dwellings,

he teaches us to establish heavenly ones.

What his hand has made, he now often builds into halls with his word.

Following farther on, after passing through the regions,

[570] Paul comes to Ephesus and teaches there, seeing certain men

[Col. 0207B] standing before him: ‘Has the holy Spirit come

upon these?’ the questioner says. They reply that they had long ago

been drenched in John’s fountain, for they are still ignorant

of this name and have been led here—those whom the sacred stream

[575] washed and whom the holy Spirit soon filled in their mouths,

giving them a rain of words with his customary powers.

The profane often move their weapons from this side

and prepare for battle. To enable me, speaking, to pour out

weapons contrary to theirs, now water my mouth more abundantly,

[580] holy Spirit, so that the doctrines you give may be worthy of you!

You are the path of speech, the way of life, the power of utterance;

come, you who through your gifts always bring about

what we may return, and at last receive back the use of your gift.

John, the forerunner of the one who was to come, displayed his baptism

[585] in the world and prepared the way for the Lord himself,

declaring to all that a future baptism would follow,

after another baptism rightly given, which the triune power

is accustomed to illuminate. But when Christ chose rather

to touch these waters, he established a pattern for all,

[590] so that the mortal race might hasten to him through the holy spring

and not abandon the sacred stream any longer; for the Lord himself

had deigned, with a pure body, to wash the river

when God, through his servant, plunged him beneath it.

Once the river had been touched,

[Col. 0208B] **213** this task passed to the disciples, whom many accounts say

[595] baptized according to the doctrines. It was right for the servants’

washing to cease when God was coming, since the forerunner

had previously proclaimed these things; at the time when Jesus

caused a complete baptism to be performed, just as John had done,

why would he give the customary and proper one? What rule

[600] compelled Paul to have them be reborn in Christ’s fountain,

when John, indicating with his finger that Christ was not merely to come

but had already come, revealed the heavenly Lamb,

singing that he would take away sins from the whole world?

Why do you wish, profane one, to counterfeit a double baptism?

[605] [Col. 0208C] Things that differ are not repeated; repetition preserves the same matter,

[Col. 0209A] [Note: [Col. 0209B]

**610. Divisa]** Vossianus 1 has *diversa*, “different.” The words are likewise transposed in Livy XXI, 55, 2. Schefferus defended *divisa Reip. membra*, “the divided members of the state,” from his manuscript in Pacatus, *Panegyric* 36, 4.

[Col. 0209B] **611. Haeretico]** Thus the Cambridge manuscript and both Vossian manuscripts; refer it to *lacu*, “lake,” and I have already defended this reading in *Miscellanea*, p. 192. The printed editions have *haeretica*, “heretical.” The Cambridge manuscript has *cum tunc haeretico*, “when then [it was] heretical.”

[Col. 0209C] **613. Fonte]** I substituted this from one Vossian manuscript because of the contrast with the lake of Avernus and the following *undam*, “wave.” All have *forte*, “perhaps.” The emendation is supported by verse 590:

“To hasten through the holy fountain.”

Nor does the fact that *lumen*, “light,” precedes it here constitute an obstacle, although it may seem somewhat unsuitable to a fountain. The same usage occurs above, verse 280:

“whom the light cleanses through baptism.”

*Forte* and *fonte* may likewise have been confused above, verse 291. N and R are frequently exchanged; hence part of Isidore, *Origins* III, 70, is corrupt, where *molestae sunt pugnationes* appears, “the struggles are troublesome.” Gothofredus read it thus; more correctly, the Groningen manuscript and the old edition have *purgationes*, “purifications,” and Almeloveen substituted the same reading from Merula’s manuscript, *Conjectures*, p. 160.

[Col. 0209C] **614. Ire]** The word is absent from Vossianus 1. Cortius had cited Hincmarus, *On the Non-Trinitarian Deity*, vol. I, p. 499, in his edition.

[Col. 0209C] **615. Qui]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *quis*, “who?”

[Col. 0209D] **619. Memorat]** Vossianus 1 has *numerat*, “numbers,” not without merit.

[Col. 0209D] **620. Et felix]** This is found in both Vossian manuscripts, Tornaesius 1, and the Antwerp edition. The others have *o felix*, “O blessed.”

[Col. 0209D] **623. Converterat]** Vossianus 1 has *convenerat*, “had assembled.”

[Col. 0209D] **625. Nutarent]** Thus the manuscripts and several printed editions. The Aldine and Tornaesius 1 have *mutarent*, “were changing.” My father often showed that these words were confused, in Pliny, *Panegyric* 5, 6, and in Silius VI, 234. The Lyon edition of 1514 has *mutat*, “changes.” I do not know whether *mutarent* was restored here from the language of Acts XIX, § 12, ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι ἀπ’ αὐτῶν τὰς νόσους, “diseases departed from them”; Duportus judges that the more Attic form would be αὐτοὺς τῶν νόσων, “them from diseases,” in his notes on Theophrastus, p. 264.—The Cambridge manuscript places the following verse before this one.

[Col. 0209D] **626. Refecerit]** The Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 2, the Aldine, and Tornaesius 1 have *reficeret*, “might restore”; Vossianus 1 has *refecerat*, “had restored.”

[Col. 0209D] **628. Absentes]** Wassenbergius conjectures *absentis*, “of an absent person.”

[Col. 0209D] **629. Calori]** Vossianus 2 has *colori*, “color.”

[Col. 0210B] **630. Semicinctia]** Σεμικίνθια—for Luke retained the Latin word in Acts—were cloths with which the dirt of the hands was wiped away; *sudaria*, “sweat-cloths,” were used for the sweat of the forehead. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 121.—The Aldine edition has *semicincia*; the Antwerp edition, *semicintina*. Vossius, *On the Purity of Speech* V, p. 297, shows how these differed from a *sudarium*, which later writers call a *facitergium*, “face-cloth.” Among the ancients it was a garment that covered the front part of a person, extending from the belt and loins down to the feet. See Taubmann on Plautus, *Aulularia* III, 6, 42, and the note on Petronius, *Satyricon* 94. Yet in that passage the word is undoubtedly corrupt. Schefferus also favored *hemicyclo*, which occurred to others as well, in the *Adversaria* preserved in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. IX, p. 191. Isidore XIX, 33: “A *cinctus* is a broad belt, a *semicinctium* a narrower one, and a *cingulum* the narrowest of all.” The old edition there has *utriusque*, “of both.”

[Col. 0210C] **631. Oblata]** Thus the Cambridge manuscript, the Aldine edition, and Tornaesius 1. Vossianus 1 and the remaining editions have *allata*, “brought”; Vossianus 2 has *ablata*, “taken away.”

[Col. 0210C] **632. Focos]** Perhaps he means the heat mentioned at verse 629. I would nevertheless prefer to read *toros*, “beds.” The *tori languorum* are the beds on which the sick lay. An abstract noun is thus used for a concrete one; I discussed this in the letter to Florianus, verse 17. *Torus* and *focus* are likewise confused in Lucan IV, 197, in the manuscripts cited by Burmannus.

[Col. 0210C] **634. Nullaeque]** Pulmann’s Schedae, Antwerp, have *milleque*, “and a thousand.”

[Col. 0210D] **636. Turba]** Vossianus 1 has *turbo*, “whirlwind.”

[Col. 0210D] **638. Plasmata]** Πεπλασμένος, “made” or “formed.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis*:

“Thus in turn is formed

a thing made of immaterial breath.”

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 105.—Christian writers derived this and many similar words from Greek. I shall spare examples; Salmasius, in his notes on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 225; Daumius, *On the Causes of the Loss of Roots*, chapter 14; and Vossius, *On the Purity of Speech* IV, 16, provide them abundantly. *Plasma* in this sense is used of a human being by Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* VII, 184, and IX, 92. In earlier authors it denotes a well-formed expression, as Salmasius notes on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 466. Gronovius rendered *plasmare* as “to form” in Ecclesiastes, chapter 15. Reinesius produced *cataplasmare* in *Various Readings* III, 12, p. 531. Compare Isidore XIX, 15, where Gothofredus incorrectly printed *pingere terra*, “to paint the earth.” The Groningen manuscript and the old edition more correctly have *fingere*, “to form”; for Isidore himself says in XX, 4: “*Fingere* means to make, form, and fashion.”]

Not another, and it would be twice that which at first

639. *Gestat* (“bears”): Vossianus I and the Antwerp edition read *portat* (“carries”).

[Col. 0211C] 640. *Hospite* (“guest”): Sedulius III, 85, says of the demon:

> Such a house was fitting for him to have as a guest.

Wopkens also compared these passages there.

[Col. 0211C] 642. *Judaea* (“Judaea”): the Aldine edition reads *Judaica* (“Judaean”).

[Col. 0211C] 644. *Proponimus* (“we set before”): Tornesianus I reads *praeponimus* (“we place before”). Vossianus I likewise does not have the reading.

[Col. 0211C] 645. *Pervasum* (“invaded”): Salvian, *The Governance of God* V, p. 97, has *Privata pervasione nudati sunt* (“they were stripped by a private invasion”). Rittershusius correctly explains *pervasiones* as *invasiones* in his note on the same work, p. 36. Johannes Cannegieterus aptly established the word for Isidore, *Observations*, chapter 17; Sedulius himself has *pervasa* at III, 309. Add Wopkens, *New Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. VIII, p. 925.

[Col. 0211C] 646. *Qui sit* (“who he is”): Cambridge and Vossianus I read *quis sit, ait, quis* (“who he is, he says, who”); the Aldine edition and Tornesianus I read *qui sit Christus ait* (“he says who Christ is”).

[Col. 0211C] 649. *Ipso* (“by this very [fact]”): Cambridge reads *ipsa*, referring it to *gens* (“people”); this reading is not displeasing.

[Col. 0211C] 650. *Placere* (“to please”): the distinguished Wassenbergius emended this to *jubere* (“to command”), and explains: “You Jews cannot frighten the evil spirit by your words, commands, or threats so as to expel him when he has been frightened by your commands.” He thinks *placere* was restored by persons who could not tolerate the dative *τῷ* joined with *jubere*. Yet the same construction occurs at Book I, 117, where I have discussed it.

[Col. 0211D] 655. *Rabido* (“raging”): Vossianus I reads *rapido* (“swift”); see above, verse 242.

[Col. 0211D] 658. *Pavore* (“terror”): Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp edition read *pavori* (“to terror”).

[Col. 0211D] 662. *Qua* (“whereby”): Cambridge reads *quo* (“whereby,” neuter).

[Col. 0211D] 663. *Edere* (“to utter”): for this expression see the note on Sedulius I, 146. Wassenbergius preferred *daemones* (“demons”).

[Col. 0211D] 665. *In* (“into”): this is the reading of the manuscripts and of the Aldine and Tornesianus I editions; the others read *ad latices* (“to the waters”), but *intrare in latices* (“to enter into the waters”) is correct. The preposition already present in a compound is often repeated, as in *inire in urbem* (“to enter into a city”). See Burmann on Suetonius, *Caesar* 18. In Orosius VI, 20, *de taberna meritoria per totum diem fluxit* (“it flowed from the shop called Meritoria throughout the whole day”), *defluxit* (“flowed down”) could be substituted, on the authority of John of Salisbury VIII, 18. *Intrare* is used as a gerund, a usage discussed in the note on the epistle to Vigilius, verse 4. Sedulius I, 39 is much the same:

> To enter through the holy waters.

[Col. 0212C] 668. *Incendia* (“fires”): it was customary to burn by fire books especially harmful to religion and the state. See Elmenhorst on Arnobius, *Against the Nations* III, p. 109, and what I said in *Miscellanies*, chapter 9, p. 104. In calling these people magicians, he reproduces Luke’s *περίεργα πραξάντων*, Acts XIX, 19 (“those who practised curious arts”). The common translator renders it “to pursue curious things”; Henry Stephanus prefers “those who had practised curious arts,” *Schediasms* II, 28. Latin writers likewise use *curiosus* of magical arts. See Gothofredus on Law 4 of the Theodosian Code, *On Sorcerers and Astrologers*, who translates Luke’s words in the same manner as Stephanus.

[Col. 0212C] 669. *Vitent* (“may avoid”): I printed this from Cambridge, Vossianus II, and the Lyon Bible; all the rest have *vitant* (“avoid”).

[Col. 0212C] 670. *Aera* (“air”): so the manuscripts and certain editions; the common reading is *aethera* (“ether”), just as *aerius* and *aethereus* are confused in Sedulius I, 134. Vossianus I reads *fulgur* (“lightning”).

[Col. 0212C] 672. *Posuere* (“they set down”): Luke’s *συμψηφίζειν*, Acts XIX, 19, means “to calculate,” as Maius notes, *Sacred Observations* IV, p. 195. By *nummi* (“coins”) understand denarii; for this is what Luke’s *ἀργύριον* denotes. See *Collection of Short Works Relating to History*, vol. II, p. 472.

[Col. 0212D] 676. *Diluit* (“washed away”): Cambridge and the Aldine edition read *deluit*; see above I, 203.

[Col. 0212D] 679. *Coactos* (“those compelled”): so Vossianus I and the Antwerp edition. Vossianus II and the Aldine and Tornesianus I editions have *coactus* (“compelled”); the remaining editions read *coactis*. Wassenbergius punctuates:

> The former owner is granted [his land], though compelled to serve.
> Lost freedom returns; the creditor remits harmful debts.

[Col. 0212D] 680. *Petit* (“seeks”): I printed this from Vossianus I and the Aldine edition. The Antwerp edition comes nearest, reading *perit* (“perishes”); the others read *redit* (“returns”), which I think has the smell of a gloss.

[Col. 0212D] 681. *Limen* (“threshold”): the Aldine and Antwerp editions, Fabricius, and the Lyon Bible read *lumen* (“light”). I suspect Cambridge and the Univers edition do as well, since Cortius wrote nothing in the margin of Fabricius’s edition. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, 21, supports the other reading:

> They are enclosed within the threshold of one homeland.

These readings are frequently confused. See the note on Sedulius I, 174, and II, 41, below at 773. I do not know whether Virgil’s *lumina Vestae* (“Vesta’s lights”), *Aeneid* II, 567, ought to have been preferred from the Juntine edition.]

[640] and be polluted by its own guest, nor the odor of the robber infect

“I know who Christ is, and who Paul is; but you are unknown. You may learn

This is the true faith. What spectacles then occurred before the people,

[655] The demon’s anger, grinding its teeth with a raging roar, harmful

only to its own adherents, tears apart its garments and cuts its faces,

while the defeated dangers flee and, stripped bare, turn their backs

in precipitous terror.

What, fierce Judaea, will you no longer fear from disaster?

[660] You perish with your ally thus, the enemy who is at once the author

and punisher of your crime, lest, while you are your own judge, he who

is guilty together with the sinner should be driven away. Soon fame,

flying throughout the city, spread everywhere the report that the demon

had uttered that God’s power is supreme.

[665] They rejoice to enter the holy

waters together, and to wash away their ancient stains in a new fountain,

and to shine with sacred streams.

From these waters one age of innocence is granted equally to all.

But others set fire to the magical books,

so that they might deserve the waters and avoid fires by means of fires.

[670] The lofty flame rises too high; its flash flies above the air,

and ashes of this kind seek heaven.

They also set down a price of fifty thousand coins for the books,

because the guilty deserved in this way to abolish their wickedness.

The reason for this figure is as follows:

[675] By sacred law the number releases sins, just as formerly

219 David washed away his crimes in the whole Psalm and drives away

obligations incurred; for when the fiftieth year arrives

as a jubilee, the alienation of one’s own land is restored to the ancient

master. Freedom, lost by those compelled to serve, seeks its return;

[680] the creditor loosens the evils owed, and the exile looks upon the

ancient threshold of his homeland.

[Col. 0213A] [Note: [Col. 0213B]

682. *Quinquaginta* (“fifty”): the Lyon Bible reads *quadraginta* (“forty”).

[Col. 0213B] 683. *Deprensa*: so the Cambridge manuscript reads. Vossianus II, with *deprehensa*, comes close. The others have *depressa*, but incorrectly. Claudian, *Against Eutropius* II, 430:

> Now caught in shallow waters.

A ship is elegantly said to be *deprensa* when overwhelmed by a storm or in some other way. See Gronovius on Seneca, *Suasoriae*, p. 11; this confusion is frequent. See Burmann on Lucan IV, 172. Dussenius excellently restored *deprenso* in place of *defenso* in the Theban Pindar, verse 978, in *Critical Remarks*, p. 42. His numerous emendations in Pindar are so pleasing that Higtius himself would certainly have approved them, had a longer life allowed him to purify Pindar by his labors.

[Col. 0213C] 683. *Tuta* (“safe”): Vossianus II reads *tota* (“whole”), as above at 334.

[Col. 0213C] 684. *Agit* (“conducts”): Vossianus II reads *ait* (“says”).

[Col. 0213C] 687. *Coepta* (“begun”): Vossianus I reads *capta* (“captured”). The same manuscript reads *funditur amnis* (“the river is poured out”). In antiquity the former, *amnis* (“river”), could be joined with *latissima*, for it was then feminine; later usage, however, required otherwise, and here *arva* (“fields” or “land”) is more correctly opposed to *freto* (“sea”). See the note on Book I, 35.

[Col. 0213C] 688. *Locabat* (“was placing”): Vossianus II reads *vacabat* (“was empty”); the Lyon Bible has *locata* (“placed”). By *locabat* he indicates that Demetrius gave craftsmen employment so that they might make these shrines. He reproduced Luke, Acts XIX, §24: *παρείχετο τοῖς τεχνίταις ἐργασίαν* (“he provided work for the craftsmen”). Later, *lucrum* (“profit”) is correctly translated by Ellysius as *quaestus* (“gain”), *Fortuitous Sacred Matters*, p. 107.

[Col. 0213C] 689. *Argentea* (“silver”): I punctuated the passage in accordance with Fabricius and the Lyon Bible. The other editions read “the shrines in places, silver,” so that the word refers to votive offerings. The other arrangement agrees better with Luke, Acts XIX, §24: *ποιῶν ναοὺς ἀργυροῦς* (“making silver shrines”). Beza understood these temples as silver coins. This was long ago rejected by those who correctly saw that they were little silver buildings containing images of Diana, which the *ναοποιοί* (“shrine-makers”) sold. See Graevius on Florus IV, 2, 91; Cuperus, *Harpocrates*, p. 131; Tomasinus, *On Votive Offerings*, chapter 3; Gutberleth, *On the Salii*, chapter 16. Richard Ellysius suspects that these objects were worn on the arms or around the neck, *Fortuitous Sacred Matters*, p. 105.

[Col. 0213D] 691. *Cedere* (“to yield”): the Lyon Bible reads *credere* (“to believe”).

[Col. 0213D] 692. *Vanas* (“empty”): so the manuscripts, the Aldine edition, and Tornesianus I. The remaining editions read *varias* (“various”), a reading that could be defended because he had stirred up various people, craftsmen and workmen. See Acts XIX, §25. I nevertheless prefer the former. Drakenborch on Livy XXII, 7, 4, and Oudendorp on Suetonius, *Caesar* 79, discuss the interchange of these words.

[Col. 0213D] 693. *Non pudet* (“are you not ashamed?”): elegantly placed at the beginning of the verse. Silius Italicus I, 342:

> Are you not ashamed of what you have begun?

The reading appears thus in the Lyon edition of 1514, where *anne* is printed. Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, 598:

> Are you not ashamed to be held again by siege and rampart?

Here see Cerda. The passage refers to Luke, Acts XIX, §27, *καθαιρεῖσθαι τὴν μεγαλειότητα* (“that her magnificence should be brought down”). This verb is used of things that are cast down and fall. See Rhoerius, *Daventer Miscellanies* II, 3.

[Col. 0214B] 698. *Numine divum* (“by the divine power of the gods”): so the Cambridge manuscript; all the others have *nomine* (“by the name”). One could explain it as “honor” or “dignity.” See the note on Pacatus, *Panegyric* 45, 2; I nevertheless prefer the other reading. Drakenborch on Silius XVI, 655, and Burmann on the *Catalecta* I, p. 103, show that these words are often interchanged. I defended the passage of Pacatus against Cortius in the additions to Sedulius, p. 272. My father truly rendered *numina* as *nomina* in Victor, *Origins of the Roman People* 6, §5, and in the anonymous *Epithalamium of Maximianus* II, §3.

I restored *Divum* (“of the gods”) from the manuscripts and the Aldine and Tornesian editions; the others have *Divae* (“of the goddess”), and the Antwerp edition, worse, *Dianae* (“of Diana”). Paul’s words apply to all the gods, not to Diana alone; for Demetrius says in Acts XIX, §26: *λέγων ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶ θεοί* (“saying that they are not gods”).

[Col. 0214C] 701. *Et* (“and”): I assigned this to Arator from the Cambridge manuscript and the Antwerp edition. All the others have *hei* (“alas”), which comes from a gloss. *Et* is elegant in exclamations, especially among poets. See Passerat on Cicero, *For Quintus*, 11. It is likewise placed at the beginning of a sentence in an interrogative expression of astonishment. See Gronovius on Seneca, *Controversiae* II, p. 176. Here an interrogative could also be inserted after *diu* (“for a long time”).

[Col. 0214C] 703. *Cinerem* (“ashes”): so Vossianus I; the others have *cineres* (“ashes,” plural). I rejected the latter because the whole ruin of the temple is meant; the singular is more suitable to indicate universal ruin, from which nothing remains. Ovid, *Heroides* I, 24:

> Troy was turned to ash, while her husband survived.

Burmann restored this reading. Previously *cineres* was read, but the meaning is that the calamity is so great that everything becomes a single ash. See the notes.

[Col. 0214D] 703. *Arcem* (“stronghold”): he seems to have taken it as “support” and “confidence,” as with the altars of liberty in Livy. See Drakenborch on Book VII, 34, 4. Otherwise I conjectured *artem* (“craft”), which also occurred to the distinguished Wassenbergius, because of verse 704:

> For whom the means of their works  
> have been cut off.

I congratulate myself on the agreement of my very dear friend in a conjecture made more plausible by the fact that these two words are frequently interchanged. See above I, 41, and those passages cited by Drakenborch on Livy IV, 56, 3. The meaning would be that they feared that, once Diana was despised, the craft and means of sustaining life would perish. Thus Luke in Acts XIX, §27: *οὐ μόνον δὲ τοῦτο κινδυνεύει ἡμῖν τὸ μέρος* (“not only is this trade of ours in danger”), where *μέρος* means the means of livelihood. See Ellysius, *Fortuitous Sacred Matters*, p. 113.

[Col. 0214D] 704. *Interclusa* (“cut off”): the Cambridge manuscript reads *interclausa* (“shut off”). See I, 17. Vossianus III begins with this verse; it is nevertheless inferior to the others.]

The ark is also extended fifty cubits,

which, caught in the shallows yet safe upon the sea, brings salvation

under the number of piety; preserved, it grows

[685] through the aid of its space-saving capacity, because Christ everywhere

built the Church, made spacious by forgiveness,

which, begun amid the seas, spreads broadly over the fields.

220 Unhappy Demetrius of Ephesus, by his craft, provided employment by making silver shrines

in sacrilegious places, accustomed

[690] to redeem his vows to his Diana at a greater price.

Seeing all the monuments of ancient madness yielding,

he groaned, and stirred up various passions with these words:

“Are you not ashamed, companions, that our Diana has fallen,

whom the honor of the world revered? What hope of salvation remains

[695] 221 for mortals, if the gods cannot remain without end through the ages?

What images can now give incense to the shrines,

what ones to the hearths? Paul, a foreigner,

terrifies them, and whatever we do on behalf of the divine powers

he calls mute metals, whose religion is departing from the world,

[700] and whose household gods, driven away, have sought flight.

Already I see our temples, built long ago, about to fall

in sudden ruins, and the noble temple itself given over

to ashes and destruction! What stronghold do we seize,

what support do we hold? For those whose means of work

[705] 222 have been cut off, it would be a crime to have made Diana.”

[Col. 0215A] [Note: [Col. 0215B]

707. *Desperat* (“despairs”): Tornesianus I reads *desperet* (“may despair”).

[Col. 0215B] 709. *Movisse* (“to have moved”): Vossianus III reads *novisse* (“to have learned”).

[Col. 0215B] 710. *Celebrant* (“celebrate”): so the three Vossian manuscripts, the Antwerp edition, and the Lyon Bible. The others read *celebrent* (“may they celebrate”). The indicative is more suitable here. The Antwerp edition also reads *qua vota* (“whose vows”).

[Col. 0215B] 710. *Reposcant* (“let them demand back”): Vossianus I reads *reposcunt* (“they demand back”).

[Col. 0215C] 711. *Magnamque* (“the great”): Alberti, *Philological Observations*, p. 258, gives three explanations of this title: either greater power was attributed to her than to the others, or because of the temple’s outstanding renown, or because she was among the great divinities. Ellysius does not approve the last explanation, *Fortuitous Sacred Matters*, p. 114, preferring to derive the name from the virtues and benefits bestowed upon human beings. One might refer here to the benefits granted in illnesses, for Diana was often invoked at such times. See Broukhusius on Tibullus I, 5, 16. Hence we find *DIANAE SERVATRICI* (“to Diana the Preserver”) in Gudius, *Inscriptions* XXX, no. 5, and *DIANAE SOSPITAE* (“to Diana the Savior”) in Reinesius, *Inscriptions*, class 1, no. 80. I therefore think that the Ephesians called her *Magna* (“Great”) not as a fixed name, but because of the aid she so often supplied in illnesses and similar circumstances.

[Col. 0215C] 712. *Vocant* (“they call”): this is correctly found in the manuscripts, in Fabricius, and in the Antwerp and Lyon editions. The others read *vocat* (“he calls”), which is either defective or contradicted by what follows. Silius IV, 20:

> Nor do the portions of the walls, with which age has struggled,  
> delay in offering aid.

A learned man wrote this in the margin of the old edition preserved in the Leiden library, a gift of Perizonius. The edition prints *nec vero muris* (“nor, indeed, the walls”). Concerning similar collective expressions, see the notes on the same author X, 307; Ruhnken on Rutilius Lupus I, p. 47, and I, p. 74. In Martial XIV, 1, from the Thuane manuscript, I would read:

> Let each guest give his own rewards to his own [host].

The preceding *fremit* (“roars”) does not conflict with this in Arator; writers commonly vary in this way. Sallust, *Catiline* 23: “Most of the nobility was seething with envy, and they thought that the consulship was being polluted.” Duker also used this passage in his note on Florus IV, 10, 3. In Florus I, 9, 6, the correct reading is: “The Roman people . . . would rush upon them . . . and reduced them.” See also Heusinger on Mallius Theodorus, *On Meters*, p. 14; and Avienus, *The Maritime Coast* 552:

> The people were moving among pathless places,  
> and extending as far as the inner sea.

Schrader, a man of the highest distinction, admirably rescued this passage in the following section in *Observations* I, 7.

[Col. 0216B] 714. *Causas* (“causes”): Vossianus I and the Antwerp edition read *alio meritum decuit causasque* (“elsewhere merit and causes were fitting”). The remaining editions have *decuit meritum causasque* (“merit and causes were fitting”). The reading I printed is found in Vossianus II and III and in the Aldine and Tornesian editions.

[Col. 0216B] 715. *Lascivos* (“wanton”): from the Cambridge manuscript and Vossianus I and III. Vossianus II, Pulmann’s manuscript, the Antwerp, Aldine, and Tornesian editions read *lascivo* (“wanton” in the singular). The others have *faedo* (“shameful”).

[Col. 0216C] 719. *Praestare* (“to provide”): so the manuscripts, the Aldine and Tornesian editions, the Antwerp edition, and Pulmann’s manuscripts. The other editions have *prodesse* (“to benefit”), but this comes from a gloss. *Praestare alicui* (“to provide for someone”) was used without the other case by later writers. Symmachus II, letter 20: *ad praestandum deesse tempus* (“time is lacking for providing”). See also Gronovius, *Observations* IV, 8, p. 119. When Wasseus therefore denies that it can be used absolutely in Sallust, *Jugurtha* 16, I would have him understood as speaking only of the purer writers. Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp edition read *cur tu* (“why do you”), which could be preferred because of the following *cur esse* (“why to be”), producing a repetition that strengthens the argument.

[Col. 0216C] 723. *Quam* (“which”): the Antwerp edition reads *qua* (“by which”).

[Col. 0216C] 726. *Solo* (“from the ground”): Vossianus II, written by a second hand, reads *solido* (“solid”), and the distinguished Wassenbergius restored this by conjecture. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 69:

> A temple of solid marble.

Ovid, *Amores* III, 8, 53:

> We dig solid gold from the earth in place of crops.

The following words, however, seem to favor the common reading through their opposition.

[Col. 0216D] 728. *Animantur* (“are animated”): so the manuscripts. The printed editions have *ut . . . animentur* (“so that they may be animated”). The Antwerp edition reads *armantur* (“are armed”). To animate is, as it were, to impart life. See Barth on Claudian, *Praise of Stilicho* IV, 19; Markland on Statius, *Silvae* II, 3, 53.

[Col. 0216D] 729. *Ingeniique* (“and of genius”): the Lyon Bible reads *ingeniis* (“by skills”); the other reading is defended by the remarks of Barth on Statius, *Thebaid* I, 440.

[Col. 0216D] 729. *Vivere* (“to live”): the Aldine and Tornesian editions read *munere* (“by a gift”). Images made with exceptional artistry are elegantly said both to breathe and to live. See Elsner on the *Epistle to the Romans* I, §23; Burmann on the *Catalecta* II, p. 225.

[Col. 0216D] 733. *Ista* (“these things”): Vossianus III reads *ipsa* (“the very things”). Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp edition have *tunc inclyte* (“then, illustrious one”); if the other manuscripts supported this, it would not be unattractive. Nevertheless, it seems that *id* (“it”) should be supplied after *licet* (“although”), since those who did not know that it is often omitted made the alteration. See Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, beginning; Oudendorp, *New Miscellaneous Observations* VII, p. 141; Ruhnken on Aquila Romanus, p. 190; Johannes Cannegieter on Ulpian, title V, §10.

[Col. 0216D] 734. *Haec* (“these things”): Vossianus I reads *hoc* (“this”). The Aldine and Tornesian editions read *dicas* (“you say”).

[Col. 0216D] 735. *Atque* (“and”): Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp edition read *et* (“and”). Vossianus I has *ferre decori* (“to bear as an ornament”); Vossianus II, *parte decori* (“in part as an ornament”); Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp edition, *deserta decori* (“abandoned as an ornament”).]

“Go on! The time has come! If the final labor despairs,

it has everything; the only way for the defeated to conquer is to fear

nothing. A sure lot of triumph remains: to move our hands on behalf

of the gods above. Rise up with weapons,

[710] and let arms demand back her whom vows celebrate as a goddess!”

At these words the people, stirred, roared, and with a common cry

called upon great Diana. With swift movement they go in riot

to the shameful theater.

It was not fitting to treat Diana’s causes and worth in any other place;

[715] the disgraceful arena receives the ugly work of the assembly.

Yet their mad impulse flowed forth like smoke that slips through empty

air before the eyes and, scattered, retains no trace.

O pitiable crowd! For whom are you laboring to provide support?

Why do you think her perpetual? With you as witness, she is being

[720] torn from her shrines in flight; by what right do you fear?

Why do you mourn her death and try to join to heaven

her whom you deny can remain upon earth? Now the order of the image

must be investigated, and its hidden meaning seen in the open.

[725] Demetrius is said to have foolishly set up halls for the Goddess

entirely of silver, although nature had brought forth more materials

from her capacious womb, metals from which he could fashion these things.

And bronzes are animated when their faces are cast, while the hands of genius promise that stones will live.

[730] If we turn the pages of the books that speak holy things,

we shall find the path, since Scripture compares gold with pure understanding

and silver with shining speech.

Although the Psalm may sing of these things, illustrious Moses,

you recall them more profoundly when you say such things to the people:

[735] “Bring gold and silver for the adornment of the temples.”

[Col. 0216B] 225 What lies within is intended for the mind: beneath the heart there lies

not the hard substance of metal that lies hidden beneath the heart; rather, it more openly sets in motion what Christ loves. The mind offers gold when faith is precious, and likewise ministers silver when the good drums of the heart sound forth in speech,
[740] so that the two together may worship the Lord: understanding from the heart, sound from speech. Thus the doctrines of the Law require

that gold and silver be prepared for these holy temples.

Because we are temples, if all crimes depart,

[745] the foreknowing words warn us of what the Apostle himself reveals:

the salvation of the believer will be in the heart,

and confession in the voice.

For the sacrilegious man there was one thing: Demetrius built temples

of silver, whose eloquence moved these minds,

so that, without a judging understanding, the rule might approve

[750] 226 that empty divinities should be worshiped, and that this work did not

come from the virtue of the heart, to which alone this part is assigned—

a part that, lacking reason, sows bare speech from the mouth.

You too, Troy, who bear standards and titles in our poem, lay aside your own claims and add triumphs,

[755] which shine more brightly for you from a true deed

than those which your wars echo in grandiloquent tragedy.

When the tongue of God, laden with seeds of salvation,

scattered them, it extended their time into the late night,

making the day brighter for the minds. Gleaming lamps shone,

[760] so that the faithful might be illuminated by the fire of the Word.

Eutychus alone, an exile from vigilant watch,

entrusted his limbs to the window, submerged in heavy sleep.

O rest badly obtained! O hearts always devoted to sleep,

227 bare of goodness! Into how many ruins does he lie open

[765] whom night alone holds and never rouses, sick, to better things!

Whoever permits God to sleep does not know how to keep watch in danger.

Why, grown man, do you seek the empty chaos of the window? Why do you rest

in this place from which you are about to fall? It is an enemy

[770] to salvation to pursue a lofty hanging place and wish to pluck

furtive dreams from a sloping couch. You could have reclined

in a better bed, in the Word of God, and, with Paul as your teacher,

desired access to the One whose threshold is directly accessible—

[Col. 0219A] [Note: [Col. 0219C]

774. *Levatae* (“raised”): Vossianus I, the Antwerp and Lyon editions, and Fabricius read *lavatae* (“washed”), since these words are confused as in I, 770; I would prefer the former. Above, I, 162:

> So that, exulting, he may raise these crowds from the fountain.

Below, 1142:

> Salvation is raised from one fountain.

[Col. 0219D] 776. *Rapidas* (“raging”): Vossianus I reads *rapidas*; see the note on verse 242.

[Col. 0219D] 780. *Dentis* (“of the tooth”): Vossianus III reads *dentes* (“teeth”).

[Col. 0219D] 783. *Acerbo* (“bitter”): Vossianus II reads *acervo* (“heap”). See I, 708.

[Col. 0219D] 784. *Erit* (“will be”): the Cambridge manuscript, Fabricius, and the Lyon Bible read *erat* (“was”). By *per adhaerens* (“clinging to”) he rendered *συμπεριλαβών* (“having embraced”); the standard translator rendered this verb *complexus* (“having embraced”) in Acts XX, §10. The word, neglected by most lexicons, was established from Lucian and the Greek translators of the Old Testament by Maius, *Sacred Observations*, part IV, p. 186; and from Plutarch by Rhoerius, *Daventer Miscellanies* II, 2.

[Col. 0219D] 785. *Vocem* (“voice”): the entire verse is missing from Vossianus III. Barthius compared this passage with Statius, *Thebaid* I, 213:

> Weight belongs to words, and fate follows the voice.

[Col. 0219D] 787. *Famulis* (“servants”): Vossianus II, the Aldine and Tornesian editions, read *famulos* (“servants,” accusative). They referred it to *facit* (“does”): “how much your power does for servants!” Yet the sixth case could also be retained with this meaning. See Oudendorp on Caesar, *Gallic War* I, 6, 3. The Aldine edition, Pulmann’s manuscript, and the Antwerp edition read *dedit* (“gave”) in place of *facit*.

[Col. 0220C] 792. *Teque* (“and you”): Vossianus II reads *tuque*. Some editions have the inferior reading *noluisse mori* (“that you did not wish to die”). See the note on Book I, 175.

[Col. 0220C] 793. *Jam* (“now”): Vossianus II, by a second hand, reads *tum* (“then”), while the first hand has *quam* (“which”). The latter reading is also found in Vossianus III and Tornesianus I; but these readings disturb the sense too much, which is clearer with the text I printed.

[Col. 0220C] 804. *Primae* (“first”): in Vossianus II and III interlinear glosses explain this as *camerae primae* (“the first chamber”). All the others have *primo* (“first”).

[Col. 0220C] 805. *Secundae* (“of the second”): from Vossianus III. The others have *secundum* (“according to the second”).

[Col. 0220C] 806. *Addicta* (“assigned”): Vossianus I reads *afflicta* (“afflicted”).

[Col. 0220C] 807. *Fontis* (“of the fountain”): so the manuscripts and the Aldine and Tornesian editions. The others have *lotis* (“washed”).

[Col. 0220D] 813. *Noe* (“Noah”): I punctuated the passage so that *jungitur* (“is joined”) would have *Noe* as its complement, producing the easier sense. Otherwise the better editions have:

> He is joined, seeking the heights; Noah stands nearby below.

[Col. 0220D] 814. *Dedita* (“assigned”): the Lyon Bible reads *debita* (“owed”).

[Col. 0220D] 821. *Epistola* (“the Epistle”): Ephesians V, §14. Concerning the verb *clamare* (“to cry out”), see Book I, 103.

[Col. 0220D] 823. *Teque* (“and you”): the Aldine edition reads *tuque* (“and you”).

[Col. 0220D] 824. *Quia* (“because”): Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp edition read *qui* (“who”).

[Col. 0220D] 827. *Solymam*: Vossianus III reads *Hierosolymam* (“Jerusalem”). The manuscripts agree here in the feminine gender. Otherwise *Solymos* could have been written; Cellarius introduced this form from Christian poets into *Ancient Geography* III, 13, p. 329. In the following passage, *quo* (“to which”) could be supplied. Some have judged that *Hierosolymam* was also used by profane writers. See Cellarius there and Duker on Florus III, 5, 30. They nevertheless seem to have preferred *Hierosolyma* only in the plural, and Oudendorp thinks the passages where the other form occurs should be emended, in his note on Suetonius, *Augustus* 93. Certainly Vossius had also written *Hierosolyma* in his copy of Florus.

I think that extremely difficult passage of Florus should be arranged as follows: “The Jews attempted to defend Jerusalem; nevertheless, she too entered it and saw that great secret of the impious people, open beneath what seemed to be a golden dome.” By *arcanum* (“secret”) understand the inner sanctuary, or holy of holies. It is said to be open, not magnificent with statues and ornaments like the temples of the Gentiles; concerning this meaning, see Burmann on Lucan IX, 6. It was open, as it were, beneath a golden dome. Temples had golden domes, as Markland shows on Statius, *Silvae* V, 1, 233. Here, however, there was not literally a dome, but it nevertheless appeared in some respect to correspond to one; hence the addition of *veluti* (“as if”). He could call it golden because everything there, skillfully made from cedar wood, had been overlaid with gold. See Lundius, *Ceremonies of the Jews* II, 6. Let the reader not be displeased by this excursus on a difficult passage.]

whose name is “Door,” through which sheep, raised from the fountain,

[775] proceed to life. Seek it, all of you, if you are concerned to avoid

the rabid jaws and bloody bites of the wolf, from whose mouth a fugitive is torn away by the shepherd—the shepherd who calls the scattered lambs

back with his voice and does not allow the flock, redeemed from its own

death,

[780] to be seized again by the enemy through ambush and the bitter wound

of the tooth. The halls resounded with mournful tumult; the crowd,

moved by pity, rushed together amid frequent lamentation to see the place,

sad because of a bitter death, which would bring about joy; and Paul,

clinging to him in an embrace,

[785] said, “He lives.” Life followed the word,

and death, repelled, fled. How much your power, Christ,

works and accomplishes in your servants! You, restored to the stars,

equal to the Father in everlasting majesty,

[790] rule the heavenly realms. But because the flesh born for you

from the body of the Virgin stripped the kingdom of Avernus,

and you recalled living limbs from their own tomb,

proving that you had wished to die, by the part in which you rise again,

and by the part in which you were born, you now loose the iron chains.

Light returns by turns to others through your agency,

[795] and is granted as an example through you, who once subjected

the infernal regions and compelled Tartarus to yield to chosen servants.

Meanwhile the happy corpse rises from death,

[Col. 0219C] and, safe by a better path, is carried through three stories

to Paul, before whose gaze the innocent boy

[800] began to stand, already worthy of the honor of life,

when he turned back the path of death. The glory of this deed

teaches us to disclose its causes according to the ancient figure.

Noah’s ark is described as supported by three chambers,

bearing the lessons of the Church. The first section contained

[805] human beings in their order; cattle occupied the second level;

the third lot was assigned to wild beasts. The square ark carried

all of them through the waters, just as now in the fountain of baptism

230 there is one salvation for all, but one place cannot belong to all

according to their morals. For Noah is said to have built nests in it—

[810] Noah, whom the Hebrew calls both “righteous” and “rest”; he is Christ,

who justly distributes fixed rewards to his own. Whoever loves virtue and seeks the heights

is joined to Noah; the one nearest below

is lesser, inferior in limited understanding; the lot assigned to the savage

[815] holds the lowest, Tartarean recess. Thus Eutychus, falling from the

first section, lost in the mouth of hell, clung there, empty of human

reason, and began to occupy the place of beasts; after Paul, with his heart, ...

Wisdom drew near and poured forth its word,

[820] Raising with its voice the soul slain under the carnal law;

He returns to the Lord from death, as the Epistle proclaims:

“You who sleep, rise quickly now!” and again it presses him:

“Lift yourself, awake, from death!” The boy has now earned the right

To stand upon the three heights, because through the threefold doctrine

[825] [Col. 0220C] He has learned what the substance of eternal life is.

And now, after Paul had traversed the regions of the world,

He was about to come to Jerusalem, where the Spirit—
