827. *Quo* (“where”): Voss. 3 has *quod* (“because”).—The same manuscript immediately afterward has *movet* (“moves”). See above, I, 924.

[Col. 0221C] 830. *Charo*: the Aldine edition has *claro* (“clear,” “bright”).

[Col. 0221C] 840. *Auctor*: “the Lord, master of all things.” See Wopkens on Sedulius V, 191.

[Col. 0221C] 841. *Discussor*: of one who examines any matter. Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, 26: “If these deaths which they inflict have been entrusted to you, examine them yourself”; and V, 13: “It is wholly improper to examine the rationale of faith.”—Voss. 3 has *reposcit* (“demands back”).

[Col. 0221D] 842. *Crementa*: see Book I, 199.

[Col. 0221D] 842. *Semina*: all manuscripts, and the Aldine and Tornesian editions, have *germina* (“sprouts”). The manuscripts of Pulmann, Antwerp, and others come close, having *gemina* (“twin”). I have retained *semina* (“seeds”), because these are soon said to have been entrusted to the furrows and scattered, verse 843. In any case, these things scarcely suit *germina*, which Sulpicius Severus carefully distinguishes from *semina* in *Dialogues* I, chapter 3, § 4: “There are no sprouts there, no sown crops.” Thus that passage should be read from both Utrecht manuscripts.

[Col. 0221D] 844. *Dolebit*: *dolere* (“to grieve”) is rightly construed with the accusative. See Burman on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII, 720. But the word seems suspicious to me here. Unless one says that the poet’s meaning is that the bad earth, or bad men, will thereafter painfully endure having produced no fruits, I truly do not know how bad earth could grieve that the fruits are meager. I once conjectured *docebit* (“will teach,” “will show”), *ostendet* (“will display”), and *proferet* (“will produce”) meager fruits, as in Florus III, 5, 16, and as in the expression “to teach a manner” (*διδάσκειν τρόπον*) in Antoninus Liberalis, *Metamorphoses* 41. Yet even this does not satisfy me, although the alteration is easy, as when Horace’s father provided a remedy for the reading in Pliny’s *Panegyric* 82, 6.

[Col. 0222C] 845. *Crucis*: Voss. 2 and 3 have *cunctis* (“all”). See above, I, 967.

[Col. 0222C] 846. *Quo*: the manuscripts of Pulmann and Antwerp have *qui* (“who”). Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 610:

“Wherever the lands call me.”

[Col. 0222C] 847. *Hic*: Antwerp has *haec* (“this,” feminine).

[Col. 0222C] 850. *Servate*: Voss. 1 has *servantque* (“and they preserve”).—The Lyon Bible has *magistri* (“masters”), incorrectly. He calls them “servants” in verse 852.

[Col. 0222C] 851. *Christi*: Fabricius, Antwerp, and the Lyon Bible have *Christus* (“Christ”), so that it is joined with what follows. Arator rightly understood Θεοῦ (*Theou*, “of God”) in Luke, *Acts of the Apostles* XX, § 28. In its place Vetstenius wrongly substituted Κυρίου (*Kyriou*, “of the Lord”), already corrected by Ernesti in *Philological Essays*, p. 335.

[Col. 0222C] 853. *Quae*: the Aldine and Tornesian editions have *quod* (“which,” neuter).

[Col. 0222C] 854. *Oro*: Antwerp has *ore* (“by the mouth”).—Voss. 1 and the Lyon Bible have *lustrare* (“to inspect”).

[Col. 0222C] 856. *Convenient*: the Aldine edition and the Lyon Bible have *conveniunt* (“they come together”). The Vulgate supports εἰσελεύσονται (*eiseleusontai*, “they will enter”) in Luke, *Acts* XX, § 29.

[Col. 0222D] 858. *Acrior*: see Weitz on Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 699.

[Col. 0222D] 860. *Ne*: the Aldine and Tornesian editions have *nec* (“nor”). The following letter has adhered to it.

[Col. 0222D] 861. *Quies*: Barthius compared this with the statements of others in *Adversaria* XXXIII, 11.

[Col. 0222D] 865. *Vestra*: Voss. 1 has *nostra* (“our”).

[Col. 0222D] 867. *Quodque*: the manuscripts of Pulmann and Antwerp have *quaeque* (“and whatever”).

[Col. 0222D] 868. *Luxu*: the Aldine edition has *fluxu* (“flow”).

[Col. 0222D] 874. *Defossis*: this passage supports Sedulius IV, 22:

“And not badly does buried gold serve thieves.”

[Col. 0222D] 874. *Claudat*: this is found in the Aldine, Antwerp, and Lyon manuscripts and editions; the others have *sic laudat* (“thus he praises”). I have often noted above that letters belonging to the following word adhere to the preceding one.]

[231] He often urges them to proceed, wishing on the familiar shore

To proclaim an everlasting farewell, and from every side he summons the holy ones,

[830] Giving back these words from his dear heart:

“O beloved band, which serves under Christ’s arms!

O people born for the supreme God! You remember the proofs

Of my love and devotion; readily I endured the pagan hosts

And the Judaic furies without end,

[835] So that I might give the precepts of life, and so that no faith

Proclaimed among the people might remain hidden. From your blood

I shall always be pure, nor shall I, owing a miserly mouth,

Pay the penalty for hoarded talents and, hungry amid the seed of the word,

Blame the sterile field; rather, it is fitting that you

[840] Render pious interest when the Lord comes,

[Col. 0221B] Who will examine merit and demand back from his servants

[232] The increase of their entrusted measure. My passion was to bring seeds

To the understanding; these, entrusted everywhere to the furrows,

I scattered, but the bad earth will grieve over its meager fruits.

[845] I am going to see the city revered among the nations for its cross,

Where the commands summon me; there I shall be given

The struggle of varied combat, for everything will be endured

By one who wishes to complete the course. Most gentle is the lot

Of the punishments which vows bring, and the power of the kingdom:

[850] To suffer perpetually for the king. Preserve, servants,

Christ’s Church, which he made for us in his own world

At the price of blood; let servants labor to retain

[Col. 0222A] What the Lord gave from death. You will no longer see

[233] My face and features; I beg you, watch more vigilantly

[855] Over the entrusted flocks, because wolves with ravenous teeth

Will come together at the fold. The guardianship fails

When a raider has carried off the spoils; through the fraud

Of an idle shepherd what the plunderer seizes perishes. But an enemy

Within will be more savage, and discord bears a heavier evil,

[860] For it creates a wound beneath peace. Do not yield to hardships:

Rest is harmful to virtue, and no secure honor crowns anyone

In the stadium. His glory will be the cause of labor for the brave,

And rare is the soldier who reaches prizes

When peace alone has been his lot; victory receives its seed

[865] [Col. 0222B] From the enemy—there it arises. The Lord is able

To make your plantations fruitful; through his own gifts he causes

His gifts to come, and whatever helps, he himself supplies.

I did not bring proud riches, deceived by luxury,

Nor did I accept gifts in exchange,

[870] Seeking you rather than what belongs to you; you know how these hands

Provided food for themselves and their companions. Accustom yourselves to bring forth treasures

Into the ways of the light, and to place the wealth of your works

In the seat of heaven. It will profit nothing to have sought gold

In buried places, if the miser locks away what he had hidden from the poor,

[875] [Col. 0223A] [Note: [Col. 0223B]

875. *Pauperе*: Voss. 3 has *pectore* (“breast”); a sufficiently obscure expression, by which he seems to have indicated what has not been distributed among the poor.

[Col. 0223B] 876. *Revolvitur*: the manuscripts of Pulmann and Antwerp have *resolvitur* (“is dissolved”).

[Col. 0223B] 877. *Laxate*: Voss. 1 has *laxare* (“to loosen”), just as the same manuscript has *lustrare* above, verse 855.

[Col. 0223B] 879. *Quo*: the Aldine edition has *in quo* (“in which”).

[Col. 0223B] 880. *Tum*: the three Vossian manuscripts have *cum* (“when”).

[Col. 0223B] 881. *Strictique*: Cambridge, by a second hand, and Voss. 2 have *strictisque* (“and having been bound”). Rufinus uses *stringi sollicitudine* (“to be constrained by anxiety”) in *Ecclesiastical History* XI, 34. He reproduced here the words of Luke, *Acts* XX, § 37, and I do not sufficiently understand why Barthius, in his note on Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 19, asserts that the Lucan passage was omitted by Arator in his poem. Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* V, 765:

“Along the curving shores there rises a mighty weeping;

They embrace one another and linger through night and day.”

[Col. 0223C] 883. *Obtutu*: Statius, *Silvae* III, 2, 78:

“Look! the ship, driven over wandering waves,

Flees, gradually growing smaller, and overcomes the distant eyes

That watch it.”

Barthius did not forget Arator there. Silius III, 155:

“Their faces remain fixed and attentive, watching the shores,

Until the sea, as the swift keel carries it onward,

Consumes the clear course from their sight,

And the land withdraws.”

Pliny’s *Panegyric* 82, 4 speaks of following the floating sails with one’s eyes; Cerda collected further parallels on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 592. Moreover, Barthius, in his note on Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 25, rightly judged that this passage of Arator, through its acuity, surpasses the Latinity even of the age in which he lived.

[Col. 0223C] 884. *Dumque*: Cambridge has *cumque* (“and when”).

[Col. 0223C] 888. *Saluti*: this is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *salutis*. It is preferable to follow the manuscripts. See the note on Book I, 344.

[Col. 0223D] 889. *Dedi*: from the manuscripts and the Antwerp, Lyon, and Fabrician editions. The others have *dedit* (“he gave”).

[Col. 0223D] 891. *Historicum*: Alcimus distinguishes two methods of interpreting sacred Scripture, the historical and the allegorical, saying:

“Whether he weaves histories or perhaps figures.”

Likewise:

“What the divine volumes of the sacred law

Display, whether by meaning or by word.”

Arator adds a third when he says:

“The historical, sounding morally, and the typical volume.”

Scholastic theologians, as they are called, count four kinds altogether, although they do not understand their names. The first is historical, which they explain as literal: it interprets the words in the simplest manner and contains a true exposition of the meaning, such as the history of the battle between David and Goliath. The second is moral, or ἠθικόν (*ēthikon*, “ethical”), which they ineptly call τροπολογικόν (*tropologikon*, “tropological”); in it the meaning is referred to some instruction concerning life and conduct. Thus, just as David did not endure the pride and slander of the impious enemy, so all pious people must resist those who blaspheme God and defend and vindicate the name of religion with all their strength.

The third follows when the history is applied to some matter because of a similarity not wholly unrelated to the event. Rhetoricians call this ἀλληγορικόν (*allēgorikon*, “allegorical”); theologians sometimes call it τυπικόν (*typikon*, “typical”), sometimes μυστικόν (*mystikon*, “mystical”). Arator calls it “hidden beneath concealments”: for example, if David’s deed is transferred to Christ, who is the perpetual champion of his Church; and Goliath’s challenge and slander to the devil, who does not cease to harass the holy people and heap upon them every accusation and curse.

Later writers added the last kind, divine and sublime, which they called by a most unsuitable name ἀναγωγικόν (*anagogikon*, “anagogical”). In it men who are truly ἀναγωγοί (*anagogoi*, “those who lead upward”) mingle earth with heaven. Thus David is the whole heavenly Church in eternal life, which wins daily triumphs over the devil and burns with everlasting hatred of him.

Philip gives this example in his *Rhetoric*: Jerusalem historically signifies the city of that name; tropologically, a well-ordered commonwealth; allegorically, the Church; anagogically, eternal life. He immediately adds: “In this way they interpreted all verses by a monstrous transformation, even when some statement occasionally resisted that transformation.” Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 73. The Pulmann manuscript and the Antwerp edition have *mortale* (“mortal”).

[Col. 0224C] 892. *Metretas*: μετρητής (*metrētēs*), a kind of measure and vessel. Juvencus II:

“Small vessels whose mouths would open to three metretes.”

Sedulius translates the term by the general word “basin,” Book III:

“Therefore Christ filled six basins with this nectar.”

The names of measures are taken for vessels by synecdoche, as *cotyle* in Homer, *amphora* in Horace, and *metreta* in Juvenal. A *metreta* and an amphora are the same. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 87.—Compare Nansius on Nonnus’s *Paraphrase*, p. 19, and Paulus Leopardus XV, *Emendations* 23.

[Col. 0224D] 894. *Sacrificii*: the second syllable is lengthened. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 118.—There are several similar instances in Arator. These poets often considered what Marius Victor writes in the preface to *Genesis*, p. 311, Fabricius’s edition:

“And if the order should offend in something against the law of meter,

The unsuitable expression and wavering sense have offended;

Let no danger to faith arise from this.”

[Col. 0224D] 895. *Offerre*: Cambridge has *proferre* (“to bring forth”), incorrectly. Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I, 7, 2: “whom he did not hesitate to offer”; chapter 19, § 4: “he had offered sacrifices.”

[Col. 0224D] 897. *Ista*: this is found in the three Vossian manuscripts and in the Aldine and Tornesian editions. The others have *iste* (“that one”).—Voss. 3 omits *est* (“is”).]

Open your hearts, I beg, to the heavenly admonitions,

[880] Thus, after he had spoken, he gave kisses; then, praying together,

[885] [235] A path is added across the sea for their eyes; the ship,

898. *Desideret*: the Aldine and Antwerp editions have *desiderat* (“he desires”).

[Col. 0225C] 900. *Sanctus*: Cambridge has *quod Spiritus unus et almus* (“that the Spirit is one and nourishing”).

[Col. 0225C] 901. *Sint*: so Voss. 3, the Aldine edition, the Pulmann manuscript, and Antwerp. Voss. 3 has *sunt* (“are”); Voss. 1 and most editions have *sit* (“is”).—The Aldine and Antwerp editions have *triplicat* (“triples”).

[Col. 0225C] 902. *Hoc*: the Aldine and Tornesian editions have *haec* (“these things”).

[Col. 0225C] 902. *Angariat*: ἀγγαρεύειν (*angareuein*), a foreign word. The *Angari*, ἄγγαροι (*angarroi*), are royal messengers in the Persian language; their relay service is called ἀγγαρεῖον (*angareion*) in Herodotus and Xenophon, both in Book VIII. These messengers were permitted to use anyone’s ship, vehicle, animal, or servant to complete their journey. Hence *angariare* among legal writers means to compel by a kind of violence and, as it were, by royal command—something that is still done in certain western kingdoms. Matthew and Mark retain that word; Erasmus altered it in his translation, while Arator retained it. Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 8.—See at length Vossius, *On the Nature of Speech*, p. 216; Alberti, *Philological Observations*, p. 160; Merillius, *Philological Notes on the Passion of Christ*, p. 639; Wissembach, *Philological Notes on Matthew* XXVII, § 32; and the further remarks made on *Digest* 2, 4, *On Summoning to Court*, chapter 7.

[Col. 0225D] 905. *Hoc*: Cambridge and the Lyon Bible have *haec* (“these things”).

[Col. 0225D] 906. *Malis*: Voss. 1 and Torn. 1 have *mavis* (“you prefer”); Voss. 3 has *mallis* (“you would prefer”).

[Col. 0225D] 908. *Almus*: this is found in the manuscripts and in the Aldine and Tornesian editions. The others have *Spiritus almus et hi numero* (“the nourishing Spirit, and these in number”).

[Col. 0225D] 909. *Vacans*: the Pulmann manuscript and Antwerp have *vocans* (“calling”).

[Col. 0225D] 911. *Quod*: this is found in the three Vossian manuscripts and in Torn. 1; the others have *quae* (“which”).

[Col. 0225D] 915. *Rabidoque*: Cambridge has *rapidoque* (“and swift”). See above, verse 242. The same confusion occurs in verses 957 and 1084.

[Col. 0225D] 916. *Conclamant*: Antwerp and the Lyon Bible have *conclamat* (“he cries out”), incorrectly. See the note on verse 712.

[Col. 0225D] 917. *Ire*: this is found in Cambridge, Voss. 1 and 2, and Torn. 1; Voss. 3 and the remaining editions have *esse* (“to be”). I have often noted above that these words are confused, I, 503.

[Col. 0226C] 921. *Teneri*: Voss. 1 and 2, the Pulmann manuscript, and Antwerp have *tenere* (“to hold”).

[Col. 0226C] 924. *Oris*: this is found in the manuscripts and in the Aldine, Antwerp, and Tornesian editions; the others have *oras has* (“these shores”).

[Col. 0226C] 925. *Omni*: the Aldine edition has *omnem* (“the whole”). He alludes here to Paul’s words in *Acts* XXII, § 3, where it is said: ἀνατεθραμμένος ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ, παρὰ τοὺς πόδας Γαμαλιὴλ πεπαιδευμένος κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν τοῦ πατρῴου νόμου—“brought up in this city, instructed at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strictness of the ancestral law.” Perizonius thus distinguishes the passage in his *Addenda to Aelian*, p. 997, as does Alberti, *Philological Observations*, p. 263, although Alberti does not mention Perizonius. Perizonius also proves from this that disciples sat at their teacher’s feet. Nevertheless, I agree with Ernesti, *Philological Essays*, p. 174, that παρὰ τοὺς πόδας Γαμαλιήλ (“at the feet of Gamaliel”) means nothing other than “with Gamaliel,” just as in *Acts* V, § 2, ἔθηκε παρὰ τοὺς πόδας τῶν ἀποστόλων (“he laid it at the feet of the apostles”) means simply “he handed it over to the apostles.” Such expressions must certainly be examined carefully by an interpreter, lest he depart from the writer’s intention. Thus I am surprised that the words of Luke’s Gospel, chapter 24, § 36, ἔστη ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν (“he stood in the midst of them”) should be understood of Christ as standing physically in the middle of his companions. They indicate only that he stood in their sight, just as *de medio*, *in medium*, and εἰς μέσον (*eis meson*, “into the midst”) are used of those who are seen, or conversely, as Burman teaches in his note on Petronius, *Satyricon* 38.

[Col. 0226D] 930. *Auctori*: in the Aldine and Tornesian editions, this verse and the next four have been confused.—I defended the dative after *certare* (“to contend”) above, I, 264.

[Col. 0226D] 932. *Acta*: I adopted this from the three Vossian manuscripts. All the others have *aucta* (“increased”), as these words are also confused in Silius XVII, 490. But if the light had been increased by this fire, how could it then have remained hidden? *Acta dies* means “the light of day driven away,” so that he was blinded by the flashing fire. Thus *lux acta est* could also be explained in Ovid, *Heroides* XIX, 33, since he himself adds *pulso die* (“the day having been driven away”), unless one prefers, with Burman, to take it as meaning “completed.”

[Col. 0226D] 933. *Orbibus*: see Book I, 731.

[Col. 0226D] 939. *Jure*: Voss. 3 has *jura* (“laws” or “rights”).

[Col. 0226D] 940. *Pronus*: the Pulmann manuscript and Antwerp have *pravus* (“wicked”).]

[237] “Pure, so that if anyone here should lack the nourishment of the word,

You may provide the food he seeks and teach the willing,

That the Father and the Son and the holy Spirit are one God,

And that the simple substance is threefold in number.

Nor do the pious commands sing this only once. ‘If anyone,’ he says,

[900] ‘Compels you, asking you to go one mile ahead,

Go with him another two thousand steps as well.’ Do these commands

Not seem to say this? If someone, wandering and ignorant of the way,

Asks you what God is, would you prefer to declare the Father,

Then willingly add that the Son and the nourishing Spirit also exist—

Three in number, and nevertheless one.

Hence Judea, empty and called a sterile tree,

[910] Did not produce fruit after three years of expectation,

[238] Because, scorning to handle the volumes in a threefold sense,

It does not know how to offer gifts to Christ in the numbers of faith.

Paul had begun to approach Solomon’s noble temple

And to fulfill the solemn rites of the ancient law.

[915] Judea seizes him, and in a savage tumult

They cry out that he is guilty of death. But the tribune

Rushes to arms and orders the bound man to proceed

In double chains,

[Col. 0226A] Which press harshly upon his fettered arms;

Yet tortures do not bind his spirit. Paul’s Epistle,

[920] Full of light, proclaims that ministers may be bound,

But faith cannot be bound, nor can the word be handed over

To punishment. And he stood upon the very steps,

Addressing the Hebrew people in their language:

“O brothers, men and fathers! You know that I came

[925] Unskilled into these regions; devoted to all the doctrine

[239] And love of the law, I was. I now call you as witnesses,

You whose writings I carried, burning to punish at Damascus

The flocks that followed Christ with slaughter

And to prevent this faith throughout the boundaries of the world.

But mortal things cannot contend with their own author:

[930] [Col. 0226B] Light came down from the stars to close my eyes,

And the day, driven away by flashing fire, vanished;

Dark shadows fell upon my eyes, and during their time

My arriving radiance grew together with the night.

One usually discerns causes after events have occurred:

[935] We saw the shadows well, soon to make use of a new sun.

But a cry from the mouth of God also clung to my ears:

‘Saul!’—Christ shakes me with terror, repeating the name—

‘Do not dare to wage war against me any longer as my standard-bearer.’

By what right can I deny it?

[940] I fall when he strikes me, by whose gift I lie prostrate,

[Col. 0227A] [Note: [Col. 0227B]

941. *Perque*: I followed Fabricius; the same reading is found in Antwerp and the Lyon Bible. Cortius had copied nothing from Fabricius’s manuscripts, so I suspect that their agreement is genuine. All the others have *per quae* (“through which”).

[Col. 0227B] 942. *Felicia*: this is found in the manuscripts and in the Aldine and Tornesian editions. The remaining editions have *felicis* (“of the happy one”).

[Col. 0227C] 943. *Movimus*: I had long suspected that this should be read by conjecture. Now Voss. 1 and 3 and the Antwerp edition agree with me, and I did not hesitate to restore it in place of *novimus* (“we have known”), which appears in the others.

[Col. 0227C] 946. *Lucete*: Voss. 2 has *lucente* (“shining”); the Aldine and Tornesian editions have *lucere* (“to shine”).

[Col. 0227C] 947. *Est*: Antwerp has *et* (“and”).

[Col. 0227C] 949. *Labores*: Cambridge and Voss. 3 have *laboris* (“of labor”). I would not reject that reading. Although rocky earth has preceded, *vacui* (“empty”) could nevertheless follow, referring to the Jews, as writers often consider the meaning more than the order of words. This has been discussed above. In that case *laboris* would belong with *vacui*, in the same construction as Hegesippus I, 40, p. 137, *vacuum ejus cujus arguebatur facinoris* (“empty of the crime of which he was accused”), and chapter 43, *otiosum nec conjurationis vacuum tentamentorum* (“idle and empty of attempts at conspiracy”). On the Greek usage, compare Vechner, *Hellenolexicon* I, part II, chapter 18, p. 274, where he also cites from Eumenius *vacuus commodorum* (“empty of advantages”). Heusinger notes that he found these words in none of Eumenius’s *Panegyrics*. They do, however, occur in *Panegyric* on Constantius 15, § 3. Here I retained *labores* (“labors”), to be understood as “idle labors,” in Arator’s customary manner of joining dissimilar things. For this meaning of *vacuus*, see Barthius on Claudian, p. 785—unless, with Wopkens on Sedulius IV, 117, you prefer to explain it as “empty and fruitless.”

[Col. 0227D] 950. *Qui*: Voss. 3 has *quae* (“which”); Antwerp has *Jesus*.

[Col. 0227D] 951. *Hac*: Cambridge has *ac* (“and”).

[Col. 0227D] 952. *Saule*: Cambridge, the Aldine, and Torn. 1 have *Paule* (“Paul”). But he himself calls himself Saul in this speech, and moreover recounts events that occurred before he went to the Gentiles, to which the name Paul does not apply. See the note on Book I, 742.

[Col. 0227D] 952. *Est*: Voss. 1 has *non hoc tibi credita* (“this has not been entrusted to you”).

[Col. 0227D] 956. *Ventosa*: “inconstant and proud.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 963:

“The crafty man would fashion him as a human being under a windy guise.”

This passage supports Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* VI, p. 195, *et, quod esse non credas, ventosa imitatione formare* (“and, what you would not believe, to fashion by a windy imitation”), where a learned man had added to my edition that *vitiosa* (“vicious”) should be read. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 8: “and so you may see her puffed up.” Sedulius II, 225:

“Those whom no windy

Glory of speech...”

He undoubtedly took this from his Virgil, who mentions a “windy tongue” in *Aeneid* XI, 390; see Cerda there. Add Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XI, 9.

[Col. 0228C] 956. *Fragore*: the Aldine and Tornesian editions have *furore* (“fury”). The former is stronger for expressing anger and the disorderly noise of a tumultuous crowd, just as Prudentius attributes a “resounding” voice to a grunting sow in *Peristephanon* X, 994. Schulting rightly asserted that the din of schoolmen is found in Seneca, *Controversiae* II, p. 161; this makes *fragor* (“roar,” “din”) especially pleasing here, since thunder is being discussed. See Heinsius on Claudian, *Consulate of Probinus*, 211. Such a multitude resembles a sky seeming to thunder; hence angry people are said to thunder. In Ovid, *Heroides* XI, 74, I would prefer:

“The mad palace calls out; it thunders.”

See Burman, who also shows that the word is used of the anger of combatants in his note on Book II of the *Tristia*, 529. Hence *circumtonat* (“thunders around”) is preferable in Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 474; it is also found in the Leiden manuscript, added by a second hand. Rhoerius restored it admirably in Manilius, *Astronomica* II, 9.

[Col. 0228C] 957. *Rabidum*: Voss. 1 and 2, and the Aldine and Tornesian editions, have *rapidum* (“swift”). From the usage of the Tornesian edition alone, I conjectured that *rabidum* (“raging”) should be restored here, as in my note on Sedulius I, 58. Compare verse 242 above.—Wopkens explains *discrimina per mortem* as “danger through death,” that is, destruction, in his note on Sedulius IV, 137.

[Col. 0228D] 961. *Paschae*: *Pascha, Paschae* follows Latin declension. Juvencus IV:

“The disciples ask where they should take the Passover meal.”

*Pascha, Paschatis* follows Greek declension, as in a hymn by an unknown author:

“Among whom the sacred Passover

Is celebrated throughout the whole world.”

Fabricius, commentary on the *Christian Poets*, p. 98.

[Col. 0228D] 962. *Electo*: the Lyon Bible has *ejecto* (“having been cast out”).

[Col. 0228D] 963. *Cuncto*: Voss. 1 has *cunctis* (“all”).

[Col. 0228D] 965. *Amictum*: the Aldine edition has *amictus* (“clothing”).

[Col. 0228D] 966. *Quia*: Voss. 2 has *qui* (“who”).

[Col. 0228D] 971. *Origo*: Voss. 1 has *imago* (“image”). The preceding *ortu* (“at the origin”) supports the other reading.

[Col. 0228D] 973. *Habitu*: Voss. 2 has *abitu* (“departure”).]

I am lifted by a better path, and I rise through the heights,

And, made sublime, I follow the happy gifts of my downfall.

[240] Enough now, citizens! We have taken up cruel weapons.

That part, blessed because it serves as witness against its enemy,

Teaches us this: why do you still wish to be guilty?

[945] Shine out from my darkness, you to whom faith,

Seen flowing from the waters of the fountain, gave power,

And whose image of death began to live in the waters. Alas,

Never has rocky earth been fertile in its own seeds,

Nor have empty labors prospered upon sterile soil!

[950] At last Jesus, who appeared to me, said:

“Prepare to go far away from this city, Saul, abandon it;

[Col. 0227B] It does not trust you because of our name.

[241] Rather, sing words of salvation to the Gentiles.”

At once the complaining ranks seized upon this voice.

[955] They throw off their garments, and, stirring up the dust farther away,

[Col. 0228A] They rage with windy lightness and varied din;

The crowd roars, frantic over Paul’s danger.

“O guilty Judea! When you wished to destroy

The author of life, you spoke thus: you had the choice

[960] To abandon the one you wanted, though he was crying out to you;

But from your bloodstained mouth you wickedly seek

A mournful crime, ill-advised, and you honor the joys of Passover

[242] With the chosen robber; you cultivate twin madness,

Savage toward the pious, appeased toward the guilty.

You strip yourself of the whole contest and make yourself empty,

Since you heap harsher tortures upon Stephen himself,

[965] Lay aside your clothing, and now are without a garment,

Because the punishment of the first parent is related to you.

You bear in your body the burden of the ancient transgressor,

Opposed to the honor of the fountain, lest you be renewed

By the waters. At the origin of his sin Adam learned

[970] That he was naked, and from this the signs of his guilt

Became clear to the wretched man. The origin of death

Repeatedly overtakes you; anger, full of evils,

Interweaves twice over the garment which guilt creates. Now the tribune

[Col. 0229A] [Note: [Col. 0229C]

974. *Ardere*: Florus III, 5, 22, has “he sees Asia burning with new disturbances.” Compare the note on the letter to Vigilantius, verse 1.

[Col. 0229C] 977. *Socios*: Voss. 2 has *socia sibi lumino* (“with the light joined to itself”); Voss. 3 has *socia sibi lumina* (“lights joined to themselves”).

[Col. 0229C] 978. *Illam*: from the three Vossian manuscripts and the Aldine and Tornesian editions; the others have *ullam* (“any”). Brouckh on Tibullus I, 4, 31, and Drakenborch on Silius IV, 435, show that these words are confused: *u* and *i* are often exchanged. In Isidore VIII, 2, write, from the Groningen manuscript, *nomen fidei unde est ductum*, “the name from which faith is derived,” not *dictum* (“spoken”).

[Col. 0229C] 982. *Feruntur*: Voss. 1 has *leguntur* (“are read”).

[Col. 0229C] 983. *Profecto*: perhaps the punctuation should more correctly be:

“Now not to have heard. Certainly

This will be a matter of reasoning.”

[Col. 0229C] 985. *Quoniam*: Antwerp and the Lyon Bible have *quomodo* (“how”).

[Col. 0229C] 987. *Stimulatus*: Voss. 1 has *stipulamur* (“we make a bargain”).

[Col. 0229C] 988. *Diverberat*: the Aldine and Tornesian editions have *deverberat* (“strikes away”).—The Aldine has *ambiguus fragor*, omitting *-que* (“and”).

[Col. 0229D] 990. *Certa*: Voss. 1 has “the other part of the sound is certainly...” The other reading is not displeasing.

[Col. 0229D] 991. *Una*: the Aldine has *illa* (“that”).

[Col. 0229D] 994. *Monet*: Antwerp has *movet* (“moves”), as these words are confused above, I, 924.—The Lyon Bible has *fungamur ab ista* (“let us make use of this”).

[Col. 0229D] 995. *Dolos*: I edited this from Voss. 1 alone. All have *dolor* (“grief”), which yields no meaning unless one reads, with some, *vetatque nefas* (“and forbids the crime”).

[Col. 0229D] 995. *Veritique*: from Cambridge, the three Vossian manuscripts, and the Aldine and Tornesian editions. The others have *vetatque* (“and forbids”).

[Col. 0229D] 998. *Satiare*: Voss. 1 has *saturare* (“to fill”). These words are likewise confused in Sedulius, Prologue 6, and in the *Acrostic of Belisarius* 16.

[Col. 0229D] 1000. *Quae*: from the three Vossian manuscripts and the Aldine, Antwerp, and Tornesian editions; the others have *quam* (“which”).

[Col. 0230C] 1003. *Parta*: from Voss. 1 and 2 and the Aldine and Tornesian editions; the others have *facta* (“committed”). Fabricius printed *quam facta caede: salubres* (“which, when the slaughter was committed, [were] salutary”). Several editions likewise adopted *salubres*. Antwerp has *sedaret* (“would calm”) in its place, but the reading I gave is supported by the manuscripts. For similar prayers, compare Rhoerius, *Ferentian Dissertations* II, 3.

[Col. 0230C] 1004. *Cordis*: Torn. 1 has *mortis* (“of death”).

[Col. 0230C] 1007. *Esuris*: see the note on the letter to Vigilantius, verse 4.

[Col. 0230C] 1009. *Tot*: Antwerp has *et tot* (“and as many”).

[Col. 0230C] 1010. *Ut*: Voss. 3 has *et* (“and”).—Several editions have *tot et* (“so many and”).

[Col. 0230C] 1012. *Rupesque*: Voss. 1 and 3 have *rupisque* (“and rocks”).

[Col. 0230C] 1013. *Quo*: “in which”; it cannot be referred to the rocks.

[Col. 0230C] 1014. *Supernis*: Voss. 3 has *superbis* (“proud”). This could be understood in a good sense as “magnificent” and “venerable”; for this meaning see Schulting on Seneca, *Controversiae*, p. 92, and compare the Greek ὑπέρβιος (*hyperbios*, “exceeding,” “lofty”). See Heinsius on Silius X, 573. Nevertheless, there is no necessity for changing the reading. Sedulius likewise mentions “heavenly nectar” in I, 133.

[Col. 0230D] 1017. *Faciat*: Voss. 3 has *facias* (“you may make”).

[Col. 0230D] 1018. *Pauli*: Voss. 1 has *Paulum* (“Paul”).

[Col. 0230D] 1019. *Parent*: Voss. 2 and 3 and the Antwerp edition have *parant* (“they prepare”).

[Col. 0230D] 1020. *Cautus*: the Pulmann manuscript and Antwerp have *cautis* (“with the cautious”).

[Col. 0230D] 1022. *Tuto*: Voss. 3 has *toto* (“whole”). See the note on verse 334.

[Col. 0230D] 1023. *Delator*: Antwerp has *delatus* (“having been carried”).

[Col. 0230D] 1024. *Rarum*: Voss. 3 has *rarus* (“rare”); the Lyon Bible has *rerum* (“of things”).—Barthius, on Statius, *Thebaid* VI, 550, explains *ad praemia* by “because of the prizes.” Perhaps it is more correct to understand it as “it is rare that you thereby attain prizes,” namely glory.

[Col. 0230D] 1026. *Quam*: this is found in the manuscripts and in the Aldine and Tornesian editions; the others have *qua sceleri servire* (“by which to serve crime”). That appears to derive from a gloss. He feared preserving his constancy for crime, so that he would not reveal that matter.]

Seeing him burning with these words, the savage tribune

[975] Added harsh chains and sent him to be tortured in the hostile camp.

We shall sing so that the noteworthy complaint may be surpassed by the events.

Paul, recounting what happened, says that his companions there

Had seen the light a little earlier, but had not heard that voice

[243] At the time when he fell blind;

[980] Yet it is said that, when he fell, his companions heard the voice.

Thus the narrator’s account varies; but both statements are necessary

And plainly harmonize. It is said that they heard then,

That they received a sound, but that now they certainly did not hear.

This is the simple path of reasoning: the voice is rightly said

[985] Not to have been understood, since it was confused in speech,

Nor is that believed to be conveyed by speech

Which the hearer does not store in his heart. Merely stimulated

By a doubtful sound from the ear, the ambiguous din strikes

Only the surrounding air.

Thus they are said both to have heard and not to have heard.

[990] One part was sound, the other certainly was voice,

And one event carries and brings back a twofold appearance.

The ranks of punishment, burning in the body of Paul,

And the grievous anger of the punishments, to unfold in verse—

The cause urges me, but my tongue is afraid. Let us flee

[995] From this part the deceits, and, having dreaded so sad a crime,

Let us restrain our utterance, lest the reader

Fill his face with tears and the page grow wet with abundant drops.

Yet these things could not satisfy their bloodthirsty spirits;

[Col. 0229C] [244] Their love of crime burns, and they desire to stain

[1000] [Col. 0230A] Their sacrilegious hands in Paul’s blood. What harsh vows of evil!

Forty men of the mad race imposed upon themselves

The vow to take neither drink nor food at all

Before the slaughter had been accomplished and food or drink permitted to them.

Hence the banquet seems all the greater. O pale image of the heart!

[1005] Judea, cups of blood are better for you

Than streams of water. Unwilling to touch any table,

You hunger for the crime and seek to make your hunger full

With the corpse of the righteous. Moses did not establish

Such fasts by his example, though they were completed through as many days

[1010] As you recount, as many weapons as you wield,

And you look upon as many years in which secret paths lay open,

Where food flowed from the rich cloud of dew,

And the dry rock in turn poured forth waters;

In this they deserved, by divine goodness, to enjoy

[1015] And nourish their souls with heavenly gifts. But you come

To rage from the very number itself, and you join

The polluted covenants of the people, so that one death

May make more people guilty.”

Lysias learned of these things, when Paul’s kinsman disclosed

Where and in what place they were preparing their attack.

[1020] Therefore he quickly ordered his commands to be secretly concealed,

And, cautious at night, forestalled the obscure undertaking.

Having selected companies, he ordered them to escort Paul

With safe and honorable protection.

Honest informer, the glory of merit from you would not be alien,

[1025] And it would be rare to win prizes by betrayal;

Nor does the steadfastness which you fear to preserve for crime injure you.

In guilt there is virtue—

[Col. 0231A] [Note: [Col. 0231B]

1028. *Tibi*: the Aldine, Antwerp, and Lyon editions, and Fabricius, have *ibi* (“there”). The final letter of the preceding word absorbed the initial letter of the following one.

[Col. 0231B] 1029. *Causa*: the Aldine edition has *culpa* (“guilt”). This is not displeasing, since it is an oxymoron of the sort Arator often uses.

[Col. 0231B] 1031. *Aure*: the Lyon Bible has *ore* (“mouth”). This is unnecessary; the same confusion occurs above, I, 124.

[Col. 0231C] 1038. *Auras*: I restored this from the Cambridge manuscript alone. All the others have *aures* (“ears”). It expresses the Lucanian ἐπισύστασιν (*episystasin*, “assault” or “concentration”), in *Acts of the Apostles* XXIV, § 12; *aura* (“breeze,” “air”) suits that better. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 6: “But you do not know how to act rightly except for popular breezes and empty rumors”; Sitzmann found *aures* (“ears”) even in the manuscripts there. Add Drakenborch on Livy VI, 11, 7.

[Col. 0231C] 1040. *Spectantia*: Voss. 2 and 3 have *exspectantia* (“awaiting”).

[Col. 0231C] 1041. *Rogo*: Voss. 1 has *jam* (“now”); Voss. 3 has *ergo* (“therefore”).

[Col. 0231C] 1042. *Eloquor*: from Cambridge, Voss. 1 and 2, Antwerp, Fabricius, and the Lyon Bible; the others have *eloquar* (“I shall speak”).

[Col. 0231C] 1045. *Patrum*: Withof compared this with Gunther in his *Specimen of Gunther*, p. 92.

[Col. 0231C] 1048. *Nomine*: that is, so that he was no longer happy, nor worthy of that name, but rather guilty of neglected justice because Paul had been thrown into chains.

[Col. 0231C] 1049. *Quem*: Voss. 2 and 3 have *quae* (“which”).

[Col. 0231C] 1049. *Obice*: anything that is placed in the way can be called an *obex* (“barrier”), a word which our Christian writers often use. Chrysologus, Sermon 65: “But what does weeping accomplish at the tomb, when the voice of the weeping person cannot penetrate such hard and piled-up barriers?” Juvencus, Book IV:

“As a bird, accustomed to shelter its chicks beneath its body,

Warms them, surrounding them with the barrier of its wings.”

Hericus, in the address of his little book:

“Nor would the insolent ranks dare to despise

The barrier of so great a name.”

Some people are ridiculous in this word, saying that it should everywhere be written with a single *i*. But whenever poets use it with a long syllable, it must be written with a double consonant; when they wish it shortened, they customarily remove the second *i* from it, just as in *adicit*, *obicit*, and other words of that kind. Hence I think that *objex*, when it is lengthened, should likewise be written with the nominative ending. Barthius, *Adversaria* XIX, 14.

*Obices*, or rather *objices*, are bolts placed against doors. Germanicus:

“As a little iron key is set against the lock with its tooth.”

Silius Italicus, Book IV:

“From the forest they strive to fetch

Strong timbers and faithful bolts for the gates.”

Valerius Flaccus alludes to this in Book I of the *Argonautica*:

“The closed cohort roars

With the bolt of Butes.”

The little word is sometimes found used in another grammatical gender. Alcimus Avitus, Book IV:

“Once the barrier is broken,

The rushing water rages forth with loosened reins.”

Sidonius, *Panegyric on Anthemius*:

> The waxen bolt gives way when its pivots have been loosened.

Learned men think that *obice* should generally be written, so that when *objice* is found it is merely poetic license. I, however, think *objex* should be written, with the consonant *j* omitted by poetic license when the word is shortened, just as poets otherwise commonly do in *adicit*, *abicit*, *obicit*, and similar words. If anyone wishes to maintain the contrary, let him produce other examples in support of his view, in which the same consonant is inserted. We have supplied examples in which it is removed. The same author, *Adversaria* XXXV, 10.

Following Fabricius and the Lyon Bible, I printed *objice*. Barthius and Weitzius rightly defend this reading in their notes on Valerius Flaccus I, 702; and it is now printed likewise in Virgil, *Georgics* II, 480, and *Aeneid* X, 377. I think the first syllable of *obice* short; hence the stronger form *objice* should be restored in Marius Victor, *Genesis*, p. 317, Fabricius’s edition. Add the notes on Lucan VIII, 796. Others, however, think that although the consonant has been removed, the syllable should be lengthened; Drakenborch discusses this properly in his note on Silius XIII, 298.

**[1051. *Linguimus*.]** Antwerp, the Lyon Bible, and Fabricius have *liquimus*, as verse 1109 soon indicates that he is omitting further material; he omits what Luke relates in Acts chapters 25 and 26.

**[1053. *Fuerint*.]** The Cambridge manuscript has *fuerant*.

**[1054. *Judaici*.]** Vossian manuscripts 1 and 2 and Tornesius 1 have *Judaei*.

**[1056. *Appello*.]** Here *appellare* and *provocare* are joined. Glareanus nevertheless distinguishes them in his note on Livy III, 56, at the end: *appellare* is used between equals, as from one consul to another; *provocare*, from an inferior to a superior, as from a governor to the emperor or from a consul to the people. I do not think this is always certain, however. Later writers also say *appellare ad populum*, “to appeal to the people.” See Cellarius’s note on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* X, 818.

**[1059. *Onus*.]** Vossian manuscript 2, written by a second hand, has *opus*. Thus the poet denies that Paul’s reason for appealing lay in fear of dangers, whereas Augustine suspected that it did. Learned men commonly offer several explanations of this matter, but I think the sole reason for this appeal was that Paul perceived justice being denied him, especially because of the Jews’ obstinacy. This is clearest from Paul’s own words in Acts 28:18–19.

A learned man recently treated the matter at greater length in the *Academy of Learned Men*, published in Dutch at Amsterdam, part III, volume II, p. 224; he further maintains that Paul did this in order to free himself from the Jews’ harassment. But this contradicts what the same distinguished author says on p. 227 against Augustine, concerning Paul’s fearless spirit, by which he would expose himself to every danger and even to death.

He adds another reason: Paul appealed all the more readily because he was convinced that no law had yet been enacted at Rome against Christians. It is indeed certain that the name of the Christians, which arose at Antioch, seems not to have become known at Rome before the last years of Claudius or the first years of Nero. See Gruner, *On the Hatred of the Human Race*, p. 137; Burmann on Suetonius, *Claudius* 25.

Even if this was known at the time of the appeal, there was still no reason for a law to be enacted against Christians. Whatever concerned the principles of the Christian religion was not yet sufficiently known to the Romans; and if any Christians at Rome were still privately practicing their rites, this was permitted at Rome. The same liberty was therefore afterward granted to Paul, once he had been released from his chains. Acts 28:30. The learned author, p. 230, attributes this to the emperor’s favor toward Paul; I rather attribute it to the Romans’ custom, since they were burdensome to no one on account of religion, even when it was ridiculous, as Athenagoras testifies, *Apology for the Christians*, p. 6, Rechenberg’s edition.

But when these rites became more widely known—especially because they assigned divine honor to God alone and not to the emperors, and because the religion itself suggested a purer form of worship—laws were first enacted, and Christians were accused of treason against the majesty of the state. Yet this too could not have been Paul’s reason for appealing. Had he done it for that purpose, he would have prepared a safer residence for himself through the appeal. Paul’s fearless spirit scarcely persuades me of this.

I am also surprised that the learned author asserts that Paul was handed over at Rome to a soldier, not to guard him but to protect him from the Jews, who might perhaps have plotted against his life. The Jews would certainly have refrained from laying plots at Rome against a man who had appealed to the emperor for the protection of his case. By doing so they would have stirred up enormous hatred against themselves on the part of the emperor, especially since the Jews had not long before been expelled from Rome by Claudius and now needed to restrain themselves, lest they expose themselves to still greater danger and hatred by provoking disturbances. Paul therefore remained under military custody. See Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* III, 22, and my father’s detailed treatment in *On Paul’s Citizenship* 5, § 5.

**[1059. *Semper*.]** I have the greatest doubt about the integrity of this passage, and the very sense of the received text stands against it. The poet says that Paul did not appeal because he was fleeing dangers in fear, and he adds the reason: an anxious mind always longs to die for a better life. These statements contradict each other. Would Paul have refused to die for a better and eternal life? What Paul himself says about this in his Epistles displays a different mind.

Arator’s verse 1042 is more suitable:

> For faith knows not dangers,  
> Nor how to fear them.

All manuscripts here retain the received text. Perhaps one should read: “An anxious mind is never [so].”

It will be a crime when the wicked band together for wrongdoing;  
Faith is counted to you as a fault, though true honor then adorns your praises  
When the cause is holy. With armed men surrounding him,

**[1030]** Paul soon approaches Caesarea, where the crowd had rushed,  
Supported by its own advocate, who, having gained the governor’s ear,  
Uttered empty words. Finally Paul spoke in reply:

“Excellent governor, we have all long known you  
To follow the proofs of justice, and that modesty accompanies  
Your counsels—she whom favor persuades us  
To trust, and under such a judge to speak without hesitation.

We have violated neither the pious custom of law and temple,  
Nor stirred the popular air with wandering speech.  
Coming from the cities of Asia, we began to discharge our offerings,  
Always directed toward a pure vow.

**[1040]** Tell me: who will be free if such acts make a man guilty?  
I speak without fear, for faith does not know  
How to fear dangers—a faith which they dare to call  
The sect that is the way of light, and does not disagree  
With the ancient laws of our fathers. It is lawful for everyone now to believe  
That bodies can rise again from the tombs, after Christ,  
Who created all things, has brought his own body forth from there.”

Felix was astonished, having lost his name; Paul,  
Whom the chains of others make guilty, is bound by their barrier,  
And is kept under the year of Governor Festus.

**[1050]** Here we omit too much, lest it delay our joy.

“Come now to Latium, Paul! [We pass over]  
What conflicts were repeatedly debated in the forum,  
And how great a stream of Jewish deceit is reported to have flowed.”  
For Paul spoke thus:

**[1055]** “I appeal to Caesar’s throne.” “To Caesar,” he said,  
“I, a Roman, appeal for aid.” Festus replied:  
“You shall go, as you wish, to see the tribunal of Augustus sooner.”

Paul did not, fleeing dangers at fear’s goad, avoid  
The burden of judgment. An anxious mind is always—

For a better life—to die. But the author of the gift  
Had once told his herald and witness  
That he was to come to Rome. Jesus’ mercy  
In every land gives draughts from its own vessel to those thirsting for faith,  
And commands all to be watered by its many-streamed word;  
The charm of the western name deserved to grow  
From the light of the Word.

The shipmaster had loosed his fleet from the eastern shore,  
Having obtained the south wind’s aid; with its breath  
The joyful course increased, and, with the sails’ wings spread wide,  
The ship cleft the sea. But when have the winds ever kept  
Their treacheries gentle? Soon the sea’s calm was shattered  
By the blasts of Eurus, and the feigned peace of the blue sea  
Glowed amid swelling waves. Everywhere the deep rages  
And, raising its masses in an angry whirlpool,  
Denies a sure track to the storm-swept keel,  
Which, suspended toward the sky and cast down, is joined to the fields.

**[1062. *Venturus*.]** Others have also proposed this as the reason for the appeal. The learned man in the *Academy of Learned Men*, part III, volume II, p. 233, rightly rejected it.

**[1065. *Venustas*.]** Thus the manuscripts and the Aldine and first Tornesian editions; the others have *vetustas*. By “the charm of the western name” I think Rome, or Latium, is meant—what poets likewise call Hesperia—celebrated for the elegance of its language and other qualities. Unless Arator had something of this kind in mind, I do not know what “the charm of the western name” could mean. The Cambridge manuscript has *numinis*. On this confusion, see above, verse 698.

**[1067. *Vector*.]** As in Lucan VIII, 39. Fabricius is therefore wrong in the Lyon Bible to print *Victor*. The same forms are interchanged in Silius XII, 119. Cerda compared this passage with Virgil in his note on *Aeneid* I, 38.

**[1069. *Crebrescente*.]** Vossian manuscripts 2 and 3 have *crebriscente*. I preferred the reading found in certain editions and in Vossian manuscript 1, following analogy and Oudendorp’s judgment on Suetonius, *Caesar* 79. Drakenborch, however, found both *crebescere* and *crebrescere* in the manuscripts, as the same authority reports in his note on Silius X, 1. It is preferable to follow the better manuscripts, especially since the similar form of other words supports this reading.

**[1069. *Alis*.]** Below, verse 1213:

> He offered winged waves upon the gentle waters,

and see what Heinsius brought together in his note on Ovid, *Art of Love* II, 45.

**[1070. *Findebat*.]** Antwerp has *fundebat*, contrary to the sense and to poetic usage. Thus Jason is said to cut through the deep in Valerius Flaccus II, 2. See Burmann on Claudian, *Rape of Proserpina* II, 158; Stephanus on Saxo Grammaticus, *History of Denmark* VI, p. 132.

**[1072. *Rupta*.]** From Lucan I, 239.

**[1072. *Incanduit*.]** Lucan X, 322:

> The foaming river grows white beneath unconquered waves.

So poets commonly speak of a foaming and troubled sea. See Burmann, *Addenda to the Catalecta*, p. 727; Bulaeus on Valerius Flaccus III, 32. Theognis, *Sentences*, verse 10:

> And the deep sea of the grey salt water rejoiced.

Add Quintilian, *Declamations* XII, p. 257. I discussed this in *Miscellanies*, p. 193.

**[1073. *Pax*.]** Florus attributes peace to a river, IV, 2, 28; Duker notes there that poets generally use the word of the stillness of inanimate things, as Burmann does in his note on Valerius Flaccus IV, 20. Lucan IV, 437, also speaks of the peace of the sea, but in a different sense, as Burmann shows. Nevertheless, I would not doubt that Arator borrowed the expression from there, as he has borrowed others.

**[1073. *Ficta*.]** Pulmann’s notes, Antwerp, have *victa*, incorrectly.

**[1075. *Abreptae*.]** The Aldine and first Tornesian editions have *arreptae*. The latter is more correct. Cornelius Nepos, *Fragments*, p. 732: “carried away by the violence of storms from the Indian seas.” This indicates more clearly the force of the storm, by which they were compelled to turn from their direct course; the other reading relates more to the winds, even though they were not rushing violently upon the ship. In this latter sense Ovidius said *arrepta vela*, “the seized sails,” *Heroides* XIII, 15. Copyists could easily err in either direction, as Drakenborch showed in his note on Livy XXII, 48, 4. In Mamertinus, *Birthday Speech for Maximian* 10, § 3, Livineius conjectured *parvos liberos arreptos* for *abreptos*. The excerpts of Vossius and the Guelferbytan manuscript support Livineius, and Schwarz likewise finds the reading acceptable.

Faith, radiating, appears; a laurel crown is made for the just  
From the reward which fear provokes, and enduring virtue  
Grows amid adversity. Having used dangers as witnesses,  
It regards peril as a means to merit. At last Paul, standing,

**[1105]** Encourages the despairing hearts with these pious words:

“O would that you, faithful company, had wished earlier  
To obey our counsels and had not left the shores of Crete,  
Destined to suffer the madness of the raging deep!

You would not have endured the threats of sea and sky,  
Nor the grievous burden of loss that lays waste to everything,  
Nor would desperate salvation have mourned the boundaries of death.

Yet joys that surpass human expectation  
God can easily grant. To him, whose gift is more powerful here  
Than anyone supposes, an angel sent from heaven  
Comes with peaceful lips and announces this:

‘The ruler of Olympus has granted you every person  
Whom this ship carries, so that she may not be wrecked  
And fixed upon the rocks. Believe it: these things will happen,  
And I shall not disappoint you with empty hope.

**[1120]** I have deserved the promises of God, and the island granted to us  
Will be a harbor. There, once we have seized the land,  
We shall be able to enjoy it and look upon  
The ship’s grievous misfortune without any danger.’”

At these words the sea’s anger fell, and the light  
That had been removed returned and shone, seeming,  
With night’s veil opened, to disclose the land  
Which, hospitable to the sailors, offered itself—Melite,  
Near the Sicilian shore, accessible by oars.

**[1087. *Libet*.]** Three Vossian manuscripts and the Antwerp edition have *refert*. I did not dare accept it, since the first syllable seemed to require lengthening for the reason given by Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 19; this is clear from examples collected by Heinsius on Ovid, *Heroides* VI, 137. Compare Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria* 30: “I shall not say everything, but shall touch lightly on each point.”

**[1087. *Conabor*.]** A harsh expression. In Luke, *ἀντοφθαλμεῖν* in Acts 27:15 is translated in the Vulgate by *conari*, that is, “to strive with the utmost effort.” Arator seems similarly to have intended that he would bring the poem to this point with the greatest care, omitting Paul’s sea-voyage, in order to describe how he safely reached the shore or land; *tangere* seems to be recalled from the preceding verse. I nevertheless doubt the integrity of the passage.

**[1088. *Praevia*.]** Antwerp has *pervia*. See the note on verse 773. *Praevia* is correct, since they were directing their course toward the stars.

**[1089. *Emicat*.]** Vossian manuscript 1 has *eminet*, but that seems less suitable, according to the distinction Burmann proposed between *emicare* and *eminere* in his note on Lucan V, 76; he also notes the same confusion there. Since Acts 27:20 says that the sun did not appear, *emicat* is more pleasing here, being appropriate to the rising sun and to light. Arator himself confirms this at verse 1125:

> The restored light shines.

So too Valerius Flaccus I, 655:

> The opened day flashed forth.

Lactantius, *On the Phoenix*, 44:

> And the gentle breath of the first light flashed forth.

Here *axis* is used for the sky. *Sidereus axis* occurs in some manuscripts in Ovid, *Amores* III, 10, 21, as Heinsius notes. Such an axis as is described here is the Greek *ἀὴρ μιχθαλόεις*, “murky air,” on which the distinguished Lennep comments in *Observations on Coluthus* II, 8.

**[1093. *Famis*.]** So that, because of fear, they did not feel hunger.

**[1097. *Venerantur*.]** Vossian manuscript 3 has *vectantur*. But the preceding *tempsisset honorem* favors the former, indicating that those who otherwise would have despised him, now oppressed by the huge storm, honored him whom they perceived to be their harbor, whose aid would enable them to escape danger. Luke says nothing of this; indeed, he says that the soldiers resolved to kill the prisoners. Unless someone wishes to refer this to the centurion, who intervened against the soldiers’ plan.

**[1097. *Victi*.]** I wrote this from Vossian manuscripts 1 and 2; all the others have *vecti*. The latter is weak. The poet indicates that they had now honored Paul because they were utterly oppressed by the storm, so that they could find no means of safety for themselves; otherwise, had the sea been calmer, they would not have cared about him. Poets commonly call those “overcome” who, driven by a violent storm, are no longer masters of themselves. Ovid, *Fasti* III, 593:

> Skill is overcome by the wind, and the steersman no longer uses the reins.

*Heroides* XIX, 183:

> Ships laboriously worked are overcome by the sea.

And *Tristia* I, 4, 11:

> The sailor, confessing his fear in icy pallor,  
> Now follows the conquered vessel and no longer guides it by skill.

**[1098. *Gerit*.]** Cortius conjectured *quaeritque ruina*. This does not seem necessary. The meaning is that the ruin possesses something by which Paul could be made manifest. The expression is not far removed from the figure in which an image is said to “bear” something, as in Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II, 3, § 1, and in *Miscellanies*, chapter 17. I suspect that it may be understood in the same way as Barthius, in his note on Claudian, *Consulship of Manlius* 146, conjectures *quos fortuna gerit*, explaining it as “brings, grants, or carries.”

**[1100. *Assertore*.]** This is a construction like *aurum corruptor* (“gold, a corrupter”), *saxum custos* (“a stone, a guardian”), and similar expressions; see Burmann on *Catalecta* I, p. 79. I previously cited several examples of the same kind at verse 134, including *bos arator*, “the ox, a plowman,” discussed by Brouckhus on Tibullus I, 11, 46, and *oculi amatores*, “loving eyes,” which should be restored from the Apuleian manuscript in *Metamorphoses* II, p. 26, as Oudendorp correctly saw in *Miscellaneous Observations* II, p. 301.

Territories and sky alike he follows; his hand, suited to the ship,  
Lacks the defenses of friendly skill. With icy fear  
They lay down their courage, and beneath the dark air, blinded,

**[1080]** They see shipwreck already at hand; and, with the deep closed around them,  
The image of death lies open. I am summoned to traverse the vast sandbanks  
In historical fashion, and to follow the torn ropes  
And fragments of the rudder; but I do not entrust my fragile tongue  
To the shoals, nor will I long attempt to confront the swift storms,  
Lest a more violent wave overwhelm my small speech as I sing.

I shall touch upon a few things; I will strive to reach the safe sands.

**[1090]** The stars that guide the wave-roaming ship lay hidden,  
Nor did the axis flash beneath the clouds with the sun’s rays.

And although the circuit of day had already properly completed many days,  
There was one night upon the sea, during which they allowed no food:  
Ah, what a punishment of fear—to be ignorant of hunger’s punishment!  
Misfortune often supplies the seeds of causes to the good: so illustrious a company  
Of sailors and soldiers would have honored the man  
In a more favorable sea, whose custody at last  
Was released, and whom, overcome by the savage sea, they honored  
As the harbor they recognized as their own. That ruin bears witness,  
So that it may not remain hidden that he was Paul, and that the saint might be revealed  
With the sea as his protector; the elements, snatched away, labor  
To show the man amid the deepest darkness.

**[1102. *Justis*.]** Vossian manuscript 1 has *justi*.

**[1103. *Agit*.]** Vossian manuscript 3 has *ait*.

**[1104. *Usa*.]** Thus the manuscripts and the Aldine and first Tornesian editions; the others have *quod testibus ipsa*. Immediately afterward Vossian manuscript 1 has *quod meritum*.

**[1106. *Conclamata*.]** Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXII, 3, explains this passage as “to compel by shouting,” “to call upon,” or “to appeal loudly.” Thus *conclamata urbs*, “a city called upon,” occurs in Hegesippus, *Destruction of Jerusalem* V, 26. I think the word rather indicates people deprived of reason and despairing of safety, like the dead, for whom this word was ordinarily used by the Romans according to ritual custom. See Drakenborch on Livy IV, 39, 3, and Gutherius, *On the Law of the Spirits of the Dead* I, 17.

**[1107. *Voluisses*.]** Fabricius, Lyon Bible, has *voluisset*. Bede used this verse in *On Metres*, p. 2355, Putsch’s edition.

**[1108. *Prius*.]** Vossian manuscript 1 has *piis*, as in the confused readings at Sedulius II, 21, and III, 44. But since Paul had warned them earlier about this matter, see Acts 27:10, *prius* is more pleasing. I read *nec dedi* from Vossian manuscripts 1 and 2; the others have *ne*.

**[1109. *Liqueris*.]** From the Cambridge manuscript and Vossian manuscript 1. Vossian manuscript 3 has *linqueris*; the others *linqueres*; the Lyon Bible *linqueret*. This was altered by those who could not tolerate different tenses, although such combinations occur frequently.

**[1110. *Minas*.]** Vossian manuscript 1 has *vias*, incorrectly. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 113:

> And he bore all the threats of sea and sky.

See Cerda’s note there.

**[1113. *Gaudia*.]** Vossian manuscript 3 has *grandia*, and this is not bad.

**[1115. *Quem*.]** I wrote this from the three Vossian manuscripts and Antwerp; all the others have *quam*, which gives no sense. I am surprised that it was retained so consistently even in the better editions.

**[1116. *Haec*.]** Vossian manuscripts 2 and 3 and all editions except the Aldine and first Tornesian have *hoc*.

**[1118. *Nullis*.]** Pulmann’s notes and Antwerp have *nullus*.

**[1119. *Fient*.]** *Fio* is very frequently shortened in disyllables, contrary to the practice of other poets. Prudentius, *The Martyrdom of Saint Stephen*:

> You shall be devoured by fires,  
> Condemned, and soon become fine ash.

Again:

> And now you command that I become yours:  
> I become another Cyprian.

*Against Symmachus* I:

> Deeming true whatever things are done  
> By authority of the senate.

Sichardus, not observing the established usage, corrected this last passage; but we follow Prudentius himself and the manuscript. The passages are: Prudentius, *Peristephanon*: “You shall be devoured by fires, condemned, and soon become fine ash”; again, “And now you command that I become yours: I become another Cyprian”; and *Against Symmachus* I: “Deeming true whatever things are done by authority of the senate.” Tertullian II likewise says:

> Stones come into being and will always be,  
> Unless a great power dissolves them.

Arator uses the same shortening. Cyprian, *Genesis*:

> “Let light come into being, and all things shone in the bright world.”

Fabricius, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 55. Three Vossian manuscripts and the Aldine, Antwerp, and first Tornesian editions have *forent*; but Heinsius also defended *fient* here in his note on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* VI, 83. See him also on the shortened syllable in book I of *Against Symmachus*, verse 223, and in the *Addenda*, p. 153; and Vossius, *Art of Grammar* II, 13.

**[1119. *Frustrabor*.]** The Cambridge manuscript has *gravabor*.

**[1123. *Casum*.]** The Cambridge manuscript has *pactum*.

**[1124. *Ira*.]** An inscription in Gruter, *Inscriptions*, p. CLXI, 2, calls the water “angry.” The expression “the anger of the sea” is rightly defended for Tibullus II, 4, 7 in *Miscellaneous Observations* II, p. 247; Drakenborch on Silius IV, 245, Burmann on Ovid, *Heroides* XVIII, 2, Heinsius on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XI, 729, and Oudendorp in *Miscellaneous Observations* V, p. 75 collect similar expressions. Elmenhorst similarly explains “the mad sea” in Arnobius I, p. 44.

**[1125. *Velamine*.]** Vossian manuscript 2 has *velamina*. He means the clouds that had covered the sun and stars, through which, as though they had been opened, the light returned.

**[1127. *Remis*.]** Bochart, *Canaan* I, p. 503, conjectures *tellus*. Certainly *remis* presents some difficulty. The manuscripts offer no change except that Vossian manuscripts 2 and 3 read *lateris*, from which I suspect that the text should be corrected to *Sicanii lateris remis*, “by the oars toward the Sicilian shore.”

**[1127. *Melite*.]** *Μελίτη*, an island near Sicily, is read twice by Arator with the middle syllable lengthened; I know of no other example of this elsewhere. Today it is Malta, the dwelling place of exiled Rhodians. Italian Ceretani now call the Maltese land “the favor of Saint Paul” and superstitiously proclaim that it cures poisonous bites. Fabricius, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 86.

There is also *Miletae* in the Cambridge manuscript, and *Milete* in Vossian manuscript 3 and Antwerp. Cellarius, *Ancient Geography* II, 12, also noted that the second syllable is lengthened here contrary to custom. Salmasius discusses various islands bearing this name in *Plinian Exercises*, p. 272.

In this matter scholars have exercised their ingenuity in two directions, one understanding the island near Sicily, the other the Adriatic island, or Meleda. Ignatius Georgius chiefly thought the latter was intended; Joan Antonius Ciantarus opposed him, although the Leipzig scholars refuted Ciantarus’s arguments in *New Acts*, supplement, volume VII, section 2, p. 55. Scaliger, Grotius, and Bochart have already brought together further evidence on the same question.

More recently the distinguished Bachiene, in *Sacred Geography* III, II, argued for Melite near Sicily, using arguments drawn from the wind, the Syrtis, the mention of Syracuse, and other considerations. I know what the eminent scholar had already replied to these arguments in his dissertation *On Paul’s Shipwreck*, § 14 and following. Nevertheless, they have not yet persuaded me to abandon the belief that Melite near Sicily is intended. The entire account of the voyage and its places points in that direction.

The greatest difficulty, however, lies in the mention of the Adriatic Sea in Acts 27:27, to which this Melite cannot be assigned. Some have extended the name farther, so that the Ionian Sea too was included under it, as the scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius IV, 304, testifies. The Leipzig scholars have learnedly discussed the boundaries of both, placing the southern limit of the Adriatic between the promontory of Iapygia and the Ceraunian Mountains.

Let this be so; a ship driven by a storm in the Ionian Sea could nevertheless be said to be tossed *ἐν τῷ Ἀδρίᾳ*, “in the Adriatic,” if those words are not understood as meaning that this happened in the Adriatic Sea itself, but in its direction. They should, I think, be translated into Latin as *ad Adriam*, “toward the Adriatic.” Thus Aelian, *Various History* XIII, 16, places Epidamnus *ἐν τῷ Ἰονίῳ κόλπῳ*, “in the Ionian Gulf.” Perizonius rightly explains this in book II, 25 as “toward the Ionian Gulf.” A still closer parallel is *ναυφραγίον ποιήσαντες ἐν τῇ Ἰταλίᾳ*, found in book 9 of the *Digest*, *On the Rhodian Law of Jettison*: “suffering shipwreck toward Italy,” as Bynkershoek interprets it in dissertation, chapter 3.

The more strongly I understand the Melite mentioned above here, the more support I find in Luke’s statement that the ship spent the winter on this island in Acts 28:11. It is called Alexandrian and was undoubtedly a grain ship, just as Paul’s ship had been, as I showed in *Miscellanies*, chapter 17, at the end.

But I do not see how a ship sailing from Alexandria to Rome, and not driven off course by a storm—for it is not apparent that it was driven by the storm to this island—could have gone out into that part of the Adriatic Sea while making for Rome. Such a detour would have been excessive, especially for sailors intending to spend the winter there, when they could more conveniently have put in at the islands nearest Sicily and lying on the route toward Rome, as this Melite did.

Apparent radiating faith; a laurel crown is made for the just  
From the reward which fear provokes, and enduring virtue  
Grows amid adversity. Having used dangers as witnesses,  
It regards peril as a means to merit. At last Paul, standing,

**[1105]** Encourages the despairing hearts with these pious words:

“O would that you, faithful company, had wished earlier  
To obey our counsels and had not left the shores of Crete,  
Destined to suffer the madness of the raging deep!

You would not have endured the threats of sea and sky,  
Nor the grievous burden of loss that lays waste to everything,  
Nor would desperate salvation have mourned the boundaries of death.

Yet joys that surpass human expectation  
God can easily grant. To him, whose gift is more powerful here  
Than anyone supposes, an angel sent from heaven  
Comes with peaceful lips and announces this:

‘The ruler of Olympus has granted you every person  
Whom this ship carries, so that she may not be wrecked  
And fixed upon the rocks. Believe it: these things will happen,  
And I shall not disappoint you with empty hope.

**[1120]** I have deserved the promises of God, and the island granted to us  
Will be a harbor. There, once we have seized the land,  
We shall be able to enjoy it and look upon  
The ship’s grievous misfortune without any danger.’”

At these words the sea’s anger fell, and the light  
That had been removed returned and shone, seeming,  
With night’s veil opened, to disclose the land  
Which, hospitable to the sailors, offered itself—Melite,  
Near the Sicilian shore, accessible by oars.

**[1130. *Et*.]** The Aldine edition has *ex*.

**[1131. *Gustate*.]** The Lyon Bible has *gustare*. He mentions the day, although the event occurred at night. Luke writes *σήμερον*, “today,” in Acts 27:33; Burmann translates it “during this night” in his note on Quintilian, *Declamations* X, chapter 14. The same expression occurs in Matthew 27:19, unless time there is reckoned in the Roman civic manner and dawn is understood, so that Pilate’s wife believed what she had seen in a dream, since dreams were thought true toward dawn. See Brouckhus on Tibullus II, 4, 2.

**[1133. *Fulserunt*.]** The Cambridge manuscript has *fluxerunt*.

**[1139. *Mosi*.]** The Cambridge manuscript has *Moyse*. Antwerp, Fabricius, and the Lyon Bible have *more*.

**[1144. *Jesum*.]** Vossian manuscript 3 has *Jesu*; Antwerp has *Jesum*.

**[1145. *Pharao*.]** The middle syllable is also lengthened below, at verse 1237:

> This people whom Pharaoh had once bound.

Victor of Africa, *On the Maccabees*, p. 450 in Fabricius’s corpus:

> Fleeing Egyptian death and King Pharaoh.

**[1148. *Salsae*.]** Vossian manuscripts 2 and 3 have *salsi*; Antwerp has *falsi*. Compare Vossius, *On Analogy* I, 32.

**[1149. *Linquitur*.]** The first Tornesian edition has *liquitur*.

**[1151. *Pastor*.]** Thus three Vossian manuscripts and the Aldine, Antwerp, and Lyon editions; the others have *pasto*.

**[1151. *Edenti*.]** The Cambridge manuscript has *utenti*; the Aldine has *edendi*.

**[1153. *Primae*.]** Vossian manuscript 1 has *primo*.

**[1154. *Quia*.]** The Aldine has *quae a—*. “Jesus” is found in Vossian manuscript 1.

**[1156. *Nimbis*.]** Some editions have *membris*.

**[1157. *Fixit*.]** Greek *καθῆψε* occurs in Acts 28:3; Bochart explains it as “bound” or “fastened,” in *Hierozoicon* I, book 1, chapter 4, and II, book 3, chapter 2. Arator appears to support him.

**[1158. *Surgentibus*.]** Antwerp has *urgentibus*.

**[1164. *Venis*.]** Vossian manuscript 1 has *vetus*, which is not unacceptable.

**[1165. *Alternis*.]** Thus the manuscripts, Antwerp, the Lyon Bible, and Fabricius; the others have *alterni*.

**[1168. *Murmure*.]** The Aldine has *munere*.

**[1169. *Insonuere*.]** In my note on Sedulius I, 11, I suspected that Arator wrote *intonuere*, in order to express a more powerful emotional effect. See below, the note on verse 1226.

**[1171. *Furunt*.]** For *furiunt*. Fabricius, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 58.

The Cambridge manuscript and the three Vossian manuscripts have *furent*; Antwerp has *forent*. I did not dare restore *furent*, because the future tense seemed to have no force here. They had already endured the sea’s fury; the fury of the land was now appearing in the viper. Fabricius is nevertheless wrong to take *furunt* for *furiunt*. See Vossius, *Analecta* III, 30, at the end.

Sulpicius Severus likewise mentions a man who had been saved from the sea but whom fate did not allow to live, *Letter* 1, § 5. Thus, on the basis of one Utrecht manuscript, we should read *siverunt*; another has *sinerent*. *Siverunt* more accurately expresses the Greek *εἴασεν* in Acts 28:4. Luke’s *δίκη* Sulpicius rendered by *fata*, “the fates.” I think Nemesis is to be understood according to the speakers’ intention, and that the word should be written with a capital letter, *Dikē* (Δίκη), following Marckland’s judgment on Maximus of Tyre, dissertation 16, p. 608.

I do not know whether the judgment of these barbarians was influenced by the custom according to which criminals were commonly killed by the bite of asps. Galen, cited by Casaubon in his notes on Athenaeus III, 8, is a witness concerning the Alexandrians. Perhaps the Alexandrians themselves were among these barbarians, since the Alexandrian ship had spent the winter on this island and Paul afterward continued his journey on it.

Before the waves of the sea’s rage could overcome them,  
Paul cried out: “Give up your fasting, exhausted men,

**[1130]** And on the fourteenth day, as we eat, he said,  
Now taste bread.” Let us examine what the holy sacraments  
Of the figurative rite are effective to accomplish.

At the time when the first lights of the month shone,  
When the day had reached this number, the people were commanded  
To feed on the flesh of the lamb; touched by its protection,  
They deserved to escape the darkness of the Nile.

Hence, after a similar interval, Paul urges those  
Whom he wishes to rescue from the world’s abyss  
To dine with him and partake of sacred food,  
Reading the footsteps of Moses and observing their pattern.

These two salvations are distinct in place  
But close in cause, and repeated salvation  
Is drawn from a single source.

Christ is present in the lamb; Christ is also held  
In the bread from heaven, as he himself teaches. Whoever receives  
Jesus in his body is free from the enemy; Pharaoh  
And Egypt no longer possess their rights over him.

**[1145]** Soon all the weapons of the demon are drowned  
In these waters, through which the captive one  
Who had been held is reborn as an infant.  
The salty flood of the abyss is abandoned,  
And the pools of the dreadful dragon are overcome.

Christ grants pasture to the flock he has rescued,  
With his proper names: now the true shepherd  
For the one who feeds.

From this the golden moon also bears the figure of the Church.  
On the fourteenth day, from the rising of the first lamp,  
She is seen full in the day, because through Jesus’ body  
She grew within her own sphere, destined to make light perpetual.

To drive away the increasing cold, Paul had brought  
Branches to the fire. A viper fastened itself upon him,  
Carrying the weapons of the demon and confronting  
The rising flames; with ancient savagery  
It inflicted upon his hand a wound of icy poison in the fire.

“What more do you seek, wickedly harmful serpent,  
By seeking to draw [the redeemed] back from the Lord  
And preparing your former plunder under the new law?  
Why, lover of death, whose own parent you are,  
Do you renew wars against the redeemed?

You come as a robber, but you lie dead as plunder;  
While administering death, wicked one, you are consumed  
By the alternating branches of the tree. After Christ’s cross,  
Death is your portion of the wood.”

Not far from there were men with savage hearts,  
Born from a barbarian stock. Together they uttered  
A dreadful muttering:

“This guilty man has shed enough blood through his crime;  
He is now safe in no land, since both sea and earth  
Are raging against him. They are dealing with mortal things—”

**[1172. *Nam*.]** Antwerp has *jam*.

**[1174. *Quam*.]** Vossian manuscript 2 has *quod*.

**[1175. *Gehenna*.]** This is a Syriac word, derived from the Valley of Hinnom in the territory of Jerusalem, where children were sacrificed to the idol Moloch. The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel fiercely attacked this idolatry, which in their time was stubbornly defended by kings and priests. The word is taken to mean the torments of hell itself. Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*:

> May the flame of greedy Gehenna  
> Not devour this soul.

Juvencus I:

> He will grant the rewards of righteousness  
> And Gehenna for crime.

Fabricius, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 58. On this passage see Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, second part, book 3, chapter 2.

**[1177. *Hic*.]** The first Tornesian edition has *hinc*. Antwerp, Fabricius, and the Lyon Bible have *rabidi*. See above, verse 242.

**[1178. *Solitas*.]** Thus the manuscripts and the Aldine, Antwerp, Lyon, and Fabrician editions; the others have *solidas*. See the note on book I, verse 299.

**[1182. *Tumore*.]** Antwerp has *timore*.

**[1183. *Currit*.]** Thus the manuscripts, Pulmann’s notes, the Aldine, first Tornesian, and Antwerp editions; the others have *fertur*.

**[1185. *Exiit*.]** From the manuscripts and the Aldine and first Tornesian editions. Other editions have *excidit*.

**[1187. *Relegans*.]** Vossian manuscripts 2 and 3, the Aldine, and the first Tornesian edition have *religans*; the quantity of the middle syllable stands against that reading. Vossian manuscript 1 has *refocans*. Perhaps it was written for *revocans*, which seems to be a gloss. Here *relegare* means “to transfer to the cross of Christ.”

**[1188. *Haec*.]** Thus the Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine, and the first Tornesian edition. Antwerp also has *haec*; the remaining editions have *hoc quoque*.

**[1189. *A sacris*.]** Thus three Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine, and the first Tornesian edition. The Cambridge manuscript has *sacris vimque*. The others read *quae sacris vim sumit*.
