**[1193. *Regnet*.]** Thus the manuscripts, the Aldine, and the first Tornesian edition. The others have: “by whose power he rules the heavens.”

[Col. 0242C] 1194. *Esse*] I restored this reading from the manuscripts and the Aldine and Antwerp editions. The others have *posse*.—Moreover, the Antwerp edition has *hos esse*. But this is more suitable if one understands “these to be servants,” namely the gods whom they supposed Paul to be.

[Col. 0242C] 1198. *Quoniam*] *Quomodo*—with the first two syllables short and the last long—is found three times in Arator and once in Prudentius, *Symm.* II. This quantity was suspect, and was generally altered in printed copies; but since I found it in the old manuscripts in more than one place, I thought it should be retained, although I do not recommend imitating it. Arator:

> He wishes to retain his hand, though supplying it suitably in this way.
>
> It is rightly called a work.

Prudentius:

> How the Vestal origin is among these ashes in the cities.

FABRICIUS, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 113.—Only the Antwerp edition, the Lyon Bible, and Fabricius have *quomodo*. Fabricius also seems to have found it in his manuscripts, since he did not alter it. In Vossianus and the remaining editions, however, the reading is *quoniam*.

[Col. 0242D] 1200. *Dominique*] Vossianus 1 and 2 have *Dominumque*; the Antwerp edition has *Deumque*, derived from a gloss. If *Dominum* refers to the enemy, it could be understood of one who exercises dominion over human beings and holds his subjects beneath his own yoke.

[Col. 0242D] 1204. *Additus*] Some editions have *additur*.—Shortly afterward Vossianus 1 and 2 read *hisque calor*. Vossianus 3 has *hicque calor*.

[Col. 0242D] 1206. *Melite*] The Cambridge manuscript has *Miletae*; Vossianus 2, *Mileti*; Vossianus 3, *Milete*, and likewise the Antwerp edition.

And they prove the divine power: for the beast hanging from his finger is shaken off, thrown upon the pyres, and properly surrendered to the flame—

[1175] the flame which it itself had previously supplied, producing the fire of guilt, from which Gehenna grows hot. The ice of poison, warmed, melts into ashes, and the pride of the frozen pest dies from the heat. This fire and its swift vapors do not assume their customary strength, yet carry dry fuel with them; rather, O faith, using your own heat, you merely boil the serpent. The cold enemy is subjected to you and, in turn making fires, blazes with smoking viperish frost.

They say that it can slip away when the swelling comes on; so far does the mind, ignorant of goodness, run through empty things!

[Col. 0241B] Already then the venom is absent from Paul’s body, when the scaly terror which the ancient serpent inflicted has departed from his eyes. Cleansed in the heavenly stream and binding his limbs anew to Christ’s cross, he does not know death from the serpent. That flame devours the venom, drawing its power from the sacred waters, by which the scorched creature pants,

[Col. 0242A] 262 grieving to see the ancient colonists return to their homeland.

The young people, astonished that he remained unharmed for so long, say: “This man must be a god.” At last, uneducated inhabitant, learn by what power he rules the heavens, he who grants such things that you may think this is what his servants are. Now the meaning of the figure must be seen more fully in the gift of the illustrious deed.

[1195] The serpent is the source of death—for death, which derives its name from this, has it from the bite of the sinner—and wishes to restrain the hand opposed to the righteous. For a hand suited to service is rightly called a work. Whoever has recognized such an enemy should cast it off without delay and burn it with the vapors of the Lord.

[1200] When Paul recognized that the theft of danger, once brought near, wished to creep upon him, he seized heavenly weapons and suppressed its deceptions in the fire. From its fuel faith grew and was kindled, and ardor was added to the senses;

[1205] from this heat proceeded to the peoples from the breast of the spring.

For three winter months in the region of Melite

[Col. 0243A] [Note: [Col. 0243B]

1210. *Coma*] An elegant expression referring to foliage. See Elmenhorst’s index to Apuleius under the word *Ciofan*; also his note on Ovid, *Nux* 20. The word can likewise mean hair. See Bunemann on Lactantius, *De Pascha* 20.

[Col. 0243B] 1211. *Juvenescit*] Vossianus 1 has *viridescit*. The other reading is more elegant, especially because of the following *senio*.

[Col. 0243B] 1212. *Cedentibus*] Vossianus 3 and Tornesianus 1 have *credentibus*.

[Col. 0243B] 1213. *Placidis*] Pulmann’s manuscript, the Antwerp edition, and others have *placidisque*.

[Col. 0243B] 1214. *Ore*] Vossianus 2 and 3 have *ora*. Arator perhaps had Psalm 125:4 in mind.

[Col. 0243B] 1216. *Prostratis*] Vossianus 2 and 3 have *substratis*.

[Col. 0243C] 1218. *Excelsae*] The Antwerp edition has *Ecclesiae sublimia culmina Romae*, “the lofty summits of the Church of Rome,” and so forth.

[Col. 0243C] 1220. *Convenisse*] This is the reading of the manuscripts, Aldine edition, and Tornesianus 1. The others have *devenisse*.—Immediately afterward, the Cambridge and Antwerp editions omit the preposition *e*.

[Col. 0243C] 1221. *Duo*] I adopted this reading from the Cambridge manuscript and punctuated the passage differently; the editions present it as follows:

> Through whom all may join their stars, who, by faith, etc.

Peter and Paul are similarly called “the lights of the world” in the poem *On the Basilica of Saint Peter*, as the distinguished Schrader correctly emended it, *Observations* I.6, p. 72.

[Col. 0243C] 1222. *Qui*] This is the reading of the three Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine, Tornesianus 1, and Antwerp editions. The others have *quae*.

[Col. 0243C] 1225. *Surrexit*] This is the reading of the manuscripts, Aldine edition, and Tornesianus 1. The others have *sacrato*.—The Cambridge manuscript has *corpora*.

[Col. 0243C] 1226. *Turrita*] See Barth on Rutilius, *Itinerary* 1.117. Savar noted on Sidonius, *Poems* II.393, that Rome was painted as turreted and long-haired. The observations of Elmenhorst on Rome at Arnobius II, p. 67, and IV, p. 128, are relevant here.

[Col. 0243D] 1227. *Majora*] This is the reading of the Vossian manuscripts, the Aldine, Tornesianus 1, and Antwerp editions. The others have *meliora*. The same words are confused in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII.102. Add Burman on Lucan I.399.

[Col. 0243D] 1228. *Dominae*] This reading comes from the Cambridge manuscript, Vossianus 1 and 2, and most editions; but Vossianus 3, the Aldine, and Tornesianus 1 have *Domino*. Nor is that reading displeasing: nevertheless, I preferred to follow the better manuscripts, especially since Rome is frequently called “mistress of the world.” If *Domino* is preferred, the meaning is clear: although Rome conquered the whole world by her arms, she was nevertheless founded upon God, the Lord of the world.

[Col. 0244B] 1228. *Sedis*] The manuscripts are remarkably confused here. The Cambridge manuscript and Aldine edition have *fundata cacumina sedes*; Vossianus 1, *fundata cacumine sedis*; Vossianus 2 and 3 and Tornesianus 1, *fundata cacumine sedes*. The remaining editions have the reading I printed.

[Col. 0244B] 1230. *Huic*] This is the reading of the manuscripts, Aldine, Tornesianus 1, and Antwerp editions. The others have *his*. Rome is meant, and also in the following line, where *quae praelata* belongs. For if *his* is adopted in this line, there is no antecedent to which *quae* can refer.—Most editions have *praeses*.

[Col. 0244B] 1231. *Intonat*] *Intonare* means to use a strong and confident manner of speaking. Prudentius, *On Stephen*:

> The profane judge could not endure the martyr thundering these words.

FABRICIUS, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 74. I would therefore not prefer *insonat* from the Cambridge manuscript. Justus demonstrated that *tonare* and *tonitru* are elegantly used in this sense, *Specimen of Observations*, ch. 12. Add Dresigius in *Acta Lipsiensia* 1740, p. 186. Burman shows on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.187, that *sonare* and *tonare* are confused, as are *sonitus* and *tonitrus*. See the notes on Sedulius I.11.—The Antwerp edition has *Quidque intonat istud*.

[Col. 0244C] 1233. *Coronae*] The Cambridge manuscript adds this word.

[Col. 0244C] 1236. *Titulis*] I adopted this from Vossianus 1 and 2. Vossianus 3 has *titulus*; the Cambridge manuscript, *titulus parvos*; the Antwerp edition, *titulus parvus*; the remaining editions, *titulos parvus*. The meaning of the reading I printed is clearer: this was worthy material for a crown, so that in Rome herself, mistress of the world, Peter and Paul might accomplish these things, lest a small enemy be given to their glory and titles. For the greater the enemy, the more illustrious the victory over him. This expression is frequently used. Ovid, *Fasti* VI.75:

> All honor accrues to me from the origin of the month.

*To Livia* 80:

> Everyone to whom virtue has accrued.

[Col. 0244D] 1240. *Idola*] The middle syllable is shortened. See above, I.269.—For the matter touched upon here, see the elegant treatment in Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 6.

[Col. 0244D] 1242. *Pharao*] See above, on line 1142.]

Paul provides manifold assistance and rescues Publius’s father from the neighboring disaster. When this deed was seen, people everywhere rushed headlong to sudden salvation.

[1210] Meanwhile, the leafy hair of shining spring sprouts forth, by which the earth grows young as the frost flees from old age. The South Wind, receiving the ship with its yielding sails, supplied winged waters upon the gentle waves.

He is rightly said to breathe, whom the prophet makes resound with his mouth, who sings of the image of faith as a torrent in the South.

So also, when storms had been laid low for our rejoicing, he came, choosing out many towns in their distinct districts, to the lofty summits of exalted Rome.

[Col. 0243B] A higher order requires that we say that the two lights of the world came together

[1220] and chose one place from such distant regions, through which the two stars might unite all things,

264 they who make all the fields of faith bright with virtues.

Although this subject extends through countless figures, wishing to report only a few, I shall publish these same eminent examples.

[1225] Peter arose as prince in the body of the Church; this turreted city bore her head about the circuit of the world.

[Col. 0244A] Greater things befit her, so that all may behold the established summits of the seat of the mistress of the lands.

Paul, chosen as an unending teacher for the nations,

[1230] more fittingly present here, spreads the reins of speech for her, who, set above the nations, instructs them; and the honor of the city compels the subjected world to hear what he thunders there,

265 and it is worthy material for the crown of Peter and Paul: to surpass imperial threats, to proclaim the laws of heaven in the tyrant’s citadel,

[1235] and to conquer the supreme tribunal in the contest, lest a small enemy be assigned to their titles.

Egypt bears the form of the world; hence the people who deserved to be called by that name were entrusted to two leaders,

[Col. 0244B] in whom brotherly origin joined their office.

[1240] All the idols of Rome, gathered from a conquered world, had oppressed hearts subject to darkness. This free people too, whom Pharaoh had previously bound, cast off the shadows of Egypt under as many leaders,

and through the baths of God—which the image of the sea then represented—

[1245] having found the path of life, it discovered heavenly food.

[Col. 0245A] [Note: [Col. 0245A]

1246. *Actus*] The reading in the Cambridge manuscript seems to have been written by a second hand; Pulmann’s manuscript and the Antwerp edition have *ictus*.

[Col. 0245A] 1247. *Quam*] Weitzius, in his note on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* VI.4, cites *cum natura*, although I have found it nowhere.

[Col. 0245A] 1247. *Edidit*] Weitzius in the same place has *addidit*; I have found this neither in manuscripts nor in printed editions, although he has sufficient grounds on which to defend it. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.535:

> And add it to your gods.

The meaning of the preceding words is that there was indeed brotherly love between Peter and Paul, but that it arose more from the glorious deeds they accomplished than from a natural bond.

[Col. 0245B] 1248. *Non eadem*] Arator seems to hold that Peter and Paul did not die as martyrs at the same time, but that one died a year after the death of the other. This was also the opinion of Prudentius and Saint Augustine. The older and more numerous Fathers, nearly all later writers, and the Roman Church itself, in the Roman Martyrology, affirm that they were victorious through their blood on the same day of the same year, namely 29 June. Saint Gelasius I, in the Roman council of seventy bishops, says the following in his decree on apocryphal books: “Paul, not at a different time, as the heretics foolishly babble, but at one time and on one and the same day, was crowned by a glorious death with Peter in the city of Rome, contending under Caesar Nero.” Consult, among others, vol. I of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the year of Our Lord 69. ANONYMOUS, in the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers*.—Prudentius, whom Arator seems to have followed, evidently placed Paul’s death one year after Peter’s. Thus, *Peristephanon* XI.3:

> This festive day of apostolic triumph returns for us,  
> renowned for the blood of Paul and Peter.  
> One day saw both crowned with glorious death,  
> yet the year had fully renewed itself.

Others report that it happened in the same year. See Weitz on Prudentius, p. 594. Cave, *Apostolic Antiquities*, ch. 7, § 9, reaches no conclusion. For the true year, see Wesseling on Simson’s *Chronicle*, p. 1669.

[Col. 0246B] 1250. *Gratia*] This is the reading of the three Vossian manuscripts. All the others have *gloria*.]

266 These too had brotherly love, to whom deeds gave more than nature did: twins whom not the same, yet one, day brought forth to the stars. Nevertheless, after the cycle of a year their passion consecrated the returning light of one day,

[1250] and their shared favor holds the eternal palm.

[Col. 0245]

# ARATOR’S LETTER TO PARTHENIUS

[Col. 0245]

[Col. 0245C] [Note: [Col. 0245C] 1. *Parthenium*] Consult what I noted about this letter in the preface.

[Col. 0245C] 2. *Daret*] There is an error at the very beginning. Juvenal has this line in mind:

> “Written also on the back, with Orestes not yet finished.”

Write *vix dat in tergo*, “it scarcely gives room on the back,” even if the reverse side of the paper is covered with verses. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2. From this conjecture it seems true that what Barthius mentions at the beginning of the chapter is that he read through this letter in one hour while walking; the alteration is so unnecessary that I suspect he had some other purpose when he reasoned in this way.—For the meaning of *tergum*, see Theodorus Ryckius on Tacitus, *Annals* XIII.5. In former times, when those sheets were made from easily available papyrus—the sheets called volumes—they did not permit writing on both sides, and thus were distinct from square codices. See Vossius on Catullus, p. 3. On the reverse surface, therefore, or back, they did not write unless the works were particularly long and exceeded the normal measure. Arator here declares that the material concerning Parthenius’ parents was of such a kind that it could not be accommodated on the reverse side of the volume but had to be pushed onto its back. Salmasius also used this passage in his note on Vopiscus, p. 447. If something was written on the back, it was called an *opisthograph*. See Britannicus on Juvenal I.6.

[Col. 0245D] 2. *Modum*] Salmasius, in his note on Vopiscus, p. 447, cites *locum*. But Sirmond printed *modum* from the manuscript, and I take it as meaning “limit” or “end,” as Schultingius does on Seneca, *Controversies*, p. 64.

[Col. 0246C] 3. *Potens*] It means distinguished, renowned, wealthy, splendid. Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of Christ*, ch. 22: “They will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory,” that is, with the greatest splendor. But here the word concerns a family. Caesar, book VII: “Vercingetorix, son of Celtillus, an Arvernian youth of the greatest power, whose father had held the primacy of all Gaul.” Horace, *Odes* I.35:

> However changed, you will leave hostile houses  
> in their powerful attire.

The same, *Odes* II.17:

> Nor do I demand a more lavish gift  
> from my powerful friend, being sufficiently blessed, etc.

A strong family is mentioned by Plautus, *Trinummus*, final scene. Ennodius’ tenth address is an abundant witness to the nobility of this Parthenius, so that no one should think this versifier a flatterer. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.

[Col. 0246D] 5. *Aevo*] “A name bestowed upon you from an age” is modest, and should be connected in that way, although the interval is rather harsh, even contrary to the lex *Pedia*. I suspected that *ab auro*, “from gold,” should be read, since Ennodius, speaking of the same man, says of Parthenius: “Gold is nothing unless it is fashioned by the craftsman’s hand, and the value of the yellow metal is joined to it by the file of the maker. When industry ceases, brilliance is insignificant.” That passage could have been in view here. But the other reading is more likely: that the author’s text read *positum cui nomen ab aequo*, “whose name was bestowed from what is just.” For it is fitting that a maidenly character should be judged by a modest name. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—Either write *impositum*, “imposed,” or take the simple form as standing for a compound. I think that by *aevum* he understood the earliest period and Parthenius’ infancy, when this name had belonged to him from birth and hence throughout his life. Writers of this period sometimes use the word in that sense. Thus, “those who have despaired in their life” are called *depositi aevo* in Hegesippus, *Fragments of the History of Jerusalem* V.24 and 27, p. 584; and the same meaning seems present in the *passages of time* mentioned by Sedulius II.135. The passage therefore indicates that Parthenius’ name was given from the very beginning of his life, but that it expressed above all the modesty of his character. I do not adequately understand what Barthius means by *verecundi*, nor why he declares the reading contrary to Pedia’s rule. Nor is it necessary to connect the word backward with *nomen*; it can also be joined with *animi*. Since the meter would not admit *verecundi*, Arator could certainly have used such a construction, while the meaning remains the same.]

267 To the illustrious, most magnificent, and exalted Parthenius, master of offices and patrician, Arator, subdeacon.

If I wished to recount, great man, the honors of your ancestors,

the page, when read, would scarcely give room on its back.

[Col. 0246C] 268 Powerful through great-grandfathers and ancestors, you surpass your lineage

in character, and your merits make your origin give way.

[5] Excellent Parthenius, whose name was bestowed from the beginning of life,

your praise is rather that of your character, by which, modest man, you are pleasing.

[Col. 0247A] [Note: [Col. 0247B]

8. *Gemmis*] Nothing is easier than to rewrite the passage:

> And so that you may double the honor by which you are called, you are present.

A prophetic tongue imposed upon you a name expressive of your character: you are what you are called, so that you may double your honor. This is from Ausonius, epigram I:

> So that he may double the titles of the man  
> who tempers battles with the Muses.

*Ades* in place of *es* is not barbarous; examples are found in Lucretius, Catullus, and Propertius. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—Perhaps the text should read:

> For the tongue that announces your name marked your modesty,  
> and, as an honor to your family, you are what you are called.

Certainly *gemmis* is worthless. *Ades* is unquestionably the correct reading; nevertheless, I did not wish to alter Sirmond’s text, perhaps out of excessive reverence. *Lingua* is used for human speech, as in book II.320:

> He deserved to grasp the life-giving tongue.

For the verb *adesse*, see above, II.300.

[Col. 0247C] 9. *Cingula*] The meaning of the passage is found in Claudian:

> Fortune adorns the man.

Arnulf of Lisieux, in the epitaph of Matilda:

> But shining more brilliantly through the glory of her virtues,  
> she surpassed the fortune of her family and marriage bed.

*Cingula* means any honors. An ancient epitaph of Pantagatus, bishop of Vienne:

> At the will of kings he received the belts of the quaestorship,  
> distinguished by ancestry, but more renowned for integrity.

Another, that of Namatius, written under the emperor Justin:

> After the fasces, Symmachus laid aside his great belts.

Freculphus II.4.24: “When he declined to do this—for he was orthodox—she invited him with greater belts.” Some, however, restrict the term to honors accompanied by the right of the sword; among them was the learned Sirmond, in his note on Sidonius, though this is not strictly correct. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2. Compare the same author on Claudian, *Letter* II.50.

[Col. 0247D] 10. *Quisque*] *Quisquis*, “whoever,” is familiar among poets of the declining age, beginning with Ausonius. The lines that follow are from Claudian, who became for later poets like a sacred anchor. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—See above, II.272.

[Col. 0248A] 12. *Solus*] Barthius compared these words with Claudian, *Adversaria* LI.12; see his note on Claudian, *Praise of Stilicho* I.33.

[Col. 0248B] 13. *Facunde*] I think *facunda* is correct, as Barthius conjectures, *Adversaria* XXIX.2. Below, line 37:

> The names that you uttered with learned speech.

Cicero, *For Archias* 10: “Poets whose utterances sound rich and foreign.”

[Col. 0248B] 15. *Multis*] *Multis opulenta*, “rich in many,” is worthless. Write *te titulis opulenta*, “you rich in titles,” through an easy scribal mistake arising from an abbreviation. The phrase is drawn from Homer, and no one would hesitate to apply it even in that age to Germany, the conqueror of the Roman world. But the fact that he calls Parthenius “a pupil of Germany” seems to oppose Sirmond’s note, which we accepted in this chapter, concerning kinship with Ennodius—unless you prefer to understand “Germans” as Goths, though I would scarcely agree. Arnulf of Lisieux speaks similarly in the epitaph of Algar:

> Filling the earth with titles and heaven with virtues,  
> he dies for us so that he may live for himself.

BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—Perhaps the text read *multis opulenta quidem Germania doctis*: “Although Germany was indeed rich in many learned men, she nevertheless, having encountered such learning in Parthenius, would regard him with admiration.”

[Col. 0248C] 16. *Gaudet*] *Tibi gaudet*, “rejoices for you,” is owed to Claudian, in whose works we find more expressions of this kind. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—One could read *plaudit*, “applauds,” but this is unnecessary. *Tibi* is used in the sense of “on your account” in Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Martin* 5.5, “to grieve more for him,” and *Letter* 3.19, “that he should rather rejoice”; Clericus compared the former passage.

[Col. 0248C] 17. *Gloria*] The following lines concerning the embassy are likewise from Claudian and were also imitated by Sidonius, as were the lines from the *Panegyric on Mallius*:

> I saw you, I saw the young man, eloquent in speech,  
> matching the Hesperian nobles, old men though they were.

The following is from Martial:

> Such as the dense toga gives to the Roman Forum.

“Never quarrelsome, toga seldom worn, mind at peace”—that is, the duties of the courts. But Arator is referring to our Claudian:

> Gaul surrounded you with learned citizens,  
> and Rome with her entire senate.

If Arator is indeed the author: for the more deeply I investigate, the more I detect a recent talent, not unpolished by reading Sidonius and Claudian, which has sprinkled only a few blemishes with cosmetic color, such as this:

> That you might demand the aid of freedom as its advocate.

BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.

[Col. 0248D] 22. *Posceres*] The article *Τό* (“the”) and *actor* are again taken from Claudian and Sidonius. If you wished to quibble, you might read *pactus es actor opem*, “you agreed to be the advocate seeking aid.” BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—Barthius’ conjecture scarcely works. These words explain the reason why he had been sent. Therefore the text should read *pactus sis*, “that you had agreed.” The fault in *posceres* is such that I scarcely believe it came from the poet; nevertheless, I have nothing with which to assist the difficult passage.

[Col. 0248D] 24. *Solum*] It means either “the sole of the foot” or the native soil of a person, which is more likely. Or would you prefer *sofum*, a word not uncommon in Sidonius? BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—I think the text read *tuos publica vota sonos*, “the public prayers made your voice resound.”]

A presaging tongue marked your modesty to come,

269 and, that you may double the distinction by which you are called, you are present.

You bear many belts of office, but you make them great,

[10] 270 for every honor given to you immediately grows.

Who could sing of such gifts? I speak briefly: all the qualities

that individually make men great, you alone possess.

You, eloquent man, resound among the peoples of the Rhône and Rhine;

[Col. 0248A] the royal court recognizes you as a man of sweet speech.

[15] Indeed, wealthy Germany, rich in many things,

welcomes you as a learned man and rejoices in native affection for you.

271 The greatest glory shines for her pupil of such distinction,

such as the crowded toga gives to the Roman Forum.

I saw you, I saw the young man, eloquent in speech,

[20] matching the Hesperian nobles, old men though they were,

whither you had been sent, having discharged an embassy,

that, as freedom’s advocate, you might seek aid.

You soothed Gothic ears with fortunate words,

and public prayers helped your native soil.

[25] [Col. 0249A] [Note: [Col. 0249B]

25. *Ovans*] Perhaps it would be better to read *nil audita novans*, “innovating nothing unheard of”: namely, the orator’s eloquence, as though renewing matters in the king’s ears. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—I retain the other reading, by which the king is shown to be victorious but to lend his ears mercifully and to offer easy access, so that he could refuse nothing to the petitioner.

[Col. 0249B] 28. *Caput*] What, I ask, do you think of the expression *assidua sustulit aure caput*, “he raised his head with a constant ear”—does it refer to fame? Or do you imagine the constant ear of that genius by which Arator’s poems were written? BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—The expression is harsh. Perhaps the text should read *assiduo sustulit ore caput*, “he raised his head with unceasing speech,” where fame began to emerge through continuous praise. I have shown in various places that Arator was especially fond of the word *os*, “mouth.” This word is also frequently referred to fame; it has been stated above, in book I.124, that it is interchangeable with *auris*, “ear.”

[Col. 0249B] 29. *Populos*] I thought this should be written by conjecture, where Sirmond printed *populo*, followed by the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*. I now see that Barthius also cites it this way, *Adversaria* XXIX.2. A following letter absorbed the preceding one, as often happens in manuscripts; and *populos* is required by the sense, since fame has been mentioned as scattering Parthenius’ praises in every direction.

[Col. 0249C] 29. *Pinguedo*] This was fashioned after the line in the epigram to the abbot Florian:

> In lean speech indeed, but weighty deeds,  
> we have written.

Certainly, anyone who wishes may judge otherwise; I do not deny that I said this poem may seem spurious. The author names himself ineptly, lest clever people thereafter doubt him. Most ineptly he flaunts his reading of Caesar’s *Commentaries*, which he composed like daily records, alluding to the testimony about them that is now well known; and he inserts the story of Ambrose, who was nourished by bees. Anyone who can digest that will have a strong stomach for other matters. BARTHIUS, *Adversaria* XXIX.2.—See above, on the letter to Florian, line 7.

[Col. 0249D] 30. *Anxia*] It is not sufficiently clear about what this crowd was anxious, unless the word is understood of the crowd’s eagerness to listen. Valerius Maximus VIII.7.7 similarly joins attentive, anxious, and never-ceasing effort. But perhaps the text read *inscia*, “ignorant,” so that this crowd, unaware of such eloquence, had gathered to hear him. *Anxius* and *inscius* are similarly confused in Valerius Flaccus I.684. Or *maxima*, “greatest,” could be substituted; the word is not far removed if one considers the small strokes placed above letters, which copyists often neglect.

[Col. 0249D] 36. *Hians*] It expresses eagerness to hear. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* III, prose 3: “For if this is always gaping and asking for something.”

[Col. 0249D] 37. *Tu*] Perhaps *tunc*, “then.”

[Col. 0249D] 37. *Docta*] The Lyon *Library of the Fathers* has *docte*, “learnedly,” as in line 63:

> And, learned man, I wish to loosen my contracted verse.

[Col. 0249D] 38. *Codicis*] This is not far removed from Longinus’ description of a learned person as a “living library” (*βιβλιοθήκη ἔμψυχος*, “a living library,” and *καὶ περιπατοῦν Μουσεῖον*, “a walking Museum”). The expression became proverbial for learned people, as Lomeyer shows more fully, *On the Library*, ch. 1.

[Col. 0250B] 40. *Ephemeridas*] These are also mentioned by Servius and others. They seem to have been written for Caesar’s private use, and the *Commentaries* were composed from them. For the distinction between the two, see Vossius on Caesar, *Gallic War* I.1. Oudendorp holds the same view in his note on *Civil War* III.34.4. Arator could call them histories because *ephemerides* was used in a broader sense, especially in the later period, for annals and history. Compare Davies on Caesar, *Fragments*, p. 999, Oudendorp’s edition. I do not know why Barthius criticizes the display of learning in this passage in his note on line 27.

[Col. 0250B] 43. *Visos*] This is worthless. Perhaps *veros*, “true,” should be read, contrasted with the deceptive art that he mentioned in the preceding line in connection with other poets. Thus Asterius, in his epigram to Macedonius, line 1:

> Accept, Father, the words of a truthful poet,  
> composed without the fault of invention.

Arator, letter to Vigilius, 20:

> Following history, I shall speak true verses.

Or one could read *missos*, “sent away,” so that Parthenius had to some extent given up his concern for Christian poets. The conjecture is indeed supported by the nearby *remeabas*, “you returned,” which implies an interruption. *Missus* and *visus* are similarly confused in manuscripts at Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* II.10.51. *Mittere* in the sense of *omittere*, “to omit,” is by no means uncommon.

[Col. 0250C] 46. *Cunis*] They imagine, following the example of Plato, that while the infant Ambrose slept in his cradle, a swarm of bees settled upon him and entered through his mouth. Hence he also seems to have called his hymns “Hyblaean,” after the mountain famous for its frequent swarms of bees, as in Martial II, epigram 46:

> As Hybla is painted with flowers of many colors,  
> when the bees ravage the brief Sicilian spring.

For these hymns of Ambrose, see Fabricius, *Commentary on Christian Poets*, p. 7. Barthius, in his note above on line 27, cannot digest the story of Ambrose inserted here and therefore judges the letter unworthy of Arator. Let it be a fable. Could the poet not have used it to describe a man’s eloquence and honey-sweet speech, when nectar, honey, and the comb flowing from the mouth are so often mentioned? See Barthius on Claudian, p. 169; Burman on Lotichius, *Elegies* IV, p. 268, and on the *Catalecta* III, p. 646; hence *honey* is used of the sweetness of speech. See the note on Liberius, *Acrostic*, line 5, and Boltius, *Critical Miscellanies*, p. 53. In this verse I would much more easily digest and even praise this elegance and poetic fiction than the many foolish figures that Arator so often inserted into his poem. If Barthius could digest those elsewhere and judge them worthy of Arator, I do not know what illness had afflicted his stomach that he could not tolerate these bees.

[Col. 0250D] 47. *Decentius*] Whether he had Licentius in mind, I do not determine, unless someone thinks that the first syllable must be shortened. These poets pay little attention to quantity in proper names, as above in *Florianus*, which is likewise neglected in the letter to him, line 2. There are other examples in Arator. For Licentius, see Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina mediae et infimae aetatis*, book XI, p. 809. Whether Decentius should be counted among the Christian poets, others may decide. Someone might perhaps suspect that *decentius* derives from *decens*, “fitting,” with the first syllable lengthened contrary to custom; such errors are sufficiently frequent in Arator. But in that case the following verse should be read *canit*.]

That king, joyfully listening, in whose power the matter then lay, could deny nothing.

272 When this flying report began to scatter with swift course

and raised its head with an attentive ear,

the rich fullness of your speech went out among the peoples,

[30] and an anxious crowd thronged your steps;

so that whenever you opened rivers with moving lips,

they might run as though to remove the thirst of summer.

Eager to touch these riches of speech,

through which, precious man, you flow like the wave of the Tagus,

[35] 273 because we were held by these household gods in the city of Ravenna,

I, a guest eager to hear, was with you night and day.

What books, what learned names you uttered to me!

How much, recalling all things together, you were like a book!

There, under your guidance, I first read Caesar’s histories,

[40] which he himself composed as daily records for his own use.

You sang poets with gentle and sweet charm,

among whom there was deceptive art and magnificent display.

Yet, excellent man, you returned to the poets you had seen,

274 whose verse faith draws back to its proper laws.

[45] Like Ambrose, who stands out in his Hyblaean hymns,

whom bees marked out when he had been placed in the cradle.

Like Decentius, who flowed into this same art,

and like the Sidonian lyre among the white-haired Arvernians.

[Col. 0251A] [Note: [Col. 0251C]

47. *Manavit*] Here too there is an error in the quantity of the first syllable.

[Col. 0251C] 48. *Sidoniana*] In the Reims manuscript, from which Sirmond printed his text, there is a [lacuna]: only “...niana celes” can be read. Hardouin supplied the mutilated verse by a certain conjecture, which I adopted into the text, understanding Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni. See the preface to Sirmond’s works.

[Col. 0252C] 58. *Seges*] See the note on the letter to Florian, line 1.

[Col. 0252C] 68. *Brevem*] “Small” or “brief.” See Cannegieter, *Dissertation on Avianus*, p. 314; Wopkens on Sedulius II.278.

[Col. 0252C] 71. *Volumina*] This word is poorly suited to stalks and pastures; he should more properly have remained within the metaphor, and the epithet *aprica*, “sunny,” does not fit. But perhaps these expressions were formed with a similar elegance, as shortly afterward in line 73, *odas mandere*, “to chew odes.”

[Col. 0252C] 73. *Davidicis*] Sirmond printed *Daviticis*. See the note on Sedulius I.7.

[Col. 0252C] 82. *Exsaturare*] I restored this reading from Sirmond’s conjecture; the manuscript has *ex saturitate*, “from satiety.”

[Col. 0252C] 87. *Patuerunt*] Perhaps *placuerunt*, “pleased.” For the rest, consult the preface.

[Col. 0252C] 92. *Bonos*] Perhaps *bonis*, “good.”]

275 and the Sidonian lyre among Arvernian swans.

For a long time, during my boyhood, I had cared

[50] to celebrate a continuous melody in verse.

I even pretended to write parts that fiction composed,

and to be carried lightly across the empty sea.

When my fragile reed had sung these things to you,

and your love had often favored me, dear friend,

[55] “Would that you preferred,” you said, “to bend the course

of this voice more rightly toward the praises of the Lord!”

And because you bear the name by which we call you, Arator,

I resolved that the harvest should not be hidden from you but open,

if ever I might perhaps deserve

[60] to pursue the fruits of my talent toward better things,

and that, wherever you might be, greatest of men,

the work I composed should be sent to you.

Now the promised day urges me finally to fulfill what was owed,

and, learned man, I wish to discharge my obligations.

[65] Accept the poem that we have sipped from the shining sea,

and kindly receive these small waters.

The Ocean of things remains deep in that vast expanse

from which I have scarcely drawn a brief drop with my mouth.

For I, mingled with the pleasant stalks of the Roman

[70] Church, have become a sheep with shorn head,

276 seeing the rich pastures and sunny volumes of Christ,

I sought to touch everything with my own taste.

Now my mind, accustomed to David’s flowers, desired

[Col. 0252A] to chew odes; now, hungry, it longed for Genesis.

[75] And while I preferred to pluck violets and lilies together,

whose ancient and new fragrance have been doubled,

the book which the rule calls *Acts* occurred to me,

a book filled throughout the world with the harvest of the apostles.

In it the Lord raised us, while Peter was fishing,

[80] from the bosom of the salty and blue sea.

He showed and gave us a ship in the image of heaven,

to satisfy the hunger of the nations he had taken aboard.

From its history, as a novice, I drew my verses,

and diligently offered my voice to my shepherd,

[85] who more generously brings new words to the singer by his aid;

without him, no one can speak anything worthy.

What was handed over to the distinguished father, the pope,

the archives of the Church rightly preserve and keep.

Come, then! Let the collation celebrate the books it has received.

[90] The heavenly cause will grant the reward of the recompense.

There are pontiffs who are teachers in religion;

learned Gaul gives many good ones.

There is Firminus, that venerable priest,

who can feed the people with the voice of doctrine.

[95] 277 His praise extends to the borders of Italy,

and beyond his homeland his glory bears his name.

Do not doubt that approved men would welcome the documents

that pleased the man of the apostolic see.

Nor should you think that you will lack the gift of fame,

[100] because you publish these writings there, prefixed to the work.

We shall both go together wherever this page has reached,

and it will always carry the honor of Parthenius on its lips.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 550.

VICTOR, BISHOP OF CAPUA.

[Col. 0251]

[Col. 0251]

# INTERPRETATION OF THE EVANGELICAL HARMONIES

## PREFACE OF VICTOR, BISHOP OF CAPUA, TO AMMONIUS’ EVANGELICAL HARMONIES
[Col. 0251D] I. When a Gospel composed from the four happened by chance to fall into my hands, and, its title being absent, I could not find the author’s name, I diligently inquired who, with no small labor of study, had arranged the deeds or sayings of our Lord and Savior, distinguished by the Gospel reading, into the order in which they seemed to follow one another. [Col. 0252D] I discovered a certain Ammonius of Alexandria, who is also said to have invented the Gospel Canons: he joined excerpts from the remaining three Gospels to Matthew’s Gospel and bound the Gospel into a single sequence. Thus Bishop Eusebius, writing to Carpianus in the preface to his edition in which he published the canons of the aforementioned Gospel, imitating that man’s diligence, reports as follows:

“A certain Ammonius of Alexandria, expending, as I believe, much labor and study, left us one Gospel from the four. From his history also I learned that Tatian, a most learned man and the most distinguished orator of his time, joined one Gospel together from the four, to which he gave the title *DIAPENTE*.”

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Fabricius, in *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, vol. I, p. 379, conjectures that *diapente* arose improperly from an abbreviated writing of *diatessaron*. This is certainly contradicted even by Victor himself as interpreter, to say nothing of the testimonies of Eusebius, Jerome, and other ancients. Accordingly, when Fabricius brings forward Victor’s words from this passage, he rewrites *diapente* as *diatessarius*. Or should it be *diatessaron*? He further observes that Casaubon, in his notes on Baronius XIII, 2, p. 211, and Ittig, following him, *De Haeresiarchis*, p. [Col. 0254D] 201, read *διὰ πάντων* (“through all”) in Victor. Nevertheless, he acknowledges that learned men were not lacking who approved the Victorine reading, hitherto commonly published, on the grounds that they supposed Tatian to have had in view, in addition to the four Gospels, the Gospel according to the Hebrews as well. See Grotius in his note on Matthew, at the beginning; G. J. Vossius, *Dissertatio de genealogia Christi*, p. 17; and Simon, *Histoire critique du texte du Nouveau Testament*, p. 74.]

This man had been a disciple of the blessed philosopher and martyr Justin while Justin was still alive. When Justin departed to the Lord with the palm of martyrdom, Tatian abandoned his teacher’s holy discipline; lifted up by the arrogance of his learning, he fell into the heresy of the Encratites, embracing rather the error of Marcion than the truth of the Christian philosopher Justin, and proved destructive to his own life by asserting, among other things, that marriage and fornication were subject to equal guilt.

II. He is also said to have laid profane hands upon the apostolic sayings by way of emendation—or, more truly, corruption. Yet because the glory of truth often triumphs, through the power of Christ our God, by the confession or activity even of faithless men—for demons too confessed Christ, and the sons of Sceva in the Acts of the Apostles drove out demons in the name of Jesus, whom Paul preached—Tatian, although entangled in profane errors, nevertheless offered students a useful example by arranging this Gospel, as it seems to me, with skillful joining.

Perhaps he was still clinging to the side of the blessed Justin and, through the merit of that instruction, brought this work to completion. For I think that the edition of the volume mentioned above belongs not to Ammonius but to this man, because Ammonius is said to have joined the account of the other evangelists to Matthew’s account in a discriminating manner, whereas this man took up the beginnings of the holy Luke and, although for the greater part he joined the sayings of the other three to the Gospel of Saint Matthew, so that it may rightly be uncertain whether the invention of the same work should be attributed to Ammonius or Tatian.

Nevertheless, even if Tatian, now a heresiarch, is the author of this edition, I gladly embrace the interpretation when I recognize the words of my Lord; if it had been his own, I would cast it far away. For he is also reported to have published magnificent books *Against the Nations*.

III. Since I had found this Gospel without the numbers which Ammonius discovered with marvelous diligence, and which Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, receiving the example from him, carefully developed—numbers by which the sayings commonly shared by the evangelists are marked with their own signs—I devoted the labor of study, with the Lord’s help, to affixing those numbers carefully in their appropriate places.

If uncertainty about a word should perhaps arise, anyone who, by means of the appended numbers, turns to the complete Gospel reading can immediately discover whether the passage in question is worded in the same way there; thus, without scruple, the mind of the diligent reader may use this volume with confidence.

Even if this work was published with the numbers by the author of the composed volume, they are nevertheless thought to have been omitted through the negligence of copyists. We, however, have undertaken the labor by which a new work is customarily brought to completion.

It must certainly be understood that this canonical number reaches only as far as ten. Nor was the total of these numbers fixed by the writer’s will; rather, it was ingeniously discovered by Ammonius according to natural reason and rule. For no other number, either below ten or above it, could in any way explain the common or distinctive sayings of the four evangelists.

This can easily be proved by the present example. For either all four must necessarily agree with one another; or Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree with one another; or John agrees with Matthew; or Matthew agrees with Luke; or Matthew speaks the same things as Mark; or Mark speaks distinctive things with Luke and John; or Mark speaks similar things with John; or Mark narrates the same things with Luke; or Luke reports things differing from John; or each is found to expound matters peculiar to himself.

IV. Thus, in the four evangelists, it has been shown by clear numerical reasoning that the common and distinctive account cannot proceed beyond ten, but must be contained within the number ten. I have nevertheless appended these canons briefly below, with each canon identified by its numbers, so that the reader may easily discover more clearly in which canon which evangelists have spoken common or distinctive things.

The order which we arranged according to the reasoning of the canons was set out for this purpose: simply to demonstrate rationally that the total of ten had been written down. As we said, we have taken care to note briefly below what their arrangement is.

I also took care to describe the numbers themselves, gathered together into one sequence, in the manner in which Saint Jerome arranged them, following only the order in which the reading of this entire Gospel is unfolded. Thus, if the curious reader wishes first to inspect the numbers mentioned above—whether the evangelists have presented the same or other things, and where they have presented material distinctive to themselves—he may easily confirm the reading he has found from the indication of the number.

We pray the holy and most blessed Trinity to deem it worthy to instruct us [Col. 0255A] in the truth of its Scriptures and to grant us the grace of discernment, so that, like excellent money-changers, we may test everything according to Paul (1 Thess. 5:21) and pursue what is good.

# The Gospel Harmony of Ammonius of Alexandria, interpreted by Victor, Bishop of Capua

[Col. 0255]

## Preface

**Luke 1:1–4.** Since many have undertaken to set in order an account of the events fulfilled among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word handed them down to us, it seemed good to me also, having followed everything from the beginning, to write it out carefully and in order for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may recognize the truth of those words in which you have been instructed.

## Chapter One. In the beginning was the Word, God with God, through whom all things were made

**John 1:1–5.** In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

## Chapter Two. Concerning the priesthood of Zechariah

**Luke 1:5–25.** There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and his wife was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. Both were righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without reproach. They had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.

Now it happened, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, that according to the custom of the priesthood he was chosen by lot to offer incense, and he entered the temple of the Lord. The whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.

Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. But the angel said to him: “Do not fear, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard; and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. He will be joy and gladness to you, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord; he will drink neither wine nor strong drink. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. He himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers toward children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfected people.”

And Zechariah said to the angel: “How shall I know this? For I *am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.” [Col. 0256A] The angel answered and said to him: “I am Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and announce this good news to you. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their proper time.”

The people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered that he was delaying in the temple. When he came out, he was unable to speak to them. They understood that he had seen a vision in the temple. He was making signs to them and remained mute.

When the days of his service had been completed, he went to his home. After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she kept herself hidden for five months, saying: “Thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to remove my reproach among people.”

## Chapter Three. The angel Gabriel speaks to Mary

**Luke 1:26–56.** In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.

The angel entered to her and said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” When she heard this, she was troubled by his saying and considered what sort of greeting this might be.

And the angel* said: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

Mary said to the angel: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” The angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.

“And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word is impossible with God.”

Mary said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her.

Mary then rose in those days and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah. She entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And it happened that when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb. Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out with a loud voice, saying to her:

“Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And from where does this happen to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy. *And blessed is she who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord will be fulfilled.”

And Mary said:

“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed, because he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. And his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him.

“He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart. He has brought down the powerful from their throne and exalted the lowly. He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty. He has received Israel his servant, remembering his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.”

Mary remained with her for about three months, and she returned to her own home.

## Chapter Four. Concerning the birth of John the Baptist

**Luke 1:57–80.** Now Elizabeth’s time to give birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son. Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.

On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zechariah. But his mother answered and said: “Not at all; he shall be called John.” They said to her: “There is no one among your relatives who is called by this name.”

They made signs to his father, asking what he wished him to be called. He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, saying: “John is his name.” And they all marveled.

Immediately his mouth and his tongue were opened, and he spoke, blessing God. Fear came upon all their neighbors, and throughout all the hill country of Judea all these things were being spoken of. All who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: “What, do you suppose, will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him.

His father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying:

“Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people. And he has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from ancient times:

“‘Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, to show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us that, delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, we might serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

“‘And you, child, shall be called prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people for the forgiveness of their sins, through the tender mercies of our God, by which the Dayspring from on high has visited us, to enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.’”

The child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and he was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.

## Chapter Five. Concerning the genealogy, or birth, of Christ

**Matthew 1:1–16.** The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.

Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac begot Jacob; Jacob begot Judah and his brothers. Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon; Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab; Boaz begot Obed by Ruth. Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot David the king.

David the king begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s wife. Solomon begot Rehoboam; Rehoboam begot *Abijah; Abijah begot Asa; Asa begot Jehoshaphat; Jehoshaphat begot Joram; Joram begot Uzziah; Uzziah begot Jotham; Jotham begot Ahaz; Ahaz begot Hezekiah; Hezekiah begot Manasseh; Manasseh begot Amon; Amon begot Josiah; Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the Babylonian deportation.

After the Babylonian deportation, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel; Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel; Zerubbabel begot Abiud; Abiud begot Eliakim; Eliakim begot Azor; Azor begot Zadok; Zadok begot Achim; Achim begot Eliud; Eliud begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Matthan; Matthan begot Jacob; Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.

**Luke 3:34–38.** Abraham was the son of Terah; Terah was the son of Nahor; Nahor was the son of Serug; Serug was the son of Reu; Reu was the son of Peleg; Peleg was the son of Eber; Eber was the son of Shelah; Shelah was the son of Cainan; Cainan was the son of Arphaxad; Arphaxad was the son of Shem; Shem was the son of Noah; Noah was the son of Lamech; Lamech was the son of Methuselah; Methuselah was the son of Enoch; Enoch was the son of Jared; Jared was the son of Mahalalel; Mahalalel was the son of Kenan; Kenan was the son of Enosh; Enosh was the son of Seth; Seth was the son of Adam; Adam was the son of God.

**Matthew 1:17–25.** Thus all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the Babylonian deportation, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian deportation to Christ, fourteen generations.

Now the birth of Christ was as follows. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly.

While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”

All this happened so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled:

“Behold, a virgin shall have a child in her womb and shall bear a son; and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is translated, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14).

When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and he took his wife. He did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son; and he called his name Jesus.

**Luke 2:1–7.** It happened in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. This registration was the first, when Quirinius was governor of Syria. And everyone went to register, each to his own city.

Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant.

While they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth. And she bore her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger, because there was no place *for him in the lodging-place.

## Chapter Six. The angel appeared to the shepherds

**Luke 2:7–20.** There were shepherds in that same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them, and they were afraid with great fear.

The angel said to them: “Do not fear. Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

When the angels had departed from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has happened, which the Lord has shown us.”

They came hastening and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger. When they saw him, they recognized the saying that had been told them about this child. All who had heard it marveled at the things that had been told them by the shepherds.

But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for everything they had heard and seen, just as it had been told them.

## Chapter Seven. The Lord’s circumcision. Jesus is brought into the temple

**Luke 2:21–39.** When the eight days were completed for the circumcision of the child, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

When the days of her purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled (Leviticus 12:6), they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exodus 13:2); and to offer a sacrifice, as it is said in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Leviticus 12:8).

And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. He had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

He came in the Spirit into the temple. When his parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him according to the custom of the law, he also took him into his arms, blessed God, and said:

“Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.”

His father and mother were marveling at the things that were being said about him. Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother:

“Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed. And a sword will pierce your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

There was also Anna the prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. She was a widow until eighty-four years of age; she did not leave the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day.

Arriving at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of *Jerusalem.

When they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.

## Chapter Eight. Concerning the Magi who came from the East

**Matthew 2:1–12.** When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem [Note: [Col. 0259] As in the current text, *τῆς Ἰουδαίας* (“of Judea”); likewise shortly afterward, below, verse 5. The Vulgate has *Juda*.] of Judea, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying:

“Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.”

When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. Gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born. They said to him*:

“In Bethlehem of Judea. For thus it is written through the prophet: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the leaders of Judah; for from you will go forth a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel’” (Micah 5:2).

Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. He sent them to Bethlehem and said: “Go and inquire carefully about the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.”

When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood above where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with *very great joy.

Entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshiped him. Opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

Having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own region by another way.

## Chapter Nine. Jesus and his parents flee into Egypt

**Matthew 2:13–15.** When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying:

“Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod is going to seek the child in order to destroy him.”

He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt. He remained there until the death of Herod, so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled:

“From Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1).

## Chapter Ten. Herod kills the children

**Matthew 2:16–18.** Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, became exceedingly angry. He sent and killed all the children who were in Bethlehem and throughout all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had learned from the Magi.

Then what had been spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great wailing: Rachel weeping for her children; and she did not wish to be comforted, because they are not” (Jeremiah 31:15).

## Chapter Eleven. Jesus is recalled from Egypt

**Matthew 2:19–23.** When Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying:

“Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Judah, for those who sought the child’s life have died.”

He rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. When he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. Having been warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee.

When he came, he settled in a city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Isaiah 11:1).

[Note: [Col. 0261D] I suspect this to be an error by the interpreter or by a copyist engaged in something else. The Greek is *εἰς γῆν Ἰσραὴλ* (“into the land of Israel”), as in the Vulgate.]

## Chapter Twelve. Jesus remains in the temple at Jerusalem

**Luke 2:40–52.** The child grew and became strong, full of wisdom; and the grace of God was in him.

His parents went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover. When he was twelve years old, and they had gone up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, after the days had been completed, as they were returning, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.

Supposing him to be in the company, they traveled a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances. When they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem in search of him.

After three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them. All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers. When they saw him, they were amazed.

His mother said to him: “My son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow.”

He said to them: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

But they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them. His mother kept all these words in her heart.

And Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and favor with God and human beings.

## Chapter Thirteen. John the Baptist appears in Israel

**Luke 3:1–3.** In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the desert.

He came into the entire region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, saying:

**Matthew 3:1–3; Mark 1:3–5.** “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. For this is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, saying—”

**Luke 3:4–6.** “The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low. The crooked places shall become straight, and the rough ways into smooth paths; and all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40:3–5).

**John 1:5–18.** He came for testimony, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light.

The true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world, was present. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.

But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name: who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God.

And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

John bears witness about him and cries out, saying: “This was he of whom I said to you—” [Note: [Col. 0261D] The final word is missing both in the text and in the Vulgate. [Col. 0262D] Moreover, in Mill’s *Codex Cantabrigiensis* there is *εἶπον ὑμῖν* (“I said to you”). But *ὑμῖν* (“to you”) is written above by another hand. See the most recent edition of Wetstein on this passage.] “*because he is to come after me and has come before me, because he was prior to me.”

From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.

**Matthew 3:4–10; Mark 1:6; Luke 3:7–9.** John himself had a garment of camel hair and a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.

Then Jerusalem, all Judea, and the whole region around the Jordan went out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.

When he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them:

“Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance. And do not think of saying within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Indeed, the ax has already been laid at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

**Luke 3:10–15.** The crowds asked him, saying: “What then shall we do?”

He answered and said to them: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none; and let the one who has food do likewise.”

Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him: “Teacher, what shall we do?”

He said to them: “Do nothing more than what has been appointed for you.”

The soldiers also asked him, saying: “And what shall we do?”

He said to them: “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay.”

While the people were expecting, and all were wondering in their hearts about John, whether perhaps he himself was the Christ—

**John 1:19–25.** The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him to ask him: “Who are you?”

He confessed and did not deny; he confessed: “I am not the Christ.”

They asked him: “What then? Are you Elijah?”

He said: “I am not.”

“Are you the prophet?”

He answered: “No.”

Then they said to him: “Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?”

He said: “I am the voice of one crying in the desert: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said” (Isaiah 40:3).

Those who had been sent were from the Pharisees. They asked him and said: “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”

John answered them, saying—

**Matthew 3:11–12; Mark 1:7–8; Luke 3:16–18; John 1:26–27.** “*I indeed baptize you in water, for repentance. But the one who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. In your midst has stood one whom you do not know. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather his wheat into the granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

With many other exhortations he also proclaimed the good news to the people.

**John 1:28.** These things happened in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

## Chapter Fourteen. Jesus is baptized by John
**MATTHEW III, 13–17; MARK I, 9–11.** Then Jesus came [Col. 0264A] from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.—**LUKE III, 23.** And he himself was beginning, about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph. But John prevented him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” But Jesus answered and said to him: “Allow it for the present; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him.—**LUKE III, 21–22.** Now when all the people were being baptized, and Jesus having been baptized and praying, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending in bodily form like a dove, and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I have been well pleased.”—**JOHN I, 32–34.** And John bore witness, saying: “Because [Note: [Col. 0263] The Vulgate: ‘Because I saw . . . upon whom you shall see.’ Nor is the Greek otherwise.] you saw the Spirit descending like a dove [Col. 0264B] from heaven, and it remained upon him; and I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ I saw, and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

## CHAPTER XV. Jesus Was Led by the Spirit into the Wilderness

**MATTHEW IV, 1–11; MARK I, 12–13; LUKE IV, 1–13.** Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry. And the tempter approached and said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.” But he answered and said: “It is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word [Col. 0264C] that proceeds from the mouth of God’” (Deuteronomy VIII, 4).

Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple, and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they shall bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone’” (Psalm XC, 11). The Lord said to him: “Again it is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’” (Deuteronomy VI, 16).

Again the devil took him onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” Then Jesus said to him: “Go away, Satan; for it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (ibid., 23).—**LUKE IV, 13.** And when every temptation had been completed, the devil then left [Col. 0264D] him until a time.—**MARK I, 13.** And he was with the wild beasts. And behold, angels came and ministered to him.

## CHAPTER XVI. Two Disciples of John Followed Jesus

**JOHN I, 35–42.** The next day John was again standing, and two of his disciples were with him. And looking at Jesus as he walked, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” And the two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus. Then Jesus turned, and seeing them following him, said to them: “What do you seek?” They said to him: “Rabbi”—which is translated “Teacher”—“where do you live?” He said to them: “Come and see.” [Col. 0265A] They came and saw where he lived, and remained with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.

Now Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who had heard John and followed him. He first found his own brother Simon, and said to him: “We have found the Messiah”—which is translated “Christ.” And he brought him to Jesus. Looking at him, Jesus said: “You are Simon, son of John [Note: [Col. 0265D] Greek, Ἰωνᾶ (*Iōna*). Other copies, Ἰωάννου (*Iōannou*). See Mill, both here and at Matthew XVI, 17, who also adduces the reading *Joanna* from ancient Latin Fathers. St. Jerome, on this passage: “They wish it to have been corrupted through the fault of scribes, so that instead of *Bar Joanno*, that is, ‘son of John,’ *Barjona* was written, with one syllable removed.”]; you shall be called Cephas”—which is translated “Peter.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Philip and Nathanael

**JOHN I, 43–51.** The next day he wished to depart for Galilee. And he found Philip, and Jesus said to him: “Follow me.” Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.

Philip found Nathanael and said to him: “We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the Prophets: Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth.” And Nathanael said: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Philip said to him: “Come and see.”

Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said concerning him: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” Nathanael said to him: “How do you know me?” Jesus answered and said to him: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”

Nathanael answered him and said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” Jesus answered and said to him: “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ you believe? You shall see greater things than these.” And he said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending [Note: [Col. 0266D] So the printed copies of the Victorine interpretation read, omitting through either scribal or typographical carelessness, ‘and descending,’ which is found both in the Greek New Testament and in the versions.] above the Son of Man.”

— **LUKE IV, 14–15.** And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and news about him went out [Col. 0265C] throughout the entire region. And he taught in their synagogues, and was glorified by all.
