Then they approached, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him. But those who were around him, seeing what was about to happen, said to him: “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”

—JOHN 18:10, 11. Therefore Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.

Then Jesus said to Peter: “Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? Put the sword into its sheath. For all who take up [Col. 0346C] the sword will perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen this way? Let it be thus far.”

And when he had touched his ear, he healed him. At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “As against a robber, you have come out with swords and clubs to seize me. Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.”

Now all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples, abandoning him, fled.

—JOHN 18:12–14. The cohort, the tribune, and the officers of the Jews therefore seized Jesus and bound him, and led him first to Annas; for he was [*autem, “however”] the father-in-law of Caiaphas, [Col. 0346D] who was high priest that year. Now Caiaphas was the one who had given the counsel to the Jews: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people.”

## CHAPTER CLXII. A certain young man, dressed in a linen cloth, followed Jesus.

MARK 14:51, 52. A certain young man was following him, clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he, leaving the linen cloth behind, fled from them naked.

—JOHN 18:15–18; MATTHEW 26:58–69, 70; MARK 14:54; LUKE 22:54–57. Simon Peter was following Jesus from a distance, and another disciple, as far as the court of the high priest. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus [Col. 0347A] into the high priest’s court.

But Peter was standing outside at the door. Therefore the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in. When the maidservant who kept the door saw him sitting by the firelight and had looked at him, she said: “Are you also one of this man’s disciples?”

He said: “Woman, I do not know him, nor do I know what you are saying.”

Now the servants and officers were standing by charcoal fires, because it was cold, and warming themselves. Peter was also standing with them and warming himself, to see the outcome.

## CHAPTER CLXIII. The high priest questions Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.

JOHN 18:19–27; MATTHEW 26:71–75; MARK 14:66–72; LUKE 22:55–62. Therefore the high priest [Col. 0347B] questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.

Jesus answered him: “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gather, and I have said nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said.”

When he had said these things, one of the officers standing nearby struck Jesus on the cheek, saying: “Is this how you answer the high priest?”

Jesus answered him: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?”

And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

Now Simon Peter was outside in the court, standing and warming himself. Another maidservant saw him again and said to those standing around: “This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.”

Those who were standing there approached and said to Peter [Col. 0347C]: “Truly you are also one of them, for your speech makes it evident that you are a Galilean.”

And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.”

And after a little while, about an hour, one of the high priest’s servants, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said: “Truly this man also was with him, for he is a Galilean. Did I not see you in the garden with him?”

Then he began to curse and swear: “I neither know him nor know what you are saying. I do not know this man whom you mention.”

And immediately the cock crowed. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord * which he had said to him: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” And going outside, he wept bitterly.

## CHAPTER CLXIV. [Col. 0347D] False witnesses were sought against Jesus.

MATTHEW 27:1; 26:59–63; MARK 14:55–61. When morning came, all the chief priests, together with the elders of the people and the scribes, gathered and held a council. They sought false testimony against Jesus, in order to hand him over to death; and they did not find any, although many false witnesses came forward. Nor were they finding any, for their testimonies were not consistent.

Finally two false witnesses came forward and said: “We heard him say: ‘I can destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days build another not made with hands.’”

But Jesus was silent. And the high priest, rising in the [Col. 0348A] midst, questioned Jesus, saying: “Do you answer nothing to the things that these men testify against you?”

But Jesus answered nothing.

## CHAPTER CLXV. The high priest adjures Jesus, saying: “If you are the Christ, tell us.”

MATTHEW 26:63–68; MARK 14:61–65; LUKE 22:66–71. And again the high priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the blessed God.”

Jesus said to him: “You have said it.” And he said to them: “If I tell you, you will not believe me; but if I also question you, you will not answer me, nor release me. Nevertheless, I tell you: from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven.”

Then the high priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. [Col. 0348B] Why do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy from his mouth. What is your judgment?”

And they answered: “He is liable to death.”

Then they spat in his face; and those who held him mocked him, covered his face, and struck him with blows. Others struck him in the face with their palms, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is the one who struck you?”

And, blaspheming him in many other ways, they said many things against him.

## CHAPTER CLXVI. Jesus is handed over to Pilate; and Judas repents.

*[The supplied source ends here.]*
MATTHEW 27:2–10; MARK 15:1; LUKE 23:1. And they led him away bound into the praetorium and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor. —JOHN 18:28. And they themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover.

[Col. 0348C] Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by remorse, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” But they said: “What is that to us? You see to it.” And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he withdrew; and going away, he hanged himself with a noose. But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said: “It is not lawful to put them into the *corban*, because it is the price of blood.” And having taken counsel, they bought with them the potter’s field, for the burial of foreigners. For this reason that field was called *Acheldemach*, that is, “Field of Blood,” to this day. Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose price had been assessed, whom they assessed from the children of Israel; and they gave them for the potter’s field, just as the Lord appointed for me” (Zech. 11:12).

## CHAPTER CLXVII. Pilate hears the Jews’ accusation against the Lord and sends him to Herod.

JOHN 18:29–30. Therefore Pilate went outside to them and said: “What accusation do you bring against this man?” They answered and said to him: “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.” —LUKE 23:12. “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” —JOHN 18:31–38.

[Col. 0349A] Therefore Pilate said: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Jews therefore said to him: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone”—so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he had spoken (Matt. 20:19), signifying by what death he was going to die.

Therefore Pilate entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him: —MATTHEW 27:11; MARK 15:2; LUKE 23:3. “Are you the king of the Jews?” And Jesus answered: “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others tell you about me?” Pilate answered: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and your chief priests* have handed you over to me. What have you done?”

Jesus answered: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not from here.”

Therefore Pilate said to him: “So you are a king?” Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.”

Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” And having said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to the chief priests and the crowds: “I find no cause* in the man.”

—LUKE 23:5–18. But they became more insistent, saying: “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee and reaching even here.” When Pilate heard “Galilee,” he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he was under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him back to Herod, who himself was also in Jerusalem in those days.

But when Herod saw Jesus, he rejoiced greatly. For he had long wished to see him, because he had heard many things about him and hoped to see some sign performed by him. He questioned him with many words, but he answered him nothing. The chief priests and scribes also stood there, vehemently accusing him.

But Herod, with his soldiers, despised him and mocked him. Having clothed him in a white garment, he sent him back to Pilate. And Herod and Pilate became friends with one another on that day; for previously they had been enemies.

But Pilate, having summoned the chief priests, the magistrates, and the people, went out to them and said: “You brought me this man as one who was turning away* the people. Behold, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no cause in him in regard to the charges you bring against him. Nor did Herod; for I sent you to him, and behold, nothing deserving death has been done. Therefore, after chastising him, I will release him.”

But the whole crowd cried out, saying: “Take this man away; crucify him, crucify him!”

—JOHN 19:6–15. Pilate said to them: “Take him yourselves and crucify him. For I find no cause in him.” The Jews answered him: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid. And he entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer. Therefore Pilate said to him: “You do not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you, and authority to release you?”

Jesus answered: “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

From then on Pilate sought to release him. But the Jews cried out, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone* who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”

Therefore, when Pilate heard these statements, he brought Jesus outside and sat down on the tribunal, at the place called the Pavement, but in Hebrew *Gabbatha*. It was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jews: “Behold your king.”

But they cried out: “Away, away with him; crucify him!” Pilate said to them: “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered: “We have no king except Caesar.”

—MATTHEW 27:12–18; MARK 15:3–10. And the chief priests accused him of many things, but Jesus answered nothing. Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor marveled greatly.

Now on the feast day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner, whomever they requested. At that time he had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Therefore, when they had gathered, Pilate said to them: —JOHN 18:39. “It is your custom that I release one prisoner to you at the Passover. Whom then do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.

## CHAPTER CLXVIII. Pilate’s wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man.”

MATTHEW 27:19–25; MARK 15:11–14; LUKE 23:17–23. While he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.”

[Col. 0350C] But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them: “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” And they said: “Barabbas.”

—JOHN 18:40. Now Barabbas was a robber. He had been imprisoned because of a certain insurrection that had occurred in the city and because of murder.

Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said: “Let him be crucified.” The governor said to them: “Why, what evil has he done?” But they cried out even more, saying: “Let him be crucified.”

When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that rather a riot was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you see to it.” And the whole people answered and said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

[Col. 0350D]

## CHAPTER CLXIX. Pilate released Barabbas and handed Jesus over to be crucified.

MATTHEW 27:26–32; MARK 15:15–21; LUKE 23:24–31; JOHN 19. Then he released Barabbas to them; but after scourging Jesus, he handed him over to them to be crucified.

And the governor’s soldiers, taking Jesus into the praetorium, gathered the whole cohort around him. And stripping him, they clothed him in a purple tunic and wrapped a scarlet cloak around him. And twisting together a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head and a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: “Hail, king of the Jews.”

[Col. 0351A] And spitting on him, they took the reed and struck his head. And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak and the purple garment, clothed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him, carrying his cross.

As they went out, they found a Cyrenian man coming from the countryside, named Simon, the father of Alexander and Rufus. They compelled him to carry the cross behind Jesus.

A large crowd of the people followed him, and women who were mourning and lamenting him. But Jesus, turning toward them, said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children. For behold, days are coming in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not nurse.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us’; and to the hills: ‘Cover us.’ For if they do these things with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?”

[Col. 0351B]

## CHAPTER CLXX. Two robbers are led with Christ to be crucified. And Jesus on the cross entrusts his mother to John and John to his mother. Given vinegar to drink, after all is completed, he gives up his spirit.

LUKE 23:32–34. And two other criminals were also led with him to be put to death.

—MATTHEW 27:33–37; MARK 15:22–26. And after they came to the place called Golgotha, which is interpreted as “Place of the Skull,” they crucified him there. And they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink; and when he had tasted it, he did not wish to drink.

But Jesus was saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

—JOHN 19:19–24. After they had crucified him, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, a part for each soldier, and also the tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. Therefore they said to one another: “Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be.” So that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Ps. 21:19). The soldiers indeed did these things.

And sitting down, they kept watch over him. Pilate also wrote an inscription concerning his charge and placed it above his head: “This is Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.” Many of the Jews read this inscription, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. And it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

[Col. 0351D] Therefore the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written.”

—MATTHEW 27:38–44; MARK 15:27–32; LUKE 23:35–43. Then they crucified two robbers with him, one on his right and the other on his left.

Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will see and believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him—for he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’”

[Col. 0352A] One of the robbers who were hanging there also blasphemed him, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” But the other answered and rebuked him, saying: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.”

And he said to Jesus: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” And Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise.”

—JOHN 19:25–27. Now standing beside the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Therefore, when Jesus saw his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he said to his mother: “Woman, behold your son.” Then he said to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own household.

—MATTHEW 27:45–50; MARK 15:33–37; LUKE 23:44–46. Now from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani” (Ps. 21:2), which is interpreted: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Some of those standing there and hearing this said: “This man is calling Elijah.”

—JOHN 19:28–30. Afterward, knowing that all things had now been completed, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled (Ps. 68:22), Jesus said: “I thirst.” Now a vessel full of vinegar had been set there. And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him to drink.

When Jesus had received the vinegar*, he said: “It is finished.”

[Col. 0352C] But the others were saying: “Leave him; let us see whether Elijah comes to free him.” Then Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

—MATTHEW 27:51–54; MARK 15:38–39; LUKE 23:47–48. And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. And the earth quaked, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose. And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many.

But the centurion and those who were with him guarding Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, glorifying God and saying: “Truly this man was righteous; he was the Son of God.”

[Col. 0352D] And the entire crowd of those who were present together for this spectacle and saw what was happening returned, beating their breasts.

—MATTHEW 27:55–56; MARK 15:40–41; LUKE 23:49. All his acquaintances stood at a distance, and many women who had followed him from Galilee and had come up with him to Jerusalem. Among them were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joseph, and Salome, the mother of the sons of Zebedee—who, when he was in Galilee, followed him—seeing these things.

—JOHN 19:31–36. Therefore, because it was the Preparation, so that the bodies might not remain on the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day—the Jews asked Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away.

Therefore the soldiers came. They first broke the legs of one and of the other who had been crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, seeing that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out.

And the one who saw it has testified, and his testimony is true. And he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you may believe. For these things happened so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “You shall not break a bone of him” (Exod. 12:46; Num. 9:12). And again another Scripture says: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10).

## CHAPTER CLXXI. Joseph asks Pilate for the body of Jesus and buries him together with Nicodemus.

MATTHEW 27:57–61; MARK 15:42–47; LUKE 23:50–56; JOHN 19:38–42. When evening had come, there came a certain rich man, a noble decurion from the city of Arimathea in Judea, named Joseph, a good and righteous man, who himself was also a secret disciple of Jesus because of fear of the Jews, and who himself was awaiting the kingdom of God. He had not consented to their counsel and actions.

He approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. But Pilate wondered whether he had already died; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. And when he had learned this*, he ordered the body to be returned.

Nicodemus also came—the one who had first come to Jesus by night—bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. They took the body of Jesus and bound him in linen cloths with spices, as is the custom of the Jews in burying.

Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been placed. Joseph laid him there and rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb, and departed.

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. They saw how his body had been placed. And returning, they prepared spices and ointments, so that when they came they might anoint him. But on the Sabbath they remained silent according to the commandment.

## CHAPTER CLXXII. The Jews seal the tomb.

MATTHEW 27:62–66. On the next day, which is after the Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver, while still alive, said: ‘After three days I will rise again.’ Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples perhaps come and steal him and say to the people: ‘He has risen from the dead’; and the last deception will be worse than the first.”

Pilate said to them: “You have a guard; go, secure it as you know how.” And they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone together with the guards.

## CHAPTER CLXXIII. On the first day of the Sabbath, Jesus rises from the dead.

MATTHEW 28:1–8; MARK 16:1–8; LUKE 24:1–9; JOHN 20:1. In the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the Sabbath was dawning, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene, the other Mary, and Salome came to the tomb, carrying the spices they had prepared. And when the sun had already risen, they said to one another: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” For it was very large.

And behold, a great earthquake occurred. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, approached, and rolled away the stone. And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, and an angel sitting upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.

Because of fear of him, the guards were terrified and became like dead men. But the angel answered and said to the women: “Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord had been laid.”

[Col. 0354B] And while they were greatly astonished in mind at this, behold, two men stood beside them in shining garments. When they were afraid and inclined their faces toward the ground, they said to them: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee, saying: ‘The Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinners, and be crucified, and rise on the third day.’”

“And going quickly, tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead. And behold, he will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him. Behold, I have told you.”

And they remembered his words. And they went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples.

—JOHN 20:2–17; LUKE 24:12. Therefore Mary Magdalene ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: “They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”

Therefore Peter and that other disciple went out and came to the tomb. Now the two were running together, and that other disciple ran ahead more quickly than Peter and came first to the tomb. And bending down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter.

Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been over his head, not lying with the linen cloths but separately, rolled up in one place.

Then that other disciple who had first come to the tomb also entered, and he saw and believed. For they did not yet understand the Scriptures, that he must rise from the dead. Therefore the disciples went away again to their own homes.

—MARK 16:9. But Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons, stood outside at the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.

They said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them: “Because they have taken my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”

When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus*. Jesus said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?”

Supposing that he was the gardener, she said to him: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him.” Jesus said to her: “Mary.”

Turning, she said to him: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.” Jesus said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”

## CHAPTER CLXXIV. The guards of the tomb announced Christ’s resurrection to the priests.

MATTHEW 28:11–15. And behold, some of the guards came into the city and announced to the chief priests everything that had happened. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping. And if this reaches the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and make you secure.”

But they, having received the money, did as they had been instructed. And this report was spread among the Jews to this day.

## CHAPTER CLXXV. Jesus appeared to the women after the resurrection.

MATTHEW 28:9–10; MARK 16:10–11; LUKE 24:10–11. And behold, Jesus met them, saying: “Greetings.” They approached, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.

Then Jesus said to them: “Do not be afraid. Go, announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee; there they will see me.”

When they had gone away, they announced all these things to the eleven who were mourning and weeping, and to all the others who had been with him. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by them, they did not believe them. And these words appeared to them as delirium, and they did not believe them.

## CHAPTER CLXXVI. Jesus appeared to two men going to a village.

MARK 16:12. After this, he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking—LUKE 24:13–35—to a village that was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus, on that very day.

And they were speaking with one another about all the things that had happened. And it came to pass, while they were talking and questioning one another, that Jesus himself, drawing near, went with them. But their eyes were restrained, so that they would not recognize him.

And he said to them: “What are these words that you are discussing with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?”

And one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answered and said to him: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem and do not know the things that have happened there in these days?”

To whom he said: “What things?” And they said: “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to condemnation to death and crucified him.

“But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And now, besides all these things, today is the third day since these things happened.

“But also some women from among us terrified us. They were at the tomb before dawn, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive.

“And some of our people went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said; but they did not find him.”

And he said to them: “O foolish men and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?”

And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

And they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he* pretended to be going farther. And they urged him, saying: “Remain with us, because it is toward evening and the day has already declined.” And he entered with them.

And it came to pass, while he was reclining with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and handed it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.

[Col. 0356B] And they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he was speaking on the way and opening the Scriptures to us?”

And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven gathered together and those who were with them, saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.” And they themselves recounted what had happened on the way and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.

## CHAPTER CLXXVII. Jesus appeared to his disciples.

MARK 16:13. Nor did they believe them. —LUKE 24:36–48. While they were speaking these things, —JOHN 20:19–23, when it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst and said to them: “Peace be with you. It is I; do not be afraid.”

But they were disturbed and terrified, supposing that they saw a spirit. And he said to them: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.”

And when he had said this, he showed them his hands, feet, and side. But while they still did not believe and were marveling for joy, he said: “Do you have anything here to eat?” They offered him part of a broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took the leftovers and gave them to them.

And he said to them: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”

Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures. And he said to them: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

“You are witnesses of these things. And I send the promise of my Father upon you.”

Therefore the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. Then he said to them again: “Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, I also send you.”

When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose you retain, they are retained.”

## CHAPTER CLXXVIII. Jesus appeared to Thomas.

[Col. 0357A]

JOHN 20:24–31. But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. Therefore the other disciples said to him: “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, while the doors were closed, and stood in the midst and said: “Peace be with you.”

Then he said to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing.”

Thomas answered and said to him: “My Lord and my God.”

[Col. 0357B] Jesus said to him: “Because you have seen me*, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus* is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life* in his name.

## CHAPTER CLXXIX. He appeared again to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias.

JOHN 21:1–14. After this he manifested himself again* at the Sea of Tiberias. He manifested himself in this way.

Simon Peter, Thomas who is called Didymus, Nathanael who was from Cana of Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together. Simon Peter said to them: “I am going fishing.” They said to him: “We are coming with you.”

And they went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing*. But when morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.

Therefore Jesus said to them: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” They answered him: “No.” Therefore he said to them: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” They cast it, therefore, and now they were not able* to haul it in because of the quantity of fish.

Therefore the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: “It is the Lord.” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded his tunic around himself—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea.

But the other disciples came in the boat—for they were not far from land, about two hundred cubits—dragging the net of fish. Therefore when they came down onto the land, they saw burning coals laid out, and fish placed upon them, and bread.

[Col. 0357D] Jesus said to them: “Bring some of the fish that you have caught* now.” Simon Peter went up and dragged the net onto the land, full of large fish, one hundred fifty-three. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.

Jesus said to them: “Come, eat breakfast.” And none of those reclining dared ask him: “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord.

And Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.

## CHAPTER CLXXX. Jesus says three times to Peter: “Do you love (*diligis*) me?”

JOHN 21:15–25. Therefore, when they had eaten, Jesus said to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love (*diligis*) me more than these?”

He said to him: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him: “Feed my lambs.”

Again he said to him: “Simon, son of John, do you love (*diligis*) me?” He said to him: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him: “Feed my lambs.”

He said to him a third time: “Simon, son of John, do you love (*amas*) me?” Peter was saddened because he had said to him a third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.” He said to him: “Feed my sheep.”

“Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.”

But he said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God. And when he had said this, he said to him: “Follow me.”

Peter, turning, saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following—the one who also reclined at the supper upon his breast [Col. 0358B] and said: “Lord, who is the one who will betray you?” Therefore, when Peter had seen him, he said to Jesus: “Lord, and what about this man?”

Jesus said to him: “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.”

Therefore this saying went out among the brothers, that that disciple would not die. But Jesus did not say to him, “He will not die,” but: “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?”

This is the disciple* who testified* concerning these things and wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true. But there are also many other things that Jesus did, which, if they were written down individually, I do not think that even the world itself could contain the books that would have to be written.

## CHAPTER CLXXXI. The disciples, going to Galilee, saw and worshiped the Lord. And he was taken up into heaven before them.

[Col. 0358C]

MATTHEW 28:16–20. The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And seeing him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.

—MARK 16:14–20. And he reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen.

And he said to them: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe everything whatsoever I have commanded you.

“And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

“And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

—LUKE 24:49–53. “But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

And he led them out as far as Bethany; and lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And it came to pass, while he was blessing them, that he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven, and he sits at the right hand of God.

And they, worshiping him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy. And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. And they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the accompanying signs.

[Col. 0359]

## FROM THE CATENA ON THE FOUR GOSPELS, TRANSLATED INTO LATIN BY VICTOR OF CAPUA

[Col. 0359] VICTOR, BISHOP OF CAPUA, FROM THE ANSWERS OF THE CHAPTERS OF SAINT POLYCARP, BISHOP OF SMYRNA, DISCIPLE OF JOHN THE EVANGELIST.

FRAGMENTS OF THE ANSWERS OF THE DIVINE POLYCARP, BISHOP AND MARTYR OF SMYRNA, ONCE A DISCIPLE OF THE BLESSED JOHN THE EVANGELIST.

[Col. 0359A] Matthew testifies that the Lord said (chap. 19:5) what Moses writes (Gen. 2:24), that Adam spoke in this manner: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; for this reason a man will leave father and mother,” and so forth.

But the Lord’s words agree with the words of Moses. Adam, performing his office by divine inspiration, prophesied; and he is reported by Moses himself to have spoken this. But God, who by divine inspiration formed these words in Adam’s heart, is rightly reported by the Lord the Father to have spoken them. For Adam also uttered this prophecy; and the Father, who inspired him, is rightly said to have uttered it.

THE SAME, ON THESE WORDS OF CHRIST: “You will drink my cup,” and so forth. Matthew 20.

By this kind of drink he signifies the Passion. James, indeed, was destined to be consummated last by martyrdom (Acts XII, 2), whereas his brother John would pass over without martyrdom, although he endured very many afflictions and exiles; but Christ judged a mind prepared for martyrdom to be a martyr. For the Apostle Paul says: “I die daily” (I Corinthians XV, 31), since it is impossible for a human being to die daily by the death through which this life ends once and for all. But because he was continually prepared to die for the Gospel, he testified that he died daily in that sense. It is also read (in the Acts) that blessed John was plunged into a cauldron of boiling oil for the name of Christ.

## THE SAME AUTHOR ON THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK

The evangelists reasonably employ different beginnings, although their one and identical intention in preaching the Gospel is evident. Matthew, writing for Hebrews, traced the order of Christ’s genealogy, in order to show that Christ descended from that lineage concerning which all the prophets had sung that he would be born. John, however, addressing those established at Ephesus, who, as Gentiles, were ignorant of the Law, took the beginning of his Gospel from the cause of our redemption. This cause is apparent from the fact that God willed his Son to become incarnate for our salvation. Luke, on the other hand, begins with the priesthood of Zechariah, so that through the miraculous birth of his son and the ministry of so great a preacher he might declare Christ’s divinity to the Gentiles. Hence Mark also, in accordance with the ancient mystery of prophecy, declares the coming of Christ, so that his preaching might be shown to be not new but proclaimed in ancient times. Or perhaps the evangelists took care to use that opening which each judged his hearers to require. Therefore nothing contradictory is found where, though the writings are different, they nevertheless arrive at the same homeland.

## THE SAME AUTHOR ON THE WORDS: “Do not invite your friends, but the poor and the crippled,” etc. (Luke XIV, 12)

[Col. 0360B]

He commanded that not friends, but every kind of infirm person, should be invited to dinner. But if a cripple or any other such person happens to be a friend, he must certainly not be invited merely on account of friendship; thus the commands themselves seem almost to oppose one another. For if not friends but the lame and blind are to be invited, and these too happen to be friends, we ought by no means to invite them. But, I think, by “friends” in this passage we should understand those whom we love for the sake of this world’s earthly concerns, not for the sake of the contemplation of divine things. These, therefore, are the friends who must be left aside. Finally, he proposed the examples of the infirm because we can desire them for no necessity of business whatsoever, but only for the fruit of eternal recompense.

## THE SAME AUTHOR ON THE WORDS: “I have completed the work which you gave me to do” (John XVII, 4)

[Col. 0360C]

How does he say that he has completed the work of human salvation when he had not yet ascended the standard of the cross? But by the settled purpose of his will—by which he had determined to undergo all the marks of the revered Passion—he rightly signifies that he had completed the work, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0359C] Victor of Capua, a man learned in Greek and Latin, around the year of the Lord 480 revised into Latin, from the Greek copy of the Responses to the Chapters of Blessed Polycarp that he had obtained, the material cited in the above-mentioned manuscript Catena, which I possess and which, when the printers permit, I shall communicate to scholars. It seemed worthwhile to insert and publish it here because, as far as I know, it has not previously been made public. Feuardentius.]

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 551: SAINT NICETIUS, BISHOP OF TRIER

[Col. 0361]

[Col. 0361]

## NOTICE (from Gallandius)

### I

From the records of ancient writers we learn that Nicetius of Trier was everywhere esteemed for the excellence of his virtues and the glory of his miracles. Gregory of Tours commended in writing the remarkable deeds accomplished by him, as reported by his disciple, blessed Aredius [Note: [Col. 0361C] Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 18.]. He is said to have professed the monastic life and then been elevated to govern the Church of Trier by Theodoric, king of the Franks, because, while still presiding over his monastery as abbot, he had been accustomed freely to admonish and rebuke the king when he sinned. Baronius, drawing his account of Nicetius’s ordination from the records of the Church of Trier preserved by Demochare [Note: [Col. 0361C] Demochare, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*.], places it in the year 529 [Note: [Col. 0361C] Baronius, under the year 529, § 14.]. In his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, Cointius writes that Nicetius succeeded Aprunculus in the year 527 [Note: [Col. 0361C] Cointius, under the year 527, § 5, vol. I, p. 351.]. He was later followed by Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0361C] Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, vol. I, p. 185, note a.], Ruinart [Note: [Col. 0361C] Ruinart, on Gregory of Tours, p. 1234.], and the authors of the *Gallic Literary History* [Note: [Col. 0361D] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 391.].

In administering his episcopate, the courage of his spirit shone out above all: for the preservation of the divine law he did not fear the faces of the powerful. He openly rebuked Theodebert, son of King Theodoric, who had often departed from justice and had nurtured the crimes of wicked men by impunity and concealment, and at length brought him back to better conduct. He also rebuked Clotarius, Theodebert’s uncle, quite sharply on account of his incestuous marriage and placed him under ecclesiastical prohibition. By Clotarius’s command he was consequently led into exile, but afterward, in the year 562, he was restored to his see by Sigibert, son of Clotarius, after Clotarius’s death [Note: [Col. 0361D] Cointius, under the year 562, § 27, vol. II, p. 18.].

He took part in the First Council of Arvernus, convened in the year 535 [Note: [Col. 0361D] Councils, vol. V, p. 953, first Venetian–Labbean edition.], as Pagi reports following Cointius [Note: [Col. 0361D] Cointius, at the cited place, vol. I, pp. 439, 443.] [Note: [Col. 0361D] Pagi, under the year 541, § 9.]. He also subscribed to the Fifth Council of Orléans, celebrated at the end of the year 549 [Note: [Col. 0361D] Councils, vol. V, p. 1384.], and shortly afterward to the Second Council of Arvernus in the same year [Note: [Col. 0361D] Councils, ibid., p. 1392.], to which ten bishops subscribed who had shortly before attended the Fifth Synod of Orléans. Finally, his name is found subscribed to the Second Council of Paris [Note: [Col. 0361D] Councils, vol. VI, p. 482.], held around the year 555 at the invitation of King Childebert in the case of Saffarac, bishop of Paris [Col. 0362A]. Cointius, however, assigns it to the year 551 [Note: [Col. 0361D] Cointius, under the year 551, § 5, vol. I, p. 778.].

There are, moreover, countless excellent deeds reported of this most blessed bishop. He finally ended his life around the year 566, as Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0362C] Mabillon, at the cited place, p. 187, note a.] and the writers just mentioned [Note: [Col. 0362C] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 193.] believe, following Cointius [Note: [Col. 0362C] Cointius, under the year 566, § 60, vol. II, p. 84.]. His memory is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on the Nones of December. Among other things, Venantius Fortunatus composed the following verses about him [Note: [Col. 0362C] Venantius Fortunatus, book III, poem 9.]:

> Splendor and summit of faith, Nicetius, revered in mind,  
> Love of the whole world and head of bishops:  
>   
> … Supreme shepherd, surpassing the apostolic fold,  
> You increased by your merits whatever honor you possess.  
>   
> Pressing on with divine work, you leave earthly things;  
> The world dies for you, but you, immortal, remain.

### II

Our excellent bishop is reported by Gregory of Tours to have been born to parents who were most devoted to study and to have been instructed in letters [Note: [Col. 0362C] Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17, § 1.]. Elsewhere Gregory testifies [Note: [Col. 0362C] Idem, *History of the Franks*, book X, chapter 19.] that Nicetius was held in the community to be exceedingly renowned for his admirable eloquence in preaching. The literary works of so great a man that have so far appeared are few, but they nevertheless sufficiently reveal the ardor of his faith, by which he was especially inflamed.

We know of two short works of his published in the preceding century by Dacherius [Note: [Col. 0362D] Dacherius, *Spicilegium*, new edition, vol. I, pp. 221–225.]. In addition, there are two important letters, first published by Freher [Note: [Col. 0362D] Freher, *Frankish History*, vol. I, pp. 189–192.], then by Duchesne [Note: [Col. 0362D] Duchesne, *Frankish Historians*, vol. I, pp. 852–855.], afterward by Sirmond [Note: [Col. 0362D] Sirmond, *Gallican Councils*, vol. I, pp. 310–322.], and finally by Cointius [Note: [Col. 0362D] Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. II, pp. 25 and 80.]; these later passed into the collection of the Councils.

The first work, entitled *On the Vigils of the Servants of God*, which Dacherius presented from an excellent manuscript of Saint-Germain, had long already been published among works falsely attributed to Saint Jerome. This escaped not only the diligent editor [Col. 0362C] but also the learned de la Barre, who prepared a new edition of Dacherius’s *Spicilegium*, and even the careful authors of the *Gallic Literary History* [Note: [Col. 0362D] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 294.].

The first person, so far as I know, to notice this was the most learned Valesius [Note: [Col. 0362D] Valesius, on Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 8.]. He also adds that the work is wrongly entitled in the cited manuscript *On the Vigils of the Servants of God*:

> “For,” he says, “the subject is not the vigils of monks but of laypeople; nor is this an abbot speaking to monks, but a bishop addressing the people, as is evident even from these words” [Note: [Col. 0363D] Nicetius, *On Vigil-Watching*, chapter 2.]:
>
> “Nor should it seem burdensome or difficult even for delicate or infirm bodies to set aside for God’s service, during the week, a portion of two nights—that is, Saturday and Sunday. For this is, as it were, a purification of the five days or nights during which we grow heavy through carnal stupor or rejoice while engrossed in worldly activities.”

Thus far Valesius.

### III

Accordingly, among the works wrongly attributed to Saint Jerome [Note: [Col. 0363D] Vallarsius, edition of Jerome’s works, vol. XI, p. 222.], this short work might more correctly be entitled *On the Observance of Vigils*. The distinguished Vallarsius, who not long ago prepared an accurate edition of the great Doctor, observed [Note: [Col. 0363D] Idem, ibid.] that the Saint-Germain manuscript [Col. 0363B] is mutilated in several places through the carelessness of the copyist, though otherwise not beyond correction. He therefore compared the old edition with Dacherius’s and recorded the variant readings. From these, accordingly, we have selected, as was proper, those that could make our copy more correct.

Nor should we omit what the learned man says at the end of his notice, as follows:

> “Saint Isidore of Seville was by no means ashamed to transcribe almost the whole of chapter 21 of *Ecclesiastical Offices* from it”—that is, from the treatise of Saint Nicetius.

Indeed, from chapter 3 of the short work of the holy bishop of Trier, that holy Father copied several passages word for word, not only in chapter 21 of book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, which we have indicated in the accompanying notes.

But what the same Vallarsius says about the author of the short work [Col. 0363C] cannot by any means be accepted: namely, that Nicetius, of whom we are speaking, was celebrated with the highest praises by Sidonius Apollinaris and was even related to him. Sidonius does indeed praise Flavius Nicetius of Lyon [Note: [Col. 0363D] Sidonius, book VIII, letter 6.], a distinguished man who had been advocate of the praetorian see and assessor; but nowhere does he recognize our Nicetius, bishop of Trier.

Indeed, what we have argued elsewhere concerning the year of Sidonius’s death seems wholly to oppose Vallarsius’s view [Note: [Col. 0363D] *Library of the Fathers*, vol. X, preliminary discussion, chapter 11, §§ 3 and 4, p. XXI.]. For this bishop of Arvernia is said to have died in the year 484, whereas the bishop of Trier, as we indicated above, departed this life around the year 566. These chronological considerations, if properly examined, increasingly confirm that our Nicetius was entirely unknown to Sidonius.

### IV

There is no need to say much about the later short work of the blessed bishop, entitled *On the Good of Psalmody*. It seems to have been attached by its author as an appendix to the former work. It therefore remains to discuss something about his two letters, which we know he wrote toward the end of his life.

The first he addressed to Chlotsinda, or Chlodosvinda, daughter of Clotarius, king of the Franks, who had married Alboin, king of the Lombards, as Gregory of Tours reports [Col. 0364A] [Note: [Col. 0363D] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 3.]. The beginning of this letter is as follows:

> “When we see your envoys traveling through the Frankish kingdoms of your brothers,” etc.

From these words it is clear that the holy bishop wrote the letter while the sons of Clotarius were ruling in Francia. Clotarius’s death, according to Marius of Avenches [Note: [Col. 0364D] Marius of Avenches, *Chronicle*.], occurred in the twentieth year after the consulship of Basil, that is, in the year 561 of Christ.

Accordingly, Nicetius wrote this letter either in that year or, at the latest, in the following year, 562, taking the opportunity presented by the embassy that Chlotsinda sent to her brothers, both to express grief at her father’s death and to wish them every good fortune in the kingdom they had assumed. This is the opinion we hold, following the learned men mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0364D] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 295.]. Others, however, believe that it was written around the year 563 [Note: [Col. 0364D] Cointius, at the cited place, under the year 563, § 7, vol. II, p. 25.]. Sirmond seems to assign it to the year 565, a date that can scarcely be accepted.

In this letter, the holy Father urges Chlotsinda to seek the salvation of her royal husband Alboin, who was devoted to the Arian heresy, and, with God’s favor, to try to bring him back to profess the true faith. At the same time, so that she might accomplish this more easily, he demonstrates to her from various passages of Sacred Scripture the falsity of Arian doctrine and urges her to present the same arguments to the king.

And because miracles are supremely powerful for persuasion, he urges the Lombards to undertake a journey into Francia in search of the truth, to visit the most noble cities of Gaul—Tours, Auxerre, Poitiers, Troyes, Reims, and Soissons—and there to behold the cures wrought by God at the tombs of the most blessed bishops Martin, Germanus, Hilary, Lupus, Remigius, and Medard, who believed the Son to be consubstantial with the Father and fought outstandingly against the heretics of their time.

These are the words of Cointius [Note: [Col. 0364D] Cointius, at the cited place, § 9, p. 27.]. He also observes that Nicetius called the peoples ruled by Alboin “Goths and Lombards” in the aforesaid letter because the Lombard people were Gothic in origin and were distinguished from the other Goths by a particular name, which they had acquired from their long beards.

### V

As for the later letter, Nicetius wrote it to the emperor Justinian, endeavoring to recall him from the heresy of the Aphthartodocetae, into which he had fallen when he promulgated his edict on the incorruptibility of Christ’s body at the beginning of the year 565—the very year in which he exchanged life for death.

Pagi discusses this chronological question at length against Cointius [Note: [Col. 0364D] Pagi, under the year 565, § 2.]. Cointius, agreeing with Baronius [Col. 0364D], believed that Justinian issued the edict in the year 563 and postponed his death to the year 566. From this corrupted chronology he conjectured [Note: [Col. 0364D] Cointius, under the year 566, § 59, at the cited place, p. 84.] that the most blessed bishop’s letter had achieved no small success with the emperor, so that it recalled his mind from publishing the edict he had written against orthodox faith. On the contrary, it is highly probable that Justinian never received Nicetius’s letter, since death overtook him first.

Whatever the truth may be, we reproduce here the words of the same Frankish annalist concerning Nicetius’s letter [Note: [Col. 0365A] Cointius, under the year 566, § 59, at the cited place, p. 83.]:

> “Nicetius, bishop of Trier, deserves outstanding praise. Although he was situated in the remotest parts of the West, where no one was infected by the poison of Nestorius or Eutyches, as soon as he heard that the emperor of the East adhered to the perverse doctrines spread by the followers of such heretics, he immediately warned him by letter to come to his senses.
>
> “He used a sharp style. He did not conceal what had been reported to him; indeed, he gathered together and reproached him with more and graver crimes than the other writers. He asserted that the Fathers whom the emperor ought to have revered had been sent to slaughter and to various crosses. Then he added how hateful the emperor’s name was among all the Italians, Africans, Spaniards, and Gauls, by whom he was anathematized on account of his heresy.”

Thus far the learned author.

Finally, we wish to inform the reader that the works of Nicetius were printed out of chronological order and placed at the end of this volume, because they had escaped us while we were occupied with other matters and preparing the remaining works of the following writers for printing.

[Col. 0365]

# SHORT WORKS OF SAINT NICETIUS (C, G)*

[Col. 0365]

## FIRST SHORT WORK: ON THE VIGILS OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0365B]

[Note: [Col. 0365D] This short work appears among the works attributed to Saint Jerome, Vallarsius edition, vol. XI, p. 222. There it begins: “It is worthy, brethren, and altogether fitting.” Then: “to deliver a discourse, when the very nocturnal study is required of the diligent.” “Behold, night is the darkness of the body.”]

It is a good, worthy, and holy matter, wholly suitable and sufficiently appropriate to speak now about sacred vigils and to deliver a discourse, since this very nighttime labor is undertaken by vigilant and religious people. Night is blind and a necessary darkness for bodies; it holds not only human beings but also animals in sleep, so that, their strength restored [Note: [Col. 0365D] Another reading: “renewed.”] through slumber, they may endure the labors of the day while awake.

Good is God, who provided and arranged things in such a way that a person going out to his work and labor until evening would have an intervening period in which to rest from hard work and great fatigue (Psalm CIII, 23). Thus he made the day for work and the night for rest. For this, as for everything, we ought to give thanks to him who granted it.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] These words were absent from the published edition of Jerome.]

We know, however, that many people, whether to please their superiors or to benefit themselves in some particular way, set aside a portion of the night for some little task and count as profit what they have been able to accomplish by stealing it from their sleep.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Jerome’s edition reads: “what they may have been able to accomplish.” Solomon also praises the woman who diligently works by lamplight at her allotted tasks and spinning. He added that from this praise for her husband at the gates and great glory arise. But if, etc.]

If those who keep watch in material pursuits—that is, pursuits necessary for food and clothing—are not reproved but rather praised, how much more ought we to observe and love sacred vigils, so fruitful in spiritual work, abounding in prayers, hymns, and readings, so that we may receive our reward from the Lord God?

[Note: [Col. 0366D] Ibid. “I confess that I am amazed that there are some who regard sacred vigils, so fruitful in spiritual work and so rich in prayers, hymns, and readings, as either superfluous, idle, or—what is worse than these—inconvenient. And indeed, if there are people alien to our religion who think this way, it is not surprising.]

### CHAPTER II

There are certainly people who criticize these practices, but they are alien to the Catholic faith and religion. That is not surprising. For how can religious observances please the impious and profane? If they pleased them, they would be ours; and we are, of course, Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0366D] Ibid. “let us be.” Another reading: “we know.”]

But if they are our own people who are offended by the salutary practice of holy vigils, so that no one may suspect anything worse of them, they are either lazy, sleepy, old, or infirm.

If they are lazy, let them be ashamed, because Solomon’s Proverbs resound against them: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and imitate its ways” (Proverbs VI, 6).

If they are sleepy, let them awaken, since Scripture cries out:

> “O sluggard, how long will you sleep? When will you rise from your sleep? You sleep a little, sit a little, doze a little, and fold your hands for a little while. Then poverty will come upon you like a traveler, and want like a swift runner” (ibid., 9–11).

If they are old, who compels them to keep vigil? Yet even without compulsion they ought to keep vigil for the sake of their very age and to pray to the Lord God more earnestly. They should therefore keep vigil sitting if they cannot stand.

But if they are infirm in their limbs, let them not criticize what they themselves cannot do. Rather, according to the prophet, let them water their bed with tears and say: “Thus I remembered you upon my bed” (Psalm LXIX, 7). Let them also commend themselves to those who keep vigil, so that the latter may assist them with their prayers. Thus, helped by the Lord, they may one day deserve to sing upon their bed of pain, saying: “In the mornings I will meditate upon you, Lord, because you have become my helper” (ibid.).

[Col. 0367A]

Otherwise it is foolish and entirely foreign to religion that, because we ourselves cannot run, we should disparage those who run well. For even if we cannot do so, we ought not to envy those who can, but to rejoice with them. Just as one who consents to wickedness becomes a participant in punishment, so from consenting to goodness one may hope to share in glory.

One person is crowned by disposition [Note: [Col. 0367D] Ibid. More correctly: “one person is crowned by achievement.”], while another is gladdened by pious willingness.

Nor should it seem burdensome or difficult, even for delicate or infirm bodies, to devote some portion of two nights in the week—that is, Saturday and Sunday—to God’s service. For this is, as it were, a purification of the five days or nights during which we grow heavy through carnal stupor or rejoice while engrossed in worldly affairs.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Ibid. “of carnal people.”]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Ibid. “we grow careless.”]

Let no one be ashamed of a good pursuit of holiness, since the wicked are not ashamed when committing shameful deeds. Scripture therefore rightly says in Proverbs: “There is a shame that brings sin” (Ecclesiasticus IV, 25). To be ashamed in a good work is sinful, just as not to be ashamed in doing evil is destructive.

If you are holy, love the vigils, so that, guarding your treasure by keeping watch, you yourselves may be preserved in holiness. If you are sinners, run all the more, so that by keeping watch and praying to God you may be cleansed, and, beating your breasts, may cry out more frequently to the Lord, saying with your whole heart: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, Lord, and spare your servant from those of others” (Psalm XVIII, 13). For those who already desire to be cleansed from hidden faults—I do not know whether they can take pleasure in defiling themselves with the same miseries.

### CHAPTER III

[Col. 0367C]

The occasion demands, dear ones, that we say a little about the authority, antiquity, and usefulness of vigils; for every labor is undertaken more willingly if the usefulness of the labor itself is placed before our eyes.

The devotion of vigils is ancient, a familiar good to all the saints. The prophet Isaiah finally cries out to the Lord:

> “By night my spirit watches for you, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isaiah XXVI, 9, according to the Septuagint).

David, sanctified both by royal and prophetic spirit and by anointing, sings as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, copied this in *Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 22. In his text we read: “David, sanctified by royal and prophetic anointing,” correctly omitting the word “spirit,” which disturbs the sense and is also absent from the published edition of Jerome.]

> “Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out, and by night before you” (Psalm LXXXVII, 2).

He also says:

> “I remembered your name in the night, Lord, and I kept your law” (Psalm CXVIII, 55).

[Note: [Col. 0368D] In Jerome’s edition the following words are immediately added: “But perhaps he sang these things while lying on his little bed. Some more sluggish people thought it sufficient if each person merely prayed or murmured a psalm while lying on his bed. That too is good: always and everywhere to remember God is salutary. But that it is better to rise and stand in the divine presence, receive the testimony of the same prophet, etc.”]

Hear another utterance of the same prophet, which reveals both the time and the posture of the one praying:

> “In the nights,” he says, “lift up your hands in the holy place and bless the Lord” (Psalm CXXXIII, 2).

And lest you think that only evening hours are called nights, he adds:

> “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm CXVIII, 62).

Here you have both the precise time and the care required for rising, and you have been shown how to give thanks to God.

As I continue to consider the zeal of the saints, something greater and more laborious presents itself, something beyond the condition of human nature, when you hear the same prophet singing:

> “If I ascend upon the bed of my couch; if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Psalm CXXXI, 3).

Who would not be astonished at such devotion of spirit in the love of God, that he entirely denied himself sleep, without which human bodies necessarily fail, until the king and prophet found a place and a temple to be built for the Lord?

This ought powerfully to admonish us: if we ourselves wish to be God’s place and desire always to be regarded as his dwelling and temple, just as the Apostle Paul says, “You are the temple of God” (II Corinthians VI, 16), then, insofar as we can, let us love vigils after the example of the saints, lest it also be said of us:

[Note: [Col. 0368D] Saint Isidore also took all these passages from this work, at the cited place, chapter 21.]

> “They slept their sleep and found nothing” (Psalm LXXV, 6).

Rather, let each one of you, full of rejoicing, already say:

> “In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived” (Psalm LXXVI, 3),

because:

> “It is good to give thanks to the Lord and sing psalms to your name, Most High, to proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth throughout the night” (Psalm XCI, 2–3).

Those holy men sang and left writings of this kind—so great and so numerous—in order that we, their descendants, might be stirred by examples equal to theirs to celebrate even at night the vigils of our salvation.

But let us pass from the ancients to the new, from the ministers of the Law to the ministers of the Gospel, so that the value of vigils may also be recorded from the New Testament.

Anna, daughter of Phanuel, a widow who served God with continual prayers and fasts, did not depart from the temple day or night. In the Gospel we read that those most holy shepherds, while keeping night watch over their flock, were privileged both to see angels in splendor and to be the first to hear that Christ had been born on earth.

And does not the Savior’s teaching rouse everyone to keep watch, whether when he teaches in the parable of the good sower:

> “While people were sleeping, the enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away” (Matthew XIII, 25)?

If they had kept watch, perhaps the enemy would not have been able to sow the weeds.

Or when he says:

> “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning; and be like those waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding. Blessed are those servants whom the master, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke XII, 35–37).

And again:

> “Whether he comes in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, and finds them watching, they are blessed” (Mark XIII, 33).

Therefore:

> “You also must be ready, because at an hour you do not know the Son of Man will come” (Matthew XXIV, 44).

He taught vigilance not only in words but also confirmed it by example. For the Gospel bears witness that Jesus spent the night in the prayer of God (Luke XI, 12). He spent the night not for his own sake, but so that we might know what all of us ought to do.

And at the time of his Passion he rebuked Peter, saying:

> “Could you not keep watch with me for one hour?”

Then he says to everyone:

> “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew XXVI, 40–41).

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Jerome’s edition reads: “These words, these examples of his—tell me, whom could they not rouse even from deep sleep, almost resembling death?”]

With such an example as these words provide, I ask you: whom could they not rouse even from deep sleep resembling death?

Instructed by these teachings and strengthened by these examples, the blessed Apostles also kept watch themselves and commanded vigils.

The Apostle Peter is awakened at night in prison by an angel, and, when the angel opened the iron gate, he reached the house of Mary, where many were gathered—not sleeping, certainly, but praying.

In his Epistle he likewise says:

> “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Peter V, 8).

Paul and Silas, while in public custody around midnight, are remembered to have prayed and sung a hymn while the prisoners listened (Acts XVI, 25). Then suddenly an earthquake occurred, the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors were opened [Note: [Col. 0369D] Ibid. “the doors were opened of their own accord.”], and everyone’s chains were immediately loosened.

Likewise, the blessed Apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0369D] Much is missing here, apparently omitted through the copyist’s negligence. It should be restored from the published edition attributed to Jerome as follows: “The same Apostle Paul, about to depart from Troas, continued teaching until midnight, with many lamps lit in the upper room. A young man named Eutychus, overcome by sleep while Paul was prolonging his discussion, fell from the third story after being lowered from a window, and was taken up dead. When life was immediately restored to him, Paul continued speaking until dawn and departed under God’s guidance. The same Apostle, exhorting the Thessalonians very fully and abundantly concerning the practice of vigils, writes: ‘Therefore let us not sleep as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night. But since we belong to God, let us be sober.’ And he concludes beautifully: ‘Whether we are watching or sleeping, we shall live together with him.’ To the Corinthians he writes: ‘Watch, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong. Act manfully.’ Likewise to the Ephesians: ‘Praying at all times in the Spirit.’ And, himself offering an example of vigilance in the catalogue of his virtues, he boasts before the Corinthians of the fruit of his many vigils.”]

exhorts the Thessalonians to practice vigils, saying:

> “Watch, stand firm in the faith, be strengthened, act manfully” (I Corinthians XVI, 13).

### CHAPTER IV

This is sufficient concerning the authority and antiquity of holy vigils. It remains, as promised, to say something about their usefulness, although their usefulness can be experienced more through practice than described in the words of a speaker.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] Jerome’s edition reads: “For it must be tasted that the Lord is sweet, as it is written. Whoever, therefore, has tasted,” etc.]

For it is perceived by tasting that the Lord is sweet (Psalm XXXIV, 9). Whoever has tasted understands and feels how much foulness is removed by keeping watch, how much mental dullness is shaken off, how great a light illumines the soul of one who watches and prays, and what grace and holy visitation gladden all the limbs of the one keeping vigil.

By keeping watch, every fear is banished, confidence is born, the flesh is disciplined, vices waste away, chastity is strengthened, foolishness gives way, prudence arrives, the mind is sharpened, error is blunted, and the devil, head of crimes, is wounded by the sword of the spirit.

What is more necessary than this usefulness? What holy benefit is more advantageous than these gains? What is sweeter than this delight? What is more blessed than this happiness?

The prophet also bears witness. At the beginning of his Psalms, when describing the blessed man, he placed the summit of his blessedness in this verse:

> “If he meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm I, 2).

Daytime meditation is good, and prayer is good, but nighttime meditation is much more welcome and effective, because during the day various necessities make themselves heard, occupations disrupt the mind, and manifold cares scatter the understanding. Night, however, is secluded; night is quiet and suitable for those who pray, most appropriate for those who keep watch, since, freed from bodily occupations and gathered in concentration, it presents the whole person before the divine presence.

[Col. 0370B]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] After these words, Jerome’s edition contains more material that is missing here, as follows: “From this the devil, ever a clever imitator of divine things, just as he gave fasting and virginity, empty baptisms and vain observances, to his own rites, so too, imitating this holy practice, added nocturnal sacred rites and vigils to his banquets. Therefore, dear faithful brothers, if they are not stirred by the instruction of their own people to hold sacred vigils, let them recognize, when they see their observance distorted into an opposing variety, that such practices are not alien to divine matters. The wicked would not imitate them for deception unless he knew them to be pleasing to God for the blessing of those who celebrate them. Yet, dear brothers, he who keeps watch,” etc.]

Therefore recognize that vigils are pleasing to God for the celebration of blessing.

Only this, beloved, is required: let the one who keeps vigil with his eyes keep vigil also with his heart; let the one who prays in spirit pray also with his mind. For it is not sufficiently useful to keep watch with the eyes while sleeping in the soul, since, conversely, Scripture speaks in the person of the Church: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2).

Above all, care must also be taken that the breasts of those keeping vigil are not weighed down by excessive food or drink, lest, belching indigestion and drunkenness, we not only be unpleasant to ourselves but also be judged unworthy of the grace of the Holy Spirit. For a certain distinguished man among the shepherds said: “Just as smoke drives away bees, so undigested belching turns away and repels the gifts of the Holy Spirit.” Therefore, as those who are about to celebrate a divine mystery, we must first prepare ourselves through abstinence, so that, restored and unencumbered, we may be able to keep vigil. Let evil thoughts also be driven away, lest the prayer of those who keep vigil badly become, as it is written, “sin” (Ps. 108:7).

For there are also vigils cursed by the wicked, as is read in Proverbs: “Sleep has been taken away from their eyes. For they do not sleep,” he says, “unless they have done evil” (Prov. 6:16). But may such vigils be absent—and far absent—from this assembly. Rather, may the breast of those keeping vigil, closed to the devil, be [Col. 0371A] open to Christ, so that we may hold in our hearts what we utter with our lips. Then our vigils will be acceptable to God; then the nightlong vigil will be saving, if our ministry is offered before the divine gaze with suitable diligence and sincere devotion.

These statements about the authority and antiquity of vigils, and also about their holy usefulness, are sufficient.
