As for how pleasing and acceptable to God is devotion to hymns and psalms, I would now have said something, however little, had a fuller treatment not demanded another volume; that will be presented, with the Lord’s favor, in the following reading.

## OPUSCULUM II. On the Good of Psalmody

[Col. 0371]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0371A] Let us speak of the good of psalmody, which God graciously deigns to bestow upon us. We, beloved, who have all been instructed by prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic teachings, should set before our eyes the words and deeds of those through whom we are everything that we are; and, beginning from the beginning, let us affirm through these same authorities how pleasing and acceptable spiritual songs are to God.

If we ask who first introduced this kind of practice, we find no one other than Moses, who offered a notable song to God when, after Egypt had been struck by the ten plagues and Pharaoh had been drowned, the people went forth rejoicing through the unfamiliar paths of the sea toward the desert, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted” (Exod. 15:1). Thus Moses was the first leader of the tribes of Israel to establish choirs, and, with himself and his sister leading, taught both sexes, arranged in distinct groups, to sing a song of triumph to the Lord.

Afterward the noble woman Deborah is found to have performed this ministry in the Book of Judges. Moses himself, however, when he was about to depart from this life, repeated a solemn song in Deuteronomy and left it written to the people in place of a testament, so that they might know what punishment and what kinds of tribulation would follow them if they departed from the Lord. Wretched—and worthy of pity—were all those who, despite such a solemn and evident warning, refused to guard themselves against sins and unlawful superstitions.

Later you will find many—not only men but also women—filled with the divine Spirit who sang the mysteries of God, even before David. David, specially chosen by the Lord for this office from childhood, deserved to become the leader of singers and a treasury of songs. While still a boy, singing sweetly and powerfully on the lyre, he restrained the evil spirit that was at work in Saul—not because such power belonged to his lyre, but because the figure of Christ’s cross, mystically represented in the wood and in the stretching of the strings, even then subdued the demonic spirit.

What will you not find in these Psalms that contributes to the benefit and edification, the consolation, of the human race—of every condition, sex, and age? In the Psalms the infant has something to drink, the child something to praise, the adolescent something with which to correct his way, the young man something to follow, and the old man something to pray for. A woman learns chastity; orphans find a father; widows, a judge; the poor, one who takes notice of them; strangers, a guardian. Kings and judges hear what they should fear.

The Psalm consoles the sorrowful, moderates the joyful, calms the angry, refreshes the poor, admonishes the rich to recognize themselves, and rebukes them lest they become proud. To all who receive it, the Psalm supplies an entirely suitable medicine; nor does it despise sinners, but healthfully applies to them a remedy through tearful repentance.

Thus the Lord our God, through his servant David, prepared a potion that would be sweet to taste through song and effective, by its power, for healing the wounds of sinners. The Psalm is heard sweetly while it is sung; it enters the mind while it delights. The Psalms are easily retained in memory if they are sung frequently, and what the austerity of the law could not wrest from human minds, these songs remove through the sweetness of their singing. For whatever the Prophets command, whatever the Gospels themselves command, is contained in these songs with the sweet delight of meditation.

God is revealed so that he may be feared; idols are mocked; justice is inculcated; iniquity is prohibited; mercy is praised; unbelief is rejected; truth is sought; lies are condemned; deceit is accused; innocence is highly praised; pride is cast down; humility is exalted; repentance is proclaimed; peace, which must be pursued, is declared.

Protection against enemies is requested; vengeance is promised; certain hope is nourished. And, greater than all these things, the mysteries of Christ are sung in the Psalms. His generation is expressed, as is the rejection of the ungodly people and the inheritance of the nations. The Lord’s mighty deeds are sung; his venerable passion is depicted; his glorious resurrection is shown; and his seat at the right hand is wonderfully portrayed.

Then the Lord’s fiery advent is revealed, and the terrible judgment of the living and the dead is disclosed. What more? Even the sending forth of the creating Spirit and the renewal of the earth are revealed. After these things there will be the everlasting kingdom of the righteous in the glory of the Lord, and the perpetual punishment of sinners.

### CHAPTER TWO

These are the songs of God that the Catholic Church of God sings. These are the songs that our assembly here practices also with the sound of its voice; they do not loosen the singer but rather bind him firmly. These songs please God when everything that is done is directed toward the glory of the Creator.

Rightly does the same prophet exhort everyone and everything to praise God, who governs all things, saying: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 150:6). Promising that he himself would also be a praiser, he said: “I will praise the name of the Lord with a song, and I will magnify him with praise” (Ps. 63:31). Praise the Lord in your life; offer to God the sacrifice of praise for your soul and your life; and through him it is shown to you in your soul by what means you may attain his salvation.

Our praise, issuing from a pure conscience, delights the Lord, just as the same writer of hymns exhorts us, saying: “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let praise be pleasing and beautiful to our God” (Ps. 134:3).

[Col. 0373A] Possessing this knowledge and knowing this office to be pleasing to God, the same Psalmist testifies: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. 118:164). And he promises something still greater: “And my tongue,” he says, “will meditate on your righteousness, on your praise, all day long” (Ps. 34:28).

Without doubt he perceived the benefit of such an act, as he himself recalls: “Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. 26:4). Armed with such protection and such a shield, he had cast down that exceedingly strong giant Goliath and had often carried away victory over foreign peoples.

### CHAPTER THREE

It would take too long, beloved, to relate individually everything contained in the histories of the saints, especially since the matter requires that certain things from the New Testament be brought forward both for confirmation of the ancient examples and for your instruction.

Thus you will find Zachariah, the father of the great John, prophesying in the form of a hymn after that long silence. Nor did Elizabeth, long barren, cease to magnify God from her very soul after giving birth to the son promised to her.

When Christ was born on earth, the host of angels sounded forth praise: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The children, proclaiming in the temple, cried out: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21:15). When the Pharisees were clamoring with envy, the Lord did not silence the mouths of the innocent but rather opened them, saying: “Have you not read what was written: ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’? And if these are silent, the stones will cry out” (ibid., 16).

The Lord himself, teacher in words and fulfiller in deeds, wishing to show that the ministry of hymns was most pleasing, went out to the Mount of Olives with his disciples after singing a hymn. Who would now doubt the religious observance of psalms and hymns, when he whom all heavenly beings adore and praise is reported to have sung a hymn with his disciples?

John also reports in the Apocalypse that, by revelation of the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of many waters and of mighty thunderclaps saying “Alleluia.” From this no one ought to doubt that this ministry of holy vigils, if celebrated with worthy faith and true devotion, is joined to the angels, who, without sleep or occupation, are constantly known to praise God in heaven and bless the Savior.

Since these things are so, brothers, let us now faithfully fulfill the mystery of hymns with fuller confidence, believing that we have obtained great grace from God, since we have been permitted to sing with so many and such great saints—that is, prophets and martyrs—the miracul… of the eternal God. [Col. 0373D] Here there is a lacuna in the printed text. With David we confess to the Lord that he is good; with Moses we sound forth the Lord’s power in those great songs; with Anna, who represents the Church—once barren, now fruitful—we are strengthened in heart in the praise of God; with Isaiah we keep vigil and sing by night; with Habakkuk, Jeremiah, and Jonah, the holiest prophets, we sing in prayer; with the three young men likewise, as though placed in the furnace, summoning every creature, we sing blessings to the Creator of all.

[Col. 0374A] What is more beneficial than this usefulness, what more delightful than this pleasure, since we delight in the Psalms, are watered by prayers, and nourished by the readings inserted between them? Indeed, just as good guests take pleasure in a variety of dishes, so our souls are fattened by varied reading and the offering of hymns.

Only this, beloved: laying aside useless stories, let us sing psalms with attentive understanding and vigilant mind, so that we may not displease God. For the psalm exhorts us, saying: “For God is King of all the earth; sing psalms wisely” (Ps. 46:8)—that is, intelligently—so that we may sing not only in spirit, that is, with the sound of the voice, but also with the mind, and may think about what we sing, lest the mind, captivated by stories and foreign thoughts, undergo fruitless labor.

Let the sound, or melody, also be sung in agreement with holy religion—not one that shouts out theatrical difficulties, but one that demonstrates true Christianity in you [Note: “In words?”]; not one that gives off something theatrical, but one that produces compunction for sins.

Your voices also should not be discordant but harmonious. Let no one foolishly prolong his voice, nor let one lower it while another raises his. Rather, let each person humbly strive to enclose his voice within the sound of the singing choir, not to raise or prolong it outside the choir and indecently project it as though for foolish display, nor to wish to please human beings.

We must celebrate everything as though in the sight of God, not from a desire to please human beings. We also have a model, or example, for this harmony of voices: those three most blessed young men, of whom the prophet Daniel reports: “Then,” he says, “these three, as though with one mouth, were singing a hymn and glorifying God in the furnace, saying: ‘Blessed are you, Lord God of our fathers’” (Dan. 3:51–52).

You see that what is set forth as instruction is that the three young men praised God together, humbly and devoutly, with one mouth. Let all of us likewise utter with one mouth the same sound of the Psalms and the same modulation of the voice, equally. Whoever cannot make himself equal to the others should preferably remain silent or sing in a quiet voice rather than disturb everyone with a loud voice. In this way he will both fulfill the duty of the ministry and cause no offense to the brotherhood singing humbly.

If, therefore, the voice of all of us is free from offense, or harmonious like well-sounding cymbals of the lips, it will delight us, edify those who hear, and make the entire praise sweet to our God, who, as we read, makes the like-minded dwell in his house.

When psalmody is performed, let everyone sing. When a reading is read, let everyone listen equally in silence, so that while the reader is reading no one at all may disturb the assembly with loud voices. Before the reading begins, all of you should assemble. If someone arrives while the reading is being performed, let him merely adore God and, having marked his forehead with the sign of the cross, diligently lend his ear to God’s reading.

The time for prayer is clear when we all pray; and there is also time, whenever you wish and as often as you wish, to pray privately. Do not complain, under the pretext of the reading, that you have lost the opportunity to read, because no one can always have it readily available. For abundant time is always at hand.

Nor should you think that little benefit arises for you from hearing sacred reading, because prayer itself becomes richer when the mind is nourished by a recent reading and runs through images of the divine things it has just heard. For Mary, the sister of Martha, who sat at Jesus’ feet and, while her sister neglected it, listened more intently to the word of the Lord, is confirmed by the Lord’s voice to have chosen the good portion.

[Col. 0376A] For this reason the deacon, with a clear voice, also admonishes everyone in the house of God through the holy proclamation, so that whether in prayer, in bending the knees, in singing psalms, or in carefully listening to the readings, unity may be maintained by all. For God loves people who are of one mind and makes them dwell in his house. Those who dwell in that house are pronounced blessed in the Psalm, because “they will praise the Lord for ever and ever” (Ps. 83:5). Amen.

[Col. 0375]

## TWO LETTERS OF ST. NICETIUS. (C, S)*

[Col. 0375]

### FIRST LETTER. TO CHLODOSVINDA, QUEEN OF THE LOMBARDS

[Col. 0375B]

Nicetius, a sinner, to his most gracious lady and daughter in Christ, Queen Chlodosvinda.

I. When we see your envoys travelling through the Frankish kings, your brothers, we are concerned for your prosperity. Yet from there we hear what we always acknowledge and proclaim concerning you: how great, how exalted, how praiseworthy, how useful, how humane and generous you are; how solicitous for the poor, how shrewd concerning the realm [Note: Thus Cointius, *Annals of the Frankish Church*, vol. II, p. 25; likewise Ruinart, on Gregory of Tours, p. 1338. But Sirmond, *Councils*, vol. VI, p. 514, reads “concerning religion” [Col. 0376D], perhaps more correctly; and shortly afterward he has *magnifica* for *munifica*, the latter being more pleasing.], how resplendent in your devout conduct among all the people. May he grant this who has already given you the spirit of wisdom and understanding. We rejoice at this; may Christ cause us to rejoice in King Alboin whom you have, and to triumph in his prosperity.

We are amazed that, while nations fear him, kings pay him reverence, powers praise him without ceasing, and even the emperor himself sets him before his own, he does not speedily seek a remedy for his soul. We read in Scripture: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all things shall be added” (Matt. 6:33). I wonder why one who shines in fame as he does does not strive to inquire into the kingdom of God and the salvation of his soul, but receives and listens to those who lead a soul rather into Gehenna than to the way of salvation. They preach that there are two Gods: one, the Father, in deity; the other, the Son, in deity indeed, but as a creature—although Scripture says: “I am the Savior, and there is none other besides me” (Isa. 45:14).

[Col. 0375D] II. Lady Chlodosvinda, I adjure you by the fearful judgment of God both to read this letter carefully and to strive to explain it well and frequently to him, and to ask him: Who is the Savior? Do they say that the Father is Savior, or the Son? How do they declare that there are two when there is one and no other? If they say the Son, then the Father is not Savior; and if they say the Father, then the Son is not Savior, because one who is not Savior cannot save anyone. If they say, “There are two Saviors,” they will find this written nowhere, except, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30): that is, the Father is in the Son and with the Son, and the Son is in the Father and with the Father.

God, because of his greatness, cannot be seen by the human eye: he is so great, so radiant, indeed so fiery. We read: “His tabernacle is round about heaven and earth” (Ps. 17:12); and this too, because of such greatness and radiance, cannot be seen by man. He expressed from himself him whom he always had with himself, who made for himself a hiding-place from flesh; and therefore Scripture says: “He made darkness his hiding-place” (ibid.). Thus in the Gospel the Word of God, of whom John says that “In the beginning was” the Word (John 1:1), “became flesh” (ibid., 14); and that which was from Mary he so joined to himself that it was one. And through Scripture he says: “From Zion comes the beauty of his form” (Ps. 49:2): that is, the human being will pass into God.

[Col. 0376C] III. In the Gospels he himself said: “I went forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:28). In the forty-seventh Psalm he said: “Mark well his steps” (Ps. 47:14). He said “his,” not “their”; for it is most plainly known that he is one, yet not alone: “that you may recount [them] to another generation.” For on the day of resurrection, one who has not believed in the Trinity in unity will be able neither to recount nor to appear. For this reason all the host of angels cries daily: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth” (Isa. 6:3). It did not say three holy ones, but three times “Holy,” Lord God Sabaoth. Holy Father, Holy Son, Holy Spirit: one Holy One, just as there is one Lord.

Therefore John the Evangelist also said: “He is the one who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Savior” (Rev. 1:8). If I proceed by names, there seem to be degrees. When you hear “Father,” he seems greater by the name; and therefore he said: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28)—but by name only. In deity, however, he is most evidently recognized, through Christ and through his apostles, as one. For when he was asked by a disciple, “Lord, show us the Father,” he replied: “You see me, and do you ask about the Father?” [Col. 0377A] (John 14:8–9). You see that he is invoked in the Trinity and found to be in one deity.

When you hear “Father,” do not believe that he is without the Son; when you hear “Son,” do not doubt that he is with the Father. Nor doubt that there are three in persons, for he is recognized as one in deity. Therefore he said to his disciples: “Go, baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). He said “in the name,” not “in the names,” because he declared one deity, not three. The Holy Spirit cannot be separated, because where the grace of God is known to be, there the gift is recognized to be. From him all good things breathe forth, as the Apostle said: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 9:36). But the Savior is “the Most High alone over all the earth” (Ps. 82:19).

Joshua son of Nun saw him, and therefore said: “Are you one of us, or of our adversaries?” [Col. 0377B] (Josh. 5:13). But he answered: “I am who I am, and there is no other besides me” (Exod. 3:14). Abraham, who is called the friend of God (2 Chr. 20:7; Isa. 41:8; Jas. 2:23), and is proved [to be so], saw three and believed one (Gen. 18:2–3). When he worships the three, he recalls the Trinity, as I have said; when he asks one to enter the house, he declares that there is one power. For how often and how often did he say to Moses: “I am who I am, and there is no other besides me”?

IV. Why need we go through matters one by one? Let us come to the twelve disciples whom he had, for the Goths themselves today pay them veneration and secretly carry off their relics; yet they possess nothing there, because they presume to annul their faith. Why is it that today they venerate their bodies in their basilicas, [Col. 0377C] but do not enter? Why is it that they dare do nothing there except secretly [Note: Cointius, *loc. cit.*, p. 26, punctuates thus: “except secretly? Like dogs, from outside, they deceive souls, when they …”], like dogs, deceiving souls from outside? Although King Alboin sends his own faithful people and brings them to the thresholds of the lords Peter and Paul, John, or the other saints, so that there they may decide, if they dare, to celebrate Masses, yet they do not dare: because the disciples of the lord Peter do not appear [to them], and they are proved to be opponents of Christ; indeed, they are found, unhappy men, to destroy what he redeemed through the cross [Note: So Cointius and Ruinart. Sirmond, in *Councils*, loc. cit., reads “which [he redeemed] through the cross.”]. [Note: These words are omitted in *Councils*, loc. cit., though they occur in Cointius and Ruinart.]

For what reason does such a king and such an age receive their poisons? Here [Note: Cointius and Ruinart read *si lubet*, “if he wishes.”], if he commands, let him send them to the lord Martin on his festival which he observes on the eleventh day of November; and there, if they dare, let them attempt something where today we see blind persons enlightened, the deaf receiving hearing, and the mute health. [Col. 0377D] What shall I say of lepers or of very many others who have been struck by whatever infirmity, and who, year after year, different persons are healed there? Perhaps they say that they feign even those blind persons who appear to have been blind from birth. [Note: Cointius reads, apparently less correctly, “What do they say?” For immediately afterward comes “What shall I say further,” etc.] What shall I say when we see those enlightened from there and see them return to their homes, by God’s mercy?

What shall I say further of the lords Germanus, Hilary, and Lupus, bishops, where such great miracles appear today that I cannot express them in words: where the afflicted—that is, those possessed by demons—are suspended in the air and tortured, and confess those whom I have named to be lords? Do they do this in their churches? They do not, because they do not perceive that God and the holy lords dwell there. A demon does not exorcise a demon. Where saints dwell, a demon is not allowed to wander; therefore it comes about that the place where God is is shown.

What of the lords Remigius and Medardus, bishops, whom, I believe, you have seen? We cannot set forth such great things as the miracles which we see God perform through them.

IV. You heard from your grandmother of blessed memory, Clothilde [Note: Clothilde, wife of Clovis I.], how she came into Francia and how she brought the lord Clovis to the Catholic law; and although he was a most shrewd man, he did not consent before he recognized the truth. When he knew that the things I have said above had been proved, he humbly fell at the thresholds of the lord Martin and allowed himself to be baptized without delay. You have heard what great things he did after his baptism against the heretical kings Alaric and Gundobad; nor are you unaware what good things he and his sons possessed in the world.

Why does such an ornamented and such a man as King Alboin is said to be, of such renown, whom the world thus prefers, not convert, or why does he appear slow to seek the way of salvation? Good God, who are the glory of the saints and the salvation of all, send yourself into him. And you, Lady Chlodosvinda, when you speak, offer encouragement, so that we may all rejoice over such a star, such a jewel, in such a manner as may enable us to please God.

I greet you as much as I can; I entreat you not to be idle: cry out without ceasing, sing without ceasing. You have heard it said: “The unbelieving man will be saved through the believing woman” [Note: Ruinart incorrectly reads “will be healed.”] (1 Cor. 7:14). For know that the first salvation, the first remission, belongs to one who causes a sinner to turn from his error. Keep vigil, keep vigil, because you have God propitious. I ask you so to act that you may make the Lombard nation strong against its enemies and grant us to rejoice over your salvation and that of your husband.

### LETTER II. TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN

He recalls him, fallen into heresy, from error.

Nicetius, humble with his [fellow bishops] but bishop by the mercy of the Lord, to Justinian, his lord always.

I. In these last times, as the Gospel saying foretold, we discern [the signs]; and although our time is always ready, we nevertheless perceive that the end is coming, as Scripture has announced. But blessed is that man whom Christ, when he comes, shall find watchful. The sun is turned into darkness from the east—that is, from on high, namely from a holy life. You shone as the sun throughout the whole world; and when all the rulers of the Church rejoiced at this by the grace of the Lord [Note: *gratia*, “grace,” is carelessly omitted in *Councils*.], all of us who shared in his counsel [Note: In *Councils*, the margin has *consiliis*, “counsels.”] are grieved and humbled to the earth by the spreading report of your fall, which we ought never to have foreseen. [Note: This period is corrupt. If these are not its very words, at least this may be its sense: “You shone as the sun throughout the whole world; and when all the rulers of the Church rejoiced at this by the grace of the Lord, we are grieved and humbled to the earth by the spreading report of your fall, which we ought never to have foreseen.” Cointius, *loc. cit.*, pp. 80–81.]

Our dear Justinian, who thus deceived you? Who persuaded you to pursue such things? Who taught you to confess Christ as a mere man? Who deceived you into enrolling yourself in the fellowship of the Jews? Who taught you that he who said, “I went forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:28), grew through circumcision, baptism, and passion? Who, when you had not formerly possessed a wretched heart, suddenly overwhelmed you? Who provoked you to send to slaughter and to various crosses the fathers whom you ought to have venerated? Who provoked you to destroy those things for which Christ was crucified and all the apostles endured? Who urged you to worship what had already been condemned once, twice, and [Col. 0379B] three times by all the rulers of the Church? Who commanded you to destroy yourself through that sect of Nestorius and Eutyches, which, as we have said, had already been anathematized time after time? [Note: *Councils* has *ipsa*, omitting the preposition *de*.] He—he who persuaded Adam to touch the tree of life, who by his own endeavour devised death—deceived you; he who, when he made Judas regard Christ as a mere man and betray him for a man, sent him into the fire which God prepared for the devil and his angels.

II. Our dear, dear Justinian, remember what you promised when you were baptized, and what in every particular you said you believed. You confessed one Son remaining in two substances, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, not two Christs. When you departed [from this faith], what did you do? What did you prepare for yourself? Examine yourself and look well to yourself, [Col. 0379C] and see whether you have not bound yourself in the place of perdition. You are still alive if you wish; if you wish, [live] by returning. “Return to me,” he says, “and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3). You sent into exile the fathers from whom you ought to have expected a blessing. When in your final old age you ought to have composed and joined yourself to your Redeemer, you yourself—not another, but you—deceived both yourself and your own people.

[Col. 0380A] When, as he says, the priest Lactantius was visiting the holy places throughout Gaul because of the Lord’s mercy, he appeared before us; we entreated concerning the things you read and adjured [you] through Jesus Christ our Redeemer. Therefore by this present letter we have adjured you before our God; moreover we solemnly testify that you should both return and urge to return those many whom you persuaded to perish in the dreadful persecution. But if you do not do this, let him be judge between us and you—the one from whom you took honours and whom you made a mere man. When you read, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), [know that] the Father is such as the Son also is, because the Father is as the Son; for how can one who is proved to be creator of all things be shown to become better by coming to circumcision, baptism, and martyrdom?

[Col. 0380B] III. Hasten, hasten—at once. For if your last day finds you as you now appear today, descending to the lower parts of the earth, you will be among the portions of foxes. Let the holy Church rejoice at your return, for she greatly mourns at your departure. Cause us to rejoice in this last age—you whom, after rejoicing at your former state, you made mourn over your perdition. Do not say even in your heart, “I have done it, I have done it; I have conquered, I have conquered.” You are conquered and bound, and indeed in the manner of a son of the devil and enemy of righteousness. For let it be known to you that all Italy, whole Africa, Spain, and all Gaul, while they weep over your perdition, anathematize your name. And unless you destroy what you have taught and cry out publicly, “I have erred, I have erred; anathema to Nestorius, anathema to Eutyches,” you have delivered yourself with them to everlasting punishments.

[Col. 0380C] We greet you greatly, adjuring you through the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; through him who appears threefold in one and is recognized one in three, that you withdraw yourself from the dreadful sect and abominable persecution, and strive to bring to a better way those who, at your persuasion, believed in it.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 552

## AGNELLUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

[Col. 0379]

[Col. 0379]

### NOTICE (from Gallandi)

[Col. 0379D] I. The only person who committed to writing the more certain records that survive concerning the deeds of Agnellus, bishop of Ravenna, was Agnellus, abbot of Saint Bartholomew, in the *Liber Pontificalis*, composed in the year 839. From a manuscript of the Estense Library, the distinguished Benedict Bacchini first published that work at Modena in 1708, illustrated with dissertations [Col. 0380D] and observations; his edition thereafter appeared at Milan in 1723 among the *Writers of Italian Affairs*, corrected and enlarged [Note: *Rerum Italicarum scriptores*, vol. II, p. 1.]. The author of the *Pontificalis* accordingly relates [Note: Agnellus, *Liber Pontificalis*, part II, ch. 1, ibid., p. 113] that Agnellus was born of noble lineage and abounded in wealth; that he first took a wife and pursued military service; but that afterward, [Col. 0381A] when his wife had died and he had laid aside the military belt, he devoted his whole self to God and cultivated the ecclesiastical life.

Accordingly, about the year 527, in the forty-fourth year of his age, he was enrolled among the clergy by Ecclesius, bishop of Ravenna, and invested with the rank of deacon; later he obtained charge of the church of Blessed Agatha. Then, at the age of seventy, he was appointed to succeed Bishop Maximian by common consent on 22 June 553. After governing the Church of Ravenna for thirteen years, one month, and eight days, he died in the year 566, on the Kalends of August, at the age of eighty-three. For more on these matters see especially Bacchini [Note: On Agnellus, *loc. cit.*, p. 88, § 2, and pp. 94, 115, 202.]; nor, I urge, should you omit Jerome Rubeus [Note: Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, book III, p. 169.] and Ughelli [Note: Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, p. 337.], who nevertheless erred in recording Agnellus’s ordination in 558, and led Oudin into the same error [Note: Oudin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 1443.].

[Col. 0381B] II. Agnellus, bishop of Ravenna, wrote a letter against the Arians to Armenius. It was first published at Basel in 1528 in Johann Sichard’s *Antidote against Heresies*, and was subsequently printed elsewhere many times. We have transcribed it from the Paris *Library of the Fathers* [Note: *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris, 1654, vol. III, p. 147.], since it is more correct than the others; and we have endeavoured to restore its reading wherever doubtful.

We also think that the fragment of a letter of Pelagius I to the same Agnellus, published by Baluzius, should not be omitted here [Note: Baluzius, *Miscellanies*, book V, p. 464.]. It is as follows: “Pelagius to Agnellus of Ravenna. We charge your brotherhood to choose as priest such a man as may prove steadfast in religion, good in morals, and effective in resisting adversaries; and send him to the holy and glorious man John the patrician, charging him above all else to name no one’s name other than mine and yours among the sacred mysteries.”

The distinguished Mansi also incorporated this same fragment, together with other letters of Pelagius drawn from manuscript codices 4047 and 4048 of the Colbertine Library and from another copy at Ripoll, which the aforementioned Baluzius published, into his *Supplement to the Venetian-Labbean Councils*, but less correctly [Note: Mansi, *Supplement to the Councils*, vol. I, p. 431.].

### III.

But the person who appended notes to the new edition of Guilielmus Cave’s *Historia litteraria* is by no means to be heeded.[^c0037-0] There he says that Agnellus whom we are discussing, besides the aforementioned letter to Armenius, also wrote the *Pontificale*, or *Lives of the Bishops of Ravenna*. Clearly confusing truth with falsehood, he judged our Agnellus to be the same as the younger Agnellus, author of the *Pontificale*, who lived almost three centuries after the other and was never honored with episcopal dignity, as we noted above.

That annotator may perhaps have been misled by Vossius, who, in a serious double error, writes that this same Agnellus, the historian of the Church of Ravenna, was its archbishop, indeed the tenth in succession.[^c0037-1] He was therefore rightly censured first by Sandi,[^c0037-2] and afterward by the distinguished author of the *Journal of the Learned Men of Italy*.[^c0037-3]

[^c0037-0]: On Cave, *Historia litteraria*, vol. I, p. 529, note; Baluze, *Miscellanies*, book V, p. 464.
[^c0037-1]: Vossius, *On Latin Historiography*, book III, chapter 4, p. 757.
[^c0037-2]: Sandi, Notes on Vossius’s *On Latin Historiography*, p. 290.
[^c0037-3]: *Journal of the Learned Men of Italy*, vol. I, p. 81.

## Letter of Agnellus to Armenius, on the Rule of Faith (C, S)

[Col. 0381]

Brother Martin demanded that a letter be sent to your Charity, asserting that your concern seeks the consolation of a defense of the catholic faith, which someone has disturbed by various assertions. But when that disturbance has been compared, all sediment is thrown away, and what has been clarified is preserved.

Before all else, therefore, one must believe that God exists (Hebrews 11:6); secondly, what God is. Why this? Because “the fool has said in his heart: There is no God” (Psalm 13:1). Therefore, whoever is not a fool does not say this, but says: “I believe in God.”

If anyone says to you, “What is the God in whom you believe?” you must answer: “This is the God who cries out in Deuteronomy: ‘See, see that I am God, and there is no other besides me’” (Deuteronomy 32:39).[^c0037-4] Likewise, when Moses asked what he should call him, he answered: “I am who I am”; and “Thus you shall say to those to whom I send you: ‘He who is has sent me’” (Exodus 3:14)—that is, the immutable one, always the same.

He was not God only yesterday, but God and Father today; rather, he was always God and Father, and there was always one of whom he was Father. For if being Father had accrued to him, he would have suffered violence in beginning to be what he had not been. But it is blasphemous to think this way.

[^c0037-4]: The Vulgate reads: “God alone.”

But someone says: “He did not suffer violence; rather, he begot the Son by his own will, because if he had not wished to do so, he would not have begotten him.” To this person one must require an answer to this question: When he wished to beget the Son, did he possess the power to beget and the wisdom to will this?

If he says, “He did not possess them,” you refute the blasphemer. If he says, “He did possess them,” you have won the argument. For the Son, as the Apostle says, is the power and wisdom of God the Father (1 Corinthians 1:24). Whoever says, “He did not possess the power,” blasphemes; whoever says, “He did not possess wisdom,” blasphemes.

Why is this so? Because Arius says at the beginning of his book: “God existed when he was not Father,” so that he may appear to introduce the Son as inferior to the Father in honor. He therefore blasphemes the Father in many ways. First, because it cannot stand to say, “He who is sent me,” since one can no longer say “He who is” of one who was one thing yesterday and another today. Therefore, if he is not another today, nor another tomorrow, but remains forever immutable, he was always Father, and there was always one of whom he was Father.

Furthermore, even if he agrees that the Son was begotten by the Father’s will, the catholic can compel him either to say that, before he wished to beget the Son, he did not wish to do so and therefore did not beget him, or that he wished to do so but could not.

If he did not wish to do so, it is good that he did not wish to do so.[^c0037-5] But if he did wish to do so, it is blasphemous to say: “There was a time when God wished something good and could not accomplish it.” It is blasphemous to say that God at any time wished and could not accomplish what he wished.

[^c0037-5]: Perhaps the better reading is *blasphemum est* (“it is blasphemous”), as the following clause suggests; the text may have been corrupted.

At this point Arius, overcome, still presses the catholic: “Did he truly beget, or only apparently?” The catholic replies: “He truly begot.” The heretic then says: “If he truly begot, before he begot, the one whom he begot did not exist.”

The answer is that many things in human frailty arise from that frailty in such a way that begetter and begotten begin simultaneously. The human voice produces speech, and there is no speech except as the son of the voice. Now, because speech is the son of the voice, should speech therefore be called inferior because it is the voice’s son? This absolutely cannot be said. Why? Because from the moment there is a voice, there is also speech.

Add efficacy within the speech, and you have completed a third person, which remains altogether undivided. Thus, the voice having gone forth, brings forth speech,[^c0037-6] and speech having gone forth, brings forth efficacy.

[^c0037-6]: Perhaps *parit* (“begets”), as above.

For example, an order is issued by the voice: “Let this man become consul,” or “Let him be stripped,” or “Let him be killed,” or “Let him be freed from danger.” See: the voice has brought forth a word, but the word has not brought forth efficacy. Rather, from the voice and the word together a power has gone forth: it made one man consul and killed another.

And therefore, from the Father comes the Son; and from the Father and the Son proceeds the Holy Spirit.

Nor does God, as some say, have two sons, Christ and the Holy Spirit. Rather, he has an invisible Son, just as he himself is invisible. In order that he might be visible, he assumed the body of our frailty—not so that he would cease to be invisible, but so that, in Christ himself, he would remain invisible to unbelievers.

For when he says, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10:23), all the Jews, then, were blessed, including those who crucified him, of whom he says through David: “But they looked upon and saw me” (Psalm 21:18). You see, therefore, that he remains invisible and is perceived by a pure and believing mind. Therefore, if the Father is invisible, the Son is invisible, and the Holy Spirit is invisible.

And to return to the point from which this argument arose, so that we may teach this from fragile human beings: these three things are invisible and undivided, gathered together into one and overflowing with the efficacy of power—namely, the voice that begets the word, and the efficacy proceeding from the word together with the voice, which makes one man consul and another be killed.

Tell me, Arian: are these three one, or are they not? If they are not one, divide the voice from the word, and the efficacy from the voice and the word.

But if, in fragile human beings, these three—voice, word, and efficacy—are so one that they are truly three and truly one,[^c0037-7] so that there are indeed three persons but one power of subsistence, then, in the most fragile human being, as we have said, if there is such power, how much more is this so in the omnipotence of God? The almighty Father is the begetter of the Son, and the power proceeding from the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit.

Can fragile man perhaps possess this, while almighty God cannot?

[^c0037-7]: Another version reads in the Trier manuscript: “They are so three in one that they are truly three and truly one; for there are truly three—voice, word, and efficacy. Therefore there are three persons, but one power of subsistence.”

## [Col. 0384B]

Thus far let reason have done its work; now let authority do its work.

The Apostle Paul set two equal forms in the Father and the Son, in order to express their equality. For he says this about the Son: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7).

Do you see that the form and equality are declared by apostolic authority? But the Arian objects and says: “Whether you wish it or not, you cannot deny what the Lord himself says: ‘The Father is greater than I’” (John 14:28).

To this one must answer with what the Apostle said: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” In this servile form he is indeed inferior, while that form remains intact in which he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.

Thus it will be possible for me to agree with you that God became inferior in assuming humanity, while you, together with me, will not deny that, with that form preserved in which he is equal to God the Father, he could not cease to be equal.

It remains to ask the heretic whether, when the Son assumed the form of a servant and came into the world, he abandoned the Father.

The answer is this: If a word that has gone out from my mouth enters your ear and, through your ear, begins to dwell in your heart, tell me: because it remains in your breast, is it no longer in my breast?

If, therefore, a word that has gone out through my mouth and entered your mind does not abandon my soul,[^c0037-8] how much more could the Word who went forth from God the Father not abandon the Father’s breast?

For the Son himself says: “I came forth from the heart of the Father” (Ecclesiasticus 24:25); and the Father says: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Psalm 44:2).

[^c0037-8]: From the preceding and following context, one might perhaps read: “If, then, while the word has gone forth through my mouth…”

They object elsewhere: “He went elsewhere,” that is, he truly came from heaven to earth. How could it happen, then, that he did not depart from the Father’s bosom?

The answer is given in Genesis 2:10: “Consider the four rivers flowing forth from one source in paradise.” The source, therefore, is the Father of the four rivers. Although they encircle the whole earth, they do not depart from the bosom of their father—that is, from that source which is in paradise.

Or, if you can, divide the source from the river. But if you cannot do this, stop dividing the Son from the Father, just as you cannot, by any reasoning whatsoever, do this with the element of water.

The heretic will also argue with you concerning passibility: “Was God there when the Lord suffered?” If you say, “God, undivided, suffered at the same time,” you fall into the heresy of Patripassianism. If you deny that the divinity was there at the same time, you create a heresy.

Since, therefore, you do not deny that God was there on the cross in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (2 Corinthians 5:19), you are compelled to teach whether God was crucified at the same time.[^c0037-9]

[^c0037-9]: Another version reads: “to say that God was crucified at the same time.”

To this you will answer that he first received the blows, but remained impassible. The sun’s radiance, remaining in a tree, receives the first blow of the axe at the moment when the tree is cut down; yet, remaining impassible, it continues whole, while the tree is cut down.

If, therefore, a creature of light possesses this power, so that, when it is struck together with the wood in which it is present, it leaves the wood to its suffering while itself escapes injury, how much more will the almighty Creator himself, the true light, remain impassible in Christ?

---

# Saint Aurelian, Bishop of Arles

## Rule of Saint Aurelian of Arles for Monks

## Ancient Testimonies concerning Saint Aurelian and His Rule

Saint Gregory the Great, book VII, letter 117, in the second indiction, to Vigilius, bishop of Arles:

“Childebert, king of the Franks, of glorious memory, inflamed by love for the catholic religion, established within the walls of the city of Arles, as we find recorded in writing, a monastery for men for the sake of his reward, and granted certain possessions there for the support of its inhabitants.

“Lest his will ever be rendered void, and lest the arrangements made for the peace of the monks be disturbed, he requested by his letters that what he had bestowed upon the legal possession of that monastery be confirmed by apostolic authority.

“Therefore, since both the royal will and the highly desired matter demanded fulfillment, our predecessor Vigilius, bishop of the Roman See, sent a written communication to your predecessor Aurelius”—read: Aurelianus—“…”

Egbert, archbishop of York, in his *Excerpt on Priestly Law*, chapter 69, in the British councils:

“Bishop Aurelian says: ‘Monks shall never take meat as food; but chickens, and so forth,’ as in chapter 51.”

Saint Benedict of Aniane, abbot, cites testimonies in the *Concordia of Rules*, chapters 6, 7, 22, 31, and 42, from the Rule of Saint Aurelian, bishop, for monks.

Smaragdus likewise uses the authority and testimonies of the same author in his *Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict*, although he almost always calls him Aurelius rather than Aurelianus.

## Critical Observation on the Following Rule

Just as Saint Caesarius composed two Rules, so also did Saint Aurelian, likewise bishop of Arles. He was not the immediate successor of Saint Caesarius, for Auxanius governed this archiepiscopal see for a few years between them.

He organized two monasteries, one for men and the other for holy virgins, and composed two Rules for them. This monastery of men was founded by Childebert, king of the Franks, and enriched with royal gifts, just as Pope Vigilius also took it under his special protection.

Saint Gregory the Great, cited above, bears witness to this. There we have a vivid example of exemption from episcopal jurisdiction, obtained from the ordinary bishop himself.

Saint Aurelian therefore wrote this Rule for monks immediately after attaining the episcopate, around the year 545. At the beginning of that year he was made archbishop of Arles, and he died in the year 545.

The Rule itself has a close connection with the Rule of Saint Caesarius. The order of the divine Office is almost the same in both, although the other is more extensive, containing fifty-five chapters, in addition to the prescribed manner of chanting and the particular regulations concerning food and drink to be observed in the refectory.

# Rule of Saint Aurelian for Monks

## Prologue

To the holy and Christ-venerating brothers established in the monastery which, by God’s mercy and at the command of King Childebert, we founded:

Aurelian, bishop.

Because God inspired us—he who anticipates us with his ineffable mercy—it seemed right to us that, having rejected the pleasures of the world and despised, or altogether spurned, temporal joys, you should choose the splendor of a most holy life; that, embracing the grace of virginity and chastity and pursuing the love of God with the full hunger of your inner being and heart, you should crucify your flesh with the fear of the Lord and say: “I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your justice” (Psalm 108); and: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6).

Therefore, with the Lord commanding and working in us both the will and its accomplishment, we determined to construct a monastery for you for the advancement of your souls, as indeed we have done.[^c0037-11] And for this reason we have established for you a rule and discipline that would make you walk rightly along the way of perfection and reach the kingdoms of heaven successfully.

[^c0037-11]: This monastery at Arles was built by Saint Aurelian in honor of the Holy Cross. Cardinal Baronius discusses it under the year 553, though with considerable hesitation because he lacked clearer documentation. The epitaph of Saint Florentinus, its first abbot, however, agrees exactly with the chronological note appended to the Rule. The monastery was founded at the end of the year 548. Florentinus presided over it as first abbot for five years, that is, until the day before the Ides of April in the year 553, as his funerary inscription records in Baronius under that year, at the final entry; the inscription also mentions his successors Redemptus and Constantinus. This Rule shows that the monastery was built not by Hilary the archbishop but by Aurelian. Aurelian succeeded Auxanius in the year 546. Hilary, however, had lived a full century earlier. According to Prosper, he died in the twenty-sixth year of Theodosius the Younger, which was the year 433.

## Chapters of the Rule of Saint Aurelian

1. If anyone comes for conversion, let the Rule be read to him in the visitors’ room.
2. He shall not leave the monastery until his death.
3. He shall not receive religious clothing unless he makes deeds of gift concerning his property, large or small, to whomever he wishes.
4. Whoever is tonsured in the monastery shall have some of his hair sent to the *confessio* (shrine), and shall reserve nothing for himself that he does not hand over to the abbot’s authority.
5. Nothing is to be received secretly. If anything is sent, and the person to whom it is sent does not need it, it shall be placed in the common fund and given to whoever needs it.
6. No letters may be given or received without the knowledge or permission of the abbot.
7. No one shall keep near his bed anything that can be eaten or drunk.
8. No one shall have a private cell or cupboard.
9. One must not swear at all.
10. One must not curse.
11. One must not lie.
12. Anger must not be retained at all.
13. No brother shall lay hands on another brother.
14. Laymen shall not enter the monastery or basilica, except only the visitors’ room.
15. Women are never to be seen at all, not even in the visitors’ room.
16. No monk may go out to greet anyone except with the provost or some other elder.
17. No one below the age of ten or twelve shall be received into the monastery.
18. A slave shall not be received; a freedman, however, may be received if the abbot so judges.
19. Even the stewards shall not be permitted to enter the monastery except for the purposes established in this Rule.
20. Infants shall not be received from baptism.
21. Those who are appointed to offices shall receive the keys above the altar or from the Gospel.
22. In every ministry they shall take turns, except the abbot, the very old, and little children.
23. They shall not choose the work they wish to do; rather, they shall do whatever is commanded by the abbot or provost.
24. While working with their hands, let holy meditation never cease in their hearts.
25. Let everything be common to you, and let no one presume to call or claim anything his own.
26. No clothing of another color shall be worn except gray, white, or natural black.
27. Secular bed furnishings shall not be used; nor shall the monastery be adorned with such things.
28. After Matins, no one may return to sleep.
29. At the vigils, care must be taken that no one sleeps; instead, let them work with their hands.
30. When the signal is given, no one shall arrive late.
31. While the psalms are being sung, no one shall speak or work with his hands.
32. Let all the monks learn letters.
33. Let all remain in separate beds.
34. The holy abbot shall remain among the community.
35. No one may speak alone with another alone; if they are found doing so, let them be punished with the severest discipline.
36. No one shall presume to speak with one who has been excommunicated.
37. They must obey the superiors.
38. If anyone is corrected or chastised for any fault, he must not presume to answer the one rebuking him.
39. Have no quarrels.
40. The proud, disobedient, and those who prolong their anger are never to be spared.
41. For any fault, the lawful number of blows must not be exceeded.
42. How those in authority are to show fatherly affection toward all.
43. The holy abbot may neither sell nor give away the monastery’s property, nor do anything contrary to the provisions of the Rule.
44. Whatever remains beyond the needs of the monastery shall be distributed to the poor by the steward.
45. Old clothing shall be returned to the abbot to be given to the poor.
46. No one shall receive an office of honor unless, by God’s favor, he has been judged worthy of the priesthood; he alone may go out.
47. Those who are underage shall be compelled to make deeds concerning their property when they have reached a proven age.
48. No banquet shall be prepared for anyone except visiting pilgrims and servants of God.
49. Those sitting at table shall keep silence.
50. The holy abbot shall not eat outside the community.
51. Meat shall never be taken as food. Chickens and other poultry shall be provided only to the sick; fish shall be served on certain feast days.
52. Nothing to eat or drink may be tasted outside the common table, except by the sick and infants.
53. How the sick are to be obeyed.
54. The holy abbot shall provide whatever is necessary in sufficient measure.
55. Let the holy community strive to fulfill everything that has been established.

# The Rule

## Chapter One

### I

By God’s command, we establish first of all that, if anyone comes for conversion, the Rule shall be read to him in the visitors’ room; and if he professes that he will fulfill everything, then he shall be received.

### II

Once received, he shall neither presume nor be permitted to leave the monastery until his death, because of the prophetic saying: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26).

### III

He shall not receive religious clothing unless, concerning all his property, whether great or small, he makes deeds of gift or sale to whomever he wishes, because of the Lord’s command, where he says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have” (Matthew 19); and: “If anyone does not leave all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

### IV

If a layman is to be tonsured, some of his hair shall be sent to the *confessio* (shrine), so that it may serve as testimony for him.

If he comes already tonsured or in religious clothing, he shall not be received unless, as we said above, he makes deeds concerning what he had possessed as his own in the world, so that he reserves nothing for himself that he does not alienate. Whatever he brings with him, he shall hand over entirely to the abbot’s authority, fearing the example of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), who offered part and faithlessly kept part for themselves.

### V

Receive nothing secretly. If a relative or friend gives or sends anyone something in clothing, gold, or anything else, it shall be under the abbot’s authority. If the person to whom it is sent needs it, it shall be given to him; but if he needs nothing, it shall be placed in the common fund and given to whoever needs it.

### VI

In particular, no letters may be given or received without the knowledge or permission of the abbot.

### VII

No one shall presume to keep near his bed anything that could be eaten or drunk. Rather, let everyone store such things in the common storeroom; and if inequality of need requires it, whatever is necessary shall not be denied him at the command of the elder.

### VIII

No one may have a cell, cupboard, or anything of this kind that can be locked privately.

### IX

Do not swear, because the Lord said: “Do not swear” (Matthew 5). Another Scripture says: “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house” (Ecclesiasticus 23).

### X

Do not curse, because it is written: “Nor will those who curse possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

### XI

It is altogether forbidden to lie, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1); and: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5).

### XII

No one shall presume to prolong anger until another day. If, as human frailty permits, a harsh word arises among the brothers, they must ask forgiveness of one another and release one another from their debts, because of the Lord’s command, where he says:

“If you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5).

And: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6).

Likewise: “If he sins against you seven times in a day and, turning back, says, ‘I am sorry,’ forgive him” (Luke 17).

And: “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven” (Matthew 18).

Another Scripture says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1). And the Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4).

But if—God forbid—someone, at the devil’s instigation, is so filled with fury that he contemptuously disregards these commands with an obstinate heart, and one of the disputants approaches the other first, he shall ask forgiveness of him. If the one from whom forgiveness is sought does not forgive him, he shall receive the lawful discipline, so that he may be corrected toward charity.

But if both despise this, both shall alike be suspended from communion or from food until they are reconciled to one another.

### XIII

If a brother dares to lay hands on another brother, he shall receive the lawful discipline.

### XIV

No layman, whether noble or obscure, shall be permitted to enter the basilica or monastery. If anyone wishes to come out of devotion or kinship, he shall meet them in the monastery’s visitors’ room.

### XV

No women whatsoever—neither religious nor secular—shall be permitted to enter, whether the mother of the abbot or of any monk, or any other female relative or acquaintance, to greet them or to pray.

Follow the example of the Lord and Master, who says: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And: “If anyone does not leave father or mother, he cannot be my disciple.”

Another Scripture says: “Those who said to father and mother, ‘We do not know you,’ kept your commandments, Lord.”

### XVI

The laymen to whom we have granted permission to come are nevertheless never to see or speak with any of the monks without the abbot, the provost, or some other elder whom the abbot has appointed. Nor shall they ever speak in a loud voice.

### XVII

No one of too young an age shall be received into the monastery, except those aged ten or twelve, who no longer need to be nursed and who know how to avoid faults.

### XVIII

A slave shall not be received. A freedman, however, if he is still of adolescent age and comes with letters from his patron, shall be received or not at the abbot’s discretion.

### XIX

The stewards of the monastery, if they are in lay clothing, shall not themselves be permitted to enter, except for the purposes established in this Rule. They may enter with masons or carpenters if something must be made or repaired, or for some specific matter that the abbot has ordered to be done. Otherwise, they shall have no permission or freedom to enter.

### XX

No one shall receive an infant from baptism.

### XXI

Those to whom the keys of the storeroom, wine cellar, granary, gate, and oratory are to be entrusted shall be persons of proven character. They shall receive them above the altar or from the Gospel, knowing that they must render an account to God for the ministry entrusted to them.

### XXII

In every ministry—whether in the order of chanting, reading, or working—they shall take turns, except the holy abbot. The very old, very young children, and those so infirm that they cannot rise at all shall not be compelled to perform these duties, because they are unable to do so.

### XXIII

They shall not choose for themselves the craft they are to learn or the work they are to perform. Rather, it shall be at the abbot’s discretion to command whatever he judges useful.

### XXIV

Throughout the day, while they work with their hands, holy meditation shall not cease in their hearts, because of the Apostle’s saying: “Singing and making melody to the Lord in your hearts with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3).

### XXV

No one shall presume to call anything his own or claim it as private. Rather, according to the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 4), let everything be common to you; let your soul be one and your heart one in the Lord.

### XXVI

Do not wear clothing of any other color except gray, white, and natural black.

### XXVII

Do not use secular bed furnishings made of colored materials. Never purchase silk hangings for the altars decorated with gold or gems. If one of the faithful offers such a thing as a votive gift, and the abbot judges it appropriate or necessity demands it, they may use it by selling it.

### XXVIII

After the prayers of Matins, no one may return to sleep. When Matins has been completed, Prime shall immediately be said; afterward, until the third hour, let everyone devote himself to reading.

### XXIX

During the vigils, while the reading is being given, work with your hands on hemp, flax, or something similar, so that sleep does not overtake you.

If it is a Sunday or feast day and sleep comes upon someone, let him be ordered to stand while the others sit, so that he may drive away the sluggishness of sleep and not be found lukewarm or negligent in the work of God.

### XXX

When the signal is given, let every task be abandoned. Like the most prudent bees hastening to the hive, strive to hurry forward with such swift haste. If anyone comes late, let him be subject to discipline.

### XXXI

While the psalms are being sung, let your holy souls take care not to wander in thought; indeed, do not presume to work or speak. Rather, “sing psalms wisely” (Psalm 46), as the prophet said: “I will sing psalms and understand” (Psalm 100); and: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14).

Fear the saying: “Cursed is the one who performs the work of the Lord negligently” (Jeremiah 48).

### XXXII

Let everyone learn letters.

### XXXIII

Let everyone remain in separate beds.

### XXXIV

The holy abbot shall not remain outside the community.

### XXXV

We especially admonish before God that this be observed: no one may speak or sit privately with another, especially during the evening and night hours.

If they are found in secret, let them be punished with the greatest severity, as though they had committed a crime, except those whose age and holiness have been proven.

### XXXVI

No one may speak with one who has been excommunicated, except the person whom the holy abbot has appointed as his keeper.

### XXXVII

Obey your superiors and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls and must render an account to God (Hebrews 13).

### XXXVIII

If anyone is rebuked or disciplined for any fault or transgression of the Rule, he shall not presume to answer the one rebuking him. The sin punished here is not punished at the eternal judgment.

You must therefore receive care of the soul as a sick person receives the care of a physician, holding to the words of Holy Scripture: “Whoever rejects discipline is miserable” (Proverbs 15); and: “I am ready for scourges” (Psalm 37).

### XXXIX

Have no quarrels, obeying the Apostle’s command, where he says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle” (2 Timothy 2).

### XL

The proud, disobedient, and those who prolong their anger are never to be spared until they are corrected.

### XLI

If, for any fault, it is necessary to receive discipline by the scourge, the lawful number—namely, thirty-nine—must never be exceeded.

### XLII

However just the discipline may be, nevertheless, according to the words “goodness and discipline” (Psalm 118), the holy abbot shall show fatherly affection toward all, following the Apostle: “As a nurse cherishes her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2); and: “I have become all things to all, that I might save all” (1 Corinthians 9).

### XLIII

The holy abbot may not give away or sell anything belonging to the monastery, nor do anything contrary to the provisions of the Rule.

If he attempts to do so, then, with holy counsel and the unanimous agreement of the brothers, and with our permission, do not comply with him. Do not permit this to be done in any way, because he should know that he will have to give an account of the matter before God.

### XLIV

If anything remains beyond the expenses or needs of the brothers—whether in gold, clothing, or the storeroom—the holy abbot shall have it distributed to the poor, pilgrims, or captives through the steward or through any trustworthy person.

### XLV

Those who receive new clothing shall return their old clothing to the abbot, so that it may be given to beginners or the poor.

### XLVI

No one shall receive the honor of the priesthood or diaconate, except the abbot, if he wishes to be ordained a priest, and one deacon and one subdeacon, whom he shall have authority to ordain whenever and whomever he wishes.

If, by God’s favor, you should progress so far that one of you is sought for the episcopate, that person alone may leave.

### XLVII

Those who are underage or enter the monastery while their parents are alive shall be compelled to make deeds concerning their property when they have reached a proven age or have obtained control of their parents’ possessions.

### XLVIII

No banquet shall be held in the monastery for anyone—not for bishops, abbots, stewards, or any religious or lay parent or relative from this city.

But if, as commonly happens, an abbot or traveling pilgrim monks arrive and wish to visit the monastery, it shall be in the power of the holy abbot to invite them to refreshment.

Because we wish your holy charity to devote itself continually to prayer and reading and to be free for God alone, we command that you be free from this preparation and disturbance.

### XLIX

Those sitting at table shall keep silence, and a reading shall be given every day, throughout the entire time when food is being eaten, so that both men may be refreshed: the outer man by food and the inner man by the word of God.

For it is written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4).

### L

The holy abbot shall not eat outside the community unless inequality of circumstances makes it necessary.

### LI

Meat shall never be taken as food. Chickens and all other poultry shall not be served to the community; they shall be provided and may be eaten only by the sick.

Fish shall be procured on certain feast days, or whenever the holy abbot wishes to grant permission.

### LII

Outside the common table, no one may taste anything to eat or drink, except the sick and those of an age that still requires especially abundant nourishment.

### LIII

The sick are to be obeyed in such a way that, if the holy abbot considers it right, they may even have their own little storeroom and a separate kitchen. Care and attention shall be devoted to them until they recover.

### LIV

Because, by God’s favor, an adequate and sufficient provision has been granted to you, capable of supplying what your monastery needs, I admonish and charge you before God and his angels, holy brother abbot, and you, venerable provost, whoever you may be, to provide the holy community—which, inspired by God and at his command, lives according to the institutions we have established in the Rule—with everything necessary for clothing and food in sufficient measure.

If you neglect this, and they begin, compelled by necessity, to murmur or suffer want, know that you and I will have to give an account of this matter before the tribunal of Christ.

### LV

And you, holy community, I adjure, by your progress and by almighty God, to preserve whole and undefiled everything that we have established in this Rule for the remedy of our soul and for the salvation of your souls.

So that you do not neglect anything through forgetfulness, read these provisions again once every thirty days—that is, on the Kalends.

We have also judged it appropriate to insert in this little book the order in which you ought to sing the psalms.

[Col. —]

[0393]

On the first day of Easter, at Terce: three times, “Lord, have mercy”; twelve psalms—that is, four brothers are to recite two psalms each and a third psalm with “Alleluia.” When the psalms have been completed, “Lord, have mercy,” and six antiphons; three readings: one from the Acts of the Apostles, another from the Apocalypse, and a third from the Gospel; the hymn *Jam surgit hora tertia* (“Now the third hour rises”), and a short reading (*capitellum*); then “Lord, have mercy.” Thus, in every work of God, say “Lord, have mercy” three times before you begin, and after the psalms and the short reading have been completed.

At Sext, the same number of psalms, one antiphon, [Col. 0393C] the hymn *Jam sexta sensim volvitur* (“Now the sixth hour slowly turns”), a Gospel reading, and a short reading. At None, let the same order be maintained: the hymn *Ter hora trina volvitur* (“Three times the hour turns”). At the lighting of the lamps, a short direct psalm (*directaneus*), namely, *Regna terrae, cantate Deo, psallite Domino* (“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God, sing praises to the Lord”; Psalm 67).

On the following day: *Laudate, pueri, Dominum* (“Praise the Lord, servants”); three antiphons; the hymn *Hic est dies verus Dei* (“This is the true day of God”), and a short reading. Recite this hymn throughout Easter at Matins and at the lighting of the lamps.

At the twelfth hour, first a short direct psalm: *Sol cognovit occasum suum* (“The sun knows its setting”; Psalm 103). Six brothers are to recite two psalms each with their accompanying “Alleluia” verses; three antiphons; two readings, one from the Apostle and another from the Gospel. At the Easter night office recite everything in the same number, as we have prescribed for the twelfth hour.

At Matins, first a direct psalm: *Exaltabo te, Deus meus et Rex meus* (“I will exalt you, my God and my King”). Then *Judica me, Deus* (“Judge me, O God”), and *Deus Deus meus, ad te de luce vigilo* (“O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the dawn”), with “Alleluia.” Then *Confitemini Domino* (“Give thanks to the Lord”), with “Alleluia”; then *Cantemus Domino* (“Let us sing to the Lord”), likewise; afterward *Lauda, anima mea, Dominum* (“Praise the Lord, my soul”). *Laudate Dominum, quoniam bonus est psalmus* (“Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good”). *Lauda, Jerusalem, Dominum* (“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem”): all three with “Alleluia.” Then the blessing is to be said.

After the blessing: *Laudate Dominum de caelis* (“Praise the Lord from the heavens”). *Cantate Domino canticum novum* (“Sing a new song to the Lord”). *Laudate Dominum in sanctis ejus* (“Praise the Lord in his holy places”), with “Alleluia.” *Magnificat anima mea Dominum* (“My soul magnifies the Lord”), either with an antiphon or with “Alleluia”; the hymn *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”), and a short reading. Complete Matins in this order throughout Easter.

Thus also on every Sunday, [Col. 0394B] and on all the greater feasts, when you will abstain from work.

On ordinary days, however, at the night office first let the direct psalm be said: *Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam* (“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy”); then eighteen psalms. Three short antiphons, two readings from the Apostle or the Prophets, and a short reading. When the night office has been completed, say Matins.

In summer—that is, from Easter until the Kalends of October—the same order shall be followed. On Friday, however, after the night office, two readings from the book shall be made in summer, and three in winter. On Sunday, at every season, both summer and winter, six readings from the book shall be made after the night office.

If it should happen that you rise later for the vigils, let as much be read as the abbot sees fit. When he gives the signal, the reader is to rise without delay, so that the canonical number of readings may be completed.

From the Kalends of October onward, additional night offices are to be added. At the first, say: *Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam* (“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy”); at the second: *Miserere mei, Deus, miserere mei* (“Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me”). A direct psalm is to be said, and eighteen psalms; two readings from the Prophets or from Solomon.

The hymn for the first night office is *Rex aeterne Domine* (“Eternal King, Lord”); for the second, *Magna et mirabilia* (“Great and wonderful”). After these have been recited, because the nights grow longer, make three readings from the book every day. One brother is to read three or four pages, according to the size of the book: if it is written in small script or in a larger format, three pages; if smaller, four. Then let a prayer be made. Again let him read the same amount, and let another prayer be made. A third time let him read the same amount; then rise, say the psalm antiphon in its order, afterward the responsory, and then the antiphon.

Again let another brother read; and when the three readings have been completed, say the canonical Matins psalms, namely: first the canticle with its antiphon, then the direct psalm: *Judica me, Deus* (“Judge me, O God”); *Deus Deus meus, ad te de luce vigilo* (“O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the dawn”); *Laudate Dominum, quoniam bonus est psalmus* (“Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good”); *Lauda, Jerusalem, Dominum* (“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem”). Then *Laudate Dominum de caelis* (“Praise the Lord from the heavens”); *Cantate Domino canticum novum* (“Sing a new song to the Lord”); *Laudate Dominum in sanctis ejus* (“Praise the Lord in his holy places”).

With the antiphon, say the hymn *Splendor paternae gloriae* (“Splendor of the Father’s glory”) one day; on another day, *Aeterne lucis conditor* (“Eternal creator of light”); then a short reading and “Lord, have mercy” twelve times. Let this be completed in this manner every ordinary day.

After Matins, at Prime, let twelve psalms be said; the hymn *Fulgentis auctor aetheris* (“Author of the shining heavens”); two readings, one from the Old and another from the New Testament; and a short reading.

After this, let everyone devote themselves to reading until Terce. During the remainder of the day, let them do their work, according to what the Lord said: *Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor* (“My Father is working until now, and I also am working”; John 5). And the Apostle says: *Operantes manibus nostris* (“Working with our hands”; [reference printed as II Thess. 4]). And: *Qui non operatur non manducet* (“Whoever does not work should not eat”; [reference printed as I Thess. 3]). For it is written: *Viae otiosorum stratae sunt spinis* (“The paths of the idle are paved with thorns”; Proverbs 15). And: *Servum inutilem projicite in tenebras exteriores* (“Throw the useless servant into the outer darkness”; Matthew 25).

Therefore, on ordinary days, at Terce say twelve psalms, an antiphon, the hymn *Jam surgit hora tertia* (“Now the third hour rises”), a reading, and the short reading *Fiat, Domine* (“Let it be done, Lord”).

At Sext, let there be the same number of psalms, an antiphon, the hymn *Jam sexta sensim volvitur* (“Now the sixth hour slowly turns”), a reading, and a short reading.

At None, the same order is to be followed; the hymn is *Ter hora trina volvitur* (“Three times the hour turns”).

At the lighting of the lamps, on every occasion—feasts and ordinary days alike—first a direct psalm, then two antiphons; the third is always to be said with “Alleluia.” On one day, the hymn is *Deus qui certis legibus* (“God, who by fixed laws”); on another, *Deus creator omnium* (“God, creator of all”), and a short reading.

At the twelfth hour, eighteen psalms, an antiphon and a hymn, a reading, and a short reading.

When you are about to retire, Compline is to be said in the school where you reside: first a direct psalm, then Psalm 90, and afterward the customary short readings. [Col. 0395C]

[Col. 0396A] On the Nativity of the Lord and on Epiphany, rise at the third hour. Say one night office, and make six readings from the prophet Isaiah; then say a second night office, and let six others be read from the Gospel.

On Epiphany proceed as follows: at the first office, say one night office; then make those six readings from the prophet Daniel, and the night offices; and likewise six Matins readings from the Gospel, in the order that we have written for Easter or for Sundays.

On the feasts of martyrs, let three or four readings be made. Read the first from the Gospel, and the rest from the passions of the martyrs.

Every Friday, after the twelfth hour, let six readings from the book be made, and three after the night office.

Every Saturday at Matins, say *Cantemus Domino* (“Let us sing to the Lord”) and *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”). At Terce, let three readings be said: one from the Prophets, another from the Apostle, and a third from the Gospel. [Col. 0396B]

Every Sunday, when the first reading is read after the night office—that is, the resurrection—let no one presume to sit, but let everyone stand. On another Sunday, another resurrection is to be read, and so, in order, all four resurrections are to be read on successive Sundays.

After Terce, say the Lord’s Prayer, and let everyone receive Communion while singing psalms. Do the same on feast days. The readings, however, are to be made whenever the holy abbot sees fit.
