When someone has died, let a few brothers keep vigil with him in the oratory until midnight, and let them make the readings. After midnight, those who kept vigil are to rest, and others are to keep vigil in turn. Make this known to the holy bishop, so that he may order him to be carried to the place where he is to be laid. But if he should disdain to provide this service, ask clergy from whatever church may be available to escort him, and give them provisions. [Col. 0396C]

We have also inserted the order of meals into this rule.

[Col. 0395]

[Col. 0395C] Every day, three portions of food are to be provided for the meal, two at midday, and two at supper. As for drinks at the meal: in summer, unmixed wine and three *caldelli*; at midday, only three; at supper in summer, during June, July, and August, let them drink three; on the remaining days, let them drink two at supper.

On feast days, and whenever the abbot wishes to grant indulgences, let as much food as he wishes be provided, together with fresh provisions. Every day, vegetables are always to be seasoned with cheese and oil. Let them receive two drinks at midday and two at supper; if they are fasting, three.

The fast is to be observed from the Kalends of September until the Kalends of October on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, they are to fast every day except Saturday and Sunday. From Epiphany until Easter, they are likewise to fast every day except on the greater feasts, Saturday, and Sunday. After Easter until Pentecost, they are to fast only on Friday.

After Pentecost, during June, July, and August, the matter of fasting or of taking a midday meal is to be left to the abbot’s discretion. According as he sees the brothers’ capacity, let him strive to regulate it. [Col. 0396D]

Aurelian, a sinner, established this rule in the name of Christ.

[Col. 0395D] In the name of Christ, a monastery of men of God was founded in the city of Arles by Saint Aurelian, bishop, at the command of Childebert, king of the Franks, of blessed memory, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh indiction, in the fifth year after the consulship of Basil the Younger, illustrious man; and a basilica was established there in honor of the holy apostles and martyrs. It contains relics deposited there, namely: of the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ; of blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ; of John the Baptist and forerunner of our Lord Jesus Christ; of Stephen; Peter; Paul; John; James; Andrew; Philip; Thomas; Bartholomew; Matthew; James; Simon; Jude; Matthias; Genesius; Symphorianus; Baudilius; Victor; Hilary, bishop and confessor; Martin, bishop and confessor; and Caesarius, bishop. [Col. 0396D]

(From the diptychs of the same monastery.)

[Col. 0395]

[Col. 0395D] At the same time, praying, we also beseech you, Lord, on behalf of the souls of your servants, our former fathers and founders, Aurelian, Peter, Florentinus, Redemptus, Constantinus, Himiterus, Hilarinus, Januarinus, Reparatus, Childebert, Vultrogotha, and all our brothers whom you have deigned to call to yourself from this place; and also on behalf of all the faithful remembered at this place, as well as our parents and those serving this place; and on behalf of the souls of all your faithful male and female servants and of pilgrims who have died in the peace of the Church: that you, Lord our God, may grant them forgiveness of sins and bestow eternal rest upon them, through the merits and intercessions [Col. 0398A] of your saints, Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ; John the Baptist and forerunner of our Lord Jesus Christ; Stephen; Peter; Paul; John; James; Andrew; Philip; Thomas; Bartholomew; Matthew; James; Simon; Jude; Matthias; Genesius; Symphorianus; Baudilius; Victor; Hilary, bishop and confessor; Martin, bishop and confessor; and Caesarius, bishop. In your mercy, deign to grant and hear these petitions, you who live and reign, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[SAINT AURELIAN OF ARLES’S RULE FOR VIRGINS.]

[Col. 0397]

TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING SAINT AURELIAN AND HIS RULE FOR VIRGINS.

[Col. 0397]

[Col. 0397B] *Roman Martyrology*, June 16: At Lyons, the burial of blessed Aurelian, bishop of Arles.

Pope Vigilius, in a letter to Aurelian of Arles: “We willingly entrust to your fraternity the administration of our vicariate, and we trust that, through the service of your charity, all matters will be diligently completed in deeds pleasing to God; since divine grace has judged you worthy of sharing in the highest priesthood, and the Christian and God-pleasing will of the most glorious Childebert, king of the Franks, has added its testimony on your behalf,” etc.

The same pope to the bishops of Gaul: “Since long ago we had entrusted the care of our vicariate to Auxanius, formerly bishop of the city of Arles, but he departed this life after completing its course, and our brother Aurelian is known to have succeeded him in that place, we have judged it very necessary [Col. 0397C] that this care should be entrusted by us to the aforementioned man. We are confident that, in accordance with the dignity of his position, he can accomplish all things that please God through good works—especially since our glorious son, King Childebert, has offered testimony to his good conscience through the devotion of his Christian will.”

Likewise, a letter sent by the clergy of Italy to the Frankish envoys, in volume 1 of Sirmond’s *Councils of Gaul*: “Therefore we ask and adjure your Glory to report all these matters quickly to your provinces, lest either those who have been sent deceive them, or a certain Anastasius—whom the holy bishop Aurelian of the city of Arles sent to the most blessed pope two years ago—lie about something there in Gaul.” [Col. 0398B]

Saint Gregory the Great, letter 117, 50, 7, indiction 2, to Vigilius, bishop of Arles: “Childebert, king of the Franks, of glorious memory, inflamed by love of the Catholic religion, established within the walls of the city of Arles, as we find recorded in writing, a monastery of men for his reward before God, and granted certain possessions there for the support of its inhabitants. So that his will might never be rendered void, and that what had been arranged for the repose of the monks might not be disturbed, he requested by his letters that what he had bestowed upon the same monastery be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See. Therefore, since both the royal will and a matter greatly desired demanded its execution, letters were sent by our predecessor Vigilius, bishop of the Roman See, to your predecessor Aurelius [read: Aurelian].” [Col. 0398C]

John Trithemius, *On the Property of Monks*, chapter 5: “Bishop Aurelian, in the Rule for Nuns, chapter 3, says as follows: ‘You shall accept nothing secretly,’ etc.”

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, also cites several chapters from this Rule of Saint Aurelian for Virgins in his *Concordia of Rules*.

[Col. 0397]

CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE.

[Col. 0397]

[Col. 0397D] We have already spoken above of Saint Aurelian’s Rule for Monks; now we come to the one he gave to the sacred Virgins. Just as Saint Caesarius founded two monasteries in the city of Arles, so also his successor in the episcopate, Saint Aurelian, built two monasteries in the same city through the generosity of Childebert, king of the Franks: one for men and the other for women. For them he composed two distinct Rules.

Just as the first Rule has a close connection with the Rule of Saint Caesarius, so this present Rule for the holy virgins contains the same monastic teaching, especially concerning the order of the divine office, food, and clothing, differing from the other only in certain circumstances and ceremonies. Besides this Rule, which comprises forty chapters and to which is added a separate exhortation concerning the divine office, Holstenius added a letter of John, bishop of Arles, an exhortation to the sacred virgins of Saint Aurelian, most worthy of reading; it both confirms and strengthens the Rule itself.

[Col. 0399]

SAINT AURELIAN’S RULE FOR VIRGINS. (C)

[Col. 0399]

PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0399A] To the holy and venerable sisters in Christ established in the monastery of blessed Mary which, by God’s command, we founded within the walls of the city of Arles, Aurelian, bishop.

Because, through the inspiration of God who in his ineffable mercy goes before us, you have judged it right, after rejecting the pleasures of the world and despising or spurning temporal joys, to choose the splendor of a most holy life; and, embracing the grace of virginity and chastity, to pursue the love of God with the full desire of your inmost being and heart; and to crucify your flesh with divine fear, holding to the words: *Juravi et statui custodire judicia justitiae tuae* (“I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your justice”; Psalm 118), and *Mihi mundus crucifixus est, et ego mundo* (“The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world”; Galatians 6)—we have determined, at the Lord’s command and with him working in us both the will and its accomplishment, to build a monastery for you for the advancement of your souls, as indeed we have done.

Therefore we have established this Rule for you as a discipline, so that through it you may learn to run along the way of God’s commandments and may happily reach the kingdoms of heaven.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE RULE BEGIN.

[Col. 0399]

1. If any woman comes for conversion and asks to be received into the monastery, let the Rule first be read to her in the reception room. Once she has been received, let her not leave the monastery until her death.

2. Let her not receive religious clothing unless she has made deeds of gift concerning her property to whomever she wishes.

3. Nothing is to be accepted secretly. But if anything is sent, and the person to whom it is sent has no need of it, let it be placed in common and given to the one who needs it.

4. No letters are to be given or received without the knowledge or permission of the abbess.

5. Let no one keep near her bed anything that can be eaten or drunk.

6. Let no one have a private cell or cupboard.

7. No swearing.

8. No cursing.

9. No lying.

10. Anger is not to be retained at all.

11. No sister is to lay hands on another sister.

12. No one may leave to visit anyone except with the superior or some older sister.

13. A slave is not to be received. A freedwoman, however, if she is one and the abbess sees fit, may be received.

14. Neither secular men nor secular women may enter the monastery, except into the basilica of the Lady Mary and into the reception room. [Col. 0399C]

15. Even the monastery’s stewards are not to be permitted to enter, except for the purposes which we establish in this Rule.

16. Infants are not to be received from baptismal fonts.

17. Those appointed to offices are to receive the keys over the Gospel. [Editorial note: Read “Gospel,” as is clear to anyone consulting the text below, column 402, line 9.]

18. They are to take turns serving, except for the abbess and the very young children.

[Col. 0400A] 19. Let no one choose work to be done according to her own preference, but let her do what has been commanded by the abbess or the superior.

20. While working with their hands, let holy meditation not cease in their hearts.

21. Let everything be held in common, and let no one presume to call or claim anything her own.

22. Let them not wear clothing of any other color except gray and white.

23. During the vigils, care must be taken that no one sleeps.

24. When the signal is sounded, let no one come late.

25. While the psalms are being sung, let no one speak or work with her hands.

26. Let them all learn letters.

27. Let the holy abbess remain within the community.

28. If anyone is corrected or punished for any fault, let her not presume to answer the one rebuking her.

29. Let them have no quarrels.

30. The proud, the disobedient, and those who prolong their anger are never to be spared.

31. The holy abbess may not sell or give away anything from the monastery’s property, nor do anything contrary to the institutions of the Rule.

32. Let them remain silent while seated at table.

33. Let the holy abbess not eat outside the community.

[Col. 0400C] 34. Let them never eat meat.

35. Chickens and other poultry are to be served only to the sick and to those who are delicate; fish, however, on specified feast days.

36. No one may taste any food or drink outside the common table, except the sick and infants.

37. How the sick are to be cared for.

38. Where they are to say the daytime or nighttime office.

39. Let the holy abbess provide whatever is necessary in sufficient quantity.

40. Let the holy community strive to fulfill everything that has been established.

THE RULE.

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399D] CHAPTER ONE. By God’s command we have first established this as an inviolable requirement: if any woman comes for conversion, let the Rule be read to her in the reception room; and if she professes that she will fulfill everything, then let her be received. Once received, she is neither to presume nor to be permitted to leave the monastery until her death, because of the prophetic saying: *Unam petii a Domino, hanc requiram, ut inhabitem in domo Domini omnibus diebus vitae meae* (“One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life”; Psalm 26).

II. Let her not receive religious clothing unless, from all her property, whether great or small, she has made deeds of gift or sale to whomever she wishes, because of the Lord’s commandments, where he says: *Si vis perfectus esse, vende omnia quae habes* (“If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you have”; Matthew 19); and: *Si quis non reliquerit omnia quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus* (“If anyone does not leave behind everything he possesses, he cannot be my disciple”; Luke 14).

III. Accept nothing secretly. But if a relative or friend gives or sends something in clothing, gold, or anything else, let it be in the abbess’s power; and if the person to whom it is sent needs it, let it be given to her. But if she needs nothing, let it be placed in common and given to whoever needs it.

[Col. 0401A] IV. We command that no letters be given or received without the knowledge or permission of the abbess.

V. Let no one presume to keep near her bed anything that can be eaten or drunk. Let everyone store such things in the common storeroom; and if inequality of need requires it, let whatever is necessary be given at the command of the superior and not be denied to her.

VI. No one may have a cell, cupboard, or anything of this kind that can be locked privately.

VII. Do not swear, because the Lord said: *Nolite jurare* (“Do not swear”; Matthew 5). And another Scripture says: “A man who swears excessively will be filled with iniquity, and plague will not depart from his house” (Ecclesiasticus 23).

VIII. Do not curse, because it is written: “Neither will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

IX. It is altogether impermissible to lie, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1), and: “You will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5).

X. Let no one presume to prolong her anger until the following day. And, in accordance with human frailty, if harsher speech should arise among the sisters, let them hasten to ask forgiveness of one another and release the debts owed, because of the Lord’s command, where he says: “If you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift before the altar and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5). And: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6). Likewise: “If he sins against you seven times in a day and, turning back, says, ‘I am sorry,’ forgive him” (Luke 17). And: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matthew 18). Another Scripture says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1). And the Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4).

God forbid that, if any woman should be filled with fury at the instigation of the devil, she should obstinately despise these commands. If one of the women who are at odds should approach the other first and ask her forgiveness, but the one from whom forgiveness is sought should not forgive her, let her receive discipline so that she may correct herself toward charity. And if both should refuse, let both equally be suspended from Communion or from food until they are reconciled with one another.

XI. If a sister dares to lay hands on another sister, let her receive discipline.

XII. No one may leave to visit anyone except with the abbess or superior, or at least with another older sister whom the abbess has instructed. In this way let them see or speak with their relatives, and let them not speak in too loud a voice. [Col. 0401D]

XIII. A slave is not to be received. If, however, she is a freedwoman, still young in age, and comes with letters from her patron, it shall be left to the abbess’s discretion whether she should be received.

XIV. Neither secular men nor secular women may enter the monastery, except into the basilica of Blessed Mary and into the reception room.

XV. The monastery’s stewards, if they are in lay clothing, are not themselves to be permitted to enter except for the purposes which we establish in this Rule: with masons or carpenters, if something must be made or repaired, or certainly for some matter on which the abbess requires them to enter. For the rest, they are to have no permission or freedom to enter.

[Col. 0402A] XVI. Let no one receive an infant from baptism.

XVII. Those to whom the keys of the storeroom, wine cellar, granary, gate, and oratory are to be entrusted must be approved persons. Let them receive these keys above the altar or the Gospel, knowing that they will have to render an account to God for the service entrusted to them.

XVIII. In every service—whether the order of singing psalms, reading, or working—let them take turns with one another, except the abbess, those who are sufficiently elderly, and the very young children; and those who are so ill that they cannot rise at all are not to be compelled to do what they cannot manage.

XIX. Let no one choose work according to her own preference, but let her do what the abbess has commanded.

XX. Throughout the day, while you work with your hands, let holy meditation not cease in your hearts, because of the Apostle’s saying: “Singing and making melody to the Lord in your hearts with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3). [Col. 0402B]

XXI. Let no one presume to call anything her own or claim it as private. Rather, according to the Acts of the Apostles, let everything be held in common: “Let there be one soul and one heart for you in the Lord” (Acts 4).

XXII. Do not wear clothing of any other color except gray and white.

XXIII. Let no one sleep during the vigils. If, however, it is a Sunday or feast day, and sleep comes upon someone, let her stand while the others sit, so that she may drive away the sluggishness of sleep from herself and not be found lukewarm or negligent in the work of God.

[Col. 0402C] XXIV. When the signal is sounded, let every task be abandoned, and, like the very wise bees to the hive, strive to hurry there with swift speed. If anyone comes late, let her be subject to strict discipline.

XXV. While the psalms are being sung, let your holy souls take care not to wander in mind; nor should they presume to work or speak. Rather, “sing wisely” (Psalm 46), as the prophet said: “I will sing and understand” (Psalm 100), and: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14), fearing the saying: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48).

XXVI. Let them all learn letters.

XXVII. Let the holy abbess not remain outside the community.

XXVIII. If anyone is rebuked for any fault or transgression of the Rule, or receives discipline, let her not presume to answer the one rebuking her, because the sin disciplined here will not be punished at the eternal judgment. Thus you ought to receive care for your soul as a sick person receives the care of a physician, holding to the words of Holy Scripture: “Whoever rejects discipline is unhappy” (Proverbs 15). And: “I am ready for scourges” (Psalm 37).

XXIX. Have no quarrels, holding to the Apostle’s command, who says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle” (2 Timothy 1).

XXX. The proud and disobedient, and those who prolong their anger, are never to be spared until they are corrected.

XXXI. The holy abbess may not give away or sell anything from the monastery’s property, nor do anything contrary to the institutions of the Rule. If she should attempt to do so, do not, with holy counsel and the unanimous consent of the sisters, yield to her in this matter with our authorization; and do not permit it to be done for any reason, because she must know that she will have to give an account of the matter before God.

[Col. 0403A] XXXII. Let them remain silent while seated at table, and let a reading be given every day, at every meal. Let both the external person be nourished by food and the inner person by the word of God, because it is written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4).

XXXIII. Unless unequal circumstances require it, let the holy abbess not eat outside the community.

XXXIV. Let meat never be eaten.

XXXV. Let chickens or any other poultry not be served to the community, but let them be provided only for the sick and the delicate. Fish, however, is to be procured on specified feast days or whenever the abbess wishes to grant an indulgence.

[Col. 0403B] XXXVI. No one may taste any food or drink outside the common table, except the sick and those who are younger in age.

XXXVII. The sick are to be cared for in such a way that, if it seems right to the holy abbess, they may even have their own little storeroom and a separate kitchen in common; and care and attention are to be devoted to them until they recover.

XXXVIII. The community is to recite the daytime and nighttime office—that is, Matins, vigils, the night office, Vespers, and the twelfth hour—in the basilica of the Lady Mary. [Col. 0404A] But if the winter is severe, say only Matins, Vespers, and the twelfth hour in the aforementioned basilica; say Prime, Terce, Sext, and None in the inner oratory, for the sake of those who wish to pray, who are meeting the abbess, or who are looking for their relatives.

When one of the women has died, let a few sisters keep vigil with her in the oratory until midnight, and let readings from the Apostle be made. After midnight, let those who kept vigil rest; then let others keep vigil in turn. Make this known to the holy bishop, so that he may order her to be carried to the place where she is to be laid.

XXXIX. Since, by God’s favor, an adequate and sufficient endowment has been granted to you, capable of providing for your monastery, before God and his angels I admonish and charge you, holy abbess, and you, venerable superior, whoever you may be, to provide the holy community, which by God’s inspiration and command lives according to the institutions we have established, with everything necessary for clothing and food in sufficient quantity. If you neglect this duty, and they begin, compelled by necessity, either to murmur or to suffer want, know that you will have to give an account with me before the tribunal of Christ.

XL. And you, holy community, I adjure you by your progress and by almighty God to preserve whole and undefiled everything that we have established in this Rule for the remedy of our soul and for the salvation of your souls. And so that you may not neglect anything through forgetfulness, reread these provisions once a month—that is, on the Kalends—and thus twelve times a year. [Col. 0404C]

We have also judged it appropriate to insert in this little book the order according to which you ought to sing the psalms.

[Col. 0403]

[Col. 0403C] On the first day of Easter, at the third hour: “Kyrie eleison,” twelve psalms—that is, four sisters shall recite two psalms each, and a third, alleluiatic psalm. When the psalms have been recited, “Kyrie eleison,” six antiphons, and three readings: one from the Acts of the Apostles, another from the Apocalypse, and the third from the Gospel; the hymn “Now the third hour rises” (*Jam surgit hora tertia*), and the capitulum; then “Kyrie eleison.” Thus, in every service of God, say “Kyrie eleison” three times: before you begin, after the psalms have been recited, and after the capitulum.

At the sixth hour, the same number of psalms, one antiphon, the hymn “Now the sixth hour is gradually turning” (*Jam sexta sensim volvitur*), a Gospel reading, and the capitulum.

At the ninth hour, let the same order be observed, with the hymn “Three times the hour turns” (*Ter hora trina volvitur*).

At the lighting of the lamps, the short directaneus: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord” (Psalm 67). On the following day: “Praise the Lord, servants,” three antiphons, the hymn “This is the true day of God” (*Hic est dies verus Dei*), and the capitulum. Recite this hymn throughout Easter at Matins and at the lighting of the lamps.

At the twelfth hour, first the short directaneus: “The sun knows its setting” (Psalm 103). Six sisters shall each recite two psalms with their alleluias; three antiphons and two readings, one from the Apostle and the other from the Gospel.

At the Easter night office, recite everything in the same number as we have prescribed for the twelfth hour. At Matins, first the directaneus: “I will exalt you, my God and my King.” Then: “Judge me, O God”; “O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn,” with “Alleluia”; then: “Give thanks to the Lord,” with “Alleluia”; then: “Let us sing to the Lord,” with “Alleluia”; afterward: “Bless the Lord, O my soul”; “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good”; “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem”—all three with “Alleluia.” Then the blessing is to be said.

After the blessing: “Praise the Lord from the heavens”; “Sing to the Lord a new song”; “Praise the Lord in his holy places,” with “Alleluia”; “My soul magnifies the Lord,” either with an antiphon or with “Alleluia”; the hymn “Glory in the highest to God”; and the capitulum. Complete Matins in this order throughout Easter.

Do the same every Sunday and on all the greater festivals on which you abstain from work.

On ordinary days, at the night office, first let the directaneus be said: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy”; then eighteen psalms; three short antiphons; two readings from the Apostle or the Prophets; and the capitulum. When the night office has been completed, say Matins.

In summer—that is, from Easter until the calends of October—the same order shall be followed. On Friday, after the night office, let two readings be made in summer and three in winter. On Sunday, at every season, summer and winter, after the night office, let six readings be made.

If it happens that the sisters rise late for the vigils, let as much be read as the abbess thinks appropriate. When the abbess gives the signal, the reader shall rise without delay, so that the canonical number of readings [Col. 0405A] may be completed.

From the calends of October, additional night offices are to be added. At the first, say: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy”; at the second: “Have mercy on me, O God; have mercy on me.” Eighteen psalms, two readings from the Prophets or from Solomon. The hymn for the first night office is “Eternal King and Lord” (*Rex aeterne Domine*); for the second, “Great and marvelous” (*Magna et mirabilia*).

After the second night office has been celebrated, since the nights are growing longer, make three readings daily from the book. One sister shall read three or four pages, according to the size of the book: if it is written in small script or in a larger format, three pages; if in a smaller format, four; and then let there be a prayer. Again let her read the same amount, and let there be another prayer. A third time let her read the same amount; then rise and say an antiphon from the psalms in order, followed by a responsory, and then another antiphon. [Col. 0405B] Again another sister shall read. When the three readings have been completed, say canonical Matins:

First, the canticle with its antiphon; then the directaneus: “Judge me, O God. O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn”; “Bless the Lord, O my soul”; “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good”; “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem”; then: “Praise the Lord from the heavens”; “Sing to the Lord a new song”; “Praise the Lord in his holy places,” with an antiphon.

Say the hymn “Splendor of the Father’s glory” (*Splendor paternae gloriae*); on another day, “Creator of eternal light” (*Aeterne lucis conditor*); then the capitulum and “Kyrie eleison” twelve times. Let this be completed in this manner on all ordinary days.

After Matins, at Prime, say six psalms and the hymn “Author of the shining heavens” (*Fulgentis auctor aetheris*); two readings—that is, one from the Old Testament and another from the New Testament—and the capitulum.

After this, let everyone devote herself to reading until the third hour. During the remaining part of the day, let them perform their tasks, in accordance with what the Lord said: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5); and what the Apostle said: “Working with our own hands” (1 Thessalonians 4); and: “Anyone who does not work shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3). For it is written: “The roads of the idle are paved with thorns” (Proverbs 13); and: “Throw the useless servant into the outer darkness” (Matthew 25).

On ordinary days, at the third hour again say six psalms, an antiphon, the hymn “Now the third hour rises” (*Jam surgit hora tertia*), a reading, and the capitulum “Let it be done, Lord” (*Fiat, Domine*).

At the sixth hour the same number of psalms is to be maintained; an antiphon is to be said, followed by the hymn “Now the sixth hour is gradually turning” (*Jam sexta sensim volvitur*), a reading, and the capitulum.

At the ninth hour this order is to be observed; the hymn, however, is “Three times the hour turns” (*Ter hora trina volvitur*).

At the lighting of the lamps, at all times, both on feast days and ordinary days, first the directaneus; afterward two antiphons. The third [antiphon] is always to be said with “Alleluia.” On one day the hymn shall be “God, who by fixed laws” (*Deus qui certis legibus*); on another day, “God, creator of all things” (*Deus creator omnium*); and the capitulum.

At the twelfth hour [Col. 0406A] say eighteen psalms, an antiphon, a hymn, a reading, and the capitulum.

When you are about to rest, say Compline in the school in which you reside. First the directaneus, and Psalm 90; then the customary capitula.

At the Nativity of the Lord and at Epiphany, rise at the third hour of the night. Say one night office and make six readings from the prophet Isaiah; then say a second night office, and let six other readings be made from the Gospel.

At Epiphany proceed as follows: first one night office; then make those six readings and the night office from the prophet Daniel; and again six readings from the Gospel.

Say Matins in the order prescribed above for Easter, or as on Sundays.

At the festivals of martyrs, let three or four readings be made: read the first from the Gospel and the others from the passions of the martyrs. [Col. 0406B]

Every Friday, after the twelfth hour, let six readings be made from the book, and three after the night office.

Every Saturday at Matins, say “Let us sing to the Lord” and “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*).

At the third hour let three readings be said: one from the Prophets, another from the Apostle, and the third from the Gospel.

Every Sunday, after the night office, when the first reading is read—that is, the Resurrection—no one shall presume to sit; all shall stand. On the following Sunday, another Resurrection shall be read. Thus, in order, all four Resurrection accounts shall be read on successive Sundays.

After the third hour, say the Lord’s Prayer, and let everyone receive Communion while singing psalms. Do the same on feast days. The readings, however, shall be held whenever the holy abbess thinks appropriate.

We have also inserted the order of meals into this Rule. [Col. 0406C] Every day, three dishes at the refection, two at midday meal, and two cups at supper. At the refection in summer, during July and August, three small bowls; at midday meal, three; at supper, two at all times.

On feast days, and whenever the abbess wishes to grant indulgence, let her arrange as much food as she wishes and add fresh items.

On ordinary days, let vegetables always be seasoned with cheese and oil.

The fast is to be observed from the calends of September until the calends of November on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. From the calends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, fasting is to be observed every day except Saturday and Sunday.

From Epiphany until Easter, fasting is to be observed every day except on a major feast, Saturday, and Sunday.

After Easter until Pentecost, fasting is to be observed only on Friday. [Col. 0406D]

After Pentecost, during June, July, and August, whether there is to be fasting or a midday meal shall be left to the abbess’s discretion. She shall strive to act according to what she sees the sisters are able to bear.

[Col. 0405]

EXCERPTS FROM THE LETTER OF AURELIAN, BISHOP OF ARLES, TO KING THEUDEBERT. (C,S)

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405D] To the illustrious, everywhere most glorious, and in Christ most devout lord and son, King Theudebert, Aurelian, bishop.

Although the service of writing at so late a time is rightly accompanied by hesitation, nevertheless, I think, my speech will in no way be judged to have escaped offense if it is weighed before the ears of your clemency solely according to the devotion of my heart. This is especially so because, while all are seeking access to your majesty, they neither draw fear from the privilege of your exalted position nor dread rejection because of the disadvantage of delay.

Your exaltation is so gracious that it is touched even by the affection of the lowly, and its heights, burdened by the accumulation of dignities, are still approached by the first devotions of inexperienced household servants. For now, with new zeal, we are being formed for the service of a religious prince, and with the testimony of perfect devotion we are admitted into the presence of your sacred mind.

Therefore, excellent Prince, measure this confidence of our love when, in your service, we withdraw neither frightened by delay nor deprived by the modesty of our poor talent. Receive kindly, then, the first efforts of your servants’ devotion, and open wide the folds of your more abundant forgiveness to those who make supplication.

For although everyone generally enjoys the favor of your noble heart, we nevertheless, even though a small portion of your service, claim for ourselves in full the abundance of the prince’s indulgence. Indeed, when we speak of you, grace is present, even if eloquence is lacking; and the subject itself is sufficient for our adornment, although learning may not be present.

Since this is so, I shall celebrate the brilliance of your character more through the wishes of my prayers than through writing. For the greatest matters always require conscience rather than tongue, and are more worthily entrusted to the judgment of the heart than of speech. Accordingly, I should not mention among my wishes what the times celebrate, but what eternity approves, etc.

THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 555

PRIMASIUS, BISHOP OF ADRUMETUM.

[Col. 0407]

[Col. 0407]

PROLEGOMENA.

NOTICE (from Cave).

[Col. 0407]

[Col. 0407B] Primasius, an African by birth, was bishop of the city of Adrumetum, which was also called Justinianopolis, in the province of Byzacena. He was one of those who were sent to Constantinople around the year 550 to manage the affairs of the African Church. There, in the following year, he took part in an assembly of bishops at which Vigilius pronounced a sentence of excommunication against Theodore of Caesarea, leader of the Acephali.

In the year 553, although he was repeatedly summoned, he refused to attend the ecumenical synod; but together with others he signed Vigilius’s decree concerning the Three Chapters, which the pope presented to the emperor during the synod.

WRITINGS.

Commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul, for the most part drawn from the writings of Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and other ancient authors. Haymo transferred much material from them into his own commentaries; hence some, being mistaken, judged that the commentaries of Primasius belonged to Haymo. They were published separately at Paris in 1543, in octavo.

Commentaries of mystical exposition on the Apocalypse, addressed to Castorius and divided into five books. They were published separately at Basel in 1544, in octavo.

Both of Primasius’s commentaries were published by Gagney at Lyon in 1543 and in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume 10.

Three books *On Heresies*, addressed to Fortunatus, bishop, in which he explained what Augustine had formerly left unfinished in his book *On Heresies*: in the first book showing what makes someone a heretic, and in the second and third what demonstrates heresy. This work has long since perished. [Col. 0407D]

There are extant today, published under the name of Praedestinatus, three books *On Heresies*, especially the heresy of the Predestinarians. In the first part the author, whoever he may be, treats ninety heresies of every kind, from Simon Magus up to the Predestinarian heresy, briefly reviewing their authors, doctrines, and practices. The second part consists of a book *On Predestination*, once falsely composed under Augustine’s name; in the third part he undertakes a refutation of that Augustinian book.

Scholars do not sufficiently agree among themselves concerning the true parent of these books. Hincmar of Reims cites them under the name of Hyginus, through an obvious error, perhaps arising from no other circumstance than that he found Hyginus’s name in the list of authors prefixed to the work. Sirmond suspected that they should be assigned to Arnobius the Younger because of the similarity of style and sentences.

More recently, Piccinardus, a theologian from Brescia, proposed as author a certain Vincentius—I do not know who—namely, the man to whose sixteen objections Prosper of Aquitaine opposed an equal number of replies. Who this Vincentius was, however, is not sufficiently known: whether that presbyter, a Gaul by nation, who commented on the Psalms and of whom Gennadius speaks in chapter 80; or Vincentius Victor, against whom Augustine wrote *On the Origin of the Soul*. Piccinardus entirely rejects Vincent of Lérins; he attributes the book falsely composed under Augustine’s name to Evodius of Uzala, whom he suspects prefixed to his little book the title *An Exposition of Augustine’s Doctrine*, and that it was consequently taken to be a work of Augustine himself.

But Piccinardus’s arguments concerning the whole matter rest upon conjectures so uncertain and slight that he will perhaps persuade very few to adopt his opinion. The work seems far more properly to be attributed to our Primasius, on the evidence of an ancient manuscript written eight hundred years ago, which the illustrious Mabillon saw in the library of Reichenau (*Itinerary through Germany*, p. 83; *Analecta*, volume 4). In it appeared the following title, written in somewhat faded ink but by an ancient hand: “The work of Saint Primasius, disciple of Augustine, on ninety heresies.”

Certainly the author seems in more than one place to suggest that he was an African. But, to state freely what I suspect, whoever added this note to the Reichenau manuscript may perhaps have been mistaken. Having read in Isidore that Primasius wrote three books *On Heresies*, and having found these three anonymous books, he immediately attached Primasius’s name to them.

Moreover, since our author mentions almost no heresy later than the recent Nestorian one, Primasius would scarcely have omitted so many heresies that arose and were condemned afterward. But we leave the whole matter for scholars to examine.

Jacques Sirmond first brought these books to light from a manuscript of Hincmar of Reims, at Paris in 1643, in octavo. In the following year, Jean Awraeus, a Sorbonne theologian, published in French a sufficiently severe critique of the entire work, in which he argued that the author had been a Pelagian and charged him with errors, heresies, lies, fables, and disgraceful ignorance. The work was soon reprinted in Holland, at Amsterdam, if I am not mistaken, in 1645, in octavo; the editor appended Awraeus’s critique in a Latin translation, and it found a place in the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum* in 1677, volume 27.

Finally, Seraphinus Piccinardus of the Order of Preachers, a theologian at the University of Padua, brought it out again at Padua in 1686, in quarto, adding various dissertations on the author, the work, and the entire controversy.

To the most Christian and most pious king of the Gauls, Francis I, greetings in Christ from John Gagney, Parisian theologian.

[Col. 0409B] Whoever has learned how completely good letters and disciplines lay in squalor and the most shameful disorder for several centuries beforehand will immediately understand, most Christian King Francis, that it was accomplished not by human effort but by the intervention of some present divine power that they were at last able to emerge and shine forth from such dreadful darkness into this splendor and brightness.

For that disastrous flood of barbarism, whether it arose through human negligence or through the injury of the times, had swallowed up not only letters and the better disciplines themselves, but, so that they might never afterward have any hope of emerging, it kept buried and entombed all good books, the most fertile parents of good letters. Thus, if anyone of refined intelligence and naturally suited to letters aspired to them and strove toward them, he was immediately excluded by the scarcity of books.

Yet I think the chief cause of this ruinous inundation was that in that age there were no princes who served as protectors and defenders of letters and disciplines. Nothing is truer than what that poet sang:

“Let there be Maecenases, and, Flaccus, there will be no lack of Maros.”

No one who possesses any judgment in assessing the monuments of learned men is unaware that this cloud of ignorance and this flood in Gaul lasted down to your own times, Francis, defender and patron of letters. Although an earlier age produced Budaeus, the one unique glory of letters, and a few others of lesser but still creditable learning, they themselves readily acknowledge that, under your leadership, they have become better and more learned than they were.

Nor is there any need to say how many myriads of learned men in the three languages your ardent desire to extend the empire of philology has produced, since your royal munificence supplied two or three professors of each of the three languages to that Parisian school of yours. Today boys speak Greek more easily and elegantly than formerly unlearned old men spoke Latin.

Moreover, not thinking it enough to enlarge the empire of philology by the expenditure of your treasury, you summoned from every quarter men who, through constant study and unwearied labor, would both defend its boundaries from barbarian incursions and extend them farther. You also added something much more useful.

For when you had long ago turned your attention to revising, restoring, and, as it were, reshaping anew all disciplines, especially the sacred disciplines that were obscured by more than Cimmerian darkness—and I count this among the chief of your praises—you wished to provide not only for your own age but also for posterity. Accordingly, you took pains to investigate good books everywhere and have countless copies made of them, so that nothing might be lacking.

I remember when I once explained to your Majesty, during a meal—as you allow scarcely any table to be without some learned or pious reading or discussion—the commentaries of Primasius, bishop of Utica in Africa, at once very ancient and very learned, rescued from that darkness in which they had lain for more than a thousand years at the monastery of Saint Theuderic, archbishop of Vienne. I remember, I say, with what favor, good God, and with what a welcoming and admiring expression you received them, astonished that they had remained hidden so long, and at the great loss this had caused the realm of letters, as well as at the rarity and value of such treasures.

Here, wishing to assist your most holy undertaking and plainly royal purpose by whatever work I could offer, I told you that your kingdom possessed many forests of the same kind, inaccessible because several barbarous peoples guarded them, with certain monks obstinately closing their libraries and denying both themselves and others access to them as though they were shrines of Vesta. You immediately promised to make a way for me, even if—as they tell in the fable of the gardens of the Hesperides—they were guarded by the constant and perpetual vigilance of dragons.

Having received, as a pledge of this outstanding promise, a public diploma by which you ordered all the libraries of your kingdom to be open to me and granted me permission to copy from them whatever monuments seemed relevant to philology, I began to search through the libraries of all the monasteries that I encountered while traveling in your company.

When I had rescued nearly a hundred volumes of no inferior quality from darkness, you conceived—unless your authority had finally intervened—a deed destined never to be erased from human memory, truly worthy of a royal and humane prince. By it you not only equaled Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, but surpassed him by many leagues; indeed, if we wish to speak as nearly as possible to the truth, you eclipsed him altogether and, as it seems to me, placed yourself above every ancient man whose glory has been commended.

For while Ptolemy gathered an outstanding and astonishing library from volumes sought from every quarter—thereby earning such a reputation among the ancients—what, in the judgment of any reasonable person, could he seem to have advanced for the public except that he once gathered scattered good and learned books into a single library, only for them to be devoured by flames? I would not wish to believe this if time, the teacher of truth, did not confirm—and would that it did not confirm—the certainty of so unhappy an event. For how many, I ask, now survive from all those thousands of books that one disaster, to the common misfortune of all, destroyed?

Even if he may seem, in the opinion of some, to have undertaken a project that was not bad and to have conceived it without evil intent, the unexpected outcome cannot obscure this fact. You, Francis, Maecenas and patron of letters, surpassed him in this respect—if I may say no more—with equal but also wiser and more provident counsel.

For, aware of the condition of mortal affairs and also knowing how many splendid buildings a sudden fire has destroyed, you resolved not to build a library of ancient books before the most carefully corrected copies of them had gone forth from the press for the common benefit of philology.

Since I had been entrusted by you with responsibility for this undertaking, and since I possessed many books worthy of the assembly and view of learned men, I decided to begin with one which I knew had long ago been approved by you through a favorable judgment, and which all learned lovers of divine matters would most willingly embrace.

This is the commentary of Primasius, bishop of Utica in Africa, the most learned, in my judgment, of all those of the Greeks and Latins that I have so far seen. For on passages that are not difficult, it is so pleasing through its fluent brevity that it is by no means tedious in matters that others, because of the great difficulty of their subject, have treated at length.

The author is further rendered attractive by what I have often heard you say, and not without judgment: a sweet and moderate style, midway between paraphrase and homily. Once you had tasted its sweetness, you ordered a vernacular translation of so excellent a book from a man not sufficiently suited to the task—one who had never practiced that fluent vernacular style, who was inexperienced in courtly language, and who until two years earlier had never been accustomed to the court.

Conscious, therefore, of my own inexperience, I would readily have declined your command under some invented excuse, had I not long known the candor and generosity of your character, and had I not considered it wrong not to assist, insofar as God might grant me the ability, so Christian a mind.

For what is more proper to the duty of a theologian than to open the sacred writings to a prince who has devoted all his efforts to advancing them and defending them against their heretical enemies? There are indeed some people of such slippery intelligence and so tossed about by every doctrinal wind that it would be much better for them to remain ignorant of these matters, except insofar as knowledge benefits their salvation.

But who would not admit you, who have offered so many and such outstanding proofs of your unconquered religion and steadfast faith, into the innermost sanctuaries of sacred Scripture?

I therefore, as a thoroughly tested witness of your piety and faith, while wishing to comply with your will, undertook a task that was certainly unusual for me but, if I foresee correctly, will not be unwelcome to you because of the dignity of its subject, which is most holy and most serious.

For I freely confess that in this work I sought no polish of language. I judged that your Majesty would be satisfied by the weight and seriousness of its thoughts, and I was convinced that your royal judgment, being as elevated as it is, delights only in matters lofty and difficult—matters of which I knew Primasius to be full. You too had already sensed this truthfully from one or two readings, and finally, as I proceeded to translate him for you, you recognized it more certainly.

Indeed, although I knew that reading this author would be extremely pleasing to you, a prince most thirsting for good things, I was nevertheless filled with admiration and astonishment at this: while most people, as is the condition of mortal minds corrupted by that original sin of the old Adam, turn in the greatest dangers to human counsel rather than seeking the heavenly powers in prayer and consulting the sacred Scriptures, those most abundant fountains of consolation, you, despite so many and such hostile diversions of war and so many struggles with uncertain and varied fortune, could not be drawn away from the reading of Primasius once you had begun it auspiciously.

While we now publish him speaking in our vernacular only to you, we have also given him, speaking in his own language—that is, Latin—under your auspices and in your name, for all scholars to study.

Moreover, since Primasius seems entirely occupied with elevating human merits and exalting faith alone, I thought it necessary to trace the argument of this matter somewhat farther back, lest anyone take from this an opportunity to slip into that ancient heresy, begun long ago by the youthful Church but patched up again in our own age.

In the time of Jerome and Augustine, and therefore of your Primasius—for you willingly call him this—two heresies arose from opposing sides: one of Pelagius and the other of Manichaeus. The former so exalted the power and capacity of free will that he left no place at all for the grace of God; the latter, by attributing everything to God’s grace, wished us to remain idle and utterly dormant, contributing nothing of our own to God—not even any assent of the will.

Accordingly, the sects of the opposing parties became so powerful in that period that they nearly penetrated and disturbed the whole Church. Whoever sought to extricate himself from the Pelagian error, unless he applied prudent and careful judgment, became entangled in the errors of Manichaeus. Conversely, whoever tried to free himself from Manichaean doctrine slipped into the Pelagian heresy.

Against these two monstrous systems of reasoning—opposed to each other in doctrine but converging in the destruction of the Church—Jerome, Augustine, Prosper, and Primasius fought manfully.

They wrote against Pelagius, the enemy of God’s grace, with such intensity of mind that, while overthrowing that heresy which flattered our powers but meanwhile undermined the grace of God, they seem almost to favor the sect of Manichaeus, especially to a man of not particularly sharp perception.

The heretics of our own time took from Augustine, Prosper, and other leaders of the Church of that age the opportunity to restore this ancient sect. They assign first, second, third, and finally last place to faith, and almost none to the sacraments; to our actions, however good, they assign absolutely nothing. These men, failing to understand their own obstinate opinion, rush from Scylla into Charybdis.

If they read—or at least did not pretend not to have read—the writings of Augustine and the holy Fathers against Manichaeus and others, they would certainly understand that those authors ascribe the root of justification and the beginning of faith [to God’s grace], while nevertheless maintaining that our actions, performed from faith and grace, are not without their reward and merit. Nor did the ancient Fathers of the Churches recoil from this terminology, which those men so vehemently reject.

I shall make this clear in the case of Primasius—to say nothing meanwhile of the others—and easily show that he does not, as some do, attribute everything to faith or abolish our merits. Rather, he has one concern: that we should not presume upon our own powers or glory in our merits, but attribute all our merits, whatever they may be, to God alone.

For, commenting on the eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where Jacob the Apostle is reconciled with Paul concerning the passage “By faith Abraham offered Isaac,” he says:

“What is the reason,” he asks, “that blessed James, when mentioning Abraham in his Epistle, praises him above all on account of his works, whereas the blessed Apostle most carefully commends not his works but his faith?

“Blessed James therefore rightly praises him for his works, since he knew that he was also perfect in faith, because he was writing to people who seemed indeed to possess faith but did not adorn that same faith with good works.

“But blessed Paul, because he was writing to people who seemed to possess the good works of the Law but did not have perfect faith, rightly commemorates Abraham’s faith more carefully, so that they might strive to imitate him.

“Thus, certainly, to show that those who wish to be children of Abraham must possess both faith and works, one Apostle rightly praises him on the basis of faith, while the other no less rightly praises him on the basis of works.”

This is what Primasius says—cleverly and learnedly. I think that this reasoning should be sufficient, in the judgment of any person not utterly obstinate, against those who insist too strongly that the Apostle so greatly commends faith in the Epistles to the Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews.

When the Apostle wrote to the Romans, he was writing partly to those who had come from Hellenism and partly to those who had come from Judaism into Christianity. The latter did not neglect the works of the Law; the former possessed actions that were outwardly admirable and earnest and, insofar as they lived under the guidance of nature alone, virtues that were not ignoble. But they did not understand that these actions were idle and of no consequence apart from faith in Christ.

The Jews, on the other hand, attributed almost everything to their Law and nearly nothing to faith. A similar error held the Galatians, whom the false apostles were trying to lead from Christianity back to Judaism.

This is why the Apostle commends faith to them with such insistence. To the others who had professed the faith of Christ with complete commitment, he mentions faith either not at all or only sparingly, because he knew that they already held it in the highest esteem. Primasius is accustomed to commend faith in such a way that he also makes room for works.

On the passage in Galatians 4, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” he explains openly, both how faith is effective without works and how works are nevertheless required, in these words:

“It is asked whether faith alone is sufficient for a Christian, and whether the person who has not kept the Gospel commandments is not accursed. Faith is sufficient first to make the believer righteous, if thereafter he remains in justification; but without works it is dead; yet the works must be those of faith, not of the Law.”

In the same place, chapter 8, on the passage “The whole Law is fulfilled in one word,” he says: “Therefore faith alone is not sufficient for life, since the many-fringed commandments of the Law are summed up in the single commandment of love.”

And on the passage “Those who crucified their flesh,” it must likewise be noted that he says those who crucified their flesh together with its desires are Christ’s, against those who think that faith alone is sufficient.

On Ephesians 5, at the passage “Every fornicator,” he argues against those who say that faith alone can suffice for salvation without works. This is rightly said only of those who are snatched away after baptism and do not have time to perform good works.

On Hebrews 4, concerning the passage “Let us hasten to enter,” he says: “Faith alone is not sufficient for salvation; it is necessary to work through the love that belongs to faith and to live worthily before God, because faith without works is dead.”

Likewise, concerning merits, on 2 Timothy 4, at the passage “I have fought the good fight,” he says: “Here he is certainly recalling his good merits, so that after good merits he may obtain the crown.”

I thought it appropriate to add these few passages, among many of the same kind in Primasius, lest when someone reads in Primasius, “Hear of grace, and be silent about works; do not glory in merits,” or something similar, he should immediately suppose that works are excluded or that our merits are entirely abolished. Rather, he should understand that these statements are written against the Pelagians, who, trusting in their natural powers, left no place for the grace of God.

But enough of this preface concerning Primasius, most Christian King Francis. I now finally conclude, having first exhorted students of good and divine letters to pray earnestly for your most Christian Majesty, through whose agency they possess long-buried letters restored to life and returned to their former dignity.

[Col. 0413]

PREFACE. (C,S)*
[Col. 0413D] First, we ought to understand to whom and for what reason the Apostle writes. For it must not be supposed that, after the Gospels—which are the fulfillment of the Law—he wrote these Epistles to the individual churches without cause, especially since in them instructions and examples for learning are set forth in the fullest manner. But at the beginning of the Church’s birth, when new circumstances arose, he excluded [or: there was a need to exclude] future questions.

Nor did the Apostle alone do this; the prophets also did so. For after the Law of Moses had been given, which contained all the commandments, they too did not cease by their preaching to restrain the people’s new sins and to transmit them in books for our remembrance, reaching down to us, who have come to the ends of the ages.

He now writes to the Romans, who, believing both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, wished by needless contention to exalt one group over the other. The Jews were saying: “We are a holy nation, whom God loved and cherished from the beginning. We descended from Abraham’s stock, from a holy lineage. We were delivered from Egypt and crossed the sea with dry feet. On our account Pharaoh and his army were submerged and perished. For us the Lord rained manna in the desert, along with the other things whose enumeration would be too lengthy. We say only this: the Lord himself, in whom you too appear to believe, was promised to us through the Law. But you, who are Gentiles, abandoned from the beginning, who never possessed knowledge of God but always served demons—is it right that today, turning away from idols, you should be compared with us, and not rather be proselytes, as you have always been under the Law? And this has happened because God is exceedingly merciful, wishing to bring you to imitate us.”

The Gentiles, on the other hand, replied: “The greater the divine benefits you recount, the more clearly you show yourselves guilty of a greater crime, because you have always been ungrateful for all these things, since, after hearing God’s voice, you fashioned a calf for yourselves. Even if you had not done this, you could not obtain pardon for this one crime alone: although the Lord promised to you through the voices of the prophets, you not only refused to receive him but even killed him—whereas we received him, although no one had foretold him to us. Therefore it is perfectly clear that our faith is better. And our service of idols was not a matter of wickedness but of ignorance. Finally, as soon as we recognized the truth, we followed it. It is not carnal birth but faith that makes children of Abraham.”

While they were thus disputing, the Apostle places himself between them, showing both peoples that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but rather faith, which works through love. At the same time, throughout the Epistle he humbles them in turn and urges them toward unity by arguments and testimonies. He shows that neither group earned this by its own righteousness, but that everything they are must be attributed to the righteousness of God. He shows that both Jews and Gentiles have sinned gravely: the Jews, because through transgressing the Law they dishonor God.

It is also asked why he wrote no more than ten Epistles to the churches. There are ten, including the one called *To the Hebrews*, for the remaining four were addressed familiarly to disciples. By this he wished to show that the New Testament does not differ from the Old and that he is not acting against the Law of Moses, corresponding to the number of the first ten commandments, by which he instructed those liberated from Pharaoh. The most learned writers have handed down that the two stone tablets represented the two Testaments.

Some indeed assert that the Epistle written to the Hebrews is not Paul’s, because it is not titled with his name and because of differences in language and style. They attribute it either to Barnabas, following Tertullian; or to Luke, according to some; or certainly to Clement, a disciple of the apostles and, after them, ordained bishop of the Roman Church.

They should be answered as follows: If it is not Paul’s because it does not bear his name, then it will belong to no one, since it is titled with no one’s name. But if that is absurd, it is more reasonable to believe that it is his, since it shines with such a brilliance of his teaching. Or perhaps, because among the churches of the Hebrews he was regarded under a false suspicion as a destroyer of the Law, he wished to write without revealing his name, lest the hatred aroused by a name displayed openly should exclude the usefulness of the reading.

It is certainly no wonder if he is more eloquent in his own language—that is, Hebrew—than in a foreign one, namely Greek, in which the other Epistles were written.

Some are also troubled by the question why the Epistle to the Romans was placed first, when the sequence makes clear that it was written later. From this it should be understood that all the Epistles were arranged so that the first placed was the one addressed to those who were less advanced, and that through the individual Epistles one would proceed gradually toward those who were more perfect.

The Romans were so weak that they did not understand; therefore he asserts that they needed to be strengthened, first recalling their former vices. To the Corinthians, however, he already says that all knowledge has been granted, and he reproves them not so much for themselves as for failing to rebuke others, when he says: “Fornication is reported among you.” And again: “When you are assembled, with my spirit, to hand such a one over to Satan.”

In the second Epistle they are praised and admonished to advance more and more. The Galatians are accused of no crime except that they believed deceitful false apostles. The Ephesians, indeed, deserve no reproach but much praise, because they preserved the apostolic faith. The Philippians are praised still more, since they were unwilling even to listen to false apostles. The Thessalonians likewise, in both Epistles, are commended with every praise, because they not only preserved an unshaken faith in the truth but were also found steadfast amid the persecution of their fellow citizens.

The Colossians were such that they did not need the Apostle to appear to them bodily. Indeed, he never promises to visit them. To them also he says: “Although absent in body, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your good order.”

What shall I say of the Hebrews, to whom he says: “For you had compassion on those who were imprisoned, and you joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions.”

[Col. 0415]

# PRIMASIUS’S COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF SAINT PAUL (C, G, S)*

## THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

[Col. 0415]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0451D]

Paul—that is, “little” and “last”—was called Paul from Saul, just as Abraham was changed from Abram, so that he might also be new in the very name.

“Servant of Jesus Christ.” As Isaiah says: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant.”

“Called as an apostle.” He was already called and predestined in foreknowledge for this purpose: to be an apostle.

“Set apart.” As he says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them.”

“For the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand.” The Gospel is called “good announcement.” And what greater good is there than that Christ was born, suffered, and rose again for us? “Through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made for him.” To nourish the faith of the Jews, he asserts that he preaches the one whom the prophets announced in the holy Scriptures. This entire passage is directed against the Manichaeans, who say that the God of the prophets is one and the God of the New Testament another.

“From the seed of David.” From Mary, who came from David’s line, as Isaiah said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son.”

“According to the flesh.” He thereby overthrows Photinus and those who speak of a solitary man, failing to understand that there are two substances in Christ.

“Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.” He was predestined to rise before all others and to open the way of resurrection to the children of God, so that, just as the head rose, so also his body might rise.

“Through whom we have received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all the nations.” Grace, so that we might believe and be baptized, and because he himself has now been justified freely, without any merits of his own. He received apostleship when he was sent to preach to the Gentiles.

“For his name.” We act as his representatives, just as he himself says: “As the Father sent me, I also send you”; and, “We act as ambassadors for Christ.”

“Among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ.” Among you Romans also we have received apostleship, just as among all the nations.

“To all who are in Rome, beloved of God.” To all the faithful of God who are in Rome, “called saints,” sanctified by God’s calling and by grace, not by the merits of their works.

“Grace to you.” His greeting is everywhere of this kind, so that he both recalls God’s benefits and prays that they may remain whole in us, since our sins have been forgiven freely, not through our merits.

“And peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” As he says to the Colossians: “He made peace between all things that are in heaven and all things that are on earth through his blood,” and those whom he redeemed he wishes to live in peace.

“First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ.” Since by nature he is the God of all, but by merit and will the God of a few, he said “my God.”

“For all of you.” Not for the Jews alone.

“Because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” He praises them subtly in order to provoke them to progress. And truly, the faith of the Romans is renowned everywhere.

“Your faith,” he says. He calls their faith theirs, although without doubt it belongs to God and was infused into them by God. But this is the custom of Scripture, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, You are gods’?” Or this: “As it is written in their Law, ‘They hated me without cause’”; and elsewhere: “Does our Law condemn anyone without first hearing him?”

Thus their faith is called theirs, just as the Law is called theirs, although no one is unaware that the Law is from God, just as faith is.

“For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit, in the Gospel of his Son.” That is, I serve him with ready devotion and complete truth, with my whole heart.

“That without ceasing I remember you, always making supplication in my prayers.” Here he shows that he will say everything with love, so that they may listen to him more willingly; and he gives an example of praying without ceasing.

“If somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey, by the will of God, to come to you.” For I do not have a prosperous journey unless the will of God—which knows all things, goes before us in every good thing, leads us, and cherishes us—directs me there, where I may bear some fruit. Thus we read concerning the apostles that, although they wished to go one way, they were directed another. They did not go where they wished, but where God sent them, knowing when and to whom they ought to go.

“To strengthen you.” Here he shows how, although he praised them above, they still needed spiritual grace for their strengthening.

“That is, to be mutually comforted among you by the faith that is common to both you and me.” Through our common faith, we may comfort one another and rejoice together in the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

“For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that I have often planned to come to you.” Through traveling brothers you may have heard of my intention.

“For I have been prevented [from coming] until now.”

[Note: [Col. 0417] We have added *sum* from the Vulgate. Here we wish to warn the reader that Primasius frequently differs from the Vulgate text in these commentaries, whether his memory failed him, or whether this should be attributed to the negligence of printers or to some other cause. In any event, we have presented the Primasius text intact, unless the restoration of the Vulgate reading was clearly demanded by the sense and syntax. For the rest, our readers, who turn over the sacred Scriptures day and night, will encounter the variants almost of their own accord. EDIT.]

That is, I have been occupied while preaching in other provinces; or I have been prevented by a revelation; or perhaps, as he says elsewhere: “Satan hindered us.”

“That I might have some fruit among you.” He calls the reward of his labor “fruit.”

“As also among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians.” “I have” is understood.

“I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish.” By the wise he means the Greeks, among whom all philosophy is found; he calls the barbarians foolish.

“So, as far as I am concerned, I am ready.” I am prepared.

“And to you who are in Rome, to evangelize.” Equally to the wise Greeks.

“For I am not ashamed of the Gospel.” This subtly applies as a reproach to the pagans, who ought rightly to be ashamed of their incestuous gods, yet are not ashamed to believe their god Jupiter, and consider it shameful to believe that the Lord was crucified for the salvation of his image, although in one case there is disgrace and in the other an emblem of virtue. It also applies against those who deny that Christ came in the flesh and are ashamed of the Lord’s birth and cross, considering these things unworthy of God and failing to understand that nothing is more worthy of God than what advances human salvation.

“For if it is foolishness to unbelievers, it is the power of God and the wisdom of God to believers.” The power of God is directed toward salvation. There is no greater power than, after conquering death, to restore to a human being the life he had lost, although weakness—that is, humanity—may appear incredible to unbelievers when joined to power, that is, divinity.

“To everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek; for the righteousness of God is revealed in it.” Just as Abraham, believing from among the nations, was saved through faith, so also may the other believers be saved.

“From faith to faith.” As it is written: “But the righteous person lives by my faith.” The Jew is justified by the faith of the Old Testament, the Gentile by that of the New, while the Jew believes that the prophets had foretold this beforehand.

Alternatively: From present faith to future faith, because faith concerns invisible things; and it was infused as God’s gift both under the Old Testament and in the New. And therefore he says: “But the righteous person lives by my faith.”

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven.” He is speaking against the Gentile portion and says that God’s wrath is revealed through the Gospel. People already knew to expect both benefits and punishments from heaven.

“Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings.” The first ungodliness is sin against God, whether through blasphemy or contempt. The second is against parents, through insult or disdain. The third is against a stranger, because everything contrary to piety is ungodliness. The fourth is against oneself, as Wisdom says: “Those who sin against me act impiously against their own souls.”

Or “all ungodliness,” because the forms of idol worship are diverse: ungodliness may refer to injury against God, and unrighteousness to all sins.

“Of those who suppress the truth in unrighteousness.” They suppress the truth of God’s name in the unrighteous matter of idols.

“Because what can be known of God is manifest in them.” Every creature shows that it is not God but that there is another who made it, whom it is necessary to obey in service. By nature a person can know of God that he exists and that he is just, and that creation itself is not from itself, since no one thing is greater in every respect than all the others. They surpass one another in different ways: some in size, such as the heavens; others in brightness, such as the sun, moon, or splendid stars.

“For God manifested it to them.” His hidden powers are manifested through what is visible.

“For his invisible things are understood and perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made.” If the things that are seen are so splendid, having been made by him—so that some people even thought them gods—how much more could they understand the eternal Creator?

“His eternal power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse.” Therefore Christ is eternal, because he is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

“Because, although they knew God.” How did they know him? Either through conscience, by the reason implanted in them, or through the making of the world, since all things are changeable and God alone is unchangeable.

“They did not glorify him as God.” They did not venerate him according to his greatness, but worshiped idols in place of God.

“Nor did they give thanks.” Because they had been made rational by him.

“But they became futile in their thoughts.” Thinking that they could comprehend God’s greatness.

“And their foolish heart was darkened.” Departing, of course, from the threshold of truth, by venerating the creature in place of the Creator, they lost the true light, that is, the wisdom of God.

“Claiming to be wise.” As though they had discovered how the invisible God might be worshiped in a visible image.

“They became fools.” Not understanding that God is not something made by human beings.

“And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible humanity, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents.” Here he refers to the worshipers of Jupiter, whom they repeatedly assert was transformed, because of his most shameful loves, into a swan and a bull.

“Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts.” God is said to hand people over when, in a just judgment, he does not restrain those who sin, because of the freedom of the will, which is exceedingly ready for evil. He abandons those who abandon him, as he says through the Prophet: “If you abandon him, he too will abandon you.” And again: “I let them go according to the desires of their hearts, and they will walk in their own pleasures.”

“To uncleanness.” This is found in the shameful rites of idols.

“So that they dishonor their bodies.” When, in the consecrations of idols, they inflict upon themselves marks and burnings.

“Among themselves.” Though loving life, they did not spare even themselves, so that in this too they might endure the penalty of their error.

“Those who exchanged the truth of God for a lie.” They transferred the worship of the true God to the lie of idols, which are falsely regarded as gods; for they deceive when they pretend to be what they are not.

“And worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.” They not only said so but also served. Whoever is overcome by desire for any creature serves that creature; for one is the servant of whoever conquers him—so much so that even the belly becomes a god.

“Who is blessed forever.” If they had served him, they too could have become blessed forever. Therefore they became accursed and temporal, having abandoned the one who is blessed forever.

For it is said of such people: “In the same way, the impious person and his impiety are hateful.” Amen—that is, truly or faithfully.

“Therefore God handed them over to dishonorable passions.” For the reasons mentioned above, they were also abandoned to these crimes, so that the passion of vice might already be the punishment for sin.
