“For their women.” He expressed the crimes themselves clearly so that you might recognize that they had lost the understanding of nature. Yet they became so deranged that they overturned everything, having been perverted against God. For those who have abandoned the author of nature cannot preserve the order of nature.

“Exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature.” They overturned everything, as it is written. For the worship of unspeakable idols is the source, beginning, and end of every evil.

“And likewise also the males, abandoning the natural use of the female.” For how could they have preserved the order of nature after abandoning the author of nature?

“They burned in their desires for one another, males committing shamefulness with males.” Unrestrained lust does not know how to observe measure.

“And receiving in themselves the recompense that was fitting for their error.” The sequence proceeds in this way: those who had forgotten the Lord did not even recognize themselves.

“And just as they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge.” They did not fail to know him, but approved of him least of all. For the one who approves of retaining the Lord in his knowledge is the person who always fears him as present and does not dare to sin.

“God handed them over to a debased mind.” That is, they were left in a debased mind.

“To do things that are not fitting.” Things that it is not fitting for a human being to do.

“Filled with all unrighteousness and wickedness.” He shows unrighteousness and wickedness to be the principal causes of vices.

“Fornication and greed.” He joined fornication and greed together because both passions are compared with idolatry, as he says in Exodus: “They fornicated against their God because of the filth of the idol.” For fornication, for a Christian, is to cling to anything other than God and to be corrupted by many desires. Hence Paul says that he betrothed us, a chaste virgin, to one husband.

“Malice.” Greed is therefore insatiable, because after the riches of God, however much anyone may possess, it is little.

“Full of envy and murder.” He aptly joined murder to envy, because envy itself is the first source of this crime: the first murder, both the Devil’s and Cain’s, arose from envy.

“Strife.” Strife occurs when something is defended not by reason but by the stubbornness of the mind, and when truth is not sought but contentiousness is wearied. The first cause of fraternal crime arose from strife.

“Deceit and malignity.” Deceit is hidden wickedness adorned with flattering speech.

“Whisperers.” Grumblers, speaking not to the face but in the ear; or those of whom it is said: “Nor should you grumble.”

“Detractors, hateful to God.” Detractors are hateful to God because nothing is so hateful to God as idolatry, to which detraction is compared, since Scripture says that both the idolater and the detractor must be uprooted.

“Insulting.” Those who are quick to inflict verbal injuries.

“Proud.” The person who wishes to rise above what he is is called proud, like the Devil, who betrayed what he had been. And whoever wishes to be above others will become beneath himself.

“Arrogant, inventors of evil.” An arrogant person is one who is carried above his own measure.

“Disobedient to parents.” In this passage teachers may also be understood, as parents of souls.

“Foolish.” Because they have withdrawn from the very source of wisdom.

“Disorderly.” Every foolish person is disordered.

“Without affection, without honor.” Affection is the fulfillment of love.

“Without mercy.” How could they show mercy to others, when they refused to be merciful even toward themselves?

“Although they knew the justice of God.” Through the fact that evil naturally displeases them, they knew God’s justice.

“They did not understand.” If they had understood, they would have feared; if they had feared, they would never have committed such things.

“That those who do such things are worthy of death.” They will not escape the future punishment of God’s judgment, even if they do not suffer it in the present.

“Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.” They consent by accepting the teaching or by conniving [variant: living together with them].

## CHAPTER TWO
Therefore you are without excuse, every human being who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the very things that you judge. All who passed judgment of this kind—and especially those who possess the authority to examine cases—are summoned not only as judges [Col. 0421D] but also as lords. For by natural judgment each person pronounces a just sentence on deeds. Everyone knows that innocence deserves a reward and wickedness a punishment proportionate to it; and therefore they are without excuse, because they recognized God’s justice.

For we know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things. Certainly the judgment by which such people will be judged is according to truth—people who thought themselves wise enough to condemn others, although they did not fear committing the same things themselves. For if you, a sinner, judge a sinner like yourself, how much more will the just God judge you, an unjust man? And therefore God’s judgment is according to truth, since we read that he spared neither his friends nor sinning angels, showing no partiality.

Human judgment, however, is corrupted in many ways. For it is distorted by love or hatred, but also by greed and fear, and sometimes even by mercy. Do you suppose, then, O man, who judge those who do such things while doing them yourself, that you will escape God’s judgment? Do you flatter yourself with impunity because God does not repay you in the present, and do you despise his patience? “The Lord,” he says, “is not slow concerning the promise, but acts patiently for your sake, not wishing anyone to perish, but all to turn to repentance.” For he is good in waiting; he is just in punishing.

Or do you despise the riches of his goodness—that is, his abundance—and of his patience and forbearance, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? People greatly deceive themselves through God’s patience, because he does not wish to punish sinners immediately. [Col. 0422B] They think either that he does not care about human affairs or that he forgives what he postpones. Many even accuse him, asking why he does not repay them in the present. Wretched and ungrateful even in this, as in all God’s benefits, they charge him with overlooking their destruction, not understanding that, if he repaid them immediately, no human being would remain, and no unjust person would become just.

What more need be said? The Church would not even have Paul himself. God therefore seems to people to wait a long time for sinners because our life is short, and we regard a hundred years as infinite. But for him with whom a thousand years are as one day, a hundred years are as an hour. And therefore this is little in the sight of the Lord, since human beings too are accustomed to wait a few days for sinners.

To offend is human; to repent of an offense is human. No one sins more dangerously than the person who defends his sins. But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up for yourself [Col. 0422C] wrath. Yet you, foolish invalid, abuse the remedy itself to produce greater wounds, as Job says: “God gave him room for repentance, and he abuses it for pride.” For unrecognized mercy prepares a greater judgment, so that the one who disdained to experience mercy may feel vengeance.

Wrath for the day of wrath. You yourself store up with the Lord wrath upon wrath against yourself; it will appear on appointed days and at fixed times, not before the day for which you are waiting [sic]. And the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who repays each person according to his works. For it is hidden, although now it is seen as through a mirror in an enigma, or appears through a veil.

To those, indeed, who with perseverance in good work—The reward of good work is awaited through perseverance [Col. 0422D], because it is not repaid in the present life. “For we walk by faith, and not by sight”; and the work will then be perfect if it endures to the end.

Glory. He proclaims that glory in which the saints will shine like the sun, and honor. The honor of the children of God. For what is more honorable than the children of God, who will even judge angels?

And incorruption. By incorruption he means the glory of immortality.

For those seeking eternal life. Whoever seeks eternal life will attain all these things; and whoever has this hope in him sanctifies himself, as he says: “Be holy, as he is holy.”

But to those who act out of contention. Those who do not believe the evangelical truth and consent to iniquity, who, having abandoned the Creator, serve the creature, and who defend what they know to be contrary—these are contentious. Beware of contention, lest you suffer what follows.

And who do not obey the truth. The evangelical truth.

But believe iniquity. They believe in the iniquity which they chose to believe, for it is not right, having abandoned the Creator of all things, to serve the creature.

Wrath and indignation. All these things are prepared for sinners in the judgment; then repentance will be great and fruitless.

Tribulation and distress. Of conscience and empty repentance, as it is written: “Then the repentant will say among themselves, and, because of the anguish of spirit, they will groan.”

Upon every soul of the human being who practices evil. Because the soul sins first, it principally experiences the punishment; or “soul” is used for the complete human being, as he says that Jacob entered Egypt with seventy souls.

To the Jew first, and to the Greek. [Col. 0423B] First, because they first acknowledged the Lord, and were the first to transgress the law more grievously. Or he uses “first” for “in particular,” since he also says: “There is no partiality with God”—thus “first” refers to priority in time, not to honor.

But glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good. Glory corresponds to wrath, honor to indignation, peace to tribulation and distress; and what he earlier called incorruption he here calls peace.

To the Jew first, and to the Greek. Where he there spoke of the soul of the Jew and the Greek, here he refers to the human being himself. And, as was said, here “first” means “in particular,” or first in the time of belief, not in honor.

For there is no partiality with God. This is so that the Gentiles might not excuse themselves on the ground of ignorance, since they are endowed with the law of nature, nor the Jews flatter themselves because of the law and circumcision, since not profession alone but conduct also is required. For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged through the law.

By “the law,” he means the law of the letter and the law of nature—that is, of the mind and conscience. For to perish seems worse than to be judged. But when he speaks here of Gentiles and Jews, who would dare say that Jews who sin under the law will not perish, since they did not believe in Christ? Since no one can be freed without faith in Christ, they will therefore be judged in this way: they will perish with respect to the kingdom, but they will not perish with respect to punishment. Who, however, doubts that whether Gentiles or Jews, if they do not believe in Christ, will perish?

For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified. He gives the reason why they are not better than the Gentiles [Col. 0423D]; hence we too must fear lest, while hearing the law and not doing it, we perish with the Gentiles. Let the Jew not say: “I lived under the law; I am better than a Gentile.” Thus the law makes hearers; grace makes doers.

For who would say that those who obeyed the law in faith were not justified? For unless they were justified, they could not be obedient. But we say that through the law it comes about that one hears what God wishes to be done, whereas through grace it comes about that one obeys the law, because not the hearers but the doers of the law will be justified.

For when Gentiles who do not have the law—So that, if it were said that they do not have the law of the letter, one might ask how they could be judged—by nature they do the things of the law, although they do not have such a law. He is speaking either of those who keep the law of nature, who do not do to others what they do not wish done to themselves [Col. 0424A]; or of those among the Gentiles who even now, while doing something good, acknowledge that they have received from God the ability by which they can please God, punishing vices.

They are a law to themselves, showing the work of the law. He shows that they were not without law, both to make the Gentiles without excuse and to remove from the Jews the glory they claim from possessing the law. For every human being is ashamed in conscience of sin and rejoices in a good deed.

Written in their hearts, while their conscience bears witness to them. Thus the law of nature is in the heart through the testimony of conscience; or conscience testifies that it possesses the law when it sins and when it rejoices at overcoming sins.

And among themselves, their thoughts accusing or even defending them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings [Col. 0424B]. He says that there are disputes among thoughts when, after long deliberation, we distinguish what ought or ought not to be done; and that we will be judged according to this on the day of the Lord, because we are shown not to have been ignorant of good and evil. Or the thoughts of our consciences will be present on the day of judgment before our eyes like histories to be recognized, and these thoughts will either accuse us or even excuse us.

According to my Gospel through Jesus Christ. According to what I proclaim through Jesus Christ; or, God will judge the hidden things of human beings through Jesus Christ.

But if you are a Jew. After addressing the Gentile portion, he now turns to the Jews, saying that the true Jew is proved to be the one whose good deeds are more hidden than public.

You are called a Jew. In name, not in deed.

And rest in the law. You trust in it, or are secure because of it.

And glory in God. You glory because God is known only in Judea, because you alone know God, or because you alone understand his will.

And know his will. “Of God” is understood. Hence we are blessed if what pleases God is known to us and we do what he commands.

And approve what is more useful, instructed by the law. By reading or examining; for many useful things are approved through nature, although nature is weak, while through the law more useful things are approved, because they are made more perfect through grace.

He again recapitulates the argument: You who rest in the law, how do you transgress the law? You who glory in God, why do you dishonor God? You who know his will, why do you not do it? You who approve what is useful, why do you pursue what is useless and vain?

A guide of the blind: how do you not see the straight road? For if you saw it, you would certainly walk along it.

A light of those who are in darkness: how do you not cast away the works of darkness? [Col. 0424D]

An instructor of the foolish: why have you also abandoned the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom?

A teacher of infants: you are childish in understanding. You possess the form of knowledge and truth in the law, yet you neither follow it yourself nor allow others to follow it by your bad example.

You rely on being yourself a guide of the blind. Of those, certainly, who have lost the way without the light of faith.

A light of those who are in darkness. In the darkness of ignorance.

An instructor of the foolish. Of those who do not possess God’s wisdom.

A teacher of infants. Whether infants in age or in understanding.

Having the form of knowledge and truth in the law. You have an example which you think they cannot live without the law; you possess the form to which, always looking, you cannot go astray.

Therefore you who teach another [Col. 0425A]—What he said to the Gentile: “In judging another, you condemn yourself”—do not teach yourself. Why does your life not correspond to your teaching? Your conduct destroys your faith, and thus the law, when it is not observed, not only benefits you nothing but also holds you guilty of a greater crime, as one who despises it.

You who preach that one must not steal, steal. Some say: “You steal Christ,” that is, you hide him from human beings; or, if you can and wish, you withhold the sacred Scriptures.

You who say that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery. Adultery is not limited to one form. For whatever you owe entirely to God, if you render it to anyone other than God, you commit adultery—whether love, fear, service, obedience, or hope. And therefore the one from whom perfection is proclaimed is offended more grievously.

You who abhor idols, commit sacrilege [Col. 0425B]. Sacrilege is what is committed specifically against God, as it were a violation of what is sacred, or a transgression of the commandments.

You who glory in the law. Saying that you are blessed because you know the will of God.

Through transgression of the law you dishonor God. He has explained sacrilege: “For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written.”

Woe to those whose evil deeds cause the name of the Lord to be blasphemed, as it is written: “They polluted my holy name among the Gentiles,” when they are called the people of God while remaining captives among the Gentiles, detained by their sins. Thus the Gentiles would say that the Lord was unable to defend his people and that they had proved victorious through their idols. They did not understand that, if Israel had held fast to the Lord, it would always have ruled over them and, through this, the Lord would have been its defender.

Circumcision indeed profits if you observe the law; [Col. 0425C] but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. It profits at its proper time, or because it causes the Jew to live and not be exterminated.

It can also be understood in this way: circumcision profits because it makes one understand that it exists, since, when it is examined, it is found that, with the circumcision of the flesh having ceased, the true circumcision of the heart is to come. He is a transgressor of the law when he does not follow what was foretold there.

A sign profits if the reality is present; otherwise a sign without the reality will be superfluous. The sign that Cain received also signified that circumcision would distinguish the Jews from the rest. And just as Cain, wandering and fugitive, endured with that sign until death, so the Jews, dispersed throughout the world with that now empty sign of circumcision, run about full of zeal and fear until the end. No one removes circumcision from them: whether under pagan or Christian rulers, they bear that sign of Christ’s murder, just as Cain, the murderer of his brother, bore his sign [Col. 0425D].

Therefore, if the uncircumcised person keeps the righteous requirements of the law—visible things need invisible things, but invisible things do not need visible things, because visible things are images of invisible things. Circumcision of the flesh needs circumcision of the heart, but circumcision of the heart does not need circumcision of the flesh, because the truth does not need an image, whereas the image needs the truth.

Why, then, was circumcision given, if it profits nothing by itself? First, so that God’s people might be recognized among the Gentiles or in war. The reason they were marked on such a member was, first, to prevent another member from being disfigured, which would have been dreadful to see; then, because of the promise of grace, in which one was to please God through chastity. Or it was given so that Christ might be signified as destined to come from circumcision; carnal circumcision was to continue until him, and Jesus the son of Nun, bearing his type, was commanded to circumcise the children of Israel a second time.

But this was a figure, so much so that it was said: “In the last days God will circumcise your heart”; and: “Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts.” It was also given so that original sin might be punished, even in the time of the law, in the member into which it had been implanted.

Will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And will it judge what is by nature. Because it possesses righteousness, of which circumcision is the sign.

Fulfilling the law through uncircumcision. Completing it.

You who, through the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the law? While you pursue the circumcision of the letter, you are not worthy to receive the Spirit.

For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly [Col. 0426B]. Everything that was previously done concerning the outward human being bore the figure of the outward human being.

Nor is circumcision that which is outward, in the flesh, but the one who is a Jew inwardly. He is the true Jew.

And circumcision is of the heart, in the Spirit. Concerning this it is written in the law: “In the last days God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring.” “In the Spirit,” he says—that is, according to the new covenant, which seeks the inner things that God alone sees—and this is true circumcision.

Not according to the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God. “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” The law of the letter was not given for the righteous but for the unrighteous, and therefore it deserved human praise. But the law of Christ no longer threatens sinners with the sword; rather, it promises a reward to those who serve freely [Col. 0426C]. Therefore it has praise from God, who alone sees the heart, because it is through faith that he is entreated.

## CHAPTER III.

What, then, is the advantage of the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? He explains that the law was not meaningless, but that the privilege of bodily circumcision is vain when supported by no works. He asks what advantage the Jew possesses. He answers, whether speaking for himself or in the person of the Jews: “Much, in every way.” For if this is his meaning—“Much, in every way”—and also “Every human being is a liar,” how does what follows agree with it, when he says: “But if our unrighteousness,” and so forth? Finally, how can he deny that the Jews have much advantage in every way? That advantage will indeed be great if they diligently preserve the oracles which they were worthy to receive.

First, certainly, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them. The Gentiles had nothing of this kind. [Col. 0426D] For what if some of them did not believe? Did their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means. The unbelief of transgressors does not prejudice those who believe; and the promise of God, which was made to Abraham, if it is nullified with regard to transgressors, is fulfilled with regard to the obedient, because Truth does not know how to lie, as it is written: “But God is true, and every human being is a liar.” For no one is without sin, except the one alone who neither had sin at birth nor contracted it by living. Therefore he alone is true, fulfilling what he promised: that the nations would be blessed in his offspring. They are blessed in Christ and through Christ, because they have believed in him through his grace. For even if the blessing of the apostolic calling was nullified in the unbelieving Jews, it was fulfilled in those from that very people who believed through the Lord’s gift, [Col. 0427A] and it is fulfilled and daily made more fully complete to the end, because he who promised is true and can in no way deceive.

“But God is true, and every human being is a liar,” as it is written: “So that you may be proved righteous in your words, and prevail when you are judged.” You prevail when you are judged, when you forgive me my sins as I confess and condemn them. “So that you may be proved righteous,” he says, “in your words.” For God is true. Even if the blessing of the apostolic office was voided in Judas the betrayer, it was fulfilled in Peter, who preserved the faith. The promise was voided in the people who perished in the desert because of their transgressions; it was fulfilled in those who, through the Lord’s gift and with faith cooperating, were led into the holy land.

He also adds testimony from Psalm 50 [Col. 0427B] [Psalm 51]: “So that you may be proved righteous,” he says, “in your words, and prevail when you are judged.” In the order of the psalm, the prophet’s wording is as follows: “O Lord, you did indeed declare, without accepting persons, that you would take vengeance upon sinners. And now, when you forgive me, they judge your patience to be a lie. But you prevail when you are judged, since you forgive me my sins as I confess and condemn them, because you do not judge twice for the same matter.” That is, when a person himself, acting as his own judge, pursues his guilt through lamentation and contrition, the indulgence of your mercy is not shown to be unjust. When through the prophet you charge me with guilt for a monstrous crime, you prove that you care about our deeds, and you prevail over those who judged you unconcerned with human actions.

For this reason I have set down the whole exposition of a certain holy man [Col. 0427C] concerning this meaning of the Apostle, so that the reader’s attention might be more fully instructed; wherever you find it in this form, I have included the full pages for the sake of instruction.

“So that you may be proved righteous,” he says, “in your words, and prevail when you are judged.” Let us see how the Apostle’s discourse at this point agrees with the testimony that he took from the prophet in order to confirm his own argument. The Apostle clearly presents this statement in the sense in which David had earlier uttered it in the voice of repentance, saying:

“O Lord, you promised that the Savior of the human race would come from my offspring. Now, when your people see me wounded by a double crime, I have caused the children of Israel to blaspheme, so that, when they perceive my guilt in adultery and murder, they may think that you have lied. Therefore accept the prayer of my satisfaction, and forgive what I myself [Col. 0427D] condemn, so that, when you have restored me through pardoning mercy and made me worthy of your promise, you may appear righteous in your words and prevail when you are judged by those who reproach you.”

And so the Apostle now follows this line, saying:

“Although the transgressing Jews have caused the name of the Lord to be blasphemed, so that it may be said: ‘This was that holy nation and chosen people, which has now entangled itself in transgression, inexpiable sacrilege, and the crime of impiety—behold, through the crime of the transgressors God’s promises have been made void’—yet it is not so. For if the transgressors have fallen away from grace, the obedience of the faithful fulfills the Lord’s truthful pledge. Thus, when those who were proclaiming that the divine oracles had been rendered void have been put to shame, the Lord is proved righteous in his words, [Col. 0428A] and prevails when he is judged, as he grants to believers the grace rejected by unbelievers.”

But when he says, “God is true, and every human being is a liar,” and again, “But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God,” let unbelievers receive both testimonies according to their rational meaning.

“But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous, who inflicts wrath?” If our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, he says, it is unjust for him to take vengeance upon those who sinned for the purpose of making him appear more righteous. For by what justice will he condemn unrighteousness, if, according to you, he is made more righteous by human unrighteousness?

At this point, while the teacher of the nations [Col. 0428B] is expounding the matter, the reasoning of two persons is presented: that of an ignorant interpreter who misinterprets, and that of the Apostle who refutes him. It is as though someone, imprudently siding with the opposing position, were to say to the Apostle:

“O Apostle, you have brought great consolation to our sins by saying that God is justified in forgiving our offenses, and that God’s truth is commended by our lies, while our sins provide God with material for mercy, so that his goodness may be exercised and his glory enlarged through our unrighteousness. Our sins, therefore, are punished unjustly, since they contribute to the manifestation of God’s patience and benevolence.”

Up to this point is the opposing objection; here the Apostle answers their reasoning: “God is unrighteous,” he says, “if he takes vengeance upon those through whose sins he appears benevolent; and I ought not to be judged, though I lie, because through my lie God’s truth is gathered and found more worthy of praise. Therefore, the greater evils we commit, [Col. 0428C] the greater goods we shall receive from him for whose praise we sinned.”

Perhaps the ignorant thought that this ought to be understood in this way because we read: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more”—as though the abundance of sin were rewarded because it provided an increase for God’s clemency. But this statement must be understood in a very different way. The abundance of sins was consumed through satisfaction and amendment, so that those who were amended might deserve not only pardon but also rewards: “So that you may be proved righteous,” he says, “in your words.”

The opposing party presented this testimony as though David had said: “For this reason I sinned, so that, when you judge me, you may appear righteous or merciful when you forgive me. Therefore you ought to spare me, because my unrighteousness commends either your mercy or your righteousness.”

The Apostle corrects their error [Col. 0428D] and destroys it by inserting several statements, saying:

“If, as some claim that we say, our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, then God is unrighteous when he inflicts wrath, since our unrighteousness proclaims his mercy. I speak according to human reasoning. By no means.” That is, according to your carnal understanding, or according to you, who think so incompetently and understand so imprudently what was said above.

“For by what justice will he condemn unrighteousness, if, in accordance with your opinion, he is made more righteous by human unrighteousness?”

But this is not so. Our God is glorified not so much by sins as by the deeds of good works. Therefore, in punishing sins, he is recognized as just, since he delights in holy works. Otherwise, how will God judge the world, [Col. 0429A] if he does not repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil, granting the just a reward for righteousness and sinners what they deserve?

“For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged?” That is: “Why am I judged as though I were doing evil? And why not, as some slanderously claim that we say, ‘Let us do greater evils, so that we may receive greater goods’?”

“Moreover”—that is, in addition—“I, as a sinner, a human being who lies, am judged,” by God on the day of judgment.

This is the meaning, as though he were saying:

“O unbeliever, from my words you construct a defense for your sins, saying that our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God and that his truth grows through our lies and appears greater and greater when compared with our weakness. But while you flatter your evils in this way with hostile severity, you will be punished by a just condemnation [Col. 0429B] by him who will judge the world according to each person’s deeds.”

For this reason this passage seems more difficult, because it is obscured by the questions of the opposing party as presented by the inexperienced. Elsewhere, likewise, the Apostle proposes and rejects irrational objections:

“What shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means.” And shortly afterward: “What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means.”

Finally, dispelling the question through the sense of truth, the Apostle says:

“And not as we are blasphemed, and as some claim that we say: ‘Let us do evil so that good may come.’” This is the objection of fools, which he then destroys by saying: “Their condemnation is just.” For what is more just than that a person should suffer the punishment of his sin? Those who accuse us falsely claimed that we denied this, although we proclaim nothing more strongly than God’s just judgment. [Col. 0429C]

“What then? Do we excel them?”—we Jews. That is: “I find no reason by which either side excels the other, because we judge all to be under sin.” Reason itself establishes this: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin, as is also confirmed by the testimony of the psalm.

“Not at all.” He answers himself.

“For we have already charged”—that is, reasoned—that “all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin,” including the Gentiles.

“As it is written: ‘For there is none righteous.’” The psalm from which he took this testimony speaks about the fool, and shows that it was fulfilled at the coming of Christ, at which time no righteous person was found—anyone at all, neither Jew nor Greek.

“There is none who understands; there is none who seeks God.” Because he does not understand, he does not seek. God is sought when [Col. 0429D] his will is inquired into and fulfilled.

“All have turned aside.” Whoever refuses to seek the foundation necessarily turns aside.

“Together they have become useless”—for the work for which they had been created.

“There is none who does good.” Therefore there was no one doing good when transgression of the commandments condemned the Jews, while the law of nature condemned the Gentiles. Whenever, then, someone on either side has done good, let him know that he owes it to grace, not to nature, as the prophet says in referring it to the Lord: “Before whom no one is innocent by himself.” And Isaiah says in a song: “Lord our God, you will give us peace, for you have accomplished all our works in us.”

“Not even one.” Some say, “Up to Christ.” [Col. 0430A]

“Their throat is an open tomb.” They intensify the violence of a pestilential odor through the stench of their teaching. Every odor of death proceeds from their mouth—that is, pestilential and flattering words which kill those who hear them. Tombs are closed for this reason: so that, among the living, they may not generate pestilence by their own exhalation.

“With their tongues they acted deceitfully.” They bring forth one thing with their mouths while meditating another in their hearts.

“The poison of asps is under their lips.” The poison of these serpents is said to be more harmful than that of the others.

“Under their lips”—that is, in their hearts.

“Their mouth is full of cursing.” Whatever is spoken with an evil intention is undoubtedly spoken evilly.

“And it is full of bitterness.” The bitterness of Antichrist is opposed to the sweetness of the word of God.

“Their feet are swift to shed blood.” They are not swift to free souls but to destroy them, killing souls—not by announcing their sins to them, but by confirming them in those sins [Col. 0430B] through flattery.

Hence Paul says: “I am clean from the blood of all.”

“Destruction and misery are in their ways.” Souls are crushed and made miserable in their ways—that is, in their teachings or in the examples of their conduct.

“And they have not known the way of peace.” They have not known the teaching of the Father, through which God would be reconciled to human beings, because Christ is our peace.

He has pursued this from the beginning of the epistle in order to show that all need the mercy of God; and mercy lies in the power of the one who gives it. No one can say that he ought to have received more.

“There is no fear of God before their eyes.” He concluded with the fear of God, because if they had always had the fear of God before their eyes, they certainly would not have sinned. For a servant does not dare to sin when his master is present.

But we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law. [Col. 0430C] The Jews were not to say that this was spoken about the Gentiles. The Jews said, “There is no God,” not in words, certainly, but in deeds: they confess that they know the Lord, but deny him by their actions. Therefore this passage does not concern the Gentiles; he had already spoken earlier about the Gentiles, and no one doubted their crimes. So that they would not say that this had been written about the Gentiles, he shows that everything said in the law about the Gentiles is also said about the Jews themselves, because their case is the principal one.

“So that every mouth may be stopped”—not only the mouths of the Gentiles but also those of the Jews, since they have no ground on which they can boast.

“And the whole world may become subject to God”—so that it may know that it cannot be saved without the grace of God; or at least, by confessing sin, it may hope for mercy, recognizing that it is in sins.

“For by works of the law”—this is directed against the Pelagians, who say that the law justifies. [Col. 0430D] By “works of the law” he means circumcision, the Sabbath, and the rest.

“No one will be justified.” He will not be justified because the law brought nothing to perfection. Here he begins to argue against those who gloried in the law and believed that they were justified through the law and not through grace. He teaches step by step that the law could not remove sin but rather increased it; grace removes it, because the law knows how to command, while weakness succumbs, just as grace knows how to help, through which charity is infused.

We do not say that those who were obedient to the law were justified because they were obedient; rather, unless they had been justified, they would not have been obedient.

“Flesh”—the human being.

“Before him.” Not every righteousness justifies before the Lord, but that which proceeds from God’s pure will, [Col. 0431A] not that whose command merely indulges human weakness—as was the case with those to whom the righteousness of God could not then be revealed, but only the knowledge of sin was demonstrated. For, seeking to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God.

“For through the law comes knowledge of sin.” Not remission, not its removal, but knowledge—either because the law of nature had fallen into oblivion, or because before the written law even the lesser matters were not recognized as sins, such as desire and other things which harmed no one else but the person himself.

“But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God”—the righteousness freely given to us by God, not sought through our own labor.

“Has been manifested.” It had been hidden.

“Witnessed by the law and the prophets.” This righteousness was proclaimed through the utterances of the law as destined to come in the last times.

“But the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ.” [Col. 0431B] This righteousness, which is bestowed through faith, is itself infused by the hidden inspiration of God as a gift of grace. It is acquired neither through human labor nor through the work of the Old Testament, because, as has been said, it is God’s gift that we believe.

“Upon all who believe.” Not upon the Jews alone. He shows that they received such a law because they did not believe; consequently, in the present they were receiving either the due of sin or that of righteousness.

“For there is no distinction.” For all have sinned and lack the glory of God—that is, there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, because both sides have been confined under unbelief and lack the glory of the Redeemer, which is extended for the salvation of believers. For Jews, by transgressing the written law, and Gentiles, by transgressing the law of nature, were found alike to be sinners, both through original sin and through actual sin.

“Justified freely.” Justified without any preceding merits, through baptism. [Col. 0431C] Since he freely forgave sins to all who did not deserve it, hear the word “freely” and be silent concerning merits.

“By his grace.” Because he paid on our behalf what he did not owe, so that he might save us, redeemed freely.

“Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” We were redeemed from the captivity of sin, not by nature, since by nature we always belonged to him. For the one who redeems shows that the person whom he redeems had been his, as the prophet says: “You were sold for nothing, and without money you shall be redeemed.”

Christ therefore redeemed us, as Peter says: “Knowing that you were redeemed, not with perishable things, silver or gold, from your futile way of life,” and so forth; and Paul says: “You were bought at a great price.”

We were therefore redeemed from death, to which we had been sold through sin, according to Isaiah’s words: “Who is the bill of repudiation? [Col. 0431D] You were sold because of your sins.” Christ overcame this death. He committed no sin, whereas we were all debtors to death through sin. He, however, surrendered himself to death, though he owed it nothing, so that by his blood he might redeem us from death. He did not purchase us, because by nature we were his; but he redeemed us, because we were being held captive.

“Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood.” He placed him openly before us, because he gives freely, so that no one may despair or exalt himself on account of his merits. Propitiation and the forgiveness of sins have been conferred through Christ’s blood; in its likeness, even in the Old Testament, the blood of sacrificial victims was offered for the sins of the people.

“For the demonstration of his righteousness.” By this he says that God demonstrated his righteousness: he patiently endured, without defense, [Col. 0432A] in expectation of our amendment. Thus the mercy of forgiveness is given to us while the one who committed no sin suffers, because God does all things justly. Therefore the devil justly lost his debtor, because he unjustly killed the innocent.

“Because of the forgiveness of preceding sins.” Why “preceding” sins, unless because of original debts?

“In the forbearance of God.” God’s forbearance had contributed to the increase of greater sins.

“For the demonstration of his righteousness.” So that he might reveal the righteousness which comes from faith—that is, Christ—in this final time.

“So that he himself may be righteous and the one who justifies.” He alone was found righteous, and he justifies those whom he himself justifies. Because he knew no sin, he condemned sins.

“Of the one who is from the faith of Jesus.” “From the faith,” he says, “of Jesus”—the faith which Jesus himself gave—and not from the works of the law or of nature.

“Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded.” [Col. 0432B] He says this to the Jews: “Where is your arrogance, in which you boasted that you were better through bodily circumcision? Your boasting has been excluded.”

“Through what law? Of works?” No, but through the law of faith. He continues: “Is it through the law of works”—that is, through the works of the law? And he answers: “No, but through the law of faith.”

He calls the grace of Christ the law of faith, through which we approach Christ and through which we receive faith.

“For we reckon that a person is justified by faith.” We define, we are certain, and we judge this to be so.

“Without the works of the law.” By adding “of the law,” he shows that there are also works of faith. How, then, does James say: “Faith without works is dead”? Paul is speaking about the works of the law, whereas James is speaking about the works which prove a person to be faithful, as he himself explains later: “Show me your faith from your works.” Works are the means by which faith is recognized. [Col. 0432C]

“Or is God the God of the Jews?” Did he not make everyone, and does he not care equally for all? Christ came not only for you but also for the Gentiles, having been promised from the law—indeed, rather, for them.

“Only?” As though the Jews were saying: “But the Gentiles abandoned God.” And the response is: “So did you. They sinned, and so did you. But we are converted, and so are they. Christ was promised to us, and to them.”

God is not therefore yours alone. Or are you unaware that all were born from Adam, and that it was written that the Gentiles would believe in Christ, as he says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations”? And again: “Hear the voice of the trumpet,” and they said: “We will not hear.” For this reason the Gentiles will hear.

“Is he not also the God of the Gentiles?” [Col. 0432D] Of Gentiles who believe, since the prophets frequently spoke of their calling.

“Indeed, also of the Gentiles.” That is, much more also of the Gentiles, because before the law holy people pleased God. He very aptly preserved the force of the words: he said “indeed” in order to show that the Gentiles were more properly included, since holy people were uncircumcised before they were circumcised, and Abraham believed and was justified before circumcision.

“Since there is one God who will justify the circumcision by faith.” He declares that both peoples are to be saved through faith in Christ—that is, from faith. For neither uncircumcision nor circumcision is justified without faith.

“And the uncircumcision through faith.” Such as Abel, Noah, and the others.

“Do we then destroy the law through faith?” By no means. Do we destroy through faith the law which taught circumcision? By no means. So much so that he says Moses was almost killed because of the circumcision of his son.

Therefore, lest they say to him, [Col. 0433A] “You are destroying the law in which all who believed were circumcised, while before the law the righteous were uncircumcised, yet under the law no one was uncircumcised,” he says:

“Not only do I not destroy it,” he says, “but I confirm it.” I confirm it by proclaiming the circumcision which that law foretold: “In the last days,” he says, “the Lord God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God.” This is faith. [Col. 0433B]

I would destroy the law if I said that it had lied—that is, that it would not come to an end—when it had promised that it would come to an end. Thus Jeremiah says: “I will give you a new covenant.” And Isaiah says: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

“But we establish the law.” We make it stand by proving that what it said concerning the ancient righteous and the Gentiles who would believe is true, and that spiritual circumcision would come. Faith brings about what the law commands; without faith, the law merely commands and holds those who do not fulfill its commands guilty. It is fulfilled only through charity, which the Holy Spirit pours into us through his grace.

### CHAPTER IV.

What then do we say that Abraham our father found? He brings them back to the origin of circumcision, so that what was established at the beginning may be accepted throughout. Circumcision is in the flesh, but faith resides in the mind. Abraham, according to faith, is father of the nations through uncircumcision; according to the flesh, he is father of circumcision. The faith by which he is father of the nations, however, resides not in the flesh but in the mind.

According to the flesh. That is, according to the circumcision of the flesh. For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory. How by works, since he himself also came from the nations? But not before God. But he has it before himself, because he fulfills the commands; otherwise, nothing. God granted it to him, but from himself; he had glory from his own works. But because faith, granted by God without presumption concerning works, justifies him, he gives glory not to himself but to the Lord, from gratuitous generosity.

He therefore says that blessed Abraham found righteousness not from works—for he lived before the law—but from faith, because he believed God’s promises. And because faith, through the grace of God, justifies not only the sinner but also the ungodly, on account of God’s goodness, when a person places confidence not in works but understands himself in every respect to be indebted to God, since he finds nothing that he can claim for himself from merits.

For what does Scripture say? Let us question Scripture. Abraham believed God. He proved it, and therefore has glory before God. So great was Abraham’s faith, by God’s gift, [Col. 0433D] that his former sins were forgiven and faith alone was counted to him as complete righteousness; and he burned with such great love that thereafter he always pleased God.

And it was counted to him as righteousness. Faith alone was accepted in compensation.

But to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt. He explains the example itself. And because the law demands works, by which the Pharisee had been exalted, when divine mercy justifies the ungodly, presumption cannot have the place of merit. For a person is already a debtor before obeying the commandments, and unless he obeys, he is condemned. If he does obey, he has no glory, because he is an unprofitable servant who does nothing more.

But if one who does not work. He speaks of circumcision and other things of this kind.

But to the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly. He justifies the ungodly by faith alone, not by works, which he did not possess; for if he is judged according to works, he must be punished, not freed. It must also be noted that it is not the sinner who is justified by faith, but the ungodly.

His faith is counted as righteousness, according to the purpose of God’s grace, just as David also says. As with Abraham, so also with us, his children, through grace.

The blessedness of the man. Great is the blessedness of obtaining faith, without the labor of the law or of repentance, through grace alone, according to God’s purpose, by which he purposed freely to forgive sins.

To whom God credits righteousness without works. Righteousness is credited to him without works [Note: The nominative case *justitia*—“righteousness”—should properly be read. EDIT.] who, through the faith by which he first believed God, is both absolved from the past and justified in the present, [Col. 0434B] and prepared for the future works of faith.

He wishes to prove that even in the law it is proclaimed that righteousness without works is beneficial, and that he does not defend this by his own authority but confirms it by the example of the prophet.

What is remitted is not present; what is covered is not exposed, and therefore it is not reckoned either.

Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven. Against the arrogance of the Jews, because blessedness and the forgiveness of sins are the work of belief, not of labor.

Some say that sins are forgiven through baptism, covered by the tears of repentance, and that no sins are reckoned in martyrdom. Although the whole matter may be understood in relation to faith in baptism, nevertheless, when offenses have been forgiven, God is loved. For the one to whom more is forgiven loves more; and therefore love covers a multitude of sins, so that love surpasses former contempt. He does not reckon them, moreover, when he takes pleasure thereafter in the person’s good works, which are performed through love, and does not remember what he did before.

And those whose sins have been covered. By love.

Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin. He does not remember it.

Is this blessedness therefore in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision? Some wish to assign this blessedness to three periods: Nature, Circumcision, and Christianity. But, in order to exclude them from the glory of privilege, he himself says that it is not in circumcision but in uncircumcision.

For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. Since we both confess Abraham to have been justified, and since we are discussing Abraham, let us accept in all cases and hold without hesitation for everyone whatever reason finds concerning him: this faith benefited not Abraham alone but all who follow the example of his belief, as we read in what follows, so that it may be counted to him as righteousness.

How, then, was it counted: in circumcision or in uncircumcision? Let us see whether he was righteous because he was circumcised, or was circumcised because he was found righteous—whether circumcision arose from righteousness, or righteousness from circumcision.

Not in circumcision but in uncircumcision. He was justified before he was circumcised. Therefore he was not justified because of circumcision.

And he received the sign of circumcision. They might say: Why, then, was he circumcised, if he did not need circumcision? It is a sign, he says, of righteousness, not an increase of it.

Alternatively: To show how righteous and faithful he was, since he did not hesitate to inflict pain upon himself at God’s command, not considering superfluous what was ordered by the Lord of knowledge, just as he did not consider the impious killing of his son to be wicked when the source of piety had commanded it.

The seal of the righteousness of faith. To signify the righteousness of Christ, which is from faith, which now exists in uncircumcision, or which was born to him in uncircumcision.

Alternatively: So perfect was his faith that it deserved to receive a seal; what is full is always sealed, and what is great is sealed.

Which is in uncircumcision. Now, in those who believe from among the nations.

So that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision. So that all who believe from among the nations might, according to faith, be sons of Abraham, since faith alone is counted to them as righteousness, and they too are circumcised—not in the flesh but in the heart; or because, before circumcision, he was the father of the righteous who were uncircumcised.

So that it might also be counted to them as righteousness, and so that he might be the father of circumcision. [Col. 0435B] Once they have been justified, they are circumcised; for if an uncircumcised person is righteous, his uncircumcision will be counted as circumcision. Now there is no need of a sign by which he may be recognized by human beings.

For God’s people are not one nation, but a congregation from all peoples, because Christ, the expectation of the nations, has already come. He is father not only of those faithful who are from circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith that was in our father Abraham while he was uncircumcised.

If they imitate him. For it was not through the law.

Not through the law, but before the law: for in the law people did indeed believe in the faith and promise of Abraham, but Moses, who wrote the law, came later. Then he himself says to the Galatians: The law came into being after four hundred and thirty years, and it does not invalidate the promise by annulling it.

The promise to Abraham, or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world. Not through circumcision, but through the righteousness of faith. So that in the seed of Abraham, that is, in Christ, all nations might be blessed; to him the Father has given the nations as an inheritance. Or so that the nations might rest with him, as the Savior says: “They will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

For if those who are of the law are heirs. If they are heirs by circumcision, according to you; if they alone are heirs, as you wish, then God did not grant Abraham what he promised—that he would be the father of many nations—and he seems to have believed without purpose. But this is not so. For God fulfilled his promise to Abraham, because nations from every part of the world believe in Christ.

Faith has been emptied, and the promise abolished. Therefore no one is justified by faith—not even Abraham. [Col. 0435D] But since faith cannot be emptied and the promise cannot be abolished, it remains that the inheritance is not from the law but through the righteousness of faith.

For the law does not forgive sins but indicates them [Elsewhere: “vindicates” or “judges”]. And therefore it cannot make children of Abraham, because, since all were found under sin, all were liable to punishment. Therefore they are from faith, so that, once their sins have been forgiven through grace, they may become children of Abraham.

For the law produces wrath. It was established for the unrighteous; it burdened sinners more heavily and did not absolve them, because it was established for the unrighteous. In the present life, it inflicted punishment on transgressors.

For what else is the law to those who know how to read it but mere letter, when they cannot fulfill it? To such people it is letter because it is not a helper of those who read but a witness against sinners. [Col. 0436A] Therefore the law produces wrath, so that, when a person is terrified and turned toward fulfilling the righteousness of the law, the mercy of God may bestow grace through Jesus Christ our Lord, who is the wisdom of God. Concerning him it is written: “He bears law and mercy on his tongue.” Law, by which he terrifies; mercy, by which he helps.

Knowledge of the law therefore makes the transgressor proud; but through the gift of love it makes one delight in being a doer of the law.

The law, he says, produces wrath, because God’s wrath is greater against the transgressor who recognizes sin through the law and nevertheless commits it.

For where there is no law, neither is there transgression. The law was established because of transgression; for when the commandment came through the law, the opportunity for transgression also increased.

Therefore it is from faith. Heirs through faith, not through the law.

So that it may be according to grace. [Col. 0436B] Observe carefully that he said “according to grace,” so that presumption may cease—presumption that flatters itself with its merits.

Let the promise be firm for every descendant. Not only for the one who is from the law, but also for the one who is from the faith of Abraham. For all nations believe, and the promise to Abraham is fulfilled.

Who is the father of us all, as it is written. The father both of the uncircumcised and of the circumcised.

Here, where Abraham is called the father of many nations, the pride of the Jews is confounded, because he is father of the Jews according to the flesh, but of the nations according to faith.

For I have appointed you as the father of many nations before God, in whom you believed. For by himself he could not even be the father of one son.

Who gives life to the dead. He speaks of bringing the dead to beget, especially Sarah, so that the expression may apply particularly to one whose womb was closed: the fruit of offspring, which age had not obtained, was secured by perfect faith. [Col. 0436C]

And he calls into existence things that do not exist as though they existed. Although at the beginning he called into existence things that did not exist, and at the command of the one who ordered them they immediately began to exist, here he signifies the conception of a son that had been despaired of.

Who against hope. It was contrary to the hope of nature that an old woman should give birth, and that his seed should become like the stars of heaven.

In hope he believed. In hope founded upon God’s power.

So that he might become the father of many nations. For at that time he was still the father of one son.

According to what was said: “So shall your seed be like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.” Since the Apostle was speaking to those who knew the law, by the sand he signified the Jews, and by the stars the nations that believe. Understand the former as earthly, the latter as heavenly; for even from that very race of the Jews the primitive Church, which believed, is rightly compared with heaven and the stars.

And he was not weakened in faith, [Col. 0436D] nor did he consider his own body, already dead, since he was almost a hundred years old, or Sarah’s dead womb. Faith considers nothing belonging to nature, because in what God promises, nature readily serves its own author.

The question is how Abraham later fathered sons by Keturah, although previously he could not do so by Sarah. He did not beget from Sarah because she was old and barren. But from the woman who was still in the vigor of youth he was easily able to procreate. In God’s promise, however, he did not hesitate through unbelief; rather, he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God.

He did not doubt either the impossibility of old age or the greatness of the promise, because he looked not to his own years but to the promises of the Almighty, giving glory to God as though he were giving thanks for something already received.

Fully knowing [Col. 0437A] that whatever God has promised, he is also able to accomplish. That is, with complete certainty. He himself therefore creates the faith of the nations, since he is able to do what he promised. He therefore works faith in our hearts in a wondrous and ineffable manner, so that we may believe.

And therefore it was counted to him as righteousness. But it was not written only for his sake, that it was counted to him. For if [Note: The conjunction *si*—“if”—appears to be superfluous and should be deleted. EDIT.] he believed.

Alternatively: It must be observed that before God not only devotion in action has merit, but also firm and perfect belief.

But for our sake also, to whom it will be counted. Not merely so that we might know what he was like, but so that he might be an example to all of us, as a father is to his children. So it is with all the examples of the saints, including their trials: they were given so that they might know themselves and we might follow their examples. Therefore the saints are tested so that they may recognize themselves; therefore those who have been proved are justified, [Col. 0437B] so that we may follow in their footsteps.

To those who believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead. Let us see in what sequence he has proceeded here to Christ’s resurrection: namely, “it will also be counted to us,” if we believe with as complete a faith that Christ rose from the dead as he believed that Sarah’s dead body could be made alive for conception.

Who was handed over because of our offenses. In his being handed over, mercy was demonstrated; in his resurrection, power. And so that an example of the new life that comes from resurrection—which is our justification—might be given to us: he died to bear our sins; he rose to display, through his resurrection, the glory of our justification.

And he rose because of our justification. He therefore died to restore life to the dead. [Col. 0437C] He appeared in the very body in which he had been crucified, so that he might confirm the faith and righteousness of believers, when he displayed the fruit of promise—or of belief—in its fullness.

## Chapter V

Therefore, having been justified. Since Jews and nations were disputing among themselves, the former presuming upon the works of the ancient law, the latter upon the new calling of Christ, the matter having been thoroughly examined—since none of them was justified by his own merit, but all by grace, which infuses faith and reveals the truth; and since neither lineage nor circumcision, but faith, makes children of Abraham, who was justified before circumcision by belief alone—having concluded the argument in this way, he exhorts them to have peace with God, because no one has been saved by his own merits, but all have been saved by God’s grace and mercy.

Through faith. Which comes from God, so that we may believe, as he also says to the Galatians: “But when faith came, we are no longer under a tutor.” And to the Hebrews: “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.”

Let us have peace with God. Or, let us be subject to God; or, let us have the peace of God, not that of the world.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Not through works, through whom we have access by faith into this grace. Through him we have drawn near, though we were far away.

In which we stand. Because before grace we were lying prostrate.

And we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. In this matter, which appears incredible, we glory through faith in hoping that we shall be the children of God, and such is the greatness of what we hope for that no one would dare to presume it from himself, since it rests solely upon God’s power that a human being can rise into the number of God’s children. He shows that we also have something in which we may rightly and safely glory.

For great is the glory of being enrolled among the children of God through faith and hope. In the hope of the glory of the children of God, that is promised to us which, as has been said, no one dared to hope for. If it had perhaps entered someone’s mind, he might have thought that he had fallen into blasphemy. It is so great that, because of its very greatness, many consider it incredible: namely, that we hope to attain the glory of the children of God.

And not only that, but we also glory in tribulations. He glories in tribulations because through them the virtue of patience is displayed, and from patience arises the testing of faith; hope, moreover, is nourished by the proving of an unconquered spirit. [Col. 0438B]

The saints therefore glory in enduring tribulation without the danger of vanity. For we glory not only in the glory of hope but also in tribulations that are most beneficial to us, knowing what reward they possess, as James says: “Consider it complete joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various trials.” And again: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life.”

We are permitted to glory in glorious tribulation; and if we do so, it is as though someone, scorning a coin of bronze or lead, were to obtain a royal jewel. Although the comparison is inadequate: here, however much the value differs, the corruption of both still remains; there, great things displace small ones, and eternal things succeed what is fleeting.

Knowing [Col. 0438C] that tribulation. What is firmly believed is now said to be known.

Produces patience. In tribulation patience appears or is increased. The faithful desire to suffer something for the Lord’s name, so that from the tribulation that must end they may gain rewards that will remain without end.

And patience, testing; and testing, hope. Whoever has been patient in all things has been proved. The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people.

But hope does not disappoint. Hope in future things drives away all shame arising from present things. Hence the one who is ashamed of Christ’s commandments is shown not to possess hope.

Because the love of God. We know how God loves us from this: he not only forgave us our sins through the death of his Son, but also bestowed in us the gift of the Holy Spirit, who cleanses and enlightens the hidden places of our hearts and already now [Col. 0438D] reveals the glory of future things.

Has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who was given to us. The greatness of benefits awakens within us a corresponding greatness of love, which, once perfected, knows neither fear nor shame. Yet this love is given to us not through our own merit but through the Holy Spirit, because love itself is recognized as the fullness of the law.

And therefore let no one glory in himself but in God, whose gift it is; nor let anyone say: “I believed the natural law, and thus I received the Holy Spirit.” For no one precedes God; rather, we are always preceded by his mercy.

For why did Christ, while we were still weak? He wishes to show here [Col. 0439A] that he died for the ungodly, and to commend the greatness of his benefits, so that we may see that, although we were loved by him without deserving it, we ought to love him just as greatly—or, if anything ought to be preferred to such a holy and great benefit, that when we were ungodly he neither preferred his own life to us nor refused us his death.

According to the time, he died for the ungodly. Either because Christ suffered at the end of the age, or because, in relation to the present time, he was dead for the period of three days, as was proclaimed.

By saying that the one who died for the ungodly, he shows that we ought to love the pious Lord even unto death, since we know that he endured the torment of death for ungodly servants. At the same time, it must be noted that he says “for the ungodly,” so that human presumption may be restrained and no one may attribute anything to his own merits.

For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person. He says this against Pelagius, who denies original sin; if sin had not bound humanity, Christ’s death would not have been necessary.

It is appropriate, however, that a human being should pour out his life without hesitation in confessing the good Lord, who died not for the righteous but for the ungodly, and that in this way we should cease presuming upon ourselves.

For if someone scarcely dies for a righteous person, who would die for an unrighteous and ungodly person, except the one who had come to save what had perished? No one gave anything to him first; rather, he received from him the ability to believe.

For perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. That is easy enough, for “good” here means “righteous,” according to that commandment: “the just and the good.”

But he commends his own love. Love is commended when something is repaid that was not owed. What, then, was so utterly beyond obligation as that the pious Lord, without sin, should die for an ungodly servant? [Col. 0439C]

God in us. From his death we understand how much he loves us.

For while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having now been justified in his blood, shall we be saved. If he loved sinners so greatly, how much more will he now preserve those whom he has made righteous? And if he intervened for strangers, much more will he not allow his own to perish. If he gave himself for the ungodly, how could he deny them what belongs to him?

He now reminds us that we are debtors not through the blood of animals, as in the law, but through the blood of the Son of God. And he wishes us to understand how much he loves those whom he has received, since he reconciled enemies.

From wrath. From the wrath of judgment.

Through him. Through him we shall be saved, not through ourselves—that is, if we are his member. For when everything burns, only the body of the Judge will be saved.

For if, when we were enemies. [Col. 0439D] We were enemies before the gift of his grace and before the sacrament of baptism. But those too are known to be his enemies who, after baptism, entangle themselves in crimes and wicked deeds and do not wish to correct their errors through repentance, as James says: “Friendship with this world is enmity with God.”

Enemies, therefore, not by nature but by a contrary will.

We have been reconciled. Because we had been alienated and had become enemies through transgression. For no one is reconciled except after enmity. The transgression of our first parent made us enemies.

Through the death of his Son: much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved in his life. If we were saved through the death of Christ, how much more shall we be glorified in his life, if we imitate both his life and his death and strive to remain under the protection of his commandments [Col. 0440A]—protection. Protection.

And not only that, but we also glory in God. Not only will Christ’s life be given to us in that transformation of the resurrection, but also glory, as the apostle John says: “It has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him.”

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. So that through his grace we may deserve his likeness and be in the glory of God the Father.

Through whom we have now received reconciliation. Now reconciliation; then glory.

Therefore, just as through one man into this world. Here he wishes to show that Christ suffered for this reason: so that those who had departed from God through Adam might be reconciled through Christ.

Sin entered. By propagation and example: just as, when there was no sin, it came through Adam, so also, when righteousness was already absent from everyone, it was restored through Christ; and just as death came through the sin of the former, so life came through the righteousness of the latter.

And through sin. In this passage, against the abrupt error of Pelagian impiety, he strives to show that death was not made by God but brought about through the fault of transgression. For just as salvation was lost through the sin of the first Adam, so it was restored through the righteousness of the second.

Here the Apostle intends to assert that Adam’s transgression was great, but Christ’s redemption is richer. Hence he said: “And not as through one man’s sin, so also is the gift.” From one sin the former brought death; the latter, through the abolition of many sins, restored life. And therefore righteousness prevailed more strongly in giving life than sin did in killing.

Death. That death of which he says: “When you were dead in sins, he made you alive together with Christ.” Death received its name from the bite of the serpent. [Col. 0440C]

And so. As in him.

Death passed into all human beings. Death, both of soul and of body, passes from original sin, even into Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; yet they were made alive by the grace of God, concerning whom it is said: “He is not God of the dead.” The Apostle likewise says that it passed even into those who did not sin.

That is, the capital sin passed into humanity in this way: not only did the one who transgressed die, but those who were begotten from transgressors are also held liable through the bond of nature. In other words, the corrupted root transmitted its own defect through all its branches.

Adam killed; Christ gave life.

In whom all sinned. Either through the sin of disobedience, or because in Adam the punishment of all sinners was foreshadowed.

For until the law, sin was in the world. It must be asked what sin this was: [Col. 0440D] namely, the one sin alone that prevailed until the law, which the transgression of the first parent introduced. Before the coming of the law, the offense of transgression ceased. In the first age, sinners enjoyed the security of the present life more freely.

There was indeed sin before the law through human action, but it was not reckoned in the same way, because knowledge of natural law had already been almost obliterated; its understanding, as though dead, revived through the law. The law came as the avenger of sin.

But sin was not reckoned when there was no law. It existed, but it was not reckoned against rustic people, nor did others believe that it was sin. But death reigned from Adam to Moses.

That is, death, coming from original evil, alone reigned until the law. He said “reigned” because it had occupied the whole world generally. Other sins did not appear to reign, because iniquity did not reign generally throughout everyone.

For a small measure of natural righteousness was still vigorous in many, as among many philosophers. And although other offenses also arose from corrupted nature, they were nevertheless voluntary. Another new thing followed: the offense of despising the law through transgression.

Therefore the liability of the one first human being, operating death by itself, reigned until Moses. From the time of the law, another kind of offense was added to the guilt: neglect of the law, which could not be reckoned before the law’s promulgation. And so, when new commandments entered, iniquity was multiplied.

For the law came not to remove sin but to display or judge it. Therefore here the Apostle’s teaching commends the abundance of grace, [Col. 0441B] because the goodness of the Redeemer forgave not only Adam’s debt—which alone, like a tyrannical domination, had reigned until the law—but also countless offenses of transgression and reprehensible conduct.

Therefore he said: “For judgment indeed came from one offense to condemnation.”

When he says “until Moses,” he means that natural debt reigned until the end of the law and the beginning of grace, just as, for example, we say: “The Huns existed until Attila.” We are not indicating the beginning of his reign but its end. So too, “until Moses” means until the end of the law and the beginning of grace.

The remaining offenses, which until the beginning of the law were not understood or recognized as sins, revived through the law when it said: “You shall not covet.” Original sin, however, still reigns today until baptism, but it has lost the use of its interest since the blood of Christ erased the original bond.

But someone may say: Why does the evil of origin still reign in many nations? He replies: That plague truly reigned when it had spread widely, when the physician was absent, when universal mortality was devastating everyone. But when forgiveness sent from heaven opened the gate of paradise, death lost its power. Thus it does not reign, because its reign has been destroyed through Christ’s grace.

Even over those who did not sin, in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come. A type of the one to come, a type by contrast: just as Adam was a type of sin, so Christ is a type of righteousness; or, Adam was a type in the living soul, Christ in the life-giving spirit.

Adam was a type of Christ: just as Adam was made without marital intercourse by the hands of God, so Christ came forth from a virgin through God’s working.

But not as the offense, so also the gift. For if many died through the offense of the one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for the many.

And not as through one sin, so also the gift. That is, righteousness prevailed more strongly in giving life than sin did in killing, because Adam’s sin killed both himself and his descendants, whereas Christ saved those whom he found in the body, his own person, and their descendants.

But perhaps someone says: The flesh, which comes from the flesh of Adam, rightly draws original sin; but the soul, which is born innocent, from where does it draw original sin, so that, if an unbaptized infant dies, it is condemned eternally? Let him hear and acknowledge that the soul first sinned in Adam, through its desire for divinity, more than the flesh did.

In this passage, however, the opinion must be avoided altogether which says: “Just as flesh is created from Adam’s flesh, so too our soul is created from Adam’s soul by God’s hidden operation.”
