As someone said: “By a hidden law nature will bring forth its work, which, unless it is liberated here through grace, will be condemned to perpetual punishment for ever.”

For the judgment. “Of death” is understood.

From one, to condemnation. “From the one who sinned,” or “from the first sin,” is understood.

But grace from many offenses to justification. As though the first liability of the ancient offense had dominated until Christ. Other offenses before the prohibition of the law did not appear, or were not understood, to be so serious. Therefore when grace came, it forgave through baptism not only the original debt but also actual sin. And therefore it justified from many offenses.

For if death reigned through the one’s offense [Col. 0442B] through the one. That is, through Adam’s transgression.

Much more those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. The redemption of the Savior is greater than the destruction caused by the transgressor, because through Christ all sins have been forgiven—not only original sins but also actual sins. For it has been granted as his gift both that we should live rightly and that we should reign with him. We hear of gifts; let us be silent about our merits.

Therefore, just as through the offense of one person condemnation came upon all people, so also through the righteousness of one person justification of life came upon all people.

Death reigned—“those who” is to be understood. Whoever, then, is freed from this condemnation should love grace; whoever is not freed should acknowledge the debt. If goodness is understood in the remitting of debt, equity is understood in its exaction. For nowhere is iniquity found to exist with God.

For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one the many are made righteous. Just as many sinned by the example of Adam’s disobedience, so many are justified by Christ’s obedience.

Great is the crime of disobedience: whatever good a Christian who possesses it may do, it nullifies. “I desire obedience,” he says, “rather than sacrifice.”

But the law entered in so that the offense might abound. They should not say to us: “The law forgave sins.” No, he says; it came to display them. When it was despised, the offense began to abound through knowledge—as though he were saying: “As I see it, the law did not lessen sins but added to them,” though not through any fault of its own but through theirs.

The law, he says, entered so that the offense might abound; this was emptied of its force by the generosity of the grace that came afterward.

Clearly, therefore, from this testimony we understand that the Apostle is speaking of two kinds of sins: those that arose from the transgression of the natural law, where he explained the natural cause, and those of the law, which he added by saying: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded even more.”

Where sin abounded. The entire meaning is this: The old Adam brought death through one offense; the new Adam granted salvation through the forgiveness of innumerable offenses.

Where, he says, sin abounded: because, once the law had been received, sin was committed not in ignorance but with knowledge. Therefore the offense began to abound.

Grace abounded even more. So that just as sin reigned in death—just as the Savior says: “To whom more is forgiven, he loves more”—the magnitude of sin might be revealed, so that they might recognize the greatness of grace, return a corresponding greatness of love, and, from the indulgence of forgiveness, increase their debt of love.

So also may grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Benefits are made manifest when they are contrasted with the merits of the undeserving: death reigned through Adam, but life through Christ. Thus, just as the kingdom of sin was confirmed through the despised law, which removed the excuse of ignorance, so the kingdom of grace is confirmed through the forgiveness of many sins.

## Chapter VI
What, then, shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound?

Here the objection is introduced of those who, still understanding little, could say: “If grace increases in proportion to the magnitude of sins, we ought to sin, so that grace may abound and its [Col. 0443B] munificence may abound more and more in sinners.” By no means. By no means. Those speak so ineptly who are still found to be weak. But let us reject this mistaken opinion, since we have already died to sin in order to live for grace. For if we have died to sin, how shall we still live in it?

He wants the baptized person to be so firm and so perfect that he may be compared, as it were, to someone who has died with respect to committing capital offenses, so that he ought no longer to sin—that is, to commit a crime.

Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus—? Do you perhaps not know the sacrament of baptism itself? In Scripture there are three kinds of baptism: that of water, as with John; that of the Spirit, which is also fire, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Holy Spirit descended as if it were fire.” Elsewhere he demonstrates the divinity of this Spirit: [Col. 0443C] “Our God,” he says, “is a consuming fire.”

The third kind is baptism in blood, by which martyrs are baptized. Hence the Lord himself, already baptized, declares in the Gospel: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, of which you do not know.” As we read in the epistle of the apostle John: “There are three that bear witness: water, blood, and Spirit.” One is so in its ministry, not in its nature. Water, by way of figure, is a witness to the Lord’s burial; blood is a witness to death; the Spirit is a witness to resurrection, because the Spirit is the author of life.

We have been baptized into his death. We are baptized into Christ’s death so that, believing in his death, we might live as though dead—people who have nothing in common with this world. The whole world, following the example of its author, was destined to die, as many saints have done or are doing, [Col. 0443D] because Christ died for all. Therefore all have died, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them.

“But I live—not I any longer; rather, Christ lives in me.” And again: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” It cannot happen otherwise than that, when the head has died, all the members should die with it. The head endured punishments for all the members, so that all the members might die in him and thus, having died to sin, live for God.

For just as a dead person cannot sin, so we, who have died with Christ, ought not to become entangled in capital sins. One who has been crucified does nothing except await the hour of death and commend his [Col. 0444A] spirit into the hands of the Father.

It must be examined more fully what is meant by “we have been baptized into his death.” The Apostle commands that, since Christ was crucified, died, was buried, and rose again for us, we too should crucify our wills and desires in imitation of his passion and should imitate, in the mystery of baptism, the example of his death, burial, and resurrection, so that if we have been companions in his sufferings, we may also be companions in his consolations.

But it must be asked how someone placed in life can die, how someone not yet dead can be buried, and how someone not yet buried can be raised. This happens in the following way: when we are transformed from sons of perdition into sons of adoption, we die beforehand to our former nature through a second birth; when we are submerged beneath the related element of earth, we are buried; when we rise from the bosom of the font, we are raised. [Col. 0444B] This, indeed, is the great sacrament of baptism.

And therefore he said: “We were buried with him through baptism into death.” And afterward: “If,” he says, “we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ.”

We must therefore strive to ensure that nothing of the filth of the old person is recognized in us. If one of us should perhaps be overtaken by it, let him be cleansed through repentance by the Lord’s gift. If, then, we become new and are transformed in our manner of life, we shall likewise be made new and transformed in glory.

Knowing that our old person was crucified together with him. The old person is called one who either does not yet appear to have laid aside the old and earthly Adam, or who imitates that same Adam by falling back into the mire of his former life. Just as that Redeemer hung an innocent body upon the cross, so let us suspend our guilty body from its vices. [Col. 0444C]

In this mystery of the cross, Moses suspended the bronze serpent on its back [Note: [Col. 0443D] Perhaps “in the desert” should be read. EDIT.], so that the body of sin might be destroyed. That is, not merely part of the vice, but every vice, must be destroyed.

For we were buried with him through baptism into death. In baptism we are buried with Christ, according to Christ’s example and in order to imitate him, so that, having died to our former crimes, we may renounce the devil and his pomp. He shows that we are baptized in such a way that we are buried with Christ.

So that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so the Father may be glorified through the resurrection of the Son, and may likewise be glorified through the newness of our manner of life. Thus let us also walk in newness of life.

He shows how we can be dead while living, and how we ought not to will or desire anything that those who are not new will or desire. For if we have been planted together [Col. 0444D] in the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection. If we have been buried with him, we shall also share in the resurrection. If we have not been planted together with him, we shall not rise together with him; and if we have become new in life, we shall be new in glory. If we have had the likeness of his death, we shall also have the likeness of his resurrection.

Knowing this: our old person was crucified together with him. The old person means those who sinned by imitating the old and earthly man. For Adam is understood as the old person, just as Christ is the new.

So that the body of sin might be destroyed. A single vice is a member of sin; the body, however, is the totality of offenses, whose beginning is original sin. But Christ was crucified whole, not in part, so that we might [Col. 0445A] die completely to sin and live for God; or so that our body might be destroyed with respect to its slavery to sin and become a servant of righteousness, whereas it had been accustomed to be a servant of wrongdoing.

So that we may no longer serve sin. For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

For the one who has died has been justified from sin. That is, he has been separated from sin and can no longer sin. For one who has been crucified, with all his members seized by pain, cannot sin; rather, he resists desires and passions.

But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ. As he says elsewhere: “If we have died together with him, we shall also live together with him.”

Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies. So also we, if we have died to vices, shall not fear the second death.

Or certainly it may be understood in this way: just as Christ cannot be crucified again for you [Col. 0445B] if you live criminally, so you cannot be baptized again. As he says elsewhere: “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened and have become participants to be renewed again for repentance, crucifying the Son of God again in themselves.” To them he forbids not repentance, but renewal—that is, the repetition of baptism.

Death shall no longer rule over him. If it shall no longer rule over him, then it has already ruled over him—against the Manichaeans, because they deny that Christ had true flesh.

For in that he died to sin. Either this means that he died for the sin of the human race, or that he died with respect to death itself, which could no longer have any place in him.

He died once. That is, just as your head died once, so you, having become his members, should follow the examples of his life, [Col. 0445C] so that you may owe nothing further to death—that is, so that the second death may have no place in you. For whoever believes that baptism can be repeated believes that Christ can be crucified again.

But in that he lives, he lives for God. He lives in his divinity—the human being who is God. So also consider yourselves in this way. Understand yourselves as his sons or members.

Dead, indeed, to sin. As his imitator said: “But I live—not I any longer; rather, Christ lives in me.”

But living. That is, following his life: we do not yet live in ourselves, but now we all live in Christ. For we have died, and our life is hidden with Christ in God.

In God, in Christ Jesus. But the one lives for God who follows Christ’s footsteps in humility, sanctification, and devotion.

Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its [Col. 0445D] desires. He shows how it reigns. For the one reigns to whom all obey.

He explained how sin reigns in the body: namely, if we offer obedience to our corrupted nature and consent to it. He did not say, “Let it not exist,” because it is already there; rather, he said, “Let it not reign”—that is, let what it commands not be done.

Anger rises: do not give your tongue to anger for cursing, nor your hand for striking, nor your members to lust. These things would not arise unless sin were in our members. Sin is indeed present in our members, but it does not reign if its desires are not obeyed.

And therefore, when he does what he does not want—when he does not want to covet but does covet—he agrees with the law, because the law is good. For he himself wants what the law wants: he wants not to covet, and the law says: [Col. 0446A] “You shall not covet.”

Nor should you present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness. If any member turns its function toward evil uses, it becomes a weapon of unrighteousness for attacking justice: the hand for theft, the tongue for lying or blasphemy, the eye for desire and for attacking chastity, and so forth.

But present yourselves to God as living from the dead. Present yourselves as though you had already risen. After the resurrection, however, one does not live according to the flesh, nor does one sin.

And your members as weapons of righteousness for God. Thus let the eye that previously looked in order to sin now look in service of a good work; let the eye that previously looked in order to strip others now look in order to clothe them. Apply the same principle to the remaining members, so that they may be changed from unrighteousness to mercy.

For sin shall [Col. 0446B] not rule over us. Let sin not conquer you. For you are not little children but mature—just as a tutor might say to a child: “Do not commit a fault in speech, for you are no longer listening to a grammarian but to an orator.”

Or, “It shall not rule” means that it has no right to rule. For you are not under the law but under grace. That is, you are under the benevolence of the Redeemer, who has granted both the effort to fight and conquer and the instruction for doing so; moreover, he has given an example and, through the consolation of the Holy Spirit, the strength by which we are freed from the dominion of sin.

What, then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law? Whoever is under the law is oppressed by the law while he does not fulfill the law; he is not under the law, but together with the law.

But under grace? By no means.

Or do you not know that, to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, leading to [Col. 0446C] death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

He anticipates the objection of the uninstructed and those inexperienced in faith: “Then, once the law’s punishment has ceased, shall we sin with impunity?” By no means. Grace, which has also granted us the means by which we conquer, does not want us to sin at all. If you want to sin, the sentence of the law—which exacts punishment from sinners—will rule over you. But if you serve righteousness, you are not under the law but under grace.

For, he says, “you cannot serve two masters.”

Here, when he says “shall we sin,” let us understand criminal and capital sins, not minor ones, without which we cannot exist. Understand this everywhere we are forbidden to sin, because he was also speaking about those sins that the law was accustomed to condemn, according to the statement: “If we say that we have no sin,” and so forth.

But thanks be to God that you were slaves of sin. Thanks be to God that you were—[Col. 0446D] but, since he himself has freed and assisted you, you are no longer slaves, because you obey and resist with God as your helper.

But you obeyed. You obeyed from the heart, from faith, so that you might live by the gift and example of Christ, who not only granted and taught the removal of sins but also the removal of the occasions of sins. “Be imitators of me,” he says, “as I also am of Christ.”

In that form of teaching into which you were delivered. Of the New Testament.

But having been freed from sin. Made free.

You have become slaves of righteousness. Through the grace of God.

I speak in human terms. For you are not yet able to hear what is divine.

Or it may be understood in this way: what I say is suited to human capacity; it also has validity among human beings and can easily be understood. This is what I mean: I ought to demand greater things from you in return for divine service, but, accommodating and adapting [Col. 0447A] myself to your weakness, I proclaim and commend things that are human and possible, so that, just as you were ready to pursue what is harmful and contrary, you may likewise be eager to carry out what is useful and favorable to salvation.

Because of the weakness of your flesh. The body that is subject to decay weighs down the soul, because whatever the soul does according to the flesh is attributed to the flesh; but when the soul does heavenly things, the whole person is spiritual.

A person is carnal when overcome by desires; spiritual when, by God’s gift, he conquers desires.

For just as you presented your members to serve, so now, with your will changed, let us present ourselves to serve righteousness—not like the Manichaeans, who say that the nature of the body has sin so inserted into it by its constitution that it cannot overcome it. Rather, renewed by grace, let us not present our members [Col. 0447B] to evil.

For the body is not evil in itself; rather, it is the wills that we are commanded to change. These are known to be present through the fault of nature caused by the guilt of the transgressor, not by nature’s constitution.

To impurity and iniquity. To luxury or idolatry.

To iniquity. To the doing of iniquity.

So now present your members to serve righteousness. Just as you were perfect in evil through original sin, so be perfect in good through the gift of grace: let the hand that previously seized things now extend mercy; let the feet that previously ran toward evil now run to visit the sick and to the prison for a good work; let the eyes that previously looked in order to covet and seize now look in order to show mercy and give generously.

Behold, in this way let our members be changed.

For sanctification. So that you may receive sanctification, [Col. 0447C] or possess it.

For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. That is, you served righteousness in no way. So now also be free from sin, so that you serve it in nothing.

Behold, it is shown that they could not serve sin at all except through another kind of freedom. They are therefore not free from righteousness except by the choice of the will. But they are not freed from sin except by the grace of the Savior.

He called them “free with respect to righteousness,” not “freed,” but with respect to sin he did not call them “free,” lest they attribute this to themselves; rather, he called them “freed.” That is: “If the Son frees you, then you will truly be free.”

What fruit, then, did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? What kind of fruit did you have in the practice of that way of life whose very recollection is a source of shame?

Whoever recognizes that he is good is ashamed that he was once evil. And whoever is ashamed of being good is [Col. 0447D] evil, because he has no fruit in the present and his end is death.

For the end of those things—the evil things, that is—is death. Everlasting punishment.

But now, having been freed from sin. Notice that he said “freed,” so that we may give glory not to ourselves but to God.

Having become slaves of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and your end is eternal life. To remain in God’s service is itself already fruit: you are alive, having been sanctified through baptism.

But God’s servant does not repay enemies in kind, like Joseph, who said to his brothers: “Do not be afraid, for I am a servant of God.”

God’s servants have as their present fruit the gift of the Holy Spirit, and as their end eternal life—or the sanctification of a good life.

Therefore, in this life, insofar as we are still servants of God, we are free from sin; insofar as we still serve the law, we are still servants [Col. 0448A] of sin.

And therefore he said: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person.” Behold from where freedom comes, and from where we delight in the law of God. Freedom gives delight; for as long as you do what is just out of fear, God does not delight you.

For the wages of sin are death. “Wage” is the term used for a reward. It is rightly called a wage, because eternal death is paid as a debt for the devil’s wickedness. Whoever serves sin receives death as his pay.

But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. The grace under which you stand.

At the same time, it must be noted that he did not say “the wages of righteousness,” because we do not possess righteousness from ourselves. Therefore, although it is not ours but comes from grace, nevertheless, when it is preserved with God’s help, it gives eternal life after this temporal life has passed.

## CHAPTER VII.

[Col. 0448B] But do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law rules over a person for as long as he lives? For a woman who belongs to her husband is bound by the law while her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.

Here he introduces an analogy: he calls the commandment of the law the husband, and the people—or the soul—the woman, in order to show that the law, which produces wrath, is ineffectual and, as it were, dead. Since we have now been put to death, it cannot prevent us from belonging to the one who rose from the dead. The law would rightly remain alive for us if it found something in us to punish. For he says that a person is under the law for as long as he lives in sin. By this sin we must understand that which arose through the law. For where there is no grace to liberate, the prohibition of sins increases the desire to sin.

[Col. 0448C] Accordingly, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man. As long as the husband lives, she must live according to his will. But if the husband should fall asleep, and the woman should be joined to another husband, she is no longer required to live according to the custom of her former husband.

[Col. 0448D] Therefore, my brothers, you also have been put to death to the law. He did not wish to say “the law has been put to death for you” in bodily terms, but left it to be understood, as in many passages. According to the analogy, he ought rather to have said that the law was dead to them than that they were dead to the law; but what still seemed difficult to say among the Jews he leaves to be understood, showing clearly enough that the law could not take sin away but rather increased it, whereas grace removes it. For the law knows how to command one whom weakness overcomes, but not how to help him; this is what the grace of Christ does.

From this point, and throughout this entire passage up to “Who will free me from this body of death?”, the Apostle is seen to have transformed into himself the person placed under the law. He speaks in his own person through that man’s words, although he had said: “We have been released from the law of death in which we were held, so that we may serve in newness of spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.” Through these words he seems to have criticized the law, but this is not so, because he added: “Is the law sin? Certainly not,” and what follows.

[Col. 0449A] But this “little ear” [auricula] is not lying. Once the flesh has been crucified, by which the law held sway over us through condemning sin, it no longer has operative force. Formerly they were imitators of Moses; now, however, they are imitators of Christ. Thus it is said, “You have died to the law,” as though it were said, “You have died to the punishment of the law.”

Why have we died to the law through the body of Christ, if the law is good? Because we have died to the law in its dominion, having been freed from the effect which the law punishes and condemns. For the law is more commonly so called when it threatens, terrifies, and exacts punishment. Thus the same commandment is law to those who fear, but grace to those who love.

Through the body of Christ, by dying with Christ, who condemned sin in the flesh. So that you may belong to another—the other husband is to be understood—who rose from the dead. So that you may bear fruit for God. A person bears fruit when, through his example, the people of God increase, as he says: “So that we may have some fruit among you.”

[Col. 0449B] For when we were in the flesh—that is, when we were living in a carnal manner—the passion of desire was active in our eyes and in our other members. These desires, nevertheless, were shown through the law to be sins, so that they might bear fruit for the death of sin. “In the flesh,” he says: that is, we were held bound by carnal desires. We were carrying out in our members the passions of sins that existed through the law. The one who now serves the law of God with his mind dies to these passions, although the passions themselves are not yet dead.

He says that desire is increased when the law prohibits it: an increase of desire through prohibition, and liability to punishment through transgression. This is what he means by saying that, through what was good, death was brought about. “So that they might bear fruit for death”: that is, so that the severity of the law might kill us, placed as we were in those same passions, and offer death fruit from our destruction, because the fruit of sin is death. We bear fruit for death when we do what has been prohibited.

[Col. 0449C] But now we have been released from the law by dying. It is called the law of death because it kills sinners, that is, criminals. It is also called the law of sin, not because it is itself sin, but because it is imposed upon sinners. It is called the law of death because “the wages of sin is death,” while “the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.”

In which we were held. We were held through sin. So that we might serve in newness of spirit and not in the oldness of the letter: obeying the commandments of the grace of the Spirit, rather than following the letter of the law.

[Col. 0449D] What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Because he had said that the passions produced through the law bore fruit for death, he raises against himself the objection, “Is the law sin?” and answers, “Certainly not.” He does this against the Manichaeans, who deny the Old Testament. If they should say, “He asserts the law here on account of the Jews, because he feared causing offense,” the answer is: Then he always feared causing offense, because he never spoke against the law.

Since in many places he has overturned the works of the law, he now rightly praises it in the respect in which it is spiritual, and by mentioning it confounds the Manichaeans.

Certainly not. The Apostle foresaw that someone might, on account of these testimonies, disparage the law and argue that it was evil. He anticipated what might occur to those who misunderstood, and proposed the question to himself: “What then shall we say,” he says, “is the law sin? Certainly not. But I did not know sin except through the law.”

He had already said above that through the law comes knowledge of sin. It is therefore not its removal, but its recognition. The law was given not to take sin away or eradicate it, but only to reveal it, so that, because sin cannot be conquered without the grace of God, the very anxiety caused by guilt might compel us to flee to grace.

[Col. 0450A] But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known desire unless the law had said, “You shall not desire.”

Here the Apostle begins to speak as though about himself and to offer himself as an example. He had lived under the law, which does not save by itself but reveals sin. It neither removes nor justifies; rather, it exacts punishment from transgressors. He does not say, “I did not commit sin except through the law,” but, “I did not know sin except through the law,” which showed that desire was sin, although I did not know that it was sin.

“I would not have known desire,” he says. He did not say, “I did not possess it” or “I did not practice it,” but, “I did not know that it was sin.” Hence it is evident that desire was not implanted by the law but revealed by it; the law teaches what each person ought to do or avoid. Yet the true human being is still drawn along by the habit of sinning. Desire belongs to our nature, entering through sin; it is not God’s creation. Therefore evil itself must not be separated from God as though it were a separate principle, but must be healed by God’s mercy.

[Col. 0450B] But when the occasion arose—here the Apostle recalls his former life, when he lived under the law, and the struggle of his youth. When he says, “I was once alive without the law,” he indicates his earliest age. “When the commandment came,” he says, “sin revived; but I died.” He testifies that he had now become capable of receiving the commandment, but not effective in fulfilling it.

[Col. 0450C] Thus, to show himself a transgressor of the law, the Apostle indicates what he knew himself to have been in his innermost being before the grace of God, which comes through Jesus Christ our Lord. He also confesses this most openly to the Ephesians: “Among whom,” he says, “we all once lived in the desires of our flesh and thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest,” and so forth. And to Titus: “We too,” he says, “were once foolish and disobedient, going astray,” and the rest that follows there. Such was he before grace.

Sin worked through the commandment. Just as an envious person receives a greater opportunity to harm when something is entrusted to the person whom he wishes to injure, so sin received an opportunity through the commandment.

Every desire in me: every desire written in the law—“You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife, nor his field, nor anything belonging to your neighbor,” and so forth. Human weakness has this tendency through transgression: what is prohibited is more difficult to observe.

[Col. 0450D] For without the law sin was dead: that is, it lay hidden, did not appear, and was unknown; it seemed dead to me. Alternatively, the natural law, which showed what sin was, had fallen into oblivion. For this reason the written law was also given, to recall the law of nature.

I was once alive without the law: I seemed to myself to live as a righteous person, free from sin. “Without the law” shows that he is not speaking strictly in his own person, but generally in the person of humanity.

But when the commandment came—that is, when the fact that sin existed, which had fallen into oblivion, was brought to light—then, when the commandment came, sin was recognized, so that everyone who committed it might recognize that he was dead.

It revived: that is, it shone forth and appeared. He says “revived,” not “lived,” for it had once lived in Paradise, when the transgression of the given commandment was plainly committed.

[Col. 0451A] “Sin revived, but I died.” This means that what had been hidden appeared. Sin had lived through natural knowledge, but had been dead through forgetfulness. For I transgressed knowingly, and through the manifestation of sin perceived that I was dead. The one who sees through the law what he ought not to do, yet does it—whether through stimulation or pleasure, even without consent—now sins through transgression. Alternatively, this is because the guilt of transgression threatens a definite punishment of death.

And the commandment was found by me to be death. The commandment, when observed, advanced one toward life; when neglected, it led to death, because I knowingly failed to observe it. All this is said to show that the law was indeed given for life, but because it did not provide help by which we could be saved, it leads us to grace, which possesses everything: mercy, assistance, and example.

What was for life became for death. If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments. The commandment, when kept, grants life; when not kept, it brings death, which is transgression.

[Col. 0451B] For sin, having received an opportunity—if he seems to say anything against the law, he attributes it to those who were unable to receive more perfect teaching. That is why he said that sin had received an opportunity.

Through the commandment. The persuasion to sin is stronger when prohibition is present; and prohibition makes a person not only a sinner but also a transgressor. Since what is forbidden is more pleasantly admitted by people who have not yet received spiritual grace, sin deceives through a false sweetness. But because the guilt of transgression arises, it kills: the person embraces the sweetness of the deadly pleasure by which he is deceived, and delights even in acting against the law. The less permitted something is, the more desirable it becomes.

[Col. 0451C] It deceived me, and through it killed me. For no sin is committed except through desiring. Therefore the law that prohibits this is good and worthy of praise. But when the Holy Spirit gives help, inspiring a good desire in place of evil desire—that is, spreading charity in our hearts—then that law, although good, nevertheless increases the evil desire by prohibiting it.

It is like the force of water, which, if it continues to flow in one direction, becomes more violent when a barrier is placed before it. When it overcomes the mass of the barrier, it plunges forward in a larger accumulation and rushes more violently down the slope. Somehow, the very thing that is desired becomes more pleasant when it is forbidden.

This is how sin deceives through the commandment and kills through it, when transgression also occurs, although no such transgression exists in the commandment itself.

[Col. 0451D] Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just. Against the opponents of the law, and against those who separate justice from goodness, the law is called both holy and good, and grace is called just. “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees,” and what follows.

God too is sometimes called good in the Old Testament and just in the New, as in the saying, “Righteous Father.” This is also directed against the Marcionites. Nevertheless, nothing is rightly accomplished through the law without grace, because it was not given in such a way that it could give life. Rather, it was established as the cause of transgression, so that it might shut up those who had been convicted under sin—not to justify the ungodly, but to convict the proud. It is a cause of transgression.

[Col. 0452A] This is also directed against the Manichaeans, because the law is praised; and against the Pelagians, because no one is justified by the law. Therefore the Spirit of grace freely comes to the aid of those whom the letter kills, so that they may be given life.

Nothing is rightly accomplished through the law, as has been said, without grace, because it was not given in such a way that it could give life.

And good. For those who keep it. What then? If what is good has become death to me, certainly not. The commandment in itself did not become the cause of death; rather, I make it so for myself when I commit what deserves death by sinning. The fault lies in the person who uses it badly, not in the commandment itself, which is good, since the law is good.

But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, brought death to me through what was good. Through the law sin appears, and through it is punished. Therefore, through what is good—that is, through the law, which is good when someone uses it lawfully—sin brings death to me when I become its transgressor.

So that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment. The magnitude of iniquity demands that a person now be called not merely a sinner but “sin.”

[Col. 0452B] For we know—that is, the law is demanding, but commands spiritual things. Yet when I am stimulated according to carnal custom, I depart from its perfection; the perfect destroys the imperfect.

For the law is spiritual. This has been explained. It commands the works that belong to the Spirit; hence it shows that the law cannot be fulfilled except by a spiritual person.

But I am carnal. Although I receive the law, I have become accustomed to living carnally: that is, consenting to the flesh, not yet freed by spiritual grace.

For it is good not to desire, and this is what the righteous person, who lives by faith, wills; yet he does what he hates because he desires, although he does not follow after his desires. If he does follow them, then he himself truly acts: he yields, consents, and obeys the desire of sin.

[Col. 0452C] Sold under sin: that is, sold for the price of temporal pleasure. At this point, a transaction between the seller and the buyer is being described. The enemy proposes a plan of iniquity and receives the consent of the will. I therefore receive as the price of lost innocence the very pleasure of sinning, the deadly sweetness arising from iniquitous pleasure.

“You were sold because of your sins,” he says, so that no one may think that the person has not yet been redeemed by the blood of Christ; rather, he awaits redemption, that is, immortality. Alternatively, he was sold under sin at the first transgression of the commandment, so that he received a corruptible body, which weighs down the soul. Now, like a purchased slave, he is compelled to serve lust.

[Col. 0452D] For I do not understand what I do. Do I not understand that the evil I admit unwillingly is evil? How can he not understand who does what he does not want and does what he hates? To hate wrongdoing is no small sign of understanding. Therefore, “I do not understand what I do” means: I do not consent, approve, or do it willingly; although overcome, I judge it to be contrary to what I decide, and I clearly understand that it is not right. I do not recognize it as belonging among the commands of truth.

For I do not do the good that I want. Up to this point, some think these are the words of a person established under the law, not yet under grace: even if he does not wish to sin, he is overcome by sin, because carnal habit and the natural bond of mortality have grown strong.

[Col. 0453A] Lest anyone, from these words, suppose that the holy Apostle consents to the desire of the flesh for evil works, let him consider what he adds: “But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good.” He says that he agrees with the law rather than with the desire of the flesh; for he calls the latter by the name of sin.

Therefore he said that he does it, not through the disposition of consenting and fulfilling, but through the very movement of desiring.

But I do what I hate. It is good not to desire, and this is what the righteous person, who lives by faith, wills; yet he does what he hates because he desires, although he does not follow after his desires. If he does follow them, then he himself truly acts: he yields, consents, and obeys the desire of sin.

[Col. 0453B] But if I do what I hate—that is, while I do not want to do what I commit, I certainly agree with the law, which neither wills nor approves evil and therefore prohibits it. In my mind I agree with it, but in my action I contradict it. Thus conscience does one thing in me, while weakness does another; weakness succumbs to the yoke of sin while judgment contradicts it.

Therefore he said that he does and performs it, not through the disposition of consenting and fulfilling, but through the very movement of desiring.

I agree with the law, that it is good. Because I do not want what the law does not want, I agree with it according to the law of conscience, because I do what I do not want.

But now—that is, now, under grace, which has freed me from consent. It is no longer I who do it: that is, I do not consent. For if he both desires, consents, and acts, how is it not he himself who does it, even if he is distressed that he acts and groans bitterly at being overcome?

“It is no longer I who do it” means: it is not the inner mind; nor do I consent to present my members as weapons of iniquity. Before the law prohibited it, I myself willingly did it; but after the law came, I sin unwillingly, because I am overcome by habit.

[Col. 0453C] But sin that dwells in me. It dwells like a guest, dominates, and, as though one thing were dwelling in another, the carnal inclination still dwells in me.

For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. By what he knows, he agrees with the law; by what he does, he yields to sin, so that sin prevails in him as though it were innate. Yet it was not created by God; it proceeds from corrupted nature.

[Col. 0453D] Here he begins to say that he himself experienced the stimulation of the flesh. It should also be noted that the Apostle testifies that he felt this stimulation himself.

But good does not dwell in my flesh. He did not say, “My flesh is not good,” but that good does not dwell in his flesh, which is weighed down by the habit of sin and which he cannot overcome, because while he trusts in the work of the law, he does not seek the help of grace.

This indwelling evil came through the transmission of mortality, through the transgressor, to all human beings.

For the will is present in me. There is indeed in me a will prepared and given by God, but there is no accomplishment, because carnal habit resists the will itself in this mortal life. Some think that these words are those of a person established under the law, not yet under grace.

But I do not find the accomplishment of the good. Without the aid of grace, I do not find the effect of good will. For that there should be willing, the will has already been prepared by God, because it is he who works in us both willing and acting.

It should be noted that he did not say, “I do not find doing good,” but “accomplishing good.” For what is the perfection of good except the extinction of evil? The perfection of good is not to desire. For what is easier for a person established under the law than to will good and do evil? To accomplish good means that a person does not even desire.

Good is imperfect when he desires, even if he does not consent to his desire for evil.

[Col. 0454A] “I do not find it” means “I cannot.” For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want. When habit prevails, I do what I do not want, just as someone who is accustomed to swearing does so without noticing.

But if I do what I do not want, he said that he does and performs it, not through the disposition of consenting and fulfilling, but through the very movement of desiring.

It is no longer I who do it. Not I, because I am unwilling; but I, because through the force of habit I myself have imposed this necessity upon myself.

But sin that dwells in me. The habit of sin dwells in me, infused into me through transgression of the first parent, from corrupted nature.

[Col. 0454B] I find, therefore, a law for me who wish to do good. In my mind I find a law that good should be done against the evil that is in my flesh. I have a law in agreement with the inner person, so that the evil present in me through corrupted nature may be excluded; but this cannot happen without the grace of God.

Therefore I say: “Who will free me from this body of death?”

For evil lies close at hand. That is, evil desires, the enemy’s counsels, or the battles of the flesh, which through an old-established consent I have become accustomed to obeying. Evil lies close at hand through desire, but the person who says, “It is no longer I who do it,” does not consent to it.

[Col. 0454C] For I delight in the law of God. Here he sets forth two laws: the law of the spirit and the law of the flesh, which resists the law of the mind—that is, either the natural law of conscience or the divine law established in the mind.

Freedom delights. For as long as you do what is just out of fear, God does not delight you. As long as he does not delight you, you continue to act as a slave. Let him delight you, and you will be free. The law delights me; what the law commands delights me; righteousness itself delights me.

According to the inner person: according to the mind.

But I see another law in my members. This is the weakness that remains, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members.

He experiences captivity in that part of himself where righteousness has not been fulfilled. “I see another law in my members”: the desires of the flesh and the movements of corrupted nature—that is, desire.

[Col. 0454D] But if this desire is called sin, it is called so because it was produced by sin, just as someone’s hand is called his writing because his hand produced it. The sins themselves, however, are the unlawful acts committed according to the desire of the flesh.

He calls the burden itself of mortality a law in his members, under which we groan, weighed down. “The corruptible body weighs down the soul.” Through it it often happens that what is not permitted gives pleasure unwillingly. He calls this burden a law because it was imposed as the rightful punishment.

Resisting the law of my mind—the law that elsewhere commands that these things be put to death in the members: “Put to death your members,” he says.

“The law of God,” he says, is in the mind, and this other law takes me captive. He laments that he is captive because he feels desires arising within him that are contrary to the purity of the mind; against these he implores the grace of the liberator.

[Col. 0455A] This can also be understood to mean that he calls it captivity according to the flesh, not according to the mind; through opportunity, not through consent. He calls it captivating because even in the flesh the nature is not foreign but our own.

It may also appear that the Apostle is describing one who still lives under the law, not yet under grace. When he says, “taking me captive,” he means “taking my flesh captive,” in the law of sin that is in his members.

But even if this is understood of the Apostle himself, it does not mean that he was polluted by immoderate lust, but that he was freed from perverse consent. Nevertheless, concerning the desire of the flesh, which he restrained by moderation, he groaned with such humility and devotion that he preferred not to have it rather than to subdue it.

In the law of sin that is in my members. This law condemns sin, or the evil habit, which is in the members—as though he were saying, “and taking me captive in its law.” He is captive because he does not do what he wants.

[Col. 0455B] As long as the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh:

Wretched man that I am, who will free me? Such are the words of a person established under grace, whose activity does indeed have the resistant mortality of the flesh, but not one that conquers him into consenting to sin.

Who could deny that, when the Apostle said these things, he was still in this body of death? From it even the ungodly are not freed, since the same bodies are restored to them for eternal punishments.

To be freed from this body of death therefore means that, when every disease of the desire of the flesh has been healed, one receives the body not for punishment but for glory, as he says elsewhere: “We groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body.”

He implores freedom from bodily and deadly vices. “If the Son,” he says, “has freed you, you will truly be free.”

[Col. 0455C] From this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. The body of death is the letter that kills. The body of death is deadly pleasure, carnal delight, bodily weakness, and the violence of habit that draws one toward death.

From this habit it is not the law but grace that frees, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Before the law there was no struggle with the pleasures of this age, because everything was permitted. Under the law there is struggle, but we are defeated. Under grace, however, we struggle and, with God’s help, conquer, because we serve not through fear but through love.

Not everyone who ends this life is freed from this body of death, but the one who receives grace in this life and, lest he receive it in vain, acts through good works and cooperates with it. For it is one thing to leave this body and another to be freed from this body of death. Only the grace of God grants the latter.

[Col. 0455D] Therefore I myself. He recapitulates or concludes.

With the mind I serve the law of God. As long as I am carnal, I am double.

But with the flesh I serve the law of sin, by desiring; with the mind I serve the law of God, by not consenting to that same desire. He is a person of twofold and divided will, that is, either carnal or spiritual, divided in himself, so to speak, according to the quality of his works.

The law is indeed one, but there are two kinds of commandments: one teaches good, the other prohibits evil. What teaches good belongs to God; what prohibits evil addresses our vice, since the law had to be given to us because we sin.

[Col. 0456A] The law of sin: the habit of sin, or corrupted nature, for as long as weakness struggles against salvation and the flesh desires against the spirit.

## CHAPTER VIII.

Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For no one is condemned except the person who consents to the desire of the flesh for evil; for when the flesh is dead, there is nothing in it that can be condemned.

“Who do not walk according to the flesh.” Those who have learned from Christ to crucify the flesh and do not live in a carnal manner.

“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free.” It should be noted that he calls grace “law.” The grace of the New Testament frees us from the habit of sin and death by removing occasions of sin and also giving assistance and an example for living, so that the desire of the flesh may not claim my consent for itself.

[Col. 0456B] “From the law of sin and death.” The law that kills and puts sinners to death—that is, the law of the letter, or that law which he earlier said ruled in the members. “For what was impossible for the law.” Since the law brings nothing to perfection, it was impossible for the law to make carnal people observe the righteousness of faith. But Christ made this possible through commandment, example, and assistance.

For it is altogether impossible to fulfill the law through the flesh. Those who are proud, ignorant of the righteousness of God—that is, the righteousness that comes from God and makes a person righteous—and who wish to establish their own righteousness, as though the law could be fulfilled through their own free choice without divine assistance, are not subject to the righteousness of God. Therefore the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in those who do not walk according to the flesh—that is, according to the person who is ignorant of God’s righteousness—but walk according to the Spirit.

[Col. 0456C] “In which it was weakened through the flesh.” It was weakened through desires, that is, through carnal longings. Therefore the law was not fulfilled, because love of that very righteousness had not yet come to be present within it, holding the mind through an inward delight so that it would not be drawn into sin by delight in temporal things. Thus the law was weakened through the flesh: that is, it did not make those devoted to the flesh righteous.

“God, sending his own Son in the likeness.” He assumed flesh like that of other human beings, without sin, because it was born neither from desire nor from intercourse, but from a virgin. He says this against Photinus, who denies that the Son existed before the Virgin gave birth.

“Of sinful flesh.” It was not sinful flesh, since it was not born from carnal pleasure; nevertheless, there was in it the likeness of sinful flesh, because it was mortal flesh.

“And by sin he condemned sin.” And from the flesh that previously served sin in us, he conquered sin by not sinning—just as someone from among barbarians might conquer barbarians. The sacrifices that they offered for sin under the law were called “sin,” although they themselves knew nothing of sin. In the same way, the flesh of sin that was offered for our sins received the name “sin.”

Some say that this refers to the sin of the Jews who killed the Lord: he condemned the devil’s sin, by which the devil had entangled humanity, as it is written to the Hebrews, “so that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death.” And death is rightly called sin, since it is clearly understood to have arisen from sin.

Others say that, because of the sin of the Jews who crucified him, he poured out his blood [Col. 0457A] for the remission of sins.

“In the flesh.” In that very flesh he conquered sin, so that by his grace he might restore the nature that had been good by creation but corrupted by transgression, enabling it, with his assistance, to conquer sin. It had originally been made in such a way that it could refrain from sinning if it wished. But this was so before the transgression, as I have said. Now, through the grace of God, it can either avoid sin or conquer it, provided that it always implores the Lord for help.

“So that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us.” Here he either calls grace itself “the law,” or certainly refers to that righteousness of the law which has been disclosed through the Spirit hidden within the letter. Since the righteousness of the law could not be fulfilled in those who had living and resistant flesh, it is fulfilled in us, who, with Christ’s assistance, mortify the flesh together with its vices.

[Col. 0457B] The commandments of the law are fulfilled through love; they could not be fulfilled through fear.

“Who do not walk according to the flesh.” That is, who do not conduct ourselves according to the flesh.

“But according to the Spirit.” The flesh was made from the earth, whereas the Spirit was given by God. Therefore each desires what corresponds to its origin: the flesh desires earthly things, and the Spirit heavenly things. If, then, the Spirit overcomes the flesh, heavenly things are accomplished; but if the Spirit consents to the flesh, earthly things prevail.

Who, then, walks according to the Spirit, except the one who is led by the Spirit of God? “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.”

“For whoever.” One human being consists of spirit and flesh. Therefore, when he walks according to the flesh, he is flesh; when he walks according to the Spirit, he is spirit.

“Those who are according to the flesh.” “The works of the flesh are manifest.”

“They set their minds on the things of the flesh.” They desire earthly and carnal goods as the highest goods.

“But those who are according to the Spirit think about the things of the Spirit.” That is, divine things. For God is Spirit. Whoever does not resist the will of God thinks about the things of the Spirit.

“For the mind of the flesh is death.” The word “mind” derives from “foreseeing.” Elsewhere he says that human prudence consists in repaying evil with evil. Such prudence, then, prepares death by transgressing the commandment. Thus the mind of the flesh is the desire of each person to avenge himself. The mind of the Spirit, however, is not to return evil for evil.

When the soul desires lower things, it is said to possess the mind of the flesh; when it desires higher things, the mind of the Spirit. This does not mean that the mind of the flesh is a substance with which the soul is clothed or from which it is stripped, but that it is an inclination of the soul itself, which will entirely cease to exist when the soul has turned wholly toward higher things.

[Col. 0457D] “But the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” The mind of the Spirit possesses peace in the present as well, by not returning evil for evil, and earns eternal life forever through obedience and peace, since by its patience it does not allow sin to increase.

“Because the mind of the flesh.” Not the flesh itself, but a carnal action.

“Is enmity against God.” Everything that is not subject to God is hostile to him. Whoever wishes to avenge himself exceeds even the measure of the old law—not because he can do God any harm, but because he harms himself.

“For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.” He says that this is completely impossible, either to recall them from the allurements and luxuries of the flesh, or—as though we were to say—that injustice cannot be just. It is as if one were to say: “Snow does not warm, nor indeed can it.” For as long as it is snow, it does not warm; but it can melt and can also boil so as to warm, and when it does this, it is no longer snow.

Likewise, the mind of the flesh is so called when it desires worldly things instead of heavenly things. But when it begins to desire heavenly things, it ceases to be a carnal mind.

“Those who are in the flesh.” From this it is proved that he was not speaking about the substance of the flesh.

“Cannot please God.” For it is impossible that those who live carnally and yield to the desires of the flesh should not sin.

“But you are not in the flesh.” That is, you are not in carnal desires, but in spiritual ones.

“But in the Spirit.” Those who have the Spirit of God live spiritually through a spiritual activity. The Spirit of God is in those in whom its fruit appears, as he says in the Letter to the Galatians, “the fruit of the Spirit.”

“If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.”

Whoever loves enemies will understand that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the substance of the Father as also from that of the Son, because he whose Spirit it is is of one and the same substance. Therefore it is called the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son. For this reason he said in the Gospel, “He will take from what is mine.”

“If anyone,” he says, “does not have the Spirit of God”—that is, so as to pray for persecutors, love enemies, and imitate him in all things, as the apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example,” and so forth.

For he himself says to his disciples: “You do not know of what spirit you are.” They were his spirits, because they lived in faith, hope, and love.

“But if Christ.” If you always imitate Christ.

“The body as though dead.” Even if it resists, it does not conquer, as David says: “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear; and you will hear me, O Lord my God.”

“In you.” Through his grace.

“Although the body.” The spirit lives and gives life, so that we may practice righteousness; but the flesh is dead, so that we may not be overcome by it. It is not enough merely for the flesh to die; the Spirit must also be brought to life. Observe likewise that the life of the soul is righteousness. Therefore we must not merely cease from carnal things, but must also do spiritual things.

“It is dead because of sin.” He calls the body dead as long as it remains such that the need for bodily things troubles the soul and disturbs it with various impulses. For this reason sin is called “desire”: it has arisen as a consequence of sin, just as a writing is called the hand of someone because that person’s hand produced it.

“But the Spirit lives because of justification.” Here he describes the person who lives under grace and does not yet possess perfect peace, which will come through the resurrection and transformation of the body. For as long as we are in this life, neither stimulation nor pleasure is absent, although the person who lives under grace does not yield: in mind he serves the law of God, but in the flesh the law of sin.

“But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you”—the one who raised Jesus Christ from the dead. If you conduct yourselves in such a way that you are worthy to be those in whom the Holy Spirit dwells, God will not allow the temple of his Spirit to perish. Rather, just as he raised Jesus from the dead, so he has also given us life.

“He will give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you.” Once your mortal bodies have been given life, there will be not only no consent to sinning [Col. 0459A], but not even the desire of the flesh to which consent might be given.

“Therefore, brothers, we are debtors.” He does all this to show that the old law is not necessary for believers, since it was given to carnal and sinful people.

“Not to the flesh, so that we should live according to the flesh.” That is, we are no longer subject to a carnal habit.

“For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.” This is according to the explanation given above: carnal people cannot keep righteousness.

“But if by the Spirit you put to death the works of the flesh, you will live.” He explains what he earlier meant by “flesh”: that you subject carnal works to spiritual actions.

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.” Those who are governed by the grace of God and the Holy Spirit. You act well if you are led by him. Conversely, the sons of the devil are led by his spirit, the one who sins from the beginning.

“For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear.” The Jews received a spirit of fear that compelled them into slavery, because the one who fears is a slave, whereas the one who loves is a son, as it is written: “A servant fears his master, and a son loves his father.” “If I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a lord, where is my fear?”

Since they were unwilling to act out of love, they were compelled by fear and necessity. But we ought to do everything willingly, out of love, as sons.

“But you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons of God.” We are adopted when we are reborn through baptism. Before that we were “sons of wrath.” And if we were sons of wrath, where is the claim that nature itself possesses faith?

“In whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Whoever calls him Father shows himself to be a son. Therefore he must imitate the Father in all things, lest, because he has unworthily claimed the name, he become subject to a greater punishment.

“Crying out”—that is, causing us to cry out.

“The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons.” This is the testimony of adoption: we possess the Spirit through which we pray in this way. No one could receive so great a gift except through the grace of the Son, which is a pledge—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit.

“But if sons, heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs with Christ.” The person who becomes a son through grace will be worthy to be an heir, and will also become a co-heir with the Son.

“If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified.” If we suffer with him, this means patience and also perseverance. For if we place before our eyes the gifts of God, and what he endured for us sinners, then, with such a helper, we ought not fear suffering for him, so that we may be glorified together with him, as Saint John says: “Now we are the sons of God; when he appears, we shall be like him.”

“For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us.” What could a human being suffer that would be worthy of heavenly glory, even if that life were like the one we now possess? Whatever he may suffer in death is no more than he had previously deserved even for his sins. But now sins are forgiven, and then eternal life will be given, together with the splendor of the sun, and so forth.

He displays the reward, by which death may more easily be despised and through which one may reach that destination more securely. For we know that human beings, which is worse, have voluntarily crept toward wild beasts for the sake of gold. With God’s help, we ought to do the same in tribulations for the Lord’s sake; and although these tribulations are temporary, they grant eternal salvation.

“If this is what he says, what of us?”

“For the expectation of creation eagerly awaits the revelation of the sons of God.” “Creation has been subjected to vanity.” Some wish “creation” to refer to Adam and Eve, whom the serpent subjected to vanity through the hope of divinity and made servants of corruption when they were unwilling to be so. This means that they were not subjected to it by themselves, since, after sinning, they were handed over by a just judgment. For, they say, they too will be freed from the slavery of corruption.

Others say that “all creation” means all human beings, because all the righteous who lived before the coming of Christ had not yet received what they awaited in hope. Not only they, but we ourselves also, in whom these things have been fulfilled, still hope. To us it was said: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it.”

Therefore he says: “They await the revelation of the sons of God.” Everything will remain in this condition as long as the resurrection continues; afterward they will cease from their present activity and will be changed, according to the Scriptures.

“Creation has been subjected to vanity”—that is, to human beings who have become empty, and whom other human beings serve. Whatever has an end is vain in comparison with eternal life. “Vanity of vanities,” he says, “all is vanity.” Nor should you think that it has provided you with anything of lasting value, since it has given you perishable and worldly things as well.

“Not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope.” Not by its own choice.

Others say that the angels are meant, since they too are creatures, and that they await human beings being transformed into the dignity of angels.

“For creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.” Those who wish to understand this of the world’s creation say the following: When the sons of God are glorified, creation itself will also be freed from slavery, because it too experiences labor, just as land that is continually sown becomes barren.

“For we know that all creation groans and labors in childbirth until now.” Those things that can groan groan because of excessive labor, since more is demanded of them than they can bear. But things that have no sense—how do they groan? Perhaps they groan because of our iniquities, just as, during the Lord’s Passion, the sun was darkened because it could not bear to see the impiety of the Jews.

“Not only it, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption.” Not only creation, which does not possess a receptacle of the Spirit, or carnal people, but we also, who know the joy of the future age, grieve because we must labor here longer.

Another interpretation is this: Not only the angels, who are more kindly disposed toward us, grieve over those who persist in sins, but we too, who possess the Holy Spirit, groan over such people.

“the redemption of our body.” The resurrection of Christ is the redemption of our body. Or we await the glorification of our body in the future resurrection, so that what is corrupt may put on incorruption.

Augustine says that this passage is obscure because it is not sufficiently clear what he now calls “creation.” According to catholic teaching, however, “creation” means whatever God the Father made and established through his only-begotten Son, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Therefore not only bodies but also our souls—that is, our spirits—are included under the name “creation.”

[Col. 0461A] Thus it is said: “Creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God,” as though we were not creation but sons of God, and as though creation would be freed from slavery into the freedom of our glory.

Again he says: “We know that all creation groans and suffers until now. Not only it, but we ourselves,” as though we were one thing and all creation another. Therefore the whole passage must be considered in detail.

“For I consider,” he says, “that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us.” This is clear, for he had said earlier: “If by the Spirit you put to death the works of the flesh, you will live.” This cannot happen without distress, for which patience is necessary. This is also the point of what he said shortly before: “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified.”

What, then, does he mean by saying: “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God”? I think he means this: Even that which suffers within us when we put to death the works of the flesh—that is, when we hunger or thirst through abstinence, when through chastity we restrain the pleasure of intercourse, when through patience we endure the wounds of injuries and the stings of insults, when, neglecting and rejecting our pleasures, we labor for the fruit of Mother Church—whatever in us suffers in this and similar affliction is creation. For body and soul suffer, and the body and soul are certainly creation. And creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God; that is, it awaits the time when what has been called forth will appear.

For since the only-begotten Son of God cannot be called creation, since all things that God made were made through him, we are distinctly called creation before that evident glory, and distinctly called sons of God, although we attain this through adoption. For that only-begotten one is Son by nature.

Therefore the expectation of creation—that is, our expectation—awaits the revelation of the sons of God. It awaits the time when what has been promised will appear, when what we now are in hope will be revealed in reality. For we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” This is the revelation of the sons of God that the expectation of creation now awaits.

For creation does not await the revelation of another nature, one that is not creation, but awaits the time when it will become what it is destined to be.

It is as though one were to say: When a painting has been placed before the painter, with colors supplied and prepared for his work, the expectation of the colors awaits the revelation and manifestation of the image—not because the colors will then be different or will cease to be colors, but because they will then possess a different dignity.

“Creation has been subjected to vanity.” This is the meaning of: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” “What profit has a person from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?” To him it was said: “By labor you shall eat bread.”

Creation has been subjected to vanity “not willingly.” It is rightly added: “Not willingly.” For human beings sinned willingly, but were not condemned willingly. Sin, therefore, was voluntary: to act against the commandment of truth. The punishment of sin, however, was subjection to deception.

Creation, then, was not willingly subjected to vanity, but because of him who subjected it in hope—that is, because of his justice and mercy. He neither left sin unpunished nor wished the sinner to be beyond healing.

“For creation itself”—that is, the human being himself—having lost the seal of the image because of sin and having remained merely creation: that creation, then, which is not yet called the perfected form of the sons, but is merely called creation, will be freed from the slavery of destruction.

When he says, “it too will be freed,” he makes us understand that it will be freed in the same way as we are. That is, we must not despair even of those who are not yet called sons of God because they have not yet believed, but are merely called creation. For they too are creation, and they will be freed [Col. 0462B] from the slavery of destruction, just as we will, who are already sons of God, although it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

It will therefore be freed from the slavery of destruction into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God. That is, those who were slaves will become free, and those who were dead will become glorious in the perfect life that the sons of God will possess.

“For we know that all creation groans and suffers until now.” All creation is counted in the human being—not because all the angels, the exalted powers and authorities, heaven, earth, and sea, and everything in them are present in him, but because creation is partly spiritual, partly animal, and partly corporeal. Thus the Gospel says: “Preach the Gospel to every creature.” And to the Colossians: “In the hope of the Gospel, which has been preached in all creation under heaven.”

If we consider this from the lower levels upward, corporeal creation is displayed through places; animal creation gives life to corporeal things; and the animal part rules them, ruling well when it subjects itself to being ruled by God. But when it transgresses his commandments, it becomes entangled in labors and hardships through the very things that it was able to govern.

Thus the person who lives by the body is called a carnal or animal person: carnal because he pursues carnal things, animal because his soul is carried along in unrestrained lust, which the spirit neither rules nor restrains within the limits of the natural order, since the soul itself does not submit to being ruled by God.

But the person who rules his soul through the Spirit, and through the soul rules the body—which he cannot do unless he too has the Lord as his ruler—is called spiritual. For just as a man cannot be the head of a woman, so Christ is the head of a man. Such a person lives spiritually, although life is now carried on with some distress; afterward he will suffer none.

And because the highest angels live spiritually, the lowest live in an animal manner, and beasts and all cattle live carnally, while the body does not live but is given life, all creation is present in the human being: he understands through the spirit, senses through the soul, and moves from place to place through the body.

[Col. 0462D] Therefore all creation groans and suffers in the human being. He does not say “the whole of creation,” but “all creation,” as when someone says that all human beings who are healthy see the sun, although they do not see with their whole bodies, but only with their eyes.

Thus all creation is in the human being, who understands, lives, and possesses a body. But not the whole of creation is in him, since outside him there are angels who understand, live, and exist; cattle that live and exist; and bodies that merely exist. Living itself is greater than not living, and understanding itself is greater than living without understanding.

When, therefore, wretched human beings groan and suffer, all creation groans and suffers with them.

He rightly said “until now,” because even if some are already in Abraham’s bosom, and the thief, on the day when he believed, was placed in paradise and ceased to suffer, nevertheless all creation still groans and suffers until now, because in those who have not yet been freed, all of it is present through spirit, soul, and body.

“Not only,” he says, “does all creation groan and suffer, but we ourselves also.” That is, not only do body, soul, and spirit suffer together in the human being because of bodily difficulties, but we ourselves, apart from the bodies, groan within ourselves.

He rightly said: “Having the firstfruits of the Spirit.” That is, our spirits have already been offered to God like a sacrifice and have been seized by the divine fire of love. These are the firstfruits of the human being, because truth first possesses our spirit, so that through it the rest may be embraced; or because, at the very coming of redemption, we first received the Spirit.

The person already has firstfruits offered to God who says: “In mind I serve the law of God, but in the flesh the law of sin”; and who says: “God, whom I serve in my spirit”; and of whom it is said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

But since he still says: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” and elsewhere: “He will give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you,” the offering is not yet a whole burnt offering. It will be one when death has been swallowed up in victory, when it is said to death: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?”

Now, therefore, he says, not only does all creation—that is, together with the body—groan, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit—that is, we who are souls, because we have offered our minds, the firstfruits, to God—groan within ourselves. That is, apart from the body, we await adoption, the redemption of our body.

This means that when the body itself receives the benefit of the adoption of sons, to which we have been called, it will reveal that, with all suffering ended, we have been wholly liberated and are sons of God in every respect.

“For by hope we have been saved.” But hope that is seen is not hope. The reality that is now hope will exist when what we shall be appears: like him, because we shall see him as he is.

If this passage is explained in the manner just presented, we will not fall into the difficulties that compel many people to say that all the angels and the exalted powers are in pain and groaning until we are completely freed, because it is written: “All creation groans and suffers.”
