Although they help us according to their exalted status by obeying God, who deemed it worthy to send his only Son for us, we must believe that they do so without groaning or pain, lest they be thought wretched and that Lazarus, one of our number who now rests in Abraham’s bosom, be considered more blessed than they.

This is especially so because he said that the same creation that groans and suffers has been subjected to vanity. It is impious to believe this of the highest and most excellent creatures among the powers and authorities.

Moreover, he said that it would be freed from the slavery of destruction. We cannot believe that those who live a most blessed life in heaven have fallen into that condition.

Nevertheless, nothing should be asserted rashly, and the divine words must be examined again and again with devout care. Perhaps, when it groans and suffers and has been subjected to vanity, the passage can be understood in another way, so that it may be thought, not impiously, to refer to the highest angels, so long as they do not assist our weakness at the Lord’s command.

But whether the explanation we have developed or another explanation of this passage is offered, only this must be guarded against: that catholic faith not be violated or wounded. For I know that many foolish heretics have made many impious and absurd claims.

“For by hope we have been saved.” “By hope,” he says; salvation is still hoped for, not yet possessed in reality, as he says to the Corinthians: “We walk by faith, not by sight.” We believe what we shall be, but we are not yet that.

“But hope that is seen is not hope.” For what does someone hope for if he sees it? What is seen is not hoped for, because it is already possessed.

“But if we hope for what we do not see.” Therefore patience has a great reward through faith, because it hopes for what it does not see. In this way we are confident as though we had already received what we have not yet received.

“Through patience we await.” Hope cannot exist without patience.

“Likewise the Spirit also helps.” In accordance with this same expectation, the Spirit helps the weakness of prayer, so that we may pray for the things of God and, because of the hope that pleases God, ask for what is pleasing to him.

“Our weakness.” Our prayer is weak unless it is not only helped by the Holy Spirit but also inspired by it. For what should we pray for? Often the things we think will prosper us are harmful. Therefore they are not granted, since God provides something better, just as Paul asked the Lord three times.

“As we ought, we do not know.” For now we see through a mirror, as he says to the Corinthians: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.”

“But the Spirit himself intercedes for us.” He tests us so that he may know—that is, so that he may make us know—just as it is said: “He built the house,” meaning that it was built at his command. In the same way, the Holy Spirit intercedes, that is, causes us to ask for the things of God by inspiring, granting, or working in us.

“With inexpressible groanings.” He makes us groan with deep, silent groanings, because to the extent that we cannot ask with the mouth, we appeal through groanings.

“But he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires.” Here he has called the grace of the Spirit the Holy Spirit, as in the statement: “If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays,” where a kind of language or an understood speech is meant.

“According to God.” Because it desires heavenly and divine things.

“He intercedes for the saints.” For holy things, not human or earthly things.

“We know that all things work together for good for those who love God.” Whatever we do or suffer because of love, everything contributes to our reward. Or “work together,” that is, they increase it. Or, with God’s help, adverse circumstances are turned to prosperity, according to the saying: “Everything that you do will prosper.”

“For those who are according to.” Just as he says that we were chosen before the foundation of the world.

“According to his purpose the saints are called.” The purpose of God is that, without the works of the law or any other merits, he should justify the ungodly through faith alone. This faith does not come from nature but is a gift of God; among the fruits of the Spirit is faith.

For not all who are called are called according to the purpose, since “many are called, but few are chosen.” Those, therefore, who are called according to the purpose are also chosen before the foundation of the world.

“For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” He predestined that the person who, by his gift, was conformed to him in life should also be conformed to him in glory: “who will transform the body of our lowliness to be like the body of his glory.” Hence John also says: “We shall be like him.”

“So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” The firstborn from the dead, because he has many others besides himself.

“And those whom he predestined.” Here predestination is understood in relation to times, not to the people of this present age: that is, before the law, under the law, and under grace. But whoever was saved at those times was saved by the grace of God, as the apostle says: “Having the same spirit of faith.”

“These he also called.” In the present age he called people to faith, because in God’s sight they were called before the world existed. They are called through the inspiration of faith, exhortation, and divine action; they are justified through baptism; they are glorified through reward, or in the present through virtue. But all these things are gifts of God, because elsewhere he says: “That he may deem you worthy of his calling.” And also: “He who called you by the grace of God.”

They are justified freely, since he works everything in everyone. For he himself rescued us from the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved—not his own kingdom, but that of the Son.

“And those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified.” “It has been made clear to you that you are called my servant.” He will glorify them after the resurrection.

All these things have already happened: he foreknew, predestined, called, and justified. For all have already been foreknown and predestined, and many have already been called and justified.

But when he says, “These he also glorified,” this glory is to be understood as the one of which he likewise says: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.”

“What then shall we say about these things?” If God is for us, who can be against us? If God helps us, who can harm us? If God freely wishes to justify us, who can say, “This cannot happen”?

He wishes to show how great is what we have received, and that no one can prevail against the will of God, who does whatever he wishes.

“He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all—how will he not also give us all things with him?” He did not spare him by permitting him to be handed over, so that freedom of choice for the sake of sin might remain even in those who handed him over, and so that he might provide us with an example of patience.

What could he have that is dearer than Christ, which he would deny us, when he did not spare his own Son for us? He was not handed over by the Father alone, but also by himself, as he says elsewhere: “He handed himself over as an offering and a sacrifice to God, for a fragrant odor.”

“Who will bring a charge against God’s elect?” Who will bring a charge against those whom God chose and made believers in him? God proves through signs and mighty works that they are already righteous, against those who say: “They are not righteous unless the law has justified them,” even though at that time everything had been confined under sin.

If you pronounce the statement as though it were a confirmation, what perversity results? It should therefore be pronounced as if the question were: “Does God justify anything?” The implied answer is: “Certainly not.”

“God, who justifies.” The implied question is: “Will God, who works signs and wonders through them and who freely justified them, condemn?”

“Who is the one who condemns?” He asks, as it were: “Who is the one who condemns?” Or, “Who will forgive?” It should be understood as: “Is it Christ?” And he answers: “He who died for us—does he condemn us?” Certainly not.

Rather, he is the one who also rose and is in the blessedness of the Father. Just as, in the form of a servant, he asks the Father for us, so also he hears us together with the Father. Will he himself accuse or condemn us?

“Christ Jesus, who died”—rather, who rose. He loved us so greatly that he even died for us.

[Col. 0466B] “Who is at the right hand of God.” Where he is, we too will come. He is speaking according to the human nature in which he died and according to which he became the firstborn from the dead.

“Who also intercedes for us.” The Arians are accustomed to say: “The one who intercedes is inferior.” The answer should be that the Lord does not suffer forgetfulness, so that he must continually be reminded about those whom he himself justified.

But he is said to intercede in this respect: he continually displays and presents to the Father, as our pledge, the glorified human being whom he assumed, as the true and eternal Priest.

Through this human being he is also called inferior. Just as soul and body, though of different substances, constitute one human being, so—
God and man, one Christ from different substances. And thus, although he himself is one from different substances, in a certain manner he asks himself, and in a certain manner he hears himself on our behalf.

[Col. 0466C] Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or persecution, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written. The Jews wanted to separate them from Christ, wishing to recall them to observance of the Law. After so many and such outstanding benefits and promises, who will give or promise us anything of the sort, so that we might rightly withdraw from Christ, who even laid down his own life for us?

“Because for your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.” “Blessed are you when they persecute you for my sake.” And, he says, “for your sake,” not because of any crime are we afflicted with death; and for your sake we endure death, although we might retaliate. This testimony is fulfilled especially in us, who are not even permitted to resist, as we follow the example of our teacher and Lord, who was led like a sheep [Col. 0466D] to the slaughter.

But in all these things we conquer, because of him who loved us. We regard all these tribulations as nothing because of him who loved us so greatly that he died for us; and when we die for his name, then we triumph most of all.

For I am certain that neither death nor life. “I am certain”: neither if someone threatens me with death, nor if he promises me eternal life. Neither angels. Nor if someone says that he is an angel sent by God, as he himself says to the Galatians. Neither principalities nor things present. Nor if he confers honor in the present. Nor things future. Nor if he promises present goods and glory in the future. Neither power. Nor if he performs miracles. Neither height. Of the kingdom of heaven or of wisdom. Nor depth. [Col. 0467A] Neither the depth of knowledge nor hell. Nor will any other creature be able to separate us.

He has named almost every creature, and was not content with these things; so he added: Even if there is another creature, it will not be able to separate us from the love of Christ. From this one must consider with what faith he believed in Christ.

From the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. The love of Christ does not consist merely in this, that someone says he loves him; rather, he himself declares that whatever is done to his saints is done to him, saying: “Whoever receives you receives me,” and so forth. And John says: “If you do not love your brother, whom you see, how can you love the Lord, whom you do not see?” Indeed, he wanted the love of God to be manifested in the brethren. “For,” he says, “God is love,” and so forth. And the Lord says: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you love one another.” “If you love me, keep my commandments.” And: “Whoever hears my words and does them is the one who loves me.”

## Chapter IX

“I speak the truth.” Some say that, since he is about to declare something incredible—namely, that he wished to be accursed from Christ for Israel—he first offers assurance by a kind of solemn affirmation. He assures the Jews that he does not hate them, but that he is deeply grieved on their account because they refuse to believe in Christ, who had been promised to them.

“I do not lie in Christ.” Therefore, whoever has been baptized either speaks the truth or tells a lie; whatever he does, he does in Christ, whose member he is. And whoever sins in baptism sins in Christ, as he says: “By thus sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak consciences, you sin against Christ.”

“My conscience bearing witness to me.” He speaks the truth whose conscience bears witness to him and does not accuse him of lying.

“In the Holy Spirit.” Not falsely.

“For I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart.” Because I have seen them refuse to believe God.

“I myself wished to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh.” I once wished this; I would not wish it now. For I knew that everything belonged to them, but when I came to know the truth, I who had been so unbelieving was converted, while they were not converted.

“Who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises.” He also recounts what he has set aside, so that you may recognize what force it was that could separate him from them.

“Whose are the fathers”—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—“and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God.”

This is directed against Arius, Manichaeus, and Photinus, but also against Nestorius, who denies that the Lord Christ is according to the flesh.

“Blessed forever. Amen.” Thomas likewise said, “My God and my Lord,” and Christ confirms this by saying, “Because you have seen me, you have believed.”

But it is not that the word of God has failed. Since above he had said that he grieved because the people of Israel were excluded from the kingdom through their own fault, although all these privileges had belonged to them, he now shows that those who do not believe are not children of Abraham. Otherwise it might have been thought that he was preaching this against all Jews and that someone might say, “Then has God lied to Abraham?” Far be it from us.

Here he begins to reason why, through the high and just judgment of God, the Gentiles were admitted after the Jews had been rejected.

“For not all who are from Israel are Israelites, nor are all who are the offspring of Abraham children.” If not all are children, nevertheless some are—those who were chosen from among them and became believers. If not all who are from Israel are Israelites, then conversely many who are not from Israel are Israelites.

The Savior says: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” Therefore, in whomever there is deceit, he is not truly an Israelite.

“But in Isaac shall your offspring be called.” The children of Abraham were called in Isaac, not in Ishmael, although Ishmael too was his offspring. That is, “It is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise who are counted as offspring”; for this word is one of promise.

Ishmael was born according to ordinary human custom from a slave woman, whereas Isaac received more than nature could give, having been born from aged parents through a promise.

So now also the promise makes Christians children of Abraham—not flesh and imitation of his faith, through which he was justified and merited that all the tribes of the earth should be blessed in his offspring, nor circumcision.

“According to this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” Not Hagar, the slave woman, so that he might show that the later people are the people of the promise; and the same was signified in Isaac.

“Not only she, but Rebecca also.” It was not only Ishmael and Isaac—although they came from one Abraham, they were born of different mothers and therefore were not one before the Lord—but also Jacob and Esau. Though they were born from one intercourse of Rebecca, before they were born they were separated from one another in the foreknowledge of God, so that God’s purpose might remain in his foreknowledge: by it he was to reject unbelieving Jews and bestow mercy on the Gentiles without any merits of theirs.

He does all this to show that before God the privilege of descent has no force and that he does not show partiality to anyone. He wishes to confirm this by examples that they could turn into an accusation against him, and through these very examples he will show that no one can oppose God when he does what he wills—whether he wished to grant something distinctive to their race or now to choose those whom he willed.

“Rebecca also, having conceived by one intercourse with Isaac our father.” For although the children had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, from one intercourse there were two. Rebecca is understood to have given birth first to twins, and, terrified because something apparently new had happened to her, she inquired of the Lord.

“It was said to her, not from works but from him who calls: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’” This was not fulfilled in Jacob and Esau, but was spoken figuratively of the Christian people, who were placed before the older Jewish people. Ephraim and Manasseh likewise prefigured the younger people, that is, the Christian people, who were blessed with their hands crossed.

“As it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’” This was spoken in Genesis. The prophet reports it as fulfilled not in the men themselves but in their descendants. The Apostle, taking up this testimony, restrained curiosity and accusation by asserting that there is no injustice with God, but that whatever he does, he does either mercifully or judicially.

“What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.” He continues his reasoning and presents to himself the character of an objector. By testimonies he proves that no one can resist the Lord’s will, with Moses himself saying:

“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy”—that is, “If I am good, why is your eye evil? Am I taking away from you what I give to another? In my foreknowledge I decided to graft the wild olive into the olive tree; what is that to you?”

For to Moses he says: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy.” For God calls the one on whom he has mercy and inspires him to believe; and to the one toward whom he is merciful so that he may believe, he grants mercy—that is, he makes him merciful, so that he may also do good works.

Thus it is clearly established that all good things come from God himself, who is the Savior of all, especially of believers.

But someone may say: “Why does he treat one person in this way and another not, and why does he not treat everyone equally? Is God a respecter of persons?”

Respect of persons is rightly spoken of where the one who judges, abandoning the merits of the case under judgment, supports one party against another because he finds in the person something worthy of honor or mercy. But if someone has two debtors and wishes to forgive one his debt while demanding it from the other, he gives to whomever he wishes but defrauds no one; and it should not be called respect of persons when there is no injustice.

Otherwise, to those who understand little, respect of persons might seem to occur where the master of the vineyard gave the laborers who had worked for one hour as much as he gave those who had borne the burden and heat of the day, making equal in reward those whose labor had been so greatly unequal.

But what did he reply to those who murmured about this apparent respect of persons? “Friend, I do you no injury,” and so forth. Here, indeed, the whole matter is just: “I wish this to be given to you; I have given that to him. I have taken nothing from you, nor have I diminished or denied what I owed you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?” and so forth.

Therefore, just as there is no respect of persons here, because one is honored freely without another being defrauded of what is owed him, so when, according to God’s purpose, one person is called and another is not, the one who is called receives a gratuitous good, whose beginning is the calling itself; while the one who is not called receives the evil that is owed, because all are guilty through the one by whom sin entered the world.

“Therefore it depends not on him who wills or on him who runs, but on God who has mercy.” He concludes the argument and introduces testimony concerning Pharaoh, so that we may tremble before God’s judgments rather than investigate them. They are often hidden, but they are never unjust. For it is true that he himself directs even the course of those who run, and that without his grace no one’s course reaches its appointed end, as Ecclesiastes says: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong”; and David says: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.”

His help, therefore, must be implored, for he works all things in all.

The Christian must therefore run and must never presume on his own strength. He must run and fulfill God’s commandments, but he must claim nothing for himself, according to the saying: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

This is directed against those who presumed upon their own merits and strength. Paul himself was running when he feared going to Bithynia, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. I believe that his running would have been in vain, but he was directed by the Holy Spirit to the place where his preaching would bear fruit.

David too cried out to the Lord: “Direct my steps according to your word.” Without doubt our running is in vain unless our steps are directed by the Lord.

A horse too can run, but if it has no guide, it rushes forward unbridled and headlong and does not travel on the right path. So it is with us without God and his grace.

But what human being has the power to attain, through such insight, to his own mind, by which his will might be moved toward faith? Who embraces in his mind what does not please him? Or who has it in his power either to encounter something capable of pleasing him or to be pleased when he encounters it?

When, therefore, the things that advance us please us, this is inspired by God and bestowed by God’s grace; it is not acquired by our will, diligence, or merits from our works. For he grants and bestows the movement of the will, the diligence of earnestness, and works fervent with love.

We are commanded to ask, so that we may receive; to seek, so that we may find; and to knock, so that it may be opened to us.

Is our prayer not sometimes lukewarm—or rather cold and almost nothing, indeed at times so entirely nothing that we do not even perceive this in ourselves with sorrow? For if we grieve over even this, we are already praying.

What else is shown to us except that he grants us even the asking, seeking, and knocking, who commands us to do these things?

“Therefore it depends not on him who wills or on him who runs, but on God who has mercy.” For we cannot even will or run unless he moves and stirs us.

Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”

Each sinner is punished when the measure and limit of his sins have been completed. Sometimes this also happens in the present, as with the Sodomites and Gomorrhaeans.

Pharaoh, therefore, had already exceeded the measure. Since he was worthy of destruction, God wished, through his example, to instill fear in everyone. He also wished the people who were about to leave Egypt to recognize his power and justice, so that they would neither sin in the same way nor fear their enemies. Through such vengeance he wished not only to free them from the impending danger but also to fortify them, by fear of his power, against committing iniquity in the future.

The passage concerning Pharaoh may also be understood in this way: he was hardened through God’s mercy. For whenever the plague ceased as Moses prayed, Pharaoh became hardened; and although God knew that he had been hardened in such a way that he could not be converted, he nevertheless displayed his goodness.

When he said, “I raised you up,” he meant, “I exposed you,” not “I made you”—just as if someone were to fan two full vessels, one containing balsam and the other dung: he reveals the fragrance or the stench, but does not produce it.

“Therefore he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.” He has mercy through great goodness, and he hardens without any iniquity. He has mercy by granting good things; he hardens by repaying what is deserved.

It is as though he said: “So you understand it in this way: if he has mercy on whomever he wills and hardens whomever he wills, then, following your understanding, you say: ‘Why are we still blamed? We do what he himself wills.’”

The Apostle perceived what might trouble their carnal understanding and set against it the words of an objector, which he would restrain by apostolic authority.

“For you will say to me: ‘Why does he still find fault?’” [The same question is asked below in this text.] “For who has resisted his will?”

He replied to the one speaking in this way: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’”

Then, following so great and hidden a mystery, he judged how much ought to be disclosed to human beings and disclosed it, saying:

“But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy…”

This is not only God’s assistance but also an example. It is assistance in the vessels of mercy; in the vessels of wrath it is an example. In them he shows his wrath and demonstrates his power, because goodness is so powerful that it makes good use even of evil things. Through them he makes known the riches of his glory to the vessels of mercy.

For what the justice of the one who punishes demands from the vessels of wrath, the grace of the one who liberates forgives in the vessels of mercy. The benefit granted freely to some would not appear unless God showed, by just judgment condemning others from the same mass, equally guilty, what was owed to each group.

Hear also the complete interpretation of this passage by the blessed Father Augustine, taken from his work addressed to Saint Simplicianus. Concerning Pharaoh he answers as follows:

“By his earlier merits, through which he had afflicted foreigners in his kingdom, he had become worthy that his heart should be hardened, so that he would not believe even the most evident signs of God’s command. From the same mass—that is, the mass of sins—he therefore brought forth vessels of mercy, whom he would assist when the children of Israel implored him; and vessels of wrath, through whose punishment he would instruct them—that is, Pharaoh and his people.

“For although both groups were sinners and therefore belonged to one mass, they nevertheless had to be treated differently: those who had groaned to the one God that he might assist them were to be treated one way; those under whose unjust burdens they had groaned were to be treated another way.

“Thus he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction. By saying ‘with much patience,’ he sufficiently indicated their earlier sins, which he endured before punishing them, when those who were being liberated had to be assisted through their punishment, so that he might make known the riches of his glory to the vessels of mercy, which he had prepared for glory.”

Perhaps, troubled by that question, you have returned to it: “If he has mercy on whomever he wills and hardens whomever he wills, why does he still find fault? Who has resisted his will?”

It is entirely so: whether you wish it or not, he has mercy on whomever he wills and hardens whomever he wills. But what impious person would call God’s will unjust, when Pharaoh himself cries out to him: “God is just, but I and my people are unjust”? For God’s will cannot be unjust. It arises from the most hidden merits by which sinners themselves are distinguished.

Although, because of the general sin, all have become one mass, there is nevertheless no lack of difference among them. For many sinners live naturally with moderation and, although they have not yet been justified, thereby become worthy of justification. In others, however, personal fault precedes, making them worthy of hardening.

The same Apostle says elsewhere: “Because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind.” This is what it means that he hardened Pharaoh’s heart.

The fact that they did not approve of having God in their knowledge is what made them worthy of being given over to a reprobate mind. Nevertheless, it remains true that it depends not on him who wills or on him who runs, but on God who has mercy. For if someone, whether for lighter sins or certainly for heavier and numerous sins, becomes worthy of God’s mercy through great groaning and the grief of repentance, this is not his own achievement—he would perish if left to himself—but the work of the merciful God, who comes to the aid of his prayers and grief.

It is not enough merely to will, although even the will by which we will is prepared by the Lord. Yet, as I have said, willing is not enough unless the Lord has mercy.

But God does not have mercy on one whom he calls to peace unless a will that has already been healed has preceded it, for “peace is for people of good will.” And just as no one can will unless he has been admonished and called—whether inwardly, where no human being sees, or outwardly through a spoken word or through some visible signs—so God brings it about that the very act of willing is worked in us.

For the Lord’s banquet, which he says in the Gospel had been prepared, was not desired by all who were called, and those who came could not have come unless they had been called. Those who came must not ascribe their coming to themselves, because they came as called; nor should those who refused to come attribute this to anyone else, but only to themselves. For they had been called to come with free choice.

The calling, therefore, works the will before merit. Consequently, if anyone ascribes his coming to the fact that he was called, he cannot ascribe to himself the fact that he was called.

The one who was called but did not come, just as he has no merit of reward for having been called, so he will fall under the merit of punishment because, though called, he neglected to come.

Thus there will be those two things: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” Calling belongs to mercy; the blessedness of those who came when called belongs to judgment, as does the punishment of those who refused to come.

Was Pharaoh unaware of how much good those lands would receive through Joseph’s arrival? Knowledge of that event therefore became his calling, so that by treating the people of Israel mercifully he would not be ungrateful.

But because he refused to obey this calling and exercised cruelty toward those to whom humanity and mercy were owed, he deserved punishment: his heart was hardened, and he suffered such blindness of mind that he did not believe so many, so great, and so evident signs of God. Through his punishment—whether by hardening or by final visible submersion—the people might be instructed, so that through that affliction [perhaps read: “that affliction”]—of hidden obtuseness and manifest submersion—they might, by the desert of disobedience, bring it upon themselves.

This calling, which operates at suitable times among individual human beings, among peoples, and in the human race itself, belongs to another and deeper ordering. To this belongs the saying: “In the womb I sanctified you,” and: “When you were still in your father’s loins, I saw you.”

So too: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” although it was said before he was born. This cannot be comprehended except perhaps by those who love the Lord their God with all their heart, with all their soul, and with all their mind, and their neighbor as themselves.

Being founded on such great love, they may already, perhaps together with the saints, comprehend “the length, breadth, and depth.”

Nevertheless, this must be held with unwavering faith: God does nothing unjustly, and there is no nature that does not owe to God what it is. For all honor, beauty, and harmony of parts are owed to God. If you remove these entirely from things, pursuing the matter even to all their remnants, nothing remains.

Since, therefore, by sinning we have lost merit, and once God’s mercy has been removed nothing but eternal punishment is owed to sinners, what does the human being born from the mass of perdition intend when he answers God and says, “Why did you make me like this?”

If you wish to know these things, do not remain clay; rather, become a son of God through the mercy of the one who gave those who believe in his name the power to become sons of God.

But divine knowledge is not given to human beings who desire to know it before they believe, according to their own wishes. The reward of knowledge is given in return for merits; merit, however, is acquired through believing.

The grace given through faith was not given because of any merits of ours preceding it. What merit does a sinner and an ungodly person possess? Yet Christ died for sinners and for the ungodly, so that we might be called to believe not by merit but by grace; and, through believing, might also establish merit.

Sinners, therefore, are commanded to believe, and by believing they are cleansed from sins. They do not know what they will see if they live rightly. Since they cannot see unless they live rightly, and cannot live rightly unless they believe, it is evident that one must begin with faith. The commandments by which believers are turned away from this world make the heart pure, so that God may be seen there.

Only then, and not in the wrong order, will you properly hear whatever may be said about the most hidden merits of souls and about the secret grace or justice of almighty God.

He also gives faith, so that you may believe; from him comes every good gift. For what do you have that you did not receive?

“You will say to me: ‘Why does he still complain? For who has resisted his will?’” It is true that he is not resisted, because no Christian doubts that God’s will is good and just.

“O man, who are you to answer back to God?” This too is the speech of an objector. Even if things were as you say, who were you to answer God? You ought to be silent and do what is commanded you. If he commands you to do what is good, you ought to understand that he too is good, since evil does not please him and he forbids it to you.

Did he say, “O man, what you have said is false”? No. He said: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” and what follows.

“Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” Does the potter not have power over the clay?

He does not say this because the thing formed can or ought to speak in such a way. He wishes us to be as silent before the Lord as clay is before the potter. When we do not understand, we must not think evil of God, knowing that no fault can fall upon God. His judgments are hidden, but they are not unjust.

“From the same mass to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.” He speaks of the mass of the sinful people from which we were all created through Adam.

“But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known…” God’s will is merciful and just, and he wills nothing except what is good, devout, and just.

“He endured with much patience.” He endured for a long time the one who blasphemed him and afflicted his people with harsh works.

“Vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory.” By completing their sins, the vessels of wrath had made themselves worthy; they were fitted for destruction by themselves, not only through original sin but also through actual sin. Wrath is not repaid unless it is deserved, lest there be injustice with God.

From this the vessels of mercy understand how freely mercy is bestowed upon them: to the vessels of wrath, with whom they share the cause of destruction and the common mass, deserved and just wrath is repaid, while to these others undeserved mercy is granted.

“Upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory, whom he also called.” For he himself wished to have mercy on them and to make them vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath.

“Not only from the Jews.” If he had called in person, he would have called the Jews alone. But we find that he neither spared sinful Jews nor prevented the Gentiles from being saved.

“But also from the Gentiles, as Hosea says.” At that time, too, some Egyptians had gone out with them.

“I will call those who were not my people, ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved, ‘beloved.’” Through the prophet he shows that it had been foretold that the Gentiles would pass over to Christ.

“And her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy.”

“And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God.”

He calls whomever he wills to such an extent that he even chose ungodly Gentiles who had never performed anything good. If he chose according to merits, Israel alone, which had always served God, ought to have deserved this. But he saves all freely, and saves no one on the basis of his own merits, because, as he says, “He has shut up all under sin, that he might have mercy on all.”

Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea…” What he threatens them with is for their good, if they believe.

“The remnant shall be saved.” Isaiah shows that only a small number of Jews would believe. These are the vessels for honor; the remaining multitude are vessels for dishonor.

“Completing and abbreviating the word in righteousness.” According to the historical sense, it is understood as follows: just as I abbreviate and bring the word to an end, so God will quickly accomplish it.

According to the allegorical sense, the New Testament receives the abbreviated word, because everything is briefly comprehended in it, as in: “I believe in God the Father almighty, and in his Son Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit,” together with the rest that follows in the Creed.

Or it may refer to: “Whatever you do not wish others to do to you, do not do to them.” That is, by the concise statement of faith he saves believers through grace, not through the countless observances by which that multitude was burdened and oppressed in servitude.

Through grace he completed and abbreviated the word for us upon the earth, saying: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

Or it may refer to: “You shall love God and your neighbor”; upon these commandments the whole law and the prophets depend.

“For the Lord will complete and abbreviate the word upon the earth.” The Lord contracted and abbreviated the people of Israel. And as Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrha.”

For he did not allow all to perish with the ungodly, but from them he made at least a few righteous, and the offspring of Abraham came, who would save what had perished. If he had not wished to save at least a few, we would all have perished together; but he did this so that he might fulfill what he had promised to Abraham.

But why should one receive and another not receive, when neither deserves to receive and whoever receives receives what is not owed? Let them measure their own strength and not investigate things stronger than themselves. Let it be enough for them to know that there is no injustice with God.

“What shall we say, then? The Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness.” If what we say is not so—if it does not depend on him who wills or on him who runs—how did the Gentiles, who had never sought righteousness, find it, while Israel, which had always pursued righteousness, could not attain the law of righteousness?

He answered: “Because the Gentiles believed, whereas the Jews did not wish to believe, but gloried in works which they did not even keep.”

What shall we say, then, in response to this objection—that the Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained it, while Israel did not attain it? Let us tremble before God’s judgments, which, as I have said, are hidden but never unjust.

“But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness.” This was the law that the Lord gave to those who were called to believe.

Why? “Because it was not from faith, but as if from works.” He says “as if” because it was not truly from works.

“They stumbled.” By cleverly defending the law, and by destroying nature and free will, like the philosophers of this world, they stumbled against the stone of stumbling.

“Against the stone of stumbling.” Whoever sees the stone finds it to be the stone of salvation if he does not stumble against it; but whoever is blind stumbles against the stone.

So too the Jews, whom their wickedness blinded so that they would not recognize Christ, stumbled against him by doing him injury. In him believing Gentiles attained righteousness.

Therefore Christ was foretold as “the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense,” because many are scandalized by his passion and birth, as it is written: “They were scandalized at him.”

Paul himself also says to the Corinthians: “Christ crucified: a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

Hence this too follows: “Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.”

Peter likewise says that for believers he is a chosen and cornerstone, but for unbelievers a stone of stumbling.

“As it is written: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.’” He said this through the prophet Isaiah.

“And everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame,” because he understands the power of God and the wisdom of God.

## Chapter X

“Brothers, the desire of my heart and my supplication to God is…” One must pray for enemies not only with the lips but also with the heart.

“For their salvation.” For the Jews.

“For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God.” They have zeal for pursuing God’s law.

“But not according to knowledge.” Unless someone does everything according to the knowledge given by God, he stumbles, even if he is fully perfected.

If the Jews had knowledge of God, they would recognize that Christ did not come against the law but according to the law. They would also understand that they cannot be justified according to the law, but that God justifies freely through faith, not through the works of the law in which they gloried.

“For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness…” They were ignorant that God justifies freely through faith and not through the works of the law in which they gloried. They claimed to have kept the law, although they had not kept it; and by justifying themselves through it, they did not submit to the remission of sins, lest they appear to have been sinners.

They were not compelled against their will to become unbelievers; but because they refused to believe, they did not escape the charge of unbelief.

“And seeking to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God.” They were seeking the righteousness that comes from the law, or the righteousness that they falsely attributed to free will. And while they ascribe to themselves what belongs to God, they are not subject to God’s righteousness.

The righteousness of the law is therefore to command what pleases God and forbid what displeases him. In the law there is righteousness in serving and in requiring no help from God outside it for living rightly.

But God’s righteousness is not presuming upon one’s own strength.

It is called God’s righteousness not because it is the righteousness by which God is righteous, but because it is the righteousness that God gives to a human being, so that the human being may be righteous through God.

“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness.” Christ is called the end of the law because he himself is, or in him is, the whole of perfection.

He is called its end from the standpoint of completing, not of destroying. For it is one thing to say, “The bread is finished,” and another to say, “The cloth is finished”: the first means that it no longer exists; the second that it has been completed.

Therefore the one who believes in Christ fulfills the law, because all our intention ought to tend and hasten toward him. Beyond him there is nothing left for us to seek, because everything that had been foretold about him in the holy Scriptures has been fulfilled.

“For every believer”—Jew and Greek.

“Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law shall live by it.” Historically, Moses spoke of the law. But the Apostle applies the statement to Christ, because the law was neither in heaven nor in the abyss; therefore he commands them always to meditate upon the law, so that they may find Christ there.

“He shall live by it.” But concerning the righteousness that comes from faith, he says as follows.

None of them therefore lives by that righteousness, because no one practices it. In comparison with their many sins, even if there were a few who practiced it, they would be regarded as none.

“Do not say in your heart: ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’”—that is, to bring Christ down—“or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead.

“But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.’” This means that you must not doubt in your heart either his passion, his resurrection, or his ascension, as though these had not been accomplished by him.

“This is the word of faith that we preach.” This is the New Testament.

“For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” The confession of the mouth is the testimony of the heart.

“For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” This concerns past sins, not future ones.

Therefore, if faith is sufficient for righteousness and confession for salvation, Jew and Greek are one in Christ.

Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame.” Not the Jew only.

“For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.” This concerns former sin or idolatry. Therefore you cannot put to shame those whom Scripture says cannot be put to shame.

---

*(Here begins an excerpted exposition from the book of Saint Augustine, taken from the work addressed to Saint Simplicianus, On Jacob and Esau. Although it may not appear to have been placed in the proper order of this treatise, it has nevertheless not been omitted because it is necessary and complete; for that reason it has been written here, so that, once the obscurity of the passage itself has been clarified, it may plainly illuminate the understanding of the reader.)*
[Col. 0477A] It was said not on account of works, but on account of the one who calls: “The elder shall serve the younger.” Grace, therefore, belongs to the one who calls; good works consequently belong to the one who receives grace—not works that produce grace, but works produced by grace. Fire does not make something hot in order that it may burn; rather, because it burns, it makes something hot. Nor does a wheel run well in order to be round, but because it is round. So no one works well in order to receive grace, but because he has received it. For how can one live justly who has not been justified? How can one live holily if one has not been sanctified? Or indeed, how can one live at all who has not been justified [elsewhere: vivified]? Grace justifies, so that the justified person may be able to live justly. Grace, therefore, comes first, and good works second, as he says elsewhere: “To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt.” [Col. 0477B] They did not understand that, precisely because it is evangelical grace, it is not owed on account of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. In many passages he repeatedly bears witness to this, placing the grace of faith before works—not in order to abolish works, but to show that works do not precede grace but follow it: so that no one may suppose that he received grace because he worked well, but rather that he cannot work well unless he has received grace through faith. A person begins to receive grace from the moment he begins to believe in God, moved toward faith either by an inward or an outward admonition. Yet it matters at which stages of time, or through the celebration of the sacraments, grace is poured out more fully and manifestly. But, to speak more directly about the matter at hand, these things are recalled in order to break and cast down the pride of ungrateful people who dare to boast of their merits. For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing either good or evil, it was said not on account of works but on account of the one who calls: “The elder shall serve the younger.” Grace, therefore, belongs to the one who calls.

If, then, election is through foreknowledge—and God foresaw Jacob’s faith—how do you prove that he did not also choose him on account of works? If it is because they had not yet been born and had not yet done anything good or evil, then neither had either of them yet believed. But just as foreknowledge saw that one would believe, so foreknowledge could also see that one would act. Thus, just as someone might say that he was chosen on account of the future faith that God foresaw, another might equally say that he was chosen rather on account of future works, which God likewise foresaw. Therefore, how does the Apostle show [Col. 0477D] that “the elder shall serve the younger” was said not on account of works? If the point is merely that they had not yet been born, then it was said not only not on account of works, but neither on account of faith, since neither existed in those not yet born. The Apostle did not, then, intend election to be understood as having been made through foreknowledge of the younger, so that the elder would serve him. For, wishing to show that it was not made on account of works, he added: “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil.” Otherwise one could have said to him: “But God already knew what each of them would do.” The question, then, is on what basis that election was made. For if it was not on account of works, which did not yet exist in those not yet born, neither was it on account of faith, since that too did not yet exist. On what basis, then? Should we say that there was no election at all, since there was no difference in the womb of their mother—whether of faith, works, or any merits whatsoever? Yet it was said: “In order that God’s purpose according to election might remain.” This is why we ask the question—unless the sentence is to be divided in this way: not so that we understand the statement, “The elder shall serve the younger,” as having been made not on account of works but on account of the one who calls, “in order that God’s purpose according to election might remain”; but rather so that this may be understood as an example concerning those not yet born and not yet active, so that no election can be understood here. For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, “in order that God’s purpose according to election might remain”—that is, they had done nothing good or evil such that an election could be made on account of the action of the one who had acted well.

When, therefore, there was no election of the one who acted well according to which God’s purpose might remain, it was said not on account of works but on account of the one who calls—that is, on account of the one who, by calling to faith, justifies the ungodly by grace: “The elder shall serve the younger.” God’s purpose, then, did not remain according to election; rather, election proceeded from the purpose. That is, God’s purpose of justification does not remain because he found good works in human beings and chose them; rather, because his purpose remains to justify believers, he finds works that he may now choose for the kingdom of heaven. For unless there were election, there would be no elect, nor would it rightly be said: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” Yet election does not precede justification; justification precedes election. No one is chosen unless he is already distinct from the one who is rejected. Thus, when it is said that God chose us [Col. 0478C] before the foundation of the world, I do not see how this can have been said except with reference to foreknowledge.

Here, however, when he says, “It was said to him not on account of works but on account of the one who calls: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’” he wished this to be understood not as an election based on merits, which come forth after justification by grace, but as an expression of God’s generosity in his gifts, so that no one might boast of works. “By the grace of God we have been saved,” and this is “not from works but God’s gift”; “not from works, so that no one might boast.” The question arises whether faith itself earns a person’s justification, or whether even the merits of faith do not precede God’s mercy, but faith itself is also to be numbered among the gifts of grace. For here too, having said “not on account of works,” he did not say, “but on account of faith it was said to him, ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’” Rather, he said, “but on account of the one who calls,” for no one believes who is not called. God, however, calls in mercy, granting this to no merits of faith, since the merits of faith follow calling rather than precede it. “How can they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without a preacher?” Unless, therefore, God’s mercy precedes by calling, no one can believe, so as thereby to begin to be justified and to receive the ability to work well.

Grace, therefore, precedes every merit. Indeed, Christ died for the ungodly. The younger, therefore, receives on account of the one who calls, not on account of any merits of his works, so that the elder might serve him; and even what is written, “Jacob I loved,” is to be understood as deriving from God’s calling, not from Jacob’s action. What, then, of Esau—that he serves the younger, and that it is written, “But Esau I hated”? By what evils of his did he merit this, when he too had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, at the time when it was said, “And the elder shall serve the younger”? Or perhaps, just as the statement concerning Jacob was made without any merits of good action, so Esau was hated without any merits of evil action? For if, because God foresaw his future evil works, he predestined him to serve the younger, then for the same reason he predestined Jacob so that the elder would serve him, because he foresaw Jacob’s future good works. In that case, what he says, “not on account of works,” is false.

But if it is true that it was not on account of works—and he proves this from the fact that it was said concerning those not yet born and not yet active—then, since faith likewise did not yet exist in those not yet born, on what merit is Esau hated before he was born? There is no question that God made the things he would love. But if we say that he made things he would hate, that is absurd, since another Scripture comes to mind and says: “For you established nothing in hatred, and you hated none of the things that you made or established.” On what merit, then, was the sun made? Or what did the moon do wrong to be so much lower than the sun? Or what did it deserve in order to be created so much brighter than the other stars? Yet all things were created good, each in its own kind. God would not have said, “I loved the sun, but hated the moon,” or, “I loved the moon, but hated the stars,” as he said, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” He loved all those things, although they were arranged in different degrees of excellence, because God saw that they were good, since they were established by his word.

But if he hated Esau for no reason other than the merit of injustice, then that would be unjust. If we grant this, Jacob begins to be loved on account of the merit of justice. But if that is true, then it is false that this was not on account of works. Or was it perhaps on account of the justice of faith? What help, then, does “when they had not yet been born” give you, since in one not yet born there could not even have been the justice of faith?

The Apostle therefore saw what might occur to the mind of the hearer or reader from these words, and immediately added: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.” And, as though teaching how this could not be so, he says: “For he says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’” By these words does he resolve the question—or rather bind it more tightly? For this is precisely what causes the greatest difficulty: if he has mercy on the one on whom he will have mercy, and shows compassion to the one to whom he will show compassion, why was this mercy withheld from Esau, so that through it he too might become good, just as Jacob became good through it?

Or was it said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” because the one on whom God has mercy in order to call him, he will have mercy on so that he may believe; and the one to whom he shows compassion so that he may believe, he will show compassion by making him compassionate, so that he may also work well? We are therefore warned that no one ought to boast or exalt himself even over works of mercy, as though he had earned God’s favor through them, since the one who will show mercy to the person to whom he is compassionate first granted him mercy itself. If someone boasts that he earned this by believing, let him know that God granted him the ability to believe—the merciful God inspiring the faith of the one on whom he had mercy—in order that he might still extend calling even to the unbeliever.

For now the faithful person is distinguished from the ungodly. “What do you have,” he says, “that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” This is rightly said. But why was this mercy withdrawn from Esau, so that he was not called in such a way that faith would also be inspired in the one who was called, and that by believing he would become compassionate, so that he might work well?

Or perhaps it was because he did not wish to? If Jacob believed because he wished to, then God did not give him faith; rather, by willing, Jacob granted it to himself and possessed something he had not received. Or is it because no one can believe unless he wishes to, and no one can wish to unless he is called? Yet no one can grant himself the opportunity to be called. God grants both calling and faith by calling, because no one can believe without calling, although no one believes against his will. “How can they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without a preacher?”

No one, therefore, believes without being called, but not everyone who is called believes. “For many are called, but few are chosen.” Those who did not despise the one who called, but followed him by believing, certainly believed willingly. What, then, of what follows? “So then it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.” Is it because we cannot even will unless we are called, and our willing is of no value unless God helps us to bring it to completion? It is necessary, then, to will to run. For it would not be said without purpose: “Peace on earth to people of good will.” And: “Run in such a way that you may obtain.”

Yet it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy, so that we may obtain what we will and reach where we wish to go. Esau, then, did not wish, and he did not run. But even if he had wished and run, he would have reached the goal through God’s help—God, who by calling would also have granted him the ability to will and to run—unless, by despising the call, he became rejected. For God grants our willing in one way, and grants what we have willed in another. He wished our willing to be both his and ours: his by calling, ours by following. But what we have willed he alone grants—that is, the ability to act well and to live blessedly forever.

Nevertheless, Esau, while still unborn, could not will or refuse any of these things. Why, then, was he rejected while in the womb? We return to those difficulties, now made more troublesome not only by their own obscurity but also by our repeated discussion. Why was Esau rejected before birth, when he could neither believe in the one who called, nor despise the call, nor do anything good or evil? If it was because of God’s foreknowledge of his future evil will, why was Jacob not approved through God’s foreknowledge of his future good will? But if you once grant that someone could be approved or rejected on the basis of what was not yet in him but what God foresaw would be in him, then it follows that he could also be approved on the basis of works that God foresaw would be in him, although he had not yet done anything. And what was said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” will not help you at all in showing that it was not on account of works, because no one had yet acted.

If you attend carefully also to those words, “So then it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” it will not seem that the Apostle said this only because we reach what we will through God’s help. He also says elsewhere: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.” There he sufficiently shows that even good will itself comes about through God working in us.

For if it was said, “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” only because human willing by itself is not sufficient for us to live rightly and justly unless we are helped by God’s mercy, then one could also say: “It depends not on God who has mercy, but on the human being who wills,” because God’s mercy alone is not sufficient unless the consent of our will is added. Yet it is evident that our willing is useless unless God has mercy. But how can it be said that God’s mercy is useless unless we will? For if God has mercy, we also will; the ability to will belongs to that same mercy. “For it is God who works in us both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.”

If we ask whether good will is God’s gift, surely no one would dare deny it. But because good will does not precede calling—rather, calling precedes good will—what we rightly will is attributed to God who calls; it cannot be attributed to us that we are called. Therefore we must not think that it was said, “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” merely because without his help we cannot attain what we will. Rather, it was said because without his calling we do not will.

But if this calling is so effective in producing good will that everyone who is called follows it, how will “Many are called, but few are chosen” be true? If it is true that the called person obeys the call, and that not obeying it lies within his will, then it can rightly also be said: “It depends not on God who has mercy, but on the human being who wills and runs,” because the mercy of the one who calls is not sufficient unless obedience follows the call.

Or perhaps those who do not perceive calling in this way [elsewhere: consent to it] can, when called in another way, direct their will toward faith, and “Many are called, but few are chosen” is true in this sense: although many are called in one way, because not all are affected in the same way, only those follow the call who are found fit to receive it. Then it would be no less true that “it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” because he called in the manner suited to those who followed the call.

To others, however, calling indeed comes, but because it was of such a kind that they could not be moved by it or were not suited to receive it, they can be called but not chosen. And would it not likewise be true that “it depends not on God who has mercy, but on the human being who wills and runs”? For the effect of God’s mercy cannot be placed in human power, as though he might have mercy in vain if a person did not wish it. If he wishes to have mercy even on such people, he must call them in a manner suited to them, so that they may be moved, understand, and follow.

“Many are called, but few are chosen” is therefore true. Those are chosen who are called fittingly; those who were not suited and did not conform themselves to the call were not chosen, because they did not follow it, although they were called. It is also true that “it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy”: even if he calls many, he has mercy on those whom he calls in the manner suited to their following. But it is false if someone says: “It depends not on God who has mercy, but on the human being who wills and runs,” because God has mercy on no one in vain. Whoever receives his mercy, he calls in the manner he knows to be suitable, so that the person will not reject the one who calls.

Here someone may say: “Why, then, was Esau not called in such a way that he would wish to obey?” We see that different people are moved to believe in different ways by the same things, whether shown or signified. For example, Simeon believed in our Lord Jesus Christ while he was still an infant, recognizing him when the Spirit revealed him to him. Nathanael, at the one statement he heard from him—“Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you”—replied: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel.” Much later, because Peter confessed this, he deserved to hear that he was blessed and that the keys of the kingdom of heaven would be given to him.

After the miracle performed at Cana of Galilee, which the Evangelist records as the beginning of the signs, when water was changed into wine, his disciples believed in him. He invited many to faith by speaking, yet many did not believe even after the dead had been raised. Terrified by his cross and death, the disciples themselves wavered; yet the criminal believed at that moment when he did not see him superior in works but equal in sharing the cross. [Col. 0482C] One of the disciples also believed after his resurrection, not so much through living limbs as through the recent scars. Many from the number of those who had crucified him—people who, while he was alive and performing miracles, had despised him—believed when the disciples preached him and performed such deeds in his name.

Since one person is moved to faith in one way and another in another way, and the same event, described in one manner, moves one person but not another, and moves one person in one description but not in another, who would dare say that God lacked a way of calling by which he could also have directed Esau’s mind toward that faith and joined his will to it—the faith in which Jacob was justified?

But if obstinacy of will can be so great that aversion of mind hardens against every manner of calling, the question arises whether that hardness itself is a divine punishment. For when God abandons someone by not calling him in the manner by which he can be moved to faith, who could say that even the Almighty lacked a way to persuade him to believe?

But why do we ask this, when the Apostle himself adds the answer? Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” The Apostle added this testimony to prove what he had said above: “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.” It is as though he were saying: “How do you teach this?” Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth”—clearly showing here that it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.

He therefore concludes: “So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” Yet the two are not stated in the same way above. For it was not said, “It depends not on the one who wills but on God who has mercy,” in the form, “It depends not on the one who wills or runs but on God who hardens.” Hence it may be understood that what he placed together below—“So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills”—can correspond to the preceding statement in this sense: God’s hardening consists in his not willing to have mercy, so that nothing is imposed by him that makes a person worse; rather, only that by which the person might become better is withheld.

But if this occurs with no distinction of merits, who would not break forth into the words that the Apostle himself put into his own mouth: “You will say to me then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’” The Spirit often finds fault with human beings, as appears throughout countless passages of Scripture, because they are unwilling to believe and live rightly. Hence the faithful, who do God’s will, are said to conduct themselves without complaint, because Scripture does not complain about them.

But “Why does he still find fault?” he says. “For who can resist his will?” This is asked when he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills. Yet let us look back at what precedes, and from there, insofar as the Lord himself helps us, direct our judgment. Shortly before he says: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.” Let this therefore be fixed and immovable in a sober devotion and steadfast faith: there is no injustice with God.

Let it be held with the greatest tenacity and certainty that the very fact that God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills—that is, that he has mercy on whom he wills and does not have mercy on whom he does not will—is the result of some hidden equity, unsearchable by human measure. This equity must also be recognized in human and earthly affairs and transactions; for unless we retained certain traces impressed by heavenly justice, our weak understanding would never be admitted into or aspire toward the innermost chamber and purest sanctuary of spiritual commands.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” In this drought of mortal life and condition, unless some exceedingly fine breath of righteousness were sprinkled upon us from above, we would quickly wither.

Therefore, since human society is bound together by giving and receiving, and what is given and received may be either owed or not owed, who does not see that no one can rightly be accused of injustice who demands what is owed to him, nor can the person who wishes to forgive what is owed to him be accused? This, as I said above, is an image—or a trace impressed upon human affairs from the highest summit of equity. All human beings, then, since, as the Apostle says, “In Adam all die,” and from him the origin of offense against God is transmitted to the whole human race, are one mass of sin, owing punishment to divine and supreme justice. Whether that punishment is exacted or forgiven, there is no injustice.

Debtors arrogantly judge from whom it should be exacted and to whom it should be forgiven. Thus those hired for the vineyard were unjustly indignant when as much was given to others as was paid to them. The Apostle therefore bluntly rebukes such shameless questions: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” For he answers God in this way when he is displeased that God complains about sinners—as though God compelled anyone to sin, whereas he merely does not extend the mercy of his justification to certain sinners. For this reason he is said to harden certain sinners: not because he drives them to sin, but because he does not have mercy on them—judging, by a most hidden equity remote from human understanding, that mercy ought not to be shown to them.

“For his judgments are unsearchable and his ways are inscrutable.” He complains about sinners as people whom he himself does not compel to sin; and at the same time, so that those on whom he has mercy may also receive this calling, when God complains about sinners they may be pierced in heart and turn toward his grace. He therefore complains justly and mercifully.

But if it is troubling that no one resists his will, because he helps whom he wills and abandons whom he wills, while both the one whom he helps and the one whom he abandons belong to the same mass of sinners, and although both owe punishment, punishment is exacted from one and forgiven to the other—if this is troubling, then: “Who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” Let this alone be held with unshaken faith: there is no injustice with God. Whether he forgives the debt or exacts it, neither can the one from whom he exacts it rightly complain of his injustice, nor should the one to whom he forgives it boast of his own merits. The former will render only what is owed; the latter possesses only what he has received.

That hardening of the ungodly demonstrates both what must be feared, so that each person may turn to God in devotion, and how great the thanks owed to God’s mercy, since by the punishment of some he shows what he grants to others. But if the punishment that he exacts from some is not just, then he grants nothing to those from whom he does not exact it. Because that punishment is just, and there is no injustice in God when he takes vengeance, who could sufficiently give thanks to the one who remits what, if he chose to exact it, no one could rightly say he did not owe?

“He also called us,” he says, “not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles”—that is, “vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory.” Not all Jews, but some from the Jews; nor all human beings from the Gentiles, but some from the Gentiles. For there is one mass of sinners and ungodly people derived from Adam, in which Jews and Gentiles, apart from God’s grace, belong to one and the same lump.

If a potter, from the same lump of clay, makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor—and it is evident that among the Jews some vessels are for honor and others for dishonor, just as among the Gentiles—then it follows that all are understood to belong to the same lump. “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved.” The remaining multitude, therefore, are vessels perfected for destruction. “For the Lord,” he says, “will make a decisive and abbreviated word upon the earth”—that is, by the brief compass of faith he saves believers through grace, not through the innumerable observances by which that multitude was burdened and oppressed in servitude.

Through grace he made his word decisive and brief upon the earth, saying: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light.” The same thing is said here shortly afterward: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart”—that is, the word of faith that we preach: “for if you confess with your mouth that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, while confession with the mouth is made unto salvation.

This is the decisive and abbreviated word that God made upon the earth. By this decisiveness and brevity the criminal was justified: with all his limbs fixed to the cross, and possessing these two things freely, he believed with his heart unto righteousness and confessed with his mouth unto salvation; and immediately he deserved to hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” His good works would have followed if, after receiving grace, he had lived longer among human beings. Yet they did not precede grace, so that he might merit that same grace; he was transferred from theft to the cross and from the cross to paradise.

“And as Isaiah foretold,” he says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.” What he says here, “He had left us a seed,” is expressed there as, “A remnant shall be saved.” The rest, however—vessels of destruction—perished by the punishment they deserved. The fact that not all perished like Sodom and Gomorrah was not due to their merit, but to the grace of God, who left a seed from which another harvest might arise throughout the whole world.

The same is said shortly afterward: “So also at the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.” “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.” What then? “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were hardened.” The vessels of mercy obtained it; the vessels of wrath were hardened—yet from the same lump. For who can investigate the works of God, who from the same lump condemns one and justifies another?

Free choice of the will has great power. Indeed, that is true—but in those sold under sin, what power does it have? “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish.” We are commanded to live rightly, with the reward set before us that we may merit blessed life forever. But who can live rightly and work well unless justified by faith?

We are commanded to believe, so that, by the gift we have received—the Holy Spirit—we may be able to work well through love.
