But who can believe unless he is touched by some calling—that is, by some testimony borne by things? Who has it within his power to have his mind touched by such a sight that his will may be moved to faith? And who embraces inwardly something that does not please him? Or who has it within his power either to encounter what can please him or to be pleased when he encounters it?

When, therefore, the things that advance us toward God please us, this is inspired and granted by God’s grace; it is not acquired by our inclination, effort, or merits of works. For he grants and bestows the movement of the will, diligence in striving, and works fervent with love. We are commanded to ask, so that we may receive; to seek, so that we may find; and to knock, so that it may be opened to us.

Is not our prayer sometimes so lukewarm—or rather, so cold and nearly nonexistent—that we do not even perceive this in ourselves with sorrow? For if we do feel sorrow over it, then we are already praying. What else, then, is shown to us except that the one who commands us to ask, seek, and knock also grants us the ability to do these things?

“So then it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” since we can neither will nor run unless he admonishes and arouses us.

But if there is some election, so that we understand the statement “A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” in this way—not that the elect of those justified are chosen for eternal life, but that those who will be justified are chosen—then that election is certainly so hidden that it cannot at all appear to us in the same lump. Or, if it does appear to some, I confess my weakness in this matter.

For I have nothing to observe when people are chosen for saving grace, if I am permitted to examine this election by some line of reasoning, unless we add either greater intelligence or fewer sins—or both—and, if it seems appropriate, honorable and useful learning. Whoever, then, is entangled and stained by the fewest sins—for who can be free of all?—and is sharp in intellect and polished in the liberal arts seems suitable for election to grace.

But when I have established this, the one who chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, will laugh at me. Looking at him and corrected by shame, I will laugh at many—those more chaste than certain sinners, and orators in comparison with certain fishermen.

Do we not observe many of our faithful walking in God’s way who are in no way comparable in intelligence—not merely to certain heretics, but even to actors? Again, do we not see certain men and women living without complaint in conjugal chastity, yet either heretics or pagans, or even people within the true faith and the true Church so lukewarm that we are astonished to see them surpassed by prostitutes and stage performers suddenly converted—not only in patience and self-control, but also in faith, hope, and love?

It remains, then, that wills are chosen. But the will itself, unless something occurs that pleases and attracts the mind, cannot be moved in any way. That something should occur, however, is not within human power.

What did Saul desire except to attack, drag away, bind, and kill Christians? What a savage, furious, blind will! Yet, struck down by a single voice from above, when a vision of such a kind confronted him that his mind and will, their violence broken, might be turned and corrected toward faith, he suddenly became from a remarkable persecutor of the Gospel an even more remarkable preacher.

And yet what shall we say? Is there injustice with God, who exacts from whomever he pleases and gives to whomever he pleases, who never exacts what is not owed and never gives what belongs to another? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. Why, then, is it so with one and not with another? “O man, who are you?” If you do not repay what is owed, you have reason to be grateful; if you repay it, you have no reason to complain.

[Col. 0487A] Let us simply believe, even if we cannot comprehend it, that the one who made and established the whole creation, spiritual and bodily, orders all things in number, weight, and measure. “His judgments are unsearchable and his ways are inscrutable.” Let us say “Alleluia” and praise the song, and let us not ask, “Why this?” or “Why that?” For all things were created in their proper time.

*(Also from the second book of Augustine to Simplicianus.)*
The Devil, moreover, wishing to harm the righteous man Job, was indeed the devil in his will to do harm; yet he was asking power from the Lord God to do so, saying: “Stretch out your hand and touch his flesh,” although, if permitted, he would have done this himself. For in this way he was asking for the permission itself, and he called it the Lord’s hand: his own hand permitted by the Lord, that is, the very power which he wished to receive.

This agrees with what the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “This night Satan has asked to sift you like wheat.” Thus the evil spirit of God was said to be the minister of God for doing evil to Saul, which the omnipotent Judge judged that he ought to suffer. For that spirit was not God’s in the will by which it was evil; but the creature by which it had been created, and the power which it had received—not from itself, but from the Lord of all, by his justice—was God’s.

Likewise, human anger is passionate and not without anguish of soul; but the anger of God, of which it is said in the Gospel, “But the wrath of God remains upon him,” exists while he himself perpetually remains in tranquility, exercising vengeance with wondrous justice through the creature subject to him.

Here he has now returned, in due order, to the Apostle’s exposition. For the same Lord is Lord of all, “rich toward all who call upon him.” For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” The one God of all, rich in mercy, possesses salvation from which he may bestow upon both peoples. How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? He asks this question and then answers it himself: “But how will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent?” For prophets were never sent to those people. As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!”

The feet of those who announce these things run well and are beautiful. But the feet of those who run after the vanities of the world are ugly. Yet not all obey the Gospel. If even those to whom these preachers were sent did not obey, how will those obey who have not heard? For Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” He says “who?” because of the difficulty involved.

Therefore, faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. The Apostle’s response is directed especially against the Jews, to whom Christ was promised both through the Law and through the prophets, but who refuse to believe that he has come. By the testimonies that follow he teaches that this is so, and that they will have no excuse.

“But I ask: Have they not heard?” Indeed, “their sound has gone out through the whole earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” He wishes this testimony to be understood allegorically as referring to the voices of the prophets.

“But I ask: Did Israel not know?” Did Israel not know that the nations were to be saved? But when they read the testimonies, they thought that they referred to proselytes, not to the whole world.

Moses is the first to say: “I will provoke you to jealousy.” Since you ought to have provided an example, so that the nations might imitate you and, abandoning their idols, worship the true God, now imitate them, since they no longer worship idols.

“Through a non-nation.” Before they believed in God, they were not God’s people. It is as though he says: “I call those who were not my nation, and they will believe in me to provoke you, so that you may rejoice if you become their equals, though you ought to have been superior to them.”

It is as though someone had an disobedient son and, in order to correct him, gave half his inheritance to a servant; then, when the son had reformed, he would rejoice if he deserved to receive the other half.

“I will provoke you to anger through an ignorant nation.” An ignorant nation is one that did not possess God’s Law; or it was not a nation, because through idolatry they were dead in sins, as he says concerning the unbeliever: “He has already been judged.”

But Isaiah dares to speak, and says: “I was found by those who were not seeking me.” He dares because he does not fear the Jewish people. These are the nations that were not seeking God and did not even possess his Law, through which they might seek him.

“I appeared openly to those who did not ask about me.” The nations did not ask God, but idols and astrologers.

But to Israel he says—he who had such a favorable opinion of the nations; see what he says about the Jews. Therefore, it was foretold not only that the nations would be chosen, but also that unbelievers from Israel would be rejected.

The extension of the hands signifies the cross allegorically: “All day long I stretched out my hands toward a people who did not believe and contradicted.” Throughout the whole time he displayed wonders, and yet you did not believe. Consider how great is the compassion of God: like a nurse who wishes an infant to make progress and walk, though it does not yet walk, stretches out her hands so that it may come to her; and while it desires to reach her, it learns to walk.

Thus God continually summoned the Jews to worship him by his benefits, but they remained in their lameness.

## CHAPTER XI

I ask, then: Has the Lord rejected his people? Since he had sufficiently humbled them, he now speaks like a good teacher, lest he appear to aggravate them further while reproving them, and consoles them as it were.

Certainly not. He did not reject them in such a way that he would no longer receive them if they believed through the Lord’s gift. For I too am an Israelite. If he had rejected them all completely, he would certainly not have drawn me to himself. Even if, so to speak, no other one of them had believed except me, God’s promise spoken to Abraham would have been fulfilled in me; I do not even mention the many thousands who believed through his gift.

“From the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.” Not from proselytes.

God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. “Whom he foreknew,” that is, whom he predestined to be saved, because many from that people believed through the gift of Christ’s grace. [F.: quia, “because.”] What is future with him has already been accomplished. Therefore he undoubtedly foreknew them; and because he foreknew them, he predestined them. But to predestine is to arrange what he himself was going to do.

Or do you not know what Scripture says about Elijah—how he appeals to God against Israel? “Lord, they have killed your prophets; they have dug down your altars; and I alone have been left, and they seek my life.”

He says this so that the nations might not again become proud because many from their own number had believed, whereas only a few from Israel had believed in comparison with the multitude of the nations.

But what does the divine response say to him? The prophets knew only what was being told them. For if they knew everything, they would more properly be called divine. The king also said to Jeremiah: “If there is a word of God in you.” “I have left for myself seven thousand men.” If so many escaped the notice of the prophet, how many do you think can escape your notice who are to be saved?

It should be noted that he did not say, “They have been left,” but “I have left for myself.” Those who have not bent the knee before Baal.

Just as God is denied by evil works, so an idol is worshiped. For not only does the one who sacrifices to it serve it, as he says concerning greed, which is the service of idols.

Thus also in the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. Therefore, just as not all perished then, so now some are saved. The time of election is now; but whoever believes now will receive his reward then.

But if it is by grace, it is not from works. The difference between grace and predestination is that predestination is the preparation of grace, while grace is the gift itself once bestowed.

What the Apostle says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works,” refers to grace. What follows, “which God prepared so that we might walk in them,” refers to predestination.

And lest they say, “Under Elijah there were righteous people, but these are sinners; how, then, does he call them chosen?” he adds: Since grace made them believers, they have been saved freely.

Grace is called grace because it is given freely, without preceding merits. For grace precedes, not as something owed but as a free gift, so that through it good works may be produced. Otherwise, if good works came first, grace would be rendered as though it were payment for works, and thus it would no longer be grace.

Whoever says that God’s grace is preceded by the merit of good works in human beings, and that God’s grace is given on the basis of merits, is a Pelagian. For it is not grace if it is not given freely, if it is returned as something owed to those who have earned it—God forbid. God has gone before us and precedes us; we do not precede God.

Scripture often testifies to this in many places, placing the grace of faith before works—not in order to abolish works, but to show that works do not precede grace; rather, they follow it. Thus no one should think that he received grace because he had acted well, but that he cannot act well unless he has received grace through faith.

Otherwise grace is not grace. If something belonging to a person comes first, by which he is saved, then salvation is no longer free. Grace is called grace, as he said, because it is given without preceding merits and because it freely forgives sins.

What, then? What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain. The whole of Israel did not obtain it because it was not seeking through faith, but thought that it was justified merely by the Sabbath and circumcision, while disregarding the other commandments. Thus, when the vessels of mercy attained righteousness, the vessels of wrath were blinded.

“But the election obtained it.” The election is the faithful people who obtained mercy, whom God chose. “I,” he says, “chose you; you did not choose me.” “God knows those who are his.” And also: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world.”

This is that election by which he chose in Christ, before the foundation of the world, those whom he wished, so that they might be holy.

But the others were blinded, as it is written. They were blinded through unbelief, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” “He gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear.”

There the prophet was speaking about unbelievers and sinners. “God gave them”—that is, God handed them over to the desire of their own heart. For God’s handing over means abandonment.

He gave them the spirit of compunction that they desired, because they had always been unbelieving toward the words of God and distrustful; therefore, by God’s just judgment, they were abandoned.

So also now Christians who doubt the resurrection, the reward, and Gehenna have received a spirit of compunction infused by the devil.

“Until the present day.” Until they turn to God. Thus he treats, in the passage addressed to the Corinthians, of the veil of the flesh: “When they have turned to God, the veil will be taken away.”

And David said: “Let their table become a snare, a trap, a stumbling-block, and a recompense for them.” He says this about those who gave the Savior vinegar and gall to drink. Yet Peter says to them: “And now, brothers, I know that you did this through ignorance; repent, therefore, and let each one of you be baptized.” And Paul himself shortly afterward says: “And they too, if they do not persist in unbelief, will be grafted in.”

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and keep their back always bent.” As long as they remain such.

I ask, then: Did they offend in such a way that they would fall? Certainly not. That is, did they fall eternally? Certainly not. Although they fell by their own will, they can nevertheless rise through the illumination of God’s grace.

“But through their trespass there is salvation for the nations.” Let the Jews imitate them. God loved the nations so greatly that, for the sake of the Jews’ salvation, the nations might be saved, so that the Jews, seeing the nations called to the kingdom of God, might be ashamed and converted.

Now if their trespass is the riches of the world—if their trespass benefited you so greatly that you became their equals—how much more would their conversion benefit you if many of them, or all of them, should wish to believe, for the sake of instruction?

The trespass of the Jews enriched the nations, so that without the labor of the Law they might become their coheirs and fellow members of the body, as he himself recalls in the Letter to the Ephesians.

“And if their diminution is the riches of the nations, how much more their fullness!” If the few who believed among them benefited you so greatly, how much more would it have benefited you if very many had believed!

I speak to you Gentiles, who have believed from the nations. He wishes to show that through them he earnestly seeks the salvation of the Jews.

“For as long as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles”—as long as I am in the body—“I will honor my ministry.” I will make my ministry illustrious and honorable if I win not only the Gentiles to whom I was sent, but also the Jews by my example.

“If somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy.” Here he calls the Jews his flesh, since he came from their race.

“If in any way I may conduct myself so that they imitate me and desire to be such as I am, and thus save some of them.” For he wishes all, or at least some, to be saved, so that the statement may be fulfilled: “The remnant will be saved.”

“For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world”—he repeats what he had said—“what will their acceptance be, except life from the dead?”

From where did the acceptance of the nations come, except from the death of the Jews? From the dead Jews, the apostles became the life and acceptance of the nations.

“If the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump.” The few who believed are holy; and all can become holy if they believe.

“And if the root is holy, so are the branches.” The root is the patriarchs; that is, the first and the last who believed from among them are holy.

“But if some of the branches have been broken off”—those who refused to believe in Christ—“and you, although you were a wild olive, have been grafted in among them.”

They were not broken off so that you might be grafted in; rather, you were grafted in because they were broken off.

Although you were a wild olive, you were grafted in among them. You were an olive tree, but uncultivated and wild, from a race without the Law and the promises.

It is contrary to nature for a wild olive to be grafted into a cultivated olive; but through God’s power all things are possible, and the work does not contradict its maker.

“And you became a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive.” The root is the Fathers; the richness is Christ.

“Do not boast against the branches.” Do not rejoice that they were broken off.

“But if you boast, it is not you who carry the root, but the root that carries you.” If you boast, you will hear that they do not stand through you, but you through them. You did not give them life; they gave life to you.

You say, then: “The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” They were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith.

You say that they were broken off so that you might be grafted in. Let us see whether this was the reason. They were broken off through unbelief, but you were grafted in through faith, freely and without any merits of your own. Do not think that he accepted your person and cast them away without cause.

“Do not be high-minded, but fear.” Do not think proudly against them; rather, grieve and pray for them.

“For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.” If he did not spare those who are from the seed of Abraham because they were unbelievers, neither will he spare you if you are unbelieving in any respect, since you were a wild olive.

Unbelief is not of one kind. Every sin descends from unbelief, as is shown in Scripture: “Because they did not believe the words of God,” even though they believed in God as sinners.

See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God—against those who assert that there is one God who is just and another who is good, and against those who deny that God punishes sinners.

“Toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, God’s goodness.” They were justified, and he showed mercy and kindness to you—not on account of any merits of yours. Therefore all presumption ought to cease.

“If you remain in his goodness”—in the faith that was granted to you through his goodness—“otherwise you too will be cut off.” If you become unbelieving, you too will experience severity; and they will experience goodness if they believe.

“And they too, if they do not persist in unbelief, will be grafted in.” But if they persist in unbelief, they will not be grafted in. He shows that by God’s gift they can return.

“For God is able to graft them in again.” Among human beings it is impossible to restore withered branches; but with God all things are possible.

For if you were cut from a natural wild olive—one that had long ago, in your ancestors, forgotten the natural Law and degenerated from nature, so that the habit of sinning continued and increased through successive generations, as though they were naturally bitter—not only through original sin but also through actual sin—and were grafted contrary to nature into a good olive, how much more will these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive?

As has been said, it is contrary to nature to graft a wild olive into a cultivated olive, since the root is usually more suited to the branch than the branch to the root.

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers. He says this also so that the Gentiles would not become proud against the Jews.

“This mystery”—this secret—“so that you may not be wise in your own eyes.” Do not say according to your carnal wisdom: “God chose us because of our merits, but rejected them; he rejected them in order to choose us.”

“For blindness has come upon Israel in part.” Blindness came upon those who did not believe; Jacob also represented them by his lameness.

“Until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved.” When the fullness of the Gentiles has believed, the Jews who are found believing will be understood as being saved at the end of the world.

The fullness of the Gentiles is the multitude of believers from every kind of people—not absolutely all nations, according to the figure of synecdoche.

As it is written in the prophet Isaiah: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns away ungodliness from Jacob”—something that no one previously had the power to do.

“And this is my covenant with them.” The new covenant, which Jeremiah promises: “When I take away their sins.” Having been cleansed through baptism, they will receive the new covenant.

“According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake.” They are enemies because I have made them your equals, and because I preach to you while they forbid us to speak to the nations.

What does “according to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake” mean, except that their hostility, by which they killed Christ, benefits the Gospel? He shows that this came about by God’s disposition, since God knows how to use even evil things well: the persecution of the Jews served the Gospel.

He permitted them to do as much as was necessary for the Gospel.

“But according to the election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers.” If they believe, they are beloved.

Another interpretation: Those who were chosen from among them by predestination love through grace; those who were left in their error exercise hostility for the sake of the Gospel. Jacob also represented them by his lameness.

“For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance”—that is, they are fixed permanently, without alteration.

All who belong to this calling are teachable by God. Nor can they say, “I believed, so that he might call me,” because the Lord does not repent of having made a promise to the seed of Abraham.

Another interpretation: Faith was given through the grace of Christ without any preceding merit or labor.

God’s repentance means change, as we read: “It repents me that I made Saul king”; or: “The Lord swore, and he will not repent,” and so forth. That is, this priesthood will not be changed as the Jewish priesthood was changed.

So here also the gifts and calling of God are without repentance: that is, “those whom he predestined, he also called.” God will not change the judgment of his calling. Rather, those whom he chose in his foreknowledge before the foundation of the world, he will say to them: “Come, you blessed of my Father,” and so forth.

“For just as you once did not believe God”—when they still believed—“but now you have obtained mercy because of their unbelief.” Not through your merit.

“So they now have not believed because of the mercy shown to you.” The mercy shown to the nations is Christ, so that they too may obtain mercy.

They did not believe to such an extent that they too are not justified by works but by mercy, just as you are, whenever they believe.

“For God has enclosed all in unbelief”—those whom he found in unbelief. That is, he enclosed all the Jews and the nations, because previously the Jews were sinners but not unbelievers; after they did not believe in Christ, they became equal to the nations. Thus all need mercy, and all obtain it.

“So that he may have mercy on all.” He did this for the purpose of having mercy on all, because he found all equally unbelieving.

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom”—he therefore praises the wisdom of God, who waited so long according to his foreknowledge until all were equally in need of mercy, so that no one might have anything from which to boast that he had been justified by works, which he had not even performed.

By God’s just judgment no one understood this. Therefore, marveling at such a profound mystery—that the nations had been admitted without preceding merits, while the Jews, after so much unbelief, had been abandoned—the Apostle cries out: “O the depth!”

And if the Apostle says this, how much more ought we to say it, rather than scrutinize God’s judgments? We should flee to this testimony as to a harbor and hold fast to it as to a very strong anchor.

“And the knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!”

It should be considered that God’s knowledge is placed above all riches. “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” “Who?” is placed here because of the difficulty.

“Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him?” Who has first done anything good without God, so that he would not glorify God’s mercy but boast that he received it by his own merit? Even our existence and life are due to his goodness, not only our faith, because in all things we are preceded by his mercy.

And let us know that if we do anything good, we already receive it from him to whom no one has first given anything.

“For from him and through him.” Not only was every creature made from nothing by him, but every good thing is from him, as James says: “From whom every perfect gift comes.”

“And in him they are.” Everything is concluded in him; he must be glorified by us.

“To him be glory forever. Amen.” If everything belongs to him, then so does faith.

## CHAPTER XII

I appeal to you, therefore, brothers. He begins the subject: since he had spoken about the mind of the Lord, he now teaches what they ought to be—how they ought to present themselves with God’s help, so that they may be deemed worthy to possess the mind of the Lord.

“Through the mercy of God”—by which you have been saved, for they had nothing greater.

“To present your bodies.” How much more your souls? Not rams and goats, which nevertheless were offered alive and without blemish.

“A living sacrifice”—alienated from every death of sin.

“Holy”—pure and chaste. For he says: “Sanctify yourselves from women.”

“Pleasing to God”—not merely to human beings.

“Your rational service.” Everything must be done wisely, because even if someone is perfected, if the knowledge of God is absent from him, he will be counted as nothing.

“And do not conform yourselves to this age.” Do not again become like the children of the world, since you have become children of God.

“But be transformed in the renewal of your mind.” Renew your mind through God’s gift, the mind by which the body is governed and all its members directed. In this way the body also will be renewed. When you have done this, then you will be able to recognize the will of God and his mind.

“So that you may prove what is the will of God.” This is revealed only through a new mind, to those reborn by grace.

“Good, pleasing, and perfect.” Good, better, and best.

“For I say, through the grace that has been given to me.” I do not speak from my own understanding; the grace of Christ speaks in me, as though forbidding me to think otherwise than the divine Law commands.

“To everyone who is among you”—to priests and teachers, whose example the others should follow—“not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety.”

He thinks too highly who investigates those things that the Law does not say, as Solomon says: “Do not seek what is too high for you.”

“To each one as God has distributed.” It should be noted that he calls the Holy Spirit God: to the Corinthians he says that he distributes gifts to each one as he wills.

“A measure of faith.” For just as in one body we have many members, we should recognize that even faith itself is given to us by God.

“And all the members do not have the same function.” The eye cannot hear, nor can the ear see.

“So we, though many, are one body in Christ.” He urges unity and peace. One person cannot have everything, lest he become proud if he needs no one.

Therefore, do not be saddened because one person does not possess what he sees another possessing. “But individually we are members of one another.” Let us provide to one another what we have, so that by giving to one another what we possess, charity may be confirmed more and more.

“Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us.” Hear about gifts, and be silent about merits. It is a gift of the New Testament, which does not come from us. A future glory is promised to all believers.

But even now, in those reborn, the Lord distributes distinctions of virtues through the giving of grace.

“Whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith.” Faith, not the Law; but that faith which works through love. This love, however, is poured into us through the Holy Spirit.

Or he may mean that true prophecy which accords with faith.

“Or ministry, in ministering.” Priestly ministry.

“Or the one who teaches, in teaching; the one who exhorts, in exhortation.” The one who teaches is greater than the one who exhorts. The ignorant too can exhort according to their abilities, but teaching belongs to teachers.

Up to this point he has discussed gifts. From here he teaches how we should use the gifts we have received properly.

“The one who gives, in simplicity.” Everything should be given simply—that is, with a pure heart. For whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward.

“The one who presides, with diligence”—over the Church or over the brothers.

“The one who shows mercy.” Mercy should be shown especially toward the sick, although it is general.

“With cheerfulness.” For God loves a cheerful giver and certainly hates a sorrowful one.

“Love without pretense.” Whoever is false in charity wrongs God, who is charity. It is a great fraud if you mix lead with gold; how much worse if, so far as you are able, you corrupt a heavenly good with the evil of hypocrisy?

There should be complete purity in a Christian, as it is said: “God is light.” A Christian should also possess serenity of mind.

It belongs to servants in the present life to be afraid and, in another’s absence, to slander. There is also the command: “Let us not love in word, but in deed and in truth,” so that, if necessary, we may even die.

“Hating evil”—whether an evil deed or the evil actions of human beings.

“Clinging to good.” As it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good.” Uproot evil so that you may sow good.

“In brotherly love.” As though born from one womb, love one another in this way.

“Kindly toward one another.” As it is written: “Considering one another superior.”

“Outdoing one another in honor.” Above all, this must always be held fast: consider yourself inferior to everyone. In this way humility and patience will be preserved, because whatever you suffer from someone greater, you will bear contentedly.

“Not sluggish in diligence.” Not only should the person responsible for the Church be energetic and eager, but you too should be concerned for one another’s progress and life.

“Fervent in spirit.” We are fervent in spirit when we flee carnal actions, because the Lord is nauseated by those who are lukewarm.

“Serving the Lord.” Not the world or vices, but the Redeemer.

“Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, persevering in prayer.” For the joy of future hope, be patient in tribulation.

“Consider it all joy,” he says, “when you fall into various temptations.”

“Blessing at all times.” In prosperity and adversity.

“Sharing in the needs of the saints.” Remember the works by which the saints served God; share in them and minister to those who despised all they possessed for Christ’s sake, so that your abundance may supply their need and their abundance likewise supply your need.

“Pursuing hospitality.” Thus Lot compelled even unwilling visitors to stay as guests. And as he says: “Do not forget hospitality, for through it some won approval, having received angels as guests,” along with the other testimonies.

“Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse.” Lest we think that both can be done, we must not merely refrain from cursing in deed but must also bless, as the Apostle Peter says: “Do not repay evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but on the contrary, bless.”

“Rejoice with those who rejoice.” But now this is perversely done: we weep with those who rejoice. If someone is praised, we envy him; if someone falls, we rejoice. If we were one body, we would grieve over one member being cut off from our body.

“Weep with those who weep.” The Lord is moved to tears by Mary’s weeping, providing us an example—not on account of Lazarus, nor because of the unbelief of the Jews, since they did not first disbelieve his signs at that time, as some think.

“Weep with those who weep”—“we ought to,” is understood. “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.”

“Having the same mind toward one another.” Just as you respond to your own need, so should you respond, in perfect charity, to the need of your brother.

“Not thinking lofty thoughts.” He thinks proudly who does not reserve his wrongs for God.

“But associating with the humble”—that is, with humility.

“Do not be wise in your own eyes.” Do not glory in human wisdom, but be foolish in this age so that you may be wise, as it is written: “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law.”

“Repaying no one evil for evil.” It is human wisdom to seek how you may return evil for evil. But in this world it is considered foolishness if, when someone strikes your cheek, you offer the other also.

If you possess such great patience and kindness, you will be approved not only before God but also among human beings.

“Providing what is good not only before God but also before all people.” Take care only that you do not do this in order to please both God and human beings—or rather, only human beings.

“If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.” Whether “if it is possible” means that it depends on you, do what is yours: live at peace with friends and enemies alike, and say with the prophet: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful.”

Therefore, we ought not to wrong anyone or harm anyone out of resentment, but rather to wish them salvation and conversion to the Lord.

Let the possibility of doing good be the reward of your will; but if it cannot be done, let the blame belong to another’s disagreement.

You, however, should declare with the prophet: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful.” You fulfill this in this way when you wish what is useful and salutary for your enemies, because through such a wish the fruit remains with the one who makes the wish, even if the other side neglects the affection.

“Do not defend yourselves, beloved.” That is, do not defend your own side with words and thereby prepare quarrels and hatred; rather, conquer the anger of the one who rages by yielding.

For to escape the force of another’s malice is to overcome it. In this way you either soothe unreasonable hostility by reason or evade it through humility.

“But give place to anger.” Either flee or permit yourselves to be harmed.

For it is written: “Vengeance is mine.” I will avenge the injury as my own, not yours, because “whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye,” and “whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” and so forth.

“I will repay,” says the Lord.

According to the historical sense, he promises them hope of vengeance, so that he may in this way provoke them to patience and mercy. Thus they might not deny what God denies to no one.

“But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink.” That is, so that you may confound evil by kindness and correct the ungrateful person through grace.

“For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head.” When he understands that coals have been heaped upon him through the undeserved mercy you have shown him, he may afterward be converted and love the one whom he previously hated.

For it is not mercy if you show it for the purpose that something worse may happen to the person for whom you are commanded to pray as for an enemy.

“Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.” In the thoughts or movements of the soul, the person is said to have conquered who draws the other over to his own side, whether the other is a heretic or a pagan.

Therefore, if he receives from you a return of evil, he has conquered you and made you subject to his vice by a like retaliation. But if through your patience you make him cease from anger or injury, you have conquered; and by winning your neighbor from sin to salvation, you have triumphed.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0496D]

Every soul [must be subject] to the authorities. This is directed against those who thought they ought to use Christian liberty in such a way that they would show honor to no one or pay taxes to no one. He speaks to them in this way in order to humble them. But it may also be understood of ecclesiastical authorities, so that we may be humble toward priests.

Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities. Ecclesiastical authorities, or those of the world.

For there is no authority except from God. And those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God. He does not want a Christian to be proud, lest he suffer not for Christ but because of pride, as he says elsewhere: “See carefully how you walk, redeeming the time, because the days are evil”; just as he himself redeemed the time when he said, “Most excellent Felix.” Not for that reason [is he] just, for it is granted to him according to his desire, because Solomon says: “For authority has been given to you by God; but although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly.” For he will be appointed to judge you justly, so that you may fear and, even so, may not sin. How, then, did the prophet say: “Because they have reigned, and not through me”? Through money and magicians they reigned by ambition.

And those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves. For they are condemned because of their pride.

For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. As he says concerning a heretic, when he has been condemned by his own judgment.

But to the evil. The evil person fears, whereas the good person does not fear to die [or: “to die for justice,” if *pro* is to be read instead of *si*] for justice.

But do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it. [Col. 0497B] The condemnation of the wicked is the praise of the good; for by nature everyone knows both that innocence deserves a reward and that wickedness deserves punishment.

Do what is good, and you will have praise from it. Even if not from it, nevertheless from what it does. For either you act justly, and a just authority will praise you, or, even if an unjust authority condemns you while you act justly, the just God will crown you. Therefore, hold fast to justice; live well. Whether it condemns or acquits, you will have praise from it.

For it is God’s minister for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid. For it is concerned for your peace. For it does not carry the sword without cause. The sword of the Spirit, which Peter carried, and Paul himself; and it has its function in your case if you sin. This is to be understood spiritually. For it is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil.

Therefore you must be subject, as in the case of Ananias [Col. 0497C] and Sapphira, and the Magus, because God wishes to correct sinners.

Not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience. Not only lest he become angry, but also because he knows that even from the righteous honor is owed to the rulers of your people, who can rise up even without cause; and also lest you be condemned because of the conscience of sin.

For this reason you also pay taxes. “Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.” For whoever has the means to pay tax, how can he not be subject in those matters that have been appointed for him by God?

This also applies to priests. For they are God’s ministers, serving for this very purpose. “The laborer is worthy of his wages.” Thus they might believe, lest Christ seem to have taught pride more than anything else: while they punish sinners, they are shown to minister to God.

Pay to all what is owed: tax to whom tax is due. Incline your ear to the poor and repay your debt; almsgiving too is called a debt.

To whom revenue is due, revenue. Our revenue is what we give to those who pass by, or what we distribute to those who sit beside the road and are in need. *Vectigal* is so called from *vehere*, “to carry.”

To whom fear is due, fear; to whom honor is due, honor. How, then, can he say, “Do not fear anyone besides God”? Rather, he says, conduct yourself so that you fear no one: for fear of God drives out human fear.

Owe no one anything except to love one another. This alone must remain: the debt of love, which is always necessary.

For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. According to the Lord’s saying, the neighbor is every person who needs mercy.

“For you shall not commit adultery; [Col. 0498A] you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not give false testimony; you shall not covet”; and if there is any other commandment, it is restored in this word:

“You shall love the Lord your God perfectly,” on account of idolatry, “and your neighbor as yourself,” on account of injustice. For injustice arises from this: that we love ourselves more than others.

“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love of one’s neighbor does no evil. The whole law and the prophets are contained in this word: just as you do not want evil done to you, so you want good done to you.

Therefore love is the fullness of the law. The completion of the law, because not doing good is also evil.

And knowing the time, because it is now the hour. Therefore you ought not always to be little children and infants, as he says in the Letter to the Hebrews. He enumerates, or recapitulates. He has put “hour” for “time.”

Now let us rise from sleep. [Col. 0498B] Let us rise from the sleep of laziness and ignorance. For the knowledge of God is already shining. For now our salvation is nearer. As the knowledge of God draws near, salvation draws near; as salvation draws near, perfect understanding draws near, and one becomes firmer through believing.

When we believed it—when we first believed. The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. He compares ignorance to night, but knowledge to day.

Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. With ignorance, let us cast off also the works of ignorance, and let us put on the weapons of knowledge—that is, good works.

“Whoever does evil hates the light, but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God.”

Let us walk honorably as in the day. Knowing that we are always seen by the eyes of God. Every sin is committed more freely at night; in the day, however, one cannot sin freely [Col. 0498C] because of fear and shame.

Not in revelries. A revelry is a gathering for a banquet. We, therefore, have not such but spiritual revelries from the Apostle: “When you come together, each of you has a psalm,” and so forth.

Not in drunkenness, bedrooms and immoralities, strife and rivalry. “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts perhaps be weighed down by excess,” and the other testimonies concerning drunkenness.

Immorality follows drunkenness, for drunkenness is the material of lust. But even if these things are absent, and jealousy and envy are present, we must not glory in ourselves, as James proves by saying: “Do not boast and become liars against the truth,” and so forth.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh. Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as he walked: let Christ alone be seen in us, not the old human being.

In desires. Solomon says: “Do not go after your desires,” and again: “If you give the desire of your soul, it will make you a joy to your enemies.” What the flesh desires must absolutely not be done.

## CHAPTER XIV

But receive the one who is weak in faith. Here he begins to discuss those among them who had believed in Christ: some were perfect in faith, while others were still less firm.

Those who were perfect also ate sacrificial meats, if someone served them, just as they ate other foods without distinction and equally. Others, however, hesitated and avoided them as unclean; they are told to eat vegetables.

Nevertheless, some think that this chapter was spoken concerning those who had believed from the Jews and from the nations. Those who had believed from the Jews still regarded certain meats as unclean according to the law, and considered certain days holier, such as the Sabbath or new moons. They are commanded, as weak people, to eat vegetables, which everyone eats without distinction.

Those who were stronger in faith—that is, those who had believed from the nations—believed that all meats and all days were equal. To them it is said to regard nothing as common through him, except to the one who considers something common, as he adds below: “I know and am persuaded in the Lord that nothing is common through him,” and so forth.

Receive him. Accept him, or bear with him. Indirectly he rebukes those who thought themselves strong because they used meat.

Not in disputes over thoughts. Do not judge according to your thoughts one whom the law does not judge.

For one person believes that he may eat everything. This is the person who is older, or who has already subdued the flesh, or who has such great faith that he cannot be moved toward lust or sin.

But the one who is weak should eat vegetables. Weak according to God, whether through youth, bodily heat, or faith.

Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat. And let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats. There was rivalry between them: those who did not eat judged those who ate as carnal, while the latter mocked the former as wishing to die quickly and as weak because they ate sacrificial meats.

For God has accepted him. In the same way that he has accepted you.

Who are you to judge another’s servant? As Saint James says: “The one who judges his brother judges the law,” [Col. 0499C] and declares himself wiser than the law.

He stands or falls before his own master. Whether he lives or dies: the one abstains for God, and the other eats for the Lord.

But he will stand, for God is able to make him stand. God, who made the three youths fed on legumes appear better than those who ate from the king’s table, can also do these things: make someone remain longer in the body, fast, or abstain from meats.

For one person judges one day to be different from another, while another judges every day alike. The Jews could not judge one day against another, because no law was established concerning fasting, but each person can or wishes to fast in his own way; the one who fasts more has the greater reward.

Let each abound in his own judgment. In such a matter alone, let each person act as he thinks best, or as he can, or as the health of his body permits.

The one who observes the day, observes it for the Lord. And the one who eats, eats for the Lord. He observes the day for the Lord who fasts for God, or who abstains while devoting himself to wisdom.

For he gives thanks to God. And the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God. He proclaims the Gospel through which thanks are returned to the Lord: for he eats for God, so that he may have the strength to build up the body of Christ—not for gluttony or lust.

For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. Through his example many are saved and give thanks to God. For the one who gives thanks with his voice gives thanks alone, but the one who does so by his conduct makes many give thanks.

For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we die for the Lord. Blessed is the one who does everything for God. [Col. 0500A] We, on the contrary, either live for ourselves or die for human beings.

Therefore, whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. For Christ died and rose again for this purpose: that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead. The coming of God will find the living and raise the dead. Therefore nothing prejudges the matter—whether he finds you alive or raises you—provided only that you are just.

But why do you judge your brother? By what authority? As though he ate not for God but for his appetite.

Or why do you despise your brother? As though he abstained for human beings.

For we shall all stand. Then the Lord will judge concerning these things, how and what we have done.

Before the tribunal of God. Do not doubt that Christ is God, who will judge. For it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”

He proves from Scripture that all will render an account to God alone. Therefore each of us will render an account to God for himself. He will not render it for another, nor will he render to human beings an account for himself concerning matters about which the law is silent. For if he remains silent while seeing someone sin, he will render an account for that person. “I have appointed you as a watchman over the house of Israel,” it is said to the prophet.

Therefore let us no longer judge one another. What you have done up to this point in ignorance is sufficient. Rather, judge this: not to place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother.

Here he subtly proceeds to abstinence and says that they ought not to eat, although they are strong, lest younger or weaker people eat by their example and fall or be scandalized.

I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common. They were not to say: “You call common what God created.” I do not say this because I consider anything common.

Through him. Through Christ all things have been cleansed. For whatever is not excepted among the Jews’ food was considered common.

Except to the one who considers something common: to that person it is common. In his conscience.

For if your brother is grieved because of food—he did not say because of fasting—whether you force him to eat or provoke him by your example, so that he eats unwillingly what he cannot endure, you are no longer walking according to love.

You no longer love your neighbor as yourself if you do not consider his ruin as though it were your own.

Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. He did not say, “By your abstinence.”

Therefore let our name not be blasphemed. It is blasphemed if disputes arise because of foods.

For the kingdom of God is not food and drink. We are not justified through food. He did not say “fasting and sobriety,” but “food and drink.”

But righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Yet these are acquired more easily through fasting. Where there is righteousness, in the sense that one should love one’s neighbor, there is also peace; and where there is peace, there is joy, because where there is dissension, there is sadness.

For whoever serves Christ in this is pleasing to God and approved by human beings. No one can doubt that he is holy.

Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace, so that we may not judge one another. And let us guard one another in the things that make for edification.

Abstinence is edification; for food, even if it does not destroy a brother, does not edify.

Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food—the human being whom God made.

All things indeed are clean. He repeats this so that he may not seem to condemn creation. But it is evil for the person who eats through causing offense. What is clean itself becomes evil for him.

The food of another, not his own.

It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine, he explains what causes the weak person to stumble. Nor to do anything by which your brother is offended or scandalized. Whatever food or drink scandalizes another must not be taken.

Or becomes weak—in faith. Wine and women make wise men apostatize.

You have faith; keep it to yourself before God. If you think yourself faithful in this matter, eat in such a way that no weak person sees you. This cannot and ought not to be done in the sense that one should eat shut away in confinement.

Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. He does not consider in what respect he proves himself weak, but fears that another may perish.

But the one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned. If he considers what he has said, he judges. He says “distinguishes,” and judgment arises from discernment, while discernment arises from judgment—or rather, they are the same thing.

Because it is not from faith—the faith that works through love. Whatever is not from faith is sin. Whatever does not edify is not from faith, and therefore is sin.

## CHAPTER XV

But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak. If you are truly strong, act as I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak.

And let us not please ourselves. Let not we ourselves but our neighbors praise us, because the Lord destroys the bones of those who please themselves. As I please everyone in every way, seeking not what is useful to me but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved.

Let each of you please his neighbor. For he cannot build up the one whom he has not pleased by his example, because those who are destroyed by examples cannot be built up by words.

For good, for edification. For Christ did not please himself. He shows the manner of pleasing, lest we please for empty glory. At the same time, by saying “for good edification,” he shows that there is also a bad kind.

Whoever is Christ’s disciple does not seek what is his own. For Christ died for the salvation of others and endured the bitterest insults from those who said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple”; and, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross and save himself,” and so forth.

But as it is written: “The insults of those who insulted you fell upon me.” Whatever insults are directed against the saints for God’s sake are directed against God, as he says: “All day long it is said to me, ‘Where is your God?’” Or: “Whoever despises you despises me.”

For whatever was written was written for our instruction. [Col. 0501D] Therefore nothing was written without cause, whether the punishments of sinners, the merits of the righteous, or the temptations of the righteous. For they were known both to God and to themselves, but their deeds are related so that we may imitate them in all things.

So that through patience. So that we too, for the edification of our brothers, may similarly endure these things if necessary.

And consolation. The consolation of our patience is this: if we know that those whom we endure were also endured by the Lord and by the saints, as he says: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you.”

Let us have the hope of the Scriptures. Through the consolation of the Scriptures we await future hope with patience, as it is written: “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no scandal for them.” Therefore those who make use of consolation cannot despair or be moved from the faith.

Now may the God of patience and consolation give you. Not of impatience or dissension, but of patience and consolation, unto completion, because without him we are nothing; for my patience comes from him.

To think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ. Let each person seek the salvation of the other as his own, so that all may persevere with one accord in the faith.

So that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is truly honored when he is praised with one mind and a harmonious voice. “If two or three are gathered in my name,” and so forth.

Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received you, for the honor of God. “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ.” If he bore our weaknesses and received us, the ungodly, because he was God, [Col. 0502B] how much more ought we to bear one another, since we are alike?

For I say that Christ Jesus. Again he brings Jews and nations to unity.

I agree with you that Christ came to you, first promised to you through the prophets, and that the nations were called because of the mercy of God. Nevertheless, you have now become one body through the death of Christ.

To have been a minister of the circumcision, for the truth of God. For he did not come to be ministered to but to minister and to give his life as a ransom for many.

To confirm the promises made to the fathers. For Christ had been promised to them, as he himself says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

But the nations are to honor God for his mercy. For the nations are unequal in giving thanks, according to the fact that God granted them mercy freely; or the nations were called to mercy because of Israel, so that they might emulate them.

As it is written: “Therefore I will confess to you among the nations, Lord, and I will sing to your name.” He shows that greater thanks are to be returned to God by the nations: “For to whom more is forgiven, he loves more.” And he removes Jewish arrogance while teaching that the salvation of the nations too was foretold, although they themselves had never heard it.

In these words Christ confesses that they have obtained mercy, because they too are in his body.

And again he says: “Rejoice, nations, with his people.” And again: “Praise the Lord, all nations, and magnify him, all peoples.” For you have been called to salvation together with them.

And again Isaiah says: “There shall be a root of Jesse.” His son is David, from whose seed came Mary, from whom Christ was born. And this passage is appropriate here: “The ruler shall not fail from the thighs of Judah”—against the Jews, because Christ truly came, in whom all the nations believed—“and he who arises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope.”

So that they might not say that this was spoken concerning proselytes.

Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy—in whom we all hope. All spiritual joy among the faithful ought to exist in hope of the future.

And with peace in believing, so that you may abound. There is joy for all where there is peace; but where there is dissension, there is no joy, but sadness.

In hope, in the power of the Holy Spirit. The consolations of the saints’ hope are the powers of the Holy Spirit.

But I myself also am confident about you, my brothers. A good teacher provokes progress by praise, so that they may be ashamed not to be what they are thought to be.

That you yourselves are also full of love. [Col. 0503A] Lest he seem to have rebuked them as quarrelsome, dissident, and foolish, he shows at the same time that Christians ought always to admonish one another.

Filled with all knowledge, so that you can admonish one another. [That is, with the knowledge] of both the Old and the New Testament.

But I have written to you more boldly, brothers, in part. Rather, for this reason I had greater confidence in writing: because I know that, as prudent people, you quickly understand the argument. “Rebuke a wise person, and he will love you.”

As though bringing you back to your memory, knowing how wise you are. A wise person even understands by signs.

Because of the grace given to me by God. Not because of human gifts, or so that I might be praised by you, but so that I might fulfill my office.

That I should be a minister of Christ Jesus to the nations, recalling to him servants who were once fugitives.

Sanctifying the Gospel of God. Immediately showing by my example that it is holy, since I minister it with such great fear. For some treat as insignificant what they preach as divine; and thus it happens that a holy thing appears not to be holy if it is not made holy. Hence it is said: “Sanctify the fast,” that is, “make it holy” or “show it to be holy.”

So that the offering of the nations may be acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit. By my example the nations may become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified and received not by fire but by the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “For it sat upon the apostles like fire.”

Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus. “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.”

Toward God. Although there may be disgrace among human beings.

For I will not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me for the obedience of the nations. I will not dare to say that I have done anything by my own power and that Christ has not worked everything through me, so that he might remove presumption from us.

By word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders. He himself spoke through me, and he himself performed signs by working powers.

In the power of the Holy Spirit. He was speaking here not of works but of the powers and signs that were performed.

So that from Jerusalem and in the surrounding region as far as Illyricum I have filled the Gospel of Christ. The Gospel is filled when the nations also believe. Thus the sufferings of Christ are fulfilled in Paul when he suffers at the hands of the nations, and the Gospel of Christ is spread everywhere.

But I have preached this Gospel not where Christ had already been named, lest I build upon another’s foundation. Not everyone who builds upon another’s foundation builds badly, for he may build with gold. Here he censures the false apostles, who always went to those who already believed and never to the nations, because they could not perform powers [or something similar must be supplied]. He shows that he labored perfectly, having both laid the foundation and built upon it.

But as it is written: “Those to whom he was not announced.” He shows that his labor was foretold beforehand.

“They shall see, and those who have not heard about him shall understand.” Christ is seen in the apostles through powers, just as the Father is in Christ, who says: “Or believe because of the works, for the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

For this reason I was hindered very much from coming to you. But now, having no further place in these regions. He explains what he had said at the beginning of the letter: “But I was hindered.”

And having a desire to come to you. It should be noted that desire can also be good.

For many years already. What necessity [Col. 0504A] caused him to be detained for many years?

When I begin to set out for Spain. He had indeed promised this, but, as God was arranging matters, he did not go.

I hope that, as I pass through, I shall see you, and be escorted there by you. For you conduct yourselves in such a way that I will have no opportunity to remain longer among you.

If I have first enjoyed your company in part. “In part,” because you have already believed; I intend to strengthen you. No length of time satisfies love.

Now I shall go to Jerusalem. This alone remains for me: that I should come.

To minister to the saints. There were saints in Jerusalem who, having despised everything and cast it at the feet of the apostles, devoted themselves to reading, prayer, and teaching. What, then, were they like, that the Apostle himself should go to minister to them, and should wish his offering to be acceptable to them if they deigned to receive it? He shows that this benefits not so much those who receive as those who give.

For Macedonia and Achaia approved. They judged that this was useful to themselves.

To make some contribution. To contribute something toward expenses.

For the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. They are called the poor among the saints because they are poor for the Lord’s sake.

For it pleased them, and they are their debtors. He urges them toward this work and shows that it was not without reason that it pleased them.

For if the nations have become participants in their spiritual things—because they received teachers from them and became companions of the root and richness of the olive tree—they ought also to minister to them in material things. Each person should give from what he has in abundance.

When, therefore, I have completed this and delivered this fruit to them, I shall go through you to Spain. If you conduct yourselves generously, I shall teach you well; for as the disciple progresses, so the teacher is provoked to teach, as it says there: “Our mouth is open to you.”

But I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ. Either because you are abundantly prepared to reap, or because Christ is blessed through my arrival.

Therefore I beseech you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ. After James had been killed, they prayed for Peter, and he was freed from prison, lest they themselves suffer loss.

And by the love of the Holy Spirit. The love of the Spirit of which he wrote to the Galatians—the love that makes us pray for one another through the Holy Spirit.

That you assist me in prayers to God on my behalf. For the persistent prayer of many has great power.

That I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, and that the offering of my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem. Either so that all may believe, or so that, while ministering to the faithful, I may not fall among unbelievers and be unable to come to you. For through the Spirit he foresaw that he would suffer many things there, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles.

That I may come to you with joy. I shall come with joy if my offering has been accepted by them, and I shall speak the word of God more freely. For sadness of spirit greatly impedes teaching, as Ecclesiastes says: “Slander troubles even the spirit of the wise.”

By the will of God, and may I be refreshed with you. If God wills—not if I proceed according to my own will without his will.

Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen. The God of peace dwells only among the peaceful. Fittingly he ended in peace, having recalled two peoples to harmony.

## CHAPTER XVI

I commend to you Phoebe, our sister. [Col. 0505A] This is now almost after the conclusion, as usually occurs at the end of a letter.

Who is in the service of the Church. Just as deacons are, or in the ministry of the word; for at that time women too taught within their own sex, as we read concerning Priscilla, whose husband was called Aquila.

Who is in Cenchreae. They say that Cenchreae was the port of Corinth.

Receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints. That is, for the Lord’s sake.

And assist her in whatever matter she may need you. For she herself also assisted many, and me personally.

And help her, whether with money or with some other consolation, because she too, as long as she had the means, assisted very many.

Greet Prisca and Aquila. They confirmed Apollos and taught him, as we read.

My fellow workers in Christ Jesus. They assisted in the work at which Paul labored, namely, in the word.

Who risked their own necks for my life. By approving my teaching, they exposed themselves to dangers.

To whom not I alone give thanks, but also all the churches of the nations. Through them I was preserved.

And their household church. He shows that wherever the brothers are gathered, there is a church.

Greet Epaenetus, beloved by me. He greets those through whom the Romans had believed; their names are not Latin but Greek.

Who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ Jesus. He was the first from Asia to believe.

Greet Mary, who labored greatly among you. In the word, for at that time she also prophesied.

Greet Andronicus and Julia [Vulgate: Junia], my kinsmen. From the Jews.

And my fellow prisoners. They had suffered tribulation together with Paul.

Who are noble among the apostles. In both mind and teaching. They were considered noble among the others sent to the Romans, through whom they would believe or be strengthened by their example.

Who were in Christ before me.

Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.

Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ Jesus, and Stachen [Vulgate: Stahyn], my beloved. They too believed before I did.

Greet Apelles, approved in Christ. Approved or perfected.

Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus.

Greet Herodion, my kinsman.

Greet those who are from Narcissus. This is a city or place.

Who are in the Lord. For not all those from Narcissus were in the Lord.

Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord.

Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored greatly in the Lord.

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. In age, not by birth.

Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.

Greet Phedologus and Julia [Vulgate: Philologus and Julia], Nereus and his sister, and Olympias, and all the saints who are with them.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you. Not falsely or deceitfully, as Judas betrayed the Savior. For this reason peace is first announced from the Church, to show that the one who is to share in the body of Christ is at peace with everyone.

Now I ask you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause dissensions. Those who dissent from the teaching were from the circumcision. They destroyed fasting and abstinence and taught new moons, Sabbaths, and festivals for the sake of the belly.

And they make offenses contrary to the teaching that you learned; avoid them. For through these things you can give offense.

For such people do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly, like Jovinianus.

And through smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent. Speaking elegantly and presenting their arguments well.

For your obedience has been reported in every place. If you obeyed those whom you ought not to have obeyed, how much more will you obey us? For this reason they came to you, knowing that you could quickly be deceived. Obedience is good, but only in what is good. For it is not always good, since evil things are often taught.

Therefore I rejoice in you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil. Think what is good by doing it; avoid evil by not knowing it; and the enemy will be placed under your feet.

“Be as shrewd as serpents and simple as doves.”

Now may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet quickly. Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions—that is, so that they may not rule over you and you may walk freely with all your members over them.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

Timothy, my fellow worker, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, greet you. This is always Paul’s subscription.

I, Tertius, who wrote the letter, greet you in the Lord.

Gaius, my host, and the whole church greet you. Tertius is a name, not a number.

Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and Quartus the brother. He clearly says to Timothy that this Erastus was a disciple and preached.

Now to him who is able to strengthen you with signs and powers, according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ. Live according to the preaching of Jesus Christ.

According to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages, but now made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures, according to the command of the eternal God, for the obedience of faith among all the nations.

The mystery of the calling of the nations had long been hidden in the law. It has now been revealed through the preaching, or revelation, of Christ and through Paul’s Gospel, by the testimonies of the prophets. For although the prophets foretold this beforehand, they themselves did not know how it would happen. [Col. 0506D] They could believe that the nations would be admitted to the faith as proselytes.

Known to God alone, who is wise. God alone foresaw these things beforehand, or he alone is wise by nature. How is he alone good, when a human being is also called good? We can be good or wise by God’s gift; he is so by nature.

It should be noted that he did not say “to the only wise Father,” but “to the only wise God,” who is the eternal Trinity.

Through the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen. Through Jesus Christ, not from ourselves.

# THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0505]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0505D]

The Corinthians are Achaeans. They too heard the word of truth from the apostles and were overturned in many ways [Col. 0506D] by false apostles. Some were led astray by the verbose eloquence of philosophy, others by the sect of the Jewish law.

The Apostle recalls them to true evangelical wisdom, [Col. 0507A] writing to them from Ephesus. Corinth is the metropolis, and therefore what he writes to them he writes to all Achaia.

## CHAPTER ONE
Paul. This is a name of authority. Called an apostle of Jesus Christ. Called on the way, so that he might be an apostle. By the will of God. Called and enlightened by the will of God, he believed. And Sosthenes the brother. Not an apostle, but he was one of them and knowledgeable. To the Church of God, which is at Corinth. There is a church that is not of God. Sanctified. Through baptism. In Christ Jesus. His grace, through which we are saved. Called saints together with all. He shows what the Church of God is: it has been cleansed by the saving washing. He rebukes the saints so that they may rebuke the others, since they themselves are not without sin; thus the Savior says to the disciples concerning the Pharisees, “See and beware of all greed”—although they possessed nothing.

Who call upon the name of the Lord Jesus [Col. 0507B] Christ in every place, both theirs and ours. To call upon is to call inwardly; this is permitted to all, but belongs especially to priests, as in the passage, “Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, calling upon my name.” And David says, “And Samuel among those who call upon the name of the Lord.” For he was a priest, and he succeeded to the priesthood, and he offered sacrifices; concerning him it is said according to the historical account: “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest.”

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. It should be noted that he always places grace before peace.

I give thanks to my God always for you, in the grace of God which has been given to you in Christ Jesus. I do indeed give thanks that you possess knowledge, but I want you to know what sort of knowledge it is: knowledge that agrees in every respect [Col. 0507C] with the catholic faith. As is his custom, he first wins them over.

Because in everything you have been enriched in him. In every teaching, by the gift of God through wisdom, which established the prophets and the friends of God. In every word and in every knowledge. Both of the Old Testament and of the New.

Just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you. The testimony of Christ, who said, “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.” Thus nothing is lacking in any grace. As Solomon says, “All things came to me together with her,” that is, with wisdom.

As you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Who, as though absent, is not now seen. He will also confirm you to the end, blameless on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. As the Prophet says, “Establish me in your words,” and also, “Great peace belongs to those who love your name, and there [Col. 0507D] is no stumbling-block for them.”

God is faithful, through whom you were called. Because faithful God has confirmed you. Into fellowship with his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. John indicates this fellowship when he says, “For God is light, and there is no darkness in him. If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie.” And Paul says, “If we die together, we shall also live together; if we endure, we shall also reign together; if we are companions in conduct and sufferings, we shall be companions also in glory.”

But I exhort you, brothers. Thus far the preface has been in praise. From this point he explains the cause of the dissension.

By the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In whose name you will see signs being performed. That you may all say the same thing, and that there may be no divisions among you. That you may think or confess one and the same thing. [Col. 0508A] But that you may be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment.
