If you both think and express one thing, then you will be able to be perfect.

For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. How did the Apostle believe reports about people who were absent, when it is written, “Do not believe a vain report,” along with many other passages? But he had this grace: that he knew what absent people were doing, as he says to the Colossians, “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order.”

Now I mean this: each one of you says, “I belong to Paul,” or, “I to Apollo,” or, “I to Cephas.” He was saying this in the person of the apostles about the false apostles, who had ensnared them through worldly wisdom, because each one claimed to belong to whichever teacher’s doctrine he loved, although they held different doctrines. [Col. 0508B] If this must not be said even of the true apostles, how much more must it not be said of those who were nothing!

But I belong to Christ. Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? A few were saying what all ought to have said. The body is divided when its members disagree. This may also be said to those who, following Christ’s example, wish to imitate Abraham: Was Abraham crucified for you? And likewise the Lord’s saying, in which he teaches that we ought not to ask what he will command another disciple; for he said to Peter, “What is that to you? You follow me.”

Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? These people therefore possessed the sacrament of baptism, but through contention and zeal they were turning it into schism; and, thinking according to the flesh, they believed differently about God. In their carnal understanding they fashioned for themselves whatever sort of God they wished, and thus believed in him as something so different from what God [Col. 0508C] is as vanity differs from truth, because “the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God.” Of such people he says, “They are carried about by every wind of doctrine.”

I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, lest anyone should say that you were baptized in my name. I baptized also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else. For Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize. This happened in such a way that I baptized none of you; for perhaps you would have said that I baptized in my own name.

Not with eloquence of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. They empty the power of the cross who glory in human wisdom, which the cross condemned. For the word of the cross is the preaching of the Gospel.

Of Christ crucified. To those who are perishing it is foolishness. To unbelievers [Col. 0508D], who do not understand the power of God, it seems foolishness to say that the Son of God was crucified; but to the faithful it is understood to be the power of God, since he conquered both the devil and death. But to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God. He saved them by pouring faith into them.

For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent.” It was fulfilled at the coming of Christ. Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? By choosing fishermen, he rejected philosophers. Where is the investigator of this age? The one who, by his wisdom, searches with others into hidden matters, such as secret things and the natures of individual beings.

From where comes this wisdom that God rejects, when all wisdom is from the Lord God? But this particular wisdom, worldly as it is, does not descend from above; it is earthly. [Col. 0509A] Therefore it is rejected by the Lord as foolish, because it thinks itself to be something and by its own wisdom to know the hidden things of God. But this wisdom is natural and demonic.

Of such wise people God says, “Because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent.” Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish? For because the world did not know God through wisdom, although God’s wisdom made all things and in it the Maker himself ought to have been known—and although he had given them wisdom in order to know him—it pleased God to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching, which was regarded by them as foolishness.

As the Jews also ask for signs. Following the custom of the prophets, although they ought to have recognized him even without signs, they did not believe when they saw them.

And the Greeks seek wisdom. The reasoning of human wisdom. [Col. 0509B]

But we preach Christ crucified. He shows that their wisdom differs greatly from his teaching.

To the Jews a stumbling-block. It is a stumbling-block to the Jews if we preach that the very one whom they crucified is the Christ. It is a stumbling-block for them to hear of Christ dead, just as they said, “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever.”

But to the Gentiles foolishness. They do not understand that this was the mercy of God, which was regarded as foolishness. For unless you believe, as the Prophet says, you will not understand.

But to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Whoever does not believe this is plainly ignorant of it; but once he has believed, he understands that what he had thought weakness is power, because in believing they understand that it is the mystery of godliness.

If Christ is the power of God, [Col. 0509C] then he is eternal. Christ is therefore eternal, because elsewhere he says, “His power, divinity, and wisdom are also eternal.” Heretics, not understanding this, blaspheme the Father as imperfect when they say that the Father once existed without the Son. Therefore he existed without power, without the Word, without wisdom, without justice. Let them recognize how foolishly they speak: God’s power, because of the signs; God’s wisdom, because of the teaching.

Because what is foolish in God is wiser than men. What seems foolish in God is wiser than all human beings, because those who were delivered through the Lord’s cross could not be saved by their own wisdom. It is like saying that a lawyer’s rustic speech is wiser than the speech of a most learned countryman.

It was judged to be God’s foolishness when they heard that God had suffered. But this was wiser.

And what is weak in God is stronger than men. The death which not even giants were able to escape was overcome by a crucified man, taken up into God.

For consider your calling, brothers. Test in yourselves what I am saying. For not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. Few wise people believed, because through the pride of worldly wisdom many desired to submit to the wisdom of God.

But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are. This means that God chose the people of the Gentiles, who were not the people of God, in order to destroy the Jewish people, who gloried in being God’s people. [Col. 0510A]

The boasting of these three classes is always condemned, as it is written: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches.”

The Lord himself also fulfilled in himself, for our example, what he had spoken through the Prophet. Finally, by being born from a poor woman he rejected riches; by not learning letters he rejected the wisdom of the world; by being handed over, he did not resist, although by one word he could have overturned the whole world. Yet he showed that human strength is nothing.

Therefore let them humble themselves before God if they too wish to be chosen with the others. But he was saying all this against those who claimed to be of priestly descent, learned in the Law, and better than the apostles, and who were leading them astray in many errors of doctrine. This can be said against the Pelagians, [Col. 0510B] who say that they were saved by their own wisdom.

So that no flesh may glory in his presence. Those who glory in their own merits are carnal; but they will quickly fall, like the flower of grass.

But from him you are in Christ Jesus. If, therefore, you are from him, do not admire those whom he did not choose.

Who became wisdom for us from God, and righteousness. So that he might make us wise, righteous, and holy. This passage is directed against the Arians, who say that the Father once existed without the Son, who is wisdom.

And sanctification and redemption. Of our body at the resurrection.

So that, as it is written, “Let the one who glories glory in the Lord.” Not in this age, nor in his own merits, as do many who believe themselves to be Christians and are deceived by the Pelagian error.

## Chapter II

And when I came to you, brothers, I did not come [Col. 0510C] with superiority of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ. For I judged that I should know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Since he had shown that they ought not to admire human wisdom, he repeats his own example: he had not preached through human wisdom. What seems foolish among human beings.

And I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling. Not in boastfulness.

And my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power. Since these Corinthians were very argumentative, he feared that they might resist him, or that this too might seem to them some kind of philosophy and they might not believe. Therefore he showed the power all the more.

So that your faith might not be in the wisdom of men but in the power of God. Human wisdom [Col. 0510D] pleases for a short time, because it is temporal, like the human being himself; but the power of God is eternal, as God is. Therefore that faith endures which has been bestowed on a human being through the power of God.

We speak wisdom among the perfect. We too possess divine wisdom, but you were not able to receive it, because you are still nourished with milk and are shown to be little ones in faith.

Yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age. Whether kings, philosophers, or certainly the Jewish rulers, or the rulers of the opposing power.

Who are being destroyed. Together with their wisdom and teaching, when the grace of Christ arrives.

But we speak God’s wisdom. This is understood to be Christ, who was also predestined, as he says to the Romans. In a mystery, which has been hidden and which God predestined before the ages for our glory. Whether in the present reality or in the work before the ages, or because many prophets desired to see it; although they knew individual things, no one nevertheless knew it fully. [Col. 0511A]

Which none of the rulers of this age knew. Pilate and Caiaphas, or certainly all the chief priests. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

But, as it is written, “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him.”

The Lord of majesty became, both by merit and by nature, Lord of every creature; and Jesus was a man in whom God, in a certain manner, could be crucified. For this reason God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, because of the unity of the person. Thus God is said to have been crucified, and the Son [Col. 0511B] of Man to be in heaven, although when the Lord said these things he was bodily on earth.

Since, therefore, Christ is true man and true God, one person from two substances—man and God, and the same one King of glory and Lord of powers—he was not crucified with respect to his inviolate divinity; and he was crucified in his humanity because of the unity of the person. Thus, in a wondrous and inconceivable manner, God suffered, but divinity did not suffer.

But God revealed this to us through his Spirit. He did not reveal it to us on account of our merit, but by his grace; through faith in him we have received the Holy Spirit, who shows us the will of God.

For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known what belongs to God except the Spirit of God. Do not doubt that he is God, since he is said to know not only human things [Col. 0511C] but also the hidden things of God.

Now we have not received the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God. Whoever thinks about worldly things—that is, whoever stains and entangles himself with worldly things—has the spirit of the world and does not have the Holy Spirit.

So that we may know what has been given to us by God, which we also speak. Through his coming, passion, and resurrection, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, which we also proclaim to you. Hear that these things were given, and say no more about merits.

Not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit. We were not taught by philosophers but by the Spirit of God.

Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. Affirming them to spiritual people who are able to receive them.

But the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. Whoever does not have the Spirit of God is natural, because he lives in the manner of animals. He thinks that there is nothing after death, but that he ought to do what animals do: eat, indulge in pleasure, and die. [Col. 0511D]

For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand it because it is examined spiritually. It seems foolishness to him, first, that God was born, suffered, and rose again; and second, that one should despise what belongs to oneself, offer the other cheek, and so forth.

But the spiritual person judges all things. He judges such a man to be vain, tests and examines him; yet he himself is understood by no carnal person, nor is the spirit by which anyone acts.

And he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him? Now he fears that they may say, “All this has the mind of God which you have told us,” that is, the mind of God is not lacking in me, but in you the power to hear is lacking.

[Col. 0512A] But we have the mind of Christ. We who receive the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter III

And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal people. They are called carnal in a certain sense, having already been reborn through faith—not like those who were still sold under sin—as though he were saying: You were not able to receive what I was saying as spiritual people but as carnal people.

For the natural man—that is, the one who thinks according to man—is called natural from *anima* (“soul”), and carnal from *caro* (“flesh”), because the whole human being consists of soul and flesh. He does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, that is, what grace conferred by the cross of Christ gives to believers.

As to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able, but even now you are not able, [Col. 0512B] for you are still carnal. He shows that they are carnal not by an age of the flesh, but that those advancing in faith in Christ (proficientis; F.: proficientes, “those advancing”) will be able, because grace had already begun in those who had been spiritually born. Therefore they were already vessels made for honor, to whom it could still rightly be said: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” And if this is rightly said to such people, it is much more rightly said to those who have either not yet been regenerated in this way or have even been made for dishonor.

Let this one point alone be retained: that there is no injustice with God. Whether he gives or exacts a debt, neither can the one from whom he exacts rightly complain of his injustice, nor ought the one to whom he gives glory in his own merits. The former will return only what is owed; the latter has nothing except what he received.

Since there is jealousy and contention among you, blessed Peter says: “Therefore, [Col. 0512C] laying aside all malice and hypocrisy, like newborn infants, desire rational milk without guile.” If, then, those who have laid aside all malice, who have not yet done good, are called little ones, what are we to think of ourselves, in whom every kind of malice rules?

Are you not carnal and walking according to man? We must consider why they are called carnal. It is not that they act carnally, but that they act according to the sense of the flesh.

For when someone says, “I belong to Paul,” and another, “I to Apollo,” are you not human beings? Whoever has nothing greater than the other human beings walks according to man. That is, the one who loves only the person who loves him, and so forth.

But in this passage, for the sake of defending particular people, they are called human beings; he clearly shows that we ought to desire [Col. 0512D] to be more than human beings. When he reproves them for being human beings, because he knew that they had contentions, he wishes us to exceed human nature, while reproving them in this way:

What then is Apollo? What indeed is Paul? Ministers of the one in whom you believed. If we are nothing, how much more are certain others truly nothing—namely, false apostles?

And to each one as the Lord has given. I planted, Apollo watered. This too comes not from us but from God’s gift, who works in you. He gave us grace both to perform signs, through which you might believe, and to have Apollo confirm you by his teaching. For just as the one who plants does so in dry ground, so every teaching grows unless God’s grace waters it.

If both the plant and the fountain are God’s, why do you attribute anything to us as though it were ours? In saying this, he commends grace.

But God gave the growth. [Col. 0513A] See how he commends grace. Yet now people dare to speak blasphemies and attribute to themselves what belongs to God, although if he does not give the growth, every human being labors in vain.

Therefore neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one.

We are hired laborers; we work with tools that belong to another. Nothing is owed to us except the wages of our labor, because we work with the talent we received.

But each one will receive his own reward according to his labor. This is directed against Jovinian, who says that the reward of all is one and the same.

For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s agriculture. Fellow workers in the word, not in power; a field and harvest belonging to God.

You are God’s building. The building of God’s temple.

According to [Col. 0513B] the grace of God that was given to me. Not according to my own power.

As a wise architect. It belongs to a wise architect to lay the foundation. Thus the Apostle, first introducing the Corinthians to faith through the grace of God, set Christ as the foundation. If he is the foundation, how do the Pelagians say that a human being makes the beginning and that Christ completes it?

I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. If Christ himself is the foundation, how do the Pelagians blaspheme by saying that they came to faith in Christ through their own merits?

But let each one consider how he builds upon it. Let a straight and strong wall therefore rise, lest through evil conduct, like stones badly cemented, you fall from God’s building.

For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ [Col. 0513C] Jesus. No one can preach another Christ to you besides Jesus, in whom, believing with complete faith, stand firm.

If Christ is the foundation, where are those who say that some good can be possessed without Christ and arrogantly presume to attribute to themselves the faith by which one believes in Christ, without giving thanks to God, from whom it is recognized that faith has been poured into them?

But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, [Col. 0513D] wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest; for the day will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire.

There are three ranks of honor in the Church: good, better, and best; and three kinds opposed to these: bad, worse, and worst, which are compared with wood, hay, and straw.

Some understand this passage in the following way: the person builds gold, silver, and precious stones who, having distributed or relinquished his possessions, seeks either a monastery or lives removed from the activities of the world; or who lives among his possessions as though he did not possess them, holding them as property lent to him by another and ready to lose them for Christ’s sake, so that if persecution comes on account of God, he may be found free and prepared.

Conversely, the person builds wood, hay, and straw who is indeed a Christian and a believer and uses his goods well, but is entangled by excessive love of his possessions. When either persecution comes or an order is given that Christians must be deprived of their goods, if they do not deny Christ, they do not value their possessions more than Christ. But because they loved them more than they ought, when they lose them they do not lose them without [Col. 0514A] pain and tribulation. Therefore they are saved as through fire—that is, through tribulation.

And the fire will test the work of each person, whatever it may be. If anyone’s work remains, what he built upon the foundation, he will receive a reward. This means either the examination of judgment or the present tribulation, which is very frequently compared with fire.

Gold and silver become brighter in fire. But wood, hay, and straw will burn. If anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss. If someone teaches carelessly, whether by example or word, he loses his labor, because he makes his work weak.

But he himself will be saved. In his own righteousness. Yet as through fire. “As through” has its true meaning, as in the phrase, “As of the only-begotten from the Father.”

If the one who is righteous will be saved through fire, why was he not careful to make what he built upon the foundation secure and lasting? [Col. 0514B] What of those who build by speech but destroy by example?

Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Do you not know whose temple you are?

But if anyone violates God’s temple. Whether in individuals or in the whole Church. Note that here he called the Holy Spirit God, whose temple we are; because we are his temple, he who dwells in us is confessed to be God.

God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are. Whether by sinning against his own body, or by leading the people of the Church astray into perverse teaching, or certainly by destroying them through his own example.

The Novatians propose this in order to exclude repentance. They must be answered: If the baptized Corinthians sinned, and repentance is not admitted, for what purpose does he write to them and say, “So that you may have a second grace”? [Col. 0514C]

Saint Jerome said to the Galatians: “I know this one thing: whoever fornicates after the faith of Christ violates the temple of God.”

Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age. Let no one flatter himself, deceived by his own vanity.

To repay evil for evil. Let him become foolish, so that he may be wise. In this age the person who fulfills the Gospel by not repaying evil for evil is judged foolish. But he becomes foolish by his will, not by nature.

For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. There is nothing more foolish than for one who cannot avenge himself to wish to do so and not to reserve his injury for God. This ought also to be done by the person who is able to avenge himself in this world, or while he seeks an account from the one whom he is commanded to trust.

For it is written, “I will seize the wise in their craftiness.” Human craftiness accomplishes nothing [Col. 0514D] by which it can escape the hand of God. A rich man seems wise to himself, but a poor man of good sense reproves him.

And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain.” Verbose eloquence contributes nothing useful to salvation.

Therefore let no one glory in human beings, in false apostles, nor in anyone of high rank, whether king or priest.

All things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollo, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death. We are yours; you are not ours.

Whether things present or things future. For all things are yours. All things were created for the saints, as though possessing nothing and possessing all things. Or, if you wish to refer it to freedom, you may choose whatever you wish, whether death or life, things present or things future.

But you are Christ’s. [Col. 0515A] And Christ is God’s. Christ is God’s just as God is Christ’s, if you apply this to divinity, although he is speaking according to the humanity of the one who was anointed.

## Chapter IV

Let a person regard us in this way: as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Not as Christ’s equals.

Here the question now arises among stewards: how may one be found faithful? This is the voice of one asking: Do you now think that you are able to judge consciences?

But it matters very little to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; nor do I even judge myself. I did not desire a human day—that is, a time. Here “human day,” understood as a discerning mind or a wise heart that can judge, is not improperly taken.

For I am conscious of nothing. Of nothing evil. But I am not justified by this. At this time or on this day—or certainly, if no one reproves me, [Col. 0515B] I ought not for that reason to flatter myself or become elated. Or, if I have committed no crime, perhaps I have not been entirely free from minor faults.

But the one who judges me is the Lord. Before the day of judgment. Therefore do not judge before the time. Judge hidden thoughts, because a human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.

Until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts. For the Lord knows me better than either I or any human being knows me.

And then each person will have his praise from God. The truly praiseworthy person is the one whom God makes praiseworthy.

Now, brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollo for your sake, so that in us you may learn. So that you may take from us an example of humility.

Not beyond what is written. What is beyond is what is not written. Let no one be puffed up against another on behalf of another. That is, when contention has arisen, you are puffed up [Col. 0515C] over who is better.

For who distinguishes you? Of what importance are you? Here he turns to those puffed up with knowledge of speech.

Or certainly: Who distinguishes you from the mass of perdition, except God? For it is not your merits or your knowledge. It is said to a human being who presumes on himself: Who distinguishes you—from the vessels of wrath, certainly, from the mass of perdition, which through one person sent everyone into condemnation?

Who distinguishes you? And as though he had answered, “My faith distinguishes me, my purpose, my merit,” he says: What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it? That is, as though what distinguishes you were your own. Therefore the one who distinguishes you is the one who grants you the means of being distinguished, removing the deserved punishment and bestowing undeserved grace.

What do you have that you did not receive? [Col. 0515D] What do you have from yourself, except perhaps sin? For whether knowledge or anything good is in you, it is God’s gift. If you believe that it comes from yourself, it will be said to you: What do you have that you did not receive?

And this happens to you if you attribute anything to yourself and not to God—the Gospel saying that is spoken concerning the ungrateful: “For whoever does not have”—that is, from God—“even what he seems to have will be taken away from him.”

Therefore let us turn away from pride and give glory to God, from whom every good gift comes, lest, if we believe that either faith or good works come from us, we lose what we seem to possess.

But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it? As though you possessed something of your own.

Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you reign without us. Doctrine or knowledge. This is spoken in the spirit of one who rebukes, because they attributed to themselves what they appeared to be.

And would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you. You need nothing from us, or have needed nothing—either if you reigned and we reigned with you, or if you counted us as companions rather than teachers.

For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, as men sentenced to death. Either as those whom he promised in the Apocalypse to send at the final time for death, or as us, who have already been sent to the Gentiles.

For we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings. Everyone awaits our injuries or our contest—Christians and pagans alike—or perhaps he simply means the angels.

We are fools for Christ, but you are prudent in Christ. We endure all things for Christ, but you wish to be Christians in such a way that you do not lose worldly prudence [Col. 0516B] and suffer nothing for Christ.

We are weak, but you are strong in Christ. As though we could not repay in kind what worldly prudence is capable of.

You are noble, but we are ignoble. For the false apostles, or certain believers, were putting forward both their knowledge and the nobility of their lineage.

Until this very hour we hunger and thirst, we are naked and beaten. From the time we began to preach until the present, we have had abundance in nothing.

And we are unsettled. We have no fixed dwelling, or at least that is how it seems to you.

And we labor, working with our own hands. We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure. He worked in this way: he taught all day and labored at night, so that he might eat bread on the following day—not so that he might store up coins (solidi) by devoting day and night to such work, but [Col. 0516C] so that both he and his disciples might live from it.

We are blasphemed, and we entreat. We entreat on behalf of those who blaspheme us.

We have become like the refuse of this world. The righteous person is unclean in the eyes of the wicked.

The offscouring of all things until now. The most humble, rejected, and despised of all, a little rag.

I do not write these things to shame you, but I admonish you as my most beloved children. They could have been shamed if he had not consoled them. I am writing not for your shame but for your progress.

For even if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers. All those who are placed over people already born cannot be fathers.

For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel. You believed when I first preached the Lord to you.

Therefore I ask you: be imitators of me. It belongs to good children to imitate their parents in everything.

[Col. 0516D] For this reason I sent you Timothy, who is my most beloved and faithful son in the Lord. The more faithful he is than the others, the dearer he is to all.

He will remind you. He will teach you both through my letters and through his own example; for one without the other cannot be complete.

My ways, which are in Christ. My life, my course, and my labors. As I teach everywhere in every Church. My ways, teaching, and conduct, in which I walk everywhere consistently and receive from no one any gain or advantage belonging to the present time.

As though I were not going to come to you, certain people are puffed up. A person remains puffed up as long as the one who possesses true knowledge does not come—not the knowledge that is foolishness with God.

But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. The power of faith, which is found in the works of Christ, or in signs.

For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. The New Testament.

What do you want? He is a kind teacher, who places the correction of his disciples in their own will: if you do not amend your ways, I will come with a rod; but if you do, I will come in consolation.

Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness? With the rod of justice, which Peter used against Ananias and Sapphira, and Paul against the Magician. At the same time, it must be considered that this anger lies within our power, not that we lie within its power; and it is brought forth when an injury against God is avenged.

## Chapter V
Absolutely fornication is heard of among you, in the Church over which you preside—and such fornication as is not found even among the Gentiles: that someone has his father’s wife, having taken his father’s concubine as his companion. [Col. 0517B]

And you are puffed up. You are puffed up with empty knowledge, or pride, and you have no concern for those who are perishing, that they may be summoned and either corrected or rejected. And you have not rather mourned. Good shepherds have always wept for the sins of the people, as Jeremiah says: “Who will give water to my head?”—for he lacked not willingness but tears—“so that the one who committed this deed may be removed from your midst.”

Whether the one who committed it, or Satan, may be removed, provided he has no one through whom to work. Although absent in body but present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, the one who acted in this way, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with you assembled. This is so that no one might think he judged merely on the basis of hearsay. And with my spirit; by the judgment of my letters. With the power of the Lord Jesus. The power of the Lord will not be lacking either. [Col. 0517C]

To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that he may have power to receive him, and thus he may be converted, when he sees that he will have rest neither here in the flesh nor in the spirit hereafter. It must be guarded against, because the person who is excommunicated is handed over to Satan.

So that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus. But if Satan has not received power over the spirit while he corrects him, the matter is reserved for the judgment of the Lord alone.

Your boasting is not good, you who admit such a person into the Church. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Do you not understand that, by the example of one wicked person, many can perish, and that through the offense of one person God’s anger came upon the whole people among the Jews?

Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, just as you are unleavened. Let nothing of your former way of life remain. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Having been cleansed through baptism, let us pass from the vices of the world to the virtues of the Lord. [Col. 0517D]

Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators.

> **[Note: [Col. 0517] The passage enclosed between the two asterisks is afflicted by an irreparable textual corruption. EDIT.]**

Not the lamb, which was a figure of Christ—and they indeed ate unleavened bread for seven days—but we always do so, if we are sincere, since the world too was made in seven days.

> **[Note: [Col. 0517] The passage enclosed between the two asterisks is afflicted by an irreparable textual corruption. EDIT.]**

The lamb is slaughtered for us every day; Passover is celebrated every day—the lamb that has no leaven of malice and wickedness. Not in the fullness of the belly, which has no relation to God, but in simplicity of mind and purity of heart. For what is leaven except corruption of nature—the same thing made bitter from something sweet? [Col. 0518A]

Not, certainly, with the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or the rapacious, or those serving idols. Not with the fornicators among the nations. Otherwise you would have had to leave this world. You would have had to leave it in another manner, not in this way; or certainly, if in this way, it would have been better for you to die.

But now I wrote to you not to associate. This is exactly what I have now written to you: if someone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or a servant of idols, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or rapacious, he is not to be called a brother merely by name, but by his conduct.

But if someone is called a fornicator—a designation that is also found in the Old Testament: “He who joins himself to fornicators will be wicked; decay and worms will inherit him”—do not even eat with such a person.

For what business is it of mine to judge those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? Nor even that common meal which I permitted, if you wish to go with the Gentiles. [Col. 0518B]

For those who are outside, God will judge. Outside the Church are the Jews, heretics, and Gentiles.

Remove the evil person from among yourselves—not from the Gentiles, but from among yourselves.

## CHAPTER VI

Does any one of you dare, when he has a dispute against another? He has dared to act against the Lord’s command, which says: “If someone wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also.” Here it is understood that they were chiefly accused of fornications in the secular court, because he introduced this matter in the middle of his discussion of fornication.

To be judged before the unjust, and not before the saints? Here it is shown that the judges were Gentiles, since they are called unjust.

Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? As the Savior says: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” But what he said to those twelve, he said to all who would imitate them. For one of those twelve perished, and another who had not heard him succeeded in his place; and Paul and Barnabas were apostles. [Col. 0518C]

And if the world will be judged among you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Whether through you yourselves or through your example.

Do you not know that we will judge angels? Those angels who sinned against nature will be judged by those who, above nature, preserved chastity with God’s help. How much more matters of this world—that is, secular matters?

If, therefore, you have secular lawsuits, appoint those who are despised in the Church to judge them. Even those who are least in the Church can judge such matters—or certainly those who disregard injuries done to themselves. [Col. 0518D]

It should be noted that he calls “least” those who are not instructed in God’s law but in worldly matters.

I say this to your shame. I say what I am about to say so that such people may be ashamed.

Is there really no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? Is there not one? But brother goes to court against brother—and this before unbelievers. They double their sin: both because they litigate and because they litigate before unbelievers.

Indeed, it is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. First, because you despise Christ’s command; you already have sin.

Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? He speaks to those who inflicted the wrong, not to those who suffered it: you ought to endure it if someone has wronged you.

But you inflict injury and commit fraud—and this against your brothers. [Col. 0519A]

Or do you not know that the unjust will not possess the kingdom of God? They are not even permitted to repay injuries to their enemies.

Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those serving idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God.

Do not be led astray by supposing that punishment is due for many sins but not also for a single sin.

And such were some of you. Do not fear because of the past; only do not commit anything criminal after baptism.

But you were washed; but you were sanctified; but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. Washed in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, sanctified through the Holy Spirit. Here understand the whole Trinity. [Col. 0519B]

“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are beneficial. Since he is treating of fornication, he wishes to point out its material cause.

“All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything. It is lawful for us to eat and drink; but if we subject ourselves to feasting, what is lawful will itself lead us to what is unlawful—that is, to fornication.

The same may be understood of marriage, wealth, and other such things, which are not sins in themselves but can lead to opportunities for sins.

“Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food”; but God will destroy both this and those—that is, both the stomach and the food—and the person himself who is occupied with them.

But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. God is with you as long as you are with him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you.

God both raised up the Lord and will raise us up by his power. If he raised up the Lord, he will also raise us up by the same power. [Col. 0519C]

If we are his members, then we ought to sanctify our members, so that we may be worthy to remain in him.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? The whole Church is Christ’s body; individuals, however, are its members.

Therefore, taking Christ’s members, shall I make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not. He did not say “of a fornicator,” but “of a prostitute,” to show that the man belongs to the same crime and name as the prostitute with whom he fornicates, since men seem to sin less than women.

It should also be noted that he first takes away Christ’s members who is about to make them members of a prostitute. In this respect the fornicator is guilty of the greater crime, because he takes away Christ’s members and makes them members of a prostitute. [Col. 0519D]

Or do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her? “For the two will become one flesh.” Just as a man lawfully becomes one flesh with his wife, so also with a prostitute one flesh is made through illicit love.

But the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit. Just as the one who performs the works of the flesh is flesh, so the one who performs the works of God is one spirit.

Flee fornication. You see how serious it is.

Every sin that a person commits is outside the body. Every other sin can be committed by one individual, who cannot be called a body but a member; in fornication, however, two perish, and two can be called a body. It is therefore more serious where two perish than where one does, because the remaining sins can also be committed without a body.

But the one who fornicates sins against his own body. Some think this was said of the body of the Church; but he says “he sins against his own body.” [Col. 0520A]

Or perhaps he means that fornication is more serious, since he knows that it occurs among them in a form they considered light because it had become customary.

Or do you not know that your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?

For you were bought at a great price. The one who is not his own ought not to live for himself, but for the one whose blood purchased him.

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.”

If a person seeks continual service from a slave purchased for a small sum, how much more does the one who had nothing greater to give for us than himself seek it?

Glorify God. Act so that God may be glorified through you and through your works.

And carry the Lord in your body. So that we may carry the heavenly image. [Col. 0520B]

It should be noted that here he calls the God whom we are commanded to carry the Holy Spirit, whose temple he previously testified that our members are, saying: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.”

And now he says: “Glorify and carry God in your body”—certainly God the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER VII

Now concerning the matters about which you wrote. Asked about this, he replies: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.”

That was good which I proclaimed as the best. If, therefore, it is good for one who has a wife not to touch her, how much better is it if he has not married?

Incontinence is prevented by circumstances, age, and weakness; chastity, however, can always be preserved, with God as helper and guardian. Therefore what is eternal ought rather to be sought.

Why then does Scripture say, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth”? But now even the earth itself can no longer contain human beings. [Col. 0520C]

“But,” he says, “could he have made everyone from the earth?” He could, but he did not wish to. For he could also have made human beings winged or horned. But he made everything perfectly according to a reason known to himself.

Finally, he did not wish to make Eve from the earth, but from a rib.

But if you think this is the way it should now be for everyone, imitate Cain and the others who married their own sisters.

If this was therefore the case, let us believe that God ordered all things according to the foreknowledge by which he is God.

This too must be believed: if even now they marry according to the law, they do not sin. For the law permits marriage for the sake of children, not for the sake of lust.

In this respect human beings make themselves worse than animals: by showing that they have taken wives not for the sake of children, since they do not spare even pregnant women.

But the one who abstains solely for the sake of children, after the woman has given birth—while the infant is being nursed, and perhaps when childbearing has ceased because of age, he also ceases from marital intercourse—understands “not to touch” according to customary usage, not according to mere physical touch. [Col. 0520D]

But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.

Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.

He permitted fornicators to marry, so that the incontinent might not fornicate. It is as though a physician said to a sick man: “It would have been good for you not to eat apples”; and if he could not restrain himself but wanted to eat figs, the physician afterwards permitted him *duracina*.

> **[Note: [Col. 0519] It would probably be read *duracina*, from *duracinum*, which in French is *bigarreau* [a type of cherry]. EDIT.]**

Only let him not eat something from which he would die.

Therefore perfection is to be praised; but for the one who cannot achieve it, the marital remedy is to be given.

The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does, because she voluntarily deprived herself of her freedom. [Col. 0521A]

Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

Let husbands recognize that they are not permitted to acknowledge any woman other than their wife, since they are mutually subject and indebted to one another on equal terms.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and then return again to the same relationship.

The incontinent person cannot devote himself to prayer.

Moreover, continence is praised not only in the New Testament but also in the Old Testament. When God was about to descend upon Mount Sinai, he commanded the people to sanctify themselves by abstaining from women for three days. How much more will the one who has wished always to be chaste be able to see God?

Likewise, the priest withheld the holy bread from David until he knew that David was clean from women; and Peter commands people to abstain even from what is lawful.

Let Satan not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. Let one person not withdraw while another commits fornication, giving Satan an opportunity to tempt. [Col. 0521B]

But I say this by way of concession, not command. I wish all people to be as I myself am.

I grant this indulgence to the weak; I do not command it to the perfect. I wish all people to imitate me in everything, since I know how powerful chastity is before God.

But each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that.

“His own gift,” because God distributes to each as he wills, since not everyone receives this word.

Moreover, if everyone can do so, how does Scripture say that no one can be continent unless you grant it?

“A gift from God: one in this way, another in that.” You hear the word “gift”; let presumption cease.

Now concerning the unmarried and widows. He begins speaking of those who have no wives and of widows. [Col. 0521C]

It is good for them if they remain as I am.

Who could say that what he himself calls good is not good? Who, I ask, except perhaps Jovinian?

But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry. Either you will suffer from incontinence, or, if you wish to be continent, you ought not to marry.

For it is better to marry than to burn. Fornication is punished by fire, as Judas says concerning his daughter-in-law: “Let her be brought out and burned.”

Therefore, in comparison with fornication, it is better to marry.

But to those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord. Here he speaks specifically to married people, so that they would not dismiss their wives and marry others, whether more beautiful or wealthier, as the Jews did. [Col. 0521D]

A wife must not depart from her husband. If anyone dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, he makes her commit adultery.

But if she departs, she must remain unmarried. She must not depart in such a way as to marry another; if she departs for some reason, she must not marry another.

Or she must be reconciled to her husband. And the husband must not dismiss his wife.

But to the rest I say—not the Lord: it is better for her to return to her husband than to marry another.

If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, he must not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, she must not dismiss her husband.

If one of the two has believed: this does not mean that he permitted an unbeliever to be joined to a believer, but he is speaking of those already joined in marriage.

For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife. It often happens that he is won through the woman.

Therefore blessed Peter says that if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives; and when they see that men have become sober from drunkenness and humble from pride, they may say: “Truly this is the law of God, which was able to change established habits.” [Col. 0522A]

I believe that it had already happened that some women came to faith through believing husbands, and men through believing wives. Although he does not mention names, he nevertheless encourages them by examples in order to confirm his counsel.

And the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.

If both of you were unbelievers, the children would necessarily imitate you; but now perhaps they imitate the believer, and they are holy. For even if they are born from two believers, they are born as though a wild olive were born from an olive tree.

I say “wild olive” because of original sin, and because of this they are under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ; for the devil is the author of guilt, not of nature. [Col. 0522B]

I believe that there were already Christian children who had been sanctified either through the influence of one parent or with the consent of both. This would not happen if the marriage were dissolved when only one had come to faith.

But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. For the husband is not greater than God.

The brother or sister is not subject to slavery. Would someone marry in such a way as to become a slave and perish on account of the other unbeliever? It should also be noted that they are servants to one another.

In such a matter—in such a case or circumstance.

But God has called us in peace. In freedom; therefore we ought not voluntarily become slaves.

For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? [Col. 0522C]

Except that each person should live as the Lord has apportioned, each as God has called him.

He placed the matter in doubt; but whenever something is ambiguous, it must always be interpreted in the better sense.

And so let him walk, as I teach in all the churches.

Whether with a wife or without a wife; whether circumcised or in the foreskin; whether a slave or free.

Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not bring upon himself a foreskin. If he was called with a wife, let him not dismiss her; if without a wife, he has no need to marry, if he is content with that purpose and can exercise self-control.

Since the circumcised person had a foreskin and cannot restore himself from having been circumcised unnecessarily, although circumcision was required in its proper time, he should not say, “It would have been better if I had not been circumcised,” nor live like a Gentile.

Was someone called in the foreskin? Let him not be circumcised. Let him not think that faith in the Lord is a cause of dissension.

Circumcision is nothing, and the foreskin is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God is what matters. [Col. 0522D]

Let each person remain with God in the calling in which he was called. It neither harms nor benefits him in the present age.

Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned. Some wish to understand slavery as marriage.

But if you can become free, make use of it. For God does not regard social conditions but the mind and will.

Nor should you say, “How can I please God? I am a slave.” For the slave who was called in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the free person who was called is Christ’s slave.

The one who is a human being’s slave is free before God; and the one who is free among human beings is God’s slave. Therefore both are one. For there is no partiality with God.

You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings.

Let each person remain with God, brothers, in the condition in which he was called. [Col. 0523A]

Do not serve human beings merely to be seen, in order to please people, but do everything for God, believing that you will receive your reward from God.

Now concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord. He answered in writing because they were saying: “Where is virginity commanded?”—as though to demonstrate that what is under command is punished if not fulfilled, while its fulfillment receives no reward.

He gives counsel, as the Savior says: “Not everyone receives this word, but those to whom it has been given.” For if it were universal, what one person can do, all could do.

The opportunity for chastity is abstinence; the opportunity for incontinence is luxury. It is given by God, because it is his particular gift, as the prophet says: “Since I know that no one is continent unless you grant it.”

But I give counsel. He fulfills what the Lord said in the figure of the innkeeper: “If you spend anything more, when I return I will repay you.” [Col. 0523B]

As one who has received mercy from the Lord so as to be faithful. He refers everything to God’s mercy, teaching by his own example that one must glory in God alone.

The faithful servant is the one who, having set everything else aside, is always occupied in the service of his Lord. By his example he urges them to desire to serve him alone.

And no one should presume upon his own merits, since he testifies that, in order to be faithful, he obtained the Lord’s mercy.

I consider this good. I consider this not doubtful but certain, just as when he says: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

Because of the present necessity—whether the necessity of preserving righteousness or of avoiding the world’s cares. For it is good for a man to be in this condition.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. It is therefore bad not to remain in that condition, because he first loses the reward of chastity—not because he sins. [Col. 0523C]

Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. Thus he says that one should not be bound, just as one should not be released.

But if you take a wife, you have not sinned. If you are free, and do not wish to be greater, be at least lesser.

And if a virgin marries, she will not sin. Marriage in itself does not contain sin, but through the cares of the world it often incurs sin.

Nevertheless such people will have tribulation in the flesh. They subject themselves to the curse of Eve, who received the curse in childbirth because God knew that human beings would be incontinent, so that fear of pain might restrain them from lust.

The cries of infants, the deaths of children, and miscarriages are also added.

But I spare you. That is why, in accordance with indulgence, I do not altogether forbid marriage. [Col. 0523D]

Now this I say, brothers. Here he urges everyone to continence.

The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none. The time of our life is short, because soon the death of one or both will dissolve the marriage.

It must be understood that, because of its brevity, this present life should be considered as nothing in comparison with future things.

And those who weep as though they were not weeping; those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. They use it in this age, because everything will soon come to an end. [Col. 0524A]

Solomon describes the brevity of the times: “A time and times.” Yet every day we see people dying and believe that we ourselves will be eternal, as though we belonged to another nature.

For the wise person is corrected by the misfortunes of others. Therefore Solomon says: “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of the foolish is in the house of feasting.”

For the form of this world is passing away. This age is a figure of the future. If the figure is such, what will the reality be? Just as a star is a figure of the sun.

But I wish you to be without anxiety. That is why a person does not marry: so that worldly anxiety may depart, lest the thorns choke the seed, and lest he say: “I bought a farm, I bought oxen, I married a wife,” and be unable to dine with the bridegroom.

> **[Note: [Col. 0523D] *Mundi* would be a better reading. EDIT.]**

The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife.

One must ask whom it is better to please: God or a woman who is going to die.

And he is divided. The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord. [Col. 0524B]

If divided, he cannot be one; for unity does not admit division.

So that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: holy in body by abstaining from intercourse, and in spirit by freedom from anxiety or the lust of thoughts.

But the married woman thinks about the things of the world. If the married woman thinks about the things of the world and desires to please the one whom she has begun to place before the Lord, she has the excuse of thinking about worldly matters because of her husband.

How she may please her husband. Such a woman is holy neither in body nor in spirit.

Moreover, I say this for your benefit. So that he would not seem to have spoken harshly to the weak, he now excuses himself; but this very excuse must be considered.

Not to cast a snare upon you. I do not impose necessity upon the unmarried, but give counsel concerning what is more beneficial for you.

But with a view to what is honorable and what grants the ability to entreat the Lord without hindrance. Therefore what they wanted was neither beneficial nor honorable. [Col. 0524C]

But if anyone thinks that he is acting improperly toward his virgin daughter because she is past marriageable age, he will seem to act improperly if, when she has reached full maturity, he makes no decision either to preserve her virginity or to marry her; or if, when she wishes to marry, he does not permit her and she then commits fornication.

For if each person applies this to his own flesh and sees that he cannot preserve virginity, let him marry, lest he appear dishonorable by fornicating.

And this is what ought to be done. It is necessary because of the girl’s will.

Let her do what she wishes: she does not sin if she marries. Parents ought indeed to guard her until mature age and teach her chastity. But if she is unwilling, let what is necessary be done; neither the girl’s father nor the girl herself sins if she marries.

For the one who stands firm in his heart. The man stands firm whose daughter’s will has strengthened his own will.

Not having necessity. From this it is recognized that he has necessity because of his daughter, of whom he said: “Having authority over his own will, and having judged this in his heart to preserve his virgin daughter, he does well.” [Col. 0524D]

He can do what he wishes. Therefore both the one who gives his virgin daughter in marriage does well, and the one who does not give her in marriage does better.

This is a concluding summary: certainly, the prudent should always pursue what is better.

A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives. Here he begins speaking about widows, since they too had consulted him.

But if her husband dies, she is free. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.

Freed from the marital bond according to the law: if even then she cannot exercise self-control, let her marry whom she wishes, provided it is in Christ.

She will be happier if she remains as she is. A married woman is blessed if she can preserve righteousness and knows her husband only for the sake of children; a widow is happier, because she labors more than a married woman, receives the reward of chastity, and can pray every day with a free conscience. [Col. 0525A]

A virgin is most blessed, because through labor of brief duration she can attain a great reward.

According to my counsel, which I give to virgins.

But I think that I too have the Spirit of God. Do not think that what I say comes from myself: the Spirit of God speaks in me, and it is not expedient to despise him.

Here “I think” does not signify doubt.

## CHAPTER VIII

Now concerning things sacrificed to idols. They had written to him about these matters as well as the preceding ones, because they ate in temples, saying: “Every creature of God is good,” and “An idol is nothing”; and by this image rather than by the truth of reason they were led astray. [Col. 0525B]

We know that all of us—“all of us,” that is, not those of whom he says, “But not everyone has knowledge,” meaning knowledge given by the Lord—have knowledge.

He has this habit: he begins gently, and at the end displays the force of his argument.

Knowledge puffs up. And that is foolishness before God. If knowledge puffs up, why does he still wish to press the matter further?

He also says of himself: “Although unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.” And he prays for the Ephesians that they may be filled with knowledge.

In this very letter he gives thanks that they have been filled with such knowledge—the knowledge that displays an image of reason rather than the truth, not knowledge that can be criticized.

But love builds up. That love which does not seek its own interests, but seeks how the body of Christ may advance through it. [Col. 0525C]

Knowledge without love puffs up; with love it builds up.

If anyone thinks that he knows something. If anyone seems wise to himself, he is not wise; for the truly wise person believes himself more foolish than everyone else. And he is truly wise who testifies that whatever good he understands he has received from God.

He has not yet understood how he ought to know. The one who attributes to himself, through foolish presumption, what he knows does not know how he ought to know.

But if anyone loves God, he is known by him. He loves God by building up the Church, because the Lord also knows this neighbor, since “the Lord knows those who are his.”

Now concerning food sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God except one. [Col. 0525D]

He repeats what he had said above—“we know”—and shows what it means: that an idol is nothing.

For even if there are those who are called gods. Something can be called by a name and not actually be what the name signifies.

Whether in heaven or on earth: indeed, there are many gods and many lords.

For us, however, there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come, and we exist for him.

Angels and saints, to whom he says, “I said, You are gods,” and lords—the saints of those whom they will judge. Or in this way, gods in heaven and lords on earth.

Here the Arians slanderously object, denying that Christ is God because he is called only Lord.

They must be answered: If he is not God because there is one God, the Father, then the Father will not be Lord either, because there is one Lord, Christ.

And one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist, and we through him. He who made all things from nothing—here understand the Trinity.

But not everyone has knowledge. Not everyone knows that you do this out of contempt; rather, they think you do it out of reverence. [Col. 0526A]

But some, with consciousness still attached to the idol, eat the sacrificial food as though it were truly idol-offering; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. In their conscience they still possess the same disposition as before they believed.

But food does not commend us to God. Neither, if we do not eat, will we lack anything; nor, if we eat, will we abound.

As the prophet Haggai says: “And if you eat and drink, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?”

But beware lest this freedom of yours become a stumbling block to the weak.

This can also be said of those religious persons or clerics who destroy by their example what they teach by word, while they cling to riches and surround themselves with costly garments. [Col. 0526B]

For if someone sees the one who has knowledge reclining at an idol, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat sacrificial food?

And the weak person perishes through your conscience—the brother for whom Christ died.

Thus, by sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.

Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be thrown into the depths of the sea; that punishment is the lighter, though it is severe.

Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble.

Not only food and meat, but all other things as well.

## CHAPTER IX
“Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?” It should be read: “Am I not indeed?” He repeats to them his own example: although he had everything in his power, he did not wish to do what he was permitted to do, for the sake of the salvation of others.

“Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?” When he appeared to him on the road. “Are you not my work in the Lord?” And if I am not an apostle to others—to whom I was not sent—yet I am one to you. “For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.” The evidence of my apostleship is that you came to believe in the Lord through me.

“My defense before those who question me is this.” By these arguments I defend my claim to be an apostle. “Do we not have the right to eat and drink?” At your expense, without our labor. “Do we not have the right to take along a believing woman?” One who would minister to us. He did not say “to lead,” but “to take along,” lest anyone think he was speaking of his own wife.

“As do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas.” He is not condemning them; rather, because they preached to more faithful people, they received their daily bread more freely, since this was also the custom among the Jews regarding teachers.

“Or are Barnabas and I alone without the right to do this?” We who were sent to the Gentiles. “Who serves as a soldier?” He gives other examples by which he proves that this was owed to him. “Ever at his own expense?” And not from public funds. “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?” By comparison he calls the people a vineyard, as in the passage, “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” “Who tends a flock and does not drink the milk of the flock?” And, “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with discipline.”

“Do I say this merely on human grounds?” I say it from my own authority. “Or does the Law not say the same?” For it is written in the Law of Moses: [Col. 0527A] “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.” He confirms everything by testimonies from the Law. “Is God concerned about oxen?” How then is God concerned about sparrows, and how is Nineveh mentioned in Jonah, where there are more than 120,000 human beings and many animals? Yet even the animals themselves were created for human beings. For when human beings perish, they too will perish.

“Or does he certainly say this for our sake?” Indeed, it was written for our sake. For “the one who plows ought to plow in hope,” and “the one who threshes ought to receive a share of the expected harvest.” The one who labors ought to hope for the fruit of his work, and the one who threshes ought to eat from the threshing floor itself. By this comparison, those who labor in the word should willingly be supported.

“If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter?” It would not be a great matter—we would not burden you—if we wished to receive support, but we do not wish to do so for your sake. “If we reap your material things,” that is, whatever is necessary. If others share in your authority, why not we all the more? But we have not used this authority.

He is speaking of the false apostles, to whom nothing was owed, since they had done nothing for them. “But we endure everything,” both disgrace, thirst, and nakedness, so that we may place no obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ. We do not wish our preaching to be displeasing in any respect, lest those to whom we preach take offense through us, while our adversaries seize the opportunity to destroy us.

“Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and that those who serve at the altar share in what is offered on the altar?” This was the practice among the Jews according to the Law. So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should live from the gospel, as he says: “The laborer is worthy of his wages.”

The Apostle says that it is lawful for him, and permitted by the Lord, that those who proclaim the gospel should live from the gospel—that is, should receive from the gospel what is necessary for this life—yet that he himself has not made use of this authority. For there were many who wanted an opportunity to acquire wealth by selling the gospel. Wishing to cut off this opportunity, the Apostle supported himself by the work of his own hands. Of these people he says elsewhere: “So that I may cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity.”

Although, like the other good apostles, he could live from the gospel by the Lord’s permission, he did not make his livelihood the end of evangelizing, so that he would not preach for the sake of obtaining food and other necessities. Rather, he accepted these things so that he might fulfill the gospel, lest he preach unwillingly under compulsion.

“But I have used none of these rights.” “I have not written these things so that this might be done for me.” I am not writing these things so that what has not been done may now be done; rather, I am giving you an example to follow. For it is better for me to die than for anyone to deprive me of my glory. Even if I die of hunger, this glory that I possess before God will not be taken from me: namely, that I receive nothing from you.

“For if I preach the gospel, there is no ground for boasting, since necessity is laid upon me.” When you have done everything, say: “We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.” “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel.” I would have punishment. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. It becomes voluntary when the obligation is nevertheless disregarded.

“What, then, is my reward?” He answers himself: that, when preaching the gospel, I may offer the gospel without expense. Where, then, do I find my reward? In proclaiming it freely, so that I do not abuse my authority in the gospel—or, alternatively, so that I do not exercise the authority I have received. Or, if I wished to receive support, I would make my authority contemptible, since I would be thought to teach for the sake of my belly.

“For although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win more.” Although I could use my freedom and care nothing for others, I have shown compassion toward everyone in order to save them.

“To the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might win the Jews.” This was when he purified himself in the Temple, although in the time of grace he knew that such purification was unnecessary. “To those under the Law, as though I were under the Law,” showing how he himself was a Jew among them, so that he might have an opportunity to preach to them, although he himself was not under the Law, in order to win those who were under the Law.

He is not under the Law given to children, since he fulfills the Law by grace; for the Law is not imposed upon the righteous. “To those without the Law, as though I were without the Law,” although I am not without the Law of God. From the Gentiles I initially sought faith alone, as though I had no commands of the Law of Christ to teach them to observe. Yet I was under the Law of Christ, in order to win those who were without the Law.

He says this against the Arians, who deny that Christ is God. For when he says that he is not without the Law of God but is under the Law of Christ, he confesses that Christ is God.

“I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak.” With the weak I ate vegetables, although I could eat meat without fear. Or this may refer to the statement: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

“I became all things to all people.” I sought nothing that was useful to myself, so that I might save everyone. We must consider that God assumed humanity and, although he was without sin, bore our sins. We, however, are sinful human beings. We ought to consider that the sickness—whether of soul or of body—that we see in another person we ourselves also could have, or may have.

Therefore, toward the person whose weakness we wish to bear, let us show the same compassion that we would wish him to show us if we were in that condition and he were not. To this belongs the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens.”

“I do everything for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in it”—so that I may have a share in it.

“Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but only one receives the prize?” We ought all to run. For if there one who wins receives the prize, how much more should we, who by God’s gift can all win and all be crowned together through his mercy? “Run in such a way that you may all obtain it.”

If we are running toward faith, let faith be accompanied by works; if toward teaching, let teaching be confirmed by example. “Everyone who competes in the games exercises self-control in all things.” They do this to receive a perishable crown: abstaining from all foods that hinder the race, or by which another person is scandalized.

Let us therefore run so that we may obtain the prize; for all who run rightly obtain it. It is not like a theatrical contest, where all run but only one receives the palm. Let us run by believing, hoping, and desiring. Let us run by disciplining the body, by giving alms, by giving good things, by forgiving evils, doing these things cheerfully and from the heart, and by praying that the strength of those who run may be aided. Let us thus hear the commands of perfection, so that we may not neglect to run toward the fullness of charity and may not attribute our running to ourselves.

“But we seek an incorruptible crown.” They run uncertainly, since they cannot all win. “I therefore run in such a way, not as uncertainly.” Whoever preaches for the sake of human approval is uncertain about his reward.

“So I fight, not as one beating the air, but I discipline my body.” I do not pretend to be fighting, nor do I fight in vain. “And I bring it into subjection,” lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified through abstinence—as Elijah in his mantle, Isaiah in sackcloth, and the others in various ways. The person who teaches only by word and not by example becomes disqualified.

## CHAPTER X

“I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud.” Let no one trust in baptism, or in spiritual food or drink, and think that God will spare him if he commits a grave sin.

Everything that happened to the people of Israel in a figure happens to us in reality. Just as they were freed from Egypt through Moses, so we are freed from the world through baptism. Then, as catechumens, we are led through the wilderness, so that through the discipline of the journey we may forget the pleasures of Egypt and learn not to return to the world. When we have crossed the sea, Pharaoh and his army die for us. Afterward we receive manna and water from the rock. Then the splendor of knowledge and the refreshment of consolation will be shown to us.

But if after all these things we commit a mortal sin, these benefits do not help us. Rather, as ungrateful people, we will be subjected to a greater punishment if we do not wash this sin away through repentance, as Hebrews says: “Anyone who set aside the Law of Moses was punished without mercy.” How much more, then, one who sets aside the baptism of Christ?
