“And all passed through the sea.” The Red Sea signifies baptism, adorned with the blood of Christ. “And all were baptized into Moses.” Moses, the leader, signifies Christ; the people passing through signify the faithful; the death of the Egyptians signifies the abolition of sins. This took place in the cloud and in the sea, and the cloud contains moisture—that is, the water of baptism.

“And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink.” They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. “And the rock was Christ.” This is understood mystically.

“But with most of them God was not well pleased, for they were struck down in the wilderness.” The manna was a type of the body of Christ. These things happened as figures for us, so that we might not desire evil things, as they desired them. For them these things were reality at the time, but they anticipated our figure.

“Nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Nor should we commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. This refers to those who reclined at idol feasts.

“Nor let us test Christ, as some of them tested him and perished by serpents.” They said, “Can God indeed?” Here Christ is shown to be God, because it is written that God said: “They tested me”—ten times. He says that they tested Christ in the same way as when he says to them: “Do you seek a test of the one who speaks in me, Christ?”

“Nor grumble, as some of them grumbled and perished by the destroyer”—in their tribulations.

“All these things happened to them as a figure.” They received everything that happened to them according to their deeds; nevertheless, these things were written so that we would not think that we may sin with impunity. If he did not spare those who were children, how much less will he spare us, who have received the perfect Law, if we do not keep it?

“These things were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” The fullness of everything falls upon us; that is, what they either foretold or prefigured has been completed.

“Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” By the very fact that he thinks he stands, he falls, while he grows proud and relies upon himself.

“No temptation has overtaken you except what is human.” Human temptations occur when someone, with a good intention but because of ordinary human weakness, falls into some error in judgment, or becomes irritated with a brother in the effort to correct him, yet goes somewhat further than Christian tranquility permits. Of such things the Apostle says: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human.”

Do not bring some temptation upon yourselves. If human beings have compelled you by tortures, you ought not to consent to abandon the faith. A human temptation is the vain presumption of free choice, or—as he himself said above—“When there is jealousy and rivalry among you, are you not human, and are you not walking according to human standards?”

What is more human than to form an improper judgment about hidden matters in other people: for a person to believe someone good whom he does not know to be evil, and again, on uncertain opinion, to believe someone evil whom he has not proved to be evil, and to judge before the proper time what he does not know?

A human temptation may also be called an evil suggestion, whether it arises in the soul or is suggested through wicked people—for example, giving false testimony, stirring up enmity, demanding revenge, and other things of this kind.

To think otherwise than perfection requires may be called a human temptation. The struggle of the flesh may also be called a human temptation, while the flesh desires what is opposed to the spirit and the spirit what is opposed to the flesh.

“God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear.” Stand firm, and he will grant you the strength to endure. “With the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.” He will bring about for you what you are able to endure, or he will bring from the tribulation itself a gain for the soul.

Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. I speak to you as prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say. For this reason you ought not to do this even unwillingly.

“The cup of blessing that we bless”—he first mentioned the cup because afterward he was going to discuss the bread at greater length. “Is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ?” As the Savior said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

“And the bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?” So also the bread of idols is a participation in demons. “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body,” all of us who share in the one bread. Likewise, if we eat from the same bread from which idolaters eat, we become one body with them.

“Consider Israel according to the flesh.” Carnal Israel offers carnal sacrifices; spiritual Israel, spiritual sacrifices; and just as the former are participants in God’s altar, so the idolater is a participant in the altar of idols. “Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?”

What, then, do I mean? That something sacrificed to idols is something, or that an idol is something? He does not want the answer to be, “You speak as though an idol possessed something, or some evil, although it is without a soul.”

But what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons. There are demons who pollute these things, who preside over images in order to lead human beings astray.

“You cannot share in the table of the Lord and in the table of demons.” You cannot be partners with God and with demons, because you wish to share in both tables.

“Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?” As in the passage: “They court you, but not rightly.” “Are we stronger than he?”

“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial.” If the one who did not do these things had known that faith was shown to be stronger by this, he too would have done it, so that in this also he might give us an example.

“All things are lawful, but not all things build up.” Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of the other. Everything beneficial is lawful, but not everything lawful is beneficial.

Following Christ’s example, we ought not to consider what is lawful, but what benefits us and builds up others. We must not seek what benefits only ourselves while benefiting another person either not at all or harmfully. Such things are not prohibited because they are inherently sinful, but because they provide an occasion for sin.

“Eat whatever is sold in the marketplace.” He said: “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine,” and again: “I will never eat meat.” How, then, does he command that everything be eaten? Rather, he permits the eating of meat, provided that they do not eat meat sacrificed to idols.

“Without asking questions, for the sake of conscience.” “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.” If they asked questions, they would be recognized as Christians, and, to mock them, everything would be declared to have been sacrificed.

“If an unbeliever invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, without asking questions, for the sake of conscience.” But if someone says, “This has been sacrificed to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who disclosed it and for the sake of conscience.

He placed this also within their own will; he did not say, “Go.” A Christian should go to an unbeliever only if there is some benefit to be gained—if he knows that he can win that person. The Savior went for this reason: either to perform miracles or to rebuke. When he went to a certain Pharisee, for example, while they were dining he first taught the man himself that the rich should not be fed but the weak. Then he taught the Pharisees, even at the meal, that humility must be observed. Third, he rebuked the experts in the Law, who claimed something more for themselves, yet neither reproved their own pride nor allowed others to do so.

“But I mean conscience—not your own, but the other person’s.” They might say: “Why do they forbid us to sacrifice, as though it were evil, while they themselves eat it, as though it were holy and clean?” “Why should my freedom be judged by another person’s conscience?” Since it benefits me nothing. “If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I slandered because of what I give thanks for?”

Everything is clean when received with thanksgiving, but the other person does not understand this and judges me as though I were pretending to say that sacrificing to idols is evil.

“Therefore, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” A Christian should do nothing else except glorify God in every work; nothing should be superfluous.

“Be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the church of God.” These groups all found the matter offensive. The Jews said, “The Christians have gone so mad that they sacrifice to idols.” The Gentiles said, “How can they forbid us to worship idols while they themselves serve idols with us?” Christians, thinking that it was permitted, followed their example.

“Just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, so that they may be saved.” I present myself in such a way as to please them. If anyone hates me without cause, let him know that it is not my fault.

## CHAPTER XI

“Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” Christ did nothing and suffered nothing for his own sake, but for the salvation of all. So also Paul seeks not what is useful to himself, but what is useful to many.

“I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in everything.” Why does he suddenly praise those whom he previously censured? Where he lacks the authority of the Law, he uses words of affection to invite them to reason. “And you hold fast to my instructions as I delivered them to you.” He speaks as though these were a law, because you know that I possess the Spirit of God, who spoke in the Law and the Prophets.

“But I want you to know”—I also want you to hold on to this—“that Christ is the head of every man.” A man is subject to no human being except Christ, who is both human and God.

“The head of a woman is the man.” A woman ought to be subject both to man and to Christ according to the order of nature; nevertheless, in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female. Yet he wished women to be subject in this respect.

“The head of Christ is God”—Christ according to his humanity, from which he also received the name. For who can know his name in his divinity, according to Solomon, who says: “What is his name, and what is the name of his son?”

“Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head.” But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head. For it is one and the same as if she were shaven. If a woman does not veil herself, let her also be shorn. But if it is disgraceful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head.

A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but a woman is the glory of man. He comes to the matter at hand because some men were growing their hair long, while women were entering the church bareheaded and taking pride in their hair. This was not only dishonorable but also a cause of scandal.

Therefore, he says, a man ought not to have a veil, since he has Christ alone as his head. A woman, however, ought to have a veil, showing that she is humble and subject to the man.

He is criticizing the custom of the Corinthians: their women went about with uncovered heads, their men grew their hair long, and they ate indiscriminately in the temples. Inflated with secular wisdom, they also denied the resurrection of the flesh.

“For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Nor was man created for woman, but woman for man.” Therefore a woman ought to have authority over her head. This is an example drawn from Adam and Eve.

“Because of the angels.” Understand “angels” as priests and ministers of the altar, or as the entire clergy who announce God’s commands. For “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature.

“Nevertheless, in the Lord neither is woman without man nor man without woman.” For Christ gave himself for everyone. Just as woman came from man, so man comes through woman. But everything comes from God.

“Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a woman to pray to God unveiled?” Does not nature itself teach you that if a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him, whereas if a woman grows her hair long, it is her glory? For her hair has been given to her as a covering.

Just as the first woman came from Adam, so Christ came from the Virgin.

“If anyone seems inclined to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the church of God.” If anyone, unwilling to accept the truth, seeks an answer and arguments on which to rely, let him know in return that he is not worthy of an answer, because he is more prepared to quarrel than to be taught.

“First of all, when you come together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and to some extent I believe it.” These are disputes. “For there must also be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may become evident among you.”

This does not mean that heresies please God, but that through them the faithful are tested and, just as they are known to God, are also revealed and become more clearly known to human beings. For how would the skill of an advocate become apparent if he never pleaded a case in which he could be tested? How would a sailor or helmsman be praised if the ship always remained in harbor or in calm waters?

“When you come together in one place, it is not to eat the Lord’s supper.” For each person takes his own supper beforehand to eat. One is hungry, while another is drunk.

“Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and shame those who have nothing?” What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

As some report, a corrupt custom had once taken hold among the Corinthians: they dishonored the churches indiscriminately with banquets. They ate before the Lord’s offering, which they offered at night; and when the rich came to the Eucharist drunk, the poor were distressed by hunger.

This custom, they say, came from pagan superstition. Hence, in certain places throughout Egypt and Syria, it is also said that people gathered in the church on the night of the Sabbath after dinner.

“For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus”—from this point he seems almost to have forgotten, and recalls how great a sacramental mystery is contained here.

“On the night when he was betrayed, he took bread.” He left us the final remembrance and memorial of himself. “And giving thanks, he broke it and said”—that is, blessing it—“This is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

“Likewise also the cup after he had eaten, saying”—as he said: “Whoever eats my body and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

Therefore, in baptism we died with him to the world, as the Apostle says: “You have died with Christ, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory.”

Therefore do not seek glory or joy here, where you have died.

“This cup is the new covenant.” The old covenant foreshadowed this through the blood of animals. “In my blood. Do this.” A covenant is consecrated through blood, because without death it is not made firm.

“Whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.” “For whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup.” The Savior God gave this example so that whenever we do this, we may remember that Christ died for all of us.

For this reason it is called the body of Christ for us: so that when we remember it, we may not be ungrateful for his grace. It is like someone who, when dying, leaves some pledge to a beloved person. After his death, whenever that person sees it, if he loved him perfectly, can he restrain his tears?

“You will proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes.” This proclamation takes place in your hearts when you hear, “the body of Christ.”

“Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily”—every clean person will eat meat, but the person who eats while unclean will be cut off. If there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your offering there.

And Jeremiah says: “Will vows and flesh take away your wickedness?” Every conscience must first be examined, to see whether it finds fault with us in anything; only then should one offer or receive communion.

“He will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” It is as though he himself had killed him, because he despises him and regards his body as nothing, just as the Jews did.

“But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from the cup.” If it cannot be placed in a soiled linen cloth or a polluted vessel, and if no one dares to use it otherwise, how much more must it not be received with a polluted heart? God detests this impurity above all, and it is the one injury inflicted upon his body.

For that righteous Joseph buried the Lord’s body, wrapped in a clean linen cloth, in a new tomb.

“For the one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” The person who approaches unworthily is guilty in two ways: both because of the sin and because of the usurpation.

“Not discerning the body of the Lord”—that is, receiving it as though it were ordinary food.

“For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many are asleep.” Bodily illnesses arise for three reasons: either from temptation, as with Job and Tobit; or from sin, as with Jehoshaphat, who is reproved in the present passage by the Apostle; or from negligence or some lack of moderation, as with Timothy and those who are commanded to honor the physician.

Only in this last case can human medicine be of benefit. Through such negligence or some other circumstance people may also die, as it is written: “The righteous man, overtaken by whatever death,” and again, “Do not be severe, lest you die before your time.”

Although this does not happen without God’s permission, it does not happen by his command; rather, it happens by his just judgment.

Correction was present then, and it is present now, but we do not understand it. We think that what is actually the result of guilt is merely customary, because many people suffer it.

“But if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged”—if we recognized ourselves. “When we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.”

Correction is the expression of paternal compassion, so that we may repent and not be condemned eternally with the faithful of the world.

“Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.” If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home. For whoever arrived first was served, ate, and departed.

“So that you may not come together for judgment.” They were gathering for judgment, not for sanctification.

“I will arrange the remaining matters when I come”—concerning the mysteries themselves.

## CHAPTER XII
Concerning spiritual gifts. As faith increased, the grace of tongues diminished, since they had received it on account of unbelievers. Therefore many became distressed and began to envy those who still possessed this grace, thinking that it was greater than all the other gifts.

I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers. You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to mute idols. [Col. 0535B] I do not want you to be ignorant of the matter. According to the prophet who says: “Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them”—things without voice and without sensation. “As you were led, going along.” By magicians or by the diviners of idols.

Therefore I inform you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus.” This is so that you may no longer be irrational and unstable: with the adoption of religion, you must also change your conduct, understand the reason for your faith, and know that no one can say, “The Lord Jesus,” except by the Holy Spirit.

How then will the Lord not recognize the workers of iniquity? Although they have confessed the Lord, the Apostle himself affirms that God is denied by deeds. This means that no one in the Holy Spirit can call Jesus Lord except one who confesses him wholly and faithfully as God and man, according to each substance—equal to the Father and [Col. 0535C] lesser than the Father.

There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit. That is, of tongues or of different things, which the Holy Spirit distributes according to his will, as true God.

There are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord. Although this passage is directed particularly against Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God—for by always saying “the same” he shows that he is speaking throughout about the Holy Spirit—nevertheless it also provides no small argument against the Arians, who continually make this objection: that the Father is named first, the Son second, and the Holy Spirit third. Here, however, he has changed that order.

He wishes to show that the grace of the divine Spirit is not itself divided; rather, it distributes the ministries of the Church, its teaching, and the other gifts.

There are divisions of activities, but [Col. 0535D] it is the same God who works everything in everyone. Through these, powers were at work. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common benefit, whether of believers or of unbelievers, so that they may believe.

To one, through the Spirit, is given a message of wisdom. This is so that it may be evident that the one who receives wisdom from God possesses the Holy Spirit, since he speaks without his own effort or reflection, and no one can resist him, as in the case of Stephen.

Wisdom means speaking wisely, appropriately, and rationally, being able to reason and teach what one knows. Wisdom may be understood as knowledge of divine things, and knowledge as human understanding.

Alternatively: among human beings, the two are usually distinguished in this way: wisdom pertains to understanding eternal things, whereas knowledge pertains to those things that we experience through the senses of the heart. But [Col. 0536A] even if this is the knowledge of God, it is not of the same kind as what is called human knowledge. Just as what is called God is something altogether different from the way human beings are called gods; and just as we speak of the wrath of God, although no disturbance falls upon God.

Thus, in the books Against the Academics, addressed to Romanianus (Augustine, Book I, Against the Academics): “For you are not now hearing for the first time that wisdom is knowledge of human and divine things.”

And later: “When knowledge of human things is mentioned, it means the knowledge by which someone knows how many or what kinds of estates we possess, or how much gold or silver we have. But that is knowledge of human things which knows the light of prudence, the beauty of temperance, the strength of courage, and the holiness of justice. [Col. 0536B] These are things that fear no fortune and that we dare truly to call our own. If that Albicerius had learned them, believe me, he would never have lived so luxuriously and disgracefully.”

To another is given a message of knowledge according to the same Spirit. Knowledge is knowledge of the mysteries of the Law, or knowing past events and judging concerning the future.

“Wisdom seems to me to be knowledge of human and divine things that pertain to the blessed life—not knowledge alone, but also diligent inquiry” (from the same book, a little later).

If you wish to divide this definition, the first part, which contains knowledge, belongs to God; the part that consists in inquiry belongs to the human being. God possesses the former; the blessed human being possesses the latter. Wisdom may be understood as knowledge of divine things, while knowledge may mean human understanding, or recalling history and recounting past events accurately.

Alternatively: wisdom pertains to understanding [Col. 0536C] eternal things, whereas knowledge pertains to those things that we seek through the senses of the body. Such wisdom pertains to the blessed life.

To another, faith by the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings by the one Spirit. As with the mustard seed, he uses the thing improperly for its effect. Here faith means not only believing but also faith for miracles, so that fire might fall.

To another, the working of powers. Power means raising the dead and cleansing lepers.

To another, prophecy: proclaiming future events beforehand or explaining obscure matters.

To another, discernment of spirits: what sort of spirit someone comes with, or which spirit suggests that something be done—whether a good spirit or an opposing one.

To another, kinds of tongues. It should be noted that among the other gifts he mentions kinds of tongues.

To another, kinds of tongues, so that he may know how to speak in languages.

To another, interpretation of messages. One person could interpret what another was saying.

[Col. 0536D] But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing them to each person as he wills. He shows that above he was speaking entirely about the Holy Spirit alone, and that he had proclaimed him to be God and Lord. Moreover, when he says “as he wills,” he likewise demonstrates that he is God: he works voluntarily, not under command; he distributes as he wills and is subject to no one.

If, then, one Spirit works everything, why are you distressed that you have received one grace and envy another, as though he had seized the greater share, when this lies not in our power but in the power of the giver?

For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. He uses the comparison of the body to show that the functions are different, [Col. 0537A] not the nature of the members, and that no one should concern himself with which function he has, so long as all are animated by one Spirit and fitted together in one body.

Thus also is Christ. It should be noted that Christ is called the Church, that is, the body of Christ.

For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, so that we might be one body. Therefore, those whose spiritual possessions are held in common ought also to share their bodily possessions, according to his own judgment. Those who have one God, the same Father, but do not hold their possessions in common, are impious.

Whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free, we were all given to drink of one Spirit. He bestowed it as a drink, according to each person’s capacity, as much as he willed.

For the body also—he returns to the example—is not one member but many. Therefore the whole body cannot have [Col. 0537B] one single function, but each member has the function for which it is suited.

If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I am not part of the body,” is it therefore not part of the body? Feet may be called those members of the Church who walk in order to intercede or preach the Gospel. The hand is the one who performs useful works in the body. They were saying that they did not belong to the body because they did not possess the grace that others possessed.

And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I am not part of the body,” is it therefore not part of the body? The ear is the wise hearer; it is also the understanding of Scripture, which was taken away from Judea.

The eye is the one who understands either future things, which he declares, or present things.

If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If all were teachers, where would the hearers be? If the whole body were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? If all were hearers, who would know how to distinguish good from evil?

[Col. 0537C] But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body. Just as the members are suitably and orderly arranged in the body, so in the Church each person is appointed by God to the task for which he is suited.

If everyone had one and the same grace, where would the others be? “As he willed.” But if all were one member, where would the body be? Now there are many members, but one body.

The will of God is good, just, and holy; it is not to be questioned but admired. O man, who are you to answer God and say, “Why is it so for him and not so for that one? What is it that he has been given, and that one has not been given?”

The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of your work.” Therefore we need one another, so that love may be preserved. For if one person possessed everything, he would become proud against the others.

Or again, the head—here the priest is the head. [Col. 0537D] It cannot say to the feet, “You are not necessary to me.” The feet are those that carry the body.

But much more necessary are those members of the body that seem to be weaker. The prophecy they despised was of greater usefulness. And the members of the body that we regard as less honorable, these we surround with more abundant honor.

Just as one can live in the body without eyes and hands, but cannot live without the inner organs, so too the parts of the body that are dishonorable have more abundant dignity, since they are covered more carefully and diligently with clothing. But our honorable parts need nothing, because they are beautiful and honorable in themselves, such as the head and the other parts.

But God has so arranged the body that the part lacking in honor receives more abundant honor, granting greater gifts to the lesser members, so that the one who is lesser in honor may be greater in grace.

[Col. 0538A] Thus there may be no division in the body. Since we need one another, we care for one another, so that no one may say that he has been deprived either of grace or of honor. Rather, the members should care for one another in the same way.

The eyes watch over the feet; the hands work for the whole body; and all the members serve one another. If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. If one member is in pain, the whole body is sick, and the remaining members hasten toward its healing.

Or if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. As Solomon says: “With a joyful heart, the face flourishes.” We, however, turn this into the opposite through sympathy and rejoicing together.

You are the body of Christ and members individually. All together are the body; each individually is a member. This means the Church, as he says elsewhere: “Of his flesh [Col. 0538B] and of his bones.” It should be noted that we are rightly called the Church.

And some God has appointed in the Church. He now sets forth the order of the members: first, apostles; second, prophets.

“In the Church,” not “in the synagogue,” lest we think that he means the prophets of ancient times, but Agabus and the others. Otherwise, he ought also to have named the patriarchs as prophets, since those from whom Agabus descended were called prophets—not those who prophesied that God would come in the flesh.

Third, teachers: both those who explain the obscurities of the prophets and those who speak words of consolation to people are rightly called teachers, since they properly establish moral conduct even if they cannot explain the mysteries.

Then, powers. Powers are greater signs, whether against demons or against illnesses.

After that, gifts of healings, helps—assistance. [Col. 0538C] For Paul is told by a Macedonian, “Come over and help us.”

Governance; kinds of tongues. Those who know how to govern individuals.

Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all possess gifts of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?

He has already said: “If all were one member, where would the body be?”

But strive eagerly. That is, endeavor to imitate.

Gifts. These gifts are gifts of grace, not rewards of merit, because what is given does not lie in our power and is not demanded from us—unlike the good life, which we ought to display with God’s help.

The greater gifts. For these too are good. And still more excellent.

Just as a public road is higher than the other roads and paths, so love is the straight road by which one travels toward the [Col. 0538D] heavenly capital. If someone possesses the other virtues but does not enter this road—that is, if he does not possess love, which is the more excellent way—he will not be able to enter the city of the Lord.

I will show you a way. The way by which you may proceed to God, that is, love. He wishes to show that we ought to seek those things that are more beneficial for life rather than signs.

CHAPTER XIII

If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, not only of human beings, but even if there are tongues belonging to angels, I have become like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal—something that produces a sound only because it is struck by another, a sound that benefits neither itself nor anyone else.

But love possesses every fruit.

And if I have prophecy and know all [Col. 0539A] mysteries—here prophecy means proclaiming future events; mysteries pertain to wisdom; knowledge means knowing all things that have been and are—and all knowledge, it is not surprising that love is preferred to knowledge, since prophecy and martyrdom are also said to be nothing without it.

And if I have all faith, so that I can move mountains. The Savior says that faith like a mustard seed can move mountains; here, however, the Apostle says that all faith is able to move mountains. From this it is understood to be perfect faith, which is compared with the mustard seed. The comparison is not made because of its smallness but because of its wholeness and fervor.

But if I do not have love, I am nothing. What will it profit me to possess the powers of foreknowledge if I do not have the works of love? For it is said to me: “Depart from me, worker of iniquity.”

And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor. [Col. 0539B] It should be noted that contempt for the world is joined to martyrdom, against those who excuse that passage from the Gospel by various arguments.

And if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing. If it is done not for God but for human glory, or if, even in martyrdom itself, he retains anger against his brother, despising God, who said, “Forget the malice of your neighbor,” then love does not arise from martyrdom; rather, martyrdom arises from love.

Love. He now describes the members and forms of love. Love is from God—or rather, it is God—and therefore it consists in such great virtues.

It is patient; it is kind. Parents, because they love their children, patiently bear all the injuries of their infants.

Love is not jealous. No one envies the person [Col. 0539C] whom he truly loves, even when he sees him enjoying whatever glory or honor; rather, he gladly embraces all his happiness as though it were his own.

It does not act improperly. It does everything in an orderly manner.

It is not puffed up; it is not ambitious. It does not seek to be greater than others and does not desire to rule over its brothers.

It does not seek its own interests. It does not seek what is useful to itself but what is useful to many.

It is not provoked; it does not think evil. It does not merely refrain from thinking of doing evil to friends; it does not repay evil with evil even to enemies.

It does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It is grieved if it sees someone either committing iniquity or suffering it.

It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things. It bears injuries, believes the one who offers satisfaction, hopes for amendment, and waits until the person is corrected.

It endures all things. Love never fails—whether [Col. 0539D] prophecies are abolished or tongues cease. This means that love alone remains in the future. Or, certainly, what is true is not changed and does not fail, because it does everything with a good intention.

Whether knowledge is abolished. Without love, knowledge puffs up, and therefore it will be abolished. For with love it builds up.

For we know in part and prophesy in part. We do not know everything, nor do we prophesy everything.

But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished. In the future, what has been promised will come—so that it will no longer be partial but complete—because the reality itself will succeed faith and hope: not something believed and hoped for, but something seen and possessed.

Love, which is greater than these three, will not be taken away but will increase and be fulfilled, beholding what it believed and [Col. 0540A] attaining what it awaited. In that fullness the commandment of love will be fulfilled: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.”

For as long as there remains some carnal desire that must be restrained by self-control, God is not loved with the whole soul.

When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. By the example of bodily growth he wishes to show spiritual progress.

When I became a man, I abolished the things that belonged to the child. He shows how the things mentioned above are abolished.

Now we see as through a mirror, in an enigma. Like children, we cannot perfectly perceive the light of truth with the most serene vision of the heart. Through the mirror of the Law, we see an image of realities.

But then, face to face. Now I know in part. He says this of the present, or perhaps plainly.

[Col. 0540B] But then I shall know, just as I have been known. Then I shall know God and the things that belong to God—but only insofar as the human mind can know God. For who can know God as he is?

Now, however, faith, hope, and love remain—these three; but the greatest of these is love. In the present there are three; in the future there will be only the love of God, of angels, and of all the saints.

Therefore what is always necessary is greater than what will at some point cease. For everything that we hope for and believe in; not everything that we believe and hope for.

CHAPTER XIV

Pursue love. Follow and hold fast to it with every effort; it is poured out through the Holy Spirit.

Strive eagerly for spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. For the one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings but to God.

I do not forbid you to strive for and [Col. 0540C] seek spiritual gifts; rather, I urge you especially to prophesy, that is, to explain, so that others too may be built up.

For no one hears; no one understands except God and anyone who has the interpretation. The Spirit speaks mysteries, through the grace of the Spirit.

But the one who prophesies speaks to human beings for their edification, exhortation, and consolation. He has explained the prophecy he mentioned; therefore whoever does this prophesies.

The one who speaks in a tongue builds himself up—himself alone. But the one who prophesies builds up the Church of God—all.

I want all of you to speak in tongues, but especially to prophesy. I do not forbid the former; I urge the latter. I want this, but I prefer that.

For the one who prophesies is greater—greater because he seeks a gift from which many will benefit, since this too is an act of love—than the one who speaks in tongues, which they considered the greatest gift.

[Col. 0540D] Unless, indeed, he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification. If he has both gifts, then he will be equal to the one who prophesies.

But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you? He discourages them by his own example from seeking as something great what does not benefit the Church. You will gain only amazement, not progress.

Unless I speak to you either by revelation, by knowledge, by prophecy, or by teaching. Then I will benefit you if I interpret, speak plainly, explain prophecies, or teach moral matters.

Or by knowledge—that is, spiritual understanding, namely discernment of what we ought to do and how we should correct our conduct. We may understand knowledge as a proper account of events.

Or by prophecy: allegorically, prophecy means anagoge, that is, when a discourse is transferred to invisible and [Col. 0541A] future things, as in what he declares concerning the resurrection of the dead. In this passage he calls exposition especially prophecy.

Or by teaching: a simple historical narrative.

Nevertheless, even lifeless things that give a sound—whether flute or lyre—unless they give distinct notes, will not be melodious. If these lifeless things are not differentiated, they will not be pleasing, and they will be rejected as empty and superfluous. How much more must you, whose spiritual sweetness ought not merely to delight the ears but the mind, provide clarity?

How will it be known what is played on the flute or what is played on the lyre? It will be understood.

For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you: unless you give a clear message through the tongue, how will what is said be known?

If the sound of the trumpet is uncertain—whether it is for a festival or for war—no one can distinguish it. [Col. 0541B] Therefore your speech must be understood, so that it can prepare Christ’s soldiers for spiritual battle.

For you will be speaking into the air. There are, let us suppose, so many kinds of languages in the world. Even if you speak as many languages as there are kinds of languages, what benefit will it be when everything dissolves into the air and benefits no one?

And nothing is without a voice—nothing is without the voice of languages. Therefore, if I do not know the force of the voice, I will be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak, and the one who speaks to me will be a barbarian. Every speech that is not understood is barbarous to the hearer.

So also you, since you are eager for spiritual gifts, as I said of myself, seek to abound in them for the building up of the Church. Just as you pursue spiritual gifts, so the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.

He should pray that he may also obtain the grace of interpretation, or he should speak in such a way as to interpret.

[Col. 0541C] For if I pray in a tongue that I do not understand, I speak as though inspired by the Spirit, in ecstasy. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays.

Here “spirit” should be understood as speech, which sometimes prays while the mind is occupied with something else. Hence the prophet says: “My heart has forsaken me.”

But my mind is without fruit, because I do not understand what I am saying through the spirit.

What then is the meaning? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing psalms with the spirit, and I will sing psalms with the mind.

For the one who interprets must first understand himself what he is going to say to others.

But if you bless with the spirit—everything that is truly and according to God spoken is blessed—who fills the place of the unlearned person? Who supplies sound knowledge in the heart of the unlearned person? How can he say “Amen” over your blessing, when he does not know what you are saying, the one who answered “Amen” in place of the unlearned, that is, the ignorant person?

[Col. 0541D] For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not built up.

The one who has blessed. “I give thanks to God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.” Do not think that I too lack this grace and that I therefore forbid you.

But in the Church I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so that I may instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue. I prefer to speak a few words for the benefit of others than many words that benefit no one.

Some ask why he says five words; conversely, they should be asked about the ten thousand.

Brothers, do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in evil; in your understanding be mature.

It is written in the Law: “In other tongues and with other lips I will speak to this people, and even then they will not hear me, says the Lord.”

At the same time he shows that no one is perfect in understanding except one who is a child in evil, because wisdom will not enter a malicious soul.

Be infants in evil, not in understanding. You ought to know how long tongues will continue or why they were given.

Therefore tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers. It is shown that as faith increases, the signs cease, since they were given on account of unbelievers.

But prophecies are not for unbelievers but for believers. Therefore prophecy is greater and more useful, since it benefits believers and is always necessary.

Therefore, if the whole Church should assemble together and all should speak in tongues—that is, if it could happen that, since you all wish this, it were granted to you—and unlearned people or unbelievers entered, would they not say that you were insane?

But if all prophesy and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted [Col. 0542B] by all and judged by all. Just as the Jews said: “These people are full of new wine.”

The secrets of his heart become manifest when his conscience is struck by the teaching.

And thus, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God truly is among you. Thus Nebuchadnezzar worshiped Daniel, saying, “Your God is truly God,” after hearing his dream and its interpretation.

What then is the case, brothers? When you assemble, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has an understanding, has an apocalypse, has a tongue, has an interpretation—has a revelation of mysteries.

Let everything be done for edification. Let there be nothing among you that does not build up one another.

If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be according to two—or at most three. Κατὰ δύο, according to the Greeks: “two at a time.”

And in turn, with one interpreting. [Col. 0542C] Either those two should speak in turn, not simultaneously, or one person should interpret in turn.

But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the Church—either he himself or another. Let him speak to himself and to God.

Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. Let him hold in his own conscience and before God that he possesses this grace.

But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be encouraged.

The one who spoke first, or the one who is first in honor.

And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace. Whether the spirit of grace agrees with another prophet, or whether the spirit of humility and love ought to be in the prophets: God is not a God of pride and dissension, who does not dwell in them, but of peace, because what they prophesy is known to them.

As I teach in [Col. 0542D] all the churches of the saints. This is the practice in all the churches, so that you may not think that I am imposing something new upon you.

Let women keep silent in the churches. For it is contrary to the order of nature or of the Law that women should speak in the assembly of men.

For they are not permitted to speak. How then does he say elsewhere that they ought to teach prudence well, so that they may teach prudence and chastity? Here, however, while indicating the place where they must keep silent, he permitted them elsewhere to speak. But he adds that they must be subject, as the Law also says.

For the man was made first, and Sarah called Abraham “lord.”

But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church.

Or did the word of God come forth from you? Or did it reach you alone?

If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual, [Col. 0543A] let him recognize that what I am writing to you are the Lord’s commandments.

Lest he seem to have forbidden them even to learn, he shows that they ought to learn at home, while in the Church all must keep silence.

It should be noted that men too must be so learned that they are able to teach their wives and instruct them in the truth of the faith.

But if anyone is ignorant, he will be disregarded. Therefore, brothers, strive eagerly to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But let everything among you be done properly and according to order.

While the Apostle was directing that everything be done properly and according to order, he said: “If anyone thinks that he has prophesied or is spiritual, let him recognize that what I am writing to you are the Lord’s commandments. But if anyone is ignorant, he will be disregarded.”

If anyone merely seems to be something, although he is not—for the one who truly is certainly recognizes it and has no need of admonition or correction, [Col. 0543B] since he judges everything and is judged by no one—then those who seemed to be what they were not were the ones creating seditions and disturbances in the churches.

He teaches them to recognize that the commandment is the Lord’s, because God is not a God of sedition but of peace.

But if anyone is ignorant, he will be disregarded—that is, rejected. For if you refer this to knowledge, God does not fail to know those to whom he will say, “I do not know you”; rather, their rejection is conveyed by this expression: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.”

Therefore we must make every effort to be equipped with the gift of God together with love.

CHAPTER XV
I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that I preached to you. Among other things, certain Corinthians even dared to deny the resurrection of the flesh; the Apostle rebukes them for this. Which you also received. [Col. 0543C] So that he might not appear to have preached only to those who did not believe. In which you also stand. You stand in whose teaching. Through which you are also being saved. Through which you are saved, provided that you believe in faith and fulfill it in deed—or because even at present they are saved from many infirmities. In what manner I preached to you, if you hold fast to it, unless you believed in vain.

For I delivered to you first what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; that he was buried; and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures. He briefly recalls the things he had preached to them, restoring them to memory. And that he was seen by Cephas. Not that he first appeared to him, but that he manifested himself to him at the third appearance. And afterward to the eleven. On the evening of the very day of the resurrection, when Thomas was absent.

Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, many of whom remain to the present. [Col. 0543D] Through them, if you wish, you can learn what I am saying. But some have fallen asleep. In the Lord. Then he was seen by James; afterward by all the apostles.

Last of all, as to one born prematurely. A prematurely born person is one who is born before the proper time, or one who is brought forth alive after his mother has died. He calls himself one born prematurely because he believed outside the proper time of the Lord’s preaching. He was seen also by me. When he was traveling to Damascus.

For I am the least of the apostles. Not in labor, since I labored more than all of them, but in rank. I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.

The whole purpose of our preaching is this: that you believe the resurrection. For this is the reward for those who serve Christ; otherwise all the labor of fasts and tribulations is useless—[Col. 0544A] things which in this life, whether prosperous or adverse, seem to be shared with unbelievers. They are accustomed to ask us what more we have than they do; and truly, if we do not hope for the reward of these labors in another life, we are worse than they are.

But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty. Rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me. That is, the grace of God gave me life and restored me; afterward I labored together with God’s grace, and it was not empty in me.

And because he had said, “I labored more abundantly than all of them,” lest he seem to attribute anything to himself, he immediately added: “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me.” For God works in us; he himself inspires us to labor; he himself helps those who labor; and he himself brings the good work to completion, because from him, through [Col. 0544B] him, and in him are all things. As he says elsewhere: “He who began a good work in you will himself bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.” And he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing.”

For blessed Jerome, too, in the *Apologeticus addressed to Pammachius*, gives this testimony in the following form: “Not I, however, but the grace of God that is in me.”

Whether, then, it was I or they, this is how we preached and this is how you believed.

But if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty as well. We are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if indeed the dead are not raised. [Col. 0544C]

For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, your faith is futile; for you are still in your sins. Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.

If our hope in Christ is only for this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings. For he burdened none of those to whom he preached the Gospel: he earned his livelihood by his own hands. Here especially what he said is fulfilled: “I labored more than all of them”; and he adds: “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me.” Thus it also appears that the grace of God must be credited with the fact that he was able, in mind and body, to labor so much more than all of them that he neither ceased preaching the Gospel nor nevertheless supported this life from the Gospel.

[Col. 0544D] But now Christ has risen from the dead. This has already been proved. The firstfruits of those who sleep. If the head has risen, the other members must necessarily follow, because he rose first in incorruptibility.

For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also came through a human being. Just as death entered through Adam, because he was the first to die, so resurrection came through Christ, because he was the first to rise. As the one was the pattern of those who die, so the other is the pattern of those who rise.

And just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. What dies is what rises. One does not speak of rising again except of what has fallen. For the soul is not mortal, although it has died through sin; nor did it lie in its own substance, since it is incorporeal. But the body—

[Col. 0545A] Otherwise, one could more properly say that it rises than that it rises again.

But each in his own order. Of time or of honor.

Christ the firstfruits. As he said above: “The firstfruits of those who sleep.”

Then those who belong to Christ at his coming. Not merely “at his coming,” but they will rise at his coming.

Then the end. When the resurrection of all has occurred, then the end of death will come.

When he has handed over. The Arians slanderously argue: If the Son hands the kingdom over to the Father, then, after handing over the kingdom, he will cease to reign. They must be answered: If the Son will not reign because he is going to hand the kingdom over to the Father, then neither does the Father reign before the Son hands it over to him. But if the Father did not begin to reign only at that time, although he then receives the kingdom, neither will the Son lose it, although he hands it over.

[Col. 0545B] Again they object that he will be subject to the Father. They are impious who even now deny that he is subject to the Father in his body. Subjection, however, does not always concern diminution. For the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets, so that God is not a God of dissension but of peace.

The kingdom. The handing over of the kingdom is our progress, when we have deserved to become fully sons in the Father’s kingdom, when he has led his chosen, made incorruptible, to that vision of which blessed John says: “We shall see him as he is.”

It must first be held that in this passage the Apostle is not speaking about the Trinity but about the resurrection, which he confirms from the example of the Lord—that is, of the human being assumed by him.

The kingdom. The kingdom of God is naturally present throughout all that he established; but God is properly said to reign when human beings have been subjected to him by their will, just as they willingly subjected themselves to the kingdom of the devil.

To God and the Father. To God according to his humanity, to the Father according to his divinity; therefore he says, “to God and the Father.”

When he has abolished every. [Col. 0545C] When we are emptied of sins, their kingdom will be emptied out from us.

Ruler. Because we followed them by doing their will.

Authority. Because they ruled over us.

Power. Because, as enemies, they conquered us.

For he must reign. He has used “reign” for “judge.”

Until he places all his enemies under his feet. When some will be subject by their will and others by necessity.

And the last enemy will be destroyed. For there will be nothing else to destroy afterward, when this mortal nature has put on immortality.

Death. In the Apocalypse, sin is called “death,” because it is the author of death.

[Col. 0545D] For he subjected all things under his feet. David says this about the human being.

But when he says, “All things have been subjected to him,” this is because of the slanderous objection: “Without doubt, except the one who subjected all things to him.” He means God, who was in the world reconciling it to himself. Or certainly understand the Father, who assumed no condition by which he ought to be subject.

But when all things have been subjected to him. When both the good and the evil have been subjected.

Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to himself. Concerning this subjection some say that, just as he hungers in those who hunger or is fed in those who are subject to him, so he himself is subjected in his body; or that human nature itself, in giving thanks, ought to be subject to that divinity which, by making it one with itself, has already subjected all things to him.

[Col. 0546A] Alternatively: At the judgment it is necessary that he again appear in the form of humility. After the judgment, however, the human being is already so subject—that is, joined or united—to God that nothing but divinity will appear, as his saying declares: “So that God may be all in all.”

The words “in all times” are understood. Or certainly, because this is not yet the case: his body is still resisted, since we do not do the things we wish; for the flesh still desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.

So that God may be all to all. The ruler who is wholly present in all things. At present he is not yet all in all, because the individual saints possess different virtues of his within themselves. Then one person will possess all of them, and he himself will be all in all.

[Col. 0546B] Let us also see what holy Bishop Augustine thought (*Augustine, in the book On Various Questions, question 66*): “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.”

The question is rightly asked here whether the Apostle spoke according to the distinct properties of the persons or according to the assumption of the human being. The surrounding passages of Scripture commonly illuminate a statement when the matters relating to the present question that occur around the passage are carefully examined.

We find, then, that the discussion has arrived at this point after he had said above: “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep.” For he was discussing the resurrection of the dead, which took place in the Lord according to the assumption of the human being. Therefore it is clear that this was said according to the assumption of the human being.

But another question commonly arises in this chapter. First, what is meant by: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father,” as though the Father does not now possess the kingdom; then what is meant by: “For he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet,” as though he will not reign afterward; and how this agrees with what was said above: “Then the end,” which heretics, in their sacrilegious opinion, understand as though he had spoken of the end or completion of his reign, although it is written in the Gospel: “And of his kingdom there will be no end.”

[Col. 0546C] Finally, what is meant by: “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him”? They wish to understand this as though now either something were not subject to the Son, or the Son himself were not subject to the Father.

The question is resolved by the form of expression. Scripture often speaks in such a way that something which always exists is said to happen at a certain time when it begins to be recognized by someone. Thus in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Hallowed be your name,” not as though it were at some time not holy.

Therefore, just as “hallowed be” means “let it be recognized as holy,” so also “when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” means “when he has shown that the Father reigns,” so that it may become clear through manifestation and disclosure what is now believed by the faithful and not thought to be so by unbelievers.

[Col. 0546D] He will abolish every ruler and authority by manifesting the Father’s kingdom, so that it may be known to all that no rulers or authorities, whether heavenly or earthly, possessed their rule and authority by themselves, but received them from him from whom all things exist—not only that they might exist, but also that they might be ordered.

[Col. 0547A] For in that manifestation no hope will remain for anyone in any ruler or in any human being. Even now this is sung prophetically: “It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in a human being.” Again: “It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in rulers.” By this reflection the soul may already rise into the Father’s kingdom, neither magnifying the power of anyone besides him nor most dangerously flattering itself.

Therefore he hands the kingdom over to God and the Father when, through him, the Father is known by manifestation. His kingdom consists of those in whom he now reigns through faith.

The kingdom of Christ is spoken of in one way according to the power of his divinity, since every creature is subject to him; and his kingdom is spoken of in another way as the Church, according to the character of the faith that is in him, in accordance with the prayer of the one who says: “Possess us.”

For it is not that he does not possess all things, as is also said: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness.”

[Col. 0547B] Therefore he will abolish every ruler, every authority, and every power, so that, when anyone looks upon the Father through the Son, there may be no need or desire to rest in the power of any creature or in one’s own power.

For he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet; that is, his kingdom must be manifested to such an extent that all his enemies confess that he reigns.

This is not understood to mean that the enemies will be under his feet in the same way. If we take the statement as referring to the just, they are called enemies because they are justified from being unjust and are subjected to him by believing. Concerning the unjust, however, who do not belong to the future blessedness of the just, it must be understood in this way: they too, confounded by the very manifestation of his kingdom, will confess that he reigns.

[Col. 0547C] Therefore, “he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet” is not said as though, once he has placed his enemies under his feet, he will not reign afterward. Rather, he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet. He must bring his kingdom, he says, to such complete visibility that his enemies will in no way dare deny that he reigns.

Sometimes the sacred writings use “until” as a conjunction, so that it can also be understood as “and” or “so that.” For it is written: “Until she bore her son,” that is, “and she bore her son.” It is also written: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God until he has mercy on us,” that is, “so that he may have mercy on us.” Yet when he has had mercy on us, we must not turn our eyes away from him.

For our blessedness consists in the extent to which we enjoy the contemplation of him. Thus this too is said: “The attention of our eyes is directed toward the Lord only until we obtain his mercy”—not so that afterward it may turn away from him, but so that it may seek nothing further from him.

[Col. 0547D] Therefore “until” is used here to mean “no further.” For to what greater extent—that is, until what greater manifestation—will the kingdom of Christ be manifested, except until all his enemies confess that he reigns?

It is one thing for there to be no further manifestation; it is another for there to be no further continuance. “No further manifestation” means that it does not become more manifest; “no further continuance” means that it does not continue any longer. But when will the kingdom of Christ be more manifest than when it has become clear to all his enemies?

[Col. 0548A] Finally, the enemy death will be destroyed. For there will be nothing else to destroy after this mortal nature has put on immortality. For he subjected all things under his feet—that is, so that he might also destroy death.

When he says that all things have been subjected, the prophet plainly said this in the Psalms. It is clear that, except for the one who subjected all things to him, he wishes the Father to be understood as having subjected all things to the Son. The same Lord commends and proclaims this in many passages of the Gospel, not only on account of the form of a servant but also on account of the principle from which he comes and in relation to which he is equal—the one from whom he is.

For, as his image, he loves to refer all things to one principle, in whom dwells the whole fullness of divinity.

But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him. This does not mean that it is not so now, but that it will then be manifest, according to the form of expression discussed above.

[Col. 0548B] So that God may be all in all. This is the end he mentioned above when he first wished to conclude everything briefly and then to explain and expound it, as it were, piece by piece. He was speaking about the resurrection, where he said: “The beginning is Christ, then those who belong to Christ at his coming, then the end.” The end itself is that God may be all in all.

“End” is used in one way when it concerns completion and in another when it concerns consumption. A garment reaches its end by being woven; food reaches its end by being eaten.

God is said to be all in all so that none of those who cling to him may love his own will against him, and so that it may be manifest to all what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “What do you have that you did not receive?”

[Col. 0548C] There are also some who understand the passage in this way: “He must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet.” They say that “reign” is used here with another meaning, not the meaning of “kingdom” in the statement: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father.”

They say that “kingdom” there refers to the kingdom by which God rules the entire creation, while “reign” here is understood as though he were leading an army against an enemy or defending a city. Thus he said, “He must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet,” because a kingdom of the kind possessed by armed rulers will have no purpose once the enemy has been subjected so completely that he can no longer wage war.

For it is certainly said in the Gospel: “And of his kingdom there will be no end,” inasmuch as he reigns eternally. But insofar as warfare is waged under him against the devil, this activity will last until he places all his enemies under his feet. Afterward it will not continue, when we enjoy perpetual peace.

[Col. 0548D] These statements have been made so that we may understand that we must examine more carefully in what sense the Lord now reigns—that is, according to the dispensation of his mystery through incarnation and passion.

For insofar as he is the Word of God, his kingdom exists without end, without beginning, and without interruption. But insofar as the Word became flesh, he began to reign in believers through faith in his incarnation. Hence also the statement: “The Lord has reigned from the wood.”

[Col. 0549A] By this means he abolished every ruler, every authority, and every power: not through his glory, but through the humility of the servant, believers are made his own. This was hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to infants, because it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. The Apostle says that he knows nothing among the infants except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

This preaching is necessary until all his enemies are placed under his feet—that is, until all worldly pride yields and is subjected to his humility, signified, I think, by the name “feet.” We see that this has already happened to a great extent and is happening daily.

But to what end do these things happen? So that the kingdom may be handed over to God and the Father; that is, so that those whom he has nourished by faith in his incarnation may be brought to the vision in which he is equal to the Father.

[Col. 0549B] He was speaking to those who had believed when he said: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

He hands the kingdom over to the Father when he will reign through that truth in those who contemplate it, the truth in which he is equal to the Father; and through himself, the only-begotten Son, he will make the Father visible.

For now he reigns in believers because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Then he will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father when he has abolished every ruler, authority, and power.

By what means will he abolish them, unless by humility, patience, and weakness? For what rule is not abolished when the rulers of this world judged the Son of God, and he therefore reigns in believers? What authority is not abolished when the one through whom all things were made reigns in believers precisely because he was so subject to the authorities that he said to a human being: “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given to you from above”?

[Col. 0549C] What power is not abolished when the one through whom the heavens were established reigns in believers precisely because he was weakened even to the cross and death?

In this way the Son is properly present in the faith of believers. For the Father cannot be called or believed to have been incarnate, judged, or crucified. But according to that vision in which he is equal to the Father, he reigns with the Father in those who contemplate the truth.

When he hands the kingdom over to God and the Father, bringing those who now believe in him from faith in his incarnation to the vision of his divinity, he does not himself lose anything. Rather, the two present themselves as one to those who contemplate them, so that they may enjoy them.

[Col. 0549D] It is necessary that this continue as long as human beings are not yet capable of beholding the equality of the Father and the Son with the clear light of the mind. During that time Christ reigns through what such people can grasp and through what he himself properly assumed—that is, the humility of the incarnation—until he places all his enemies under his feet; that is, until all worldly pride is subjected to the humility of his incarnation.

It is true that the statement, “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him,” is spoken according to the assumption of the human being, since the question arose while he was discussing the resurrection of the dead. Nevertheless, it is rightly asked whether it was spoken only of Christ himself, who is the head of the Church, or of the whole Christ, with his body and members included.

[Col. 0550A] When he says to the Galatians: “He does not say ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ,” we should not understand Christ in this passage as only the one who was born of the Virgin Mary. For afterward he says: “For you are all one in Christ Jesus. But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed.”

To the Corinthians, when he spoke about love and drew an analogy from the members of the body, he says: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ.” He did not say, “so also are Christ’s members,” but “so also is Christ,” showing that Christ may rightly be called the whole—namely, the head together with his body, which is the Church.

[Col. 0550B] We find Christ called in this way in many passages of Scripture, so that he is understood together with all his members, to whom it was said: “You are the body of Christ and members.”

Therefore we understand it without absurdity in this way: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him,” so that by “the Son” we understand not only the head of the Church but all the saints together with him, who are one in Christ and one seed of Abraham.

He is subject according to the contemplation of eternal truth, in order to obtain blessedness, with no movement of the mind and no part of the body resisting, since in that life no one loves his own power, but God is all in all.

Otherwise. Furthermore.

What will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they also baptized for them?

[Col. 0550C] All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For all who are baptized are baptized as though we had already died for the dead.

What benefit is there, then, in our dying to this world if eternal life does not follow this labor? Why do we also endanger ourselves every hour?

Daily I die because of your glory, brothers. If there were nothing in the future, we would not be so foolish as to suffer such things for others.

Which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. I possess the reward of my labor even if you do not wish to make progress.

If, in human terms, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what benefit is there for me if the dead are not raised? If you hope for no reward from God for me, then I fought for nothing, perhaps in order to please human beings.

Alternatively, the beasts are understood allegorically as hostile powers. As in the Psalm: “Do not hand over to beasts the one who confesses you.”

[Col. 0550D] Many things are said in the Epistles that are not found in Acts, and many things in Acts that are not said in the Epistles.

“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” The prophet Isaiah rebukes those devoted to gluttony because of their despair concerning future things, and he denies that the crime of this blasphemy is forgiven them as long as they live.

Do not be led astray. By those who do such things.

“Evil conversations corrupt good morals.” They might say: “Do you therefore think that we can be led astray?” He responds to their thought: “No, I am not afraid of you; rather, I fear their evasion.”

Conversely, good conversations restore evil morals.

Awake. Be sober, you righteous. He proves that those who surrender themselves to gluttony and pleasures do not believe in the resurrection.

And do not sin. For some possess ignorance of God.

The righteous person is the one who does not sin—that is, who does not commit a capital sin—or, if he is suddenly overtaken by one, erases it through repentance, because he believes that he will have to give an account at the judgment. For the one who does not believe in the resurrection, despairing of everything, commits every unspeakable act.

[Col. 0551A] Many commonly ask whether weak bodies will rise again in the same condition in which they died. They must be answered that in the resurrection it is not the defect of weakness that is restored but nature itself. For the body is never so weak as when it lies hidden in dust. Therefore, if it is believed that God restores the whole, why should it be doubted that he restores part? Why should he not restore the eyes, when he will restore the whole body?

I say this to put you to shame.

But someone will say: “How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body will they come?” They do not know the power of God, thinking that he cannot raise the dead and measuring divinity by their own weakness. Thus you should be ashamed that I must instruct you with such arguments as though you were children.

Foolish person, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. Foolish person, who ought also to have been taught by natural things not to doubt the resurrection.

Are you still unbelieving in the divine promises? From the regularity of your own work you ought to have considered what we are saying.

[Col. 0551B] And what you sow is not the body that will be, but a bare grain—for example, of wheat or of one of the other kinds of seed. But God gives it a body as he wills. Just as from a grain an ear rises, more fruitful and filled with grains, so the corruptible body will rise to an increase of glory.

And to each kind of seed its own body. Hence blessed Job says: “And in my flesh I shall see God.”

Not all flesh is the same flesh. Pay attention: he said “its own body,” not “another’s.”

But there is one flesh of human beings, another of cattle, another of birds, and another of fish. Understand the same thing concerning the waters, which have produced such a diversity of birds and fish.
