[Col. 0551C] And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. Since he made such bodies out of the elements, why should he not restore the small human body?

But the glory of heavenly things is one kind, and that of earthly things another. The brightness of the moon is one kind, and the brightness of the stars another. Every difference in comparison serves this purpose: that you may believe that the one who made so many things from nothing can easily restore one.

For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead. He compares the diversity of the stars with the difference among the righteous, whom virtues, not sins, will make diverse. There will be no diversity of sinners in heaven, but in punishment.

It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. So that it may suffer neither fevers nor other afflictions.

[Col. 0551D] It is sown in dishonor. What is more dishonorable than a dead body? It will rise in glory. It will rise in the glory of splendor, like the sun.

It is sown in weakness. In human frailty. It will rise in power. In the power of angelic eternity.

It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body. Here it is an animal body because we do not always have the Holy Spirit; then he will always be in us.

If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one. One that can go to meet Christ. As it is written: “The first man, Adam, was made a living soul.” This testimony is from the Law.

“The last Adam was made a life-giving Spirit.” Why is the second human being, or the last Adam, so called after so many human beings? The first Adam is whoever imitates his footsteps; the last is the one who follows the footsteps of the Lord. [Col. 0552A]

He is called “last” from the first because, until him, death descended from the first human being, and until the cross the fall of the first human being held power. Therefore he is first in relation to death and last in relation to salvation: the one was first as living, the other as giving life.

But it was not first the spiritual, but the animal; afterward the spiritual.

The first human being was from the earth, earthly. It should be noted that, when he speaks of two Adams, he demonstrates that both are of the same nature: just as the first was without generation, so the second was without seed.

The second human being was from heaven, heavenly. Christ is human from heaven for this reason: that in the baptism of John it was not water but grace that descended from heaven. And because he assumed flesh without sin, and God deigned to be born from a Virgin.

As was the earthly one, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly one, so are the heavenly. Understand Christ as heavenly because he is entirely without sin, not because he brought flesh from heaven.

[Col. 0552B] Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly. The old human being before baptism; the new after baptism.

Now I say this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption. Scripture frequently uses “flesh” for the substance itself, as in the statement: “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit.”

Alternatively: Flesh as it now exists will not possess the kingdom of God unless it is clothed with immortality.

Behold, I tell you a mystery. By naming it a mystery, he indicates something obscure.

We shall all rise. All of us who are found dead when Christ comes will rise. But we shall not all be changed.

[Col. 0552C] Those who are found in the body, because the saints will be taken up, while sinners will be left for eternal fire. For sinners who are found alive will first be consumed by fire; then they will rise.

But we shall not all be changed. Because the righteous will rise to glory, while sinners will rise for punishment.

In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. He wishes to indicate the brevity of the moment.

At the last trumpet. Some understand two trumpets and two comings of Christ. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise. The dead will rise first, and then the saints will be changed; hence it is called the last trumpet.

Incorruptible. So that they may endure forever in punishment.

And we shall be changed. For this corruptible nature must put on incorruption, and this mortal nature must put on immortality.

[Col. 0552D] When this corruptible nature has put on incorruption and this mortal nature has put on immortality. There is what will clothe and there is what will be clothed.

Then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” The causes of death having been abolished.

“Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death? Where is your contention, O death?” What contention, except that now the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh? This is the struggle, this is the contention; but he speaks in the person of the righteous, who taunt death.

The sting of death is sin. The arrow of death is sin, by which souls are slaughtered.

The power of sin is the law. Through knowledge, sin becomes stronger.

Why is the law the power of sin if the law is good? Because sin, through what is good, worked death, so that it might become exceedingly great—that is, so that it might receive greater strength through transgression.

[Col. 0553A] But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. The victory over that sin in which the law was weakened, through our carnal desire, which Christ destroyed by his cross.

Therefore, my beloved brothers. Having given the reason for the resurrection, about which they were uncertain, he exhorts them to remain steadfast in God’s work, now confident of the future reward.

Be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord. Let no one move you any farther from this step of hope.

Knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord. That is, you do not labor without cause.

## Chapter XVI.

Concerning the collections made for the saints: just as I ordered the churches of Galatia, so also you are to do. He speaks of the funds collected throughout the individual churches and sent to Jerusalem for the poor among the saints.

**On the first day of the week, each of you**—“the first day of the week” means the Lord’s Day, just as it is written in the Gospel that the Lord rose on the first day of the week—**should set something aside at home, storing up whatever seems good to him**, so that collections will not have to be made when I come. When I am present, I will send those whom you approve by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. Thus, by setting it aside little by little, they will not think themselves burdened all at once, so that the givers may be cheerful, since God loves cheerful givers.

If it is worthy that I should go as well, they will travel with me—if your offering is such that it may suitably be presented through me.

I will come to you after I have passed through Macedonia. For I will pass through Macedonia. But I may remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go. I do not wish to see you now merely in passing, because the Macedonians are situated in such a way [Col. 0553C] that there is no need for me to remain longer among them. But it is necessary that I remain with you, or spend the winter there, for there are many matters among you that need correction; indeed, a physician remains where more people are sick.

For I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. But I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

If Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you, for he is doing the Lord’s work just as I am. Therefore let no one despise him. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am expecting him with the brothers.

Concerning our brother Apollos, I urged him at length to come to you with the brothers; and certainly it was not his will that he come now [Col. 0554A]. But he will come when he has the opportunity.

Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strengthened. Let everything you do be done in love.

That is why I will remain there: because an evident opportunity for preaching has arisen for me, and many are resisting, while God has opened the door of the heart to many, and many who do not believe have resisted.

I appeal to you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas and Fortunatus, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia—either firstfruits in faith or firstfruits in honor. They have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints, whether for teaching the saints or for supplying their necessities. You also should submit to such people, and to everyone who cooperates and labors.

Those who cooperate with us or with them in the Gospel of Christ.

I will rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, who are present among you, because [Col. 0554B] they supplied what was lacking in you—in knowledge. They supplied it through teaching or example. For they refreshed both my spirit and yours: mine with joy at your progress, and yours through instruction in doctrine.

Therefore acknowledge those who are such.

The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca [Vulgate: Priscilla] greet you very warmly in the Lord, always.

As he says elsewhere: “Acknowledge those who walk in this way, just as you have our example.” Here “acknowledge” means “honor,” recognizing their labor.

Together with their household church. A household gathering of the brotherhood is called a church.

All the brothers with whom I am also staying greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss—not a deceitful one, as Judas gave.

The greeting is by my own hand, Paul’s.

If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: *Maranatha* (“the Lord has come”).

Just as Christ will come as redemption for those who love him, so an anathema comes upon those who do not love him—that is, so that he may abhor and destroy them.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

This is the subscription: that is, may grace always be with you, without whose help you cannot stand or do anything good.

My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus—not worldly love, so that, just as I love you, you may love one another in Christ, who said: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you love one another.”

Amen. Amen is the confirmation of the blessing. As he says above: “How does he say ‘Amen’ over your blessing?”

# THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0553]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0553D]

After they had done penance, he writes to console them from Troas; praising them, he exhorts them to better things.

## CHAPTER ONE

Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ. It is asked why, contrary to the custom of writing, he places his own name first in all the Epistles, and then the names of those to whom he writes. This is because of apostolic authority and rank: he writes to those beneath him, just as judges customarily send commands to those whom they govern.

By the will of God. As he says to the Galatians: “Not from human beings, nor through a human being.” At the same time, he shows that he was not sent without the will of the Father [Col. 0554D]. No one is unaware that God’s will is just and reasonable.

And Timothy, the brother. He did not say “Paul and Timothy,” because they were not both apostles. But to the Philippians, where such authority was not equally necessary, he begins in this way: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ,” because both are servants.

To the church of God that is in Corinth. For there was a church there, but not one belonging to God.

With all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. Here “saints” may be understood not only as the baptized, but also as God’s priests, as in the First Epistle: “With all who call upon the name of the Lord.” And to the Philippians: “With bishops [Col. 0555A] and deacons.” He placed the priests afterward so that those who understood less clearly would not appear to have excluded them from the church.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Just as we customarily pray for health at the beginning of our letters, the Apostle always places grace instead.

Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. He gives thanks to God because they receive consolation so that they themselves may console others.

The Father of mercies. Because every mercy comes from him.

And God of all consolation. “Of all consolation,” because he consoles perfectly, and consolation is not less than tribulation.

Who consoles us in all our tribulation. Not in some tribulations only.

So that we too may console those who are in every distress. For this reason he frees us, so that we may console others, and thus gives us a model for consoling others [Col. 0555B] through the exhortation by which we ourselves are exhorted by God.

And through the exhortation by which we ourselves are consoled by God, we recognize that God abandons no one, and that in the future he will reward even those whom he does not abandon in the present.

For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us—sufferings endured for the name of Christ—so also through Christ our consolation abounds. As Peter was freed from prison, and Paul was confirmed by the Lord’s vision and voice in the temple.

Whether we are afflicted for your exhortation and salvation, or whether we are consoled for your consolation. We exhort you to salvation, or so that we may offer you an example of endurance.

Or whether we are exhorted for your exhortation, which produces endurance of the same sufferings that we also endure [Col. 0555C]. For this reason we are freed, so that you may be confirmed in the knowledge that you ought not fear sufferings; or so that we may urge you patiently to bear these things, which have both present and future consolation.

So that our hope for you may be firm, knowing that just as you are partners in the sufferings, so also you will be partners in the consolation. For we are certain.

For we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation that occurred in Asia. He recounts his sufferings so that they may recognize that they themselves suffer little—especially since those who were sent in Christ’s place endured such things. In comparison with their teacher, the disciples should be ashamed to grieve over their own injuries when they know that their teacher endured greater ones.

For we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength. By the pressure of tribulations.

So that we were even weary of living. So that we wished to die.

But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death [Col. 0555D]. Death itself taught us that every human help had failed, and that a remedy must be hoped for from him alone to whom it is also possible to raise the dead.

So that we would not put our trust in ourselves—or even despair of life. This passage is directed against those who are Catholics yet presume to attribute something to their own merits.

But in God, who raises the dead, who rescued us from such great dangers and continues to rescue us. Not in our prudence or caution, nor in our virtues, because cursed is the one who places his trust in the flesh of his arm.

In him we hope, because he will still rescue us. One who hopes to be delivered knows beforehand that he will still suffer.

With the help of you also. Just as Peter was freed from prison through the prayers of the Church [Col. 0556A]. At the same time, it should be noted that no one is said to be helped unless he is laboring.

In prayer for us. The prayer of the whole Church is very powerful.

So that thanks may be given for us by many people for the gift bestowed on us through the grace of many. That is, so that, through the gathering of many people—children, young people, and old people—thanks may be returned to the Lord because we have been given to you.

For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that we have conducted ourselves in the simplicity and sincerity of God. That is why I glory in tribulations: because my conscience does not reproach me for preaching for the sake of profit or glory, but for seeking your salvation in simplicity.

And not in carnal wisdom, but in the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world. We did not teach deceitfully, as carnal wisdom does, which is sold for payment, but freely, just as we received from God or preached for God’s sake [Col. 0556B].

And more abundantly toward you. From you we did not even receive the food that was rightfully due to us.

For we write nothing else to you. I am not ashamed, because you yourselves know that what I say is certain.

Than what you have read and understand. These are the things that you understand as you read them in the letter and recognize them in your conscience.

But I hope that you will understand fully to the end. I will not change my purpose.

Just as you have understood us in part. For the end has not yet come; but when the end comes, then you will understand us completely.

Because we are your glory, just as you are ours. Just as disciples glory in a good teacher, so also a teacher glories in good disciples.

On the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. There true teachers and good disciples will be tested.

And with this confidence I wished to come to you first. With this conscience, because we sought nothing of yours except your salvation.

So that you might have a second grace, and pass through Macedonia by way of you. And again, from Macedonia, come to you, and be sent on by you into Judea. At my first coming you had the first grace; or certainly, by “a second grace,” he meant penance, because the first is baptism.

When I therefore intended this, did I use fickleness? Because he had not fulfilled his promise, lest they think this was fickleness, he excuses himself truthfully and wisely.

Or do I make my plans according to the flesh? According to carnal desire. It is carnal, when there is no reason, not to do what one promises, as many carnal people are accustomed to do.

So that with me there should be “Yes” and “No”? Therefore I do not think according to the flesh, so that I may not lie.

But God is faithful: for our word that was preached among you was not “Yes” and “No,” but “Yes” was in it. There is no uncertainty in it, nor have we ever lied to you.

For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not “Yes” and “No” in him [Col. 0556D], but “Yes” was in him.

This is directed against the Manichaeans, who assert that Christ had false flesh, and against the Arians, who deny that the Son always existed, although he himself spoke to Moses: “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you.” For he both was, is, and always is, because he never does not exist.

But “Yes” was in him. That is, truth and immutability, as Moses says: “He who is has sent me.” For he truly is who is always the same.

For however many promises of God there are, in him is “Yes.” Therefore through him we also say “Amen” to God [Col. 0557A]. The fulfillment of truth.

For our glory. Every truth of the promises is in Christ, and through us it is fulfilled for the glory of God.

Now the one who confirms us with you in Christ. Because he had said, “through us,” he now shows that God does all this, who worked all these things in them, so that human weakness would claim nothing for itself.

And who anointed us is God. With the Holy Spirit, or with chrism.

And who sealed us. Everything precious within is sealed.

And who gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. Every pledge is given in proportion to the value of the price. How great, then, is the reward whose pledge is so great? That is, the grace of the Spirit.

But I. He explains why he did not go, so that it might be attributed not to his fickleness but to their weakness.

I call God as witness against my soul. He alone does not fail to perceive the secrets of the soul [Col. 0557B].

That, sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth. So that I would not exercise a harsher judgment among you.

Not that we lord it over your faith. Not because you believed so that we might lord it over you, as priests do under the Law, and therefore frighten you; rather, we do everything for your correction, so that you may rejoice both here in your conscience and forever.

Not that you are again compelled through fear as slaves, but we assist your freedom, so that, while you do not know how to preserve its proper measure, you may not fall into something worse.

But we are helpers. Co-workers.

Of your joy. For you have stood firm in the faith. You are free if you do not sin. Conscience rejoices when it remembers good works. The joy of a teacher is the progress of his disciples.

## CHAPTER TWO

But I determined this within myself. I considered it [Col. 0557C], or decided it.

Not to come to you again in sorrow. I who had first come in joy, when you believed.

For if I cause you sorrow, who is there to make me glad? I cause you sorrow for this purpose, so that I may rejoice over you.

Except the one who is saddened by me? For the one who is saddened understands that he has sinned; just as a sick person who still feels pain can recover health.

And I myself wrote this to you. I wrote in order that, corrected by the letter, you might make me rejoice when I came.

So that when I come I may not have sorrow upon sorrow. For I am sorrowful because you sin; therefore my sorrow increases if you do not correct yourselves completely.

Concerning those over whom I ought to have rejoiced. Over whom I should never have had cause for sorrow—or concerning whose correction I ought to rejoice.

Confident in all of you, because my joy is the joy of all of you. Confident that you all understand that you have true joy when I rejoice.

For out of great tribulation and anguish of heart. Here one should understand how concerned the apostles were for the salvation of everyone.

I wrote to you with many tears—the earlier Epistle—not so that you might be saddened, but so that you might know what love I have for you. Not because your pain pleases me, but because you cannot otherwise be healed.

That I might have more abundantly in you. They might say: “We alone have not sinned.” From a more abundant concern you can discern a greater love.

But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has not caused sorrow to me. Because through his sin you, having also been corrected, make greater progress; or because, since he has reformed, he has not caused sorrow in every respect.

But only in part. As though he had caused harm in a good cause.

So that I do not burden all of you. That is why [Col. 0558A] I write that he should be received, so that he may not burden you if, because of your harshness, he should despair.

This punishment, which has been imposed by the majority, is sufficient for such a person. He is speaking not only of the man who polluted his father’s marriage bed, but of every sinner, since many sinned, as the First Epistle shows.

So that, on the contrary, you should rather grant forgiveness and consolation, lest someone of this kind be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Grant him pardon and console him with the words of the Prophet: “I do not desire the death of a sinner, but only that he should turn.” And: “On whatever day the wicked person turns.”

Lest, through despair, he be swallowed up by the refusal of pardon, engulfed in the depth of vices, or swallowed by the devil and led to the precipices of unbelief and blasphemy.

For this reason I appeal to you to confirm your love for him. So that, through the prophecy, he may recognize that he has received pardon [Col. 0558B], by which God said: “I do not desire the death of the one who is dying.”

For this reason I wrote, so that I might learn by experience whether you are obedient in everything. I write this second letter so that I may see whether, just as you obeyed in excommunicating him, so you also obey in receiving him. For that obedience is perfect and true which despises nothing.

But to whomever you have forgiven—that is, “whomever you will have forgiven”—I forgive also.

And I. Just as I exercised judgment with you, so I forgive together with you.

For what I have forgiven, I have forgiven not in my own person, but in the person of Christ, who said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

If I have forgiven anything, I have done so for your sake, so that you may not be burdened.

In the person of Christ. For we represent the person of Christ.

So that we may not be outwitted by Satan. For he outwits us through excessive severity, so that souls may perish by despair, just as he does through excessive kindness, when we fail to correct them. Hence Solomon says: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left.”

Although the entire Epistle is directed against the Novatians, here it is shown most clearly that they have been outwitted by the devil by refusing penance.

For we are not ignorant of his designs. These are his stratagems: to deceive the unwary through excessive acts of apparent goodness.

When I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ. He now wishes to prove to them how much more he loves them and how concerned he is on their account. Although everything was prosperous for him, he had no rest because he did not find Titus, whom he had sent to them so that Titus might report whether they had corrected themselves. By this they should understand that he had done everything out of love.

And when a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit. “Door”: an entrance or opportunity for preaching; or because God had opened the hearts of those to whom he preached [Col. 0558D].

Because I did not find Titus, my brother. Because he had not returned to me to inform me about you.

But saying farewell to them, I went away to Macedonia. From there I departed, although I had an opportunity to preach; and I said farewell to those who had believed, whose heart God had opened.

To Macedonia. From there I would hear more quickly about you. Macedonia is nearer to Achaia.

But thanks be to God, who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus. He makes us triumph, or he himself triumphs over us.

And through us manifests the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place. At first, those who were beginning to believe could know only something slight, as though it were the fragrance of faith.

For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God [Col. 0559A]. The fragrance of the knowledge of God is manifested through teaching and signs. It is called a fragrance because it is sensed rather than seen.

The good fragrance is holy preaching and a good life. Those who love such things live by the good fragrance; those who envy them die by the good fragrance.

Among those who are being saved. His grace.

And among those who are perishing. His most just judgment. Among those who are being saved, as with Tabitha; and among those who are perishing, as with Hymenaeus and Alexander.

To some we are the fragrance of death unto death, but to others the fragrance of life unto life. How can one fragrance bring both life and death? Just as the sight of the sun brings brightness to healthy eyes but blindness to diseased eyes, so Christ’s teaching is life to those who obey and death to those who contradict it.

Again, in another sense: Christ’s baptism is a good fragrance. Whoever receives it in the Catholic Church lives by the good fragrance; whoever receives it in heresy dies by the good fragrance.

Again, in another sense: you loved one who acted well, and you lived by the good fragrance; you envy and slander one who acts well, and you are dead by the good fragrance.

And who is so capable of these things? Who can do so by himself or by his own strength, unless that one inspires and gives, without whom we can do nothing? For who can comprehend how the grace of God saves some and leaves others?

For we are not like the many who adulterate the word of God, but we speak from sincerity. He censures the pseudo-apostles, who mix human understanding into divine preaching, as he says in Isaiah: “Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine”—that is, they mix words of flattery with pure doctrine, so that people do not become fervent through intoxication but grow lukewarm through pleasure.

As from God, before God. He has gone before, and we know that we speak from him and before him.

We speak in Christ—in the person [Col. 0559C] of Christ, just as he himself taught.

## CHAPTER THREE

Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we perhaps need letters of recommendation, as some do? We do not praise you in order to be commended to you, but because we are compelled to recall these things lest you be led astray by others.

Letters of recommendation to you, or from you? Those whom the grace of virtues does not commend, letters from friends commend suitably.

You are our letter. As he says in the First Epistle: “You are the seal of my apostleship”—a letter of recommendation.

Written in our hearts. It is in our consciences that you believed when we preached to you.

Which is known and read by all people as having been made manifest. It is evident to everyone that you believed in Christ through us, with the Holy Spirit confirming our teaching through miracles; or, from this, you will truly be known to be Christ’s [Col. 0559D], because you have received his Spirit.

For you are the letter of Christ, served through us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. With the invisible Spirit.

Not on stone tablets. The Jews received the Law on hard material, signifying their hardness, just as the veil of Moses displayed the veil over their hearts.

Although we too possess the Law of Christ written down, at first we received the Lord’s words in our hearts not as absent people but as those who were present before written tablets. The Gospels, however, were later written for the remembrance of posterity.

Here he now introduces the distinction between the Law and grace.

But on tablets of fleshly hearts. Where faith and the grace of the Spirit are found.

He wishes to show that more has been bestowed on us, since we have received the Law in our hearts. If therefore they were inexcusable who had the Law externally [Col. 0560A], how much more are we, who have received Christ’s words from his mouth into our hearts?

Now we have such confidence. By which we know that you believed in Christ through us; or because it is not a human letter but God’s grace that commends us.

Through Christ toward God. Not through ourselves, who are nothing without him.

Not that we are sufficient to think anything. If we are not sufficient even to think, how much less to act! As the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing.”

From this let us understand that we are nothing through ourselves unless we are governed by the Lord’s mercy and grace. He therefore wishes to show that he does nothing by his own strength or wisdom, since, unless by God’s grace, even a few people could never have saved the whole world.

He prefaced this because he was about to say that he had undertaken a ministry much greater than Moses’, insofar as the New Testament is greater than the Law, lest he appear to claim anything for himself. He said this both to recall them from the false apostles and to prevent them from attributing anything to their own merits.

From us, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God. As though it came from our own wisdom or strength, so that human weakness may attribute nothing to its own powers.

Who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament. He made us competent to fulfill this.

Not of the letter but of the spirit. Not of the letter of the Law, but of spiritual commandments.

Nor is the letter itself evil because it kills; rather, those whom it convicts through transgression are evil. For the sting of death is sin, while the power of sin is the Law. It increases the desires of sin, and thereby kills. The Law is merely letter for those who know how to read it but cannot fulfill it: it is not a helper of those who read, but a witness against sinners, and it puts sinners to death.

Yet he himself said: “The Law is holy, and the commandment is holy.” Why then is it called a ministry of death, if the Law is good?

Do not be surprised, since it was also said concerning the preaching of the Gospel: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing,” and so forth.

The Law was called a ministry of death with reference to the Jews, for whom it was also written on stones, to represent their hardness—not with reference to those who fulfill the Law through love.

For the Law itself, which is represented in letters engraved on stone, says: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not commit fornication,” and the rest. But it kills sinners when they transgress.

How, then, is the Law spiritual? Some think that the literal meaning of the text kills, failing to understand that neither can history be preserved everywhere nor allegory be preserved everywhere [Col. 0560D]. For some things are spoken figuratively.

If we wish to turn every commandment into allegory, we weaken all its force and open the door to wrongdoing. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life, by making believers and infusing spiritual understanding, so that each matter may be understood appropriately.

But if the ministry of death, formed in letters on stones, was in glory—on insensible materials, as the hard hearts of the Jews deserved—so that the children of Israel could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, this is directed against the Manichaeans. The Apostle could never compare contrary things, nor proclaim his own glory as less than Moses’ glory, unless the same God were the creator of both Testaments.

Which is being brought to an end. The visible glory is brought to an end by the glory of the Gospel, but it is brought to an end in such a way that it advances, just as childhood is brought to an end in youth and the seed in the fruit. The fruit is indeed better than the seed, but there is never fruit without seed; the seed does not perish but is multiplied in the fruit. Thus it is brought to an end, as he says in the First Epistle when he prophesies that knowledge and prophecy will be destroyed: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be brought to an end.”

How much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory? Just as injustice is done to the Old Testament if it is said not to have been created by the same God by whom the New Testament was created, so injustice is done to the New Testament if it is compared with the Old.

Will it be in glory? Our ministry, whose glory is not brought to an end because it is perfect.

For if there is glory in the ministry of condemnation. He has explained the ministry of death.

Much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. By this righteousness he justifies freely, or waits for repentance.

In eternal glory. For even that which shone in this part was not glorified, because of the surpassing glory. In comparison with the glory of the Gospel, the glory of the Law is overshadowed, just as, when the sun rises, the light of a lamp is blinded, although in its own time it appears to possess great brilliance.

The Lord showed this when, ascending the mountain alone, he is said to have radiated with the splendor of the sun; yet Moses and Elijah are reported to have appeared in glory, and for this reason the Father’s voice commanded us to listen to him alone.

For if that which is brought to an end was given through glory, much more will that which remains be in glory. If the Testament that was to be brought to an end was given through glory, how much more is the Testament that remains in glory?

Therefore, having such hope. Such hope of glory, through which we walk by faith.

We use great confidence. In that God has made us competent.

And not as Moses placed a veil over his face. We no longer act in this way, because here all Christians see the glory.

So that the children of Israel could not look intently at his face. Until its revelation. In the same way, the Law is not understood until, at its conclusion, one believes in Christ, because he is the end of the Law, to which we must come.

Which is brought to an end. The veil is brought to an end in the consummation, and now in Christ.

But their minds were dulled until the present day. “Unless you believe, you will not understand.”

The same veil remains in the reading of the Old Testament, the figure of which he bore on his face. It is not revealed as long as he does not believe in Christ.

Which is brought to an end in Christ. He is the end of the Law.

But to this very day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart [Col. 0561D]—the veil of ignorance in the hearts of the Jews.

But whenever one turns to God, the veil will be removed. Someone among them will turn, as Moses used to turn.

Now the Lord is Spirit. There is nothing obscure or contrived in him. The Spirit is free, and for this reason cannot receive a veil; rather, he himself reveals.

Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Whoever has the Spirit of the Lord sees everything freely, for the Spirit searches all things.

But we—the faithful—all, with unveiled face. Not a few, as Moses did.

Beholding the glory of the Lord. We understand the Lord’s glory openly and clearly, or see it by faith.

Into the same image. The image that Christ displayed on the mountain, as he says elsewhere: “Who will transform the body of our lowliness.”

We are transformed. We strive toward this every day [Col. 0562A].

From glory. From the present glory, which does not come to an end but advances toward the future glory.

Into glory, as from the Lord’s Spirit. From glory to glory.

## CHAPTER FOUR
Therefore, since we have this ministry—the apostolate—according to the mercy we have received. Since we were not capable of so great a ministry through ourselves, we continually implore his mercy, which went before us.

We do not grow faint. We do not grow faint amid all tribulations. But we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in cunning. By the grace of God we cast away from men the hidden things of vice. For it is shameful for a Christian to live disgracefully.

Nor do we adulterate the word of God. This is like those who please men with the word of God, mixing a worthless discourse into it and creeping along the ground by excusing sins through flattery. But by the manifestation of the truth, commending ourselves to every human conscience. Yet what we say is so manifestly true to everyone that even the conscience of those who resist bears witness for us.

Before God. We do this before God, not for the sake of men, although by this very fact we also please men.

But if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing. As though someone had said to him: “But not everyone understands your preaching.” “The unbelievers,” he says, “or the false apostles, do not understand it.” For believers understand it when God reveals it.

In whom is the god of this age. Among the false apostles, the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers. “The god of this age” can be understood in the same way as “the ruler of the world,” because he claims sovereignty for himself among unbelievers. But, on account of those who bring accusations, it should be pronounced in such a way that we say: God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age on account of the merit of their unbelief, just as the Savior himself says: “For judgment I came into the world, so that those who see may become blind.” And the Apostle himself says elsewhere: “Because they did not believe the truth, God will send them a spirit of error,” because he permits it to be given to those who do not believe in him. It is as when a physician abandons a disobedient sick person: the physician is said to have prolonged his illness, although the whole responsibility belongs to the one who refused to listen to him. If, however, he should obey again, he will come to health.

So that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ may not shine. Because they are blind, they cannot see the brightly shining sun.

Who is the image of God. Either the expressed image of his substance, or because he is without sin.

For we do not preach ourselves, but the Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever seeks his own advantages does not preach Christ but himself, like those who serve their own belly.

But ourselves as your servants through Jesus. We serve your interests through the example of the one who took the form of a servant—not because of greed or glory.

For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness. This is directed against all the enemies of the Old Testament.

Who has shone in our hearts. First through Christ, so that through us he might enlighten others.

For the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God. Manifestation.

In the face of Jesus Christ. In the person of Christ. But observe also that here he indicated the Trinity. “God, who said that light should shine out of darkness”: the Holy Spirit is understood. In the phrase “for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God,” recognize the Father. In “the face of Jesus Christ,” he designated the Son.

[Col. 0563A] But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may belong to God and not come from us. We carry in a fragile body the treasure of spiritual grace by which we perform signs. In that body, even while we frequently heal others, we ourselves become weak, so that what we do may be understood to belong not to our own power or merits but to the greatness of God.

In everything we suffer tribulation. The tribulation of persecutions or labors.

But we are not distressed. Through beatings or insults.

We are at a loss, but not destitute; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken. Through the consolation of hope we are not destitute.

We are cast down, but we do not perish. We come even to despair of life, but we do not die; and even if we die, we do not perish.

Always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. The dying brought about by tribulations, as he says elsewhere: “I die every day, by your glory”; for if we die together, we shall also live together. But those who do not die together will not live together.

For we who live are always being handed over to death. We who are in the body. Because of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. If we suffer for his body what he suffered for us, our mortal flesh will receive the life of Jesus—that is, incorruptibility—so that it may become immortal.

May it be manifested in our mortal flesh. Because “it has not yet appeared what we shall be,” or so that his power may become known through us.

Therefore. Is it therefore that death works in us, but life in you?

He rebukes them because they had believed the false apostles, who said that Paul was subjected to persecutions because he was weaker in faith, while they themselves could not suffer tribulation because of their faith. He therefore shows, on the contrary, that he suffers these things not because of unbelief but because of faith. They, however, have no cause for hatred except through flattery and negligence, as he says to the Galatians: “So that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ, for this reason they compel you to be circumcised.”

But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written. The spirit possessed by David and the other patriarchs or prophets; for they lived by the same faith by which we live, believing that the incarnation, passion, and resurrection of Christ were still to come, whereas we believe that they have already occurred—even up to John the Baptist.

“I believed, and therefore I spoke”; and we believe, and therefore we speak. By this testimony he proves that he believes. For if the former spoke because he believed—for no sane person affirms to others what he himself does not believe—then we too, he says, who speak, believe. We are also afflicted for this reason: they believed that these things would come to pass, whereas we believe that they have come to pass.

Knowing that he who raised Jesus. Holding this most firmly: this is perfect faith, from which not even death separates us.

Will also raise us with Jesus and establish us with you. He will raise us likewise if we die for him.

For everything is for your sake. We suffer everything because we are entirely concerned for your salvation. They, however, suffer nothing of this kind because of their negligence.

So that abundant grace, through the thanksgiving of many, may abound to the glory of God. So that, through the multitude of believers, thanksgiving may abound to the glory of God because of the abundant grace.

For this reason. Therefore we do not cease.

We do not grow faint. In tribulations and insults. They do not grow faint amid tribulations; but we, if we are not praised, grow faint.

But although our outward person is being corrupted, the inward person is being renewed day by day. Although the body is corrupted by tribulations and sufferings, the soul is strengthened each day by hope of the things to come, so that it may endure everything.

For this momentary and light affliction of ours. However great the present punishment and however long it lasts, in comparison with the immense and eternal glory it is both easy and brief, as he says elsewhere: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us.”

Beyond measure in sublimity. For no comparison is possible.

It produces for us an eternal weight of glory. Because he had called it “light,” here he says “weight,” preserving the metaphor of the scales.

While we do not contemplate the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal. We consider neither the good things that are seen nor the evil things, because neither of them is eternal.

## CHAPTER V

For we know that. As though someone were saying: “If I suffer these things in this life, when will I receive them, since I am dying?” He therefore begins to show the glory of the resurrection.

If our earthly house. That is, the body, which was made from earth and in which we dwell in this age.

Should be dissolved. If it should be dissolved before the Lord’s coming, either through sufferings or through the condition of nature.

We have a building from God. That is, incorruption itself, because it is immortal: a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens. This bodily house is said to have been made, as it were, by a bodily hand; therefore this spiritual house will be made through the Spirit.

For in this also we groan, longing to put on our dwelling that is from heaven. We groan for it and labor for it, because no one labors without groaning, just as childbirth is used to signify pain.

Desiring to be clothed over. Therefore we are already clothed with something, so that we may be clothed over with it.

If indeed, when clothed, we shall not be found naked. If, after being stripped of the body, we shall not be found naked of works.

For we who are in this tent also groan, being weighed down, because we do not wish to be stripped but clothed over. Those who are found alive at the Lord’s coming also groan and labor for this reason: that they may not be stripped by the fire together with sinners, but may deserve to be clothed over with immortality together with the righteous.

So that it may be swallowed up. What is swallowed up does not appear, although it exists. Thus iron, if it is thrown into fire, remains iron in substance, yet the whole becomes fire, because the iron itself has taken on the brightness and heat of the fire.

What is mortal. As though he were touching upon the body.

By life. Eternal life.

Now the one who brings about this very thing is God. He says that God does this, so that it might not seem incredible to anyone.

Who gave us the pledge of the Spirit. He has already given us the Spirit as a pledge, so that we may know that he does not permit the temple of his Spirit to perish, and so that you may believe that what we say belongs to him.

The passage continues: Therefore, always confident, and knowing that while we are in the body. For this reason we dare to hope.

We are away from the Lord. We are away as exiles because we are not yet in the paternal inheritance. Therefore, as exiles, we ought not to care greatly about the things of this age, but, content with what is necessary, we should direct every desire and effort toward how we may reach our homeland.

For we walk by faith and not by sight. We still hope by faith; we do not yet possess by sight.

But we are confident and have a good will. We choose this with complete confidence, as he says elsewhere: “Having the desire to depart and be with Christ is much better.”

Rather to be away from the body. Properly, “to be away,” because we shall return to him again.

And to be present with God. He is present everywhere, but we are in some way more present with him then, when we have been separated from the frailty of the flesh.

And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. We strive already to be in action what we shall be in substance in the kingdom: incorruptible and, without doubt, perfect.

[Col. 0565B] For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ. The greatness of the tribunal and of the judgment must be estimated according to the greatness of the judge’s power. For the greater the judge’s power, the greater necessarily is the terror of the judgment.

So that each may receive. “Receive” is understood.

What is proper to the body, according to what he has done. What does “according to what he has done through the body” mean except “according to what he did during the time when he was in the body”? Because he is dealing with the resurrection, he wishes to show that the soul worked through the body in everything, as long as it lived in the body. For the soul sins without the body, but the body cannot sin without the soul.

Whether evil or good. “Depart from me, accursed ones”; “Come, blessed ones of my Father.” It should be noted that the punishment of the wicked is called evil.

Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade men, but we are manifest to God. Knowing how great is the fear of God’s judgment, we persuade men to beware of falling into it. But we are manifest to God.

If we teach one thing but act otherwise. I hope, however, that we are also manifest in your consciences. Although something bad may have been suggested to you about us, I nevertheless think that your conscience does not allow you to suspect anything else about us than what it knows, nor can it place greater faith in others than in itself.

We do not commend ourselves to you again. For above he had said that he had no need of letters of recommendation.

But we give you an occasion to boast on our behalf. Against the false apostles, who first attempted through disparagement to implant hatred of him in them, so that they themselves might more easily be believed.

So that you may have an answer for them. Something to say to those who boast in appearance and not in heart. When they boast to the face of their own justice and our weakness, they are refuted by the testimony of their heart, or in the carnal works of the law.

For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you. Some say: whether we have wisdom beyond humanity—that is, whether we are in ecstasy—it is for God, because what we say is more than human; or whether we speak according to our ordinary judgment, it is for you.

A teacher is said to be “beside himself” when he speaks lofty and spiritual things, as blessed John did: “In the beginning was the Word,” and what follows. He spoke soberly when he humbled himself, saying: “The Word became flesh.” This was also signified by the angels on the ladder Jacob saw, ascending and descending—that is, teachers. Thus blessed Paul ascended when he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect,” and: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people.” He descended when he said: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

For the love of Christ urges us. We must repay some portion of his love with our own, so that we may suffer for his body, since he deigned to die for our death.

Judging this. Considering or supposing this:

That if one died for all, then all died. And Christ died for all. He alone was found worthy to die for all as an immaculate sacrifice, for those who were dead in sins.

So that those who live. We owe our life to him who restored it to us through his death.

May no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them. If someone does his own will and not God’s, he lives for himself. Hence the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” and what follows.

And he rose again. He always joins resurrection to death, because of slander.

Therefore, from now on we know no one according to the flesh. They were presenting the Corinthians with examples from former times. We know no one who has been circumcised according to the flesh or who observes a carnal Sabbath; we follow no example from the former age.

And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh. Even if Christ himself was circumcised bodily and celebrated everything with the Jews.

Yet now we no longer know him in that way. After his resurrection, the New Testament exists. We no longer know Christ as one who will suffer in the future; rather, after the resurrection, we understand him spiritually as wholly God.

Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away. If anyone is new, a new creation in Christ, let him understand that all the old things have been separated in their proper time and that now one must live according to a new way.

Behold, they have come to be. According to Isaiah.

All things are new. For even the commandments have been renewed when they are fulfilled through the grace of Christ.

But all things are from God. Both the new and the old were brought about by one God according to the diversity of times.

Who reconciled us. Because through sins we had been turned away from him.

To himself through Christ. Through Christ’s blood and example, because he both redeemed and taught.

And gave us the ministry of reconciliation. So that we too might reconcile others.

For God was indeed in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. Christ was not merely human but also God; that is, as God, the human Christ is everywhere present according to presence, not according to effect. In Christ, however, the whole fullness of divinity dwells.

Not counting their trespasses against them. That is, forgiving them through faith alone, which was freely given.

And he placed in us the word of reconciliation. The preaching, so that in Christ’s place we might reconcile people to God.

Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ. We are God’s ambassadors in Christ’s place.

As though God were exhorting through us. We do not speak from ourselves; God speaks through us.

We beseech you. That is, as though Christ were beseeching you.

To be reconciled to God. Because we were enemies; for no one is reconciled except after hostility. Sin, not nature, made us enemies; hence we became his enemies and therefore servants of sin. But how are we reconciled unless what separates us from him—namely, sin—is removed? For this reason the Lord Christ is the mediator: he became a sacrifice, offering himself for sin.

[Col. 0567A] Be reconciled to God in Christ’s place. That is, in Christ’s stead we ask you to turn back and believe.

Him who knew no sin. God the Father, namely, made the Son.

He made him sin for us. That is, he made him a sacrifice for sin; for our sake he made him “sin.” In the law, a victim offered for sin was called “sin,” although it committed no sin, as it is written: “And he shall place his hands upon the head of his sin.” Through whose blood that blood which was poured out for us was prefigured. Thus Christ, offered for our sins, also received the name “sin.”

So that we might become the righteousness of God. Not our own righteousness.

In him. Not in ourselves.

## CHAPTER VI

And adjuring you, we exhort you. By the word of God.

Not to receive the grace of God in vain. He receives the grace of God in vain who does not labor with God’s grace and does not add his own effort, so that, with God as helper, he may fulfill the commandments of God. He is not made new in the New Testament and does not pursue a new life; for such a person the grace of God accomplishes nothing. He says the same thing to the Galatians: “I do not set aside the grace of God.”

For he says. God, through the prophet Isaiah:

“At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” For me, the acceptable time in which one is heard and the day of salvation are this present life, as the Savior says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you.”

Behold, now is the acceptable time. As he says elsewhere: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good.”

The day is called this life because it is suitable for working, and it is closed by the night of judgment, in which no one will be able to work. This life is also called summer, in comparison with which ants are said to hope for the coming winter.

Behold, now is the day of salvation. Here alone, with God granting it, we can find salvation.

Giving no one any occasion of offense, so that our ministry may not be criticized. Let no one be offended by our example, lest the fault be thought to belong not so much to us as to the ministry.

But in everything. Not in some things only.

Let us present ourselves. This shows that, once restored by the grace of God, we can, with God’s help, present ourselves as ministers of God in the virtues described.

As ministers of God. Ministers of God ought to imitate God in everything, and true worshipers of God should be recognized by their life and conduct, just as he allows himself to be blasphemed by everyone and, in the present life, does not withhold his benefits even from the ungrateful.

In great patience. Not in a small measure.

Now he describes the members of patience:

In tribulations. Every injury is a tribulation.

In necessities. Whatever is necessary, let us bear it as necessity requires.

In distresses. Every deprivation is a distress.

In beatings, in prisons, in disturbances. Caused by the rulers of the places.

In labors, in vigils. In the labors of journeys or activities, which ought to be more mental than bodily. For honorable vigils discipline the flesh.

In fastings. It should be noted that he counts fastings among the virtues.

In chastity. That is true chastity which is preserved both in heart and in body.

In knowledge. Knowledge is a form of virtue, provided that one is instructed by it and not puffed up.

In long-suffering. True long-suffering is enduring perseverance over a long period.

In gentleness. Gentleness exists when we generate bitterness toward no one by our words and fulfill what the same Apostle says: “Let all bitterness, anger, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice.” And let it be said of you: “His palate is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable.”

In the Holy Spirit. That is, we can present ourselves as such through his gift if we prepare ourselves to be worthy of his gift and do not violate his temple, which he commanded us to preserve in baptism.

In unfeigned love. Love is truly unfeigned if we do for others everything that we want done for ourselves, as blessed John says: “Let us not love in word and tongue, but in deed and truth.” Love is also unfeigned in this respect: if we correct offenses and faults in our brothers with a kindly disposition.

In the word of truth. The word of truth is the word of Christ, brought forth from the Scriptures, provided that it is brought forth appropriately. We must beware lest we make a lie out of the truth, or violate the command: “Do not lie to one another.”

In the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness. In the power of Christ we fight against the devil through the weapons of righteousness; or, in the power of God, who overcame the devil through the weapons of the law.

On the right and on the left. Let us neither be lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity.

Through glory and disgrace. The glory of virtues, the disgrace of prisons.

Through ill repute and good repute. Let us pass through all these things equally with patience. Let neither those who praise us exalt us nor those who slander us cast us down, because it is sometimes necessary that both groups lie.

As deceivers, and yet truthful. He explained “ill repute” and “good repute,” because some called them deceivers, while others called them not only truthful but even gods. It is therefore no wonder that the apostles were called deceivers, since the Jews spoke in this way even of the Lord himself.

As unknown. By unbelievers.

And yet known. By believers.

As dying, and behold, we live. That is, coming to the point of despairing of life, as when Paul was thought to have died after being stoned, yet rose and taught at Lystra. It should also be noted that adversity and temporal things are spoken of as though they were like a dream: “I seemed to myself to be there.” Eternal rewards, however, do not have this “as though.”

As chastened, and not put to death. “The Lord has chastened me severely, but he has not given me over to death.”

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Sorrowful in the severity of their appearance, but rejoicing in their hearts even amid tribulation because of hope.

As needy, yet enriching many. In the very things in which we are needy, we abound for others, since almsgiving is done through us. Or, being needy in earthly possessions, we make others rich, as though receiving in return the reward of eternal life.

As having nothing, and possessing everything. As Solomon says: “For the faithful person the whole world is a wealth of riches,” except that everything belongs to the Lord. No one possesses more than the one who needs nothing. The one who needs nothing is the person who seeks nothing beyond what is necessary.

Our mouth is open to you. We have been so encouraged by your progress that we cannot remain silent. The progress of a disciple opens the mouth, enlarges the heart, and magnifies it.

O Corinthians, our heart. As it is written: “God gave Solomon breadth of heart”; may he grant it to you also.

It has been enlarged. In understanding and teachings.

You are not restricted by us. The restriction of speech does not come from us.

But you are restricted in your own affections. The cause of the restriction proceeds from you.

But, having the same recompense. You will have the same recompense if you have the same God as helper and run the same course; or certainly, if you receive from God, who inspires us, as much as we teach.

As to children I say: be enlarged yourselves. Like children, following my example and imploring the grace of God, be enlarged in understanding so that you may receive greater things through his gift. Alternatively, he is teaching priests by his example to enlarge themselves or to advance in the breadth of love.

Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Do not be joined or made equal to them; for equals draw the yoke together.

For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? He shows that no one can be simultaneously just and unjust, setting forth contrary examples.

Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? None—just as light has no fellowship with darkness.

And what agreement does Christ have with Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? They cannot agree. By Belial he means the devil or the Antichrist.

And what agreement is there between the temple of God and idols? By “idol” he means the very people who worship idols.

For you are the temple of the living God, as God says. They are the temple of dead idols, which demons possess. Although God is everywhere, he dwells in those who recognize his benefit and believe that whatever they are is his gift.

For I will dwell in them. He proves by this testimony that we are God’s temple, teaching that, with God as helper, we must offer him a clean dwelling in our heart.

And I will walk among them. I will possess or traverse all their senses.

And I will be their God. God is God of all by nature, but of few by their will. For he is not the God of the dead but of the living.

And they will be my people. Those who are servants willingly, not unwillingly—that is, by faith and obedience, not merely by nature.

Therefore, come out from among them and be separated, says the Lord. By conduct and way of life, or by intimacy—not by physical location.

And what is unclean. Everyone who sins is unclean; for every unrighteous person is unclean before God.

Do not touch. Do not touch through union, association, agreement, or imitation of wicked deeds.

And I will receive you. If they cast you out.

And I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me. He says: If unbelieving parents disown you, you will have me as your eternal Father.

Says the Lord Almighty. He added “Almighty,” so that you may not say: “How can human beings become children of God?”

## CHAPTER VII

Therefore, since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves. Since we possess such great and such promises, with what diligence must the house that is to receive such a guest be cleansed! And how ought the children of God to imitate their Father in everything?

From every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness. The defilement of the flesh is what is committed through the flesh; the defilement of the spirit is what is sinned by thought alone. We therefore perfect holiness when we keep both clean.

In the fear of God. Not in the praise or fear of men.

Receive us. Accept what we say, or accept our example as something to be imitated in all these matters; or, consider us.

We have wronged no one. We have corrupted no one; we have defrauded no one.

I do not say this to condemn you. For we said above that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. I am not condemning you while excusing myself, as though you were such people. I cannot think that way about you, whom I love so greatly, as I said above; or, your love makes me have such confidence.

I have great confidence in you. You have given me great confidence to speak because you obeyed in everything; or, I do not fail to recognize that I am greatly loved by you.

I have much reason to boast about you. In all the churches I boast of your reform.

I am filled with consolation. After the sadness I had on your account; or, my speech of consolation abounds because your progress encourages me.

I overflow with joy in all our tribulation. For even when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest. My joy is so great that I forget all my pressures. He shows how greatly the magnitude of joy surpassed the magnitude of the pressure.

But we suffered every kind of tribulation. We experienced no kind of tribulation that we did not undergo.

Battles outside. Battles against unbelievers; and fear from false brothers—or, we were altogether afraid lest believers should suffer scandal.

Fears within. Lest you should be embittered.

But God, who comforts the lowly, comforted us. He comforted us who were afflicted.

By the arrival of Titus. Not only by his arrival, but also by his consolation. Not only because the one desired had arrived, but also because he reported those things for which we had been awaiting his arrival.

By which he comforted us concerning you, reporting your longing. He comforted us after the grief that he shared with us on your account.

Your weeping, your zeal for me. For our sadness and for the sins of some.

So that I rejoiced all the more. Because you not only corrected yourselves but also made further progress.

For even if I saddened you by the letter, I do not regret it. And if I did regret it, seeing that the letter saddened you, although only for a time, now I rejoice—not because you were saddened, but because you were saddened to repentance. Even if I regretted having rebuked you too severely, your progress makes me not regret it.

For you were saddened according to God. Not according to the world or the devil.

So that you might suffer no loss through us. For what is sadness according to God? Either our negligence, or the fear that, when we came, we might condemn someone.

Repentance leading to salvation. For there is also repentance that leads away from salvation.

Steadfast: not to be regretted.

It produces. It produces enduring repentance. We must not be without fear concerning the forgiveness of sins; even when God does not remember them, we must remember them through repentance.

[Col. 0570D] But worldly sadness produces death. Worldly sadness is being tormented over lost present possessions, things not seized from others, or another person’s happiness. Sadness according to God, however, is mourning one’s own sins or the sins of others.

For behold, this very thing—that you were saddened according to God—how much it has produced in you. What has now happened can teach you what difference there is between worldly sadness and sadness according to God.

Diligence. Our diligence is inspired by God; and where there is diligence, there is neither inertia nor sleepiness nor false security.

But defense. Defense either of discipline or of faith.

But indignation. Either we are indignant against those who sin, or we endure the indignation of the nations.

But fear. Not security toward those who sin.

But if anyone is scandalized, I burn. But longing, and zeal. Our longing, not disgust.

But—some say that in this place the conjunction “but” is superfluous in Latin; among the Greeks, however, it has a syntactical function.

Vengeance. Not an evil pardon. It is better to exact vengeance justly than to pardon wickedly; for the person who spares the wicked wishes to destroy the good.

In everything you have shown yourselves to be uncontaminated. You have proved yourselves free from guilt. For a contaminated person has no authority to exact vengeance from another.

In the matter. The matter under discussion.

Therefore, even if I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who acted. Or: not for the sake only of the one who injured his father and was excommunicated, nor for the sake only of the one who suffered the injury, as though these things alone had pleased me.

The injury. To the father.

Nor for the sake of the one who suffered. “Only” is understood.

But to make manifest our diligence, which we have for you before God. Do not think that anything can escape us because of our diligence.

For this reason we were comforted. Because you proved yourselves to be pure in the matter.

In our consolation. Because we receive consolation from you.

We rejoiced all the more abundantly over the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. We rejoiced even more that Titus’s spirit was so refreshed by you that you never left his thoughts. For the progress of disciples is the refreshment of the teacher’s spirit.

And if I boasted to him about you, I was not put to shame. Boasting in progress does not bring shame, as worldly boasting does.

But just as we spoke everything to you in truth, so also our boasting before Titus proved true. Whoever boasts in righteous things boasts in truth and in God, whose gift they are.

And his heart is even more abundantly disposed toward you, as he remembers the obedience of you all. All his members long for you, as eyes long for your presence, ears for your speech, the mouth for conversation, and so forth.

How you received him with fear and trembling. Obedience does not know how to exist without fear; for one who obeys out of love fears offending the one whom he loves.

I rejoice that I have confidence in you in everything. As a skilled physician uses the gentlest medicines on a wound that is already almost healed, so that it may be cured without cauterization by burning.

You have made me rejoice, because I never distrust your obedience.

## CHAPTER VIII
Now we make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia. He appeals to mercy by the example of the churches of Macedonia, so that they may not think it burdensome when they see that the Philippians or others have already done so. And in the midst of a great trial of affliction, their abundance of joy overflowed. They rejoice most when they have suffered greatly, just as the apostles went away rejoicing because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus.

And their deepest poverty abounded in the riches of their simplicity. “I know your poverty and affliction, but you are rich”: they are very poor in possessions, but still richer in simplicity, and they desire to give more than they possess. Therefore God tests the disposition more than what the right hand extended. For whoever does whatever he can, does everything; rich and poor give equally, although the rich may appear to give more.

For I bear them witness according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing. He has placed the words in the wrong order, for the meaning is this: “I bear witness that they acted according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing.”

With much exhortation, they begged us for the favor and fellowship of the ministry performed for the saints. They earnestly pleaded with us to receive gratefully their participation in the ministry to the saints.

And not as we hoped. Rather, more than we hoped. But they first gave themselves to the Lord, and afterward to us. They surrendered not only all they possessed, but first themselves to the Lord in this work, and afterward to us; that is, God saw their intention, while we saw its accomplishment.

According to the will of God. Not so that they might please us against the will of the Lord; rather, it was the will of God that they should do this, since he inspired them to do it.

So that we urged Titus that, just as he had begun, so also he should complete this grace among you. Inflamed by their example, we were moved to send Titus to you, so that by his teaching or arrangement he too, with God’s help, might complete this work among you, lest you should have anything less than the others.

But just as you abound in everything—in faith, speech, knowledge, every kind of earnestness, and your love for us. He does not merely join speech to faith and knowledge.

So that you may abound in this grace also. Lest, while you surpass the others in everything else, you should be found inferior in this matter.

I do not speak as one commanding, but by means of the earnestness of others also testing the genuine quality of your love. I do not command or demand it, but give advice: that, just as you are an example to others in everything, so you may be an example here as well. For we know that you possess such obedience and mercy that you seem not to have learned them, but to possess them naturally.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. You are not ignorant that he became poor for your sake, although he was the maker and Lord of all, so that by his grace you might be enriched with heavenly goods. If, then, he despised everything that was his for your sake, how much more ought you, for your own sake, to give what is small—not what is yours, but rather to restore to him what is his! For whatever is offered for his sake is given to him.

For he became needy for your sake. God became man. Although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich.

And I give advice in this matter. For this is useful to you. He also says this against Photinus, because Christ was rich before he became poor.

Who not only began to do, but also to desire, from the previous year. He shows that some can act without willingness, when either the persistence of the one asking or the authority of the one commanding has compelled them.

But now complete the work also in deed, so that your willing disposition may be as ready. Complete by action what you began to do willingly. The end of every undertaking should also be sought. For just as an action performed unwillingly is not acceptable, so a resistant will is fruitless.

So let there also be completion from what you have. To the end. For if the will is ready according to what one has, it is acceptable. Do not think that I am demanding anything beyond your means, or expecting as much from a poor person as from a rich one. For all give equally, if each gives according to what he possesses.

Not according to what he does not possess. “As you have, my son, so perform almsgiving.”

Not that there should be relief for others. They were such people that it was necessary to say this to them: “Not so that you yourselves may have nothing left, but so that there may be sufficiency both for them and for you!”

But for you, affliction. Poverty. But by equality, in the present time. The saints and servants of God are pilgrims and poor in this age, but in eternal life they have a homeland and riches. The laity, however, or those who abound in possessions, seem here to possess a homeland, if they share with the saints; there, the saints restore these things to them, in their own homeland, where they are proved to be rich.

Let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance also may supply your need. Give them material things, so that, being free for God, they too may be able to return spiritual things to you. These two ranks cannot stand without one another. The former will not be perfect if he thinks only about material things, nor will the latter be merciful when he has no one to whom he can give, or from whom he may be taught to give.

Let it be a supplement to your need, so that there may be equality. In this age the rich are like an elm supporting a vine: with the elm’s assistance the vine produces abundant fruit, and through the vine’s fertility the elm is seen to be fruitful. So the servants of God, who are poor in spirit, are like the vine. They are supported by the resources of the rich and share with one another what they possess in abundance; both, filled with good things, arrive at eternal life.

As it is written. This was said about the manna, whose example teaches us that every excess produces worms; at the same time it is shown that what God gives ought, in the present, to be common to all.

He who gathered much did not have too much. By this testimony he wishes us to possess everything in common, so that the perfect do not conceal their teaching and those who have material substance do not deny them food. For “the laborer is worthy of his food.”

And he who gathered little did not have too little.
