But thanks be to God, who gave Titus the same earnest concern for you. Just as, in the matter of manna, if God gives someone the zeal or concern to care for others, who else will give him the concern to care for himself?

Since these things are so, nothing is commanded to a person by the Lord in the Holy Scriptures for the testing of free will that is not found to be given by his goodness. Nor does anyone at all begin to be changed from evil to good through the beginning of faith unless God’s undeserved and gratuitous mercy works this in him, because the change is not from our power but from the right hand of the Most High.

For he indeed accepted the exhortation, but, being more earnest, he went to you of his own will. He accepted the favor of the exhortation, but also hastened of his own accord, so that he might receive a reward without being unwilling, as though the administration had been entrusted to him.

We also sent with him our brother, whose praise in the Gospel is known throughout all the churches. This is understood to refer to Luke, who has praise in the Gospel above the others because he wrote both the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

And not only that, but he was also appointed by the churches as our companion in our journey. This is said to demonstrate that he is suitable.

For this grace, which is administered by us for the glory of the Lord. Whether this refers to the ministry of the saints or to teaching, everything is done for the glory of the Lord.

And our declared intention. That is, our proposed or prepared intention.

Avoiding this: that anyone should blame us in this abundance that is administered by us. Lest anyone say, “How did Christ fulfill the law, when we see Christians not giving as much alms as the law commanded to be given?”

For the glory of the Lord. Every godly person glorifies God for the glory of the Lord.

For we provide what is good. We do nothing for human glory; nevertheless, we do not want anyone to be scandalized and perish through us, but, seeing our good works, to glorify our Father who is in heaven.

Not only before God, but also before human beings. Our conscience is sufficient for us on our own account, but reputation matters for the sake of our neighbors. It ought not to be polluted, but to shine. These are two things: conscience and reputation. Conscience is for you; reputation is for others. Whoever, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation is cruel.

And we sent with them our brother. Some say that this refers to Apollos, but it is uncertain.

Whom we have often proved to be earnest in many matters. He gives them this testimony so that he may be heard more readily.

But now much more earnest. We commend him, confident that your obedience will be stirred up.

There is much confidence in you. He already knows you well enough to have confidence in you.

Whether concerning Titus, who is my companion and helper among you; or our brothers, apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ. The meaning is this: either because Titus told him about you—he who has found your obedience approved—or because the apostles of the individual churches also reported the same to him, to the glory of Christ.

Therefore show them, before the face of the churches of God, the proof of your love and of our glory concerning you. So that, when they see that what is said is true, they may report it for the consideration of all the churches.

Or else, show them the love that you possess, of which we glory on your behalf, as an example to all the churches.

## CHAPTER IX

Now concerning the ministry that is performed for the saints. He seems to change the subject. Some say that above he spoke about lay saints, but here about priests. Others say that earlier he dealt with almsgiving, whereas now he reminds them about the ministry of the word, which is offered to those sanctified through baptism. These two interpretations must be carefully observed until the end of the discussion.

It is excessive for me to write to you. I remind you of this unnecessarily, because you either do it willingly yourselves or minister to the priests, and you do not refuse mercy even to the others.

For I know your ready disposition. In this work. On account of it I glory in you among the Macedonians.

For Achaia also has been ready since the previous year. All Achaia, through you, who are its head, has been stirred up to this ministry.

And your zeal has stirred up very many. Here “zeal” means imitation.

But we sent the brothers. Those whom he named above.

So that our boasting about you might not be emptied of its content. They will either prepare you or remind you.

In this matter, so that, as I said, you may be ready, lest, when the Macedonians come with me, they find you unprepared. Lest I find you otherwise than I expected.

In the matter either of the ministry or of the teaching.

Let us be put to shame. If we are put to shame, as though we had falsely boasted on your behalf, how much more will you be ashamed, both because of your negligence and because of our disgrace! It is a great humiliation if the person who loves you is put to shame on your account.

So that we may not say that you are unprepared in this matter.

Therefore I considered it necessary to ask the brothers to go to you beforehand. This refers to what he had said above, “in this matter.”

And to prepare the promised gift. The gift that we promised them from you.

A blessing. Either from the act of blessing, or because through almsgiving a blessing from God arises among human beings.

That it should be ready. A sufficient blessing.

Thus, as a blessing and not as an act of greed. It will be a blessing if it is given with a grateful heart. For God loves a cheerful giver, but a greedy person cannot abound.

A greedy person is also greedy in knowledge when he delays putting into practice or carrying out the understanding he has begun to possess. Hence the Lord also says, “Greet no one on the way”; that is, do not preach the word of salvation to anyone merely in passing.

But this I say: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. It should be noted that here too a gradation is shown.

And whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings. Conversely, one who sows in a curse may also reap the same.

Each one according to what he has determined in his heart. Not as one compelled, but willingly.

Not from sadness or from necessity. “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with an administration”—and I have learned it without pretense and share it without envy.

All this refers to the ministry of the word. For if the subject were almsgiving, the rule would be: “Each one according to what he has.”

For God loves a cheerful giver. Conversely, without doubt, he hates a sad one.

And God is able. Do not fear poverty.

To make every grace abound. The gift of grace, that is, an abundance of fruits, because from it graces are returned for your works; or else, the grace of knowledge.

But it is rightly understood as a gift, because grace is given freely; and this too is God’s gift, that we should be generous.

To make it abound in you. “They have been multiplied from the fruit of his grain, wine, and oil.”

So that in everything always. Whether in kinds of gifts, or in graces, or in teachings.

Having every sufficiency, you may abound in every good work. Having every sufficiency, both spiritual and material, so that you may fulfill every good work.

As it is written: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” From temporal possessions eternal righteousness is acquired: whoever distributes present things will receive eternal things.

And he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply. This refers more especially to the seed of the word: the one who gave the office of teaching will also provide food, provided that you devote yourselves to teaching. Or else, the one who gave you something to distribute will not allow you to suffer hunger.

And he will multiply your seed. Whether of the word or of righteousness.

And he will increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that you may be enriched in everything. The fruits of righteousness are the word of God. Possessions too are fruits of righteousness when righteousness is practiced through them. But when they are gathered unjustly, or unjustly used for pride or greed, they are fruits of iniquity.

“For placing a price on grain and oppressing the people, he is accursed.” Or this refers to those who swell with the ambition for money.

May you abound in all simplicity. So that you may give generously to everyone without distinction, not asking to whom you should give, but for what reason you should give.

Which produces through us thanksgiving to God. This is the simplicity of giving.

For the ministry of this service. That is, of this administration.

Not only. It not only supplies the saints’ needs, but thanks are also returned to the Lord, who has enriched you with such wisdom.

It supplies what the saints lack. You give so much that it not only supplies the needs of the saints, but also leaves something from which it may be distributed to others.

But it also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord. You can receive a double reward: both the refreshment of the saints and thanksgiving offered to the Lord.

Through the testing of this ministry. Through this ministry you are proved to be Christians. For you teach and demonstrate perfectly that the matter is divine, in which you glorify God through obedience.

Glorifying God in the obedience of your confession of the Gospel of Christ. They glorify God who confess him through obedience, just as some deny him by their deeds.

And in the simplicity of your sharing. Either by teaching simply or by giving simply.

Toward them and toward all. For you share with them and with all rather than merely giving, since you are certain that you will receive these things back with manifold increase.

And in their supplication for you. This too is an abundant result of the administration of this ministry.

As they long for you. Who would not long to see people of this kind?

Because of the surpassing grace of God in you. Whether the grace of knowledge or of mercy.

Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift. The understood expression is “as they give thanks”: he who by his inspiration has bestowed such grace upon you.

It should be noted that whatever good we either do or possess is proved to be his gift.

## CHAPTER X

Now I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ. I appeal to you with the meekness with which Christ, although he could have avenged himself, endured those who wronged him in order to correct them.

I who am humble in person among you, but when absent am confident toward you. As though I possessed no virtues, as he says elsewhere, “like a nurse always.” The presence of the saints, because of excessive humility, can be treated with contempt; but when absent, if necessary, they confidently display their authority.

But I ask you not to make me bold when present, with the confidence that I am thought to possess against some. Act in such a way that, when present, I may not begin to reveal my power by taking vengeance.

Who am thought to be bold against certain people. Not every opinion is false, as in the saying, “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

Who think that we walk according to the flesh. They think that we possess no power beyond human nature.

Although we walk in the flesh. As human beings.

We do not wage war according to the flesh. As ministers of Christ. It can also be understood in this way: those are said to wage war “in the flesh” who explain the Old Testament in a humble, literal manner. Those who follow the spiritual understanding are indeed in the flesh, because they have the same letter as the Jews, but they do not wage war according to the flesh, passing from flesh to spirit.

For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God. Our weapons are not a shield or sword, but the power of God, by which we accomplish more through the word than others do with carnal weapons.

And because our struggle is not against flesh and blood.

For the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments. The false apostles fortify and surround their teaching with crafty plans and subtle arguments, which the apostolic ram destroys by the power of spiritual grace, just as he struck blind that great Magus who was overthrowing the ways of God by his disputations.

And every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God. For what is more arrogant than to oppose divine teachings?

And taking every understanding captive into the obedience of Christ. We destroy the false apostles who, under the name of Christ, desire to take everyone’s understanding captive and subject it to their own teaching, as heretics attempt to do.

And being ready to avenge every disobedience, when your obedience has been fulfilled. When obedience has finally been fulfilled through us, if they are not listened to, they falsely claim that they have received from the Lord the authority to take vengeance.

Look at what is according to outward appearance. The proof of the matter is evident, and the meaning is easy to understand.

If anyone is confident in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him think this again within himself: that just as he belongs to Christ, so do we. No one is so foolish as the one who boasts that he alone belongs to Christ.

For even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave for your edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be put to shame. Even if I say that I have received greater authority from Christ, as a true apostle, to take vengeance, I shall not be put to shame, because I shall be speaking the truth. Nor will I do this from being lifted up by glory, but because I am compelled for your edification.

They, therefore, wish to exercise an authority that they have usurped, and to exercise it for your destruction.

But so that I may not seem to be terrifying you through letters—for, they say, the letters are weighty and forceful, but bodily presence is weak and speech contemptible—I say this so that no one may think that I threaten what I cannot fulfill, as your deceivers boast about me.

Let the one who is such a person consider this: that what we are in word through letters when absent, such we are also in deed when present. Whoever thinks this should know that I can do everything, through him who remains in me, if it should be necessary—everything that I promise. For toward those who obey through humility I am found to be weak, but toward those who sin, through severity, strong.

For we do not dare to insert ourselves among or compare ourselves with certain people who commend themselves. We cannot boast greater things about ourselves than we are. We do not dare to despise God so far as to be like certain people who prefer to be commended by their own praises rather than by the grace of God.

But they measure themselves by themselves among themselves. We do not exceed the limits of our measure.

And comparing themselves with themselves. Not with those who are greater, as do those who, although they are nothing, not only make themselves equal to others but even put themselves before them.

But we will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule by which God measured us—the measure of reaching even to you. For we do not stretch ourselves beyond our measure as though we had not reached you.

We claim nothing beyond human measure, but only insofar as God has deigned to grant us, that is, the grace of apostleship, through which we preach also to you Corinthians. We do not do this by usurpation, but by command.

For we have reached even you in the Gospel of Christ. Not in our own Gospel.

Not boasting beyond measure in the labors of others. It is beyond measure to boast in the labors of others, because they were always going to believers who required no signs at all.

But having hope, as your faith grows, of being magnified among you. We are the ones who teach you.

According to our rule. Not another’s.

To preach the Gospel even in the regions beyond you, in greater abundance. It is not enough to have reached only you. When your faith has grown, we shall move elsewhere also, preaching the Gospel to the peoples who are beyond you.

Not according to another’s rule. That is, in places.

To boast in things already prepared. Either they enter into prepared glory, or we proceed to the glory of the Lord among those who have already been prepared.

But whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord. Whoever boasts should boast in the Lord, whose gift is what we are and whose powers have worked in us.

This is directed against the Pelagians.

For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved. Our preaching, unless it is confirmed by the Lord’s powers, is not received by unbelievers, so that we may know that faith too is from God, who gives powers so that signs may occur through which unbelievers may believe. Self-commendation is by praising oneself; but the one whom God commends is approved, God commending him by displaying signs.

## CHAPTER XI

I wish that you would bear with me. Bear with me for a little while, since you bear greatly with others.

A little foolishness of mine—but indeed, bear with me. He calls himself foolish because he had to say certain true things about himself in order to show that those who falsely praise themselves, without any necessity compelling them, are much more foolish.

For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God. For I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ. I am not inflamed by human jealousy, but as a father I guard you with divine jealousy, so that we may join you to Christ undefiled—preserved with the greater devotion, the more excellent the bridegroom to whom you are to be united.

But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted. The serpent deceived Eve by lying about God, saying that God had threatened merely to inspire fear and would not actually inflict death if they sinned. So now also the false apostles said that the precepts of the Gospel had been added to the law either so that it might thus be observed, or because the observance of the law alone was sufficient.

Even now the serpent deceives in the same way, asserting that Gehenna is mentioned only as a threat, and maintaining either that it does not exist at all or that it is not eternal.

And may fall away. From true chastity.

From simplicity. A chaste mind is one that desires to please one husband and is satisfied with the promise once made to him alone.

Which is in Christ. That is, to believe that these are the words of God.

For if the one who comes preaches another Christ whom we did not preach, or if you receive another spirit that you did not receive, or another Gospel that you did not accept, you would rightly bear with him. If they provided you with anything more than what you received through us, you would rightly admit them even when they came against us and disparaged us.

For I think that I have done nothing less. Among you.

Than the great apostles. If he is speaking of the great apostles, how much more does this apply to those who are nothing! Or else, so that you may not think that you received less than the other churches, to which Peter and the others preached.

For even if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not so in knowledge. He shows that these men, unskilled in knowledge, boast in inflated speech.

But in everything we have been made manifest to you. He shows his integrity, because he did everything according to God, never seeking avarice, gluttony, or glory from them.

Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted? Perhaps this is the only thing in which I sinned: that, for your benefit, I even omitted what was permitted.

Because I preached the Gospel of God to you free of charge, robbing other churches and receiving support. For I did not even receive from you the daily bread that the Lord ordained for ministering to you, while I was ministering the Gospel to you.

And when I was with you. While I was with you and did not receive from you, I received from the Macedonians, who were far away, so that you would not think that I preached the Gospel for the sake of earthly profit.

And when I was in need, I was a burden to no one. This is an additional point: although I was in need, I did not want to receive.

For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked, which I had not made up by the labor of my hands.

And in everything I kept myself from being a burden to you. They did not have false apostles, nor were they weak.

And I shall continue to do so. Because you still have such people, so that they may not find an opportunity through us.

The truth of Christ is in me. Just as Christ did not change what he once decreed and never lied.

For this boasting will not be broken off. Boasting is, for the sake of God, to despise even what is permitted, especially if one is suffering want.

In me in the regions of Achaia. He received elsewhere, then. Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. God knows whether I love you or not—or rather, it is precisely because I love you that I do not receive.

But what I do, I will continue to do, in order to cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity. Here he gives the reason why he himself does not receive anything.

The false apostles were teaching, evidently, while pursuing gluttony or greed and seeking glory, so that, if he accepted bread, they might demand gold; and so that, if they claimed to preach for God’s sake, it might immediately become apparent—for surely, if they do not receive anything, neither will they teach.

So that in what they boast they may be found to be like us. Such are they.

For such people are false apostles. They say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them, and they speak visions from their own hearts.

They are deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ—and no wonder. A deceitful worker avoids one thing and does another; beneath the simple appearance of preaching Christ, bestial greed is concealed. To please others and, by pleasing them, receive from them, such people must flatter, and by flattering deceive, saying what pleases the hearer rather than what is useful.

For Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is not so easy to place faith in dreams and certain apparently angelic visions, lest Satan disguise himself as an angel of light and deceive and mislead the unwary.

Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. It is no wonder if ministers of greed pretend to preach righteousness.

Their end will be according to their works. Evil works await an evil end.

Again I say, let no one think me foolish. Above he had already said, “Bear with a little foolishness of mine,” and had given the reason: because he was jealous for them with the jealousy of God, not because he desired glory, he was about to relate certain things about himself—lest, having turned against him, they should follow false apostles.

Otherwise, accept me as a foolish person, so that I too may boast a little. Receive me in whatever way you wish.

What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as though in foolishness. If the Apostle, compelled by necessity for the sake of the people of God, says that boasting is not “according to the Lord” but belongs to foolishness, it is clear what must be said about those others.

In this matter of boasting. There is another substance of true glory.

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. For to boast in nobility of birth is carnal.

For you gladly bear with fools, since you yourselves are wise. I see that, although you have been taught that these things are of no importance, you so readily agreed with fools.

For you bear it if someone enslaves you. To the slavery of the law, or of priests who exercised dominion over the people.

If someone devours you, if someone takes from you. If someone devours you—that is, consumes your possessions by taking or plundering them.

If someone exalts himself. Through money, Jewish pride, lineage, or knowledge.

If someone strikes you in the face. If someone rebukes you even in person or attacks you with insults.

I speak according to dishonor. The greatest dishonor is for the children of God to boast of earthly nobility.

As though we had been weak in this respect. As though in this matter we possessed something less than they, and did not preach to you things that were truer and stronger.

Whatever anyone dares—in foolishness I speak—I also dare. I can dare it if I wish.

They are Hebrews, and so am I. They are Israelites, and so am I. They are the seed of Abraham, and so am I. If they boast of being Hebrews, I too belong to this race.

They are ministers of Christ, and so am I. I speak as one less wise.

It should be noted that if anyone boasts even of the ministry of Christ, he boasts carnally.

I am more so. More than they.

In far greater labors; in prisons more abundantly; in beatings beyond measure. He did not say, “I preached so much,” but, setting aside all his glorious deeds, he enumerates what he endured.

In deaths often. From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one. In the Acts of the Apostles it is mentioned once: five times thirty-nine lashes, as though he were a transgressor of the law.

Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned. Not all these events are found in the Acts of the Apostles, because the Epistles also do not contain everything that is found there.

Three times I suffered shipwreck. There it is mentioned once.

I have spent a night and a day in the deep sea. In the final danger, when we thought that the mass of the waves would cover the ship, which had been driven into the deep.

In journeys often; in dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles. He speaks of dangers from his own people and from the Gentiles.

In dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea. When those sailing were in danger and drove the ship onto the shore, because the prow remained fixed and motionless, while the stern was being torn away by the force of the sea.

In dangers among false brothers. They secretly entered in order to spy out our freedom.

In labor. Of the hands.

And hardship. Misery.

In many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness. Hunger arises from necessity; fasting from the will.

Besides the things that are external, there is my daily anxiety. As if he were saying: besides the things that have already become customary and are considered lighter because of their familiarity—

The anxiety for all the churches. He shows what that anxiety is.

Who is weak in faith, and I am not weak? I am weak with those who are weak; with those who perish, I believe that I perish too.

Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed? With sadness.

If it is necessary to boast. If they wish to boast in these matters, let them boast in the things in which I boast, although I was compelled to do so. But because they do not possess these things, they boast in carnal matters.

I will boast of the things that concern my weakness. He designated all the sufferings mentioned above by the name “weakness,” since they prevail over human weakness.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. Since he is about to say something that may seem difficult—that the Jews had even fought against the rulers of the Gentiles on his account—he first calls upon God’s testimony, lest it be thought that he was boasting falsely because kingdoms had risen against him and had not been able to prevail. He enumerates these things in order to show the difference between true and false apostles.

In Damascus, the governor of the people under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes. In order to seize me, I was lowered through a window in a basket along the wall, and so I escaped his hands. He was governor of that people over whom Aretas reigned.

## CHAPTER XII
If it is necessary to boast, it is indeed not expedient. Nor is it expedient for me, since I am compelled by necessity. But I shall come to visions and revelations of the Lord. As though he were saying: “The infirmities are mine; the visions, however, are not mine but the Lord’s.”

I know a man in Christ. Whether he is speaking of himself and, for the sake of humility, speaking as though of another, or whether he is truly speaking of someone else, either interpretation can stand. Fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—such a man was caught up as far as the third heaven. Consider how great the necessity pressing upon him must have been, since he was compelled later to disclose what he had concealed for fourteen years.

And I know that such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—was caught up into paradise. By repeating again “whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know,” he shows that this was a different vision. And he heard secret words—hidden things—which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. Either: things that no human being is permitted to utter, or things that it is impossible for human nature to recount.

On behalf of such a one I will boast; on my own behalf, however, I will boast of nothing except my infirmities. Either “on behalf of such a vision” or “on behalf of such a man.” But on my own behalf, nothing—or, “on behalf of my own virtue,” since it is not mine but the Lord’s revelation.

For even if I should wish to boast, I shall not be foolish, for I shall speak the truth. Here he seems to show that, although he is speaking as though of another, he too has grounds for boasting, but does not wish to boast.

But I refrain, lest anyone should think me to be—There are also hidden things that I could truthfully bring forward, but I refrain, that is, I do not do so. Beyond what he sees in me—what is manifest is sufficient, even if what is hidden remains concealed. Or, “what he hears from me”: let each person judge me only by what he sees in me or hears from me.

And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan. How great are the things I conceal! Thus a thorn was rightly necessary for me, one that would remind me that I am human. To buffet me. Satan buffeted him either by stirring up tribulations or by inflicting pains. For some say that he suffered from frequent headaches; others say that he was goaded by an irritation of the flesh; [Col. 0582A] but it is more credible that the reference is to continual tribulations.

For this reason I pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from me. We understand also that the saints have requested certain things contrary to their good; and at the same time we learn that an importunate request may merit an answer even when it does not merit fulfillment. For when God does not grant what is not expedient, then he hears us all the more.

And he said to me: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.” The grace that you possess—or the grace that frees you—which power, unless it belongs to him, does not exalt. And who doubts that this pertains to righteousness? The Apostle certainly did not yet possess this perfection of power; he was not yet equal to the angels of God. But there remained in him a weakness tending to exalt himself, which had to be restrained through the angel, even Satan’s angel, lest he should be exalted by the greatness of the revelations.

Why through Satan’s angel? Because an antidote is frequently prepared even from serpents against the poisons of serpents. What, then, does “My grace is sufficient for you” mean except: “so that you do not fail and succumb beneath the buffeting of Satan’s angel”? And what does “power is perfected in weakness” mean except that, in this condition of weakness, the perfection of power can exist to the extent that pride is restrained by the presence of weakness itself, so that the perfection of power includes both the knowledge, in truth, and the confession, in humility, of that very imperfection?

Therefore I will most gladly boast of my infirmities, after learning that what I had thought harmful is beneficial. So that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Not in worldly power.

For this reason I am pleased with myself in infirmities, in insults—not in honors; in necessities—not in leisure; in persecutions—not in greetings; in distresses—not in riches; for Christ—not for avarice or any crime, just as the Savior says, so that we may suffer for the cause of righteousness alone.

For when I am weak, then I am powerful. To be weak for Christ is the greatest power.

I have become foolish; you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you. It is characteristic of a fool to recount his own labors and boast of his own virtues. But you compelled this, since you ought to have defended me before others, because I was in no respect inferior to the great apostles; now once again you require us ourselves to commend ourselves to you.

For I was in no respect inferior to those who are “super-apostles.” Even though I am nothing, the signs of my apostleship were nevertheless performed among you, with all perseverance, in signs, wonders, and powers. I indeed am nothing because I am human; but the signs of apostleship displayed their power among you—that is, the power of miracles and wonders.

For what is it in which you were inferior to the other churches? Those to whom other apostles preached. Except that I myself did not burden you? Because I received nothing from you. Forgive me this wrong. If you consider it a wrong, pardon me.

Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not burden you. For I do not seek what is yours, but you. For children ought not to store up treasures for their parents, but parents for their children. I seek your salvation, not gifts. I ought rather to give you what I have.

But I will most gladly spend what I have, and I will spend myself besides for your souls. Even if, loving you more, I am loved less. Whatever I have, I expend through labor, and I will spend myself besides for your souls. For perfect love not only freely spends all that it has, but also gladly spends itself.

Where it is necessary. But let it be so: I did not burden you. In every respect he clears himself by continually questioning their conscience, while at the same time showing them how they should guard against such things.

But, being crafty, I caught you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus and sent the brother with him. Perhaps—did Titus take advantage of you? Certainly not. Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did he take anything from you to bring to me, or did he teach otherwise than you see me teaching? Did we not follow the same footsteps?

Do you think that we have been defending ourselves to you for a long time? No—as I said above, we do not say these things in order to please you, but so that, when we come, we may not have to act more severely against you. Before God, in Christ, we speak; and everything, beloved, is for your edification. Which it is impossible to deceive.

For I fear that, when I come, I may perhaps not find you as I wish, and that I may be found by you to be someone whom you do not wish. If I do not find you righteous, I too shall be found severe by you. He makes no use of flattery.

I fear that there may perhaps be among you contentions, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, conceits, and disorders. If he said that he would punish these things with the utmost severity, what would he do if he encountered them in our times, when, by comparison with other crimes, these things are scarcely even considered sins?

Contention exists where something is defended not by reason but by obstinacy of mind. A whisperer is one who murmurs and speaks evil of someone to others, not to his face.

And again, when I come, may God humble me before you. This too I fear. And that I may mourn over many of those who sinned previously and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication—against the Novatians, who deny repentance. If he mourns those who do not repent, then certainly he rejoices over those who do repent.

And over the shamelessness that they committed. Shamelessness is more serious, a kind of monstrous fornication, as in the case of the man who took his father’s wife.

## CHAPTER XIII

Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you. For he had already come twice. “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand,” according to the Law.

I have already said, and I say beforehand, as though present, and now absent, to those who sinned previously and to all the others: if I come again, I will not spare them. Those who sinned afterward I will not spare either, because the downfall of the former should have made the latter more cautious.

Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me? Or do you test Christ in me, to see whether he is able to exercise judgment against you? And it should be noted that his teaching is shown to be not human but Christ’s; whoever censures it is undoubtedly found contumacious toward God.

Who is not weak among you. It may be said that he is not weak but powerful, and you yourselves are not unaware of this. But he is powerful among us. If he is powerful even among you, how much more powerful is he in us, who are more capable of receiving him!

For although he was crucified—what was crucified belongs to us; what lives belongs to him—from weakness, that is, from human nature; yet he lives by the power of God. For we too are weak in him. But we too are weak in the present, and in the future we shall live with him—not by our own power but by God’s power. We shall live with him through the power of God in us.

If you challenge us as weak, you will find us living with Christ in the power of God when we begin to exercise judgment against you.

Examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. If you are in the faith, recognize us from your own condition: pronounce judgment upon the sinner and see whether punishment does not immediately proceed through the word.

Or do you not recognize yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you—unless perhaps you are rejected? Or do you not know that Christ, the power of God, is in you, provided that you are not rejected—that is, provided that he has not abandoned you because of your negligence?

I hope that you will recognize that we are not rejected. I hope that we shall perceive the way in which I see you conducting yourselves.

But we pray to God that you do nothing evil. For if you do anything evil, we shall appear approved when we punish you; but we would rather appear rejected, provided only that you do what is good. Not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good. “I pray” is understood. We, however, are to be as rejected.

For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth. For our sentence has no power against an innocent person, but only against one who has sinned.

We rejoice when we are weak and you are powerful. We rejoice if there is no need for our power to appear, as it appeared in the case of Peter’s Ananias and Sapphira, and as ours appeared in the case of the Magician. This too we pray for: your perfection—that you may be complete and powerful.

For this reason I write these things while absent, so that, when present, I may not act more harshly according to the authority that the Lord gave me. For if you do not correct yourselves, I shall act even more harshly than I say.

For edification, so that you may amend yourselves and others may fear to sin; and not for destruction—your destruction, as those men arrogate to themselves.

Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfected. It should be noted that, writing to the whole Church, he says that they ought to be perfect, and that he commands laypeople to exhort one another. As he says elsewhere: “I wish that all people were as I myself am.” But because he then adds: “Each person has his own gift from God,” perfection lies in the power of the giver, not of the recipient.

Exhort one another; agree in your thinking; maintain peace. This is the one thing. And the God of peace and love will be with you. But if the author of dissension and hatred is with you, you will also be with him forever.

Greet one another with a holy kiss—not a false one. All the saints greet you, not the rich.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with all of you. Against the Arians, who slanderously argue that the Father is greater because he is always named first. Let it be with all of you. Amen. As it is with some of you who are more righteous, so may it be with all of you.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 0583]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0583D]

The Galatians are Greeks. They first received the word of truth from the Apostle, but after his departure they were tempted by false apostles to be overthrown into the Law and circumcision. The Apostle recalls them to the faith of truth, writing to them from Ephesus.

As the argument makes clear, the Galatians had been persuaded and deceived by pseudo-apostles. They heard that Paul, through whom they had believed the true Gospel, was not an apostle—presumably because he was neither among the twelve chosen apostles nor had followed Christ at some time, as Peter and the others had. He therefore needed to refute this disparagement with true arguments grounded in the authority of the Holy Spirit, proving in due order that he had been sent neither by human beings nor through a human being, but by the one who had chosen him, and the others, for the order of apostleship.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, an apostle. As has often been said, “little,” from humility. Not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ. Not through human presumption, nor through the apostles, as Aaron was appointed through Moses, but through God and the Lord himself, as Moses, the apostles, and the prophets were.

Many are ordained by human beings with the favor of the people, though unworthy, despising the Lord’s patience. And to show his greater authority, he added: “Through Jesus Christ”; and God the Father, who raised him. For the operation of the Son and the Father is one. And so that you may know that Christ is God, through whom he was made an apostle, carefully observe that he named the Son before the Father, against the slanders of the Arians.

From the dead. According to that by which he was able to die, namely, the flesh.

And all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia. Otherwise, if he were alone, they might be thought to resent the trampling down of his teaching.

Grace to you. Because you have been saved by faith alone, through the grace of God. And peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. Because, with all their sins forgiven, they had been reconciled to God.

Who gave himself for our sins, in order to rescue us. He displays Christ’s benefits, toward which they are ungrateful, wishing to live under the Law, which was given to sinners, for whom all sins have been forgiven.

From the present evil age. From the evil works of the age that are carried out in it. According to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory. Not according to our merits.

Forever and ever. Infinite benefits deserve infinite glory. Amen. He concludes the prologue with his own “Amen,” in Hebrew speech. The Septuagint translated *Amen* as Γένοιτο (*genoito*), “let it be”; Aquila as πεπείσθωμαι (*pepeithōmai*), “let me be persuaded.” We, however, render it “truly” or “faithfully.” The Savior also always uses it in the Gospel, confirming his words by “Amen.”

I am astonished that you are transferring yourselves so quickly from the one who called you. After enumerating the benefits, he says that he is astonished that they could be drawn away from the one from whom no tortures ought to have separated them, by words alone.

Into the grace of Christ, into another Gospel. Not into the Law. Which is not another Gospel, except that there are some who disturb you. For there cannot be another Gospel. And they wish to transform the Gospel of Christ. In a perverse order: whereas the Law ought to advance toward the Gospel, they are trying to recall the Gospel to the Law.

But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should evangelize you contrary to what we evangelized to you, let him be accursed. He briefly passed judgment upon every person, since he allowed neither the apostles to be heard against what he had once preached, nor the voice of an angel speaking from heaven. He does this also against all heretics who attempt to alter the apostolic traditions.

Let him be accursed. Let him be abominable to you. As we have said before, and now I say again: if anyone evangelizes you contrary to what you received, let him be accursed. He repeats this in order to commend it more forcefully.

For now—he wishes to show that he does not fear human hatred and ought to preach the truth freely. Am I now persuading you for human beings, just as previously I acted for the sake of Jewish traditions? I persuade human beings—I satisfy them—or God? God. Or do I seek to please human beings?

Whenever human beings are mentioned without any qualification, the word is especially understood in a negative sense, as in: “Every human being is a liar”; “Who do human beings say that I am?”; and “Are you not human beings?” Therefore whoever wishes to please such people must do their will. The holy, however, please God alone and those who love God, who are now said to be more than merely human.

If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ. For they hated me because I am Christ’s servant.

For I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was evangelized by me, because it is not according to human beings. He wishes to cleanse himself of usurpation and the disgrace of human tradition.

For neither did I receive it from a human being. I neither invented it myself nor received it from another: namely, that the Gentiles are saved by faith alone. At the same time, it should be noted that here he calls Christ God, from whom he received the Gospel.

I received it neither from a human being nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. The distinction between receiving and learning is this: one receives the Gospel when it is first made known to him and he is led to faith in it, so that he believes the things written in it to be true. One learns when he comes to understand, explained and expounded, the things figuratively represented in it through riddles and parables.

For you have heard. Nor are you yourselves unaware of what I am saying. My former way of life in Judaism. Here he recounts how firmly he had held to Judaism and how he had attacked the Church on behalf of ancestral traditions, to show that he could not have been separated from it by human counsel, but only by divine revelation and mercy.

For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, that I persecuted the Church of God beyond measure and was destroying it. He offers his own example: if I, who was born a Jew and educated there, do not follow the ceremonies of the Law, what ought you to do?

And I advanced in Judaism. Not in the Law of God, but in the tradition of the fathers. Beyond many of my contemporaries among my people. He did not say “beyond all,” lest it appear an occasion for boasting.

Being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers. He mentions ancestral traditions, not the Lord’s commandments.

But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb. He who had already set me apart from the womb in the present, when he willed, did what he knew would happen. His mother’s womb may also be understood as the Synagogue.

And called me through his grace. Not through my merits. To reveal his Son in me, so that I might evangelize him among the Gentiles. Through me, or in me. He revealed him not only on the road but also in the other places.

Immediately I did not consent. Immediately I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, because I heard not the voice of flesh and blood but of the Lord, nor did I confer with flesh and blood. “Flesh and blood,” that is, my own people.

Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away to Arabia, and returned again to Damascus. He did this not to learn something from them, but went from Damascus to Arabia to teach what had been revealed to him.

Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem. He went after three years so that we may understand that he did not need instruction, since he had already been teaching for three years.

He went to see Peter, as it is reported that he attempted to join the disciples. To see Peter—for the sake of seeing, not of learning. And I remained with him fifteen days. He shows that Peter received him with love, and that in so short a time he could not have learned anything.

But I saw none of the other apostles, except James, the brother of the Lord. By kinship through Mary.

Now concerning what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie. Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. But I was unknown. It should be noted that after three years he saw people who were unknown to him.

I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. They had only heard that the one who formerly persecuted us now evangelizes the faith that he once tried to destroy.

Those who at that time, as believers from among the Jews, had their churches separately and did not mingle with those who were from the Gentiles.

And they glorified God in me. In a difficult matter this is a great miracle: God, who alone can make an apostle from a persecutor and make the good from the evil.

## CHAPTER II

Then after fourteen years I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. This was when the question concerning the burdens of the Law arose.

I went up according to revelation. Not according to my own will. And I laid the Gospel before them. I did not learn it from them, but laid it before them. To confer is one thing, to learn another. Among those conferring there is equality; between teacher and learner, the one who learns is inferior.

The Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles—that they are saved by grace and faith alone. Privately, lest the disciples think that they doubted.

Before those who seemed to be something—those who were superior. Lest perhaps I should be running, or had run, in vain. This does not express doubt but confirmation.

But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised. Nor does “not” always carry its usual negative force. But because of the false brothers who had been brought in, who slipped in secretly.

They slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to bring us back into slavery. He gives the reasons why, according to the Latin copies, he circumcised Titus: not because circumcision benefited him, but in order to avoid scandal. By which we are free from the yoke of the Law.

To them we did not yield in submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you. The Latin text has: “To them we yielded for an hour, in order to avoid danger, and so that there might be those among you who would confirm the truth of the Gospel.” It does not complete the sense with which he had begun and introduced another one; after completing that, he returns to what he had begun.

But from those who seemed to be something I received nothing. If, then, even among so many Jews, with brothers pressing in from every side, some of them looking on with partiality, we could not be compelled by any force or argument to observe circumcision, which we knew had come to an end, how can you, who are Gentiles, who are in Galatia, and against whom no force can be brought, voluntarily depart from grace, cross back into the antiquity of a Law that has already been abolished, and observe ceremonies that are no longer necessary?

Whatever they once were makes no difference to me. I do not care that they lived with the Lord. For God does not accept a person’s status. But those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me. For time does not prejudice faith.

On the contrary, when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, just as the Gospel of the circumcision had been entrusted to Peter—so that I might preach to the Gentiles, just as Peter preached to the Jews—he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles. I am not inferior to him, because we both were appointed by one person to one ministry.

And when they recognized the grace that had been given to me—James, Cephas, and John. Here he gives the reason, and names those whom he had called “those who seemed to be something” above.

Those who seemed to be pillars—the foundation of the Church, and those upon whom it rested—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship. They agreed that we should teach in this way.

That we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision. “Should go” is understood.

Only that we should remember the poor. Those who sold their possessions and laid the proceeds at the apostles’ feet, or whose goods had been seized by the Jews, as it is said to the Hebrews: “You joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions.” This was the very thing I was eager to do.

In every epistle he does this.

But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face. The weakness of the Galatians compelled him to relate that he did not spare Peter himself when Peter was not freely defending the truth of the Gospel, just as, for the benefit of the Corinthians, he made known the vision that he had concealed for fourteen years.

He does all this to show that he was never an advocate of circumcision, as the pseudo-apostles boasted about him.

Because he was blameworthy—from the Gentiles, because he was compelling them to Judaize. For before certain people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. He ate with those who were from the Gentiles, knowing that the Lord had said to him that he should call no human being unclean.

But when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision; and the other Jews joined him in his pretense. He is not reproved because he ate with them, but because afterward he withdrew from them.

So that even Barnabas was led by them into that pretense. He had been sent with me to the Gentiles and had preached that there was no difference between Jew and Gentile.

But when I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel—although he did this because of the Jews’ offense, I confronted him publicly, so that both Jewish pride and Gentile despair might be removed.

I said to Cephas before everyone. A public scandal could not be healed privately.

If you, although you are a Jew—he gave a reason; he did not offer an insult—if you do not observe what you were born into, how do you compel those who were not born into it to observe it?

You live like a Gentile and not like a Jew. You know that you possess life not from works but through faith alone, by grace. How do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?

We are Jews by nature, and not from the Gentiles. By withdrawing from them as though they possessed something ἄλιον (*alion*, that is, evil).

Sinners. Yet sinners, because Scripture has enclosed everything under sin.

But knowing that a human being is not justified by works of the Law—of the Law, not works of righteousness. The works of the Law are circumcision, the Sabbath, feast days, baptisms, and the rest, which were commanded not for the sake of righteousness but to occupy the people.

Except through faith in Jesus Christ. And we have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by the faith of Christ and not by works of the Law—that is, by the faith given by Christ.

Therefore by works of the Law no flesh will be justified. At that time, according to the plain understanding, not every flesh but only those human beings who were in Palestine were justified by the Law. But now every flesh is justified by faith in Jesus Christ, while his Church is established throughout the whole world.

But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were found to be sinners—if faith alone did not save the Gentiles, neither does it save us, since no one will be justified by works. Therefore we are still sinners, and Christ is a minister of sinners, as though he were unable to forgive sins.

Is Christ therefore a minister of sin? Certainly not. He ministers to sinners, as Moses did, because through Moses—that is, through the Law—sins were increased, not removed.

For if I rebuild the very things that I destroyed, I establish myself as a transgressor. I destroyed the idea that a Jew had anything more; if I rebuild this again, as they say, I am found to contradict my own judgment.

For through the Law I died to the Law. Through the Law of Christ I died to the old Law, or through the old Law itself I died to it, because it foretold that it would come to an end.

So that I might live for God, not for the world. I have been crucified with Christ, crucified to all sins, for which the Law was given. Therefore the Law is in no way necessary for me.

But now it is no longer I who live. The old person does not live—the one who formerly lived under the Law and persecuted the Church. But Christ lives in him: wisdom, strength, the Word, peace, joy, and the other virtues. Whoever does not possess these cannot say: “Christ lives in me.”

But what I now live in the flesh—being in the flesh is one thing, living in the flesh another. For those who are in the flesh cannot please God; hence it is said to those who live rightly: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit.”

I live in faith in the Son of God. In faith alone, because I owe nothing to the Law. He loved me and gave himself for me, in order to carry out the will of the Father and his own will. Himself for me, not something else.

I do not reject the grace of God. I ought not to prove ungrateful to the one who loved me so greatly that he did not refuse to die for me. For I reject grace if this alone is not sufficient for me.

For if righteousness comes through the Law—if the Law could justify, Christ died for nothing. Let those who say that the Law has led people to the kingdom be ashamed.

Therefore Christ died for nothing. Up to this point he has been speaking against Peter, or against the Jews; now he returns to the Galatians.

## CHAPTER III
O foolish Galatians! He does not contradict the Savior, who forbids calling a brother a fool; for this is not said without cause. He calls them foolish because they are unable to distinguish the spirit of the law from its letter.

“Who has bewitched you?” Who has envied you? As Solomon says: “The envious eye torments the house” [the Latin text appears corrupt here]. “Has the fascinator caused you not to believe the truth?” Among us the one who envies is called *invidus*, but in Greek the more expressive term is used, **βάσκανος** (*báskanos*), “fascinator” or “bewitcher.” Properly speaking, a *fascinus* is said to harm the weak, tender childhood, and those who have not yet set their feet firmly as they walk. Hence the saying: “Who bewitches the tender lambs with his eye?” [Col. 0590A] Just as a tender age is said to be harmed by the evil eye, so also the Galatians, newly born and nourished in faith in Christ, were harmed by a kind of fascination [Note: [Col. 0589D] A passive participle of *noceo*, a verb commonly understood only as intransitive. EDIT.]. They became nauseated at the food of faith and vomited out the nourishment of the Holy Spirit.

Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed. Through my preaching, his passion was made so clear to you that you seemed to see him hanging before your eyes. And crucified among you. He received the sentence; or, you still regard him as one condemned and therefore contemptible.

This alone I wish to learn from you. This one question I ask you: Did you receive the Holy Spirit through works of the law or through hearing with faith? Did you receive the Holy Spirit from works of the law, or from hearing with faith? If you received the Spirit through faith, what more will the law provide for you?

Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being brought to completion in the flesh? While the Jews receive the Spirit in no other way than through faith, you, by contrast, think that the Spirit is insufficient for you unless you also submit yourselves to the law.

[Col. 0590B] Did you suffer so many things for no purpose? Observe that one who follows Scripture according to the letter is said to be brought to completion in the flesh. If indeed it was for no purpose. If you suffered for Christ, nevertheless you did not suffer in vain. Here “if indeed” does not express doubt, but confirmation, as in the saying: “If indeed it is just before the Lord to repay those who trouble you with trouble, and you who are troubled with rest together with us.”

He, therefore, who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you—did he do this through works of the law or through hearing with faith? You received the Holy Spirit solely through power, and the Spirit is received only by the righteous. It is therefore clear that you were righteous without works of the law.

[Col. 0590C] Works of the law are the Sabbath rest, observance of circumcision, and the superstition of the ceremonies.

As it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Thus faith alone is sufficient for you also for righteousness.

You know, then, that those who are from faith—whether Jews or Greeks—are the sons of Abraham. Not those who have been circumcised according to the flesh.

But Scripture, foreseeing this—that God would justify the nations by faith—announced the good news beforehand to Abraham: not by works, but by faith, which God himself inspires by his grace: “In you all the nations shall be blessed.” Not Israel alone.

Therefore those who are from faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham. For not all the nations have been circumcised, so that they could be blessed on the basis of works.

For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse. The habit of sinning has become so prevalent that no one now [Col. 0590D] keeps the law; and therefore they are not unjustly subject to the curse.

For it is written: “Cursed is everyone.”

The question arises whether faith alone is sufficient for a Christian, and whether the person who does not keep the evangelical commandments is not accursed. Faith is sufficient to make the one who first believes righteous, provided that he thereafter remains in justification. Otherwise faith without works is dead—but the works required are works of faith, not works of the law.

The person who does not believe God does not heed the commandments; and the Savior also taught that those who despise the commandments of the Gospel are accursed, saying: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” The apostle James likewise showed that whoever transgresses one commandment is guilty of all.

But learned interpreters understand this “one” commandment to mean charity, on which the whole law and the [Col. 0591A] prophets depend.

Some say that faith without works is beneficial because, if a baptized person should immediately depart this life—or if he should lack the means by which to perform works—faith without works is sufficient; for works without faith are nothing.

“Whoever does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, so as to do them.” That is, whoever does not keep all the commandments of the law to the end.

But that no one is justified before God by the law is clear. At the present time the law justifies no one; nor was it previously beneficial without faith.

“For the righteous person shall live by faith.” Faith is perfect when one believes not only in Christ but also in Christ himself.

He lives: he possesses life.

But the law is not from faith, because it does not justify. The righteous person, therefore, lives by faith; and the phrase does not add “in these things” or “in those things.”

But “the one living in the law, who does these things, shall live in them”—that is, in the things he has done, which he considered [Col. 0591B] good. He receives the reward of his labor only for the works he performed in the present life: either length of life, as the Jews think, or escape from the present punishment by which the transgressor of the law is killed.

“But whoever does them shall live in them.” He lives by his own labor; he lived under fear in the law for as long as the law remained in force.

Christ was not under the curse, because he alone fulfilled the law in every respect. Therefore his undeserved curse was exchanged for our curse, so that, passing freely over to faith, we might no longer concern ourselves with the works of the law.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.

One who buys purchases what belongs to another; one who redeems, however, properly purchases what was his own and had ceased to be his. Christ therefore redeemed us from the curse of the law, which was established for sinners, as it says: “Behold, you were sold because of your sins,” [Col. 0591C] and so forth.

For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.”

It must be considered that not everyone who has hung on a tree is accursed before God, but the one who has sinned and, because of his crime, has been sentenced to death. A wicked person is not accursed merely because he was crucified, but because he deserved to be crucified for his guilt; for it is not the punishment that makes a person guilty, but the cause.

Thus it is written: “If a sentence of death is imposed on someone, you shall hang him on a tree, and his body shall not remain on the tree, because everyone who hangs on a tree is accursed.” He is not accursed because he hung there; rather, he hung there because he was accursed.

Christ, therefore, for whom there was no sentence of death and no cause for crucifixion or for a curse, underwent the curse for us, because we were all guilty of death and liable to the tree. We were accursed because we had not remained in all the things written in the book of the law; [Col. 0591D] for the same law had decreed both matters.

So that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the nations in Christ Jesus. So that the nations might be blessed in Christ by faith alone, just as had been promised to Abraham.

So that we might receive the promise of the Spirit. The Spirit was promised through Joel to all flesh—that is, to the entire human race. This is a case of the whole being designated by a part, according to synecdoche.

Through faith: faith alone.

Brothers, I speak in human terms. I am speaking by comparison with human affairs. Human things can be compared with divine things for the sake of clearer understanding, but they cannot be made equal to them.

Yet no one rejects or adds to a humanly confirmed testament. That is, a testament legally drawn up is not considered valid apart from the death of the testator.

[Col. 0592A] The promises were spoken to Abraham. He calls the promises made to Abraham the New Testament.

“And to his seed”—that is, to the seed appointed by God. He does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “And to your seed,” who is Christ. He interprets the seed of Abraham as Christ.

Now this is what I mean: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, cannot annul a testament previously confirmed by God. The law, given after so long a period, cannot invalidate the testament that God confirmed to Abraham in Christ.

If we ask whether this testament, which he says was confirmed by God and could not be weakened by the law made four hundred and thirty years later, is the Old or the New Testament, no one can doubt that it is the New—though it was hidden in prophetic mysteries until the time came when it would be revealed in Christ.

Those who belong to the Old Testament are the people who, after [Col. 0592B] receiving a holy and just law, think that the letter is sufficient for them unto life. They seek to establish their own righteousness and do not submit themselves to the righteousness of God.

Someone may say: How can that which was made through Moses after 430 years be called old, while that which was made with Abraham so many years earlier is called new?

If anyone is moved by this question not contentiously but earnestly, let him understand, first, that one is called old because of its earlier time and the other new because of its later time. In these names their revelations are being considered, not their institutions.

Through Moses came the Old Testament, through whom the holy and good law was given—a law through which there would be not the abolition but the recognition of sin, and through which the proud would be convicted.

This law had been hidden from the beginning, when nature itself convicted unrighteous people because they did to others [Col. 0592C] what they did not wish to have done to themselves.

The revelation of the New Testament, however, took place in Christ, when he was manifested in the flesh. In him the righteousness of God appeared—that is, the righteousness that comes to human beings from God.

For he says: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law.”

This, then, is why it is called the Old Testament: because it was revealed earlier.

Furthermore, the Old Testament belongs to the old human being, from whom it is necessary for a person to begin; the New belongs to the new human being, into whom a person must pass from oldness. In the former are earthly promises; in the latter, heavenly promises.

It does not annul the promise in order to make it void. “For if the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from the promise.”

The promises made earlier to Abraham cannot be destroyed by the law given later, nor can what came later prejudice what came first, [Col. 0592D] since the promises were given to Abraham 430 years beforehand, so that all the nations might be blessed in him.

God granted the promise to Abraham. Therefore the inheritance does not come from the law, which did not yet exist; when it came, it revealed sin but did not remove it.

What, then? Why was the law given, if the weak needed it? It was given to restrain the unstable and wandering by the severity of a saving commandment and to confine them through careful observance.

But the law is good because it is spiritual. Therefore, he who does not consider it spiritual [the text is uncertain here]. The law is good if you raise your mind above the letter, because “the letter kills.”

The law was established because of transgression: to teach us not to transgress, or to constrain us until Christ came.

Until the seed should come to whom he had made the promise.

[Col. 0593A] After the people’s offense in the wilderness, after they worshiped the calf and murmured against the Lord, the law that forbade transgression was brought in.

The law was not established for the righteous. For this reason it gives commands so severe that it might tame the pride of the Jews. He says, “because of transgression,” not “because of justification.”

Let those who rave that the law by itself sent anyone to the kingdom of heaven hear this and fall silent.

Ordained through angels. He wants us to understand that throughout the Old Testament, whenever any angel was seen, the Mediator was speaking through that angel—the one who says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

Nor is it surprising that God speaks through angels, since the Lord also speaks through the angels who are in human beings, namely, through the prophets. Haggai says: “And the angel who spoke in me said,” and then adds: “Thus says the Lord God [Col. 0593B] Almighty.”

We may understand Moses, Aaron, and Joshua as angels, since they were messengers of God, through whom God gave and ordered the law through angels.

The law was ordered through angels. For we read that angels were present either with Moses, as some think, or with Christ. They also say that Moses stood between God and the people.

For “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature.

In the hand of the Mediator: in the authority, power, and strength of Christ.

But a mediator does not belong to one party alone, whereas God is one.

Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. The word “substance” or “one party” is to be supplied, because he existed as mediator between God and human beings.

He added, “But God is one,” so that no one might separate Christ from the unity of the divine substance on account of the office of the flesh he assumed.

“A mediator does not belong to one” means that “substance” is to be supplied, because [Col. 0593C] in Christ there is one person and yet a twofold substance.

For if a law had been given that could give life—as he says in the Epistle to the Romans—then righteousness would truly have come from the law. For what was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened, was impossible because no one was now keeping it. If it did not give life, how could it send the dead into the kingdom?

He called righteousness the inheritance, or at least the righteousness that comes from the faith of the New Testament.

But Scripture confined everything under sin. It exposed everything, so that the promise of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe, and so that believers would necessarily be saved by grace through faith alone.

Before faith came, however, we were being guarded under the law—before the one came in whom we were to believe, or before the faith through which we were to believe.

If faith came, where are those who say that faith is derived from nature?

We were confined within that faith which was to be revealed. We were preserved by the law [Col. 0593D] for this faith, which was to be revealed.

Therefore faith is not derived from nature, since it was revealed at a later time, after the law.

Thus the law was our pedagogue leading to Christ. Disciples who have reached maturity no longer need a pedagogue.

So that we might be justified by faith.

But when faith came, we were no longer under a pedagogue.

Pay close attention to how often he says “from faith,” so that those may be confounded who say that the law sent people to the kingdom without grace. They do not understand that all who were saved under the law were saved by grace, because they were saved through the faith that grace bestows.

For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. All of you equally—Jews and nations—are sons through the one faith by which, as God’s gift, you believe in Christ.

For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. Having put on the Son of God and having become wholly his [Col. 0594A] members through the sanctification of baptism, you must be sons of God.

Why, then, do you need the law, which was given to sinners, when your sins have already been forgiven?

There is neither Jew nor Greek. At that time there was a distinction between Jew and proselyte, and even between tribe and tribe; among all these groups there was diversity.

There is neither slave nor free. They are not separated by social condition, but by faith; for a slave may be better than a free person, and a free person may surpass a slave in the quality of faith.

There is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus.

They are separated by the strength and weakness of their bodies. Faith, however, is assessed by the devotion of the mind; often a woman becomes the cause of salvation for a man.

But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise. If you have all become one body of Christ, you are Abraham’s seed [Col. 0594B] and true heirs—not through carnal descent, but through divine promise.

## Chapter IV

But I say this: for as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of everything; rather, he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father.

He is speaking according to the comparison he has begun. Because priests and rulers exercised authority over those whom he calls guardians and stewards.

Now they are commanded not to rule but to display a pattern, because we are all a priestly race and possess everything in common, although we receive the sacraments through them.

Guardians and stewards may also be understood as the prophets, whose words instructed us daily concerning the coming of the Savior, just as the law of Moses was previously called a pedagogue.

Those who possess the spirit of fear and have not yet deserved to receive the spirit of freedom and adoption are rightly said [Col. 0594C] to be under guardians and stewards.

The age of infancy fears sins and is afraid of the pedagogue. It does not trust that it is free, although by nature it is a ruler.

So also, when we were children, we were enslaved under the elements of this world.

This may be understood to mean as long as someone is a child and has not fulfilled the time appointed by the father, so that he may be called a son and heir.

We accepted the observance of days and times because of weakness and so that we might not observe idols. He called those whom he had previously called guardians and stewards “the elements of the world,” because at first we were placed under these governors and could not yet receive the coming of the Son of God.

Others have said that the elements of the world are heaven and earth and the things within them.

Others interpret “elements” as [Col. 0594D] the law and the sayings of the prophets: through these, as beginnings and elementary lessons in God’s writings, we receive the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom.

Nevertheless, in a simple sense “elements” may be understood as letters, or as the law and the prophets, because through them human beings are initiated. They are taught not so much for their own sake as for the usefulness of another matter: so that we may be able to read a connected sentence, in which the meaning and order of the words are considered rather than the initial elements of the letters.

But when the fullness of time came—when no one could any longer keep the law through habit, or fulfill what he had resolved to do in its presence—God sent his Son.

The sending of the Son is understood as his incarnation, not as any diminution of his majesty.

Born of a woman. “Woman” signifies not corruption but sex. Indeed, Eve is called a woman immediately after she was made.

[Col. 0595A] How was he made under the law? So that he might redeem those who were under the law.
