For if they could not otherwise be saved, he wished to be born of a woman and female nature for the sake of those who had been born under the law.

For this reason he also received baptism as though he were repentant, although he was free from sins: to teach the others that they must be cleansed through baptism.

He was made under the law in order to redeem those who were under the law. For if he had not been made under the law, he could not have saved the Jews. He could, however, redeem the nations who were placed under the law.

So that we might receive adoption as sons. We would not all have received adoption if he had not been made under the law.

And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.”

He proves that we are sons of God so that we might receive the Spirit that he himself [Col. 0595B] possessed—the Spirit crying, that is, making us cry out.

Therefore you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then also an heir through God.

Why do you wish to become a slave, when, having received the Spirit of the Son, you have become a son and heir—not through your own merit or by nature?

But at that time, when you did not know God—he turns to those who were believers from the nations and rebukes them because they wish to observe Jewish days and seasons, just as previously they had observed idols.

The Jews were also granted these days so that, through love of festivals, they would not offer them to idols.

You served those who by nature are not gods.

But now, since you have known God—or rather, since you have been known by God—how are you turning back again to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved once more?

For he does not know the wicked. Therefore it was not you who sought him, but he who sought you.

[Col. 0595C] You observe days, months, and seasons. We do not do so in the same manner; we do not worship the Kalends, nor celebrate feast days with revelry and banquets as they do, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

And years. Perhaps he is speaking of the seventh year of remission, or of the fiftieth year, that is, the jubilee.

I fear that perhaps I have labored among you in vain. For I have accomplished nothing by making you Christians if you observe these things again.

Become as I am. Be holy and think more perfectly.

For I also became as you are: I, a man who lived in the law without accusation, regarded everything as refuse in order to gain Christ.

Brothers, I beg you: you have done me no wrong.

This is so that you may rightly think that I am moved not by hostility but for the sake of your salvation.

A disciple wrongs his teacher if, through his own negligence, he despises the teacher’s instructions and labor.

You know that it was because of an infirmity [Col. 0595D] of the flesh that I preached the Gospel to you previously.

This may refer either to bodily sufferings or to natural weakness, because he had the treasure in earthen vessels.

He teaches through an infirmity of the flesh when he says, “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry”—that is, I gave you more humble instructions, as to children.

It may also be understood in this way: when I came to you, I did not come with lofty speech or wisdom, but in a humble and despised condition.

And you did not despise or reject your trial in my flesh.

It is a great trial for disciples if their teacher is either weakened or injured with impunity.

But God permits them to suffer these things so that power may be perfected in weakness, and so that, experiencing corruption, they may desire incorruptible life with greater ardor.

But you received me as an angel of God—as Christ Jesus.

When he compares himself with an angel, [Col. 0596A] he shows that the angel is greater. “As Christ Jesus”—not merely as an angel, because you received me in this way.

Where, then, is your blessedness? For I bear witness that, if it had been possible, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me.

He shows with what great love they received him and how completely they handed themselves over to his teaching, so that they wished to give him the members of their bodies that were most precious, in order, by giving him their eyes, to repay in some measure the light of the Gospel.

So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?

Such is the nature of truth: it is pursued by hostility, just as harmful friendships pursue it through flattery. People gladly listen to what pleases them; everything they do not want is offensive.

So these people too had begun to love Sabbath rest and the banquets of feast days, preaching against [Col. 0596B] the Apostle, who taught all self-restraint by his own example.

They are zealous for you, but not rightly; they want to exclude you so that you may become zealous for them.

“Zealous” may be understood to mean both “imitator” and “enemy” or “envious person.”

One is not rightly zealous when one strives to bring another down rather than to advance oneself.

But be zealous for what is good, always and in what is good, and not only when I am present with you.

Do not imitate them; always pursue what is good, not merely for a time.

My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.

You were brought into the light through the Gospel and begotten through teaching.

He shows that it is possible to be born again through repentance.

You have made me undergo pain again.

Christ is formed in the person who understands the power of his faith, in whom his entire manner of life is expressed and depicted.

Christ is formed in the hearts [Col. 0596C] of believers when all the sacraments are disclosed to them and the things that seemed obscure become clear.

I wish that I could be with you now, because I cannot write as much as you would marvel to hear.

And I would change my voice: I would turn the voice of a gentle father into the anger of a teacher rebuking you.

The teaching of divine Scripture builds up and delights, but it is much more beneficial when it passes from written letters into the spoken voice. The living voice has great power, since it is explained in the manner in which it is generated in the heart.

For I am perplexed about you.

Tell me, you who wish to be under the law: have you not read the law?

The confusion and disgrace of disciples are the confusion and disgrace of the teacher, just as their progress is the glory of their instructor.

He is confounded in them because, having already become sons, they desire to be slaves.

For it is written that Abraham [Col. 0596D] had two sons: one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.

But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through the promise.

Ishmael was the son of the flesh; Isaac was the son of faith. Abraham begot Ishmael according to carnal custom; Isaac he received against nature through the promise, by believing.

Who are those born according to the flesh if not lovers of the world? Who are those born through the promise if not lovers of the kingdom of heaven? For eternal life has also been promised to those who desire it and worship God freely.

These things were spoken allegorically—that is, one thing was figured through another.

The Apostle established a rule for how we ought to allegorize: while the truth of the historical account remains, we should understand its figures.

For after saying that Abraham truly [Col. 0597A] had two wives, he then showed what these very women prefigured. He did the same wherever the deeds of holy people are recounted, but not where sins are condemned.

To call sins mysteries, however, is to accuse God either of inability or of ignorance: either he could not display his mysteries in another way, or, not knowing what was necessary for him, he condemned certain people’s sins beforehand in general and then, later, would not have reproved and punished them if he himself had wished those sins to be committed for the sake of his mysteries.

As for the commandments, it is difficult to find them interpreted in such a way that their force appears to be nullified.

For these are the two Testaments: one from Mount Sinai.

The Old and New Testaments are like two mothers; one was given at Mount Sinai through Moses.

Into slavery—“of the law” is to be supplied.

Generating. The Jews [Col. 0597B] were compelled to serve even by fear of the present; they were driven onward by the threats of the law, whereas Christians are invited to freedom by rewards.

The Jews, as slaves, were occupied not only with moral commandments but also with various works. For us, as sons who have fulfilled the moral admonitions, all servile burdens are removed.

They were required to serve the priests as a matter of obligation and were also compelled to pay taxes; we, who owe nothing except charity, honor them voluntarily.

Those who crucified the gift and remained in the same unbelief came from that very people. They have been scattered throughout all the lands so that Christian truth might not lack testimony from their books.

Therefore God established the New Testament from the Old, because it pleased God to reveal the heavenly promises, which were set forth as a reward, only when the fullness of time had come. To a people [Col. 0597C] longing for earthly goods he gave the law on tablets of stone.

Which is Hagar—the slave woman of Abraham.

For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia. He wishes the diversity of the Testaments to be understood from the character of the places.

It is joined to the Jerusalem that now exists and is enslaved with her children. It is adjacent to it.

But the Jerusalem above is free. For this reason the Mediator and High Priest of the New Testament also came from heaven. The Gospel was preached not in one place but throughout the whole world.

Jerusalem is free. The children of a free woman ought not to be slaves.

She is the mother of us all—that is, of the multitude of believers.

For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear.”

He proves that we have another and better mother than the Jews have, for Jerusalem is full of iniquity.

“Break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail.” Cry out because of the greatness of your joy.

“For the children of the [Col. 0597D] deserted woman are many”—as Hannah prefigured when she said: “The barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children has grown weak.”

More than she who has a husband—she who boasts of her fertility, thinking that she has a husband; or because she did have one at that time, before the slave woman was cast out with her son.

But we, brothers, are children according to Isaac. Just as the promise was made to Abraham concerning Isaac, so it was also made concerning us, because all the nations would be blessed in him.

We are children of the promise, not children according to Ishmael of the flesh.

But just as then the one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so also now.

Not only Jews, but also carnal Christians today persecute the Church—either by slander, by bringing accusations against it, or by living wickedly. The last is by far the greater persecution.

Those who are carnal always persecute those who are spiritual. [Col. 0598A] We should not be surprised if such people persecute us, provided that we understand ourselves to be spiritual.

He persecuted the one who was according to the Spirit.

In Genesis it is written that Ishmael was playing with Isaac. Here, however, it is shown that the play was not innocent, since it is called persecution. Ishmael wanted to make Isaac appear vulgar and insignificant, as he himself was, so that Isaac would not be placed before him in the inheritance.

Perhaps Ishmael, being the elder and circumcised at an age when he could already understand and feel, claimed the rights of the firstborn. Scripture called the quarrel of the children “play.”

Even today the Jews persecute the Church more than the nations do.

So also now these people, who resemble their ancestors, desire you to be slaves.

But what does Scripture say? [Col. 0598B] “Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.”

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of a slave woman.

However much iniquity exalts itself, it is a slave woman and must be subjected to the saints, however much such people exalt themselves and boast that they are children of Abraham.

As long as they remain children of the slave woman, they cannot share the inheritance with you.

But we are children of the free woman.

Therefore we must not abandon our mother and follow the slave woman. Although she was the wife of the same husband, she was so only for a time, because Sarah was not yet able to bear children.

Christ has set us free with this freedom.

He redeemed us from the hand of the enemy.

## Chapter V
Stand firm. Be firm in the faith of the Gospel. And do not again allow yourselves to be held under the yoke of slavery. For the time of this age has already run its course; the darkness has passed, and the true light now shines. You ought no longer to draw the yoke [Col. 0598C] with slaves.

He calls the yoke of slavery the harsh, difficult, laborious Law, which exhausts its adherents with a heavy burden. Christ removed from us that exceedingly oppressive yoke of many observances, so that we should not be circumcised according to the flesh, or observe other things of that kind, but hold them spiritually understood; and, when the symbolic shadows have been removed, remain watchful in the light of the realities signified. For this also concerns us: “Do not remember the injury of your fellow citizens”; and, “If anyone finds another’s property, let him return it,” and the rest. Above all, the Decalogue itself—apart from the observance of the Sabbath—is to be understood according to the flesh.

“Behold, I, Paul, say to you.” I, Paul, boldly say this to you, fearing no one and not concealing my name, so that those who hear may be moved not so much by the authority of the one sent as by that of the one who sent him.

“For if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.” You do not think that Christ alone is sufficient for your salvation.

“But I testify again to every person who circumcises himself.” Whoever has undertaken the chief work of the Law must necessarily fulfill the whole Law and be subject to its curse.

“For he is a debtor bound to perform the entire Law.” He is obligated not only to circumcision, but also to attend the feasts at Jerusalem, offer burnt offerings of victims, and observe the remaining requirements.

“You have been emptied of Christ.” If you place your hope in the Law, you judge Christ’s grace to be ineffective; and what you have already received freely, as though you did not possess it, you wish to obtain by your own labors.

“You who are justified in the Law have fallen away from grace.” You wish to be justified and to follow the shadow rather than the truth. Who could be so deaf to the Apostle’s [Col. 0599A] words as to dare to say that the Law is grace, when the Apostle cries out: “You who are justified in the Law have fallen away from grace”?

“For we, by the Spirit.” By spiritual actions, not carnal ones.

“From faith.” Not from the Law.

“The hope of righteousness.” For we have been saved by hope.

“We await.” In a moral sense he has placed “spirit” in distinction from “letter.” The hope of righteousness is to be understood as Christ, because he himself is truth, patience, hope, righteousness, and every virtue. We await his coming, when he will judge all things and will appear not only in patience but also in terror and righteousness.

“For in Christ Jesus.” This had force under the Law; it did not have force in Christ.

“Neither circumcision has any value, nor uncircumcision.” Circumcision does not benefit, and uncircumcision does not harm.

“But faith.” Faith, therefore, also acts: for whoever believes God attends to his commandments. Whoever believes in future things does more than one who fears a present punishment.

“Which works through love.” Not through fear.

“You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” By the steps of faith and moral discipline you were progressing well. Who was it that called you back and hindered you with the burdens of the Law, which even those who imposed them could not bear?

“This persuasion is not from him who calls you.” He does not say that this persuasion is from God, but from those who assert such things; and he exhorts them not to listen to any of them.

“A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.” So that no one might say, “Why do you rebuke everyone, when not everyone has gone astray?”, he foretells that a little leaven of wickedness can corrupt the whole lump of the Church. Do not think that the plots of the few men who come from Judea and teach something different may be disregarded, because a little leaven corrupts the whole lump.

“I have confidence in you in the Lord.” In you, who have not yet been corrupted by perversity.

“That you will think nothing else.” You will think nothing other than what the truth holds.

“But whoever is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.” Whoever troubles you by drawing you away from the truth of the Gospel will bear judgment.

“But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision.” This is what the deceivers have falsely told you about me: that I preach circumcision to others. If I still preached it, “why am I still suffering persecution?”—as though I were an enemy of the Law and circumcision.

“All the hatred,” he says, “of the Jews is directed against me; and while they rage against me in their madness, the reason is nothing other than that I teach the Gentiles that they ought not to be circumcised or, though abolished, preserve the burdens of the Law, because when the truth came, the shadows ceased.”

“Then the offense of the cross has been removed.” They are offended because I say that salvation rests on faith in the cross alone. Consequently, those who say that righteousness comes through the Law are enemies of his cross, since the Law commands but does not help.

“I wish that those who are troubling you would even mutilate themselves.” Some say, “May they be cut off from error and grafted into the truth”; others say, “If they think this benefits them, let them not merely be circumcised, but even mutilated, if the removal of the member is useful.”

“For you were called to freedom, brothers—only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.” You were called to the freedom of the New Testament; only do not, under the pretext of circumcision, allow yourselves to be recalled to the service of the Law. Nor should you use freedom of conduct as an opportunity for the flesh—that is, do not live according to the flesh.

“Let them be circumcised according to the flesh.” Let them observe the commandments of the Law according to the flesh. [Col. 0600A] If they stand more firmly in the Spirit, let them cut away the foreskin of the flesh spiritually; and, attending more deeply to spiritual understanding, let them abandon the humility of the letter.

“But through love serve one another in the Spirit.” I am not teaching pride; service ought to be voluntary, not forced, because love seeks not its own interests but those of its neighbor.

“For the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying.” Even the moral requirements of the Law that are sought can be summarized in one saying and fulfilled in one commandment. Faith alone is therefore not sufficient for life in such a way that the many-fragmented commandments of the Law are summed up in one chapter of love.

“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Charity, or love, is fulfilled in four ways: first, God must be loved; second, we must love ourselves; third, our neighbors; fourth, our enemies. God must be loved more than ourselves, our neighbor as ourselves, and our enemy as a neighbor. Unless we have first loved God, we cannot love ourselves—that is, refrain from sinning. And if we do not love ourselves, according to what model will we love our neighbors? If we do not love our neighbor, how much less our enemy?

If, therefore, we wish to possess love, let us first love God more than our souls. This is proved as follows: if for God’s sake we despise even our salvation and our very souls, is faith alone then sufficient for life?

“As yourself.” Whoever says that he loves his neighbor not only does not do him the evil he does not wish for himself, but also does him the good that he wishes another to do for him. Thus he fulfills the whole Law, which has two kinds of commandments: not to do evil, and to do good.

“But if you bite and devour one another.” This happens through contention, because you judge yourselves better than one another; when you slander one another; when you are tormented by another’s prosperity and make another’s good your own evil; when you bite one another; and when you think to avenge yourselves by cursing. Or perhaps, according to the Law—“an eye for an eye,” and the other commandments of the Law prepared for retaliation—you seek to make a bite follow a bite, so that what appears to be justice becomes destruction: it does not avenge one person but consumes both.

“See that you are not consumed by one another.” This happens when one becomes an occasion of destruction for another.

“But I say, walk by the Spirit.” By the spiritual actions that he describes below.

“And you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” This does not mean that the flesh desires without the soul; rather, when the soul thinks about carnal things, it is called “flesh,” and when it thinks about divine things, it is one spirit with God. As long, therefore, as there is a double desire or will within us, we do not accomplish everything we wish. When one part builds and another destroys, we do not accomplish our purpose while we struggle against our desires.

This also must be noted: he did not say, “Do not have them,” but “Do not fulfill them”—that is, do not give consent to them and cease from carrying them out.

“For the flesh desires.” It desires carnal actions. The flesh does not desire without the soul, although the flesh is said to desire because the soul desires carnally. A person will then be righteous without any sin at all, when there is no law in his members resisting the law of his mind, but the whole soul and mind entirely love God, which is the first and greatest commandment.

“Against the Spirit; and the Spirit against the flesh.” These oppose one another. Against a spiritual action, the flesh desires adultery, while the Spirit desires chastity.

“So that you do not do whatever you wish.” Reason brings this about, so that the effect may follow the will, because in this life the flesh fights against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh.

“But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.” If you devote yourselves wholly to spiritual things, you have no need of the Law, which was given to carnal people. “If you are led by the Spirit,” he says, “you are not under the Law”—that is, under the Law which inspires fear, not the Law which bestows love. “God’s love has been poured into our hearts,” not through the letter of the Law, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. This is the law of freedom, not of slavery.

To the extent that someone is led by the Spirit, he is not under the Law, because to the extent that he delights in the Law of God, he is not under the fear of the Law. Fear has torment, not delight.

“But the works of the flesh are manifest.” It is not difficult to distinguish carnal works from spiritual ones.

“Which are fornication.” Fornication is the beginning of the works of the flesh.

“Impurity, indecency, debauchery, idolatry.” This was practiced by Onan, the son of Judah.

“Sorcery, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, anger, disputes, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries.” He calls enmities and the other similar things carnal, although they belong to the soul rather than to the flesh, so that the Manichaeans would not think that he was accusing the flesh. He defined every evil as carnal because it is produced by thinking about carnal things. Every good thing, however, is spiritual because it descends from above.

“And things like these.” You yourselves can gather the remaining things from these examples.

“Which I forewarn you, as I forewarned you, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.” It must therefore be noted and mourned that he has utterly excluded those who quarrel, dissent, and become angry, together with idolaters, sorcerers, and murderers, from the kingdom.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love.” Love is the first of all the virtues. As we have observed, it is divided into four parts: love of God, love of oneself, love of one’s neighbor, and love of one’s enemy.

“Joy.” Spiritual joy.

“Peace.” When the tranquil mind is disturbed by no passions.

“Patience.” Bearing injuries inflicted upon us.

“Goodness.” Always wishing to do good.

“Kindness.” Doing injury to no one, and patiently enduring injury done to oneself.

“Gentleness, faith.” It must be noted that faith also is given by God. The Apostle placed it seventh among the fruits of the Spirit. This too must be noted: faith is from God, whether it means believing in God or fulfilling promises made to human beings.

“Moderation.” Not becoming angry.

“Self-control, chastity.” Self-control is for a time; chastity is everlasting. One must abstain not only from fornication but from every iniquity.

“Against such things there is no law.” The Law did not prohibit these things; and whoever fulfills the new Law is not in the Old Testament.

“But those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” If all vices have been crucified together, and the flesh, as though hanging, desires nothing, why do we need the Law, which was given to restrain vices? This too must be noted: he says that those belong to Christ who crucify the flesh with its vices and desires, against those who thought that faith alone was sufficient.

## CHAPTER VI

“If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.” [Col. 0602A] We have life through the Spirit if we conduct ourselves spiritually and do not serve the Law carnally. But who is it who lives by the Spirit, except our hidden person, who sometimes also is accustomed to live according to the flesh? When he has lived by the Spirit, he walks by the Spirit. When he wishes to walk in the flesh, he is alive yet dead.

The perfect person in Christ always lives by the Spirit; he obeys the Spirit and never lives in the flesh. Conversely, whoever gives himself entirely to the flesh and assigns himself to the passions never lives in the Spirit. Between these are those whom we can call neither spiritual nor carnal: wavering between virtues and vices, they are now drawn back toward better things and are spiritual, and now are overthrown by the slippery path of the flesh and are carnal.

“If we live by the Spirit,” he says, “let us obey the Spirit,” serving one another not through the Law but through love. [Col. 0602B]

We ought not to dispute over the interpretation of the Scriptures and say, for example, “Circumcision is better”; “No, uncircumcision is better.” We ought not to despise the historical sense and follow allegory; indeed, allegory is empty and shadowy, unsupported by any foundations of truth. Hence envy arises among them. “They wish to exclude you,” he says, “so that you may emulate them”—not wishing so much to teach the truth of the Law as to conquer.

“Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another.” These extensive explanations are from Saint Jerome’s commentary on Galatians.

Empty glory arises when people impose things that are not commanded in the Law—for example, when we compel everyone to abstain from all flesh, and, once we ourselves can no longer do this, call such practices superfluous. I will speak plainly and will not conceal my own passion, a passion that is almost universal. We must not glory in riches, power, beauty, or bodily attractiveness, for these are clearly counted among the works of the flesh.

If almsgiving is done for praise, it is empty glory; so too prolonged prayer and the pallor that follows fasting. These are not my words, but the words of the Savior, thundered in the Gospel.

Even chastity in marriage, widowhood, and virginity often seeks human applause. And what I have long feared to say, but must say, is this: even martyrdom, if undertaken so that we may be admired and praised by our brothers, has shed its blood in vain.

The Apostle speaks—let the Vessel of Election speak: “If I hand over my body so that I may glory,” [sic] “but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

He who had said, “I know a man in Christ, whether in the body or outside the body I do not know—God knows—who was caught up to the third heaven,” and the rest—he, I say, who labored more than all the others, was given a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet him, so that he would not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations.

Certainly he asked the Lord three times that it might depart from him, but it was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.”

What is more truly the work of God than reading the Scriptures, preaching in the church, accepting the priesthood, and ministering before the Lord’s altar? Yet these things, unless someone guards his heart with the utmost care, arise from the desire for praise.

You may see many people—something Cicero also says—entitle their books “On Despising Glory,” while placing the titles of their own names at the front for the sake of glory. We often interpret the Scriptures and write things worthy of reading; but unless these works are done for Christ’s sake, rather than for remembrance among posterity and fame among the people, all our labor will be fruitless, and we shall be like a sounding drum and a clanging cymbal.

You may see many people disputing among themselves about the Scriptures and turning the word of God into an athletic arena. They provoke one another, and, if defeated, envy one another; for they are desirous of empty glory.

“Brothers, even if someone is overtaken in some offense, you who are spiritual, restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness.” Human weakness is overtaken in lesser matters that happen unexpectedly. But there is no being “overtaken” where something is committed after long and deliberate planning. He does not say that those who were not persuaded should not gently correct those who were overtaken.

Paul knew that he worshipped the God who did not wish the sinner’s death but repentance, and that every creature, though it may not sin, is nevertheless capable of sinning. Therefore he exhorts even the spiritual person to fear for himself, lest he sin, and to extend a hand to the one who has fallen.

Beautifully, he calls the person overtaken in an offense “a human being,” who can die; by the very name he displays the frailty of his condition, so that he may be worthy of pardon—like a human being deceived by error and plunged into an abyss, unable to raise himself without help and assistance.

It must be noted that he does not say that the person has been overtaken by many sins, but that someone who has gone astray after being overtaken by a particular fault should be corrected with a spirit of gentleness and mildness. One must not wish to correct the erring person harshly, angrily, or sorrowfully, but should willingly draw him toward salvation, promising pardon.

One should present Christ’s testimony, by which he invites those weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law and sins to his easy yoke and light burden, so that they may learn that he is humble, mild, and gentle of heart, and may find rest for their souls.

Let us use this testimony against heretics who invent various fables and say that a spiritual tree is so by nature and never bears evil fruit. Behold, the Apostle, whose authority they themselves follow, says that those who are spiritual can sin if they are inflated by the pride of their hearts and fall. We also acknowledge this, and we acknowledge that they may become spiritual if they return to better things.

Someone may object with what is written to the Corinthians: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” If there he says that he will come to sinners not in a spirit of gentleness but with a rod, how does he now, for those who have been overtaken by some sin, apply not a rod but a spirit of gentleness?

The answer is that he is speaking there of those who, after sinning, did not recognize their error and refused to submit to their superiors and be corrected by repentance. But when a sinner recognizes his wound and hands himself over to a physician to be healed, a rod is not necessary; rather, a spirit of gentleness is needed.

There is also perhaps this question: If someone must therefore restore a sinner in a spirit of gentleness because he must consider himself, lest he too be tempted, does a righteous person who is certain of his own mind and knows that he cannot fall fail to restore the sinner in [Col. 0604A] a spirit of gentleness?

We answer that even if the righteous person has conquered, knowing with how much labor he overcame, he will grant greater pardon to the one who sins.

If someone has remained a virgin into old age, let him forgive the person deceived by the heat of youth, knowing through how many difficulties he himself passed through that age.

If someone has seen a person deny Christ while being tortured under torment for confessing Christ’s name, let him sympathize with the wounds of the one who denied him, and let him marvel not so much that the other was defeated as that he himself conquered.

Observe also the care of the writer: he did not say, “Considering yourself, lest you also fall,” but, “lest you be tempted.” To be defeated or to conquer, with God’s help, is in our power. But to be tempted lies in the power of the tempter. If the Savior himself was tempted, who can be secure that he will cross the seas of this life without being tempted?

Paul therefore does not despair of salvation, but extends a hand to the one who pleads for mercy; as far as he is able, he weeps with the one who weeps, becomes weak with the weak, and judges another’s sins as his own.

Through love he fulfills the Law of Christ, which is this law: “This is my commandment, that you love one another.” What is the Law of the Son of God? “Love one another, as I also have loved you.”

Whoever lacks mercy and is not clothed with compassion and tears does not fulfill the Law of Christ, even if he is spiritual.

If someone is weak in faith and is still nourished with the milk of infancy, unable to pass so quickly from legal observance to spiritual mysteries, you who are stronger should bear his burdens, lest your knowledge cause the brother for whom Christ died to perish.

The person who helps a poor man burdened by the weight of poverty also bears his brother’s need and makes friends for himself from unrighteous mammon.

“Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.” You too are human and can be overtaken in some matter and need assistance. The healthy support the sick and bury the dead because they believe that they themselves can become sick and die.

“Bear one another’s burdens.” For example, you bear your brother’s anger when you do not become angry against him. And again, when anger has overtaken you, let him support you with gentleness and tranquillity.

Certainly, if one person has conquered loquacity in himself but has not yet conquered stubbornness, while another is still talkative but no longer stubborn, the first ought to bear the second’s loquacity, and the second the first’s stubbornness, in love, until the one fault is healed in one and the other in the other.

“And thus you will fulfill the Law of Christ.” The Law of Christ is love, for he says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.”

“For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” Whoever thinks he cannot be tempted, or trusts someone praising him more than his own conscience, deceives himself.

If someone does not wish to bear another’s burdens and, without mercy, is content only with his own work and virtue, seeking not what belongs to others but what belongs to himself—that is, if he loves only himself and not also God—he deceives himself.

“But let each person test his own work.” Whoever has a good conscience concerning his work and, examining himself, does not condemn his own work ought not to boast about it before another, pour out his praise abroad, share it with everyone, and seek ostentation from human favor. [Col. 0605A] Instead, let him possess his glory within himself and say: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

Whoever seeks glory from another has neither the world crucified to him nor himself crucified with Christ. He has received from human beings the reward he was seeking.

Thus he will have glory only in himself, and not in another—in his own conscience, not in another’s flattery.

Alternatively, this means carrying oil with oneself: not depending on another’s praise, but possessing whatever glory one has in oneself. Yet what glory will he have except in him to whom it is said, “My glory and the one who lifts up my head”? He who glories in his own righteousness does not glory in another’s sin. For he gains nothing through another’s loss, nor will he appear more righteous on the day of judgment because of another’s offense.

“For each person will bear his own burden.” If each person will bear his own burden, one person will not be able to bear another’s burdens. But we must observe that the command there was that, in this life, we support one another when we sin and assist one another in the present age.

Here, however, he speaks of the Lord’s judgment at the resurrection: we shall be received not according to another’s sin but according to our own work. That will occur on the day of judgment. In this life, however, let us support one another when we sin; therefore he said, “Bear one another’s burdens,” and so forth.

“He will bear his own burden.” Another person’s praise will not remove the burden from the one who deceives himself.

“Let the one who is being instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.” Let him share either obedience in word and actions, imitation, or the means of bodily sustenance. You who receive spiritual things from teachers should provide teachers with material things.

“Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.” A human being can be mocked by the serpent, who denies God’s vengeance, as Eve was. But God provides what he promises. Indeed, to defeat every stratagem of the devil, he gave Adam and Eve more than he had promised. He also did for Lot’s wife what he had not foretold.

“For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.” And in proportion to what he has sown.

“For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh.” This is the person who places his hope in carnal circumcision, or who sows vices in spiritual conduct or in faith.

“But the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.” Everything we say, do, and think is sown in two fields, flesh and spirit. If the things that proceed from the hand, heart, and mouth are good, having been sown in the Spirit, they will overflow with the fruits of eternal life. If they are evil and arise from the field of the flesh, they will cause a harvest of corruption to sprout for us.

Alternatively: whoever understands the Law carnally also expects carnal promises, things that perish in the present age. But whoever is a spiritual helper sows in the Spirit and will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

It should also be observed that the one who sows in the flesh is said to sow in “his own” flesh, with the addition of “his own,” whereas the one who sows in the Spirit is not said to sow in “his own spirit,” but simply “in the Spirit.” Whoever sows good things does so not in his own spirit but in God’s Spirit. Therefore no one should attribute anything to himself, because whatever good things there are are gifts of God.

“And in doing good, let us not grow weary.” As it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not be hindered from praying always, and do not fear being justified until death, for God’s reward remains forever.”

An unfailing reward will therefore follow unfailing righteousness. For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.

He exhorts them to devote themselves to perseverance. In this life they await the reward of good work, not knowing that just as in seed there is one time for sowing and another for harvest, so in the present life the work is the sowing that is reaped either in the Spirit or in the flesh.

The harvest is the future judgment. According to the quality and diversity of the seed, it produces different harvests: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold. No one can reap that crop if he grows weary. Whoever perseveres to the end, as was said above, will be saved.

What is more unreasonable than for sinners to increase daily in evil works while we grow weary in doing good? [Col. 0606B]

“For in due season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary.” Now is the time for sowing, not for harvesting. Let us not seek to receive our reward here. Nor should tender grass be left out in winter in the present, lest it be trampled and nothing remain to be harvested in the future.

For it will be said to us: “You received your good things during your life.” And again: “You received your reward.”

“Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to everyone.” The time of sowing, as we have said, is the present time and the life we are living. In this life we are permitted to sow whatever we wish.

When this life has passed, the time for working will be taken away, whether we are sick or healthy, humble or powerful, obscure or honored. Let us do everything in the name of the Lord with patience and equanimity, and what is written will be fulfilled in us: “For those who love God all things work together for good.”

If we ought to loosen the reins of generosity indiscriminately toward everyone, how much more toward the members of the household of faith and toward Christians, who have the same Father and are known by the title of the same teacher?

It seems to me that this passage can be joined to what precedes, so that he calls teachers members of the household of faith, to whom above he had commanded that all the things considered good should be supplied by their hearers.

This is the final time for sowing. Let us hasten to sow all the fields, and let us fill especially those that are most fertile, lest at harvest time we begin to hunger while others feast.

“Especially toward the members of the household of faith.” Let us show mercy to Jews, pagans, and Christians, to good and evil alike, lest we deny them what God does not deny. Nevertheless, let us show it especially to those who render distinctive service to the faith.

“See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.” Understand how confidently I have written, fearing no one, since I have written this letter with my own hand.

“As many as desire to please according to the flesh.” They wish to please carnal Jews and fear suffering persecution for the cross of Christ; they provide nothing for your salvation.

“They compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.” Gaius, who was also Julius Caesar; Octavian Augustus; and Tiberius, Augustus’s successor, had promulgated laws that the Jews dispersed throughout the Roman world should live according to their own rite and ancestral ceremonies.

Therefore, whoever was circumcised, even if he believed in Christ, was regarded by the Gentiles as a Jew, and no one persecuted him. The Apostle now calls this circumcision “confidence,” and therefore says: “As many as desire to please according to the flesh, they compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.”

“For those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the Law; rather, they wish you to be circumcised.” If circumcision caused the Law to be kept, this persuasion might appear to have some reason. But they act for the sake of earthly prosperity, or from the desire to obtain something, or from fear of losing it. They do not truly keep the Law, because carnal desire, through which sin is committed, is changed rather than increased; one desire does not heal another. Carnal fear and desire make them slaves, because they think they observe everything carnally.

“So that they may glory in your flesh.” That is, because they have drawn disciples over to themselves.

“But far be it from me to glory except in the cross.” Among the Jews.

“Of our Lord Jesus Christ.” I glory not in my own righteousness or teaching, but in the faith of the cross, through which all my sins have been forgiven, so that I might die to the world. Only the person who takes up Christ’s cross and follows the Savior can glory in the cross of Christ—he who crucified his flesh with its vices and desires, who died to the world and regards not the things that are seen but those that are unseen.

“Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” I have died.

“For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any value nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.” At this time circumcision does not benefit and uncircumcision does not harm. The only thing that benefits is for someone, having been reborn, to live by a new way of life, as the prophet says: “Renew your new fields, and do not sow among thorns; circumcise yourselves for your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your hearts.”

“And whoever shall follow this rule.” This rule by which hope must be placed in faith alone.

“Peace and mercy be upon them.” Upon Christians, for the Jews are Israel according to the flesh.

“And upon the Israel of God.” There is an Israel that is not of God—that is, a carnal Israel. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israelites.

“From now on let no one trouble me.” Let no one question me any further as though doubtful. I have explained the whole truth.

“For I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ in my body.” I bear in my body signs and marks not of circumcision but of the cross, through suffering; I carry the wounds and scourges that I endured for Christ.

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.” Such is Paul’s subscription.

He wishes the Lord’s grace, not the works of the Law, to accompany them. “With your spirit,” he says—not in the flesh, in whose circumcision carnal people glory. You, however, have been circumcised spiritually and conduct yourselves spiritually.

# THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 0607]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0607C]

The Ephesians are Asians. Having received the word of truth, they persevered in the faith. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from prison at Rome.

The Ephesians believed through the Apostle’s preaching, both Jews and Gentiles, and he writes to them because they stand firm. At the beginning of the Epistle, addressing the Jews, he explains the mysteries of Christ’s Incarnation. Afterwards he turns to the Gentiles and exhorts them not to be ungrateful for such great benefits. Then, commonly and continuously to the end, he commands moral regulations.

# CHAPTER ONE
Paul, apostle of Christ Jesus.

As in all the Epistles, apostolic authority is placed first. “By the will of God”: the Father’s will is understood—“not by my merits.”

“To all the saints who are in Ephesus”: every saint is faithful, but not every faithful person is holy—namely, baptized believers or those who faithfully preserve holiness; not catechumens, who possess faith because they believe but do not possess holiness. [Col. 0607D]

“And to the faithful in Christ Jesus”: those who make legitimate use of things.

“Grace to you”: this is understood to mean, “may grace be present.”

“And peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Grace will be yours if you are not ungrateful to him, assigning your salvation not to your own merits but to his grace. We have preserved the peace of reconciliation if henceforth we do nothing contrary to his goodness or justice. His customary greeting is this: when grace is wished from both, they are shown to be one.

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He begins with praises of God, who has granted them the blessings described below.

“Who blessed us with every blessing”: not with merely one, so that nothing might be lacking in any grace.

“Spiritual”: not with carnal prosperity or earthly abundance.

“In the heavenly realms”: in heavenly things, not earthly ones.

“In Christ.” In the Head he blessed and chose all the members, [Col. 0608C] so that he might make us holy and blameless—not because we were going to be so, but so that we might become so.

“Just as he chose us in him”: in Christ he predestined us.

“Before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless.” Nothing is new to God, with whom all things existed before they came into being—not, as some dream, because souls were chosen in heaven before the world; rather, his Church, without stain or wrinkle, was foreknown, predestined, and chosen in them, because he knows those who are his.

It is not as the Pelagians understand this passage: that, after receiving the commandments, people can be blameless by free will alone. They say: “Because God foreknew that we would become such, therefore he chose and predestined us in Christ before the foundation of the world.” But this is not so. It was not because he foreknew that we would become such, but so that we might become such, that through this very election of his grace he himself would make us such, by which he “graced us in his beloved Son.” When, therefore, he predestined us, he foreknew his work, by which he makes us holy and blameless. [Col. 0608D]

“In his sight and in love”: not in the sight of human beings.

“Who predestined us.” He predestined this: that, by pouring faith into them, he might make all believers children of God. They were indeed proclaiming the word of God with confidence to everyone willing to believe; but in order that they might believe, God had already touched their hearts, as we read in the Acts themselves: “And Lydia, the seller of purple, believed; the Lord opened her heart to understand what was being said by Paul.” Also: “The Lord knows those who are his”; and: “The will is prepared by the Lord.”

“For adoption as children”: not as a matter of nature.

“Through Jesus Christ to himself”: so that we might be his members.

“According to the purpose of his will”: not according to [Col. 0609A] our merits.

“For the praise of the glory of his grace”: so that we may praise the glory of his justice and mercy, which he bestowed on those who did not deserve it.

“By which he graced us.” By his grace or will he made us pleasing to himself in him. It is said “graced” (*gratificavit*) from “grace,” just as “justified” (*justificavit*) comes from “justice.”

“In the beloved”: in him, that is, in his Son.

“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.” He did not merely redeem us, but also forgave our sins, so that we might be righteous without our own labor.

“In accordance with the riches of his grace.” “We have redemption” is understood: not according to our merits. Where are those who say that they can be saved by their own diligence?

“Which he lavished upon us in all wisdom [Col. 0609B] and prudence”: so that he might make known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure. He lavished it more than abundantly—not only forgiving the sins of those redeemed from death, but also granting us such great wisdom that we might know the hidden mysteries of his will. By revealing it in his mercy, he placed in this mystery of his will the riches of his grace, according to his good pleasure, not according to ours.

“Which he purposed in him”: in Christ, in whom we have been chosen and predestined, so that he himself might make us holy—not because he foresaw that we would be holy.

“For the dispensation of the fullness of times”: in the last times, when the entire dispensation of the times of the law and of nature, and likewise of the prophets, had already passed, as he says elsewhere: “When the fullness of time had come, the Lord sent his Son.” [Col. 0609C]

“To restore all things in Christ.” This is what he purposed: “the things in heaven and the things on earth,” in him.

Many have held different opinions about this matter. Some say that “heaven” means souls and “earth” bodies. Others say that heaven means the Jews, who had received heavenly commandments, and earth the Gentiles. Others assert that in heaven it was not angels who were restored, but that their knowledge advanced from the time of Christ: they had asked, as though ignorant, “Who is this King of glory?” and were taught that he is the Lord of hosts.

But since something is not said to be restored unless it has fallen, it is better to say that their joy was restored through the salvation of human beings, a joy which they had possessed before human beings had completely turned away from righteousness. And who could doubt that the human race was restored on earth?

Again, in another way: that portion of the angels which fell in heaven with its prince is restored through the increase and fellowship of the saints, of whom it is written: “But they are like the angels in heaven.” Likewise, all things on earth are restored when believers from the Gentiles are admitted in place of the Jews who have fallen away.

And again, in another way: the things on earth are restored while we are restored through the blood and reconciliation of our Mediator. The heavenly things are restored when joy over our salvation arises among the angels.

“In whom we too have been called to share.” We who have believed from among the Jews.

“Predestined”: appointed beforehand, or foreknown and foreseen—not because we existed as such, but because through him we, who would be evil, would become good. [Col. 0610A]

“According to his purpose.” He purposed first to restore the Jews and then the Gentiles, although only a portion of the Jews believed.

“Who accomplishes all things.” The cause of all things is God’s will, which no believer fails to recognize as rational and undoubtedly good. If he accomplishes all things, where is Pelagian pride? He therefore also brings it about that we begin to believe—he who accomplishes all things.

“According to the counsel of his will”: not according to our merits. Let those who say, “My good will made me a Christian,” be silent about merits when they hear, “According to the counsel of his will.”

“So that we should be for the praise of his glory”: so that through the signs we perform God’s glory may be praised.

“We who first hoped in Christ”: we who were Jews and believed first, or who hoped from the law.

“In whom”: in whom salvation was also announced to you.

“And you, when you had heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation”: “Gentiles” is to be supplied.

“In whom also, when you believed, you were sealed.” [Col. 0610B] In that Gospel, or in Christ, you were sealed with one mark; and by this you are recognized as one flock, because you too, like us, perform powers through the Spirit. These powers are the pledge of the inheritance to come. If raising the dead is a pledge, how great will the possession itself be?

“With the Holy Spirit of promise”: the one promised through the prophet Joel.

“Who is the pledge of our inheritance.” A pledge is given so that people may believe the promises.

“For the redemption of the acquired possession”: of those whom he acquired for himself by his blood.

“For the praise of his glory”: so that his name may also be glorified by us in this matter.

“Therefore I too, having heard of your faith, which is in the Lord Jesus, and your love toward all the saints.” You believe firmly in the Lord Jesus, and you love all the saints without respect to person or familiarity.

We are commanded to beware of false prophets and not to believe every spirit, and not to judge before testing.

“I do not cease giving thanks for you.” That is, I prove faith by works, because he infused into you, by the gift of his mercy, the faith by which you would believe and the love by which you would love.

“Making remembrance of you in my prayers.” In prayers—not, as some do, in the pleasure of feasting. For me, nothing is more pleasing than prayer.

“That the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory”: the Father of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ—

“May give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation.” How does he ask God to give wisdom to the Ephesians, when he said to the Corinthians that knowledge puffs up? The difference lies in the effect, not in the name. There he speaks of worldly knowledge, which is foolishness before God; here he seeks heavenly and divine wisdom. Whoever possesses it can be humbled rather than puffed up; and through it, by God’s gift, all virtues can be acquired. For just as knowledge without love puffs up, so with love it builds up. [Col. 0610D]

“In the knowledge of him.” How does he wish them to know God, whom they knew so well that, believing in him, they loved all the saints for his sake? He wishes them to know perfectly that they were saved by God’s grace, not by their own merit, and how great his power and greatness are.

His power is shown in that he can fulfill the promised rewards or punishments; his greatness, in that he is everywhere and nothing can be hidden from him. Whoever knows and firmly holds these things fears to commit grave sins. For if someone is ashamed in the presence of human beings, much more in the divine presence. Hence the sons of Eli the priest are said not to have known God, because they did not fear his presence [Col. 0611A] and power at all.

“Having the eyes of your heart enlightened.” Spiritual promises are foreseen only with spiritual eyes.

“So that you may know what is the hope of his calling and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance.” If you know to what hope you have been called, you will easily despise every hope of the world. And if you see the riches of God’s inheritance, every earthly inheritance will seem filthy to you. No one who hopes for a kingdom together with its wealth considers himself worthy to possess bronze or lead.

“In the saints”: in the righteous and holy, not in all human beings.

“And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe.” Who can comprehend the greatness of his power and his ineffable goodness, which he bestowed both on those who believed from the circumcision and on those who believed from the Gentiles, making them believers and making them members of his Son, who is the head of his Church, and placing them at his [Col. 0611B] right hand in the heavenly realms?

“According to the working of his power”: not according to law or nature.

“Which he worked in Christ.” This is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us.

“Raising him from the dead”: through the assumption of our nature.

“And seating him at his right hand in the heavenly realms, above every principality, authority, and power.” “Right hand” signifies honor and blessedness; it is not to be understood that God is corporeal. For the Father too is said to be at the right hand of the Son, as it is written: “The Lord at your right hand has shattered.” Both, therefore, are at the right hand, because there is nothing left-handed in the Godhead.

The right hand of God is therefore blessedness; “sitting” is to be understood as dwelling.

“And dominion”: because he is one with God, or in God.

“And every name that is named”: if there is some other name of which we are unaware.

“Not only in this age but also in the age to come.”

“And he subjected all things under his feet.” “In the future,” that is, in the heavenly reality that is future for us, not for God or for Christ himself.

“And he gave him as head over the whole Church.” Christ is the head of the Church, the fullness of all its members.

“Which is his body and his fullness”: the fullness of the Head.

“Who is filled with all things in all things.” He is wholly filled in all the members, not in each individual member, lest there be any disparity of merits. When all have believed and have been perfected, then the body will be perfect in all its members.

## CHAPTER II

“And you, when you were.” Here he wishes to show them how great a benefit has been bestowed on them.

“Dead in your trespasses and sins.” Dead through the death of sin—against the Pelagians, who defend nature to the extent that reason does not permit and say that faith arises from nature. For what good can a dead person do?

“In which you once walked”: but now you no longer walk in them.

“According to the age of this world.” For this reason we call human beings “people of the world,” just as we call a house good or bad while understanding that the people living in it are meant. He calls idol-worshipers “the world,” just as he calls them “serpents,” whose likeness we bore when we followed the will of the devil.

“According to the prince of the power of this air.” According to the prince of that power who was cast down from heaven into this windy air.

“The spirit who now works”: by persuasion, not by force.

“In the sons of unbelief”: in those who do not believe. Each person becomes the son of the one whom he imitates, or of the one to whom he is worthy—just as there are sons of wrath, death, and Gehenna. [Col. 0612A]

“Among whom we too”: not you alone.

“We all once lived.” The Gentiles lived without believing in God; the Jews lived badly. We were all held by original sin.

“In the desires of our flesh, doing the wishes of the flesh and of our thoughts.” This was when our soul clung to earthly and carnal things, not only desiring what it thought of, but also doing what thought suggested.

“And we were by nature.” The evil habit of our ancestral origin so possessed us that we were all born for condemnation.

“Children of wrath, like the rest.” Children of wrath, as above, children of unbelief; children of Adam, children of vengeance.

Let those who attribute so much to corrupted nature that they contradict the Apostle and depart from the faith hear this and be ashamed.

“But God, who is rich in mercy.” Not only rich in power, but also in mercy. “You have mercy on all,” he says, “because you can do all things, and you love the things you have made; for you established nothing while hating it.”

“Because of his great love.” Great love is to love rebellious and impious servants as though they were sons. From this we should consider how greatly he loves those who have already become holy, since he loved sinners and the impious so greatly.

“With which he loved us”: and had mercy on us.

“And when we were dead in sins.” We were liable to death and lived as though already dead, not only in original sin but also in actual sin.

“He made us alive together with Christ.” He made us free from sin through baptism and raised us up. We should not despair that what our nature already possesses in Christ may come to be in you.

“By whose grace you have been saved.” Freely, not by our merit, so that human pride—which boasts of its merits—may be humbled and may know that grace is given freely. [Col. 0612C]

“And he raised us up together and seated us together in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus.” Where the Head is, there the body will also be, just as he himself says: “I desire that where I am, they too may be.”

“So that he might show in the ages to come.” He predestined beforehand what he was now going to do.

“The abundant riches of his grace in goodness.” Truly abundant grace: he not only forgave sins, but also raised us with Christ. Nor was this enough unless he also placed us at God’s right hand in the heavenly realms, in the human being whom he assumed.

“Toward us in Christ Jesus”: in the body of Christ or by his example.

“For by grace you have been saved.” Not by your merits, but by grace freely given. This is directed against those who say that they are saved by their merits.

“Through faith”: through faith alone, which the Holy Spirit infuses by his gift.

“And this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift.” It is a gift of grace, so that they might not say that faith came from themselves and not from God.

“Not from your works, so that no one may boast.” No one should boast that he received it through his own merits.

“For we are his workmanship.” We have recently been reborn in Christ so that, with God’s help, we might walk in the good works revealed in the Gospel.

“Created in Christ for good works.” He is not speaking of that creation by which we are born in Adam or from Adam, but of the creation by which we are reformed through grace in baptism, so that with his help we might walk in good works.

All these things happen or are prepared by grace. For what follows—“which God prepared”—means “which he predestined.”

“Which God prepared so that we should walk in them.” God prepared them in his presence, and now he has given them through his grace, so that we might walk according to the new human being. That is, he predestined them; predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge. [Col. 0613A]

“Therefore remember that formerly you, Gentiles.” He reminds them from what great ignobility they were brought to the summit of the kingdom, so that they may not be ungrateful to him who graciously chose to bestow this on them by his grace.

“In the flesh, you who were called the uncircumcision.” The Gentiles were called “uncircumcision,” and the Jews “circumcision.”

“By what is called circumcision”: not circumcision in the heart through the Spirit.

“Made in the flesh by hand”: human circumcision.

“For at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the society of Israel.” They had Christ promised to them in many mysteries and sacraments; but you, following blind and mute idols, did not even know Christ by name, nor were you regarded as God’s people.

“And strangers to the covenants.” Even if some believed, they were regarded as proselytes—that is, foreigners—because the Gentiles were strangers to Israel and to Christ. [Col. 0613B]

“Having no hope of the promise.” The Jews hoped for God’s promises, by which he had promised Abraham that salvation would come in Christ.

“And without God in this world.” For, following many false gods, they had lost the one true God.

“But now in Christ Jesus.” You are one in his body, that is, the Church.

“You who once were far away have been brought near.” You have been brought near to God.

“So that you have been made equal to the Jews.”

“By the blood of Christ.” Believe that you have been freed by his blood, by which he made you equal to them.

“For he is our peace”: the reconciliation of both peoples with one another and with God.

“Who made both one”: one flock.

“And the middle wall of the dividing fence.” Like a middle wall and fence, the burdens of the law enclosed the two peoples, deterring the Gentiles from joining the Israelite people. [Col. 0613C]

“That wall is called hostility.” Or certainly the actual and original sins which are known to separate us from God are rightly called hostility.

“By abolishing hostility in his flesh, the law of commandments.” That is, the law of circumcision and the other commandments, which were demanded not by God’s will but by the people’s stubbornness. The Lord removed these hostilities and poured out peace, nullifying the law so that he might create the two in one new human being.

In this he signifies not only the inner and outer person, but also the Jew and the Greek, so that he might be “all things in all.” For the Lord, who is lord of the Sabbath, removed the superstition of the bodily Sabbath and, as it were, dismantled the middle wall of the law, which by the difficulty of its decrees prevented us from practicing that piety which is according to God. It was impossible for the Gentiles, according to the law of Moses, to serve God as soldiers.

“By abolishing the decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new human being.” Justifying by faith alone; and, while making this determination, he destroyed only these moral matters, so that not only the outer and inner person but also the two peoples might be made into one Christian people.

“Making peace, and reconciling both in one body to God.” Both had been alienated through sin.

“Through the cross.” Through faith alone in the cross, which deters no one. For it is not burdensome; even the crucified thief was able to receive it suddenly.

“Putting to death the hostility”: the hostility of separation.

“In himself”: in his flesh.

“And coming, he proclaimed the Gospel.” For this purpose he came.

“Peace to you who were far away.” He speaks to the Gentiles, who had departed far from God—not spatially, but by worshiping idols.

“And peace to those who were near”: to the Jews.

“For through him we have.” “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

“Both have access”: both peoples.

“In one Spirit to the Father.” One body has one Spirit.

“Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.” You are no longer outsiders or proselytes. He did not separate you from his people, as Isaiah foretold. Citizens of the same city share both origin and dwelling.

“Built upon the foundation.” Christ is the foundation of the apostles and prophets, and he is also called the cornerstone, as it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected,” joining and holding together the two walls. [Col. 0614B]

He is both the foundation and the summit, because the Church is founded and completed in him.

“Of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.” “Prophets” means the prophets of the New Testament, not the Old; otherwise he ought to have mentioned the earlier prophets.

“In whom every structure, joined together, grows.” He says that the body of Christ, that is, the Church, is constructed in comparison with Solomon’s temple, so that truth may possess far greater purity and holiness than the image.

“Into a holy temple in the Lord.” Stones that have not been sanctified cannot be placed in a holy temple.

“In whom you too.” So that you too may be God’s spiritual dwelling, that is, not made by hand.

“You are being built together into a dwelling of God in the Spirit”: together with the apostles and prophets.

## CHAPTER III

“For this reason.” For the reason mentioned above: that the Son of God, descending from heaven, saved both Jews and Gentiles and made one flock.

“Grace”: the gift of God. [Col. 0614C]

“I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus.” Whether imprisoned in chains or bound by the love of Christ, I cannot do my own will unless the Lord grants it.

When he calls himself a prisoner, he confirms the Gospel, showing how great is the hope for which he willingly embraces such sufferings, even though among the Jews he could have been a teacher of the law, possessed great wealth, and been held in the highest honor.

“For you Gentiles.” According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake, because he said that they were one.

“If indeed you have heard.” If you retain it firmly.

“The dispensation of God’s grace which was given to me for you.” “Who is the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord appointed over his household, to give it food at the proper time?” This is the dispensation of preaching.

Pay close attention: he attributes what he is to the grace of God, so that no one may be lifted up by his merits; and one who ascribes to himself what he has thereby proves ungrateful for God’s gift.

“For according to revelation the mystery was made known to me.” That Jews and Gentiles are one in Christ, according to revelation, not according to human teaching.

“As I wrote above briefly, as you can understand when you read.” Not as much as I could have written, but as much as you were able to understand.

“My understanding in the mystery of Christ”: not in worldly eloquence.

“Which was not made known to other generations to the sons of men.” The ancient prophets did know that the Gentiles would be called, but they did not know that there would be no distinction between Jew and Gentile; or else the prophets did not speak as human beings.

“As it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets.” “Prophets” means the prophets of the New Testament, to whom he now asserts that it was revealed. [Col. 0615A]

“In the Spirit”: through the Spirit.

“That the Gentiles are fellow heirs.” Not merely “fellow heirs,” which can refer to people of different kinds; nor merely “of the same body,” since children may be of the same kind but not share the same substance of inheritance.

“But also fellow members of the body and fellow participants in the promise in Christ Jesus”: members of one body.

“Through the Gospel, of which I became a minister.” It is made known to all that this gift was specially bestowed on me.

“According to the gift of God’s grace which was given to me.” Not according to my merit. From this we learn that we must not glory in merits, since the gift is given freely.

“According to the working of his power.” His power strengthened me; or the Gospel is confirmed through miraculous works.

“To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given among the Gentiles.” He is therefore least among the saints—that is, last in rank—and greatest through grace. Although he humbled himself, nevertheless each person has a work in which he humbles himself.

“To proclaim the Gospel”: to announce the riches of the inheritance to come.

“The unsearchable riches of Christ.” Unsearchable to human understanding by itself, but not to divine revelation.

“And to enlighten everyone concerning the dispensation of the hidden mystery.” So that I might teach Jews and Gentiles the meaning of this mystery.

“Hidden for ages in God”: hidden within God from former ages, that is, known only to him.

“Who created all things”: both Jews and Gentiles, or every creature, against Marcion.

“So that the manifold grace of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly realms.” Through me, to those who rule over heavenly matters through the whole Church, the manifold grace of God might be made known.

“Through the Church, the manifold wisdom of God, according to the preordination of the ages which he made in Christ Jesus our Lord.” He determined that at this time, when human beings could not otherwise be saved, they would be saved through faith alone in Christ.

“In whom we have boldness and access with confidence.” We do not have boldness and access to God through our own righteousness, but in him whose faith forgave our sins.

“Through his faith.” Hear “his faith,” and do not arrogate to yourself that you possess faith from yourself, unless it has been given by him.

“Therefore I ask that you not lose heart at my tribulations for you, which are your glory.” Do not, on hearing that I am imprisoned and abused without cause or impunity, think that my injury has nothing to do with God. Rather, you ought to glory, understanding that I could not suffer so much without fruit, because he will repay a reward in the future. [Col. 0615D]

“For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.

“From whom every fatherhood has received its name,” or “from whom every reality is called fatherhood,” because since he is our first and true Father, the name is derived from him, after whom other fathers are called.

“That he may grant you according to the riches of his glory.” That he may strengthen you through the illumination of the knowledge of the riches of his glory.

“To be strengthened with power through his Spirit”: with the wisdom and protection he provides.

“That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person.” Where the inner person is made strong through faith, there Christ dwells—not where the outer person is fattened.

“In love.” So that, having come to know his benefits, you may love him.

“Rooted and founded, so that you may be able to comprehend.” So that you may be able to comprehend the greatness of knowledge from every side.

“With all the saints.” You seek wisdom among the wicked, and you will not find it.

“What is the breadth and length and height and depth?” Some say that breadth signifies the spacious way; length, eternal life; height, heaven; depth, the lower regions. Thus, possessing knowledge of all these things, they may know what to choose and what to reject.

Again, in another way: breadth signifies good works of love; length, perseverance in goodness to the end; height, hope of heavenly rewards; depth, the inscrutable judgments of God, from which this grace comes to human beings. This interpretation fits the mystery of the cross.

Length means that, through long-suffering, troubles are endured for the breadth of love. Height is the eternal reward. Depth is the origin from which God’s freely given grace exists according to the secret of his will.

“And to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge.” The love of Christ surpasses knowledge, so that knowledge arises from it, just as fruit surpasses the root.

“So that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” So that you may be perfected in all the virtues of Christ.

“Now to him who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand.” He frequently grants more than we ask, and more even than we understand.

“According to the power that works in us.” We understand this through the power of signs that works in us; or, whatever good is done through us, he himself works in us.

“To him be glory in the Church.” For we have nothing from which to glory.

“In Christ Jesus throughout all generations.” When Christ came, he gathered the Church for the glory of God.

“Of the age”: immense benefits are to be celebrated with immense praises.

“Of the ages. Amen.”

Thus far he has spoken about the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, the calling of the Gentiles, and their unity with the Jews accomplished through the Gospel. He himself undertook this mystery, and through every aspect of it taught them, by God’s grace, word, and prayer, to present them as perfected.

## CHAPTER IV
Therefore I beseech you—I, a prisoner in the Lord—to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called. I, who am bound on your account, beg you: recognizing that you are sons of God, conduct yourselves worthily of so great an honor. For every dignity has its proper rules by which it is recognized, both in mind and in body, lest it be feigned.

With all humility and gentleness. Humility claims nothing [Col. 0616D] for itself; the gentle person harms no one and returns no evil for evil. With patience, bearing with one another in love. Philosophers also endure hardship, but not in love, nor for God’s sake, but for human praise.
