We, however, must suffer not in order to be praised, but so that the one whom we support may make progress; we should bear with him not in sorrow, but with love.

Be eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Through the bond of peace the unity of the Holy Spirit is maintained. We all receive the one Spirit, and wherever there is unity and harmony, let us not doubt that there is the Holy Spirit and his gift. But where there is discord and dissension, there is the contrary spirit—that is, the activity of Antichrist, who is already working the mystery of iniquity.

One body and one [Col. 0617A] Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. The whole structure of the members must have one agreement in one body, since they have been called to one hope. This can be said against those who think that they themselves may sin while others may not, although they too, baptized in one body, have received the same Spirit; and so also with the other things that follow.

One Lord, one faith. One faith belonging to all, in which you have all believed. One baptism, one God. Let heretics who rebaptize take note.

And Father of all. Of all believing nations also, not only of the Jews. Who is above all, and through all, and in us all. Above all virtues, because he is almighty; through all his works, because he is immeasurable; in all Christians, because he graciously dwells in them according to their sanctification.

But grace was given to each one of us. There are not many bodies, but different members through the variety of graces. According to the measure. According to the measure of his gift and the distinction of his generosity: “measure,” that is, faith. “Of Christ’s gift,” which is why he says: His gifts are given so that we may each be prepared for the grace assigned to us, and he distributes them as he himself wills. Let us recognize the gifts; let us not presume upon merits.

“Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.” Those whom the devil held captive unto death, Christ took captive unto life, carrying the head of our nature upward.

But what does “he ascended” mean except that he also first descended? He explains why he is said to ascend, although he is everywhere: namely, according to the form of a servant, to which descent is not a matter of place but of gracious condescension. For he who is everywhere according to his divinity—where could he ascend or descend? The Lord’s body, in which he suffered and rose again, can be in one place; his truth and divinity are everywhere.

Into the lower parts of the earth? Therefore hell is beneath the earth. He who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill all things. He who descended with his soul into hell ascended with soul and body into heaven, so that he might fulfill everything that had been written.

And he himself gave some as apostles. Against the Arians: the Son’s operation is one with the Father’s. For in the Letter to the Corinthians he says that God the Father appointed, first, apostles and, second, prophets. Here, however, he records that Christ gave them.

And others as prophets. Of the New Testament.

And others as evangelists. Every apostle is an evangelist, but not every evangelist is an apostle, as in the case of Philip, who was one of the seven.

And others as shepherds and teachers. Shepherds are priests; teachers are all who are qualified to instruct others. Therefore all shepherds are also teachers [Supplement: but not all teachers are also shepherds].

For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ. He appointed all these for this purpose: that they might build up the Church, which is Christ’s body, and bring all people to the reception of the faith.

Until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God. I want all people to be as I am. The one who has recognized the Son of God does not resist God’s commandments, commit deadly sins, or defend [Col. 0618A] his own evils. This will happen when Christ is all in all, and every schism or contention of death and flesh has passed away, so that the righteous may say with free voice: “Where is your contention, O death?” and the rest.

To a perfect man. Like Christ. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked.

To the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. We are not to imitate the measure of his age in years, but of his fullness; we are to hold fast to the perfection of his faith.

So that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine. So that we may not be ignorant, doubtful, or wavering, spreading the sails of our minds to every wind like an inexperienced helmsman, and thus easily suffering shipwreck or failing to reach the harbor.

By human wickedness. Human wickedness [Col. 0618B] and cunning turn those whom they deceive away from the straight course of faith.

By craftiness for the circumvention of error. Promising an easy remedy to those who are wandering, they cause them to remain in error; or they think that the remedy for their error lies in making more people err along with them.

But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in him. Let us do everything in the truth for the sake of Christ’s love, and nothing in hypocrisy.

Who is the head, Christ, in every respect. Let us grow in every way into his perfection.

From whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to its working. The body, joined and knit together from the head through every subordination of operation, grows as the members build one another up by loving one another, so that each member increases according to its measure. That is, the one who is an eye grows among those who perform the function of the eyes, and the individual members make progress in their proper place.

According to the measure of each member, the body produces its growth for its own building up in love. As the individual members grow, the body becomes greater, while the members build one another up in love.

Therefore I say this and testify in the Lord. What he urged above, here he reinforces with the Lord’s solemn testimony.

That you should no longer walk as the Gentiles walk. “I do not want you,” he says, “to be Christians in name only, confessing God with your mouth while denying him by your deeds. Just as great as the difference between the devil and God must be the difference separating the sons of God from the sons of the devil—not merely in name, but also in works. Otherwise, while honoring God with our lips, we may stand far from him in heart—that is, in affection and fear—and it may be said of us: ‘They worship me in vain,’ that is, they derive no fruit from my worship.”

In the futility of their mind. All human beings are vain who do not have knowledge of God.

Having their understanding darkened by darkness. They possess natural understanding, but it is darkened by the shadows of ignorance, so that they worship idols instead of God. We, by contrast, have been illuminated by the light of knowledge through the gift of grace.

Alienated from the life of God. They have been alienated from the life of God because they are ignorant of God. You, however, who have come to know God, must follow him.

Through the ignorance that is in them. It should be noted that ignorance gave birth to idolatry.

Because of the blindness of their heart. Their foolish heart was blinded when they said: “There is no God.”

Who, having become hopeless. Having lost hope of punishment for the ungodly and reward for the righteous, [Col. 0619A] or of the future life.

Have handed themselves over to immorality. Those who despair of the future must cling to present pleasures, as is said in the Book of Wisdom in the person of those who presumed that the soul could be dissolved into air: “Come, let us enjoy the good things that exist,” and so forth.

For the practice of every impurity, in greed. He includes all crimes under the name of greed.

But you did not learn Christ in this way. That is, you were not taught to live as they—the Gentiles—do. For the one who truly heard Christ and learned from him is found in no vice to be like the Gentiles.

If indeed you heard him and were taught in him, as truth is in Jesus. Just as he truly died and truly rose again, so that we might truly walk in newness of life, as he says to the Romans: “Let us walk honorably as in the day,” and so forth.

To put off, according to your former way of life, the old man. He explained what the old man is and how he is put off: namely, when one rejects former errors and is changed according to Christ’s way of life.

Who is corrupted according to the desires of error. Doing the will of the flesh and of thoughts.

But be renewed in the spirit of your mind. As Jeremiah says: “Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit.” We may also understand “spirit” as “mind”: be renewed in soul.

And put on the new man. Understand the new man from the old one.

Who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness. He explained what it means for a human being to have been created in the image of God: namely, to be righteous, holy, and truthful like God.

Of truth. Not of vanity, which hunts after the empty glory of human beings, since it is written: “You shall pursue what is just, what is just”; and again: “Those who keep just things justly will be justified,” not those who keep just things unjustly.

Therefore, having put away falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbor. Having put away the falsehood of the world’s writings, speak the truth of God’s law. He describes the forms of holiness by which the new man is recognized; but he also teaches us to flee falsehood.

For we are members of one another. Let no one deceive his brother, because we are one body, and the members cannot deceive or tear one another apart. The hand does not lie to the mouth, nor do the teeth tear the body—unless an unclean spirit dwells there.

Be angry, and do not sin. Let anger not intoxicate the mind, but let severity be exercised with restraint. Do not take notice of your own injury, but of your brother’s sin; or, “Be angry with yourselves, because you have been overtaken in something” [sic].

Let not the sun go down upon your anger. Do not give place to the devil. Do not let the light of faith or knowledge fail in your indignation. We give place to the devil by retaining anger, or if indignation is changed into hatred.

Let the one who used to steal steal no longer. By becoming angry or stealing, or by any sin whatever, we give place to the devil. Robbery is the devil’s doorway, just as righteousness is the doorway of the Holy Spirit.

Rather, let him labor, working with his hands. Let him compensate through his own labor for the labor he has seized from others, and by working give to those in need what he made many poor by stealing.

What is good, so that he may have something to give to those suffering need. Not what is evil. For there are many dishonorable or evil occupations, such as magic and those that serve pleasure.

Let no evil word proceed from your mouth. Not one, not two, but none at all.

But if there is any good word for the building up of faith. It should be noted that, although he gives this command to the whole Church, he addresses it especially to the priestly office. He did not impose silence, but changed the quality of speech, so that every word might build up Christian faith and our mouth might open only for the word of God.

So that it may give grace to those who hear. So that those who hear may receive grace from our speech, as he says elsewhere: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt.”

And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God. He speaks by comparison with human beings, so that from ourselves we may understand how great an injury we do to the Holy Spirit when we pollute his dwelling [elsewhere: “gift”] in us with some stain of sin; and because he grieves over our conduct in his dwelling, he therefore departs sorrowfully.

For the rest, sorrow, anger, and other things of this kind are passions in us, because we are capable of suffering; in God, however, they are dispensations. We suffer these things unwillingly, whereas he assumes them willingly for our correction. This is the difference between God and human beings in these conditions, and also in their natures.

Alternatively: For the substance of the Holy Spirit itself—which is whatever he himself is—cannot be grieved, since it possesses eternal and unchangeable blessedness, and is itself rather eternal and unchangeable blessedness. But because he dwells in the saints in order to fill them with love, by which spiritual people must rejoice in the progress of the faithful and in their good works, it is therefore necessary that they also grieve at the fall or sins of those whose faith and progress had brought them joy.

For this reason the Holy Spirit is said to be grieved by those who act in such a way that the saints are grieved by their deeds—nothing else being intended than that they possess the Holy Spirit, whose gift has made them so good that evil things cause them sorrow. Thus God is also said to do whatever we do under his direction; so he is rightly said to rest when we rest by his gift, to know when he causes us to know, and to groan when he causes us to groan.

In whom you were sealed. You have begun to bear a new seal.

For the day of redemption. On the day of baptism you received the seal of the Holy Spirit.

All bitterness. He shows what grieves the Holy Spirit, namely bitterness—that is, provocation.

And anger. He removes every occasion for our becoming angry.

And indignation and shouting. Indignation arises from pride, when we judge someone unworthy and therefore do not tolerate him.

The good man will neither shout nor quarrel. Shouting descends from fury, which Christ did not possess. Nevertheless, Isaiah is commanded to shout, and the Lord shouted in the temple: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink.”

And blasphemy. So that you may blaspheme no one.

Let it be taken away from you, together with all malice. Malice can repay even an enemy in kind.

But be kind and merciful to one another. He preserves the order of the law: not only must malice be removed, but kindness must also be planted in its place.

Forgiving one another. Otherwise it may be said to us: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt,” and so forth.

As God also did in Christ. Through Christ.

Forgave us. All sins.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. You are God’s children by imitation or adoption, not by nature, as the Lord says: “So that you may be sons of your Father,” and so forth.

And walk in love, just as Christ also loved you. As John also says: “In this we have known his love, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.”

And he handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God. He handed himself over voluntarily.

For a pleasing fragrance. Love is the sweetest fragrance to God.

But fornication. He briefly includes all crimes by naming two roots.

And every impurity or greed. Just as in the old law, concerning disgraceful crimes committed in secret—and which it is most shameful even to name, lest those who speak of them pollute the mouth and ears of their hearers—Scripture included them generally when it said: “Make the children of Israel modest, or reverent, concerning every impurity.” So here other extraordinary pleasures, including even the acts of marriage, if they are not carried out modestly and honorably, as though under God’s eyes, merely for the sake of serving children, are called impurity.

Nor should it be named among you, as is fitting for saints. Let us consider whether it is permissible to do what it is not permissible even to name.

Or obscenity or foolish talk. Foolish talk is also reproved among the children of human beings.

Or vulgar joking, which is irrelevant. Vulgar joking arouses laughter and is unsuitable to Christian seriousness, because it has no connection with heavenly and divine matters.

But rather thanksgiving. You ought rather to do and discuss this, so that you may not be ungrateful to God.

For know this, understanding that every fornicator. He argues against those who say that faith alone can suffice for salvation without works. This is rightly said only of those who are taken away after baptism and have no time to perform works.

Or impure person, or greedy person, who is a worshiper of idols. Such acts are offered not to God but to demons. For the greedy person, while hoarding coins and serving money, providing neither for himself nor for others, in effect venerates a human likeness; in the manner of images, he is rightly said to serve idols.

Has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. The kingdom is prepared for God’s children, not for the devil’s.

Against the Arians, who say: “The one named first is the greater.”

Let no one deceive you with empty words. By saying that faith is sufficient, and that once a person has received only Christ’s baptism, no matter how much he sins, he cannot perish.

Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Know the future from the past: [Col. 0621D] if he spared the Sodomites and those who perished in the flood, he will spare you as well.

Therefore do not become their partners. If you share in their sins, you will also be companions in their punishment.

For you were once darkness. When you did not know the Lord’s will; but now you have come to know everything. As great as the difference between light and darkness is, so great must be the distance between your former way of life and your present one.

But now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light. It must be carefully observed that we are darkness, whereas light is in the Lord, so that no one may glory in his own merits.

For the fruit of light consists in goodness, righteousness, and truth. True knowledge bears such fruits.

Testing what is pleasing to God. Test from the law what God wills, not what human beings assert.

And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness. For light cannot participate with darkness. Whatever is done without fear or knowledge of God, or whatever is not done for God’s sake, is of no benefit.

Rather, reprove them. Do not merely refuse to participate; reprove them as well.

For the things done by them in secret. In houses or in temples.

It is shameful even to speak of them. It is shameful for us to speak of things that they do without shame, as though in darkness.

But everything that is reproved is made manifest by the light. The light begins to exist when a person believes and is joined to you. For everything that is made manifest is light.

As he says to the Corinthians: “Even the secrets of his heart become manifest, and then, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.”

Therefore he says: “Rise, you who sleep.” He introduces the voice of some wise person striking the conscience of a pagan.

And Christ will shine upon you. When you have believed in him, you will become light.

Therefore watch carefully, brothers, how you walk—not as unwise, but as wise. As children of wisdom and children of light, so that you may not give anyone an occasion for stumbling and begin to become the cause of that person’s destruction.

Redeeming the time. Through your wisdom or prudence, and for the sake of your own peace, it is necessary that something perish for your accusers.

Because the days are evil. The days themselves are not evil, but human beings are, just as a place is called evil when something evil is committed there.

Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is. Search the Scriptures, because there his will is recognized.

And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery; but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to yourselves. He explains the value of self-control: it is not fitting for those crucified to desire the material of debauchery, but they should be filled with the Holy Spirit, since drunkenness is the mother of vices.

In psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing. Not about worldly matters, as David says: “So that my mouth may not speak of the works of human beings.”

And singing psalms in your hearts to God. Let us not sing God’s words with the mouth alone.

Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father. For everything that happens, whether good or evil, like Job, say: “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” according to David: “I will bless the Lord at all times.”

Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ. Not from human fear or for the sake of greed, as some flatter their patrons.

Wives, be subject to your husbands as to the Lord. He did not, as with the Corinthians, nourish incontinent people with milk, but fed them with the solid food of self-control. He feared that, when the duty of the flesh ceased, either the submission of wives or the affection of love in husbands might also cease in many cases, and that he might seem to have taught not self-control but divorce.

Moreover, how would it be fitting for a preacher of the new life to teach, without any reason, what nature itself demanded?

For the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church. He himself is the Savior of his body. He gives the reason for submission: the husband is first, and he ought to be the savior of both bodies.

But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything. They ought to obey every pious command.

Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church. With such holy love.

And he handed himself over for her. So you too should not refuse to die, if necessary, for the holiness of your wives.

That he might sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water. Water washed the body; sanctification of the word—or teaching—washed the soul, as he says to the Hebrews: “Having washed the body with clean water.”

In the word, so that he might present the Church to himself in glory. So you also should cleanse your wives’ bodies through self-control and their souls through teaching.

Not having spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind. Thus Christ cleansed the Church for himself, removing both former crimes and new stains.

But so that she might be holy and without blemish. If she is without blemish in all her members, those who are stained are not considered to belong to her unless they are again cleansed through purifying punishments. But in the future she will be without spot or wrinkle; for now she is mixed, like straw and wheat on the threshing floor before the winnowing.

So husbands ought also to love their wives as their own bodies. They should present their wives as they themselves wish to be found.

He who loves his wife loves himself. For the two are one flesh.

For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church. He does this not to inflict toil and pain upon it, but to make it secure and peaceful.

He does not condemn marriage, but exhorts to self-control.

Because we are members of his body. His members ought to imitate him in everything.

Of his flesh and of his bones. We are of the whole substance of his body.

Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This mystery is great. It concerns love, not merely place.

But I speak of Christ and of the Church. Nevertheless [Col. 0623C] let each one of you love his own wife as himself. “I understand this,” he says, “with reference to Christ and the Church; nevertheless, you must not therefore fail to love your wives—indeed, love them even more, as Christ loved the Church.”

For Christ left his mother—that is, by leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh—and clung to his Church, which he gathered from all nations.

How did he leave the Father? Not because he withdrew from the Father, but because he appeared in that form in which he is equal to the Father.

But let the wife fear her husband. Let her be subject as the weaker, so that she may be governed.

## CHAPTER VI

Children, obey your parents in the Lord. Prepare them through discipline, because he commands that they be instructed by their parents according to God.

For this is just: that you repay mutual duties.

Honor your father and your mother. [Col. 0623D] But honor good parents; for Moses himself taught that those who oppose God must not be followed, although we ought to show them honor out of fear of God.

Which is the first commandment with a promise. It is the first commandment of the second tablet, which contained six commandments concerning human relations. The first tablet demanded duties belonging specifically to God.

So that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth. Not upon this earth, on which even the impious and wicked grow old, but upon that earth which the Lord promises to the meek, in which the righteous will dwell, and which the Psalmist believes he will see.

And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger. This may be understood simply: do not provoke them to anger by correcting them excessively and without cause.

But raise them in the discipline and correction of the Lord. Do not, while living wickedly either with your wives or after your wives, destroy them through your own wickedness.

Servants, obey your bodily masters. Servitude was not given by nature, but was invented by captivity. Nor did it begin with the curse of Ham, as some think, since we read that kings were born from him; rather, it was fulfilled among the Canaanites, who were subjected to the sons of Israel.

The Apostle took care that God’s teaching should not be blasphemed in any respect, if believing servants became useless to their masters. And someone who might perhaps have been ready to allow other slaves to become Christians would begin to regret those who had already become so. But if he saw them improve and become faithful, he would not only wish others to believe, but would himself also be saved. For Christ did not come to change social conditions, but character.

With fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your hearts. That is, with complete humility, once your former pride has been set aside.

As to Christ. Whatever you offer to human beings for Christ’s sake, you offer to Christ.

Not serving merely when observed, as pleasing human beings, but as servants of Christ. That is, do not work only in the presence of your master.

Doing the will of God from the heart, serving with goodwill, as to the Lord and not to human beings. In matters that are not contrary to God’s will. For in many things the minds of masters naturally coincide with the law: they wish to have servants who are faithful, sober, chaste, and kind.

Serve your master without murmuring. Knowing that each person will receive from the Lord whatever good he has done.

Whatever benefit you have done to anyone for God’s sake, expect your reward from God. [Col. 0624C]

Whether servant or free. Your condition of servitude should not make you despair.

And you, masters. Listen to me: if you want them to listen to you as well, give them an example.

Do the same things for them. Otherwise, if they flee, you will begin to attribute it not to religion but to your own wickedness.

Give up threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven. Threaten for the sake of discipline, but give up threats for the sake of mercy, so that your own Lord may also forgive you.

And there is no partiality with God. Before the Lord you are so completely one that you were bought equally, and one inheritance has been promised to you all.

Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power. He concludes the Letter with a general exhortation, following the Lord’s example and relying on his strength.

Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. Spiritual weapons must be taken up against spiritual enemies, so that the difference in the nature of the weapons may be protected by their spiritual strength.

For our struggle is not against flesh and blood. “Flesh and blood” means a human being.

But against rulers and powers. Those who have usurped rule over the human beings of this world, and who incite ignorant and impious people to commit sins and seem to govern them.

Against the world-rulers of this darkness. So that no one might suppose that wicked spirits, together with their author and prince, the devil, rule heaven, earth, and sea, he added and specified what was appropriate: “of the world.” “Of this darkness,” he says—that is, of the darkness of unbelievers and impious people, to whom it was already said when they came to believe: “You were once [Col. 0625A] darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” You were darkness—that is, unbelievers; but now, through the Lord, you have become believers.

Against the spiritual forces of wickedness. For there are also spiritual forces of goodness.

In the heavenly places. In the air, in which flying birds are called the birds of heaven.

Therefore take up the armor of God. Because you have such enemies.

So that you may be able to resist on the evil day. The evil day is for us when we are attacked by evil.

And in all things. Not in one thing only.

To stand perfected. So that, with God’s help, we may resist the devil’s schemes, fully armed with spiritual weapons; with the loins of the mind girded—that is, chaste, prepared manfully for every battle, and free from all worldly cares.

Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth. Not in hypocrisy.

And clothed with the breastplate of righteousness. Just as a breastplate is woven together from many bracelets or rings, so righteousness is joined together from various kinds of virtues. It protects not only the conscience of the breast but also the self-control of the belly, and it reaches even to the thighs, restraining lust.

And having your feet shod for the preparation of the gospel of peace. Just as feet that are shod walk confidently, so you should preach without fear.

In all things taking up. In every battle let us be covered by faith, because the shield is also the defense of the other weapons, and without it they are all weak. In the same way these virtues cannot save without faith.

The shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. Just as a shield repels and shakes off everything cast against it, so faith extinguishes all his suggestions, even though, as if they were rational, they may seem to possess light.

And take the helmet of salvation. May it protect or conceal all the senses of the head from wicked activities.

And the sword. No soldier dares to go into battle without a sword. He can defend himself to some extent, but he cannot kill the enemy; sometimes he is even stripped of his weapons by a bold enemy and killed. So without God’s word every righteousness is exposed and defenseless.

Of the Spirit, which is the word of God. A spiritual sword.

Through every prayer and supplication. Now ask for the sword, and always possess it.

Praying at every time in the Spirit. [Col. 0626A] Do not allow yourself to be hindered from praying always, but pray for spiritual matters.

And keeping watch in him with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints and for me. It is useless for the body to lie inactive like that of a sleeping person while the mind wanders about, since through such vanity nothing is obtained even from a human being.

That speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, so that with confidence I may make known the mystery of the gospel. So that I may explain freely and without fear of persecution or the hatred of the Jews the order of the people united in Christ.

For which I am acting as an ambassador in chains. All ambassadors of the word must necessarily endure such things.

So that in it I may dare to speak as I ought. My confidence will then be greater if what is said is reasonable and abundant enough to express the argument.

“In it,” he says, and not in my own strength.

But so that you too may know what concerns me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know what concerns us and that he may comfort your hearts. He acts diligently not only so that they may make progress, but also so that they may not fail amid his tribulations or be saddened in any way.

Peace to the brothers. Peace, love, and faith together make the Christian perfect. It should also be noted that he confirms that these things come to us not from ourselves but from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, so that no one may glory in his own merits or say that he does not receive faith from God. From the one, therefore, from whom peace and love come, faith also comes. For this reason we ask him not only to increase it in those who possess it, but also to grant it to those who do not possess it.

And love. Love is greater than peace; someone may possess peace and nevertheless not be loved.

With faith, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. For without faith everything is fruitless. And observe carefully that faith itself, together with the other virtues, is also given to us as a gift.

Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. Amen. Whether “in chastity,” or among those whose hearts contain no adulterous love of the world by which their love of Christ is violated.

Written from the City.

# THE LETTER OF THE HOLY APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 0625]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0625C]

[Col. 0625D] Let us see what Saint Jerome said about the holy Paul in his *Apology to Pammachius*: “I shall bring forward the apostle Paul, whom, whenever I read him, I seem not to hear words but thunderclaps. Read his Letters, especially those to the Romans, Galatians, and Ephesians, in which he is wholly engaged in the contest; and you will see, in the testimonies he takes from the Old Testament, how skillful, how prudent, and how concealing he is concerning what he is doing. His words seem simple, like those of an innocent and rustic man who knows neither how to set nor how to avoid ambushes; but wherever you look, there are thunderbolts. He clings to the case; he seizes everything he touches; he turns his back in order to conquer; he pretends to flee in order to kill.”

The Philippians are Macedonians. After receiving the word of truth, they persevered in the faith and did not accept false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Rome. In the Acts of the Apostles we read that the Philippians believed when he himself preached; and they had made such progress in faith and knowledge that they even preached and defended the Gospel boldly. Therefore he records that he received from these people alone, even while preaching to others.

Praising them, therefore, he urges them not to be terrified by his sufferings. Through them the Gospel of Christ is not destroyed but strengthened, since everyone understands that he could not endure so much for something false or doubtful. He exhorts them, following his example, willingly to struggle for Christ even unto death.

## CHAPTER ONE
Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ. Every apostle is a servant, but not every servant is an apostle.

To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi. Not indiscriminately to all the Philippians, since there were also pagans there.

With bishops and deacons. Here we understand “bishops” to mean not only overseers, but also presbyters. For there were not several bishops in one city; this too is found in the Acts of the Apostles.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The remembrance of good things is celebrated with thanksgiving.

I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you, always in all my prayers, for you all. He displays his affection for them, for whom he always prays.

Making supplication with joy. Not with sorrow, as for sinners.

Because of your fellowship in the Gospel. Because you share in the preaching of the Gospel.

From the first day until now. From the beginning of your faith I pray that you may persevere.

Confident of this very thing. I am confident that I shall obtain this.

That he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion. It should be noted that, when we begin, this is due to his grace, so that human pride may claim nothing for itself; for faith, teaching, and knowledge are given by him, and he himself begins and completes the work in us.

Until the day of Jesus Christ. Until the day of death.

As it is right for me to think this about all of you. For love hopes all things.

Because I have you in my heart, and in my bonds. I love you so much that neither the memory of you nor the anxiety of defending you can remove you from me, even amid my tribulations.

Both in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel. The confirmation of the Gospel is the steadfastness of the preacher, with God confirming him.

That you are all partners in my joy. This is what I think about you, and I believe that, just as you are partners in my tribulation, so you will also be partners in my joy.

For God is my witness, how I long for you all in the affections of Christ Jesus. This may mean either that you are in his affections, or that he desires you as though you were his own affections.

And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more. It should be noted that he not only commands them to do this, but also prays for them, so that we may know that the law is not sufficient by commanding unless grace comes to its aid by helping.

In knowledge and every kind of discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent. It should be noted that he asks for still greater knowledge from those who already know, so that they may prevail in being sincere; and this knowledge, together with love, builds up.

So that you may be sincere and without offense until the day of Christ. Sincere, as the grace of baptism has restored you.

Filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ. So that you may not merely be free from corruption, but may also abound in the fruits of righteousness through Christ’s gift—he who not only has no wickedness, but overflows with goodness.

To the glory and praise of God. So that God may be glorified in us, not human presumption and empty glory, attributing to itself whatever good it seems to possess. Rather, let people see good works and glorify God, whose gift is what we have.

But I want you to know, brothers, that the things concerning me—[Col. 0627D] He consoles them concerning his tribulation, because they had heard that he was bound and kept under guard in Caesar’s household—have turned out rather for the advancement of the Gospel. They not only do no harm, but even do good, since it is made clear that I endure everything not for some crime, but for Christ.

So that my bonds have become manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorium. Before every judge.

And in all other places. “Places” is understood.

So that most of the brothers, trusting in the Lord because of my bonds, dare much more fearlessly to speak the word of God. They have been encouraged by the example of my bonds, seeing me gladly endure these things for Christ.

Some indeed preach Christ because of envy and rivalry, but others because of goodwill. They desire to take glory from me among believers, as though I alone claimed for myself the knowledge of preaching. Others, desiring that others also be saved, faithfully announce Christ; some help me defend the Gospel out of love. But others preach deceitfully in order to burden me further, as though I were making more disciples and striving to fill the whole world with my teaching, so that they might heap greater envy upon me.

Some do so out of love, knowing that I have been appointed for the defense of the Gospel. They know that I have been appointed to this not by myself, but by God.

But others announce Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, supposing that they are stirring up affliction for me in my bonds. They lacked a sincere conscience, for they preached for the sake of present profit; by their preaching they aroused envy, increased the punishments of his imprisonment, and rejoiced in his sufferings.

[Col. 0628B] But he rejoiced, because through the deceitful Christ was truly preached, and through the mouths of wicked men Christ was announced.

What then? So long as Christ is announced in every way, whether through pretext or through truth, Christ is proclaimed. I do not care with what intention they preach, provided that what I desire occurs: that the name of Christ becomes known to everyone and is believed by many.

For this reason I rejoice now, and I shall rejoice in the future. I rejoice in this, and I shall also rejoice.

Whether through a pretext of hatred or envy—not because he was malicious and rejoiced in another’s evil, but because the word was preached even by the wicked, and Christ was announced through the mouths of the wicked.

For I know that this will turn out for me. Not only through the Word and my suffering, but also through hatred the Church of Christ is increased, because the Lord knows how to work good from evil.

For salvation, through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. The Spirit governs everything for my salvation and turns adversity into prosperity.

According to my expectation and hope. For from all these things I expect a reward, and I endure them so that they may be converted.

Because I shall be put to shame in nothing. He is put to shame neither by insults nor by reproaches, whereas we are put to shame in everything, even though it is according to God; by this we show that we serve human praise, not Christ.

But with all confidence, as always. Nothing frightens me.

And now Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death. Both my life and my death contribute to the glorification of Christ, who strengthens me in everything. He insults his enemies by the great fruit he will have if he preserves me for announcing Christ.

For to me, living is Christ, and dying is gain. I have no desire to live here except that I may build up his body by my example. I count it the greatest gain no longer to be held by worldly snares, and no longer to be subject to any sins or vices of the flesh—something that will undoubtedly occur after this life.

But if living in the flesh here is the fruit of my work—because even here I live without being fruitless in soul, by the Lord’s gift—

And what I should choose, I do not know. Both alternatives are so advantageous to me that I do not know what to choose, although they are thought harmful to me.

But I am hard-pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is much better. But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake. The former is better for me; the latter is necessary for you. By his own example he teaches them not to fear death but to choose it; and, so that they may not be saddened, he promises prophetically that he will remain in the flesh.

And, confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all. I do not merely believe it; I know it.

For your progress and the joy of faith, so that your rejoicing in Christ Jesus because of me may abound. Through my progress, you will have joy in the fruit of your faith.

Through my coming to you again. When you see me, you may rejoice more abundantly again.

Only live worthily of the Gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you—whether you keep all his commandments—or, being absent, I hear about you, that you are standing firm in one spirit, as we read that they had one heart and one soul, and did not call anything their own, but had everything in common—

United in striving together for the faith of the Gospel. All who are united in a struggle achieve victory.

And in nothing be frightened by your adversaries—which is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation. He wants his own to be crowned after being tested. Thus the apostles went away rejoicing because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus. Job too is permitted to be tested, because, protected by God’s help, he could not be overcome, and his glory was to be increased when the adversary had been defeated and confounded.

And this is from God: for it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him. The opportunity for faith has been granted by God, because unless Christ had come and not only taught but also touched hearts, our preaching would have been empty. Although in the Acts we read that faith is voluntary, he nevertheless teaches clearly here that it is God’s gift that we believe. Therefore we should attribute nothing to ourselves, since both believing and persevering, and even suffering for him, are his gift. Thus it is clearly evident that the faith by which we believe is his gift; indeed, he said that both things are gifts: both believing and suffering.

But also to suffer for him. We have received from him not only the gift of faith, but also the gift and reward of martyrdom.

Having the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear about me. You are suffering nothing new, but what you saw in me when I was present and now hear about while I am absent.

## CHAPTER II

If there is therefore any consolation in Christ. In every tribulation, be consoled in Christ alone.

If there is any comfort of love. Not of friends.

If there is any fellowship of the Spirit. Of spiritual things, not carnal ones.

If there are any affections of compassion. Have compassion on your own, not on your relatives.

Complete my joy. A teacher rejoices in such disciples.

By thinking the same thing. This very thing.

Having the same love, united in soul. All toward one another.

Being of one mind. “I feel toward another what I feel toward you” [the text reads *tibi*, “toward you”; possibly an uncertain or corrupt reading].

Doing nothing through rivalry or empty glory. Let us not do anything in rivalry with God, nor let anyone seem better than we are.

But in humility considering one another superior to oneself. If we considered all from whom we suffer injuries superior, we would bear them patiently; for no one thinks it wrong to receive an injury from a father or master. We must also consider that there is no person who cannot possess some good that you do not yet have, even if it is hidden; in that respect he may undoubtedly be superior to you. This thought is useful for crushing and taming pride, so that you do not suppose that, because certain qualities are prominent and visible, another has nothing hidden within him—perhaps goods of greater weight by which he surpasses you without your knowing it.

Not each looking to his own interests, but to those of others. Not what benefits us alone, but what benefits others as well.

Have this mind among yourselves. Let there be such humility among you; for however much anyone humbles himself, he will not be humbler than Christ. He wishes to show that Christ suffered not for his own sake, but for the sake of others.

Some understand this passage in the following way: that Christ humbled himself according to his divinity, that is, according to the form of God, in which he did not seize as plunder the equality with God—which he naturally possessed—and that he emptied himself, not by abolishing his substance, but by concealing his honor, taking the form of a servant, that is, assuming human substance, appearing in every way merely as a man, and, through humble obedience, refusing not even death on the cross.

But we must consider how this interpretation escapes Arius’s slander. For it does nothing except assert that the Son is lesser, as though he were said to have been exalted by the Father according to his divinity and to have received a name that he did not previously possess—unless perhaps the words spoken of the person according to the form of man are attributed to God. Since Christ is rightly believed to be God and man, the one who understands it in this way understands it well and does not think contrary to the faith.

And this in Christ Jesus. According to that by which Christ is Christ, and Jesus is Jesus.

Who, though he was in the form of God. That is, in the image of God without sin, or in whom God was present—that is, the fullness of divinity.

Did not regard it as plunder to be equal with God. He concealed what he was through humility, giving us an example so that we might not glory in anything concerning ourselves. He did not seize what he possessed—that is, equality with the Father, which he naturally had.

But emptied himself. By assuming what he was not, not by losing what he was.

The form of a servant. Thus he washed feet, claiming no power for himself, although he possessed dominion over all as the Father’s Only-Begotten.

Taking it. Our sinful flesh, without sin.

Being made in the likeness of human beings. Likeness is not always true likeness; for Adam begot a son according to his image and likeness, and called his name Seth.

And being found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. He did this to show us an example of perfect obedience.

And the death of the cross. For no death is worse, because of its prolonged torture.

Therefore God also exalted him, and so forth. Divinity is not exalted, because it cannot be humbled; and what is given is given to one who does not possess it. Thus this can be understood more appropriately according to the human nature than according to the divine nature.

If we too desire to be exalted, let us serve our brothers by Christ’s example. For if he, the Lord and Teacher, ministered to servants and disciples, how much more ought we to serve our superiors and equals, and obey God and the saints even unto death, lest proud disciples fail to follow a humble teacher!

So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. So that all together may adore the human being assumed into the Word.

And every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. That is, in the nature and glory of divinity: his glory and equality are the same.

We have inserted here the complete exposition of Saint Augustine concerning this passage.

“Being found in appearance as a human being.”

We use the word “appearance” in many ways: either for the disposition of the mind, such as the acquisition of some discipline strengthened and confirmed by practice; or for the condition of the body, according to which we say that one person is more well-nourished and stronger than another—something more properly called bodily form; or for what is externally fitted to our limbs, according to which we speak of someone as clothed, shod, armed, and so forth.

In all these categories, since this word is derived from the verb meaning “to have,” it is clear that “appearance” is said of something that happens to someone in such a way that he can also not have it. For instruction happens to the mind, nourishment and strength to the body, and clothing and weapons to our limbs. Thus a person may have an uneducated mind if instruction has not come to it; a thin and weak body without nourishment and bodily strength; and he may be naked without clothing, unarmed without weapons, and barefoot without shoes.

“Appearance,” therefore, is said of something that happens to us so that we may possess it. Yet there is this distinction: some of the things that happen to us and produce such a condition are not changed by us; rather, they change us, while remaining themselves whole and unshaken. Thus, when wisdom comes to a person, wisdom itself is not changed, but changes the person, making him wise instead of foolish.

Other things happen in such a way that they both change and are changed, as food does. Food changes its own form and is turned into our body, while we, restored by food from thinness and weakness, are changed into strength and vigor.

There is a third category: when the things that happen to us are themselves changed in order to produce such a condition, as with clothing. When a garment is cast aside or put away, it does not have the form it assumes when it is put on and fitted to the limbs. When it is worn, therefore, the garment receives a form that it did not have when unworn, while the limbs themselves remain in their own condition both when clothed and when unclothed.

There can also be a fourth category, when the things that happen to us to produce such a condition neither change the things to which they happen nor are themselves changed by them, as with a ring on a finger, if one does not examine the matter too minutely. Yet this category either does not exist at all, if carefully scrutinized, or is exceedingly rare.

When the Apostle was speaking of the only-begotten Son of God, therefore, insofar as his divinity is concerned, according to which he is true God, he said that he was equal to the Father. This was not for him as plunder, as though he desired something belonging to another.

The work of mercy would have remained hidden if, always remaining in that equality, he had refused to assume humanity and appear to human beings as a human being. But he emptied himself, not by changing his own form, but by taking the form of a servant. He was neither converted nor transformed into a human being, abandoning his unchangeable stability; rather, by assuming a true human being, he himself—the one who assumed—was made in the likeness of human beings, not for his own sake but for the sake of those to whom he appeared in human form. He was found in appearance as a human being—that is, he was found as a human being by having a human being.

He could not be found by those whose hearts were unclean and who could not see the Word with the Father, except by assuming what they could see and through which they might be led to that inner light.

This appearance, however, does not belong to the first category. For the human nature, remaining in itself, did not change the nature of God. Nor does it belong to the second, since the human being did not change God and was not changed by him. Nor does it belong to the fourth, since the human being was not assumed in such a way that he neither changed God nor was changed by God. Rather, it belongs to the third category: he was assumed in such a way that he was changed for the better and ineffably fashioned by him, more excellently and more closely than a garment is fashioned by a human being when it is put on.

By this word, therefore, the Apostle sufficiently indicated what he meant when he said, “Being made in the likeness of human beings.” He was not transformed into a human being, but was made such in appearance when he was clothed with humanity, joining the humanity he assumed to immortality and eternity, as it were, by living and conforming it to himself.

But the appearance that consists in the acquisition of wisdom—or rather of discipline—which the Greeks call *hexis* [ἕξις] or *schesis* [σχέσις], they call *schema* [σχῆμα] instead when referring to the condition in which we speak of someone as clothed or armed. From this it is understood that the Apostle spoke of this kind of appearance, since the Greek manuscripts read *schēmati* [σχήματι], whereas in Latin we have *habitu*, “appearance” or “condition.”

By this term we must understand that the Word was not changed by assuming humanity, just as limbs are not changed when clothed, although that assumption united the one assumed ineffably to the one assuming. Since human words can be adapted to ineffable realities only so far, so that God may not be understood as changed by assuming human weakness, it was chosen that this assumption should be called in Greek *schēma* and in Latin *habitus*.

Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed. After the example of him who was obedient unto death.

Not only in my presence. As servants who serve only when watched.

But much more now in my absence. For if you did anything more freely while I was present, you could be corrected.

With fear and trembling. Not carelessly, as Job says: “I feared all my works.”

Work out your salvation. Take care of one another’s salvation. Since he had said, “Work out your own salvation,” lest human weakness claim something for itself and attribute salvation to its own effort, he immediately added: “God,” he says, “who works in you.”

Not merely with you, but inwardly in you he is wonderfully infused and given. When they are commanded to work, their free will is addressed; but they are to do so with fear and trembling lest, attributing to themselves what they do well, they become exalted over good works as though those works were their own.

For it is God who works in you. Let human pride be silent and not say, “From myself I have the will to do good,” because God also produces this in you by hidden inspiration. He gives not only faith, but perseverance as well.

But perhaps someone will say: “Then nothing is mine; everything is yours.” Let the answer be: “But thanks be to the giver, because good will is prepared by the Lord.”

Both to will and to accomplish. Accomplishment unquestionably belongs to him who said, “Without me you can do nothing.” He accomplishes it in us when he fulfills what he said: “Behold, I am with you until the completion of the age.” He who began a good work in us will bring it to completion, even to the end.

For his good will. “His”—that is, God’s—is to be supplied.

Do everything without murmuring and hesitation, so that you may be without complaint. An ungrateful servant complains that his master’s commands are burdensome; everyone who murmurs expresses doubt concerning the commands.

And innocent children of God, without reproach. Consider whose children you are: since he is of a simple nature, he does not want to have degenerate children.

In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation. It overturns and destroys every rational order through its unbelief.

Among whom you shine like lights in the world. Let the people of God shine among the human race as the sun and moon shine in the world—that is, all Catholics among heretics, Jews, and pagans.

Holding fast the word of life. So that they may be enlightened both by your example and by the word.

For my glory. “A wise son is the glory of his father,” says Solomon; the perfection of disciples is proven to be the glory of their teacher.

On the day of Christ. On the day of Christ’s judgment.

Because I did not run in vain, nor labor in vain. For I acquired such a people for God.

But even if I am poured out upon the sacrifice. Even if I am killed, because I have offered to God the sacrifice and service of your faith, the joy of your progress overcomes the justice of punishment or death.

And the service of your faith: I rejoice and congratulate you all. Either because I ministered to your faith, so that you believed through God working in you and through my preaching—

And in the same way, you also rejoice and congratulate me. To be killed for your sake is a reward.

But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly. He gives the example that we should not fear, but promise everything under the hope of the Lord.

So that I too may be encouraged when I learn what concerns you. Provided your lack of fear in the face of my sufferings is known.

For I have no one of such like mind who will sincerely be concerned for you. Who will be concerned with me in this way for the salvation of all.

For everyone seeks his own interests. At that time there was no one in the Church of Christ, apart from the Apostle Paul and Timothy, who was genuinely concerned for the flock. It happened that, at the time when he sent Timothy, he had no other son with him; rather, mercenaries were with him—that is, people seeking their own interests.

They seek their own advantages or ease, unwilling to suffer for the salvation of others.

Not the things of Jesus Christ.

But you know his proven character. He did not refuse to die for the salvation of all.

Because, as a son with his father, he served with me in the Gospel. According to his humanity, for humanity’s sake he became obedient unto death. Or, alternatively: he served as though I had begotten him bodily.

I hope, therefore, to send him immediately, as soon as I see what concerns me. But I trust in the Lord that I myself will also come to you shortly. For at present I am still uncertain, since I am speaking about Timothy.

Yet I considered it necessary. Necessary for you.

To send Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow worker. For the work of the Gospel.

And my fellow soldier. Because of the apostolic rank that he received among you.

But your apostle and minister of my need, to send him to you. He came to minister to my need on your behalf.

For he was longing for you all. He seeks to commend his love for them, so that he himself may be loved by them more.

And he was distressed because you had heard that he was ill; for indeed he was ill to the point of death. He was distressed because he feared that you had been saddened by news of his illness.

But God had mercy on him, and not only on him, but also on me. He had mercy on him in order to produce greater fruit by teaching.

So that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow. So that the sadness of prison would not be increased by desolation.

Therefore I sent him more eagerly, so that when you saw him you might rejoice again. You had been saddened by his absence.

And I might be without sorrow—the sorrow I had because of your grief.

Receive him, therefore, with all joy in the Lord. Receive him as the Lord, and do not allow any doubt to arise concerning his delay.

And hold such men in honor. Not only him, but people of this kind.

Because of the work of Christ. He was not afraid to minister as though to one condemned.

He came close to death, surrendering his life. He was ready for death.

To complete what was lacking in your service toward me. So that he alone might fulfill, on behalf of all, your duty toward me.

## CHAPTER III

Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. Not in worldly things, or in anything apart from the Lord.

For me to write the same things to you is not burdensome, but for you it is necessary. To repeat the same things, even when present, is not useless, just as repeatedly leveling plants is not useless.

Beware of the dogs. Those barking against the Gospel.

Beware of evil workers. They try to destroy whatever we build.

Beware of the mutilation. This is mutilation, not circumcision.

For we are the circumcision. We are the true Jews, because we have cut away not the skin of one member, but the vices of the whole flesh together.

We who serve God in the spirit. We who, according to Jeremiah, have circumcised the foreskin of the heart.

And glory in Christ Jesus, and do not place confidence in the flesh. We have been justified by faith in him alone, not by bodily circumcision.

Although I too have confidence in the flesh. Let no one think that I say this as though I have no reason for glorying and therefore glory.

If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I have more. Circumcised on the eighth day. Perhaps some of those people were proselytes.

Of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews. Benjamin was always joined with Judah.

According to the law, a Pharisee. A teacher of the law.

According to zeal, persecuting the Church of God. I possessed such zeal and love for the law that I even became a persecutor of the Church of God.

According to the righteousness that is in the law. According to all its justifications and ceremonies.

Living without reproach, and so forth. I fulfilled the law except in this one respect: I did not believe in Christ, whom the law had promised. I was first in everything in which they glory; but because I have now learned that those things have no value, I regard them as losses and consider them worthless.

For someone could be a transgressor of the law inwardly, in his affections, while still performing the law’s visible works, either through fear of human beings or of God himself, but from fear of punishment rather than from love and delight in righteousness. Indeed, he sins in his inward will if he refrains from sinning not willingly but through fear. He knew that he had been such inwardly, even while he thought that by these things he was acquiring life.

“These things,” he says, “I cast away as impediments for Christ.”

In comparison with discovered gold, bronze is despised, although each is useful in its own time. The knowledge of Christ will be esteemed among human beings when the world has been despised by him for Christ’s sake.

I cast away all the ceremonial matters of the law. Dung consists of the remnants and refuse of things that were once useful.

So that I may gain Christ and be found in him. So that I may have Christ as my head and, remaining in him, be found as his member.

Not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law. A righteousness sought by my own labor, as though natural or legal.

But that which comes through the faith of Christ. The righteousness that comes properly from God through the faith of Christ alone, which he himself has given.

The righteousness that comes from God through faith, for knowing him. Whoever recognizes this acts sufficiently to prevent himself from claiming anything for himself. Whatever has been given to him by God’s grace, he must attribute neither to the law nor to nature, but to God alone, whose gift it is.

And the power of his resurrection. So that I may perfectly know the benefit and power of his resurrection, since he rose for this purpose: that we too might rise in the same way.

And fellowship in his sufferings, being conformed to his death. For if we suffer with him, we shall also live with him.

If somehow I may attain to the resurrection that is from the dead. To the resurrection of the perfected, not to that resurrection which even the unwilling will have.

Not that I have already received it. I have not yet received perfection, because the end has not yet come.

Or am already perfect. With regard to this perfection and to such a resurrection, I am still uncertain, because there is another perfection after this life. This is the perfection of which he says to the Corinthians, “When that which is perfect has come,” and elsewhere, “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man,” and so forth. For no one placed in this world possesses true perfection, since he himself said, “Now we see through a mirror,” and so forth.

Perfect: with regard to the perfection that the saints can possess in this life, he was perfect; but with regard to the perfection that will exist after the resurrection, he was imperfect. Thus he should be understood to have possessed here a certain imperfect perfection, because he saw through faith, not through sight, and through a mirror, not face to face.

But I pursue, if I may apprehend that for which I was also apprehended by Christ. If I may apprehend the merit of the apostleship, in which apostleship I was apprehended by Christ.

Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. By humbling himself he bestowed glory on everyone and urges them toward progress.

I have apprehended it. I shall be certain then, when the end has come.

But one thing. In fact, one thing is necessary.

Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, toward the goal. This alone I know: by God’s gift I make progress daily, not counting my former labor, but hastening toward better things. Or, forgetting the law, I stretch myself toward the perfect commandments of the Gospel.

I pursue the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. Christ promised the perfect prize in heaven.

Therefore, whoever is perfect, let us think this way. Whoever is perfect should think this: that the old things must be forgotten and the new pursued, because Christ’s disciples ought to be perfect.

There is therefore now an imperfect perfection, while in the future there will be perfect perfection. Someone may be perfect in one respect and imperfect in another. For example, someone may already be a perfect hearer of wisdom, although he is not yet a perfect teacher.

Someone may be perfect in loving enemies, although he is not yet perfect in enduring them. And one who is perfect in loving all human beings, having even attained to love of enemies, may still be asked whether he is perfect in that love itself—that is, whether he loves those whom he loves as much as the unchangeable rule of truth prescribes that they should be loved.

This shows that, according to the condition of this life, there is a certain perfection, and that it also belongs to this perfection if someone knows that he is not yet perfect. No one possesses perfect perfection in this life, because the flesh desires against the spirit.

Here, therefore, the command is that we not obey the desires of sin. There, it will be that we do not have the desires of sin. Then, according to this weakness, righteousness is perfect in this world in proportion to its capacity.

This is a small righteousness, because it also understands what it lacks. Therefore the Apostle calls himself both imperfect and perfect: imperfect in considering how much he lacks of righteousness, whose fullness he still hungers for; perfect in that he is not ashamed of his own imperfection.

If we run perfectly, let us think this way: that we are not yet perfect, so that there we may be perfected, while we continue to run perfectly here. When that which is perfect has come, then what is partial will be abolished.

And if you think anything differently. If God has revealed something to you in another way. “Differently,” not “something else”: that is, with another understanding.

God will reveal this to you also. Even if you think something less perfectly, wait humbly and ask God. He can reveal it to those who walk and make progress along the way of the true faith.

Nevertheless, to what we have attained. To the perfection of the New Testament.

Let us think the same thing. The same thing, even if it is asserted in different ways.

And let us remain in the same rule. For knowing is not sufficient without action.

Be imitators of me, brothers. Imitate me, not the false apostles.

And observe those who walk in this way, as you have our example. “Observe” is used in two senses: either for imitation, as here, or for avoidance, as he says to the Romans: “Observe those who cause dissensions and offenses.”

For many walk—of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears—that they are enemies of the cross of Christ. He is speaking of the false apostles, who, by removing the hope of Christ’s passion through which sins were forgiven, placed it in the ceremonies of the law.

This can also be understood of the Jovinianists, who turned bodily discipline into feasting and luxury.

Their end is destruction. It should be noted that, even in relation to his enemies, he desires their salvation.

Their god is their belly. They think that they serve this god if they feast.

And their glory is in their shame. In the circumcision of the shameful member.

They set their minds on earthly things. Our citizenship, however, is in heaven. Someone enslaved to earthly vices cannot say this.

From there also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ. He is our head.

He will refashion the body of our lowliness, making it conform to the body of his glory. He prefigured this on the mountain when he conformed one of the living and one of the dead to the glory of his body, showing an example of the resurrection.

According to the operation by which he is also able to subject all things to himself. Or, according to this power, it is also possible for him to do this, by which he subjected all things to himself.

## CHAPTER IV
Therefore, my most beloved and most greatly desired brothers. More than the others, because you are more perfect. My joy and crown. For through you I am to be crowned and rewarded. [Col. 0637B] So stand firm in the Lord, beloved. As I said above, placing hope in faith in Christ alone and in a heavenly manner of life.

I urge Euodia and I entreat Syntyche. They were women possessing knowledge; he admonishes and exhorts them to think alike. To have the same mind in the Lord. The same thing that I said.

And I also ask you, true companion, help them. “Germanus” is the man’s name; “companion” refers to his office. They labored with me in the Gospel. He says that women, not men, labored; and that they taught not in the church but in the house.

With Clement and my other fellow workers. Clement was a man of great learning from philosophy, who was bishop at Rome. Whose names are in the book of life. They should not be displeased that they have not been written in this Epistle, since they are written in the book of life, which book Moses also mentions [Col. 0637C], as do David and the Lord.

Rejoice in the Lord always. Since in this world you have no joy, but affliction. Again I say, rejoice. He repeats this in order to confirm it.

Let your gentleness be known to all people. Both to Jews and to Gentiles, and also to all who trouble you.

The Lord is near; be anxious about nothing. See whether anything is lacking for you; do not consider what you will eat or what you will wear. Or, “the Lord is near” to deliver; do not fear your persecutors. For the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart.

But in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known before God. Not with murmuring and sadness. Then your prayer will be worthy of God, if you give thanks for everything you suffer, as the apostles did.

And the peace of God, which surpasses [Col. 0637D] all understanding. It sustains the wicked and the ungrateful; or, the peace of Christ, by which he prayed for his persecutors, when considered surpasses and bends every furious mind.

May it guard your hearts and your understandings in Christ Jesus. May it guard these hearts and understandings of yours according to the example of Christ.

Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are modest, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy. To say everything briefly at the end: whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report. For every human nature knows how to love and praise what is good.

If there is any virtue, if there is any praise of endurance, think on these things. Meditate on them and think of nothing else.

The things that you learned. By word or example.

And received. By the gift of Christ’s grace.

And heard. You heard these things through preaching. [Col. 0638A]

And saw in me. With your eyes.

Do these things, and the God of peace will be with you. Then the God of peace will be with you, if you are found to be such.

I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because at last you have again begun to think of me as you used to think. Again you have blossomed with the flower of good work, which forgetfulness had not withered but preoccupation had hindered.

You were indeed preoccupied—not that I say this because of want. I do not say that I rejoiced because of my want, but because of your fruit.

For I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. From Christ I have been taught to endure all things equally. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer want. Thus I am neither elated by abundance nor broken by poverty.

I can do all things through him who strengthens me. He gives understanding [Col. 0638B] so that one may know how to be humbled and how to abound, while he says, “I can do all things through him who strengthens me”; for he attributes nothing to himself, but continually implores help so that he may fulfill his commandments.

Nevertheless, you did well by sharing in my tribulation. For my equanimity ought not to have hindered your reward.

You yourselves know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, you alone were chosen as those from whom we would receive necessities, since we judged you more faithful than all the others.

No church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone. They gave, and I received; that is, by giving material things, they received spiritual things.

For even when I was in Thessalonica, you sent something for my needs once and twice. You sent not only to Corinth but also to Thessalonica.

Not because I seek the gift, but I seek the abundant fruit credited to your account. The superabundant fruit of prayer, even when offered for absent saints, is itself called a gift; the thing you give is the gift, but the fruit is the good and upright intention of the giver: that he may give what he gives for the Lord’s sake, so that, like one who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet and a righteous person in the name of a righteous person, he may receive the reward of a prophet and of a righteous person.

I have everything and abound; I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus what you sent. By praising them and giving thanks, he urges them toward a similar work.

As a fragrant offering. The fragrance does not consist in the thing offered but in the devotion of the mind, just as Scripture says that God gratefully smelled Noah’s sacrifice, although he later says that he takes no delight in the flesh or blood of animals.

An acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God. It should be noted that almsgiving is called a sacrifice; and just as it is accepted when offered by holy people, so it is rejected when given by those who have persisted in sin.

And my God will fill every desire of yours. Since perfect people were not thought to desire anything evil.

According to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. Now to our God and Father be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

The phrase “according to the riches of God” pertains to the glory of Christ.

Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the saints greet you. There were therefore saints whom he alone wishes to greet before the others, whom he also named in all the Epistles; they are to be understood as not having had capital sins. For who is without sin? Scripture, however, frequently calls a baptized person a saint. Especially those who are of Caesar’s household.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. So that he might encourage them, and they might persist more freely in the faith or preach with greater confidence, when they heard that many even from Caesar’s official household had been converted.

# The First Epistle to the Thessalonians

[Col. 0639]

## Argument

The Thessalonians are Macedonians. Having received from Christ Jesus the word of truth, they persevered in the faith, even amid the persecution of their fellow citizens. Moreover, they neither accepted false apostles nor the things that were said by the false apostles.
