Therefore, why do they seek something new there when they also have it in the Law? At the same time he demonstrates that the Law agrees with the Gospels.

I give thanks to him. So that they would not say, “Who is this person to whom it was entrusted?” He strengthened me in Christ Jesus our Lord. When I was weak and useless. Because he considered me faithful, appointing me to the ministry. Appointing me to the ministry.

I who was previously a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent person, but I received mercy. A righteous person is, at the beginning, an accuser of himself, so that when the adversary begins, he may be put to shame. But this man spoke the truth, as we read in Acts.

Because I acted ignorantly. Those who act ignorantly sin more lightly. In unbelief. In which I had been born.

But the grace of our Lord overflowed with faith and love. His grace was, or is, so abundant that it overcame the mass of my sins; it also gave me faith and love, so that I might serve not from necessity but from love. Which is in Christ Jesus. Through Christ, who forgave me greater things—for it was not by nature.

And the saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into the world. Everyone believes this, and the conscience of everyone recognizes it as true. To save sinners. Therefore he also saved me among the other sinners.

Of whom I am the foremost. “I am” is customarily used in place of “I was.” But for this reason I received mercy, so that Christ Jesus might first display in me all patience. As David says: “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn to you.” That is, if you forgive me, I will teach that no one ought to despair.

All patience. He not only forgives his persecutors but also bestows upon them the honor of apostleship. For the formation of those who are going to believe in him for eternal life. So that no one may despair.

But to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God. Who granted me forgiveness though I did not deserve it. Honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

A king of short duration, mortal, visible, and capable has temporal, not eternal, honor and glory among his companions.

This commandment. This teaching. Up to this point he has spoken about his own status; now he grants authority to teach.

I entrust this charge to you, my son Timothy, according to the prophecies previously made about you. For even before this you possessed this grace. So that you might wage a good warfare in them. Good warfare is that in which one fights against the devil and vices and obeys God’s will.

Having faith and a good conscience. Perfect faith in Christ and a good conscience in one’s conduct, or doctrine. Some, having rejected this, have suffered shipwreck with regard to the faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander. They did not keep it intact; already entangled in vices, they stained both faith and life.

I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme. They were handed over so that they might be corrected, not destroyed, and so that others might be frightened by their example.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, first of all, I urge that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made. A supplication is firmer than a prayer.

Alternatively: supplications are made for past or present sins; prayers for obtaining the things we hope for; petitions when we intervene on behalf of others; thanksgivings when we obtain what we ask for, or certainly when we render thanks and praise for God’s immeasurable benefits.

Thanksgivings. Let us give thanks to him who has made us worthy to obtain things even for others.

For all people. Even to pray for persecutors.

For kings and all who are in positions of high authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. So that they may know God; or, so that they may keep the nations subject. For our repose consists in their peace: if they are Christians, the violence of persecution will cease.

For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior. So that you also, like him, may desire all people to be saved.

Who desires all people to be saved. From this it is proved that God forces no one to perish; rather, whoever perishes perishes by his own merit, and whoever is saved is saved by God’s grace and mercy. For here, according to the figure of synecdoche, we ought to understand “all” as the whole from a part.

He desires them to be saved. But why are not all saved? Because God is just and merciful: the fact that many are condemned is the merit of those who perish; the fact that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. For when the guilty person is condemned, God’s justice is blameless; when the guilty person is justified, it is God’s ineffable grace. For many are hardened by benefits.

And to come to knowledge of the truth. It is clear that God wills all good things, but human beings are plunged into evil by their own fault.

For there is one God. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the one God of all human beings; therefore he desires all to be saved, since he created them. Whoever is saved, however, is saved by his gift. Let it be enough for us that there is no injustice with God and that his judgments are inscrutable.

And one mediator between God and human beings. Just as there is one God, so there is one mediator—that is, no other mediator of this kind, neither Moses nor any of the prophets.

The human being Christ Jesus. Against the Manichaeans: because he was about to speak of the betrayer, he therefore named him only as a human being.

Who gave himself as a ransom for all. Christ’s blood was indeed poured out for all, but it benefits believers; for unbelievers it will be condemnation. As he himself says elsewhere: “To some we are an odor of life unto life; to others an odor of death unto death.”

His testimony was confirmed at its proper times. For the prophets also bore witness in their own times. Finally he sent his Son to them, in whom I have been appointed preacher and apostle.

As a testimony that Jesus is the Son of God. I speak the truth; I do not lie. I am a teacher of the gentiles in faith and truth. Therefore I want men to pray in every place. As teacher of the nations, he gives a law of prayer. He would never have established a rule concerning prayer unless some question had begun to be raised by Jews who wished to worship only in the temple that was in Jerusalem.

Lifting up. Prayer with the hands is a testimony of innocence. Pure hands. Free from slaughter and blood, and from every evil deed.

Without anger and disputation. Not merely in deed.

Likewise women. In everything he said concerning men.

In modest and proper dress, with reverence and sobriety. These are the ornaments of a Christian woman. Adorning themselves not with braided hair. She ought not to provide an occasion for desire. Nor with gold or pearls. These are ornaments of the earth, whose god is the human being. Or with expensive clothing. So expensive that not even one person is warmed by it, although many people of the same nature could be clothed from its cost.

But with what is fitting for women who profess piety through good works. Therefore these are not the adornments of those who profess chastity, but of those who deny it.

Let a woman learn in silence, with complete submission. Let her learn, certainly, but with complete humility and silence.

But I do not permit a woman to teach. She ought not to teach a man. Nevertheless, he himself said that younger women should be taught by older women; and she may also admonish privately a male child or a brother.

Nor to exercise authority over a man. By usurping the role of teacher or placing herself above her husband. But to remain in silence. So that they may not speak in the church.

For Adam was formed first, then Eve. He gives reasons for wanting them to be subject: namely, because they are later in order and earlier in guilt.

And Adam was not deceived. By the serpent. But the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression. In the transgression of the commandment. But the woman should not therefore despair, because she too will be saved through baptism.

But she will be saved through the bearing of children. Not Eve, but “woman,” because Eve is introduced as an example, and the statement was not spoken specifically of her. Through the bearing of children: by nurturing them, not by killing them or aborting them.

If she remains. Just as above he passed from the plural number to the singular, so here he returns to the plural.

Otherwise, how will the righteousness of the righteous be upon him, and how will Noah, Job, and Daniel not at all deliver their sons and daughters, if Eve is saved through children? Rather, all women will be saved in this way, if they remain in the faith of Christ through good works, faith, chastity, and love pleasing to God.

And love. Of God and neighbor. And sanctification. Of mind and body. “Sanctify yourselves for three days, and do not approach a woman.” Therefore chastity is called sanctification.

With sobriety. Because without sobriety it is difficult to preserve it.

## CHAPTER III

The saying is trustworthy. If anyone desires the office of bishop. He speaks here about the person who is to be ordained, specifying what kind of person should be chosen. First he instructs lay people of both sexes, because priests are also chosen from among them.

He desires a good work. He says “work,” not “honor.”

Therefore a bishop must be blameless. As he said to Titus, “without accusation”: first in general, then the individual qualities themselves are distinguished specifically.

The husband of one wife. Vigilant. If he may not do what is permitted even to a lay person, what must be thought concerning the rest? Sober. Free from every kind of drunkenness. Prudent, orderly, hospitable. Adorned with every spiritual ornament.

Able to teach. So that he may teach both by word and by example. If everyone ought to know how to answer each person, how much more a priest, from whose mouth they will seek the Law, because he is the angel of the almighty Lord?

Not a drunkard. So that he may be able to teach sobriety with confidence. Not violent, but gentle; not quarrelsome. Either so that he may not be provocative in his behavior, or so that he may not wound the consciences of the weak by his example.

Not greedy. For greed provokes quarrels and disputes.

Managing his own household well, keeping his children subject with complete chastity. He explained this in what follows. That is, if he has raised his children in chastity and humility, so that his diligence may be proved by this. For if he did not know how to educate his own few children, how will he govern so many children of God—that is, the whole people—whose characters differ according to their number?

But if someone does not know how to govern his own household, how will he show concern for the Church of God? So that he may not admonish them negligently. Otherwise, if those who were well brought up become insolent, the fault will not be the father’s.

Not a recent convert. Newly reborn. Lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. For through ignorance he can quickly become exalted and imagine that he has undertaken not an office of humility but the administration of worldly affairs; and because his sins were forgiven in the baptismal font and he has only recently been taken in, pride may arise from this very fact.

Into the judgment of the devil. Who was cast down through pride.

Moreover, he must have a good reputation. “Be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the churches of God.” For all people naturally know how to condemn vices and praise virtues.

From those who are outside, so that they may not fall into reproach. Outside the Church. And into the snare of the devil. So that through him the devil may ensnare many who could have become Christians.

Deacons. The question arises why he made no mention of presbyters. But in the bishops he also includes presbyters, because the second rank is almost one and the same, as is demonstrated by many testimonies of Scripture.

Likewise, chaste and self-controlled. Blameless. Not double-tongued. So that they may not also slander; for this is to double the office of one tongue. Or, speaking one thing in the heart and another with the mouth.

Not devoted to much wine. He allowed a little on account of necessity, because he prohibited much.

Not pursuing shameful gain. Shameful gain is acquiring earthly wealth from heavenly sacraments.

Holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience. The mystery of faith is that Christ’s passion is the remedy of human salvation. If he understands this purely and is not ashamed of Christ’s humiliations. Or else, so that he may not think that piety is a source of gain merely because this alone ought to be preached.

And let these also first be tested, and then let them serve. Not only the bishop, but these men also.

Having no accusation. He says that it is an accusation if a priest or Levite of Christ lacks any of these virtues, or certainly if he is guilty of capital sins. It should be noted that he did not say, “having no sin.”

Women likewise must be chaste, not slanderers, sober. He commands that they also be chosen in the same way as deacons. Hence it is clear that he is speaking of those whom in the East they call deaconesses.

Faithful in everything. Doubting nothing.

Let deacons be husbands of one wife. Not so that, if they have not had a wife, they should take one, but so that they have not had two. For if a wife makes a man more worthy, why should bigamists not also be ordained?

Those who manage their children and their own households well. He repeats what he had said more briefly. For those who have served well acquire a good rank for themselves. There are indeed lesser ranks. He has used “good” here in the sense of “great.”

And much confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus. Confidence both in petitioning God and in teaching human beings.

I am writing these things to you, my son Timothy, hoping to come to you soon. And to instruct you more fully. But if I delay, so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the household of God. So that you may have the authority to arrange everything properly on my behalf.

Which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and support of the truth. In it alone the truth now stands firmly established, and it alone supports the whole structure of truth.

And confessedly great is the mystery of piety. The incarnation of Christ, through which piety has been brought about in all things.

Which was manifested in the flesh. When the Word became flesh.

He was justified in the Spirit. “The Spirit of God will come upon you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

He appeared to angels. When the multitude of angels said, “Glory to God in the highest,” and when they ministered to him in the wilderness.

He was preached among the gentiles. As Simeon says: “A light for revelation to the gentiles.”

He was believed in the world. By both peoples.

He was taken up in glory. In the sight of the apostles he was taken up into heaven.

## CHAPTER IV

But the Spirit says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error. The Holy Spirit says this in the manner of the prophets.

And to doctrines of demons. Every heretical doctrine is composed by the art of demons.

Speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience branded. They speak in hypocrisy: although they are not afraid to fornicate, they wish to appear so chaste that they even condemn marriage; and they are so abstinent that they judge the creature of God while eating sparingly, although they themselves devote themselves to banquets.

Paul, however, preaches chastity and abstinence in such a way that he condemns neither nature nor creation: he exhorts the stronger to the former and grants the latter to the weak. For those people did this not out of love of chastity and abstinence but to obscure his preaching, wishing to appear more righteous and holier than the one who permitted lawful marriage for the sake of children, lest they incur the crime of fornication. Yet while pretending to chastity, they acted against it.

Forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.

If you attend to the precise meaning of the wording, some monstrous teaching will be proclaimed, since they prohibit both marriage and abstinence by saying the things that follow.

By setting these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus. Holding the balance in all things, and administering everything rationally and moderately.

Nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine that you have attained. For from childhood he had been instructed in the sacred writings, that is, in the Law.

But avoid foolish and old-womanish myths. Things unsuitable to religion or faith.

Exercise yourself for piety. Piety also consists in helping another person even at the cost of one’s own hardship, as the widow of Zarephath did for Elijah.

For bodily exercise. Of food, baths, and other such things, or of bodily labor. Is useful for a little. For a little time.

But piety is useful for everything, holding a promise of the life that now is and of the life to come. Piety is useful both for the present time and for the future. The widow was nourished in the present, and her reward remains in heaven.

The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance. True in the conscience of everyone, and one to which no one can object.

For to this end we labor and are reviled. Since it is certain to everyone that we have done nothing deserving hatred, what follows except that we are blasphemed because of our different way of life?

Because we have hoped in the living God. And by hoping we preserve righteousness. He is the Savior of all people. In the present life. Especially of believers. To whom he will grant eternal salvation. “Come, you blessed.” For the Lord knows those who are his.

Command and teach these things. Command them to do them, and teach how and why they should be done—that is, for the reward of eternal life.

Let no one despise your youth. Act in such a way that you may be regarded with admiration rather than contempt.

But be an example to the faithful. It is a small thing to be an example to unbelievers, among whom anyone who does not commit the more serious crimes is considered great. But this is truly great: to present oneself in such a way that even the perfect may make progress through him.

In word, in conduct, in love. That is, in teaching. He wants to provide the faithful with an example in speech. At the same time, let us say nothing other than the word of God; this applies especially to everyone, but above all to priests and those devoted to religion within the Catholic faith.

In chastity. The marks of which are displayed even in the simplicity of one’s dress.

Until I come, attend to reading. Be diligent to understand what you read; attend to this, and do what you read.

To exhortation and teaching. Exhort them so that it may be done; teach how obscure things are to be understood, or how the things that are read can be accomplished.

Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you. He neglects grace who does not exercise the talent he has received.

Through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. He possessed the grace of prophecy, or of teaching, together with his episcopal ordination; or he received grace at his ordination, either for teaching or for understanding.

Meditate on these things. For constant meditation produces every kind of progress.

Be devoted to them. For not everyone who meditates is actually engaged in the things on which he meditates.

So that your progress may be manifest to all. Progress will be manifest if you are always attentive in meditation.

Attend to yourself and to teaching. First to yourself, then to teaching: be diligent in both, so that you may save yourself by your life and strengthen them by teaching confirmed through example.

Persist in these things. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you—those whom you teach.

## CHAPTER V
Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father. Do not take offense at the rebuke of a younger man, so that, irritated, he may make no progress; rather, by his own example, let him correct the younger men. Young men as brothers. Brothers may be admonished more freely, as they are of the same age; likewise, sisters. Older women as mothers, with reverence. Younger women as sisters, in complete chastity, both of mind and of body.

Honor widows who are truly widows. They are to be honored by providing what they need or by offering consolation. But if any widow has children or grandchildren—he defines true widows as those who are completely desolate and free from every other concern—let her first learn to manage her own household and to repay her parents in kind; for this is acceptable before God. Let her manage her household for as long as she is instructing young children or grandchildren, so that she may repay her children what she received from her parents. Yet she must take care not to use this as an excuse for avarice, but preserve only what is sufficient for herself and her children, and not herself give them an opportunity to indulge in luxury in the world.

But the woman who is truly a widow and desolate hopes in the Lord. Such women are to be honored. And she persists in supplications and prayers night and day, as did Anna, the daughter of Phanuel. For the woman who lives in luxury is dead while she lives. And command this also, so that they may be irreproachable. Here he touches upon the widows of his own time, who, although they do not clothe a man of their own nature with even some sort of garment, adorn their walls with costly slabs of marble. Whatever exceeds the limits of nature is luxury.

But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith. This refers to anyone who rejects widows, orphans, or the poor, and especially parents. He is worse than an unbeliever, because even unbelievers show devotion toward their neighbors. If any widow has left children orphaned, she is worse than an unbeliever. It should be noted that some Christians are worse than unbelievers.

Let a widow be chosen. Those whom he calls deaconesses are the women he wished to be chosen—women who would be an example to everyone. Not less than sixty years old. This concerns several widows. She must have been the wife of one husband and have a reputation for good works. This means that she has maintained all these qualities from the time of her widowhood. If she has raised children—if she has raised those born to her, neither accepting an abortion nor killing a child already born. If she has welcomed strangers. If she has washed the feet of the saints—not merely welcoming them, but washing their feet with her own hands, something that women devoted to luxury scarcely do. If she has assisted those suffering tribulation, whether those placed in prison or the sick. If she has followed every good work. He has summarized the matter briefly.

But avoid younger widows. Avoid appointing them, lest what is evil become an example in place of what is good. Or, at least, do not choose them for ministry; certainly avoid intimacy with them. For when they have become wanton, they desire to marry in Christ. This means through lack of self-control; or, at any rate, when they begin to be dishonored, saying that they merely wish to marry in the Lord. They incur condemnation because they have made their first faith void. They have made illicit for themselves what was permitted, by vowing chastity. This rule must be observed not only with widows, but also with virgins and other women who practice continence.

At the same time, being idle, they learn to go about from house to house. They have no household duties to occupy them, are not bound by a husband’s authority, and are not restrained by fear of God. They are not only idle, but also talkative and inquisitive, saying things that ought not to be said. Desiring to excuse their own will, they offer others a bad example.

Therefore I desire—indeed, I grant this before they promise what they cannot fulfill—that younger women marry, women of the kind he mentioned above; that they bear children and be heads of households. “Not kill” means that women who conceive children from adultery frequently kill them. Let them give the adversary no occasion for slander. Or, let religion not be blasphemed on their account if they are incontinent.

For already some have turned back after Satan. He gives the reasons why he said that he wanted them to marry, lest you think he wished this for its own sake: either they have denied the faith of God or have committed fornication.

If any believer has widows, let him provide for them, so that the Church may not be burdened. This may refer to widows in his own household or to poor relatives. The purpose is that provision may suffice for those who are truly widows—that is, those who have been left desolate by human beings.

Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor—that is, those who fulfill their duty, both in office and in labor concerning the word. Especially those who labor in preaching and teaching doctrine. He did not say, “especially those who possess the word,” but “those who labor.” For he commanded that all who possess it—those who are teachable—should be given something. Scripture says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing,” and: “The laborer is worthy of his wage.”

He wishes material benefits to be supplied to those from whom spiritual benefits are received, because, occupied with teaching, they cannot provide themselves with necessities.

Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter unless there are two or three witnesses. It is unjust to accept an accusation against anyone who is absent, since even secular courts do not do this; how much more should this not be done concerning the priest of the Lord?

Reprove sinners before everyone. This is done if the charge has been proved against them, so that either the person being punished may be corrected by the experience or others may be frightened by the example. So that the rest may have fear, seeing that you did not spare even a presbyter who was sinning.

I charge you before God and Christ Jesus. He binds him by a divine and heavenly adjuration, so that no consideration may prejudice him against observing these instructions. And before the elect angels, that you may keep these things without prejudice—that is, without turning aside to either side. The angels either attend the sacred altars or have preserved their dignity.

Do nothing by inclining toward one side or the other, neither to the right nor to the left.

Lay hands quickly on no one. For it is no small sin to cast pearls before swine, to give what is holy to dogs, and to bestow clerical ordination not upon holy men who are deeply learned in the law of God, but upon one’s own followers and servants of lowly offices—and, more disgracefully still, at the petitions of little women.

Here one must consider the wisdom of Christ’s Apostle in his own words. To demonstrate the danger of ordination, he joined to it the punishment of sinners: “Do not share,” he says, “in the sins of others.” Therefore, just as in ordaining evil men the person who appoints such men becomes a participant in their sins, so in ordaining holy men the one who chooses good men becomes a participant in their righteousness. “Do not share in the sins of others”: he says that one shares in the sin of the person who is ordained without having been tested.

Keep yourself chaste, so that you may be able to rebuke others boldly.

Do not continue to drink only water, but use a little wine, because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses. He advises him to care more for the progress of others than for his own abstinence. Illness could impede his preaching.

The sins of some people are manifest. This is so either when they are exposed and excommunicated, or when they are condemned beforehand by present punishments—what they will receive at the future judgment. These sins precede judgment. They are sins that each person has committed here beforehand; for example, if some whom you have deprived of their resources are afflicted by poverty even after our death.

But some people are followed by their sins. Likewise, good works are manifest. The sins that precede judgment are those that are known to everyone. But some follow afterward, when they are subsequently established at the judgment.

Alternatively, the meaning is this: those sins precede us into judgment which each person committed here beforehand; those follow us to which we gave occasion, but which are completed after our departure. Therefore sins of this kind follow us. For example, if we have caused someone’s poverty, and that person is consumed by hunger and want after our death.

Or they are judged in the future judgment because they cannot remain hidden for long. “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed.” Even things that remain concealed for a time cannot be hidden at the judgment. Things of another kind also cannot be concealed—from what is manifest, whether evil or good.

## CHAPTER VI

Let all who are under the yoke consider their masters worthy of every honor, even if they are unbelievers, so that the name of the Lord and the doctrine may not be blasphemed. Otherwise you may appear to have fallen away into something worse through your religion.

But those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers. They must not claim equality for themselves. Rather, they should serve all the more, because their masters are believers and beloved, sharing in God’s benefit. If they served unbelievers through hateful fear, how much more ought they to serve believers through love, since they have been deemed worthy to share in their benefits?

Teach these things and exhort others to them. Teach that all the things I have said ought to be done, and exhort them by displaying the reward.

If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ—the Lord who speaks through me, Christ—and to the doctrine that accords with piety, he is arrogant and knows nothing, but is diseased with regard to disputes. He raises himself above others, knowing nothing, since that wisdom is not from above.

He is diseased with disputes about words, from which envy arises. Having abandoned the meaning of truth, such people are ensnared by the ambiguities of words. From these come quarrels and blasphemies, which generate disputes, and evil suspicions. Either they suspect heresy in one another, or those who hear them think that the truth is being abandoned.

These are conflicts among people whose minds are corrupted and who have been deprived of the truth—that is, of the integrity of the Gospel or of nature—people who think that piety is a means of gain. They suppose that the New Testament came for the sake of their profit.

But if piety is a great gain, whoever has piety together with sufficiency gains much—not with avarice, but with what nature requires. Piety is the worship of God; impiety, therefore, is contempt of God.

For we brought nothing into the world; there is no doubt that we can take nothing out of it. We were born naked, and we shall also die naked. Whatever has been acquired here will be left here; it is not ours, since we are strangers and travelers. Therefore, content with sufficiency, let us acquire those riches that we may carry with us to our homeland.

Having food and clothing, we are content with these things. By “sufficiency,” which he mentioned above, he means that whatever is beyond these things is wealth.

But those who desire to become rich—that is, those who are rich should use their riches well, whereas those who desire to become rich are not free from temptation—fall into temptation. For what increases for them necessarily diminishes for others.

They fall into temptation and the devil’s snare. It is therefore an occasion of temptation and a snare of the devil to possess riches that even one’s parents did not possess, since whatever parents have left behind ought to be distributed in good works.

They also fall into many desires, useless and harmful. The desires for riches are never satisfied, because a person is always in need: whatever he sees, he desires. These desires are not only useless but harmful, and they plunge people into destruction and perdition. Swollen with ambition for possessions, they are lifted up even to heaven and plunged down to hell; or, desiring the wealth of others, they carry their schemes as far as murder.

For the love of money is the root of all evils, because it is either the source or the instrument of every crime. By desiring it, some have wandered away from the faith; they have departed from faith in God’s promises. And they have pierced themselves with many sorrows. The more one possesses, the greater are the torments of anxiety one endures.

Hence the Lord also affirmed that the word is choked by the troubles of riches and by the surrounding desires. In the end, such people do not rule their riches but serve them, so that one may say, “How rich that man is!”—as though one were saying, “How enslaved to riches!”

But you, man of God—not a man of riches, but a man of God, whose all things are, and who is enslaved to God alone—flee these things, which are the cause of faithlessness and sorrows. Pursue righteousness, piety, faith, love, patience, and gentleness. I desire you to be rich in these riches.

Fight the good fight of faith. The good fight is not a fight for possessions, but a fight for faith. Take hold of eternal life, as he says of himself: “If somehow I may attain that for which I was attained.”

You were called to this life, having renounced the world and its spectacles. And you confessed the good confession in baptism, before many witnesses—before priests and ministers, and also before heavenly and divine powers.

I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who gave the good confession under Pontius Pilate. “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God.”

Keep the commandment without stain, as he kept it to the end, irreproachably. Whoever pollutes himself with capital sins stains himself and causes himself to be seized.

Keep it until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” Which the blessed and only mighty One, the King of kings and Lord of lords, will show in its own times. When he wills, he will show it, since he alone is mighty enough to do this.

He alone possesses immortality. Properly speaking, he alone possesses it, since he gave angels and human beings the ability to possess it. We do not possess it either alone or from ourselves, as he does.

He alone likewise possesses unchangeableness, because he alone has true eternity. The soul is indeed immortal, but it is changeable; in God there is no change at all.

He dwells in inaccessible light, inaccessible to every creature. For “no one knows the Father except the Son.” No human being has seen him, nor can anyone see him. To him belong honor and everlasting dominion. Amen.

No one has seen him in the fullness of what he is, but each person sees according to his merit; for we see that much more the purer the sharpness of our eyes has become.

Command those who are rich in the present age. There are also rich people of the age to come, who buy for themselves gold refined by the Lord.

Command them not to be arrogant, not to set their minds on high things. Above all, cure their first and chief disease, for you will find it exceedingly difficult to find a rich man who is not proud—one who acknowledges the poor or his parents and does not take it hard that the least honor is not rendered to him by someone inferior.

They must not hope in riches: by not hoping in them, riches become cheap; once they have become cheap, they are given away. They must not hope in the uncertainty of riches. They are uncertain whether they will be taken from their riches more quickly, or their riches from them. Many have had their riches taken away together with their life; others have foreseen with their own eyes that their possessions would pass to strangers; some have unwillingly left them to outsiders.

Rather, let them hope in the living God, who provides us with all things, since all things belong to him, abundantly. He provides abundantly so that we may use his gifts, also giving generously to others—not so that, by great labor, we may destroy what we have in order to build larger storehouses.

He gives them for enjoyment, not for storing away and brooding over them.

Let them do good and become rich in good works, not in gold and silver. Let them give readily. Whoever gives readily will soon cease to be rich.

Let them share. This means either making what is one’s own common property or giving here in order to receive in the future.

Let them store up for themselves a good foundation for the future. “Sell everything, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” This is the foundation of perfection.

So that they may take hold of true life. The present life is not true, because it does not remain in its own condition; for everything under the sun is vanity.

O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Preserve the commandment entrusted to you by us; or, guard the deposit of faith.

Avoid profane novelties of words. Things you have not heard from me, do not readily accept, even if they are spoken by an angel.

And avoid oppositions—that is, dialectical questions raised against the faith, and claims to possess limitless knowledge of things. This is the knowledge falsely so called. Some, by promising such knowledge, have fallen away from the faith.

These are the heretics who, like the serpent promising Eve greater knowledge, have fallen away from the truth of faith.

Grace be with you. Amen. May it remain forever.

# THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0671]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0671D]

He writes again to Timothy concerning the exhortation to martyrdom and the whole rule of truth, what will happen in the last times, and his own suffering. When Paul was being held in chains at Rome, he wrote to Timothy, warning him, because of Paul’s absence, not to be frightened either by his own tribulations or by those of his teacher, and not to be ashamed of the Lord’s testimony, for which Paul himself contended even unto death. He also writes about avoiding heretics and those who preach their own fables rather than the truth of God.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God. With his customary humility and truthfulness, he asserts that he was made an apostle not by his own merit but by the Lord’s will.

According to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus. For eternal life comes to us through Christ.

To Timothy, his most beloved son: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. Such is Paul’s greeting, so that he might obtain all the benefits of Christ and the Father; for this reason he always commends grace.

I give thanks to God, whom I serve. I give thanks to the one who granted us such love for one another and made us worthy of the apostolate.

With a pure conscience, as my ancestors did. My entire ancestry worshiped God alone; for this reason I persecuted the Church of God out of zeal for the law. I continually remember you in my prayers.

Night and day, desiring to see you. He both displays his love and gives a continual example of prayer.

Remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy. These are the tears you shed when I departed, and by which you moved me to sadness—a sadness which I desire to have eased by your presence.

Receiving the recollection of the sincere faith that is in you. This faith first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice. Its reality in you is proved by works, as James defined it; and from that life it descended to you through the succession of instruction, by God’s gift, as though by hereditary right.

I am sure that it is also in you. I have tested your faith. You need to be stirred up, not taught.

For this reason I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is in you. “To rekindle” it means as though it had fallen asleep through tribulations. It was previously given to you by the infusion of faith.

Through the laying on of my hands. This refers to the blessing he received in the episcopate through the laying on of Paul’s hands.

For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control. Those who practice injustice have the spirit of fear, as he says elsewhere: “If you do evil, be afraid.” Or this may refer to the spirit of the law, which punished sinners.

Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner. Christ did nothing deserving shame; nor did I, whom you know to be suffering all these things not because of any crime, but for his sake.

But suffer together with the Gospel according to the power of God. His power always strengthens us and, for his own sake, assists those who labor.

He saved us from sins and from the power or captivity of the devil.

And he called us with his holy calling—that is, a pious calling. “Those whom he called, he also justified.”

Not according to our works, but according to his purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus. In him he purposed to save us freely through Christ, with no preceding merits.

It should be noted that he says “not according to our works,” so that no one may boast.

Before eternal times. Insofar as God’s foreknowledge is concerned, he already gave this before the ages. Even human beings, although uncertain, customarily designate estates for their children before they are born. Elsewhere he likewise says: “He predestined us for adoption as sons before eternal times,” because with God all future things are already known as accomplished.

But it has now been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ. What was previously hidden and granted to only a few in a single people has now been revealed.

He indeed destroyed death. By the power of his grace he destroyed the sins that generated death, and he granted and showed how life and incorruption are to be sought.

He brought life and incorruption to light through the Gospel, in which I was appointed a preacher and apostle. That is, when he brought it to light and I preached it, they believed; for “neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase.”

And teacher of the nations. People are called teachers in comparison with other people; but in comparison with Christ no one is a true teacher except Christ alone.

For this reason I also suffer these things—not because of any crime, as Peter likewise exhorts us to suffer.

But I am not ashamed. Paul is not ashamed of his chains, while we are ashamed of mere reproaches. Not only do we fail to act if we are not praised, but we also grow lukewarm.

For I know whom I have believed. I know that he is a faithful rewarder.

And I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit for that day. He will preserve the faith, since he himself entrusted it to me; it cannot be preserved by my strength without his help.

Hold to the pattern of sound words that you have heard from me. Live and teach according to this pattern, since you received it from me in brief form.

In faith and love in Christ Jesus. This is how we are to believe in integrity and love one another.

Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit. This is what I entrusted to you through the Holy Spirit; the deposit is understood as the faith that is named among the fruits of the Holy Spirit in the Epistle to the Galatians.

Who dwells in us. He has been given to us.

You know this: all who are in Asia have turned away from me. For this reason I remind you, because those whom I did not think would abandon me have left me. Among them are Phygelus and Hermogenes.

May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain. He censures those who deserted him and praises those who persevered, in order to stir good people to imitate them.

But when he arrived in Rome, he searched for me diligently and found me. May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day. And how much he served in Ephesus, you know better.

He found me because he sought me diligently. From this it is shown that not everyone who seeks finds, because some search carelessly.

## CHAPTER II

You, therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus and in what you heard from me through many witnesses. Either I gave you instructions in the presence of many people about how you should teach, or I confirmed what I said by many examples and testimonies of the prophets.

Entrust these things to faithful people who will be able faithfully to administer God’s grace—that is, teaching for God’s sake and not flattering others for worldly advantage or seeking their own glory.

They will be competent to teach others as well—people who not only do these things but also teach them.

Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. We are called soldiers because, with God’s help, we fight against his enemies with spiritual weapons. Since you have already been armed and equipped by God’s gift, labor so that you may receive rewards worthy of your labor.

No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. He uses the comparison with soldiers to show that we must be much more free from worldly affairs in order to please Christ, since even soldiers of this world abstain from their other activities so that they may please their ruler perfectly and seek to stand in his presence.

And if anyone competes in the athletic contest: many compete, but the one who conquers is crowned. We, with the Lord’s help, ought to act so that through his grace we may all triumph.

He is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully—that is, perfectly.

The laboring farmer ought first to receive a share of the fruits. He says this so that the farmer may not ask, “From what shall I live if I devote myself entirely to teaching?” He also shows that the first fruits must be received here from the people, in addition to the harvest-wage that he will receive from the Lord in the future.

Understand what I am saying; for the Lord will give you understanding in all things. He would not admonish him in this way if everyone were able to understand. “In all things” means not only in these matters. Observe carefully that the Lord gives understanding so that we may understand. We must not attribute anything to ourselves, but give thanks to the giver, who has made what belongs to him become ours.

Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David. This is directed against those who, denying the resurrection of the flesh, consequently denied Christ’s resurrection as well, and also against those who denied that Christ came in the flesh—those whom John calls antichrists.

According to my Gospel—that is, according to what I preach.

For which I suffer hardship even to chains, as though I were a criminal. Not truly a criminal, but as though I were one.

But the word of God is not bound. I teach the word boldly to those who are present, and by letters I instruct and strengthen those who are absent.

Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with heavenly glory. For this reason I sought help from the tribune; for this reason I appealed to Caesar, so that the elect might be strengthened through me, although by dying I could now have brought these sufferings to an end. The salvation is in Christ, and it is not bare salvation but salvation with glory—not earthly but heavenly.

The saying is trustworthy, founded upon the reason of truth.

For if we have died with him, we shall also live with him. If we have died to vices and pleasures, we shall live for Christ; otherwise, how do we live with him? For there is no agreement between Christ and Belial.

If we endure, we shall also reign with him. If we endure what he taught both by word and by example, then at last we shall be able to reign together with him. If not, may we at least obtain forgiveness!

If we deny him, he will also deny us, just as he himself promised in the Gospel that he would deny before the Father and the angels those who denied him before human beings.

If we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself. Whether we believe or do not believe, the truth does not change; but if we believe, we benefit ourselves. He cannot give each person anything other than what he promised, because the Truth does not lie, nor does he make his promise void even if not everyone has believed, as he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Did their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God?” For he remains faithful.

Remind them of these things, charging them before the Lord. Bind them under God’s testimony.

Do not quarrel about words, for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear. Without the testimonies of Scripture, such contention does not build up but destroys those who hear.

But take diligent care to present yourself approved to God. Above all, labor to present yourself before God as one deserving that the people should obey you.

An unashamed worker. Do not be ashamed in good work.

Rightly handling the word of truth. The person who confirms what he says by his example. For just as doctrine is an ornament of life, so a good way of life is an ornament of doctrine. People are not taught well by words if they are destroyed by examples.

But avoid profane and empty talk, for it advances greatly toward impiety. These are the irreligious fables of heretics who deny the resurrection. Once fear of judgment has been removed, this leads to every form of impiety and to every crime.

And their word spreads like cancer. Cancer is said to be a wound that arises in women’s breasts, and unless help is given immediately, it spreads to the heart, after which there is no remedy. In the same way, conversations with heretics must be avoided, lest they wound the mind irreparably through the ears.

Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth. Their names are identified so that he may know whom to avoid.

They say that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overturn the faith of some. They place the resurrection in children, or in the soul when it rises from vices. To deceive those whom they destroy, they also take that testimony from Ezekiel concerning the bones. He says that such people must be avoided altogether.

But the firm foundation of God stands. Those in whose hearts the faith of Christ was founded were not shaken or deceived.

It has this inscription: “The Lord knows those who are his.” This is the sign that was made in the time of Moses concerning those whom Dathan and Abiram were utterly unable to overthrow.

“The Lord knows those who are his.” These people did not perish with the sinners because they did not consent to them. The Lord knows those who are his because he is not deceived in his foreknowledge. He chose us before the foundation of the world and does not permit his people to become entangled in those errors. For those who do not persevere to the end cannot, without doubt, be his.

And let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity, so that he may not perish with the wicked.

But in a great house. Some might ask, “Why then do heretics or evil Christians enter the Church?” He gives the comparison of a great house, such as the Church is now, before the resurrection. He calls the Church a great house in which good and evil, genuine and false, righteous and unrighteous people are mixed, just as grain and chaff are threshed together with weeds on the threshing floor until the winnowing.

After the resurrection the Church will be without stain or wrinkle, when the weeds have been separated from the grain. But now, what is worse, many false Christians enter the Church and are mixed with God’s people, such as the Manichaeans and others.

There are not only vessels of gold and silver, precious and strong, but also wooden and earthen vessels. Some are for honor, others for dishonor—cheap and weak.

If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor. If anyone cleanses himself from these heretical deceivers, believes that the resurrection and God’s judgment are to come, and therefore strives with God’s help to fulfill every good work, he will be a vessel of gold and silver, which is purified by fire rather than consumed by it.

Sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work. This does not mean that he commits no minor sins, for we cannot be without lesser sins; rather, he does not commit capital sins.

Flee youthful desires. Such desires can exist even in old men if they do what is inconsistent with Christian dignity. Young people, with God’s help, can overcome them if they guard against frivolity.

But pursue righteousness, faith, and love. Here he calls faith the integrity of faith.

Pursue peace with those who call upon the Lord, the peace owed to religion, pure and simple, from a pure heart. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

But avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate disputes. All questions that are without the discipline of Scripture are foolish.

The servant of the Lord must not quarrel. The servant of Christ ought to imitate Christ, who did not cry out or contend, and no one heard his voice in the streets, and so forth, as the prophet foretold concerning him.

But he must be gentle toward everyone, not only toward friends; teachable and patient. He must be able to teach everyone patiently, and he must not be ashamed to learn.

He must correct opponents with modesty—not with anger or shouting—in case God should perhaps grant them repentance for acknowledging the truth.

This is directed against the Novatians, who deny repentance. It should likewise be noted that repentance is God’s gift. Through your gentle and gracious correction—this too is said against the Novatians, who deny repentance—forgiveness is promised even to those who are held in such heresy.

And they may return to sobriety from the devil’s snare, by whom they are held captive for his will.

Having accepted the reasoned understanding.

## CHAPTER III
But know this, that in the last days. Do not be surprised that things grow worse day by day. Perilous times will be at hand. Difficult. For people will be lovers of themselves. When we seek our own advantage and glory, we love ourselves and not God. For the more someone delights in what is below, the more he is separated from what is above. Covetous, boastful. Greedy and vainglorious. Proud, blasphemous. Unwilling to learn, yet arrogating to themselves [the right to teach] doctrine. Disobedient to parents. That is, to true teachers, who begot or instructed them through the Gospel. Ungrateful, wicked, without affection. That is, without devotion. Without peace, slanderers. Of the saints: for corrupt nature is such that, when it cannot excuse itself, it seeks accomplices for itself through false accusations against others. Incontinent, fierce, without kindness. Whether toward vices or toward avarice. Traitors, insolent, swollen with pride. Against one another. Lovers of pleasures rather than of God. By this it is recognized what we love more: that in which we are found to have greater concern.

Having indeed an appearance of piety. An appearance of conduct or doctrine. But denying its power. Denying the reality of it by their deeds. And avoid these people. For among them are those who enter houses. So that evil conversations may not corrupt good morals. And take captive little women weighed down with sins. They capture those burdened with sins, promising them impunity and forgiveness; or weak souls, who are compared with women. Who are led by various desires. Always wishing to hear something new. Always learning, and never arriving at knowledge. For no one who wants to hold everything, even what has not been tested, holds anything definite; what one hears from one person is destroyed by another. [Never] arriving at the truth. As if one were to say: always walking, yet never reaching the road.

But just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth. As those men did so through the deception of magic, so these do through the illusions of arguments and the subtleties of words. People corrupted in mind. Corrupted either in the integrity of doctrine or in faith. Reprobate with regard to the faith. Although perhaps they may seem to people to lead a commendable life.

But they will make no further progress, for their folly will be made manifest to all. He is not speaking of all heretics, but only of those whom he foresaw would then soon be destroyed. As was also the case with those men. When they confessed that they had been overcome by the finger of God.

But you have followed my doctrine, instruction, purpose, faith, steadfastness, love, and patience. Believe more about me than about them; or, for this reason I have no fear concerning you, because I know that you have come to know my life very well. Persecutions, sufferings, such as befell me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra: what persecutions I endured, and from all of them the Lord rescued me. From these things you could recognize that I do nothing for the sake of human beings, since I have suffered so much—not by my own strength or ingenuity.

And all who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution. Not I alone, but all who do not kill souls by flattering them. Hence we must fear that we are not living devoutly, since we suffer nothing for God.

But evil people and impostors will advance from bad to worse, themselves erring and leading others into error. He says this either of flatterers or of heretics, who, while they are loved and praised by people, are themselves more greatly deceived and deceive others.

But you remain in the things that you have learned and that have been entrusted to you. I do not want these things to frighten you. Knowing from whom you learned them. From a true apostle of Christ. And because from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. Without the faith of Christ they cannot now instruct anyone for salvation.

All Scripture is inspired by God. For whatever things were written in the Law were written for our instruction, as he himself says elsewhere. It is useful for teaching, for reproving, for correcting, and for training in righteousness, so that the person of God may be complete. Through the Law the ignorant person is taught, the insolent person is reproved, the erring person is corrected, and the one who does not know how to keep the proper measure is trained for righteousness.

For every good work. Not merely for one. Instructed. For this reason the instruction of the Scriptures has been given.

## CHAPTER IV

I testify before God and Christ Jesus. He adjures him by all that he believes. Who is going to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom. For he will raise the dead and will find the living.

Preach the word; persist without ceasing. Fervently. In season and out of season. It is “in season” for one who listens willingly, and “out of season” for one who is unwilling. Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and instruction. Reprove those who sin, entreat them not to sin, rebuke those who resist; but do all these things with patience, according to the teaching of the Law.

For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine. Unwilling to hear the truth, like the people of Israel with regard to the prophets. But they will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires. They will seek such teachers for themselves as say what they themselves desire, so that they may sin without fear. Itching in their ears. Desiring to be entertained, not to be pierced by remorse.

And indeed they will turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn to fables. Away from the truth of Scripture, by which we condemn vices, and toward human arguments that contrive reasons why God does not punish.

But you, keep watch; labor in all things. In matters that pertain to the benefit of those who hear. Do the work of an evangelist. So that your word may be confirmed by your deeds. Fulfill your ministry. The episcopate; or, let each person fulfill his ministry in his own vocation.

For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is near. “I am being poured out”: that is, “I am being sacrificed.” He said that his death would be offered as a sacrifice to God, in order to urge him on to martyrdom.

I have fought the good fight; I have finished the race. Now he says this confidently, standing at the final limit of life. Thus he now recalls his good merits, so that after good merits he may obtain the crown, just as after evil merits he obtained grace.

Finally, note what follows. “There remains for me,” he says, “the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day.” To whom would the righteous judge give the crown, if the merciful Father had not first granted grace? And how would this be a crown of righteousness, unless grace, which justifies the ungodly, had preceded it? How would this debt be repaid, unless that free gift had first been given?

I have kept the faith. In what remains, the crown of righteousness has been laid up for me. The faith that I received I have kept to the end through his grace. He will give it to me on that day—the righteous judge, who knows that, with his help, I have fought for his righteousness even unto death.

And not to me alone, but also to those who—who, with God as my helper, will have imitated me. Love his appearing. They rejoice that Christ has come and taught righteousness; or every day they say with full faith: “May your kingdom come.”

Hurry to come to me soon. For Demas has deserted me, loving this present age, and has gone to Thessalonica. It was necessary that one who loved the pleasures of the age should leave the one who did not love it, because every creature joins itself to what is like it.

Crescens went to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia; Luke alone is with me. These men did not love the age; otherwise he ought to have said collectively that they loved the age.

Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in the ministry. Also in the ministry of speech and preaching.

But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books—especially the parchments. The *paenula* was the consular garment of the ancient Romans. He did not say that this cloak had been his; for someone converted to the faith of Christ might have placed it for sale at the Apostle’s feet, among other things.

Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; may the Lord repay him according to his works. Since he resisted the words of God, let him give an account to God. You too avoid him, for he greatly resisted our words. If he resisted ours, how much more yours? He warns him to beware of perverse people.

At my first defense no one stood by me; everyone deserted me. May it not be counted against them. When I first began to defend the Gospel. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me. When he says that the Lord was with him while everyone else deserted him, he commends grace and exhorts him not to be afraid. So that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear. Not because I feared death, since I was continually defended by the Lord’s help.

And I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. The Lord rescued me from the mouth of Festus, who was raging against me; or from the devil. The Lord delivered me from every evil work and will save me. From all their snares. Into his heavenly kingdom, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. Since he has delivered me from here, he will also bring me into the kingdom.

Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth. But I left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Here it is shown that the apostles did not heal their own companions because of weakness of the flesh, but in order to display signs, since they did not heal their own disciples.

Hurry to come before winter. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, and Claudia greet you, as do all the brothers. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen. He who has died in the flesh is alive spiritually. Written from the City.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE DIVINE PAUL TO TITUS

## ARGUMENT

He reminds Titus and instructs him concerning the appointment of a presbyter, spiritual conduct, and the avoidance of heretics who believe in the Jewish Scriptures.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, a servant of God. He was a servant of God, not of sin. But an apostle of Jesus Christ. He distinguished apostleship, because not everyone who is a servant is immediately also an apostle. He was an apostle because he had been sent through him to preach.

According to the faith of God’s elect and the acknowledgment of the truth that accords with piety, in hope of eternal life. According to the faith that he himself infuses and causes people to believe—those whom he also chose in his foreknowledge, as he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.”

Which he promised. “You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free,” because Christ is the truth. God, who does not lie. If he does not lie, he offers nothing other than what he promised, both to the righteous and to the unrighteous, although this may seem harsh to human beings. Or in this way: What he promised to Abraham and to his seed, he will fulfill in Christ.

Before eternal times. Before all times, through the Son, to save those who believe—those whom he chose before the foundation of the world.

But he manifested his word at the proper times in the preaching that was entrusted to me. He manifested his plan then, when he brought into faith the whole world, which he had foreknown would turn away from righteousness.

According to the command of God our Savior. To Titus, his beloved son. This was the command by which he ordered Paul and Barnabas to be set apart so that they might preach to the Gentiles.

According to the common faith: grace and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ our Savior. “According to the common faith” refers to a son by faith, not by nature.

For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters throughout the cities. Correct what is lacking according to the proper order; then you will be able to ordain presbyters, once everyone in the Church has been set right. As I also directed you.

According to the order in which I instructed you in person. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife. It must be noted that even what is lawful is forbidden in a priest.

Having believing children, not accused of debauchery or disobedient. So that he may not be able boldly to rebuke those who sin; or so that the proof of his teaching may arise from the discipline of his own household, and he may fear the example of Eli.

For a bishop must be blameless. He calls the same person a bishop whom above he called a presbyter. As God’s steward. If trustworthy stewards of human laws are sought, what ought those to be like who administer divine rights?

Not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine. Not self-pleasing. Not violent, not greedy for shameful gain. A disciple of Christ must not strike for the sake of him for whom Christ was struck.

Alternatively: he must not wound the conscience of others through his evil conduct; nor is he commanded to pursue shameful gain through flattery, since he hopes for heavenly things.

According to the custom of the Scriptures, he first condemned vices and then introduced virtues, as in: “Turn away from evil and do good.”

But hospitable and kind. So that he may receive guests with kindness. Sober, chaste. Free from every accusation. Just, holy. Just in judgment, holy in conduct through self-restraint. Self-controlled. He says this so that, because he had spoken of one wife, no one might think that he had made room for lack of self-control.

Holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the doctrine. So that he may love the teaching and always speak from it, rather than pursue empty and idle fables. So that he may be able to exhort. Such a person must be chosen who can both exhort and refute those who contradict.

In sound doctrine, and to refute those who contradict. That doctrine is sound which heals those who hear, so that what someone possesses as a gift from God may not make him ungrateful because he attributes it to himself.

For there are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers. Disobedient to apostolic doctrine, they speak without producing any benefit. Especially those of the circumcision, whom it is necessary to refute, because they overturn whole households. They speak human traditions, not God’s commandments.

Teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain. Things that are already superfluous in the time of Christ—namely, the ceremonies of the Jews.

One of them said it. Such things that they even receive this testimony from one of their own. Their own prophet. Epimenides, or Callimachus. “Cretans.” The verse of Epimenides is a hexameter, which in Greek stands according to its own metrical feet:

> Always liars, evil beasts.

Lovers of falsehood, and not merely in the way one ordinarily falls into it, but always; also gluttons and idle. Lazy bellies. For this reason they willingly accept holidays and idleness.

This testimony is true. If only this statement is true, he says that the others are false.

For this reason rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in the faith. Severely. Not paying attention to Jewish fables and human commandments. To human traditions, about which they are reproved by the Savior, according to Isaiah, honoring God not with the heart but with the lips.

Turning themselves away from the truth. All things are clean to the clean. For they still called certain things unclean according to the Law. But to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled.

The defiled and unbelieving are those who do not believe that Christ, by granting faith, removed the yoke of the Law from the necks of believers—that is, all those things that had been given temporarily in figure.

They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him. They say that they know Christ, who was promised to them from the Law; but by their deeds they deny his coming, turning themselves away, as he says, from his truth, since they think they cannot be justified without the aid of the Law.

They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for every good work. In this they claim to be more religious, while they do not do what they command.

## CHAPTER II

But speak the things that befit sound doctrine. That is, the things that pertain to the life of Christ.

Older men. Here he calls the elders of the Church “older men,” whom it is necessary to make an example for everyone. Let them be sober, dignified, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in patience. Let them be vigilant, so that they may not provide younger men with an example of drunkenness.

Older women likewise. Those who were chosen as an example for other women. In holy conduct, not slanderers. Therefore there is also conduct that is not holy. Not enslaved to much wine. But drinking sparingly. Teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence. He permitted them to teach, but women.

Young women. Either because they were to be self-controlled, or lest the word of God be blasphemed as though it preached discord. To love their husbands. Not other men. To love their children; to be prudent, chaste, keepers of the household, kind, subject to their own husbands. So that through negligence they may not distress their husbands in anything.

So that the word of God may not be blasphemed. Either so that they themselves may not blaspheme it, if they are Gentiles, or so that others, seeing them become worse, may not blaspheme it.

Likewise exhort young men to be sober. Remove the cause of lust from young men by taking away drunkenness.

In all things present yourself as an example. “In all things,” either in the things that are fitting, or not only in body but also in mind. An example of good works. So that by your example you do not destroy the word, or rebuke others boldly.

In doctrine, integrity and dignity; a sound, irreproachable word. So that they may know how to teach. So that the one who is opposed may turn back, having nothing evil to say about us. Who could contradict him if he noticed anything of that kind?

That slaves are to be subject to their masters, pleasing them in all things. In all things that they justly command. Not contradicting, not defrauding. So that, by doing things with murmuring, you may be ungrateful both to a human being and to God, and may have no reward with God.

But showing good faith in all things. Either in the things entrusted to them, or so that they may demonstrate by their works that what they believe is good. So that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things. And so that it may be praised together with their deeds, when people see your good works and glorify your Father.

But the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us. Excluding no condition or sex, both through commandments and through example. So that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires. Every desire and every ambition that is temporary is worldly. That we may live soberly and justly. For this reason the Savior also says: “Take care that your hearts are not weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of this life.”

And that we may live devoutly in this age. Let us join piety to righteousness, so that it may not be without proper measure.

Awaiting the blessed hope. The one who lives as he has commanded awaits these things with confidence. And the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. He called Christ himself the great God, of whom the angel said to the blessed Mary: “He will be great,” and the rest. He too will come with glory to judge the living and the dead.

Who gave himself for us, to redeem us from every iniquity. As Isaiah says: “He gave his life over to death, and was reckoned among the transgressors; and he himself bore the sins of many.” And to cleanse for himself a people acceptable to him, zealous for good works. For this reason he gave himself, to cleanse us from every iniquity; therefore let us beware lest we make his benefit fruitless and empty.

Speak these things and exhort. Let all your speech be exhortation toward this. And rebuke with all authority. He rebukes sharply who does not live as he teaches. Let no one despise you. Present yourself as someone who cannot be despised, for life gives authority to doctrine.

Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey the command, and to be ready for every good work. Not for any evil work. To slander no one. Not even those who deserve to be slandered. Not to be quarrelsome, but modest, showing every gentleness. A quarrelsome person is one who provokes a quarrel by returning the blow.

Toward all people. Not only toward the good.

For we too were once such people. So that they might not despair of correction, he offers his own example. Or because, he says, we too were such people, we ought to bear their folly patiently.

Once foolish and unbelieving. It must be noted what Christ found us like; let us not presume upon our merits or glory in the goodness of nature. Erring, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, acting in malice and envy; hateful, hating one another. See what we were before grace through the freedom of the will.

But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared. “Humanity,” either Christ according to his humanity, or the generosity of God. Not from works of righteousness. It must be noted that we were saved by none of our merits, but solely by the mercy of the Redeemer. Let those who are more eager to destroy than to defend free will be silent.

Which we ourselves performed. Which we Jews performed—how much more, then, the Gentiles! But according to his mercy he saved us. Not according to our diligence or labor, but according to the mercy of him who both goes before us in every good work and brings it to completion.

Through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior. More abundantly than in the case of the righteous of former times. So that, having been justified by grace, we might be his heirs. It must be observed that we are justified by his grace, not by our merits.

According to the hope of eternal life. Not according to a carnal inheritance.

This saying is trustworthy, and I want you to affirm these things, so that those who believe in God may take care to excel in good works. To excel in teaching good works. These things are good and useful for people. These things, not those that follow.

But avoid foolish questions and genealogies. He does not want us to occupy ourselves with superfluous questions and disputes that arise from genealogies in the Law; rather, we should always speak about those things by which the hearers may progress.

And avoid disputes and fights about the Law, for they are useless and empty. As though they were contradictions that heretics eagerly seize upon.

After one and a second admonition, avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a person is perverted. He does not want us to occupy ourselves even with those who, after being admonished twice, are not corrected, lest we waste time in useless contempt.

And he sins, since he is condemned by his own judgment. Because, after hearing and recognizing the truth, he persists in his obstinacy; for each person is bound by the cords of his own sins.

When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, hurry to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Carefully send ahead Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they lack nothing. So that, by delaying, they may lose nothing of the fruit of their teaching.

Let our people also learn to excel in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful. He repeats the same thing that he said above: Let those who believe in God take care to excel in good works.
