All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. The grace of God be with you all. Amen. Truly, or faithfully. Written from Nicopolis.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE DIVINE PAUL TO PHILEMON

## ARGUMENT

He writes a familiar letter to Philemon on behalf of his slave Onesimus, writing to him from prison at Rome.

Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon, our beloved and fellow worker, and to Appia, our dearest sister. He was a fellow worker in the Gospel. Appia, however, is believed either to have been his sister or his wife. And to Archippus, our fellow soldier, and to the Church that is in your house.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Archippus was either a bishop or a deacon. Concerning him he says to the Colossians: “Say to Archippus: See to the ministry that you have received, so that you may fulfill it.”

I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers. He prays for them with joy. Hearing of your love and the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus. A faith that becomes known through good works. And toward all the saints. Whoever loves the head ought to love all the members.

So that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the acknowledgment of every good work among you, in Christ Jesus. Or I ask this so that your works in Christ may shine forth. Alternatively: He loves all the saints so greatly that everyone among us may clearly recognize you as faithful in Christ.

For I have had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother. Those whom you received as guests.

Therefore, although we have great confidence in Christ Jesus. Although your love has given us confidence to command you, we preferred to entreat you. To command you in what pertains to the matter, because of love. In what pertains to Christian love.

I entreat you rather, since you are such a person, as Paul, an old man—and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I entreat you for my son, whom I begot in my imprisonment, Onesimus. In all things like me. He who was once useless to you is now useful both to you and to me, whom I have sent back to you. When he was carnal. But receive him as my own heart. That is, as a son.

I had wished to keep him with me, so that he might minister to me on your behalf in the bonds of the Gospel. From this you may recognize what sort of person he is, since he pleased me so much that I believed he could minister to me on your behalf.

But I wished to do nothing without your counsel. He speaks in such a way as to send him back to Philemon himself, or so that his usefulness might be commended more strongly. Thus your good deed would not be as though it were forced, but voluntary. For perhaps he departed from you for a time for this reason, so that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave.

For he will no longer serve as though by necessity, but voluntarily. Rather than a slave, [receive him as] a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord! He owes you service both in the flesh and according to what he has believed.

Therefore, if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has harmed you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand: I will repay it—not to say to you that you owe me even your own self.

Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in the Lord. Confident of your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. If you love me, receive him as you would receive me, because I regard him as I regard myself.

At the same time, prepare lodging for me, for I hope through your prayers to be given back to you. Here it is shown that he was sent from the City on the first occasion.

Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you; and Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. Written from the city of Rome.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE DIVINE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS

## PREFACE

At the beginning of this epistle it must be explained why the apostle Paul did not follow his usual practice in this letter, namely, why he did not set out either the designation of his name or the dignity of his office.

The reason, therefore, was that he did not title it with his name because he was writing to Jews, his own brothers, to whom he was hateful because he taught that circumcision, the Sabbath, and the other sacrifices that the Law commanded to be observed ought not to be observed in a carnal manner after the Lord’s Passion.

For those Jews who had believed argued that they should hold both things: namely, that they should be baptized according to the grace of the Gospel and circumcised, and that they should also observe the Sabbath according to the commandment of the Law.

Therefore, if the Apostle had placed his name at the beginning of this Epistle, it could have happened that his rivals, seeing his name at the very front, would disdain to receive it, and thus the benefit of reading would have been delayed.

He did not place the title of apostleship for this reason: because, having been appointed the apostle of the Gentiles, if he had prefaced the letter addressed to them with the title of his apostleship, calling himself an apostle, he might have seemed to them to wish to place himself above the apostle Peter, who had been appointed their leader by the Lord, just as the same distinguished preacher says elsewhere: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also through me among the Gentiles.”

Perhaps they would also have said: “Why does Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, place himself above our apostles Peter and James? Let him write to those to whom he was appointed an apostle; the writings of our apostles can abundantly instruct us.”

By doing this he showed that he was not unaware of their pride, and at the same time displayed his own humility. In a similar way, the apostle John also, because of humility and for the same reason, omitted his name in his epistle.

Or certainly some say that he did so because he was going to name Christ in the Epistle as the Apostle, saying: “We have Jesus the Just as the High Priest and Apostle of our confession.” He did not wish to place the title of his own apostleship at the beginning of this Epistle. For he did not think it fitting that, where he was going to call Christ an Apostle, he should also call himself an apostle, especially in the title, lest he seem to place himself above Christ.

Some say that this Epistle belongs to Barnabas, some to Luke, and some to Clement. They say that if it were Paul’s, he would certainly have prefixed his name in his customary manner, as in the other letters and likewise in this one. But if it is not Paul’s because it is not titled with his name, then it belongs neither to Barnabas, nor to Luke, nor to Clement, nor to anyone else, since it bears no one’s name.

To which of these, then, should it be attributed? Certainly to the distinguished preacher. For it is proved to be his by its lucid meaning and its manner of expression, although it is composed in a subtler and clearer style than all the Epistles. For it is said that the Apostle sent this to the Hebrews and wrote it in the Hebrew language, in which he was especially skilled, whereas he wrote the remaining letters in Greek.

After the Apostle’s departure, however, the evangelist Luke rendered it in Greek. From Greek it was later translated into the Latin language, as were the others.

## CHAPTER I
In many ways and by many means, God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son.

The whole purpose of the blessed Apostle in this Epistle is to lead the Jews, his kinsmen—who are also called Hebrews, from Heber, in whom they were taken up—from the law of Moses to the grace of the Gospel, from carnal observance to spiritual observance. At the same time, he distinguishes the eminence of the grace given through the Son to the faithful from the legal shadows that were presented through angelic ministrations.

Accordingly, he first states here that the prophets spoke to the fathers in different ways and with various expressions, saying: “In many ways,” that is, with many forms of speech; “and by many means,” that is, through many kinds of manifestation; “formerly,” namely, in time past. God the Father spoke through the prophets to our fathers. Then, to show how great the difference was between the grace given to them and that given to their fathers, he added: “In these last days,” that is, in the final age, “he has spoken to us through the Son.”

When he says, “He has spoken in the prophets, and in the Son,” this has the same force as if he had said, “through the prophets and through the Son,” because one preposition is often used in place of another; and in many passages of the Epistle he is found to use these prepositions indiscriminately.

Let us therefore consider how God the Father spoke to the fathers of the Covenant through many expressions and in many ways. He spoke to them with many expressions and in many forms because he did not always reveal his secrets to them uniformly.

At one time he spoke openly and through an angel, as to Abraham, to whom he said: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” He also spoke to Moses when he gave the legal commandments: “You shall not kill”; “You shall not commit adultery”; and other things of this kind. He spoke likewise to Lot when he led him out of Sodom, and on many other occasions.

At another time he spoke obscurely and through riddles, as to Moses, to whom he said: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” [Col. 0686D–0687A]. At times he appeared in the form of a soldier, as to Joshua; at times in the heart, as to David, who said: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me”; and likewise to the other prophets. At times he spoke through a dream, as to Daniel.

As great as the difference is between the grace of the Gospel, which was given through the Son, and the law, which was administered through a servant, so great is the difference between the ministers and assistants of the law—for servants were sent to servants—and between the promise and grace that was given through the Son to the sons and was afterward administered through the sons to the sons.

“He appointed him heir of all things.”

“Heir” is derived from *hero*, that is, “lord,” because the heir rules over an inheritance with free authority. God the Father therefore appointed the Son heir of all things—that is, of the whole world, or of all creatures. This was not, however, according to his divinity, by which he is coeternal with the Father and equal to him in the omnipotence of the Godhead, and by which he eternally possesses all things with the Father. Rather, according to his humanity assumed by the Word, he was appointed Lord and heir over every creature, just as God the Father promised him, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth.”

And the Son himself, rising from the dead, speaks in the person of his humanity: “All authority,” he says, “has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” Let us not therefore divide the persons, but distinguish the natures.

Accordingly, we must carefully observe that the Apostle now speaks in this Epistle of the substance of his humanity and now of the substance of his divinity. When he said that he had been appointed by God the Father heir of all creatures, he referred this to his humanity. But wishing to distinguish between the nature of his divinity and his humanity, and to show what properly belonged to each nature, he added: “Through whom he also made the ages.”

The ages are so called from “following,” because they follow one another by returning and coming back upon themselves. Here, however, by “ages” we should understand all things that were made in time. Thus, to show that the same one who came into the world in the last days and temporally received an inheritance had been with the Father before all ages, the Apostle said: “Through whom God the Father made all things that were made in time.” For what the evangelist John said, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” the Apostle signified by saying, “Through whom he also made the ages,” referring this to his divinity.

Then, elegantly employing certain stages of ascent, he arrived at that which is greater than all these things and proclaimed: “Who, being the radiance of his glory and the likeness of his substance.”

God the Father is light, as the same Apostle says when speaking of the Son: “Who dwells,” he says, “in inaccessible light”; and the Son is light, and the Holy Spirit is light. The Father is also radiance, and the Son is radiance; but it is impossible to define how radiance proceeds from radiance.

The Son is called the Father’s radiance because, just as in fire there are three inseparable things—namely, fire, heat, and radiance—yet fire and heat are shown to us through the radiance, although human things must not be compared with divine things [Col. 0687D–0688A], so the nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, inseparably joined and united, has deigned through its Word, as through its radiance, to reveal itself. It has also revealed the mystery of the Holy Trinity, as the Son himself says: “I and the Father are one,” and: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

In a wondrous manner, therefore, the Apostle displays the entire substance of the divinity of the Father and the Son, so as to disclose two persons in glory and radiance. Through the radiance he declared unity of essence with God the Father; in the name of glory he expressed the person of God the Father; and in the radiance, the person of the Son. Thus the Son is radiance from radiance, just as light is from light, God from God, brightness from brightness, and beginning from beginning.

He continues: “And the likeness of his substance.”

As far as human beings are concerned, likeness and substance are different. When the image and likeness of a man is painted on a wall, what is there is not the substance itself, but its likeness. The Apostle, however, used “likeness” here for the very substance and equality of essence. Elsewhere he used “form” for the same thing, saying: “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” For “form” there and “likeness” here declare one and the same quality of essence.

Christ, therefore, is the radiance of the Father and the likeness of his substance, because through him the Father was manifested, as he himself said: “Father, I have manifested your name to the people.” He is also equal to the Father in the substance of the Godhead.

He continues: “And sustaining all things by the word of his power.”

By saying “sustaining,” he wished to express the ease with which he contains all things; he used “sustaining” for “governing and directing.” The Word of God the Father therefore sustains all the things he made by the word of his power—that is, by the power of his might and by the word of his command he governs and directs all things.

For governing the world is no less than creating it. In creating, the substances of things were brought forth from nothing; in governing, the things that have been made are held together so that they do not return to nothing. Thus, while all these things are governed and things opposed to one another are fitted together, the great and wondrous judgment of God’s power is revealed.

After such a lofty account of the divine majesty in the Son, he descends to the lowliness of his incarnation and at the same time distinguishes the nature of his divinity from that of his humanity, saying: “Having made purification for sins.”

When he said, “Sustaining all things by his governance and by the direction of his power,” he referred this to his divinity. But what he added, “Having made purification for sins,” properly pertains to his humanity—namely, through the redemption of his passion and through the water of baptism. Thus John says in his Apocalypse: “He washed us from our sins in his blood.”

“He sits at the right hand of his majesty in the heights.”

The order of the words must be considered. First he declared that the Lord procured purification for us through his passion; afterward he said that he sits at the right hand of majesty in the heights. Christ first redeemed us by the blood of his passion, and afterward penetrated the heights of heaven, where he now sits at the Father’s right hand [Col. 0688D–0689A].

His sitting here means dwelling and being present in that place; likewise, “right hand” means the highest honor and dignity. We must not suppose that the almighty Father, who is uncircumscribed Spirit and fills all things, has a right or left hand as we do, or that his Son sits at his right hand as the sons of kings customarily sit beside their father on a throne placed next to his. Rather, as we have said, “right hand” is understood as glory and the honor of dignity.

Indeed, the Father is also written to be at Christ’s right hand, as it says in the Psalm: “The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings in the day of his wrath.” Both, therefore, are at the right hand, because there is nothing left-handed in the Godhead; for the human being assumed by the Word has already become one with God in glory and was exalted to the heavenly places on the fortieth day.

What, then, does “he sits at the right hand of majesty” mean, except that he dwells in the fullness of the Father’s majesty? And when he says “in the heights,” he shows that this man has been exalted above every angelic and human creature. Hence he continues:

“Having become so much superior to the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than they.”

Here “made” or “become” should be understood as “having assumed,” as though he were saying: “He inherited a name of sonship more distinguished and excellent than theirs.” For just as great as the difference is between the name of son and that of servant, so much greater is his dignity than that of the angels, since he is the Creator—I speak according to his divinity—whereas they are creatures.

That man also is greater than all the angels and every creature in this respect: the power that was in the Word before all ages came to rest in that man assumed by the Word from the time of his conception [Col. 0689B–C]. Therefore the angels are his ministers and servants, as was shown at his temptation and passion, and also at his resurrection and ascension.

He, however, exists as the proper Son and heir. The Apostle also intimates this to us when he adds: “For to which of the angels did he ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?”

“None of the angels” is understood. This must be understood of the Word of God, who is eternal and consubstantial with the Father, not of any creature, although we read in the Book of Job that angels are called sons of God. They are called sons also in Genesis; but whenever this occurs, it is an improper use of the term.

When, therefore, he said to him, “You are my Son,” at the time of baptism and on the mountain the paternal voice thundered from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son.” In saying, “You are my Son,” he makes clear that he was begotten from the Father’s very essence.

It should also be noted that he did not say, “I begot you before all ages,” or “in past time,” but “today I have begotten you.” “Today” is an adverb of the present time. In God, past things do not pass away and future things do not succeed them; rather, all times are joined together for him, because he possesses all things as present.

The meaning is: “Just as I am always eternal, having neither beginning nor end, so I always have you as coeternal with me.” The same is meant by what he said elsewhere: “Before Lucifer I begot you”—that is, before the angelic creature and before all ages.

And again: “I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a son.”

Do you see how he distinguishes the twofold nature in Christ? What he said shortly before, “Today I have begotten you,” refers to the divinity of eternity; but what he added, “I will be to him a Father,” refers without any doubt to the essence of his humanity. Accordingly, he appropriately used the future tense, saying: “I will be.”

For when God the Father said to David, “When you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring, which shall come forth from your loins, and I will establish his throne over your throne; he shall be my son, and I will be his Father,” it was still future that the Word of God the Father should assume a human being in the virgin’s womb in the unity of his person. Or the wording may be understood in this way because he would be the Son of God in truth, not adopted but proper.

This statement may also refer back to what precedes, so that it is read as a question: “Again, to which of the angels did he say, ‘I will be to him a Father’?” The answer is understood: “To none.” Or it may be read absolutely and affirmatively in this way: “Again, God the Father says of him: ‘I will be his Father.’”

And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: “And let all the angels of God worship him.”

Every only-begotten son can be called firstborn, because he is the first to open his mother’s womb; but not every firstborn is only-begotten, since a firstborn may have other brothers born afterward.

The Lord Jesus can be called both only-begotten and firstborn, according to both his divinity and his humanity. He is only-begotten according to his divinity, because in the nature of the Godhead he has no brothers born afterward. According to his humanity also he is the only-begotten son of blessed Mary, who bore no others after him, as Helvidius falsely alleges.

He is also firstborn according to the essence of his divinity, as Solomon testifies, saying: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature” [Col. 0690B–C]. According to his humanity he is firstborn among many adopted brothers, concerning whom he said to Mary: “Go to my brothers and say to them.”

When the Apostle says, “When God the Father again brought his firstborn into the world,” the words seem to imply that he had already been brought in once before. But how this is to be understood the evangelist John clearly explains, saying: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.”

The Word of God the Father, through whom all things were made, being of one essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is everywhere and fills all things. By encircling, he fills all things; he encircles the things to be filled. He presides by governing, and governs by presiding.

Because he was in the world, where he assumed flesh, and because he was inaccessible to our sight, since he could not be seen, he calls the assumption of flesh a second entry. For when he who was invisible to human sight made himself visible by assuming flesh, he was as though brought in again.

It should also be noted that what the Apostle calls an entry, Truth himself in the Gospel calls an exit, saying: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world.”

He rightly calls the assumption and manifestation of his incarnation an exit, because we were outside, expelled from God and placed outside the court of paradise, the palace of the eternal King. We had been placed in the prison of this world and banished into exile.

For example, just as criminals who incur the king’s displeasure are excluded from the royal court, sent into exile, and shut up in prison, but a good mediator, wishing to obtain pardon for them, does not first bring them into the king’s court. Instead, he goes out to them, there engages them in conversation, and then, after they have been corrected and chastised, brings them into the king’s presence.

In the same way the Lord Jesus presented himself. He came forth to us from the presence of the Father’s majesty by assuming flesh and making himself visible. He spoke with us the commandments of the eternal King. Then, having corrected and chastised us through his preaching and miracles, confirmed us in his faith, and cleansed us from sins through his passion, he brought us into the court and presence of the Father’s majesty when, ascending to heaven, he opened for us the entrance to the heavenly kingdom.

When he says that he was brought into the world, this signifies that the world was entrusted to him; he shows that he is Lord of the whole world. He will possess the world when he is acknowledged by all as Lord of the whole world.

Understand this statement, however, not of the substance of the Word but of the essence of the man.

What follows, “And let all the angels of God worship him,” has this meaning, as though he were saying: “Let all my angels, and his, worship him,” because they were made through him.

They worshiped him when they announced his birth, and when they came to him in his hunger and ministered to him; likewise when they guarded his tomb. They worship him daily because they obey his vision.

But did God the Father command only the angels to worship him? No, rather, he commanded every creature.

To the angels he says: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire.” When God the Father—or divine Scripture—says this to the angels, it is as though he were speaking “of angels,” using *to* in place of *of*. For the Apostle does not preserve the order or sense of the prepositions. The meaning is: He whom the angels are commanded to worship makes angels from those spirits of his whenever he wishes; he also makes his ministers a flame of fire, because those who stand in his presence he makes burning and aflame with his love, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “Into whom the angels desire to look.”

When he said, “He makes his angels spirits,” he expressed the words in an inverted order. He ought to have said: “He makes his spirits angels.”

It must be understood that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. They are always spirits, but they are by no means always called angels, except when they are sent. For *angel* (Greek: ἄγγελος) is rendered in Latin as *nuntius*, “messenger.” If you ask for the name of their nature, it is “spirit”; from the fact that one is sent, it is “angel.” For example, “human being” is the name of a nature, whereas “soldier” is the name of an office.

The passage may also be understood in another way: the ministers of almighty God are priests and ecclesiastical superiors, in accordance with what Malachi said: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

The priests of the Church are therefore angels when they announce the joys of the heavenly homeland to their hearers, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near”; and: “The righteous will shine like the sun and will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

They are a flame of fire when they threaten their hearers with the terror of the fire of Gehenna, saying: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” [Col. 0691D–0692A].

“But to the Son”—the Psalmist is understood to say:

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom.”

Observe how, and with what clarity, he distinguishes the angelic creature from the Son, who created all things.

“Throne” (*thronos*, Greek: θρόνος) is rendered in Latin as *sedes regia*, “royal seat,” just as it is also called a *solium*. By “throne” we may understand the kingdom in one sense; by “scepter,” which is a golden rod, the power of the kingdom is understood.

The Psalmist therefore says, addressing the Son of God: “O God, your kingdom and the power of your rule will remain for ever and ever.”

Gabriel says something similar to Mary: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

This is the kingdom concerning which the crowds cried out: “Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that has come,” and of which the Lord himself said to Pilate: “My kingdom is not of this world.”

Alternatively, we may appropriately understand “throne,” as the seat of judges, to mean the judgment that proceeds from the seat. This is the judgment of which the Son of Man says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”; and of which the Psalmist says: “O God, give your judgment to the king and your righteousness to the king’s son,” that is, to Christ.

The throne of God, therefore, will remain for ever and ever, because the final judgment that he will give to the elect, saying, “Come, blessed of my Father,” and to the reprobate, “Go into eternal fire,” will stand between the two groups with eternal separation, as the Gospel testifies, saying: “Then these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

What follows, “The rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom,” is understood as the uprightness of his sentence and judgment, or as the just power of his kingdom. This rod rules the righteous with justice and strikes the wicked justly and rightly, governing and judging all without partiality.

“You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.”

This rod makes things upright, so that righteousness is loved and iniquity hated. No one can perfectly love righteousness unless he has hated iniquity.

Iniquity, which is also called ἀνομία (*anomia*), is understood as whatever is done against the divine law. For love of truth is hatred of falsehood.

Because the Lord loved righteousness, since he did not sin, and hated iniquity, he explains what he first deserved to receive, saying: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

The Psalmist addresses the Son of God and says: “O God, God—your God, the Father—has anointed you with the oil of exultation, because you hated iniquity and loved righteousness.”

We must not understand this to mean that the Son of God, according to the nature of his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, can have God as his God, since he himself with the Father is the true God. According to the fact that he is human, however, he has God the Father, because he was made by him. Therefore the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you.”

He was anointed not with visible oil but with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, who from the day of his baptism rested upon him in the form of a dove [Col. 0692D–0693A]. Nor did the fullness of the Holy Spirit remain in him only from the time of his baptism; rather, it was present from the time of his conception, as Isaiah testifies, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding,” and so forth.

He says that he was anointed with the oil of exultation or gladness because Christ never sinned and never experienced sadness from the recollection of sin. For what does it mean to be anointed with the oil of gladness except to have no stain of sin?

The conscience of the saints becomes increasingly cheerful and bursts into gladness when it is not tormented by the recollection of any grave sin. The Holy Spirit, therefore, who rested in Christ guarded him, so that he was conceived without sin, born without sin, and passed from this world without the stain of sin, in accordance with what is written of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

But what does the Psalmist mean when he says: “God has anointed you above your companions”? Who are his companions?

In the Old Testament, the patriarchs were companions of Christ in this anointing, as it is written in the Psalm, where the Lord says of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to Abimelech and the other kings of the Philistines: “Do not touch my anointed ones.”

Kings, priests, and prophets were also his companions, because anointing especially belonged to them, through which they were deemed worthy to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For we read that Saul was anointed, as were Samuel and David. Solomon too was anointed at Gihon.

Priests were anointed, as Aaron was anointed by Moses, when the Lord said to him: “You shall anoint Aaron and his sons for me as priests by perpetual right.”

Prophets likewise were anointed, as Elisha was anointed by Elijah, to whom the Lord said: “You shall anoint Elisha the prophet in your place.”

These three orders prefigured the Lord, who is the true King, Priest, and Prophet.

In the New Testament, his companions are the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and all who, washed by the grace of baptism, receive the gift of the Holy Spirit and are called Christians from Christ.

Christ, therefore, was anointed with the oil of gladness above all his companions because all others receive the Holy Spirit according to a measure, whereas he does not receive him according to a measure but in fullness, in accordance with the statement: “For God the Father does not give the Spirit by measure to his Son”; and: “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” [Col. 0693C–D].

“And: ‘You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.’”

After speaking of the excellence of the humanity of the Son of God, he turns again to the eternity of his divinity, saying: “You, Lord,” he says, “in the beginning of the creatures founded the earth.”

Where did he found the earth? If we consider the matter carefully, we shall see that by the divine will and disposition it subsists, founded upon nothing except itself.

When he said, “The heavens are the works of your hands,” we must not suppose that the Word of God the Father works with hands, since there are no bodily features in the nature of the Godhead as there are in us. We must therefore understand “the works of his hands” as the power of his command: by the word and power of his command he works whatever he wills, in accordance with what the Psalm says: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

By the power of the Word of God, therefore, heaven and earth subsist, because all things were made by the power of his command, and without him nothing was made.

But since Moses, at the beginning of Genesis, says that heaven was made first and earth afterward, saying: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” the question arises why the Psalmist places earth first and heaven afterward, as though earth had been made before heaven.

The question is resolved as follows: what Moses placed before the earth, the Psalmist placed after it. This was done to show that the two were made together. Yet what the divine majesty made together, the human voice could not utter together; therefore it was necessary to name one before the other.

“They will perish, but you will remain.”

Here the plural number is used for the singular, as in many other places of divine Scripture. This should not be understood of the firmament in which the stars are contained, nor of the ethereal heaven through which the courses of the seven planets are carried out. Rather, it should be understood of this aerial heaven, from which the birds of heaven are named.

On the day of judgment this aerial heaven, from which we draw and release breath, will perish—not so that it completely ceases to exist according to its nature, but so that it will be changed from its present form into a better one, and from its present density into the subtlety and brightness of the ether. Hence the Apostle said elsewhere: “The form of this world is passing away.”

If the form passes away, the substance will remain. For as much space as the waters occupied at the time of the Flood—so that they rose fifteen cubits above all the mountains under the whole heaven, and, as some say, reached as far as the circle of the moon—so much space the fire will occupy on the day of judgment, accompanying the Lord’s coming, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “Fire will go before him.” For it will consume all the clouds and all the density of this air, and there will be a new heaven and a new earth [Col. 0694B–C].

The Lord also speaks of this transformation in the Gospel, saying: “Heaven and earth will pass away.” They will indeed pass away from this form and appearance into something better through renewal, but they will remain in their own substance.

“And they will all grow old like a garment.”

By “garment” here we should understand the human body, which is worn down by the length of time and the pain of illness and is reduced to dust. Just as the human body grows old and is reduced to dust but will be renewed through resurrection on the day of judgment, so this aerial heaven, through excessive longevity, has in a certain sense already grown old; but on the day of judgment it will be renewed through the kindling of fire.

“And like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed.”

A cloak is called *amictus* from *amicire*, “to surround.” Heaven is therefore appropriately compared with a cloak by which we are surrounded. For just as a cloak encircles the human body on every side, so heaven encircles the earth, which is balanced in equal measure. Elsewhere it is compared with the skin of a living creature, when the Psalmist says: “Stretching out the heavens like a skin.”

“You will change heaven,” he says, “like a cloak,” as though he were saying: Just as a cloak, if it has been spread out, is easily folded and, once folded, is easily spread out again, and if it has been soiled, can easily be cleansed, so the heaven stretched out and arranged by you will be changed with incomprehensible ease on the day of judgment from this form and appearance into something better.

And to show that the things made by the Lord would remain under eternity, he added: “And they will be changed,” as though he were saying: After they have been changed, they will remain in that renewal and will never return to this corruptible state [Col. 0694D–0695A].

“But you are the same, and your years will not fail.”

Here is the difference between a creature made temporally and the Creator, who remains equally in his eternity. No past or future, nor any mutability, affects almighty God; all things are present to him, and he is always immutable.

Therefore the Psalmist, carefully contemplating the eternity and immutability of the Word of God, used the substantive verb of the present tense when speaking of him: “Heaven and earth,” he says, “will be changed, but you are the same”—that is, you are now what you were before all ages.

“And your years,” that is, your eternity, “will not fail.”

He who always possesses being therefore says of himself to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

Therefore every rational creature, which is mutable in itself or temporal, must strive with all its strength to be joined and attached to him who always remains the same.

“To which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’?”

After showing that the majesty of divine eternity exists in the Son, the blessed Apostle again turns his speech to the glorification of his humility, saying: “To which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand’?” “None” is understood. For God the Father granted this glory to no archangel, no dominion, power, or principality, so as to say to him: “Sit at my right hand”—that is, “Dwell with me and rest in the fullness of my majesty.”

But to the victorious Son, the triumphant conqueror of the whole world through the dispensation of his incarnation, after the glory of his resurrection, on the fortieth day he says: “You labored in your passion; you labored in the redemption of the human race. Rest with me in glory until I make your enemies your footstool.”

“Until” or “as long as” does not here signify the end of a period of time but is used for what is infinite and eternal, as though he were saying in other words: “Dwell forever in the fullness of my majesty, because I will always subject your enemies—the Jews and other unbelievers—to your eternity.”

The feet of the Lord signify the stability of eternity, where he stands, as upon firm footprints, by the power of his omnipotence.

We may also appropriately understand the feet as the mystery of his incarnation in two ways. His enemies are subjected to him daily when, abandoning the opposition of vice and unbelief, they voluntarily submit themselves to him for salvation, so that they may be protected under him. Or else, when they refuse to believe in him, they are compelled to submit to him and are trampled beneath the dominion of his power.

“Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?”

If all the spirits of the heavenly powers are sent for the salvation of believers, why did Daniel say: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him”? For how can all be sent if ten thousand times ten thousand stand before him?

We must understand that almighty God, who is uncircumscribed Spirit, fills all things and is wholly everywhere. Therefore the angelic spirit, which is circumscribed, wherever it is sent runs within the Lord and always has the Lord present. Consequently, those who are sent also stand before him.

Or else they are called “all” because, as Didymus the Greek says in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, they are sent from all the orders of the heavenly dignities. Thus we read in the book of Daniel that the archangels Gabriel and Michael were sent; Raphael was sent to Tobit; and one of the seraphim was sent to Isaiah when he touched his lips with a coal. Angels are also frequently read to have been sent to the saints [Col. 0696A–B].

In general, as the teachers say, each of the faithful receives from God, from the time of birth—or rather, from the time of baptism—an angel for his protection and to urge him to do good. Hence the Apostle says here: “They are sent for the ministry of salvation, on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of the heavenly homeland.”

In this passage, therefore, as we have said, all are sent because they are sent from all the orders. Those who are sent possess the same dignity as those who stand before him. Or else they are all of one will; and while those who always stand before him agree with those who are sent, in a certain sense all come and all are sent in those who are sent.

The meaning is: What wonder is it if the angels offer their ministry to the only Son of God, when it is also clear that they have been made ministers of our salvation? Therefore he said to none of them: “Sit at my right hand.”

## CHAPTER II.

Therefore, we ought to observe more carefully the things that we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away.

Therefore—what wonder is it that the Son of God is superior to all the angels, since he has given us his Gospel? Or certainly, because the angels minister to us and continually report our deeds to God, although he is everywhere, we ought to observe more carefully and more fully the things that we have heard from Christ in the Gospel and from his apostles than we formerly observed in the Law, which was given through a servant. And why “more carefully”? Lest perhaps we drift away—that is, lest perhaps we perish and fall away from salvation. Or lest perhaps we vanish, passing into destruction like a river flowing into the sea, while our thoughts wander through empty things. [Col. 0696D]

He joins his own person to theirs, as is his custom. And he gives the reason why he said “more carefully” when, in the words that follow, he explains it, saying: “For if the word spoken through angels was made firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we have neglected so great a salvation?”

The word of the Law and of the prophets was spoken through angels to our fathers, because he spoke to Moses and the prophets through a subordinate creature, in accordance with what blessed Stephen also declares in his dispute concerning Moses: “This is Moses who was with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai.”

The word spoken through the angel was made firm—that is, true—because everything happened just as it had been foretold there, whether good or evil. Every transgression, or violation of the Law, and every disobedience committed against that word received a just recompense of reward, namely, the judgment of eternal condemnation. Thus it happened to those who murmured.

It should be noted, however, that although “reward” is generally understood in a good sense, here the Apostle used it for evil, according to his customary practice, without concern for the proper meanings of words, placing one term indifferently for another: here, for example, “reward” for evil, and elsewhere “captivity” in a good sense, where he said: “Take every thought captive to obey Christ.”

The Apostle therefore makes a comparison between the word of the Law, which was spoken through an angel, and the grace of the Gospel given through the Son, and says: If the word of the Law spoken through angels was shown to be true in all the good things that it promised or the evils that it threatened, how much more firm will be the word of the Gospel given through the Son! And if those who were disobedient to the Law received condemnation and could not escape judgment, how shall we escape the vengeance of God if we have neglected so great a salvation—namely, the faith of the Gospel and eternal life, so great because it was announced and promised to us through the Son? One must understand: in no way.

By these words the Apostle makes clear that the Law did not contain as great a salvation as the Gospel. The Law promised the earth, saying: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land.” The Gospel promised the kingdom of heaven, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” The Law inflicted vengeance upon earthly enemies; the Gospel inflicts it upon spiritual ones. The Law promised a long temporal life; the Gospel grants life that will endure without end.

“Which”—understand, “salvation.”

When it first began to be proclaimed by the Lord, it was confirmed to us by those who heard him. The salvation contained in the Gospel therefore received from God the beginning of its proclamation: he himself first announced it through his own person, saying, “Repent,” and so forth, and, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” Then it was confirmed—that is, believed—by those who heard him, namely, by the apostles who were with him and by their successors. Or certainly, it was confirmed, that is, consolidated and perfected in us, by those who received it from the Lord himself, because the salvation given to us through the Holy Spirit remains forever. [Col. 0697D]

For the sake of humility he joins his own person to theirs, saying: “It was confirmed in us by those who heard.” Someone might then say: How was it confirmed by them? He answers: “God bearing witness by signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.”

“It was confirmed,” he says, “in us by those who heard,” with God bearing witness—that is, giving simultaneous testimony to their teaching and preaching, not by voice but by power, by the display of miracles, and by the variety of tongues. For when one of the apostles said to a dead or sick person, “Rise; be alive or be well,” that person immediately rose up whole.

Here “signs,” “wonders,” and “powers” are understood as one and the same thing. But when he adds “distributions of the Holy Spirit,” he signifies the abundance of graces that the fathers of the Old Testament did not possess, which was given after Jesus had been glorified, as the Gospel bears witness, saying: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

These are the distributions, or divisions, that the Apostle recalls elsewhere, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom,” and so forth, listing the gifts that follow, until he adds: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills.”

Hence here also he says: “According to his will.” For he apportions all things according to the divine will and counsel, so that no one may trust in his own merits. The Holy Spirit himself knows what benefits each person and what is advantageous for each.

For God did not subject the world to come to angels, concerning which we are speaking. He refers to what he said above, that God the Father said: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet”; but he handed the world over to his Son. To him he said in the psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

Therefore the Son himself, rejoicing that the world destined to believe had been handed over to him, says: “But I have been appointed king by him,” that is, by God the Father.

But he testified in a certain passage, saying—[Col. 0698C]

In this epistle he suppresses the names of the prophets whose testimony he knows. He does this not out of envy or from a desire to conceal them, but from an intention to honor them and to show that the Hebrews to whom he was writing possessed great knowledge of the divine Scriptures, so much so that he did not even need to name the one who spoke.

This testimony, then, was taken from the Psalter of David. He speaks to God the Father as follows: “What is man?” This must be pronounced softly and with contempt. “What is man?” Understand: fragile, mortal, transitory, and overcome by the inherited corruption that came from Adam’s ancient sin.

“That you are mindful of him.” Understand: and therefore you lavish upon him the gifts of your mercy.

It follows: “Or the son of man”—understand, “what is he?” The teachers refer this same expression to Christ, who very frequently calls himself in the Gospel “the Son of Man,” that is, the son of Mary. For this reason the voice should be raised in the form of a question. The meaning is: What merit did that man assumed by the Word possess, that he should become the Son of God?

But what follows—“that you visit him”—they refer to the human race, of which it was said shortly before, under the name “man”: “What is man?” The meaning is: That you visit the human race through your Son and continually bestow benefits upon it is not due to its merit but to your grace; and it endures because it is visited by you.

Visitation pertains to a physician and to a sick person. A physician is said to fulfill the duty of visitation when he enters to see someone who is ill. The human race, which was sick and weakened, was visited by God the Father when he sent his Son, who became flesh as the Word and dwelt among us. Concerning this visitation, Zachariah, the father of blessed John, also said: “The dawn from on high has visited us.”

Some teachers refer everything in the words, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you are—that you visit him?” to the human race; [Col. 0699A] but what follows they unanimously refer to Christ.

“You made him a little lower than the angels.” Through the death of his body and the shame of his Passion, God the Father made his Son lower than the angels, although according to his divinity he was equal to the Father in omnipotence, since the angels are immortal and incapable of suffering.

He was made lower, not by necessity but by voluntary compassion, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross.” In that respect in which he could die, the Creator of the angels was made lower than the angels.

He rightly said, “a little lower,” because although he assumed a mortal body, he had no stain of sin.

“You crowned him with glory and honor.” The Psalmist speaks to God the Father about the Son’s humiliation and exaltation, saying: “You made your Son a little lower than the angels”—that is, when you made him mortal—“but because he remained obedient to you unto death, you crowned him with glory and honor.”

The same is expressed by what the Apostle says elsewhere: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth.”

God the Father crowned him with glory in the resurrection, and with honor in the ascension, when, on the fortieth day after his resurrection, he exalted him above every creature.

Alternatively: He was crowned with glory in the multitude of believers, when, after the triumph of the resurrection, he received the inheritance of the whole world insofar as he is man; and with honor in the confession of his eternal majesty, that is, in the fact that he dwells in the fullness of the Father’s glory.

“And you appointed him over the works of your hands.” Because he became man, he was appointed by God the Father over the works of creation: over heavenly, earthly, and infernal things. According to the power of his divinity, just as he had created all things together with God the Father, so also he possessed all things together with him.

By saying, “You appointed him over the works of your hands,” every creature is shown to be subject to him. For just as all things were created by the Word, so that man assumed by the Word possesses all things with the Word.

“You subjected all things beneath his feet”—that is, to his eternity and power, so that every creature might adore him. This is what he himself said to them when he appeared after the glory of the resurrection: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him. In this gift, or act, by which he subjected all things to him, he appears to have excluded neither heavenly nor earthly things. He did not say, “after the angelic creature,” but concluded in this way: “He subjected all things to him.”

“But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.” What does blessed Paul mean? For after saying that all things were subjected to Christ, he immediately added: “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.”

If all things are subject to him, how are they not subject? This must therefore be understood as follows. Above, where he said, “He left nothing that was not subject to him,” we should understand universal subjection: voluntary subjection, namely through faith, and necessary subjection, by which every creature is compelled to be subject to its Creator.

But here, where he said, “We do not yet see all things subjected to him,” we should understand only voluntary subjection, which consists in faith and which those who refuse to believe in him do not possess.

Because, at the time when the Apostle said these things, the preaching of the Gospel had not yet been spread throughout the whole world, and not all those predestined to life had yet believed, he rightly says, “Now they are not yet all subject to him.” And not only at that time: even now, not all the predestined believe.

“But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.” Here he clearly shows that Christ’s glory and honor were his cross, on account of which he was made a little lower than the angels by dying for our salvation. Therefore elsewhere, after the Apostle had said, “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross,” he immediately continued: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.”

So also the Lord himself called the cross glory when he said: “That the Son of Man may be glorified.” If the one who is Lord calls those things glory which he suffered for servants, much more should you, a human being, have no doubt that what you suffer for God pertains to your everlasting glory.

“This one,” I say—that is, Jesus—we see crowned, not with bodily eyes but with the eyes of the mind, while he sits in the fullness of the Father’s majesty.

“So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.” The Son is called the grace of God the Father because he was freely given to us by God the Father and because he freely endured death for us. It was not owed to us on account of our merit that the Son of God should taste death for us; rather, he did this by ineffable grace.

When he says that he tasted death for everyone, some teachers understand this absolutely, so that “for everyone” means for all for whom he tasted death—that is, for the elect predestined to eternal life.

Others, however, understand it universally, so that it means that he died for everyone, even though not everyone will be saved. And what if not everyone believes? He nevertheless did what was his to do.

Blessed Prosper therefore offers the following comparison. Suppose there is a most skilled physician who comes to a populous city in which there are many sick people. He prepares a potion against every kind of illness and summons everyone, saying: “Come, all you people who suffer from various illnesses, and drink from this potion, which I have prepared for your healing. I assure you and solemnly declare that whoever drinks from it will immediately obtain healing.”

Those who believe his words come, drink, and are cured; those who refuse to drink are not cured but waste away in their illness. Thus, as far as the physician’s devotion is concerned, he prepared the potion for the health of all of them, although it benefits only those who drink from it. So also Christ, insofar as it depended on him, died for everyone, although his Passion benefits only those who are willing to believe in him. [Col. 0701A]

At the same time, it should be noted that the Apostle did not say, “He was subjected to death,” but specifically, “He tasted death.” By this he wished to show the swiftness of the resurrection. For he could be held by death only for a short time, and once death had been conquered he immediately rose as victor.

“For it was fitting that the one for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, who had brought many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering.”

He says that it was fitting for him—that is, for the author of their salvation—to perfect, or complete, the salvation of all through the Passion of Christ. Christ is the author of the salvation of all believers, and before his Passion he had brought many adopted sons into the glory of faith, hope, and charity. They possessed a firm hope that they could attain the joys of the heavenly homeland and receive the inheritance of the eternal King.

Or certainly, through his Passion it was fitting for him to complete everything that had been proclaimed concerning him. Hence, hanging on the cross, he himself said: “It is finished.”

“For whom all things exist”—that is, through whose death all heavenly and earthly things have been restored: the human being has been redeemed and the number of the angels has been restored.

“And through whom all things exist”—understand, “were made,” in accordance with what John says: “All things were made through him.”

Do you see how he is in our midst and joined to us? He is a son, and we are sons: he is the proper Son, we are adopted; but he saves, and we are saved.

Do you see how he both joins and distinguishes us? When he says, “He had brought many sons to glory,” he joins us to himself. But when he adds, “the author of their salvation,” he distinguishes us from him.

“For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.”

Who is the one who sanctifies? Christ, through faith in his Passion and through the gift of baptism.

Who are those who are sanctified? All who believe, who are sanctified by faith in Christ’s Passion and by the grace of baptism.

But Christ, who sanctifies, and we, who are sanctified, are from one God the Father, because all things received their origin from him: for there is one God, from whom all things come.

Yet he is one kind of son, and we are another. He, as the proper Son, can sanctify; we, as adopted sons, are sanctified by him. Nevertheless, we have one Father in heaven: he the proper Son, we adopted.

“For what reason”—understand: because both he and we are from one God the Father, although distinctly.

“He is not ashamed to call them brothers.” Who are the adopted sons? He says: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.”

He is not ashamed to call them brothers, showing that this brotherhood is not the same as the brotherhood arising from our humanity, but that it proceeds from his great mercy and supreme humility, by which he chose us as brothers.

He also confirms this by prophetic testimony, lest it be thought something new and not foretold long beforehand. For he says: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.” That is, he promises that he will proclaim the sacred Passion and glorious resurrection, as well as the glory of the Father’s divinity and even the name by which he was called Father.

“I will proclaim,” he says—that is, “I will have it proclaimed by my preachers, so that you may believe in me.” For, rising from the dead, he says to the women: “Go and proclaim to my brothers.” And to Mary: “Go to my brothers.”

They are called brothers both because they love and because they are loved.

He added: “In the midst of the Church I will praise you”—in the midst of the Church, that is, in the assembly of the faithful.

The Son praised the Lord Father when, after the apostles had returned from preaching, he said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth”—that is, “I praise and glorify you”—“because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

He also praises God the Father in the midst of the Church when all his faithful, redeemed by his Passion and washed by his baptism, offer unceasing praises to God the Father in heart and deed.

God must be praised in these three ways.

And again: “I will put my trust in him”—that is, in God the Father.

This is the voice of the Son of God speaking of God the Father in his humanity. For the man assumed by the Word placed all his trust in God the Father. Hence he said: “Father, glorify your name.”

And when he prayed for his faithful, he said: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me.”

He also exhorted them to have confidence, commanding them: “Take courage; I have overcome the world.”

And again: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.”

These two testimonies are taken from the oracle of the prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Son of God.

These children are the saints, namely the apostles, to whom the Lord said: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” They are rightly called children because of their innocence and humility. Concerning them Truth itself says: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.”

Therefore, because the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same.

This was said concerning all the apostles and all the faithful: they were the Lord’s brothers because he had a true body and true blood, just as they did.

In this passage Marcion is manifestly confuted, since he dared to say that our Lord did not have a true body, whereas the Apostle says that, by assuming flesh, he became a participant in what they possessed. For just as those children—and we—consist of flesh and blood, so Christ likewise shared in flesh and blood by becoming man.

And just as Christ shared in our substance by assuming humanity, so we are participants in him through the assumption of his body and blood.

Why Christ shared in flesh and blood he makes clear in what follows, when he adds: “So that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their whole life.”

Here the Apostle presents something marvelous, showing that the devil was conquered by Christ through the very thing by which he held power in the world—the weapons that had once been strong against the world. This was death: through death Christ struck him.

It was like David, who took Goliath’s sword and cut off his head with the very weapon by which that former victor was accustomed to prevail.

Therefore, because the devil had presumptuously seized dominion in the world through the death of man, he was conquered through the temporal death of Christ.

For this reason Christ shared in flesh and blood, so that he could die for a time. Thus, when he died, although he had committed no sin, he destroyed the devil and death, because he was always dead to sin in that he did not sin.

Once the devil’s dominion had been destroyed, he freed his elect, who through fear of death throughout their life, while they lived in this world, were subject—that is, indebted and bound—to the slavery of death and the devil. [Col. 0703A]

They feared death because they were servants of death, since all were subject to death.

“For surely he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.”

He develops further the point he had made above, that the children shared in flesh and blood and that Christ participated in the same. He wishes to show from what source he shared in them, and he says: “He did not take hold”—that is, nowhere, neither in heaven nor on earth, did he assume the angelic creature; rather, he assumed a human body from the seed of Abraham.

By these words he speaks soothingly to them. Whom of them did he assume? Since the human being had to be rescued from death by the Son of God, he therefore did not assume an angelic nature, which cannot suffer death, but a human nature, in which he could die.

Nor was such dignity and honor conferred upon the angels that the Son of God should be joined to their nature in one person. Divine grace bestowed this dignity and honor upon human nature, so that God and man should be one person.

And why did he say “he took hold,” a word that pertains to someone fleeing? Because, as it were, we were withdrawing from him and fleeing far away, and he pursued and seized us.

“Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.”

“For this reason,” he says—that is, because he did not assume an angelic nature but a human nature from the seed of Abraham—“he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.”

What does “in every respect” mean? He was brought up and grew, he hungered, suffered, and died. In all these things he was like his brothers, because they are subject to the same condition.

But perhaps someone asks: Why was the fallen human being restored rather than the fallen angel?

The answer must be that the human being sinned less than the devil. The human being sinned after being persuaded by the devil; the devil fell through pride, without being persuaded by anyone.

Moreover, because the human being had a body, he needed to eat; but because the devil is a spirit, he is altogether without excuse.

There was also a third reason: the human being had not yet reached the place where he would reign eternally with God, but was dwelling in an earthly paradise, from which he was to be transferred to heaven after the number of the elect had been completed. The devil, however, had already been placed in heaven.

“So that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.”

He is called merciful from “a wretched heart,” namely, one who endures wretchedness and knows how to show mercy through experience.

Thus there was no other reason for his being made like his brothers in every respect except that he might show us mercy by redeeming us and become a faithful, true, and powerful high priest, interceding with God the Father for us and making propitiation for our sins.

This was the reason for this pitiable dispensation. He saw the human race doomed to death and bound by the chains of sins, and he took pity on it as a faithful high priest, reconciling us to God the Father and, by reconciling us, cleansing us.

For the ministry of a priest and high priest is to be faithful, so that he may free from sins those whose priest he is.

He is called a high priest because he provides a bridge—that is, a way—for those who follow him, through his good example.

Thus the Lord also made a bridge for us, that is, he showed us the way of life, when he said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.”

He also made a bridge for us because he opened for us the door of the heavenly homeland, where he now stands, interceding for us with God the Father. [Col. 0704A]

For in that in which he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able also to help those who are tempted.

“In that,” he says—that is, in his humanity, in which he himself was tempted, though not overcome, and suffered at the hands of his ministers.

He is able to free those who are bound and to assist those who are tempted, so that they may not be overcome, because he knew temptations not only as God but also tested them by experience as man.

Therefore he is able to have mercy on us not only because he is God, but also because he is man, since the man assumed by the Word possesses the same power as the Word himself.

CHAPTER III.

Therefore, holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the Apostle and High Priest of our confession [Col. 0704B], who is faithful to the one who made him, just as Moses was in all his house.

He calls them brothers both according to the flesh and according to the spirit: they were of the same race and held the same faith. He calls them holy because they had been sanctified by faith in Christ’s passion and by the water of baptism. They were sharers in the heavenly calling—that is, in the heavenly homeland—to which he called everyone when he said: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

“Consider,” he says, “Jesus, the Apostle and High Priest of our faith.” *Apostle* is Greek; in Latin it means “one who is sent.” The Lord Jesus was an apostle because he was freely sent by God the Father, as he himself testifies: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”; and: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” Hence the outstanding preacher says elsewhere: “God sent his Son, made from a woman” [Col. 0704C].

He is the High Priest of our confession because he presents the confession of our faith before God the Father. He is faithful to that same God the Father who made him, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “He was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.”

This statement is not concerned only with the substance of his humanity, in which he himself was faithful, obedient to God the Father even unto death. Was he not faithful to God the Father when he did not attribute anything he did to his own glory, but to the Father’s, saying: “The Father, remaining in me, himself does the works”?

“Just as Moses,” he says, “was—or was found to be—faithful in all his house.” Here we must understand the house of God as the people of God, namely, the Israelite nation, over which Moses was placed by God. Isaiah speaks of this house: “The vineyard of Sabaoth is the house of Israel.” Again, exhorting them, he says: “House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord” [Col. 0704D].

In that house Moses was faithful—that is, devoted and well-intentioned—delivering what belonged to God and not appropriating God’s glory for himself.

“For this man was considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the one who built the house has greater honor than the house.” Here there is a hypallage in the meaning, or a sufficiently necessary ellipsis. The sentence should be supplied in this way: “Christ was found worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as he has greater honor”—understand, “the Lord of the house, who built that same house.” Or: “Christ was found worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder has greater honor than the house that he himself built.”

He then gives the reason why the Lord has greater glory than the house built by him [Col. 0705A]: every house is built by someone, but God is the one who created everything. Here he distinguishes the builder from the building, intending us to understand God as the author of both houses, namely, of the people as well.

Moses, indeed, was faithful—that is, devoted and well-intentioned—in his whole house, like a servant, for testimony to them—understand, to the words that were to be spoken. Christ, however, is like a son over his own house: he dwells in it, ordering and arranging it.

There is as much difference between a servant whom the master of a household places over his house and a son whom he leaves as heir as there is difference and distinction between Moses and Christ. Moses was a faithful and devoted servant in the house of almighty God [Col. 0705B], that is, among the Israelite people, for testimony to those words that were to be spoken through him to the people, since he was a witness both to God’s words addressed to the people and to the people’s words addressed to God.

Christ, however, freely orders his own house, like a son receiving his paternal inheritance. Concerning this the Apostle adds immediately:

“We are his house, if we hold firmly to the confidence and the glory of our hope to the end.”

The Apostle again urges the Hebrews to stand firmly in the faith and to persevere in good works, joining himself to them in his customary manner. “We are,” he says, “the house of God, if we retain firmly to the end of our life, or until the day of judgment, confidence—that is, right faith—and the glory of our hope.”

The glory of our hope is that by which we glory in the hope that we are already children of God, and, as we possess it in hope, believe that we shall possess it in reality. For we can in no way possess in this painful life the good things promised to us. Therefore, possessing right faith, let us patiently await the certain rewards promised to us by the Lord.

It follows: “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,’” and so forth, up to: “They shall not enter into my rest.”

A little earlier the blessed Apostle had spoken of hope: that we ought to hope for the things that are to come. He then adds prophetic testimony, comparing how those who despaired of the power of almighty God perished and what the few who believed in God’s promises with certain hope obtained. Since, therefore, the Apostle spoke obscurely [Col. 0705D], it is necessary to rehearse the history of the Old Testament so that his discourse may become clearer.

The Israelite people had been led out of Egyptian slavery through the Lord’s signs and wonders. After they had traveled a long way through the desert, been fed by the Lord with manna, given water from the rock, and protected by him, they all took counsel to send leaders and scouts from each tribe to spy out and examine the land granted to them by the Lord.

These men traversed the land among its peoples. After forty days they returned to the multitude, reporting that the land was exceedingly fertile and produced abundant crops, but that it had impregnable cities and extremely powerful men—men of the race of Anak, that is, giants.

The Israelites, however, were ungrateful and foolish. They ought to have remembered God’s many benefits: how he had rescued them when they were enclosed amid such a great army of Egyptians; how he had delivered them from the dangers of the rivers; how he had given them inexhaustible springs from the rock; how he had supplied manna; and how he had bestowed countless other benefits upon them. Yet they still did not believe. Despairing of his power and remembering none of these things, they were overcome by desperate fear and murmured:

“Would that the Lord had not brought us into that land! Let us return to Egypt.”

God was therefore angry because they had so quickly forgotten his works and wonders, and he swore that that generation would not enter the rest and homeland once promised to their fathers. Thus the six hundred thousand who had gone out of Egypt perished, except only Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun, who had tried to restrain the people’s rebellion because they believed the Lord’s promise [Col. 0706B].

It should be noted that the Apostle mentions three rests in this epistle. The first is the Sabbath, on which God rested from his works. The second is Palestine, into which the Israelites entered and in which they were to rest from misery and many labors. The third is the true rest, namely, the kingdom of heaven. Those who are granted the opportunity to reach it will rest completely from the labors and troubles of this age.

The Apostle speaks here of this third rest prophetically and spiritually when he says: “Therefore”—understand, because we are the house of God, if we retain right faith and the firm glory of hope—“do not harden your hearts,” lest you suffer what your ancestors suffered when they were deprived of the promised rest [Col. 0706C].

By these words the Apostle urges the Hebrews not to be faithless and unbelieving and thus lose the eternal rest promised to them by the Lord, just as their fathers lost the temporal rest. “Do not harden your hearts,” he says, “as your fathers hardened theirs, in the provocation”—that is, in the bitterness, when they provoked me to bitterness—“according to the day of temptation in the desert, where your fathers tempted me.”

They did so in many ways, saying: “Can God prepare a table in the desert?” and: “Can he bring us into the land promised to our fathers?”

When the Psalmist says “today,” he is not speaking to those who died in the desert while murmuring against God and remaining unbelieving, but rather to those who lived during the time of the Lord’s preaching and of the apostles, and to all who will live until the end of the age [Col. 0706D].

“Today,” he says—that is, in the day of the New Testament, or at every time so long as it is called “today”—“do not harden your hearts.” For “today” stands for eternity, as long as the world and the present life remain.

It follows: “They tested and saw my works, for forty years.”

When he says, “They tested my works and wonders,” this must not be understood as though “they tested” meant that they chose them as a cause for thanksgiving. Rather, this testing must be referred to curiosity and temptation. “They tested my works,” he says: that is, out of curiosity they investigated them while tempting me, asking whether I was almighty.

But what happened? They saw those works for forty years and remained ungrateful.

The phrase “for forty years” can also be joined to what follows. The number forty is understood to be mystical in divine Scripture. The Lord fasted for forty days in the desert in order to triumph over the one through whom those people had murmured against God for forty years in the desert.
