After the completion of these things, he remained with his disciples for forty days in the glory of victory, through his passion and resurrection, before he entered the heights of heaven [Col. 0707A].

In the first forty days, therefore, he showed the temptation of this pilgrimage; in the later forty days, the consolation with which they are to be consoled in the homeland. For his body, that is, the Church, must suffer temptations in the present age so that afterward it may reach the joys of the heavenly homeland. Nevertheless, even in the present life the Consoler is not absent, for he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” [Col. 0707B].

It follows: “Therefore”—understand, because they tempted me and out of curiosity tested my works for forty years—“I was offended with that generation.”

To be called offended, or hostile, is stronger than to be called angry. Someone who becomes angry can easily be recalled from anger; but one who is hostile or offended can scarcely, or not at all, be appeased. Thus almighty God was offended—that is, extremely and implacably angry—with those six hundred thousand who perished in the desert.

“And I said”—to Moses and Aaron, or even to Joshua—“They always err in their heart.”

Almighty God chastised them in many ways, but they always went astray in their hearts, deviating from the way of truth and uprightness. Whoever does not obey God’s will goes astray from the uprightness of justice.

“But they did not know my ways” [Col. 0707C].

When he says, “They did not know,” he means that they did not approve me, nor did they choose my actions and commandments. Or, “They did not know” because they still refused to know them, so as to hold and observe them.

“To whom I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest.”

“Si” sometimes expresses affirmation, sometimes doubt, and sometimes negation, as in the present passage, where it means “not,” and in the Psalm where the prophet says: “If I repaid those who repaid me evil”—that is, “I did not repay.”

The order of the words is: “They shall not enter into my rest, as I swore in my anger.”

God’s anger is his vengeance. To speak of God is a great matter; to say that he swears is exceedingly fearful. Since every word of his ought to be accepted as an oath, because he is truthful, he is nevertheless sometimes said to swear in order to intensify the force of the matter and to instill terror in his hearers. Likewise, he is said to become angry in the human manner, although he himself always remains the same, so that when we hear that he is angry, we may fear to sin.

When he said, “They shall not enter into my rest,” we must understand here, as was said above, a twofold rule: one rest is the rest of the earthly promise made to Abraham, which they lost because of their unbelief; the other is eternal life, of which the Apostle speaks spiritually, into which the Jews who remain in unbelief will not enter [Col. 0707D].

“See to it, brothers, lest there be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing you to depart from the living God.”

The Apostle again urges them by gentle exhortation, calling them brothers and giving them advice on how they may enter into the rest.

“My brothers according to the flesh, and brothers also according to faith, see”—that is, take care and attend with the utmost diligence—“lest there be in any one of you an evil will and an evil heart of unbelief, causing you to depart from the living God,” as happened to those who went astray in the desert by worshiping idols, and lest you perish as they perished [Col. 0708A].

“But exhort one another each day, while it is called ‘today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.”

Because he was writing to Jews who had already believed, among whom there were people able to exhort others in faith, hope, and good works, he speaks in this way: “Exhort,” he says, “one another, and correct one another each day, while it is called ‘today’”—that is, throughout the whole period of the present life, in which there is opportunity for repentance.

If anyone has sinned, let him not despair of pardon as long as he lives. Let none of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin—that is, by the despair produced by the deceit of unbelief, as though pardon could not be obtained through repentance [Col. 0708B].

The one who does not fully believe in salvation often falls into despair. He then gives the reason why no one should despair of pardon, saying:

“For we have become sharers in Christ.”

What does “we have become sharers in Christ” mean? We are made sharers in Christ and joined to him, as one with him and existing in him. We share in him because he is our head and we are his members, coheirs and fellow members with him according to the spiritual person who was created in him.

We also share in him because we receive his body and blood for our redemption [Col. 0708C]. Therefore, we must not despair, provided that we hold firmly to the beginning of his substance until the end, as it is said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts in rebellion against God, as in that provocation.”

Understand: their fathers hardened their hearts.

By “the beginning of his substance” he means faith in Christ, through which we subsist and are reborn, because he is the foundation of all virtues. He rightly calls it “substance,” because just as the body subsists and is given life through the soul, so the soul subsists in God through faith and lives by this faith, without which it is nothing. Hence the prophet says: “But my righteous one lives by faith.” The same outstanding preacher says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.”

The substance of Christ is called faith either because it is given by him or because he himself dwells through it in the hearts of the faithful, in accordance with what the same Apostle says elsewhere, praying that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, in the inner person [Col. 0708D].

We are therefore truly sharers in Christ if we retain his faith firmly until the end of our life or until the day of judgment—in other words, throughout the whole time for which it is said through the prophet: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

For some who heard provoked him, but not all who departed from Egypt through Moses.

He silently recalls that history when, after the scouts returned, the people murmured: “Would that the Lord had not brought us into that land!” Joshua and Caleb, however, glorified God, saying to the whole multitude: “The Lord is powerful in faith” [Col. 0709A]. Therefore, it profited them nothing that they heard, because they were not found worthy to enter it.

## CHAPTER IV

[lacuna]

After these words of exhortation the Apostle adds, saying: “For we who have believed shall enter into his rest,” just as he said: “As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest.” At this point, for the completion of the meaning, something must be added. “Let us enter,” he says, “into the rest of the heavenly homeland promised to us by God, lest, if we should be unbelieving, it be said to us as it was to those who did not enter: ‘They shall enter into my rest’”—that is, they shall not enter into my rest. By these words he exhorts everyone to enter into the Lord’s rest, lest, because of our unbelief, what was said to those people be said to us also. For just as it is certain that unbelievers will not enter, so it is held as certain and fixed that believers will enter.

“And indeed, his works were completed from the foundation of the world”—that is, the adornment of the world was completed. For in a certain passage he spoke in this way about the seventh day: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” In Genesis God said this through Moses. By these words the Apostle wishes to show that the rest to which we have been called is different from the rest that existed in Palestine, to which the Jews were called. He does not say that we shall enter into that rest which existed in Palestine; rather, he shows that they did not enter because of the hardness of their hearts—neither into Palestine nor into the heavenly rest. Thus he speaks of the first rest: “The Lord rested on the seventh day from all his works.”

He did indeed rest from the creation of new creatures, but he did not rest from governing what he had made, nor from producing from them even now, day by day, what comes forth from them. Hence Truth says to the Jews in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” For it was no greater act for God to create the world from nothing than to govern what had been made.

Having therefore mentioned the first rest of the seventh day, on which God rested, he added a second rest, which was promised to the people of God, saying: “Of that rest he said in a certain passage through Moses.” And in this place—“place” being understood—he says again: “If they shall enter into my rest.” The conjunction *if*, as has already been said above, can be understood as affirmation, doubt, or denial. Above, it was placed in two passages as a denial, where he said that God had sworn because of their unbelief: “If they shall enter into my rest”—that is, they shall not enter. Here, however, it can be understood as an affirmation, in another sense, as John Chrysostom and other teachers explain it, as though he were saying: “If they shall enter into my rest”—that is, they shall prosper. And understand this of the rest that existed in Palestine. Hence he immediately adds: “Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief.”

Because only a few entered that rest which existed in Palestine—namely, only two, Caleb and Joshua, out of all those who came out of Egypt—he therefore says: “Since it remains,” or “since it is left,” for some to enter into the rest of the promised land; and these, that is, the six hundred thousand to whom it was first announced, did not enter it, but their corpses were laid low in the wilderness.

Again, he marks out a certain day as “today” in David, saying, after so long a time, as was said above: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” The order of the words is: After so long a time—the time after they murmured and died in the wilderness—the Holy Spirit marks out, that is, establishes and defines, another certain day, namely, the time of the New Testament, saying through David: “Today,” and so forth.

Here the Apostle speaks in the person of the prophet: “Today, if you hear his voice,” as though he were saying in other words: “O Jews, my fellow citizens, do not think that what David said—‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts’—refers to the time when they murmured in the wilderness, or that he said it for the sake of the salvation of those who were already dead. It refers to another time, namely, the time of the New Testament. For from the day of their murmuring in the wilderness there was a long interval until David, and until us, to whom David spoke these words. At the same time, the day must be understood as referring to the time of the Lord’s coming and of the New Testament.”

What he says, “in David,” is equivalent to “through David,” the preposition being changed in the customary manner. What he said can also be understood in this way: “He marks out a certain day”—that is, the Holy Spirit establishes a limit and an end to the former time, which lasted from the day of their murmuring, and gives a beginning to another time, saying through David: “Today.”

He continues: “For if Jesus”—the son of Nun, leader of the Israelite people—“had given them rest”—understand, true rest—“he would never have spoken afterward of another day.” “Afterward,” that is, from that day onward, after they had obtained that rest.

Here he indicates a third kind of rest, of which David spoke when he said, “Today,” and so forth. He does not mean the rest into which Jesus the son of Nun led the people, but another, far more excellent rest, into which not the typological Jesus but the true Jesus daily leads those who belong to him. For if Jesus the son of Nun had given true rest to the people whose leader he was, David would never afterward have spoken of another rest.

It is therefore certain, as something still future, that some will receive the rest prefigured by that rest which existed in Palestine. Thus—understand, because Jesus the son of Nun did not provide true rest for the people over whom he presided—“a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God.” A true rest is reserved for the future, namely, eternal life, which surpasses the Sabbath of the law. In that Sabbath only bodies rested; in this rest, the souls of the people of God rest.

Hence it also follows: “For whoever has entered into his rest”—the rest of almighty God, which is eternal life—“has himself also rested from his works,” earthly works and all labors, “as God did from his.” God rested on the seventh day.

God’s rest is to be understood as the completion of his works: when the primordial creation of things had been completed on the sixth day, he ceased on the seventh from creating new natures. Through that rest of God—which is not eternal—he earnestly urges us to strive with all our strength toward the rest of eternal blessedness, which he calls the sabbath-rest.

Whoever, therefore, enters this Sabbath of God rests forever from every labor and work, just as God rests from the creation of new things. Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest, lest anyone fall into the same example of unbelief.

Faith is indeed a great and saving reality, since without it no one can be saved, as it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” But faith alone is not sufficient for salvation. It is necessary to work through the love that belongs to faith and to conduct oneself worthily of God, because faith without works is dead.

Considering, therefore, the faithfulness of eternal life, the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Let us hasten, through right faith and holy conduct, to enter that rest of the heavenly homeland promised to us, lest any of you fall into the same example of unbelief and despair into which those people fell.”

“Let us hasten,” he says, because faith alone is not sufficient; a life worthy of faith must also be added. We are sufficiently instructed by the example of our ancestors, lest, falling into the same condition into which they fell, we suffer what they suffered.

“For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword.” The Apostle says this while exhorting us to hasten, through faith and conduct, to enter the rest of the heavenly homeland, lest any of us fall into the same example of unbelief into which those people fell, and lest what happened to them happen to us—those who were laid low in the wilderness.

Those Jews might have answered: “Such things will certainly not happen to us, because we do not have prophets and judges through whose mouths the Lord may speak to us, as they had. Therefore, whatever we do, we shall be excusable.”

In response, the Apostle wishes to show that we have the same judge whom they had, the one who condemned them because of their unbelief, and says: “It is not so, for the word of God is living and effective.” The word of God the Father is the Son, the Word, who by his power killed those six hundred thousand in the wilderness because of their unfaithfulness and because they refused to believe him.

This is the Word who never dies but always remains the same, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.” This is the Word who says of himself: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.”

If those people had kept the word of God by believing rightly and living well, they would have lived both temporal and eternal life and would have entered the promised land. Likewise, if we keep his word, we shall live and shall enter the heavenly rest.

This word of God the Father, who always lives with God the Father and through whom the Father judges all things, is effective—that is, readily operative—because he works without difficulty. For “he spoke, and they were made,” and “he did all that he willed.”

He is also sharper than any two-edged sword—that is, a sword sharpened on both sides. For a material sword, sharpened on both sides, can separate limbs from the body and penetrate the hidden parts of the flesh, even to the point of causing the soul to depart from the body and reducing the body itself to death. Yet it cannot divide the soul into parts or penetrate its secrets. Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul.”

It follows: “And reaching”—the same word of God—“to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

We live through the soul, and through the spirit we understand rationally. Bodily life is shared by us with the beasts; spiritual reason is shared with the angels. There are certain sins that belong more particularly to the body, such as hatred, deceit, envy, and other things of this kind, which do not exist without bodily action. And because the soul gives life to the body, we may appropriately understand bodily sins through the soul, while spiritual sins, which take place in the secrecy of the mind, may be understood through the spirit.

Again, by “joints” we should understand thoughts, which are joined to one another as one follows another; by “marrow,” subtle intentions. This is what he adds: “Discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

The word of God the Father is therefore so effective and sharper than any two-edged sword that it distinguishes between the works of the flesh and the works of the spirit, between bodily and spiritual sins, between good and bad thoughts, and between good and bad intentions.

A thought may be in some way good while the intention is bad. For example, to speak by comparison: There is a widow whose hereditary property is seized by someone stronger. She approaches a judge and teacher of the law, asking him to undertake her case and assist her in recovering the inheritance that has been taken from her. She promises him either one hundred solidi or a substantial portion of that same inheritance.

He enters the church of God, prostrates himself with his face to the ground, and prays, saying: “Eternal God, because you judge all things justly, and because you have said, ‘Judge the people and defend the widow,’ grant me help today, so that I may be able to win this widow’s case.”

In this prayer, the thought and words are good, but the intention is wicked, since, unless the widow had promised him something that he hoped to receive, he would never have undertaken her case.

The word of God discerns and judges this subtlety of thoughts and intentions of the heart. It considers with what disposition and desire each person serves in his heart. Its gaze is so penetrating that all the things we do or think are known more certainly by it than by ourselves.

Let us therefore have as witness of our actions, thoughts, and intentions the one whom we shall have as judge. Let us fear the presence of him whose knowledge we can in no way escape.

Hence it follows: “And no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes”—that is, to his presence. How, then, could anything be unknown to him by whom all things were made? It is not surprising that he, who is wholly everywhere, knows his entire creation everywhere.

By this especially the Apostle terrified the Jews when he said: “All things are naked and open to his eyes.”

“To whom we must render an account.” To whom? To the Son. For we ourselves shall render an account of our actions, thoughts, and intentions.

“Having therefore a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast the confession of our hope”—that is, faith in his name.

Having spoken briefly above about the divinity of the Son of God, he said: “All things are naked and open to his eyes.” But since he is now speaking about the flesh and discussing the priesthood of the one who offered himself on the altar of the cross for our salvation—for he himself is both priest and sacrifice—

He is called “high priest” because he provides a bridge and a way for the people. The Lord himself has shown us the way of righteousness on which we must walk, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.” He also provided a bridge by which we may reach the heavenly homeland, through the blood of his Passion together with the water of baptism, or because he himself was the first to pass through the heavens.

Thus Moses, the leader of the people, to whom a temporary rest was promised, did not enter into the rest promised to the people entrusted to him. Hence the Apostle calls Christ the great high priest, one who possesses an eternal priesthood, always living to intercede for us.

For the angel said of him to Mary: “He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High,” showing that he is the Son of God. He called him Jesus, the Son of God, a title he nowhere wished to give to Moses; rather, he called Moses his servant.

It follows: “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize”—or “to suffer with”—“our weaknesses.”

This means: He is not ignorant of what belongs to us. He came by way of the human condition, in all things without sin. Therefore, not only because he is God and knows all things does he know the weakness of our frailty and have the power to show mercy; he also knows it and is able to forgive because he became a participant in the frailty of the flesh, without sin.

Many high priests are ignorant of those who are in tribulation and do not know what the tribulation of each person is. It is impossible for one who has not experienced affliction and has not physically endured all things to know the afflictions of the afflicted.

But our high priest fittingly endured all the things that were inflicted upon human misery after the sin of the first man. Then he entered within the veil and ascended to the throne of the Father’s majesty.

Hence it follows: “Tempted”—understand, “we have a high priest”—“in all things,” that is, in every temptation, “according to the likeness of sinful flesh, yet without sin.”

Christ was tempted in many ways through every kind of temptation, but he was not overcome by temptations; rather, he emerged as a tested victor.

The temptations by which he was tested were hunger, thirst, the devil’s temptation, persecution by the Jews, spitting, accusations, slanders, rejection by his own people, and finally crucifixion and death.

He was tempted in these ways in the likeness of flesh, but without sin. Yet since Christ had true flesh, why does he say that he was tempted in the likeness of flesh?

In this respect, that he became human, he had true flesh. In this respect, however, that he did not have sinful flesh but was without sin, he had the likeness of our flesh, which is sinful flesh. For he had no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.

If it had been possible for him to have sin, then he would have had not merely the likeness of sinful flesh but sinful flesh in reality. Our flesh is sinful flesh because we are conceived in sin and born in sin. But his flesh was not sinful; it was characterized by purity, chastity, and innocence.

Therefore he was not tempted in sinful flesh so that he might commit sin, but in the likeness of sinful flesh so that he might remain without sin.

Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help.

Because we have a high priest who knows how to sympathize with our weaknesses, since he endured all things like us, and who can help us because he is God, who by his own power has already penetrated the heights of heaven, the Apostle exhorts us to approach his throne with confidence.

He says: “Let us approach”—in mind and contemplation, and also through faith adorned with good works—“the throne of grace,” that is, faith in the Son of God, who was given to us by God the Father and who sits in the fullness of the Father’s majesty. He can freely forgive us our sins.

The Son of God is called “grace” because he was freely given to us. Accordingly, the same Apostle says plainly in this very Epistle: “So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.”

He then explains why we ought to approach his throne with faith and devotion, saying: “So that we may receive mercy”—that is, forgiveness of sins—and “find grace,” the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or indulgence, “for timely help”—that is, in the present age.

Now is the time of his help and mercy, of which the Apostle says elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” And the prophet says of it: “At an acceptable time I heard you.”

For when, in the present age, he grants his mercy by forgiving a person’s sins and receives him through the grace of spiritual gifts, he will also permit him, in the future kingdom, to reign with him. Since our high priest sits upon the throne of the Father’s glory, he grants everything that will most certainly contribute to our salvation.

## Chapter V

“For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He is able to sympathize with those who are ignorant and wandering, since he himself is surrounded by weakness. Because of this, he must offer for sins, just as for the people, so also for himself.”

In these words the Apostle sets forth certain features common to Christ and to the priests of the old law. For when he says, “Every high priest taken from among human beings,” just as Aaron was, “is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God,” praying for their salvation, this is common to Christ and to those priests.

The office of the high priest is to stand between God and the people and to entreat God for the people’s sins. Christ did this because he is both human and God, offering himself for our sins and always living to intercede with God the Father for us. Once taken from among human beings, he intercedes for all forever.

Again, when he says, “to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins,” this is partly common and partly not common or similar. Insofar as Christ offered a sacrifice for the people’s sins, as those priests also did, there is a likeness. But in that he did not offer for himself, whereas they offered sacrifices for their own sins—oxen, rams, goats, and other such animals—there is no likeness.

Christ offered a rational victim for the salvation of the whole world, namely himself, who is the Lamb, in accordance with what John says: “Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world,” and the rest that follows. These things are no longer common to them and to Christ.

When he says, “who is able to sympathize with those who are ignorant and wandering, since he himself is surrounded by weakness of flesh, in which he could be tempted in all things in the likeness of sinful flesh yet without sin,” this is an excellence belonging to Christ, concerning which we spoke more fully above. Because he suffered similar things, he can sympathize; and because he is God in both substances, he is able to show mercy.

But what he adds—“and because of this he must offer for sins, just as for the people, so also for himself”—belongs more to the priests of the law, or to the priests of our own time, than to Christ, who committed no sin.

The statement, “since he himself is surrounded by weakness,” may also be referred to the priests of the law or to those of our own time, so that “weakness” is understood as sin. Since they are surrounded by weakness of flesh—that is, by sin—they need to offer both for the people and for themselves.

By these words the Apostle wished to show what a high priest is, to demonstrate what belongs to the high priest and what his ministry and marks of priesthood are—namely, that he offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, knowing how to sympathize with those who wander in ignorance.

He then began to discuss how one ought to approach the priesthood, saying: “And no one takes the honor”—of the priesthood—“for himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was.”

Understand: Aaron was called by the sign of the flowering rod, or by the sign of the burning of those who, out of envy, attempted to seize his dignity by invading his priesthood. Through these two signs the priest chosen by God was demonstrated.

The blessed Apostle condemns and strikes down priests who are greedy for honor and eager for priesthood, who thrust and force themselves into the priestly ministry of their own accord—not by God’s calling or will, but rather through the intervention of gifts—because they do this not for the salvation of the people but out of worldly ambition.

“So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’”

“Glorify,” “honor,” and “make glorious” are three expressions with one meaning. The Greek term placed here for the Latin is δοξάζω (*doxazō*).

For when the evangelist reports that the Lord said, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing,” the Apostle here mentioned glorification. Christ therefore did not glorify or exalt himself so as to become high priest by his own initiative or to possess the honor of the priesthood from himself, because he was not from himself.

This is what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I have not come from myself, but he sent me.” And again: “I do not seek my glory”; and: “It is my Father who glorifies me.”

Just as he did not come from himself, because he was not from himself, and did not seek his own glory, so he did not glorify himself in order to possess the honor of the priesthood from himself. Rather, he was glorified by the Father, who said to him on the day of his baptism: “This is my beloved Son.”

This glorification or exaltation had been foretold long beforehand through the prophet, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in the person of the Son of God and said: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

Since all future things are, for almighty God, as though they were already past or present, what he was going to say to him after his baptism he regarded as though it had already been said. Therefore he used the past tense, saying: “The Lord said to me.”

By the name “Lord” we must understand God the Father. And so that we may believe that there is one person in Christ, he added: “Today I have begotten you”—that is, he expressed what properly belongs to God.

It follows: “As he also says in another place: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’”

This depends on the preceding verse, where the Apostle says: “Because Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but God the Father, who said to him, ‘You are my Son,’ glorified him.” In the same way, another passage of the Psalm says to the Son: “You are a priest forever,” and so forth.

It must be considered that Christ is not a priest according to the fact that he was begotten by God the Father before all ages—coeternal and consubstantial with the one who begot him, remaining true God with the Father—but according to the fact that he was born from a virginal womb and became human at the end of the ages, not because of the victim he offered for us, which he received from us, namely, flesh and blood.

But why is he said to exist as a priest “according to the order of Melchizedek,” and not according to the order of Aaron? There are various reasons.

The first is that Melchizedek was not a priest according to the legal commandments. Rather, according to the dignity of a singular priesthood, he offered bread to God, not the blood of irrational animals. Christ became a priest according to the order of this priesthood—not a temporal priest but an eternal one. He does not offer legal victims, but, in imitation of Melchizedek, bread and wine, namely his flesh and blood.

Hence he said: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

He also entrusted these two gifts—bread and wine—to his Church, to be offered in remembrance of him. Thus it is clear that the sacrifice of animals, which belonged to the order of Aaron, has passed away, while that which belonged to the order of Melchizedek remains, because Christ strengthened it and taught the Church to maintain it.

The second reason is that Melchizedek was both king and priest, and he was anointed not with visible oil, as were the priests of the law, but with the oil of the Holy Spirit. Christ remains marked by this double dignity.

That he possesses royal dignity he himself plainly declares: “I have been appointed king by him”—that is, by God the Father. And after his resurrection he says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

The Psalmist also says to God the Father: “Give the king your judgment.”

That he exists as a priest is sufficiently clear, since he offered himself on the altar of the cross for us and now intercedes with God the Father for our salvation.

That he was also anointed, not with visible oil but with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, the Psalmist indicates to us when he says to him: “O God, your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions”—that is, with the fullness of the Holy Spirit.

There is also a third reason why Christ is said to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek and not according to that of Aaron: just as the divine Scripture speaks only once of Melchizedek and of his priesthood, so Christ offered himself once as a sacrifice for us.

It follows: “In the days of his flesh, he offered prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears.”

“To God,” that is, to God the Father.

The days of our Lord’s flesh are the days in which he assumed flesh, in which he was born and suffered, and in which he inhabited a mortal body. Everything he did in the flesh was prayer and supplication for the sins of the human race.

The sacred shedding of his blood was a loud cry. In this cry, “he was heard”—by God the Father—“because of his reverence,” that is, because of his willing obedience and most perfect love.

Did he not pour out prayers with tears when he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death,” and, “Father, take this cup from me”?

And because he was voluntarily obedient to God the Father unto death, the Father heard him by raising him on the third day, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption.”

He is said to have poured out prayers and supplications not because he feared the death that he willingly accepted, but because, for the sake of our salvation, he placed the will of the Father’s dispensation above the will of his own flesh, so that he might show that the true nature of our humanity existed in him.

It should be noted that “reverence,” according to Cassiodorus’s interpretation, is sometimes understood as love and sometimes as fear. Here it signifies the highest love with which the Son of God loved us, and the highest obedience by which he was obedient to the Father unto death.

“And although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from what he suffered, and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, being called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.”

“Although,” he says, “he was truly the Son, he rendered obedience through the insults and torments that he suffered.” That is, in his humanity he voluntarily displayed obedience to the Father.

The obedience that the Apostle here says the Son of God gave—that is, voluntarily assumed—he shows elsewhere when he says: “Although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death.”

When he says, “and having been perfected”—that is, having been made perfect in priesthood and in every form of obedience—“he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him,” he shows how great a gain his Passion and obedience brought: they are sufficient to grant eternal life to all who believe.

It follows: “Concerning him”—not concerning Melchizedek but concerning Christ—“we have much to say, and it is difficult to explain.”

This difficulty does not arise from any fault in the Incarnation, since the mysteries hidden from the ages have been revealed, but from the slowness of those hearers, because they were weak—that is, infirm—in faith and fragile in understanding when it came to grasping the profound mysteries. Yet, considering the time, they ought to have been teachers.

Hence he gives the reason, saying: “For you have become weak in hearing.”

Then he adds: “For although you ought to be teachers by this time”—during which you have possessed the law and the prophets almost from the beginning—“you again need someone to teach you,” namely, me and the other apostles, “what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God. And you have become people who need milk, not solid food.”

He is addressing those who, having remained for a long time in the law, ought to have possessed trained understanding concerning Christ’s coming through the sayings of the law and the prophets, and also through the grace brought to believers through him.

Although, because of the time that had passed—during which they had received all the things mentioned above—they ought to have been teachers of the Gentiles, they again needed him and the other apostles to teach them what the elements of the beginning of God’s words were.

The elements are called *elementa*, as though they were *elevamenta*, because other things take their origin from them—namely, the beginnings and foundations of created things.

Some also say that the term derives from *elimenta*, as though they were structures, from *elimo, elimas*, as if everything were constructed from them.

Here, however, we can understand “elements,” or “foundations,” in two ways: either as the actual characters and pronunciations of letters, from which speech begins, or as the beginnings and foundations of faith.

It is as though he were saying: “You need to be taught what the elements of letters or the beginnings of faith are, although you ought to be investigating the depth of the mysteries through understanding and to be perfect in faith.”

“You have become,” he says, “like infants who need milk”—that is, simple teaching—“not solid food,” that is, perfect teaching and profound mysteries.

The blessed Apostle customarily designates simple teaching by the name “milk,” while he calls perfect teaching “solid food.” Hence he says to the less-perfect Corinthians: “I gave you milk, not food, because you were not yet able to receive it.”

Milk, therefore, is simple teaching: the incarnation of the Son of God, his Passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

Solid food, however, is the mystery of the perfect word: how there are three persons and one substance of divinity.

But whoever cannot understand what the Evangelist says—“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—how will he be able to reach the height of what he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word”?

It follows: “For everyone who partakes of milk”—that is, of simple teaching alone—“is unacquainted with the word of righteousness.” That is, he is alien to the discernment of perfect righteousness, because he is not yet able to penetrate the secret things of the mysteries, nor does he know how to make the necessary distinction between good and evil.

He gives the reason: “For he is an infant”—in sense and understanding.

“But solid food belongs to the mature”—that is, to people who possess mature understanding. To them they disclose the lofty and obscure mysteries concerning the divinity of almighty God.

Hence it also follows: “Those who”—I say—“through habitual practice have their senses trained.” That is, their senses have been extended through study.

This is “for the discernment of good and evil,” not for the discernment of heretical depravity.

Just as an infant does not know how to distinguish one food from another and often comes to harm by eating harmful foods if an elder does not restrain him, so every unlearned person who does not know how to distinguish teachings is easily deceived and imperiled by error.

Therefore he says: “For everyone who partakes of milk is unacquainted with the word of righteousness.” What distinguishes the unlearned from the wise is analogous to what distinguishes milk from solid food.

Just as milk suits infants and solid food those mature in age, so humble speech suits the unlearned, while the wise, whose senses have been trained by devoted reading, ought to know the hidden mystery.

Through habitual reading and frequent meditation on the divine Scriptures, our senses become trained and extended so as to understand greater things. Hence the Psalmist calls blessed the person who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 0719B]

Therefore, leaving aside the elementary word of Christ, let us advance toward perfection. Since it is fitting that we have senses trained in the law of the Lord, let us leave aside the elementary word of Christ and be led to the profound and lofty mysteries of his divinity. He calls the elementary word of Christ the beginning of faith, namely instruction concerning Christ’s human birth, his passion, resurrection, ascension, and the grace of baptism. For just as one who is to be instructed in letters must first hear the elements of reading and writing, so a Christian must first be instructed in these matters and afterward come to the mysteries of divinity.

Not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God. He calls the foundation of repentance that from which the person who is to be baptized must first be instructed—provided that he has reached an age of understanding [Col. 0719C]. This means that he should believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was begotten from God the Father before all the ages; was born of a Virgin at the end of time for the salvation of the human race, without the seed of a man; suffered, died, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judgment to repay each person according to his works; that there will be a resurrection of bodies and an unchangeableness of souls; that the good will remain in glory and the wicked in punishment; and that Almighty God has Trinity in persons and unity in substance.

After he has confessed that he believes all these things, he must confess his sins, and repentance must then be imposed upon him for forty, twenty, or even seven days, as we read in the *Passions of the Saints* [Col. 0719D]. He must then be baptized, renouncing the devil, all his pomp, and all his works. After baptism, he must be instructed more fully concerning divinity: he must believe that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from both; and he must learn the rule of life according to evangelical and apostolic teaching—what good things he ought to do and what evils he ought to avoid.

Since, then, the Jews to whom the Apostle was writing had already been baptized and had already received the foundation described above, he exhorts them to strive toward these greater matters. There was no need for them to repeat that foundation of repentance, which he calls by this name because, as has been said, repentance was first imposed upon those being baptized. Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, Paul says to the Jews coming together for the faith [Col. 0720A]: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized.”

“It should not be necessary,” he says, “for us to lay again the foundation of repentance from dead works”—that is, the foundation of faith by which one approaches God—which was laid in you before you came to the grace of baptism. To practice repentance from dead works is to erase through repentance the evil works that were killing the soul. For sins are works of death: just as the soul is given life by faith and the other virtues, so it dies through unbelief and sins.

He continues: not laying again a foundation of the teaching of baptisms. The foundation of the teaching of baptisms is the institution and teaching of baptism—namely, what baptism contains in itself and what it confers upon those who approach in faith. But when he called it the foundation of baptisms in the plural [Col. 0720B], he used the plural because of the variety of those who receive it, not because several baptisms are to be understood, but one: for just as there is one God and one faith, so there is one baptism.

Nor should we lay again the foundation of the laying on of hands. He calls “the laying on of hands” that through which the gift of the Holy Spirit is believed to be received in its fullness, an act customarily performed by bishops after baptism for the confirmation of unity in the Church.

When these things have therefore been received in the Church, one must hold the faith in the resurrection and in the future judgment. Hence the Apostle adds: “And of the resurrection of the dead and of eternal judgment.” You must not lay the foundation again, as though you needed to be instructed once more concerning faith in the universal resurrection and eternal judgment, which will be given equally to the just and the unjust—as though you had not already been instructed in these matters [Col. 0720C]. It should be noted that in all these expressions one must always supply the words “not again.”

And this we will do, if indeed God permits. That is, we will lead you on to greater things and teach you most fully about all the matters we have listed, so that it will not again be necessary to lay the foundation from the beginning and in its entirety.

But lest anyone should think that baptism could be administered a second or third time after sins, he immediately added: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened.” They were enlightened under the light of the Holy Spirit in the baptism of faith. They “tasted the heavenly gift”—that is, they received remission in baptism, or they shared in the body and blood of the Lord after baptism. And they “became participants in the Holy Spirit,” namely, in the distribution of his gifts [Col. 0720D].

They “tasted the good word of God,” that is, they understood evangelical teaching. And they tasted “the powers of the age to come”—that is, glorification, resurrection, and future life. And they “fell away”: from the faith of Christ by denying him, or even into criminal sins.

“To renew again to repentance”: that is, to be made new through repentance. From what precedes, the words “it is impossible” are to be supplied: “It is impossible,” he says, “for those who, after receiving all the things mentioned above, have fallen into the uncleanness of criminal sins or even into unbelief, to be renewed again through repentance and baptism.” He did not say, “It is difficult,” but “it is impossible.” What is difficult can nevertheless somehow be done; what is impossible is what cannot be done in any way.

What then? Is repentance after baptism, and forgiveness of sins, excluded [Col. 0721A]? Far be it from us. There are indeed two kinds of repentance. One is before baptism, which may be called the plea for baptism. We spoke above about this: it is imposed upon those who are being instructed before they reach baptism. The blessed Apostle excludes this kind when he says that those who have once been renewed cannot be renewed again through repentance, so that, after repentance has been completed, they might be baptized again.

The other kind of repentance is that through which sins committed after baptism are erased. The blessed Apostle does not exclude this. He therefore terrifies everyone, so that they may fear entangling themselves in more serious sins after the grace of baptism, because a second renewal through the baptismal washing cannot take place. For just as Christ died once and rose once and no longer dies, so the grace of baptism is to be administered once [Col. 0721B] and cannot be repeated—unless there is uncertainty as to whether someone captured by enemies had been baptized.

He said “to be renewed” in the sense of “to be made new.” To make a person new belongs to sacred baptism, concerning which the Prophet says: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.”

I say, it is impossible for anyone to be renewed again through repentance—which takes place through baptism—in order that he might be baptized again after completing his repentance, because those things mentioned above have already been received and “the powers of the age to come” have been tasted.

His statement, “They tasted the powers of the age to come,” is equivalent to saying: If they have learned that at the resurrection the elect will be like the angels of God in heaven, and that the just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, they cannot in any way be made new again through repentance and repeated baptism if they commit a criminal sin, just as they were made new in the first baptism [Col. 0721C]. For there were people who wanted to repeat baptism, saying: “Whatever sin I commit does not concern me, because I will order myself to be baptized again and will be made wholly new, as before.”

The Apostle completely denies that this can in any way happen. And because the power of baptism rests especially upon the cross and burial of Christ, he therefore adds: “Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt.” To hold him up to contempt means to subject him to mockery.

Nevertheless, repentance is not thereby denied. Although they are not renewed again in baptism, they will nevertheless receive pardon through confession of sins, humility, repentance, almsgiving if they have the means, and forgiveness of those brothers who have sinned against them.

This refers to those who wish to be baptized again and to hold the Son of God up to ridicule—for this is what “holding him up to contempt” means. But it cannot happen. Just as Christ died once in the flesh upon the cross, so we too can die for sin only once in baptism [Col. 0721D].

“For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it and producing suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated, receives blessing from God.” By this example he reproves the Jews, who had often drunk the rain of heavenly teaching but had never produced the shoots of faith and good works.

He first gives a comparison involving good soil and then one involving bad soil. “The earth,” he says, “drinking in the rain”—that is, the soul of good will receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit and the rain of divine words—and “producing suitable vegetation,” that is, bringing forth virtues and perfected faith, for its own preachers, by whom it is cultivated, or for itself, receives from God the blessing of eternal life, or an abundance of virtues, so that it may bear thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and likewise a hundredfold fruit. Nothing is more suitable than perfected faith in the Son of God together with an upright life [Col. 0722A].

Having presented this example of a soul flourishing in virtues and worthy of God’s blessing, the Apostle immediately adds another example concerning the soul that neglects its salvation, although it could frequently receive the rain of heavenly teaching.

“But if it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse.” By thorns and thistles we can understand the pricks of sins by which the soul is pierced. Concerning these the Lord said to Adam: “Your earth will produce thorns and thistles for you”—that is, your flesh will produce for you the pricks of sins and the barbs of vices [Col. 0722B].

Alternatively, by “thorns and thistles” we should understand excessive cares and the anxieties of this age. Concerning these the Lord says in the Gospel: “The cares of this world and the anxiety of riches.” The rejected earth is therefore unworthy of praise and near to a curse.

It should be noted that he did not say, “It is cursed,” but, “It is near to a curse.” As long as it is being reserved for repentance, it is, as it were, not cursed; but if it refuses to repent, it will then be cursed.

Hence he continues: “Whose end”—that is, the end of that soul in evil action and persistence in wickedness until the end of life—“is for burning.” Supply: “It will be for the fire of eternal punishment.” While it still has time for repentance, it is near to a curse; but if it persists in its iniquity, it will be subjected to the burning of eternal punishment [Col. 0722C]. This burning will belong only to those who remain in their sins to the end, because: “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die.”

After sufficiently reproving, frightening, and striking them, he addresses them soothingly, lest he drive them to despair. Yet he neither flatters them in every respect nor strikes them in every respect. He therefore says:

“But we are confident concerning you, beloved, of better things and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.” Since he had no basis for praising them in the present, he praises them on the basis of the hope for the future that he held concerning them. It is as though he said: “We do not speak as though we think you are full of thorns, but because we fear that you may become such. It is better for you to be frightened by words than to suffer through the realities themselves. We are confident that you will do the best things, things beneficial to your salvation, although we speak in this way.”

For what we said above concerning the rejected earth and its nearness to burning, we did not say about you, because we believe better things concerning you. He also recalled their former good deeds to their memory, so that through what they had done in the past he might lead them toward every good thing. Therefore he added:

“For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love that you showed in his name.”

See how he revived and strengthened their spirits by recalling their former good works. Since forgetfulness cannot befall Almighty God, he does not forget the works and labors of his faithful servants. In this he is just, because he rewards those of his elect who labor for him. If he forgot their works and did not reward them, he could somehow be considered unjust; but it is wholly impious to say this.

Hence the Apostle says: “God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and labor, and the love that you showed for the sake of the love of his name, toward one another and toward all.” You “ministered to the saints, and still minister”—as far as you are able [Col. 0723A].

He is speaking of those saints who, when they came to the faith of Christ, were stripped of their possessions by the Jews. He praises them in this Epistle, saying: “You joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions.” They are the ones of whom Isaiah had previously foretold: “The one who departed from evil,” he says, “was exposed to the plunder of the Jews.”

When such people had been stripped of their possessions, those who had not been stripped ministered to them as far as they were able.

How great and intense his desire was for their salvation, he expresses in part in the words that follow:

“But we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness”—supply: “that you showed previously”—“unto the fulfillment of hope to the end” [Col. 0723B].

That is, to the end of your life, or until the day of judgment. “So that you may not become sluggish”—that is, idle and lazy in good works and in fulfilling God’s commandments.

“We desire,” he says, “that you conduct yourselves not only in words but also in virtues.” He does not say this as though he were blaming what belonged to them personally, but as one admonishing them out of concern for the future. That is: “As you were at first, so we desire you to be now and in the future.”

He did not say, “I want,” which would express divine authority, but “we desire,” which expressed paternal affection. That is: “We desire each one of you always to show the same greatest care toward the brothers that you formerly had, unto the completion of human hope”—the eternal resurrection.

For the completion of hope is the attainment of the things that we hope we shall obtain.

“But we desire you to be imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises.”

Again he exhorts them to await, with unfailing faith and perfect patience, the promises of God and the inheritance that he promised to his saints. This may be understood in two ways. It may refer to the patriarchs and saints of the Old Testament, who received many promises concerning Christ and the inheritance of the promised land. Because they possessed perfect faith, by which they believed that God could fulfill what he had promised, and steadfast patience, because they waited for the promises to be fulfilled not in themselves but in their children, they deserved to be friends of God and to inherit those same promises in their children.

It may also refer to the apostles and other saints, who through faith and patience deserved to attain and inherit from the Lord the promises of eternal blessing made to themselves and to all the faithful [Col. 0723D].

For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: “Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.”

To strengthen more firmly what he had said above concerning the saints—that they inherited God’s promises through faith and patience—he therefore uses examples. Yet his wisdom is marvelous. At one time he wins them over by exalting them with praise; at another he frightens them with threats. Above, he frightened them lest they should be unbelieving and insufficiently trusting in God’s promises. Now, however, he exhorts them by examples to repentance and faith, so that they may believe without doubt not only because God speaks, but also because he swears by himself [Col. 0724A].

If it is wicked not to believe when God makes a promise, how impious it is not to place faith in God when he swears! God the Father swore to Abraham by himself, because he had no one greater by whom he could swear, saying: “Surely, blessing I will bless you,” and so forth.

The repetition of the word confirms the matter. In this passage, “surely” (*nisi*) is used affirmatively in the sense of “certainly” or “because.” The meaning is: “I will certainly always bless you in your children, and I will always multiply you.”

“And thus, having patiently endured, he obtained the promise.” That is, by believing for a long time and enduring patiently, he obtained the promise in his children concerning the promised land, which God promised them, saying: “I will give this land to you and to your children.” In addition, he obtained the promise concerning Christ, of whom God said: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.”

He continues: “For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the oath is the end of every dispute for confirmation” [Col. 0724B].

It is as though he said: If people place future trust in human beings, concerning whom the Prophet says, “Every human being is a liar,” how much more ought we to trust God’s oath, since he is truth and can neither be deceived nor deceive, and since he ought to be believed even without an oath!

“Human beings,” he says, “swear by one greater than themselves”—that is, by the Lord, who is their creator. An oath is also the end of all their disputes for confirmation, because an oath establishes what must be believed. After an oath has been fulfilled, no complaint should subsequently be made; rather, the oath, under confirmation, should be the end of the dispute.

“In which”—supply: “in which oath”; or, “for this reason,” because confirmation of a matter is provided by an oath [Col. 0724C].

“God, wishing to show more abundantly the unchangeableness of his purpose to the heirs of the promises”—that is, to the fathers, or to the heirs of the promise—“interposed an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest consolation.”

That is, so that we might firmly believe him.

“We who have fled for refuge”—by believing—“to hold fast the hope set before us.” That is, to receive the promised reward.

Here we should understand the two unchangeable things as God’s promise concerning Christ, in which he said, “In your seed all the nations will be blessed,” and his oath, in which he said, “By myself I have sworn to you.” His promise is unchangeable because it could not be altered, and his oath is truthful.

Some also wish one unchangeable thing to be understood as his promise together with his oath, and the other as the fulfillment of that very matter [Col. 0724D].

By “the hope set before us” he means the truth of the things accomplished—namely, the promise of the heavenly homeland, to receive which we have fled for refuge through faith.

“We have this hope as a sure and firm anchor of the soul.” Just as an anchor cast from a ship does not allow it to be carried about or endangered, even if the winds stir it, but, having been cast, holds the ship firmly amid storms and waves, so faith, strengthened by hope in future goods, steadies our mind amid the prosperity and adversity of this age and introduces us into the reality of the things that we now hold by faith and hope.

Therefore the Apostle added: “And entering into the interior of the veil.”

By “the interior of the veil” he calls the secrets of the heavenly kingdom and the joys of the heavenly homeland. The veil that stood before the Holy of Holies signifies heaven; the things that were within the veil signify the secrets of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0725A]. Hope penetrates into the interior of the veil when, through contemplation of the mind, it beholds future goods; when it believes without any doubt that heavenly rewards will come to it; when it hopes, loves, and shows through its works what it believes and what it hopes.

If we do not possess this hope, we shall certainly be submerged, not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily ones, just as a ship without an anchor cast into the sea is submerged. But if we obey the Prophet’s voice, which says, “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you,” then our hope, fixed within the interior of the veil, will be unable to sink through any unbelief.

He continues: “Where Jesus, having become and been appointed High Priest by God the Father forever according to the order of Melchisedech, entered as forerunner on our behalf.”

To give us firmer hope, he added this concerning Christ [Col. 0725B].

He is called a forerunner from going before and running ahead. Someone is the forerunner of another, as John was the forerunner of Christ.

It should be considered that he did not simply say, “Jesus entered into the interior of the veil,” but added the words, “Where the forerunner entered on our behalf,” as though it were beyond doubt that we ought to follow our forerunner. The one who goes before and the one who follows ought to be on the same road.

Thus Christ, rising from the dead, went before us to the height of heaven. He became our forerunner by opening heaven for us and restoring to us the joys of the heavenly homeland. If, therefore, we wish to follow our forerunner, we must walk as he walked.

This refers to the nature of the Son of God’s humanity, in which he offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross as the sacrifice of our salvation [Col. 0725C].

Why Christ is said to exist as a priest according to the order of Melchisedech has, as I think, been shown sufficiently clearly a little earlier. But when he says that Christ entered into the interior of the veil, he speaks in the manner of the Jewish high priests, who entered once a year within the veil and into the Holy of Holies to pray for the people. Christ, however, penetrating the secrets of the heavenly kingdom, prays continually for the salvation of his faithful.

## CHAPTER VII.

Here indeed Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of the Most High God. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him; and Abraham apportioned to him a tenth of everything. The Hebrews relate that Melchizedek himself was Shem, Noah’s firstborn, and that at the time Abraham was born he was 292 years old. At the time Abraham died, he was 575 years old, and thus he outlived Abraham by thirty-five years; when these had been completed, all the days of his life amounted to six hundred years. Nor is it surprising if he went out to meet Abraham and offered him bread and wine, since he owed the rights of fatherhood to his great-grandson; and if he blessed him and accepted from him a tenth of the spoil and victory, as priest of the Most High and supreme God—not of false gods and idols. He was also king of Salem.

Salem, however, as blessed Jerome says, should not be thought to be Jerusalem, as Josephus the historian and very many of our people suppose. Rather, it is a town near Scythopolis which to this day is called Salem or Salim. Concerning it, blessed Jerome testifies that the Gospel reads: “John,” he says, “was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there.” This variation in names occurs because in many places the Hebrews write only the consonants, omitting the vowels; and so, according to the reader’s judgment, the word is pronounced not always in one and the same way.

In that same town the palace of King Melchizedek is shown, its great ruins displaying the excellence of the ancient structure. Jacob is also said to have gone down to this city, or town, which was in the land of Canaan, in the region of Shechem. It should likewise be considered that when Abraham returned from the slaughter of the enemies whom he had pursued as far as Dan, he did not have Jerusalem on his route of return, but rather the Salem mentioned above.

First, Melchizedek, whose name is interpreted as “king of righteousness”; and then also “king of Salem,” which means “king of peace”; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life. Blessed Paul frequently introduces Melchizedek as a type of the Lord and Savior. Although almost all the saints, patriarchs, and earlier prophets expressed in some respect a figure of the Lord and Savior, Melchizedek nevertheless went before him more particularly as a type of the priesthood of the Son of God, concerning whom God the Father says in Psalm 109: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

We can interpret his order in many ways, as was said above: namely, that he alone was both king and priest; that he exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that it was not the Gentiles who received the priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the Gentiles; that he was not anointed with visible oil, as the Mosaic precepts prescribe, but with the oil of gladness and purity of faith; and that he did not offer victims of flesh and blood, but dedicated the priesthood through bread and wine, a simple and pure sacrifice of Christ.

But first, as the Apostle says, he is made like the Son of God because he is interpreted as “king of righteousness.” For *Melchon*, or *Melchi*, means “king,” while *Sedech* means “just” or “righteousness.” And who is the true king of righteousness except Christ, who says in the Psalm: “But I have been appointed king by him”? For he rules and governs his elect justly and rightly, making them lovers of righteousness.

Then he is made like the Son of God by what is said of him as “king of peace,” which pertains to Christ: for Salem is interpreted as “peace.” Christ, therefore, justifies us, being the king of righteousness; and he himself makes peace between all things in heaven and on earth. By his birth and death, resurrection and ascension, he brought peace to the world. According to his divinity he is king without end and without beginning, eternal from the eternal Father, although from a temporal mother he was temporal.

We do not read in Sacred Scripture of the beginning or end of this Melchizedek; likewise, we do not read of a beginning or end of the Son of God. Nothing of this kind exists in the nature of his divinity. The likeness consists in this: neither the beginning nor the end of the one or of the other is read of. In Melchizedek’s case, because it was not written; in Christ’s case, because it does not exist at all. We do not read under whom Melchizedek was born, nor is it related when he died; rather, he is introduced suddenly, as Elijah also is.

Nor should it be believed at all that Melchizedek was without father or mother, since Christ also, according to both natures, had both a mother and a father. This is said of Melchizedek because he is introduced suddenly in divine Scripture, as we have said, and because his genealogy is not mentioned. Of him it is also said: “But, being made like the Son of God in all these matters mentioned above, he remains a priest forever.” Not in himself, but in Christ. For Melchizedek died, but his figure remains eternally in Christ. Here “likeness” does not refer to age, but to typological representation.

Consider, then, how great this man was, to whom the patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest things.

He turns his discourse toward those who glory in calling themselves sons of Abraham and boast that they derive their nobility from him. For this reason, in the Gospel they attempted to place Abraham before the Lord when they said: “Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died?”

Therefore, to confound their pride, the Apostle said: “Consider and pay close attention to how great this Melchizedek was, the priest of the Most High God, to whom the patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest things,” that is, of the better spoils. By these words he wishes to show that Melchizedek possessed greater dignity and honor than Abraham, and consequently that the priesthood of Christ would be greater and holier than that of the Jews. It is as though he were saying: “The one whom you regard as more excellent than all other human beings offered a tenth to Melchizedek, who went before as a type of Christ.”

Indeed, those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi have a command to take tithes from the people according to the law—that is, from their brothers—although they themselves also came forth from the loins of Abraham.

Such, he says, is the excellence of the priesthood that even those who had the same ancestor and descended from one father, because of the merit of their excellence—which made them better than their brothers, as Aaron was, who, standing between the dead and the living, appeased the Lord’s wrath—were deemed worthy to attain the dignity of the priesthood. Therefore, unless Melchizedek were of greater dignity than Abraham, Abraham would never have given tithes to a foreigner, just as Aaron was of greater merit than his brothers of the other tribes.

He therefore says: “Those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi, as Aaron and his sons received it, have a command and precept according to the law to take tithes from the people, as though they were better than them, and to take them from their brothers, although they had one and the same ancestor.” In accordance with this the Apostle declares: “Although they too, the brothers descended from Levi, came forth from the loins of Abraham.”

But whose descent is not counted among them—that is, among the sons of Levi—he took tithes from Abraham, and he blessed him who had the promises—that is, Abraham, who had the promises concerning the Son of God. “He blessed him”—that is, Melchizedek blessed Abraham.

Here he shows that an uncircumcised priest was far superior to a circumcised priest. How does he show this? Clearly, because Levi himself, from whom the priestly line arose, was tithed by Melchizedek while still in the loins of his ancestor; and Abraham had already been circumcised and had already received the promises concerning Christ—that all the nations would be blessed in his offspring—when he was blessed by the uncircumcised priest Melchizedek, giving him a tenth of the entire spoil.

When Melchizedek blessed him, he said: “Blessed be Abraham by God, under whose protection his enemies are in his hand,” and other words that follow in the same passage.

Without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the better. It is as though he were saying: “It is clearer than daylight to everyone that the lesser is blessed by the greater.” Therefore Abraham, as the lesser, is blessed—or received a blessing—from Melchizedek as the better. Consequently, Melchizedek is a greater and better type of Christ than Abraham, who possessed the promises concerning Christ.

Here, indeed, mortal men receive tithes; but there it is testified that he lives.

To put it so: through Abraham, Levi also, who received tithes, was tithed.

“Here,” he says—that is, in the present age, or in the temple that was still standing—mortal men, namely the sons of Levi, who are mortal and subject to death, receive tithes. “There,” however, that is, in the other life, in the place where it is said of Christ, “You are a priest forever,” God the Father testifies with an oath that Christ lives. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

For Levi was still in the loins—that is, in the propagation of the seed—of his father when Melchizedek met him.

How does he say that Levi was tithed by Melchizedek, when Levi had not yet been born, especially since he was also the natural son of Jacob? Clearly, he was not tithed in himself, but in Abraham, from whose offspring he descended. When Abraham offered tithes to Melchizedek, all his sons gave tithes in him. Therefore the Apostle says: “He who received tithes in his sons from his brothers was tithed through Abraham,” or “in Abraham.”

By these words it is declared that, unless the priesthood of Melchizedek—which went before as a type of Christ’s priesthood—had been of greater dignity, Abraham and all his sons would never have been tithed by him. For when one priesthood is tithed by another, one is shown to possess greater dignity than the other.

If, therefore, perfection came through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, there must also be a transfer of the law.

Here he begins to show more fully the differences of the New Testament, saying: If perfection—that is, perfection of life and justification—came through the Levitical priesthood, what need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek?

There is no doubt that Aaron was the first priest of the tribe of Levi after the law had been given. For this reason the priesthood which he exercised was called the Levitical priesthood. Or perhaps it was so called because Levi himself exercised that priesthood through his sons: his descendants received it, namely Moses and Aaron, together with the other brothers of the same tribe. For Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; and Amram begot Moses and Aaron.

He says that the people received the law under that priesthood because Moses and Aaron were leaders of the people at that time, administering the law itself while belonging to the priestly tribe. Therefore the order of the priesthood of Melchizedek, who bore the type of our priest, is much better than the Levitical priesthood. He would never have said “according to the order of Melchizedek” if the priesthood of Aaron, under which the Jewish people received the law, had been better.

But if the priesthood of the law has been transferred to Christ according to the order of Melchizedek, the law too must necessarily be transferred. That is, it is necessary to pass from the law of Moses to the law of the Gospel. For a priest cannot exist without a law, nor without a testament, nor without commandments.

The Apostle strives with all his strength to make the transition from the law of Moses to the law of the Gospel, from bodily things to spiritual things.

For the one concerning whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one attended the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe concerning which Moses said nothing about priests.

“Of whom,” he says, “are these things spoken?” That is, concerning whom do they say that he is “a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”? They indicate that the Lord and Savior belongs to another tribe than the priestly one, namely the tribe from which no one attended the altar—that is, the tribe of Judah.

The change occurred not only in order, testament, or commandments, but also in tribe. And how was the priesthood transferred from one tribe to another? It was transferred from the priestly tribe to the royal one, so that in Christ the same person might be both priestly and royal, since he is both king and priest.

Consider the mystery. First there was the royal priesthood of Melchizedek, according to the sequence of this discourse. Second was the priesthood that was solely priestly, in Aaron. Third, again, there was a royal priesthood in Christ, as there had been at the beginning.

Hence the Church now possesses a royal priesthood, as the Apostle Peter says: “You are a holy race, a royal priesthood.”

Thus, in the tribe of Judah, from which the Lord arose through the Virgin Mary, although it had always been royal and never priestly, Christ possessed both offices, royal and priestly. The priesthood was completely transferred from the tribe of Levi, which had previously been priestly.

And this is still more clearly shown if another priest arises according to the order of Melchizedek, one who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life.

For God the Father testifies, speaking to the Son: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

A deficiency in the wording occurs at this point, and it is quite necessary to supply it. The passage should therefore be understood as follows: “And this is still more clearly shown”—supply, “that the priesthood of the law has been abolished”—by the fact that Christ is said to be a priest forever not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek, because he was not from the tribe of Levi.

When he says, “If another priest should arise according to the order of Melchizedek,” he is not speaking doubtfully but affirmatively. It is as though he were saying: “This demonstrates still more clearly that the priesthood of the law has been abolished, because Christ, another priest, has arisen according to the order of Melchizedek. He was made a priest not according to the law of a carnal commandment, as Aaron was.”
