He calls it the law of a carnal commandment because for the most part it was carnal, prescribing bodily matters in circumcision, bodily purification, sacrifices and offerings, distinctions of foods, days, and seasons. It said: “Remain outside the camp”; “Wash your body”; “Offer this or that”; “Abstain from these foods”; “Observe these seasons”; and other things of the same kind, all of which were destined to end in death.

Christ’s priesthood, however, is spiritual and according to the power of an indestructible life—that is, according to the power of a life that cannot fail, which no intervention of death can destroy. Christ possesses indestructible life. Although he died in the flesh for a time, he nevertheless lives eternally in his divinity, and also in his humanity after rising victoriously from the dead.

Therefore God the Father testifies with an oath that he lives, saying through the Psalmist: “You are a priest forever.”

There is indeed a setting aside of the former commandment—that is, of the law of Moses—because of its weakness and uselessness.

The law had weakness in this respect: it was unable to help those who practiced it. It had uselessness in this respect: it was unable to open the kingdom of heaven to anyone.

Hence what follows: “For the law brought nothing to perfection.”

Why, then, did the law accomplish nothing? It did accomplish something, by cleansing bodies and remitting certain sins; but it accomplished nothing toward making those who served under it perfect. It did not remove the more serious sins, nor did it open the gate of the heavenly homeland to anyone. Therefore it was set aside, so that room might be given to the grace of God, in which perfection consists.

The law was useful to those who had faith in Christ, but not to those who placed all their hope in bodily observances.

But the introduction of a better hope—supply, “now exists in grace”—through which we draw near to God.

The law had hope, but not the kind that grace provided. Those who pleased God and kept the law hoped to possess the land, according to the saying: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land.” They also hoped to suffer nothing grievous and to live prosperously, as it is said: “Whoever does it shall live.”

But now we hope that, while mourning and keeping the commandments of the Gospel, we shall possess not the earth but heaven. Moreover—and heaven is much better—we hope to stand near God, to reach the very throne of the Father, and to minister to him with the angels, according to what the Savior said in the Gospel: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father,” and “they will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

This priesthood, through which we shall possess this glory, is not without an oath, so that we may believe God’s promise to be firm. Hence the Apostle adds: “And how much greater”—supply, “is this priesthood of Christ of which we speak”—namely, very much greater, because it “was confirmed with an oath.”

Others indeed became priests without an oath, such as Aaron and his sons, to whom God did not swear that they would be priests forever according to the order of the law.

But this one became a priest with an oath, through him—that is, through God the Father—who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” that is, “he will not change his oath”: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

[Col. 0731A] Jesus became the guarantor—or promisor—of a better covenant.

Supply: he became so insofar as he holds his priesthood with the oath of God the Father, and insofar as Christ’s priesthood, sanctioned by God’s oath, surpasses the law of Moses even through the grace of the Gospel.

Many others indeed became priests according to the law, because they were prevented by death from continuing. But this one—Christ, to whom the Father said with an oath, “You are a priest forever”—because he remains forever, possesses an everlasting priesthood.

Blessed Paul sets forth two distinctions here: our priest has no end, unlike the priests of the law; and he will possess his priesthood with an oath. Since the priests of the law were mortal, many became priests under that law, such as Aaron and his sons, because death prevented them from continuing in the priesthood. When the fathers died, the sons succeeded to their place. Jesus, however, alone possesses an everlasting priesthood because he is immortal, and he can have no successor, since he himself remains forever.

It follows: “Therefore he can save forever those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for us.”

“Therefore,” he says, because Christ remains forever and possesses an everlasting priesthood, he always intercedes for us and is always able to save.

Some manuscripts, however, read: “He who draws near through himself to God”; others have the plural: “those who draw near.” Either reading may be accepted.

Our high priest Christ, therefore, does not himself draw near to God the Father through another, greater high priest, but through himself; and for this reason he is able to save those who believe in him.

The statement may also be understood in this way: “He can save forever those who draw near through him to God.” Since we are mere human beings, we approach God the Father through him, because, being the mediator, he stands before God’s face on our behalf, directing our prayers through him to the Father. Therefore the priests of the Church, standing at the altar, say: “Receive, O Lord, the prayers of your people, through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.”

And because he always lives, he always intercedes for us. The other high priests, however, because they did not always exist, did not always intercede.

He intercedes for us because he assumed human nature for our sake, which he continually presents before God’s face on our behalf; and he has mercy according to both substances.

For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.

We were not worthy, nor had we earned it, to have such a high priest. Yet it was necessary for us to have a high priest who would be holy in the inner person, innocent in his hands, undefiled in body, and separated from sinners: one who would likewise be free from every sin and separated from the conduct of sinners.

He was separated from them in this respect: other human beings are conceived and born with sin and depart from this age with sin; but he was conceived without sin, born without sin, and passed from this world without sin, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

He was exalted above the heavens when, on the fortieth day after his wondrous resurrection, he was raised above all the heavens and above all the orders of heavenly spirits to the session of the Father’s majesty, where he now sits in the fullness of honor and glory.

The statement, “Such a high priest was fitting for us,” may also be understood in this way—as though he were saying: The Jews, serving God as slaves through fear of the law, had legal high priests who were fellow servants, mortal and sinful, and who likewise needed to offer sacrifice for themselves. But we, to whom it was said, “I no longer call you servants, but my friends,” and because we are sons of God, serving him with the love proper to children, ought to have an immortal high priest separated from sinners.

It follows: “Who did not have the daily necessity, as the priests of the law did, first to offer sacrifices for their own sins and then for those of the people; for he did this once for all by offering himself.”

What did our Lord Jesus Christ do? He offered a sacrifice not for his own offenses but for ours, and he did this once, not repeatedly. Having died once for our sins, he does not die again; death no longer has dominion over him.

Here he shows the greatness of Christ’s sacrifice: offered once, it prevailed as greatly as all the legal sacrifices could not prevail. For it was one sacrifice, offered once, and it suffices forever to remove all the sins of believers.

The Jewish high priests were sinners, and therefore they needed to offer sacrifices for their own offenses. For this reason those sacrifices could not justify a human being, since it was inappropriate that an irrational animal should be offered for a rational human being.

A sinless high priest and a rational victim were sought, but none was found. One was found who was without sin, God and man, and he offered himself as a rational sacrifice for the salvation of rational humanity.

The law appoints as priests men who have weakness. The Lord said to Moses: “You shall anoint Aaron and his sons as priests for me.” But because they possessed weakness—that is, sins—they offered sacrifices for their own offenses as well as for those of the people.

This one, however, is so powerful that he did not need to offer for himself; moreover, by the one-time offering of the sacrifice of his flesh, he was sufficient for the salvation of all.

But the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son perfect forever.

Supply: it “shows,” or “establishes,” him as a perfect priest, not burdened with weakness, as the law established its own priests after the law was given. The word of God the Father was addressed to David concerning Christ with an oath, where it says: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever.”

Here the Apostle uses the name “Son” to distinguish him from the servants who were under the law. They were weak, either because they were sinners or because they were mortal; but he shows the Son to be perfect, because he always lives and is without sin.

## Chapter VIII.

## Chapter VIII

“Now, the chief point concerning the things being said.” That is, a recapitulation concerning what is being said about Christ. By this statement he signifies something supreme and great, and, as though by a recapitulation of the preceding arrangement, he leads the hearer to the matter itself.

“We have such a high priest.” Supply: such as we described above—namely, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners—and such as we shall further describe in what follows. “Who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of holy things and of the true tabernacle, which God established, and not man.”

We should understand “the throne of Majesty in the heavens” as the fullness of the Father’s majesty, in which the Son of God sits; this is also indicated by “the right hand.” We must not childishly understand this as meaning that God the Father has a right or left hand, since he is spirit and fills all things, so that the Son sits at his right hand as a son ordinarily sits beside his father who is king. Rather, as we have said, by “the right hand” we should understand the fullness of majesty and the highest glory of blessedness and prosperity, in which the Son sits. “To sit” is used here in the sense of “to dwell.”

Our high priest, therefore, who has taken his seat in the highest glory of the Father’s majesty in the heavens, is a minister of holy things. This can be understood in two ways. When the Lord came into the world through the manifestation of his incarnation, he ministered to the holy apostles and to the other faithful—including those who were still to come—the bread of nourishment, the spiritual word, and the drink of evangelical teaching, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

He also ministered to them the instruction of faith and the grace of baptism, and, beyond this, what was greater: the sacrament of redemption through his passion, together with knowledge of the mysteries contained in the Law and the Prophets. After his ascension, he ministered to his chosen ones by appearing in the world.

It may also be said in another way: he will be a minister of holy things in the future, when he will minister himself to them and they will know him with the Father and the Holy Spirit as he is—namely, when he has handed over his kingdom to God and the Father. Accordingly, in the Gospel, speaking of himself under the figure of a master of a household, he says: “Truly I tell you, he will gird himself and make them recline at table, and, coming by, he will minister to them.” He is said to “come by” because he will make his chosen ones pass from judgment into the kingdom; or because he will raise us from contemplation of his humanity to knowledge of his divinity.

He will minister to them when he manifests himself and the Father with the Holy Spirit to them. For their food and life will be the vision of the Holy Trinity, as he himself says to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they may know you with the Holy Spirit, and Jesus Christ whom you sent, the one true God.”

He is also the minister of the true tabernacle, which God established or constructed, and not man—that is, of heaven, which he himself administers to us, so that we may be illumined by the radiance of its stars. For the tabernacle that Bezalel constructed in the wilderness, or the temple that Solomon made in the Promised Land, was not the true one; it was consumed by age and could not endure forever. Therefore he calls heaven the true tabernacle, because it will stand forever and will not be consumed by any old age.

It can also be understood in a higher sense, so that the souls of the saints are taken as the true tabernacle—souls to which the Son of God ministers the joys of the heavenly homeland and in which he deigns to dwell, in accordance with what he says through the Prophet: “I will dwell in them and walk among them.” And the Apostle says: “Christ dwells through faith in our hearts, in the inner man”; and: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.”

[Col. 0734A] For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; hence it is necessary that this one also have something to offer. He cannot be a priest unless he has something to offer. The priests of the former priesthood, according to the command of the Law, offered gifts and sacrifices for the sins of the people; but Christ, in the eternal nature of his divinity, since he had nothing that he could offer, took from us something to offer for us—that is, human flesh, namely himself, whom he offered upon the altar of the cross.

What, then, is so suited to sacrifice as rational flesh offered for irrational flesh? And what is so pure for those being cleansed as flesh without any stain, offered undefiled? And since four things must be considered in every sacrifice—namely, to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—we can also find all these here in a most fitting manner. Since sacrifice is owed to no one except God alone, our high priest offered a pure victim to God the Father for us.

While himself remaining the priest at the sacrifice, he also offers to God the Father a sacrifice acceptable through his Church. Therefore, while we offer the sacraments of his body, he himself offers.

“If, then, he were on earth”—supply: a priest on earth according to the order of Aaron—“he would not be a priest” according to the order of Melchizedek, “since there are priests of Levitical descent who offer gifts according to the Law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, as Moses was instructed when he was about to complete”—that is, finish—“the tabernacle of the oracle.”

If there were on earth a high priest like Aaron, or another according to the order of Melchizedek—immortal and without sin—who could cleanse the human race through sacrifices and make it perfect, then there would certainly not be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek forever, because there would be enough priests to offer the gifts prescribed by the Law.

But because Aaron and his sons were mortal and sinners, they could not make the human race perfect. Therefore Christ came, without sin, to hold his priesthood forever and, by his sacrifice, to cleanse the human race most perfectly—not like those who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.

A “copy” is a figure and likeness by which another reality is displayed, just as an image expressed on a wall is a copy and figure of the true light. The priests of the Jews, therefore, served a copy—that is, a figure and shadow—of the heavenly mysteries, because all those things were likenesses and figures of what is now enacted in truth within the Church.

By “heavenly things,” however, he means spiritual mysteries, which in truth lead those who observe them to heavenly realities. Is not our faith a heavenly altar, on which we offer our prayers to God every day?

“See,” he says, “that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.” Since our hearing seems less suited to receiving instruction than our sight—for we do not impress upon our minds what we hear in the same way as what we perceive with our own eyes—the Lord showed Moses on the mountain not only through hearing but also through sight what he was going to make with Bezalel’s assistance. Hence he says: “See that you make everything according to that likeness which was shown to you on the mountain.”

What he says is to be understood both of the construction of the tabernacle and its vessels and of the sacrifices and victims that they were going to offer there.

[Col. 0735A] “But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry”—namely, the dignity of the priesthood—“inasmuch as he is also the mediator of a better covenant, which has been established upon better promises.” That is, confirmed, established, and strengthened.

You see, he says, how much better this observance is than the one practiced at that time: the former was a copy and figure, whereas this is the reality, as the Gospel says: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

“Now”—that is, in the final age of the world—Christ has obtained a much better priestly ministry than the legal priesthood, just as he is the mediator of a better covenant. As heavenly things are better than earthly things and eternal things than temporal things, so Jesus is the giver of a better covenant, and it has been confirmed by better promises.

That covenant promised temporal and earthly things, saying: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land”; and: “Observe what I command you, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth”; and it promised other similar temporal and earthly things.

But the New Covenant, given through Christ, promises and grants heavenly and earthly things, as well as perfect life through the grace of baptism and faith in the Lord’s passion, and the remission of all sins. “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved”; and: “The chosen will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

Beyond this, there is something greater, which is said in the Gospel of John: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God.”

See how Christ is the mediator and giver of the better covenant, and how it has been confirmed by better promises. In this too he has obtained the better priesthood, because the former was temporary, whereas this is eternal. The former could neither justify a human being nor open the kingdom of heaven to those who observed it; but this one both justifies a person perfectly and immediately opens the kingdom of heaven.

The Lord is called the mediator of the covenant because, just as Moses was mediator between God and the people, conveying God’s words to the people and then the people’s words to God, so Christ conveyed to us the words of God the Father and in turn conveys ours to him.

The Apostle moves on from priest and sacrifice and finally makes a distinction between the covenants, saying:

“For if that first”—covenant—“had been without fault, there would have been no occasion sought for a second”—covenant.

That is, if the covenant of the Law had been able to remove sins, so that those who observed it would be blameless, there would have been no place left for the second covenant. But because the former was not perfect, once it had been removed, a suitable place was found for the second covenant.

The text continues: “For finding fault with them”—that is, not approving them as worthy of praise—“he says through the Prophet: ‘Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah.’”

[Col. 0736A] As far as the literal sense is concerned, the ten tribes are understood by “the house of Israel”—the tribes that separated themselves from the house of David in the days of Jeroboam. By “the house of Judah” are understood the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, together with the priestly tribe, which remained attached to the house of David.

In a higher sense, however, by both houses we should understand all believers, both from the Jews and from the nations, who, by rightly confessing God—which is the meaning of “Judah”—are true Israelites, that is, people who see God with the mind. To them God perfected and completed the New Covenant, namely, the grace of the Gospel.

It is called the New Covenant in distinction from the Old. To speak more profoundly, the Old Covenant is so called because it could not make new the human being who was placed in the oldness of sin. But the New Covenant is so called because it makes new the old person—namely, the person defiled by the sin of the old Adam—through baptism and faith in the Lord’s passion.

It is not like the Old Covenant that he made with their fathers. The former promised earthly and temporal things and commanded carnal observances; this one promises eternal and heavenly things and commands spiritual observances.

When he said, “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt,” almighty God displayed the great intimacy that he showed toward that people. The divine speech speaks in the manner of women, who customarily take little children by the hand and often lead them along, and often support them here and there so that they do not fall, since they do not yet have firm steps.

So almighty God, when that people was childish and small—for it possessed neither the steps of good works nor the strength by which it could free itself from the yoke of its oppressors—stretched out his hand to it, namely, the great assistance of his mercy, and drew it out from the iron furnace. He led it to knowledge of himself, embraced it with the most gracious affection, and at the same time guided it through the vastness of the wilderness and brought it into a land better than all others.

But because they did not remain in his covenant—that is, because they did not keep what had been commanded them in the covenant—he disregarded them; that is, he allowed them to go according to the desires of their hearts, as the Psalmist said.

It should be noted that, when the divine speech had said, “I will complete a covenant,” it added: “Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers.” Lest the Jews, by their objections, be able to say that the covenant of which he said to Abraham, “In your seed all the nations will be blessed,” was to be destroyed, he clearly indicated which covenant he meant when he added: “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.”

For he said this about the Law, which, as is known, was given on Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day after their departure from the land of Egypt. Their fathers did not remain in it, but made a calf at Horeb and worshiped it.

But the covenant that he made with Abraham was fulfilled in Christ, in whom all the nations would be blessed.

“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel”—that is, with all believers—“after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws into their minds, and I will write them upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And no one will teach his neighbor, and no one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all will know me, from the greatest to the least of them; for I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sin no more.”

[Col. 0737A] Great is the difference between law and law, between writing and writing, between teachers of the Law and teachers of the Gospel, between the letter and the grace of spiritual understanding.

For the letter of the Law was written on tablets of stone, whereas the grace of spiritual understanding was given to the faithful by the Holy Spirit in the heart. Through that Spirit the love of God has been poured out into the hearts of the faithful.

What he says here—“I will give my laws into their minds, and I will write them upon their hearts”—refers especially to the holy apostles. They did not have the grace of the New Covenant written on tablets of stone or on parchment, but divinely engraved in their minds and hearts.

First, indeed, [they received] the Lord’s passion [reading uncertain], when, as Matthew relates, he went up the mountain and there delivered to them that lengthy sermon in which the instruction of the whole perfect life is contained.

Second, after his resurrection, as Luke testifies, “he opened their understanding, so that they might understand all the things that had been written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.”

Then, on the tenth day after his ascension, they learned everything concerning God that mortals needed to know.

How could the evangelists, after his ascension, have written down such great miracles and heavenly words unless these things had been divinely engraved upon the tablets of their hearts? This is especially true of blessed John, who wrote the Gospel sixty-five years after the Lord’s ascension. How could he have set forth so great a divinity of Christ, which the Lord himself had revealed to them, especially on the night when he was arrested?

We, however, have it written partly in our hearts, but more fully on parchment, handed down to us by them, so that we may exercise ourselves by meditating upon it.

What he adds—“No one will teach his neighbor, and no one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’”—must not be referred to the present time, when we teach one another. Rather, as blessed Augustine says, when the prophet Jeremiah was speaking about the Lord’s first coming, he suddenly turned the eye of his mind toward the second coming, after which no one will teach his neighbor to know the Lord. For all the chosen, placed in his contemplation, will see and know him as he is. In the present, as we have said, we teach one another.

[Col. 0737D] Afterward, he says, he will remember their sins no more, because all, stripped of every sediment of mortality and corruption and of the body’s mutability and sin, will be endowed with the glory of the resurrection and will shine like the angels of God in heaven.

[Col. 0738A] “By saying ‘new,’ he has made the former old.” The Apostle, taking confidence and authority from the prophetic words in which it is said, “I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel,” shows that the former covenant must now more clearly be brought to an end.

“By saying,” he says, “through the Prophet, ‘I will complete a new covenant,’ he has made the former old.” That is, he reduced it to oldness, or showed that the covenant that existed previously was old.

Hence he adds: “And what is becoming old and growing aged is near to disappearance.” It is as though he said: By saying that a New Covenant would come, the divine word showed that the former covenant was old.

It is therefore understood that, if the former covenant is becoming old and is old, it is close to perishing and reaching its end.

This should not, however, be understood of the commandments concerning life and morals, in which the Law remains, agreeing with the Gospel, but of the commands concerning carnal sacrifices. With the coming of the one whom those sacrifices prefigured, the Law was destined to receive its end.

## Chapter IX
He did indeed have earlier ordinances of worship and a worldly sanctuary.

“Earlier,” he says, “the Testament had ordinances of worship”: for through divine worship [Col. 0738B] people were justified from lesser faults. It also had a worldly sanctuary, in which it received worldly people—that is, Gentiles passing over to Judaism. It was open not only to Jews but also to such Gentiles. Thus he calls the worldly sanctuary the place of the courts where the Gentiles stood to pray after the Jews.

For the first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called holy. The Apostle is not here going to discuss that tabernacle which Moses made in the wilderness, where there was only one lampstand, but the Temple that Solomon later built in Jerusalem, where there were several lampstands. Therefore, when he says “first,” this should not be referred to time but rather to place. For the blessed Apostle says that Solomon’s Temple had two tabernacles. [Col. 0738C] He calls the first tabernacle that part of the Temple where the lampstands were, and the table on which twelve hot loaves were placed—six on one side and six on the other. Above the loaves were two golden dishes full of incense, one on one side and the other on the other side, and they remained there from Sabbath to Sabbath.

There was also a golden altar where incense was offered morning and evening. Together with this part of the Temple he includes the altar of burnt offering, which stood in the open air before the doors of the Lord’s Temple. In this tabernacle the priests and the other ministers were permitted to enter daily.

By the second tabernacle, however, he wishes the Holy of Holies to be understood: that part of the Temple which was separated by a wall twenty cubits long and by the veil hanging before the wall. Inside it was [Col. 0738D] Moses’ ark, containing the tablets of the Law, a golden urn in which the manna was kept, and Aaron’s staff, which had blossomed. The ark itself had been made in a flat form, and therefore above it was a golden slab called the mercy seat, because from there the Lord spoke to Moses and the priests. Above the ark were two cherubim, which overshadowed the mercy seat with their wings and, with their faces turned, looked upon the mercy seat.

No one entered this second tabernacle—that is, the Holy of Holies—except the high priest, once a year. Having taken blood in a vessel, he entered within to pray for the people, namely on the seventeenth day—described in the text as the seventh after the Passover festival; [the chronological wording is uncertain] that day was called the Day of Atonement. On the following day the festival of Tabernacles began.

[Col. 0739A] Spiritually, the first tabernacle, where the priests were permitted to enter, signifies the condition of the present Church. In it are many lampstands, namely the holy preachers, who shine for themselves and for others through word and example. Or it signifies the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which the hearts of the faithful are illuminated—those who abide in the Church through faith.

There is also God’s table, namely Scripture, of which the Psalmist says: “You have prepared a table before me.” There is also the presentation of the loaves upon the table, namely the understanding of Holy Scripture, by which the souls of the faithful are daily refreshed. We may also understand the bread as the body and blood of the Lord, which is consecrated in the church.

Behind the veil is the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies. [Col. 0739B] It has a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold. In it were the golden urn containing the manna, Aaron’s staff that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant. How and in what manner each of these was arranged has been explained somewhat earlier according to the literal sense; therefore let us consider the spiritual mysteries.

The veil behind which the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies stood signifies heaven, on account of its dignity, just as the Song of Songs does. Beyond it is God, in the inner regions of the heavenly homeland. When the veil had been raised, the high priest entered the Holy of Holies with blood to pray for the people. So also our High Priest, the Lord, entered the Holy of Holies with the blood of his passion. After completing that passion and opening heaven, he penetrated there, where he continually pleads with God the Father [Col. 0739C] for us.

In the Holy of Holies there was a censer, because Christ dwells in the hidden places of the heavenly homeland; through him we direct our prayers to God the Father. The ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold, is the flesh of the Lord and Savior, who is the author of both Testaments. Within, he was full of divinity; outwardly, he shone with the power of miracles and heavenly words. Gold commonly signifies the brightness of speech, as Wisdom says: “Desire wisdom as gold.”

The golden urn containing the manna is Christ, in whom is the manna of divinity. He said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” Aaron’s staff that had blossomed signifies the dignity of the priesthood, which always flourishes in Christ; or it signifies imperial power. The two tablets of the covenant in the ark are the two Testaments abiding there.

[Col. 0739D] It follows: “Above which were”—that is, above the ark—“the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat.”

The two cherubim covering it—whose name is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge”—are the two Testaments, in which there is the fullness of knowledge. They cover Christ, who is the atoning sacrifice for sins, because he lies hidden in divine Scripture.

“Concerning which things”—that is, what mystery each of them contains—“it is not now possible to speak individually.” Perhaps he was silent for this reason, because they required many words; or because his hearers were not yet capable of bearing everything.

“Now when these things had been arranged”—that is, when the things we have said were arranged in both the first tabernacle and the second, namely the Holy of Holies—“the priests always entered the first tabernacle,” that is, that part of the Temple where the altar of incense was and [Col. 0740A] before whose doors the altar of burnt offering also stood, “completing the services of the sacrifices.”

This should not be understood to mean that they offered victims upon the altar of incense in the Temple or completed the sacrificial rites there. Rather, by the services of the sacrifices we may understand the offering of incense, for which the priests always entered in the morning and evening. Or, after the sacrifice had been completed and perfected before the Temple on the altar of burnt offering, they always entered the Temple with incense. It can also be understood in a third way: as we said above, he included the altar of burnt offering together with the Temple and thereby wished to comprehend the whole by reference to a part. Either interpretation, however, may be accepted as correct.

But into the second tabernacle the high priest alone entered once a year, and not without blood, which [Col. 0740B] he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people.

The second tabernacle, into which the high priest alone entered with blood, signifies the inner regions of the heavenly homeland. That high priest signifies Christ, who entered the Holy of Holies once, within the veil, after completing his passion, so that he might now stand before God’s countenance and pray for us—not for his own sins, but for ours.

Unless perhaps it is said that he prayed for his own sins because of the communion he has with his body, which is the Church. Hence, during his passion, he says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation.” For what are “the words of my sins” except those of his body, which we are? He himself committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

The Holy Spirit signified by this that the way of the saints had not yet been made manifest. [Col. 0740C] That is, by signifying this to Moses, the Holy Spirit indicated that Christ had not yet come, Christ who would enter the secrets of heaven once with the blood of his passion.

It is as though he were saying in other words: “For this reason the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies once with blood, so that we might learn that the heavenly kingdom was still inaccessible to mortals until Christ came. After completing his passion, he would open for us the gate of the heavenly homeland by opening the veil—that is, heaven. For the way into the heavenly homeland had not yet been made manifest,” or its meaning had not yet been revealed, because people did not know what those mysteries signified.

Nor should we think that we cannot enter there because our High Priest entered first. For he himself says to the Father: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me.” And elsewhere: “Where I am, there also my minister will be.”

Because the Temple was still standing when the Apostle said these things, and legal offerings were being made there, although without purpose, he therefore added: “While the first tabernacle still had its place”—where [Col. 0740D] “things” should be understood.

“It is a parable”—that is, a figure and likeness—“for the present time,” or the time then existing. For what was being done in the Temple at that time was a figure and likeness of this truth, which was also being fulfilled in the Church.

It follows: “According to which”—that is, according to the parable or figure—“gifts and sacrifices are offered” there still by the priests. “Which gifts or sacrifices cannot perfect the worshiper according to conscience.”

Conscience means “knowledge of the heart,” by which the human [Col. 0741A] mind is understood. Those carnal gifts, he says, could not make the worshiper perfect according to the perfection of the mind, because they could not justify the mind, since they did not remove sins. For the Law brought no one to perfection. But after indicating the matters in which the purification of the Law principally consisted, he continues: “Only in foods and drinks and various baptisms and ordinances of the flesh”—“seemed,” by implication, “to make the worshiper perfect”—“until the time of correction,” that is, improvement and amendment.

These ordinances of the flesh—distinctions among foods and drinks and various baptisms or washings—were imposed until the time of the Lord’s coming, as were the other things performed in figure. When the Lord came, they were corrected, that is, amended and changed for the better. [Col. 0741B]

For by the clean animals that the Law commands to be eaten are signified clean works; by the unclean animals, unclean works, from which one must abstain. By clean drinks we should understand the teaching of ecclesiastical men; by unclean drinks, likewise, the teaching of heretics.

Concerning the Jews’ baptisms, the Gospel of Mark gives a fuller account, where the Pharisees criticized the Lord and his disciples for eating with unwashed hands. For he designates all their washings by the name “baptism.” Sometimes they washed only their hands, sometimes their feet, and sometimes the whole body, whenever they touched something unclean or even entered where there was a dead person.

But they wash their hands and [Col. 0741C] body in vain while they disdain to be washed in the Savior’s font. For when the Prophet says, “Wash yourselves, be clean, and cleanse yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the Lord,” they understood this only in a carnal sense, whereas it was spoken rather of the washing of Christ’s baptism and the purity of works.

All these things were imposed until the time of correction—that is, until the time of the Lord’s coming. Afterwards Christ changed them for the better. While they were observed carnally, they fulfilled bodily cleanliness; but when they began to be observed spiritually, they likewise began to preserve the purity of the soul.

“Christ, however, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation.”

[Col. 0741D] The Jewish high priest, who entered once a year with blood within the veil into the Holy of Holies to pray for the people, signified Christ the Lord, as has already been explained in many places. With the blood of his passion, after opening heaven, he entered the secrets of the heavenly homeland, where he now stands before God’s countenance for us.

He is called High Priest of the good things to come in two ways. The good things that he himself administered to us were the heavenly words, his birth, baptism, passion, resurrection, remission of sins, and perfect justification. They are called “good things to come” either because they were prefigured in the mysteries or because they were foretold in the divine oracles.

In a higher sense, however, we may understand the good things to come as the joys of the heavenly homeland, which have been provided for us through Christ. He is therefore also called High Priest because he has offered us a bridge—that is, the way of righteousness—by which [Col. 0742A] we may ascend to the heavenly homeland.

Another translation reads: “Christ, having come, High Priest of the good things to come.” For if he had not come, he would in no way have administered the good things to come to us, nor would he have stood before God’s countenance for us.

It should be noted that the Apostle did not simply say that he stands there, but that he does so through a tabernacle. He also used the comparative expressions “greater and more perfect.” The tabernacle through which he stands before God the Father is his humanity, for unless he had become human, he could in no way stand before God the Father.

Thus the Lord’s body is a tabernacle greater than Moses’ tabernacle and also greater than Solomon’s tabernacle. Those were made by the hands of mortal men; this one was formed within the Virgin’s womb without the seed of a man, through the work of the whole Trinity. [Col. 0742B]

Or it is greater and more excellent than those tabernacles because the divinity of the Word—which in its entirety cannot be contained in a tabernacle made by hands—rests most fully in that man. It is more perfect, or holier, than those tabernacles because neither of them could sanctify those who ministered in them or make them perfect.

What he said—“not made with hands”—he himself explained by adding, “that is, not of this creation,” of which we are, because it was not formed from human seed.

This is the stone that Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands: that is, born from the Jewish people without the seed of a man or sexual union with a male.

“Nor through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption.”

He did not enter with the blood of the animals prescribed by the Law, through which perfect justification [Col. 0742C] could not be given, but with the blood of his passion he entered the heavenly homeland. By that blood all have been perfectly redeemed and justified—not with a temporal redemption but with an eternal one.

Of this redemption it is said through Zechariah: “He visited us and accomplished the redemption of his people.” Redemption pertains to captives, and we were captives, having been taken captive by the devil in our first parent.

“For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctifies for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?”

If the blood of irrational animals could cleanse the flesh, and if, as it seemed at that time, anyone who had been unclean was sanctified [Col. 0742D] when sprinkled with that blood, much more could the blood of Christ cleanse the soul and justify it completely. But lest anyone think that full justification and cleansing came through the sprinkling of that legal blood, the Apostle added that it provided only cleansing of the flesh according to the Law. It is as though he said: “The flesh is indeed sanctified and cleansed because of the commandment of the Law; nevertheless, the soul is not purified.”

He also added the reason for the distinction, by which he showed that the blood of those animals was not without blemish, saying of Christ: “Who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God.” The Holy Spirit, who filled that man in the Virgin’s womb, guarded him so that he might pass from this world without sin and become a spotless sacrifice, a pleasing fragrance to God the Father. [Col. 0743A]

“He will cleanse our conscience”—that is, our mind—“from dead works.” Dead works are sins that kill the soul. For just as the soul lives through virtues, which are called works of life, so it dies through vices and sins and is at the same time dragged toward the death of eternal destruction. He rightly said “from dead works.” For if someone touched a dead person under the Law, he became polluted, yet was later cleansed by the sprinkling of blood. Similarly, whoever imitates the work of a dead soul is defiled, yet is cleansed through faith in the Lord’s passion.

“He who touches pitch will be defiled by it.” That is, if someone has been washed from dead works through repentance and the grace of baptism, but touches them again, he will be contaminated.

It follows: [Col. 0743B] “To serve the living God.”

Here he most appropriately shows that those who possess dead works cannot serve the true and living God, because those works are dead and false. For if someone who had touched a dead person or anything unclean was not permitted to enter the Temple, how much less will someone who possesses dead works be able to enter heaven?

“And therefore he is the mediator of a new Testament, so that, death having taken place”—or intervening—“for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first Testament, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.”

“For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene”—or take place. “For a testament is confirmed upon the dead; otherwise”—that is, in another way—“it is not yet valid,” that is, the testament is not firm “while he who made it is alive.”

Here the Apostle appears to touch upon human laws, [Col. 0743C] under which a testament that one person makes for another concerning his inheritance is customarily made firm only when the testator has departed through the death that intervenes. Once the testator who made the testament has died, it remains entirely firm.

In this way, the testament of eternal life that we have received from Christ could not otherwise remain firm for us unless he had strengthened it by his death. Our sin was so great that we could not otherwise have been redeemed and saved unless the only-begotten Son of God died for us. And because we were unworthy to obtain what he had promised, he became our mediator through his death, so that by his undeserved death he might remove the death that was owed to us.

Since many who were less perfect might perhaps have doubted [Col. 0743D] the Lord’s promises, especially because he died, as though he were weak, the blessed Apostle explains the matter. Drawing upon the common practice of human laws, he shows that testaments are made firm and receive their force not while the testators are alive but when they are dying. For as long as the testator lives, he can change his decision.

Therefore, wishing to establish firmly the testament that Christ left us, the Apostle says the same thing, declaring: “Christ is the mediator of the new Testament, so that, by his death intervening for the redemption of those transgressions that could not be removed or erased under the first Testament, but were erased through his passion, those who have been called with an eternal calling may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.”

Here he is not speaking of the general calling [Col. 0744A] of which the Lord says, “Many are called, but few are chosen,” but of the calling concerning which that outstanding preacher says, speaking of the elect: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified.”

At present we already possess in part the title to the eternal inheritance, given to us by the Lord: namely, the Gospel of that inheritance which makes those who observe it live eternally with God; the grace of the Holy Spirit; the remission of sins; knowledge of him; and the peace that he left us when he went to his passion: “Peace,” he says, “I leave you.”

We have this title to the inheritance in the present as a kind of pledge, but it will be supplied to us more perfectly when God is all in all; when Christ has handed the kingdom over to God and [Col. 0744B] the Father; and when we have been brought to the joys of the heavenly homeland, where the elect will be like the angels of God in heaven, seeing God as he is.

This will be the perfect inheritance of the elect, which Christ confirmed by his death.

Hence even the first Testament was not inaugurated without blood—that is, confirmed and consecrated. For after every commandment of the Law had been read by Moses to the whole people, he took the blood of calves and goats, together with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people.

All these things were performed in figure. For that calf, which often belonged to the priest, signified Christ, who, being the true Priest, offered the calf—that is, himself—to God the Father upon the altar of the cross. This is the calf that the father slaughtered for the return of the prodigal son.

The goat that was offered for sin likewise signifies [Col. 0744C] the same Christ, who was offered for sinners, according to what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Him who knew no sin, God the Father made sin for us”—that is, a sacrifice for sin.

Just as the Old Testament was sprinkled with blood for its confirmation, so the people were symbolically signified by the blood of Christ’s passion: the new Testament was to be confirmed and the believing people cleansed. The water with which the people were sprinkled is the water of baptism, with which the faithful are drenched.

The scarlet wool signifies the love of Christ, through which he suffered for us, and of which it is said elsewhere: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world.”

Hyssop is a low-growing herb that grows on a rock; through it Christ’s humility and [Col. 0744D] strength are signified, by which our inner parts are cleansed. For preparations of this herb are customarily used to cure diseases of the lungs. Hyssop may also be understood as repentance, which, when carried out earnestly, cleanses the inner faults of the mind.

Saying: “This is the blood of the Testament that God commanded for you,” he means: “This is the confirmation of the Testament that God commanded for you.” This blood prefigured the blood that flowed from Christ’s side on the cross. With this blood Christ sprinkled us and confirmed his Testament, just as he himself said: “This is the blood of the new Testament, for the remission of sins.”

He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry with blood.

By the tabernacle are to be understood those of whom God says through the Prophet: “I will dwell in them and walk among them,” and of whom the Apostle [Col. 0745A] says elsewhere: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.”

The various vessels are the faithful of the Church, who have different ministries. Some are vessels of preaching, such as Paul, concerning whom the Lord says to Ananias: “This man is a vessel of election for me.” Others possess different ranks and various ministries, as the same outstanding preacher recalls: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another kinds of tongues, to another the gift of healings,” and others have various gifts, which the Holy Spirit distributes to each as he wills.

Thus the tabernacle and all its vessels are sprinkled with blood, because the universal Church, together with all those who minister within it, is cleansed by the blood of Christ’s passion.

“And almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the Law, and without the shedding of blood [Col. 0745B] there is no remission.”

Why does he say that almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the Law, and that without the shedding of blood there is no remission? Because there was neither perfect cleansing nor perfect remission in those rites. The bodies were cleansed, so far as the Law was concerned, by the sprinkling or shedding of the blood of animals, and lesser sins were forgiven. But because it did not remove greater crimes or make a person perfect, the cleansing was not perfect.

Perfect cleansing and remission consist in the blood of Christ, which was poured out for us for the remission of sins. Without the shedding of his blood no one is redeemed.

“It is necessary, therefore, that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed with these sacrifices and sprinklings, but that the heavenly things themselves be cleansed with better sacrifices than these.”

[Col. 0745C] He calls the legal sacrifices “copies,” that is, figures and likenesses. But the things now celebrated in truth in the Church he calls “heavenly,” that is, spiritual, because they are to be performed spiritually. Or he calls them heavenly because they lead those who celebrate them in truth to heavenly things.

The copies of the heavenly mysteries and realities, he says—of those things that were performed in the Law as figures of what is now fulfilled in the Church—necessarily had to be accompanied in the Law by such typical sacrifices and figurative sprinklings, which prefigured the truth.

But the heavenly things themselves, that is, the spiritual things now celebrated in truth in the Church, are cleansed by better sacrifices than those prescribed by the Law, namely by the blood of Christ’s passion.

Since people were seeking true sacrifices by which they could be perfectly cleansed, and such sacrifices were not found, it was necessary for those former rites to remain until the true sacrifices came.

[Col. 0745D] “For Christ did not enter into a sanctuary made with hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us.”

He did not enter, he says, into sanctuaries made with hands—understand, those that are copies of the true ones. He calls the Holy of Holies “made with hands,” because it was first made by the hands of Bezalel in the wilderness and later similarly by the hands of craftsmen in Solomon’s Temple. Jesus did not enter these, but heaven itself, which was not made by human hands but stretched out by the command and will of God the Word.

Those sanctuaries were therefore copies and figures of the true ones, because they prefigured the true Holy of Holies into which Christ entered once.

We say that Jesus entered according to that in which he is human. [Col. 0746A] For according to that in which he is God, he is everywhere and fills all things. He did not enter sanctuaries made by human hands, but heaven itself, created by God’s command.

He showed not only this distinction but also the high priest’s immediate office (pontificem proximum factorem; the wording is uncertain): to appear before God’s face for us—that is, so that he might present himself before the Father and make him favorable toward us. Hence John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins.”

“Nor was it necessary that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters the Holy Places every year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer often from the foundation of the world.”

Christ did not enter the Holy of Holies for the purpose of offering himself repeatedly, as the Jewish high priest entered the Holy Places every year. He entered neither with another’s blood but with his own, [Col. 0746B] because he himself—the priest and the sacrifice—offered himself once upon the altar of the cross.

But after rising again he no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him. Nor is it necessary for him to die again, because his one passion is sufficient for the salvation of all believers.

“Otherwise”—that is, if the matter were otherwise, so that his having suffered once did not suffice—“he would have had to be crucified repeatedly from the foundation of the world.” That is, for every elect person who has existed and for every one who will exist, he would have had to die separately if he wished to redeem them. But he willed to die only once, because redemption was accomplished by his one death.

“But now once, at the consummation of the ages”—that is, at the end of the ages, in the final age—“he has appeared for the removal of sin through his sacrifice.”

That is, through his [Col. 0746C] body, which he made a sacrifice for sin. “Once,” he says, “at the end of the ages he appeared for this purpose: to destroy sin through his sacrifice.” He appeared appropriately at that time, when sins were many, in order to display the riches of his grace. For if this had happened at the beginning, perhaps no one would have believed it. And this occurred once, at the consummation of sins, through his own blood, not another’s.

“And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment, so also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, apart from sin, to those who await him for salvation.”

Just as it has been appointed and decreed for human beings that they cannot die except once, and afterwards receive judgment—that is, according to what each has done in the body, whether good or evil—so Christ was offered once [Col. 0746D] by himself to take away the sins of many. He cannot die again, nor do we need him to do so.

It should be noted that he was offered to take away the sins of many, and not of all, because not all will believe. The Lord himself said something similar to the Apostles: “This is my blood of the new Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins.”

What follows—“He will appear a second time, apart from sin, to those who await him for salvation”—means this: At first he appeared through his sacrifice, that is, through his mortal body, which was a sacrifice for sin. But the second time he will appear without a sacrifice for sin, because there will no longer be a sacrifice for sin as there was before; he will not be able to die thereafter.

For just as each of us [Col. 0747A] receives after death according to his works, so Christ, having conquered death and obtained the kingdom, will appear a second time to those who await him for salvation, so that he, who suffered unjustly at the hands of others, may justly vindicate his own.

This appearing to those who await him for salvation is better than the universal sight of which it is said: “Every eye will see him, even those who pierced him.”

Thus “to appear a second time without sin” means that he will no longer be seen in the likeness of sinful flesh, nor will he bear the sins of others in his body upon the cross as he did at his first coming. Nor will he intervene again for sins; rather, he will exercise vengeance against sinners.

## CHAPTER X.

For the law, possessing only a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of those things, can never, by the same sacrifices that they continually offer year after year, make perfect those who draw near. The order of the words is: “The law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of those things, can never make those who draw near to it perfect by the same sacrifices that they continually offer year after year.”

The future good things are to be understood in two ways: either as the sacraments that have been fulfilled in truth in Christ and in the Church—things that were future, in order that they might come—or as the joys of the heavenly homeland. He calls it a “shadow” because it is a figure and likeness; “image,” however, he uses for the truth. In many ways he displayed the sacraments of Christ and the Church until Christ himself, the Truth, should come, who, by the grace of the Holy Spirit bestowed upon his Church, would disclose the inner meaning of that same figure, and, by dying in the flesh, would at the same time unfold all those sacraments.

[Col. 0747C] Yet those who drew near could never be perfectly cleansed by the same sacrifices, which the priests themselves always offered year after year. Every year they offered the same irrational victims: rams, oxen, goats, turtledoves, and pigeons.

It follows: “Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, once cleansed, would have no further consciousness of sin; but in them there is a remembrance of sins every year.” “Otherwise,” that is, if they had been freed from all sins and those victims had ceased to be offered because the worshipers no longer had any consciousness—that is, memory and recollection—of the sins from which they had once been cleansed. But because this could not happen, and because greater and criminal sins could never be cleansed by those sacrifices, a remembrance of sins is made every year in those very victims. For example, if someone had offered a sacrifice for the sin of adultery, sacrilege, or parricide in the present year, it was necessary for him to do the same every year, since he could not be perfectly cleansed from that offense. Thus what took place was an accusation of sins, not their removal; an accusation of weakness, not a display of strength. In the very fact that something was offered there was a rebuke of sins; in the fact that it was always offered, there was a rebuke of the weakness of that same sacrifice. Why, then, did he command it always to be offered? Because of its weakness: it could not cleanse perfectly, so that both the memory and the rebuke of sins might be produced.

What, then, are we to say? Do our priests also not do the same every day, since they do not continually offer the sacrifice? They do offer it, certainly, but in remembrance of his death. And because we sin every day and every day need to be cleansed—because he cannot now die again—he gave us this sacrament of his body and blood, so that, just as his passion was the redemption and release of the world, so also this offering might be redemption and cleansing for all who offer it in true faith and with a good intention.

[Col. 0748A] This is how our sacrifice differs from that ancient sacrifice, which was repeated frequently, although this too is repeated: ours is the truth, whereas that was a figure; ours makes a person perfect, whereas that did not; and ours is not repeated because of its weakness, as though it could not confer perfect salvation, but in remembrance of Christ’s passion, just as he himself said: “Do this,” he said, “in remembrance of me.” And this is one victim, not many, as theirs were.

How is it one and not many, when it is offered by many different people in many places and at different times? We must therefore observe most appropriately that the divinity of the Word of God, which is one, fills all things, and is wholly everywhere; it is this divinity that makes the sacrifices not many but one, although it is offered by many. It also makes the body of Christ one with the body that he received in the virginal womb, not many bodies. Nor shall we now offer one body greater and another smaller, one today and another tomorrow; rather, we always offer the very same body, possessing equal greatness. Therefore this is one sacrifice of Christ, not different sacrifices, as theirs were.

For if it were otherwise, since it is offered in many places, there would be many Christs—which God forbid. He is therefore one everywhere, fully present here and fully present there, possessing everywhere one complete body. And just as the one who is offered everywhere is one body, not many bodies, so also there is one sacrifice.

It follows: “For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.” What reason could there be for a rational human being to be cleansed by the blood of an irrational animal? Therefore lesser sins were cleansed, and the body was purified insofar as the law was concerned; nevertheless, it was impossible for criminal and graver sins to be cleansed by those sacrifices. Hence the law brought no one to perfection.

Therefore, when he entered the world, he said: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me. You were not pleased with burnt offerings for sin. Then I said: Behold, I come—in the heading of the book it is written concerning me—to do your will, O God.”

[Col. 0748D] By these words the former sacrifices are shown to be useless for complete and perfect cleansing; they were rather a form and were not acceptable to God, since from the beginning he was not pleased with them. We must not think that almighty God was ever delighted by the smell of flesh or by the burning of animals, although it is written that he smelled “the fragrance of sweetness”—that is, on account of the faith and desire of the one offering. Hence through Jeremiah he says: “Your burnt offerings are not acceptable to me, and your sacrifices have not pleased me.” And through Isaiah: “Do not continue to offer sacrifice,” he says; “incense is an abomination to me. Whoever slaughters an ox is like one who brains a dog.”

A considerable question can arise from this: Why did he command that they be offered if they did not please him and it was not his will?

This can be resolved in two ways. Almighty God, seeing that the minds of the Jews were inclined toward the worship of idols and the imitation of pagan rites, commanded them to offer many sacrifices, lest, sitting idle without sacrifices, they should fall into the worship of foreign gods when they saw others making offerings. He preferred that they offer to him things created by him rather than to idols and demonic apparitions. He imposed servitude upon them, not justification, because it was not his will that such things be offered.

In a similar way the excellent preacher, following the Creator in dealing with creatures, acted in his own statements when he said: “I want all people to be like myself,” that is, chaste and continent. And again: “I want,” he says, “young men to marry and beget children,” because of fornication and adultery. Behold, he established two wills; yet both are not his will. In the first statement—“I want all people to be continent like myself”—he expressed his own will. In the second—“I want young men to marry”—he spoke in the interest of indulgence, because of the weakness of the flesh.

Similarly, it was not the will of almighty God that such sacrifices be offered, but because of their weakness he commanded them. Hence earlier he said that he not only did not will them, but did not even desire them.

The matter can also be resolved in this way: because the true sacrifice of Christ in the Church was destined to come, he commanded types and figurative sacrifices to precede it. Indeed, it was necessary that, just as it was foretold in words, it should also be prefigured through mysteries, so that they might pass from figures to the truth.

[Col. 0749C] But because those sacrifices did not please him, he came again—the one of whom the Apostle says: “Therefore,” he says, “because it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of goats, and because such sacrifices did not please God, when entering the world”—there is no doubt that he means Christ.

This entrance is nothing other than his mission and his appearance, namely, the appearance of his humanity. For when the one who was everywhere present, yet invisible, later became human and appeared visibly to the world, in a certain manner he entered the place where he already was.

And what does he say to God the Father? “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared”—or “perfected”—“a body for me; I shall offer it to you as an acceptable sacrifice. You were not pleased with burnt offerings for sin. Then I said: Behold, I come through the mystery of the Incarnation, so that by my sacrifice I may redeem the human race.”

A “holocaust” was called a sacrifice that was entirely burned upon the altar, as though wholly consumed by fire. For ὅλον (*holon*) means “whole,” while καυστόν (*causton*) means “burnt,” as in *holovitreum*, “entirely glass.”

But if burnt offerings for sin did not please him, one may ask how people were cleansed by them. The answer is that they were cleansed by faith and worthy repentance, just as David was cleansed from the sin of adultery and murder. Perfect cleansing, however, was given at Christ’s coming.

“In the heading of the book it is written concerning me, to do your will, O God.” The teachers dispute in various ways about the heading of this book. Some understand it as the beginning of Genesis, where it is written, “In the beginning”—that is, in the Son God made heaven and earth. Some understand it as the first Psalm, which some refer to Christ and others to any chosen person, in which it says: “His delight is in the law of the Lord.”

[Col. 0750A] But since none of these contains anything prefiguring Christ’s death, about which the Apostle speaks throughout this passage, it seems better to understand the statement as referring to the beginning of the book of Leviticus. Since that book is entirely concerned with sacrifices and victims, it first commanded a sacrifice to be offered from a calf, saying: “If anyone among you offers a sacrifice to God from the cattle, let him offer a male without blemish”—that is, a calf from the oxen or from the herd.

This calf, taken from the oxen and offered as a sacrifice, is Christ, born from the line of the patriarchs and sacrificed for the salvation of the human race. For it was the will of God the Father that the Son redeem the human race through his passion. Thus the Son himself, as his passion drew near, says: “But that the world may know that I love the Father”; and: “As the Father commanded me, so I do. Rise, let us go from here”—that is, let us go to the passion.

Earlier he said: “You did not desire sacrifices, offerings, and burnt offerings for sin, nor were those offered according to the law pleasing to you. Then I said: Behold, I come to do your will, O God.”

“He takes away the first”—understand, the first Testament—when he rejects its offerings, “in order to establish the second,” namely, the Testament, that is, to make it stand and remain.

“In this will”—the will of God the Father, which the Son fulfilled—“we have been sanctified.” In baptism. “Through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” What he says by “once for all” is as though he were saying: We have been sanctified in baptism through the passion that Christ underwent once for all.

[Col. 0750C] “And every priest of the law stands ready.” At the altar, ministering daily and offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins—understand, criminal and capital sins.

“But this one”—there is no doubt that he means Christ—“offering one sacrifice for sins forever, sits at the right hand of God, henceforth waiting until his enemies are placed as a footstool beneath his feet.”

To minister, or to offer, is a sign of ministry, by which Christ’s humility is understood. The altar, however, is a sign of the one who judges and rules, so that service may be rendered to him. Through this is shown the exaltation and glory of Christ, who appeared in humility but now, exalted above every creature, dwells in the fullness of majesty, waiting and considering the time that remains until he judges.

He explains the reason for this delay when he says: “Until his enemies are placed as a footstool beneath his feet.” His enemies are the Jews, heretics, false Christians, and all unbelievers, who are to be subjected to his power. Here one may also understand a necessary subjection, which pertains to the reprobate who remain in wickedness, and a voluntary subjection, which pertains to the elect, who abandon the way of wickedness and willingly subject themselves to Christ.

Those Jewish priests, by offering many sacrifices every day, could not take away sins; but Christ, offering himself once for all, took away the sins of the world. He now sits in the glory of God the Father. “By one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified.”

The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us. For after he had said, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will place my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds; and I will no longer remember their sins and iniquities,”

[Col. 0751A] the Holy Spirit, he says, also bears witness to us—that is, he confirms our words by his testimony—not only through the Psalmist but also through the prophet, showing that those sacrifices are no longer to be offered.

In the following words there is a necessary omission in the sentence; therefore it should be supplied as follows: After almighty God had said through the prophet Jeremiah, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will place my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds,” he immediately added: “And I will no longer remember their sin,” showing that figurative sacrifices would no longer be necessary.

This too the Apostle makes clear when he adds: “Where there is forgiveness of these”—that is, of sins—“there is no longer any necessary offering for sin.” For after this covenant, which God had promised through the prophet, was fulfilled, those sacrifices immediately came to an end, because when the truth came, the shadow departed.

It must therefore be noted that where there is no remembrance of sins—which are forgiven in baptism through faith in the Lord’s passion—there is no longer any need for the offering of the law for sin.

“Therefore, brothers, having confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Christ, the new and living way that he opened for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh, and having a great Priest over the house of God…”

[Col. 0751C] Up to this point he has shown the distinction and great difference between the high priest and the sacrifices, the tabernacle and the covenant, and the promise. Now, by inviting them, he exhorts them to those things that have come to us in truth through Christ, giving authority concerning the great High Priest and saying: “Therefore,” he says, “we have greater confidence because we have been cleansed through the blood of Christ than those who offered sacrifices according to the flesh, because our victim is true and rational.”

We have confidence of entering heaven through the blood of Christ in proportion as we have become more fully co-heirs. No one can attain the gifts of the Holy Spirit except through faith or confidence—that is, through the new and living way that Christ opened for us. He gave us the beginning of using this way. He calls faith “a new way,” because it was given through Christ; or it may mean the example of humility by which Christ himself proceeded, humbling himself even unto death.

We may also understand the new way as the entrance to the heavenly homeland, opened to us through Christ. It is called new because it was accessible to no one before.

By calling it “new,” he attempts to show that all greater things are now new: the way of faith is now open to us, through which we receive complete justification, and the gates of heaven have been opened to us—something that had previously been granted to no one.

He also called it “living,” that is, always enduring and always open, because right faith will remain eternally and the gate of heaven will always stand open.

Christ opened this way for us—that is, he dedicated and confirmed it, or gave it—“through the veil,” that is, through his flesh. He first opened that way by ascending to the heavenly homeland, and he himself first gave us the beginning of using it.

[Col. 0752A] The Lord’s flesh is appropriately designated by the name “veil.” For just as the veil concealed the ark and the things beyond it, so the divinity of the Word lay hidden beyond Christ’s humanity. And just as one reached the inner things through the veil, so through his humanity one reaches knowledge of his divinity.

By the “great Priest over the house of God,” Christ is understood, for he was appointed by God the Father over the Church, in accordance with what he himself says: “But I have been appointed king by him.”

It follows: “Let us draw near with a true heart and in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.”

These words depend upon what came before, where the Apostle says: “Therefore, brothers, having confidence to enter the holy places through the blood of Christ, let us draw near to God with a true heart.”

What does it mean to draw near to Christ with a true heart? He explained this by adding: “In the fullness of faith,” so that we may believe that there will be a general resurrection. It is as though he were saying: Since we now have confidence to enter the heavenly homeland, we must not hesitate, as though some would rise and others would not; rather, with true faith we must believe that all human beings will rise, some to glory and others to punishment. For anyone who hesitates about this does not possess true and complete faith.

It may also be understood in another way: full faith is conceived in the heart, confessed with the mouth, and adorned with good works. Whoever wishes the entrance to the heavenly homeland to be opened must draw near to the Lord with this faith.

[Col. 0752C] It is therefore necessary that hearts be “sprinkled,” that is, cleansed from an evil conscience through the heart—from sins and from an evil will—or that we possess pure hearts. At the same time he shows that not faith alone is sought, but also a life accompanied by virtues, since faith without works is dead.

The Jews cleansed their bodies, not their consciences. “And washed,” he says—that is, possessing a body washed with pure water—which means the water of baptism. He says that the body must be washed with baptismal water because, when the body is washed with water, the soul is sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

“Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.” We hold the confession of hope without wavering if we do not despair of the heavenly homeland and of all that the Lord promised us, or if we firmly observe what we professed in baptism.

For just as Christ is a faithful and true rewarder in his promises, so he wants us to be faithful in our promises, which we made at the time of baptism: to renounce the devil and to serve Christ.
