“And let us consider one another, for the provoking of love and good works.” That is, let us look carefully among ourselves, and whenever we see someone possessing greater love and devoting himself to better works, let us be provoked by his example, so that we may imitate him with the greatest zeal. Let us direct our attention toward him so that we may be loved, for good works proceed from love.

Therefore love is a great good, and nothing is good that is not done through love, since love is the fullness of the law.

“Not forsaking our assembly”—that is, the congregation of the faithful—“as is the custom of some, but comforting”—understand, one another.

[Col. 0753A] In this passage he not only admonished but also blamed and frightened those who were splitting the unity of love. For there were many who disturbed the congregation of the faithful, as though, because of their holiness, they could not live among the others. They abandoned their assembly and lived alone, so that they might seem to devote themselves more freely to God.

Such people, filled with pride, despised the others and divided charity. The Apostle both admonishes and frightens them, urging them not to abandon the fellowship of the faithful, but rather to desire to comfort the simpler members and to strengthen them by their example. So powerful is the fellowship of the faithful that wherever two or three are gathered in the name of the Savior, he himself is in their midst.

It follows: “And all the more”—pursue love and comfort one another—“as you see the day approaching,” the day of judgment, on which the merits of each person will be examined; or the final day of our life. For he says elsewhere: “Do not be anxious about anything, for the Lord is near.”

“For if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth”—that is, after receiving knowledge of the true faith and the grace of baptism—“there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.”

If we sin willingly and deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the true faith and after being cleansed in baptism, no sacrifice for sin is reserved for us to be offered on our behalf, as it was granted in the Old Testament that sacrifices should be offered repeatedly for sin.

For Christ, who is our sacrifice, is not to be sacrificed again for our sins. This happened once, and there is no need for it a second time. Rather, after receiving grace, we must remain in right faith and in the purity of good works.

[Col. 0753C] You were cleansed in baptism; you were freed from all crimes and sins; you became a child of God. If you return to your former state, an exceedingly severe judgment will await you unless you are recalled through worthy repentance.

By these words he does not exclude repentance, nor the reconciliation that takes place through repentance; nor does he repel or cast sinners down into despair. Rather, he excludes a second washing of baptism. He was not so hostile to our salvation as to say that there is no longer any repentance or forgiveness of sins. Instead he says that there is no longer a sacrifice—that is, no longer a cross, so that Christ might be crucified again and we might be baptized again.

For just as Christ died once and no longer dies, so we, once baptized in the likeness of his death and burial, cannot be baptized again, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “Buried with him through baptism into death.”

How much greater will his grace be among them when there are more of them?

But there is a fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal—or “jealousy”—of fire that will consume the adversaries. “Zeal” is sometimes used for imitation and sometimes for envy; here it means consumption and vengeance.

The Apostle therefore frightens everyone, so that after the washing of baptism they may fear falling back into vices, since they cannot be baptized again. He also frightens them so that, if they sin, they may immediately strive to perform worthy repentance. For whoever neglects the medicine of repentance will be devoured by vengeance and the consuming fire of eternity.

Therefore each person should flee to the remedies of repentance while he has time, lest he be handed over to eternal fire.

“A person who sets aside the law of Moses, convicted on the testimony of two or three witnesses”—understand, after being convicted—“dies without mercy. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as polluted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

It is called the law of Moses because it was given by the Lord through Moses. In the same way, in the Lord’s Prayer we customarily say to the Lord: “Give us this day our daily bread”—not because it belonged to us beforehand, but because, when it is given by him, it becomes ours.

[Col. 0754B] The Apostle instills terror in Christians by taking his comparison from the law of Moses. If anyone had transgressed that law, making it void and empty, and had been convicted by two or three witnesses, he was judged by the authorities without any mercy or pardon and was immediately put to death.

He therefore says: If the person who transgressed the law given through a servant was killed without mercy, how much greater punishment will be endured by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God?

Since Christ is so much greater than Moses, and the grace of the Gospel given through the Son is so much greater than the law given and administered through a servant, so much greater and worse punishment will be deserved by the one who tramples upon Christ.

But how can we trample upon him who sits at the right hand of God the Father, raised above all the heavens? When we regard his commandments as worthless and disdain to fulfill them, then indeed we trample upon him.

For just as we regard as worthless and without honor the things we trample upon, so those who sin freely, without fear and without repentance, trample upon Christ—or despise and scorn him—and have no fear of him as the future judge.

Or certainly anyone who receives his body unworthily tramples upon Christ.

Or, to state a third interpretation, the one who expels Christ from the tabernacle of his heart by living wickedly tramples upon him—Christ who said: “I will dwell in them and walk among them.”

[Col. 0754C] He also regards the blood of the covenant as polluted—or, as it is found in Greek, as “common” or “unclean”—when he treats the blood of Christ’s passion as worthless, the blood by which the New Testament was confirmed and by which he himself was sanctified from the time of the passion.

In yet another way, to regard the blood of the covenant as polluted means to receive the mystery of Christ’s blood unworthily and to make no distinction between it and other things, although through it he was sanctified at the time of baptism and could also be sanctified daily if he received it worthily.

Of such people the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not distinguishing or discerning the body and blood of the Lord from other foods and drinks.”

He also insults the Spirit of grace—that is, the Holy Spirit—who expels him from the tabernacle of his heart by living wickedly. Or he does so by refusing to believe that through the Spirit forgiveness of sins takes place in the Church. Or certainly he insults him by blaspheming against him, denying his works and attributing them to the devil.

Hence the Lord says: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

He is called the Spirit of grace either because through him sins are freely forgiven us, or because, through his distribution, the graces of spiritual gifts are divided among the faithful. The Apostle mentions these when he says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,” and so forth, until he concludes: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills.”

“For we know the one who said: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay.’” Almighty God speaks through the prophet: “I will repay with vengeance the one who does me injury and insult, and I will requite them according to what they deserve.” And again: “For the Lord will judge his people.”

This was said concerning enemies. “I will repay those who do evil,” not those who suffer evil—that is, those who live negligently and refuse to purify themselves through repentance, but, while doing evil, approach the Lord’s table without concern.

The people whom the Lord is said to judge can be understood in two ways: the statement can refer to the chosen people or to the reprobate. For “the Lord will judge his people” means that he will separate his own people and distinguish the good from the evil, the faithful from the unfaithful. If it is referred to the reprobate, “to judge” must be understood as “to condemn.” The people of the Lord are called his people not by grace but by creation.

“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” The person who fears human judgment but disregards the judgment of almighty God falls into the hands of the Lord. Whoever, after sinning, scorns to perform repentance also falls into his hands—that is, into the power and judgment of almighty God.

Therefore every sinner who does not repent of his sins will fall into the fearful and greatly dreaded judgment of almighty God, who will repay each person according to his works.

“Recall the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings.”

The best physicians, when they have cut into a wound and increased the pain through the incision, apply comfort and remedy to the place where the pain is present and disturbing, and restore the troubled soul. Once they have recalled the patient to health, they do not make another incision; rather, they soothe and comfort what has been done with gentler and effective medicines that lessen the severity and calm the pain.

[Col. 0755D] In this passage the Apostle acts in the same manner. After he had shaken their souls and pierced them with the mention of Gehenna, affirming in every way that those who at any time insult God’s grace would perish, and teaching this from the law of Moses and other testimonies, and saying that it was fearful to fall into the hands of the living God, he immediately consoles them—lest they collapse into despair through excessive fear—with praise, encouragement, and prayers, bringing their former good works back to their memory.

“Recall,” he says, “the former days, in which, after being enlightened through faith and strengthened by divine grace, you endured a great struggle of sufferings.” It is as though he were saying: When you were introduced to the faith, when you were at the beginning of faith, you displayed such strength that you endured a great struggle of sufferings for Christ’s name at the hands of your fellow countrymen.

For some of the Jews who believed were stripped of their possessions by those who did not believe; others were not. Those who were not stripped of their possessions supplied the others from their own resources. When the unbelievers learned of this, they inflicted many evils upon them both [*utriusque*; the manuscript reading may perhaps be *utrisque*, “both groups”]. Hence the Apostle does not simply say that they endured a struggle, but adds “a great” one; nor does he say “temptations,” but “sufferings.”

“And in one respect you were made a spectacle through reproaches and tribulations.” You were. “In another respect you became companions of those who lived in this way.”

“In one respect,” he says, “you were made a spectacle through reproaches”—that is, insults and mockery—and through tribulations. This means that you were mocked publicly and in the sight of many. “In another respect you became companions in the suffering of those who lived in this way”—namely, the apostles and those who had been stripped of their own possessions, afflicted with blows, and thrust into prison.

He shows in two ways that they had labored well: either because they had been publicly afflicted with various insults and tribulations—for the human race finds it especially difficult to endure suffering something shameful, whether in words or deeds, in the sight of many—or because, when others were imprisoned, they shared their suffering and supplied them with food and clothing as far as they could. Hence they became their companions, because the reward and recompense received by a preacher of the truth who is imprisoned and afflicted by other torments for Christ’s name will also be received by the one who provides him assistance, so that he does not fail amid his tribulations. The Truth himself promises this when he says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward.”

It must also be noted that he did not simply say, “afflicted by tribulations,” but added the reason, saying: “You were made a spectacle.” For when someone is reproached secretly, he seems to endure it more easily. But that they had endured the things we have enumerated he now shows more openly when he continues:

[Col. 0756C] “For you also had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions.”

He praises them wonderfully in the faith. For if they did not have faith that they would receive better things in return for the substance taken from them, they would not have accepted its seizure with joy.

As long as it was permitted to them, they shared the suffering of others who had been stripped of their possessions and placed in prison. Those who were stripped of their possessions, however, accepted with joy the seizure and loss inflicted upon them, believing that they would receive better things. Hence he adds:

“Knowing that you have a better and enduring possession.”

It is as though he were saying: Seeing that spiritual riches were destined for you in place of these temporal ones, you endured with joy the seizure of your temporal possessions.

All this was an apostolic work and worthy of courageous souls: to rejoice in the scourging. As it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “They went away from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus.”

And to show that this temporal possession would not last forever, he therefore said that they had a better possession, and one that endured—as though he were saying: firm, substantial, and perpetual, incapable of perishing, unlike this earthly possession, which perishes.

“Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.” That is: Do not fail amid your tribulations, because the reward is great.

It is evident that they possessed great confidence before God, and he urges them most earnestly not to lose it. For things that are kept intact are more easily preserved than recovered once lost. Therefore whatever is held and has cause for fear must possess courage.

“You have no need,” he says, “of anything except to stand firm in your faith and remain in your courage, which has a great reward with God.”

“For you need endurance, so that, after doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.”

O what a great exhortation and consolation! It is as though someone were saying this to an athlete and contestant who had overcome everyone and had no one left who could compete with him. For example, if he were to say: “Since I have now overcome everyone, and there is no one who will compete with me, give me the crown,” anyone might say to him: “Wait a little, until the judge—or even the king—comes to award you the prize for your victory.”

But if that athlete impatiently endured neither thirst for water nor the heat, saying: “Either give me what I deserve, or I will withdraw,” he would be told: “Endure this brief delay patiently. The emperor is about to come, and he will give you your reward.”

He is indeed saddened, but much more so if it happens publicly and in the sight of many. For just as the human race greatly delights in public praise, so it is easily ensnared by reproaches openly inflicted upon it.

In this way the Apostle urges them not to fail but patiently to await the Lord’s coming: “You need endurance,” he says. That is, what you truly need is to persevere in the contest until you receive a crown worthy of your labor.

For it is not the one who has begun who will be crowned, but the one who perseveres in the contest to the end; he will be saved.

“In your endurance,” says the Lord, “you will possess…”
your souls. “You will receive,” he said, “the promise”—that is, you will receive the glory of everlasting blessedness. For yet “a very little while, and the one who is to come will come, and will not delay.” There is no doubt that he signifies Christ: he consoles them as though only a little time remained until he comes. For it is no small consolation amid toil to hope that the judge and the one who rewards steadfastness and struggle will come soon.

“But my righteous one lives by faith. And if he draws back, he will not please my soul.” The Apostle introduced this prophetic testimony to encourage faith, for the gaining of the soul. Just as the soul is the life of the body, so faith is the life of the soul: it is conceived in the heart, confessed with the mouth, and adorned by works, since faith without works is dead. If anyone withdraws from this faith, he will not please the will of God.

For one must not suppose that God the Father, or the Holy Spirit, or even the Son, possesses a soul in the nature of divinity. Rather, divine Scripture speaks in human fashion; in condescension to us, it expresses God’s will under the name “soul.” It must also be considered that, just as the one who hesitates will displease God, so the one who believes will please him, living by his sound faith.

“You have labored,” he says, “in the contest; await that hope. Do not seek here what you hope for, because the righteous one lives by faith.” But we are not children of withdrawal, destined for destruction, but children of faith, destined for the gaining of the soul. “We,” he says, “that is, I and you, are not children of those pagans and Gentiles who withdraw from the life of faith and from everlasting light, to the destruction of their souls. Rather, we are children of the patriarchs, who had been proved by faith and perfected in faith, so that they might gain their own souls for salvation—and, moreover, the souls of others through their example.”

## Chapter XI.

Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. The order of the words is: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for,” namely, the evidence of things not seen. Faith is to believe what is not seen; and when we believe in truth that things we have not seen either existed, exist, or will exist, faith itself makes them present in our heart, as though before our bodily eyes. In matters that are seen, however, neither belief nor unbelief can properly be spoken of, but rather knowledge.

Indeed, faith is for the mind to be as firmly convinced about things that are not seen as about things already seen; and when this happens, faith makes them present within us through believing. For example, to use at least a few examples from many: the general resurrection has not yet taken place; and although it does not yet exist in substance, hope makes it present in our soul, as though we had it before our eyes. This is what I meant when I said that faith is the substance of those things that are hoped for, not yet of those that are seen. And if the same faith is the evidence of things that do not yet appear, why do they now wish to see it? The ancients used *arguere* to mean “to show”; from this comes *argumentum*, as though it meant the showing and foreseeing of future things and of things that are not seen. Properly, however, an *argumentum* is a reason that establishes belief in a doubtful matter.

[Col. 0758B] It is therefore perfectly clear that faith is the evidence of things that cannot appear. For things that appear no longer require faith, as we said above, but knowledge. When Thomas therefore saw and touched, why is he told, “Because you have seen me, you have believed”? He saw one thing and believed another. The Divinity cannot be seen by mortal man. Thus, by seeing, he believed: contemplating the true man, he exclaimed that he was God, whom he could not see.

“In this”—understand, “by this faith”—“they obtained a testimony.” “Of righteousness.” “The elders.” Here we must understand by “elders” the fathers of the Old Testament: namely, the patriarchs, prophets, and other righteous men who, through the faith by which they believed God and his promises, advanced a testimony of praise and righteousness. Hence, because Abraham believed God, it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called God’s friend.

This faith must be understood as something believed in the heart, confessed with the mouth, and adorned by works. For the one who truly believes is the one who practices in action what he believes. Conversely, concerning those who retain faith in name only, Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him.”

By faith we understand that the ages were prepared by the word of God, so that visible things came into being from invisible things. Because the souls of the Hebrews were still weak, and although they had begun from faith, they became fainthearted through the sufferings of tribulations and bore with insufficient patience the evils inflicted upon them, the Apostle first encouraged them from their own experience, saying: “Remember the former days”; then from divine Scripture, which says: “The righteous person lives by faith”; and thereafter by arguments, showing that faith is the substance of things not seen. Now, however, he begins to speak of their ancestors, wonderfully setting them before them as an example: just as all those people were saved through faith, so we too are all saved through faith. For when the soul finds a companion in the same sufferings, it rests and breathes again; and this commonly happens amid faith and tribulations of whatever kind.

[Col. 0758C] The human race is exceedingly fragile and overly hesitant in thought; therefore consolation from the faith and patience of those who preceded us is necessary. The Apostle accordingly encourages them from the fathers, but first from the common beginning, saying: “It is evident,” he says, “that God did not make the things that exist from things already existing, but visible things from invisible things, and existing things from things that did not exist.”

By reasoning, therefore, we cannot discover how he made everything from nothing, or visible things from invisible things, since we were not present when they were made. How, then, is it held to be certain? Certainly, it is evident that believing this is a matter of faith. For by faith we believe that the ages were prepared—that is, perfected or made—because the things that are seen were made not from visible things but from invisible things.

By “invisible things” we may understand unformed matter, of which it is said at the beginning of Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” By the name “heaven,” however, we must not understand this bodily heaven that is called the firmament, but the angelic nature and the spiritual heavens. By “earth” is understood the unformed matter from which all things were subsequently made: namely, all bodily things, which were then in a certain sense invisible, when darkness was over the face of the abyss.

From invisible matter visible things were made, when everything was divided and distinguished according to forms and appearances. What he says—“so that visible things might come into being from invisible things”—can also be understood in another way: before the world was formed, it existed invisibly in the wisdom of God; yet through the completion of the work it became visible to human desire.

When he says that the ages were perfected by the word of God, by “ages” we should understand all things made in times or ages by the word of God the Father, in accordance with what John said: “All things were made through him.” The ages, as Ovid Naso says, are called *saecula* from “following,” because they follow one another and revolve, as Varro bears witness. They can be called *saecula* from the time when variety began to exist in time.

By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks.

[Col. 0758D] He places first the one who suffered evil—and suffered it from his brother—offering an example particularly suited to them, since they too had suffered the same things from their fellow tribesmen and brothers. Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain, that is, a better sacrifice—not because that sacrifice was materially greater, but because whatever better thing Abel possessed, he presented to the benevolent God with a devout spirit, and from this his gifts were multiplied. We understand that he pleased God by this, for he did it through faith: he believed that the things he offered with good will were pleasing to God and that God would reward him.

God also bore witness to his gifts—either because fire descended from heaven, as Theodotion records: “The Lord set fire upon Abel and upon his gifts”; or because he was approved as righteous through that judgment by which the Lord praised him in the Gospel. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Truly I tell you, the blood of the righteous that has been shed upon the earth will be required of you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah.”

Through that sacrifice the dead man still speaks, and it is said: “The blood of Abel cries out to me from the earth.” Or “he still speaks” means this: although Cain killed him bodily, he could not kill his glory along with him. For while his glory is proclaimed throughout the whole world, while his praise is spoken by human lips, and while everyone admires him, the dead man still speaks every day. For one who admonishes others by his example to be righteous—how does he not speak?

By faith Enoch pleased God, and he was transferred so that he would not see death; and he was not found, because God transferred him. Enoch pleased God through faith because he was adorned with good works, believing that through it he would altogether please God. Therefore he was transferred to the earthly paradise, from which Adam was once expelled, so that he might not undergo bodily death until the time established by God has run its course. It is not for us to inquire in what manner of life or in what condition he now exists in paradise. This, however, must be believed: he rests in that paradise without any distress, pain, or labor.

[Col. 0759A] And just as he lives without any assault of the flesh or any lust of the flesh, so, if the first man had not sinned, when the full number of the elect had been completed, he would have been transferred from the earthly paradise to the heavenly paradise. The reason he was transferred was that he had pleased God; but the reason he pleased God was his faith. For if he had not believed that God would repay him for his labor, how could he have pleased him? Before his translation he had testimony that he had pleased God. Scripture says: “Enoch walked with God,” obeying his will.

Without faith it is impossible to please God. Enoch believed that if anyone believed that God exists and approached him, he would receive a reward. Since faith is therefore the foundation of all good things, no one can please God without faith. The one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

Thus, whoever approaches God by believing must believe that he is God—that is, that he always possesses being—in accordance with what he himself says to Moses: “I am who I am”; and, “He who is has sent me to you.” He must also believe that he is, according to the Psalmist, an eternal and true rewarder of those who seek him through good works: “Seek the Lord, and be strengthened.”

By faith Noah, having received a revelation concerning things not yet seen—that is, concerning the rains—in fear prepared an ark for the salvation of his household, through which he condemned the world. This was by comparison with the better faith and deed. And he was made heir of the righteousness that comes through faith.

Noah believed by faith that God would bring waters upon the earth, when God said to him: “The end of all flesh has come before me, and I will bring waters upon them. Make for yourself an ark of smoothed wood,” followed by the other instructions. Therefore he was saved with his whole household, that is, his family.

The completion of the work or the rational explanation achieved nothing in this case by experience: “They were marrying,” as the Lord says in the Gospel, “and the air was clear”; no signs of the Flood appeared. Nevertheless, Noah feared and, through faith, fearing things he did not yet see, built the ark for the salvation of his family. Through this faith he condemned the world by comparison with his own faith, which the world refused to possess. For he showed that those people were worthy of this punishment, since they did not wish to be corrected even through the hundred years during which the ark was being built.

[Col. 0759B] Through faith, not through the law, he was made heir of righteousness, since he alone held the faith of the fathers while the others departed from it. He is called heir of the kingdom of heaven, or heir of the world, because through his offspring the world was restored; and he appeared righteous because he believed God.

By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. It is as though he said: Abraham too pleased God through faith. As soon as God said to him, “Go out from your land and go to the land that I will show you; I will give it to you and to your seed,” he believed God and went out to the place that God had commanded him, not knowing where he was going. The place and habitation of that land were unknown to him; and insofar as he walked, he walked by faith. Or he did not know where he was going because he had no one to imitate.

By faith he dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in huts with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. *Casula* is a diminutive noun from *casa*, meaning “house.” Here it is used for tents and tabernacles in which Abraham lived with Isaac and Jacob, like travelers and pilgrims, teaching them the faith of God, since they were co-heirs of his promise.

For the promise made to Abraham was made to Isaac and Jacob, and all three together are co-heirs in Abraham’s promises. It was said to Abraham: “In you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,” and, “In Isaac your seed shall be called.” To Isaac God said: “Fulfilling the oath that he swore to your father Abraham, God will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and I will give your descendants all these regions.”

To Jacob also he said: “I am God Almighty; I will make nations grow and multiply from you, and I will give you the land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac.” Behold how all are co-heirs in the promises made to Abraham.

It should be noted that Abraham’s faith is doubled on account of the greatness of his faith; hence he is also called the father of faith. For just as he went out from his land by faith, not knowing where he was going, so by faith he remained and dwelt in his own land as though it were foreign. He saw his son living there as a stranger; he saw his grandson; he saw himself wandering in a foreign land, and he was not disturbed.

[Col. 0759C] Although it had been said to him, “I will give it to you and to your seed,” neither he, nor Isaac, nor Jacob were placed in possession of this promise, but their succession was. And because when he obeyed God by going out from his land he was not called Abraham but Abram, the Apostle carefully said: “By faith he who is now called Abraham”—for at that time he was called Abram—“dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land.” At first he was called Ram, then Abram, and finally Abraham.

For he was awaiting the city that has foundations, whose craftsman and builder is God. The heavenly city is said to have foundations because of its stability and firmness; whoever once finds a place in it can never be disinherited or torn away. Therefore, he says, they dwelt by faith in the land of promise as in a foreign land. They did not attend to the promises made concerning the earthly land, but sought the future rest.

They showed themselves worthy of greater things; for this reason he did not allow them to receive these things, because he wished to give them greater ones.

By faith Sarah herself, although barren, received power to conceive offspring, even beyond the proper time of life, because she believed that he who had promised was faithful.

Here a question arises: Why does he say that Sarah received by faith the power to conceive, when she was rebuked by the angel for laughing, as though this were a matter of unbelief? For although that laughter was laughter of joy, it did not arise from complete faith. Abraham’s laughter, however, was both joyful and full of faith. The matter is resolved as follows: although she initially doubted, afterward she was strengthened in faith by the angel’s words; the cause of her doubt was removed, and faith was introduced. This gave her power to conceive offspring, since she was already barren through age.

There were two obstacles: one of time, for she had already grown old; the other of nature, for she was barren. Yet she received power both to receive and to retain the seed.

Women ordinarily become barren chiefly for two reasons: either because they do not possess in the womb the power of heat by which they can digest the man’s seed, as happens in old age when the functions of womanhood fail; or because the womb is closed even in youth, so that the seed does not reach the places of conception. Against both conditions God gave power—that is, against barrenness and old age.

[Col. 0759D] The seed reached the place of conception sufficiently, and after it had arrived, he gave the woman firmness for childbirth. Thus, through the firmness of faith, her infirm womb was strengthened, and all things became possible for the believer.

Therefore, from one person—and that person as good as dead—there arose descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore, which cannot be counted. “For this reason,” he says, because both Abraham and Sarah possessed true faith, innumerable peoples arose from the one body of Abraham and Sarah.

By these words he wished to show that Sarah not only bore a child but bore more descendants than any fertile woman. He says that they had one body because it is said in Genesis: “The two shall become one flesh.” He added: “And from this body, as dead, they were born”—not dead in life, but dead with respect to seed. An old man can indeed discharge seed, but it lacks the firmness necessary to beget children, unless perhaps with a young woman, as some report.

“Like the stars of heaven” or “the sand of the sea” is spoken hyperbolically. By the stars of heaven are understood the good, the children of Abraham from both peoples through faith. By the sand of the sea, however, are understood the reprobate children of Abraham from the Jewish people according to the flesh, who, always seeking earthly things, are weighed down by the burden of sins. Although the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea—and likewise those represented by them—are innumerable, they are nevertheless numbered by God, to whom all things are open.

“According to faith”—that is, “with faith.”

All these died without receiving the promises, but seeing them and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth. “Those who say such things”—understand, “that they are strangers upon the earth”—show that they are seeking a homeland.

And if indeed they had remembered that homeland—that is, the land from which they had departed—they would certainly have had an opportunity to return. But now, since they do not wish to return to the land from which they departed, but remain in a foreign land as pilgrims, they seek a better one, that is, a heavenly one.

Here it is fitting to raise two questions. Above he had said: “Enoch was transferred, and was not found, so that he would not see death”; here he says: “According to faith all these died.” Again, he had said that they did not receive the promises but saw them from afar; yet earlier he said of Abel that “he obtained testimony that he was righteous,” and of Enoch that he was transferred, and of Noah that he was saved from the condemnation of the world. Of Abraham, and likewise of Isaac and Jacob, no one doubts that they received many promises concerning both Christ and the promised land.

These two points admit the following solution. When he first said, “All these died in faith,” it is to be understood as follows: all these died except Enoch alone, whom we know to have been transferred. As for what he added, that they did not receive the promises, it is clear that they received them in some matters but not in others, nor did they receive them in their fullness.

Enoch received the promise that he would not see death; Noah received the promise that he would be saved; and many others received promises as well. But these were for them partial offerings and first tastes of future things, not the fullness of the promises.

[Col. 0760A] For God not only grants us the things that are to come but also provides the necessities of this life, just as he said to his disciples: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these temporal things will be added to you insofar as they are useful to you.”

Since in the present age they earned in part the praise of righteousness, did not perish with the wicked, and were rich in temporal goods although they were pilgrims—as we read of Abraham, that he was rich in silver and gold—they received certain tastes of the promises.

But because they saw from afar, without possessing the full promise, the promises that Christ, when he came, proclaimed—saying, “If anyone leaves house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother for my sake, he will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life”—they did not attain this promise before the Lord’s coming, although they had left everything of their own, as the apostles did.

Or they did not attain the promises concerning the Lord’s coming: although he had been promised to them, they did not see him present in the world.

They also greeted those same promises—that is, they desired them—as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

He used the metaphor of sailors when he said “greeting”: those who see desired cities from afar and, before entering them, anticipate them with a greeting and make them familiar to themselves. They looked upon these promises in faith, greeted them with desire, and confessed in speech that they were pilgrims, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “For I am a stranger with you, as all my fathers were.”

“Pilgrim” comes from *peregre*, that is, from traveling from afar; for we say *peragrare* for “to travel through” or “to walk about.” They lived in tents, those who bought tombs with money.

[Col. 0760B] It is clear how much they were pilgrims, since they did not even possess a place where they might bury their own dead. Therefore, it is more righteous first of all to be a pilgrim and stranger in this world, to have nothing in common with the kings of this age, and to be removed from them like a foreigner.

For this reason God is not ashamed to be called their God—that is, he is not embarrassed. He prepared a city for them. Because they believed in that God and placed no confidence in earthly things or set their hope upon them, the almighty God is not ashamed to be called their God.

For he himself said: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” namely, through faith and the merit of their life. He is glorified when he is called the God of kind and excellent people, people who cultivate virtue. Conversely, he is put to shame and disgraced when he is invoked by the foolishness of the wicked. Hence he says through the prophet: “Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations.”

Those men, however, were so distinguished by their virtues and so full of confidence that he was not put to shame but rather glorified when he was called their God.

He speaks generally of the God of earth and the God of heaven, since he is also the God of the nations, and not only of the nations but of the whole world, because he himself created everything. But he is called the God of those saints not merely by creation, but as a friend.

He is also now called the God of Christians. “He prepared a city for them”—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore he did not give them an inheritance in the present Church. Or he is not ashamed to be called their God because he predestined them to reign with him in the heavenly city.

By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he offered his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises. It had been said to him: “In Isaac your seed shall be called,” because he reckoned that God was able even to raise him from the dead.

Why is it that blessed James, mentioning Abraham in his Epistle, praises him most highly for his works, whereas the blessed Apostle commends not his works but his faith with the greatest care?

Blessed James rightly praises through works the man whom he knew to be perfect also in faith, because he was writing to people who seemed to have faith but did not adorn that faith with good works. Blessed Paul, however, was writing to people who seemed to possess the good works of the law but did not have perfect faith; therefore he rightly recalls Abraham’s faith with particular emphasis, so that they might strive to imitate him.

Thus, to show that those who wish to be children of Abraham must possess both faith and works, one Apostle fittingly praised him for faith, while the other likewise praised him for works.

“By faith,” he says, “Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested.” Although he had no free son except Isaac, and through Isaac had received the promise that he would become the father of many nations, he was nevertheless not disobedient to God.

Although he heard a second command that seemed contrary to the first—when the Lord said to him, “Offer your son Isaac to me,” after he had already heard, “In Isaac your seed shall be called”—he did not doubt the promises. He believed that God could raise Isaac from the dead and multiply from him a multitude of peoples.

[Col. 0760C] For this reason he immediately wished to offer his son, because he believed that God would promptly raise him again. But lest anyone should say that he had another son from whom he hoped the promise would be fulfilled and that he therefore offered Isaac confidently, the Apostle says: “Abraham himself offered his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises concerning him.”

Why, then, did God test him? Did he not know that Abraham was a strong and proven man in faith? Certainly he knew. He tested him not so that he himself might learn this, but so that he might demonstrate it to others and make Abraham’s strength manifest, just as he himself showed when he said: “Now I know that you fear the Lord”—that is, “I have made it known to others that you fear God.”

Hence he took him in a parable. *Parabola*, a Greek word, is called in Latin *similitudo*, “likeness,” or *figura*, “figure.”

He received him back from death from God in a parable, when God said to him: “Do not stretch out your hand over the boy.” For when the ram was killed, Isaac was saved. Isaac was killed insofar as the father’s will was concerned.

Then God returned him to the patriarch in a parable—that is, in a figure and likeness of Christ’s passion. Everything that was then done with Abraham existed as a likeness of what the true Abraham—namely, God the Father, creator of all nations—had determined to do for us at the end of the age.

Abraham bore the figure of God the Father, while Isaac bore the figure of Christ. Abraham carried, as Scripture says, fire and a sword, because God the Father in a certain sense carried the sword of Christ’s passion when he permitted him to be killed. Hence the Son says to him in the Psalm: “For those whom you struck”—that is, “whom you permitted to be struck”—“they persecuted.”

And God the Father says through Zechariah: “I will strike the shepherd”—that is, “I will permit him to be struck.”

The fire he carried signifies the fervor and favor of that supreme love with which he loves us, of which it is said: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for us.”

For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son to God as a victim, so God the Father delivered his only Son for us all.

Isaac himself carried the wood on which he was to be placed, because Christ also carried the wood of the cross on which he would be crucified. The ram signified Christ’s flesh. Isaac was offered but was not killed; only the ram was killed. Thus Christ was offered in his passion, but his Divinity remained incapable of suffering.

By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning future things. He blessed them concerning future things because, in accordance with what he invoked upon them, he believed that everything would afterward happen to them as he had blessed them, and by blessing he wished for the things that were to come.

It can also be understood otherwise: he blessed them concerning future mysteries, because Jacob bore the figure of Christ or of the Christian people, while Esau bore the figure of the Jewish people.

By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped the top of his staff. We read in Genesis that Joseph, hearing that his father was ill, came to him and presented his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, to receive a blessing. Jacob, possessing faith that everything would happen to them according to what he prayed for them, blessed them.

[Col. 0760D] It is therefore said that he blessed each of them because he poured a separate blessing upon each and placed the younger before the elder, since he foresaw that matters would turn out in this way.

What follows—“And he worshiped the top of his staff,” that is, Joseph’s staff—can be understood in two ways. Filled with prophetic spirit, Jacob understood that Joseph’s staff signified the kingdom of Christ; by the top, that is, the summit of the staff, he understood the power and honor of Christ’s kingdom, of which the Psalmist says: “Your rod is a righteous rod, the rod of your kingdom.”

Thus he did not worship the staff as a god, according to the rite of the pagans who worshiped idols; rather, in the staff he worshiped Christ, whose kingdom and power he foresaw represented there.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, perhaps he worshiped Joseph’s staff according to the custom of that time, since he saw Joseph as lord of the entire kingdom of the land of Egypt. For the same reason Esther is read to have worshiped the staff of Ahasuerus.

By faith Joseph, when he was dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel and gave instructions concerning his bones. He spoke of the departure of the children of Israel, believing that everything God had promised to their fathers was true, especially what he had said to Abraham: “Know with certainty that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own, and they will mistreat them for four hundred years. Nevertheless, I will judge the nation that they will serve, says the Lord, and afterward they will return to the land of their fathers.”

Joseph would certainly not have given instructions concerning his bones unless he had confidently hoped, with complete faith, for their return to the land of promise. For he said to them: “God will surely visit you after many days; carry my bones away from here with you.”

And not only did the tribe of Joseph carry their father’s bones with them through the wilderness into the land of promise; the other tribes also carried all the bones of the patriarchs and buried them at Shechem, which became the possession of the tribe of Joseph.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried in the double cave at Hebron, which Abraham had purchased from the sons of Heth, together with Sarah, Rebekah, and Leah. Adam and Eve also rested there, having been buried there.

Perhaps someone may ask why all those holy fathers preferred to be buried in the land of promise rather than in another place. The answer is that they did not do this out of concern for tombs, but because, foreseeing by the Holy Spirit that the Lord would redeem the human race through death in that land and would rise there, they desired with the greatest longing to be buried there with him, so that when he rose they might rise together with him.

[Col. 0761A] We, however, should not become fainthearted wherever we are buried, since we do not know where the glorious bodies of many martyrs lie buried.

By faith Moses, after he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that he was a beautiful child and did not fear the king’s edict.

Moses was not hidden through his own faith, since he could not yet speak, but through the faith of his parents, his father and mother. Believing that the almighty God could free and protect him, they kept him hidden for three months. Then, when they could no longer conceal him because of his crying, they placed him in a basket of rushes and set him among the reeds of the river.

The king’s edict had been that all the male children should be thrown into the river. But what does it mean that they are said not to have feared the king’s edict? If they did not fear it, why did they hide him?

They feared it in this respect: they did not dare to keep him openly. Yet in another respect they did not fear it: they did not throw him into the open river but placed him in a basket and put him among the reeds of the river, hoping and trusting that the almighty God would protect him. Thus they are reckoned as though they had not feared.

How, then, did they hope that the child would be saved, except through faith? “They saw,” he says, “that he was a beautiful child.” From the moment of his birth, a great grace of beauty had been infused into him. This was not the work of nature, by which he was born a handsome infant, but a gift of divine grace, which also moved that barbarian Egyptian woman—the daughter of Pharaoh—to love him, take him, and raise him.

By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasure of temporary sin, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked toward the reward.

It is as though he said to those to whom he was writing: None of us has abandoned a spacious and splendid royal palace, or such treasures, nor has anyone, although able to be a king’s son, despised them as Moses did. He not only despised them but renounced them. With heaven set before him, he refused to admire the beauty of the Egyptian kingdom. He chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasure of sin.

For he considered it sin if he remained in the king’s palace, enjoying temporal happiness while abandoning his brothers in tribulation. He considered it sin, I say, not to suffer affliction with the others.

[Col. 0761B] If, then, Moses judged it sinful not to suffer gladly with the others, how great a heap of sins will those have who abandon the assembly of the faithful? “You,” he says, “suffer for your own sake.” Moses, however, chose this not merely for himself, looking only toward his own reward, but also for the sake of others, so that he might receive a greater reward. He voluntarily cast himself into such great dangers, although he could have lived devoutly while also enjoying secular goods.

“Considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt.” He calls it the reproach of Christ because Moses endured reproach for Christ, who is of one essence with the Father according to his Divinity.

Or he calls it the reproach of Christ in the sense of the reproach that Christ endured from his own relatives. Just as Christ endured reproach from his own people, whom he had come to redeem, when they said to him, “You have a demon,” and inflicted other evils upon him all the way to his passion, so Moses endured reproach from his brothers, whom he wished to free. For they said to him: “Who appointed you ruler or judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”

Likewise, whenever anyone suffers reproach from members of his household or from those to whom he has done a kindness, he suffers the reproach of Christ.

He looked toward his reward, he says, and toward the reward of the people. Therefore, whenever someone suffers anything adverse, he should call to mind what reward he will receive from the Lord for it.

By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; for he endured the invisible One as though he were present.

We read in Exodus that when a certain Hebrew man who was wronging his brother said to Moses—whom Moses wished to rebuke—“Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Moses fled because of this statement, since Pharaoh, on hearing it, sought to kill him.

But since it is clear that he fled to Midian, what does blessed Paul mean when he says: “Not fearing the king’s anger”? If he did not fear, why did he flee?

In fleeing, therefore, he was confident, believing that God would deliver him. He feigned outward fear while inwardly possessing no fear; therefore he is reckoned as though he had not feared. For he did not wish to remain there, lest he appear to be acting boastfully by rushing into open danger and tempting the Lord.
their God, which it is wholly [Col. 0768C] impermissible to do. For as long as the saints have something they can do, they ought not to tempt God; rather, they ought to imitate their Lord, who frequently gave the Jews an opportunity to escape, hearing him command: “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another.”

Moses’ flight, therefore, was entirely outward, since he possessed the greatest faith in God’s help. Hence the Apostle says: “He endured the invisible Lord as though he were present.” That is to say: He was so confident in God’s assistance and so secure in his protection that he seemed always to behold as present the omnipotent God, who by nature is invisible.

By faith he celebrated the Passover and the shedding of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them. By the faith with which Moses believed that the people would be saved through that blood, he celebrated the [Col. 0768D] Passover. He celebrated the Passover by the shedding of blood, with which he smeared the doorposts, so that the angel who was destroying the firstborn of the Egyptians would not afflict the Israelites—as though he were saying to them: If the blood of the typical lamb preserved the Jews unharmed amid the Egyptians and amid such great devastation, whose doorposts had been sprinkled with that blood, how much more will the blood of the true Lamb, that is, Christ, save us, whose sacrifice—that is, whose foreheads—are marked with the sign of Christ’s Passion.

For the angel feared that blood, understanding in it the Lord’s death; and for that reason he did not touch the doorposts, although what was being done was nothing in itself, whereas what was signified through it was great. The doorposts of the Israelites were smeared with the lamb’s blood, so that the destroying angel would not dare to inflict death; the faithful people are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s death [Col. 0769A] for the protection of salvation, so that they may be freed from destruction.

By faith they crossed the Red Sea as though through dry land; when the Egyptians attempted the same, they were swallowed up. It is as though he were saying to those for whom he was writing these things: We must hold faith so firmly that whenever our spirit wavers into some despair, even then we may be of faith (sic) and be delivered—as though we had come right up to death, as though everyone had despaired of us. What hope could they have had? On one side there was the sea; on another they were enclosed by very high mountains; on the third were their enemies. If they wished to flee, they would either perish in the sea or fall into the hands of the Egyptians. Yet, possessing faith, they overcame everything.

For by the faith with which Moses believed God, he struck the sea at his word and divided it into twelve divisions, according to what is said in the Psalm: “And believing [Col. 0769B] that all those tribes could cross with dry feet, they entered the sea”—but the tribe of Judah first. According to what is read in Hosea: “Praise,” he says, “O prince, with God in the sea”; for because of that sea the Hebrews had it on their right and left as a wall, providing them with a dry path, while it drowned the Egyptians. Hence the Apostle says: “The Egyptians, attempting it, were swallowed up.” For they learned that it was truly the sea: from the fact that they came and were swallowed up, it became clear that the water was real; and from this it became clear that it was not an apparition but the reality of things, because the Egyptians, attempting it, were swallowed up.

Allegorically, however, the Red Sea is baptism, consecrated by the redness of Christ’s blood. The Hebrews who went out from Egypt and crossed the Red Sea are the faithful, who, abandoning the darkness of unbelief, crossed through the font of [Col. 0769C] baptism. Pharaoh and the Egyptians died in the sea, because in the baptismal font the devil died, losing the power that he possessed; original and actual sins also died there, if any had previously existed.

By faith the walls of Jericho fell after a circuit of seven days. It was not by the sound of trumpets that he cast down the stones of the walls—not even if someone were to sound trumpets for ten thousand years—but by the faith with which they believed God, they cast them down. We read that the Lord had commanded Joshua to carry the ark around Jericho for seven days and thus to sound the trumpets. On the seventh day, when they had blown the trumpets, the walls of Jericho fell; and this is not without a great mystery.

Jericho, which is interpreted as “Moon,” represents the form of this world, because just as the moon wanes through its monthly cycles, so this world falls through daily declines. [Col. 0769D] In the ark the Church is represented. In the bronze trumpets are understood the strong preachers. Joshua, who leads the ark around, is Christ, who governs his Church through this world.

The Israelites, carrying the ark and sounding the bronze trumpets, go around this city of Jericho for seven days, and its walls fall through the presence of the ark and the sound of the bronze trumpets. For in this age, which revolves through the succession of seven days, while the ark is carried—that is, while the Church, circling the world, is renewed at the voices of the preachers as though at the sound of trumpets—the walls of Jericho, that is, the arrogance of this world, its rulers, and the obstacles of unbelief’s pride, fall, until [Col. 0770A] at the end of time the last enemy, death, is destroyed.

By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace. The blessed Apostle offers everyone great consolation and exhortation at this point: if a prostitute and idolater was saved by faith alone, much more will those be saved who have not fallen into more serious sins. It is as though he were saying openly: It is shameful if you are more unbelieving than a prostitute. She heard only men announcing these things and immediately believed; but you hear not only men, but also the voices of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, and in addition you do not recognize the Son of God himself, sent to you.

For in Rahab also the effect of faith was achieved: while everyone else perished, she alone was saved. Rahab, whose name is interpreted as “the enlarged one,” represents the [Col. 0770B] Church, which has been enlarged from East to West and from north to south. She possesses the breadth of charity, so much so that she pours out prayer even for her enemies.

And rightly that Rahab was a prostitute from foreign and alien nations, serving young men in the desires of the flesh and in fornications: for before the Lord’s coming the Church was alienated from God, living according to the desires of the flesh and serving fornication and idolatry. But after the true Jesus sent two spies to her—that is, Peter and Paul, or the two Testaments—she became faithful, abandoned the fornication of idolatry, and so was saved and is saved daily, lest she perish with the unbelievers.

Thus far he has spoken of the lawgiver and of the ancient fathers; now he is going to speak of the judges who existed [Col. 0770C] after Joshua, mentioning only their names because of the brevity of his discourse: those who fought by faith and conquered very many nations.

And what more shall I say? For time will fail me as I tell of it. That is, the time allotted for writing the epistle will fail me if I wish to recount all the deeds of those whom I have mentioned thus far, or the things I could relate about those who succeeded them.

Of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms. The fact that he mentions them all together means that the works of each were performed by the same faith, since all of them together conquered kingdoms through faith.

Gideon, having received a sign from the Lord, conquered with the three hundred men who drew water, concerning whom the Lord said to him: “With these you shall overcome Midian.” Moreover, through the wet fleece, filled with dry [sic; reading uncertain], he overthrew Zebah and Zalmunna and won victory over the enemies. [Col. 0770D]

Allegorically, however, Gideon, whose name is interpreted as “going around in the womb,” signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who through the mystery of the Incarnation was placed in the Virgin’s womb and, by the fullness of divinity with which he fills all things, surrounds the whole world: for by filling all things, he surrounds all things.

The three hundred men who drew water with their hands, received fire in jars, and went against Midian; when the jars were broken, the fire shone forth, and they sounded the trumpets, while the enemies were simultaneously put to flight—these represent the holy preachers, who possess faith in the Holy Trinity and are marked with the sign of the Lord’s Passion. This is represented [Col. 0771A] by the letter Tau, which expresses the number 300 and among the ancient Jews bore the likeness of a cross.

The jars, which are earthen vessels, signify the frail bodies of those same preachers, concerning which the distinguished preacher says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” The sound of the trumpets expresses the voice of the preachers.

When the jars had therefore been broken, the fire shone forth and the Midianites were put to flight. They represent rulers, because after the holy martyrs depart from this world, miracles increase; and thus, shaken by the power of miracles, they are put to flight, either submitting themselves to the faith or even ceasing from their tortures, defeated by fear of the signs.

It is also not without mystery that when Gideon prayed, the fleece was first wet and the ground dry; but the second time [Col. 0771B] the fleece was dry and the whole ground wet. The fleece represents the Jewish people, while the ground represents all the nations. Rightly, therefore, the fleece was first wet and the ground remained dry: for when the Jewish people had been moistened by the dew of heavenly wisdom before the Lord’s coming, all the nations were parched and dried up through lack of faith and wisdom. Again, when after the Lord’s coming all the nations had been made wet with the dew of wisdom, Judea perished through aridity.

Barak. He is Lapidoth, Deborah’s husband, who, by the faith with which he believed the prophetess, overcame Sisera and all his chariots.

Samson, by the faith with which he believed that he would obtain from God what he prayed for, killed more people in his death than during his life. For he said: “Lord God, remember me, and now restore my former strength to me, my God, that I may avenge myself on my enemies; and for the loss of my two eyes let me receive a single vengeance.” [Col. 0771C]

Jephthah had faith when he fought against the sons of Ammon and offered up his daughter, although in this he acted foolishly, thinking that he could appease almighty God by shedding human blood. For he vowed that if the Lord granted him victory over the sons of Ammon, he would sacrifice to him whoever first came out to meet him from his house. He did so: his daughter came out to meet him, and after she had mourned her virginity, he killed her.

But one may ask for what reason the custom arose that every year the virgins of the Hebrews should mourn Jephthah’s daughter. The recognized explanation is this: when they see her mourned by her own daughters, no one may dare to rush into such folly and such abomination as to shed human blood for God.

David, full of faith, went out against the Philistine and killed him; and because he believed God, he merited many promises concerning Christ.

The prophet and priest Samuel possessed perfect faith [Col. 0771D], because at the word of the Lord he anointed David king and killed the king of Amalek.

They practiced righteousness. That is, they completed in action what they believed, adorning that same faith.

They obtained the promises. Concerning Christ, or concerning the heavenly homeland. Abraham received a promise concerning Christ, when the Lord said to him: “In your seed,” that is, in Christ, “all the nations shall be blessed.”

David also received very many promises, among them this one, which the Lord said to him: “When you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed, which shall go forth from your loins, and I shall establish his throne over your throne.” And elsewhere: “From the fruit of your womb I shall place him upon [Col. 0772A] my seat.” And with an oath: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: If I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever.”

They shut the mouths of lions. Such were Samson, David, and Daniel, who was twice sent into the pit.

They extinguished the force of fire. Thus the three youths, Daniel’s companions, were sent into the furnace of blazing fire at Nebuchadnezzar’s command, while Chaldean madness pressed the order upon them; yet it caused them no harm.

They escaped the edge of the sword. That is, by fighting valiantly they drove the strength of their enemies back from themselves, as did Joshua, Gideon, David, and other princes and kings of the Jews.

They recovered from weakness. Such were Job and Hezekiah, who, when he had fallen sick unto death, was restored to his former health by the Lord’s favor for a period of fifteen years. We may also understand by “weakness” the evil of captivity, from which they were delivered when the Lord willed it, Cyrus commanded it, and Ezra and Nehemiah arranged it.

They became strong in war. Such were [Col. 0772B] Jesus the son of Nun, Moses’ successor; Samson, who killed many of the Philistines with an ass’s jawbone; King David; Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers, in whose time six thousand Jews also killed one hundred thousand enemies; and three thousand men sent to Antioch to aid Demetrius killed one hundred and twenty thousand.

They turned the camps of foreigners to flight. That is, they frequently forced them to flee. Camps are said to derive their name from *castrare* (“to castrate”), because lust is castrated there: for it is not military custom for men going into battle to take their wives or other women with them.

Once two princes of the earth went to war with a retinue of wives: Darius, namely, and Antony; but both fell there. [Col. 0772C] Darius was defeated by Alexander, while Antony was defeated by Octavian Augustus.

Women received back their dead through resurrection. He means those women whose sons were raised by Elijah and Elisha. After their resurrection, the women received them—not as husbands, but as living again those whom they had lost through death.

Others were stretched out, refusing release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Very many of the saints were stretched out—that is, extended on a cross and bound with ropes, as was the blessed Andrew; or stretched out, that is, tied to the tops of two trees and torn apart; or even stretched out and killed by the arms of untamed horses, torn apart by them; or certainly stretched out, that is, beheaded. All these things are seen to have been fulfilled in the holy martyrs.

They did not accept release—that is, liberation in the present [Col. 0772D]—for the purpose of being saved from their torments, so that they might obtain a better and more glorious resurrection in the future, since the greater the torments someone endures for God in the present, the more glorious he will appear in the resurrection.

Others experienced mockeries and lashes, and in addition bonds and prisons. Mockeries are so called from *ludus*, that is, ridicule: first the holy martyrs were made sport of through mockery and derision; then they were afflicted with lashes. Thus bound in chains, they were placed in prison; finally they were killed by various and elaborate tortures.

They were stoned. Such were Naboth, Jeremiah in Egypt, by the remnants of the deportees; Ezekiel in Babylon; and many others in the New Testament.

They were sawn apart. Here the plural number is used for the singular [Col. 0773A], for we read of no saint in the Old Testament who was sawn apart except the prophet Isaiah, whom King Manasseh had sawn with a wooden saw. Manasseh had taken Isaiah’s daughter as his wife.

They were tested. Such were Abraham and many others—not for deception, but rather for testing, namely, the testing of which it is said: “The Lord your God is testing you,” that is, proving you; for God is not a tempter of evils.

They died by the killing of the sword. Such were Uriah, Josiah, and many others.

They wandered about in *melotae*, in goatskins, needy, distressed, and afflicted. Here we should understand Elijah and others who lived in this manner; afflicted everywhere by want and tribulations, they endured everything in distress through faith, so that they might reach the desire for higher things.

[Col. 0773B] Every need and poverty is called distress, because a person is distressed—that is, afflicted—either by hunger or by some other deprivation. Some say that a *melota* is a kind of garment made from goatskins, hanging down on one side; because of the garment’s roughness, monks in Egypt are said to use this kind of clothing. Elijah too is read to have used it. In Greek, *mēlon* means a sheep, or any four-footed animal; hence *mēlōtē* means a sheep’s skin.

Others, however, say that it is a kind of garment made from the skins of badgers. For there is an animal called a badger, accustomed to live in underground caves, whose skin is said to be shaggy; the name of this garment is derived from that animal, namely, from *melo*, *melota*.

Of whom the world was not worthy. [Col. 0773C] By “the world” here, in one sense, we can understand the lovers of the world, who, desiring earthly things alone, were far removed from love of their Creator; therefore they were not worthy to have such companions as those whose great deeds the Apostle described above.

Alternatively, by “the world” may be understood everything contained between heaven and earth—gold, silver, gems, and all precious things—as well as the reprobate themselves, deceived by love of worldly affairs. The world, therefore, was not worthy of these saints: that is, even if the whole world were reduced to a price, it could not rightly be compared with one of them; nor, even if all those things could be offered as payment, could they purchase such a man.

To recall, then, the memory of a few from among the many: how could such a great man as Moses have been compared with anything? Whenever he wished, he divided the sea; whenever he wished, he drew back [Col. 0773D] its waters; whenever he wished, he caused manna to descend from heaven, brought water forth from a rock, and performed countless other deeds.

Or how could such a great man as his successor Joshua have been compared with anything? Whenever he wished, he caused the sun and moon, those two greatest lights, to stand still in one place, saying: “Sun, do not move against Gibeon; and moon, against the valley of Aijalon.”

Perhaps, however, someone will say that they could not be purchased because they could not be found. This is certainly true, because nowhere in the whole world could people like them be found. And if they could have been compared with anything, how could one of them accomplish by a word what the whole world could not accomplish? For when the whole world had labored under drought for three years and six months in the time of Elijah and had been unable to obtain rain, at Elijah’s word the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain came upon the face of the earth.

[Col. 0774A] Wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and caverns of the earth. Here he wishes Elijah, the outstanding prophet, and the sons of the prophets to be understood. They were driven into hiding in the time of Ahab and Jezebel, because Jezebel wished to kill them. At that time Obadiah fed them by fifties in caves and caverns of the earth; and for this he deserved the gift of prophecy, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward.”

And all these, having been approved through the testimony of faith, obtained no promise, God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected without us.

Who are all those approved through the testimony of faith—found approved—if not all those mentioned above? [Col. 0774B] Their splendid and praiseworthy faith has been recalled: earthly human beings like stars and the firmament, and heavenly angels; living stones and shining pearls, whose deeds confirm their faith, since without faith it is impossible to please God. Through the testimony of faith, therefore, they were approved—that is, through holy action, which worked through faith—and were found worthy of praise.

For their faith was made manifest by their pure works. Yet, although they were thus perfect, they did not receive the promise. Someone may therefore say: What benefit did it bring them to serve God, if they remain without reward to this day? Far be it from the hearts of the faithful to believe that they remain without reward. While still clothed in mortal flesh, they received a great reward: namely, the ability to live, to know God, and to perform many wonders. [Col. 0774C] Now, however, they rest in soul, enjoying ineffable joy in the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom.

But let us see what John says about them in his Apocalypse, and thus it will become clear to us which promise they did not receive: “I saw,” John says, “under the altar of God the souls of those who had been killed for the word of God, which they possessed; and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?’ And individual white robes were given to them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be fulfilled.”

At present the souls of the saints possess individual robes, rejoicing in their immortality and exulting in the happiness they enjoy. They will possess double robes [Col. 0774D] when, in the general resurrection, they receive immortality and incorruption in the body, which at present they possess only in the soul.

They have not yet received this promise, concerning which Isaiah says: “In their land they shall possess double things,” after the general resurrection. And truly it is fitting that those who served God in body and soul should receive their reward in body and soul alike.

What follows—“God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected without us”—means that they would not attain perfection. This is expressed in human terms, for example: Just as certain sons returning from the field say to their father, “Father, we have worked today and endured the sun’s heat; it is time for you to give us refreshment,” and he replies to them, “Wait a little, my sons, [Col. 0775A] until your brothers arrive, who are working in the same way, and then you will feast fully with them,” so almighty God acted, in a certain sense, when he did not give the elect immortality in the body, so that there might be greater glory and greater desire when all together, on the day of judgment, receive double robes. This is what he says: “So that they should not attain perfection without us, who are still pilgrims here, in the resurrection of the bodies.”

## Chapter 12.

Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and the sin that besets us, and let us run with perseverance the contest set before us.

By “a cloud of witnesses” he means the multitude of patriarchs and prophets, and the rest of the faithful who were witnesses to perfect faith; also witnesses to the Son of God, whom they foretold as coming into the world. They are rightly called clouds because of the height and multitude of their merits. For just as a cloud is illuminated by the sun and suffused with its warmth, and afterward warms the earth, often waters it with rain, and at other times sends forth flashes of lightning, so those holy fathers, warmed and illuminated by the true Sun, warm and illuminate human hearts by their example; in their own time they poured down rain through their words and flashed with miracles.

A cloud of witnesses so great has therefore been set before us as an example, so that we may strive to imitate their faith and works. Let us therefore lay aside, through repentance, every weight of vices, as well as the sleep of sloth and feeble thoughts. By adding, “and the sin that besets us,” he shows that the Jews were tempted by the devil on every side, served carnal desires, and abounded in many sins.

Let us run with perseverance the contest set before us, so that, just as they patiently endured the adversities of this age, we too may endure them.
