He did not say, “Let us add something to our running,” but, remaining in the same course, let us run the contest appointed for us, according to what the Psalmist says: “I have run the way of your commandments.”

In the present age we have been placed in a contest against the vices of the flesh, against demons, and against false brethren. We must therefore run patiently—or complete this contest—in order that we may reach the promised reward of the contest.

“Looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising its shame.”

Thus sons look to their parents, and disciples to their teacher, in diligence of work and in contests, shaping their minds according to their teachers and receiving certain rules from them by observing them. So too, if we wish to run and to learn how to run well, let us look to Christ, the author and finisher, who said to us: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart”; and elsewhere: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you”; and: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more his servants?”

Let us therefore look to Christ and receive from him an example of patience. He said: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” He himself is indeed both the author and the finisher of faith. He is the author of faith for us because he himself infuses faith into us; we cannot believe unless he first comes before us. Hence he says to the faithful: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.”

He is the finisher, or perfecter, of faith because he grants us completion or perfection, namely, that we may persevere in faith. Or he is the perfecter of faith because he gives the will and the ability to complete the good work by which faith itself is adorned; for faith without works is not perfect but dead.

In him we all possess perfection, for he endured the cross for the joy set before him. The Son of God, setting before himself—that is, establishing in the present—the joy of the resurrection and ascension into heaven, and of all the glory he received after the resurrection, endured the cross because he saw that it would ultimately benefit him.

“Despising its shame”: that is, counting its disgrace as nothing, since he endured that dishonor without shame or embarrassment. It was a very great joy for him that he suffered for us in order to fulfill the will of God the Father, through which he afterward received power over every creature. Hence he himself says: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you.”

If, then, he who had no necessity of being crucified was crucified for us, how much more is it right for us to endure all things courageously?

For this reason the Lord appeared in the flesh: to rouse human life by admonition, to kindle it by providing examples, to redeem it by dying, and to restore it by rising again. He died, therefore, in order to teach us to regard as nothing the glory bestowed by human beings.

“And he sits at the right hand of the throne of God.”

That is, he is in the prosperity of eternal life and in the fullness of the Father’s majesty. If there were no other promise or exhortation, this one example that the Apostle presents here concerning Christ ought by itself to suffice to persuade us to endure every adversity patiently, so that we may deserve to sit with Christ.

“Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, fainting in your minds.”

The Apostle wished to indicate by the single term “contradiction” all the adversities that Christ endured from the Jews: scourging, mockery, spitting, blows, slaps, blasphemies, and death itself. He says in effect: Remember Christ, who endured such and so great opposition for sinners, though he had committed no sin, so that you, who are known to be transgressors and sinners, may not grow weary and faint in your minds, but may imitate him and endure similar things patiently.

Christ endured contradiction against himself; that is, he allowed them to do what they wished against him, contradicting them in nothing.

He exhorts them not to fail in their tribulations, since they had not yet reached martyrdom and the shedding of blood. Hence he adds:

“You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.”

It is as though he said: Even if you have lost your earthly possessions, having been stripped of them by your fellow citizens, you have not yet suffered death; you are still alive. Whoever resists unto blood, fighting against sin, is one who fights against unbelievers for the truth of the faith even unto death, as the apostles and their successors did. For unbelief is the greatest sin. When someone, wishing to deceive or to win another either by flatteries or by terrors, fights for the faith against an unbeliever, he is certainly resisting sin.

This may also be understood of every sin: namely, of evil suggestion, perverse will, and impure desire. Whoever resists these by refusing to consent to them fights against sin.

“And you have forgotten the consolation by which he speaks to you as sons, saying: ‘My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him.’”

The Wisdom of God the Father, which spoke through Solomon, among other things also uttered this through his mouth. The blessed Apostle now takes it up as an example, exhorting the Jews not to fail in tribulation when they are reproved by the Lord for the sake of testing.

He therefore says: “My son, do not neglect”—or, “do not treat negligently”—the discipline of the Lord. Discipline is so called from learning; in another term, it may be called correction of morals. When someone is afflicted by hardships and tribulations, he ought not to grow weary or fail, but rather to bear them patiently, reflecting that he is being corrected by the Lord.

“For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives.”

The Apostle sets forth these testimonies so that, just as sons are scourged by their fathers in order that they may be worthy to approach their paternal inheritance—and are often commanded to stand throughout the night in the cold and trained in various ways—so these people too may endure God’s corrections with a cheerful spirit, in order that they may be made fit to reach the true inheritance of the eternal homeland.

For many serve the Lord in prosperity, but go astray in adversity. Such people have not yet been perfectly tested so as to attain the inheritance. Therefore the Apostle, who taught them to live well in prosperity, exhorts them not to fail under correction, since the Lord chastises the son whom he loves in order to establish him as an heir of the kingdom of heaven. He scourges every son whom he receives into glory, whether by illness, poverty, persecution, or torments.

It should be noted, however, that not everyone who is scourged is a son; rather, everyone who is a son is scourged. Which of the saints do we read to have passed from this age to the heavenly inheritance without divine scourging?

Therefore, the less we ought to murmur about the scourging by which we are chastised, the more closely we feel in it the affection of paternal love. Hence he himself says: “Those whom I love, I reprove and chastise.”

Many, however, are scourged, like Antiochus and Herod, not so that they may be received into the inheritance, but so that it may already be shown in part what evils they will suffer after death.

“Persevere in discipline.”

“As sons.”

“Very dear ones, God offers himself to you.”

Supply: “as the inheritance of the heavenly homeland.” It is as though he said: It is better for you to pass through discipline and correction, which are carried out with paternal affection, to the heavenly inheritance, than to be outside discipline and thus descend to punishments. For you think that God hates and has abandoned you because of the things you have suffered. If you had not suffered these things, then you would have had greater reason to think so; for if he scourges every son whom he receives, whoever is not scourged is undoubtedly not numbered among the sons.

By these words he shows them that the very thing by which they thought themselves abandoned gave them greater reason to believe that they were loved by him. For what son is there whom his father does not correct?

A master of a household sometimes neglects the children of others, but chastises and corrects his own, lest negligence overwhelm them. There is no wise father who does not correct his delinquent children; sometimes he even reproves those who are doing good, so that they may be stirred to better things. Thus Eli, because he did not correct his sons, did not deserve to leave them as heirs of the priesthood after him.

“But if you are without that discipline of which all have become partakers”—namely, all the good sons or holy fathers mentioned above—“then you are adulterers and not sons.”

Whoever remains outside that discipline of the Lord, of which all good sons destined for the heavenly inheritance have become partakers, is an illegitimate son and does not belong to the paternal inheritance, because he is not a free son.

Beware, then, lest you be illegitimate sons. For all unbelievers and negligent persons who despise the discipline of the Lord are regarded as illegitimate and not as sons.

“Furthermore, we had fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we respected them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?”

Supply: We ought to consider that we had fathers as instructors and feared them. Shall we not much more obey God, the Father of spirits, and live in eternal glory?

The Father of spirits—that is, the creator of souls—is almighty God, who first created good things from nothing, and afterward created the bodies of human beings and of other animals from the elements. He created the human soul from nothing, and he still creates it. We must not think that the soul is a part of the Godhead, since the Godhead is uncreated, whereas the soul is a creature.

He calls almighty God the creator of souls, rather than of bodies, although he is the creator of all things, because our body is formed from paternal and maternal seed, whereas the soul is always created by God from nothing.

He says, in effect: If we feared our carnal fathers, by whom we were instructed temporarily so that we might deserve to become their heirs, how much more ought we to obey and submit to the creator of souls, so that we may live with him in the glory of eternal blessedness?

There is not only a difference between them because of the distinction of persons—these fathers are earthly, whereas the other is heavenly—but also in the very purpose of their discipline and instruction. They do not instruct us for the same purpose or in the same spiritual matters, but for whatever seems suitable to them, as the Apostle makes clear when he says:

“And they indeed, our fathers, from whose seed we received our bodies, instructed us for a few days according to their own will; but he, the Father of spirits, instructs us for what is useful”—that is, for the salvation and benefit of our soul.

“In receiving his sanctification.”

Our carnal fathers instruct us so that we may be useful to them according to their will, which is not useful in every respect. Almighty God, however, trains us for everything beneficial, so that we may attain the salvation of our soul and receive his sanctification: namely, so that we may be holy, as he himself is holy in a certain manner, according to what he says: “Be holy, because I too am holy.” For this purpose, I say, he instructs and chastises us, so that he may make us worthy of his gifts.

For every nation instructs its children according to its own will. Thus it was customary for the Romans to train their sons in military matters, and for the Greeks to educate theirs in letters.

“Now every discipline, while it is being received, does not seem to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.”

Every discipline, he says, both human and divine, when it is being learned, does not seem to be a discipline of joy but of sorrow. He called all of this discipline, both divine and human, because whatever is learned is called discipline.

It does not seem at present to be a discipline of joy but of sorrow because the person being scourged is very often constrained, endures hunger, suffers cold, and bears every hardship. But when he has reached perfection, he rejoices and exults, receiving a most welcome reward, as the Apostle says.

“Afterward,” he says, “when it has reached the summit of perfection, that same discipline will yield the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it”: that is, to those who have been tested and perfected by that same discipline.

He calls the fruit “most peaceful” because it is the most welcome and acceptable recompense received by those who are trained and tested through that same discipline. For example, Roman recruits who have been trained in military discipline first endure many hardships, but afterward rejoice, possessing dominion over the whole world.

The same should be understood of those who are afflicted by discipline and who will receive eternal rewards, such as the holy apostles, martyrs, and teachers of the Church.

“Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and strengthen the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be turned aside but rather may be healed.”

Therefore—because the reward of recompense is given for discipline and joy follows—or in order that you may be able to receive the supreme inheritance with the good sons—lift up hands that have fallen away from good work and have grown sluggish through the idleness of laziness. “Strengthen the feeble knees” for the performance of good works.

By feet and knees we should understand works, just as by hands; by paths, understanding and the intention of the mind. The meaning is: Perform works that possess perfect understanding and that are done with a good intention. “Walk rightly,” he says; let praise not increase further, but rather let it raise you to a state of uprightness.

He commands that hanging hands and feeble knees be strengthened, just as Isaiah orders when he says: “Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees,” so that no one who is wavering may go astray—that is, so that no one who is hesitant in faith and good works may wander from the way of uprightness, but may rather be healed of sins by believing rightly in God.

It is as though he said: Whoever does not believe rightly ought to believe more firmly and tenaciously, so that in every way he may find healing for his soul.

By these words he touches upon their hesitations, so that they might believe in him without any doubt.

“Pursue peace with all”—supply: “with all good people”—“and holiness, without which no one will see God.”

There are many things that display the form and character of Christianity, but above all and better than all are the affection of mutual charity and peace, which unites human hearts. Therefore the Truth itself says: “I leave you peace”; and again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

For this reason the Apostle also says: “Pursue peace with all good people.” By “peace” we should understand love and concord.

“Holiness” means purity of mind and body. It is as though he said: Love all good people as yourselves, and let there be in you chastity, or purity, of mind and body, because without peace and holiness no one will see God.

“For blessed are the peacemakers, because they will be called sons of God. Blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God.”

“Watching carefully lest anyone fall short of the grace of God.”

By “watching carefully” he means diligently attending and considering, lest any one of you fall short of the grace of God. He speaks to them as to travelers who journey over long roads in a company and in a group. The person in charge customarily says to them: “See that no one remains behind who does not proceed with you.”

It is as though he said: I do not require merely that you alone obtain grace and enter the heavenly homeland, but also that you look after the others.

By “grace” he means faith, hope, and charity, through which a person deserves to find the grace of God, since whoever possesses these also possesses the remaining virtues. Or by “the grace of God” he means the remission of sins, which is given to us freely in baptism, or through perfect faith and the other virtues.

“Lest any root of bitterness spring up above and cause hindrance, and through it many be defiled.”

He calls an evil will and a perverse intention the “root of bitterness,” from which the sin of bitterness proceeds. For just as a bitter root cannot produce sweet fruits but only fruits like itself—that is, bitter ones—and just as a sulfurous spring produces water unfit for drinking, so an evil will and a perverse intention emit from themselves evil action and the sin of bitterness. By these the road to the heavenly homeland is obstructed.

Through that evil will, from which the seeds of wickedness proceed, many are defiled, because a little leaven corrupts the whole lump, and by one sin of unbelief all the works that could have been good are corrupted; by one sinner many are defiled.

He particularly intended the “root of bitterness” to mean the sin of unbelief, although, as we have said, it also refers to an evil will and perverse intention.

He appropriately called sin bitter, because nothing is more bitter than it after it has been committed. Those who are tormented by the sorrow of conscience after committing an offense know this by experience, and are consumed by a sufficiently dreadful bitterness, so much so that the bitterness of the offense sometimes overturns both the understanding and reason, as we read concerning Cain, who fell into despair.

“Lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright.”

Esau is called a fornicator because, against the will of his father and mother, he took foreign wives. “Profane” properly means irreligious, as though one were far—*porro*—from the shrine and temple of God.

Here, however, “profane” is used for a glutton, or for one who sells something useful for something useless. This aptly applies to Esau, who was a glutton and a gourmand, selling his birthright for cheap food, namely, red lentils.

In this passage “birthright” means the honor and dignity of the priesthood. Before the priesthood of Aaron, which was established by God in the Law, all firstborn sons were priests, as was Shem, who was also called Melchizedek, the firstborn of Noah.

It was a great dignity to possess the birthright, since the firstborn also received the larger portion of the paternal substance and inheritance, and, adorned with clothing, shone in greater wealth.

Hence we read in Genesis that Rebekah, taking Esau’s very fine garments that she had at home, clothed Jacob in them and brought him to his father. When Isaac perceived the scent and fragrance of his garments, he said: “Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a field.”

Since, therefore, there were among the Jews certain followers of Esau in fornication and gluttony, the Apostle recalls to their memory what happened to Esau, exhorting them to beware of all such conduct, lest anyone become like him who, out of love for temporal things, went so far as to sell his birthright.

Through his own negligence and greed he sold the honor he had received from God, and for a small thing lost great glory. He became last although he had been first, and, although he had been second, he remained first.

“For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected.”

Supply: “by God.” The history in Genesis relates that Esau, returning from the field, learned that his brother had forestalled him in receiving his father’s blessing. He said with tears and a great cry: “Do you have only one blessing, father? Bless me also.”

Isaac replied to him: “I have made him your lord; and for you, my son, what more can I do?” At last, overcome by his cries, Isaac gave him a blessing in the riches of this age and in the produce of the earth, saying: “In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above shall your blessing be.”

It is therefore evident that when he wished to inherit and receive his father’s blessing—namely, the dignity of the priesthood, which he had already lost, as well as his father’s holiness together with the spirit of prophecy—he was brought by his sins to the point of being rejected by God and deprived by his brother of the paternal blessing.

Hence it follows:

“For he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.”

Why did he not find a place for repentance—that is, forgiveness through repentance—which he sought with tears? Because he did not seek it as he ought. Those tears were tears of indignation over his lost honor and of resentment against his brother, rather than of humility and true repentance. Hence he also said: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and I will kill my brother Jacob.”

Therefore, although he sought it with tears, he could no longer reach that place of blessing as his brother had. He ought to have repented in the manner we read of Peter: when he had denied the Lord, he went outside and wept bitterly. His great sin was forgiven because he repented as he ought.

“For you have not come to a tangible and accessible fire, and to a whirlwind, and gloom, and storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words.”

It is customary for those who make a comparison to diminish and weaken one side so that the excellence of the other side may stand out. Thus the Apostle, by comparison with the things that occurred in the Old Testament, declares that our realities are greater, clearer, gentler, better, and more worthy of admiration.

He now contrasts Christ with Moses, the Law with the Gospel, heaven with Mount Sinai, the sprinkling of legal blood with the cleansing of Christ’s blood. These things are far better than those were: there the shadow rested; here the truth is held and revealed.

“You have not come to a tangible and accessible fire”: that is, you have not come to a visible and palpable light of fire that can be handled by bodily sight, as we read concerning the ancient Jewish people, but to the invisible and incomprehensible God.

These things are reported to have taken place on Mount Sinai when the Law was given: fire, namely, the whirlwind, darkness, storm, the sound of the trumpet, and the voice of words.

“He was seen,” it says, “on Mount Sinai.”

A whirlwind is a powerful wind that carries away straw and wraps lighter things in the dust of the earth. It often also carries away heavier things. Darkness is the obscurity of smoke and fire. A storm is tempest and rain.

These things occurred when the Law was given so that the hearts of the Jews, inclined to sin, might be shaken, lest they dare transgress the Law itself. Hence an earthquake also occurred there, so that, struck with complete terror, they might flee for refuge to the God of heaven.

The darkness, or gloom, signifies the obscurity of the Law itself. The whirlwind, or agitation of the winds, signifies the threat of the Law, which says: “If anyone does this or that, let him be killed.” The storm signifies the punishment itself. The sound of the trumpet signifies the presence and coming of almighty God.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “At the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, he will descend from heaven.”

By the trumpet is understood the voice of the angels themselves. We must not think that the angels rebuked with a bronze or horn trumpet belonging to God.

The voice of words is likewise understood not as the voice of almighty God himself, but as that of the angels. For God spoke to Moses through a subordinate creature, that is, through an angel. That it was not the voice of God is demonstrated by the Lord in the Gospel when he says to the Jews: “You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form.”

That Moses spoke with an angel, not with the Lord, is shown by blessed Stephen in the sermon he delivered to the Jews: “This is Moses,” he says, “who was with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai.”

The Gospel, however, was not given amid trembling or threats. Rather, the Lord spoke to the faithful with paternal affection, as to sons. For when he ascended the mountain and, among the other precepts of life, presented to them the eight beatitudes, they did not obey, nor were signs seen by which they might be terrified, as there were when the Law was given.

It follows:

“Which”—supply: “the voice of the trumpets and of the angels”—“those who heard excused themselves, so that no word might be spoken to them.”

That is, so that he might not speak to them. For they could not bear what was being said to them; that is, they could not endure the voice of the angel because of fear. Hence they said to Moses: “Speak to us yourself, and let the Lord not speak to us, lest perhaps we die.”

They had been struck with excessive fear, seeing the whole of Mount Sinai smoking, together with storms, thunderclaps, and the sounds of trumpets.

“And if even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”

Supply: “with stones of hail sent from heaven.” For the Lord had commanded: “Let the children of Israel keep far from the mountain, because if a human being or any beast approaches the mountain, it shall be killed with stones of hail.”

And what was seen was so terrifying—supply: that they did not dare either to hear or to approach the mountain.

For Moses said: “I am terrified and trembling.” If Moses was terrified, what should be said of the others?

“But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.”

These words depend on what was said above: “You have not come to the tangible and accessible fire of Mount Sinai, but you have come to Mount Zion.”

The remaining matters have already been explained in their several parts. By Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” and by Jerusalem, which is called “vision of peace,” he wishes the heavenly homeland to be understood—namely, the Church above, which consists of angels and righteous human beings, and to which one approaches by faith and desire.

“You have come,” he says, “to Mount Zion,” that is, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, by faith and desire.

“And you have come to the assembly”—or “multitude”—“of many thousands of angels,” united with them in faith and to be united with them again in glory, according to what the Lord says: “The elect will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

“And you have come to the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.”

By the Church of the firstborn we should understand the apostles, who first believed, and to whose faith those others were joined by believing; their names are written in the memory of almighty God, according to what the Truth himself said to them: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

“And you have come to God, the Judge of all”—that is, to the Lord Jesus, who says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

Through him God the Father will judge not only the Jews but all human beings.

“And you have come to the spirits of the perfected righteous.”

By “the spirit of the perfected” he calls the Holy Spirit, through whom all are called righteous when, in baptism, they receive from him the remission of all sins. They are rightly called righteous because they are then called righteous when they have been cleansed from every defilement.

Or by “the spirits of the perfected righteous” he means the souls of the saints who have proved acceptable to God, to whom those others were joined by faith and desire.

“And you have also come to Jesus, the mediator of the New Testament.”

The Lord Jesus, because he is at once human and God, is our mediator. Just as Moses was mediator between God and the people, conveying God’s words to the people and those of the people back to God—according to what he himself says: “I am your intermediary and mediator between God and you”—so the Lord Jesus conveyed to us the words of God the Father, and now conveys ours to him, continually interceding for us. At the same time, by his passion he confirmed the New Testament for us.

“And to the sprinkling of blood”—you have come—“which speaks better than Abel.”

According to the usage of the Law, by the term “sprinkling” he indicates the cleansing of Christ’s blood, since the cleansing accomplished through blood was called sprinkling.

They therefore came to the blood of Christ, or to cleansing—that is, to his passion—because they were cleansed by faith in his passion.

The blood of Christ speaks better than the blood of Abel, because Abel’s blood demanded vengeance from God against his brother, whereas Christ’s blood implores life and forgiveness for his persecutors, as he said to the Father: “Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing.”

Or it speaks better in that it makes us speak, namely, that the Lord himself is the Son of the living God, by whose passion we have been redeemed and by whose baptism we have been washed, and because through his blood we have been made sons of God.

“See that you do not refuse him who speaks.”

That is to say: Beware lest you despise Jesus speaking through his Gospel, since he sits at the right hand of God, considering what each one of us does.

“For if those did not escape who refused him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven.”

Supply: “we shall not escape.” It is as though he said: If your fathers did not escape the vengeance of almighty God when they transgressed his commandments by making an idol—commandments given to them through Moses or through an angel, both of whom spoke on earth—much less shall we be able to escape his vengeance if we despise the commandments given through the Son.

“They,” he says, “heard him speaking on earth; we hear him from heaven.”

Because of the unity of person that the Son of God possesses in two natures, he is said to speak to us from heaven. On earth he appeared to speak through his humanity, but in his divinity he was on earth and in heaven. Hence he himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

Likewise, while the Gospel is preached on earth, he himself speaks to us from heaven. Therefore he must be heard much more than Moses.

It follows:

“Whose voice then shook the earth”—supply: “when the Law was given”—“but now he promises, saying: ‘Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.’”

He who then shook Mount Sinai by his command, and the earth around it where the people stood when he gave the Law to Moses, now promises that he will shake not merely part of the earth, nor only the whole earth, but heaven also.

Therefore, the greater the things he promises to accomplish, the more he must be feared.

Although there have been earthquakes in various places and different regions of the world, there has not been one so great throughout the whole world. And even if the earth has been shaken, heaven has not. Hence he rightly says that this will happen once, on the day of judgment, showing that they will never be shaken again.

Therefore it follows:

“Now the expression ‘yet once more’ indicates the removal of things that can be shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.”

This shaking of heaven and earth concerns their renewal and improvement. As the day of judgment approaches, the earth will undergo shaking; but heaven and earth will be renewed together, and they will be moved from their present form into a better one, according to what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The form of this world is passing away.”

When its form has been changed, its substance will remain, and afterward there will be a new heaven and a new earth.

By “heaven” here understand not the starry or ethereal heaven, but this aerial heaven, from which birds are also called birds of heaven.

“Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom”—supply: “now in hope, which we shall receive in reality”—“let us have grace, through which we may serve God acceptably, with fear and reverence.”

The unshakable kingdom is the heavenly Church, which consists of holy angels and righteous human beings. This Church is the kingdom of God, and almighty God is the kingdom of the Church.

We now receive this kingdom in hope, but then we shall receive it in reality, when Christ hands the kingdom over to God the Father.

It is called unshakable because, if heaven and earth will remain immovable after their transformation, much more will the elect, after the resurrection, receive immortality immovably in the body and unchangeability in the soul. They will reign eternally with God, and they themselves will be the unshakable kingdom of almighty God, while their kingdom will be the contemplation of the Holy Trinity.

And because we now receive this unshakable kingdom in hope, the Apostle exhorts us to have grace through which we may serve God acceptably. By “grace” he means right faith, certain hope, and perfect charity together with holy conduct. Through these we must serve God with fear, fearing him as God and Judge of all things, and with reverence, loving him as Father.

We must fear lest we be scourged here and afterward excluded from rest.

“For our God is a consuming fire.”

Almighty God is called fire, not as matter…

…which he made, it may consume, but that which a human being draws in from without, namely, the rust of sins; for it does not consume that which he himself made, but that which human malice has brought in.

This fire also accomplishes another thing: it kindles human hearts, namely, toward the love of God. Concerning this fire the Truth says: “I came to send fire upon the earth, and what do I will but that it burn?” For “earth” means earthly hearts [Col. 0785D]; since they are always occupied with the lowest thoughts and earthly desires, they are trampled by evil spirits as though they were earth. But the Lord casts fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he kindles the hearts of carnal people toward the love of God and neighbor.

Behold why almighty God is called fire: namely, because he consumes the rust of sins and kindles human hearts toward charity.

But one may still ask why he is compared to fire. The answer, however, is this: Because just as fire lies hidden in flints and stones, so almighty God remains in his creation, yet is not seen.

## CHAPTER 13

“Let brotherly love remain among you.” This means: Love everyone as yourselves, remembering that you have one Father, God almighty, and one mother, the Church—or that you were born from one father, Adam, and one mother.

“And do not forget hospitality.” He did not say, “Be hospitable,” but, “Do not forget hospitality.” Before they had been completely stripped of their possessions, they had been sufficiently devoted to hospitality; but after they had been almost entirely deprived of their property, they had again become excessively tightfisted. Therefore the Apostle urges them to fulfill the duty of hospitality according to their means, saying to them: “Do not consign your former hospitality to oblivion.”

Hospitality, however, must be practiced with a cheerful mind and joyful spirit, as blessed Peter says: “Be hospitable to one another without complaining.” And elsewhere: “God loves a cheerful giver.”

He continues: “For by this some have pleased God, receiving angels as guests”—such as Abraham, who deserved to receive the promise, and Lot, who was rescued from the destruction of Sodom. Hence the Judge of all himself will say on the day of judgment: “As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me.”

“Remember those in chains as though you were chained with them.” That is: Just as you would wish assistance to be given to you and yourselves to be remembered if you were imprisoned in chains, so remember those who are held in bonds for the faith of Christ.

“And those who suffer, as though you yourselves were still living in the body.” This means: Since you still remain in the body, through which you learn by experience what those who suffer need, remember those who labor in teaching and holy activity, supplying them with food and clothing, just as you would wish to be remembered if you were laboring in such a way. For by remaining in this mortal body, as they do, you prove by experience that “a man’s life upon earth is warfare,” and that “man is born to labor, and the bird to fly.”

“Marriage is honorable in all things”—may it be so for you, if it pleases God—“and the marriage bed undefiled.”

Marriage (*connubium*) is so called from *conhabere*, “to dwell together.” At that time there were certain people who condemned marriage, saying that the marital union was unclean and that one could not rise pure from a spouse’s bed. Therefore blessed Paul calls legitimate marriage that which is undertaken for the sake of love for children, not for the satisfaction of lust. He not only permits it but also says that it pleases God.

Marriage is honorable when a man lawfully takes a wife for the love of children, abstains from her at appointed times, and does not have several wives. For at the beginning, as Scripture says, “God created male and female, and said to them: Increase and multiply.” It is also said in what follows that the two would become one flesh. Such a marriage bed is undefiled—that is, a lawful union without the purpose of fornication—and the bed is undefiled, as are those who rise from it undefiled: they do not carry away from it the stain of sin.

Hence blessed Matthew says in one passage that a lawful marriage and a lawful marriage bed have, in a certain sense, uncleanness in the mingling of semen, but do not have the stain of sin. For it is better to take a lawful wife than to fornicate with prostitutes or even to violate other men’s wives.

But if the marriage is not legitimate—if it is entered into not for the love of children but for the satisfaction of lust, and if there are several wives—then it is no longer an honorable marriage or an undefiled bed.

“For fornicators and adulterers God will judge.” To fornicate is to pollute oneself and satisfy lust in any manner; to commit adultery is to violate another person’s marriage bed. Hence an adulterer is so called, as it were, because he violates another’s bed.

But will almighty God judge—that is, condemn—only fornicators and adulterers, while passing over murderers, sacrilegious persons, thieves, and others entangled in various crimes? Certainly not. Why, then, did the Apostle specifically say that fornicators and adulterers would be judged? Clearly because there is no doubt that murderers, sacrilegious persons, robbers, parricides, and others weighed down by grave sins are to be condemned.

But concerning fornicators and adulterers, there were at that time some who doubted, saying that males and females had been made for intercourse and therefore that it was not sinful to lie with any woman. This is entirely far from the truth. Thus, after the Apostle had first said, “Marriage is honorable and the undefiled bed is pleasing to God,” he immediately added: “For God will judge fornicators and adulterers,” showing that fornicators and adulterers are rightly judged. If marriage has been permitted, fornicators are rightly subjected to punishments and adulterers are rightly punished.

“Let your conduct be without avarice; be content with the present.” Conduct (*mos*) means uprightness of life and good living. He did not say, “Possess,” but “Let your conduct be”—that is, let your life and manner of living be without avarice.

A miser is called *avarus*, “greedy for gold”: he is tightfisted in giving, eager in receiving, and has a hand closed when giving but extended when receiving. Concerning such a person a certain wise man gives this warning: “Do not let your hand be extended to receive and closed to give.”

Perhaps, after they had been stripped of their own property by unbelievers, they desired to gather wealth again under the pretext of almsgiving. Therefore the Apostle warned them to let their conduct be without avarice, content only with the necessities present to them and not anticipating the future. In accordance with what he had urged elsewhere, saying: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these.”

And lest they should say, “What shall we do if the things necessary for us should fail?” he immediately added consolation, introducing a testimony from the Book of Joshua son of Nun. For almighty God himself said: “I will not forsake you, nor abandon you.”

After the death of Moses, the Lord said to Joshua: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. Be strong and courageous. I will not forsake you, nor abandon you.” This example applies to Joshua, but likewise to every elect person who places his hope in God. For he does not lie in any way if we place our hope in him.

“So.” Understand: “He is with us.” Thus we may say confidently: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.”

Here “man” means not only any fleshly adversary but also the ancient enemy, who is called “man,” taking his name from his function, since he deceives man; just as Christ is called a lion because of his strength. Hence the prophet says: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man”—that is, from the devil.

Therefore, in all tribulations and temptations, we ought to cry out this verse of the Psalmist or Apostle, saying: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what any enemy or adversary can do to me.”

“Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.”

All prelates and teachers, insofar as they preach what is good and practice what is good, are to be heard and imitated. But insofar as they either do not preach rightly or live badly, they are neither to be heard nor imitated. For example, one who lives well while preaching rightly is both to be heard and imitated; but if he does neither, he is neither to be imitated nor heard.

If, however, he preaches rightly although he lives badly, he is not to be rejected so that he will not be heard. Hence the Lord says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.”

Since these people had good leaders—namely, the holy apostles and their successors—the Apostle urges them to remember them and, considering the outcome of their way of life, to imitate their perseverance in the true faith and in good works, even to the end.

“Faith”—that is, the steadfastness of all good things. Since the conduct of those leaders had a good end, imitate their faith. By “faith” he means their steadfastness or perseverance.

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.”

These words belong to what precedes, where he testified that the Lord had said: “I will not forsake you, nor abandon you.” They might have replied: “This does not apply to our help, because it was not promised to us; rather, God promised it to Joshua.”

To this the Apostle responds: Do not lose heart. Just as this promise applies to Joshua, so it applies to you, because Jesus Christ, who exists as one essence with the Father, was himself then, is himself now, and will himself be forever.

Do not suppose that the one who was then is not now. The same one who was yesterday will be the same forever. “Yesterday” signifies past time, “today” the present, and “forever” the future without end. It is as though he said: Before the ages, throughout the ages, and after the ages, he will always remain, just as the prophet says of him: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.”

“Do not be led away by various and foreign doctrines.” Various and foreign doctrines are the new teachings of heretics, by which simpler people are led away and separated from the truth of the faith. They also include the superstitions of the Jews, who teach that one must abstain from certain foods, which the law prohibits, while permitting others.

Since among them there were some who were wise according to the flesh and who misled certain people through the observance and distinction of foods, drawing them away from the evangelical teaching that says, “All things are clean to the clean,” the Apostle addresses them, warning them not to be led away by that foreign doctrine. He makes this clearer by adding:

“For it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those who walked in them.”

“It is best,” he says, and perfect, to establish the heart and strengthen the mind in the grace of the new covenant, so that you may possess a perfect faith, believing that all things are clean to the clean—not to establish yourselves in distinctions and observances of foods by saying that certain foods are clean and others unclean. Such observances benefited no one who walked in them.

After the Lord’s coming, all those things that occurred figuratively came to an end, and especially after the Lord said: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person,” but “all things are clean to the clean.” For he saw everything that he had made, and it was very good.

It is better to retain faith together with perfect works than to dispute about distinctions among foods, rejecting what God created clean. There is one perfect observance: abstaining from sin. For it is of no benefit to abstain from foods if one does not abstain from sins.

Although they devoted themselves to such observances, they gained nothing if they did not have faith. Their observance of the law benefited them; their refusal to eat certain foods brought them no benefit.

“We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat.”

He refers to the legal custom, its mystery, and its spiritual meaning. The commandment of the law required that on the tenth day of the seventh month, during the festival of Passover—namely, the festival of Atonement—they should take a bull calf and a goat and sacrifice them in the camp.

The high priest alone was to carry the blood of those animals into the Holy of Holies and pray for the people; their flesh, however, was to be carried outside the camp and burned there. No one serving the tabernacle was permitted to eat of it.

Spiritually, those two animals—the bull calf and the goat—prefigure the Lord the Savior. He is the calf whom the merciful father sacrificed at the return of the prodigal son; he is also the goat, because he was offered for sinners.

That high priest who entered the Holy of Holies with the blood of those animals to pray for the people represented the true High Priest, who entered the inner regions of the heavenly homeland with the blood of his Passion to pray for his faithful.

Those animals were sacrificed within the camp, but their flesh was burned outside the camp, because our Redeemer was sacrificed in Jerusalem, as though within the camp, by the voices and judgment of the children of Israel; but their flesh was burned outside Jerusalem, on the cross, by the fire of his Passion.

When he was condemned to death, while the Jews cried, “He is guilty of death! Crucify him, crucify him!” he was, so far as concerned them, in a certain sense sacrificed. Mark the Evangelist, wishing to show us that this was so, says: “It was the third hour when they crucified him”—namely, with their tongues. For at the sixth hour he was raised upon the cross outside Jerusalem, and there his body was consumed by the fire of his Passion.

That altar of the Jews, which was situated outside the camp, where the flesh was consumed, is the altar of the Church, where the body of Christ is consecrated daily.

We therefore have the altar of the Church, where the Lord’s body is consecrated. Those who serve the tabernacle of their body have no authority to eat from it: namely, fornicators, adulterers, drunkards, the unclean, those who sow discord among brothers, and all who serve the pleasures and desires of their flesh.

“For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.”

The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the Holy Place for sin by the high priest are burned outside the camp. How these things apply to the Lord has, I think, been sufficiently explained.

But since he himself is the head of all the elect, by the flesh of those animals we can understand all the elect, who outside the camp—that is, outside the manner of life of worldly and carnal people—put their members to death with vices and desires, or who, while following the example of the Lord’s Passion, undergo the crown of martyrdom.

As blessed Peter urges, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps.”

Their blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest when their praiseworthy life is presented to God the Father through the true Priest, Jesus, who is our advocate and intercedes for us. Blood properly signifies life, because “the life of man is in the blood.”

Or their blood is brought into the Holy Place when their souls are carried to the heavenly realms in the triumph of their Passion. They are rightly consumed upon the altar, because the holy martyrs fulfill all these things in faith, by which they believe that they will be rewarded by God.

Those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat what is consecrated upon this altar, because those who live carnally and are held fast by love of this world do not dare approach what the holy martyrs fulfill by enduring in perfect faith.

“Therefore”—understand: “the mystery must be fulfilled”—“Jesus also, to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.”

That is, he suffered for those who believe in him. As the Gospel books testify, the Lord suffered outside the gate of Jerusalem, in the place of those beheaded, which was called Calvary.

Therefore, so that the Lord might transform the shadow and figure into the reality that had been prefigured concerning him and his members, and so that he might redeem and cleanse through his blood the people who believed in him, he suffered outside Jerusalem.

“Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.”

Since the Lord suffered for us, the Apostle urges us to imitate him, saying: Since he suffered outside the camp to sanctify us, let us go out to him outside the manner of life of carnal people, putting our members to death with vices and desires. Let us also imitate his Passion by enduring martyrdom for him.

This is to bear his reproach: to suffer the same things that he suffered. His cross appears to the pagans to be his reproach, but to us it is sanctification and redemption.

Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, despising present things, loving future things, scorning visible things, desiring eternal things, and following him. For “we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come.”

It is certain that in this world we cannot have an eternal dwelling or a city that always remains, since the world will pass away, and so will its desire. Therefore we must strive with all our strength toward the heavenly city, Jerusalem, whose inhabitant is God, who will remain eternally.

“Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God”—that is, “the fruit of lips confessing his name.”

Through him, that is, through Christ, we ought to offer God the Father a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving for all good things. He calls it “the fruit of lips” because those same praises and thanksgivings merit the fruit of rewards.

Hence the Apostle says: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” They offered animals; we offer none of these things, but ought to offer God thanksgiving alone. Concerning this sacrifice the Psalmist says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise.”

“And do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for God is pleased by such sacrifices.”

A beneficent person is one who is generous and devoted to almsgiving; hence beneficence means generosity in almsgiving.

“Do not forget,” he says, “beneficence and fellowship”—that is, generosity in almsgiving and the sharing that you ought to extend and distribute to others from your possessions. Do not forget this.

Even if others have seized your property, do not forget to give alms from what you possess, as the prophet says: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor.”

By such sacrifices and gifts of alms God is made propitious. Hence he says through the prophet: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.”

One should not consider the poor person, who appears to receive, but rather the one who commanded the gift to be made. The alms given to the poor on earth are received from God in heaven.

Do not look to whether the recipient will return to you what he has received. You gave earthly things; you will purchase eternal things.

“Obey your leaders and submit to them.”

Prelates and preachers are to be obeyed in every respect insofar as their doctrine and conduct are holy and devout. But if they depart from the path of righteousness, as did the scribes and Pharisees, let us not do what they do but what they say—unless they should prove contrary in the faith.

For if they prove contrary in the faith, they are not only to be avoided but also fled. But if they teach rightly while differing in conduct, hear Christ speaking of such people in the person of the scribes and Pharisees: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do.”

“For they keep watch as those who must give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning.”

All prelates and leaders are to be obeyed unless they have perhaps departed from the truth of the faith. Above all, however, obedience is owed to those who keep watch—who watch without interruption in setting a good example, preaching, and caring for external matters, being concerned about how they will give an account for their people.

Therefore we ought to be subject to our prelates, who are concerned for us, since they must give an account for us, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning—that is, so that they may exercise care for you with gladness and a cheerful mind, and not with complaint and disturbance of spirit. For the bad conduct and disobedience of subjects often provoke the minds of prelates to bitterness, so that they become slower and sadder regarding their progress.

Alternatively, we ought to obey them so that on the day of judgment they may give an account for us with joy, secure concerning their reward, and not with groaning, anxious about our condemnation.

“For this is of no advantage to you.” Understand: It is not advantageous for you that they should care for you with groaning or give an account for you with sadness.

“Pray for us.”

Here he destroys the pride and arrogance of mind found in certain bishops, who, swollen with the appearance of pride, disdain to ask their subjects to offer prayers for them.

If, then, the one who was called by God to become the teacher and master of all nations did not disdain to ask that his subjects—those whom he had acquired for the Lord—pray for him, how much more do those who are filled with envy and covered with robbery and other vices need the assistance of their subjects’ prayers?

He continues: “For we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to conduct ourselves well in all things.”

The Jews accused the Apostle of not loving his own people as he loved the Gentiles. Therefore he addresses them gently and imploringly, showing that he had good will toward all—that is, toward both Jews and Gentiles.

“We are confident,” he says—both I and my companions—that we have good will toward all people, desiring to conduct ourselves well toward Jews as well as Gentiles.

Do not bring forward any accusations or slanders, for our conscience reproves and condemns us in nothing on the ground that we lack good will toward you.

“But I urge you more earnestly to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.”

It is my desire to come; therefore I earnestly ask you to pray for me, so that my desire to come to you may be fulfilled quickly.

It should be noted that he first asks them for the assistance of prayer; then, not merely and casually, but with complete intention and every possible effort, he pours out a devout prayer for them to the Lord, saying:

“May the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ…”

Here “the God of peace” means God the Father, from whom true peace proceeds, who loves peace, and who reconciled us through the blood of his Son.

He brought the great shepherd of the sheep back from the dead—that is, from the tomb, which is properly the place of the dead—and raised him on the third day. In accordance with this, as the Son himself drew near to his Passion, he prayed, saying: “Father, glorify your Son”—that is, raise your Son.

And what does that same God the Father say to him in the Psalm? “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery”—that is, the chorus of all virtues. To him the Son says: “I will rise at dawn.”

God the Father therefore brought his Son back from the dead—that is, from hell or from the tomb—according to what the Psalmist had foretold: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption.”

And, so to speak, the Son himself raised himself by the power of the Word. For the whole Trinity brought him back from the dead, since those three persons work indivisibly.

The Lord Jesus is the great shepherd because he leads his sheep to the pastures of life and the pleasant meadows of the green paradise. He is the shepherd who says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd.”

His sheep are the elect, of whom he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life.”

“May he make you fit”—that is, prepare you and make you perfect—“in every good thing, so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

“May the God of peace,” he says, “make you fit in every good thing”—that is, make you fit in true faith, sound doctrine, and perfect works, so that you may fulfill his will, himself accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ.

You can possess no good from yourselves unless he goes before and follows after you, in accordance with what the Psalmist prays: “His mercy shall go before me, and his mercy shall follow me.”

The Apostle likewise says elsewhere: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish,” because through him we were made and redeemed, and through him whatever good we possess is supplied to us.

“To whom be glory”—that is, to God the Father and Jesus Christ—“through all future ages. Amen.”

“Amen” is a confirmation, meaning either “Let it be,” or “It is true as I have said.”

“But I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation, for I have written to you only very briefly.”

Note that he calls the whole epistle “one word.” He did not say, “I ask you to bear patiently the word of admonition,” because they were fainthearted, but “the word of consolation”—that is, a word of comfort and exhortation.

I have not written much to you, but little in comparison with what I would say to you if I were present, because I fear being a burden to you.

“Know that our brother Timothy has been released.”

Timothy was the blessed Apostle’s fellow bishop and assistant in preaching. He says that Timothy had been released by him and sent to preach, or perhaps from Athens, where the Apostle had left him.

It may also be understood that Timothy had been detained in prison and had then been released.

“With whom”—that is, with Timothy—“if he comes more quickly, I will see you.”

He wishes to make them gentler by saying that he too will come to them.

“Greet all your leaders and all the saints.”

Just as he had written this epistle generally to all the Hebrews, so he greets all generally and wishes them well—not only the prelates but also all their subjects, whom he calls saints. At the same time he flatters them by greeting them honorably, so that they might recognize that he loved them not merely outwardly but with the full affection of his heart.

“The brothers from Italy greet you.”

By these words he very clearly indicates to us that he wrote this epistle at Rome, which is situated in the region of Italy, and, as the teachers think, was at that time in prison.

“Grace be with you all. Amen.”

Grace is so called because it is freely given. Here, under the name of grace, we must understand perfect faith together with the performance of good works, the remission of sins—which the faithful receive at the time of baptism—and also the gift of the Holy Spirit, which is given in baptism through the laying on of the bishops’ hands. All these things are given freely by God.

The Apostle therefore prays that those to whom he was writing might possess all these gifts. Let us also pray to the Lord with devout supplication that, through the intercession of the outstanding Apostle, he may make us possessors of these gifts in the present, guarding with complete integrity the faith he taught and adorning it with good works, so that, with Christ as our guide, we may deserve to attain the contemplation of the heavenly vision. Amen.

---

[Col. 0793D]

# The Five Books of Primasius’s Commentaries on the Apocalypse of Blessed John

[Note: Cassiodorus, in *The Book on Divine Readings*, chapter 9: “In our own times, the Apocalypse mentioned above has also been expounded in five books, minutely and diligently, through the efforts of blessed Primasias, an African bishop.”]

(C, S)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0793C]

Yielding to your persuasion, illustrious and devout Castor, I have undertaken to expound, with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, the book of the Apocalypse of blessed John, veiled in many mysteries, although with scant strength. I have not been content merely with discoveries of my own; rather, although few in number, whenever I happened to find testimonies concerning it expounded by the holy Augustine, I added them without hesitation.

I also culled certain passages from Tichonius the former Donatist that accord with sound understanding. From these materials I suppressed what overflowed, cut away what was inappropriate, and composed what was rough, tempering everything with Catholic moderation.

For in his work I found many things that were both superfluous and foolish and contrary to sound doctrine. Concerning the dispute that exists between us and them, he sought out harmful passages according to the perversity of his heart and thought that he could maliciously mock our Church by an injurious interpretation.

It is not surprising that a heretic made a work suited to himself. But whatever could be culled from it—although he attempted this unjustly—it was our concern, when we found suitable opportunities, to set forth truthfully and, by refuting their error, to nullify it.

Just as a precious gem found in dung ought to be cared for, gathered up, and restored by a prudent person to its noble worth, so wherever truth shines forth, it must be defended for the Catholic unity. For whatever truth may have proclaimed outside also belongs to this unity alone.

Faith rightly gathered from the faithless whatever it recognized as belonging to its own right. What has been usurped cannot benefit strangers, but it can benefit sons once it has been returned to its true mother.

The Donatists, however, ought not to become exalted on this account, just as the Jews ought not to glory in Caiaphas’s statement, by which he said, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John 11).

Nor should this cause offense to our own people. If anything should prove useful for ecclesiastical purposes, it must be applied to our instruction. One must not consider the person of the speaker, but the quality of what is said.

Thus Moses (Exodus 18), having been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians after the address of the divine word, by which he had previously deserved fellowship with the blessed (*beati*; F. *beari*, “to be blessed”), listened to his father-in-law Jethro: the meek man listened to the uneducated, the skilled to the ignorant, the teacher of a great multitude to an individual, and the devoted Israelite to a Gentile.

Following his advice, he soon discovered the utility mentioned above, when the burdens of governing the people were distributed among many and thereby made specifically lighter. In the same way, sound statements made by pagan authorities and joined to apostolic preaching have, by a better command, contributed to our progress; yet the Gentiles are not thereby permitted to glory.

This work extends through five books. What benefit its reading will bring to diligent students will be proved better by experience than by our promise.

Yet, because of the differing opinions of critics, I expect to be blamed in different ways: some will begin to complain about the length of this work, while others, weighing the depths of the book, will be more inclined to accuse it of brevity.

I think that the former may first be appeased by saying that I confess it is more fitting to criticize me for its shortness, since I have neither been able adequately to penetrate the fullness of the divine mysteries hidden there nor been capable of expressing in suitable language even those things that could be understood.

To the latter I offer this answer as satisfaction: I have not maliciously withheld anything from my masters and fellow servants. Rather, I prefer to ask pardon for my shortness by confessing my ignorance.

Even if I had not believed one experienced in this matter, I would nevertheless have learned from the judgment of Saint Jerome, who, speaking about this book, says: “The Apocalypse of John has as many mysteries as words. I have said too little, and in keeping with the worth of the volume every praise falls short.” Within each of these individual words lie many levels of understanding.

Through these considerations, humble confession earns pardon, and the excellence of the book becomes known at least to believers, even if they do not yet understand it.

For whereas elsewhere a narrative with figurative meaning is rarely inserted, here it is either frequently interwoven, or a denser figure is gradually generated from another, or one and the same matter is presented under various veiled figures, so that it might seem impossible for the same thing to have been repeated rather than another. This is also found at the beginning of Ezekiel and in certain visions of Daniel, but here more extensively.

For this reason, you know that I, who am weak, must be assisted all the more by your prayers.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795B]

With the Lord’s assistance, as we are about to undertake this exposition, we must necessarily interpret the title, identify the place, recount the discourse, and indicate the person, so that its contents may be announced by its name, recognized by its location, and [its] time [F. “in time”] designated.

Through the subject, the excellence of its merits should become clear; the person should signify one among the company of the others, to whom the particular task entrusted should appropriately be assigned.

Since it is clear that individual books are given titles by different names, it was fitting to call the *epigraphē*—that is, the superscription—of this one the Apocalypse.

Although he was placed among the Greeks, he was a Hebrew; nevertheless, he expressed the character of the book in the proper language of the Greeks. For *apokalypsis* [ἀποκάλυψις] is interpreted as “revelation.”

To whom would the Lord Jesus Christ reveal such and such great things except to the one whom he loved with such exceptional affection above the other disciples that, while still present in the body, he graciously caused him to recline upon his breast and abundantly draw from that spiritual fountain of life the secrets of truth?

Thus, with this indication of his love preceding, no one could doubt that John was worthy of such a revelation.

It was fitting first to commend the greatness of the revelation by the greatness of love.

He deserved to see these things at the time when, for Christ’s sake, he had been sent into exile on the island of Patmos by the emperor Domitian and condemned to the mines, confined within its boundaries.

Time and place are fittingly added: there, and at the time when he was thought to be confined by human custody, he deserved to transcend the limits of humanity in mind and see divine things with a free gaze; and he to whom it was then forbidden to exceed certain earthly spaces was granted access to penetrate heavenly secrets.

Thus the faith of Christ claims heaven for itself even on earth, when, making good use of temporal evils, it enjoys eternal goods.

The universal goods of the universal Church are therefore revealed to one person, but proclaimed for the benefit of all. Finally, what he alone saw, he sent in writing to the seven churches, so that one person might serve unity and show that he had labored not only for himself but also for all.

Later he wrote the Gospel, when, after Domitian’s death, a gathering of many priests entreated him, now free from exile, not to allow the ignorant to be deceived by the defilement of false preachers.

For Valentinus, Cerinthus, and Ebion had already begun to entangle many of their followers in falsehoods. These had rightly to be refuted by the novelty of the true Gospel.

## CHAPTERS OF BOOK ONE

[Col. 0795D]

I. The title, subject-matter, time, and place are indicated. II. The beginning of the book. III. The address to the seven Churches, their interpretation, and their significance are recalled. IV. Beginning the sequence of the visions, he expounds what concerns the golden lampstands and the rest. [Col. 0796D] V. The character of the seven angels of the Churches is intimated by praise, with blame interposed, together with mention of the twenty-four elders and the door opened in heaven. VI. He says that flashes of lightning and thunder come forth from the throne. VII. Concerning the seven lamps and the four creatures with eyes.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0795D]

The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known openly to his servants.

This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God the Father is therefore said to have given him, although every work of the Father and the Son is [Col. 0796D] proved to be inseparable—indeed, also the work of the Holy Spirit, whose name he frequently indicates here—because, even in the form of a servant, one and the same person both receives from the Father and grants together with the Father what must shortly come to pass. Every event that takes place in time has a beginning, a course, and an end. [Col. 0797A] After the emergence of the Church, which had already been founded through the preaching of the apostles, it was necessary to reveal how it would be propagated more widely, and by what kind of end it would be confined, so that the preachers of this truth, relying on the confidence provided by this knowledge, might boldly set out—the few against the many, the unarmed against the armed, the humble against the proud, the weak against the noble—yet spiritually alive against those who were spiritually dead.

With God, indeed, whatever is prolonged in this life, however long its delays, is said to be “short.” Thus the prophet says (Ps. LXXXIX): “For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed away.” And he signified these things, which were to be announced through his angel, to his servant John, who preached the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ—the things that he saw. By saying “he signified,” he also [Col. 0797B] showed that the things concerned the future and mysteries; nor did he wish us to remain satisfied with the surface of the letter. Rather, by the word “signification,” he directed us to scrutinize the mysteries more deeply.

When he says “to his servant John,” he wished it to be revealed to the whole Church in one person—the Church that he founded in unity. Therefore he says “to make known openly to his servants,” not merely to one among many, but rather through one person to all, just as Peter alone received the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI), although the whole Church, exalted by that authority, has deserved to use them.

Quite properly he added that these things were shown by Christ to the disciple through his angel, since Christ has always appeared clearly to mortals through an assumed creature, not through the essence of his divinity, both before the Incarnation and after the Ascension. Therefore the one who had known him as teacher in the humanity he had assumed bore witness [Col. 0797C] to the invisible Word. And lest anyone should think that only the Word was to be understood, he again added the name “Jesus Christ,” which everyone knows pertains to the form of the man he assumed.

Blessed is the one who reads, and those who hear the words of this prophecy and keep what is written in it.

By saying “the one who reads” and “those who hear,” he indicated the persons of teachers and learners: by the effort of reading he might remove idleness, and upon those who keep these things he might bestow blessedness. The words that follow also correspond to them: “and they keep what is written in it,” because keeping belongs to both groups and is appropriate to both. “For not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. II).

Because the time is already near—that is, the time when each of the things that must be said will be fulfilled—and because the Church already planted [Col. 0797D] was to receive the increases of its propagation, he introduces what he is about to discuss in this way: “John to the seven Churches that are in Asia.” That is, to one sevenfold Church.

The number seven often represents universality, because the whole universe is, as it were, composed from the first odd and even numbers—that is, from three and four—as from unlike elements. For the diversity of soul and body likewise embraces the unity represented by this number. Three pertain to the soul, and four to the body. Thus it is said (Deut. VI): “God is to be loved with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the mind.” As for the body, we recognize four qualities: hot and cold, dry and moist.

For this reason it is also sung [Col. 0798A] (Ps. CXVIII): “Seven times a day I have praised you.” Elsewhere he says (Ps. XXXIII): “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.” And Wisdom “built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars” (Prov. IX), together with the other passages that foretell that the Church will possess the world, which Christ likewise received as one possession for an inheritance. “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

Hence it uniquely bears the name “catholic,” because by hereditary dignity it alone possesses the whole world. This Church now hears John and, through the greeting, as one redeemed hopes for perpetual salvation:

“Grace to you and peace from God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.”

Although, according to the Apostle (II Cor. V), “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,” and although he himself testifies (John VIII), “The one who sent me is with me,” because of the unity of one and the same nature, this passage must nevertheless properly be referred to the person of the Son. [Col. 0798B] He “is,” because he remains the same; he “was,” because he created all things with the Father and did not begin from the Virgin; he “is to come” to judge.

And from the seven spirits who are before the throne of God.

Because of the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold (Isa. II)—that is, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord. The gifts of one Spirit are commended according to the law when peace and grace are desired from the seven spirits for the devout.

And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead.

In the humanity he assumed, he bore witness to the Father, when, preaching, he said (John XVII): “I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known.” Showing that this name had formerly been withheld from the Jews, [Col. 0798C] he says (Exod. VI): “And I did not make my name Adonai known to them.” Once the Son is believed, knowledge of the Father is likewise revealed; for he would not be called son unless he had a father, nor father unless he had a son. Each, therefore, is known through the proclamation of the other, because the Father is truly approved in the Son, and the Son in the Father. “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V).

For this reason the same John also says in his Epistle: “Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself; whoever does not believe the Son makes him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has testified concerning his Son” (I John V).

And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, who also, having suffered, freed us from sin by his own blood; [Col. 0798D] and, having risen, is rightly proclaimed the firstborn from the dead (Col. I). And he made us a kingdom and priests for his God and Father, as the apostle Peter also says: “A holy nation, a royal priesthood, an elect race” (I Pet. II), and so forth.

Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him.

The one who first came secretly to be judged will come openly to judge. He will be seen by unbelievers in the flesh in which he chose to suffer, not in the divinity that remained impassible and invisible. Therefore he added: “and those who pierced him.”

And all the earth will see him.

All earthly people, or all the wicked in general—especially the Jews, [Col. 0799A] who considered him insignificant and worthy of death—when they see him as they did not believe he would be, will lament themselves with belated repentance and will mourn when he comes.

So be it, Amen.

By inserting “Amen”—which, through God’s revelation, he knows most certainly will happen—he confirms without doubt that he will come.

I am Α and Ω, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.

Through him the ages were made, and he is proclaimed to have been absent from no age. For this reason he is also taught to be the Almighty.

I, John, your brother and sharer in tribulation, and in the kingdom and endurance in Christ Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ.

I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.
