So that what we have promised may be confirmed, here he indicates the place, the time, and the cause. Lest anyone should think that he had been deceived by a carnal fantasy, he testifies that he was in the Spirit and saw these things. Those whose citizenship is in heaven [Col. 0799B] (Phil. III), and who do not live for themselves but for the one who died and rose for all (II Cor. V), are always to be understood as keeping the Lord’s day.

And I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet, saying to me: What you see, write in a book, and send it to the seven Churches—to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum and Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.

I think it is fitting for the work undertaken if, since we cannot investigate everything, we at least examine the names of the seven Churches, to determine how their interpreted meanings resound in our language. Once clear indications have been opened to us by their titles, the subsequent words of the divine discourse, when considered, may also be fitted with a suitable meaning to the persons or Churches mentioned.

First, we must deal with Asia, in which these seven Churches are enumerated as though in the world. For Asia is interpreted as “exaltation.” Thus the whole Church, as though placed in the exaltation of this [Col. 0799C] world’s province, is admonished to reject that exaltation and approach in gentleness, ready to submit to Christ’s easy yoke—or, if it has already begun to advance, to progress through a more abundant cultivation of piety.

Thus Saul is rebuked in his pride so that he may be gained in humility. When the Lord rebuked Saul, he made him Paul—“little”—to such an extent that the man who had recently been a ravening wolf, breathing out a desire to seize spoils from Christ’s disciples, submitted his neck in devotion even to Ananias, whose name is interpreted as “sheep.” Though he was to become a teacher, he humbly undertook discipleship in order to preach the faith.

Ephesus, therefore, is said to be interpreted as “my will” or “my counsel.” We frequently know that “will” is used for charity, and “counsel” for the correction of negligence. This is clear there, since things pleasing to the will, [Col. 0799D] which soothe through charity, are recounted, while things requiring correction are bound with threats according to better counsel.

Pergamum is interpreted as “dividing their horns,” or “cutting apart valleys in speech.” Since, concerning its angel, he showed two kinds of people—some holding the faith, others holding the teaching of the Nicolaitans—he not without reason divides the horns of the righteous and the sinners, since the same name is expressed in both cases. This is so that, as we read (Ps. LXXIV), “the horns of sinners may be broken, and the horns of the righteous exalted.”

And “cutting apart the valley.” [Col. 0800A] The humility of confession was certainly to be discerned under the name of “valley,” distinguished from the ruin of those who are said to be entangled in Satan’s doctrines. He was rightly to repent for mere negligence, whereas they were to be reproached and pierced with compunction for a grave fall.

Sardis is interpreted as “prince of beauty.” In this Church he recalls the dignity of the elect, saying: “They have not defiled their garments; they will walk with me in white.”

Philadelphia is interpreted as “saving the one who clings to the Lord.” Therefore such a discourse is directed to its angel, so that he may know both that he is loved and that he is to be protected from the hour of temptation.

Laodicea is said to be interpreted as “a tribe beloved by the Lord,” or “they were in vomit.” Here he shows what is bestowed there through the gift of divine charity, and what is more justly charged to the fault of human exaltation in those who boasted that they were rich.

Finally, the Lord who loves says (Apoc. III): “I reprove and discipline those whom I love.” But again it is reproved for lukewarmness, so that, once the foulness of transgression has been rejected, it may remain beloved. To it, when converted, he promises both gold refined by fire and a white garment (ibid.).

But those who have an impenitent heart there were themselves in vomit. [Col. 0800B] To them he also says: “I am about to vomit you out of my mouth,” so that the word and the deed may agree with the name.

And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me. And I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like the Son of Man.

That is, Christ, who frequently wished to be called by this name. This Christ is clothed in the seven lampstands themselves. Whether the seven lampstands or the seven stars are mentioned, the Church is meant.

It is rightly said “in the midst.” For, as the Psalm says (Ps. LXXV), “All who are around him will offer gifts.” Or, as Ezekiel says: “So that the nations may know that I am in the midst of Israel.”

But because of figurative expressions, he divides the genus [Col. 0800C] tropologically into species, so that in certain species only the genus is found expressed. In particular passages, because of subtle details and the profundity of divine eloquence, the genus cannot be clearly demonstrated; it can more easily be seen than expressed.

He divides the genus into parts in this way: Noah’s ark is the Church, and the eight souls within the ark are the Church, although there is one Church. The man Judah, the one who dwells in Jerusalem, and the judges between the house and its vineyard likewise belong to this pattern, since Jerusalem and those who dwell in it, as well as the Lord’s vineyard, are the Church. Thus he concluded, saying: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V).

And in the great house, which is the Church, there are vessels of gold and silver (II Tim. II), although those same vessels are the house of God. Again: “Go out from the midst of it, you who bear the vessels of the Lord,” [Col. 0800D] although those who bear them are themselves the vessels. And: “Who will dwell in the tent of God? The one innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. XIV), since there is no other tent of God on earth than the innocent and pure in heart.

So now also he distinguishes the Church among the seven lampstands [Col. 0800D] in the Son of Man. “The two,” says the Apostle (Eph. V), “will be one flesh; but I speak of Christ and the Church.”

And, as was said above, in certain species the genus is present as a part. In another sense he says “one like the Son of Man,” when, after conquering death, he had ascended into heaven with the body of the Church joined to him. He says that the Church deserved even more to sit in heavenly places, not yet in reality but still in hope, as though the Son of Man were walking in the midst of the golden lampstands.

He says “in the midst” of the Churches, just as in Solomon he says: “I will walk among the paths of the righteous.”

[Col. 0801A] The antiquity and immortality of his majesty are shown by the brightness at his head. “He was clothed,” he says, “in a long robe,” indicating the priesthood. According to Zechariah, the long robe is priestly clothing. Christ exercised the priesthood through the singular sacrifice of his flesh, when, offering himself to the Father on the cross for us, he permitted himself to be crucified.

And he was girded above the breasts with a golden belt.

He says that the two breasts are the two Testaments, as we read in the Song of Songs: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns feeding among the lilies,” and, “Your breasts are like clusters of grapes.”

In this figure the genus may also be understood [Col. 0801B] in the Testaments, so that the Testaments receive their comparison from what they accomplish. For the Testaments are not nourished; rather, the Church is nourished through the Testaments.

Examples of this trope are found in the Scriptures, in which the agent receives a name from what he does. Thus the breasts are the Testaments, while the golden belt signifies the chorus of the saints, who cling to and embrace the Testaments—or Christ, whom they proclaim. It also signifies the charity by which they are bound to one another, preserving, as the Apostle says, “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

His head and his hair were white like wool or snow.

By the white hair he means the multitude of the candidates, exalted and shining with the virtues of righteousness, whom grace has whitened beyond snow. He signified them by wool because of the sheep that are at the right hand, and by snow because of the innumerable throng of those who have been whitened and given to heaven. They are Jerusalem, which daily descends from heaven, so that those who are still pilgrims sigh as they press toward it.

Alternatively, the reference to wool may rightly be understood [Col. 0801C] as concerning the holy garment made from it, without stain or wrinkle.

His eyes were like a flame of fire.

At one time he calls the eyes of the Church the commandments of God; at another, spiritual people, as Solomon says (Prov. I): “The commandment is a lamp, and the law is light.” And concerning spiritual people the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V).

That the commandments themselves are fire, he says as follows: “Your word is exceedingly refined by fire” (Ps. CXVIII); and concerning Joseph: “The commandment of the Lord set him on fire.”

The fire of the commandments provides light to the faithful, but burning to unbelievers: “Fire will go before him and burn up his enemies round about.”

His feet were like burnished bronze of Lebanon, as though refined in a fiery furnace. [Col. 0801D]

By the feet of fire he means the Church of the final age. The foot is the final part of the body. Thus the Church is foretold as being tested by the intensity of the persecutions at that time (Dan. II), just as the stone cut from the mountain struck the statue at its feet—that is, by its blow crushed the entire body of the kingdoms of the world.

But it is at the feet because this will occur at the end of time. He compared them to burnished bronze because it is made from bronze, which, with much fire and the application of a treatment, is brought to a golden color.

He says “of Lebanon” because the elect are meant; for Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening.” And because Lebanon is a mountain in Judea, this signifies that, near the end of the world, the body of Christ will be tested by persecutions there, where the Lord is believed to have suffered.

And his voice was like the voice of many waters.

[Col. 0802A] By the voice he shows the Church preaching. To it is said: “Cry out, do not cease” (Isa. LVIII). The many waters are the many peoples. But the gift of baptism, which he sent through the apostles for salvation by his command, is also rightly understood here.

This is expressed in the Psalm: “The Lord dwells over the flood” (Ps. XXVIII); and, “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered” (ibid.), together with the other passages that support this interpretation.

And he held seven stars in his right hand.

In Christ’s right hand is the spiritual Church. Therefore: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in various colors” (Ps. XLIV). To her, standing there, he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV).

These seven Churches are the seven stars that he names individually [Col. 0802B]—not because they alone are Churches or leaders, but because what he says to one he says to all who are placed in unity, according to the interpretation given above, by which we said that the number seven signifies universality.

And from his mouth came forth a two-edged sword.

It is two-edged because the sword arms the soldier, kills the enemy, and punishes the deserter. Hence the Apostle says (Eph. VI): “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.”

“For every scribe who has been instructed,” says the Lord (Matt. XIII), “is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old”—namely, the New Testament and the Old.

Through this twofold Testament, like a two-edged sword, the Church is now instructed, so that, being destined for eternal goods, it may know how to use present goods properly.

The Apostle, girded with this sword, says (II Cor. VI): “By the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left.”

And his face was shining like the sun in its strength.

He says that his splendor manifests [Col. 0802C] his presence in the flesh, in which he spoke with human beings face to face (Exod. XXXIII). The comparison with the sun is applied because of its appropriate significance: because of rising, setting, and rising again—because he was born, suffered, and rose again.

The Lord also promises the future likeness of glory to his Church, saying: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. XIII).

By comparison with this, the brightness of Christ’s head must be understood as far more exalted, since he himself is the splendor of the righteous. For this reason, after the resurrection, he concealed that splendor from his disciples, lest they be unable either to recognize or to endure him.

This should not be recognized or called blindness, but rather a kind of invisibility, which in Greek is more appropriately called ἀορασία (*aorasia*). [Col. 0802D] Through this invisibility, the army did not recognize Elisha, nor did the raging people recognize the door, although they saw everything else besides these.

Finally, they were unable to endure an example of this glorification on the mountain.

And when I saw him, I fell at his feet like a dead man.

John, who saw these things, bears the figure of the whole Church. But individual apostles and prophets also do so, those who say: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

The Church, therefore, is as one dead to the world before the Lord Christ.

And he placed his right hand upon me.

This is certainly because of the priesthood, through which we know that rulers of the Churches are ordained. Or it is because the whole body belongs to one priest, who says:

Do not be afraid, John. I am the first [Col. 0803A] and the last.

The first, because all things were made through him (John I); the last, because in him all things are renewed; and the living one, because “I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever.”

The whole sum and hope of consolation is shown when he says to the one who lies dead: “Do not be afraid.” Thus in the Gospel he says (John XVI): “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world.”

I am the living one who was dead.

The Head of the body truly promises the same hope of resurrection, whose going before us is the hope of the struggle undertaken by the good.

And I have the keys of death and of the underworld—that is, of the devil and of his entire body, which he designates by the name “death,” and of the underworld, in which he reigns. None of these escape the power of divine judgment, which is like a key.

And to the Church he says: “In me you have the keys of death, which you have rightly received from me and possess.”

You who are like one dead, because although the Church is still a pilgrim, [Col. 0803B] the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification (Rom. VIII), have nevertheless received the power, in your God, of binding and loosing. This is so whether the Church administers all things with sound judgment, or whether faith in those who receive them is hindered by no obstacle of unbelief.

“To whomever,” he says (John XX), “you forgive sins, they will be forgiven; to whomever you retain them, they will be retained.”

Therefore write what you have seen, what is, and what must take place after these things: the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands.

The seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches. And the seven lampstands are the Church. He said that the stars are the angels of the Churches and the lampstands the Churches; [Col. 0803C] these things must be considered carefully.

For if there is one sevenfold Church, as it is described (Song of Songs VI): “My dove is one; my perfect one is one,” then the angels will not be seven. For if there are seven, these alone—which he specifically named—have angels, while the others do not.

Nor should it be thought that in this passage angels are assigned to individual human beings, as some have incongruously judged. Rather, the angels of the Churches here are to be understood as the leaders of the people, who preside over the individual Churches and announce the word of life to all. For the name “angel” is also interpreted as “messenger.”

## CHAPTER II

[The supplied source ends here.]

And to the angel of the church at Ephesus write:

Here the dative case, [Note: [Col. 0803D] See whether *Ecclesiae* should be read, although the sense is not even entirely clear.] is used for *angelo*, not the genitive. It is as though he said: “Write to this angel of the church,” so that he may seem to have spoken not so much of an angel and a church separately as to have wished to explain what an angel is, making the person of the angel and the church one. For although he is placed over it by the administration of the sacrament, he is joined to it by the unity of its structure. Since he observes this rule from the beginning, John would have written not to seven angels but to seven churches: “John,” he says, “to the seven churches that are in Asia”; and the Lord whom he saw says, “Write in a book what you have seen and send it to the seven churches.” Yet afterward he commands that it be written to the angels, to show that they are one.

Even if he addresses something separately to the individual churches, the whole church in general is taught to be included. For he does not say, “What the Spirit says to the church,” but “to the churches.” By signifying the church through the angel, therefore, he shows two aspects in him, since he both praises and rebukes. In what follows, however, it becomes clear that he does not rebuke the same part that he praises. Thus the Lord in the Gospel (Luke 12; Matthew 24), speaking of the whole body of leaders, called one servant both blessed and wicked; when he comes, the Lord himself will divide him, and he says that he will place not merely the servant but “his portion” with the hypocrites.

Beginning, therefore, to show the internal conflicts and the various works of the sevenfold church that were to occur in the present age, he did not say, “Write what is,” but, “What must take place,” announcing that until the end of the world the wicked would be mingled with the good in the church. This church must undoubtedly be embraced for the sake of the good, though it must not be abandoned because of the wicked.

“To the angel of the church at Ephesus write: These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand”—the same one who holds you in his hand and rules and preserves you by his authority—“who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands,” that is, in the midst of you.

“I know your works, your labor, and your endurance, and that you cannot bear the wicked; you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and have found them liars; you have had patience and endured for my name’s sake, and have not grown weary.”

“You have tested them,” he says. Only those within are tested. Those who are outside are plainly outside without any testing, and there is no need to test them. Rather, those within must be tested to determine whether they are outside; they are recognized as schismatics not only by their fruits but also by their dwelling-place.

It is not praise that he said the church could not bear the wicked, but an indication of weakness. Praise lies in the statement, “You cannot,” together with the fact that she endured this weakness for his name’s sake. He distinguishes this from perseverance: by the former he does not mean that she succumbed through human frailty, but that she endured, strengthened by the power of patience, what she could not bear by herself for God’s name.

She is also said to be unable to bear the wicked so that she would not imitate those whom she recognized; she is said to have endured them so that, by abandoning them, she herself would not become alienated from the bond of unity. For he is judged reprobate who, because of openly wicked people, abandons the good who remain hidden.

He then attacks a part of the angel, saying: “But I have this against you, that you have abandoned your first love.” Far be it from us to suppose that he rebukes the one whom he had just praised. Rather, retaining the rule already stated, he teaches that the pilgrim church contains the worst mingled with the best.

One person, then, abandons the love he had begun; another is said, for God’s name, to preserve patience even toward the wicked. To the one he says, “You have patience and have not grown weary”; to the other:

“Remember from where you have fallen, repent, and do the former works. Otherwise I will come to you soon and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.”

He says that he will move the lampstand of the one whom he invites to repent. What the angel is, that the lampstand is. He says that he does not remove part of it, but moves it from its place, signifying one who, although not cut off from the church until he is separated by the winnowing-fan of the final judgment, has nevertheless lost his own salvation and all the light of the lampstand. Even if he appears honored with charisms, he is known to be dead in himself. For what lives in him is another’s.

To another part he speaks well: “But you have this good thing, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate”—that is, idolatry and fornication, as he shows subsequently.

Teaching all the churches, therefore, he says: “Let the one who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life,” that is, from the fruit of the cross, “which is,” he says, “in the paradise of my God.”

Paradise can also be understood as the church, for everything was made in figure, and Adam preceded as a shadow of what was to come, as the Apostle teaches (Romans 13). The tree of life is the wisdom of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who hung upon the cross. In the church and in the spiritual paradise he provides the faithful with living nourishment and the sacrament of the heavenly bread. Of this we read (Proverbs 3): “Wisdom is life to those who embrace her.”

And to the angel of the church at Smyrna write:

“These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and poverty, but you are rich.”

He speaks to the whole church, which is poor in spirit and possesses everything; hence the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 6): “As having nothing, yet possessing everything.”

“And you are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.”

Here also it is shown that he is not speaking only to one particular church, since Jews who blaspheme did not exist or do not exist only at Smyrna. The name “Jews” may be understood in two ways: either as referring to Jews who are openly outside, or to those placed within, that is, false Christians. For “Jew” is a religious name. Hence the Apostle says (Romans 2): “He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter.” Likewise (Philippians 3): “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit and place no confidence in the flesh.”

Yet even these people must not be abandoned, although they are called a synagogue of Satan, since we know that the Lord, by enduring Judas to the end (John 13), provided us with an example of patience.

“Fear none of the things that you are going to suffer.” He certainly warns the whole church not to fear in any way the entire body of the devil.

“Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, so that you may be tested, and you will have tribulation for ten days.”

These words apply to the universal church, against which the devil always exercises unrelenting hostility. Therefore the period of ten days signifies the course of the present life, because of the Decalogue, in which the sum of the law is briefly contained. Divine commandments are necessary here, where self-restraint is required.

Hence the divine instruction (Matthew 5): “Agree with your adversary,” that is, with the law, “while you are with him on the way of this world.” This signifies the whole period during which, under the instruction of the law, one struggles against the various enticements of desire, so that victory may be gained after the five bodily senses have been subdued by God’s grace. Because of the double sense, these senses are doubled and thus make ten.

“Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24).

“Let the one who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be harmed by the second death.”

The eating of the forbidden tree (Genesis 2–3) brought this death upon posterity. Christ, however, causing water and blood to flow from the sanctuary of his side and watering the wood of the cross, made the first fruits of salvation spring forth from the place where he knew original evil had arisen. He said: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world.” Therefore, if anyone conquers, he will be able to conquer in him.

And to the angel of the church at Pergamum write:

“These things says he who has the two-edged sword.” Let enough now have been said about the double-edged sword.

“I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is.”

He speaks to the whole church, because the tempter is everywhere, of whom it is said: “She will watch your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel” (Genesis 3). “The world lies in the evil one.” Satan’s throne is the human beings whom he wickedly possesses.

He returns to the particular image. Although the whole sevenfold church is represented in these seven places, particular events nevertheless took place in them, which he either praises or rebukes.

“And you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny my faith. In those days Antipas, my witness and faithful one, was killed among you.”

Christ is also killed among many people: either by those who do not believe that he rose again, or because people deny him within themselves by damnable vices, where Satan dwells.

“But I have a few things against you to say”—certainly against other members who deserve blame, not against those to whom he says, “You did not deny my faith.”

“You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam” (Numbers 24), “who taught Balak to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat sacrificial offerings and to commit fornication.”

These are the two principal things to which hypocrites devote themselves for enjoyment: eating and fornication, as the Lord says: “Within you are full of robbery, self-indulgence, and every iniquity” (Luke 12; Matthew 23). Idolatry is spiritual fornication. “You have destroyed,” he says (Psalm 72), “all who fornicate away from you.”

“Likewise, you have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Therefore repent likewise. Otherwise I will come to you soon and fight against you with the sword of my mouth.”

That is, “with the sword of the mouth,” which must be understood as belonging to the church, in accordance with the preceding form of interpretation. The sword is the precepts of both Testaments, by which contemptuous people are overcome by divine judgment. For “all who sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Romans 2).

“Let the one who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna”—that is, the invisible bread that descended from heaven so that man might eat the bread of angels (John 6).

The manna in the wilderness preceded this in figure. Those who ate that manna are said to have died by the Lord because they remained unbelieving. They did not eat of that hidden and spiritual manna in a singular sense, which promises immortality to the faithful, when he says (ibid.): “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

Those who at that time were able to be nourished spiritually by that food also deserved to obtain the same immortality, as did Moses and the others. For, as the Apostle teaches (1 Corinthians 10), they ate the same spiritual food, because visible manna did not harm those who used bodily food spiritually. Nor will the spiritual manna of the Lord’s body benefit people of the present time if they receive it unworthily, because they eat and drink judgment upon themselves.

“And I will give him a white stone,” that is, adoption as a son of God (1 Corinthians 11). For a stone is a precious gem, understood in the manner of the pearl that the merchant found and purchased after selling everything (Matthew 13). Another translation has “pearl.”

“And upon the stone a new name, which the mouth of the Lord named.” Alternatively, this may refer to baptism and martyrdom, which, he says, no one knows except the one who receives it.

For although hypocrites appear to possess the outward surface to some extent, they cannot penetrate the power of understanding it (Isaiah 62). “Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power.” Hence the same John says (1 John 2): “Whoever says that he knows him but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him.”

And to the angel of the church at Thyatira write:

“These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire and whose feet are like orichalcum.

“I know your works, your love, your faith, your ministry, and your patience, and that your latter works are more numerous than the former.”

Here it is more fully declared that, in the one body of the church, the part belonging to the good is comforted with praise and the part belonging to the wicked is reproached with rebukes. He both approves, by praise, works together with love, faith, ministry, and patience, and says that the latter works have been increased beyond the former.

“But I have many things against you: you tolerate your wife Jezebel” (1 Kings 16), “who calls herself a prophetess, and you tolerate her teaching and seducing my servants to commit fornication and to eat sacrificial offerings.”

“Angel,” that is, “church,” is a general designation; but the character of the statements shows to whom the speech applies: what part, what kind, and what office correspond to the angel, and how the speech passes from a part of one body, or from a figure, to a proper referent, and from the proper referent returns to the figure.

These events took place, and it is conjectured that a woman actually existed in the church mentioned above. From the special form of that woman, the discourse is now figuratively transferred to the general Jezebel of the whole world.

The angel, therefore—that is, the church—because it still consists of the good and the reprobate, is understood here in a twofold manner. But because it has both leaders and peoples, the office of preachers is signified in the angel. It is as when, in reporting that a person has undertaken some work [F. *peregisse*, “performed”], our account indicates the quality of the individual members referred to: if, for example, we say that he saw something or spoke words, the former is certainly assigned to the eyes and the latter to the tongue.

This is shown to apply to the person of the angel, since the angel is known to be a messenger. As a watchman, it is fitting for him both to see what must be corrected and to announce what must be preserved. In the same way, through the other works named, the functions of the members are signified.

When, therefore, he now praises works greater than the former, he introduces the person of all in general. Since among all those placed in authority there are also negligent ones, he adds that the angel tolerates Jezebel’s fornication. Thus, from the figure of the saints—those to whom divine power is given to permit or restrain—he passes to the whole church. He thereby makes the leader guilty, not because he himself committed the act, but because he permitted it to be done and, by permitting it, became a participant in the transgressions.

Therefore he continues:

“I gave her time to repent, and she did not wish to repent of her fornication.”

He did not say, “I gave you,” or “I gave you, the leader.” For can the one who consents to a fornicator’s fornication not himself be a fornicator? But because he passes from the particular figure to the genus, he shows the saints to be so alien from this crime that, through the reproach of the wicked, he always wishes the members to remain vigilant. This is so even though what their right hand does is unknown to their left, as we readily recognize.

We readily understand this if we distinguish spiritually the flocks from the shepherds and the lower members from those who are eminent, or if we fit each thing to its proper time.

Jezebel’s fornication in general foreshadowed both bodily and spiritual adultery, when, under the name of Christ, she taught fornication and idolatry. “For you have destroyed,” he says, “all who fornicate away from you.”

“Behold, I cast her into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works.”

The bed here is understood as the security of sinners, which wicked people often promise themselves amid the impurity of their crimes. Since they have sinned without experiencing the vengeance of present anger, they neglect repentance until sudden destruction overtakes them, like the pain of a woman in labor, and they will not escape.

This neglect of security is said to be given by God because they are abandoned to a hidden but not unjust judgment. Of this security we read elsewhere (Proverbs 1): “The turning away of the inexperienced will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them.”

Another translation has “mourning” in place of “bed,” by which it signifies eternal misery, unless they repent of their works.

“And I will kill her children with death.”

Here we understand the woman’s authority and works to be represented by her children. The death threatened is not a momentary bodily death but the eternal death of the soul.

After such excesses have been recalled, and no repentance has corrected them, apostolic authority often testifies that eternal punishment rather than temporal discipline is deserved. For they are not among those of whom it is said, “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12), but among those to whom it is said: “Israel, I will no longer be angry with you,” and, “My jealousy has departed from you” (Ezekiel 16).

This is not because they had obtained reconciliation, but because they would be judged unworthy of being scourged temporarily.

“And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches the kidneys and the heart” (Jeremiah 17).

Do the churches not know, even before he exposes the adulterers and kills them, that God is the searcher of kidneys and heart? Or how can it be said to the church that it will come to know this, if from the beginning of its faith it did not know God as the knower of hidden things?

Therefore it must be held by certain faith—not as something learned through experience—that he will punish with death not the obvious but the hidden idolater and adulterer. For he says that these people will be punished by eternal condemnation.

“And I will give to each of you according to your works.”

Now he does not rebuke the whole on account of a part, but the whole on account of the whole, when he makes a promise to each according to his own condition. “Each one,” says the Apostle (Galatians 6), “will bear his own burden.”

Turning to the good part of the same angel, he says:

“But I say to you, the rest who are in Thyatira: all who do not hold this teaching, who have not known the depths of Satan, as they say.”

“Have not known” is used in place of “have not approved,” as though he said, “You have approved them by no consent.” The Lord may also testify that he does not know those whom he has not received into his discipline.

It follows:

“I will not lay upon you any other burden; nevertheless, hold fast what you have until I come.”

That is, “I will not impose upon you the burdens of the law,” about which the Apostle says (Galatians 5): “Stand firm, and do not again be held by the yoke of slavery.” Therefore hold fast the light burden, or the light yoke, of Christ (Matthew 11), which becomes light through the spirit of adoption. Wishing us to persevere under it, he says: “But hold fast what you have until I come.”

“And to the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end, I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod; they will be broken like a potter’s vessels, just as I also received from my Father.”

In Christ the church has this authority, as the body has it in the head. If anyone adheres worthily to his body, he is truly said to possess what the Son acquired by hereditary right; in him, as the Apostle says, God has given us all things.

The iron rod is wholly inflexible justice. It rules the gentle and destroys the obstinate.

“And I will give him the morning star.”

It is appropriate to understand the morning star both as Christ and as the first resurrection. When he appeared, he drove away the darkness of error; and when the resurrection hastens, the darkness of the world’s night will flee. This star appears to provide the beginning of the day just as it provides the end of the night.

## CHAPTER III

And to the angel of the church at Sardis write:

“These things says he who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars:

“I know your works: you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead. Be watchful and steadfast, and strengthen what remains, which was about to die. For I have not found your works complete before my God.

“Remember how you received and heard; keep it and repent. For if you do not repent, I will come and raise up my advent against you as a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come to you.”

If you are negligent at the call itself, the unforeseen hour of the summons will overtake you.

He continues:

“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments. They will walk with me in white, because they are worthy.”

It is great praise for a few people, amid wicked and defiled persons, to remain in undefiled garments through the continual brightness of their virtues. God calls them to such conduct when he says:

“The one who conquers will be clothed in a white garment.”

The few saints knew that a multitude of defiled people were in their midst; nevertheless, remaining undefiled, they groaned and mourned, as Ezekiel says (Ezekiel 3), because of the iniquity committed among them.

“And I will not erase his name from the book of life, and I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels.”

As in the Gospel (Matthew 10): “I will confess him,” he says, “before my Father who is in heaven.” And (Luke 10): “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

And to the angel of the church at Philadelphia write:

“These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David,” that is, royal authority.

He calls it the key of David either because Christ was born from David’s line or because David himself foretold many things about Christ. Through Christ’s administration, like a key, the secrets of the law, the prophets, and the psalms were opened, as he himself testifies when he says (Luke 24): “It was necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled.”

“He who opens and no one shuts, and who shuts and no one opens.”

The secrets of divine law are disclosed to the faithful only by Christ’s authority and shut to unbelievers. When he loosens, no one binds; when he binds, no one releases.

“Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut, because you have little strength.”

The door that Christ opens began to be opened to the church when he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (ibid.). No force has ever closed what, through their preaching, is now opened throughout the entire world.

Hence the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 16): “A great door,” he says, “has been opened to us in the Lord, and there are many adversaries.”

When he says, “You have little strength, and you have kept my word and have not denied my name,” he shows the reason why the church deserves these gifts: because it does not trust in its own strength, but, confessing that it has little strength, glories in the Lord who redeemed it, not in itself.

“Behold, I will make some from the synagogue of Satan—those who call themselves Jews and are not, but lie—come and fall down before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you, because you have kept the word of my endurance.”

At that time he promised this particularly to the church at Philadelphia. The remaining period, especially the time near the end of the world, is foretold here: Jews who believe in Christ will be joined to his church, which truly says (Psalm 56): “Foreigners have become subject to me.”

The Apostle also speaks of the Jews (Romans 11): “A hardening has come upon part of Israel, until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved.”

“And you will know that I have loved you,” when I subject to you in faith those Jews who were once exalted because of the nobility of their ancestry. You will recognize, and they themselves will recognize, what love I show you.

Many Jews come to the church, saying, as it is written: “Cast me to one side of your priesthood, that I may eat bread.”

“Because you have kept the word of my endurance, I also will protect you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole inhabited world, to test those who dwell on the earth.”

Although the church is continually exercised by internal and external conflict, and although individuals are attacked partially and the church as a whole generally by various temptations, the time of Antichrist is also signified. From him the Lord Christ promises to free the entire church that consists in his own people, so that the temptation may be recognized as ruin and deception.

“I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one else may take your crown.”

Here, with astonishing consideration, we understand that he speaks of the number of the elect, whom the Apostle mentions as called according to the purpose. “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” He shows that nothing can be added to or taken away from this number, since he says that this person will lose his own crown in such a way that another will come to receive it.

Hence it is understood that no one else can succeed if the person who holds it preserves it with persevering faith.

In the same way the pride of the Jews was frustrated, since they gloried in the lineage of Abraham. “For God,” he says (Matthew 3), “is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham,” so that the promise might remain certain through a gift and carnal boasting might be emptied in its lineage.

“The one who conquers, I will make a pillar in the temple of my God.”

A pillar in a building contributes both strength and beauty. So those who conquer the world stand out in the church through the gift of dignity and bear its burdens through the service of love.

“And he will go out no more.”

The younger son had gone out (Luke 15), that is, the people of the nations. But through the death of the fattened calf—that is, through Christ’s blood—he was reconciled and redeemed. He no longer goes out, since the king has brought him into his chamber (Song of Songs 3:8). Even if he is shaken by whatever battering-rams of schisms or persecutions, he is not moved.

“For the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal (2 Timothy 2): The Lord knows those who are his.”

“And I will write upon him the name of my God,” by which we are called children of God through adoption (Romans 8), “and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which descends from heaven from my God, and my new name.”

The title of the name indicates eminence, dignity, and the vision of peace. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace” (Romans 6). It is “new” because of the newness of life in which we are commanded to walk.

This name of Christ, which is above every name (Philippians 2), did not come to the Son of God in time so that it might be thought new, since he remained coeternal with the Father in the same glory. Of that glory he says to him (John 17): “The glory that I had with you before the world existed.”

Rather, it is new in respect of his humanity, in which he wished to die and, having died, rose again. Hence through the prophet (Isaiah 43): “Behold, I make all things new, which now will arise.” And the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 5): “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.”

Through this we also have deserved to be reckoned by the name “Christian.”

And to the angel of the church at Laodicea write:

“These things says he who is Amen, the faithful and true witness.”

We should pay attention to the fact that here “is” and “Amen” are placed together. *Amen* is interpreted to mean “true” or “faithfully.” Therefore, in this passage, it must without doubt be referred to that essence of divinity about which God speaks to Moses, saying (Exodus 3): “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

For he truly is who is always the same.

But because the humanity assumed in the one person of Christ also had to be proclaimed, he accordingly says (chapter 3): “He who is the beginning of God’s creation.”

The beginning of God’s creation is appropriately understood as the Lord Christ because of the mystery of the incarnation. Of him we read (Job 10): “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways.” And the Apostle says (Hebrews 10): “Having confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Christ, by a new and living way that he inaugurated for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh, and having a great priest,” and so forth.

For he is the way and the homeland; he is the author of faith and also its perfecter; he is Alpha and Omega; he is the beginning, whom no one precedes; he is the end, and no one succeeds him in the kingdom.

“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you from my mouth.”

Here the person of certain nobles of the world may be recognized. He says that they are neither hot nor cold, but rather lukewarm, because, although such an abundance of riches flows around them, they are found barren in works of mercy and are not kindled to good works by any impulse of compassion.

For this reason the poor are denied the description “cold” as well as “hot”: they do not abound in the riches by which the lukewarm grow torpid through use, and because they do not share those riches with the needy, they are rightly judged to lack the fervor of good works.

The passage may also signify the person of those among whom Scripture is discussed inside the chamber, while outside it is unknown whether they are faithful. Presuming boldly and securely, they are found empty of works. Therefore he says that they are neither cold nor hot—that is, neither unbelieving nor faithful.

Because people of this kind, through their lukewarmness, cause disgust to both sides, he says: “I will vomit you from my mouth.” But since this is a time for repentance, they must not flatter themselves with the false name of rich and powerful people, whose poverty, blindness, and nakedness are rebuked. Let them hear the one who counsels them and promises true riches, namely, knowledge.

Both groups must take care not to be vomited from the deepest inward parts.

Now let them buy gold for themselves, of which it is said (Proverbs 16): “Receive wisdom as gold and knowledge as silver”—[OCR: *Kelimet* [*Kemite*]].

If they are able to draw something from the springs of the divine Scriptures, radiant like the light of wisdom, let them perfect it through action: one group through generosity of substance, with the inward parts of compassion set aflame; the other through the spiritual formation supplied by learned knowledge.

For it is written (Proverbs 13): “A man’s riches are the redemption of his soul.”

Of the latter it is said (1 Timothy 3): “From infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation, which is in Christ Jesus.”

He rightly speaks of gold refined, because of the pressure of persecution. If they should be called to endure it for Christ, they should willingly receive it with devotion. For people such as these, converted from the great ruin of lukewarmness by useful remorse, may become fruitful not only for themselves but also for others. They themselves are gold purified and at the same time refined by the fire of tribulation.

“That you may be rich,” he says, “and be clothed in a white garment, and the shame of your nakedness may not appear in you; and anoint your eyes with salve, so that you may see.”

He marks as naked those who are deprived of works of righteousness, and he also rebukes them for blindness.

The one who is clothed in white garments is clothed in Christ’s baptism and possesses the faith that works through love (Galatians 5). “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Romans 6).

When he says that the eyes must be anointed with salve, he urges the heart to incline toward the divine testimonies (Galatians 3). “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18).

“Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline.” For “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12).

Therefore believe and repent.

He shows that there were people at Laodicea who were worthy of imitation, or others who needed correction.

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door for me”—the door of the heart, certainly, for receiving Christ through faith and obedience to his commandments.

It follows:

“I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me.”

Hence the Lord also says (John 14): “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

“To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sit with my Father on his throne.”

He calls the one who sits with him a participant in authority and judgment. Of this John says (John 1): “He gave them authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God.”

And (Matthew 19): “You will sit with me on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

“Let the one who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

Here “ears” should appropriately be understood as the ears of the heart, directed toward obedience to the commandments.

He shows that what he had urged upon the church by naming each one individually he now applies generally to the churches as things that must be proclaimed. Having described the works of the church—what it was and what kind it would be necessary to foretell—he will now, after recapitulating Christ’s birth, say the same things in another way.

## CHAPTER IV
Afterward, he says, I saw. Certainly, after that vision he recalls having seen another. It is not the time of the events that differs, but of the visions; just as, if someone narrates one thing in different ways, the narratives will have different temporal settings, though the event itself occurred at one time. So he repeats the whole period of the Church for narration under different figures.

“Behold,” he says, “a door opened in heaven.” By the open door he means Christ, born, having suffered, and raised again; he is the door, as he himself says: “I am the door.” He calls heaven the Church, because it is God’s dwelling place, where heavenly things are carried out. This is what we ask: that God’s will be done on earth as it is in heaven (Matt. VI). At times, however, he calls heaven and earth the Church (Luke XI), because the earth also comes to be heaven: whether when unbelievers are won over by the upright preaching of the faithful, when the flesh is subjected to the spirit, or when earthly things, reconciled with heavenly things, are joined to them.

“Behold,” he says, “that first voice which I heard speaking with me like a trumpet: Come up here, and I will show you what must take place afterward.” The voice is preaching; therefore it is said (Isa. LVIII): “Raise your voice like a trumpet.” The ascent occurs when, with contempt for the world, someone is either compelled or found worthy to come to the Church. One ascends from the valley of weeping to the summit of this dignity; hence we read (Isa. II): “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways.”

The faithful, too, are invited to ascend to heaven when they are commanded and taught to desire and understand not earthly things but heavenly ones. For when someone still inexperienced in the Church is taught that Christ suffered, rose again, and ascended to the Father, and when someone spiritually instructed and a teacher of these things contemplates that same Christ according to the form of God, he is said to ascend in the portion of the righteous, in order to see the secrets of the mysteries entrusted to him. Hence the Lord says (John XX): “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” wishing “touch” to be understood as belief.

“Immediately I was in the spirit, and behold, I saw a throne set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne. And he who sat there was like the appearance of jasper,” and so forth. These comparisons apply to the Church. I think that the jasper in which the Lord is clothed signifies water, and the sardius fire—by these two we know judgment to be carried out: first through the flood, and at the end of the world through fire.

“And a rainbow,” he says, “was around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.” The rainbow, because after the flood it preceded as a sign of security, is now appropriately applied to the Church for the propitiation of God. For when rain-bearing clouds are illuminated by the splendor of the sun, they produce the appearance of a rainbow. In comparison with this, when the souls of the saints have been illumined by the Sun of righteousness, who is Christ, the Divinity deigns to be propitiated through their intercession.

“And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the seats were twenty-four elders seated, clothed in white garments, and upon their heads golden crowns.” By the elders he means the whole Church, as through Isaiah (Isa. XXIV): “The Lord has reigned in Zion and in Jerusalem, and he will be glorified in the sight of its elders.”

By the twenty-four he encompasses both the rulers and the peoples, doubling the twelve tribes of Israel on account of the two Testaments, because the same Church is formed in both the Old and the New. That is, he shows the Church in the twelve apostles, namely, the whole body of its rulers, as we also find in the description of the city Jerusalem descending from heaven (Rev. XXI).

Apart from the distribution of offices, these twenty-four thrones are twelve, because the rulers are promoted from the twelve tribes. But the twelve thrones, apart from the mystical number, are one throne—that is, the Church. For only the Lord Christ will sit to judge; he will sit on the seat, that is, the Church, judging the twelve tribes. But in Christ, in whom the whole Church exists, the members will also sit and judge, in unity and through the one head.

Alternatively, the twenty-four elders may be understood as those who complete the perfection commended by the number six through the clear preaching of the Gospel; for four times six makes twenty-four.

“And from that throne proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and peals of thunder.” The thunder and voices signify the preaching of truth; the flashes of lightning signify the marks of miracles, as in the Gospel (Mark XVI): “But they went forth,” he says, “and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.” Likewise (Ps. LXXVI): “The voice of your thunder was in the wheel; your flashes appeared to the world.”

Through these things, as though through clouds thunderous with commands and shining with miracles, the world was shaken, feared, and believed.

“And seven fiery lamps were burning before the throne.” These seven lamps are the seven Spirits of God. If he did not explain himself, we ought to understand the Holy Spirit in these seven burning lamps—either because he was poured out upon the apostles in the form of fiery tongues, or because of his notable sevenfold operation. How much more must we understand this now, when he himself adds: “which are,” he says, “the seven Spirits of God”?

Where, moreover, would the Holy Spirit more appropriately be said to be present than at the time of baptism, when we believe that each of the faithful rightly receives him? This is what the mention of waters now appears to signify. For what follows says: “And before the throne there was a sea of glass, like crystal.”

In the sea of glass baptism is understood, where one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confesses with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X). It is related to glass because of faith, since nothing other than what it contains within is seen outwardly in glass. Nor does he commend this baptism as being before the throne without reason, except because heretics too can possess or administer it outwardly.

Thus he says (Exod. XXXIII): “Before the throne,” just as we read that it was said to Moses: “There is a place beside me.” Or he himself gives warning in Deuteronomy, saying (Deut. XII, XIV, XVI, XXVI): “In the place which the Lord your God will choose, so that his name may dwell there.” Through all these passages we know the singular unity of the Church to have been declared: there the baptism of the Trinity can be held for salvation, whereas one generated outside has it for destruction—not because what is given is evil, but because the recipient uses badly what is given, just as with the morsel handed to Judas by the Lord’s hand (John XIII).

But because another edition places “the sea of glass” before the throne, the seat may beneficially prefigure the seat of future judgment. Thus we see that, before the time of judgment, the remedy of saving baptism is granted, so that judgment may find people not guilty and naked but justified and protected. For who would be saved if God wished to anticipate the world with judgment before baptism had been granted?

By crystal is signified pure water and steadfast belief, not carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV), since it has its foundations secured in Christ, who founded the earth upon the waters (Ps. XXIII).

“And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind.” The four living creatures are the four evangelists. Because of the particular excellence evident in each narrative, a distinctive characteristic appears to be assigned to each, as some have wished: to Matthew, the human being; to Mark, the lion; to Luke, the calf; and to John, the eagle.

Since, however, there is one Gospel belonging to all, they are principally shown as four on account of the four rivers of paradise, by which the whole world is said to be watered, just as the whole world is believed to be instructed by their preaching. Indeed, the Church is often understood as paradise.

The creatures are said to have eyes before and behind either because they are full of the lights of knowledge, or because they perfectly contain all the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments. The faith brought forth by the two Testaments is completed by the vision of all times.

Thus, when we consider what previously belonged appropriately to the Old Testament alone, what became clear when the New succeeded it, and what is known to be hoped for through the teaching of both, these creatures are proved in every respect to shine, as it were, with lights.

The dispensation of Christ the Lord is assigned to the past as promises lying before us: it is read as foretold by the prophets and also taught as accomplished. To the present belong the increases of faith and the growth of the Churches. To the future belongs the separation of the good and the wicked, because we believe that the righteous will be assigned to life and the impious to punishment (Matt. XXV).

We also know that the harmony of both Testaments is prefigured when the later things are proved by the earlier—that is, the new things by the old—through the same eyes. They shine together and harmonize with one another in the full truth of faith. For example, in the Old Testament, after the slaughter of the lamb and the completion of fifty days, the law was given for fear, written by the finger of God on stone tablets (Exod. XXI, XIX, XX).

Now, when our Passover has been sacrificed, Christ (I Cor. V)—that is, as John says (John I), “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world”—after fifty days he sends from heaven the Holy Spirit promised to the disciples (Acts I). In the sacred pages we often read that he is called the finger of God (Exod. VIII:13). Through him the ancient hardness of the heart of stone is removed (Luke XI), and charity is given, by which fear is immediately driven out (I John IV), so that the law, which had previously been difficult for the weak, might be fulfilled.

“For the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V). Through his working, God is worshiped freely, no longer through fear of punishment but through love of righteousness.

Our very head, too, when we solemnly preach that he suffered, rose again, now sits at the Father’s right hand, and will come as judge, illuminates the Church with these four lights, as with the eyes of the four living creatures.

By the evangelists’ preaching, the reader learns all these things. He is also attentively taught and warned that the text mentions the creatures both in the midst of the throne and around the throne, as though it were saying: In the midst of the Church is the Gospel, and around the world the fruitful Church—that is, the Gospel. For although the number of preachers increases, the truth of the one Gospel is never changed by any diversity of novelty. What persists in the world as it grows is the same as what remains undefiled at its origin: in the midst of the throne and around the throne.

Earlier he said that he saw one seated upon the throne and, around the throne, twenty-four seats on which twenty-four elders were seated, clothed in white garments. Subsequently he says: “In the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures.”

Since he wishes us to understand by the diversity of names that the one seated, the elders, and the four living creatures are different, yet by the name of one throne he appears to combine them all in one place, it is understood that the Gospels are in the elders and the elders in the Gospels, for they cannot be separated from one another.

Thus the creatures could be around the seat where he had already said the elders were, and also in the midst of the throne—that is, in the body of Christ, which is the Church. There sound understanding permits neither the elders to exist without the Gospel nor the Gospel without the elders.

“The first living creature was like a lion.” Although above I preferred to set forth the interpretation of many Fathers concerning the living creatures, here I attend to the order of the account. When he says that the first living creature was like a lion, I assert that the face of a lion is more appropriate to Matthew, who first wrote the Gospel in Judea and prominently recounts and proclaims in Christ both royal dignity and lineage.

Blessed Augustine, too, urges that this order be followed, assigning the person of the lion to Matthew and that of the human being to Mark, who appears especially to have narrated Christ’s human deeds. The third is the calf, which corresponds to Luke because of the distinctive sacrifice of the fattened calf. To John, however, the symbolism of the eagle is more rightly assigned, since he deserved both to see clearly and to proclaim truthfully the loftiness of the Word of God.

Accordingly, the Church possesses the strength and beauty of royal majesty, because “the lion from the tribe of Judah” has conquered. “A lion’s cub is Judah” (Gen. XLIX), from whose tribe kings customarily ruled over the people.

“And the second living creature was like a calf.” The power of this Church is also signified in the calf, the first victim, for this reason: each of the faithful still conquers when he is slaughtered for Christ. “Present your bodies,” he says, “as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God, your reasonable service” (Rom. XII), so that what the head accomplished for the body, the body may be worthy to fulfill for the head.

For this reason he also began with Zechariah the priest (Luke I).

“The third living creature had a face like a human being.” I think that the humility of the Church is commended here: having received the spirit of adoption as sons of God (Rom. VIII), and possessing this treasure in earthen vessels (II Cor. IV), it nevertheless preferred humbly to glory in its weaknesses (II Cor. XII) rather than to be exalted by acquired virtues, piously following the footsteps of its teacher, who, “becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. II), said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI).

“The fourth living creature was like a flying eagle.” The Church is described as flying through its spiritual members who contemplate heavenly things. Enticed by no sight of earthly desire, it is governed by the guidance of the two Testaments and lifted upward to be raised on high.

The person of Christ, too, appropriately corresponds to these likenesses of faces: to the human being, whom he truly and veritably assumed, not merely imaginatively. The remaining three likenesses he bore for the sake of figurative comparison: he himself is the lion from the tribe of Judah, victor over the death inflicted upon him, because the lion is the strongest of beasts and fears no encounter; the calf, because he was sacrificed for the salvation of the world and is commended as the more distinguished victim; and the eagle, because he descended from above to the depths of our mortality and from there again ascended to the heavenly seat.

“And the four living creatures each had six wings around them.” In the living creatures he shows the twenty-four elders, for the four creatures’ six wings make twenty-four wings; and he saw the creatures around the throne, where he had said that he saw the elders.

How, however, can a creature with six wings be like an eagle, which has two wings, unless the four living creatures are one? They have twenty-four wings, in which we understand the twenty-four elders, who are the Church, which he likened to the eagle. Its two wings are the two Testaments, by which it is carried aloft, so that, entangled in earthly affections, it may not be delayed.

Alternatively, I think that the six wings were placed on account of the perfection of the number six, because in the sixth age—that is, when the fullness of time had arrived—the Apostle says that these things were accomplished (Gal. IV).

In the last living creature he concluded everything, for there are four, just as there are four evangelists. Each creature possesses both its own form and the forms of the other three, just as these seats and the same living creatures are described through Ezekiel.

He said that each creature had four forms, and the forms which here in the Apocalypse are those of the lion, calf, human being, and eagle were possessed by each creature, so that if someone saw one of them, he would see all four. Hence it is understood that each is complete in itself.

He describes the wheels of the same throne in such a way that one wheel faced the four parts of the world. It is both like a wheel and, in its construction, all four are one, so that there would be no place where the perfect throne was absent, nor would it withdraw from any part of the world; thus, surrounding everything, it was to possess the whole terrestrial world.

“They were full of eyes before and behind.” Or, as another translation says, “inside and outside.” “Inside,” because the light of the Gospel is worthy to be hidden. For if our Gospel is veiled, he says, it is veiled among those who are perishing (II Cor. IV).

Alternatively, “before and behind” means that wherever the Church bears fruit and spreads, it walks in the light of God’s countenance and, with unveiled face, beholds the glory of God.

Alternatively, the six wings before and behind, which together make twenty-four, indicate the books of the Old Testament, which we receive with the canonical authority of that same number, like the twenty-four elders presiding over tribunals (II Cor. III). The preaching of the New Testament is fruitful because it is strengthened by the testimonies of the Old.

This is what the Church holds before and behind—that is, then under the law and now under grace.

“They had no rest day or night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and is, and is to come” (Isa. VI). As the Church, spread everywhere through its individual members and diverse confessions, cities, regions, provinces, languages, and peoples, continually praises God in word and deed, in adversity and prosperity, it does not cease to praise the Lord day and night. The perpetual praise of the intellectual creation remains in the heavens, above Jerusalem, after whose likeness the pilgrim Church rejoices to be formed.

“And when those living creatures gave glory, honor, and thanksgiving to him who sat upon the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders immediately fell upon their faces before the throne and worshiped him who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the throne.”

According to the form of interpretation already set forth, the Church appears to be built from diverse members into one whole. When the living creatures resound with praise—that is, when the evangelists preach Christ’s dispensation, which consists in the sum of three times—the twenty-four elders, that is, the whole Church, consisting of rulers and peoples, immediately fall [the text has singular “falling”] upon their faces and worship him who lives forever and ever.

The Apostle Paul finally bears witness to this understanding and says (I Cor. XIV): “If the whole Church comes together in one place, and all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an uninstructed person enters, he is convicted by all, judged by all, and the secrets of his heart become manifest. And so, falling upon his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.”

“Casting their crowns before the throne” means assigning to God whatever virtue and whatever dignity they possess. For whatever good is acquired is rightly attributed to him by whom the one who conquers is assisted.

A figure of this action preceded in the Gospel, when the people who went before the Lord spread their garments on the road, and, taking branches of palm trees, went out to meet him and said: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (Matt. XXI; Mark XI; Luke XIX; John XII). Victory is appropriately compared with the sign of crowns and palms.

“Saying: You are worthy, our Lord God, to receive glory, honor, and power, because you created all things, and by your power they were established.”

Or, as we find it translated in another edition: “Because you created all things, and on account of your will they existed, and they were created.” They existed, that is, in the art of God before they were formed in actuality. They were created so that they might also visibly exist in their own natures according to the limits prescribed in God’s wisdom.

What follows should be taken as the beginning of the treatment of another book.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0819]

## CHAPTERS OF BOOK TWO

[Col. 0819B]

I. The dignity of the book sealed with seven seals, its reception when opened, and the vision are recounted.

II. At the first seal, the appearance of a white horse is described.

III. At the second seal, a red horse, and at the third, a black horse, are mentioned.

IV. At the fourth seal, a pale horse.

V. At the fifth seal, the souls of those who were slain beneath the altar of God.

VI. An earthquake; the darkening of the sun, with its light changed into blood; and stars about to fall.

[Note: [Col. 0819B] Blood. The change of the moon.]

VII. Four angels are said to hold the four corners of the earth.

VIII. The number of those sealed from each of the tribes is mentioned.

IX. An innumerable multitude coming from the nations is proclaimed.

X. The Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will rule them.

[Col. 0819C]

That the law of God can be understood in three ways, and indeed in many ways, yet recognized through a straightforward exposition, is demonstrated repeatedly by its own testimonies. For just as we read in Solomon (Prov. VII): “Write these things for yourself threefold,” so in the book of Job (ch. XI) we remember it to be written: “Would that God would speak with you and reveal to you the secrets of wisdom, and that his law were manifold!”

But because things proved by one Spirit can in no way be opposed to one another, it is easily demonstrated by reasonable argument that both statements stand together. The chief concern to be preserved is this: in expounding the sacred books, we must take care to employ meanings that do not depart from the truth of the passages themselves. Rather, penetrating the author’s intention with sober attention, they should bring it forth profitably, and, fitted to the rules of faith, always correspond harmoniously to the truth.

Nor should we think that the following appears contradictory: the Spirit of God is first presented as one or simple when he is introduced according to the law (Wis. VII), and soon afterward is described as manifold or multiple, as the diversity of translations has it. He is simple in the singular uniqueness of his nature, but manifold in the distributions of grace.

Alternatively, forgiveness of sins may be read as being accomplished in three ways: through baptism, repentance, and martyrdom, according to the psalm that we sing (Ps. XXXI): “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.” Thus sins are believed to be forgiven in baptism, covered by repentance, and not imputed in martyrdom.

Other Fathers, however, have said that forgiveness is granted in seven ways, adding almsgiving toward obtaining the remission of debts, restraining one’s neighbor from error, and the abundance of love, through which we read that the abundance of sins is covered (Prov. X).

These too can remain included within the three modes, which can be explained more broadly and clearly. The purpose of this preliminary discussion will soon be taught by the course of the following reading: as we hasten to expound difficult passages, we do not wish either to be marked by rash progress or to be judged forgetful of the tradition of the Fathers.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0820D]

And I saw a book in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne, written within and without, sealed with seven seals. “In the right hand,” he says, “in Christ”: for he himself is the arm of God, he himself is the right hand of the Father; or else, in supreme blessedness. The book written within and without is the two Testaments. On the outside was the Old Testament, which was visible; within was the New Testament, which lay hidden inside the Old.

Hence the Apostle addresses the Hebrews, saying (*Hebrews* 12): “For you have not drawn near to a tangible fire, and to a whirlwind, and to darkness, and to a storm, and to the sound of a trumpet, and to the voice of words; which those who heard excused themselves, so that the word might not be spoken to them; for they could not bear what was commanded,” and so forth. But now, “comparing spiritual things with spiritual,” we do not contemplate the things that are seen, but those that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

It is called one book because neither can the New exist without the Old, nor the Old without the New. For the Old is the announcement and veil of the New, and the New is the fulfillment and revelation of the Old; since, although the Old was on the outside, it was neither wholly apparent nor wholly hidden. Or, to express it more clearly, the whole dispensation of the Savior is repeatedly designated by the name of this book, since in both Testaments it is read either as promised or as accomplished.

“Sealed with seven seals”: covered by the manifold fullness of hidden mysteries, and therefore also by the shadowy and dense mountain. Although the number seven carefully embraces totality, I nevertheless think that seven modes, as though seven seals, ought to be openly sought in the divine Scriptures through disciplined study and necessarily found according to their own character—not merely the modes of expression, which even secular authors, with God’s revelation, could regularly discern in their own compositions, but also the modes of saving understanding, which are said to have remained specially reserved for Christ alone.

For as long as the same Lord had turned the water in those six jars, as though in six ages, into wine—that is, as long as he was teaching that the Old Testament was to be understood spiritually—the law could not make anyone drunk with the fervor of the Spirit. Those signs also remained closed until that time. Therefore, after carefully searching the sacred pages, we readily see that the first seven modes are comprehended in forms of speech: the indicative, declarative, imperative, optative, subjunctive, infinitive, and impersonal.

Thus, for example, the indicative occurs in what we read (*Micah* 6): “I will show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: namely, to love judgment, to practice mercy, and to walk carefully with your God.” And: “I am the Lord your God, teaching you what is useful, guiding you on the way in which you walk” (*Isaiah* 48). Likewise, when the question is asked: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (*Isaiah* 63), the answer is given indicatively: “I am he who speaks justice, and I am the defender for salvation” (*ibid.*).

The declarative mode is found in: “Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God” (*Isaiah* 48).
