Likewise: “Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: ‘My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed away from my God’? Do you not know, or have you not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, who created the boundaries of the earth, will neither faint nor grow weary, and there is no searching out his wisdom? He gives strength to the weary” (*Isaiah* 40). Or: “Behold, the days will come, says the Lord, and I will conclude a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (*Jeremiah* 21).

The imperative mode is found in: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”; and: “You shall have no foreign gods besides me” (*Exodus* 20), or similar passages. Also: “Cry out; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (*Isaiah* 58).

The optative mode is found in: “Would that you had heeded my commandments, and your peace had become like a river, and your justice like the waves of the sea” (*Isaiah* 48); and: “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances” (*Psalm* 118 [119]); and: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and rest?” (*Psalm* 58 [59]).

The subjunctive mode is found in: “If you will hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples; for the whole earth is mine, and you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation” (*Exodus* 19). Elsewhere also: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (*Leviticus* 26). Or: “If they had stood in my substance, I would surely have turned them away from their evil thoughts” (*Jeremiah* 23).

The infinitive mode, which is sixth in order, is found in: “To know and understand the Lord, and to practice judgment and justice in the midst of the earth” (*Jeremiah* 9). Likewise: “To restrain oneself from evil is understanding” (*Micah* 6).

The impersonal mode is found in: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord? With whom did he take counsel, and instruct him, and teach him the path of justice, and show him the way of prudence?” (*Job* 28). Or in what is written: “Who among you will hear this, attend, and listen to things to come?” (*Isaiah* 40). And: “Who is the man who fears the Lord? He has established for him a law on the way which he has chosen” (*Psalm* 24 [25]). Or: “To understand the law is the sense of the excellent”; and: “Who speaks of the mighty deeds of the Lord?” (*Psalm* 105 [106]); and other similar passages, which can appropriately be applied more extensively to each of these modes.

These modes, I say, are easily found in words. But now the proper order requires that we fit regular forms of understanding, as though seven seals, to the things themselves through suitable testimonies—or rather, that we show plausibly that the testimonies themselves serve those same rules. For although the modes of speech mentioned above may appear to correspond to what we seek, they are judged insufficient for it. He therefore says that the book is sealed with seven seals because he indicates that another mode, more secret and profound, which had previously lain hidden there but was asserted to have been opened through Christ’s own dispensation, must be identified.

As we inquire into Scripture, the first text that meets us is the historical action; the second is the allegorical deed; the third is recognized as the mode belonging to both. The fourth concerns the unchangeable essence of the divine Trinity, and when it is introduced properly or figuratively in the sacred oracles. The fifth concerns parables, since it is accomplished both by narration and by action, so that when one thing is said and another is found in writing, the mind may be raised to the nourishment of spiritual understanding. The sixth concerns the Savior’s two comings, or matters belonging to them, so that the first may not be understood as the second, nor the second as the first; here the rule of discernment must be applied with great care.

For this reason the minds of the Jews were darkened when the Lord came, and to this day they suffer from the same blindness of ignorance, to such an extent that sometimes even the sins of particular people and the transgressions of certain persons are presented prophetically as signs of future works or as secrets of spiritual meanings.

The seventh mode is that by which we are instructed through divine commandments in such a way that a definite pattern for conducting life is made known, while to others a figure for signifying life is regularly disclosed. It must be treated with attentive care, so that in these matters one may distinguish what is written outwardly from what lies within.

But now it is fitting to teach these modes by examples.

The historical mode, which is the first, indicates to us in this way that there is one God: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (*Deuteronomy* 9), and that all things were made by him, together with similar passages.

The second, allegory, is found in the passage where Abraham holds his servant to an unusual and extraordinary oath, saying: “Put your hand beneath my thigh and swear to me by the Lord God of heaven” (*Genesis* 24). This is recognized as figurative because it is not generally practiced by everyone, but only by Abraham and Jacob, the prophetic patriarchs, from whose thigh Christ was expected to be born bodily.

Again, when a young woman is sought and found from among all the faithful people of Israel for King David, so fervent that she warmed the limbs of the aged man, chilled with cold, by an appropriate heat, yet so chaste that, although she warmed him, she did not arouse him to lust (*1 Kings* 1); or when the people in the wilderness, scourged by fiery serpents, were freed from the serpents’ bite by looking upon a bronze serpent (*Numbers* 21); and when David figuratively changed his appearance before Abimelech, who dismissed him and he departed—although in the Book of Kings David is read to have changed his appearance before King Achish (*1 Kings* 21), when he beat upon the doors of the city, carried his own body in his hands, caused saliva to run down his beard, and performed the other actions of a madman, thereby expressing a type of the Lord’s Passion.

When the name is changed from Achish to Abimelech, the reader is warned, through the meanings of the names themselves, to penetrate more deeply into the hidden mystery. For Abimelech is interpreted as “the kingdom of my father.”

Thus Jesus Christ, the Son of God, changed his appearance before the kingdom of his Father—that is, before the Jews—when, coming in the humble form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (*Philippians* 2), which is properly signified by the drum, he disregarded the unbelief of the Jews and wished to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles, from whom he gathered a Church for himself.

This is what is meant by: “He dismissed him, and he departed.” The Apostle Paul plainly says this (*Acts* 13): “To you indeed this word was sent, but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.” Or there is the passage in the parable of the vineyard (*Matthew* 21): “He will destroy those evil men evilly, and will lease his vineyard to other farmers.”

I think that an example of that mode of speech also descends from nearly the same rule, in which we read: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep” (*Psalm* 113 [114]); and: “The rivers clapped their hands” (*Psalm* 97 [98]); likewise: “The trees walked to anoint a king” (*Judges*).

In these modes, what actually happened is not being reported, since nature plainly denies that such things are possible; rather, something is described figuratively through an appropriate signification. By these modes also, I think, parables of things are distinguished from parables of words.

The sixth mode, by which Christ’s coming is recognized—namely, which matters are to be referred locally to the first coming and which to the second—is something else to discern. The first coming claims for itself the passages concerning humiliation, such as what Moses says (*Deuteronomy* 18): “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you heard me.” Likewise: “Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (*Baruch* 3). And again: “He had neither beauty nor splendor; we saw him, and he had no appearance that would attract us, despised and last among men, a man of sorrows” (*Isaiah* 53). A little later: “He himself bore our weaknesses” (*ibid.*), and so forth. Again: “He will be led like a lamb to slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (*ibid.*).

But concerning the second coming we read: “God will come openly; our God, and he will not keep silence” (*Psalm* 49 [50]). And: “They will look upon you whom they pierced” (*Zechariah* 12). Malachi also says: “I will come to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers, and against those who oppress the wage of the hired worker” (*Malachi* 3), and so forth.

As for what we said about the sins of certain people often figuring something prophetic, it is especially there that signs appear to flash within and without. David’s public sin concerning the wife of Uriah the Hittite (*2 Samuel* 11–12) was evident; yet through his evil deed a prophecy of something good was figured for us.

For Bathsheba is interpreted as “the well of satiety,” or “the seventh well,” by which the Church is specifically signified. Christ joined her to himself from the Gentiles after separating her from the devil and killing him, from whose unlawful union she had been held. Concerning her we also read in the *Song of Songs* (*Song of Songs* 4): “A well of living water.” This number is joined to her because of the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit.

Even in the name of Uriah the Hittite, it is clearly shown that the person of the devil is signified. For Uriah is said to be interpreted as “my light is God”; but “Hittite” means “cut off”—either because he did not stand in the truth but was cut off, through the merit of his pride, from his heavenly light, which he had from God; or because, having fallen and lost his true powers, he transforms himself into an angel of light (*2 Corinthians* 11), still daring to say, “My light is God.”

Thus King David, the strong-handed one, saw from the roof of the house a woman washing herself, looked upon her wantonly, desired her, and took her (*2 Samuel* 11). Christ, however, the King of kings, saw with foreknowledge the Church, cleansed by the bath and by the word, trampling earthly things and longing for heavenly things; the provident bridegroom loved her as one called, so that, justified, he might join her to himself in a spiritual marriage as her lawful husband.

Likewise Moses (*Exodus* 2), in the person of Christ, having been received from the water, struck down with a blow of his heel the Egyptian lying in wait for the Hebrew—that is, the devil hostile to the Israelites—and hid the slain man beneath the sand.

“For all of you,” says the Apostle (*Galatians* 3), “who were baptized have put on Christ.” In him we shall perform a mighty deed, so that we may confidently say: “I will stretch out my sandal over Idumea; foreigners have been subjected to me” (*Psalm* 59 [60]). He crushes Satan beneath our feet, but permits his corpse to lie hidden only in those whom he knows not to be steadfast, rightly comparing them to shifting sand.

We know that this was also enacted in Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law (*Genesis* 38), and in many others, so that although they fell through guilt before God, who knows how to make good use even of our evils, something else might be accomplished through them as a mystery.

For the Apostle teaches that everything done at that time among the same people was a prophecy of things to come, saying (*1 Corinthians* 10): “All these things happened to them figuratively.” And although they either paid purifying penalties for what they had committed or obtained forgiveness through the remedies of repentance, divine clemency nevertheless prepared for us the effect of Christ’s dispensation.

Thus sins appeared outwardly, while mysteries lay hidden within. I preferred to pass over the matters concerning Judah’s daughter-in-law and similar examples, lest I lengthen this work far beyond its proper extent by a much fuller discussion.

Finally, concerning the deed of one person—namely, Lot and his wife (*Genesis* 19)—I thought that what blessed Augustine said in his argument against Faustus the Manichaean should be woven into this work for the general understanding of similar passages. He says:

“Just as another kind of people was figured in Lot’s wife—namely, those who are called by the grace of God but look backward, unlike Paul, who forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what lies ahead” (*Philippians* 3). Hence the Lord himself says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (*Luke* 9). Nor did he omit that example by which he seasoned us, as it were, with salt, so that we might not foolishly neglect but wisely guard against this evil (*Luke* 17). Therefore, to warn us of this, she was turned into a pillar of salt (*Genesis* 19).

So too in Lot himself, when his daughters lay with him, something other than what occurred when he was rescued from Sodom was figured. At that time Lot himself appears to have borne the person of the future law. Certain people born from it and placed under the law, understanding it wrongly and, as it were, being made drunk by water which they use unlawfully, produce works of unbelief. “The law is good,” says the Apostle (*1 Timothy* 1), “if one uses it lawfully.”

Yet we do not therefore justify that deed, whether of Lot himself or of his daughters, because it signified something else that foretold the future perversity of certain people. For they intended one thing in doing this, while God, who permitted it to happen so that he might also reveal something through it, intended another, while his righteous judgment concerning the sins of those people then present and his providence concerning the signification of future events remained active.

Accordingly, one thing is the deed when it is narrated in Holy Scripture: it is prophecy. But when it is considered in the lives of those who committed it, it is a crime. Blessed Augustine prefaced these matters as being understood in this way, so that he might teach that this is what should be thought concerning Judah’s daughter-in-law and similar cases.

The seventh mode, therefore, which retains the twofold character of the commandments, concerns the conduct of life. For example: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (*Leviticus* 19). Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law, as the Apostle discusses more fully (*Romans* 13). It also concerns the figurative meaning of circumcision and the Sabbath, or of the carnal sacrifices.

Although this mode may appear similar to the second, it is distinguished by this consideration: the present mode is to be referred only to morals, whereas the other must also be referred to faith. Therefore the Apostle James also distinguishes the two from one another, saying (*James* 2): “Faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.”

For by the circumcision of the flesh the cutting away of vices is understood; by the Sabbath, the rest of souls, of which it is said: “Be still and see that I am God” (*Psalm* 45 [46]); and by the sacrifices, that we should present our bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God (*Romans* 12). Other things that were commanded in the Old Testament were to be fulfilled through the actions of life; others were shadowed forth through the signification of life.

Christ declared that he had come to extend his grace for the fulfillment of the former and to remove the latter at their appointed time. “The law was given through Moses” (*John* 1), as something outward and external, for example: “You shall not covet” (*Exodus* 20), or rather: “Do not follow your desires” (*Ecclesiasticus* 18). “But grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (*John* 1), as something hidden within, revealed when the fullness of time arrived.

In those commandments that openly instructed love of God and neighbor, although the plainly evident form of the unchanging commandment remained, the weak people nevertheless needed grace, since they groaned under the burden of the law. In the figurative sacrifices of animals, however, that coming Lamb was awaited, and these sacrifices truly foretold that he had been appointed for them. When he came, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (*Colossians* 2), the commandments governing the conduct of life were fulfilled by the grace that had been given, while the figures, like shadows (*Hebrews* 8), immediately fled once the truth had been revealed.

For one thing belonged to the Old Testament: the letter, in its killing form, commanded it, so that through the life-giving Spirit it might be fulfilled—for example: “Do not follow your desires” (*Ecclesiasticus* 18). Hence Paul says (*Romans* 4): “The law produces wrath. But where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” Although this was clear to anyone hearing it outwardly and without a covering, human weakness was nevertheless unable to fulfill it by its own powers.

Another thing was covered within by a mystical veil and demanded the Lord’s coming, for which the model and shadows served (*Hebrews* 8). In him the pattern of heavenly life consists, from whose faith the righteous person lives (*Habakkuk* 2).

Through the things made plain, the law convicted the guilty and exposed the weak, so that salvation might be sought. Through the things that signify, however, as though within the inner chamber of the veil, they gave birth to Christ as the one who was to come. When he came, the celebration of the figures ceased, since it had been the shadow of future things. It must not be sought any longer, now that the truth of his living body has been made manifest (*Hebrews* 8). “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (*Romans* 10).

I think that the twofold distribution of those commandments belongs to this distinction. In discussing them, the Apostle says, with a sound enumeration (*1 Timothy* 1): “The law is good, if one uses it lawfully.” He had said previously (*ibid.*): “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.” By this statement he clearly introduced the law of faith; then he immediately expressed the law of works, saying: “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous, the ungodly, sinners,” and others opposed to sound doctrine.

Thus one may ask: if the law is not laid down for the righteous, how is the righteous person said to use it lawfully? The answer is that we do not need to be terrified by the punishment of punitive commandments, since through grace we already freely enjoy the perfection of virtues. Faith has already obtained for us what no one could attribute to his own powers. The Apostle says (*Romans* 3): “All have sinned and lack the glory of God.”

The law first shows in us a firm will; grace healed the will, and the will fulfilled the law. Therefore the law is imposed upon the ungodly who do not wish to fear, so that they may not be permitted to sin with impunity. It is not imposed upon the righteous because, through the love of the Holy Spirit, they are instructed by the commandments and are no longer permitted to sin.

The righteous use the law either to instruct others through the warnings of the commandments or to form them through the example of virtues worthy of imitation. The Apostle distinguishes both uses when he says (*Romans* 8): “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Delighting in this prayer according to the Apostle’s counsel, we also say that, setting lesser things aside, we have loved what is more excellent.

Hence he says again (*1 Corinthians* 7): “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel.” He does this by exhortation, not by compelling through a commandment, following the teaching of the Lord who gives counsel, when he said (*Matthew* 19): “Let him who is able to receive it, receive it.”

Since the present task is now being carried forward, the purpose of this undertaking does not allow us to discuss it further. For the present, let it suffice that we have said that this example is contained within this mode according to its own kind: “written within and without.”

It is rightly asked, however, concerning the seven modes we have set out, which should be counted as inward and which as outward.

The first, the historical mode, is outward. The second, the allegorical mode, is wholly inward. The third retains within itself the double form of both, so that it might fulfill the appropriate task of the present time and also figuratively enact something belonging to the future.

The fourth concerns God, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration. Both senses must be understood inwardly, for they cannot be comprehended by understanding. “The peace of God,” says the Apostle (*Philippians* 4), “surpasses every understanding,” because his essence exceeds the limits of our capacity, and no one can adequately attain his mercy, through which he has narrated many things about himself figuratively.

The fifth mode, in which something other than what is read is found, often diffused through parables, is so concealed and obscurely ambiguous that it must in every respect be counted as inward.

The sixth, concerning Christ’s two comings, shines clearly through certain testimonies and lies outwardly in plain sight; yet through certain hidden testimonies it lies concealed within, so that what is open removes doubt, what is hidden exercises the faithful, and it clears away weariness.

The seventh appears outwardly in commandments concerning the conduct of life, as we have already said; but in commandments concerning the figurative signification of life it lies hidden within.

Hence we also read that it was said to Daniel (*Daniel* 12): “Close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time. Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied.” It is sealed with seven seals.

Our fathers also discerned seven ages of the inner human being, in which, through God’s grace, we are healthfully renewed in the spirit of our mind. Blessed Augustine speaks of these in his book *On True Religion* as follows:

“The first is at the breast: a useful history, by which one is nourished through examples.

“The second is according to Jacob, forgetting human things and tending toward divine things; in it one is not confined within the limit of human authority, but relies by the steps of reason upon the highest and unchangeable law.

“The third is already more confident, marrying carnal desire to the strength of reason, and rejoicing inwardly in a certain conjugal sweetness, when the soul is joined to the mind and is veiled by the covering of modesty, so that it is no longer forced to live rightly: even if everyone should approve, it does not delight in sin.

“The fourth now does these things much more firmly and orderly, shining forth as a perfect man, fit and able to withstand and break all persecutions and storms and waves of the world.

“The fifth lives in peace and tranquility in every respect, and in the abundance of the unchangeable kingdom of the highest and ineffable wisdom.

“The sixth is a perfected form passing in every way from change into eternal life, even to the complete forgetfulness of temporal life, made according to the image and likeness of God.

“The seventh is eternal rest and perpetual blessedness, not to be distinguished by any ages. For just as death is the end of the old human being, so eternal life is the end of the new human being. The former is the person of sin; the latter, of righteousness.”

The same most excellent teacher Augustine also mentions these seven stages by which we are said to advance, writing finally to Maximus. He says:

“Thus, through the commandments of God—which we have received so that we may act well—you strengthen your life and conduct, beginning with religious fear. For ‘the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’ (*Psalm* 110 [111]). Here human pride is broken and weakened.

“Then, becoming gentle and mild through obedient piety, you do not inwardly resist with contention even those things that you do not yet understand and that seem absurd and contradictory to the unlearned (*Proverbs* 1) in the Holy Scriptures. Nor do you impose your own meaning upon the meanings of the divine books; rather, yield and bring a gentle understanding to them instead of accusing the mystery harshly.

“Third, when human weakness begins to open itself to you for the knowledge of yourself, and you know where you lie, what penal bonds of mortality, propagated from Adam, you drag along with you, and how far you are wandering from the Lord, and when you perceive another law in your members resisting the law of your mind and taking you captive in the law of sin that is in your members, you cry out (*Romans* 7): ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?’ Thus the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord may console you as you mourn, promising that very deliverance.

“Fourth, you now desire to fulfill righteousness much more vehemently and fervently than the most wicked people ordinarily desire the pleasures of the flesh—except that this desire rests upon hope in divine assistance. In this appetite there is a tranquil ardor and a more secure flame.

“At this fourth stage of life one applies oneself earnestly to prayers, so that fullness of righteousness may be granted to those who hunger and thirst for it, and so that abstaining from every corrupt pleasure—whether one’s own or another’s—may be not only burdensome but even delightful, and, by struggling against it, this may easily be granted by God.

“To this is joined, fifth, the counsel of showing mercy: help the needy insofar as you can, because you desire to be helped by the Almighty in what you cannot yet accomplish. The gift of mercy is twofold: when punishment is remitted and when kindness is shown. The Lord briefly included both when he said (*Luke* 6): ‘Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.’

“This work also serves the cleansing of the heart, so that, insofar as it is possible in this life, we may be able to see the unchangeable substance of God with a pure understanding. Something is held against us that must be released, so that our vision may burst forth into the light. Hence the Lord himself says (*Luke* 11): ‘But give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.’

“Therefore the sixth stage follows: the cleansing of the heart itself. So that a straight and pure gaze may be directed toward the true light, neither those things that we do well and laudably nor those that we cautiously and wisely reject should be referred to the goal of pleasing people or relieving bodily needs. For God wishes to be worshiped freely, since nothing should be desired except himself.

“When through the stages of a good life we have arrived at this purity of understanding, whether more slowly or more quickly, then we may dare to say that we have attained, to some degree, the mental capacity to touch the unity of the supreme and ineffable Trinity. There will be supreme peace there, beyond which nothing remains to be awaited, when children of God, made from human beings and reformed according to the image of their kind, enjoy the Father’s unchangeableness.

“First, ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit’ (*Matthew* 5), where there is the fear of God; then, ‘Blessed are the meek,’ where there is teachable piety; third, ‘Blessed are those who mourn,’ where there is knowledge of one’s own weakness; fourth, ‘Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,’ where there is the strength to strive to keep desires subdued; fifth, ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy,’ where there is the counsel to help, so that you may deserve to be helped.

“Then one reaches the sixth stage, in which it is said: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,’ where there is a pure intellect, capable of understanding. We cannot preserve the Trinity, even in the smallest degree, unless we also cease to desire human praise, although we may do praiseworthy things (*John* 14).

“Accordingly, by the seventh stage we arrive at the tranquility of that peace which the world cannot give. For even those four virtues that I mentioned earlier—prudence, courage, temperance, and justice—philosophers were able to recognize through their own diligence. If, joining to these three things for the perfect practice of religion, we add faith, hope, and love, we certainly find the number seven. These three are rightly not omitted, since without them we know that no one can worship God or please him.”

Since these things are so, whether the saving knowledge and the mysteries placed in the sacred books, lying hidden in those seven modes as though in seven seals, are shaded by deeper obscurity; or whether the whole perfection and fullness of the virtues, through which the inner person advances by inward growth—not confused indiscriminately but specially arranged in stages; or whether the promised assistance of eternal salvation, through Christ the Lord mercifully suffering, truly rising again, wondrously ascending, and always working in each person—has been and can be revealed, known, acquired, and perfected: those seals are truly proclaimed to have been revealed and perfected in him and through him.

I think this should be taught fully by testimonies. Among others, the Apostle says as follows (*Colossians* 1): “The mystery that was hidden from ages and generations has now been manifested to his saints, to whom God wished to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles: Christ in you, the hope of love. Him we proclaim, rebuking every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ. For this I labor, striving according to his operation, which he works in me with power.”

In the Old Testament he says: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (*Proverbs* 8). Since he himself is principally the way in which we must walk for our salvation, we nevertheless know that from him the ways themselves—that is, the progress of the stages, the rules of life, and the mysteries of the law—are opened and bestowed.

And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice: “Who is worthy to open the book and to break its seven seals?”

By “the mighty angel” he means the herald of the law, since we remember, from the preaching of Saint Stephen, that the same law was given and received through the ministry of angels, yet was not kept by the whole people. Its herald now rightly demands that it be kept and testifies that he has found no one worthy of its opening.

Since the seals are first broken and the book is then opened, the customary order has been reversed for a definite reason. Christ opened the book when he fulfilled the work of his voluntary Passion, abolishing enmity in his flesh and annulling the law of commandments in decrees (*Ephesians* 2). He proved that the proclamations of both Testaments were fulfilled in himself, and through his Passion the veil of the Temple was drawn back. Thus, with the veil of the legal figures removed, he is understood to have revealed the seven seals—that is, all the profound mysteries of the divine law—by his purpose and is proved to have done so by his deed.

Therefore no one was found worthy—not in heaven, that is, indicating that the power of the angels was exceeded. This does not mean that the angels were ignorant of the future mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and dispensation, but that it was not to be accomplished through an angelic creature. Since the Son of God was going to redeem human beings by assuming true humanity, he wished everything to be fulfilled through himself.

Hence Isaiah says (*Isaiah* 63, according to the Septuagint): “Not an angel,” he says, “not a messenger, but the Lord himself saved them.” Nor was anyone found upon earth—not even any of the perfectly righteous who remain alive in this life. For the restoration of humanity required the help of the Creator alone.

Nor was anyone found beneath the earth. None of the holy dead was found worthy to open the book, nor even to look upon it. By “look upon it” he means “to comprehend it.”

Hence Paul says that the riches of Christ are incomprehensible (*Ephesians* 3), and that he proclaims them to the Gentiles. These riches are the love of the New Testament, because it lay hidden in the law, and Christ reserved it for the time of his presence. No one was able to behold it with a vision sufficiently capable to carry it out in action as well, because Christ alone, through his dispensation, could fulfill it. Those earlier people could foresee it, but could not bring it to completion.

And I wept greatly because no one was found worthy to open the book or to break its seals. The Church, in John, wept, burdened by the works of sins, imploring the redemption of herself, which [the help of the Redeemer, which] he showed to consist in the opening of the book.

And one of the elders said to me: “Do not weep. Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and break its seven seals.”

By “one of the elders” we recognize the whole body of the prophets, by whose certain oracles the Church was consoled: Christ, from the tribe of Judah, would redeem the world by his blood.

Concerning him we read beforehand (*Genesis* 49): “A lion’s cub is Judah; to the prey you have gone up, my son. You have lain down and rested like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him?”

The same person is called both a lamb and a lion: being innocent, he underwent a voluntarily offered death and killed the power that had been taken up [the exact referent is textually uncertain]. Against death he had earlier directed a just threat through Hosea, saying (*Hosea* 13): “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O underworld.”

And Isaiah says (*Isaiah* 11): “Behold, the root of Jesse will rise for the salvation of the peoples; him the nations …

[The supplied source ends here.]

They will entreat him, and his sepulchre will be glorious. For each of the faithful in particular, when he strives to mourn his sins and remembers the promised redemption through the consolation of the Scriptures, is recognized as possessing the hope of eternal salvation and is strengthened by a similar response from one of the elders, so to speak. He therefore promised both what was past and what was future, because the Spirit subtly relates the past [the reading *in rita* is uncertain] and discloses the future through it (Rom. XV).

And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and in the midst of the elders. What the throne is, so are the living creatures and so are the elders—that is, the Church. For the Church is in the midst of the things that follow and that he describes, saying: The Lamb standing as though slain [Col. 0831C]. Whenever Christ is proclaimed as slain in the midst of the Church, the same Lamb is seen to be offered as though sacrificed for the world’s sin. What is unknown to the unlearned is laid open, and the Son is engraved in the memory of the faithful [F. *fidelium*] by devoted worship; for even when the Church, whom Christ has put on, mortifies herself to the world so that she may live to God, the Lamb is said to be offered as the head for the body.

Finally, it follows: Having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent throughout the whole earth. The diversity of the terms teaches that one meaning is being expressed: by the horns, the most excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified, through which Christ reigns throughout the world in his Church.

It follows: Which are the seven spirits of God. For there is no one who rules justly, eminent throughout the whole earth, and who specially glories in being enlarged by the gift of the Holy Spirit, except the Church of Christ. We remember that “seven” is used for the whole. But because horns are above the head, rightly is the singular exaltation of the Church placed upon Christ. Therefore he says: Upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt. XVI), as though he were saying: “Upon me I will build you” (Wis. I).

Now the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole earth (Ps. LXXIV). In order that this might come to pass, when the horns of sinners had been broken, the horns of the righteous are said to be exalted. Concerning this Isaiah had foretold (Isa. XXIV): From the ends of the earth we have heard praises announcing the glory of the righteous. Thus he is understood to have seven horns, as possessing the whole world, in which the sevenfold-graced Spirit rules, on account of his memorable sevenfold operation. He mentions it here in connection with the illumination of the eyes, concerning which I think Zechariah said (Zech. IV): These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which run throughout the whole earth.

Moreover, he seems not inappropriately to express the dignity of his excellence by horns. For natural horns arise as though by breaking through the places where they grow; nor, content with the level of the flesh, do they remain there, but as they grow they reach ever higher and higher. The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one (I Cor. II). Nor could he judge anyone unless, no longer carnal in the body, he presided over the others, raised up to a more excellent watchtower. Hence the Apostle also says (Rom. VIII): You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit.

And he came and took the book from the right hand of God who sits upon the throne. The Son of Man is said to have received from the right hand of God the book—that is, the dispensation arranged by the Father and by himself—because each of them dwells upon the throne with his Spirit. Here, too, we must understand “right hand” as the happiness of victory; it must not be understood carnally, as though he were said to receive the book from some other right hand of the Father, since the Son is himself the Father’s Son and is himself the right hand.

But since he who says, Rejoice, because I have conquered the world (John XVI), always conquers in his own people and caused his Church to exist as victorious, he is declared to receive the book from that Church.

And when he had taken the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each having golden harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. The living creatures and the elders—that is, the whole Church—falls before the Lamb, not without a narration of the virtues that have been accomplished [Col. 0832C]. Therefore each has golden harps and golden bowls. In harps, on which strings are stretched over wood, the passion of Christ is represented: the Church continually imitates it for Christ, so that, according to the Apostle, she may complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in her flesh (Col. I).

In the bowls is a devout confession offered to God, in which nothing is shut up with a double heart but is openly disclosed in its effect. These are also the golden vessels in the great house (II Tim. II), fragrant with the sweetness of Christ’s good odor. The prayers of the saints, moreover, are thanksgivings of those who rejoice together on account of the world’s salvation, and intercessions for the steadfastness of the little ones.

Christ, he says, suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (I Pet. II). Therefore, when those who belong to Christ crucify their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V), they sing together with Christ as though on harps, so that what he did for them, they may do for him, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith (Heb. XII).

When he wished to reveal himself for recognition under those seven notable titles, he is shown to have accomplished seven hidden signs: when he taught that he was God coeternal with the Father; when, born of a virgin, he assumed humanity; when he suffered; when he rose again; when he ascended into heaven; when, after sending the Holy Spirit, he acquired the Church from among the Gentiles; and when he announced that he would be the future judge.

Finally, let us hear what Isaiah says to the Jews (Isa. XXIX, according to the Septuagint): All these words will be for you like the words of a sealed book. There he says that the learned and the ignorant alike are deprived of the fruit of knowledge: the one is prevented by the seals from penetrating the inner secrets, while the other is hindered by ignorance.

The Lord rebukes the rulers of the Jews for having taken away this key of knowledge, saying (Matt. XXIII): Woe to you, teachers of the law, who have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you did not allow to enter. For by denying Christ, whose coming is the work of the prophets, they were taking away the key of knowledge. The knowledge of the law, which contains Christ, is closed off by the faith that has been denied.

And singing a new song. In harmony with the truth of both Testaments, Christ renders a new song when the Word, remaining the same in the beginning, is born through the virgin in a new birth; when God, clothed in a new manner, assumes humanity; when by his own power he is handed over to those who kill him; when he is wondrously raised from death; when, whenever he wills, he is lifted above the heavens; and when, sending down the Holy Spirit, he acquires the Gentiles. To the whole Church he acquired, he left a new song to be sung continually, by which she could confidently hope for the Judge who is to come, so that we might walk in newness of life (Rom. VI), saying: If anyone wishes to be my disciple, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me (Luke IX).

Saying: Worthy are you, Lord, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood, from every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and you made us a kingdom and priests for our God, and we reigned upon the earth.

They pursue with praises that very dispensation of Christ, designated by the name of the book, which they confess belongs to Christ alone. Here it is more clearly shown that the living creatures and the elders are the Church, since they say: You redeemed us by your blood. For this cannot be said except by the Church.

He also shows in what heaven the living creatures and the elders are, when they say: You made us a kingdom and priests for our God, and we reigned upon the earth. And if, while the understanding of the higher regions remains, some such powers in heaven too are believed to rejoice together, he nevertheless shows that the Church receives the book in Christ, since those redeemed from every people, tribe, nation, and tongue confess that they have received power and a kingdom.

For whoever clings to God is one spirit. They will be, he says, two in one flesh (I Cor. VI). But I speak of Christ and of the Church (Eph. V). Therefore he himself received in her what he gave; he himself is crowned in the one whom he crowns. Therefore Isaiah says: He adorned me like a bridegroom with a crown, and like a bride he adorned me with her ornaments.

And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne and around the living creatures and the elders. He showed what the throne, the living creatures, and the elders are, in whose midst he heard the voice. If the righteous are called sons of God, why should they not be called angels? In both cases this is by grace, not by nature. Nevertheless, the heavenly host of angels too can, with its proper united proclamation of praise, sing these things together with the living creatures and the elders, rejoicing over the greatness of our redemption.

And their number was thousands of thousands—that is, innumerable—saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing, and every creature that is in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that are in them [Col. 0834A].

Although these things properly belong to Christ, our Head, they can nevertheless be understood not inappropriately of his Church as well, provided that some things which belong to the Head alone also belong to the body (Col. II). Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches, and so forth. For he is himself the treasury of all good things and the wisdom of God. He makes him rule over all the nations, saying (Ps. LIX): Foreigners are subject to me; and, You have placed all things under his feet (Ps. VIII); and, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI).

Then he passes to the Head, saying: And every creature that is in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that are in them. Nor should it seem difficult that the Church received these things with him with whom she rose, since it is not difficult for a member to possess what the head possesses.

Nor can it seem unjust that he says the Church is worthy of every creature. For although each member, in religious humility, judges himself unworthy of this, nevertheless we say that the whole body shares in its Head, concerning whom we read: He gave us all things with him. Likewise: He made us sit with him in the heavenly places.

Alternatively, we frequently know that “creature” signifies human beings, as the Apostle says: The creature itself will also be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. VIII). And the Lord says (Mark XVI): Preach the Gospel to every creature. For everything that belongs to all creatures is found in the human being: to exist, to live, to move, to perceive, and to understand [Col. 0834C].

Therefore here too, by “every creature,” he means the entire human race, that is, the whole world. Hence he himself also says (Matt. XXVIII): All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. He did not mean to signify that he had received his authority in time, but rather the dignity of the Church among human beings.

He is indeed the one who teaches himself to be equal to the Father in all things, so that even when he says, “who is in heaven,” the human nature in Christ, exalted above the angels, rules in heaven; proclaimed to human beings, it reigns and rules on earth; and, prevailing when the groans of the underworld are loosed, it is also taught to have ruled beneath the earth.

I heard everyone saying: To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb—that is, to the Father and the Son—blessing and honor and dignity and power forever and ever.

And the four living creatures said: Amen. The Church indeed says “Amen,” that is, “truly,” faithfully [Col. 0834D]. And the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and worshiped him who lives forever and ever.

The same living creatures are the elders who bore witness, saying: Amen.

After the Church had been described together with the duties and works of her rightful praise, it was necessary to hasten onward, so that the things signified by the opening of each seal might become clear. For nothing could be lacking in these seven seals, so that in their mystery the whole perfection of feeling, understanding, and action might be taught to be present.

Finally, he describes the contents of each seal, at times taking up the end from the beginning, and in his customary manner passing through both Christ’s triumph and the Church’s future struggles, so that he might give consolation concerning the prosperity of victory, and announce concern regarding the future conflict and the terrifying judgment.

# Chapter VI

And when the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals. The opening of the seal is the revelation of a mystery. Yet because the mysteries are not one but many, and not of a single kind—as the apostle Paul says (Heb. 1): “In many parts and in many ways God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son,” and so forth—and because it would take a long time to discuss the diversity of the mysteries by which Christ’s future dispensation and the salvation soon to come to the Church were being prepared, everything can certainly be briefly summed up in the three modes we have mentioned above: speech, understanding, and action. Thus speech embraces within itself all the commands of the entire heavenly oracle. Therefore, he says, “in many parts and in many ways he spoke,” so that this knowledge might indicate the forms of understanding that must be applied according to rule.

Hence in the Gospel the Lord is said (Luke 24), after the resurrection, to have opened the minds of the disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures, and to have salutarily inflamed their hearts so that they might preach to others what had been revealed to them, fulfilling nonetheless, according to the Apostle, “what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in his flesh” (Col. 1), and truly saying: “We have become an example to all believers” (1 Thess. 1). Likewise: “That we might give ourselves as an example for you to imitate” (2 Thess. 3). If they had not done this, they would have sung from memory the Scriptures they had retained in vain, since they would have been unable to penetrate them by understanding or complete them in action.

And since in our preceding discussion we have dealt with the formerly hidden modes of speech and saving understanding, let us now listen more attentively to what was hidden in action, as each seal is opened. For if the opening of the seal is believed to be the revelation of a mystery, and if we say that its mystery consists in speech, understanding, and action, let us see how these three can likewise be found, plausibly, spoken, understood, and carried out in particular passages, so that what is spoken may be grasped by sober understanding, and what is understood may be confirmed by works.

For example: “Behold, I come” (Ps. 39); “at the beginning of the book it is written of me.” By saying “I come,” he still foretells that he is to come. But when it is asked who this person is, he is understood to be Christ, desired by all the nations, especially since he is read as written both at the beginning of the book of the Psalter and at the beginning of the book of Genesis: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” For, he says (Ps. 103), “you made all things in wisdom”; and when those who asked who he was sought an answer, he declared himself to be “the beginning” (John 8).

But when it is asked why he came, what follows is: “To do your will, O my God; I desired it” (Ps. 39). Concerning this the same person says in the Gospel (John 4): “My food is to do the will of him who sent me.” We understand him to have expressed the same thing about the hour of his Passion (John 14): “That the world may know that I do the will of my Father: rise, let us go from here.”

Accordingly, he is understood to have revealed the deeds of this sealed book when he taught that he remained one with the Father as the Beginning; when, born of a virgin, he assumed a true human being; when, accepting an undeserved Passion for the salvation of the world, he rose again in triumphal death, opened the tomb after he had broken the power of hell; and when, as though returning to heaven, he sent the Holy Spirit promised to the disciples. By filling the whole world, the Spirit won for him a multitude of the nations, and he taught that he was to be awaited as the future Judge.

And when he had opened one of the seven seals, I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as though with a voice of thunder: “Come and see.” And behold, a white horse, and the one sitting upon it held an arrow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out to conquer, and he went forth victorious.

First, as we have indicated, there is a variation in the speech; understanding is joined to it, and immediately supplies the inner meaning of the action itself. What proceeds in action agrees with the word and with the account given by understanding. I want the attentive reader to observe this in the other seals as well.

For he said: “I heard one of the four living creatures saying: Come and see.” This one living creature is the whole Church, which thunders with the loud voice of preaching, inviting the Church that is succeeding it to faith: “Come and see” (John 1); “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink” (John 7); “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33); “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5).

“And behold, a white horse, and the one sitting upon it held an arrow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out to conquer, and he went forth victorious.” This horse can be understood as the apostles and preachers of the truth of the Church, whitened beyond snow by grace (Ps. 50), whose rider is Christ. Therefore the prophet says to him (Hab. 3): “Because you have mounted your horses, and your riding is salvation.” For this reason he is also said to hold an arrow, which is aptly compared with the preaching of the word of God, by which the inner parts of human beings, pierced through, can bring forth the fruit of faith. Hence we read (Ps. 44): “Your arrows are sharp, O Most Powerful; peoples shall fall beneath you.” It signifies, moreover, that the crown belongs to preachers.

And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying: “Come and see.” The same words of exhortation to come and see are repeated here for a different purpose. Since the white horse is presented as good, but the reddish horse as evil, I think the point is that just as the former promises joy concerning the Church’s victory, so the latter announces caution in view of what is foreknown to come.

For it follows: “And another horse went out, a red horse, and to the one sitting upon it was granted that he should take peace from the earth, so that they should kill one another; and a great sword was given to him.” This red horse, as though bloodstained with another’s blood and not his own, is proclaimed to oppose the victorious Church, when it is indicated that he removes from the earth the peace that surpasses all understanding—a thing taught both by action and by the sword.

And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: “Come and see.” And I saw a black horse, and the one sitting upon it had a balance in his hand. In this measure the appearance of a counterfeit judgment is signified, by which they weigh the merits of individuals. For whatever belongs to a just judge, transgressors also arrogate to themselves. Hence the saying: “I will set my throne toward the north” (Isa. 14). And because, with God permitting it, they were able to prevail for a time, Scripture teaches this in the following words: “You shall not harm the wine and the oil.”

And I heard a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: “A two-pound measure of wheat for one denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for one denarius; but you shall not harm the wine and the oil.”

In the wheat and barley he signifies the Church, whether in the great and the small, or in rulers and peoples. Yet one two-pound measure is not less than three. For the same perfection exists both in singularity and in the Trinity. Thus the Lord (Matt. 13; Luke 13) says that leaven was hidden in three measures of flour, showing that from a small amount the whole people are consecrated by the mystical, indivisible number of the Trinity.

But he also teaches that the price of the wheat and the barley is one and the same. Although one surpasses the other in merit, both have nevertheless been redeemed at one price. Alternatively, I think the unequal number—one and three—was set down on account of the diversity of professions.

In the denarius, however, eternal life is signified, which is common to all among the many dwelling places. Thus, although through the difference of merits one person may be higher than another and enriched with a greater reward, no one there is long-lived in comparison with another: there will be one immortality for each, while a common eternity remains for all.

In the wine and oil, therefore, he forbids the power of the sacraments to be violated, namely, the anointing and the precious blood. Hence we read (Zech. 9): “What is his goodness, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the chosen and the wine that makes virgins flourish?” And in the Psalm: “Wine gladdens the heart of man, and the face is brightened with oil” (Ps. 103).

And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the fourth living creature saying: “Come and see.” And I saw a pale horse, and the one sitting upon it was named Death, and hell followed him; and power was given to him over a fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, famine, death, and the beasts those who dwell on the earth.

There are two parts in the world: one belonging to God and the other to the devil. But the devil’s part is divided into three: within and without—that is, the pagans, false brothers, and those separated by open error or schism. Thus there are three parts that wage war against one. He foretold that power would now be given over a fourth part, and he calls this the Church, which in one part is to be exercised by various evils and swords.

This must also be recognized in the number of the angels: against one and the same good power he set three evil powers in opposition—the red one with a sword, the second black one with a balance, and the third pale one with the sign of death—announcing war by the sword, famine by the black horse, and death by the pale one.

And while he assigned afflictions to each individually, he also foretells the future afflictions by the third itself, or by counting everything through it, adding the name of the beasts.

And because even in this way it might remain hidden whether the speech is literal or figurative—for a sword can be brought against the visible body and against the soul in a spiritual sense, and likewise it may be uncertain whether famine refers to the word of the Lord or to the body, and whether death here threatens souls with eternal punishment or bodies with momentary death—it is nevertheless clear that the good fourth, against which he sets three evil powers, is to be exercised by all these visible and temporal persecutions.

For those who have been called according to the purpose of God’s will (Eph. 1) will remain in the fullness of the elect, especially those concerning whom he wished the sacraments of the wine and oil to be preserved unharmed, saying: “You shall not harm the wine and the oil”—signifying in the wine the price of redemption, and in the oil the chrism of baptism.

Moreover, by mentioning barley and wheat, he demonstrates that the Church cannot perish through any persecution of the wicked until the end of the age, since he counts these same kinds not contemptibly but together with a sacred number and a specified quantity of price.

Finally, what the wicked inflict upon the Church as a punishment for their own evil, the supremely good God turns to the benefit of his people and thereby provides us with an opportunity for spiritual triumphs.

It follows: “And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and their testimony. And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth? And white robes were given to each of them.”

He says that he saw the remaining ones of the martyrs—whom God, even amid adversities, makes safer through the hidden counsel of his working—namely, the relics [or: remaining ones] of the martyrs, that is, their souls. He saw them not in a lowly or ordinary place, but beneath the altar of God: either persevering in the unity of the Church, or fighting bravely to the point of death beneath the testimony of the name of Christ, as beneath the altar of God.

Thus it is said concerning the Maccabees, under the covenant of God: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”

How much more, then, are those said to intercede who, knowing that in the Lord they have a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens, desire to be clothed over with their dwelling that is from heaven (2 Cor. 5). We understand these things in such a way that, through the Lord’s Passion, the groans of hell having already been released, we do not think that the souls of the saints come any longer to the underworld.

I think this is more appropriately signified here: just as in the Old Testament an inner golden altar is described, so here, through the memorable name of the altar, an intellectual secret is to be understood, like the inner parts of the Holy of Holies. Having received here the pledge of salvation, those who are still pilgrims sigh, possessing hope “as a sure and firm anchor of the soul,” reaching into the interior of the veil, where Jesus, our forerunner, entered on our behalf, according to the Apostle’s statement (Heb. 6). In this way he was indicating the presence of Christ while explaining the figurative expressions.

“How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?”

This is not to be understood in a carnal sense, as though they were inflamed by a desire for vengeance, since we know that those who are here love even their enemies through the abundance of charity (Mark 5). Rather, it is clear that they prayed against the kingdom of sin and asked for such things out of their longing for that kingdom, concerning which we say: “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6).

We understand that the presence of divine wisdom revealed this to them: that the wicked will inevitably be punished with eternal punishment, and that, while the fountain of heavenly grace continues to flow until the end of the age, many more are still to be joined to the fellowship of the holy martyrs.

When they receive this answer, they are filled with indescribable joy, which we rightly believe to be represented by the white robes. Therefore each received a white robe—that is, being content with this consolation through the perfection of charity poured into the hearts of believers by the Holy Spirit, they themselves preferred to be delayed until the number of their other brothers should be made complete.

For what they do in their benevolent desire, inspired by God, they are said to request; and they are immediately instructed by the answer. It is not right to believe that they desire anything contrary to God’s will, since their desires depend upon his will.

And I saw, and when he had opened the sixth seal, there was a great earthquake; and behold, the sun became black like a sackcloth garment.

By the sixth seal the sixth age of the world is understood. Near its end the final persecution is announced, whose violent assault, like an earthquake, is said to shake the whole world.

The sun and the moon signify Christ and the Church. Because many, terrified by the final persecution, will deny the Church, the sun is therefore said to be darkened. For if, he says (2 Cor. 4), “our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, may not shine.”

Hence it is said (Matt. 24): “So that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray.”

In this way the sun is said to have become black, as though Christ’s works and power, or his teaching, were temporarily obscured, or his defense delayed, when the wicked are permitted to rage against the saints.

Hence the prophet says (Hab. 1): “Will you be silent in this, so that the wicked may devour the just?”

Finally, concerning Christ himself we read (Luke 2): “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many, and as a sign that will be opposed.” In him some certainly make progress, while others, turning away from him, suffer decline.

The moon is said to become blood because the Church is proclaimed to shed blood for Christ more abundantly than usual, as the great tumult of persecutions presses upon it. Thus it is by its own blood, not by another’s, unlike the red horse, which is described as red with another’s blood.

The stars fell to the earth in the manner in which a fig tree, shaken by a great wind, loses its unripe fruits.

Those are signified by the stars who, in the Church, when they are judged by all to belong to the number of the elect, appear for a time to stand out. Yet when the fury of persecution presses more fiercely, they are said to fall from the height of their position, as from heaven. The Lord foretells this in the Gospel, saying (Matt. 24): “There will be tribulation such as has never been and never will be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened.”

He presents the Church as a tree, and the unripe fruits—which another translation calls “figs”—as human beings. The winds signify the agitation, or upheaval, of persecution, by which people, shaken, are torn away from the Church.

They are properly compared with unripe fruits either because of their unbelief, since, having turned into a crooked bow (Ps. 77), they prefer, after abandoning the faith, to return to unbelief, or because of the immaturity of the time. By this it happens that, although the Church has sought their happy birth by conceiving them, it nevertheless suffers a lamentable miscarriage concerning them through an unfortunate outcome.

“And heaven withdrew like a scroll when it is unrolled.”

He rightly indicates that heaven—that is, the Church—withdrew like a scroll that has been unrolled rather than one that is rolled up. For whatever is rolled up cannot be recognized by anyone at all. But what is unrolled is immediately revealed as exposed.

Thus, when this persecution has become manifest and distinct, the Church withdraws in avoidance, so that it may not be seen by outsiders in its hiddenness. It is known only to itself—that is, to those to whom it is able to entrust itself—through the unity of the Spirit. It guards itself against the unknown and foreign, and through the spirit of discernment conceals itself, lest, once understood, it be betrayed.

Hence John says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4).

“And every mountain and island was moved from its place, and the kings of the earth, and the magistrates, and the tribunes, and the rich, and the strong, and every slave and free person.”

The Church too is represented by mountains and islands. For it is “the city set upon a mountain” (Matt. 5). Therefore we read (Ps. 124): “The mountains surround it”; and (Isa. 24): “On the islands of the sea, the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.”

He foretells that it will be moved from its place by the force of persecution. This can be understood in either direction: among the good, it moves by taking precautions through flight; among the wicked, moved for the worse by a faithless will, it is transformed, as it says (Rev. 2): “I will move your lampstand from its place.”

We understand the kings of the earth as the powerful, namely, those capable of standing firm in the sure judgment of their own discernment. By magistrates, tribunes, rich and strong, he wishes all such people to be understood according to the diversity of their offices and the quality of their strength. He foretells that no one will be free from the distress of that persecution, although no one doubts that the number of the elect will be delivered.

“And every slave and free person.” The free person is recognized as free from the bond of marriage, while the slave is understood as joined in marriage.

“They hid themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains, saying to the mountains and rocks: Fall upon us” (Luke 23), “and hide us from the face of the one seated upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of his wrath has come. And who will be able to stand before him?”

We appropriately understand the caves and rocks of the mountains as refuges of the Christian faith. For it is written (Prov. 30): “The weak people, the rabbits, make their burrow in the rock”; and the Psalm agrees with this meaning, saying (Ps. 103): “The highest mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs and rabbits.”

Here too we recognize that those who are lofty in the Church are designated by the name of mountains, because of “the surpassing knowledge of the charity of Christ” (Phil. 3).

The little ones, therefore, now seek the help of these people, as the roar of persecution presses upon them. Seeking remedies of protection, they are said to desire the shelters of the firm rock. For whatever such mountains they flee to, they are said to flee to the rock dwelling in them. “The rock,” he says (1 Cor. 10), “was Christ.”

When, therefore, they are fortified by the counsel of those mountains, and are to be protected by saving admonitions and shaded by counsel, they implore those very mountains to fall upon them through the affection of compassion. For each person is sheltered beneath the protection of the one whose remedy of exhortation fortifies him.

Hence Isaiah (chap. 2): “And then,” he says, “enter into the rock, hide yourself in a pit in the earth, from the face of the fear of God and from the face of his fury, when he rises to strike the earth.”

What he says these people, compelled by severe persecution, seek, the prophet appears to urge us to seek: even in that persecution which has no equal, let us seek the refuge of Christ and of the Church, of the unconquered Head and the glorious Body.

But when he says, “from the face of the Lamb seated upon the throne,” this means that he may find them not rejected but steadfast in the faith when he comes.

Moreover, attention must be paid to the manner of expression that the Holy Spirit has woven into this book. Up to the sixth seal he preserved the order; then, setting the seventh aside for a short time, he recapitulates the same matters, and, interweaving two narratives as though following the order, he concludes with the seventh.

But this recapitulation must be understood according to the passages involved. For sometimes he recapitulates in order to speak from the beginning of Christ’s dispensation; sometimes from the Passion; sometimes from the intervening period; sometimes from the persecution itself alone, or from a time not long before it.

Now, having described the sixth seal, he returns to the beginning, intending to speak of the same things briefly and in another way.

# Chapter VII

[Col. 0841B]

After this, he says, “I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, so that they might not blow upon the earth, or upon the sea, or upon any tree.” In these four corners the Church understands four kingdoms to be signified in John: those of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, and Romans. By their power, in a certain sense, suffocating everything, they would allow nothing to breathe freely according to its own will. Therefore he says, “so that they might not blow upon the earth,” that is, upon the inhabitants of the earth, “or upon the sea, or upon any tree.”

The number four is used because of the four best-known regions of the world, which are the four corners; that is, four winds are to be understood, in accordance with the prophecy of Daniel (chapter VII), who says: “Behold, four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea, and four beasts were coming up from the sea, different from one another” [Col. 0841C]. And because the Church, throughout all four quarters of the world, appears still to have her portion mingled with the kingdoms of this world, and is known to have both her own among foreigners and foreigners within herself, he wished “upon the earth” to indicate the diversity of provinces, “upon the sea” that of islands, and “upon the trees”—since a tree is a kind of forest—the various offices and qualities of people, according to their diversity.

“And I saw an angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God.” Here the first coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is declared; elsewhere he is called “the Angel of the great counsel” (Isaiah IX). Therefore it says “from the rising of the sun,” in accordance with what we read about him in Zechariah (Zechariah VI): “Behold, the man whose name is Rising.”

“And he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels, to whom it had been given to harm the earth and the sea, saying to them: Do not harm the earth, or the sea, or any tree, until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads.” He is said to cry out because, by the power of saving proclamation, he restrained the hostile powers, so that they would not oppress the world with the customary cruelty of an unlawful domination.

In those kingdoms in which fervent idolatry held sway, the strength even of the four harmful angels is frustrated, as though the authors were being restrained through their ministers, by that voice: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew III). Some of the demons themselves confess this, saying to the Lord (Matthew VIII): “Have you come here before the time to torture us?”

Of this coming Daniel says (chapter II): “A stone cut from the mountain without hands,” which struck the statue revealed to him [the reading *oramate* is uncertain], whose head was of gold, its chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, and its legs of iron. In this statue the four kingdoms mentioned above are signified: in the gold, that of the Assyrians; in the silver, that of the Medes; in the bronze, that of the Persians; and in the iron, that of the Romans, as Daniel related when the angel explained it (chapter II), continuing:

“But in the days of those kingdoms the God of heaven will raise up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and its kingdom will not be handed over to another people. It will shatter and consume all these kingdoms, but it will itself stand forever.”

That stone, having struck the four kingdoms—as though the brow of an unlawful tyranny had been destroyed—grew; “and it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” [Col. 0842B]. Thus he now says that these four angels are restrained by this power, so that they are not permitted to harm the kingdoms mentioned above with their customary assaults, until the number of the elect known to God has been certified by an inviolable seal. Of these the Apostle says (Ephesians I): “He chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight, predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in himself.”

Now, appropriately indicating this multitude through the number of the mystery, he continues: “And I heard the number of those who had been sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed, from every tribe of the sons of Israel.” By this number the whole Church is signified. For the Trinity is also represented by a fourfold calculation: three times four, and twelve times twelve, make one hundred and forty-four. The city itself is described as having twelve stadia on every side, and the circuit of the city, in its solid measure, as one hundred and forty-four cubits. Hence it is clearly recognized that, through this indication of a mystical number, an innumerable multitude of the elect is foreshadowed, as a definite number is significantly used to represent an indefinite one.

Finally, he continues by specifying the number of those sealed and mentioning each tribe. “From the tribe of Judah,” he says, “twelve thousand sealed.” He proceeds similarly through the others, from whose stock the lineage of the Israelite people is handed down.

“From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed. From the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Gad, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Asher, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Naphtali, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Manasseh, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Simeon, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Levi, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Zebulun, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Joseph, twelve thousand. From the tribe of Benjamin, twelve thousand.”

As he proceeds through the names of all the tribes, it is not surprising that, having begun with Judah, he has repeated the same names [“naming them individually”]. For the Lord Jesus Christ willed to be born from the tribe of Judah. This order is not constructed according to earthly generations, as though he were presenting the eldest sons according to custom and arrived at Judah, who is fourth; rather, it follows the appointed number of the redeemed, by which he wished to signify the fullness of the elect. Since he wished to direct our attention toward this intention by necessary reflection, he did not preserve (variant: *custodivit*, “keep/observe”) the order of birth even in naming the other brothers, but placed those younger by birth before those older than themselves after Reuben. This can be demonstrated by comparing the books of Genesis (chapters XXVI, XXX, XXXV) and Exodus (chapter I) [Col. 0843A].

If we wished to speak more fully, we would burden this work further. Judah, properly interpreted, is said to mean “praise” or “confession,” as is also taught in the paternal blessing: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” Reuben means “seeing a son,” or “those seeing a son.” Simeon means “he has heard sadness,” or “the name of a dwelling place.” Levi means “added.” Issachar means “there is a reward.” Zebulun means “dwelling place of strength.” Benjamin means “son of the right hand.” Dan means “judgment,” or “judging the Hebrews who are passing over.” Naphtali means “breadth.” Gad means “temptation,” or “girded,” or “a raider.” Asher means “blessed.” Joseph means “increase.” Manasseh means “forgotten,” or “necessity.”

Since we know that various virtues dwell in individual believers—for example, that in one the fullness of saving knowledge stands out, while in another gentleness alone excels—we nevertheless see that these twelve names must necessarily be arranged according to the order of gifts and the stages of souls making progress. They are not arranged as they were begotten, nor as they were named when entering Egypt, because in the first case the origin of earthly generation is being recalled, while in Exodus the dwelling together in the land of Egypt is remembered.

Therefore I have taken care, after setting out the sequence of names written in this book, to add also the order of their birth, together with the interpretations of each, to see whether I might somehow demonstrate that this order was not changed without reason.
