We must also warn the little ones beforehand, lest they think this number refers to the infants whom Herod killed (Matthew II), as we have discovered some ignorant people supposing [Col. 0843C]. To say nothing of the rest, it is known that Herod killed infants from only one tribe, Judah, where, according to the extent of the jurisdiction over which he was permitted to rule as tetrarch, the madman raged as he pleased. Here, however, he mentions all the tribes. If we append the meanings of their names to their respective tribes and adapt them to the number, we shall be able, by examining the secrets of this passage, to clarify still further the significance already given concerning the fullness of the elect.

In Judah both confession of sins and praise—praise that proclaims virtues—shine forth; and this is fitting for the number of those sealed who are born from that same tribe. For in the sacred books confession is not only applied to sins, but is also very often understood as praise. Hence the psalm of the dedication of David’s house, that is, Psalm Twenty-Nine: “Let my glory sing to you, and let it not be pierced; Lord my God, forever I will confess to you”; and the Lord has no sin at all. “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.”

Reuben means “seeing a son,” or “those seeing a son.” We understand that works are often signified by sons. To the sons of light who walk in the light it is said: “May you see the sons of your sons; peace upon Israel” (Psalm CXXVII), whose sons are now taken up spiritually in this discussion. The Apostle also says this (Galatians VI): “Peace upon the Israel of God.”

Therefore the number of those sealed is rightly associated with the name of this tribe, since “seeing a son” also suits them. For to such people the Lord says (Matthew V): “That they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” [Col. 0844A].

Simeon means “he has heard sadness,” or “the name of dwellings.” I think those are signified here of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V). They hear sadness in this way: they prefer obediently to embrace it here, sowing in tears so that they may reap in joy (Psalm CXXV). They do not place the aim of their dwelling here below, but have their hearts above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Colossians III), desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling that is from heaven, like Abel, who awaited the enduring city in heaven, whose architect and founder is God.

Thus Simeon is also said to be interpreted as “the name of a dwelling,” so that he may hear both what is to be possessed here and what is to be awaited by the faithful: for now is the time for mourning and for sighing after another, better dwelling. Hence the Lord said to his disciples: “You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI).

Levi means “added.” What we read in Solomon also applies to these (Ecclesiasticus XXVI): “The number of his days is doubled”—those who use the good things of the present life in such a way that they purchase eternal things rather than temporal ones, lest, hindered by earthly things, they be deprived of heavenly ones.

We know that Job provided them with a praiseworthy example (Job XLII). He had rightly possessed temporal things, yet later despised them in such a way that the number of his years and the measure of his substance were doubled and added to him. Hence Isaiah says (Isaiah LXI): “In their land they shall possess double, and everlasting happiness shall be theirs.”

Issachar means “there is a reward.” Hence Jeremiah says: “Let your voice cease from weeping, and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your works” (Jeremiah XXXI). And when we hear the Apostle, like a spiritual athlete who does not fight uncertainly, saying (Galatians VI): “Brothers, let us not grow weary, for in due time we shall reap”; and the Lord himself saying (Matthew VI): “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys them,” we certainly know what the reward is for the faithful. Their number also shines forth in this tribe, and plainly, by the judgment of the elect and the sacramental meaning of the name, it is especially to those people that this is said: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matthew V).

Zebulun means “dwelling place of strength.” I think the army of those people is signified here who, fighting spiritually in martyrdom, overcome the rage of the enemy even with their bodies, as with a dwelling place of strength. Aided by God and, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians XII), recovering strength from weakness, they prove themselves strong in battle. Therefore, famous both by the title of their name and by the accomplishment of glorious virtue, they gain titles of glory as victors.

Benjamin (Genesis XXXV) means “son of the right hand.” It is not difficult to recognize as sons of the right hand those whom the Truth represented in the Gospel under the name of lambs, saying (Matthew XXV): “The lambs at the right hand”—so that those whom his right hand strengthens in this age may enjoy his happiness in the age to come.

Dan means “judgment,” or “judging the Hebrews who are passing over.” I think the judgment of those people is placed here who spiritually discern between the times of the New and Old Testaments in such a way that they neither think the Gentiles ought to become Jews nor suppose that anything should be mutilated in condemnation of the Old Testament [Col. 0845A].

Concerning this question, such a dispute arose not only among the apostles, as blessed Paul records to the Galatians (chapter II), but also later among spiritual men. As we recognize (*dignoscimur*; variant *dignoscimus*) from the great significance of the name inserted here, this question required judgment. Accordingly, by Dan—“judgment,” or “judging the Hebrews who are passing over”—we understand either a time or a type: that is, the figurative actions of the Jews who were passing over, serving Christ and the Church that was to come. They are called “passing over” because they are to be referred not to themselves but rather to something else.

“For all these things,” the Apostle says, “happened to them in a figure” (1 Corinthians X); and again (2 Corinthians V): “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.” This follows the same line of thought concerning those ceremonies that I mentioned above, and there is no need to repeat everything each time the necessity of explaining these matters arises.

Naphtali means “breadth,” as we read in the blessing of Shem and Japheth (Genesis IX): “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem,” which is interpreted as “named.” Christ is understood here, who is so renowned throughout the whole world that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

For this reason we also read that the poured-out ointment is his name (Song of Songs I). He did not permit that name to be denied by being confined in silence, but commanded it to blaze forth far and wide through unceasing proclamation. Thus here too we see the breadth of the fruitful Church displayed in the children of adoption, whom we rejoice to see enlarged through good works [Col. 0845C].

Gad means “temptation,” or “girded,” or “a raider.” Since, as we read (Job VII, according to the Septuagint), this life is a temptation, it befits the soldiers of Christ to fulfill what he himself commands and to fight continually, girded against every temptation. For he says (Luke XII): “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,” so that by restraining unlawful desires we may keep them in check, and by devoting ourselves to good works we may shine, as he likewise says: “Let your light shine before men” (Matthew V).

And because we ought to direct the end of good works toward God rather than turn it toward the favor of human praise, the name is also interpreted as “a raider,” as one who secretly acquires the good things of the heart, offering them to God for his approval and not exposing them to human eyes as things to be displayed. Thus, according to what he himself promised (Matthew VI): “Your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly.” It is called “a raider,” therefore, because it remains hidden from the eyes.

Asher means “blessed.” I think the kind of blessedness that the Lord mentions in the Gospel is signified here, saying (Matthew V): “You will be blessed when they curse you and persecute you, and speak every evil thing against you falsely, because of me.” Thus the sacred number among the elect is designated.

Joseph means “increase.” An increase is understood here that ought to be applied both to superiors and to various members within the unity of the Church: to those, namely, whom the Lord says (Matthew XXV) will gain twofold from the spiritual substance entrusted to them; and to others when they fulfill either the purpose of virginity or the celibacy of professed continence [Col. 0846A]. To vow these things is not counted as a fault if one does not do so, but to fulfill what one has undertaken advances one toward the crown, because they appear to set aside lawful things by choosing what is better.

Hence the Apostle says (1 Corinthians VII): “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord.” This also applies to the one who, like Zacchaeus, says (Luke XIX): “I give half of my goods to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” If some people arise in the Church who act similarly out of love for eternal life, they may rightly be associated with the character of this name, being inflamed by an increase of the fullest devotion.

Or it may be because superiors, through diligent industry, double the money that the Lord commanded to be given to the money-changers (Matthew XXV), so that when he comes he may demand it with interest; or because celibates, preceded by divine grace, overcome the incentives of the flesh by the abundance of the spirit; or because those who, from their resources, offer not merely the tithes required by commandment but a greater portion.

Stirred by an increase of virtue and an accumulation of devotion, they hasten not only to obey the commandment but also to commend themselves to God through a more excellent worship of virtue—not now merely to avoid punishment, but to acquire a reward. To these, I think, the name Joseph—that is, “increase”—properly belongs. Joseph, exalted among foreigners, is known to have increased through prosperous success and to have received Manasseh as a son, whose name is interpreted as “forgotten” or “necessity,” since he had forgotten the harshness of slavery and captivity.

Now, if we wish to follow the order of their birth according to the qualities of the names and the various correspondences of things applied to the names mentioned above, we find no adequate conclusion to the exposition already given. For example, if we begin with Reuben, the firstborn, whose name means “seeing a son,” or “those seeing a son,” and then insert Judah in the fourth place of his birth, this is entirely contrary to sound understanding. No one reaches the summit of good works before the beginning of confession, because unless through confession we renounce evil deeds, we are not formed in what is right and pleasing.

Therefore, to prove that the sequence of their names was not changed here without reason, but so that its significance might be clearly recognized, we must distinguish how great is the difference between the origin of a culpable nature and the orders of saving grace.

Following the order of this book, let us briefly connect, as though with little chains, the same meanings that we arranged according to the interpretations of the names, recapitulating them in this order [Col. 0846D]:

To our confession and divine praise there follows, as is customary, the perfection of works, as Reuben follows Judah, so that one may neither wish to repeat what ought to be repented of nor be reluctant to fulfill what is worthy of belief and by which God is praised. Therefore Reuben is placed after Judah in the order, so that the one who acts may rejoice in hope, and those who see may refer the one acting to the praise of God.

But because “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wisdom IX), and “we groan, being burdened” (2 Corinthians V), and “while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (ibid.), and “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV), as it is written, Gad follows, that is, temptation. I say that it follows not by the origin of birth but by the course of spiritual warfare. Even such people are not without the temptations of the present life, by which they are exercised in the contest and, girded with a spiritual belt, are not permitted to wither through the torpor of idleness.

Although temptation is often used both for good and for evil, here it is proposed that it be understood as being directed toward virtue through good use. Therefore he is also recognized as “girded,” since he fights spiritually: “You have girded me with strength for battle,” he says (Psalm XVII). Hence we read (James I): “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life,” just as Abraham also shone forth when tested.

Although temptation is indeed evil, we rightly call those blessed who conquer temptation, or emerge victorious from temptation. Therefore after Gad, Asher—that is, “blessed”—is placed, in accordance with the rule of truth received from the Lord, who says (Matthew V): “You will be blessed when people hate you, and when they persecute you, and speak every evil thing against you falsely, because of me” [Col. 0847B].

Secure in the faithful promise of this blessedness, they are not distressed but say with the Apostle (2 Corinthians VI): “Our heart has been enlarged.” And they sing with the psalm (Psalm CXVIII): “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.”

Therefore Naphtali follows, which means “breadth,” so that not only may we not grow faint, but, forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, may extend ourselves in it, according to the Apostle, so that, bound only by the necessity of human condition, we may not provide for the flesh in its desires. “Our citizenship,” he says (Romans XIII), “is in heaven.”

Although our desire is “to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians III), nevertheless we still carry this treasure in earthen vessels (2 Corinthians IV). Therefore Manasseh is placed after Naphtali, that is, “forgotten” or “necessity.”

The Apostle speaks of this necessity (Romans XIII): “Do not provide for the flesh in its desires.” He warns that we must not serve our lusts but attend beforehand to our necessities. Concerning these the prophet prayed, sighing after better things, saying (Psalm XXIV): “Deliver me from my necessities.”

Simeon is placed after him, that is, “I have heard sadness,” or “the name of a dwelling place,” so that through the character of this name he might impress more clearly both what is to be possessed here and what is salutarily to be awaited. The joy of the heavenly dwelling will be given to those whose spirit here is saddened by fruitful repentance, to whom it is also said: “Your sadness will be turned into joy” (John XVI).

Next Levi is joined, that is, “added.” By him we understand either those who purchase eternal things with temporal things, as Solomon says (Proverbs XIII): “The wealth of a man is the redemption of his soul”; or those who, following the Lord’s counsel (Matthew XIX), receive a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the age to come.

What is written also suits these people: “Whoever adds knowledge adds labor.” The bitterness of tribulations was likewise added to holy Job so that, once he had been tested, a greater reward of recompense might be returned to him.

Nor does Issachar wrongly follow him in the proper order, whose interpretation is said to be “there is a reward,” because, as the Apostle teaches (Romans VIII), “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” The battle is more fruitful when a reward is proclaimed.

God works and perfects this in the dwelling place of strength, which is called Zebulun, when strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians XII). The body, which enemies think weak and through whose material they attempt to bring destruction upon the soul as well, is found, when God strengthens it, to be unconquered.

Then a fortunate increase follows, namely Joseph, whose name means “increase.” In this sequence it signifies increases of grace. You may understand this either as the interest from the double return of the talents, or as the increase of spiritual profit in those things that are offered to God the Redeemer through the devoted religion of the faithful.

And so that you may understand all those who are significantly placed here by both the order and the interpretation of the names as destined to stand at the right hand of Christ, the eternal King, in the future judgment, Benjamin is placed last: “son of the right hand.” It is as though he were the end of the order, the happiness promised as the perfect reward.

Then “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians XV), so that either each of the faithful may rightly be called a son of the right hand, or the whole Church, concerning which we sing: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded with variety” (Psalm XLIV).

I certainly do not think that we should pass over the fact that here in the Apocalypse Manasseh, who was not a son of Jacob but his grandson, although adopted among the sons, is placed in sixth position, while Dan, who certainly is a son and is shown to be numbered with his other brothers both in Genesis and in Exodus, is entirely omitted. This is as though the Church adopted from the Gentiles were being shown, in the sixth age of the world, to reject the unbelief of the Jews [Col. 0848C].

Nor is it without significance that Manasseh, born in Egypt among foreigners, is inserted in the sixth place through the merit of adoption and for the sake of the signification, while Dan is given no place. Thus it may be demonstrated even more clearly that everything here is arranged for the sake of signification and not composed through a passing account, so that in Dan—“judging the Hebrews who are passing over”—the time may be more plainly indicated when the law of ceremonies, in circumcision, bodily sacrifices, and other such matters, was passing away and was recognized as no longer necessary.

The Apostle teaches this when he says (2 Corinthians V): “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new”; and again (Hebrews VII): “There is an abolition of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness.”

These things being so, I declare that it must be understood that I in no way contradict the words of the Lord, by which he showed that three parables of profession alone had been set forth: thirtyfold for married people, sixtyfold for widows and the continent, and a hundredfold (Matthew XIII; Mark IV; Luke VIII) for virgins or even martyrs.

When he signified in the field the active warfare of the clergy, the contemplative leisure of the elect among monks, or the course of those who grind at the mill among the laity [*Sic*], although with varying significance, he does not appear to exceed the same number. Both the doctrine of salvation and evident experience demonstrate that all these ways can be found or understood within those same three categories.

For I do not know how often we find such people among the number of monks, in the order of clergy, and in the ranks of married people: people who shine in confession, as in Judah, with praise; who are effective in works, as in Reuben; strong in the exercises of temptation, as in Gad; blessed, as in Asher; enlarged by generous works of mercy, as in Naphtali; forgetful of what lies behind, as in Manasseh; and, as in Simeon, still sorrowful in the valley of weeping, yet always rejoicing and, in the name of a dwelling place, sighing for the heavenly Jerusalem.

They rejoice with Levi in the promise of the present and future life, founded upon eternal good through the temporal goods added to them; they are strengthened in Issachar by contemplation of the future reward; in Zebulun they fight for Christ and lay down their souls; in Joseph they strive to increase their spiritual substance and offer something beyond God’s commandments, either in virginity or from the measure of their possessions; and in Benjamin they receive the right hand of eternal happiness.

When the last enemy, death, has been destroyed (1 Corinthians XV), God is all in all. Thus the Lord himself cannot be thought to contradict his own words when elsewhere, recalling the eight beatitudes, he describes them with an altogether remarkable arrangement.

He did not separate them from those three professions, but taught that they are found within them and shine forth from their members. In these we shall also be able to perceive the understanding of these patriarchs drawn from their names and to adapt the names themselves correspondingly to the same degrees—not by equality of office, since the one group consists of eight and the other of twelve, but by relating the quality of their meaning and setting them opposite one another in corresponding order.

He called the first beatitude “the poor in spirit,” that is, the humble, who, endowed with the fear of God, are saved through confession of their weaknesses. To them it is said: “Do not be wise in your own sight, but fear” (Romans XI). Thus the poor in spirit are suitably understood in Judah through praiseworthy and truthful confession. Hence Isaiah says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?”

The second beatitude is assigned to the meek. The meek are those who obey the sacred words, believe without resistance what they hear, and accept without criticism the things they see handed down in the Church as things to be followed. They are not incongruously represented in Reuben, whose name means “seeing a son,” or “those seeing a son.”

The third is: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V). Gad, whose name means “temptation” or “girded,” placed third, corresponds to this according to the exposition already given [Col. 0849D].

The fourth is: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.” To this number Asher is also compared, placed in the fourth position, whose name means “blessed.” No better blessedness can be found than that the lover of this very righteousness should be filled by its author, who refreshes without failing, sufficient for each person and remaining whole for all.

In the fifth place comes: “Blessed are the merciful.” Corresponding to this fifth order is Naphtali, truly “breadth,” who exercises works of piety in such a way that, with narrow greed removed, he is continually enlarged through generous liberality and joy.

In the sixth place it says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Manasseh also appears sixth in his own order, that is, “forgotten” or “necessity.” This Manasseh, adopted from a grandson as a son, also represents here that Church to which it is said: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm XLIV).

It also suits such people to see God with a pure heart. They have forgotten what lies behind and stretch toward what lies ahead (Philippians III), saying: “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Romans VII).

Or does it seem relevant that the single cluster of grapes carried from the land of promise between two men (Numbers XIII) represented these two peoples: the earlier people, the Jews, as having the cluster—that is, Christ—behind them, while the Gentiles follow, always having Christ before their eyes?

In the seventh place it says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Simeon corresponds to this in the seventh position, that is, “he has heard sadness,” or “the name of a dwelling place.” Such people, already enriched by the abundance of wisdom, say: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Psalm CXIX).

They are saddened by the zeal with which the prophet said: “I saw the foolish, and I wasted away” (Psalm CXVIII); and: “Faintness of soul has seized me because of sinners who abandon your law” (ibid.).

In the eighth place it says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness” (Matthew V). To this beatitude Levi, who occupies the corresponding place in the numerical order, or, I think, Zebulun according to the proper meaning of the name, is to be joined: “dwelling place of strength,” by which martyrs of the truth are shown to conquer the devil, naturally the stronger. Nevertheless, the meaning is not incompatible with Levi if the honor of martyrdom is understood as added to baptism.

Yet, lest anyone think that the merits of these gifts are to be attributed to human strength, they must instead be shown to belong to the gift of the one who distributes them individually as he wills (1 Corinthians XII) [Col. 0850C].

The sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, compared with each beatitude or name, also seems to correspond along a harmonious path, provided only that, when we desire to reach the harbor of wisdom, we know that we must begin from fear. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm CX).

Thus, from the point at which the prophet begins his enumeration, each person will advance to its completion. Fear therefore belongs to Judah, to whom the poor in spirit are compared; piety to Reuben, to whom the meek are suited; knowledge to Gad—that is, “temptation” or “girded”—to whom the mourners, the third order, are joined.

Fortitude is assigned to Asher in the fourth place, to whom those who hunger and thirst for righteousness correspond. Counsel is assigned to Naphtali, to whom the merciful rightly belong in the fifth beatitude. For the person who wishes to be helped by what is above is governed by saving remedy so that he may hasten to help others below, as far as he is able.

Understanding is joined to Manasseh, who forgets earthly things and looks upon divine things with a pure eye of heart; the sixth beatitude, concerning seeing God, corresponds to him.

Wisdom, however, belongs to Levi, to whom it especially pertains to bear the *logion*, that is, the rational principle, because solid food belongs to the mature. “We speak wisdom,” he says, “among the perfect.” Through contemplation of divine things it perfects the soul capable of God in such a way that it is found effective; and, coming as a composition from both, like an action added to theory [*theoria*], it says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you.”

This especially suits the one from whose tribe priests were commanded to be lawfully appointed to the altar, who clung to God in such a way that they also cared for their neighbor—or rather, for the people—through the duties of sacred worship.

For the Lord himself, born from both the priestly and royal tribes—that is, Levi and Judah—made peace between earthly and heavenly things. “He is our peace” (Ephesians II), and he taught that he is both the true king and the true priest. Hence Elizabeth is said in the Gospel to be related to Mary (Luke I).

But because the Lord Christ acquired the Church for himself from both circumcision and uncircumcision—that is, from Jews and Gentiles—when he grafted the Gentiles, like a wild olive branch, onto the richness of the olive tree of the Israelite people (Romans XI), the redemption of both peoples is clearly displayed in the enumeration by name of all the tribes, chiefly the tribes, so that he might also mention the salvation of the Gentiles, saying:

“After this I saw a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation and from every tribe and people and language.” Those whom he had previously named individually he now joins together in unity, standing before the throne and in the presence of the Lamb. “They were clothed in white robes, and palm branches were in their hands, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.”

By the robes he indicates baptism, and by the palms the triumph of the cross; and he also indicates that they conquered the world in Christ, although the robes may likewise signify the love that is given through the Holy Spirit (Romans VIII).

This multitude of the elect, whom God foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, he foretells through the sign of the sacred number. For those who come from the Gentiles also become Israel, and are rightly called children of Abraham—not according to the flesh but according to faith, in that seed which is Christ, the cornerstone. Concerning him the Apostle says (Ephesians II):

“He himself is our peace, making both one and breaking down the middle wall of the enclosure, abolishing in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments expressed in decrees, that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross.”

As for the statement that they carry palms in their hands, this either signifies perseverance in good works through the hands. Hence we read: “The Lord strengthened his arms for good work” (Psalm LXXVI); and: “With my hands at night before him, and I was not deceived.”

Or it signifies that power through the hands which, in order that…

…might become sons of God by adoption, received [this power], as is said of Joseph (Gen. 41): “And the Lord had given everything into his hand,” that is, into his power.

And with a loud cry [Col. 0851D] they were saying: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” Advancing with a great voice, profound devotion, and unceasing praise, they declare that the Father and the Son reign upon the throne, that is, in the Church, while the Holy Spirit likewise reigns with them. The order of the words is in fact this: “Salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb sitting upon the throne,” just as we read a similar expression in the Gospel (John 17): “That they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent”—as though he had said, “That they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the one true God.”

By the one throne, the power of one nature is signified; by the name “Lamb,” however, the personal distinction in the Father and the Son is indicated. Likewise, when only the Holy Spirit is named, both the Father [Col. 0852A] and the Son are to be understood there. For when we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Pay attention to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops,” he immediately adds: “to shepherd the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.” But we know that the shedding of blood for us belongs only to the person of Christ. Hence it is quite clear that, even when one alone is named, the whole Trinity must be understood.

And all the angels were standing around the throne, around the elders, and around the four living creatures. Explaining what that very multitude was, he made it clear by these names: for he distinguished the whole Church. “All,” he says, “who are around him shall offer gifts,” and immediately they fell upon their faces before the sight of the throne and worshiped God, saying: “Amen.” To show that the same innumerable multitude which he saw standing in the presence of the throne—as something plausibly known to him—consisted of the angels who fell upon their faces and worshiped, he does not say here that the multitude itself, the living creatures, or the elders worshiped, but only the angels. They themselves are the multitude; they themselves are the elders and the living creatures; they fell down and worshiped God, saying: “Amen.”

Therefore, too, we read (Rom. 15): “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people, and let all the angels of God worship him.” Therefore also: “Blessing and glory and wisdom and grace and honor and power and strength belong to our God forever and ever.”

Having enumerated the sevenfold number of virtues, we are especially encouraged by this reason to seek what he intended by naming here those virtues of which God willed his Church to be a participant, so that, when these things are offered to God in praise, each person may confess that he has received them from him. For it must be considered that he does not name here things belonging exclusively to God, but things which he also deigns to bestow upon the faithful: blessing, glory, wisdom, grace, honor, power, and strength. We rejoice that Christ’s Church possesses a share in all these.

Here he has not spoken of omnipotence, nor of majesty, nor of eternity, which God alone has always possessed by right; rather, he names those seven virtues in which all the virtues granted to the faithful may likewise be understood—granted by him who gave them power to become sons of God—so that, if we acquire any good things, we may truly know that we possess them by God’s generosity.

I see that the same may readily be proved from the other virtues. Blessing, for instance, belongs especially to the Church, as we read (Ps. 3): “Your blessing is upon your people.” For he will give blessing to those to whom he also gives the law; and glory, of which we sing (Ps. 89): “Let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us,” so that, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, we may be considered light, being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory (2 Cor. 3).

And wisdom—not that wisdom begotten and coeternal with God the Father, but that wisdom created [or: believed to be created] in us and in the angels—which, distinguishing one from the other, the Law says (Ecclus. 1): “Wisdom is from God, and has always been with him, and exists before the age”; and it adds concerning created wisdom (ibid.): “Before all things wisdom was created, and the understanding of prudence from eternity.”

And grace, of which it is said: “By grace you have been saved through faith” (Eph. 2); and honor, of which we read: “But glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good” [Col. 0853A] (Rom. 2); and strength, concerning which Isaiah says (Isa. 40): “He gives strength to the weary, and to those who have no strength he increases vigor and power.”

And one of the elders answered and said to me: “Those who are clothed in white robes—who are they, and from where have they come?” And I said to him: “You know, Lord.” And he said to me: “These are the ones who came out of the great tribulation, and they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

By “one of the elders” he means either the body of the prophets or the Church, as though those set over the lower members were declaring what reward of future recompense workers ought to hope for, just as the Apostle says concerning the Gospel (Rom. 1): “The righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith”—namely, from the faith of those who preach to the faith of those who hear.

When the number of the faithful is said to have come out of the great tribulation, what else is demonstrated except what we read elsewhere (Acts 14): “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations”? Therefore the Apostle also says (Gal. 1): “Brothers, let us not grow weary, for in its own time we shall reap.” For the number of the faithful is refined through exercises of pressure, just as oil is carefully produced by applying the weight of presses, and as grain destined to be stored in the granary is gathered after being threshed beneath the tribulum.

But when they are said to have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb, the fruit of their reward is shown, so that the labor of the struggle mentioned above may be endured with equanimity. He aptly adds: “And they made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” It is as though he said: “The robes which others stained, either through neglect, ignorance, or contempt after the grace [Col. 0853C] of baptism, these made white in the blood of the Lamb”—that is, in the grace of Christ, or also through the acceptance of martyrdom.

This merit ought to be assigned especially in the Church to those who happen to shed their blood for Christ and to make the baptismal robe brighter through the Lamb’s blood by a more excellent form of devotion. But if this grace must be applied generally to all the faithful, the point must be considered in summary: even if someone is cleansed in the font of his Lord, nourished by the flesh of the Lamb, and kindled by spiritual fire, he is aided in this way. For there are those who, although they do not appear publicly to possess martyrdom in deed, are nevertheless proven before God to possess it in disposition.

For this reason they are before the sight of God’s throne and serve him day and night in his temple. And before the sight of God’s throne is the Church, for which he established ascents in the heart (Ps. 83), in the valley of weeping, in the place he appointed; it serves him day and night—that is, in prosperity and in adversity. It is understood as the temple because it is said to serve in the temple, just as it is also understood as the throne.

Finally, it follows: “And the one who sits upon the throne will dwell among them.” For the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. Wisdom, however, is Christ; and Christ is God. It follows:

“They shall hunger no more, nor thirst ever again; neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor shall they suffer any heat.” They shall not hunger, because they feed upon the living bread. “I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven.” Nor shall they thirst, because they are made drunk with such a splendid cup, as the Truth said (John 6): “Whoever believes in me shall never thirst”; likewise (John 4): “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

Neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor shall they be burned by the deadly incitements of heat. God promises something similar to his Church through Isaiah, saying (Isa. 25): “A refuge from the storm, a shelter from the heat,” where he declares that the integrity of his mysteries flourishes in his people and cannot be disturbed by any scorching of temptation [Col. 0854B].

Because the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them. Above, he had said that the Lamb received the book from the right hand of the one seated upon the throne. Now, however, he says that the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them, in order to teach that the Father and the Son have one throne: for the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father—that is, in the midst of the Church, in which the one God, the whole Trinity, dwells through faith.

“And he will lead them to the fountain of the waters of life, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” This is the fountain of which we read (Ps. 35): “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.” Christ leads his own to it by shepherding them, making himself the way, and revealing the homeland as he brings them there, so that he may fulfill what he formerly promised through the oracles of life; for he called the waters something like proclamations.

Designating this fountain, Solomon says (Prov. 18): “An overflowing torrent, a fountain of wisdom.” And “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes,” while they say: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 41). They are said to be removed at the time of consolation, when, having attained the fullness of immortal joys, every sorrow can be consigned to oblivion.

“For behold,” Isaiah says (chap. 65), “I create Jerusalem as rejoicing, and her people as joy; and there shall no longer be heard in her the sound of shouting or the sound of weeping.”

## CHAPTER VIII

And when he had opened the seventh sign, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour. “In heaven,” that is, in the Church, the silence lasting half an hour indicates the beginning of eternal rest; and he saw only a portion of the silence, because he was still going to see the same things. With the seventh sign he did not see how long the future period would be, so that many things might be shown to him more clearly. The silence was interrupted; for if it had continued unbroken, this would have been the end of the narration. But since it still had to be repeated, the sequence of the narrative, after my silence as well, would appropriately receive its beginning again in the following book.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0853]

## TABLE OF CONTENTS

[Col. 0853D]

I. The seven angels with an equal number of trumpets, and another angel over God’s altar with a golden censer; when the first angel sounds the trumpet, hail and flame mixed with blood are hurled down.

[Col. 0854D] II. When the second angel sounds, a fiery mountain is thrown into the sea, and a part of the sea is turned into blood.

III. When the third angel sounds, a burning star is said to have fallen from heaven.

IV. When the angel sounds the trumpet, a third of the sun, moon, and stars is said to be darkened.

[Col. 0855A] V. “I saw another angel flying like an eagle in mid-heaven, saying three times: Woe, woe, woe!”

VI. When the fifth angel sounds, a star falls from heaven, and the key of the abyss’s well is given to it; from there smoke and locusts emerge.

VII. Concerning the torment of five months or six, in the form of scorpions.

VIII. Where the horse prepared for battle, resembling locusts, signifies the heresiarchs.

IX. He announces that one woe has passed and two are to follow.

X. When the sixth angel sounds, the release of the four angels formerly bound over the Euphrates, and concerning the number eighty thousand or twice ten thousand times ten thousand.

XI. Concerning the horsemen who have fiery, thorny, and sulphurous breastplates.

XII. Concerning the error of paganism.

XIII. The angel seated and clothed with a cloud, whose face was like the sun, and concerning the seven thunders.

[Col. 0856A] XIV. Concerning the days of the voice of the seventh angel and the completion of the divine mystery.

XV. Concerning the bitterness which he is foretold to feel after eating the book, and the measurement received for the reed.

XVI. Concerning the two martyrs who will prophesy for 1,260 [1,290] days.

XVII. It is said that the third woe has come.

XVIII. The voices made by the elders at the trumpet blast of the seventh angel.

XIX. God’s temple opened in heaven, and the ark of the covenant seen.

XX. The red dragon and the woman in labor.

XXI. The devil, the accuser of the brothers, being sent from heaven to earth.

XXII. The woman receiving two wings, with which she would flee into the wilderness to be nourished.

[Col. 0855B] “And I saw seven angels standing in the presence of God, and seven trumpets were given to them.” We should understand that in the seven angels the Church is repeated according to the preceding rule, since it is very often commended through the number seven on account of its universality. It is said to have received the most steadfast trumpet of preaching; when this prevails, we confidently believe that the whole world believes. For we read (Isa. 57): “As a trumpet, raise your voice.”

“And another angel came and stood over God’s altar, holding a golden censer, and many petitions were given to him, so that he might offer the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar of God, which is in the presence of the throne.” This kind of narrative must also be observed. Frequently someone relates something briefly in a manner different from the plan he has set out; and when he has finished what he inserted to obscure the matter, he returns to his original subject.

[Col. 0855C] For he had proposed that the seven angels had received trumpets, and another angel came, so that one might suppose that this angel came after the seven, whereas he saw it all at one time. When the angel came, the seven received trumpets—that is, when Christ the Lord came, his Church received the authority to preach. We understand that he himself came over the altar, that is, over the Church; and the Church is understood as the body of that priest. To it Peter says (1 Pet. 2): “A holy nation, an elect race, a royal priesthood.”

“Having a golden censer”: that is, an immaculate body conceived when the Holy Spirit came upon it. He offered it to God as an offering and sacrifice, for the redemption of the whole world, as a sweet-smelling fragrance; and he cleansed the conscience of all from dead works.

He is said both to have received the prayers of the saints and to have offered them, because through him the prayers of all can reach God pleasantly. Hence the Apostle says (Heb. 13): “Through him we offer continually to God a sacrifice of praise,” that is, “the fruit of lips confessing his name.”

For this reason he is said to intercede not only for our sins but also for those of the whole world [or: “age”], as blessed John likewise says: “And he himself,” he says, “intercedes for our sins.”

“And the smoke of the prayers, the prayers of the saints, rose from the angel’s hand before the presence of God. And the angel took the censer, filled it with the fire of God’s wrath, and threw it upon the earth.” He rightly says that the censer was full of fire. For God, he says (John 3), “does not give the Spirit by measure.” We know that this was fulfilled especially in Christ’s humanity, in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Col. 2).

And because he willed that only his Church should share in that same Spirit, he demonstrated this here in particular. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel (Luke 12): “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” I think that this fire is signified here.

By this fire we know that sinners, like fragile vessels collapsing in a furnace, are rejected. For through one fire—though not with the same result—the portion of the wicked shares with the righteous, just as straw and gold do not have the same outcome: one is consumed, while the other is tested. Likewise, under one press, oil is known to obtain a different quality from the dregs.

This fire, then, sent upon the earth, kindled the minds of preachers. “And it is said to have burned a third of the earth, of the trees, and of the grass and green vegetation,” as though he were saying: rejecting and destroying the portion of useless vessels, whether situated outside the Church or within it. For if anyone builds upon the foundation wood, hay, and straw, all these things perish by fire (1 Cor. 3).

Alternatively: “And the angel took the censer, filled it from the fire of the altar, and threw it upon the earth.” The Lord took his body, that is, the Church; and, by fulfilling the Father’s will, he filled it from the fire of the altar—that is, from the authority to bind and loose, which consists in sacrifices and God’s propitiation.

Hence it is also said (Ps. 103): “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire.” In these matters the Church received all authority in heaven and on earth, when it completed God’s sacrifice: the Lord offering himself principally, and the saints presenting their bodies as “a living and holy sacrifice” (Rom. XI).

“And he threw it upon the earth.” For through the Church’s preaching the world will receive knowledge of the coming indignation, as Zechariah says (Zech. 12): “I will make the leaders of Judah like a torrent of fire,” and so forth.

What follows can be fitted to either interpretation: “And there were thunderclaps and voices and flashes of lightning and an earthquake.” All these things are spiritual; they belong to the Church. They are the voices of those rebuking in fire: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. 3), and so forth; or: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”

The thunderclaps are the preachings of the Christian faith; the flashes of lightning are miracles of healings; the earthquakes are persecutions, which he both preached as coming and suffers when they arrive at various times.

He repeats what he had proposed, being accustomed to dictate the same things in sections. “And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets,” he says, “prepared themselves to sound the trumpets.” The Church, commended through the number seven, prepared itself confidently for preaching.

“And the first angel sounded the trumpet, and there was hail and flame mixed with blood, and it was thrown upon the earth; and a third of the earth was burned up [Vulgate: ‘was consumed by fire’], and a third of the trees was burned up, and all the green grass was burned up.”

What is the earth is also the trees, but he says that only a third of the trees was burned, whereas he says that all the grass burned. Here the earth represents earthly people; the trees represent people wavering through unbelief, shaken “by every wind of doctrine” (Eph. 4). Concerning them the apostle Jude says (ch. 1): “Autumn trees, fruitless, uprooted, twice dead.”

The grass, moreover, and the green vegetation represent flesh fattened by pleasures; for “all flesh is grass” (Isa. 40).

Although he had previously placed three quarters against the one quarter that is the Church, he has now confined the part opposed to the Church to two thirds: one third consists of the wicked mixed with the good within the Church, in the form of false brothers; the other is separated in open schism into the error of paganism and the depravity of heresy. Thus the Church—that is, the one third—fights against a twofold evil, like simplicity resisting duplicity.

So in the Gospel (Luke 14) a king is said to have gone out to fight against one who has twenty thousand with ten thousand; and so God promises through Zechariah, saying (Zech. 13): “And it shall be in all the land, says the Lord: two parts in it shall be cut off and perish, but a third shall be left in it. And I will lead the third part through fire, and I will burn them as silver is burned, and I will test them as gold is tested. He shall call upon my name, and I will answer him. And I shall say, ‘You are my people’; and they shall say, ‘The Lord is my God.’”

Scripture frequently mentions the portion of evils consisting of the two thirds as one body and therefore as one person, sometimes introducing it in the singular.

“And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea; and a third of the sea became blood; and a third of the fish died; and a third of the ships perished.”

The burning mountain in the sea is the devil, thrown among the peoples. “A third of the sea became blood”: he uses “blood” for the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God. For this reason it is said that through it the human soul is killed. Hence the Apostle says (Rom. 8): “To set the mind on the flesh is death,” because “flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

By the name “sea,” as well as by “trees,” “ships,” and “fish,” he embraces the world, together with its inhabitants, according to his customary manner. Finally, after saying that one third had been turned into blood, signifying that souls had been consumed by death, he subsequently divides that same portion into two thirds, saying: “And a third of the fish died, and a third of the ships perished.” In the one he showed the kind of death; in these he assigned the number.

Another edition, by saying “those having souls,” shows clearly that they were killed by spiritual death, just as the Apostle says of the widow (1 Tim. 5): “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives.” Thus, as the wording sounds, it is as though one third killed another third, through a harmful tradition and the imitation of useless teaching.

“And the third angel sounded the trumpet, and a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven upon a third of the rivers and upon the springs of water. And the name of the star is said to be *absentius* (“wormwood”), or, as it is said elsewhere, *absentium* (“wormwood”); and a third of the waters became like *absentium* (“wormwood”), and many people died from the bitterness of the waters.”

He indicates that people had fallen from heaven, as though from the Church—people whom others thought to shine forth through good merits. Therefore they are compared with stars and torches; the apostle Jude rebukes them, saying (Jude 1): “Stars of deception.” For they deceive by the very outward appearance of their brightness. The Lord also compares them (Matt. 23) to whitewashed walls and tombs.

And because the fall of the great usually troubles many, he says that the star fell upon part of the rivers and springs. Its name, *absentium* [Note: “*Absinthium* ought to be read, and *absinthio*, unless the archetypes resist it.”], he uses for great bitterness.

When such people fall, we know that many are weakened and corrupted by imitating their worst teaching. He rightly compared them with wormwood (*absentia*), since, if a little of its bitterness is mixed with a sweet drink, everything is turned into bitterness.

Scripture signifies this elsewhere also when it says to such people (Jer. 2): “I planted you as a choice vine; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?”

He places this as a third part of the wicked, since others who ought to have been made more cautious by the example of those who fell instead suffer failure through imitating them.

“And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and a third of the sun, a third of the moon, and a third of the stars was struck, so that they might shine less; and the day lost that same part, and the night likewise.”

The sun, moon, and stars represent the Church. It was fitting that, when the fourth angel was mentioned, he should speak of those things which are narrated as having been made on the fourth day in the creation of the world, to rule the day and the night and to divide light from darkness.

Thus, when these wicked people—one body, outwardly manifest and inwardly concealed—are separated from the Church, and by their transgressions cause the Church’s dignity to shine less, they are convicted of acting against the Creator’s ordering, as though by their darkness they were taking away a third of the sun, a third of the moon, and a third of the stars.

For just as he willed the sun, moon, and stars to surpass the other visible created things in place or appearance, so he commanded his Church, distinguished by dignity and glory, to rule throughout the whole world. They are observed to wish to darken it. “For the name of God,” the Apostle says (Rom. 2), “is blasphemed among the nations because of you.” Through those by whom our good is blasphemed, the native light seems to be darkened.

But lest anyone think that this could happen at will and without measure, he sets a kind of limit to the measure, indicating that same portion of the wicked through a different account. What he had mentioned as one third under the third angel, he here mentions in a threefold manner: a third of the sun, a third of the moon, and a third of the stars were diminished.

Thus in these luminaries two parts remained intact in their own condition, and that destruction or darkness did not affect anyone belonging to the number of the elect. For, as Job says (17), “only the son of destruction perished.” And (2 Tim. 2): “The Lord knows those who are his.”

Alternatively: The perfection of every kingdom consists in the sum of twelve ounces. Therefore he says that a third of the sun, a third of the moon, and a third of the stars was darkened—that is, four ounces each, from which the body of all the wicked is composed, represented in many ways.

In the case of the good, it is understood that eight ounces remained in each: three times eight, twenty-four, representing the perfection which consists in leaders and peoples.

Here “third” is the name for the portion of the wicked: two portions, one of the day and the other of the night. To this Jeremiah says: “I compared your mother to the night.”

Therefore it was struck so that the third of the day and the third of the night might appear—that is, which belong to Christ and which to the devil. He did not say, “Their third was struck and darkened, and the third of the day and night appeared,” but “that it might be darkened and appear,” because it did not appear in the condition in which it was struck; rather, it was struck for this purpose: having been handed over to its own pleasures, it would be revealed in due time when sins overflowed.

“Authority was given to their tails to harm people for five months.” We remember what is written in Isaiah (ch. 9): “The long-lived and honored one, he is the head; and the prophet who teaches falsehood, he is the tail. And those who bless my people are those who lead them astray, and those who are blessed are thrown down.”

Hence it is clear that these people wish to rule in the sphere which all the saints and teachers of truth strive most earnestly to avoid: secular glory and the error of harmful preaching.

Therefore, by “their tails” and “their authority for five months,” he again indicates this present life, in which falsehood can prevail, either to capture the useless or to torment the spiritual temporarily. Hence we read (Ps. 118): “I saw the senseless, and I was wasting away, and weariness seized me because of sinners.”

“And they had over them as king the angel of the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Armageddom, in Greek Apollyon (‘Destroyer’), and in Latin he bears the name Destroyer.”

Although God is supremely good, he permitted an angel suitable for such people to preside over them, through hidden but nevertheless just judgments. For whoever has been defeated by someone is assigned as that person’s servant. Therefore the Apostle says (2 Pet. 2) that they are handed over to every deception of unrighteousness, because they did not receive the love of truth so that they might be saved.

And for this reason God sends them into the working of error (2 Thess. 2), so that they may believe a lie and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness.

The nature of his activity agrees with the expressed meaning of his name, namely, “Destroyer.”

“One woe has passed, and behold, two other woes are coming.”

“And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet.” He says that the first woe has passed and that the trumpet of the sixth angel has sounded. Here the final preaching of the sixth age is announced.

“And I heard one of the four horns of God’s altar—the altar which is before God’s eyes—saying to the sixth angel who held the trumpet: ‘Release the four angels who are bound over that great river Euphrates.’”

Here he shows that the winds and the angels signify the same things. Earlier he had said that the winds were held by angels; now he says that the angels are released by an angel—that is, by the Church, which retains the authority to loose and to bind (Matt. 16; 18; John 20).

Therefore, he says, it has the trumpet, that is, the power of preaching. Hence it is said: “Like a trumpet, raise your voice” (Isa. 58).

“Release the four angels who are bound over the river Euphrates.” Earlier he had said that they were at the four corners of the earth, to show that by the name Euphrates the power of worldly rule and the multitude of persecutors are signified. In that power the devil’s harmful will is said to be bound because he is not permitted to harm as much as he wishes.

For the Euphrates is a river of Babylonia, which we know is frequently used negatively in the divine Scriptures. Jeremiah also says (ch. 46): “That day is a day of vengeance for the Lord our God, to avenge his enemies; the sword shall devour them and be filled with their blood, for there is a sacrifice for the Lord of hosts in the land of the north, at the river Euphrates.”

Here “sacrifice” announces not propitiation but slaughter. For the final persecution is foretold to be more violent than the others because then, when the devil has been released with his ministers, he is permitted to harm and afflict more greatly.

Then follows: “And those four angels were released.” This signifies the beginning of the persecution. They had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, so that they might kill a third of humanity.

Here he foretells, with an appropriate symbolic significance, the four periods during which the persecution will rage—that is, three years and six months. He said “for the hour, the day, the month, and the year” because hours gradually complete days, days complete months, and months are known to complete years.

By saying “prepared,” he expressed the character of the devil and his angels. They maintain unrelenting hostility against Christ’s Church and have a continual desire to harm, but divine power restrains them, so that they cannot harm as much as they wish. Properly, therefore, he had previously said of the locusts that they were like horses prepared for battle. For when he says that angels were released, he says that he saw horses.

“And the number,” he says, “of the mounted army was eighty thousand; I heard their number, so that they might kill a third of humanity.” Once again he indicates the entire body of the wicked in many ways.

Eighty thousand, just as the number sixty, arising from the perfection of the number six, prefigures for us an example of the good—for we read (Song 6), “There are sixty queens”—so eighty is sometimes used negatively.

It arises from four because of the four well-known qualities of the body: cold and hot, moist and dry; or because of the four disturbances by which life is often grievously afflicted: fear, desire, grief, and joy. These, doubled on account of the two sexes, make eight.

This number, rising likewise through ten, forms eighty; in it he shows, in a certain manner, the portion of the mounted wicked who fight against the body of Christ, which is the Church. Hence there too it follows: “And there are eighty concubines,” as though they were joined not in a legitimate marriage but rather in a fraudulent one.

This properly applies to all heretics, because they handle the mysteries of the faith temporarily, cloaked under Christ’s name, so that, just as concubines are not destined to remain always in the house, they too desire to possess from Christ’s name only a momentary authority or human applause.

Nor is it difficult to distinguish correctly between the merits of queens and concubines, since the very names of queens reveal their dignity, while the deformity of concubines is evident.

Another translation, which Tychonius expounded, has: “And the number of the mounted army was twice ten thousand times ten thousand.” Passing over the exposition, he added only this: “He did not say how many ten-thousands.”

It seems to us, however, that in this translation also the entire portion of the lost is represented not inappropriately. Twice ten thousand makes twenty thousand. The Lord uses this number in the Gospel concerning a king who has twenty thousand, as though the duplicity of the wicked resists Christian simplicity.

According to this rule of interpretation, by which a simple ten is opposed by a doubled twenty, he added “of ten thousands.” By remaining silent about how many, he represented that many were being counted beyond the number, as though they had been gathered but had not been reckoned. Concerning them the prophet says (Ps. 39): “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number.”

The undifferentiated confusion of this multitude was also signified in the first catch of the disciples (Luke 5), before the Lord’s passion. Through it the boats were weighed down and the nets were torn, so that these may properly be recognized as heretics and false Christians—people concerned only with contention. For the Church is often burdened by internal disputes and exercised by the attacks of heretics, so that the torn nets may be understood as schisms that had been committed.

In that catch too the number is left unspoken, just as here there are “twice ten thousand times ten thousand.” It is as though he were saying: They were indeed called, but they were not to be counted among the fullness of the elect. “For many are called,” he says, “but few are chosen.”

In the other catch, after the Lord’s resurrection (Matt. 20; John 21), both the number and the great size of the fish are mentioned, and the net is said to have remained unbroken.

Therefore, just as “twice ten thousand times ten thousand” should be applied to heretics and false Christians, so it should be applied to the remaining wicked, whom the preceding exposition says are also among the Gentiles and whom the following order now mentions. From all these persons the entire body of the devil consists—or rather, is shown to consist: Jews, heretics, false Christians, and pagans.

A little later he follows by indicating the error of paganism itself: “And the rest of humanity who were not killed by these plagues, and did not repent of the works of their evil deeds, so as not to worship demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood,” and the rest by which he shows that the whole body of the wicked is here fully circumscribed.

“And I saw horses in the vision, and those seated upon them had breastplates of fire, and of thorn, and of sulfur, and their heads were like lions’ heads.”

The horses are human beings; here the riders are evil spirits. For just as we previously read in connection with the good, “You who ride upon your horses,” that is, preachers, “and your cavalry is a sound,” so here, conversely, cavalry is joined to evil spirits.

Enough and more than enough has already been said about the lions’ heads. What must not be passed over, however, is that although some resemblance of locusts is found in horses, and of horses is not found in locusts, just as neither is found in lions, both figures nevertheless aptly correspond to the persons of heretics through their symbolism. The breadth of divine speech has distinguished one thing in dissimilar ways.

In the description and qualities of the breastplates, the punishments of the wicked are signified, as we read that fire, sulfur, and smoke from their torments are promised to those who worship the beast: “The smoke of their torments rises for ever and ever.”

And because this translation added “thorny,” it showed beforehand the merit that deserved the punishments, signifying vices by thorns. The Apostle also expresses the order of this interpretation (Heb. 6), speaking of similar soil: because it produces thorns and thistles, it is accursed, and its end is burning.

Hence that original punishment of sin is also stated: “It shall produce thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). And Solomon says (Prov. 26): “Thorns grow in the hands of a drunkard.”

“And fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths.” Here what is produced is rightly signified by the one who produces it. They are introduced as having and uttering from their mouths those things by whose harmful preaching people are deceived and perish, to be tormented by the fire, smoke, and sulfur that came out of their mouths.

Thus they are said to incur these plagues through the words of their heads, that is, through the teachings of their leaders. For “the power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails,” that is, in the office of speech. He calls reprobate preachers “tails.”

“For their tails were like serpents, having heads of dragons; and with these they harm.” Here he appropriately mentions serpents as a likeness of the ancient transgression: deceived by the serpent’s hissing, the woman boldly did what was forbidden and justly lost what she had received.

So these have the heads of dragons—that is, the rulers of the world. Dragons are earthly creatures, often dwelling in waters and larger than almost all beasts. Therefore, when they preach harmful doctrines under the patronage of rulers, they harm more greatly than if they persuaded by speech alone. Hence he says that they have the heads of dragons, by which they harm.

Now he speaks of the Gentiles: “And the rest of humanity, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their evil deeds, so as to worship demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders or their sorceries.”

He anticipated this and placed it earlier, so that by enclosing all who would be destined for the left hand he might circumscribe them completely. Here he mentions sorceries negatively; for we often call sorcerers “evildoers.”

The sequence of the narrative must therefore be considered. After describing the final conflict and the manner of the nations, he passed over the seventh angel, under whom the final persecution and the manifest coming of the Lord are expected, and he mentions the Church of the present time. By indicating this in different ways, and by recapitulating what he had omitted, he seemed to narrate two endings.

Let us therefore remember that, when he has carried the discourse through to its end, a compressed conclusion must be attached to the order. For he did something unusual by not concluding both narratives with one ending. He distinguished the preaching of the future peace, showing how powerful it would be and how clearly visible on land and sea.

## CHAPTER X
And I saw, he says, another mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow over his head; his face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire.

He understands the Lord Christ descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud—that is, the Church—or clothed with the cloud of flesh, which elsewhere (Rev. XXI) is said to descend from heaven as a newly married bride. Or, as Daniel says (chap. VII), the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven. And the rainbow over his head signifies the enduring promise of mercy toward the good, but it also signifies those who, before the Lord’s advent, happened to be honored with martyrdom, such as Abel and the others.

He rightly says that the rainbow was over his head, because another translation has *iris* (Gen. IV), by which the Church is described as surrounded, as though members had been sent ahead in such a way that they are nevertheless shown to remain joined to the head. And his face was like the sun: the Lord Jesus Christ was manifested through the glory of the resurrection. Of him we read (Ps. XVIII): “He placed his tabernacle in the sun,” namely, where he would shine forth. For in the face the manifestation of his presence is signified; desiring this, the Psalmist said (Ps. LXXIX): “Show us your face, and we shall be saved.”

His feet—that is, the apostles—are kindled for preaching by the words of God and by the Holy Spirit. “Was not our heart,” he says (Luke XXIV), “burning within us on the way, while he spoke to us and opened the Scriptures?”

They are called pillars because of the firmness of the churches. Of them the prophet says: “I have strengthened its pillars” (Ps. LXXIV); and again: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one announcing and preaching peace!” (Isa. LII). The Apostle also says: “Those who were considered to be pillars of the Church” (Gal. II).

And he had in his hand an open book, and he placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth.

If, in the earlier passage, profound secrets are understood to have lain hidden in the sealed book of the Old Testament, it is more fittingly believed that here grace, revealed and made manifest, shines forth in the open book of the New Testament, so that the Apostle could confidently say (II Cor. III): “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.” Therefore, too, his face is said to have shone like the sun.

His right foot upon the sea means that he wisely sent his stronger members to endure the assaults of persecution, as though into the dangers of the sea; his left upon the earth means those who are not to be committed to greater dangers. For God does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that we may be able to endure it. It is certain, nevertheless, that his preaching extends over land and sea.

And he cried out with a loud voice, like a roaring lion—that is, he prevailed as he was proclaimed with strength and confidence through his servants. Hence the prophet says: “And he established,” he says, “the firm love of his strength.”

And when he cried out, the seven thunders spoke.

Because the operation of the number seven is known, I think that the seven thunders signify the manifold adaptation of ecclesiastical preaching. The Apostle Paul, observing this, said to some (I Cor. III): “As infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.” But of others he says (Heb. V): “Solid food belongs to the mature.” And of still others (Tit. III): “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition.”

Thus the Church is said rightly to proclaim through the customary offices of preaching.

And when the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to write, and I heard a voice from heaven saying: “Seal what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it.”

He is commanded not to describe openly what he heard, but to temper it by discreetly marking and moderating it, lest it either lie indiscriminately open to everyone or, being too easily understood, produce distaste. Therefore he says: “Mark it for yourself”; or, as another translation has it: “Seal it for yourself, and do not write it,” so that by the seal he might indicate the allegory without denying nourishment to understanding.

For this reason Daniel is also told (Dan. XII): “Seal the book and close the words until the appointed time; many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied”—that is, either the matter is to be deferred until its proper time or distributed according to the capacity of those receiving it. Hence the Lord says (John XVI): “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth, he says, lifted his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who established heaven and the things in it, and the earth and the things in it: “There shall be no more time, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God will be finished, just as he announced through his servants the prophets.”

The trumpet of the seventh angel is the end of persecution and the advent of the Lord. Therefore the Apostle also says (I Cor. XV): “At the last trumpet—for he will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible.”

Thus he foretells the future time of the Church, when the promised eternity of heavenly blessings will have received her, so that she will no longer be subject to the changes of time but will enjoy the stable eternity of blessedness. “The mystery is finished”: he means that what was promised is brought to completion, not that what was taken away is consummated.

And I heard a voice from heaven speaking with me again: “Go and take the open book from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth.”

The voice from heaven is the command of God, who inspires the heart of the Church and orders her to receive what the Church has preached from the open book concerning the future peace. It also seems to us that receiving the open book from the angel’s hand means understanding the truth manifested in Christ through the Law and the Prophets. Therefore he says that the book is received not as earlier, sealed, but open.

For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. This Christ—that is, the Truth—then chose to be born from the earth, that is, from Mary, when righteousness looked down from heaven (Ps. LXXXIV).

For this reason I think the words “I heard a voice from heaven speaking with me” are said here, just as he himself says (John VIII): “I am the beginning, who also speak to you.”

And I went to the angel, telling him to give me the book.

The Church is pierced by divine inspiration so that she may be thoroughly instructed concerning this mystery.

And he says to me: “Take it and eat it”—that is, store it in the secret recesses of your inward parts—“and it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet like honey.”

That is: when you receive it, you will delight in the sweetness of the divine word, in the hope of promised salvation, and in the pleasantness of divine righteousness; but you will certainly experience bitterness when you begin to preach this both to the devoted and to the undevoted.

When the preaching of divine judgment is heard, some are changed for the better by the bitterness of repentance, while others, offended, become still more hardened and fiercely harbor hatred against the preachers. “Reprove a wise man,” he says, “and he will love you; rebuke a fool, and he will add to his hatred of you” (Prov. IX).

The preacher receives bitterness from both groups: either through the feeling of compassion, sharing the tears of those who repent, or by drawing the torment of bitterness from the failure of those others. Hence the Apostle says (Rom. IX): “I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers.”

He refers here to this bitterness. But if sweetness is to be attributed to the devoted and bitterness alone to the undevoted, I think that interpretation fits better. For spiritual people can say: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

And when I had received the little book from the angel’s hand, he says, and had eaten it, my stomach was immediately filled; and he said to me: “You must again prophesy among peoples and nations and languages and many kings.”

Just as divine Scripture often turns its discourse from a genus to a species, but also subsequently embraces both together, so now its definite intention is directed toward John, who, after being freed from exile, was still required not only to bring this revelation to the knowledge of the Church of Christ, but also to preach the Gospel more profoundly among peoples, nations, languages, and many kings.

Nevertheless, no one doubts that this voice also applies to the whole Church, which must never cease from preaching.

He showed this confidence in evangelizing by the reed he received, in the likeness of a rod, not without a reasonable significance: from what produces something, he indicates the thing produced. The Gospel is written by the function of a reed; but, lest any emptiness be thought to be present in the reed, it is rightly said to resemble a rod, in which, because of its natural strength, solidity is signified.
