This solidity is to be referred either to the firmness of faith or to the extended rule of belief that can be crossed, in which measurement is necessarily mentioned because of the varying distribution of graces. The Apostle refers to this, saying (Eph. IV): “To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.”

In this faith, recognize also the brightness of wisdom in gold, received together with the manifestation of the flesh, which Christ deigned to bear in one person. John both deserved to recognize this and took care to preach it.

Appropriately, the gift of graces is here described as being given to the members according to measure, so that it may be expressly declared that to Christ the Head it was not given according to measure. Concerning him John says in the same passage (John III): “For God does not give the Spirit by measure.” In him are “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” and in him “all the fullness of divinity dwells” (Col. II); no measure therefore limits him.

## CHAPTER XI

“He gave me,” he says, “a golden reed like a rod, saying: ‘Rise and measure the temple of God, and the altar of God, and those who worship in it.’”

“Rise.” An awakening of zeal is enjoined, to be applied to John or to the Church, so that, freed from secular impediments, we may be more fit for the duties of eternal blessings.

“Measure the temple, the altar, and those who worship in it.” He commands the Church—that is, the temple of God—to be spiritually formed according to the measure of divine gifts already set forth, especially in the altar, that is, in faith, without which it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI).

By saying “those who worship in it” he emphasized more explicitly those who strive to worship the Lord in spirit and truth, so that faith may shine forth in truth and a life worthy of approval in spirit. “For the Father,” he says, “seeks such people to worship him, true worshipers.”

Alternatively: by the altar he signifies priests, and by the temple the faithful. For many appear to worship only outwardly, and will not be written in the book.

Indicating this, he continues: “But do not measure the court that is outside the temple.” For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is inward” (Ps. XLIV), because it has been given to the nations, and “they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.”

The evil doctrine of false belief and the contagion of an ill-omened way of life among heretics, Jews, and nations are commanded to be expelled outside, because it is unworthy for such people to hasten toward the Holy of Holies. “What business is it of mine,” the Apostle says (I Cor. V), “to judge those who are outside?”

For all Jews, heretics, and Gentiles continually attack the Church in various ways, as though trampling upon her.

The number of months does not signify only the final persecution; it also designates the entire period of Christianity, because of the six ages of the world and the seven days through whose passing and return all time unfolds. Six times seven makes forty-two, but I think the number should be referred to both meanings.

“And I will give,” he says, “to my two martyrs, and they will prophesy for twelve hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

What he had said, “You must again prophesy,” is equivalent to this: “I will give to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy.” For what John is, these two witnesses are: the Church preaching and prophesying through the two Testaments.

Alternatively: Truth bears witness that there are two kinds of martyrdom, one in disposition and the other in action. The first, known to God alone, is carried in the heart, even if the time of suffering does not at some point arrive. The second is fulfilled publicly before human beings when the opportunity for persecution arises.

Sometimes martyrdom seems to be lacking in the intention, and at other times the intention seems to be lacking in martyrdom. Hence blessed Cyprian says:

“First in the title of victory is to confess the Lord when seized by the hands of the Gentiles; the second step toward glory is to withdraw prudently and preserve oneself for the Lord. The former is a public confession, the latter a private one. The former conquers the judge of the world; the latter, content with God as his judge, preserves the integrity of his heart with a pure conscience.”

This is most clearly confirmed in the case of the two sons of Zebedee: James, killed by Herod, is dedicated to martyrdom by a public confession, while his brother John the Evangelist (Acts XII) is crowned with martyrdom secretly before the Lord. It is clear that the Lord had long ago said to both: “You will indeed drink my cup” (Matt. XX)—one in action, the other in disposition.

“Clothed in sackcloth”: humility is shown in confessions (*exomologeseis*).

Accordingly, since he speaks not of future events but of those present, he says: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth.”

This can be understood of the Church, which is formed, illumined by the light of the two Testaments. It can also be understood of the two kinds of martyrdom just mentioned, which are divinely granted to armed members in different ways.

For the two lampstands are the Church; but he said “two” because of the number of the Testaments. Or he said it because the Church, gathered from circumcision and uncircumcision, stands joined to the cornerstone. Thus, even if he names one or more of the seven lampstands according to their locations, the whole Church is signified.

And if anyone wished to harm them, fire would come out of their mouths and consume their enemies; and if anyone wishes to injure them, he must likewise be killed.

This means that if anyone desires to injure the Church, he is consumed by fire, condemned according to the reciprocal judgment of that injury, receiving justly what he unjustly seeks to inflict.

Or, in a good sense, he is spiritually consumed by the fire of the Church’s prayers and changed for the better, when the person is saved by being converted from error while the error perishes.

They have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy.

“He says,” not “they will have,” as though they did not possess this power now. Since all power in heaven and on earth was given to the Son of Man (Matt. XXVIII), this can also be understood of his body, which is the Church: she shuts heaven when blessing does not descend from her upon the barren earth, just as the Lord says concerning a part of his vineyard (Isa. V): “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it.”

They have power over all waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague whenever they wish.

They not only suspend the waters, but also make those that had descended useless. This means turning waters into blood because of those who interpret carnally the things that the Church presents for spiritual examination. Rightly struck by the Church with a just anathema, they die; from the source from which spiritual life and progress come to others, they themselves incur the failure of death. For, as the Apostle says (Rom. VIII), “to set the mind on the flesh is death.”

Thus the good fragrance of Christ, wafting from the Church, becomes for some “the fragrance of death unto death,” and for others “the fragrance of life unto life” (II Cor. II).

Hence it is also said that they strike the inhabitants of the earth with plagues, when, according to the differences of merits and sins, having received the power of binding and loosing, they judge each person with a right decree.

And when they have finished their martyrdom, the beast that ascends from the abyss will make war against them, conquer them, and kill them.

Here it is plainly evident that these things occur before the final persecution, since he says “when they have finished their martyrdom”—that is, the martyrdom which they are said to sustain until the revelation of the beast that is to ascend from the abyss, from the hiding places of the wickedness of the hearts of the Jews. For Antichrist is reported to be born from the tribe of Dan.

“He will conquer them”: he means those who will have succumbed in these matters. “He will kill them”: he signifies those who will have been slain for the name of Christ with praiseworthy patience.

And he will place their bodies in the middle of that great city which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was also crucified.

Another translation has “body” in the singular. He spoke of the one body of the two, and later of bodies, both to preserve the number of the Testaments and the two martyrdoms and to show the Church as one body. He spoke not only of those who were killed but also of the living.

“It will be thrown out,” that is, it will be despised, as in: “You have thrown my words behind you” (Ps. XLIX).

“In the middle,” that is, in the open. This is that Jerusalem which killed the prophets and stoned those sent to her, according to the word of the Lord rebuking her (Matt. XXIII). Therefore she deserved to be rejected rather than restored.

And people from the nations and tribes, languages and peoples will see their bodies and will not permit their bodies to be placed in tombs.

When bodies are prevented from being gathered into their proper places, they do not permit the days commemorating them to be marked by the sacred celebration of the living.

Alternatively, this expresses the desires of those impious people who strive to remove the Church of Christ from the world, as the Psalm says (Ps. CVIII): “Let his name be remembered no more.” Although they cannot fulfill this desire, they nevertheless manifest their harmful will.

And those who dwell upon the earth will rejoice over them, and celebrate, and send gifts to one another, because these two tormented those who dwell upon the earth.

It is not surprising if those who think according to earthly things rejoice at the deaths of the righteous. For, besides the plagues by which the human race will be reproved because of the testimony of God, the very sight of the righteous burdens the unjust, as it is written (Wis. II): “They are burdensome to us even to behold.” It not only burdens them but also makes them waste away.

Hence the Psalm says (Ps. CXI): “The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away.”

And after three and a half days, the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon those who saw them.

We can understand the three and a half days as three years and six months, which Daniel’s prophecy also foretells as coming in the final week (Dan. IX). Following the manner of Scripture, we use what we read concerning the forty days during which the spies traversed the land of Canaan (Num. XIII): a year is reckoned for a day, so that here, conversely, a day may be understood to stand for a year.

And so that our interpretation may not arise from uncertainty, we ought principally to set forth the words of the passage itself together with a suitable exposition, if in any way we may be able to penetrate the hidden things of this passage.

For when he speaks of the seventy weeks, he says as follows (Dan. IX): “So that Jerusalem may be rebuilt, until Christ the leader there shall be sixty-two weeks; and after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed, and the people that will deny him shall no longer be his, and the people with the coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary” (ibid.).

And a little later: “He will confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease, and there will be in the temple the abomination of desolation.”

Although these statements refer to the first advent of Christ, in which the completed events receive their fulfillment, nevertheless what follows the division of the weeks—distributed by a more hidden figure of heavenly inspiration, first mentioning seventy, then sixty-two, and finally one, which it itself divides into two parts—can appropriately be applied also to the end of Christ’s first advent, when the second advent begins.

To make this clearer, I think it must necessarily be referred to both meanings with a suitable exposition.

That Christ, coming after seventy and sixty-two weeks, should be killed, and that the same people, by killing him, should be rejected so that it is said they are no longer his; and that he should confirm the covenant with many for one week—all this is rightly understood when all the words and deeds of the Old Testament that served typologically for Christ’s advent were completed by the reality of his presence, since he is the end of the Law (Rom. X).

Nevertheless, I think it is especially appropriate to apply the understanding of this week also to the final course of the world, since immediately afterward I hear: “In the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease.”

For he also says in what follows (Dan. IX): “For a time, times, and half a time.” And: “When the dispersal of the hand of the holy people has been completed, all these things will be fulfilled.” A little later: “When the continual sacrifice has been removed and the abomination of desolation has been set up, there will be twelve hundred and ninety days”—a number that corresponds approximately to the course of three years and six months.

At that time the two kinds of martyrdom which, as we have already stated, consist in disposition and action will be strengthened by Elijah’s preaching in the middle of the week, so that they cannot be overthrown by the assault of the persecution soon to come. For, just as the persecution will then be more severe, so greater strength will shine forth in the soldiers of Christ who fight invincibly.

John speaks of these same witnesses: “And I will give to my two martyrs that they may prophesy for twelve hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

Although during the remaining three years and six months, before the violence of Antichrist, they may withdraw as though dead by retreating to other places, or, suitably sheltered in hiding places, may not appear because they conceal themselves after being divinely warned, they are nevertheless said to be strengthened and restored for that contest, so that through the spirit of life they remain firm upon their feet.

Then, when by the final preaching or persecution he confirms the covenant with many for one week, and while some are killed after completing their martyrdom and others are driven into flight, they are proclaimed to rise again as one body, because, armed with one spirit and established in one faith, they depart spiritually as one. For “if one member suffers, all the members suffer together” (I Cor. XII).

Therefore the Lord also says concerning John (Luke I): “In the spirit and power of Elijah”; or that other saying (Matt. XVII): “Elijah has already come, and they did to him whatever they wished,” intending John to be understood by this statement. Of John, whose birth he had promised, it was said that he would go before in the spirit and power of Elijah, so that through the grace of the same spirit and the likeness of one office, one person might be more suitably indicated in place of the other—Elijah in place of John—because just as John precedes the first advent, so Elijah precedes the second.

Here too the Lord says: “Elijah will come, and he will restore all things” (ibid.). When he fulfills the promises, he will restore what was foreshadowed.

Then also he will confirm the covenant with many for one week. All these things are prophetically understood to have once been foreshadowed in the person of Elijah, when, during the same period of time—that is, three years and six months—he hid himself so that it would not rain (III Kings XVII), and then appeared by divine command to obtain rain again. Through the sacrifice that had been offered, he reconciled to God and won back the estranged hearts of the Israelite people (III Kings XVIII).

Nor do I think that mention of that rain was made here without reason, except so that from the preceding events we may expect truth to be rendered in future deeds. This concerns the remaining three years and six months, during which, after Elijah has been killed by the persecution of Antichrist and the persecution is raging, the sacrifice and offering will cease in the middle of the week—the sacrifice that is now solemnly offered in the Church—when the violence of Antichrist then prevails.

Finally, when he preaches, the Jews will believe in Christ; when he rebukes them, they will deserve to be converted from idolatry, as they once were.

It may now be asked whether the resurrection of these witnesses should be joined to the time of Elijah’s preaching, lasting three years and six months, or to the remaining three years of Antichrist’s persecution. This is suggested by what was said earlier: “He will not permit their bodies to be placed in tombs, and those who dwell upon the earth will rejoice over them,” together with the other statements that are either narrated in advance, when future events are written as though past, or perhaps are woven ambiguously because such people will exist both in the half-week of preaching and in the half-week of persecution.

And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell; and seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake.

By the earthquake he signifies persecution, either by way of recapitulation, or he declares more clearly that it was intensified for those who, having already been thought dead, were seen again. For an hour signifies the whole period of time; the number ten is a perfect number, as is seven. If that were not so, the whole would have to be understood from a part.

He says that the city perished in part, namely, the portion belonging to the wicked collapsed, so that those too may be understood of whom we read (I John II): “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

There are two buildings: one upon the rock and the other upon the sand (Matt. VII). He says that this latter one fell.

And the rest were thrown into fear and gave glory to the God of heaven and earth.

These are the ones built upon the rock (Luke VI), who, while others fall through the earthquake—that is, through persecution—from the stability of their uprightness, glorify God by their confession.

Having finished the recapitulation that he had inserted while passing over the seventh angel, he resumes the order, saying: “The second woe has passed, and behold, the third woe will come quickly.”

He had said, after the battle of the locusts was completed, that one woe had passed and that two others were coming, lest it immediately be thought that he was describing the third, since a recapitulation had to be made.

Now, with that recapitulation completed, he says: “The second woe has passed”—not the woe of the recapitulation, but that of the horsemen, whose description had followed and to which he had not assigned a woe. Thus the second woe belongs to the horsemen, and it is followed by the third woe.

And the seventh angel, in whom the end is contained—here he seems to have made two endings, one belonging to the recapitulation and the other to the sequence. For he says that the end occurs in the resurrection as the third event, and he announces another end belonging to the battle, saying: “The second woe has passed, and behold, the third woe will come quickly.”

And the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and great voices arose in heaven, saying:

“The kingdom of our God and of his Christ has come, and he will reign forever and ever.”

And the twenty-four elders who sit before God upon their thrones fell upon their faces and worshiped God, saying:

“We give you thanks, Lord God Almighty, who are and who were, because you have taken your great power and have reigned. The nations were angry, and your wrath has come, and the time has come to judge the dead and to give their reward to your servants the prophets and to those who fear your name, both small and great, and to destroy those who corrupted the earth.”

Enough, and more than enough, has already been said concerning the elders and what should be understood.

Now he has mentioned the beginning and the end of Christ’s dispensation. For by saying “you have reigned” and “the nations were angry,” he demonstrates Christ’s first advent. But what follows—“Your wrath has come, and the time of the dead”—or, as another translation has it, “the time when the dead are to be judged”—shows the second advent, when the saints, the prophets, and those who fear his name, both small and great, receive their reward: the perfect and the little ones alike, because, as he says, “your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

And lest the wicked promise themselves impunity, he adds: “And to destroy those who corrupted the earth,” as the Psalm says (Ps. XXXIII): “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

“Behold,” he says, “the third woe has come in the voice of the seventh angel.” When he sounded, he spoke only of the Church praising and giving thanks to the Lord. From this we understand that the reward of the good is not without the woe of the wicked.

Hence the Psalm says (Ps. II): “When his wrath is kindled in a little while”—surely against the wicked—“blessed are all who trust in him.”

Thus now the Church herself says: “Your wrath has come, and the time to judge the dead, and to give your servants their reward,” and so forth. This is the final woe.

Having recapitulated the Lord’s bodily birth, he intimates that he will now speak of the same matters in another and fuller manner.

And the temple of God in heaven was opened—that is, the Church.

The temple of God may be understood as the body of Christ. Therefore the same Lord says: “Destroy this temple,” he says (John II), “and in three days I will raise it up.”

Alternatively, a definite understanding can be sought here through the variety of multiple meanings, so that each thing, more suitably assigned to its own character, may be recognized more clearly.

Since the ark often signifies the Church, here, by mentioning the ark of the covenant within the temple, he urges us to understand something higher. By saying also “in heaven,” he persuades us to penetrate a certain hidden meaning. The sense, then, is this: the temple is the Church; the ark of the covenant is the mystery of Christ’s incarnation—he who bore within himself, unto death, that ark and the tables of the covenant [the Latin syntax is uncertain]; he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. V). For “whatever promises of God there are,” the Apostle says (II Cor. I), “in him they are.”

And it had one golden vessel containing manna (Heb. IX), because it bears within the body spiritual food—an understanding adorned with the splendor of wisdom, to be preferred above others. For “the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John VI).

And it had Aaron’s rod, because he was uniquely begotten in a new birth from an undefiled virgin and is said to possess hidden within the covering of flesh, like an almond, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II).

Hence the Psalm says: “Arise, O Lord, into your resting place, you and the ark of your sanctification,” and the other words that harmonize with the same meaning.

For thus God promises through Jeremiah that the ark of the covenant will be abolished from human hearts—that ark, namely, of the Hebrews—and that Jerusalem, that is, the Church, will be called the throne of the Lord. He says:

“When you have been multiplied and have increased upon the earth, says the Lord, they will no longer say, ‘The ark of the covenant of the Lord,’ nor will it come upon their heart. In those days and at that time they will call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord, and all the nations will be gathered to it in the name of the Lord” (Jer. III).

And there were flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder, and an earthquake, and great hail.

The flashes of lightning are the powers by which Christ the Lord caused his disciples to shine. The voices and thunders are the proclamations by which the apostles, like clouds, thundered over the peoples.

The earthquake is the tumult of the peoples, aroused as they repeatedly brought persecutions upon the growing Church.

Hail always causes harm by breaking itself still more as it strikes against the waves, and by destroying itself it is reduced to fragments. In the same way the savage multitude of the Gentiles that persecuted the faith of Christ, later by following it became so reduced in number that it was either small or nothing.

He had said that these things took place in the description of the preaching of the seven angels, from the Lord’s advent itself and generally from beginning to end. Then, by sections, he described how they occurred; so now likewise he says that the temple of God in heaven was opened and that the battles followed, saying:

## CHAPTER XII
A great sign appeared in heaven. This is likewise now seen in the Church: namely, that the wisdom of God, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, is joined to human nature, and that from the two there is made one and the same Christ, mediator between God and human beings, proclaimed or believed. He himself says (John II): “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”; and the Evangelist adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet. It has frequently been stated that a genus is divided into many species which nevertheless constitute one thing. For what is heaven is also the temple in heaven; and what is the woman clothed with the sun and with the moon beneath her feet is the Church clothed with Christ, trampling all mutable things because of her love for him. For she is not carried away by these mutable things, but, cleaving steadfastly to the truly good, she says (Psalm LXXII): “But for me it is good to cling to God.” Hence are those words that we read concerning the Church (Song VI): “Beautiful as the sun, perfect as the moon”; and again: “Like the perfect moon forever, and a faithful witness in heaven” (Psalm LXXXVIII).

He plainly speaks of the Church as journeying in exile. Alternatively, after Christ’s human birth we have seen many opinions of heretics—and equally false ones—being put forward. For concerning this temple, Valentinus said one thing, Bardesanes another, Apollinaris another, Nestorius another, Eutyches another, and Timothy Hilarus another—heresiarchs who lied as it pleased them—so that, as though truth had arisen from the earth, conflicts followed. Thus, from the very source from which the orthodox and faithful obtain their reward, the heretics, thinking wrongly about Christ’s incarnation, incur the punishment of eternal condemnation.

Hence we remember that it was said of him by Simeon in the Gospel (Luke II): “Behold, this one is appointed for the falling and rising of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed.”

And upon her head was a crown of twelve stars—that is, of the Church. By the number twelve of the apostles he says that the beginnings of the Church, founded soon afterward, are adorned. Hence the Psalm says (Psalm XX): “You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.”

And she was pregnant in mind, not in the womb, and she cried out. In the valley of weeping, lamenting, she gives birth to those whom she labors to bring forth, and she does not cease to labor over those already born. Hence the Apostle says (Galatians IV): “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

[Col. 0873B]

And another sign appeared in heaven, and behold, a great red dragon, namely bloody and savage, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon its heads seven diadems. The seven heads are seven kings, while the horns are kingdoms; these will be discussed more fully in their proper place. And its tail dragged down a third of the stars of heaven, and cast them to the earth.

The tail signifies wicked prophets, through whom the enemy accomplishes his wickedness. Hence Isaiah says (Isaiah IX): “The prophet who teaches falsehood is himself the tail.” Those who cling to their teachings are said to be hurled down to the earth. By the third part of the stars of heaven he refers to the entire body of the wicked, whether among the angels whom he dragged down with himself from heaven in a like ruin, or among human beings whom he deceived. The stars are those whom the devil makes apostates from the good.

And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she had given birth, he might devour her child. That is, the devil, lying in wait, strives to kill the new human being who has been created according to God, in whom we are renewed in the spirit of our mind through the righteousness and holiness of truth (Ephesians IV), within the Church. In each of the faithful he craftily attempts to conceal the one who has arisen, or to extinguish his progress.

We also remember that this happened in a certain heretic, who is said to have suffocated his offspring through deadly sleep, even unto death. In him the birth of life—through which we are commanded to walk—is prophetically represented as being killed.

[Col. 0873C]

He is said to have stood in the woman’s presence because of the words: “She will watch your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel” (Genesis III).

And she gave birth to a male child who was to rule all the nations with an iron rod. He is called male because we know that victory is rightly assigned to the male sex, as the superior one. Here Christ, the head of the Church, is rightly said to be born in each of the members, since he is known to rule. For he is the author and perfecter of faith, in whom we shall perform mighty deeds.

With an iron rod—that is, with inflexible justice. He will rule over the good; he will break the wicked. This is also fitted to his Church as to his body and to the head. For, he says, “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III); and, “The two will become one flesh.” The Apostle says that this is to be understood both in Christ and in the Church (Ephesians V).

[Col. 0873D]

And her child was taken up to God and to his throne. Although this took place first in Christ the head, who, having completed the dispensation, ascended to the Father, it nevertheless also applies to the body. Hence are those words of the Apostle (Ephesians II): “He raised us up and made us sit together in the heavenly places”; and (Philippians III): “Our citizenship is in heaven”; and (Colossians III): “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.”

If you also wish to understand this specifically of Christ’s person, then, except for the suffering which Blessed Mary is not believed to have undergone in childbirth—for we know that she contracted no sin of lust in conception—you may rightly apply the other details, provided that we recognize in the ambushes of the red dragon the persecutions which Christ endured from Herod himself, from his earliest infancy (Matthew I), and thereafter willingly underwent even to the death of the cross. When the dragon, eager for his death, had sought it, but was frustrated by his resurrection, it groaned that he had been taken up to God’s throne, that is, to the Father’s right hand.

And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that he might nourish her there, for 1,260 days. He calls the wilderness the pilgrimage of this present life. In it the Church lives with the singular hope of blessed recompense, like a solitary sparrow (Psalm CI). From her King she has received power to trample upon serpents and scorpions, and upon every power of the enemy, now represented by the red dragon (Mark XVI; Luke X). For the people of Israel, too, when led through the wilderness, were able by looking upon the bronze serpents to overcome the fiery serpents (Numbers XXI). “All these things,” says the Apostle (I Corinthians X), “happened in figure for us”; and just as manna visibly nourished those people, so now he nourishes the Church with heavenly bread.

[Col. 0874A]

She has a prepared place, of which the prophet says (Psalm LXXXIII): “In the place which he appointed”; and also, “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Corinthians III). For the human heart ought to ascend there. By the peace of mutual human speech, he could express both “the appointed place” and “the prepared place,” since he had previously said (Psalm LXXXIII): “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; he has appointed ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping, into the place which he appointed.”

The same place is both a refuge for pilgrims and food for the refreshment of hungry servants; it is the reward promised to those who will reign.

[Col. 0874B]

These things, then, which God has prepared, as the Apostle says (I Corinthians II), “for those who love him”—“God,” he says, “has revealed to us through his Spirit.” Since this Spirit alone reveals them, blessed John too was able to penetrate these depths.

By this number of days, which makes three years and six months, he also signifies here the entire period of Christianity, from the time when Christ’s preaching began until the end, as it bears fruit and grows.

And a battle took place in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and so forth. We must not suppose that God’s angels dared to attack in heaven, since even Job could not be tested there except by God’s permission (Job I). Here “heaven” more clearly signifies the Church, where each of the faithful continually fights against spiritual wickedness.

Hence the Apostle says (Ephesians VI): “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world.”

He says that Michael fights here against the devil together with his angels because he is rightly understood to fight on behalf of the pilgrim Church, praying according to God’s will for her and ministering assistance to her. “Are they not all,” says the Apostle (Hebrews I), “ministering spirits sent into service for the sake of those who are to inherit eternal salvation?”

Indeed, the name Michael is said to be interpreted as “the help of God,” and this work is fittingly assigned to him in particular. Daniel too said that he would come to the Church’s aid in the final distress. “At that time,” he says (Daniel XII), “Michael will arise, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there will come a time such as has not been since the nations began to exist, even until that time. And at that time your people will be saved, everyone who is found written in the book.”

[Col. 0874C]

As for the statement that they are “his angels,” he uses here the same manner of expression in which we read (Matthew XVIII): “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” These are, of course, those whose fellow citizens they began to be through believing in Christ; so here too they are called “his angels,” because they are believed to be rewarded by one presiding King and blessed by one Spirit who gives them life.

And the dragon fought, and his angels, but they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven. The devil and his angels are to be understood here: those who are like him in nature and will, but also human beings who, ensnared in their traps, become followers of such beings.

For according to the qualities of their wills, it is said both of the devil, “An evil man did this” (Matthew XIII), and of Judas, “He is a devil” (John VI). The devil is handed down as existing in his own people with a twofold body. Yet he is said to be overcome and expelled by those who, after renouncing him and receiving the faith of Christ, no longer return to his errors, but in whom love perseveres “from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” (I Timothy I).

Alternatively, this may refer to the time when the Church, completely separated from every mixture of evil and glorified in the blessedness to come, will grant the devil and his angels no place at all, either for deceiving the wicked or for testing the good.

Therefore the Psalm, marking him out, says (Psalm XXXVI): “I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found.”

[Col. 0874D]

And that dragon was cast out—the great and ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole inhabited world. He was cast down to the earth, and his angels were cast down with him to the earth.

Here those who think according to earthly things are understood: among them, when that sentence prevails, the devil is known to dwell—“You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Genesis III). Excluded from spiritual beings, he invades those earthly people who are suited to his deserts; this is what it means for him to be cast down from heaven and thrown upon the earth.

And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying: “Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come.” It is clearly shown in what sense we ought here to understand “heaven.” For we know that Christ’s victory has brought salvation in the Church, through which she has also received the recognized authority to bind what has been loosed and to loose what has been bound. In the person of one Peter, the whole Church heard this in a general sense: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose will be loosed” (Matthew XVI).

[Col. 0875A]

Concerning this the Lord says (Matthew XXVIII): “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” He does not mean authority which he himself always possessed, but authority which, from the time he willed it, he began to possess in the Church as the head in the members.

For the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before our God day and night. They overcame him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony.

Using the manner of expression introduced shortly before, he speaks from the person of the angels: “the accuser of our brothers,” that is, of those who will be our fellow citizens in the future but are now pilgrims. For the faithful are now journeying toward that heavenly city, Jerusalem, which the angels happily inhabit.

As for the claim that he was excluded from heaven and cast down to earth, and that they are said to proclaim this with joy, they rejoice in the redemption of those whom the Lord has graciously deigned to prepare as a temple for himself to inhabit. For the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

Concerning the earthly people into whom he is said to have descended, the angels, by recognizing the inner sanctuaries of divine justice, praise God together with understanding, and sing of mercy and judgment over the blessed, since divine goodness is displayed in the redeemed and divine equity in the lost.

Those who conquer are likewise said to have been able to overcome the devil through the Lamb’s blood. And as for what follows, “They did not love their lives even unto death,” they are to be understood as having received that love which is poured into our hearts—not from ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans V).

[Col. 0875B]

Teaching that we ought to rejoice in so great a good, he says: “Therefore rejoice, heavens, and you who dwell in them.” If, as above, “heaven” is understood as the Church in the angels, then this applies fittingly to both, who rejoice together harmoniously in the Lord, since human beings are believed to be joined to the angels, and the angels minister to the human substance in Christ.

It follows: “Woe to you, earth and sea, because the devil has come down to you with great anger, knowing that he has only a short time remaining!” Just as exultation was due to the redeemed, so lamentation ought to be offered for those who perish.

Hence Ezekiel says (chapter II) that he received a book containing “lamentation, song, and woe.” In “lamentation” he signifies the weeping of penitents; in “song,” the joy of the saints; while “woe” properly reveals the condemnation of the wicked.

This too he mentions here, saying: “Woe to you, earth and sea,” and so forth, up to “knowing that he has only a short time remaining.” Hence, compelled by the Lord’s unconquerable power to confess, he says: “Have you come before the time to torment us?”

[Col. 0875C]

And when the dragon saw that he had been cast down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. This is what we previously stated: that the devil wages an irreconcilable enmity against the Church. For when he is excluded, destined to be overcome, he does not cease multiplying his cunning devices all the more fiercely.

And two wings like those of a great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the wilderness, to her place. The Church uses the two Testaments as wings. Taught by them, she strives to flee the enemy’s ambushes through the commandments and overcomes them through the examples they provide.

She is also governed by the twofold love of God and neighbor. The place of the wilderness is the pilgrimage of this worldly existence. For as long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord (II Corinthians V). The heart is directed there most effectively by one who departs from the world not in place but in affection. Thus the prophet says (Psalm LIV): “Behold, I have fled far away, and I remained in the wilderness. I was waiting for him who would save me.”

[Col. 0875D]

Appropriately, he mentions here the likeness of an eagle. Although it is known to fly higher than other birds, when it sees food from far away, conquered by its natural need, it immediately descends to the lower places. So the Church, in her spiritual members, seeks and savors in her mind the things that are above (Colossians III), yet, weighed down by the weakness of the body, she remains subject to bodily need, for which she groans and labors even now. For creation was subjected to vanity (Romans VIII), not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope.

Again: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (II Corinthians V).

Where she is nourished for a time and times and half a time, away from the presence of Antichrist—that is, of that serpent—for three years and six months. This again signifies the period during which the Church of Christ God is extended to the end, fleeing the worship of idols and every error of the serpent. This is what is meant by “from the presence of that serpent,” whom he previously calls the dragon, whom she conquered by the Lamb’s blood, so that she may truly sing (Psalm XC): “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk; you will trample the lion and the dragon.”

And the serpent cast water from its mouth after the woman like a river, so that it might destroy her. The water signifies the onrush of persecutors. Hence the Psalm says (Psalm CXXIII): “When people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When their anger was kindled against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us like water. Our soul passed through the torrent,” and so forth.

[Col. 0876A]

But the earth helped the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from its mouth. Although “earth” can also be understood here as the Church, as in the Psalm (Psalm CII): “He founded the earth upon its stability; it will not be moved forever and ever”—that is, in the saints, whose prayers, teachings, and salutary administration expose and nullify the enemy’s cunning—it is better understood here as the human nature in Christ.

That nature is itself the truth that arose from the earth (Psalm LXIV). Always appearing before the face of God, as the Apostle says (Hebrews IX), it intercedes for us. This earth, swallowing up the death assumed into itself, is said to open its mouth like a mouth when, through the abundance of its life, it is recognized to have swallowed the author of death (Romans VIII). Likewise, it is said to have taught [absorbebam; perhaps *absorbendum*, “that which is to be swallowed”], when, sitting on the mountain (Matthew V), it opened its mouth and gave greater commandments to the disciples, nullifying the law of commandments (Ephesians II).

And the dragon became angry with the woman and went away to make war with the rest of her offspring, those who keep the commandment of God and possess the testimony of Jesus Christ.

Seeing that the persecution could not be continued and that the harmful desires by which he thought—or wished—that Christ’s Church could be removed from the world could not be brought to fulfillment, namely, since the trophy of the Lord’s body had prevailed in the heavenly places, ruled in earthly places, and exercised authority over the realms below.

[Col. 0876B]

For, as the Apostle says (Romans XIV), “Christ died and rose again for this purpose, that he might rule over both the living and the dead”; and likewise (Philippians II): “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.”

Seeing this, I say, he continually attempts to wage war against the rest of the Church’s offspring in each generation. He now knows that he cannot entirely uproot her from the world, because, he says, “the gates of hell will not prevail against her” (Matthew XVI).

Christ makes marvelous use of him to acquire for himself, at the proper time, a multitude of martyrs. But he has decreed that the dragon and his fiercer associates be punished by more severe judgments.

[Col. 0876C]

For this reason, I think that this book is more fittingly concluded with the memorable victory of that same Church, whose memory cannot perish from the world.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0877]

## CHAPTER XIII
And I saw a beast rising from the sea, having ten horns and seven heads, and upon its horns diadems. Here he has designated as “the sea” what he previously called the abyss, from which he said that this beast would rise. In both instances, however, a people is signified: he sees a people rising from the people, and the beast arising from the people.

“Beast” is a general designation, opposed to the Lamb; but in the exposition it must be understood according to the particular passages, indicating which part of the beast is meant. For at one time he calls the devil the beast, at another his body, at another one of the heads of that beast, which, as though slain, rose again from death—an imitation of the true faith—and at another he calls only the rulers the beast.

Now, by the beast rising from the sea he means the body of the devil, having ten horns and seven heads, with diadems upon its horns and the name of blasphemy upon its heads. Since it wishes to be regarded as God, it is rightly said to be titled with the name of blasphemy. Concerning the ten horns and seven heads, a more suitable explanation is given in the following passage, where it is shown that each of the two designations is sufficient everywhere.

And the beast that I saw was like a leopard, and its feet were like those of a bear, and its mouth was like the mouth of a lion. It is compared with a leopard because of the diversity of the nations, with a bear because of its bestial wickedness, and with a lion because of the strength of its body and the pride of its speech.

And the dragon gave it his power, his throne, and great authority. Thus the Apostle speaks concerning the body of the devil: “Whose coming,” he says (II Thess. II), “is according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders, among those who are perishing.”

And one of its seven heads seemed to have been slain unto death, and the wound of its death was healed. By one of its heads he means the Antichrist, because the seven are not seven in number but signify the universality of the earthly kingdom opposed to the Lamb. It is certain that the dragon—that is, the devil—gives him his power and his throne. For just as, in the good, the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, so, in evil, the enemy is said to give his throne to those whom he chiefly possesses and uses to seduce others. Through them he frequently performs astonishing deeds, God permitting it. Such is the impiety to which he advances: in order to deceive the minds of the simple, he dares to present one of the seven heads, in imitation of the true Head, as though slain and risen again, to be received in place of Christ, who truly accomplished this.

And the nations dwelling on the earth were amazed. He transferred the names from the beast, so that he would not say, “The beast, having marveled, followed the beast.” He called the earth “the earthly,” meaning those who preferred to follow and worship him—that is, his own people, who are said to worship the devil in the Antichrist as in an image.

This is what he says: “And they worshiped the dragon, because he had given all his authority to the beast. And they worshiped the beast, saying: Who is like the beast? And who can wage war against it?”

When it is praised by its own followers as preeminent—as we read—and when it opens the mouths of the nations, displaying the virtues of the good and producing admiration for a living being turned toward the earth, then, I say, when it is praised by its own and exalted in grandiloquent speech, the entire body of the beast is being described.

And authority was given to it to act for forty-two months. In these months, three years and six months are completed, during which the severity of the present persecution—and now, specifically, of the final persecution—is foretold. For, because the world has four well-known regions, if one takes the legal decad four times, in which there is a sign of perfection, one completes the number forty. When two commandments of charity are added to these and fulfilled in practice, they complete forty-two. For the words announced would have been of no benefit if they were not fulfilled in deeds. During these months the Church is said to be protected for a time like an eagle’s wings, fleeing into the wilderness from the dragon’s snares and being nourished for 1,260 days, by which the forty-two months are fulfilled, so that the same number may clearly not have been assigned without significance.

And it opened its mouth in blasphemy against God, to blaspheme his name and his tabernacle and those who dwell in heaven—that is, against God and the Church that dwells in heaven. For this reason the Apostle says (Phil. III): “Our citizenship is in heaven”; and elsewhere (Rom. VIII): “Now you are not in the flesh.”

Alternatively: I think that the glorified body of Christ is here also signified as a trophy. The Antichrist is then said to blaspheme it when he dares to assign to himself the dignity that properly belongs to Christ.

For this reason the Lord says in the Gospel: “So that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led astray”; but he immediately adds: “Yet for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened” (Matt. XXIV).

And authority was given to it to wage war with the saints, and to conquer them. By saying, “It opened its mouth,” he shows that it had burst forth into this damnable confidence, so that what it had previously blasphemed secretly it now dared to blaspheme publicly, when it dared to assign to itself the dignity specifically owed to Christ and to speak wickedness in high places, wishing, as Christ’s adversary, either by force to insert itself in his place or by fraud to substitute itself for him.

It will receive authority for a time. Abusing it, and wishing to harm the body of Christ, it will be exalted still further, like the persecutors were against Christ in his suffering, and will be tormented more severely with its followers. Concerning this the Lord says (John XIX): “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above.” If, then, Christ granted such authority for a moment to his persecutors concerning his own passion (John XIV), when the prince of this world found nothing in him worthy of death, what is surprising if he permits the wicked to rage against his Church for a time, so that Scripture says that they conquered it? Yet the part must be understood as being meant by the whole, for only a part can be conquered.

And authority was given to it over every tribe and people and language and nation; and all who dwell on the earth worshiped it, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world.

It would have seemed too little if it had been said of that beast, so often presented as opposed to the Lamb: “It is not the Lamb,” or “It is not Christ,” whom it pretends to be. Rather, neither it nor those who consent to it have deserved to be written in the Lamb’s book. Yet the body of the beast may also be understood, because he had first said: “All who dwell on the earth worshiped it”—that is, the earthly, who worship the devil, to whom it was said, “You shall eat earth” (Gen. III). Concerning them Jeremiah says: “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. XXXII); and the Psalm says: “And let them not be written with the righteous” (Ps. LXVIII).

If anyone has ears, let him hear. Whoever leads into captivity will himself go into captivity. Whenever the Spirit says here things that must be heard with particular attention, he introduces them in this way.

Having mentioned the authority that the devil and the beast would receive, lest we should regard the momentary arrogance of a ruinous height as something important, he instructs us—as though anticipating human thoughts—by saying: “Whoever leads into captivity will himself go into captivity.” It is as though he said: The devil and the beast, who now seem to be taking the nations captive in their nets, will himself, together with his followers, soon be a captive.

And whoever kills with the sword must himself be killed with the sword. Knowing that such things would immediately be avenged at the Lord’s coming, he therefore says: “He himself must be killed with the sword.” He speaks absolutely of the person of the devil and the Antichrist, as though dwelling together with his habitation. For this reason he says indefinitely: “Whoever leads into captivity,” he says, “will himself be taken captive; and whoever kills with the sword must himself be killed with the sword.”

For this reason the Apostle says (II Thess. II): “Then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming.” This will occur when death has been swallowed up in victory (I Cor. XV), when all the saints must patiently and steadfastly wait. Therefore he adds: “Here is the patience and faith of the saints.” Hence the same Apostle says (Gal. VI): “Brothers, let us not grow weary, for in due season we shall reap, if we do not fail.”

And I saw another beast rising from the earth, having two horns like those of a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon; and it exercised all the authority of the first beast on the earth.

It attempted to usurp for itself the two horns resembling those of the Lamb—the two Testaments that properly belong to the Lamb. Yet it is said to speak like a dragon because, in hypocrisy—that is, in a pretense of truth—it deceives those whom it seduces. It would not resemble the Lamb if it spoke openly like a dragon. But now it pretends to be a lamb in order to attack the Lamb, that is, the body of Christ. It speaks like a dragon because it drives from the way of truth those whom it deceives while they seek him.

And it exercised all the authority of the first beast on the earth. He said “of the first,” namely, the beast that he had previously said he saw rising from the sea, to which the devil had given his great authority. He said that this beast exercised that authority in the presence of the first beast.

For in the rulers whom he appoints lies the whole authority of the people, like that of locusts and horses in their tails. While the people stand by, the rulers do what advances the devil’s will, under the cloak of the Church’s hypocrisy.

It is so evident that the two beasts are one body and practice the worship of one wickedness that the hypocrisy of the second beast is said to serve the first beast. Therefore he adds:

So that those who dwell on the earth would worship that first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed. And it performed signs, so that it even made fire descend from heaven in the sight of human beings; and it deceived those who dwell on the earth—or, as another translation has it, “the earth and those who dwell in it.”

Again he transfers the names. He called the beast with the heads “the earth,” and its head “the beast.” For he had said that the wound of its head had been healed. Now he says “the beast whose wound was healed,” showing that he calls all the parts of the beast “the beast,” because in all its functions it is the devil who is the beast.

Thus the beast with two horns, which is a part of the beast, causes the beast to worship the beast, because he said “the earth” in order to transfer the name “beast” to the head, as though slain; otherwise he would have said: “The beast caused the beast to worship the beast.” For the beast is one thing and the earth another, since the beast is the people, while the earth has killed.

He rightly said “the earth and those who dwell in it.” For it would have been sufficient to say either “the earth” or “those who dwell on the earth.” But he shows the force of the deception and that they have miserably enslaved both soul and body to themselves. Whoever falls by force, without being deceived, is captive in body alone. Whoever is deceived is taken captive both in body and in mind.

Therefore he said: “It causes the earth and those who dwell in it to worship the beast whose mortal wound was healed, and it lived.”

Let us examine the matter more closely. Our Lord Jesus Christ has a wound from the sword, and he lived. But here he says that the beast has a wound inflicted by the sword, and it lived. He says that the dragon was worshiped and that the beast was worshiped.

[The text is uncertain here.] When the dragon alone is worshiped by its own, For just as the Church has a mediator bodily between itself and God, so the devil does not have a mediator between himself and his own, except in name, by imitation of Christ. This beast that he has mentioned has no personal existence between the devil and his own, because it exists only in the term by which they say that they worship Christ, who died and rose again (Rom. VIII). In that term they worship the devil, who devised this image for his own followers.

Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light (II Cor. XI), deceitfully presenting Christ to his own in name only. Thus he himself fills both his own place and the place of the mediator; he has no mediator except the image of Christ.

He says that this very imitation has a wound from the sword and lives. It is a beast because it is by this name that it moves among itself and its followers. Therefore, whenever he says that the beast which has a wound from the sword and lived is worshiped, he indicates the devil. Concerning him the Apostle says (II Thess. II): “He who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.”

Thus there are three: the devil; the beast, as though slain; and the people with their rulers; through the image, however, they are two. Whenever he says that the intermediary is worshiped, the matter falls back upon the devil, who fills both his own place and that of this intermediary name when he presents himself to his followers for damnable worship, by a simulated imitation and deceptive shadowing of the term.

And it performed great signs, so that it made fire descend from heaven in the sight of human beings. Although he says that it will perform many signs, he gives this sign precedence over the others as especially memorable.

This translation speaks as though of the past, although it announces the future. Elsewhere, signifying the future, it says: “So that it may make fire descend from heaven”—that is, from the Church to the earthly. Whether from the diversity of nations or from the enemies’ deceptive cunning, it will make its ministers speak in new and many tongues, so that by this sign, as it were, they may boast that they have received the gift of the Holy Spirit—he who is truly read to have once caused Christ’s disciples to proclaim the form of fiery tongues over each of them (Acts II).

For the Lord himself commends this sign above all in believers, saying (Mark XVI): “These signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues,” and so forth.

It is therefore no wonder if that beast, which falsely assumes the name of the slain and living Lamb, also fraudulently claims, by imitation and merely in appearance, this gift of the Holy Spirit, and pretends to grant condemnation through its ministers, just as we remember that Simon once desired this but was unable to accomplish it.

For when those ministers of Satan themselves, enumerating exorcisms and many signs, say (Matt. VII), “Did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons?” and so forth, the Lord does not approve their boasting but condemns and rejects them as defiant.

Perhaps for this reason he wished especially to name this outstanding sign of fire, by which the Holy Spirit is symbolized, since nothing more powerful than it could be found. For although many heresies appear to share many things with us, the Church of Christ boasts that it alone possesses this gift in particular.

Finally, the magicians of Pharaoh, who performed miracles resembling those of Moses (Exod. VIII), are read to have been confounded by the Holy Spirit. When they succumbed in their assertions and, defeated, confessed the truth, they said: “This is the finger of God.”

That the finger of God is called the Holy Spirit is attested by the Gospel: one says (Matt. XII), “By the Spirit of God I cast out demons”; another (Luke XI), “By the finger of God I cast out demons.”

For this reason the intensity of the deception is shown: the beast is thought to possess that Spirit by whose resistance the fraud of the magicians was emptied of power.

For this reason it follows:

And it deceived those who dwell on the earth because of the signs that were granted it to perform in the presence of the beast. And it says to the inhabitants of the earth that they should make an image of the beast that has the wound inflicted by the sword and lived.

It is as though he said: This imitation prevailed to such an extent that the earthly, deceived because of the signs of the beast and miserably favoring the beast with their consent, urge one another by mutual devotion to fashion an image of the beast in the imagination of their hearts. They no longer think that doubt is permissible; confirmed, as it were, by the certain judgment of the fire just mentioned, they conclude that he truly is Christ, although the devil is in the Antichrist. The same malignant spirit is in the image, and, God permitting it, he displays such pools of deception that he is said to give spirit to the image of that beast and to cause the image of the beast to speak.

This passage can be understood in two ways. First, because the whole body of the wicked has already been persuaded, as though the devil were at work and the rulers were pressing upon the people, so that there might be one identical confession for all, just as a uniform observance is to be proclaimed by everyone. If anyone did not speak through the image of the beast—that is, through mutual imitation—he would be killed.

Thus he says:

So that the image of the beast might speak and cause those who did not worship the image of the beast to be killed.

Alternatively, just as, when the first human being was being deceived, the serpent spoke to the woman with its mouth (Gen. III), so at that time he will deceive many by a similar fraud, when he causes his counselors to receive responses through an image—that is, through the Antichrist, to whom they think honor should be rendered as to God, although he is the man of sin and the son of perdition (II Thess. II).

This is the meaning of: “And it was granted to him to give spirit to the image of that beast, and to cause the image of the beast to speak, and to cause those who did not worship the image of the beast to be killed.”

And it caused all—the great and the small, the rich and the slaves—to bear a mark on their right hand or on their foreheads. He wished to divide individuals according to individual members, whom he frequently embraces together indistinguishably in one body and under the name of the beast.

The hand signifies works; the right hand, the imitation of truth; the forehead, the profession of faith. Because they have been deprived of both good things, they are therefore said to be marked in both places.

So that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark of the name of the beast or the number of its name. By mentioning buying and selling, he taught that just as, in the good, the Church hands down a symbol that will benefit our salvation, so those people in evil know themselves to be constrained and bound by such a defense, as it were, so that they are not permitted to buy or sell. They resemble merchants who appear to be carried in one ship and are recognized as being held by a uniform sign.

Unless he has the mark of the name of the beast and the number of its name.

Here is wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast. For it is the number of a human being, and its number is six hundred and sixty-six.

There is one expression: “Whoever has the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of its name.” Earlier he mentioned only the mark; afterward he explained it by synonyms, saying both “mark” and “name” and “the number of the name.” “Here is wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast.” For, he says, “it is the number of a human being.”

Let us therefore accept the number he mentioned, so that in the number we may also recognize the name and the mark. “Its number,” he says, “is six hundred and sixty-six.” We shall calculate it according to the Greeks, especially since he was writing to Asia and according to the idiom of their language: “I am,” he says (below, XXII), “the alpha and the omega.”

Having presented as far as possible the imitations of the opposing party, by which the devil strives to usurp for himself the honor of divinity that does not belong to him, he expresses the Antichrist as opposed to divine honor and warns that his character is to be investigated either through the mark or through the number of his name—that is, of the beast’s most wicked will and action.

There is a name which, when measured by its letters—the characters by which the Greeks read numbers—will plainly be found to amount to six hundred and sixty-six. When interpreted, it is also said to mean “opposed to honor,” by which is meant something unsuitable, inappropriate, or incongruous. For honor does not belong to him; anathema does.

Thus, through the number, the name is found, and from the name the number is calculated; through the interpretation of the name itself, the character of his merits is recognized.

Another name, which likewise contains the sum of that number, may prudently be considered. Its letters, taken together, produce six hundred and six. Their interpretation, however, is “I deny” (*nego*). Nor is it surprising that the Antichrist is said to be worthy of this designation, namely, “of denial,” since the name of Christ corresponds to belief. He himself testifies to this when he says (John VI): “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent”; and again (John XIV): “You believe in God; believe also in me.”

Accordingly, whether you say “opposed to honor,” which is **ἄντεμος** (*antemos*), or “I deny,” which is **ἀρνυμαι** (*arnymai*), both may rightly be referred to the Antichrist, since through two parts of speech—namely, a noun and a verb—the quality of the person and the severity of his work are indicated.

For the name of Christ, whom the Antichrist desires to be accepted through a false imitation, also properly completes the number of days that this passage repeatedly foretells as destined to occur during the persecution of the Antichrist: namely, 1,225 days, in whose appearance the adversary fraudulently sets himself forward.

This is expressed in the mark, that is, in the monogram, which is formed in this manner, in which the entire name of Christ is included in abbreviated form.

Yet the name’s number, written out in full as previously given, again completes the sum of 1,225 days, because in the number forty-six we remember that the form of the Lord’s body is signified. The second Adam, Christ, received this body from Mary in order to correct the errors of the first Adam. For this reason he says in the Gospel (John II): “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” When the Jews replied, “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” the evangelist explains: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

And not without reason. For the name Adam, written in Greek letters, completes the number forty-six in this way, the letters together making XLVI. When this number itself is also expanded, written out and multiplied by itself—that is, forty-six—it likewise completes the number in Greek letters, in a manner which, when the parts are reduced to one, produces 1,225.

Above we spoke of the monogram. Now, in the orderly sequence of the name written out, the sum of the same number is demonstrated to be contained in it. Since both correspond to one another, they unquestionably indicate not an empty but a certain mystery.

Perhaps this is related to what the Apostle says concerning the imitation of the Antichrist (II Thess. II): “So that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.” For in this book also he says: “The temple of God in heaven was opened”—namely, the temple of the one born from the Virgin—so that, just as there is a false imitation of the slain Lamb and of similar realities, so the temple of God may also be transformed by artifice rather than truth.

I do not doubt that some may be troubled by the number 1,225, since three years and six months do not produce that same total. But it must be understood that Scripture does not always indicate this period in one manner or under the definition of one and the same number.

For in this very book, speaking of the woman who is suffering, it says (above, XII): “And she will be nourished for a time and times and half a time.” Elsewhere, concerning the dragon and the beast, it says (above, XI): “Authority was given to it for forty-two months.” Again it says: “I will grant my two witnesses that they may prophesy for 1,260 days.” Yet it is clear that between forty-two months and 1,260 days there is a difference of seventeen days.

Nor do we know that this number is placed variously only in this book, since in Daniel’s visions also this period is signified by different quantities. For he says (Dan. IX, XI, XII), “a time of times,” that is, one year and two years, according to the Hebrew manner of expression. Again he says, “1,290 days.” Elsewhere, in the tenth vision, he gives 1,395 days.

All these things concerning the significance of the period seem to be set forth in such a way that neither the day of judgment nor the second coming would be disclosed to human knowledge, and that the abundance of divine speech and its varied presentation might exercise the devout.

When the disciples asked whether he would restore the kingdom of Israel at that time, the Lord answered: “It is not for you to know the times that the Father has established in his own authority.”

Moreover, when the Greek expression—that is, forty-six—is written through its letters and added by its component numerical values, it does not depart from the significance of the period. For it produces 1,317.

## Chapter XIV
And behold, I saw a Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand; and they have his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads.

After the likeness which the adversarial power reveres and to which it makes itself similar had been shown, it was also necessary to declare the unconquered camp of the Church, lest a weak mind should suppose that this same Church had either succumbed to so violent an assault of persecution or perished, and lest anyone should think that one of the number of the elect had fallen. He therefore preferred to mention those who had resolved to seize the path of the narrower way and the more constricted track [Col. 0886B], and, to show that the imitation belonged to the adversaries, not to the truth, which the men of God knew that good men rightly bear: “They had,” he says, “his name”—that is, the Lamb’s—and “the name of his Father written on their foreheads.”

This finite number, however, ought to be understood as standing for the infinite, and as consecrated by the significance of a hidden mystery. For when the number three is tripled, it becomes nine; and when four is multiplied by four, sixteen results. Nine times sixteen produces one hundred and forty-four. In this number the fullness of the virgin choir is mystically indicated, so that, when such a great multitude is spoken of among these, there may be no doubt concerning the other members of the Church.

“And I heard a voice from heaven, like the sound of many waters or of a great thunder; and the voice that I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps [Col. 0886C], and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. No one could sing the song except the one hundred and forty-four thousand, who had been purchased from the earth. These are they who did not defile themselves with women, for they remained virgins. These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.”

Some have thought that this passage should be explained in such a way that it be understood not only of those who are virgins in faith and in the flesh, but also of those who were able to use lawful marriage temperately. They add the examples of the prophets and patriarchs, whom we know to have pleased God through the greatest zeal for holiness, lest men of such outstanding life be judged excluded from the company of virgins.

But when the matter is examined with careful attention, the evident distinction of merits in the Church of Christ appears from the distribution of divine gifts: a distinction differing in profession, order, and vow. Set apart is the singular and special dignity of those who, though they had marriages, are shown not only to have contracted no offense, but also—by using marriage solely for the begetting of offspring—to have acquired great merits, because the prophetic purpose of such marriages served the coming of Christ. To say nothing of the other virtues in which, as Scripture testifies, we learn that they flourished: with their eminent rank, I say, set apart, no one will ever have thought that the glory of virginity can be made equal either to conjugal chastity or even to widowly continence.

Although this is established by many testimonies of divine Scripture [Col. 0887A], it is especially declared in this passage. When the blessed Augustine hastened to explain it and undertook its exposition, I have taken into this work what he had previously said or understood, from his book which he composed on holy virginity, so that it may be clear that virgins hold an honorable place above others. In addition to the integrity of faith, according to which the whole Church is a virgin, they have vowed themselves to Christ while preserving the integrity of the flesh.

For he says:

“Let marriages have their own good—not because they beget children, but because they beget them honorably, lawfully, chastely, and in companionship, and because they bring up those whom they have begotten together, healthfully and diligently; because they keep faith with one another in the marriage-bed, because they do not violate the sacrament of marriage. Yet all these are gifts belonging to human duty. Virgin integrity, however, and freedom from all intercourse through pious continence, is an angelic portion, and in corruptible flesh it is a continual meditation on everlasting incorruption. Let all fruitfulness of the flesh yield to this; let conjugal chastity yield. The former is not within one’s power; the latter is not in eternity. Carnal fruitfulness is not subject to free choice; heaven does not possess conjugal chastity. Surely those who already have something not of the flesh in the flesh will possess something great beyond others in that common immortality.”

And a little later:

“Therefore,” he says, “I have no command from the Lord concerning virgins”—by which the preacher is taught to look toward eternal salvation; from what is announced, the one who announces is indicated.

Hence the Psalm [Col. 0887C] (103): “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire.”

He continues:

“Fear God instead, and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come.”

Although from the beginning of the Christian faith we have known that the kingdom of heaven is drawing near, here he announces with the greatest urgency that the hour of God’s judgment is already, even now, about to arrive. For this reason he necessarily placed this kind of preaching first, to be proclaimed to all, just as the Lord also says (Matt. 24): “This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world, and then the end will come.”

And to show the moment of time in which the hostility of the final persecution would arise, he added “instead,” as though he were saying that the temporal power of the beast should be considered of little account, and that the Lord should be feared rather than human beings—the Lord whom his aforementioned creature acknowledges to be eternal [Col. 0887D].

“And worship him,” he says, “who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of waters.”

And another, a second angel, followed him, saying:

“Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, from the wine of the wrath of her fornication.”

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” In it is signified the city and people of the devil, together with every corruption of vices, which he continually exercises to its own destruction and to that of the human race.
