He says that this Babylon, which is destined to fall, has already fallen, using the customary language of Scripture, which often constructs the past tense in place of the future when it knows that what it foretells will inevitably be fulfilled—for example, “They divided my garments among themselves” (Ps. 21), and similar passages—or because the proud are then recognized to have fallen when they dared to act proudly.

Hence the Psalm (72): “You cast them down,” he says, “when they were lifted up”—that is, they were cast down precisely when they had become exalted.

In its customary manner, Scripture says, “All the nations fell from the wine of her fornication,” although this city, which is desired and is assembled from nations gathered from everywhere, itself drank from the wine of fornication. For all the nations, intoxicated by errors, are that city; yet in its customary manner he divides the one city.

And a third angel followed him, saying in a loud voice:

“If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives its name on his forehead or on his hand, he too will drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed in the cup of his wrath.”

Enough and more than enough has already been said about the beast and its image. But because certain heretics depart from us through an evil credulity, while others, straying through the discordant perversity of their conduct, diverge from our traditions, they are all briefly included here in the inscription of the beast placed upon the living, whether on the forehead or on the hand. They are shown to perish by an enemy evil.

The cup of wrath, however, ought not here to be understood only of that wrath of which the Lord says (John 3), “The wrath of God remains upon him,” indicating original sin; it also refers to that of which he says, speaking to the obstinate Jews (John 8), “You will die in your sin,” thereby signifying the added merits of damnable actions.

“And he will be punished with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb, and the smoke of their torments will rise forever and ever.”

He says “in the presence of the Lamb,” whose judgment they will suffer—he whom they proudly despised and whose members they unjustly desire to rule—and, indeed, in the presence of his angels, who, by God’s revelation, know that these people are paying just penalties [Col. 0888C].

“And they will have no rest day or night, those who worship the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name.”

By this manner of narration he has constructed the whole body of the beast from the dead and those still living. What is now said to be tormented in the dead is understood still to be worshiped in the living. But when it says that those who worship the beast and its image—that is, the devil—will have no rest day or night, this refers either to that slain head or to the whole body.

“This is the patience of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.”

Hence the Lord says (Matt. 10), “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved,” and the Apostle (Heb. 10), “You have need of patience.” So here too the patience of the saints is said to consist in this: that, persevering to the end, they flee from fellowship with the beast and from the mark of its name.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me:

“Write: Blessed are those dead who die in the Lord.”

Those are said to die in the Lord who, proven in faith and life, have deserved to be called away from here.

Then it follows:

“From now on, the Spirit also says, let them rest from their labors.”

Just as, by contrast, he said that the wicked would have no rest day or night, so now he says that the faithful have deserved rest from their good works. For after mentioning the deeds of the wicked, it was fitting also to proclaim the blessedness and fullness of the good. Since this blessedness consists in leaders and peoples, he briefly embraces both here, first speaking indefinitely:

“Blessed are those dead who die in the Lord.”

But for those who labor in the vineyard he says, “Let them rest from their labors” (Matt. 20), thus promising happiness to all, while assigning the special fruit of rest after labor to those who work in the vineyard.

Hence the Apostle says (1 Thess. 20): “We ask you to recognize those who labor among you, who preside over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work.”

Or also concerning himself (1 Cor. 15): “I labored more than all.”

“For their works,” he says, “follow them.”

Of these the prophet says (Ps. 89): “Establish the work of our hands upon us.”

And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and seated upon the cloud was one like the Son of Man, having on his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle [Col. 0889B].

In the cloud he shows the incarnation of our head, Jesus Christ, or the body of the Church which Christ assumed, made white after the fires of persecution, and having a golden crown on its head. These are the elders with golden crowns, or the twelve apostles, whom he principally acquired in faith at the beginning of his preaching.

Hence we read (Ps. 20): “You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.”

The sharp sickle signifies the judicial sentence of separation, owed to the wicked and inflicted upon them more justly by divine judgment on account of the Church, for whose defense Christ the Shepherd is always vigilant.

Hence Zechariah says (Zech. 5): “This is the devouring that has gone out over the face of the whole earth.”

And another angel came out, crying to the one seated upon the cloud:

“Send your sickle and reap, because the hour of reaping has come, because the harvest of the earth is already dry.”

We know from the Lord’s explanation (Matt. 13) that the reapers of the earth will be angels, and that the end of the age is marked beforehand by the judgment of the ripe harvest. Since in this harvest both straw is recognized in the fragile stalks and ears, and grain in the kernels, we appropriately recognize that the due ends of the good and the wicked are signified here, when he says that the sickle is to be applied to the ripe harvest.

To whom, however, could this especially be made known if not to the Church? Then the one seated upon the cloud sent his sickle over the earth, and the earth was reaped.

At the time of the final examination, after the spiritual battles with the beast have been completed, the Church will be able to recognize with greater illumination whom it ought to regard as its own and whom it ought firmly to consider alien. For this is what it means to sit upon the cloud: having received divinely granted judicial power, to distinguish between the good and the wicked.

The Lord says (Matt. 19): “You will sit with me upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

What follows concerning the other angels clearly seems to express the Lord’s judgment, when he says (Matt. 13), “The reapers are angels.”

What threshing is for the harvest, the winepress is for the pressing of grapes, so that the time may come for the burning of the straw and the casting away of the grape-skins, while hidden receptacles of heavenly dwelling receive the fruits to be stored.

And another angel came out of the temple that is in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. Then another angel came, having authority over fire.

The one who has the harvesting sickle also has the vintage sickle; and the one who said to the harvester, “Reap,” said also to the vintager, “Gather the vintage.” For it is one event, and it will take place at one time.

But in harvest and vintage, just as in the cultivation and building of the Church, the figurative breadth of divine speech is displayed when the Apostle says (1 Cor. 3): “You are God’s cultivation; you are God’s building.”

And he cast it into the great winepress of God’s wrath, and the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from it as high as the horses’ bridles for a distance of one thousand six hundred stadia.

By saying “of God’s wrath,” he has here placed the sentence in place of God’s wrath—the sentence inflicted upon the proud one, whom he also calls “great.” “You,” he says, “humbled the proud one as one wounded” [Col. 0890A].

For he used “winepress,” as the Greek copies contain it, in the feminine gender, and “great” in the masculine.

“Outside the city,” that is, outside the Church: after the future separation has taken place, the trampling of every sinful person will be outside.

This winepress, or threshing-floor, gathers together what is useless and tests what is imperishable, like fire tests vessels, and tribulation tests the righteous (Eccl. 27).

The blood flowing as high as the horses’ bridles signifies vengeance reaching as far as the rulers of the peoples. For when the devil and his accomplices begin to pay the penalties of the persecution they inflicted, it is not unfittingly said that the blood of the saints which was shed reaches him and his princes—that is, those horses through whom wars are stirred up in the persons of heretics, and all who follow whatever errors are theirs.

As it was previously proclaimed: “You have sinned in blood, and blood will pursue you.”

The one thousand six hundred stadia signify the four parts of the whole world. For there is a quaternity multiplied by four, as in the four faces of the fourfold creatures and in the wheels. Four times four hundred makes one thousand six hundred.

## CHAPTER XV

And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wondrous: seven angels possessing the seven last plagues.

Having once again restored the order, and about to narrate the same plagues of the final persecution, he wished to make the hearer attentive by saying, “A great and wondrous sign.” We understand the Church to be represented by the seven angels, because in them the indignation of God is brought to completion.

“And I saw,” he says, “something like a glassy sea mingled with fire.”

This means the water of baptism consecrated by the fire of the Holy Spirit, or else, insofar as it pertains to the quality of fire, reddened by martyrdom.

Hence we read: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and tribulation tests righteous people.”

And I saw those standing upon it who had won the victory over the beast and its image.

By “those who stood above,” he demonstrates that they were stable in faith. The Psalm describes such people in almost similar language. After saying, “He made the heavens with understanding,” thereby designating spiritual people who enjoy the serene understanding of heavenly truth, it adds, “He founded the earth upon the waters”—that is, upon baptism—“immovable.”

Although they may appear to have been nourished with milk, they are nevertheless not carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4). Therefore here too they are said to triumph over the beast and its image.

They had the harps of God.

Their hearts were devoted to praise and were harmonious and melodious in the consonant truth of both Testaments; or this signifies the flesh stretched upon the wood of the Passion, where not only the sound of the voice but also the effect of good work is indicated.

For this reason he also inserted mention of that great man Moses, just as God testified, saying (Num. 12): “Moses my servant, who is faithful in all my house.”

And they were singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.

Here he expressed more fully the intention of the elect, who say from the heart: “Remove from me the way of iniquity, Lord, and have mercy on me according to your law” (Ps. 118); or, “Because of your law I have waited for you, Lord” (Ps. 129), and similar words. Thus he wished these people also to be understood as belonging to the number of the faithful, since they share in the victory just mentioned.

In Moses’ song the Old Testament is signified; in the Lamb’s song, the New Testament. Thus he teaches that the fullness of the elect, armed from both, has existed as perfected in both, saying:

“Great and wondrous are your works, Lord God almighty; your ways are just and true, King of all nations.”

The text of both Testaments bears witness to this for us in harmonious truth, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24).

He is more appropriately called King of all nations because God is no longer known only in Judea, nor does heavenly dew still appear to descend upon the fleece alone (Judg. 6). Rather, as Malachi says (ch. 1): “From the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place an offering is sacrificed and presented to my name.”

The following also belongs here:

“Who will not fear and glorify your name? For you alone are merciful; all nations will come and worship before you, because your judgments have been revealed as just.”

These things are explained at length because they can already be seen being fulfilled in deed [Col. 0891C].

After this I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened.

Here he says that the hidden secrets of the testimonies concerning Christ and the Church, which had been promised, are now being disclosed.

And seven angels with seven plagues came out of the temple.

They came from the Church, against which the opposing party had rebelled with unceasing plots. For this reason he says that plagues proceed from it: either for the defense of the saints, in whom the Lord Christ formerly endured insults—as was said to Paul (Acts 9), “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”—or because, as Peter recalls (1 Pet. 4), the time has come for judgment to begin from the house of God.

It is certainly known that people are scourged in two ways: either God justly chastises sins, as in Pharaoh (Exod. 14), or, as in Job, he tests them through a greater exercise of virtue (Job 1).

Nor without reason do we read that he said (Ps. 118): “The Lord tested me as gold that passes through the fire; I kept his ways and did not depart from the commandments of his lips.”

By the number of the angels or of the plagues, I think the universality of the consummation is prefigured, just as he frequently says in Leviticus: “And I will strike you with seven plagues.”

They were dressed in clean and shining linen.

Mortification is usually symbolized by linen. Therefore, if irreproachable judgments of God are also recognized in its brightness, the meaning is appropriately understood in clean linen: those who have been mortified use this brightness when, with unveiled face, they contemplate the glory of God’s judgments (2 Cor. 3).

And they were girded around their chests with golden belts.

We are taught by Scripture that wisdom is represented by gold, which says (Prov. 16, according to the Septuagint): “Receive wisdom as gold.”

And appropriately around the chest, where the priestly breast is often commanded by the law to bear the *logion*, that is, the rational breastpiece, so that a mind conscious of its own goodness may not dare to reproach divine judgments but praise them, and by the splendor of that gold may confidently urge others also to praise.

And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven bowls, full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever.

Earlier he mentions seven angels with an equal number of bowls, bearing the prayers of the saints; now he says that they are full of the wrath of God. These same bowls are said to contain both the sweetness of supplications and the wrath of punishments, when the saints pour out their prayers for the coming of God’s kingdom. At that time the judgments of God, no longer hidden like the abyss but open like bowls, are foretold as bringing salvation to the righteous and destruction to the wicked (Ps. 35), just as the Apostle says (2 Cor. 2): “We are the good fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the former, an odor of death unto death; to the latter, an odor of life unto life.”

For if it was said concerning our Lord (Luke 2), “Behold, this one is appointed for the falling and rising of many,” what is surprising if the bowls provide sweetness to the righteous but inflict the punishment of plagues upon the wicked—provided that here we ought to understand these bowls themselves, and not others?

And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory and power of God.

I think that by the smoke is signified the fact that not everyone can penetrate the hidden things of God’s judgments, and that mortal minds grow dim and tremble when considering the plagues inflicted. These plagues he now undertakes to recount, and he asserts that the smoke remains in the temple until those bowls have reached their end [Col. 0892C].

It rightly follows:

“And no one could enter the temple”—that is, that inner sanctuary—“until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.”

Hence the Psalm (72): “This became labor before me,” he says, “until I entered the sanctuary of God and understood the end.”

Alternatively, confession is commonly signified by smoke. For just as smoke precedes a fire, so confession of sins precedes the flame of faith and charity.

Therefore the Psalm, indicating such people, says (Ps. 103): “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they smoke.”

Finally, the Lord looked upon Peter (Matt. 26) and washed away through tears of confession what he had contracted through fearful denial. Thus the meaning is:

“No one could enter the temple until the seven plagues were completed”—that is, no one could yet say, “I walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of your house” (Ps. 100), or, “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song 1), unless he had taken care to erase all his past offenses by confessing his reproba­ble acts.

“For the thought,” he says (Ps. 75), “of a human being will confess to you.”

Behold, the smoke and the remnants of thought will celebrate solemn rites for you, like a secure praise of justification obtained.

Thus, until all the plagues are completed, the Church is shown in mournful confession: in those whom we have mentioned, paying fruitful penalties for an earlier offense; and in those whom he has established to be tested by a better form of worship.

## CHAPTER XVI
I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels [Col. 0893A]: “Go and pour out upon the earth the seven bowls (which you have received) of the wrath of God.” Here the unavoidable outcome of the divine command is revealed, but also that power which the Church has specially deserved to receive from God: to inflict judgment upon the condemned and mercifully to grant absolution to those who turn back.

And the first went and poured out his bowl upon the earth, and a grievous and most evil sore came upon all who had the inscription of the name of the beast and who worshiped its image. The nature of a deadly wound is such that the small area it occupies in the body has greater power to inflict death than the remaining, healthy part of the body, however extensive, has to preserve a person’s health. And although the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ serves the believers as an aid to salvation, so it serves unbelievers as a testimony to their condemnation [Col. 0893B], a most evil wound inflicted by this plague may be understood to affect the whole body of the lost. For of Christ we read (Luke II): “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many, and as a sign that will be opposed.”

Yet the Jewish people in particular, from whom Antichrist is said to be destined to be born (Gen. XLIX), by this one sin lost whatever observances of the law’s righteousness they might have possessed, and they themselves perished irremediably, because they refused to receive the Christ promised to them. In their person the elder brother is represented as saying to the father (Luke XV): “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment; yet you have never given me a young goat, that I might feast with my friends,” and so forth.

For that people which despised the Lamb, as though scorning the things on the right because of the lambs on the right, embraced [Col. 0893C] the young goat (Matt. XXV), straying, as one destined for condemnation, toward the left: that is, despising Christ and receiving Antichrist. Perhaps for this reason he says here: “A grievous and most evil sore came upon those people who have the inscription of the name of the beast and who worship its image,” so that, convicted by the guilt of this one wound, they might be judged worthy to be punished with eternal punishment.

Of this sin, as of a most evil ulcer, the Lord says (John XV): “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin. If I had not done among them works which no one else has done, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.” This is the irremediable wound.

But because many will have followers after them in their most evil imitation [Col. 0893D], therefore at the end he said, “upon those people who have the inscription of the name of the beast,” lest it be thought that he had spoken only of the Hebrew people. For just as, in the good sense, the law also calls the Gentiles children of Abraham through imitation of faith—not by being born of his flesh, but by confessing that Christ, from the tribe of Judah, rose victorious from the dead—so in the evil sense the Jews must be believed to have followers from among the Gentiles. By receiving and following Antichrist, who is said to be destined to be born from the tribe of Dan (Gen. XLIX), they will be marked as accomplices in the guilt of those whose partners they will be in the punishment of eternal condemnation.

And the second poured out his bowl upon the sea, and it became blood, and every living creature in the sea died. When water is changed into blood [Col. 0894A], it is easy to perceive that this refers to thinking carnally about spiritual things; by this we readily recognize what was symbolized in that first plague which we read was inflicted upon the Egyptians (Exod. VII). But there he says that the sweet waters were changed into blood—whether the rivers of Egypt or the rainwaters, as certain translations show, saying, “And their rainwaters into blood,” which the Greeks likewise rendered *ebremata*.

What is now brought into question, however, is that in this passage he says that the second bowl was poured out upon the sea, that is, upon bitter and salty waters. “And it became,” he says, “blood, and every living creature in the sea died.” Therefore I think that those are signified who among the Jewish people not only strove to understand the spiritual law carnally, and consequently could not recognize Christ in it—for, as the Apostle says (I Cor. II), “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory”—but were also driven so far by the weight of their merits, as though struck by a second wound and a worse plague, that they desired the image of the beast and, bearing the inscription of its name, thought that Antichrist should be worshiped in place of Christ.

For this reason perhaps what is described in Exodus (chapter VII) as having occurred in the first plague is placed here in the second bowl: as though they passed from barren waters even further into the foulness of blood. Through this, it is said, every living creature in the sea—that is, in this world—was killed, the part standing for the whole, as in: “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII). Their manifest barrenness is indicated, concerning whom it is said: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isa. V). These are surely those over whom their tongue was so weakened [Col. 0894C] that, to their own condemnation, they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

And the third poured out his bowl upon the rivers and the fountains of waters, and they became blood. He now includes the remaining Gentiles in general. Just as they had been forestalled by natural error and entangled in muddy desires, so they added to this a carnal understanding even of divine things. Hence the fountains may be understood as the teachings of the Gentiles. Therefore he says: “They became blood,” as also in Genesis: “My spirit,” he says (Gen. IX), “will not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh.” In the Book of Wisdom also he says: “Disturbed by filthy blood in their rebuke”; and because, as the Apostle says (Rom. VIII), “to think according to the flesh is death, and the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God.”

Therefore concerning such people [Col. 0894D], who are said both to offend through sins of this kind and again to incur punishable crimes, he says: “I heard”—may a voice resound in the praises of God [sic]—“the voice of the angels.” And I heard, he says, the angel of the waters saying: “You are just, who are and who were.” The angel of the waters is the messenger of the peoples, inwardly resounding with divine praises; and “you are gracious, because you have judged thus,” for “they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and therefore you gave them blood to drink, because they are worthy.”

Although Jews and Gentiles bodily shed the blood of the saints, which the Lord declares must be avenged—“From the blood of righteous Abel,” he says (Matt. XXIII), “to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah”—the plague of blindness [Col. 0895A] may nevertheless also be understood, so that those too may be recognized as having shed the blood of the prophets who, abusing them, diverted their meaning toward something else. It is as though he were saying: Those who understood the spiritual law carnally are justly handed over to the corruption of flesh and blood, where both the sin and the punishment of sinners are recognized.

Hence the Apostle says (II Thess. II): “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity.”

And I heard another voice saying: “Yes, Lord God almighty, your judgments are true and just.” Here too there is something like what is often said in the Psalms (XL, LXXI, LXXXVIII, CV): “Let it be, let it be.” We ought to say this by imitation, not by delaying over an evident meaning through exposition [Col. 0895B].

And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and power was given to it to scorch and burn people. And people were scorched with great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has authority over these plagues. This power was given not to the sun, but to the angel who poured out the bowl upon it. Nor should this be thought to be the fire of Gehenna; there will no longer be any opportunity there for anyone to blaspheme, when the time of unfruitful repentance comes upon the condemned, so that they will say, as the Law records: “What did our pride profit us? And what did the boast of riches contribute to us?” (Wis. V).

Therefore I think that the fire and heat here should be understood as follows: the body of the devil will be irremediably tormented by the steadfastness of the saints, and, stirred up by that very heat, its members will be compelled to blaspheme. For perhaps “upon the sun” is said with the ablative sense, “from the sun,” namely from the sun [Col. 0895C] of righteousness; just as in: “I will watch over my word to accomplish it” (Jer. I), and Daniel says (Dan. II): “Let us seek mercy from the face of almighty God concerning this mystery,” so that from the source from which the elect receive the firmness of illumination, the impious are said to derive burning.

And they did not repent so as to give him glory. The very death of the blasphemers consists in preferring to accuse God of iniquity rather than themselves of impiety: they do not repent after the plagues but, though scourged, heap insults upon him. For just as bronze vessels, subdued by a great fire, leap up from within and boil over outwardly, exceeding the limits of their capacity, so the part of the beast, resisting in its vastness, when it sees Christ’s Church fighting with tireless steadfastness [Col. 0895D], inflamed by the torches of unbearable envy, exhales through its impure mouth in blasphemies the fire conceived in its heart. Of this fire we read: “Zeal has seized an uneducated people, and now fire will consume the adversaries.”

And the fifth angel poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was darkened, and they gnawed their tongues because of the pain. The throne of the beast, or its kingdom, is said to be darkened as a judicial power, because, deprived of the brightness of eternal happiness, they praise one another while possessing present goods as the highest happiness and suppress the truth in iniquity; therefore they gnaw their tongues.

The Psalm agrees with this meaning (CXLIII), saying: “Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity,” and elsewhere (Ps. LXXII): “They have spoken iniquity on high” [Col. 0896A]. For, lifted up like smoke by the pride of momentary prosperity, they rejoice in darkness, although they ought to have been converted through repentance. “They spend their days in good,” as Job says, “and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI).

And the sixth angel poured out his bowl upon that great river, the Euphrates, and its water was dried up, so that the way might be prepared for the king who comes from the rising of the sun, that is, for Christ, concerning whom we read: “Behold the man; his name is Rising,” for whom, when he comes to judge, the way is prepared.

By the name of the river Euphrates, just as by the sea, the rivers, the fountains of waters, the sun, and the throne of the beast, upon which the angels are said to have poured out their bowls, unclean people are signified. “And its water was dried up,” that is, they will no longer retain anything in themselves from the former people that does not correspond to the fire [Col. 0896B] of the approaching judgment. Just as above he says that the harvest dried up when it was ripe and that the vintage had arrived, so here too he says figuratively that the water of the river was dried up: nothing green remained, but everything was now to be tested by the fire of divine judgment, by which either the impious are consumed like hay or the saints are approved like gold.

And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet. Although malign spirits are said to possess different qualities according to the various passions, afflictions, and vices—for in the Gospel he said in one place, “deaf and mute spirit” (Mark VI), elsewhere “unclean spirit,” and the prophet said elsewhere (Hos. IV), “The spirit of fornication destroyed them”—not for any other reason than that it drives them to commit filthy crimes, nevertheless [Col. 0896C] here he called all three unclean because he represented one body of the devil, composed according to its customary distinctions. He mentioned that body’s greater authority by introducing the dragon as the devil and the beast as Antichrist together with the teachers of his doctrines.

Thus he saw one spirit, but, according to the number of the parts of one body, he speaks of three, so that it might be revealed that the entire number of the lost is driven by one evil spirit. Perhaps for this reason also, comparing their temerity with the terrible foulness of frogs, he added: “For it is fitting for these false prophets, gathered together like living creatures in the manner of frogs, to resound at night with the barking of error, to their damnation.” Frogs are hated because of their place, their appearance, and their troublesome croaking; so the devil with his followers is recognized as abhorrent to the truth [Col. 0896D], and rightly destined to be condemned to eternal fire.

Although the blessed Apostle speaks in equally clear language by way of comparison when he says beforehand (II Cor. IX): “Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has the believer with the unbeliever? What accord has the temple of God with idols?”

So here too, when he says that an unclean spirit comes forth from their mouths in the likeness of frogs, it is as though he were saying: “Why should you compare filth with heaven, which is suited to the dwelling place of frogs, that is, to the dreadful blasphemies of the false prophet?” He asserts that the teachers of truth differ from them as frogs differ from holy human beings, so that even those who are not capable of recognizing and repelling [Col. 0897A] their frauds by the power of discernment may nevertheless, struck by the horror of frogs, strive to avoid such people, who, like frogs, obstruct the ignorant so that they may not receive the truth through the peaceful practice of devotion.

“For they are spirits of demons,” he says, “performing signs.” They too, like the magicians of Pharaoh (Exod. VII), must be believed to perform signs. He does not mention them without reason after mentioning frogs, unless he were also predicting that the ministers of Satan would then perform similar signs. The magicians were permitted by their incantations to have power even to the sign of frogs.

And they go out to the kings of the whole earth to gather them for battle—not because they gather them from the entire world into one place, but because they wish to make each nation, seized by their superstitions in the place of its habitation, serve in battle.

For the great day of almighty God [Col. 0897B]. The day of the Lord must be understood according to the diversity of contexts. Sometimes it refers to the whole period beginning with the Lord’s Passion, during which those destined to be condemned at the final judgment are now said to be gathered, as though it meant “being prepared.” Sometimes the day of the Lord must be understood as the day of judgment; sometimes as the time of persecution. Hence it is clear that such people are gathered throughout the whole period of the present life.

Who comes suddenly like a thief. Hence the Apostle says (I Thess. V): “He will come like a thief in the night.” “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and see his shame.” “All you,” he says (Gal. III), “who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ.” I think that these undefiled garments are commended here for preservation, so that they may neither be torn by a second baptism nor stained by the splashes of the reprobate [Col. 0897C]. In both cases the shame of transgressors is exposed, which a vigilant and persevering purpose avoids.

And he gathered them into the place called in Hebrew Armageddon. In another recapitulation he interpreted the place, saying (below, XX): “He gathered them for battle, whose number is like the sand of the sea.”

And the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying: “It is done; it is finished.” And there were flashes of lightning and voices and thunder, and earthquakes, and great signs. Recounting the same persecution again, he mentions an incomparable commotion in which he says that miracles and proclamations are present. But whether those signs that he mentions continue on the side of the good, who oppose falsehood, or on the side of the wicked, to exercise the good and harden the wicked, or whether the signs call to one another from both sides [Col. 0897D], is not sufficiently clear here, just as happened between Moses and the magicians of Pharaoh (Exod. VII). Whatever the case may be, signs too, such as the earthquake, should be understood as becoming incomparably more striking as the crisis approaches.

And that great city was divided into three parts. “The great city,” because of the multitude of peoples and the arrogance by which it was carried along through immoderate ventures, will be divided into three parts: one of the Gentiles, another consisting of heretics and Jews, and a third consisting of false brothers, who confess that they know God but deny him by their deeds, since they are detestable and unbelieving and disqualified for every good work (Titus I).

For it follows [Col. 0898A]: “And the cities of the nations fell”—that is, all the strength and confidence of the Gentiles. And that Babylon the great was remembered and came before God’s sight. He indicates the confused multitude of all the lost. “To give her,” he says, “the cup of the wine of the wrath of his indignation.” The repayment of due vengeance is prescribed for the wicked.

And every island fled, and the mountains were not found. By the name of the islands and mountains alike, the knowledge of the Church is represented because of their eminence in stability. Concerning them it is said through Isaiah (chapter XXIV): “Glorify the Lord in doctrines, in the islands of the sea the name of the Lord God of Israel.” Likewise (Isa. II): “And it shall be in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared upon the peaks of the mountains.”

This flight is to be understood as occurring when the fellowship of the wicked will finally be fled in such a way that thereafter that confused mingling of the Church with the wicked will no longer be found. Hence the Prophet says (Jer. LI): “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul.” Babylon falls then when, finally, it has received [Col. 0898B] the power to persecute the saints. Therefore, as he says, “before ruin the heart will be exalted, and before glory the spirit will be humbled.”

And a great hail, weighing a talent, fell from heaven upon the people, and the people blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, because the plague caused by the hail was exceedingly great. He places the wrath of vengeance in the hail, concerning which we read elsewhere: “The wrath of the Lord descends like hail.” The Lord promises to protect his own from it, saying through the Apostle (I Thess. I): “Who has rescued us from the coming wrath.”

Nor does he mention the weight of a talent without reason, unless it is because, according to the equity of divine judgment, each person is struck in accordance with the diversity [Col. 0898C] of his sins. Among the Greeks a talent is weighed according to one quantity, and among the Romans according to another. But because sins differ, scourges differ, and sometimes both are found together—a matter that would take too long to discuss here—blaspheming the Lord because of the hail is recognized as both sin and the punishment of sin. Through it the impious are cut down in such a way that, though not corrected, they do not come to their senses; rather, made even worse by the scourges themselves, they rage madly.

Isaiah finally says: “Lord, you were angry, and behold, we sinned” (Isa. XLVI).

## CHAPTER XVII.

And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great prostitute who sits upon many waters.”

Isaiah likewise presents something similar concerning the devil, whom, under the figurative person of the prince of Babylon, he foretells will fall [Col. 0898D] (Isa. XIV): “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn,” etc. The Holy Spirit, considering the body of all the lost—which he calls by various but appropriate names—advancing after long arrogance through diverse excesses, being corrupted by crimes and swept along by errors, and raging with such impiety that it even opposes the meek, depicts it as destined for a fitting confinement, calling it a prostitute because, having abandoned the Creator, it prostitutes itself to demons to be defiled.

“Great,” because of the enormity of its transgression, by which it had long insulted the saints. “Upon many waters,” that is, many peoples, “with whom,” he says, “the kings of the earth committed fornication,” that is, while proudly seeking earthly kingdoms. [Col. 0899A] Thus he divides her among kings and earthly people so that we may understand her to arise from them.

“From the wine of her fornication.” What precedes indicates the corruption of vices: just as wine exalts the mind, so the lust of vices blinds those who are wavering.

“And he led me,” he says, “into the desert in the spirit.” He calls the desert the absence of Divinity, whose presence is paradise. “In the spirit,” because these things can be discerned by the spirit.

“And I saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast.” In what form would the divine Word most appropriately adorn her, if not that of a woman from whom sin began and because of whom, as it is written (Eccli. XXV), we all die? She is said to sit upon the beast because she is exalted by the arrogance of presumption.

“Scarlet”—a blood-red beast, as has been said: the body opposed to the Lamb, in which now the devil, now the head as though slain, and now his people are to be understood. The whole of this is Babylon, that is, confusion. Scarlet, therefore, through its impiety and blood-red through its corruptions, as though intoxicated by blood, it is “full of names of blasphemy.” Although accomplishing blasphemy by deed is worse than being called blasphemous, nevertheless he says here that she abounds fully even in names, so that she may in no way be thought to lack excesses. And because it is one thing to sin against God and another to sin in God—that is, to blaspheme—he sins against God with the greater guilt.

“Having seven heads and ten horns.” As the final persecution hastens on, the prophecy of the holy Daniel also testifies that there will be ten kings (Dan. VII). This book frequently designates these by the beast’s seven heads and ten horns. It says above that diadems are also upon them because, after all the kingdoms have been destroyed, they alone will be able to reign throughout the whole world. He says that the diadems—the signs of conquered kingdoms—are carried before the heads of the proud like trophies.

For this reason it subsequently instructs us to understand the seven heads as seven mountains, so that, by signifying Rome, which presides over seven mountains, it might bring the whole dominion that had ruled the world under the likeness of their kingdom, and under the name of Rome might figure the power of the entire kingdom. By the number seven he wished to show the universality of that dominion, since it is composed of three and four—that is, of odd and even, as though from different elements—and thus signifies universality. As has already been sufficiently stated, we previously set forth the figure of the seven churches in a favorable sense, when the one Church of Christ is foretold as destined to possess the lands of the world. Now the same number appears oppositely in these seven heads mentioned here, in which it is said that a universality of power will rule. Holy Scripture testifies that the number seven is frequently applied both to good and to evil.

For when the Holy Spirit is believed to be sevenfold in a good sense because of his sevenfold operation, as the prophet Isaiah testifies (Isa. XI), the evil spirit is also more often represented as sevenfold. And because the monarchy of these powers and the kingdom of Christ are frequently set in opposition, he not only attacks the faithful by open oppression of power, but also desires to ensnare them under a false appearance of truth. He therefore designated its manifest power by the ten horns and its plausible deceit by the seven heads. For this reason that same persecution is foretold as violent: the art of deception is aided by power, and what is lacking in pretense is supplied by force.

Above he mentions the tricks of this deception, saying: “And one of its seven heads was as though it had been slain unto death, and its deadly wound was healed”—that is, from the whole power of the secular kingdom opposed to the Church there is one head, namely the Antichrist, who wishes to be received in place of Christ, asserting that he has risen again as one who had died, while impiously separating the unwary from Christ, who truly died and rose again.

He had also said earlier that the dragon—that is, the devil—gave him his power, throne, and great authority; therefore he also says that he is full of names of blasphemy. No worse blasphemy can be found than for one opposed to Christ—as his name Antichrist itself indicates—to wish to be regarded as Christ, so that those whom he cannot break by violent terrors he may strive to seduce by a shadowed imitation of the truth, and may cause those who avoid open error to fall into plausible falsehood.

The Lord taught in the Gospel that this plague must be guarded against, saying (Matt. XII; Luke XI): “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, he walks through waterless places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then he says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came out.’ And then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.”

Was he not speaking above of one unclean spirit? Why did he say “seven others more wicked than himself,” unless the unclean spirit is recognized as sevenfold, so that even hidden evils may be found seven times more wicked?

And so that what we are saying may become clearer, the reader should pay close attention. The good spirit is the spirit of wisdom; opposed to it is the evil spirit of foolishness, and worse than that is the imitation of wisdom. The good spirit is the spirit of understanding; the evil spirit is the spirit of stupidity, and worse than that is the imitation of learning. The good spirit is the spirit of counsel; the evil spirit is the spirit of imprudence, and worse than that is the imitation of prudence. The good spirit is the spirit of fortitude; opposed to it is the evil spirit of open cowardice, and worse than that is weakness concealed under the shadow of virtue. The good spirit is the spirit of knowledge; opposed to it is the evil spirit of ignorance, and worse than that is the usurpation of knowledge. The good spirit is the spirit of piety; the evil spirit is the spirit of impiety, and worse than that is the pretext of false piety. The good spirit is the spirit of the fear of God; opposed to it is the spirit of rashness, and worse than that is the deceit of feigned religion.

For this reason he wished to dwell somewhat more extensively on the simulation of the opposing party, so that this exposition might assist us in understanding many passages.

The Apostle also announces that this multifaceted persecution will come either through power or through deceit, saying (II Thess. II): “Then that lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming; whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders, and with every deceit of unrighteousness among those who are perishing.” By “power” he signifies the force of authority; by “deceit,” the hypocrisy of falsehood.

“Surrounded with purple and scarlet.” In purple the substance of pretended rule is shown; in scarlet the bloodstained appearance of impiety. And she was adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls—that is, with every enticement of feigned truth, which we have already sufficiently displayed in those wicked spirits.

Finally, he explains what is within this beauty, saying: “And she had a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations and the uncleanness of the fornication of the whole earth.” Gold, therefore, signifies hypocrisy, because, as the Lord says, “Outwardly they appear to people as righteous, but inwardly they are full of all uncleanness.”

“And upon her forehead a name written, a mystery: Babylon, mother of fornications and of the abominations of the whole earth.” So that the superstition of error might not openly deceive those who were unprepared for the truth, let them know from the title on her forehead that they must be on their guard.

“And I saw that woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus Christ.” Appropriately the abundance of the divine Word shows her raging inwardly.

“And when I had seen her, I wondered with great astonishment.” And the angel said to me: “Why did you wonder? I will show you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The beast that you saw was, and is not, but is about to rise from the abyss and is going to destruction.”

From the beginning of the world, Scripture teaches that the origin and succession of two cities have continued until now: one belonging to God and the other to the devil. This is what is designated here by the beast, as the entire body of the wicked. [Col. 0901C] Therefore it says, “It was, and is not,” because it is constructed and completed through the succession of generations that depart and follow one another.

For this reason it follows: “And it is about to rise from the abyss, and it is going to destruction.” This is carried out by divine judgment, hidden indeed but just. Hence the psalm says (XXXV): “Your judgments are a great abyss.” Or it may mean that it is to come forth from the hearts of the wicked. Hence the psalm says (XLI): “Abyss calls to abyss.”

“And all who dwell on the earth will wonder—those whose names have not been written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world—when they see the beast that was, and is not, and is to come.” He presents these as the very ones from whose members the body destined for condemnation is constructed. But if the names cause ambiguity, the same author says in his epistle, using the singular number: “As you have heard that the Antichrist is coming, so now there are many Antichrists.” And shortly afterward: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

Therefore their names are not written in the book of life. These, then, are the people whom the end of the world will find alive; experiencing the destruction of their own condemnation, they will wonder too late in their thoughts that the one they supposed to be Christ was not Christ, deceived by the beast’s shadowy seduction. But they will recognize our Christ, whom as judge they will certainly feel condemning them with perfect justice.

It follows: “From the foundation of the world.” Just as the Lord knows those who are his, to whom he also promised that he would say, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV), so he will condemn those who are not his—those whose names he has not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world—to the punishment of eternal fire. They are unknown to him and foreknown from afar, and he will condemn them to the fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

For the Lord is exalted and regards the lowly, while he knows the proud from afar (Ps. CXXXVII). Hence he says (Matt. VII): “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.”

“Seeing the beast that was, and is not.” Here is the meaning, which requires wisdom. Those seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. We have frequently said in another way that a genus is shown in each species. For what the entire beast is, that the seven heads are. Finally, he says that they are seven mountains and seven kings—that is, the entire portion of the wicked, consisting of rulers as though of kings and of subjects.

It is called by various names because of the diversity of its actions: it oppresses by force and deceives by fraud, when it creeps into unstable minds after they have been captured by the pleasures of visible things. As we read in Scripture (Jerem. IX): “Death has entered through your windows.” I think this should properly be referred to the five-part sense: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

Hence the Lord says to that Samaritan woman (John IV): “You have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband.” What is meant there by husbands, understand here as kings, whose governance we recognize as ruling and administering the beginnings of human life, which beasts seem to have in common with us.

There it continues: “And the one whom you now have is not your husband,” signifying that she does not use a husband lawfully—that is, error. Here it has already said the same thing: “Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come.” By saying “the other has not yet come,” he indicates that the remaining part of the same evil body will succeed the departing generation and will likewise be possessed by the same evil spirit, which we previously said is sevenfold.

The five whom he says have fallen, the one whom he says remains, and the other whom he announces will come make seven. “And when he has come,” he says, “he must remain for a short time.”

“And the beast that was, and is not, is itself the eighth, although it is one of the seven, and it goes into destruction.” So that you would not think this eighth to be of another kind, he added: “It is of the seven, and it will go into destruction,” showing both that it is of the same wicked kind and that, by exceeding the number seven, it represents those more wicked in hypocrisy.

For just as, in the Lord’s testimony mentioned above, after speaking of one unclean spirit he suddenly added, “He takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself” (Luke XI), so now, beginning with seven, he wished to designate another seven in one of the same kind—that is, the eighth.

Therefore he says: “It is of the seven, and it will go into destruction.” And so that the merit of one kind might be brought to the same punishment, he rightly says that it is of the seven, although he also places it numerically as the eighth, and adds, “and it goes into destruction.” He says that in the future judgment all the wickedness of the wicked will be ended.

And he explains how: “And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings; these have not yet received a kingdom.” He designates the entire kingdom of the world, which, as a little earlier, he describes in terms of kings and subjects. But they receive royal authority for one hour with the beast.

Here “hour” is understood as a period of time, as both example and meaning teach, namely from the Lord’s Passion, from which the apostolic voice cries: “It is the last hour.” Therefore, as long as the future events are being fulfilled, he says that they have not yet received the kingdom, because although even now they rule over many, their mad power of boasting will be more intense when they have deceived many even through signs.

“All these have one purpose, and they give their power and authority to the beast.” What he earlier said, “with the beast,” he now states more openly: “They will give their power to the beast”—to that head, namely, which pretended to have risen again though it had been slain. With equal consent they will offer it the worship of all their purpose and render it service.

“They will fight against the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings.” When he was describing the power of the opposing party, he appropriately proclaimed here the victory of the Lamb. To indicate that he triumphs in his own people, he added: “And those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”

He rightly placed “chosen” first, because the Lord says (Matt. XX): “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

And he said to me: “The waters that you saw, upon which the prostitute sits, are peoples, crowds of the wicked, and tongues.”

That waters are frequently represented as peoples is easily demonstrated here.

“And the ten horns that you saw, and the beast, will hate the prostitute and will make her desolate and naked.” It is as though he were saying: The corruptions of carnal desires, which they now love as though they were the woman herself, will be turned into hatred against them when, near the end, they recognize that they are to be condemned by inevitable judgment and see the manifest victory of the Lamb.

Accordingly, the beast is divided into parts. This can be understood in two ways: either because, as we read (Prov. XIII), “There are always quarrels among the proud,” or because “everyone who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X). “Who will be good to one who is bad to himself?” (Eccl. XIV).

“And they will devour her flesh and burn her with fire.” It is as though the angel were saying in the person of the Church: Those who harm me and rise up against me to eat my flesh (Ps. XXVI) will eat their own flesh and burn it with fire. After God, provoked to anger by their excesses, has desolated the world, he says that they themselves do what has justly happened to them [the intervening wording concerning the angel and the devastation is textually uncertain].

“For God put it into their hearts to accomplish what pleased him, and to be of one accord and to fear, and to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.” What the Apostle says (Rom. I)—“God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is improper”—is also said here: the Lord put it into their hearts to do what pleased him.

For justice pleases God, through which we know that he inflicts vengeance upon the wicked; and those who have given their kingdom to the beast will pay just penalties with it until the words of God are fulfilled, words that consist in judgment and mercy. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV).

“And the woman whom you saw is the great city that has kingship over the kings of the earth.” This is the very woman whom he previously presented as devoted to the corruptions of flesh and blood and flourishing in the power of worldly rule. Since she consists of those very kings, he says that she reigns over them, dividing one entity according to his custom into parts, as from genus to species: into the woman, the city, and the kings.

Over this the words of the Lord will be fulfilled, when he both mercifully redeems his own and justly condemns the rebellious.

Wherever there is mention of consummation, there the fitting conclusion of this book should also be made.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0903]

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0903C]

And after these things I saw another angel descending from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was illuminated by his glory.

This signifies the destruction of worldly wisdom, as the destruction of Jericho also signifies. But when he is about to speak of the ruin of the earthly kingdom, he says that this angel has great authority, as I think to indicate that he has come against a strong one as a stronger one and has come prepared to wage war against him. Overshadowing the trace of worldly wisdom, he testifies that the true light of wisdom has now come, which would show itself unconquered both in power and in knowledge to the wise of the world and to earthly kings who trust in the strength of their own power.

“And the earth,” he says, “was illuminated by his glory.”

And he cried out with a loud and powerful voice, saying: “That great Babylon has fallen, and has become a dwelling place and refuge of demons, and of every unclean spirit, and of every unclean beast, and of every unclean and hateful bird.”

I think that the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is signified—the angel of great counsel whom we read of in Isaiah (Isa. IX). At his first coming, when he said (Matt. III), “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near,” he was destroying the schemes of secular power.

But the earth was illuminated by his glory because he is the true light that illuminates every person coming into this world (John I).

What follows may disturb the reader. He says: “And it has become a dwelling place and refuge of demons,” etc. If it has fallen, how is it said to have become a dwelling place and refuge for demons, unclean spirits, and birds? Unless it is because, by falling through the enormity of its transgressions, it made itself worthy to be a dwelling place of demons, while a part of it was destroyed through wholesome conduct; and because it, which was rising up against the faith of Christ in the sea of this age with the strong waves of persecutions, now groans, restrained within narrower boundaries and roaring like a wineskin enclosed.

Hence we sing in the psalm (Ps. XXXII): “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin, placing the abysses in storehouses.” For the very power that Christians once feared now fears Christians, when it sees even the broad decrees of religious rulers mobilized under their privilege.

Nevertheless, the remaining part of it has become a dwelling place and refuge of demons. By this means it is destroyed so that it may be rebuilt everywhere for the better, and, cast down among the proud, may be shattered; rightly it is said to have fallen after being destroyed.

That spiritual wickedness is also signified by birds is affirmed by that passage in the book of Genesis where Abraham is said to have driven away the birds that swooped down among the divided pieces of flesh (Gen. XV).

“For all the nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxuries.”

Here he names three kinds of vice and introduces an equal number of persons of transgression: avarice, which according to the Apostle is called the worship of idols (Eph. V); lust, under the name of fornication (Col. III); and, in the name of luxuries, gluttony, which the Lord warns us to avoid when he says (Luke XXI): “Let not your hearts be weighed down with overeating and drunkenness.”

“And the kings of the earth,” he says, “have committed fornication with her.” In saying that the merchants grew rich, he signifies avarice. Although some have preferred to understand wealth here as sins rather than possessions [Sic], he signifies by “nations” the mixed multitude of the common and insignificant people; by “kings,” those who seem to excel among them in temporal power; and by “merchants,” those who, yearning for earthly profits, exchange their souls in an unhappy bargain for temporal abundance, doing the opposite of what the Lord teaches when he says (Matt. XVI): “What will a person give in exchange for his soul?”

And I heard another voice from heaven saying: “Come out of her, my people, so that you may not share in her sins.”

The heavenly voice that was heard is the one of which Scripture says: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. VIII), and, “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II), and similar passages.

It follows: “Come out of her, my people, so that you may not share in her sins.” Up to this point, it seems to me, the passage refers to the first coming, when, until the end of the age, the good endure the wicked mingled with them in such a way that they neither regard the good as needing to be abandoned for the sake of the wicked nor follow the wicked in harmful imitation.

Thus that prophetic word is also fulfilled (Isa. LII): “Come out from their midst, and do not touch what is unclean.” The righteous person is not mingled with the wicked by a bodily departure, but by departing from the most wicked will.

It follows: “And do not be struck by her plagues, because her sins have reached as far as heaven, and the Lord God has remembered her iniquities. Therefore he repays her double, and in what she mingled with the people, double has been mixed back into her. To the extent that she glorified herself and lived in luxury, to that extent give her torment and mourning, because she says in her heart, ‘I am a queen, and I am no widow, nor shall I see mourning.’ Therefore her plagues will come in one hour: death, mourning, and famine; and she will be burned with fire, because strong is the Lord God who judges her.”

All these things are believed to pertain to the second coming, when, after the company of the wicked has been excluded by the examination of the supreme judgment, it will be punished with just retribution, so that those who sinned temporarily may be punished eternally.

This is what he says: “Repay her double, and double has been mixed back into her,” so that the one who enjoyed passing luxuries may be tormented by eternal punishments.

And Christ is foretold in the psalm as freeing his own from usury (Ps. LXXI): “From usury and iniquity,” he says, “he will redeem their souls.”

But they are also said to be burned by perpetual fire and afflicted by hunger—then, certainly, when those who now hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. V) will receive incorruptible satisfaction.

They die because God abandons them. For just as the body dies when the soul departs, so the soul must be understood to die when God abandons it.

Their mourning is that which Christ says in the Gospel (Luke VI): “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.” Wishing to show that his own are unharmed by these plagues, God says: “And do not be struck by her plagues,” as though he were saying: Since, after your conversion, you did not wish to have a will like theirs in sins, you will not receive an equal punishment.

Nor can we escape these same plagues by our own strength, since this is granted to us solely by the grace of God. But the Holy Spirit, maintaining the proper order, wished to declare that those who are not taken captive in their hearts by impiety are in no way struck by the torments of the wicked through consent.

“For the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of wickedness shall not touch them” (Wis. III).

He circumscribes these things, which will occur then, in such a way that he expresses the works to be inflicted. Nevertheless, these punishments are not to be thought of as belonging to this age, since they will soon bring its course to an end, as is shown by what follows.

When the Lord foretold the world’s destruction, he also added (Luke XXI): “But the end will not come immediately.”

“And the kings of the earth who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury with her will weep and mourn over her when they see the smoke of her burning, standing far away because of fear of her punishment, saying: ‘Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city, for in one hour your judgment has come.’”

And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her because no one buys their merchandise.

How can it be certain that the same Babylon is signified by different names, and that it exists either among the kings of the earth, or among the nations, or among the merchants, if, after she has been burned, they are said to stand far away and to mourn her—not sharing her common suffering, but lamenting her miserably from a free consideration—unless, as I stated above, we should understand that the complete end of the world is not yet meant here, but rather the diminution of human affairs and the destruction of various nations?

He says that the pomp of secular riches is to be taken away, through which the opportunity provided by an abundance of carnal luxuries somehow assisted the importunity of those who sought to fulfill wicked desires.

When this has been removed through the decline and desolation inflicted by divine judgments, certain survivors are said to mourn the destruction of others. For this reason they are said to stand far away and to fear, dreading a similar punishment.

Perhaps this is also why they are said to see the smoke of her burning, as though it were a specimen of eternal fire. Smoke gives an indication of flames to come.

Accordingly, he enumerates whatever he knows to be necessary for human use, whatever worldly utility the greedy and carnal greatly desire, and also those things that he knows are pleasantly taken in through the five most familiar bodily senses. He declares that these things will be absent in this way:

“The merchandise of gold and silver and precious stones and pearls and silk.” Thus far he proceeds according to the utility of places [Sic]. “And purple and scarlet cloth, and every kind of cedar wood, and every vessel of ivory, of precious wood, of bronze, of iron, and of marble.”

Up to this point he also mentions things pertaining to the sense of sight. The same passage then concerns smell: “And cinnamon, incense, and ointment.” With the ointment he also introduces touch: “and frankincense,” he says.

Then he adds what belongs to taste and use, saying: “and wine, and oil, and wheat.” He lists beasts of burden and cattle, and the conveyances of horses and chariots, as well as slaves and animals of various kinds, for the sake of utility.

“And the desire of your soul for your fruits,” he says, “has departed from you.” This too he referred to sight and taste.

“And all the fat and splendid things have perished from you, and you will never find them again.” Your merchants also, who became rich through her, will stand far away because of fear of her punishment, weeping and mourning, and saying: “Woe, woe, that great city, clothed in purple and linen and scarlet, adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls! In one hour such great riches have been destroyed.”

That “hour” is used for a period of time is demonstrated by the judgments of many testimonies.

“And every helmsman, and everyone who sails by sea, and sailors, and those who work at sea, will stand far away, seeing the smoke of her burning and saying: ‘What city is like this great city?’ And they will throw dust upon their heads,” that is, reproaching the face of their rulers, by whom they were deceived and perished. They will cry out, weeping and mourning, and saying with a loud voice: “Woe, woe, that great city, in which all who had ships at sea became rich because of her splendor! For in one hour she has been destroyed.”

But because we often know many people to be deeply moved by this destruction, if those passages by which we are admonished should be applied to their persons, it may appropriately be understood in this way: They will “stand far away and cry out, seeing the smoke of her burning,” so that “standing far away” means not falling together with the lost, but rather attaining stability through sudden conversion.

Therefore, what stands or falls for its Lord must not be understood bodily, but as a stable conversion of the mind in faith. And when they are said to mourn over the destruction of others, they themselves are to be understood as performing fruitful repentance.

For the Apostle says this (Eph. II): “When you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the children of disobedience, among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of our flesh and thoughts; and we were by nature children of wrath, just as the others,” and similar words.

According to these words of the Apostle, I say, this passage can be applied to the persons of the converted. For no one can be found good who was not first evil.

Hence the psalm says (CXVIII): “I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors.”

Perhaps this is why the following occurs here: “Rejoice over her, heavens and saints, apostles and prophets,” as though these converted people, delighted by God’s judgment, rejoice because God has judged her judgment on their behalf.

And the strong angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: “With such force that great Babylon will be thrown down, and it will never be found again.”

We know that the Lord said in the Gospel (Matt. XVIII): “Woe to the world because of scandals,” and added: “Woe to the person through whom the scandal comes; it is better for that person if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should scandalize one of these little ones.” By this he signifies that the authors of scandal will be punished with such a penalty.

I do not think this should be understood only of the scandal of strife, but of every kind of sin, according to that rule which Holy Scripture gives, whether through the Lord’s saying (Matt. I), “If your eye causes you to stumble, or your foot, or your hand,” or through the Apostle Paul (I Cor. XI), “Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?”

The psalm agrees with this meaning (CII), saying: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” Here one may understand the sun and moon as bad belief concerning Christ and the Church; or the sins of adversity and prosperity, with the latter referred to the moon and the former to the sun. All the species of transgression seem to be included under the general name of scandal.

Here too he indicates that the author of scandal—that is, of every sin—is to be plunged like a millstone. The millstone here, I think, is placed as a symbol of the weight of sins contracted from temporal things. The Lord teaches that a millstone belongs to the circuit of secular affairs when he says: “Two women will be grinding at the mill.”

“And the voice of harpists, musicians, flute-players, and trumpeters will no longer be heard in you.”

He had postponed the sound associated with the five senses; now he expresses it fully, having also foretold among the other things that it would be taken away, as though he were saying: Whatever is beautiful to sight, melodious to hearing, pleasant to touch, sweet to smell, and delightful to taste will pass away from the world.

And so that he would not allow them to be content with these things, he also added those that pertain to the use of human life, saying: “No craftsman of any craft will ever again be found in you, and the sound of the mill will no longer be heard in you; the light of a lamp will no longer shine in you; and the voice of bridegroom and bride will no longer be heard in you.”

And he says for what reason: “Because your merchants were the rulers of the earth, because by your sorceries all the nations were led astray.” It is as though he were saying: Because you used temporal goods badly during your life, you will justly be deprived of them forever and confined under eternal punishments.

“And in you was found the blood of prophets and saints and of all those slain upon the earth.” Here it is more openly declared that the entire body of Babylon—the body of the devil—is reproved for its excesses in one city. For we do not know that the prophets were killed in the same city in which the martyrs were killed, so far as the signification of the place is concerned, although there is one city in the fellowship of the wicked.

It follows.

## CHAPTER XIX
After this I heard the voice of immense crowds crying out with a loud voice in heaven, saying: “Alleluia. Salvation and glory belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just, for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth by her fornication, and he has avenged the blood of his servants at her hands.” And again they said: “Alleluia.” In the Gospel the Lord likewise testified something similar, saying that the blood of the righteous in general was to be exacted with regard to the person of this body [Col. 0909A]: “From the blood,” he says (Matt. 23), “of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah”—briefly indicating and encompassing the whole sum of peoples and priests. Therefore there too he mentions the place, saying, “whom you killed between the temple and the altar,” referring “temple” to the people and “altar” to the priests. As for their saying “Alleluia” again, the Church praises God continually and fervently for his judgments. For *Alleluia* means “Praise the Lord.”

It follows concerning that prostitute: “And smoke from her ascended forever and ever.” While the Church perseveres in the praise of that joy, the smoke of the wicked’s destruction remains. For just as smoke marks the beginning of a fire, so, when the fire continues, he says that smoke remains within it. I think that the Lord represented an example of these good and evil things [Col. 0909B] in the poor man and the rich man (Luke 16).

And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sat upon the throne. He is referring to the Church. It follows, saying: “Amen,” that is, “truly,” “faithfully.”

And a voice came out of heaven, saying: “Praise your God, all his servants, and you who fear God, both the lowly and the great.” By commanding that this be done while also recording that it had been done, he gave an indication that God had accepted the pleasing praise of his elect—approving what had been offered and commanding that it continue forever. The great in the Church are those of whom the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2). And the Lord says: “Whoever teaches people in this way shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). The lowly are those of whom he says: “[Col. 0909C] As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3).

And I heard the voice of great trumpets, and something like the voice of mighty thunderclaps, and something like the sound of many waters, saying: “Alleluia.” The preaching which Isaiah describes is signified by the trumpets: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58). In that preaching the dread of divine judgment is also intimated. I think that this is signified by the name “thunder,” since thunder is appropriate to human beings. Accordingly, it is certain that he ordinarily represents peoples by many waters—peoples who praise God, saying: “Alleluia.” Thus, when the Church both preaches, fears, and praises, she rejoices with trembling, as it is written: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling.”

“For the Lord Almighty has reigned.” Here he rightly mentions his omnipotence. For he made from [Col. 0909D] nothing the things that did not exist; he sought those who had perished through sin; he found those deserving punishment; and from those whom he chose he mercifully made the righteous. Finally, building the Church from them as from his own members, he bestowed upon her such a gift [of dignity]—redeemed at such a price—that he made her his bride, although she had not even deserved to be a slave.

Finally it follows: “Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give him glory, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself. And it was granted to her to clothe herself in clean, shining linen.” For the clean linen is the righteousness of the saints. No spiritual person doubts that all these things apply to the Church of the elect. Those, certainly, are said to prepare themselves for her spiritual marriage who have preferred always to devote themselves to works of righteousness.
