And he said to me: “[Col. 0910A] Write: Blessed are those who have been invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” Concerning this the Lord says: “And they will recline with Abraham and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8); and likewise: “Passing by, he will serve them,” signifying those who have been called saints according to the purpose and who pass into the fullness of the elect. “For many are called, but few are elect” (Matt. 22).

And again he said to me: “These words of God are true and just.” This is said divinely to the Church when the Word of God, which is also the truth, is revealed.

And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said to me: “See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers who possess the testimony of Jesus Christ. Worship God.”

[Col. 0910B] Although at the beginning of this book I said that the Lord Christ revealed everything to John through the assumed creature of an angel, which is also especially clear here when he does not permit himself to be worshiped as God but rather instructs him to regard him as a fellow servant and teaches that the one God alone is to be worshiped, nevertheless this may trouble the reader, since that same figure also says: “I am the first and the last” (above, 1). But we should understand that the angel spoke this in the person of Christ. Finally, at the end he says: “I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches” (below, 22).

It follows: “For the sanctification of the testimony is the spirit of the prophets.” Indeed, the whole sum of prophecy and the sanctification of the Spirit consists in the testimony of Jesus Christ, whom the whole Law and prophecy serve. For this reason, when he manifested himself on the mountain (Matt. 17; Mark 9; Luke 9) between Moses and Elijah, he shone with the brightness of his face and clothing, and truly declared that he had testimony from the Law and the [Col. 0910C] prophets. For he himself testifies that whatever they foretold served Christ and the Church, saying concerning Moses: “He wrote about me” (John 5).

And after rising, he says: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24). Perhaps the mysteries of Christ do not appear there, do not sound there, or are not signified there. They are inserted for this purpose: so that the whole sequence of that Scripture, rising through the instrument of speech, may be more suitably constructed, like an organ. For whatever places they have touched resounds; but so that a sounding place may produce the song of the necessary modulation, the entire arrangement of those instruments, bound together, serves that purpose.

Then he unfolds again at greater length what was stated above, with a brief recapitulation:

[Col. 0910D] “I saw heaven opened; and behold, a white horse, and the one seated upon it was called Faithful and True.” This is the one whom he had earlier said had received the crown due to victory, the equitable and just one who judges, and who will wage war as the King of all ages wages war—he who always suffers together with his members, fights when he conquers, and crowns in himself, while providing strength to those who struggle; he promises a reward to the victors (Wis. 2).

“His eyes were like a flame of fire, and upon his head were many diadems.” In him “we shall perform valiantly” (Ps. 59); in him, amid the multitude of the saints, he is said to possess the splendor of one crowned.

“And he had a great name written which no one knows except himself.” The perfect knowledge of the Word of God is revealed to those who have deserved to be Christ’s body and members. For, just as the head specially imparts knowledge of itself to the body, so he himself knows what the Church has deserved to know in him. “Whoever is joined to the Lord,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. 6), “is one spirit.” For “the two will be one flesh.”

[Col. 0911A] Neither the Jews, nor the foreigners, nor the heretics have known this name. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). Likewise he says: “The world did not know you” (John 17); and again he says to his own disciples: “But you will see me, because I live, and you will live. On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you” (John 14). Hence the disciples also respond: “Lord, what has happened, that you are going to manifest yourself to us and not to the world?” (ibid.).

As for the heretics, he says to them again: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to those who are outside everything is presented in parables, so that seeing they may see and not understand” (Matt. 13; Mark 4).

[Col. 0911B] “He had a great name written which no one knows except himself.” Care must certainly be taken lest, when carnal reasoning steals in, the name of the Son under discussion be thought unknown either to the Father or to the Holy Spirit. Rather, taking the customary mode of expression in Scripture as our guide, let us understand that this passage expresses purely that, although the Son alone is said to know, the whole Trinity is taught to know—just as, if the Father alone is said to know something, he is nevertheless undoubtedly shown to know it together with his Wisdom, who is Christ, or together with his Spirit, who is believed to be the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

For when the Father alone is said to know the day of judgment, [Col. 0911C] the Son and the Holy Spirit are certainly not thereby denied knowledge. Likewise, when the Holy Spirit alone is said to know something, and the name of the Father or the Son is omitted through a similar mode of expression, they are nevertheless shown in every way to know it. The Apostle says: “No one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him; so also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). It would be madness to separate either the Father or the Son from that knowledge.

For when elsewhere he says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption” (Eph. 4), he does not, by remaining silent about the Father and the Son, exclude their persons from the work of our redemption, since the inseparable works of the Trinity are taught to proceed through the undivided power of one nature.

When the Lord says in the Gospel that neither the Son but the Father alone knows that day of judgment [Col. 0911D] (Mark 13), this is said according to that rule of expression: the one who knows something makes others know it, and by not knowing makes them not know. Therefore, through the rule of understanding just indicated, we recognize that the name of the Son, which is said to be known by him alone, is also manifestly known to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The evident continuation testifies that this is said about the Son, when it says: “And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called the Word of God.” If no one is permitted to know his name, why is he now openly proclaimed to be the Word of God? But just as we read: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3), so we should understand that, if any of the members ascends, he deserves to ascend in and through the head. The head both gave this hope to his members by promising it and will make them possess it by fulfilling it.

[Col. 0912A] So here too Christ alone is said to know what his bride is granted to know in him—through whom and in whom the Church is fully instructed.

By saying that Christ’s garment was sprinkled with blood, the signs of his passion are described, whether in the head himself or in the body, which is the Church. Hence the Apostle teaches the Hebrews (Heb. 9) that, from the beginning, remission of sins was not celebrated without blood in those legal sacrifices of animals.

He also says concerning the Church: “That I may fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1), mindful of the voice that was heard: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9). Whatever the Church suffers is truly said to be suffered by Christ. Concerning him the same Apostle says: “He suffered once to take away the sins of many” (Heb. 9).

[Col. 0912B] Isaiah likewise describes the appearance of this garment: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one is beautiful in his robe, striding in the abundance of his strength. I am the one who speaks righteousness, and I am the defender who saves. Why then is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one treading in the winepress? I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man from the nations with me,” and so forth (Isa. 63).

“And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses.” Heaven means the Church, where, with unveiled face, they contemplate the glory of the Lord (2 Cor. 3). All who are pure in heart, whitened by grace beyond snow (Ps. 50), are said to follow Christ. They wear clean white linen, which he defined above as the righteousnesses of the saints. As [Col. 0912C] they distribute to each person what is his own and subject both body and mind to God, they proceed on white horses—that is, they always advance pure in body and mind—going before [F. supp. and] following the footsteps of Christ, to whom it is said in the Song of Songs: “We will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

“And from his mouth came a sword sharp on both sides, so that with it he might strike the nations, and he himself will rule them with an iron rod.” “Sharp on both sides” signifies either the two-edged blade of the two Testaments, or what we read concerning Wisdom: “He carries law and mercy upon his tongue” (Prov. 31), namely, judgment and mercy. The iron rod is the unchanging straightness of righteousness.

“And he himself has trodden the winepress of the wine of the wrath of God Almighty.” Just as, when threshing is applied, grain stripped of its chaff is stored in barns, so in a winepress, by applying the weight of pressure, wine is customarily and thoroughly separated from grape skins, or oil from dregs. The prophet describes this concerning the vineyard, saying: “And I dug a winepress in it” (Isa. 5).

[Col. 0912D] This takes place in the Church when, whether forced out by the adversity of persecution or removed by the occasion of some calamity, some fall headlong like dregs in an irreparable collapse, while others, shining more brightly through approved devotion, become more radiant.

“And on his garment and on his thigh he has a name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.”

“On his garment”: in the Church which Christ has put on, which, according to the Apostle (Eph. 5), he cleansed “by the washing of water in the word,” so that he might present the Church to himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle. For, like a garment, she is cleansed so that she may not acquire a spot; she is stretched so that she may not contract a wrinkle.

But “[Col. 0913A] on his thigh” the posterity of the seed is signified—the one in whom all nations will be blessed, according to the Apostle’s teaching: “He did not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though to one, ‘and to your seed,’ who is Christ” (Gal. 3).

To him, as to a dead brother, the same Apostle spiritually raises up offspring according to the law of ancient custom (Deut. 25), saying: “Let no one say that you were baptized in my name” (1 Cor. 1), although he says that he filled all things with the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum (Rom. 15). To these peoples he could truly say: “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4).

Therefore, in this thigh—as in sons propagated from Christ—the knowledge of Christ is written, not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts (2 Cor. 3). When they confess him as King of kings and Lord of all lords [Col. 0913B] (1 Tim. 6), this inscription of the thigh is reckoned to believers in him, and they will be blessed together with faithful Abraham.

And I saw an angel standing in the sun. He calls the Church an angel preaching. He rightly added “one.” “My dove is one” (Song 6), because of the mystery of preserving unity. She is in the sun, where she already shines clearly and no longer hides on account of fear.

And he cried out with a loud voice. In the loud voice, great freedom born of confidence is to be understood. He said to all the birds of heaven. Birds are sometimes understood in relation to their qualities and circumstances as evil, sometimes as good. Here, just as earlier (above, 8) the figure of a flying eagle was introduced, so now spiritual beings are invited to the supper.

Concerning this Peter, who bore the figure of the present Church, was told [Col. 0913C]: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). What they had been is killed, so that they may become what he himself was—that is, faithful—and, passing into the body of the Church, be grafted into the members of Christ and reign with him. For whatever we eat, we transfer into our body.

“Come,” he says, “to the great supper of God, so that you may eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of tribunes, the flesh of the mighty, the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them, and the flesh of all free persons and slaves, of the lowly and the great.”

The flesh of “horses and those seated upon them” may be understood as that of the leaders of error and of those whom they had previously deceived by their frauds, since the Church also receives converts from their number. The free are those who maintain celibacy; the slaves are the married; the lowly are the common and undistinguished crowd; and the great are either philosophers or those elevated by birth or wealth.

[Col. 0913D] And I saw the beast—that is, the devil—and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to wage war against the one seated upon the white horse and against his army, that is, against Christ and the Church. In light of the exposition of similar passages given above, this passage too can be understood.

And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet—the devil and Antichrist, or the leaders together with his entire body—who had performed signs before it, by which signs those who worshiped the image of the beast and had received its mark had been deceived.

These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire burning with fire and sulfur. The two are the head and body of the devil and his association, as the narrative had already anticipated—something that was still to take place at the end of time.

And the rest were killed by the sword of the one seated upon the white horse, which had come out of his mouth. [Col. 0914A] He divided one body into parts, wishing to show that those whom Christ’s second coming finds alive had long since been dead, as we read: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2).

And all the birds were filled with their flesh. We must not understand this so carnally as to believe that the saints, who seek higher things, are filled with the flesh of the wicked. Rather, once the divine equality of judgment has been revealed to the saints—the judgment by which, having redeemed the fullness of the elect, God has decreed that the others be condemned—they are said to be filled with knowledge of this justice, which in this life one may hunger and thirst for (Matt. 5), but not perfectly comprehend.

Isaiah too, speaking of the wicked by God’s command, says: “And they will be, until the satiety of vision, for all flesh” [Col. 0914B] (Isa. 66). I think that this is the satiety here ascribed above to the birds. The Apostle also confesses that he had not yet perfectly attained it, saying: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, to see whether I may grasp that for which I have also been grasped by Christ” (Phil. 3).

They will not therefore rejoice in the wicked’s condemnation, but because, satisfied with the light of divine justice, they already rejoice.

Alternatively, the birds may also be understood in an evil sense as transgressing angels. After leading their own followers to destruction, they are said to be satisfied with the flesh of the lost, their evil desire having been fulfilled, as they seek satisfaction in the condemnation of those whom they had supplied with the means of error.

## CHAPTER XX.

And I saw a mighty angel descending from [Col. 0914C] heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. And he seized that dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.

By the angel descending from heaven we understand our Lord Jesus Christ, who is called the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. IX), and who, visiting the region of mortals, being stronger, desired to bind the strong one, so that he might make vessels of mercy out of those who had formerly been vessels of wrath. In this he carried out by deed what he had earlier promised by preaching: “No one,” he says (Matt. XII; Mark III; Luke XI), “can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man”—that is, the Devil.

The key of the abyss is the profundity of the divine judgments. For “the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV). It is known only to him who calls people from the multitude of sins into the fullness of understanding. Hence elsewhere we read: “You closed up the abyss and sealed it over him.”

He is said to have bound the Devil with chains in that he restrained and curbed his power to lead astray human beings who were destined to be liberated. The thousand years may be understood in two ways. Either this event is said to last a thousand years because it takes place over many years—that is, during the sixth millennium of years, for however long it may be extended until the end of the age, whose latter periods are now passing—followed by the Sabbath that has no evening, namely, the rest of the saints that has no end. In that case, the final part of this millennium, like the final part of a day, which will remain until the end of the age, is called “a thousand years,” according to the manner of speaking in which a part signifies the whole; or else he used “a thousand years” for all the years of this age, so that the fullness of time might be indicated by a perfect number.

For the number one thousand makes the solid square of the number ten. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, which already has the form of a square but is not yet solid; and when one hundred is again multiplied tenfold, it becomes one thousand. This is perhaps more clearly understood in the psalm (CIV): “He remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations”—that is, for all generations.

“And he cast him,” he says, “into the abyss.” Clearly, he cast the Devil into the abyss, by which name the innumerable multitude of the impious is signified, whose hearts are deeply sunk in wickedness against the Church of God. This does not mean that the Devil had not previously been there; rather, he is said to have been sent there because, excluded from believers, he began to possess the impious more fully. For the Devil possesses more completely the one who is not only alienated from God but also freely hates those who serve God.

“And he closed it and sealed it over him, so that he would no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were finished.” By saying “he closed it over him,” he means that he forbade him to presume to transgress the prohibition any further. By adding “he sealed it,” he seems to me to have indicated that he wished it to remain hidden who belong to the Devil’s portion and who do not. For some fall away from those who are steadfast, while some of the reprobate are saved through a fruitful conversion, after being pierced by remorse.

The Devil is prohibited and restrained by this bond of prohibition and confinement from deceiving those nations who belong to Christ, whom previously he either deceived or held captive. For God chose them before the foundation of the world to rescue them from the power of darkness and transfer them into the kingdom of the Son of his love, as the Apostle says (Eph. I).

Who among the faithful does not know that even now he deceives nations and drags them with him into eternal punishment—but not those predestined to eternal life? “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II). Of these he leads no one into eternal damnation. The Devil was therefore bound and shut up in the abyss for this purpose: that he might no longer deceive the nations from which the Church is constituted, whom he had previously held deceived before they became the Church.

For it was not said that he should no longer deceive anyone, but, he says, that he should “no longer deceive the nations,” in which he undoubtedly wished the Church to be understood.

“Until the thousand years are finished”—that is, either the remainder of the sixth day, which consists of a thousand years, or all the years during which this age is thereafter to run its course. When he says “until,” he does not mean that afterward he will deceive those nations alone from which the predestined Church consists and from deceiving whom he has been restrained by that bond and confinement, as was already said in the expression. Thus also in the psalm (CXXII): “As our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.” We are not therefore to suppose that, once he has shown mercy, the eyes of the servants will no longer be directed toward God.

Alternatively, this may be the order of the words: “And he closed it and sealed it over him until the thousand years were finished, so that he would no longer deceive the nations”; that is, he closed him in order that, until the thousand years were finished, he would no longer deceive the nations.

“After this,” he says, “he must be released for a short time.” If the binding and confinement of the Devil mean that the Church cannot be deceived, then his release would mean that he could deceive it. Far be it from us to think so. The Church, predestined and chosen before the foundation of the world (Eph. I), is never deceived by him; concerning it has been said: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II).

Rather, the Devil’s binding consists in his not being permitted to exercise all the temptation that he is capable of, whether by force or by deceit, in order to draw human beings over to his side—either compelling them violently or misleading them. If he were permitted to do so, during so long a period and amid the great weakness of many, he would overthrow very many people of the sort whom God does not wish to permit to suffer this; therefore he was bound.

He will then be released when the time is also short. For it is read that he will rage with all his strength and that of his followers for three years and six months, and those with whom he must wage war will be such that they cannot be defeated by the violence and schemes of his assault.

If he were never released, his evil power would be less evident, the steadfast endurance of the holy city would be less fully tested, and finally it would be less apparent how greatly Almighty God had used him for good despite the magnitude of his evil.

This binding of the Devil occurred not only from the time when the Church began to extend beyond Judaea into other nations; it is also occurring now and will continue until the end of the age, when he is to be released. For even now, whenever people turn from the unbelief in which he held them to faith, the strong one is bound, since his goods are being plundered from him (Matt. XII; Mark III; Luke XI).

“And I saw,” he says, “thrones in the vision [Col. 0916C], and those seated upon them, and judgment was given to them.” Having said that, with the Devil bound for a thousand years, his customary power to deceive had been taken away, and having foretold that he would later be released for a short time, he then recapitulates what the Church does, or what is done within it, during these thousand years: “And I saw thrones and those seated upon them, and judgment was given to them.”

This should not be understood as referring to the final judgment, but rather to the administration of those placed in authority, through whom the presiding Church is now governed. From its King it has deserved to hear, with authoritative force: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

Hence the Apostle says (I Cor. V): “What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those who are inside whom you judge?”

“And the souls,” he says, “of those who were slain for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God.” What he will say here afterward is understood: they will reign with Jesus for a thousand years—namely, the souls of the martyrs, not yet restored to their bodies. For the souls of the righteous dead are not separated from the Church, which even now is the kingdom of Christ; otherwise their commemoration would not be made at the altar of Christ in the communion of Christ’s body.

Although they are not yet reigning with their bodies, their souls already reign with him while these thousand years run their course. Hence in this book it is said above (XIV): “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”

The Church therefore now reigns with Christ, first in the living and the dead. For this reason, as the Apostle says (Rom. XIV), “Christ died so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead.”

He mentioned the souls of the martyrs alone because they reign especially after death—those who contended for the truth even unto death. But, taking the part for the whole, we should understand also the other dead who belong to the Church, which is the kingdom of Christ.

What follows—“And those who did not worship the beast or his image, and did not receive his inscription on their forehead or on their hand”—we should understand as referring collectively to the living and the dead.

What this beast is, however, must be sought with greater care. Nevertheless, it is not contrary to right faith to understand it as the impious city itself, and as the people of unbelievers opposed to the faithful people and to the city of God. Its image, it seems to me, is its pretence, found in all those who appear to profess faith while living unbelievingly. They pretend to be what they are not; they are called Christians with a truthful likeness but a deceptive image, and thus belong to the same beast.

These include not only the open enemies of the name of Christ and of his most glorious city, but also the weeds that are to be gathered from his kingdom, which is the Church, at the end of the age.

Who are those who do not worship the beast or its image except those who do what the Apostle says (II Cor. VI): “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers”? They do not worship—that is, they do not consent or submit. Nor do they receive the inscription, namely, the mark of crime: on the forehead because of profession, and on the hand because of action.

Separated from these evils, whether they are still living in this mortal flesh or have died, they reign with Christ even now, in a manner suited to the present age, throughout the whole interval signified by the number one thousand years.

“The rest of them did not live,” he says. “For the hour is coming now when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John V). The rest, therefore, will not live.

What he added—“until the thousand years are finished”—is to be understood as meaning that they did not live during the time when they ought to have lived, namely, by passing from death into life. Therefore, when the day comes on which the resurrection of the bodies also takes place, they will not come forth from the tombs into life but to judgment, that is, to damnation, which is called the second death.

Until the thousand years are finished, whoever has not lived—that is, throughout this whole period during which the first resurrection is taking place—and has not heard the voice of the Son of God so as to pass from death into life will surely, in the second resurrection, which is the resurrection of the flesh, pass with that very flesh into the second death.

Then it follows: “And he said: This is the first resurrection.” Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in this first resurrection—that is, who has become a participant in it.

That person is its participant who not only rises again from the death in which he is through sins, but also remains in what he has revived into.

“Over these,” he says, “the second death has no power.” It therefore has power over the others, concerning whom he said above: “The rest of them did not live until the thousand years were finished.” For throughout this entire interval of time, which he calls a thousand years, however long any of them lived in the body, he did not rise again from death.

When he had said, “Over these the second death has no power,” he added: “They were priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.” This was not said only of bishops and presbyters. Just as we call all Christians “christs” because of the mystical chrism, so we call all priests, since all are members of the one Priest. Of these the Apostle Peter says (I Pet. II): “A holy nation, a royal priesthood.”

“And when the thousand years are finished,” he says, “Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and he will draw them into battle. Their number is like the sand of the sea.”

He deceives them then for the purpose of drawing them into battle; previously also he deceived them by the various means available to him, through many and diverse evils.

“He went out,” it is said, meaning that he burst forth into open persecution from the hidden recesses of hatred, in the final persecution, by judgment, before the whole Church and the cities of Christ suffer from the entire city of the Devil, whatever the extent of each may be upon the earth.

As for these nations, Gog and Magog, some suppose that they are the Getae and Massagetae, on account of the first letters of these names. But when we attend to the interpretation of the names, we recognize that a better meaning can be fitted to them.

For Gog means “roof,” and Magog means “from the roof,” as though they were the house and the one who proceeds from the house. The nations, therefore, are those in whom we understood the Devil above to have been confined as in an abyss; and he himself, in a certain way, rises up and proceeds from them, so that they are the roof and he is “from the roof.”

If, however, we refer both terms to the nations—rather than referring one of them to the nations and the other to the Devil—then the nations themselves are the roof, because the enemy is now enclosed and concealed in them; and they will be “from the roof” when they burst forth into open hatred.

But when he says, “They went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city,” this does not signify that they came or will come to one particular place, as though the camp of the saints and the beloved city were to exist in some single location, since this is none other than the Church of Christ, spread throughout the whole world.

Therefore, wherever at that time the Church exists—which is to be found among all nations, signified by the term “the breadth of the earth”—wherever the camp of the saints exists, there will be the city beloved by God. There it will be surrounded by all its enemies with the savagery of that persecution; that is, it will be compressed, harassed, and hemmed in by the straits of tribulation. Yet it does not abandon its military service, for it is called by the term “camp.”

But when he says, “And fire came down from heaven and consumed them,” this should not be thought to be the final punishment with which we know the impious will be tormented (Matt. XXV). Rather, it is the fire of envy by which the hostile power will be tormented because of the steadfastness of the saints. For their steadfastness is a firmament; since stability comes to the saints from it, fire is rightly said to come from there also upon their persecutors.

Hence we read: “Jealousy has seized an undisciplined people,” and, “Now fire will consume the adversaries.”

This final persecution, which is to come from the Antichrist, will last three years and six months. Although this period is brief, it is rightly questioned whether it belongs to the thousand years during which he says the Devil is bound and the saints reign with Christ, or whether this short interval is added within those years and lies outside them.

For if we say that it belongs to those same years, the reign of the saints with Christ will be found to extend for not merely that length of time but for a longer period than the Devil’s binding. Clearly, the saints will reign with their King even during that very persecution, especially by overcoming such great evils, when the Devil will no longer be bound and will therefore be able to persecute them with all his strength.

How then does this Scripture assign both events to the same thousand years—the binding of the Devil and the reign of the saints—when it first designates the Devil’s binding as lasting three years and six months, before the reign of the saints with Christ ends within those thousand years?

If, on the other hand, we say that this brief period of persecution is not counted within the thousand years but is added after they have been completed, so that the passage may be understood in its proper sense: after saying, “The priests of God and of Christ will reign with him for a thousand years,” he added, “And when the thousand years are finished, Satan will be released from his prison.”

In this way he indicates that the reign of the saints and the Devil’s bond will cease simultaneously. Therefore, if the period of that persecution is believed to belong neither to the reign of the saints nor to Satan’s imprisonment—both of which are included in the thousand years—but to be added afterward and counted outside them, we are forced to admit that the saints will not reign with Christ during that persecution.

But who would dare say that his members will not then reign with him, when they will cling to him most closely and most steadfastly, and when, the more violent the assault of the battle, the greater will be the glory of not yielding and the denser the crown of martyrdom?

Consequently, the years of the saints reigning with Christ are more numerous than the years of the Devil’s bond and imprisonment, because they will reign with their King, the Son of God, even after the Devil is no longer bound, throughout those three years and six months.

It remains, therefore, that when we hear, “The priests of God and of Christ will reign with him for a thousand years,” and, “When the thousand years are finished, Satan will be released from his imprisonment,” we should understand either that the thousand years of this reign of the saints are not being brought to an end, but rather the thousand years of the Devil’s bond and imprisonment; so that each part has its own thousand years, to be completed with different and proper durations—the reign of the saints being longer, and the Devil’s bond shorter—or else that the very brief period of three years and six months was not counted, because it seemed too short, or because the reign of the saints appears to be longer, as we often find such usage in the sacred Scriptures.

After this brief mention of the final persecution, he summarizes everything that, at the final judgment, the Devil and the hostile city with its ruler will suffer. For he says: “And the Devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet will be tormented day and night forever and ever.”

The beast is rightly understood as the impious city itself; the false prophet is either its Antichrist or that image, that is, the fiction about which he spoke here: “And I saw,” he says, “a great white throne and the one seated upon it, from whose face heaven and earth fled, and no place was found for them.”

He says that he saw seated upon the throne the one from whose face heaven and earth fled. For afterward, once the judgment has been completed, heaven and earth cease to exist, when the new heaven and the new earth begin to exist—through a transformation of things that will not altogether perish. This world will pass away; hence the Apostle also says (I Cor. VII): “For the form of this age is passing away.” It is therefore the form that passes away, not nature.

“And I saw,” he says, “the dead, great and small, and the books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of the life of each person; and the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works.”

He said that books and a book were opened, but he did not leave unspecified what kind of book it was. The books, therefore, are understood to be the New and Old Testaments, so that, when what God commanded to be done is shown in them, it may become clear in that book what each person did or did not do.

This book should not be understood in a carnal manner, nor should it be thought to contain the lives of individuals written out for examination at the judgment. Rather, a certain divine power is to be understood, by which it will come about that all a person’s works, whether good or evil, are recalled to memory and perceived by the mind’s gaze with marvelous speed, so that knowledge accuses or excuses the conscience, and all together and each individually are judged. This divine power has received the name “book.”

For in it, in a certain sense, whatever is recalled through its operation is read.

To show which dead, small and great, were judged, he recapitulates, as though returning to what he had passed over—or rather, postponed. “And the sea,” he says, “gave up the dead who were in it, and death and hell gave up the dead whom they held within them.”

This clearly occurred before the dead were judged. Therefore he recapitulated what he had interrupted; but now, maintaining the order, he says: “And they were judged, each according to his works.”

But who are the dead whom the sea gave up except those whom the second coming of Christ found placed in this age? The name “dead” signifies both the good and the wicked: the good, to whom it is said (Col. III), “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God”; and the wicked, concerning whom it is said (Matt. VIII; Luke IX), “Let the dead bury their own dead.”

The dead may also be called dead because they bear mortal bodies. Hence the Apostle says (Rom. VIII): “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness,” showing that both are present in a living human being within this body.

The sea, therefore, he says, gave them up because they appeared just as they were found. But death and hell gave them up because they recalled them to the life from which they had already departed.

Perhaps it was not without reason that it was insufficient to say “death” or “hell,” but both were mentioned: “death” on account of the good, who could suffer death alone but not hell; and “hell” on account of the wicked, who also undergo punishments among the dead.

For if it does not seem unreasonable to believe that the ancient saints who held faith in the coming Christ were also in places among the dead, far removed from the torments of the impious, until the blood of Christ and his descent to those places rescued them from there, then afterward the good faithful, already redeemed by that blood once the price had been poured out, know hell no longer, until, having also received their bodies, they receive the good things they have deserved.

After saying, “And they were judged, each according to his works,” he briefly added how this occurred: “Death and hell,” he says, “were cast into the lake of fire.” By these names he signifies the Devil, since he is the author of death and infernal punishments, together with the entire fellowship of demons.

This is what he had already stated more explicitly above by anticipation: “And the Devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur.” But what he had added there more obscurely, saying that the beast and the false prophet would also be there, he expresses here more clearly: “And those who were not found written in the book of life were cast into the lake of fire.”

He does not mention this book as though it could be deceived by forgetfulness; rather, it signifies the predestination of those who will receive eternal life. God does not fail to know them and read them in this book in order to know them. Rather, his very foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived concerning them—is the book of life in which they are written, that is, foreknown beforehand.

When the judgment has been completed, by which he foretold that the wicked would be judged, it remains for him to speak also about the good.

**CHAPTER XXI**
And I saw, he says, a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and earth passed away, and the sea is no more. This will happen in the order that he already anticipated above when he said that he had seen the one seated upon the throne, before whose face heaven and earth fled. When the impious have been judged and condemned, then the form of this world will pass away in the conflagration of worldly fires, just as the flood came about through the inundation of worldly waters. Thus, when heaven and earth have been changed for the better, [Col. 0921C] the bodies of the saints, through incorruption and immortality, will correspond to the fitting quality of this twofold change, and the world, renewed for the better, will be suitably adapted to people who themselves have likewise been renewed for the better.

But when he says, “And the sea is no more,” I would not readily say whether it will be dried up by that immense heat, or whether it too will be transformed for the better. For we read that there will be a new heaven and a new earth (Isa. LV). As for a new sea, I do not recall having read anything of the kind anywhere. Yet if, as is customary, prophetic language mingles transferred expressions with its proper words, and in some way veils what it says, he could have been speaking of that sea whose name is understood to signify this age. For then this age, turbulent and stormy as the life of mortals is, which he represented under the name of the sea, will no longer exist.

[Col. 0921D] “And I saw,” he says, “the great city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared by God like a new bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying: Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more, nor mourning nor crying, nor will there be any pain, because the former things have passed away. And the one seated upon the throne said: Behold, I make all things new.”

This city is said to descend from heaven because the grace by which God made it is heavenly; therefore he also says to it through Isaiah: “I am the Lord who makes you” (Isa. XLV). It did indeed descend from heaven from its beginning, since, throughout the time of [Col. 0922A] this age, its citizens have continually increased as the grace of God came from above through the washing of regeneration in the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. But through the judgment of God—which will be the final judgment, carried out through his Son Jesus Christ—such great and such new splendor from God’s gift will appear in it that no traces of antiquity will remain, since the bodies too will pass from the old corruption and mortality into incorruption and immortality.

For this reason he promises, saying: “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor will there be any pain.” It is certain that all these things pertain not to this life but to the life to come. For now, in this life, the holier someone is, and the fuller of holy desires, the more abundant [Col. 0922B] that person is in tears during prayer. Thus we read (Ps. XIV): “My tears have become my bread day and night,” and (Ps. XLVI): “Every night I wash my bed,” and similar passages.

And he said to me: “These words are most faithful and true.” And he said to me: “It is accomplished.” These things ought to be believed, not explained, especially since he says that they have been accomplished in the past in such a way as to leave no one uncertain about the future.

“I am Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω), the first and the last” (above, I). Just as he testified at the beginning of the book that he is this, it was appropriate that it be repeated in this third part, so that no god might be believed to exist before him, as Isaiah says (Isa. XLI), nor any other after him.

[Col. 0922C] “I will give to the thirsty, freely, from the fountain of living water.” From this fountain he waters those who do not believe along the way, while in the homeland he provides it abundantly for the victorious to drink. Thus strangers may not perish from thirst in this desert, but, once watered and made citizens, may continually be filled from the torrent of God’s delights. Both are given freely, because, as the Apostle says (Rom. VI), eternal life is the grace of God.

It follows: “The one who conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son.” Here he recalls that generation of which the Apostle says (Gal. IV): “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’” “And if sons, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ. But we have been saved in hope” (Rom. VIII). When one arrives at the reality through hope, God himself will be the reward of eternal blessedness for the elect, so that those who have been possessed by him may possess him forever.

[Col. 0922D] “But for the doubtful and unbelieving”—by “doubtful” one must here understand the double-minded person of whom the Apostle James says (Jas. I): “A double-minded man,” he says, “is unstable in all his ways.” “And for the detestable, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, those who serve idols, and all liars, their portion will be in the pool of fire that burns with sulfur, which is the second death.” These things—whether the vices of crimes or the scourges of punishments—are not to be explained merely so that they may be understood, but rather pondered in terms of how they may be avoided through God’s grace.

And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven final plagues came. Just as the totality of good things is very often represented by the number seven, so in evil the totality of the plagues may also be comprehended by the same number. If he now declares those plagues that he previously mentioned as having been poured out to be full, it is surprising how he could have remained silent about their infliction upon the world—unless perhaps here he preferred to touch briefly upon a meaning that he knew he had already set forth more fully, [Col. 0923A] so that he might neither omit mention of the evil things nor fail immediately to turn his attention toward the good figure of the Church, concerning which he sings (Ps. XXVI): “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

Finally, it follows: “And he spoke with me, saying: Come, I will show you the new bride, the wife of the Lamb,” that is, the Church. “And he led me onto a great and high mountain, and he showed me the holy city Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God.”

This is, according to the testimony of Truth, the city set upon a mountain (Matt. V). [Col. 0923B] Hence Isaiah says (chap. III): “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the summit of the mountains, and it will be lifted above the hills.” This may refer either to that summit of righteousness about which we read (Isa. XLI), “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God,” or because mountains are called both apostles and prophets.

Yet the Lord Christ rises above all of them, like a mountain at the summit of the mountains. From his fullness, he says, “we have received, and grace upon grace.”

And it is rightly said to be “from heaven, from God.” For then it appears more beautiful, when, through the Spirit by whom her bridegroom is believed to have been conceived and born, she has been deemed worthy to bear a heavenly image.

Thus the bride herself is also the city. “Having,” he says, “the glory of God as her light.” To her the Lord says (Matt. V): “You are the light of the world.” This declaration applies to the whole body of Christ, which the apostles, prior in merit and in time, then received from the mouth of Truth.

“And the one who illuminates it is like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone, shining like crystal.” Although jasper and crystal are different in kind and color, he rightly joined them here on account of their resemblance. [Col. 0923C] And when he soon compares it with the most precious stones, he wished it to be understood as Christ revealed under this image, concerning whom blessed Peter says (1 Pet. II): “A precious cornerstone, laid as a foundation.”

“And it has a great and broad wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written upon them—the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.”

The wall of the Church is Christ, whom we also read to be great and exalted: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain,” and “the Lord is exalted above all nations” (Ps. XLVII; Ps. CXLIV; Ps. CXII).

[Col. 0923D] The prophet Isaiah speaks of the wall (chap. XXVI): “On that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: ‘The city of our strength is Zion; the Savior will be placed in it as wall and rampart. Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, keeping the truth; the ancient error has passed away.’”

These passages appear to narrate similar things while expressing them in one spirit. Finally, he also speaks of the gates, saying: “And twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written upon them—the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.”

We certainly know that through the twelve apostles our Lord formerly provided the beginnings of entrance into faith for all people in another sense. Nevertheless, the context of this passage drew us away from that interpretation when it inserted the mention of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, as though wishing the twelve patriarchs to be understood here first. From their stock we know the whole Israelite people to have been specially propagated, and from them, according to the Apostle Paul [Col. 0924A] (Rom. XI), “a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace,” while he adds in the same place that “God has not rejected his people.” Therefore we ought to understand the twelve patriarchs as corresponding to the twelve gates, especially when we hear: “You do not bear the root, but the root bears you.”

For he clearly says: “And names written upon them—the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.” Hence the Apostle confidently cries (Rom. IX): “Who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, whose is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenants, and the legislation, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.”

[Col. 0924B] I think that the angels here signify those elders and leaders by whose administration and guidance that people was wonderfully governed. If we remember that they are often called gods (Ps. XLVI), why should we be surprised if we believe them to be called angels? “He shall be brought,” it says (Exod. XXII), “to the gods”; and (Ps. LXXXI), “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” Thus he showed that he was embracing the whole community of the people, which consists of leaders and peoples.

“Three gates on the east, three gates on the north, three gates on the south, and three gates on the west.” Here he embraces the number twelve, which is often presented to us as sacred, both in the apostles and in the seats, for the fullness of universality. “You will sit with me upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). For the odd number, that is, three, multiplied by the even number four—three times four—produces twelve.

[Col. 0924C] It follows: “And the walls of the city have twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the apostles of the Lamb.”

After mentioning the patriarchs, he recalls the apostles. Since we know that the Church has only one foundation, namely Christ, we should not be troubled by his saying here that it has twelve foundations. For in Christ the apostles were worthy to be the foundations of the Church. Concerning this the Apostle says (1 Cor. III): “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.”

In the same way the apostles are also said to be light, when he says to them (Matt. V): “You are the light of this world,” although Christ is the sun, the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I). Christ, therefore, is the illuminating light, while they are illuminated light. Holy Scripture frequently conveys many such things to us through similar expressions.

[Col. 0924D] Finally, the Apostle James says (Jas. I): “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of first-fruits of his creation.” Yet the Apostle Paul, confident [the printed reading is uncertain: *praebendi*], says (1 Cor. IV): “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you.”

God begets through the adoption of grace, while Paul begets in Christ either through the administration of the sacrament or through the preaching of doctrine. He nevertheless remembers the divine admonition that says (Matt. XXIII): “Do not call anyone your teacher on earth, for one is your teacher, who is in heaven.” The same applies to fathers.

Elsewhere the same Paul says (1 Cor. I): “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” Thus, by withdrawing the intention and hope of all the faithful from everyone else, he fixed them in God through sound teaching.

[Col. 0925A] In this sense Psalm CXX also sang, saying: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come.” By the mountains he wished the apostles and prophets to be understood, whom Christ, the Sun of righteousness, principally illuminated. And lest anyone think that he should trust in their names, he immediately followed by adding: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXX).

Thus here too we ought to recognize the twelve foundations as the apostles, though all are called upon the one foundation, Jesus Christ. This is also why the name of the Lamb is not omitted here, when he says: “And upon them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.” The apostles are therefore foundations, but upon the one foundation, Jesus. Christ alone is rightly called the foundation without the apostles; but the apostles without Christ can in no way be called the foundations of the Church.

[Col. 0925B] The same applies to the other comparisons that we have thought appropriate to apply to this passage. For they were worthy, in Christ, to beget the faithful spiritually—those whom Christ alone, without them, could have adopted incomparably if he had wished. They were also worthy to be teachers and shepherds of peoples in Christ, but so that their service might serve the heavenly Father, their teacher and shepherd.

They acted according to the measure that Christ distributed to them through the gift of their Lord; Christ himself acted through his uniquely natural power. Concerning him we remember what was said in the Gospel: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John III). “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II), and “from his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace” (John I).

It follows:

[Col. 0925C] “And the one who spoke with me had a golden measuring reed, in order to measure the city, and its gates, and its walls. And the city is laid out as a square, and its length is as great as its width.”

Earlier John says that a reed was given to him, as though the administration of preaching had been entrusted to him. But now he says that the angel who spoke with him had a golden reed, “in order,” he says, “to measure the city, its gates, and its walls.”

Therefore Christ must be understood, for he is the wisdom of God (1 Cor. I), “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII). Hence we read (Prov. XVI): “Receive wisdom as gold.” Indeed, only Christ may measure the city, since he distributes the gifts of grace to each of the spiritual faithful. As we read, he has also ordered all things “in number, measure, and weight” (Wis. XI).

This measurement of the city is recalled by the Apostle when he says (Eph. IV): “According to the measure of Christ’s gift”; and again (Eph. III): “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach the Gospel among the Gentiles.”

[Col. 0925D] For this reason the city is said to be laid out as a square, and established with equal dimensions on every side, so that it may not be altered by any unequal variation. According to the Apostle (1 Cor. I), to be perfect, to have the same understanding, and to possess peace is truly to stand securely in a solid square.

This is the city that the Lord declares in the Gospel to have been built upon a mountain—that is, founded upon himself (Matt. V). For this reason he also says to Peter, who bore the figure of the whole Church [Col. 0926A] (Matt. XVI): “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” It is as though he were saying: “Upon me I will build you.” For the rock was Christ; thus Peter takes his name from the rock, just as Christian takes its name from Christ.

He teaches us to flee the inventions of human error and to follow only the defenses of divine truth.

“And he measured,” he says, “the city with the reed: twelve thousand stadia, equal in length, width, and height.” Here is that solidity of unconquered truth by which the Church of Christ, properly supported, is not allowed to be carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV).

The number twelve produces one hundred forty-four when multiplied by itself: twelve times twelve makes one hundred forty-four.

It follows: “And he measured its wall: one hundred forty-four cubits, a human measure, which is also an angel’s measure.”

[Col. 0926B] That the angel here often signifies the Church is plainly demonstrated by the frequent occurrence of this interpretation throughout the passages. And because the Church is gathered from human beings and exalted by the promises of Christ, it hopes for equality with the angels, and all its desire sighs toward their fellowship.

Therefore he says, “a human measure, which is also an angel’s measure.” This may mean either that the city will consist partly of angels already dwelling there in perpetual happiness and partly of pilgrims, that is, human beings, who will reign there in fuller measure; or, alternatively, that we trust what was lost from the heavenly habitation of the angels through a certain number of transgressors will be restored by the number of the redeemed. It will easily be replaced by a more abundant multitude, though it will not be diminished.

For this reason it is sung in Deuteronomy (chap. XXXII): “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” and so forth.

[Col. 0926C] “And the structure of its wall was of jasper stone.” Blessed Peter exhorts the people (1 Pet. II) to be built, like living stones, into a spiritual house.

It follows: “But the city itself was of pure gold, like pure glass.” He also mentions things that do not naturally correspond, so that, by attributing singular dignity to the one singular stone, Christ, through all the comparisons, he might teach that everything serves him. For who does not know that gold properly differs from glass and is distinguished from it in color?

And although it is not a new thing for the Church to be represented by gold—since it is often described in golden lampstands and bowls on account of the cultivation of wisdom—what is striking here is that pure gold is likened to pure glass.

[Col. 0926D] I think this signifies what the Apostle foretold, saying (1 Cor. IV): “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts.” For in glass nothing is revealed outwardly except what is contained within.

Accordingly, announcing here that time when thoughts will be clearly disclosed to one another, this book confidently wished to compare gold with glass. Whatever will then be present in the thought of the saints will shine, adorned with the beauty of wisdom, to which the comparison rightly corresponds.

For now, however great a person’s excellence in virtue may be, “no one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him” (1 Cor. II). Alternatively, this may mean that glass, according to its own nature, completely excels within its kind.

“And the foundations were made of every precious stone.” [Col. 0927A] In the Song we also read in Tobit (chap. XIII): “All your walls are precious stones.” And in Isaiah (chap. LIV): “Behold, I will arrange your stones in order, and I will lay your foundations in sapphires, and I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates of carved stones, and all your boundaries of desirable stones.”

And, as though explaining what he had said, lest you should think carnally about the extent of an earthly structure, he added (Isa. XLV): “All your sons will be taught by the Lord, and great will be the peace of your sons,” and so forth.

Blessed Paul, agreeing with these meanings, says (Eph. II): “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.”

[Col. 0927B] The first foundation is jasper. What he earlier said—“the foundations were made of every precious stone”—he now proceeds to enumerate by name:

The second, sapphire; the third, chalcedony; the fourth, emerald; the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, topaz; the tenth, chrysoprase; the eleventh, hyacinth; the twelfth, amethyst.

Through these comparisons with all the stones, the beauties and supports of the virtues are signified, by which each of the saints is spiritually adorned. The whole city too is described as firm through these stones, as through strength, and adorned with the splendor of their variety.

[Col. 0927C] “And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate being made from a single pearl.” What we have said sufficiently and more than sufficiently concerning the one foundation, Christ, and the twelve apostles of the Lamb, the reader should also consider here concerning the one pearl—that is, Christ—which the merchant found and purchased after selling everything (Matt. XIII)—and concerning the twelve pearls.

“And its streets were of pure gold, like transparent glass.” He had already said that the city was of pure gold, like pure glass, and that its foundations were made of every precious stone. I think this refers to the powerful members of the Church.

Now he adds concerning the streets, saying that they too were of gold, “like transparent glass.” It seems that the streets do not belong to the city described earlier, but that here the little ones are signified, concerning whom it is now said (Ps. CXXXVIII): “Your eyes saw my unfinished state, and in your book they will all be written.” Likewise (Prov. III): “And with the simple is his conversation.” That is, they too will not be deprived of this gift, but will contemplate their thoughts in mutual exchange.

[Col. 0927D] Just as streets are placed in a lower position, so such people seem to be saved in a humble position. But if breadth is to be understood in the streets as charity, he wished to signify the perfect by different names.

Then, however, no one unworthy will be there, and no one will be found little or weak, although one may surpass another in the unequal elevation of rewards. For “star differs from star in glory,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. XV); so also is the resurrection of the dead.

[Col. 0928A] “And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.” Just as the body is constructed from its individual members, so the temple is constructed from precious stones. And because he does not want us, being devoted to material constructions, to imagine anything bodily here according to our accustomed habit, he restrains us from that interpretation, saying: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.”

For the Church, especially when the weeds have now been removed, rejoicing in the elect alone, remains consecrated in the Lord, resting more securely as though in a temple. From him she received the origin of her existence and experienced the tenderness of redemption; in him she also obtains her blessed dwelling.

Her whole being is completed in these three things: to exist, to know, and to love. God created her to be formed, illuminated her when called, and blessed her when chosen, when he causes himself to dwell in her through the promised glorification once she has been perfected—not now walking by faith, but rejoicing in direct vision.

“And the city,” he says, “does not need the sun or the moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God illuminates it, and its lamp is the Lamb.”

[Col. 0928B] Desiring to withdraw us completely from the customary alternation of daytime and nighttime light, and to recall us to that unchangeable light, he says: “It does not need the sun or the moon.” Nor does he assert that the city is illuminated in the same manner, but by a far better and ineffable light—namely, by the Sun of righteousness, whom the prophet recalls, saying (Mal. IV): “And healing is in his wings.”

For he is the true Son, eternal life, and the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I). Of this light, in his divinity, “no eye has seen in this age, no ear has heard, and it has not entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. II). Nothing better, or more fittingly than what is said here, could explain it: “The glory of the Lord illuminates it, and its lamp is the Lamb.”

For what more excellent gift could be given to the victor than to be deemed worthy to possess the very giver of gifts? In the homeland he will enjoy the light by which we are now guided as we walk along the way. Formed by that same light, we distinguish between good and evil; then, glorified, we will see only the things that are good.

[Col. 0928C] “And the nations,” he says, “will walk in its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it.” By these words he wished it to be understood that the same Lamb is the way for those journeying abroad, and the life for the citizens who have arrived.

Whatever dignity they may have obtained, they must necessarily confer it, with fitting praises, upon the honor of the giver. Here he calls spiritual people kings, concerning whom we read: “He is mighty, and gives strength to our kings, and exalted the horn of his Christ” (1 Sam. II).

“And its gates will not be shut by day, for there will be no night there.” He says that the perpetual light of the Lamb—or rather, the Lamb himself as everlasting light—will be beneficial in that city once the time of night has been removed.

[Col. 0928D] Thus Isaiah says (chap. LXVI): “From month to month and from sabbath to sabbath they will come,” signifying light by the month, because of the moon’s fullest radiance, and perpetual rest by the sabbath. It is as though he were saying: light for them proceeds from light, and eternal rest is continued for them from rest.

The fact that the gates will not be shut indicates the condition of complete security. There it will no longer be said, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI), but rather, “Be still and see that I am the Lord” (Ps. XLV).

There what is seen is loved honorably, and what is loved will be praised without ceasing. No one there withers through idleness, nor is anyone wearied by the labor of perpetual praise.

“And they will bring the honor and majesty of the nations into it,” because it will be gathered from all nations.

[Col. 0929A] “And nothing unclean will enter it, nor anyone who practices the abomination of life, except those who are written in the book of life of the Lamb.” Here he describes the Church in the future, when it will no longer, as now, tolerate the wicked dwelling together with the good in a mixed community. For only the good will reign with Christ, with whom and in whom they will faithfully remain as that same Jerusalem, the heavenly mother of all.

He says that they are written in the Lamb’s book, concerning which he says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

It follows:

**CHAPTER XXII**
And he showed me a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing out from the throne of God and of the Lamb, through the middle of its street. In the middle of the city’s river of life, running through it [*per mediante*, thus], the celebration of baptism is not yet indicated, but the fruit of the sacrament itself will already be revealed. For now, what will then be reaped with joy is sown in tears (Ps. 125). And therefore the Church now sows in the Spirit, so that from the Spirit she may reap eternal life (Gal. 6). When, then, experience has shown us when the fruit of the sacrament received by grace has benefited us, the river of the water of life, bright as crystal—that is, steadfastness in faith—is said in John to be revealed to the Church. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10; 24).

Signifying this, he continues: “And on either side of the river was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit in each month, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations, and there will no longer be any curse.” By the twelve months he indicates all time and signifies complete perpetuity. Accordingly, where there is eternal vigor, no withering is ever understood to be present; where there is perfect and enduring health, no infirmity interrupts anything at all. The prophet promises this, saying (Isa. 35): “They will obtain joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning will flee away.”

That tree is the one which we read was planted beside streams of water (Ps. 1), concerning which Jeremiah also says (chap. 17) that it will send out its roots toward moisture—the one who places his hope and trust in the Lord. Alternatively, by “the river of the water of life,” etc., the Lord Jesus Christ himself, rightly understood as the fountain of life, is signified, of whom we read (Ps. 35): “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.” For he is, as we read (Wis. 7), “the image of God’s majesty, all-powerful and abiding in himself; he renews all things and, through the nations, rests in holy souls.”

That fountain, therefore, is also a river: a fountain because it remains unchangeable in itself; a river because it generously and continually offers itself for fellowship with the saints. Indeed, where he is called a fountain, he is also called a torrent. For when the psalm said (Ps. 35), “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delights,” it immediately added: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.”

Appropriately, it is said to be “through the middle of the street,” as a common good for all the saints, denied to no one who is worthy and granted to no one who is unworthy. “Those who dwell in Jerusalem are mountains around her, and the Lord is around his people” (Ps. 124). Likewise: “God, who is glorified in the assembly of the saints, is great and awesome above all who surround him.” For he is in the midst, as an undivided inheritance visible to all who see God. Hence we read (Ps. 121): “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in unity.”

But if the fruit of death is received as blessed immortality, the leaves are rightly understood as the song of perpetual praise, which falls upon those already singing in blessed condition. For there the healing of the nations is true, redemption complete, and happiness everlasting.

“But the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it.” He did not say “they will be,” nor “thrones.” For where there is natural and undifferentiated unity, the glory of the Godhead ought especially to be commended: one indivisible throne of session, which cannot be divided by the cunning of Arian depravity or confused by the suspicion of Sabellian vanity, but belongs solely to catholic truth. The remaining corrupt wording appears to concern adoption and its confession in right belief.

“And they will see his face.” He is considering the vision of God promised to the saints in the future, a cause of great merit and something to be valued with entirely exceptional estimation. I have chosen [*Legi*, perhaps *elegi*] to extract sayings of Saint Augustine appropriate to this passage, so that, with him as our teacher, we may recognize without doubt what is promised for the future.

For, writing to Paulina about the vision of God, he says:

> Until, through careful inquiry, if the Lord helps, it is discovered what should more probably be believed according to the Scriptures concerning the spiritual body promised in the resurrection, for the present let it suffice us that the only-begotten Son, who is also the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2), sees the Father in the same way as he is seen by the Father. But as for that vision of God promised to us in the resurrection, let us not attempt to transfer to it from this world the lust of the eyes; rather, let us devote ourselves with pious affection to the purification of our hearts. Nor should we imagine a bodily face, when the Apostle says (1 Cor. 13): “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face”; especially since he said more explicitly: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known.”

How, then, could anyone fail to understand that in this passage he also wished to signify our face, of which he says elsewhere (2 Cor. 3): “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord”—that is, from the glory of faith into the glory of eternal contemplation? For this is what that transformation effects, by which the inner person is renewed from day to day (2 Cor. 4). Concerning this the Apostle Peter also says, when he urges that person to be adorned:

> Not with what is adorned outwardly, he says (1 Pet. 3), with the curling of the hair, or gold, or pearls, or expensive clothing, but with the hidden person of the heart, which is precious before God.

Likewise, in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*, he says:

> The vision of God is reserved for us as the reward of faith. Concerning it the Apostle John also says: “When he appears,” he says (1 John 3), “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

But the face of God is to be understood as the manifestation of God, not as some bodily member such as we possess; it is called “face” by this designation. A little later he says:

> Thus God will be known and visible to us that he may be seen by each of us in spirit, seen by one through another, seen in himself, seen in the new heaven and the new earth, and in every creature that will then exist.

“And his name will be written on their foreheads.” He declares that this temple is justified through faith, through which the merit of eternal life is also conferred, when he causes the name of God and of the Lamb to be borne written upon their foreheads, as though it were recognized and gloriously displayed as a title. This faith he embraces in a single name. For he did not say, “the names of God and of the Lamb will be written on their foreheads,” although he appears to have signified a twofold person, in order to preserve the rule of that doctrine when speaking of the reigning saints—a rule which the Lord had earlier handed down for his disciples to maintain among the nations: “Go,” he says (Matt. 28), “baptize all nations, immersing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

This had to be carefully commended: that the saints would see and possess in visible form what, while living, they had believed through faith.

“And night will no longer exist, nor will they need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord God will shine upon them, and they will reign forever and ever.” The frailty of our bodies now uses the alternations of time and the disturbances of the elements, so that night’s rest may make us fit for the works of the day; it also uses a lamp during the night as a consolation. But then, when God will be “all in all” (1 Cor. 15), he who is the true light, no one there will need these elements, nor will anyone ever be subject to them. He himself will be the light of the reigning saints, he who is the author of the whole work. Nor will there be any need of the exhortation and preaching of the divine law which are now said to be a lamp in a dark place, because, with all things completed in the contemplation of God, the promise will be held in perfection.

“And he said to me: ‘These words are most trustworthy and true.’” He was not expressing doubt about John, but was commending the true vision to the whole Church, in which he knew that children too would be present.

“And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must take place.” In brief, he taught that he had generally provided for the benefit of all. He himself is the Spirit of the prophets, who is also the Holy Spirit—indeed, the Lord—and for that reason the prophet. “I will hear,” he says (Ps. 84), “what the Lord God will speak within me”; and the beginning of speech belongs to the Lord in Hosea (chap. 1). For, because of the essence of the one divine Trinity, he appropriately also named the Holy Spirit here, after recently mentioning the Father and the Son. What we read (John 4), that “God is spirit,” applies to the whole Trinity.

“Behold, I am coming quickly. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.” Here “to keep” means to believe reverently and to guard through a commitment to a purer life.
