“And I, John, who heard and saw these things.” The attestation of the revelation is presented as being confirmed by human judgment. “And when I had heard,” he says, “and had seen, I fell down before the feet of the angel who showed me these things, to worship him. And he said to me: ‘See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers the prophets who keep the words of the prophecy of this book. Worship God instead.’”

Either he repeated an action he had performed only once and did not repeat after being restrained, or, struck by the great astonishment of the visions, he confesses that he wished to worship again, just as the prophet says: “My belly trembled at the voice of the supplication of my lips, and trembling entered my bones, and my strength was disturbed within me.”

“And he said to me: ‘Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, because the time is near; let the one who persists in doing harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is in filth continue to be filthy.’” Here he shows God’s hidden but just judgments, by which wicked people are permitted to advance toward worse things. “To do harm” here should be understood not only of harming others but rather of harming oneself. Hence it follows: “Let the one who is in filth continue to be filthy.” For if a person is wicked toward himself, toward whom will he be good?

Another translation has: “Let the one who is unjust continue to act unjustly; but let the just person do what is more just, and likewise the holy person what is holier.” I think he says, “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book,” because, as the judgment approaches, it was necessary for the divine commands, judgments, and promises to be revealed, so that the gentle may acquire a reward through observing them, while the negligent and obstinate may incur punishment.

Earlier he had said: “Do not write the signs spoken by the seven thunders”; now, however: “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.”

“Behold, I am coming quickly, and my reward is with me, to repay each person according to his deeds.” This has been sufficiently stated.

“I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.” This is a faithful proclamation of the truth. Whenever the irreproachable pattern of virtues is confirmed through repetition, the spiritual mind is shaped with greater devotion. This is expressed briefly but suitably at the conclusion of the book: in Alpha he assigns the divinity of the Word, and in Omega the humanity assumed—beginning without end.

But when I see Alpha and Omega repeated so often in the present book, I recognize that this was not done without purpose. Whether it was to suggest more frequently the divinity and humanity of the one Christ, in which, as we have stated earlier, the whole sum of Christian faith consists; or so that the whole Trinity might be intimated as one in nature—the one who says through the prophet (Isa. 43), “Before me no god was formed, and after me there will be none. I am God, and there is no savior besides me”; or the one to whom the prophet says, “You are God, and before you and besides you there is no other God”; or whether some other, better and more hidden mystery lies concealed, I nevertheless do not doubt that it was repeated so often so that it might remain fruitful for the faithful for the sake of understanding.

The Greek alphabet’s own elements, Alpha and Omega, also produce the sum of the same number, which we know is contained in the Greek word for “dove.” For “dove” is called [the Greek word is absent from the supplied text], from whose name the number eight hundred and one is summed; this number they also complete [the text is corrupt here]. Under the appearance of a dove, we rightly understand the person of the Holy Spirit to be signified (Matt. 3), since, descending in that form, he wished to appear. Thus the madness of the Arians and other heretics would be confounded: they assert that he is alien from the nature of the Father and the Son, although through the correspondence of this number the heavenly revelation here too manifests the Holy Spirit as consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son, and speaks of those in washed robes as guardians of the divine commandments.

John also composed the beginning of his Gospel with the same meaning, although he began with different wording, saying (John 1): “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; and a little later: “And the Word became flesh.” Here the whole sum of faith consists: that in one and the same Christ perfect divinity and true humanity are believed.

As for moral integrity, he says (John 1): “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name,” adding, of course, love to faith. He appears to have narrated the reward of these things also through corresponding paths, signifying Christ in Alpha and Omega, and signifying an immaculate life by white robes. He promises the same reward to this life, saying: “That their authority may be over the tree of life.”

The tree of life is Christ, as we read: “Wisdom is a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Prov. 3). But these people are not to be thought of as being above Christ, because “a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord” (Matt. 10). He says “over the tree of life” in the same way as if he were to say: Their strength will rest upon the tree of life—that is, upon the Lord Christ—of whom the prophet also says: “And upon the Holy One of Israel they are established.” From the source of their strength, then, they are said to be above them.

In the same sense it is also said to Saint Peter (Matt. 16): “Upon this rock I will build my Church,” that is, upon me. And the prophet, using different words but the same meaning, says (Ps. 58): “I will keep my strength toward you.”

“And let them enter the holy city through the gates.” Concerning these gates, I think it is written (Ps. 117): “Open for me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter through them and confess to the Lord; this is the Lord’s gate; the righteous will enter through it.” For that city cannot be entered in any other way except through Christ, who said (John 10): “I am the door, and no one comes to the Father except through me.”

“But outside will remain the dogs, and sorcerers, and fornicators, and murderers, and those who serve idols, and poisoners, and all who love and practice falsehood.” With respect to these people, diligence is not to be spent on explaining them, but care is to be devoted to avoiding them.

“I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the seven churches.” As he is about to resume the sequence of the book, he assigns the intention of the first account, so that the later parts may correspond to the earlier ones.

“I am the root and offspring of David.” Having first proclaimed Christ’s divinity, as I explained earlier, he also proclaims the form of a servant which he assumed for us, saying: “I am the root and lineage of David, the bright and morning star.” As the grace of the New Testament shines forth, he indicates the time of the first resurrection, when Christ rose from the dead. Hence we read (Ps. 129): “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.”

“And the Spirit and the new bride say”—Christ and the Church—“‘We exhort: Come!’ And let the one who hears say: ‘Come!’” Explaining himself, he discloses the disposition of his exhortation and says: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink; and let the one who wishes take the water of life freely.”

How can the one who wishes take it, when he said (John 6), “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”? Only because we know that one who was previously unwilling becomes willing through divine inspiration. Here too he appropriately affirms free choice by saying, “Let the one who wishes take,” so that grace may immediately be proclaimed in the words, “the water of life freely”: let him take the water of life freely, with no preceding good works.

For what do you have, the Apostle says (1 Cor. 4), that you did not receive? Therefore we also receive freely from God the will to come, although we contributed nothing as a reward for being created—how much more, then, for being made righteous from sinners!

“I, John, testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book.” He says this who commanded the testimony to be given. The one whom he earlier calls the faithful witness now says that he commanded testimony to be given, lest the usefulness of so salutary a book be thought contemptible. With commendable humility he places his own person second and sets Christ before those who despise it.

Therefore, what the faithful witness, the head, fulfilled when he said (John 4), “My food is to do the will of him who sent me,” or words of similar meaning, may he help the body also to fulfill.

“If anyone adds to these things, God will add upon him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away, the Lord will take away his share from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book.” Solomon also says (Prov. 30): “Do not add anything to his words, lest you be reproved and found a liar.” Here, however, he also added the terror of plagues, so that he might not only urge them by the weight of his authority in admonition, but also, through threats, either rouse the negligent or restrain the rash.

He who testifies to these things says: “Yes, I am coming quickly.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

The same Christ bears witness, announcing that he will come to the Church. In the manner of the *Song of Songs* (Cant. 2, 4, 5, 7), the devoted Church replies: “Yes, come, Lord Jesus Christ.” She says in prayer, “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6), and, “You will come to me on the blameless way.”

Since I know that the fullness of the work undertaken must therefore be concluded with a devoted and fitting ending, and that what has been spread broadly and arranged in many ways is difficult to comprehend—for neither an adequate memory supports everyone, nor can swift attention readily fit the passages related to each individual matter together—I think it necessary to proceed by useful abridgements. After traversing the authority of the entire book, the sequence of the conclusion should be unfolded again in a brief recapitulation, presented in sections, so that the text of all five books may be clearly defined in summary at a single point, since it has both received the division of its individual parts and appears to obtain fullness throughout.

In the seven angels of the seven churches, therefore, the unity of the universal Church is described, with the necessary insertion of their names. He teaches that this Church, also represented in the golden lampstands, has the wicked mixed together with the good; their differing quality is either soothed by praises for their advancement or censured by rebukes for their disgrace. He also describes her, in a repeated signification, as to be recognized in the twenty-four elders through Christ’s dispensation and the preaching of the evangelists. This is in the first book.

In the second book, the dignity of the sealed book is said, by the merit of the completed dispensation, to be bestowed upon Christ the head, so that Christ and the Church may be understood as “two in one flesh” (Eph. 5), and so that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge may be understood to have previously lain hidden in him, in whom they are taught (Col. 2) to have shone forth when their time came.

The same one earlier appeared in action on the white horse, sent forth; he is said to have proceeded, revealed to sight. After Christ’s triumph over death, he enumerates the future assaults upon the Church and the wounds of the human race, which he says will be inflicted under the symbolism of the red, black, and pale horses. He recalls the martyrs who arise beneath God’s altar and announces, under the sixth sign, the sixth age of the world, which will come at the end with a great force of persecution.

In the four angels he attests, in words corresponding to Daniel, the four kingdoms of the world. The first, ancient advent of Christ declares that these kingdoms harm the number of the elect; nor were they to be passed over in a transitory account, since he also gave the names of the twelve tribes together with the number of those sealed. And, to show that the Church exists as one Church from the race of Israel and from the nations, he immediately added the calling of the nations. From their works he wished faith to be related, and from faith its reward.

In the third book also, in a pleasing repetition characteristic of him, he describes the Church in the seven angels and the trumpets. He recalls that she will be exercised by external and internal persecutions and dangers. After one angel who stood upon God’s altar with a golden censer, he appears to have set against him a second, third, and fourth antagonist. With the mention of the eagle inserted again, he says that heretics emerge from the well of the abyss in the locusts, the smoke, and the warlike horses. Their bites are like those of scorpions, in which he says that the first woe has passed.

The release of the four angels, together with the number eighty and twice ten thousand times ten thousand, by which he describes the constant heresiarchs in various ways as horsemen with breastplates of fire and sulfur, is followed by the error of paganism, which is to be assigned to the second woe.

In the angel clothed with a cloud, the first advent of Christ is signified. Through his preaching, he says, sweetness is produced from what is good in the mouth, and bitterness from what is evil in the weakness of the belly. In the voice of the seventh angel, the end of the sixth age and the beginning of the seventh are announced. In the two witnesses, two kinds of martyrdom are to be recognized, and he says that the third woe has come.

After inserting a mention of the second advent, he relates that Christ’s birth again took place when God’s temple was opened in heaven—that is, the Church—which, following the footsteps of her head and victorious in the struggle, is said to have emerged from the battle with the dragon.

In the fourth book, therefore, he discusses the beast, which he says has seven heads and ten horns. In it is signified the opposition directed against Christ and the Church. Although he says that it will prevail for a time through the signs of Antichrist, he nevertheless teaches that it must be endured with the patience and wisdom of the saints. He warns that the mark, or the name, or the number of the beast must be investigated.

After this he circumscribes the Church as steadfast among the elect, marked with the name of the Lamb and titled with a sacred number. Likewise, he asserts that Christ is seated upon a white cloud in another form, crowned, with the sickle of harvest, after a mention of seven plagues. He relates the victory of the saints and, while the hardness of the Jews remains, recalls the future condemnation of the prostitute, whom he describes in the adorned attire of a woman. In her seven heads and ten horns he says that both worldly power and hidden wickedness reside.

In the fifth book as well, Christ’s same advent is indicated in a different account. He says that Christ descends from heaven under the name of an angel and illuminates the earth with his power and splendor. He recalls that Babylon has been destroyed. Signified by many names, she is foretold as destined to fall; she is shown to be punished with the vengeance owed for the iniquity committed. There the dignity of the saints was certainly to be commemorated in the elders, in the marriage of the Lamb, and in clean linen.

Then he describes the one wearing the insignia of a diadem and seated upon a white horse as having fought against the beast. He says that he bound the devil with his own chains for a thousand years, so that the devil lost his customary power to deceive the nations. He presents the form of the future judgment, with one sitting upon a white throne.

Mentioning Christ himself, he again signifies the second advent, when, through the renewal of the elements, the new heaven and the future earth are described, together with the new Jerusalem, the bride of the Lamb. Solidly founded upon the patriarchs and apostles, she is said to obtain the promised reward, to be illumined by the Lamb’s light, to drink from the fountain of life, and to enjoy his vision.

He therefore repeatedly emphasizes Alpha and Omega in his proclamation, so that he may intimate the Trinity of the one divine nature, and so that the language of his future Gospel may appear to agree with this book. By repeating the mention of the seven churches, he assigns the purpose of the book, that is, its intention, and Christ announces that he will come to the Church.

Considering the extent of this work, I think that some may complain about its length, as they imagine it, while others, burning with zeal for the divine law or for reading, may instead demand greater depths from so profound a book. But as I long wavered between those who are weary and those who are eager, I feared either that through excessive outpourings I might have imposed error upon the idle, or that I might be judged grudging for having withheld what was necessary through brevity. Thus I thought the style should be moderated, with the Lord guiding it, so that I might devote more words to illuminating the more obscure passages and few to those that are clear—so that I would neither defraud the hungry of what they might discover nor, by what I brought forth, offend the learned.

Nevertheless, I confess that I have rendered these services not as much as the dignity of the difficult mysteries required, but as much as the poverty of my powers, with divine assistance, was able to provide.

**In the year of our Lord 555**

**Victor, Bishop of Tunnuna.**

[Note: Elsewhere it is read *Tunonensis*; either form is valid. — Editor.]

## Notice (from Gallandius)

### I.

Around the middle of the sixth century Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna in Africa, became renowned. There is considerable disagreement among scholars concerning the city whose bishop Victor was; Wesselingius discusses the matter at greater length [Note: Wessel., *Dissertation on the Gospel, etc., in Victor of Tunnuna*, chap. 4, pp. 158 ff.]. For the present, we follow Victor himself, who calls the Church he governed “Tunnunensis” [Note: Victor, *Chronicle*, under the year 555; below, col. 860]. Nor does Isidore of Seville say otherwise, calling Victor bishop of the African Church of Tunnuna [Note: Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 25], although elsewhere in the same author, clearly through a scribal error, he is called “Turonensis” [Note: Id., *Etymologies*, book 5, chap. 39, at the end].

Because of his vigorous defense of the Three Chapters, as the same bishop of Seville reports [Note: Id., *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, cited above], he was expelled from his church by the Emperor Justinian Augustus and transported into exile in Egypt. Recalled from there to Constantinople, when he resisted the Emperor Justinian and Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, who opposed the same Three Chapters, he was sent to a monastery in that city to be held in custody, and, remaining under that condemnation, as they say, he died.

But our African bishop himself must be heard above all. Under the year 555, in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of illustrious rank, he writes the following about himself in detail [Note: Victor, *Chronicle*, cited above]:

> Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna and author of this work, after the confinements and also the blows which he suffered from Sala and Valericus, and likewise in the monastery of Mandra, was sent into exile, first and second, on the island of Ega in Mauretania, and third to Alexandria together with Theodore, bishop of the Church of Cebarsus, in defense of the aforesaid Three Chapters; he was thrust into the prison of the castle of Diocletian, at the praetorian prison.

And again, under the year 556, in the sixteenth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of illustrious rank [Note: Id., same passage]:

> Victor, he says, and Theodosius, the aforementioned African bishops, were expelled from prison; and after continuous disputations in the praetorium lasting sixteen days, they were sent to another custody, the monastery of the Tabenesiotes, which is near Canopus, twelve miles from the city of Alexandria.

Referring to these words, Breulius, the editor of the works of Isidore of Seville, writes as follows [Note: Breul., note on the works of Isidore of Seville, p. 786, Paris edition, 1601]:

> There he laments his exile, which he seems to me to have richly deserved. For he stubbornly resisted the decrees of Pope Vigilius, the Emperor Justinian, and the Council of Constantinople while defending the Three Chapters.

For the rest, we think that Victor died shortly after the year 566, in which he completed his *Chronicle*.

### II.

There exists a *Chronicle* of this African bishop, continuing from where Prosper ends, which we have mentioned from time to time. “He,” says Isidore [Note: Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, cited above], “published from the beginning of the world up to the first year of the reign of Justin the Younger a brief but most distinguished history of military and ecclesiastical affairs, arranged by annual consuls, illustrious for praise and critical observation, and eminently worthy of remembrance.”

In the same sense, elsewhere [Note: Id., *Etymologies*, book 5, cited above], after praising Eusebius of Caesarea and Jerome, who published a varied history of the chronicles arranged simultaneously according to kingdoms and times, he adds concerning our writer:

> Thereafter came various others, among whom especially Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna, after reviewing the histories of his predecessors, completed the record of succeeding ages down to the consulship of the Emperor Justin the Younger.

Honorius of Autun briefly abridged Isidore, whom Trithemius also copied [Note: Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 214] [Note: Honorius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, book 3, chap. 29]:

> But if both truly say this, says Vossius [Note: Vossius, *On Latin History*, book 3, chap. 3, p. 748], that the *Chronicle* began from the beginning of the world, then the same thing happened to Victor as to Prosper. Although Gennadius says that Prosper began his *Chronicle* from the creation of the world, everything he wrote concerning the period before the point where blessed Jerome stopped has nevertheless perished. Certainly, we have no more of Victor than what follows the times described by Prosper, as the words prefixed to Victor’s little book indicate. Nor should one be misled by what is read in Henry Canisius [Note: Canisius, preface to Prosper’s *Chronicle*], namely, that both Gennadius concerning Prosper and Isidore concerning the same man were mistaken. Neither began from the creation of the world; rather, Prosper began where Jerome ended, and Victor where Prosper ended. The opportunity for Gennadius and Isidore to err was supplied by the fact that, in both their works, the years from the creation of the world are counted up to the time at which they had finished writing. None of these points, I say, ought to move us, since that same most learned man later retracted this opinion in his notes on Prosper.

Thus far Vossius. Influenced by the authority of Isidore and Honorius, he evidently conjectured that Victor had composed his *Chronicle* from the beginning of the world; and we understand that Cave and others later followed him in this [Note: Cave, *Literary History*, vol. 1, p. 528]. But the opinion seems more convincing which was first approved by Canisius and subsequently by other learned men, and which rests upon the title of the work as it appears both in printed and handwritten manuscripts: namely, that Victor continued the history from the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger, at the point where Prosper left off.

### III.

We have just heard the bishop of Seville, who greatly extols the value of Victor’s *Chronicle*. Yet his praise appears to require qualification according to the criticism of Norisius:

> Certainly, says he [Note: Norisius, *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chap. 8, works, vol. 1, pp. 669–670], with regard to the truth of historical events, I grant Victor complete credibility; but as regards the designation of the years, his *Chronicle* is full of errors—not Victor’s errors, as I think, but the ignorance of some corrupter.

The judgment of this most distinguished writer is confirmed by the learned editors of his works [Note: Ballerini, note on the works of Norisius, *Observations*, book 3, chap. 4, vol. 4, p. 956]:

> To diminish Victor’s authority, there is no reason for anyone to heap together more things wrongly written by him in chronological matters. But as regards history and events, he deserves the fullest confidence; for it is not easy to find errors in that portion or to demonstrate them by certain testimony. This, they add, should especially be noted by readers in relation to what we shall shortly write against Garnerius on behalf of Norisius, lest, preoccupied by a lengthy enumeration of the chronological errors that are widely exaggerated, they should think that no confidence can be placed in so great a historian even in historical matters.

This they wrote, pointing to the *Defense of Norisius’s Dissertation on the Fifth Synod against the Dissertation of Father Garnerius*, which they published at the end of volume 4 of the works of Norisius. Garnerius’s dissertation, which they undertook to refute, appears in his *Supplement to Theodoret*.

Nor should we omit what the celebrated Garnerius thought fit to note [Note: Garnerius, *Supplement to Theodoret*, p. 166]: Victor did not permit himself to remain unpraised in his own *Chronicle*—“if,” he says, “the final part of the *Chronicle* is actually his; which I do not think it is.” He was referring, of course, to the words which we transcribed earlier from the author himself.

But since Isidore of Seville and others recognized those words as Victor’s, and since they all especially transmitted that he carried his *Chronicle* down to the first year of the reign of Justin the Younger, we leave this kind of conjecture to that learned man.

## IV

Victor’s *Chronicle* was first published by Canisius, before he undertook his *Ancient Readings*, from a manuscript of the Toledo library which Andreas Schott had copied and sent to Marcus Welser, the Augsburg magistrate, as Schott himself informed the reader in his preface. Later Scaliger incorporated it, after Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, into his *Thesaurus temporum*. He testifies that he had copied the same *Chronicle* from a manuscript three years before the Ingolstadt edition of Canisius was published [Note: [Col. 0939C] Scaliger, *Thesaurus temporum*, following Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, p. 1 ff.]. That both editions abound in no small number of errors is sufficiently clear from the notes which we have taken care to append to our text. Wesselingius complains especially of Scaliger’s edition [Note: [Col. 0940C] Wesselingius, *Dissertation on the Gospel, etc., in Victor of Tunnuna*, p. 149 ff.].

But concerning what the same author of the dissertation brings forward about Vigilius the prevaricator, as though it had been recorded in writing by Victor [Col. 0940B] after the consulship of Basil, a man of senatorial rank, in his seventeenth year [Note: [Col. 0940C] Victor’s *Chronicle* below, col. 861, and in Scaliger, p. 11]—concerning this, I say, which the same disputant adduces [Note: [Col. 0940C] Wesselingius, cited work, pp. 148, 153] from a certain book copied by the hand of M. Welser and lent to him by Hemsterhusius, and which he suspects Canisius deliberately suppressed out of hostility toward the Roman pontiff, we first point out that Canisius, as we have just indicated, used a manuscript copied by Andreas Schott from the Toledo library and sent to M. Welser, from whom he received it; it was not, as Wesselingius says, a manuscript written in Welser’s own hand.

Furthermore, the manuscript which Scaliger claims to have copied three years before Canisius published his edition was plainly different, it seems, from the one which Canisius himself committed to print. Yet in neither manuscript is there any trace of the words which Wesselingius presents from the Welserian exemplar in capital letters [Col. 0940C]:

> Vigilius, Bishop of Rome, after he had prevaricated, under the excommunication of all the bishops of the African Church, died on the island of Sicily.

If Scaliger had found these words in his own manuscript, he certainly would not have wished to pass them over or neglect them. What, then, should be thought of the manuscript copied by Welser’s hand, from which the critical scholar drew his material? Welser must have happened upon a copy of Victor which had been interpolated by someone more zealous than our African bishop in defending the Three Chapters—as I myself would suppose. Consequently, in view of what has been observed thus far, that note must wholly disappear, both the charge of prevarication and that of heresy which a sufficiently rash man dared to affix to the Roman pontiff.

# VICTOR’S CHRONICLE, CONTINUING WHERE PROSPER ENDS (C)

From the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger, Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna in Africa, continues the history where Prosper left it.

### In the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius and Albinus (A.D. 444)

After John, Diaconus assumed the episcopate of the Church of Antioch.

### In the third consulship of Aetius and the consulship of Symmachus (A.D. 446)

### In the consulship of Callippius and Ardabur (A.D. 447)

Eutyches, a presbyter and archimandrite of a certain monastery in Constantinople, appeared. He founded the heresy named after himself. For he asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ was born from Mary, his ever-virgin mother, in such a way that he confessed nothing in him belonging to human nature. Summoned to a synodal hearing in Constantinople, where a council had assembled under the presidency of the holy Flavian, bishop of that city, he refused to confess Christ as existing in two natures after his birth from the Virgin and to acknowledge him as consubstantial with us according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0941D] This reading reveals the great carelessness of the copyists and editors. With Cotelerius, *Ecclesiastical Greek Monuments*, vol. I, p. 787, read “consubstantial” (*consubstantialem*).]. He therefore incurred condemnation together with his own error, and the holy Roman prelate confirmed it by apostolic authority. In support of this, with the emperor Theodosius as patron, came Leo of Rome, Dioscorus of Alexandria, Diaconus of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0942D] Who could tolerate this? With the same authority, Cotelerius, cited work, read *Domno Ant.* The same correction should be made above under the year 444, reading “Domnus assumed [the office].”], Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Flavius of Constantinople, prelates of their respective sees.

### In the consulship of Posthumian and Zeno (A.D. 448)

A second general council was convened at Ephesus. There Dioscorus of Alexandria, usurping the chief place with imperial favor, absolved Eutyches after his lawful condemnation. He condemned, with impious authority and despite the opposition of the legates of the Apostolic See, those who opposed Eutyches—teachers of the two natures in Christ: Flavian of Constantinople, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, Theodoret of Cyrus, Ibas of Edessa, and other bishops—and by the riotous action of the monks and military violence bent the entire council to his own support.

### In the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes (A.D. 449)

[Note: [Col. 0941C] During these days the Goths fought the Huns in the Catalaunian Plains. In that battle King Theodoric fell [Col. 0941D], and the Goths were victorious, with King Thorismund fighting [Col. 0942C]. Attila, king of the Huns, appeared nowhere. *Schol.*]

After Attila, king of the Huns, had been defeated in battle by the generals of the emperor Valentinian Augustus and put to flight, he recovered his strength and proceeded with overwhelming force toward Italy; the Roman state brought his aggression to an end by a treaty of peace. After accepting the embassy of Pope Leo, Attila not only ceased ravaging the Roman state but also withdrew beyond the Danube after peace had been granted.

### In the seventh consulship of Valentinian and the consulship of Avienus (A.D. 450)

The emperor Theodosius died at Constantinople in the sixty-second year of his life. Chrysaphius, the emperor’s chamberlain, having abused his friendship with Eutyches, was killed; and Marcian was made emperor by the unanimous consent of the whole state.

He was the forty-seventh Roman emperor and reigned five years and six months. At the very beginning of his reign, seeking peace for the Churches, he announced by imperial authority that a council should be held at Chalcedon.

After Flavian, Anatolius assumed the episcopate of the Church of Constantinople.

### In the consulship of Marcian Augustus [Note: [Col. 0942C] After Theodoric, his son Thorismund ruled the Gothic kingdom for ten years. *Id.*] (A.D. 451)

On the eighth day before the Kalends of October, with Leo of Rome, Dioscorus of Alexandria, Maximus of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Anatolius of Constantinople as prelates, a general council of 632 bishops assembled at Chalcedon. There the second council of Ephesus—if it should even be called a council—was repudiated. Eutyches, together with his patron Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, and Nestorius, was condemned. The Catholic bishops unjustly condemned by that same Dioscorus in the aforementioned second Ephesian council were restored, and the faith of the holy Fathers who had assembled at Nicaea, Constantinople, and the first council of Ephesus was expounded by the holy councils.

When these matters had thus been defined and confirmed by the signatures of the entire council, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, Theodoret of Cyrus, and Ibas of Edessa were restored to their own Churches, while those whom the heretic Dioscorus had substituted in their place were expelled. Everything pertaining to the condition of the Church was arranged and received a definitive settlement.

### In the consulship of Opilio and Vincomalus (A.D. 453)

After Dioscorus had been banished to exile at Gangra, Proterius assumed the episcopate of the Church of Alexandria.

At that time Attila died. While his sons fought over his kingdom, the Huns were devastated and subsequently diminished.

### In the consulship of Aetius and Studius (A.D. 454)

Aetius the patrician, first struck down inside the palace by the hand of the emperor Valentinian Augustus, was brutally killed by the swords of those standing around him; Boethius the prefect was likewise killed.

### In the eighth consulship of Valentinian and the consulship of Anthemius (A.D. 455)

The emperor Valentinian was killed at Rome on the Campus Martius through the treachery of the patrician Maximus and the chamberlain Heraclius. Maximus himself, formerly consul and patrician, seized the empire for sixty-seven days. Thus the evil that had been concealed came to light. Soon afterward he took Valentinian’s widow, the Augusta, in marriage, not allowing her to mourn her husband’s death. But worse things followed these evils: fearing the arrival of Genseric, king of the Vandals, he granted everyone permission to leave the City. Before he could undertake the flight he was planning, he was killed, cut limb from limb, and thrown into the river Tiber.

### In the consulship of Aetius and Studius, and in the prefectures

On the third day after Maximus was killed, Genseric, king of the Vandals, entered the city of Rome and for fourteen days stripped it of all its resources. He carried away with him Valentinian’s daughters and wife and many thousands of captives. The intervention of Pope Leo induced him to refrain from fire, torture, and the sword. During this captivity, on the seventy-fifth day, Anicius Avitus, a man of complete simplicity, assumed the empire in Gaul.

### In the consulship of John and Varane (A.D. 456)

The patrician Ricimer defeated Avitus. Out of respect for his innocence, he made him bishop of the city of Placentia.

### In the consulship of Constantine and Rufus (A.D. 457)

The emperor Marcian of the East died at Constantinople, and Leo became Roman emperor in his place. He was the forty-eighth Roman emperor and reigned sixteen years.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] During these times Theodoric, the brother of Thorismund, ruled the Goths for nine years. *Schol.*]

Alexandria and Egypt, languishing in the error of Dioscorus, did not accept the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. The Dioscorite populace, instigated by Timothy, surnamed Herulus or Aelurus, revolted and killed Proterius, the successor of Dioscorus and guardian of the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April [read: the sixth day of the year 457], the sixth day of the final week of the fast, the day on which our Savior and Lord was crucified by the Jews. For the Lord’s Passover was then celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of April. After Proterius had been killed, the aforementioned Timothy, surnamed Herulus or Aelurus, an opponent of the Council of Chalcedon, seized his episcopate and the Church.

### In the consulship of Leo Augustus (A.D. 458)

[Note: [Col. 0943D] During these days the Goths fought the Suebi in the field of Paramo, beside the river Orbigo, and the Goths were victorious. *Id.*]

Majorian assumed the empire at Rome. Timothy, the usurper of the Church of Alexandria, pursued the defenders of the Council of Chalcedon.

### In the consulship of Patricius and Ricimer (A.D. 459)

Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, was armed by letters from Leo, the Roman prelate, against the error of Eutyches and Dioscorus.

### In the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius (A.D. 460)

[Note: [Col. 0943D] During these days the emperor Majorian came to Caesaraugusta. *Id.*]

Timothy, the bishop who had killed Proterius, was forcibly removed from the see of Alexandria by order of the emperor Leo and banished to Chersonesus. After five months, another Timothy, surnamed Salatratatus or Salafaciarim, a defender of the Council of Chalcedon, was ordained bishop of the Church of Alexandria in his place.

### In the consulship of Dagalaiphus and Severinus (A.D. 461)

### In the second consulship of Leo Augustus (A.D. 462) and the consulship of Vivianus, a man of senatorial rank [Note: [Col. 0943] In the consulship of Leo Augustus II and Severus Augustus; Basil and Vivianus were consuls.] (A.D. 463)

In the Church of Carthage, after Capreolus, Eugenius was ordained bishop [the intervening name Quodvultdeus is textually uncertain] [Note: [Col. 0943D] Add from the edition of Canisius: “Majorian is killed at Rome, and the emperor Severus assumes power on the ninth day before the Ides of July.” *Basnage.*].

### In the consulship of Olybrius and Rusticus (A.D. 464)

[Note: [Col. 0944D] In this consulship the emperor Majorian was killed by Ricimer. *Schol.*]

Genseric, king of the Vandals, died in the fortieth year of his reign, after the devastation of many provinces and the plunder and slaughter of the Christian population in Africa. His son Huneric succeeded him and reigned seven years and five months. His father Genseric gave Huneric in marriage Valentinian’s daughter, whom he had carried away captive from Rome.

### In the consulship of Hermineric and Basiliscus (A.D. 465)

After Maximus, Alexander assumed the episcopate of the Church of Antioch. After Juvenal, Anastasius presided over the Church of Jerusalem.

### In the third consulship of Leo Augustus (A.D. 466)

Huneric, king of the Vandals, aroused by Arian fury, persecuted the Catholics throughout Africa more severely than his father. He confiscated the churches of the Christians and sent the Catholic priests into exile.

### In the consulship of Buseus or Pusaeus and John (A.D. 467)

A sign appeared in the sky from a cloud, resembling a pole, for ten days. Anthemius assumed the empire at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0944D] During these days Theodoric, king of the Goths, was killed by his own men with a sword, and his brother Euric became king. He reigned sixteen years. *Id.*]

### In the fourth consulship of Leo and the second of Anthemius (A.D. 468)

Moved by the petitions of the Egyptians, who asked that a council be held to pass judgment on the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon, Leo Augustus wrote separately to the prelates of each Church to ascertain the faith of each one. He received from each of them letters agreeing as though they had been composed in a single conference, declaring that such a council could in no way be held and that the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon should remain ever more firmly established. These letters exist and are called *encyclicals* in Greek, τὰ ἐγκύκλια.

### In the consulship of Zeno and Marcian (A.D. 469)

After Leo, Hilarus assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church.

### In the consulship of John or Jordan and Severus (A.D. 470)

[Note: [Col. 0944D] In this consulship Arles and Marseille were occupied by the Goths. *Id.*]

Leo Augustus made Patricius, the son of Aspar, Caesar.

### In the fifth consulship of Leo Augustus and the consulship of Probinus (A.D. 471)

Aspar and his two sons, Patricius Caesar and Ardaburius, were killed at Constantinople by order of Leo Augustus.

### In the sixth consulship of Leo and the consulship of Probinus (A.D. 473)

Leo Augustus made Leo, his grandson—the son of Zeno and of his own daughter—Caesar, and he ruled for two years. After Hilarus, Simplicius was ordained bishop of the Roman Church, and after Simplicius came Felix.

Gennadius succeeded Anatolius in the episcopate of the Church of Constantinople, and Acacius succeeded Gennadius.

After Alexander, Martyrius was ordained bishop of the Church of Antioch, and after Martyrius, Julianus. Martyrius was ordained bishop of the Church of Jerusalem after Anastasius [Col. 0945B]. In this consulship Olybrius came to Rome and seized the empire through the faction of the patrician Ricimer, while Anthemius was reigning. When Anthemius recognized this, he fled and was killed. After some days Herculanus, the son of Orestes, seized the empire and was killed together with his father; his nephew assumed his kingdom.

### In the consulship of Leo the Younger Augustus (A.D. 474)

Leo the Elder Augustus died at Constantinople. Zeno was crowned by Leo Augustus, his son, in the Seventh district, contrary to custom.

### The forty-ninth Roman emperor: Zeno (A.D. 475)

Zeno reigned seventeen years after the consulship of Leo the Younger Augustus. When the emperor Zeno sought to kill Leo Augustus, his own son, and seize his empire, his wife, the Augusta Ariadne, offered another boy resembling him to be put to death in his place. She secretly cut the hair of that same Leo Augustus and made him a cleric of one of the churches of Constantinople. This Leo lived until the time of the emperor Justinian.

In the same consulship, Basiliscus seized the empire at Constantinople with his son Marcus, acting as a tyrant.

Augustus Zeno fled into Isauria, from which he had originated, and the Augusta Ariadne followed him by sea despite the dangers of winter.

In this consulship the tyrant Basiliscus issued a law ordering that the Council of Chalcedon be condemned and that the second Council of Ephesus be absolved and accepted.

The bishop Timothy, surnamed Hellurus or Aelurus, both successor to and slayer of Proterius, returned from exile at Chersonesus. After he had driven out the other bishop, Timothy surnamed Salafatiatius or Salafaciarius, a defender of the Council of Chalcedon, he also seized the Church of Alexandria.

### In the consulship of the tyrant Basiliscus and Armatus or Harmatius (A.D. 476)

In the twentieth month, after an army had been granted to him, Zeno Augustus returned from Isauria to Constantinople. He resumed the empire and sent Basiliscus, with his sons and wife, into exile at Sasima in Cappadocia, where he miserably ended his life.

Since no consul entered office during these events (A.D. 477), and the tyrant Basiliscus withdrew from the consulship, Armatus remained consul for the present year.

### After the consulship of Armatus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 478)

Timothy Hellurus, an opponent of the Council of Chalcedon and the slayer of Bishop Proterius, died. Another Timothy, Salafatiatius, a defender of the Council of Chalcedon, resumed the episcopate of the Church of Alexandria. Sallustius succeeded Martyrius as bishop of the Church of Jerusalem. In the Church of Antioch, Peter, surnamed the Fuller, was ordained bishop after Julianus, who had succeeded Martyrius.

### In the consulship of Zeno Augustus (A.D. 479)

Huneric, king of the Vandals, carrying persecution throughout Africa to an extreme, banished to harsher exiles approximately four thousand Catholics—not only priests and clerics of every order, but also monks and laypeople—from Tubunnis, Macri, Nippis, and other parts of the desert, and made confessors and martyrs of them. He also cut out the tongues of the confessors. The royal city, where their bodies lie, bears witness that these confessors continued to speak perfectly to the very end even after their tongues had been cut out.

At that time Laetus, bishop of the Church of Neptis, was crowned with martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of October. Eugenius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, after dreadful exiles in the desert, was regarded as illustrious through his many afflictions and punishments. Thus, amid the countless massacres of Catholics which Huneric perpetrated in his impiety, in the eighth year of his reign he miserably ended his life, with all his internal organs poured out, like his father Arius. Guntamund succeeded him and reigned twelve years; he immediately recalled our people from exile.

### After the third consulship of Zeno (A.D. 480)

Timothy, surnamed Salafatiatius, defender of the Council of Chalcedon, died. In his place John Tabennesiota, a presbyter and steward of the Church of Alexandria and defender of the Council of Chalcedon, was ordained bishop.

By order of the emperor Zeno, Peter expelled him. Peter had been ordained by the heretics while Timothy Salafatiatius was still bishop and then seized the Church of Alexandria. Immediately, with the favor of the emperor Zeno, he condemned the Council of Chalcedon from the pulpit before the people. He removed the names of Proterius and Salafatiatius from the ecclesiastical diptychs and entered the names of Dioscorus and Hellurus, who had killed Proterius. He also expelled the body of the aforementioned Timothy Salafatiatius from the church and threw it outside the city in a deserted place.

### In the consulship of Tricundio, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 482)

The emperor Zeno, lulled to sleep by the cup of Eutychian error, associated Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, with Peter, bishop of Alexandria, and Peter, bishop of Antioch, who had condemned the Council of Chalcedon, through the *Henotikon* issued by him. He was polluted by communion with them and departed with them from the Catholic faith.

### After the consulship of Tricundius, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 483)

The tyrant Leontius seized the empire in Isauria through the faction of the patrician Illus and ruled as a tyrant.

### In the consulship of Theodoret, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 484)

Felix, prelate of the Roman Church, wrote to the monks and clerics living throughout the East, Egypt, and Bithynia, instructing them to avoid Peter, bishop of Alexandria and opponent of the Council of Chalcedon, and those in communion with him as heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] During these days King Euric died, and his son Alaric became king in his place. He reigned twenty-three years. *Schol.*]

### After the consulship of Theodoret, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 485)

The Eastern bishops, with few exceptions, polluted by communion and agreement with Zeno through the *Henotikon*, renounced the Council of Chalcedon together with Peter, bishop of Alexandria; Peter, bishop of Antioch; and Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

### In the consulship of Longinus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 486)

Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, was admonished by letters from Felix, prelate of the Roman Church, to abstain from communion and association with those condemned by the Council of Chalcedon. He handed Felix’s legates over to custody.

### After the consulship of Longinus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 487)

Acacius of Constantinople, Peter of Alexandria, and Peter of Antioch, bishops hostile to the Council of Chalcedon, were condemned by Felix, prelate of the Roman Church, and by a council held in Italy. The condemnation itself was delivered to Acacius at Constantinople by legates sent through the monks of the monasteries of the Aceemetes, Basanius and Dius.

### After the second consulship of Longinus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 488)

The body of the holy apostle Barnabas was discovered in Cyprus, together with the Gospel according to Matthew written in Barnabas’ own hand, the discovery being revealed by Barnabas himself. The tyrant Leontius and Patricius were captured through the betrayal of a fortress and died a most shameful death. Peter of Antioch died under condemnation, and Calendion was ordained in his place. The Eastern bishops, pretending ignorance, consecrated John, surnamed Codonatus, as bishop of that same Church; Peter the heretic succeeded him.

### In the consulship of Eusebius, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 489)

Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, died under condemnation, and Flavian was ordained in his place. When Flavian died in the third month of his episcopate, Euphemius, guardian of the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, succeeded him.

### After the third consulship of Longinus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 490)

Peter, the usurper of the Church of Alexandria, died under condemnation. Anastasius succeeded him in both his episcopate and his error. Calendion, bishop of Antioch, gathered the remains of his predecessor Eustochius, bishop and confessor, from Philippi—Philippopolis—in Macedonia and brought them to Antioch with the greatest honor.

At this time Annianus healed sufferers from gout by prayer above the river Euphrates; Auxentius drove out demons; Daniel and Anastasius, Vindemiolus, Manasseh, Severus, and many others became renowned in various parts of the desert for diverse miracles and foreknowledge.

### In the consulship of Olybrius, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 491)

The emperor Zeno died at Constantinople in the forty-second year of his life. The Augusta Ariadne, Zeno’s widow, designated Anastasius Silentiarius, an Illyrian from Dyrrachium, whose father was Dyrrachian and whose mother was Arian, as emperor.

But Anastasius’ faith—or rather his perfidy—had long been known to his father. Since the bishop Euphemius of Constantinople insisted, he was compelled to promise in writing that he would do nothing contrary to the apostolic faith and the Council of Chalcedon. Bishop Euphemius received the written document and placed it in the church archives.

### The fiftieth Roman emperor: Anastasius

Anastasius reigned twenty-seven years. When he assumed the empire, he forcibly recovered his written document from Bishop Euphemius and savagely persecuted the bishops who defended the Council of Chalcedon. Among them was Peter, bishop of Antioch, who had been ordained by the heretics during the reign of Zeno while Calendion, a defender of the Council of Chalcedon, was still alive. After Peter’s death, Anastasius changed the situation for the worse, so that Calendion was led from bad to worse, and Palladius was ordained in his place.

### In the consulship of Anastasius and Rufus (A.D. 492)

Gelasius succeeded Felix in the Roman Church, and Anastasius succeeded Gelasius. Athanasius the heretic presided over the Church of Alexandria. Palladius had also been made bishop of the Church of Antioch while Calendion was still alive, and Sallustius presided over Jerusalem.

Foreseeing the cunning of the emperor Anastasius, Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople, convened a council and confirmed the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] In this consulship the Saci entered Spain. *Id.*]

### In the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius (A.D. 494)

John, bishop of Alexandria, came from the Roman Church and pleaded with the emperor Anastasius to restore him to his throne on account of their ancient friendship. But when he could not obtain this because he defended the Council of Chalcedon, he secretly returned to Rome, from which he had come.

### In the consulship of Victor or Viator, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 495)

When the Isaurian War broke out, the tyrants Athenodorus and Longinus were killed. After Athanasius of Alexandria died, John, surnamed Hemula, succeeded him. When he died, another John, surnamed Nicetas, succeeded him as bishop a few days later.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] In this consulship Burdimelus assumed tyranny in Spain. *Id.*]

### In the consulship of Paulus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 496)

The emperor Anastasius, holding a council of heretics, confirmed Zeno’s *Henotikon* and deposed Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople and defender of the Council of Chalcedon. He sent Euphemius into exile at Euchaita and made Macedonius bishop in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] In this consulship the Goths established settlements within Spain, and Burdemalus was betrayed by his own men and sent to Toulouse, where he was burned in a bronze bull. *Id.*]

### In the consulship of Augustus Anastasius (A.D. 497)

Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, convened a council and condemned both those who accepted the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and those who defended Nestorius and Eutyches.

After the Roman bishop Anastasius died, Symmachus succeeded him, while Laurentius was ordained on the other side. Since Laurentius, who was bishop of the city of Nuceria—or, as should be read, who was unwilling to remain content with the episcopate of Nuceria—was expelled from the priestly assembly by a council held at Rome.

Palladius of Antioch died, and Flavian was ordained bishop in his place. John, surnamed Nicetas, still presided over the Church of Alexandria. At Jerusalem, Elias assumed the episcopate after Sallustius.

After Guntamund, king of the Vandals, died at Carthage, Thrasamund reigned for twenty-seven years and four months. Filled with Arian madness, he persecuted the Catholics. He closed the Catholic churches and sent 120 bishops from the whole African Church into exile in Sardinia. At that time Fulgentius, bishop of the city of Ruspe, became renowned for our doctrine.

### In the consulship of John the Scythian and Paulus (A.D. 498)

A certain Arian named Olympius blasphemed the holy and consubstantial Trinity in the baths called the Helian Baths, near the royal city. Through the ministry of an angel, he was invisibly drenched by three fiery projectiles in a pool of cold water and ended his life impiously and at the same time miraculously.

### In the consulship of Gibbo, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 499)

The emperor Anastasius convened a council at Constantinople under the presidency of Flavian of Antioch and Philoxenus of Hierapolis. He persuaded it to pronounce anathema against Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his writings, Theodoret of Cyrus, Ibas of Edessa, Andrew [Note: [Col. 0949D] Andrew—plainly Andrew of Samosata—Eucherius, which should be corrected to Eutherius, and Quirus, or Cyrus. So Lequien, *Dissertation III on Damascus*, p. 52. Garnerius likewise previously read it this way in the *Appendix to Theodoret*, p. 152.], Eucherius, Quirus, and John, bishops who proclaimed two natures and two forms in Christ, and those who did not confess that one of the Trinity had been crucified [Note: [Col. 0950D] Garnerius, cited work, reads *confiterentur*, “would confess”; that reading is preferable], together with Leo, bishop of Rome, and his Tome, and the Council of Chalcedon.

### In the consulship of Patricius and Hypatius (A.D. 500)

A certain bishop named Barbas, of Arian error, presumed to say over a person already baptized, contrary to the rule: “Barbas baptizes you in the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.” At once the water from which he was about to baptize the man disappeared completely, and the vessel itself in which the water had been was shattered. Seeing this, the person who was to be baptized immediately ran to a Catholic and received baptism according to the rule.

### In the consulship of Avienus and Pompeius (A.D. 501)

The emperor Anastasius dragged Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, from the church and sent him into exile, because he and certain clerics refused to condemn the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. He made Timothy the presbyter bishop in his place, and Timothy immediately received into communion those who condemned the Council of Chalcedon.

### In the consulship of Avienus the Younger (A.D. 502)

A great earthquake occurred, accompanied by great flashes of lightning and hail, and by the shaking of the whole sky and earth.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] In this consulship the circus at Caesaraugusta was awaited. *Schol.*]

### In the consulship of Cethegus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 504)

Flavian of Antioch, repenting too late, abandoned the emperor Anastasius and, leaving his throne, withdrew to an estate called Platanus. The emperor Anastasius replaced him with Severus, an enemy of the Council of Chalcedon, and thereby brought great scandals upon the Eastern Church.

### In the consulship of Theodorus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 505)

Eugenius, bishop of Carthage and a confessor, died. Julianus of Bostra and John of Paltus voluntarily withdrew from their own Churches, and others were substituted for them.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] During this consulship Dertosa was entered by the Goths. Petyrannus was killed, and his head was carried to Caesaraugusta. *Id.*]

### In the consulship of Messalla, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 505)

At Constantinople, by order of the emperor Anastasius, the holy Gospels were criticized and corrected as though they had been composed by ignorant evangelists.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] During these days there was a battle between the Goths and the Franks at Boglodoreta. King Alaric was killed in battle by the Franks. The kingdom of Toulouse was destroyed. *Id.*]

### In the consulship of Venantius and Celer (A.D. 508)

The peoples of Alexandria and of all Egypt, small and great alike, free and enslaved, clerics and monks, except for foreigners, were possessed by an unclean spirit. Deprived of human speech, they began to bark like dogs throughout all the days and nights, so that afterward they had to be dragged to the churches in iron chains to recover their health. For all of them were eating their own hands and arms alike.

When these things occurred, an angel appeared to some of the people in the form of a man and said that this had happened to them because they had pronounced anathema against the Council of Chalcedon. He warned them thereafter not to presume to do anything of the kind.

### In the consulship of Venantius the Younger, a man of senatorial rank

Cawades, king of the Persians, captured through the prayers of the Christians the fortress of Zumdaber, which from the beginning of its foundation had been filled with many treasures, entrusted to demonic lions, and fortified with a guard; no one had ever been able to enter it. Entering it, he carried away all its treasures.

### In the consulship of the younger Importunus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 509)

Elias, bishop of Jerusalem and defender of the Council of Chalcedon, refused, at the command of the emperor Anastasius, to receive Severus of Antioch, an enemy of the apostolic faith, into communion. He was thrust into exile at the fortress of Paraxton. John, guardian of the Cross, was ordained bishop in his place; he immediately received Severus of Antioch into communion and condemned the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 0950D] In this consulship Gesalicus killed Gaiseric at Barcelona in the palace. In the same year Gesalicus, driven from Spain by Helbanus, the general of Theodoric, king of Italy, went to Africa. Count Veilicus was killed at Barcelona. *Id.*]

### In the consulship of Boethius, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 510)

Vitalianus, son of Patriciolus, learning of the overthrow of the Catholic faith, the condemnation of the Council of Chalcedon, and the removal of orthodox bishops together with the succession of heretics, gathered a strong force of brave men and rebelled against the empire of Anastasius.

### In the consulship of Felix, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 511)

Vitalianus, the count, engaged in battle with Patricius, nephew of the emperor Anastasius and master of the Roman army. After killing sixty-seven men from the Roman army, he captured Patricius alive, bound him with bronze chains, and delivered him into the custody of an iron cage; afterward he tore him apart.

### In the consulship of Paulus and Muschianus (A.D. 512)

Alamundarus, king of the Saracens, baptized by defenders of the Council of Chalcedon, brilliantly formulated and overcame the barbarous proposition of the Theopaschite bishops sent to him by Severus, bishop of Antioch, and demonstrated the immortality of God.

[Note: [Col. 0951D] Flavius Clementinus had Anicius Probus as his colleague. Concerning this passage, P. Wesselingius, in the dissertation on the Jewish Archons appended to his *Dissertation on Victor of Tunnuna*, reports the following on p. 152 from a manuscript copied by the hand of M. Welser and lent to him by Hemsterhusius:

“Everyone knows,” he says, “who has used this *Chronicle* even cursorily that notes capable of illuminating the succession of the Visigothic kings were added in the margin by a Spanish copyist. Neither Scaliger nor Canisius considered them to be neglected, although neither extracted them all. Thus, under the consuls Probus, a man of senatorial rank, it is written: ‘In this consulship Gelasicus, returning from Africa, went to Aquitaine out of fear of Helbanus and hid there for one year.’ This should have been taken into account because of what the copyist had noted under the consul Boethius concerning Gesalicus’ flight to Africa; it also agrees well with Isidore’s Gothic Chronicle, year 545 of the era.”]

### In the consulship of Probus, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 513)

By order of the emperor Anastasius, Plato, prefect of the city, and Maximus ascended the pulpit of the Church of Saint Theodore and newly added **τὸ σταυρωθὲν**, “the one crucified,” to the hymn which the Greeks call the Trisagion. While they were singing this as they proceeded through the Forum of Constantine toward the great church, a cloud suddenly sent down ashes upon them instead of rain and covered the entire city and province.

Because of this strange event, many evils befell the city of Constantinople, and many people were killed disastrously. For the factions of the Greens and the Blues united against the emperor Anastasius and, amid a thousand insults and calamities, set fire to the city. The city was burned from **ἀπὸ τῆς ΧΑΛΚΗΣ**, “from the Chalke,” as far as the Forum of Constantine, for a distance along the street exceeding ninety-four columns.

[Note: [Col. 0952D] Wesselingius, cited work, p. 149, likewise testifies that the manuscript mentioned above reads **ὁ σταυρωθέντι ἡμᾶς**. Hence, since the formula was **ὁ σταυρωθεὶς δι’ ἡμᾶς**, that is what it ought to have read. See Photius, *Bibliotheca*, pp. 610 and 747.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] After Alaric, Theodoric, king of Italy, ruled the Goths in Spain for fifteen years, acting as guardian of the young Amalaric. *Schol.*]

### In the consulship of Senator, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 514)

Count Vitalianus came to Constantinople with a powerful force of barbarians and took up position at Sosthenion. He promised peace to the emperor Anastasius only on condition that the defenders of the Council of Chalcedon who had been banished be restored to their own homes and that all the Churches of the East be united with the Roman Church.

### In the consulship of Florentius, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 515)

The Huns violently ravaged Armenia, Cappadocia, and Galatia, as well as Pontus. At that time Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople, died at Ancyra in Galatia, and the Augusta Ariadne died in the royal city.

### In the consulship of Peter, a man of senatorial rank (A.D. 516)

All the archimandrites and monks of the desert beyond Palestine and the Jordan River write to the emperor Anastasius [Col. 0952A] on behalf of the status of the Council of Chalcedon and against the impieties of Severus, bishop of Antioch.

## Agapitus, consul (A.D. 517)

John, bishop of Alexandria, dies, and Dioscorus is ordained in his place. Timothy, bishop of Constantinople and detractor of the Council of Chalcedon, dies on 5 April, and John the Cappadocian, in his own cell [Note: [Col. 0952D] Wesselingius thinks that this should be emended to “to John the Cappadocian, his own Syncellus.” He confirms his restoration by the authority of Theophanes, *Chronographia*, p. 140, where we read: “After Timothy had died, they appointed John the Cappadocian, a presbyter and Syncellus.”], and presbyter, assumes the episcopate. Before his ordination Anastasius had compelled him to condemn the Council of Chalcedon beforehand.

## Agapitus II and Magnus, consuls (A.D. 518)

The emperor Anastasius, driven from his palace by terror of thunder and struck by a bolt of lightning, dies in the bedroom where he had hidden himself; and, in disgrace and without the customary funeral rites, he is carried to the tomb [Col. 0952B] in the eighty-eighth year of his life.

Justinus, the fifty-first Roman emperor, reigns for 8 years and 9 months.

Illyricianus was a Catholic and a lover and defender of the Council of Chalcedon. His wife was called Lupicina, whom the Constantinopolitans later called Euphemia. Their nephew was Justinian, who had served in the guard of the *candidati*.

## Justinus Augustus and Heraclius, consuls (A.D. 519)

Amantius, the chamberlain, stirred up seditions among the people and demanded another emperor. By order of the emperor Justinus, he was killed together with Andrew the chamberlain and thrown into the sewer.

## Rusticius, consul (A.D. 520)

John, who had been chosen for the imperial office before Justinus, is ordained bishop of Heraclea, and Justinian, the nephew of the emperor Justinus, is appointed ordinary master of the soldiers, having previously served among the *candidati*.

## Valerius and Justinian, consuls (A.D. 521)

When Dioscorus, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, dies, Timothy succeeds him. In the Church of Antioch, Severus becomes the chief of heresy [Note: [Col. 0952D] Victor of Tunnuna repeatedly calls Severus “the chief of heresy”; but in one place the editions have “heretic.” COTELER, *Ecclesiae Graecae Monumenta*, vol. II, p. 659.], and John becomes bishop of the Church of Jerusalem.

The emperor Justinus reunites the Eastern churches with the Western prelates under an appropriate satisfaction, excepting the wicked bishops: Acacius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, Peter of Antioch, and Peter of Alexandria, who were entangled in their former error [Note: [Col. 0952D] Who would not see at first glance that the true reading is “wicked bishops” (*pravos pontifices*)? COTELER, *Ecclesiae Graecae Monumenta*, vol. I, p. 787.]. He revives the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0953A], which had been renounced during the reigns of the emperors Zeno and Anastasius.

## Symmachus and Boethius, consuls (A.D. 522)

Vitalianus, having taken the oath, returns to Constantinople. The emperor Justinus receives him graciously, appoints him master of the soldiers, and permits him to be given the consulship.

## Maximus, consul (A.D. 523)

Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, dies at Carthage. His wife Amalafrida, fleeing to the barbarians, is captured at Capsa near the desert after an encounter and dies in private custody.

Hilderic, born from the daughter of the emperor Valentinian, who had been captured by Gaiseric and married to Huneric, reigns for 7 years and 3 months. Before he became king, his predecessor Thrasamund had bound him by an oath not to open churches to Catholics in his kingdom or restore their privileges. In order not to exceed the terms of his oath, he ordered Catholic priests to return from exile and churches to be opened, and, at the request of the entire Church of Carthage, consecrated Boniface, a man sufficiently vigorous in divine doctrine, as its bishop.

Vitalianus is said to have been killed at Constantinople within the palace, in the place called *Delphicum* in Greek, by the faction of the patrician Justinian.

## Justinus Augustus and [Note: [Col. 0953D] Eduardus Corsinus, in Dissertation 3 *Ad Notas Graecorum*, p. XLV, considers this certainly a passage of Victor’s text that must be corrected: in place of *Apio*, which entered the text recklessly through Victor’s or the copyist’s error, he would restore *Opilio*, who, together with Flavius Anicius Justinus, is entered in the consular fasti for the year 524. Victor himself certainly designates the year 539 by the consulship of Apio, a man of senatorial rank; yet he does not indicate by a doubled consular notation that Apio was consul for a second time, although Victor is seen to have done this in other consulships. “For these consuls,” says Wesselingius, loc. cit., p. 152, “the prefatory manuscript offers the following scholion: ‘Under these consuls Amalaric became king of the Goths; he reigned 5 years.’ This ought not to have been disregarded, since after the consulships of Lampadius and Orestes, Scaliger and Canisius appended that Amalaric was defeated by Childebert, king of the Franks. Indeed, even that statement was not reproduced quite faithfully: both editions read, ‘and there he died, struck by a Frankish spear.’ But the written book has: ‘struck by the spear of a certain Boson the Frank,’ etc. Isidore would be a weighty witness that *angone* and *Narbone* are corrupt, since he reports that Amalaric was killed at Narbonne, *Chronicle of the Goths*, year 564—unless *angon* in the Frankish language was a shorter weapon, covered for the most part with iron. Eustathius, in his commentary on Homer, p. 1854, writes: ‘*Angon*: a kind of Frankish spear, neither very small nor large, most of which is encased in iron.’ Eustathius’ own passage is cited by Cangius under *Odyssey* T in the *Glossarium Graecum*, vol. I, p. 9, s.v. *Angones*, where he also makes further observations. Thus, I think, *angone* should be retained. See Hadrianus Valesius, *Rerum Francicarum*, book VII, under the year 531, vol. I, p. 369.”] Apio, consuls (A.D. 524)

After Symmachus died, Hormisdas succeeds him in the episcopate of the Roman Church. Timothy still survived in the Alexandrian Church. Severus of the Antiochene Church, a detractor of the Council of Chalcedon, fled when the emperor Justinus sought to punish him; Paul was appointed in his place [Col. 0953C]. John presided over the Church of Jerusalem. In the Church of Constantinople, Epiphanius succeeds John as bishop.

After the second consulship of Justinus and Apio, the emperor Justinus Augustus, reluctantly and in response to the senators’ supplication, appoints his nephew Justinian Caesar.

## Philoxenus and Probus, consuls (A.D. 525)

## Marbotius, consul (A.D. 527)

The emperor Justinus dies.

Justinianus, the fifty-second Roman emperor, reigns for 39 years and 7 months. His wife was named Theodora.

[Col. 0954A] Justinian Augustus, consul (A.D. 528)

At the command of the same emperor, the Eastern churches publicly accept, with present sacrifices, the four councils—the Council of Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and the Council of Chalcedon—and the faith of the 150 holy Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0953C] During these days Stephen was made prefect of the Spains. In the third year of his prefecture he was stripped of office in the city of Gerunda at a council. SCHOL.]

## Decius, consul (A.D. 529)

Through the faction of the empress Theodora, he imposes upon everyone by a general law that the statement “one of the Trinity suffered” must be accepted not in a qualified sense but absolutely, and he violently extorts subscriptions from clergy and monks. For this reason many withdrew from the Church, and monks departed from their own monasteries, asserting that the faith of those who had assembled at the four aforesaid holy councils was sufficient for them.

## Lampadius and Orestes, consuls (A.D. 530)

[Col. 0954B] Epatius [Hypatius], the nephew of the emperor Anastasius, assumes tyranny at Constantinople. After many thousands of people have been slaughtered with military swords during the circus spectacle, he is captured and killed at night together with Pompeius, and thrown into the sewer.

After the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes [Note: [Col. 0953C] Under these consuls Amalaric, the king, having been defeated in Gaul by Childebert, king of the Franks, in a battle near Narbonne, fled to Barcelona, where he was struck by a Frankish spear and died. ID.] (A.D. 531), Gelimer seizes the kingdom in Africa by tyranny. Entering Carthage, he deprives Hilderic of the kingship, commits him and his sons to custody, and kills Oamerdigus and many nobles.

In the third year after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, Belisarius, master of the Roman army, having defeated the enemy in two battles, remarkably defeated the Persians in battle at Tracium.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] Cl. Montfaucon, in *Palaeographia Graeca*, book II, chapter 7, pp. 174 ff., discusses an inscription from Trapezus, recovered by D. de Tournefort at the gate of the citadel, in which Justinian’s third consulship is recorded.]

## Justinian Augustus, third consul (A.D. 533)

The tyrant Gelimer cruelly destroys many nobles of the province of Africa, and removes the property of many through Boniface.

## Justinian Augustus, fourth consul (A.D. 534)

The emperor Justinian, prompted by the visitation of Bishop Laetus, who had been made a martyr by Huneric, king of the Vandals, sends an army to Africa under the command of Belisarius, master of the soldiers. Belisarius defeats the Vandals in battle, kills Gunthimer and Gebamund, brothers of King Gadinges, and, after King Gelimer himself has been put to flight, captures Africa in the ninety-seventh year after the Vandals’ invasion. At the very time of Belisarius’ arrival, before the invasion itself took place, the tyrant Gelimer killed King Hilderic together with certain relatives of his family. Belisarius, master of the soldiers and patrician, captures the tyrant Gelimer and brings him to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople, together with the riches acquired from the plunder of Africa.

## Belisarius, consul (A.D. 535)

Reparatus succeeds Boniface in the episcopate of the Church of Carthage. In the Church of Jerusalem, Peter succeeds John, who had died, in the episcopate.

After the consulship of Belisarius, in the second year (A.D. 536), the emperor Justinian publishes books on the Incarnation of the Lord and compels the Illyrian bishops to subscribe.

[Col. 0955B] After the consulship of Belisarius, in the third year (A.D. 537). When Epiphanius, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, who had succeeded John, dies, Anthimus, an Eutychianist bishop of Trapezus, by the faction of the empress Theodora, seizes the Church of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0955D] Thus erroneously in both editions of Scaliger and Canisius. “But everyone sees that *Eutychianist* must be read here,” says Cotelerius, *Ecclesiae Graecae Monumenta*, vol. I, p. 786.]

## John, consul (A.D. 538)

After Hormisdas, John; after John, Felix; after Felix, Boniface; after Boniface, another John; and after John, Agapitus are ordained bishops of the Roman Church. When Timothy of the Alexandrian Church dies—the Timothy who had succeeded the younger Dioscorus—two perverse men, namely Theodosius and Gaianus, are ordained bishops on the same day by popular election. Once they have been ordained, Alexandria is divided between the two enemies of Christ. The followers of Theodosius wished to be called Theodosians, and those of Gaianus Gaianites [Col. 0955C], although neither group accepts the Council of Chalcedon and both make the errors of Eutyches and Dioscorus their own.

## Apio, consul (A.D. 539)

[Note: [Col. 0955D] The learned Montfaucon makes several observations on this consulship of Apio, loc. cit., pp. 173 ff., where he explains another inscription found at Gortyna in Crete by the same Tournefort. But Corsinus, a man of senatorial rank, does not approve his conjectures in Dissertation 3 *Ad Notas Graecorum*, pp. LXII ff.]

Severus of Antioch, the chief of the heresy from whom the Severians are named, and Julian, bishop of Halicarnassus—both opponents of the apostolic faith and of the Council of Chalcedon—are sent into exile at Alexandria by Justinian’s order [Note: [Col. 0956D] Read “by order,” with Cotelerius, *Ecclesiae Graecae Monumenta*, vol. I, p. 788. From him also we have restored this entire passage, which previously suffered from corruptions and faulty punctuation, to its integrity: formerly it read, “formerly Severus, and uncorrupted Alexandria,” etc.]. There they write against the followers of the Council of Chalcedon and say that there is one nature in Christ from two natures. While Severus asserts that this nature is corruptible and Julian that it is incorruptible, Alexandria, Egypt, and Libya are divided between the two enemies of Christ. The Theodosians followed Severus, and the Gaianites followed Julian.

From the Theodosians two other heresies arose: one of the Agnoitae and the other of the Tritheitae. The Agnoitae add to the perverse teaching from which they arose the claim that Christ’s divinity is ignorant of future things written concerning the day and hour of the end. The Tritheites assert that, just as there are three persons in the Trinity, so there are three gods, contrary to what is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one.” And again: “There is no God except one”; and, “I am God, and there is no other besides me.”

## Justinus, consul (A.D. 540)

Agapitus, archbishop of Rome, comes to Constantinople and deposes Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, a perverter of the Church and an enemy of the Council of Chalcedon. He deprives the empress Theodora, Anthimus’ patroness, of communion, and immediately makes Mena bishop of the Church of Constantinople.

[Col. 0956B] The Alexandrian bishops Theodosius and Gaianus are condemned together with their error and transported into exile. But Theodosius, banished to Sycae at Constantinople, infected nearly the whole palace and a large part of the imperial city with his perfidy.
