This gave almost all heresies an opportunity for license, so that not only the Theodosians but also the Gaianites built monasteries and oratories near the imperial city. The aforesaid heretic Theodosius lived until the first consulship of Justinian the Younger. In that year, while Paul, bishop of Antioch, was still alive, Euphrasius was substituted for him.

## Basil, consul (A.D. 541)

When Agapitus, archbishop of Rome, dies at Constantinople, Silverius is ordained bishop in his place. In the Alexandrian Church, while Theodosius and Gaianus are in exile, Paul [Note: [Col. 0955D] Paul the praetor is ordained bishop in their place by the Tabennesiot monks, defenders of the Council of Chalcedon; he who [was] of Dioscorus. SCHOL.], first in their place, while celebrating the deposition of Dioscorus, the heretic and predecessor of the Zabinnesiots, is deposed by a Palestinian council; Zoilus is ordained bishop in his place.

In the aforesaid consulship [Note: [Col. 0955D] In this year five Frankish kings entered the Spains through Pamplona, reached Zaragoza, and, after besieging it for three days, ravaged the whole province of Tarraconensis. ID.] Stutzas seizes a kingdom in Africa, with tyranny, in the regions of the desert.

After the second year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 543), snares of proscription are prepared through the faction of the empress Theodora, who, from the time she began to reign, never ceased to be a secret enemy of the Council of Chalcedon. Silverius, bishop of Rome, is sent into exile, and Vigilius is ordained in his place. Before his ordination, the aforementioned empress Theodora extracted from him by a secret written agreement that, once he had become pope, he would condemn the Three Chapters in the proscription of the Council of Chalcedon: namely, the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Maris the Persian [Note: [Col. 0956D] Thus we read it. The editions have *Murim* incorrectly.]—a letter approved and judged orthodox by the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon and incorporated into its synodal acts; next, Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, likewise praised synodally in the acts at Antioch under John, bishop of that Church, and at Chalcedon; and the statements of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus [Note: [Col. 0957D] Scaliger’s edition in the *Thesaurus Temporum*, p. 9, correctly has *Cyrensis*. Other editions incorrectly have *Cypri*.], which, together with Theodoret himself, were highly praised in the pronouncements of the Council of Chalcedon.

After he had become pope, Antonia, the patrician wife of Belisarius, compelled him to write as though they were Catholics to Theodosius of Alexandria, Anthimus of Constantinople, and Severus of Antioch, who had long before been condemned by the apostolic see, and to think about the faith as they did. The text of his letter is attested as follows:

> To my lords and brothers united in the love of Christ God our Savior, Theodosius, Anthimus, and Severus, bishops: Vigilius, bishop.
>
> I know what the credulity of my faith previously brought to your holiness, with God’s help [Note: [Col. 0957D] Liberatus has “because … previously … with God’s help.” Baronius also reads this way under the year 538, §14, where he transmits the same letter from Liberatus.]. But because now my glorious lady and my daughter, the most Christian patrician [Note: [Col. 0957D] Liberatus does not acknowledge this, nor does Baronius. Liberatus instead immediately has, “made what was desired by your fraternity come to pass.”], causes my desires to be fulfilled, so that I may send the present writing to your fraternity, I, greeting you with the grace by which we are joined in Christ our Lord and Savior [Note: [Col. 0957D] Liberatus: “Therefore, greeting you with the grace that joins us to our God Christ the Savior.” Baronius likewise.], declare that, with God’s command [Note: [Col. 0957D] Liberatus: “with God’s help.” Baronius likewise.], I have held and do hold the faith that you hold. Know this among us [Note: [Col. 0957D] Liberatus: “Knowing that what we preach among you …” Baronius agrees, but has “among us.”]: that what we preach and read is that we have one soul and one heart in God.
>
> I have hastened, with God’s help, to announce to you the joys of my advancement, which is yours, and my heart freely embraces your fraternity, which desires this [Note: [Col. 0957D] Liberatus: “I have hastened, with God’s help, to announce to you the joys of my advancement, which is yours, knowing that your fraternity, which desired it, would gladly embrace it.”].
>
> Therefore, let your wisdom recognize what I write to you [Note: [Col. 0958D] Liberatus, with Baronius: “Let no one recognize it.” This is certainly correct, since the context requires it.]; but rather let it judge me, above all others, as suspect to you [Col. 0957C] [Note: [Col. 0958D] Liberatus: “let it consider me suspect.” Baronius likewise, although shortly before he reads, “here let my wisdom …”], so that God may more easily complete what he has begun to work [Note: [Col. 0958D] Liberatus: “so that I may more easily complete what I have begun to work.” Baronius likewise, except that he reads *concepi* (“I conceived”) instead of *coepi* (“I began”), perhaps more correctly.].
>
> And the subscription: Pray for me, my lords and brothers, joined in the love of Christ our Lord and Savior [Note: [Col. 0958D] Liberatus: “Pray to God for us, my brothers, united in love in Christ our Lord.” Baronius likewise.].

[Note: [Col. 0957D] After Thiudus died, Thiudisolus ruled the Goths for 1 year and 7 months. SCHOL.]

The beginnings of these evils are followed by a general mortality throughout the world, and the greater part of the population dies from the bubonic plague.

After the third year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 544), the tyrant Stutzas, having organized a multitude of peoples, comes against Solomon, master of the soldiers and patrician, and against Aedecius, commander of the Roman army, at Cilium. When the engagement takes place, because of the sins of Africa, the Roman army is defeated, together with Solomon, commander of both forces.

[Col. 0958A] [Lacuna.]

After the fourth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 545), the emperor Justinian, incited by the intrigues of the Acephali, subtly compels Vigilius, bishop of Rome, to hasten to the imperial city and, under the pretext of an assembly of those who are divided from the communion of the Church, to condemn the Three Chapters.

[Note: [Col. 0958D] After Tudis died, Agila ruled the Goths for 5 years and 7 months. ID.]

Macarius succeeds Peter in the episcopate of the Church of Jerusalem.

After the fifth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 546), the tyrant Stutzas, engaging at the harbor of Tacae in Africa, is struck by the spear of John, commander of the Roman army; John, in turn, is struck by Stutzas. Each falls immediately by the sword of the other, and both die on the Lord’s day on which the battle took place.

[Col. 0958B] After the sixth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 547), Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, is held in high regard. Guntarith, master of the soldiers, kills the patrician Ariobindus, commander and chief of the Roman army in Africa, who had been sent there by the emperor, at night within the palace at Carthage, and seizes the kingdom by tyranny. Artabanus, commander of Carthage, kills him while he is dining on the thirty-sixth day of his rule.

After the eighth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 548), the emperor Justinian writes with great urgency throughout the various provinces established within the boundaries of his kingdom and compels all the bishops to condemn the aforesaid Three Chapters. Donninus succeeds Euphemius as bishop of Antioch.

After the ninth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 549), the Illyrian council writes to Justinian Augustus in defense of the Three Chapters and condemns Benenatus, bishop of the First Justinian City, a detractor of those same Three Chapters.

The empress Theodora, an enemy of the Council of Chalcedon, her whole body covered by the plague of cancer, ended her life in a remarkable manner.

After the tenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank [Note: [Col. 0958D] Wesselingius, often cited above, loc. cit., p. 153, notes that the following was written in the margin of the mentioned manuscript: “After Agila died, Athanagild, who had earlier seized tyranny, became king of the Goths; he reigned 15 years.” Scaliger and Canisius omitted this.] (A.D. 550), the African bishops synodally exclude Vigilius, bishop of Rome and condemner of the Three Chapters, from Catholic communion, while reserving for him an opportunity for repentance; and, in defense of the aforesaid Three Chapters, they send highly suitable letters to the emperor Justinian through Olympius, the *magisterianus*. At that time the seven books [Note: [Col. 0959D] Seven books must be understood. Shortly afterward one should perhaps read “in the proscription.”] of Facundus, bishop of the Church of Hermiana, shone forth. In them he demonstrated most clearly that the aforesaid Three Chapters had been condemned in the proscription of the faith of the Catholic and apostolic Council of Chalcedon.

After the eleventh year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 551), Reparatus, archbishop of the Church of Carthage; Firmus, primate of the Numidian bishops; and Primasius and Verecundus, bishops of the Council of Byzacena [Note: [Col. 0959D] Byzacena. SCAL.], are summoned to the imperial city by order of the same emperor for the sake of the faith. Apollinarius is substituted for Zoilus as bishop of the Alexandrian Church because Zoilus refuses to condemn the aforesaid Three Chapters.

After the twelfth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 552), Reparatus, accused by numerous slanders because he had not consented to the condemnation of the aforesaid Three Chapters [Col. 0959B], is deprived of office and property and banished into exile at Euchaita. His deacon and *apocrisiarius*, Primasius, after condemning what had been defended synodally and universally, is ordained bishop of the Church of Carthage, while Reparatus is still alive, against the wishes of both clergy and people.

Firmus, primate of the Council of Numidia, corrupted by the emperor’s gifts, consented to the condemnation of those same Chapters. But, returning to his own country by ship, he died a most disgraceful death. Primasius too was banished to the monastery of Aquimetum. But when Boethius, primate of Byzacena, died before him, Primasius, in order to succeed him, immediately consented to the aforesaid condemnation; and, once he had returned home, he attacked with the most violent persecutions what he had previously defended, generating accusations against the faithful and confiscating their property. But the things in which he sinned could not remain hidden. After he was condemned by the Catholic bishops of his own council for his acts of betrayal, he died a miserable death; and what he had acquired by fraud was faithfully taken away by the judges.

Verecundus, however, bishop of the Church of Nicaea, persevering in the defense of the aforesaid Chapters, died in the city of Chalcedon, where he had taken refuge, in the inn of the glorious mother [Note: [Col. 0959D] Cotelerius rightly advises that this should be emended to “of the martyr” Euphemia, *Ecclesiae Graecae Monumenta*, vol. II, p. 609], and passed to the Lord. Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, is expelled, and while he is still alive Eustochius is ordained in his place.

After the thirteenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 553), a council is assembled at Constantinople by order of the emperor Justinian [Col. 0959D]. The bishops present were Vigilius, bishop of Rome, ordained while Silverius was still alive; Apollinarius of Alexandria, promoted while Zoilus was still living; Domnus of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0959D] Also called Domninus. SCAL. Above, in the eighth year after the consulship of Basil, he is called Donninus.]; Eustochius [Note: [Col. 0959D] Eutocius. ID.], made bishop of Jerusalem after Macarius had been removed; and Eutychius of Constantinople, who had been substituted for Mena [Col. 0960A].

There they subject the aforesaid Three Chapters, together with their defenders, to condemnation, and penally bar themselves from returning to repentance, binding themselves by a perpetual anathema if they should ever attempt to grant absolution. Rusticus, a deacon of the Roman Church, and Felix, abbot of the monastery of Gillium in the province of Africa, contradicted these decrees in writing and were sent into exile in the Thebaid together with their companions.

After these events, an earthquake shook the imperial city from its foundations, threw down many buildings and porticoes, and, although the basilicas remained standing, overturned nearly all their altars.

After the fourteenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 554), Bishop Frontinus, summoned to the imperial city, is assigned to exile at Antinoe in the First Thebaid for defending the same Three Chapters [Note: [Col. 0959D] Antinoe. ID.]; in his place the heretics ordain Peter to the Church of Salona.

The priests of the province of the Proconsular Council of Africa, deceived by the strategy of the detractors of the bishops Rufinus and Vinus and of Archbishop Reparatus, approach them as though they were defenders of the faith, and, with very few exceptions, pollute themselves by communion with Primasius, the betrayer of the Church of Carthage.

Dacius, bishop of Milan, comes to Constantinople and, consenting to the condemnation of the same Three Chapters, dies on that very day after being struck down.

Narses the eunuch, formerly a chamberlain and now a patrician, remarkably defeats and kills Totila, king of the Goths, in battle in Italy [Col. 0960C], and takes all his wealth.

After the fifteenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 555), the bishops of the Council of Numidia, assembled in the manner of the priests of the Proconsular province, come to Carthage. Polluted by communion with Primasius, the usurper of that Church, and having become betrayers, they return to their own sees.

Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna and author of this work, after the imprisonments and beatings he endured at Sala and Valericis, and likewise in the monastery of Mandra [Note: [Col. 0959D] Wesselingius, loc. cit., p. 151, says: “These words could indeed appear sound and well-colored, if the manuscript did not contain *de Mandracium*.” Mandracium was the harbor of the city of Carthage, according to Procopius, *Vandalic War*, book I, chapter 20. The same Procopius reports, *On the Buildings of Justinian*, book VI, chapter 5, that the emperor Justinian founded a monastery near this harbor, which accordingly took the name Mandracium: “He built the monastery within the enclosure, beside the sea, very near the harbor which they call Mandracium.”], is sent into exile in the Mauritanian island of Egi for a first and second exile, and in a third exile to Alexandria, together with Theodore, bishop of the Church of Cabarsus, for defending the aforesaid Three Chapters. After his imprisonment in the praetorian prison, he is thrust into the prison of the castle of Diocletian [Col. 0960D]. Anastasius succeeds Domninus as bishop of Antioch.

After the sixteenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 556), Primosus [Note: [Col. 0960D] Thus the edition of Scaliger. Is *Primasius* intended, as shortly before?]—the usurper of the Church of Carthage—afflicts those unwilling to give him their consent, sometimes with beatings, sometimes with imprisonment, and sometimes with exile.

[Col. 0961A] The aforesaid African bishops Victor and Theodosius are released from prison. After fifteen continuous days of disputations in the praetorium, they are sent to another custody, the monastery of the Tabennesiots near Canopus, twelve miles from the city of Alexandria.

After the seventeenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 557), Vigilius of Rome dies on the island of Sicily. At that time Felix, abbot of the Gallitan monastery [Note: [Col. 0961D] Above, under the year 553, it reads “of Gillium.”], departs this life and goes to the Lord in exile at Sinope.

After the eighteenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 558), Pelagius, Roman archdeacon and defender of the aforesaid Three Chapters, returns from exile through the persuasion of the emperor Justinian. He condemns what he had previously defended with the greatest firmness and is ordained bishop of the Roman Church by the betrayers. He held the office for 5 years [Col. 0961B].

After the nineteenth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 559), the Illyrian bishops, apart from a few small monasteries and a few faithful, after suffering persecutions give their consent, nullifying their former faith. At that time the Ugni ravaged Armenia with the greatest severity.

After the twentieth year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 560), the Bulgars invade Thrace and come as far as Sucae, near Constantinople. They capture Sergius, the patrician who had formerly been commander of the African army, and drag him away with them. But, vigorously defeated by the arms of the patrician Belisarius and put to flight, they crossed the Danube together.

After the twenty-first year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 561), the body of Saint Antony the hermit is discovered and brought to Alexandria with the greatest honor, and is reverently placed in the basilica of Saint John [Col. 0961C] the Baptist.

After the twenty-second year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 562), Frontinianus, bishop of Salona, is transferred from exile at Antinoe to Ancyra in Galatia. Peter, the usurper of his Church, dies, and Prodinus is substituted for him.

After the twenty-third year following the consulship of Basil, of senatorial rank (A.D. 563), Reparatus, archbishop of the Church of Carthage, passes from exile at Euchaita to the Lord in a glorious confession, on 7 January.

In that year the emperor Justinian sends the envoys of the people of the Avars [Note: [Col. 0961D] Avars. SCALIG.] back whence they had come . . . [lacuna].

In the thirty-second year of the reign of the aforementioned emperor Justinian, Pelagius of Rome is ordained bishop. He presided for 11 years.

[Col. 0962A] Eustochius, bishop of Jerusalem, who had been ordained while Macarius was still alive, is expelled; and Macarius is restored once again.

In the thirty-eighth year of the same emperor (A.D. 564), the bishops Musicus, Brumasius, Donatus, and Chrysonius from Africa, and Victor and Theodore, bishops likewise from Egypt, are summoned to the imperial city by imperial command. Because, in the presence of the emperor Justinian himself and later in disputation with Eutychius, bishop of the imperial city, they resist the new superstition, they are separated from one another and sent into custody in monasteries throughout that city.

In the thirty-ninth year of his reign (A.D. 565), Justinian sends into exile Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, condemner of the Three Chapters and of Evagrius the hermit, a deacon [Col. 0962B], and Didymus, the Alexandrian monk and confessor, whose praises we have cited above among illustrious men on the authority of the sources; in his place he makes John, a bishop sharing the same error.

In that year the Greens wage civil war in the imperial city and, in frequent engagements, strike down many men of the state with the sword. But many of them were later destroyed by Julian the prefect because of their atrocities.

In the fortieth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0961D] See Mansi on Baronius, vol. X of the *Annals*, [Col. 0962D] p. 232. Against Pagi, who assigns Justinian’s death to the year 565, he proves that the following year, 566, existed.] (A.D. 566), Justinian reached the end of his life in the fifteenth indiction.

Theodore, bishop of Cabarsus, defender of the Three Chapters, dies in exile at the imperial city in the same month and on the same day as Justinian. He is buried beside the confessors whose tongues Huneric, king of the Vandals, had cut out [Col. 0962C].

Justinus the Younger, son of Vigilantia, the sister of the emperor Justinian Augustus, and born to Dulcissimus, peacefully assumes the scepter of the empire amid great tranquility among the people. His wife is said to have been Sophia, niece of the empress Theodora.

All the years are reckoned from Adam, the first man, to the birth according to the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, which occurred in the year 5,699. From the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, which occurred in the forty-third year of the reign of Augustus Octavian Caesar, to the first year of Justinus, the first Roman ruler to succeed Justinian in the empire, there are 527 years. From Adam to the first year of the aforesaid Roman ruler there are altogether 5,766 years.

## In the Year of Our Lord 556

## Liberatus, Deacon of Carthage

[Col. 0963]

[Col. 0963]

# Preface to the *Breviary* of Liberatus the Deacon

[Col. 0963A] I. Liberatus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage and one of the African defenders of the Three Chapters, wrote a short book on the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies. In it he teaches from what parents each of them was born and what offspring each subsequently had, down to the Fifth Council—whether propagators or principal defenders.

II. He openly reveals at the end the purpose for which he wrote. After setting out throughout the work the struggles of the Nestorians and Eutychians and the arts of warfare learned through long practice, and finally explaining the secret machinations of the emperor Justinian and his wife Theodora, he attempted, with a certain crafty subtlety, gradually and imperceptibly to lead the unwary reader’s mind to the opinion that the Fifth Council should not be regarded as a legitimate judgment of the Church but as a political gathering of bishops flattering the emperor.

III. Since he was inclined toward Nestorius—or at least toward Theodoret, the friend of Nestorius—he was less than fair-minded toward Cyril and the emperor Theodosius. This led the man, indulging his partiality, [Col. 0963B] to make Cyril guilty of envy and Theodosius guilty of perverse rule, as though each had been the occasion of disturbances or, as he himself puts it, scandals—or even their author.

### IV

He does not provide a fully explicit chronology. For, content to narrate the events themselves and the succession of bishops, he does not always carefully record the periods of years in which individual events occurred. Yet if Facundus of Hermiane, his fellow African along with the other two, who wrote twelve books on the affair of the Three Chapters, and Victor of Tunnuna, who wrote a Chronicle, are joined with him, a more reliable history of the events relating to the Fifth Synod will be obtained than from Theophanes or Nicephorus—whether the Constantinopolitan or Callistus. Those men committed to writing events of which they were largely a part; the latter authors were far removed from them, since Theophanes was separated by three centuries and Nicephorus by nearly eight.

### V

He gave the work the title *Breviary*, partly because it was compiled by abridging more extensive records, and partly because in twenty-four chapters, none of them particularly lengthy, it embraces a history of 125 years. For that many years intervened between the ordination of Nestorius, from which it takes its beginning, and the Fifth Synod, at which it appears to stop; Nestorius’s ordination is said to have occurred on 10 April 428, and the synod is said to have begun on 4 May 553.

### VI

From where he obtained the material presented in the *Breviary*, he partly reveals himself and partly allows us to discover through none-too-obscure indications. “From an ecclesiastical history,” he says, “recently translated from Greek into Latin, and from the acts of synods or the letters of the holy Fathers, I assembled this *Breviary*, joining together, in the course of time, those things which I received from a Greek work written at Alexandria, or learned from the faithful account of very eminent men.” We shall speak shortly about each of the sources he mentions and about several others.

### VII

How much the *Breviary* has gained from the *Little Breviary* of the Eutychianists, the readers’ own eyes announce; for it often uses the very words and preserves the continuous discourse. But since the *Little Breviary* extends no farther than the condemnation of Acacius, he obtained the events of the following years partly from John the rhetor and others, and partly from what he himself saw or learned through the reports of his contemporaries, whether while he was staying at Rome or in the East. Therefore we have prefixed the name of no author to the last five chapters.

### VIII

But the *Little Breviary* itself, as we have said, embraces a history of nearly fifty years, during which many events took place. Since the author could not have witnessed these with his own eyes, he certainly obtained them elsewhere—namely, from the archives of the Roman Church, in which the acts of synods, the reports of *apocrisiarii*, letters which the popes had either received or sent, and many other documents of that kind were preserved.

### IX

I know that the fifth and sixth centuries were exceptionally fertile in writers who committed to memory the same events that Liberatus recorded; nor do I deny that such writers may have been read by Liberatus, if he knew Greek sufficiently well, or consulted through another interpreter—which is quite probable, though I can scarcely affirm that he did so. Apart from the three most famous authors, Theodoret, Sozomen, and Socrates, histories were written by Priscus Panites under Theodosius the Younger; John the Aegean under Zeno; Candidus the Isaurian under Zeno; Eustathius the Syrian under Anastasius; Theodore the Lector under Justin the Elder; John the rhetor, Basil the Cilician, and Zachariah the rhetor under Justinian; and others whom Evagrius, Theophanes, and Nicephorus, excerptors of earlier authors, mention.

### X

Baronius accuses Liberatus of having sometimes believed too rashly historians favorable to Nestorius and therefore insufficiently fair toward Catholics. Some inquire—perhaps more curiously than usefully—who such historians were, and think that they should not be sought beyond the eight just listed; for what other historians could one suspect? Nothing is more natural than to suppose that Zachariah the rhetor was one of them, because Evagrius says that he was impelled by partiality to write, among other things, and especially that Nestorius himself had been summoned to the Council of Chalcedon.

It might also be conjectured that this Zachariah was identical with the Nestorian historian mentioned in the Alexandrian Chronicle. But Evagrius, *Book* III, chapter 7, demonstrates that Zachariah followed the side of the Eutychianists, and at the same time shows that the partiality which impelled him to write his history was directed not toward Nestorius but toward Eutyches. He also says that Nestorius was summoned to the council as a defendant to be judged, not as a bishop who was to sit in council.

### XI

The conjecture concerning the Nestorian heretic is very weak, indeed, unless I am mistaken, entirely groundless. For this historian is praised in the Alexandrian Chronicle, which was certainly written by Catholics, as a man of exceptional wisdom. I therefore think that this is the very man whom Liberatus calls Nestorius of Phlagonea, who condemned Dioscorus at the Council of Chalcedon and, after Proterius’s return, ordained him together with three other Catholic bishops.

This opinion is supported by the date, the name, and the man’s reliability. For this chronicler, of whom we are speaking, brought his history down to Leo the Younger—that is, to the year 474—which was the twenty-third year after the Council of Chalcedon. He could easily have lived until then, and, being about fifty years old, could also have attended the council in 451.

Furthermore, the similar name shared by the chronicler and the bishop provides a substantial basis for conjecture, especially since I remember reading nowhere among the Fathers of the council of any Nestorius of Phlagonea. What is more, both were Catholics. Add that it is quite credible that a man who had been deeply involved in events concerning the Alexandrian Church would have committed their history to writing. Finally, since no one except Alexandrian writers mentions a Nestorian chronicler, it should not seem contrary to the truth to believe that this same man wrote in Egypt.

### XII

This little book appears to have been written after the year 564. First, in chapter 22, mention is made of the death of Pope Vigilius, who died at Syracuse at the beginning of 555. Second, the journey mentioned in chapter 1 was certainly none other than the journey during which the deacon accompanied his bishop Reparatus after the latter had been expelled to Euchaita. Reparatus was expelled in 553 and died there at the beginning of 563.

This chronology agrees with the other circumstances. Liberatus says that he was writing while Apollinarius was governing the Alexandrian Church and after Primosus, the condemner of the Three Chapters who succeeded Reparatus in the see of Carthage, had died. Apollinarius was still governing the Alexandrian Church in 564, since he is said to have been ordained in 551 and, according to Nicephorus of Constantinople, to have held the see for seventeen years. Primosus, however, died around 562, at which time Theodosius of Alexandria was still alive, since he died in the first year of Justin the Younger, that is, in the year 566 of Christ.

### XIII

Some assign the greatest importance to this *Breviary*, others less. The former praise the brevity of the book and the breadth of its subject—two attractions that draw minds to reading. The latter complain that it is less thorough than it ought to be in examining the evidence for so important a controversy on both sides, and that it is excessively ready to place confidence in men whose faith was not entirely sincere. Indeed, they also charge it with excessive partisanship, for Liberatus was involved in the schism because of his obstinate defense of the Three Chapters.

### XIV

Although the lowliness and almost incredible unevenness of its style—caused by the insertion of passages from authors rendered from Greek in less-than-Latin fashion—might repel a fastidious reader, it ought not to repel one devoted to history. Whatever defect there is, is compensated by the variety of the events, which are scarcely found anywhere else either in their entirety or gathered together in this way; for many of the records from which he drew have largely perished.

### XV

The work has recently appeared with countless errors, from which it is now free through the assistance of three manuscript codices of the finest quality: Tellerian, Bellovacensis, and our own. The printed editions have been of considerable help, at least in giving weight to conjectures, as have the Greek authors themselves, whose works have been condensed into this epitome.

We preferred to remove the errors of the old editions from the text altogether rather than, as is customary, retain them to the great disadvantage or annoyance of readers. Nevertheless, it seemed appropriate to print what has been emended in a different type, so that it may be more easily recognized and, if desired, compared with the printed books.

### XVI

Scholia have been added that correspond to the work—that is, very brief notes, which were greatly needed either to shed light on the text when its brevity had rendered it obscure, or to correct the author’s judgment when it differs from that of better writers of a nearer age.

### XVII

The work I have undertaken may be regarded as a kind of continuation of the Nestorian history which I prefixed to the latter part of the works of Marius Mercator; indeed, it may also be regarded as an appendix to the life of Theodoret, which will shortly be published. For in order to make both works accurate, I applied myself to a more careful examination of Liberatus, for several reasons, but above all for this one: having sometimes been led into error by this author, I thought that others should be warned, lest, because of a preconceived opinion about him and a greater credulity than he deserves, they should either put themselves at risk or even be deceived.

### XVIII

What I said above, in section 4, namely that what is lacking in Liberatus should be supplied from other authors, especially Facundus of Hermiane and Victor of Tunnuna, must be understood of events that took place in the sixth century and in which they themselves participated. For other matters, better sources must be consulted: the acts of councils, the letters of popes, and the imperial decrees, on which dates are inscribed. One must also consult the most trustworthy writers who have set out the succession of bishops of each major Church and who have attached more carefully determined chronological markers to the events.

### XIX

But when exact chronology is at issue, take care not to rank Theophanes and Nicephorus of Constantinople among these writers. The former composed chronological tables, the latter a catalogue of five patriarchates; but each did so in such a way that, although Theophanes is a credible historian, neither is a commendable chronologist.

These authors therefore ought to be read with eyes that are not overly learned, despite the recommendation given them by a recent writer, who praises them under the name of “excellent chronology.”

### XX

But lest I seem to speak slanderously of Nicephorus and Theophanes, two very clear examples must be demonstrated. The first is how far Nicephorus departs from the truth in assigning the years during which each bishop in his catalogue held office, especially those mentioned by Liberatus. The second is how extensive is the partnership of error between Theophanes and Nicephorus in this matter.

### XXI

When Nicephorus drew up his catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, he placed forty-eight years between the death of Anastasius and the death of Celestine. For he assigns fifteen years to Innocent I, who succeeded Anastasius; eight to Zosimus; four to Boniface; and twenty-one to Celestine. Yet it is established by indisputable evidence that no more than thirty years intervened, since Anastasius died on 27 April 402 and Celestine on 6 April 432. Nicephorus’s computation therefore exceeds the truth by eighteen years.

Furthermore, if the eight years assigned by Nicephorus are attributed to Zosimus, Zosimus must have held the apostolic see until the year 425, since he began to sit in it in 417, after the death of Innocent I. How far this is from the truth everyone knows, since in 425 Celestine, who succeeded Boniface, the successor of Zosimus, had already begun to sit in the see, as is established by Augustine’s Letter 262 and other reliable records.

Again, if Celestine held the see for twenty-one years, as Nicephorus reports, and began to do so on 3 November 423, he must have held it until 444. Yet Saint Leo began to exercise the pontificate as early as 440; nevertheless, he did not succeed Celestine immediately, but succeeded Sixtus, who followed Celestine.

There is another obvious fault in Nicephorus’s catalogue of the Roman pontiffs. John Mercury ascended the apostolic see in January 532, while Pelagius I did so in 555, or, as others think, in 556. Thus twenty-three or twenty-four years elapsed between the accession of the two. Yet in Nicephorus’s catalogue, according to the edition of Contius, only eleven years are assigned: three years to John, one to Agapetus, two to Silverius, and five to Vigilius. Nothing more outrageous could be said, for on this reckoning the entire history of the Fifth Synod insofar as it concerns Vigilius would collapse.

But if we consult the same catalogue in the Royal edition, the total will not fall short by thirteen years; rather, it will exceed the truth by three or four. For, in a plainly astonishing error, eighteen years are assigned to Silverius. Thus Silverius, having succeeded Agapetus in 536, would have continued until 554—that is, beyond the period of the Fifth Synod. What could be more unbelievable?

If it is said, as indeed it ought to be said, that a double fault has entered the Greek text—namely, that the years belonging to Vigilius have been assigned to Silverius, and that one should write *Σιλβήριος ἔτος ἕν* (“one year of Silverius”), not *ἔτη εʹ* (“five years”)—everything will at least fit together in some fashion. But who would place confidence in books that must first be corrected before they can usefully be praised? I pass over many other far more serious offenses in the same catalogue.

### XXII

Nor is he more accurate concerning the bishops of Jerusalem than concerning those of Rome. I shall give one example, but a highly effective one, in which he commits a very serious fourth error in computing the years of the three bishops John, Praylius, and Juvenal.

It is established by a certain calculation of dates that seventy-one years elapsed between John’s ordination and Juvenal’s death, since Cyril died and John succeeded him in 386, while Juvenal died under Anastasius in 457. Nicephorus reports that seventy-four years elapsed. This is his first error.

He assigns John only fifteen years, although John sat for thirty. For John died in 417, as is clear from the letters of Augustine and Zosimus, and succeeded Cyril, whose death occurred in the eighth year of Theodosius the Great—that is, in 386—according to Jerome, chapter 19 of *On Illustrious Men*. This is the second error.

The third is much more remarkable, if not more absurd: he assigns twenty years to Praylius, who succeeded John. On this calculation Praylius must be said to have held office until 436 or 437. But what could conflict more sharply with history? Juvenal, who succeeded Praylius, attended the Ephesian synod in 431, received letters from Saints Celestine and Cyril in 430, and governed the Church of Jerusalem in the year when Theodoret says Theodotus died—that is, in 427. Indeed, as will soon be shown, he began to exercise the episcopate in 424. Praylius therefore governed the Church of Jerusalem for scarcely eight years. This is a fourth error equal to the preceding ones.

Nicephorus assigns thirty-eight years to Juvenal. On this reckoning Juvenal ought to be said to have died in 462, since he began to sit in 424. Yet he died in 457, since the eighth year of Anastasius, who succeeded Juvenal, coincides with the ninth year of the emperor Leo I and therefore with the year 465 of Christ, as is clearly gathered from Cyril the monk’s *Life of Saint Cyriacus*.

### XXIII

What shall I say about the Alexandrian bishops? Nicephorus invents things that no one even moderately skilled in ecclesiastical history could read patiently. It is established by indisputable calculations that Dioscorus succeeded the deceased Saint Cyril in 444, that Zoilus was deposed, and that Apollinarius succeeded him in 551. Thus nearly 107 years elapsed between the ordination of Dioscorus and that of Apollinarius. Nicephorus, however, gives only eighty; he is therefore short by twenty-seven years.

Nor is the deficiency remedied if one adds the seventeen years which others assign to Timothy Asterius, for Nicephorus assigns no number of years to his episcopate. Nearly ten years would still be missing.

Moreover, Nicephorus assigns only five years to Dioscorus, although he was ordained at the beginning of February 444 and deposed at Chalcedon on 13 October 451. Thus he held office for nearly eight years.

He assigns only fifteen years to Timothy Salophaciolus, or “the White,” whereas Liberatus reports that Timothy died after a pontificate of approximately twenty-three years.

He assigns one year to Gaianus; Liberatus assigns 103 days, or, according to another reading, sixty-three days.

He assigns two years to Theodosius; Liberatus assigns one year and four months. Why should I pursue more carefully the remaining matters written with such carelessness? I pass on to the Antiochenes.

### XXIV

It is certain, on the authority of Theodoret, near the end of Book V of his *History*, that Theodotus of Antioch died in 427. It is equally certain from Evagrius that Euphrasius perished when the city collapsed in 526, on 29 May, which was a Friday. Thus exactly ninety-nine years elapsed between the deaths of the two.

Nicephorus counts 106 years and seven months. This is his first serious error, and the following is another.

As has been said, it is established by Theodoret’s indisputable authority in this matter that Theodotus was succeeded by John in 427. It is equally established from the acts both of the Ephesian Robber Synod and of the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon that Domnus was deposed in August 449.

Thus twenty-two years elapsed from the accession of John, who succeeded Theodotus, to the accession of Maximus, who was substituted for Domnus. Nicephorus counts twenty-six years, assigning eighteen years to John and eight to Domnus. On this reckoning—an error more outrageous than the preceding ones—John would have to be said to have held the see of Antioch until 445 and Domnus until 453, which is utterly opposed to the truth. For Maximus, who replaced Domnus, attended the Council of Chalcedon in 451, as the acts establish. Domnus was deposed at Ephesus in the Robber Synod in August 449, as the proceedings show.

Domnus was in charge of the Church of Antioch in 444, the year in which Cyril died, as is clear from the fragments excerpted by Marius Mercator.

Moreover, he received from Cyril letters concerning the case of Athanasius, bishop of Perrha, and he also received from Theodoret letters concerning Caelestiacus, a distinguished African, in 442. Furthermore, Theodoret—no one knew John’s years more certainly because of their exceptional friendship and intimate association—demonstrates in his letter to Dioscorus, Cyril’s successor, that John held office for only thirteen years.

### XXV

Yet Nicephorus was astonishingly mistaken even in computing the years of his own predecessors. It is established from the acts of the Council of Ephesus that Nestorius was deposed in June 431. It is equally established from the letters of Pope Vigilius and from the confession of Eutychius that Menna died in 552. It is therefore beyond doubt that 121 years elapsed between the deposition of Nestorius and the death of Menna.

Nicephorus nevertheless counts only 110 years, and thus errs by a deficiency of eleven years. He then writes that Proclus held office for twelve years and three months. It is nevertheless certain that he held office for thirteen years and six months. For he was ordained on the very day on which Maximianus departed this life, the fifth day of Holy Week, the day before the Ides of April, which belonged to the year 434; and he himself went to heaven on 24 October 447. He therefore held office for thirteen years and six months.

### XXVI

From what has been demonstrated clearly, unless I am mistaken, concerning Nicephorus, anyone may easily infer what opinion to hold about Theophanes: namely, that he made the same errors as Nicephorus.

### XXVII

To begin with the Roman bishops, Theophanes assigns eight years to Zosimus, four to Boniface, ten to Celestine, and eight to Sixtus. On this calculation Sixtus ought to have died in 447, Celestine in 433, Boniface in 449, and Zosimus in 425.

Zosimus succeeded Innocent in 417, which is as far from the truth as possible, since Leo, the successor of Sixtus, began to sit in 440. Certainly Leo wrote to the bishops throughout Campania in 443. Sixtus wrote to John of Antioch and Cyril in 433. Celestine held the apostolic see for a considerable time before the ordination of Nestorius, which occurred in 428. Boniface sent a letter to the bishops of Gaul concerning Maximus of Valentia during the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta, that is, in 419.

### XXVIII

Regarding the bishops of Jerusalem, Theophanes makes the same error as Nicephorus. He assigns sixteen years to John, twenty to Praylius, and thirty-eight to Juvenal. These are three enormous anachronisms (*ἀντιχρονισμοί*).

He is similarly mistaken concerning the bishops of Antioch and also those of Alexandria, indeed even those of Constantinople, so that Nicephorus’s catalogue appears to have been copied from the chronological tables of Theophanes.

### XXIX

Since matters stand thus with Theophanes, it is plainly evident how prudently the learned interpreter Goar called him “a more credible historian than tolerable chronographer.” For nothing is more careless or more corrupt than his chronological tables.

[Col. 0969]

# The Breviary

[Note: [Col. 0969B] The manuscript codex of Tellerius begins: “The *Breviary* …” “[The printing of several sheets had already been completed,” says Garnerius, “when a manuscript codex came into my hands, which in its preface was named after the most illustrious archbishop and duke of Reims and first peer of France, Maurice Tellerius. From it I extracted sixty-five variant readings, though not all are of equal value. Some entered through scribal error, while others may still serve to correct the text. All are presented alongside the text *παραλλήλως*, ‘in parallel.’ We preferred to place these variants n[.....]s beneath the text. EDIT.”]]

The Causes of the Nestorians and Eutychians, collected by Liberatus, archdeacon of the sixth ecclesiastical region of the Church of Carthage. (C)

[Col. 0969]

# Titles of the Chapters

[Note: [Col. 0969B] The same manuscript says: “The following are the contents of this *Breviary*.”]

[Col. 0969A]

1. Introduction.
2. Paul of Samosata, and that he is the author of the Nestorian heresy.
3. Apollinarius, and that he is the author of the Eutychian heresy.
4. The ordination of Nestorius and his heresy.
5. The First Synod of Ephesus and the condemnation of Nestorius.
6. The disagreement between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch.
7. The ordination of Maximianus, bishop of Constantinople.
8. The peace between Cyril and John.
9. Cyril’s letters written on behalf of the Eastern bishops.
10. The scandal of the Nestorians and the monks of Armenia.
11. The presbyter and abbot Eutyches, his heresy, and his condemnation.
12. The Second Synod of Ephesus and the death of Flavian.
13. The Council of Chalcedon and the condemnation of Dioscorus.
14. The exile of Dioscorus and the ordination of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria.
15. The ordination of Timothy Aelurus and the death of Proterius.
16. The ordination of Timothy the Catholic and Peter the heretic.
17. The ordination of John the Catholic and the condemnation of Acacius.
18. The Alexandrian bishops.
19. Severus, Julian, and Macedonius.

[Note: [Col. 0970B] In the same manuscript, “Macedonius” is absent.]

20. Gaianus and Theodosius.
21. Pope Agapetus and Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople.
22. Silverius and Vigilius.
23. Paul, bishop of Alexandria, and the monks of Jerusalem.
24. Pelagius and Theodore of Cappadocia.

[Note: [Col. 0970B] In the same manuscript, “of Cappadocia” is absent.]

# Chapter One: Introduction

[Col. 0969C]

Exhausted by the necessities of travel, and with my mind to some extent released from temporal cares, I have compiled this *Breviary* of the two heresies—that is, of the Nestorians and Eutychians—from an ecclesiastical history recently translated from Greek into Latin, from the acts of synods, and from the letters of the holy Fathers. I have joined together, in the course of time, those things which I received from a Greek work written at Alexandria or learned from the faithful account of very eminent men.

In doing this, for my own instruction and as a response to the false speakers among the followers of both parties, who in their customary zeal speak differently about their authors from the way the truth requires, I willingly offer it to Catholic brothers who are ignorant of the acts of these heresies and wish to read them.

[Note: [Col. 0969C]

“On the necessities of travel,” etc.] On this journey he showed himself a faithful companion to Reparatus, bishop of Carthage, whose deacon he was, even in exile, so that he did not leave Euchaita until after the bishop’s death.

“Exhausted,” etc.] The reading may be corrupt. For how do these two words, “exhausted” and “released,” fit together? What if the reading were “deceased”? Nevertheless, the old reading may be retained, provided that “exhausted” is taken to mean “restored after weariness”—an unusual sense, but one that may be pardoned in an African writer.

“Recently translated from Greek into Latin,” etc.] By Epiphanius the Scholastic, at the urging of Cassiodorus, who compiled what is called the *Tripartite History* from the histories of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret.

“From a Greek work written at Alexandria,” etc.] It is not permissible to guess what work this was, unless the statements made in the preface about Nestorius, bishop of Phlagonea, are true.

“For my own instruction and as a response,” etc.] That is, “to instruct me and so that I might readily answer those who ask.”]

# Chapter Two: Paul of Samosata, and that He Is the Author of the Nestorian Heresy

*(From the Epitome of the Chronicles of Lucentius and Book VII of the History of Socrates.)*

Thus Paul, bishop of Samosata, is recognized by many as the author of the Nestorian doctrine. Following the teaching of the ancient heretics, he asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ was born and suffered as a mere man. Regarding the holy and supremely blessed Trinity, he followed, as the Greeks report, the opinion of Sabellius.

For this reason, they say that the Council of Nicaea decreed that the Paulianists were to be baptized absolutely, distinguishing between the teaching of Paul and that of Nestorius on the grounds that Nestorius, while confessing the existence of the divinity of the Son of God, believed Christ to have been conceived and formed as a mere man and afterward advanced into Godhood—that is, a deified man—and not that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, as the Gospel proclaims and the Catholic Church confesses.

For this reason Lucentius places and says the following in his *Epitome of the Chronicles*: “During the consulship of Felix and Taurus, Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, attempted to introduce a new error into the Churches, preaching that Christ was born a man only and not also God, and saying that divinity had been bestowed upon him as a reward for his merit.”

[Note: [Col. 0971D] The Tellerian codex reads: “He says this altogether.”]

Socrates, however, distinguishes Nestorius from Paul and sets out their difference as follows:

“It is evident,” he says, “that Nestorius was ignorant of the readings of the ancients. Therefore, as I have said, he lingered only over the term. And he not only subjected the term to examination, but also altogether denied that the one who was born was God. We, however, confess that the one who was born of the holy Virgin Mary and was crucified is the Lord of glory, as the Apostle says: ‘For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Cor. 2:8).

“Moreover, Nestorius says: ‘Do not boast, Jew; you did not crucify God,’ as though the Lord of glory were not himself God. The fact that he does not call Christ a mere man, as Photinus and Paul of Samosata did, is also shown by the homilies he composed. For nowhere does he destroy the subsistence of God the Word, but everywhere he confesses that he subsists and possesses subsistence, and that he is not like Photinus and Paul of Samosata, who destroyed his subsistence” (Socrates, Book VII, chapter 32).”

[Note: [Col. 0971D] The same codex reads: “not only that term.”]

[Note: [Col. 0971D] The same codex reads: “was born, the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] The Tellerian codex reads: “he destroys the substance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] The same codex reads: “and possesses substance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] The same codex reads: “destroying his substance.”]

This is what Socrates says about Paul and Nestorius. Using his testimony, I shall proceed to what another reading says:

“Unfamiliar with the expositions of the holy Fathers, who teach that the Son of God received into his person, through the union of his nature, the manhood which he does not share with the Father, Nestorius—ignorant in his madness—was unwilling, because of the indivisible and inseparable nature of the Father and the Son, to call blessed Mary the Mother of God, lest he should also apply birth to the Father. He did not understand that the Father and the Son are one in nature but distinct in persons: the one who begets is not begotten, nor does the one who is begotten beget.”

Because the Nestorians do not understand this, they have until now shamelessly set before us, as though it were a knotty and insoluble question, the objection that the Father was born together with the Son if we confess blessed Mary to be *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”). But since this is how matters stand concerning Nestorius, let us continue the work we have begun.

[Note: [Col. 0972A]

“As many maintain …”] Several have charged Nestorius with this shameful origin, first of all two laymen, Eusebius, who later became bishop of Dorilaeum, and Marius Mercator; then Pope Celestine in his letter to Nestorius; and finally, indiscriminately, others. Among these, however, one must not count Cyril of Alexandria, for nowhere did he trace the origins of the Nestorian heresy farther back than Photinus, Diodorus of Tarsus, and Theodore of Mopsuestia.

“Ancient heretics.”] Mercator mentions Ebion, Paul’s teacher, in his *Refutation of the Anathemas of Nestorius*; Theodoret mentions Artemon in Book II, chapter 8, of the *Fabulous History of Heresies*; and the author of the *Predestinatus* mentions him under heresy 44.

“Following the opinion of Sabellius.”] Mercator treats this very differently and more satisfactorily in his dissertation on the twelfth anathema of Nestorius.

“Paulianists.”] The author of the *Predestinatus*, in the passage cited, says: “It is known to all that when heretics come to us, we do not rebaptize them, but extend the hand of reconciliation and thus deliver them to the divine people to be joined to them. Regarding the Paulianists, however, the holy Council of Nicaea decreed that they should be baptized completely and only then joined to the Catholic people. Hence I believe that they do not preserve the rule of baptism intact, and that this decree was established by the pontiffs of Christ.”

“Afterward advanced into Godhood.”] Nestorius himself objects to this in Mercator. See the first dissertation on the second part of the works of Marius Mercator, where the popular opinion is overthrown by the clearest testimonies.

“A deified man.”] Nestorius again objects to this in his first letter to Celestine, in which he accuses his opponents of using the word “deification.”

“Lucentius.”] This reading must certainly be retained, despite the futile objection of the highly learned collector of the councils, Labbe. For it indicates the continuator of Prosper—if indeed it is Prosper—not that the Aquitanian author had a better view on this matter. He too was deceived by Cassian, who presented the Lepotian heresy as Nestorian. See Mercator’s letter cited immediately below and the first dissertation cited immediately above.

“It is evident.”] This passage is either mutilated in the Greek edition, even in the latest edition of Valesius, or it was inserted into the *Tripartite History* only up to the words “destroying his subsistence.”

“The homilies he composed.”] Since they had previously lain hidden, they have now been published for the first time in the second part of the works of Marius Mercator, including the very homily Socrates mentions.

“What another reading says.”] Whose reading is that, after all? This entire section (*περικοπή*, “passage”) is certainly quite confused. I am scarcely prevented from believing that it belonged to some annotator who imposed it upon Liberatus.]

# Chapter Three: Apollinarius, and that He Is the Author of the Eutychian Heresy

*(From Theodoret, Book V, chapter 3, of the Ecclesiastical History.)*

After the condemnation of Paul of Samosata, when a generation of time had passed, Apollinarius, bishop of Laodicea, followed the Arians’ blasphemy concerning the Lord’s incarnation. Asserting doctrines contrary to Paul’s, he preached that the flesh and the omnipotent Word of God were of one substance, insisting with the utmost contentiousness that the Word became flesh, or that some part of the Word was converted and changed into flesh, rather than that flesh was taken and assumed from the Virgin Mary. Thus Christ would be acknowledged as sinless, consubstantial with us, and in every respect like us, as the Apostle says (Heb. 4:15).

Theodoret, bishop, records Apollinarius and his heresy in his *Ecclesiastical History* as follows:

“Apollinarius, bishop of Laodicea,” he says, “while assuming the appearance of piety and pretending to preserve the apostolic doctrines, soon appeared openly as an enemy. For he used fraudulent arguments concerning the divine nature, generating certain degrees of dignity and presuming to explain the mystery of the dispensation as incomplete, while asserting that the rational soul, through which the body rises again, was deprived of salvation.

“According to his reasoning, if the Word of God did not assume a soul, he neither provided medicine for the soul nor bestowed honor upon it. Rather, the earthly body is worshiped by the invisible powers, while the soul, made according to the divine image, remained in an inferior state, clothed in the insults of sin. In his madness he also asserted many things beyond this. At one time he himself confessed equally that flesh had been assumed from the holy Virgin; at another, that it had descended from heaven together with the Word of God; at another, that the Word itself had become flesh and had assumed nothing from us. He joined many other empty fables to sacred opinions, which I have judged it superfluous to mention at present.

“By saying such things, he not only filled his own followers with the plague, but also made some of our people sharers in this leprosy.

“After a short time, when nearly all of them saw their own disgrace and the splendor of the Church, they returned. Yet they did not put aside their former sickness; rather, they secretly wounded many of those who remained steadfast.”

[Note: [Col. 0973D] The Tellerian codex reads: “Theodoret in the *Ecclesiastical [History]*.”]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] The same codex reads: “Apollinarius, bishop of Laodicea, while …”]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] The same codex reads: “sacred promises.”]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] The same codex reads: “to make [them] sharers in the leprosy.”]

«From this root, therefore, there sprouted in the Churches the one nature of flesh and divinity, so that suffering might be joined to the divinity of the Only-Begotten, and it generated whatever other controversies among peoples and priests (Book V, chapter 3).»

And shortly afterward: «But after Apollinaris had been stripped of his episcopate, he proclaimed the novelty of his teaching in the Church with open shamelessness [Note: The same codex has, “he proclaimed it to the Church,”], presenting himself as the leader of the heresy.»

Therefore, from all that was said and brought forward above [Col. 0973D], it is evident that the Nestorians were propagated by Paul, and that the preachers of one nature—such as the Acephali and Eutychians—were propagated by Apollinaris.

At that time Bishop Diodore of Tarsus [Note: [Col. 0974D] The same codex: “Diodore of the Tarsians.”] replied to his statements and letters; afterward, Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil, and Theodore of Mopsuestia did so as well. They convincingly demonstrated from divine testimonies the distinct properties of the two natures in the one person of Christ, as their own works themselves prove.

Now that the authorities of both heresies have been demonstrated [Col. 0974A], it remains to narrate their proceedings, as the preface promises.

[Note: [Col. 0974A]

**On Apollinaris.** See what has been written about him and his heresy in Dissertation 1, on the second part of Mercator’s works; it is useful for refuting certain popular prejudices and for correcting Liberatus himself.

**In one generation of time.** He used “generation” for “age.” For Paul was condemned in the year 270, whereas Apollinaris began to teach around the year 360.

**The flesh and the almighty Word of God.** Apollinaris and Theodoret object. The latter does so partly in his *Ecclesiastical History*, in the words that Liberatus will soon quote, and partly in Dialogue 4 against Apollinaris, which is falsely attributed to Athanasius. The former does so in his confession of faith: “Let him be anathema who does not say that the flesh is from Mary, and who says that this flesh is of an uncreated nature and ὁμοούσιον—consubstantial—with God.”

**Certain ranks of dignity.** See Epiphanius and the cited dialogue of Theodoret concerning the bishop, presbyter, and [Col. 0974B] deacon, to whom those heretics likened the three divine persons.

**Nazianzenus.** I am surprised that Nyssenus was not added to the others, for Nazianzenus never disputed against Apollinaris more explicitly than Nyssenus did.

**Authorities.** This word is used for origins, or authors—a usage not unusual among Africans after Tertullian.]

## CHAPTER IV. On the Ordination of Nestorius and His Heresy

*(From Socrates and the acts of the Council of Ephesus.)*

After the condemnation and deposition of Apollinaris, when some time had passed and Sisinnius had died—the man who, after the death of blessed Atticus, had assumed the episcopate of the Church of Constantinople—the emperors decided [Col. 0974C] not to appoint a pontiff from the Church of Constantinople, but to summon some foreigner from Antioch in Syria, from which that Church had previously received John, and to make him bishop.

And as Socrates relates in his *Ecclesiastical History*: «There was a certain presbyter at Antioch named Nestorius, a Germanician by birth, eloquent in speech, whom the rulers summoned to Constantinople as a man useful for teaching. After three months had passed, Nestorius came from Antioch. He was regarded as outstanding among many for his chastity. What sort of character he had, however, the wise learned from his very first homily. Anastasius the presbyter had also been sent with him; Nestorius honored him greatly and kept him as his adviser in his affairs (Socrates, Book VII, [Col. 0974D] chapter 29).»

Accordingly, when Nestorius was ordained on the first day of April, in the consulship of Felix and Taurus, Anastasius taught before the Church: “Let no one dare to call Mary *God-bearer*, for Mary was a human being, and it is utterly impossible for God to be begotten by a human being.” When many clergy and laypeople heard this together, they were greatly disturbed. For from ancient times they had learned to confess Christ as God, and they did not at all believe that, through the dispensation, the human being had been separated from God.

[Col. 0975A] When an uproar therefore arose in the Church, Nestorius, wishing to strengthen Anastasius’s sermon because he honored him, refused to rebuke him as a blasphemer. Instead, he repeatedly taught this before the Church and stirred up the controversy through disputes, denying the confession of the *God-bearer*. Hence division arose in the Church, and Nestorius’s lukewarm proceedings caused a great disturbance throughout the world. Since he did not correct himself, the Church of Constantinople was in scandal and, like a nocturnal quarrel filled with every kind of confusion, could distinguish neither allies nor enemies, with different people now agreeing with one side, now with another, and changing their own statements. For Nestorius held the opinion that Christ was altogether a mere human being, introducing into the Church the doctrine of Paul of Samosata and Photinus [Col. 0975B].

When Bishop Cyril of Alexandria heard this—for at that time he was assigned primacy in dealing with such matters—some people from Constantinople who were not in communion with Nestorius came to him [Note: The Codex Tellerianus has, “some of the people of the Constantinopolitans”] and reported to him what had taken place at Constantinople. Cyril therefore sent Nestorius a letter beginning, “Venerable sons and worthy of faith,” and so forth, persuading him that, if his statement had slipped out before the people, it should be corrected in his discourses, and that he should call the holy Virgin the *God-bearer*, that is, Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), so that the offense of the whole world might cease. For the illustrious pope Celestine had already received from a certain Antiochus four-book volumes of Nestorius’s expositions, had read and examined the doctrine signed by Nestorius’s own hand and sent by him, and the entire East [Col. 0975C] already knew it from his writings.

But since Nestorius refused to correct himself, Cyril again sent him a second letter, beginning, “Some people complain about me to your Fraternity,” and so forth. In it he gave him a full account of the Incarnation of Christ, asking him to share the same mind with him, so that the peace of the Churches might remain unharmed and unbroken concord might continue among the priests.

In reply, Nestorius wrote Cyril a contrary letter, beginning, “The insults directed against us in your remarkable letters,” and so forth. Nevertheless, he refused to call blessed Mary Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), nor did he correct his statement.

John of Antioch also sent Nestorius a letter beginning, “My intention regarding your Reverence,” and so forth. In it he urged him not to reject a counselor who would be beneficial to him, merely because he was reluctant to call the blessed Virgin the *God-bearer*, as the holy Fathers had taught and written. In that letter he mentioned Theodore of Mopsuestia, showing him an example of retraction: how, while he was speaking and an uproar had arisen, that most courageous man had risen and, without confusion, retracted his opinion, and how he quickly corrected for the benefit of the Church what seemed of little use to the ignorant [Note: The same codex has, “what seemed of little use to those who were ignorant”].

But Nestorius despised this and became hateful to his own city [Col. 0976A]. Cyril, through his deacon Possidonius, reported the matter to Pope Celestine and informed him by letter of what was being done at Constantinople.

The same Cyril [Note: The Codex Tellerianus repeatedly has, “to whom Cyril”] sent Nestorius a third synodical letter, in which he also composed and inserted twelve chapters against his doctrine. It begins: “The Lord says, ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’” (Matthew 10).

When a copy of this letter reached John of Antioch, he was offended by Cyril’s chapters themselves. He thought that, in confronting Nestorius excessively, Cyril had fallen into the sect of Apollinaris.

He therefore instructed Andrew and Theodoret, bishops of his council, to respond in writing against the twelve [Col. 0976B] chapters themselves, as though they were restoring the doctrine of Apollinaris.

Nestorius, realizing that Cyril would not tolerate the Church’s remaining in such disturbances and the people in scandal, secretly approached the pious emperor Theodosius, asking him to send a formal imperial letter to Cyril and restrain him from his persecution. The emperor did indeed write to him, rebuking him as a restless man who pursued scandals and acted and wrote without the cooperation of the priests.

[Note: [Col. 0976B]

**After the condemnation and deposition of Apollinaris.** He is recorded as having been condemned in the Alexandrian council under Athanasius, in the Roman council under Damasus, and in the Constantinopolitan council in the year 351. So far as I know, only Theodoret said that he was deposed.

**When some time had passed.** From the death of Apollinaris, [Col. 0976C] which occurred in the year 373, to the ordination of Sisinnius, which fell on the Sunday that was the last day of February in the year 426, fifty-three years intervened.

**The emperors decided.** This was because the clergy had been divided into factions, with some stubbornly supporting Proclus and others Philip of Side. See the history of Nestorius prefixed to the second part of M. Mercator’s works.

**On the first day.** Yet Socrates gives the tenth. See Dissertation 2 on the latter part of M. Mercator’s works, and marvel at the inconsistency of a recent scholar who, after following Liberatus in his *Pelagian History* for a trivial reason, returned to Socrates in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod, guided by better judgment.

**For the illustrious pope Celestine had already received them through Antiochus.** Certain historical facts contradict this. See the preface to the second part of M. Mercator’s works.

[Col. 0976D] **John of Antioch also.** Either these words were inserted in anticipation—and quite improperly—or the history is at fault. For, as the letter itself makes clear, John wrote to Nestorius only after receiving the letters of Saint Celestine, and therefore several months after Cyril sent the deacon Possidonius to Rome. For through Possidonius Celestine gave both his reply to Cyril and his letter to John.]

## CHAPTER V. On the First Synod of Ephesus and the Condemnation of Nestorius

*(From the acts of the Council of Ephesus and the Letter of Ibas.)*

After this he wrote another imperial letter to all the bishops [Col. 0977A], ordering them to assemble at Ephesus and to deliver judgment concerning the books of Nestorius and Cyril.

The emperor also sent a formal letter through the *magistrianus* Ebagnius to blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius, asking him to honor the council with his presence. When Ebagnius came to Carthage, he heard from Capreolus, the bishop of that city, that blessed Augustine had departed from this world to the Lord. Having received from him a letter to the emperor reporting [Note: The Codex Tellerianus has, “reporting”] the death of blessed Augustine, he returned to Constantinople, from which he had come.

But Archbishop Capreolus, unable to assemble a universal council because of the attacks of the Vandals besieging the African regions, sent his deacon Bessula to Ephesus as his legate to the council.

Pope Celestine of Rome wrote Nestorius a letter of rebuke, together with exhortation and censure, because he ought not to have gone astray; Celestine had rejoiced at his ordination [Note: The same codex has, “from his ordination”]. The letter begins, “For some days of our life,” and so forth. It granted him a period of ten days—from the first day on which he received the letter [Note: The same codex has, “from the first day on which he received his letter”] to the final day—so that, if Nestorius did not correct his expositions and restore to the Church those whom he had expelled because of Christ, who is its head, he would know that he had been separated from Celestine’s fellowship and from the company of all the holy bishops.

Celestine informed him that he had appointed Cyril to act in his place at the council, through a letter beginning, “The letters of Your Holiness have brought sorrow to us,” and so forth. In it he instructed Cyril that, if Nestorius did not correct his doctrine within those ten days, Cyril should arrange for him to be removed from the common body and should provide for that Church.

He wrote about the same matter [Note: The same codex has, “about the same man”] also to John of Antioch, Rufus of Thessalonica, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Flavian of Philippi, the archbishops. He also wrote to the Constantinopolitan clergy, admonishing them to stand firmly against Nestorius’s doctrine and to endure his persecutions patiently, since they would bring forth the fruit of crowns; and they should know that those whom Nestorius had excommunicated or deposed remained in communion with the Apostolic See.

Immediately after the paschal festival, Nestorius came to Ephesus with a very large crowd and found many bishops assembled. Cyril of Alexandria, delayed for a short time, arrived around Pentecost [Col. 0977D], as did Juvenal of Jerusalem.

But while John of Antioch was delayed, the bishops who were present raised the question of blessed Mary, the *God-bearer*.

Cyril was making certain excerpts from Nestorius’s books, wishing to disturb him; for, it is said, he was his enemy.

When many were confessing Jesus Christ as God, Nestorius said: “I will never confess as God one who was [Col. 0978A] two or three months old; for this reason I am thrice clean of your blood, and from now on I shall not come to you” [Note: The Codex Tellerianus has, “I shall not come to you”].

After saying this, he joined the other bishops who followed his opinion. Thus the bishops who were present were divided into two groups.

Cyril, together with his party, exercising the authority of the Apostolic See, summoned a council of two hundred bishops and called Nestorius. But he refused to come, postponing his appearance until John of Antioch arrived [Note: The same codex has, “until John’s presence”]. For John himself had written to Cyril from his sixth stopping-place, reporting his journey, his haste, the hardships of the road, the deaths of the animals, and the needs of the bishops who were with him [Note: The same codex has, “who had been with him”].

The bishops who were with Cyril, repeatedly rereading Nestorius’s homilies, which he had delivered on this question, condemned Nestorius as a blasphemer of the Son of God before the council of the East and the bishops of certain provinces who had joined the council arrived at the synod.

After this had been done against Nestorius, John and the bishops who were with him held another council among themselves and condemned Cyril, together with Memnon, bishop of Ephesus.

[Note: [Col. 0978B]

**After this he wrote another imperial letter.** Rather, this was either done simultaneously with, or before, the event described. The first part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 32, mentions this very letter: “Your Piety shall take care that, once the coming holy Easter has passed, you hasten to the city of Ephesus in Asia on the very day of Holy Pentecost, bringing with you those most holy bishops of your province whom you judge suitable.” It later adds: “Concerning this most holy synod of ours, Our Serenity has written letters to all the bishops who are metropolitan and beloved of God” [Col. 0978C].

**The letters to the emperor.** Three letters of Capreolus are mentioned. One was addressed to the emperor Theodosius; nothing from it has been published except a fragment preserved by Ferrandus in his letter to Pelagius and Anatolius. A second was addressed to the Council of Ephesus and is preserved in the acts, Act 1. A third was addressed to Vitalis and Constantius against Nestorius; P. Sirmondus published it complete, whereas previously it had been mutilated.

In my opinion, a certain recent writer on Pelagian history had not remembered this passage of Liberatus when he said that Theodosius, in the imperial letter sent to the Ephesian Fathers through John, count S. L., had included Augustine’s name because he had not yet learned of Augustine’s death and therefore believed him to be present. But those who are not strangers to ecclesiastical history know the reason for this event. This is precisely why the supreme pontiff Celestine, Rufus of Thessalonica, and others are mentioned in the same imperial letter, although their absence was known and news had also been heard in the royal city of the arrival of the legates.

**Universal.** That is, of the entire African diocese. See the dissertation on the synods in the Pelagian controversy, in the first part of Mercator’s works.

**But Pope Celestine.** The chronology is disturbed. Celestine wrote to Nestorius a full three months before the imperial letter by which the synod was convened, since the letters of the supreme pontiff are dated August 11, whereas the imperial letter is dated November 19.

**He had appointed Cyril to act in his place at the council.** If this refers to the Council of Ephesus, the error is obvious. Celestine could not have heard anything about the Council of Ephesus when he gave these letters, for he gave them on the third day before the Ides of August, whereas the council is recorded as having been convened on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of the following December. Liberatus is therefore speaking of the Roman council at which the pontiff wrote letters to Nestorius, Cyril, and other bishops, which Liberatus mentions. To have appointed someone to act in his place at the council thus means the same as writing letters at the Roman council by which the pontiff ordered them to exercise his authority—not at the Council of Ephesus, which had not yet been convened, but in carrying out the pontiff’s command to depose Nestorius if he did not submit, and to appoint another in his place.

**With a very large crowd.** Yet he brought only ten bishops from his own diocese and two courtiers from the palace. The bishops’ names are subscribed to Nestorius’s report to the emperor. The courtiers were Candidianus, *comes domesticorum*, who came as an investigator, and Irenaeus, who was closely connected with Nestorius by friendship. See Theodosius’s imperial letter to the synod.

[Col. 0979B] **Certain excerpts.** They were published in the second part of M. Mercator’s works, p. 103, although previously they had been entirely unknown.

**For he was his enemy.** It is not surprising that Ibas’s defender wrote the same things about Cyril as Ibas did, since he took what he wrote from Ibas’s letter. It is surprising, however, that Isidore of Pelusium, a holy man whom Cyril honored as a father, believed the same popular report and wrote to Cyril: “So that neither I may be condemned, nor you yourself condemned by God, cease from contention. Do not demand from the living Church, under the pretext of piety, vengeance for your personal injuries, which you are owed by mortal men, and build for it an eternal discord” (*Facundus*, Book II, chapter 1).

**Two hundred bishops.** The better authority is Marius Mercator, who was able to count those present. He stated that 274 Catholics assembled, in the preface to Theodore’s creed.

**The bishops who were with him.** There were thirty-three, as is clear [Col. 0979C] from the following chapter; Theodore himself was among them. Liberatus does not, however, count him, since he evidently names only seven metropolitans together with John.
