**Among themselves.** In the very lodging-house, before the dust of the journey had been shaken off and scarcely after John had descended from his carriage, as the report of the Fathers to the emperor relates, in the second part of the Council of Ephesus.

How extensively Liberatus errs in this account of the Council of Ephesus has been shown in Dissertation 2 on the latter part of M. Mercator’s works, where the accounts handed down by earlier historians of Ephesus have been examined. When I investigated Theophanes’ chronography, I called Cerameus to mind, being deceived by memory. Cerameus is in fact entirely different.]

## CHAPTER VI. On the Discord between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch

*(From the acts of the Council of Ephesus, Socrates, and the Letter of Ibas.)*

After two days, John of Antioch arrived and learned what had been done as described above [Note: The Codex Tellerianus has, “and, learning this, he did the following”], as well as what had been done in the condemnation of Nestorius and the acceptance and confirmation at the council itself of Cyril’s twelve chapters. He was very angry with Cyril as the author of sedition, because he had condemned Nestorius with such fervor. The bishops who had assembled with John—that is, Alexander of Apamea, John of Damascus, Dexianus of Seleucia, Alexander of Hierapolis, Himerius of Nicomedia, Helladius [Col. 0980A] of Tarsus, Maximus of Anazarbus, and the other thirty-four who had then arrived at Ephesus with him—complained about Cyril, saying: “In accordance with the rulers’ command, why were the bishops of the other provinces not awaited, so that, just as he judged Nestorius’s books, the council might also judge Cyril’s statements?”

When they had assembled at Ephesus, John inveighed against Cyril and Memnon as follows: «We had hoped that, in accordance with the rules of the holy Fathers and the letters of our most pious and Christian emperors, the synod would be held in peace. But since, using audacity, sedition, and a heretical understanding, you alone sat in council while we were approaching, and, in accordance with the letters of our most pious emperors, filled the holy synod with the entire crowd, so that the chapters corresponding to the perfidy and impiety of Apollinaris, Arius, and Eunomius might not be investigated, and you did not await the presence of the holy bishops who had been summoned from every direction by the most pious emperors—even though the most illustrious Count Candidianus had ordered you in writing and orally to presume no such thing, but to await the common council of all the holy bishops—know therefore that you have been deposed and excluded from the episcopate: you, Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and you, Memnon, bishop of this city. You are excluded from every ecclesiastical ministry as authors of the entire sedition and injustice, because you gave the occasion for the Fathers’ rules and the imperial decrees to be trampled underfoot. But all the rest of you who consented to the seditious, acting against the laws and contrary to the imperial decrees, are excommunicated until, recognizing your own offense, you do penance, accept the faith of the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, introduce nothing new, anathematize the heretical chapters set forth by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria [Note: The Codex Tellerianus has, “the chapters set forth by Cyril of Alexandria”], against evangelical and apostolic doctrine, and follow the letters of our most pious and most Christian emperors, which command that an inquiry be made and that a careful examination of the faith be conducted in peace.»

John and those who were with him publicly presented this statement of theirs against Cyril and Memnon at Ephesus and informed the emperor by their letters of the condemnation of both. The letters begin: “Your radiant Piety, for the benefit of the whole world,” and so forth.

After this, the legates of Pope Celestine arrived at the council from the West: the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, and Philip, a presbyter of the Roman Church.

When these men had taken their seats, Cyril and Memnon presented petitions to the council, filing a protest against John of Antioch and the bishops who were with him, so that they might be summoned and give the reasons for their deposition. When they were summoned by the council through Daniel, bishop of Colonia Secunda in Cappadocia, Commodus of Tripolis [Col. 0981A] in Lydia, and Timothy of Terma in the Hellespont, together with the notary Musonius and the reader, through the deacon who carried the message, they received this response: “Neither send to us, nor let us come to you, for we are awaiting the emperor’s response concerning you.”

Cyril and Memnon, wishing to take revenge, therefore condemned John and all who had assembled with him, and both parties endured many evils at Ephesus with equal arrogance.

The emperor, through John, count S. L., sent an imperial letter to the entire council and to the place, saying: “We accept the condemnation of Nestorius, Cyril, and Memnon; but we censure the other things that have been done among you, while preserving the Christian faith and the rectitude which we received from our fathers and ancestors.”

But when fourteen bishops departed from the council [Note: The same codex has, “seven and seven bishops”], they satisfied the emperor because the great and universal council, conducting everything according to the rules, had condemned Nestorius. When he learned this, the emperor ordered them to enter the church and ordain another bishop in place of Nestorius.

After this he ordered all the bishops to depart, each to his own region. John and his party therefore went to Antioch, where, gathering many bishops, he again condemned Cyril, who was already in Alexandria.

And, as Socrates says, when Nestorius realized that his party had reached a certain ruin through contention, he called Mary the *God-bearer*, saying: [Col. 0981C] “Let her also be called the *God-bearer*, and let the things that caused grief cease” [Note: The same codex has, “Let her also be called the *Christ-bearer*, and let the things that had caused grief cease.”] But no one received him when he said such things in repentance. Thus he remained condemned and was sent into exile at Oasis.

After his condemnation, the crowd at Constantinople was stirred up violently against the Church, and the people were divided because of his lukewarm, as has been said, teaching; the clergy, however, anathematized him by common decree.

[Note: [Col. 0981C]

**After two days.** Rather, on the fifth day after Nestorius’s deposition, as Socrates relates in Book VII, chapter 33, he who committed to writing events placed before his own eyes.

**The chapters accepted and confirmed.** Yet Cyril’s third letter to Nestorius, together with its chapters, was indeed read; but the Fathers passed no judgment on it. Their judgment concerned only the second letter, as is clear both from the acts of the council [Col. 0981D] and from the Council of Chalcedon and the Fifth Synod. Nor is this surprising, for only the second letter had a response from Nestorius with which it could be compared, so that Cyril’s ὀρθοδοξία (*orthodoxy*) and Nestorius’s ἑτεροδοξία (*heterodoxy*) might be demonstrated.

**Publicly presenting.** The acts of Ephesus contradict this, postponing the publication until the time when the Catholic Easterners struck the schismatics with anathema. Only then was the publication first made, so that the Easterners might show that they had been condemned by those who were absent and whose authority was null.

**Summoned by the council through Daniel.** This was the third summons. The first was carried out by Archelaus of Myndus, Paul of Lampsae, and Peter of Parembolae. The second was carried out by Timothy of Termessus, Eustathius of Docimus, and Eudoxius of Chomatis, bishops. Council of Ephesus, Act 4.

**Wishing to take revenge.** These words suit a defender of the Three Chapters, a copyist of Ibas.

**The emperor ordered them to enter the church.** Either the sentence is mutilated and a word distinguishing the bishops of the Catholic party from the Easterners is missing, or all the bishops mentioned are said, contrary to the truth of the history, to have entered Constantinople in order to ordain a bishop. For, as is clear from the letters of the schismatics themselves to their own party, only those of the Catholic party entered.]

## CHAPTER VII. On the Ordination of Maximian as Bishop of Constantinople

*(From the acts of the Council of Ephesus and Socrates.)*

When matters had proceeded in this way, the question of the election of a bishop arose again [Note: The Codex Tellerianus has, “the question arose”]. Many were seeking the presbyter Philip, who had been ordained deacon by blessed John, surnamed Chrysostom, and who had written many volumes against the apostate emperor Julian. Others were seeking the presbyter Proclus, whom Sisinnius had ordained bishop of Cyzicus. Before he departed for Cyzicus, the citizens of that city had ordained the monk Dalmatian as their bishop, because it seemed that only Atticus, Sisinnius’s predecessor, had been granted this authority. But the nobles of the palace were displeased that it should be done, although it happened afterward. Proclus remained without a church of his own, although he flourished greatly in ecclesiastical teaching at Constantinople [Note: The same codex has, “in the teaching of the Churches”].

When four months had passed since Nestorius’s [Col. 0982C] condemnation, Maximian was ordained bishop. In life he was a monk, but in rank a presbyter; he was steadfast in the true faith, but uneducated in speech [Note: The same codex has, “steadfast in the faith, but uneducated”], and preferred to live quietly.

[Note: [Col. 0982C]

**Because this had been granted to Atticus, his predecessor.** The people of Cyzicus had granted this to Atticus as an arbitrator freely chosen when discord arose among them. Sisinnius, Atticus’s successor, tried to claim it for himself by right of his see. The people of Cyzicus therefore resisted at that time, and rightly so; nevertheless, after the Council of Chalcedon they yielded, overcome by the power of the rulers who favored their new Rome.

**Maximian is ordained bishop.** On October 25, which was a Sunday in the year 431. In the Western Church ordination was performed on Sundays, as can be gathered from canon 49 of the African Church Code; but this custom was not observed so strictly in the East. Chrysostom, for example, is recorded as having been ordained on January 27 in the year 398, when the Sunday letter was C, and therefore January 27 fell on a Wednesday. Nestorius was likewise ordained on a Wednesday in the year 428, when the Sunday letters were AG.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Peace between Cyril and John

*(From the third part of the Council of Ephesus and the Letter of Ibas.)*

After a short while, the emperor saw that the discord between Cyril and John continued and judged their disagreement intolerable. He summoned Maximian, then bishop, and many other bishops who were in Constantinople, and considered how the dissension of the Churches might be removed. They replied that it could happen in no other way than by first going and presenting the bond of one faith, and by John, bishop of Antioch, anathematizing Nestorius and his rejected doctrines.

The emperor rejoiced greatly at this, and the tribune Aristolaus was sent to accomplish the matter. He carried an imperial letter to John and Cyril, in which he threatened both with exile to Nicomedia unless they made peace with one another.

The bishops in Constantinople also wrote Cyril that friendship and peace among the holy Churches could not properly be achieved unless everything that he had written in the matter—in letters, treatises, and books—were annulled. Cyril considered it intolerable to do this.

John of Antioch, however, sent the emperor this message: “Because of those chapters of his, I shall send my confession of faith to Cyril; if he accepts it and signs it, I shall communicate with him. Otherwise, I shall not be able to be at peace with him.”

John again assembled a council at Antioch and composed a confession of faith as follows: «We confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and a body: before the ages, begotten from the Father according to divinity; but in the last days, the same one, for us and for our salvation, from the Virgin Mary according to humanity; and [Col. 0983C] consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us according to humanity. For a union of two natures has taken place, and therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, and one Lord.

«According to this understanding of an unconfused union [Note: The Codex Tellerianus has, “of an unconfused union”], we confess the holy Virgin as the *God-bearer*. For this reason the Word of God became incarnate and was made man, and from the very conception united to himself the temple which he received from her. We know that the evangelical and apostolic statements about the Lord, spoken by men who proclaimed divine things, sometimes join matters together as belonging to one person and sometimes distinguish them as belonging to two natures, handing down the more divine and exalted statements according to Christ’s divinity, and the humbler ones according to his humanity.»

[Col. 0983D] John therefore inserted this rule of faith in this form into his letter, which begins, “Some time ago, through the decree of the most pious rulers,” and so forth. He delivered it to Paul, bishop of Emesa, and sent it to Cyril at Alexandria.

When Paul came to that city, Cyril received him most graciously. Without difficulty or dispute, as many thought, he accepted the aforementioned faith of the Eastern bishops [Note: The same codex has, “the inviolate faith”]. Then, on a Sunday, Paul delivered a sermon to the people in Cyril’s presence and [Col. 0984A] expounded the passage from John’s Gospel: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). «Observe,» he said, «John proclaiming two natures and one Son. For the dwelling-place is one thing, and God who dwells is another. Pay attention, I ask, to what has been said. He did not say “one and another,” as though there were two persons, or two Christs, or two sons, but “one thing and another,” as in two natures. Therefore, when he said, “And he dwelt among us,” and proclaimed two natures, he then added, “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”»

In what followed, he expounded the faith that he had brought to Cyril, openly proclaiming two natures in the Lord Christ, in one person.

And when the people cried out, “You have come well, orthodox one,” [Col. 0984B] Cyril immediately discussed similar matters and said, among other things:

“What could be said more clearly about these things? [Note: [Col. 0984D] Codex Tellerianus reads, ‘What of these things [is] clearer?’] What need have they of explanation? He has aptly taught us that the one who dwells is one thing, and the one who is indwelt is another; human nature is one thing, divine nature another.”

And, concluding his sermon in confirmation of what Paul had said, he declared:

“Behold John proclaiming two natures and one Christ: two natures of the Only-Begotten, and one person. And when he said, ‘And he dwelt among us,’ he proclaimed two natures; then he added this: ‘And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.’”

Cyril discussed these matters in Paul’s presence and taught the Alexandrian church to believe concerning Christ just as it had learned when Paul had earlier expounded the matter.

[Col. 0984C] After this Cyril inserted into his own letter the confession that he had received from Paul. Its beginning is: “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult,” etc. In order to satisfy certain reports that had been circulated about him—that he did not maintain that Christ had taken a body from heaven, nor that he understood his natures as fermentation or mixture—he wrote and subscribed the aforesaid confession and sent it to the Eastern bishops.

Paul, therefore, going up to Antioch, presented Cyril’s letter to Archbishop John and to his entire council. When they learned that Paul had accepted the faith sent by them and had subscribed to its confirmation, they made peace with him and his council, condemning Nestorius and receiving Maximian, who had been made bishop in his place. Some of the bishops among them, however, still hesitated [Col. 0984D] to enter into communion with Cyril, thinking that he had erred and later recognized the truth, and blaming John [Note: The same codex reads, “and blaming John”] for having sought from him the condemnation of his Chapters.

On the other hand, certain members of the imperial court, through Eulogius, presbyter and apocrisiarius of the Alexandrian Church, blamed Cyril for having accepted from the Eastern bishops the confession of two natures, which Nestorius had stated and taught.

Valerian, bishop of Iconium, and Acacius, bishop of Melitene, likewise held this view concerning Cyril.

[Note: [Col. 0985A]

A little later.] After approximately six months had elapsed. For in the preface to the second part of the works of M. Mercator we have shown that the emperor’s mandate—which in the printed books lacks a date—was issued at Constantinople at the beginning of April.

And then summoning Maximian to himself.] We have discussed fully this entire consultation of the bishops at the imperial palace in Dissertation 2 on the same part of M. Mercator’s works.

Unless one first went.] These words are obscure, unless perhaps they mean that someone was to be sent by the emperor to both disputing bishops, either to deliver to them the bond of one faith or, in the emperor’s name, to order that a bond of one faith be established by the common agreement of both bishops.

But they wrote from Constantinople.] Cyril protests this in his letter to Acacius of Melitene; for he reports that the writing came from Acacius of Beroea, where the Easterners’ council was being held. See the dissertation cited immediately above.

But John of Antioch.] The fragment of a certainly much longer letter written by John to the emperor deserves careful attention [Col. 0985B]. In it Cyril’s Chapters were accused of heresy. Theodoret mentions this letter in his second letter to Himerius of Nicomedia, preserved by M. Mercator.

We confess.] The detailed discussion of this confession—which even the Catholics themselves regarded with suspicion, and which Theodoret certainly asserted to be Nestorian—you will find in Dissertation 2 cited immediately above.

Without difficulty or contention.] This conflicts with the truth at this point. For from the time the Emesene arrived in Alexandria, four months and more were spent in negotiating the matter of peace, with the Emesene employing every device by which he might appear to have drawn Cyril toward repentance. It is unnecessary, in order to avoid this conclusion, to invent the explanation accepted by some that the Emesene made two journeys to Alexandria, as though, because his business had been interrupted, he had needed to return once to Antioch and then bring back from there an amended confession of faith. Those who thought this were deceived through their failure to consider an ambiguous expression in John’s letter to Cyril. For when John said that he had already returned with concord and peace, they interpreted this as referring to the Emesene, of whom the discussion had been held, as though he had returned with peace. *Apology 3 for Jansenius of Ypres.*

On the Lord’s Day.] Everything here is confused and obscure. He mentions only one homily delivered by Paul, although Paul actually addressed the people twice in the Alexandrian church, with Cyril presiding: once on the twenty-ninth day of the Egyptian month Choiak, and again on the sixth day of the month Tybi. In the first speech he did not explain John’s saying, “The Word became flesh,” whereas he devoted a large part of the other speech to its explanation. What is reported as having been said by Paul and accepted by Cyril belong to the second speech. Accordingly, the printed editions of the councils should be corrected, since they append to the second homily what Cyril added to the first. Both sermons, moreover, were delivered on a Sunday. The year 432 had the Sunday letter CB, while the following year, 433, had the letter A. Thus, in that year, the twenty-fifth of December—which was the twenty-ninth of Choiak—fell on a Sunday, and thus the first homily was delivered that year.

Some of them still hesitating.] This refers to Theodoret, as we demonstrated from Cyril’s letter to Acacius of Melitene in the second part of M. Mercator’s works.

The confession of two natures.] The popular opinion, or rather error, had gained such strength, with the men of the Nestorian faction supporting it, that anyone who confessed two natures was regarded as a Nestorian, while anyone who confessed one was regarded as a Cyrillian. Cyril himself clearly teaches this in his memorandum to Eulogius, discussed below.

## CHAPTER IX

### On Cyril’s Letters Written on Behalf of the Easterners

*(From the same third part of the Council of Ephesus.)*

Cyril therefore wrote to them in defense of the Eastern bishops and in support of the two natures of the one Christ. I do not think it superfluous to insert into this work some passages from those letters, for the refutation of the Alexandrian Phantasiasts or Corrupticolae, who boast of Cyril as though he were their father and author.

Cyril therefore admonishes his presbyter Eulogius and says:

“Some criticize the exposition made by the Easterners and say: ‘Why did the Alexandrian bishop permit them to speak of two natures, or even praise them for doing so?’ [Col. 0986B] Others say that Nestorius said the same thing, and they secretly insinuate this subtlety among the ignorant [Note: [Col. 0985D] Codex Tellerianus reads, ‘slipping it in unawares’].

“For we must teach those who blame us that we ought not to flee from or reject everything that heretics say. They confess many things just as we do. For example, when the Arians say that the Father is the Creator and Lord of all [Note: The same codex reads, ‘because he is the Creator’], is it therefore appropriate to flee from such confessions? So also with Nestorius: although he asserts two natures, signifying the distinction between flesh and the Word—for one nature belongs to the Word and the other to the flesh—nevertheless he does not confess unity with us. We, however, by uniting these things, confess one Christ, one Son, the same one God” (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 37).

[Col. 0986C] And again:

“Thus, in his expositions Nestorius pretends to say, ‘One Son, one Lord,’ but he refers sonship to the Word of God alone. When, however, he comes to the dispensation, he again speaks of another Lord, who is from a woman, a man by himself, joined by an equal honor of dignity because he has a conjunction with Christ. How is it not obvious that he speaks of two Christs, if Christ has conjunction with Christ—one with another?

“But those who are from the East say nothing of this kind [Note: The same codex reads, ‘have learned nothing of this kind’]. They merely divide the expressions. They divide them in this manner: they say that some expressions are ‘sayable of God’ [*Deo decibiles*; Note: [Col. 0986D] Codex Tellerianus reads, ‘sayable of God’], others human, and others common, as though they simultaneously possessed what is proper to Christ as God and what is human; [Col. 0986D] yet they say that both kinds of expression were spoken by one and the same Christ. They do not, like Nestorius, attribute some expressions separately to the Word of God and others to him who is from a woman, as though to another Son.”

Writing also to Acacius, bishop of Melitene, he says among other things:

“For Nestorius says that Christ is named separately as the Word of God, but that he has a continuous conjunction with Christ. Do you suppose that he is not most openly speaking of two Christs? The Easterners, however, confess that they worship one Christ, Son, God, and Lord [Col. 0987A], the same one from the Father according to divinity and the same one from the holy Virgin according to humanity. For they say that a union of two natures has taken place; nevertheless, they openly confess one Christ, one Son, and one Lord” (ibid., chapter 34).

And in what follows Cyril agrees to some extent with Pope Leo’s Tome and says:

“There are some expressions that are especially sayable of God, while others are suitable to a man; still others possess a certain order, showing the Son to be God and man simultaneously.”

And in the same place:

“When he says to Philip, ‘I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Whoever sees me sees the Father also’ (John 14:9), and, ‘I and [Col. 0987B] the Father are one’ (John 10:30), we affirm these as expressions most befitting God. But when he rebukes the Jewish people, saying, ‘If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which Abraham did not do’ (John 8:39), we say that these words were fittingly spoken of a man.”

The continuation of this letter contains a plausible exposition of the two natures. For the sake of brevity in this work, however, we have omitted the necessary evidence in full.

To Valerian of Iconium he replied as follows:

“All the Eastern bishops, together with my most religious lord John, bishop of the Antiochenes, have clearly established in a written and manifest declaration for all that they condemn and anathematize with us the polluted innovations of Nestorius [Col. 0987C]. They never deem them worthy of speech, but follow the evangelical and apostolic doctrines and in no way dishonor the confession of the Fathers. For they too have confessed with us that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God, and they did not add that she is the Mother of Christ, as those say who defend the wretched and rejectable notions of Nestorius. Rather, they openly say that there is one Christ, Son, and God from God: the Word of God, ineffably begotten from the Father before all ages; and, in the last times, this same one also from a woman according to the flesh, so that the very same one is simultaneously God and man, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity. The very same one is one person, in no way divided into two sons, or Christs, or lords.

[Col. 0987D] “Therefore, if some liars say that these men hold some other opinion, let no one believe them; but, as impostors and deceivers, following their father the devil, let them be cast out, lest they disturb those who desire to walk rightly.

“But if some also circulate letters composed for one another, as though written in the name of distinguished men, one ought by no means presume upon such documents. For those who once confessed the faith in writing—how could they write another letter, as though recalled by repentance, so as no longer to wish to hold the right opinion? Greet the brotherhood that is with you. Those who are with us in the Lord greet you” (ibid., chapter 40).

[Col. 0988A] From this conclusion of his letter, in which Cyril says, “But if some also circulate letters composed for one another,” etc., Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, proves in the disputation he undertook against the Acephali, at the command of the emperor Justinian and through the agency of Strategius, count of the sacred largesses, in the palace place called the Heptaconchus, that Cyril referred to a letter written to Maris the Persian. Cyril neither judged that this letter ought to be condemned nor identified it in the letter itself as Nestorian.

These, then, are the things Cyril wrote in defense of the Eastern bishops in support of the two natures of the one Christ. I believe that those who at that time did not accept them were the founders of the Acephali, who neither acknowledge Cyril as their head nor show whom they follow.

[Col. 0988B] At that time Evoptius, bishop of Ptolemais in the region of Pentapolis, received a copy of the letters of Theodoret, who had written against Cyril’s Twelve Chapters, and sent it to Cyril so that he might answer it and explain his own Chapters.

Cyril received this most gladly and composed an exposition [Note: Codex Tellerianus reads, “composed an explanation”] of his twelve Chapters, adding explanations by which he seemed to provide a full account of them.

Thus, when Cyril accepted and defended the faith of the Eastern bishops and explained his own Chapters, peace and unity were restored to the churches. While the Church rejoiced in this peace, the enemy of peace and rival of unity did not cease to stir up his weapons against her and to sow [Col. 0988C] tares.

[Note: [Col. 0988C]

On Cyril’s letters.] The defender of the Three Chapters deliberately inserted this entire chapter, although it was not particularly necessary—at least not in such a lengthy form, so richly filled with carefully selected testimonies from Cyril—in order to conclude from Cyril himself, first, that the doctrine of two natures is Catholic; second, that Cyril retracted his former position concerning the one incarnate nature of the Word after the union; and finally, that Theodorus and Theodoret, and also Ibas, were free from wrongdoing, since, as it seemed to him, neither Theodoret nor Ibas had attacked Cyril except when he was following his former error, and Theodorus had taught nothing against the Apollinarians other than the two natures of Christ.

The Alexandrian Phantasiasts and Corrupticolae.] The former originated with Gaianus and the latter with Theodosius in Alexandria around the year 537. The Phantasiasts were also called Aphthartodocetae and Schematics. For while they made Christ’s body incorruptible, they asserted that it was like ours only in form and appearance, but in reality unlike it [Col. 0988D]. Concerning them, see Anastasius the Sinaite in the *Hodegos* (*Guide*) and Photius, codex 162. Each faction falsely claimed Cyril as its parent, by the same fraud with which Eutyches and the other defenders of one nature acted.

They confess unity with us.] Namely, the unity *καθ’ ὑπόστασιν* [“according to hypostasis”], whose confession we have shown in Dissertation 1 of the second part of M. Mercator’s works to have been the only indisputable rule of faith in this controversy. For whatever else one might say could be twisted by obstinate men into a heterodox meaning.

Thus Nestorius in his expositions.] The words of Nestorius cited here are taken from Sermon 2, which should be consulted in the second part of M. Mercator’s works. Cyril cites these same words in his letter to Acacius of Melitene.

[Col. 0989A] If therefore some liars.] He attacks Theodoret without naming him. Theodoret had boasted that the faith of the Easterners was the same as that of Nestorius, and that neither differed from the faith of the Fathers. Thus, when Cyril agreed with the Easterners, he claimed that Cyril had gone over to the side of Nestorius. See Cyril’s letter to Acacius of Melitene and Theodoret’s letter to Andrew, a Constantinopolitan monk, in which these words occur:

“For behold, those who had confused the natures of Christ the Savior by impious reasoning, and had dared to proclaim one nature and to add sufferings to the divinity, therefore also insulted the most holy and venerable high priest of the Most High God, Nestorius. But, with their jaws completely shattered, as though by a bit and bridle, according to the Prophet, and having been led from crooked things to straight, they have again learned the truth, using the assertion of him who suffered battles for the truth. For instead of one nature they now confess two, anathematizing those who proclaim mixture or confusion. They venerate the divinity of Christ as impassible and explain that the sufferings belong to the flesh. They divide the evangelical expressions, assigning lofty and sayable-of-God expressions to the divinity [Col. 0989B] and humble ones to the humanity. For such things have now been brought in writings from Egypt.”

But if some also circulate letters.] Cyril means forged letters attributed to John of Antioch, to Philip, a presbyter of the Roman Church, and also to himself, as though he had revoked his former position.

Hypatius proves.] Hypatius was undoubtedly mistaken. Cyril could not have been speaking of Ibas’s letter to Maris, but of some other letter that he was said to have written before he actually wrote to Valerian. Yet Cyril wrote to Valerian in the year 433, at which time Ibas was neither a distinguished man nor anyone of note, but an obscure presbyter. Nor had he actually written to Maris, since in the letter to him he mentions the disturbances that arose on account of Diodorus after the year 435, when the emperor Theodosius issued the decree concerning the burning of Nestorius’s books. It was then that the great controversy concerning Diodorus first arose, when the faction in question substituted his books for those of the Nestorians [Col. 0989C]. But more on this matter in the dissertation.

In the disputation.] It was held at Constantinople in the year 533, by order of the emperor Justinian, in the palace triclinium called the Heptaconchus. Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, disputed with four other Catholics against Sergius, bishop of Cyrus, and five other Severians. Strategius, master of the offices, served as examiner. The acts are found in volume IV of the final collection of the general councils.

Founders of the Acephali.] This should not be passed over without comment, for it makes Theodoret the leader of a faction of men called Acephali because, since they did not accept Cyril’s defense of the Easterners, they had neither Cyril as their head nor John of Antioch, although those two were the leaders of the opposing parties. Perhaps the name Acephali was first heard at that time. Afterward, when it became attached to certain defenders of the two natures, it passed to the Monophysites [Col. 0989D] and was applied to them. Observe that in the Arabic Chronicle of Eutychius the Acephali are called Jacobites, and the orthodox are called Melchites.

Then Evoptius of Ptolemais, etc.] There is at least a chronological error of two years here. Cyril answered Theodoret before the Council of Ephesus, as we demonstrated in Book II of Part 2 of M. Mercator’s works.

## CHAPTER X

### On the Nestorian Scandal and the Monks of Armenia

*(From the letters of Saint Cyril and the acts of the Fourth and Fifth Synods.)*

For when the followers of Nestorius saw that his blasphemous books could not be publicly produced because [Col. 0990A] they had been condemned by the Council of Ephesus, which had anathematized them [Note: Codex Tellerianus reads, “because they had been condemned”], and because imperial law had forbidden anyone to read or defend them, they began circulating the works of Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, and Theodorus, bishop of Mopsuestia, as well as those of other bishops who had composed books against Eunomius and Apollinaris, defenders of one nature. These works demonstrated two natures in Christ in one person—something Nestorius had not said in this way—and, wishing to deceive the simplest people, they claimed that Nestorius had taught nothing new but had followed the doctrine of the ancient Fathers. They devoted such zeal to this cause that they maliciously translated these very works into the language of the Syrians, Armenians, and Persians.

But when Acacius of Melitene and Rabula, bishop of the city of Edessa, learned of this—concerning Rabula, his successor Ibas says in his letter, “He who presumes upon everything dared openly to anathematize him in his own church” (speaking above of Theodorus of Mopsuestia)—they wrote to the bishops of Armenia, warning them not to receive the books of Theodorus of Mopsuestia, as belonging to a heretic and the author of the Nestorian doctrine. The bishops of Cilicia accused Rabula and Acacius of having done this not out of charity but out of rivalry and contentiousness.

The venerable bishops of Armenia therefore assembled together and sent two presbyters, Leontius and Aberius, to Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, according to custom, with their petitions and one volume of Theodorus of Mopsuestia. They wished to know whether the doctrine of Theodorus or that of Rabula and Acacius was proved to be true.

Proclus, therefore, after receiving the petitions of the Armenian bishops and the volume of Theodorus, carefully examined both and wrote and sent to the Armenians a Tome. In it, to destroy the tricks of the Nestorians, who introduce two persons in Christ, he placed the expression, “one of the Trinity incarnate.” He also sent it to John of Antioch through his deacon Theodorus. The Tome contained below it the Chapters put forward by the heretics. Proclus asked John, for the sake of preserving the common faith, to receive and subscribe it together with his council.

John and the bishops assembled with him read the Tome, praised its composition, subscribed it, and sent it back to Proclus.

[Col. 0990D] The Council of Chalcedon likewise, in its report sent to the emperor Marcian, received and confirmed this Tome among the letters of the holy Fathers, as evidence that the faith was established not only by the synodal acts but also by the letters.

The same Proclus wrote a letter to John, to whom he had sent his Tome, in which he says:

“While declaring God passible again—that is, Christ—we confess that he did not suffer in what he is, but in what was made, that is, in his own flesh. In proclaiming this we are in no way deceived, since we confess that one of the Trinity was crucified according to the flesh, and we by no means blaspheme by calling the divinity passible [Col. 0991A]” (Facundus, Book I, chapter 1, from which the passage has been corrected).

But a certain deacon named Basil, taking the Tome that Proclus had written to the Armenians, came to Alexandria. He attached the petitions of the Armenians to his own petitions and presented them to Cyril, bishop of that city.

Moved by these reports, as the rumors relate [Note: Codex Tellerianus reads, “Moved by these rumors, as they relate”], Cyril wrote four books: three against Diodorus and Theodorus, as authors of the Nestorian doctrine, and another book on the Incarnation. These books contain uncorrupted testimonies of the ancient Fathers, namely Pope Felix of Rome, Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, and Gregory surnamed *Thaumaturgus*, “Wonderworker.” Although Theodorus’s statements published against the Arians are praised in these books, they nevertheless maintain that he was the teacher of Nestorius.

[Col. 0991B] Against them the defenders of Catholic truth [Note: The same codex reads, “the defenders of the Catholic faith”] answered the Acephali as follows:

“Those books are not Cyril’s, since he did not use against Nestorius, who was alive, the testimonies that he is said to have set down in them against the dead—neither at the synod nor in any letters.” Hence they say that “Cyril neither dictated those books nor published them.”

Thus, when the deacon Basil came to Constantinople, he composed petitions and presented them to Archbishop Proclus, attaching all the documents that he had previously presented to Archbishop Cyril. But Proclus had already sent his Tome to the Armenians, and in that Tome he made no mention of any condemnation of Theodorus.

When Basil learned this, he wrote a petition in which he taught [Note: Codex Tellerianus reads, “he wrote a petition and taught in his work”] that the books of Theodorus should be avoided like the blasphemies of Arius and Eunomius [Col. 0991C]. To prudent people, however, it appears that he wrote this inappropriately, since Arius and Eunomius proclaimed in Christ one substance alien to that of the Father. Theodorus, on the contrary, as his accusers claim, taught two natures in Christ.

After this, taking the opportunity, certain monks from Armenia, followers of Apollinaris—two or three, as John of Antioch reports in his letter—arose. They carried excerpts of Chapters, as they claimed, from the books of Theodorus of Mopsuestia or of other holy Fathers who at that time, as we said, had written against Apollinaris. Entering the imperial city and defiling the hearing of many, they threw everything into confusion by their cunning. Then, traveling through the cities of the entire East and all the monasteries, they loudly proclaimed that the works, together with their authors, ought to be condemned, accusing them of having been written in a Nestorian sense.

“For if Nestorius was justly condemned,” they said, “let these works also be condemned together with their authors.”

They did this in an effort to strengthen the doctrines of Apollinaris, who, by means of one nature, did not explain Christ as consubstantial with us. With the support of certain persons, they terrified by threats the clergy, people, and monks who were pursuing a peaceful life.

John of Antioch then convened a synod and dictated three letters on behalf of Theodorus of Mopsuestia [Col. 0992A]. He sent one to the emperor Theodosius, another to Cyril of Alexandria, and a third to Proclus, bishop of Constantinople. In them he praised Theodorus and explained his wisdom.

In response, the emperor sent a sacred letter to John and judged that those detractors of Theodorus were acting against their own salvation.

Cyril, however, in his reply, favoring Theodorus, issued this judgment concerning his accusers: they were held by a doctrine contrary to the truth. He also inserted a passage from the creed presented to him at the council because of the Tesseracaedecatites by the presbyter Charisius.

Nevertheless, Proclus, writing to John through his deacon Maximus, asked whose the Chapters said to belong to Theodorus actually were. John, in order to excuse him, replied that he did not know. Yet the Council of Chalcedon, in its report sent to the emperor Marcian, received and confirmed two letters of the aforementioned John—the first and the third, containing praises of Theodorus of Mopsuestia—together with Proclus’s Tome, which he sent to the Armenians, and the other letters of the holy Fathers.

When these matters had been quieted and settled, Cyril died in the thirty-second year of his episcopate. Dioscorus was ordained bishop of Alexandria. He had been the archdeacon of that same Cyril, who had neither wife nor children. Common opinion says that he had a greater affection for his fellow citizens, since, after oppressing Cyril’s heirs and extracting money from them through many calumnies, he gave it without interest to the bread sellers [Col. 0992C] [Note: The same codex reads, “he gave it to the bread sellers”] and wine merchants of the city, so that they might provide the people with the purest bread and the finest wine at a cheaper price.

After Archbishop John’s death, Domnus was ordained archbishop of the Church of Antioch. After Proclus’s death, Flavian obtained the see of the Church of Constantinople.

At that same time, certain presbyters and deacons accused Ibas, bishop of Edessa, before Domnus the archbishop in petitions of their own, as a Nestorian, because, addressing the clergy, he had said: “I do not envy Christ because he was made God, for if I wish, I too become one.” When they had gone up to Antioch, Ibas excommunicated them. But when the feast of the Ascension, on the fortieth day, arrived, Domnus ordered that they be released from excommunication [Col. 0992D], on the condition that they not leave Antioch; otherwise they were to be deposed from their order.

Some of them, however, disregarding the commands of Archbishop Domnus, went to the imperial court and obtained sacred letters for bishops Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, so that they might be heard at Berytus. With them were Eulogius, a Constantinopolitan deacon, and Damascius, a man of rank, tribune and notary. When it became known that those clerics had gone to Constantinople, they were condemned by Domnus and his council.

After this Ibas appeared at Berytus for the hearing [Col. 0993A]. When the accusers, as the proceedings show, had been unable to prove anything against him, a report and petition arrived from the clergy of Edessa, demanding the presence of their bishop on behalf of the Church. In it they took upon themselves all the penalties of the dreadful Gehenna if they remembered that anything of this kind had been said in the discussion for which Ibas was accused and had not made it known to the judges. Therefore the judges had the accusers themselves communicate with their bishop in the secretariat, and then dismissed them in peace.

[Note: [Col. 0993A]

Tenth chapter.] This is divided into three parts. It deals with the case of Diodorus and Theodorus, the death of three patriarchs, and the judgment concerning Ibas of Edessa. The first and the last parts are treated much better by Facundus.

First observe that everything narrated in this chapter concerning the books of Diodorus and Theodorus occurred in the interval between the emperor’s decree [Col. 0993B] concerning the burning of Nestorius’s books and the death of John of Antioch. The former was issued in the year 435, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the third indiction; the latter occurred in the year 441. Next, this history is exceedingly entangled because of the disturbed chronological order, which must be restored from the exchange of letters among Cyril, John, and Proclus. Finally, Baronius warns the reader not to allow himself to be deceived by Liberatus, who reports matters he had received from some Nestorian; more on that warning below.

Imperial law.] It was enacted under the consulship of Theodosius XV and the man who had been designated consul, on the third day before the Nones of August—that is, in the year 435. It is found in the final collection of the Councils, in the third part of the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, and in the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*, law 66.

Then they began circulating the works of Diodorus.] There is considerable suspicion that the entire affair was carried out either through Theodoret’s efforts or at least with his advice. We give the reasons for this suspicion in the dissertation on Theodoret’s faith. For the present, let this one point suffice: Cyril writes to Acacius of Melitene [Col. 0993C] and to Valerian of Iconium that Theodoret, when he disapproved of the peace established between the churches, boasted that the faith of the Easterners was the same as Nestorius’s faith, and that neither differed from the faith of the Fathers.

And of the other bishops.] Athanasius, both Gregories, Basil, Amphilochius, and Theophilus, as can be gathered both from Cyril’s second letter to Acacius of Melitene and from John’s synodical letter to Cyril and Cyril’s reply to John, in the third part of the Council of Ephesus.

Their very volumes.] Just as Ibas translated these works into Syriac, so Eulalius, Theodoret’s friend, translated them into Armenian, and Maris into Persian. (Proclus, in his letter to John of Antioch and in the Fifth Synod, Collation 6.) Even now the works of Diodorus and Theodorus are found among the Syrians, as we learn from the catalogue of books written in the Syriac language, which Habediesu compiled under Julius III and which Abraham Echellensis published at Rome in 1653.

Acacius and Rabula.] The identity and importance of that Acacius of Melitene are clear from the acts of the Council of Ephesus. Concerning Rabula, Theodorus the lector tells something remarkable in his collected works:

“Rabula,” he says, “the bishop of Edessa, was blind, and Andrew of Samosata accused him, as though he had written against Theodoret’s Twelve Chapters.”

These matters are explained in our dissertations on Theodoret. If they are read as they should be, they contain much material useful for history that escaped Valesius, otherwise a diligent editor of Theodoret.

In his letter.] It is inserted both in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, Session 10, and in the Fifth Synod, Collation 6. It is also found in Facundus, Book VI, chapter 3, everywhere without a preface and everywhere in a different version.

The bishops of Cilicia.] They were friends of Theodoret and disciples of Theodorus, who had died eight years earlier. Theodoret’s eighty-fourth letter is addressed to them.

Out of rivalry.] It is clear from the history of the period that Rabula opposed Ibas, and Acacius opposed Theodoret, both for the sake of the common faith and for private reasons [Col. 0994A]. The Church of Edessa had been divided into the parties of Rabula and Ibas, and at Chalcedon Theodoret had attacked Acacius with extraordinary vehemence, since Acacius represented the schismatic synod while Theodoret represented the Catholic one.

The venerable bishops of Armenia therefore assembled together.] Baronius supposes that a notable council was convened in Armenia. At it, “after the Catholic faith had been established, and after the writings of Theodorus of Mopsuestia had been examined and found impious and contrary to the path of the orthodox faith, they sent an embassy from the synod to Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, so that they might not appear to have condemned him alone, but rather the entire Eastern Church,” and so forth.

But I do not see how this agrees with Liberatus’s words:

“They sent two presbyters, Leontius and Aberius, to Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, according to custom, with their petitions and one volume of Theodorus of Mopsuestia, wishing to know whether the doctrine of Theodorus or that of Rabula and Acacius was proved to be true.”

[Col. 0994B] For if the Armenians had condemned Theodorus after a careful examination of the case, why were they inquiring which faith was superior, that of Theodorus or that of Acacius? If they wished their judgment to be approved by the entire Eastern Church, why did they send an embassy neither to the bishop of Antioch nor to the bishop of Alexandria, nor to the other autocephalous primates?

### “According to custom.”

Which custom? That of sending two presbyters, and not one together with a deacon? Or that of referring to the bishop of Constantinople matters conducted in a council concerning the definition of faith? Or that of questioning the bishop of the principal see about the faith? For it was customary, when a matter was referred from a lesser synod to the bishop of the diocese, to delegate two presbyters; it was also customary to refer matters of greater importance to that same bishop. Moreover, in the Eastern Church it was customary not to ratify any definition in matters of faith in provincial synods, but to consult the bishop of the entire diocese; for this matter was considered one of the greater matters, which therefore belonged to the greater [Col. 0994C] see.

### “The volume of Theodore.”

The volume contained no complete work, but only certain excerpts, as is clear both from what follows—“containing below the chapters produced by the heretics”—and from the refutation made by Cyril, whose fragments are found in the Fifth Synod.

### “He wrote a tome to the Armenians.”

In the commonly circulated editions, it is read that it was sent during the consulship of the most pious emperors Theodosius XV and Valentinian IV. This chronological notice may reasonably appear suspicious, not only because a date is scarcely ever appended to the letters of bishops, except those of the supreme pontiffs, but much more because between the imperial decree issued in August of the year 435 and the sending of the tome by Proclus to the Armenians there occurred events that could scarcely, or barely at all, be compressed into the intervening period, even if the tome is said to have been sent toward the end of December.

First, after the decree had been put into execution and the books of Nestorius had been wrested from everyone’s hands, excerpts [Col. 0994D] were taken from the books of Diodore, Theodore, and others, which would publicly repair the loss suffered by the Nestorians. These were then translated into Armenian, Syriac, and Persian. Later, when Acacius and Rabula learned that these materials had been sent to the Armenians, they warned them to beware of an error concealing itself beneath great names. Then the Cilician bishops accused Acacius and Rabula before the Armenians for this reason. Finally, the Armenians were summoned by a formal notice from their primate to a council; they assembled at the proper time and sent from there two presbyters to Proclus with petitions and Theodore’s volume. Proclus then examined both the petitions and the volume with great care and wrote a tome in which scarcely anything could have been more thoroughly treated concerning the matter.

For these and many other reasons, one might suppose either that the chronological notice should be removed altogether as spurious, or that it should be corrected to read “given after the consulship of the most pious [emperors],” and so forth. For it is not unheard of for acts to be dated after the consulship of illustrious consuls, especially when they were emperors. Thus the acts of Ephesus are headed: “After the consulship of our lords, ever august, Flavius Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III,” although the names of Bassus and Antiochus, who held the ordinary magistracy, were everywhere known, as is clear from the letters of Pope Celestine and from several laws of the Theodosian Code.

### “One of the Trinity incarnate.”

If these words do not allude to a certain futile subtlety of the ancients, by which they denied that one could say “one of the Trinity,” and held that no substantive noun could safely be joined to that numeral adjective *one*—for they reasoned as follows: if one says “one of the Trinity” and adds “God,” tritheism is introduced; if “Father,” many fathers; if “Son,” several sons, and so forth, since *one* is the beginning of number and one can never say “one God” except with a continuation, while one may go on to say “a second God,” etc.—if, I say, these words do not allude to what we have just described, there is undoubtedly an error, with *incarnate* written in place of *suffered* or *crucified*. For Nestorius himself never denied either that the Word was [Col. 0995B] one of the three divine persons or that he was incarnate. Nor was the question ever debated whether one of the three persons was incarnate, but whether one of the Trinity had suffered and been crucified, as is gathered from Liberatus’s words about Proclus that follow.

### “Through the deacon Theodore.”

And likewise through the deacon Maximus, as is understood from the correspondence exchanged between Proclus and John.

### “Composition.”

The synodical words are these: “What gave us pleasure was not merely the beauty of the composition, nor the multitude of arguments discussed against both opposing parties, but the care and piety with which the sacred doctrines themselves had been handled.”

### “Faith is established not only by the acts but also by letters.”

That is, faith is established not only by the canons themselves, which had been inserted into the acts, but also by letters issued from the synod by the bishops of the principal sees. Proclus sent his own tome to the Armenians from his synod. They were striving to establish this point so that they might assert the decretal force of Leo’s letter to Flavian by the example of Proclus’s letter, in which they perhaps favored the bishop of New Rome more than was proper, as though he possessed authority to define matters equal to that of the pontiff of Old Rome.

### “Not to have suffered in what he is.”

Observe the ingenuity of the man who is defending three chapters. He carefully notices the words that favor Theodore and Theodoret: he had observed that Proclus had previously said that one of the Trinity had become incarnate, but now said that Christ had not suffered in what he is, but in what he had become.

### “But the deacon Basil.”

Who this man was, and to which Church he belonged, is difficult to know. What he had in mind, and that he was a forerunner of the turbulent monks, is clear from what follows. He attempted to have Theodore condemned by name, just as Arius and Eunomius had been, not because Theodore had uttered the same blasphemies—for Liberatus misunderstood this—but because they were equals in a different matter. This deacon was indignant that excerpts from an author whose name was suppressed had been condemned by Proclus, whereas Arius and Eunomius had been expressly named by him.

### “As rumor has it.”

He agrees with his fellow countryman Facundus, in Book III, chapter 3, and elsewhere throughout, who denies or doubts that those books were written by Cyril. Yet that entire body of people—whether Asians or Africans—who deny this does not possess enough authority to deprive a general council, and Cyril himself, who recognized the work, of credibility. It was in the interest of those who defended the three chapters to remove from themselves the odium of defending Theodore, whom Cyril had condemned.

### “Cyril wrote four books.”

Of these four books, three, directed against Diodore and Theodore, have for the most part perished. The fourth, concerning the Incarnation, is contained in volume IV, part I, of Cyril’s works in the edition of G. L. It is composed in the form of a dialogue and with such learning that scarcely any other work of Cyril on this subject is superior to it, or even equal.

### “In which are contained.”

No testimonies of any Father are cited in the book *On the Incarnation*. Whether any were cited in the others, no one can know with certainty, since nothing of them except fragments has come down to us. It is nevertheless remarkable that the Constantinopolitan compilers rejected the first three books because they praised Fathers whom Cyril had not praised in his other works against Nestorius or at the Council of Ephesus itself.

Of the three Fathers who are cited, one was Felix, whose testimony was brought forward in the first session of the Council of Ephesus. Then, in the first book *On the Right Faith to the Queens*, commonly attributed to Cyril, the testimony of Antiochus, Chrysostom, Vitalis, Ammon, and Severian is employed, although none of them is mentioned at the Council of Ephesus. Finally, there may have been some reason for calling upon Dionysius and the Thaumaturge—for example, if they had been praised by the defenders of Diodore and Theodore. For it is clear from Liberatus himself, and indeed from the better witness Cyril, that many Fathers were praised.

### “Of Felix.”

Although Cyril calls him as a witness, it is not nevertheless certain that the letter from which the passage is taken is genuine. Leontius reports that it was fabricated by the Apollinarists.

### “Of Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians.”

The word *Areopagite* had been added in the published manuscripts, but it had to be removed, on the testimony of Dionysius of Corinth himself. In Eusebius, in his letter to the Athenians, Dionysius of Corinth mentions that he was older in age than Dionysius the Areopagite, the first bishop of the Athenians.

I would not wish to draw anyone into that tangled dispute concerning the various Dionysiuses. I am content to venerate Dionysius the martyr, the father of my faith; wherever he may ultimately have come to Paris, he was certainly sent by God to consecrate the capital of the Gallic empire. As for the renown of Dionysius of Corinth, who flourished around the year 175, and what he wrote for the edification of the Churches, consult Eusebius in the passage just cited.

### “Of the wondrous Gregory.”

From what book were the twelve chapters of anathemas attributed to the Thaumaturge taken? Henry Canisius published them in Latin and Greek in Book III of *Antiquae Lectiones*. From this, some may suppose that Cyril derived a testimony against Diodore and Theodore for dividing Christ, for four of the chapters plainly support unity—the third, fifth, sixth, and eighth.

But these twelve chapters were falsely attributed to Gregory, and do not seem to have been written until after the heresy of the Incorruptibles had arisen, as chapter 4 indicates, if the appended explanation is accepted. It is therefore better to suppose that Cyril, if he did use the testimony of the Thaumaturge, received it from tradition—whether the tradition called *revealed*, or that called *κατὰ μέρος* (“in part”), although both are suspect in the form in which they now appear in the works of Gerard Vossius. Leontius attributes the former to Apollinaris, while Bellarmine and others attribute the latter to an uncertain author.

For the faith of Gregory the Thaumaturge, which Nyssenus mentions in the *Life of the Thaumaturge*, contained matters not reported in the work published by Vossius. See Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year of Christ 233.

### “Let the statements be praised as directed against the Arians.”

Cyril’s meaning is reported in bad faith. For in the Fifth Synod, collection [Col. 0996D] 5, the passage reads as follows:

“Thus twenty or more books were written by the good Theodore against the heresy of the Arians and Eunomians, as well as other books interpreting the evangelical and apostolic writings. No one would wish to criticize these labors, but rather would honor them with discerning zeal, if only they contained correctness of doctrine.”

These words do not approve the books written by Theodore; they accuse them on account of the heresy.

### “Published against the Arians.”

It is clear from the catalogue of Hebedjesus that these works were burned by the devices of the Arians.

### “Defenders of Catholic truth.”

Their leader was Hypatius of Ephesus, in the conference held at Constantinople, concerning which see the notes to the preceding chapter.

### “Followers of Apollinaris.”

Baronius calls this into doubt under the year 435, no. 9. He supposes that the monks had been falsely accused because Liberatus had been deceived by the account of some Nestorian. But he does not prove his opinion, although he would need to do so, since it seems possible to refute it from the fact that Apollinaris’s opinion had gained strength in Armenia, especially in the monasteries. Hence the Armenians’ question to Proclus, as they wondered which opinion should be preferred, that of one nature or that of two.

### “They say that Cyril did not even dictate them.”

Cyril contradicts this in his letter to Acacius of Melitene. After John of Antioch had written to him about the books of Diodore and Theodore, as though they contained nothing that could not, by a kindly interpretation, be understood in a Catholic sense, Cyril says:

“I have neither ceased nor shall I cease to rebuke what they wrote. But since it was necessary that written refutations also be made against them, after examining the books of Theodore and Diodore, which they wrote not concerning the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten but rather against the Incarnation, I set down some chapters and contradicted them as best I could, declaring everywhere that their sect was full of abomination.”

### “Two or three.”

In the printed books, the reading is “two or three,” with no sense at all, since the numerals cannot refer to chapters. For it is certain that far more than two or three chapters were excerpted from Theodore’s books, since these are the very passages reported either at greater length in the Fifth Synod or more briefly by Mercator and refuted by Cyril.

### “In his letter.”

It was addressed to Saint Cyril. It is found among his works, copied in Book VIII of Facundus of Hermiane, and is extremely worthy of reading for the history.

### “Entering the imperial city.”

What if Eutyches himself had been corrupted by those errors? Someone might very plausibly conjecture this. From it the subsequent events can easily be understood—namely, how, using the patronage of certain persons, they terrified clerics with threats, and so forth. That patronage was undoubtedly provided by Chrysaphius, whom Eutyches had received from the sacred font because of his reputation for holiness, and who, because of the emperor’s favor, could accomplish anything.

Moreover, the opinion of one nature was attributed to Cyril by the courtiers, who understood little but nevertheless adhered to Cyril, as is clear from Cyril’s memorandum to Eulogius.

### [Col. 0997C] “By his rescript.”

These words once led me astray when I was writing notes on the second part of the works of Marius Mercator, causing me to believe that Cyril, in his response to John of Antioch, had mentioned the creed written by Theodore, although in reality he did so only in Letter 2 to Acacius of Melitene.

This and other matters later made me, repenting of my credulity, investigate more carefully the wording and the reliability of Liberatus’s Punic text. If Liberatus understood by “rescript” a single letter in which Cyril replied to John, his memory failed him. Cyril addressed three matters in three letters, one in each: his judgment concerning Theodore in the letter to John; his judgment concerning the monks in the letter to the Fathers of the monks, which is an exposition of the Council of Nicaea; and his recollection of the creed in the letter to Acacius of Melitene.

### “Concerning the creed presented to him at the council.”

Marius Mercator refutes this creed in a separate work. We, however, have explained its author and history, against Facundus and many others, in the notes to the later part of Marius Mercator’s works. From these notes, as well as from other writings, someone—whose name I deliberately consider it best to conceal—profited in a less favorable direction, as much as he himself admitted.

### “Because of the Tesseracædecatic heresy.”

In the commonly circulated editions the reading was “*Tessera decadas factas*,” and so forth. Guided by history, we have arrived at the true reading. The creed in question was presented by two presbyters, emissaries of Anastasius, who had been an administrator of Nestorian impiety concerning the Mother of God, for subscription by those who abjured the Tesseracædecatic heresy. Read the sixth session of the Council of Ephesus.

### “After Cyril’s death.”

A considerable reversal of affairs occurred when three patriarchs in the East died. Cyril died in 444, John of Antioch in 441, [Col. 0998A] and Proclus in 447. Dioscorus succeeded Cyril, Domnus succeeded John, and Flavian succeeded Proclus.

### “Cyril’s heirs.”

Baronius orders the clergy to take warning from this example against dissipating ecclesiastical property among relatives, who, as commonly happens, grow rich on the patrimony of the poor and revel in Christ. Woe to this wicked age!

### “Ibas, bishop of Edessa.”

Concerning Ibas, whose case was one of the Three Famous Chapters, take the following. He was at Ephesus when the council was held, as he testifies in his letter to Maris. He was not yet a bishop, for he mentions the bishop who at that time occupied the see of Edessa.

He succeeded Rabula either at the beginning of the year 436 or toward the end of the preceding year. It could not have been earlier, since Rabula was still alive in 435 and was writing to the Armenians and Cyril after the dissemination of Theodore’s excerpts. Nor could it have been later, because in a letter to John, written in 436 toward its end or at the beginning of the following year, Proclus mentions Ibas as bishop of Edessa.

He received a letter from Theodoret in 441 concerning Caelestiacus of Carthage. In 446, [Col. 0998B] he was accused before Domnus of Antioch, John’s successor, by four of his own clerics—not only of heresy but also of improperly performed ordinations and plundering the Church’s property.

With Domnus conniving, he appealed to the emperor, who in 447 ordered that the trial be held at Tyre. It began at Tyre in February 448 and was completed at Beirut in September of the same year; the matter was settled amicably. But since the clerics did not remain quiet, he was again accused in the Ephesian Robber Council in August 449, while absent, and was deposed. Toward the end of that year he received a consolatory letter from Theodoret, who had shared the same fate.

In 450 he presented petitions of complaint to the emperor Marcian. In 451 he was restored to his see by the Council of Chalcedon, in its tenth session.

### “Ascension”

*ἀναστάσεως*, not *ἀναλήψεως*—that is, “resurrection,” or an ascent from the tomb, not an ascension into heaven, according to Theodoret, Letter 87.

## CHAPTER XI [Col. 0998C]

### Concerning Eutyches the presbyter and hegumen, his heresy, and his condemnation

*(From the acts of the Council of Constantinople under Flavian, which are inserted into the acts of the Council of Chalcedon.)*

At this time a certain presbyter and archimandrite named Eutyches, presiding over the famous monastery at Constantinople, preached, under the pressure of Satan, that our Lord Jesus Christ was not consubstantial with us according to the flesh, but had received a body from heaven. Again changing his position, he said that before the union there had been two natures in Christ, but that after the union they had become one.

When Eusebius, bishop of the city of Dorylaeum in the province of Phrygia Salutaris, heard him teaching and preaching such things—and Eusebius was orthodox, pure, and also his friend—he forbade him to hold and teach such opinions. But when Eutyches stubbornly refused to listen, Eusebius referred the matter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

He even entered the council of Flavian, which had been convened concerning Florentius, metropolitan of Sardes, against the bishops subject to him, John of Hyrcanum and Cossinius of Hierocaesarea. [Note: Col. 0997D: Codex Tellerii reads, “who also entered.”] After a ruling had been given concerning some of their cases, Eusebius presented petitions to Flavian and the entire council, adjuring everyone to come against the presbyter Eutyches, so that in their presence he might be convicted of holding and teaching heretical doctrines.

When Bishop Flavian heard this, he ordered Eutyches to come to his council through the presbyter and defensor John and the deacon Andrew. [Note: Col. 0999D: Codex Tellerii reads, “Upon this, Bishop Flavian, through John …”] When they went to him, Eutyches gave them this reply: “He had determined within himself never to leave his community, but to live in the monastery as though in a tomb.”

At the second meeting, Eusebius requested that two synodical letters of Cyril be read: one which he had sent to Nestorius, beginning, “Certain people are speaking against me to your fraternity,” and another which he had sent to John of Antioch, beginning, “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult.” The Council of Chalcedon later also accepted these letters.

When this had been done, Eutyches was summoned to the council in writing a second time through the presbyters Mama and Theophilus. They did not enter to him, but heard from his monks that he was ill and therefore could not see them. Nevertheless, they later entered to him and offered him the synodical document.

He again gave them this reply: “I have determined within myself not to leave the monastery except under the necessity of death. But accept this document, written in my own hand, and present it to the synod.”

After this, when he continued to refuse, they reported his excuse to the council. [Note: Col. 0999D: The same codex reads, “and after this, when he reported his refusal, they reported [it].”] Eutyches sent tomes containing his doctrines throughout the monasteries to the abbots, for them to subscribe to. Bishop Eusebius informed the council of this.

[Col. 0999C] Again Flavian, together with his council, summoned him in writing for the third time through the presbyter Memnon and the deacons Epiphanius and Germanus. When Eutyches once more excused himself on the ground of illness, those who had been sent nevertheless compelled him to request a delay of one week, so that after the number of seven days he might appear for the hearing. [Note: Col. 0999D: The same codex reads, “after the seventh number of days.”]

He fled to the emperor Theodosius and, as is reported, obtained through the eunuch Chrysaphius—whom Eutyches had received from the sacred baptismal font—that he might enter Flavian’s council together with the patrician Florentius and the *Magister Silentii*. For he claimed to fear Flavian’s accusations.

After he was permitted to take with him the *Magister Silentii*, [Col. 0999D] and had received from the emperor’s written order both the officers of the *excubitores* and the *chlamydati*, he came to the council. When he entered it, the *Magister Silentii*, who was with him, read in the synod the emperor’s mandate, which was as follows: [Note: Col. 1000D: Codex Tellerii reads, “Magnus in the synod.”]

“If we desire peace among the holy Churches, and wish to preserve the soundness of the Catholic faith and the faith inspired by God and preached by our fathers who assembled at Nicaea—three hundred and eighteen bishops—and by those who were present at Ephesus for the condemnation of Nestorius, then this is what we wish: [Note: Col. 1000D: The same codex reads, “at the condemnation of Nestorius.”] that no scandal be introduced into the aforesaid Catholic faith. And since we know the most magnificent patrician Florentius to be faithful, approved, and of correct faith, we wish him to be present at the synod’s hearing, since the subject is faith.”

When the patrician Florentius arrived and took his seat, the bishops demanded that Eutyches confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was consubstantial with us according to the flesh, in the union of two natures. But he requested that his own petition be read and said that he believed according to the faith of the Council of Nicaea.

The patrician Florentius asked Eutyches whether he said that Christ, who was from the Virgin, was consubstantial with us and that there were two united natures in him. He answered that he confessed this before the union, but after the union he confessed one nature.

The synod said to him: “You must confess this and anathematize every doctrine contrary to this faith.” He replied: “I did not say this earlier, but I can say it because they were saying it. Nevertheless, I claim to follow the Fathers, since I have not found this explained in the Scriptures, nor have the Fathers said it in this way.”

The holy synod then rose and anathematized him.

The patrician Florentius repeatedly said to him: “Whoever does not confess two natures in Christ does not believe correctly.” He replied: “I have the rule of the holy Cyril and Athanasius, who said that Christ was from two natures before the union, but after the union and the Incarnation they did not say two natures, but one.” [Note: Col. 1000D: The same codex reads, “because [he is] from two natures.”]

The holy synod then rose and anathematized [Col. 1000C] him again.

The venerable Flavian, because Eutyches had fallen ill through the error of the heretics Valentinus and Apollinaris, stripped him of the dignity of the presbyterate, anathematized and condemned him. When the acts had been closed, the council subscribed to his condemnation.

The venerable Flavian appended his letter to these acts and sent it to Pope Leo, faithfully reporting what had been done in the council. Eutyches, writing to Pope Leo concerning his condemnation, posted edicts at Constantinople and publicly declared that he had suffered injustice.

Leo sent Flavian a tome containing the sound doctrine of Christ’s Incarnation and wonderfully destroying Eutyches’ assertions. Its beginning, after the preface, is: “Having read the letter of your affection,” and so forth.

Eutyches then presented a petition to the emperor, complaining that the acts had been falsified, as though some things had been added by the notaries and other things had been said but not inserted into the acts. [Note: Col. 1000D: The same codex reads, “for some things had indeed been said.”] He requested that a council be convened again in the palace, in the presence of Bishop Thalassius and the patrician Florentius, with Flavian appearing, so that the truth might be revealed through the questioning of the persons involved.

The emperor consented and subscribed the petition with his own hand as follows:

“Let them deposit it before the most reverend bishops—not only those who previously assembled, but also the most reverend Thalassius—so that, with all these persons present, the truth of the matter may be investigated concerning what the petition alleges.”

When the council was assembled, Eutyches was absent and sent the deacon Constantine in his place, so that by answering for him before the judges who were conducting the examination, he might challenge the falsity of the acts. But when the acts were examined, and the notaries insisted, together with the God-fearing bishops, although some persons were for the time supporting Eutyches, no falsity could be found. The only action taken was that records were prepared before the *magister officiorum* concerning the alleged falsity of the notaries, with certain laymen from the emperor’s service present, who had been present at the acts themselves during the council.

Afterward the emperor requested from Flavian a confession of his faith, written and subscribed by his own hand. Flavian therefore wrote his faith in his own hand and sent it to the emperor in the following form:

“Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, sends greetings to our emperor Theodosius, lover of Christ. [Note: Col. 1001D: Codex Tellerii reads, “lover of Christ” (*amator Christi*).]

“Nothing is so fitting for a priest of God and one instructed in the divine doctrines as to be ready to give an account to everyone who asks for a reason concerning the hope and grace that are in us (1 Peter 3:15). For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of God, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes (Romans 1:16).

“Since, therefore, by the mercy of Christ our God, King of all, we too have received such a priesthood, we think rightly and blamelessly, always following the divine Scriptures and the exposition of the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, of the one hundred and fifty who assembled here, and of those who assembled at Ephesus under the holy memory of Cyril, who was bishop of the Alexandrians.

“We preach our Lord Jesus Christ as, before the ages, born without beginning from God the Father according to his divinity; and in the last days, the same one, for us and for our salvation, born from the Virgin Mary according to his humanity.

“Confessing Christ, therefore, after the Incarnation and embodiment from the holy Virgin, to be from two natures, in one substance and in one person, we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord.

“We do not deny that we speak of the one nature of God the Word as incarnate and made man, since our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ is from both natures.

“But we anathematize those who proclaim either two sons, or two substances, or two persons, and who do not preach one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God; and we judge them alien to the Churches.
