“Above all, we anathematize the impious Nestorius, and those who think and speak as he did. Let such persons be cut off from the adoption of sons, which has been promised to those who believe rightly.”

And the subscription: “Lord Jesus Christ, help us.” And again: “I have written this with my own hand to satisfy your authority, so that those who bring accusations against our simple conduct may be confounded.”

### “At this time.”

That is, in the year 448, after the year 447, in which Flavian ascended the see of Constantinople, and before the year 449, in which Ibas was summoned to trial. For when Eutyches had been made the defendant in Flavian’s council, he contrived an accusation against Ibas, who complained about this matter at the Council of Chalcedon, session 10.

### “A certain Eutyches.”

For the history of Eutyches, besides Liberatus, it is worthwhile to consult the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* edited by P. Sirmond; the *Chronography* of Theophanes; the Council of Constantinople under Flavian; the Ephesian Robber Council; the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon; the Second Council of Constantinople, which is the Fifth Universal Council; and the letters, both those exchanged between Leo the Great and Flavian and others pertaining to the matter.

### “He preached the Lord.”

What Eutyches actually believed can scarcely be known with certainty, because of the incompetence and inconsistency of the delirious old man; these led different authors in different directions. He wished to follow Cyril’s Catholic teaching that, after the union, there was one nature of the incarnate Word of God, but he could not grasp it because of the sluggishness of his understanding.

Consequently, he appeared to incline toward the heresy of Apollinaris, although what he said was fundamentally opposed to it: namely, that Christ was from two natures but not in two—that there had been two natures before the union and one afterward. This reflects Polemius’s confusion more than Apollinaris’s doctrine.

The mind of this ignorant man was unsettled by hatred of Nestorius. Inflamed by that hatred, he had worked with extraordinary zeal for the faith alongside the Ephesian Fathers several years earlier, as had the other archimandrites of the imperial city, whose leader was Dalmatius.

Nevertheless, what men of great reputation report on this matter—namely, that Eutyches himself had brought the Fathers’ letters from Ephesus to Constantinople—is neither credible nor affirmatively attested by any ancient writer. For when John and Andrew summoned him to the council, he replied that from the beginning of his conversion he had determined not to leave the monastery, “having said that this had been predetermined for him and that he had been bound by a certain rule from the beginning, namely, that he should in no way leave his community,” and so forth.

### “Eusebius, bishop of the city of Dorylaeum.”

The *Brief History of the Eutychianists*, edited by Sirmond after the appendix to the Theodosian Code, says:

“When Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, discovered that this Eutyches, presbyter and abbot of the city of Constantinople, was persuading people of such things, he reported him to Bishop Flavian with zeal for the faith—a zeal he had shown even when he was an imperial agent, for he had also rebuked Nestorius at the proper time when Nestorius was preaching sacrilegious things in the church—and he demanded that he be brought to judgment.”

Later, where it deals with the Ephesian Robber Council, it says:

“Eusebius [Col. 1002D] the bishop, who had accused that same presbyter, was also condemned as a Nestorian, although earlier, while still a layman, he had been an accuser of Nestorius.”

The author of this *Brief History*, from whom Liberatus drew, was writing in the year 486. He plainly confirms what we stated in the preface and notes to the second part of the works of Marius Mercator concerning this Eusebius: that, while he was still a *scholasticus* of the imperial court—*σχολαστικὸς τῆς βασιλίδος*—he publicly accused Nestorius both in an assembly and through a posted protest.

### “And after a ruling had been given.”

In Greek, *τύπου δὲ δοθέντος φανεροῦ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀναγνωσθεῖσιν*, that is, “after the matter had been readily settled,” concerning the case that had arisen between Florentius, the metropolitan, and the two subordinate bishops.

### “His council.”

This was the ordinary council, held in accordance with the prescription of the Nicene Synod during the autumn season. It held seven meetings, as is clear from the acts inserted both in the Ephesian acts under Dioscorus and in those of Chalcedon, session 1, volume V of the final collection of the Councils. There the chronological notice “after the consulship of Zeno,” and so forth, which appeared in the earlier editions, has rightly been corrected.

The letters of Pope Leo to Flavian and others of his letters, both those issued before the Ephesian Robber Council and those issued after that council, demonstrate the correction by clear reasoning. The consuls were Asterius and Protogenes, who succeeded Zeno and Postumianus. Thirty-one bishops and twenty-two archimandrites assembled.

### “At the second meeting.”

It was held on the day before the Ides of November, which was Friday. The first meeting had been held on 8 November, according to custom, namely on Monday, since in that leap year the dominical letter was D C. The third was held on the 15th, which was Monday; the fourth on the following day; the fifth on the 17th; the sixth on the 20th, a Saturday; and the seventh on the 22nd, a Monday. Thus the synod lasted fifteen days.

### “Cyril’s synodical letters.”

Read what we have said at length on this subject, to overturn a certain popular opinion, in Dissertation 2 to the second part of Mercator’s works, which is entirely concerned with the synods held in the case of Nestorius.

### “He sent tomes.”

He sent them through his deacons Constantine and Eleusinius, men certainly not of the best character. They claimed that the tomes contained only what had been defined at Nicaea and Ephesus or written by Cyril. But they must have been altered, since the deacons refused to allow those who requested it to compare them with the copies preserved in the monasteries.

### “A delay of one week.”

For all the details to fit together properly, this request must have been made in session 3, held on 15 November, and then either repeated or confirmed in the subsequent sessions. For Eutyches appeared on the 22nd.

### “The synod rose.”

Observe the custom of rising when a sentence of excommunication was being pronounced. You will see this practice observed in all the councils.

### [Col. 1003C] “He sent [the letter] to Pope Leo.”

This seems to imply that Flavian’s letter reached Saint Leo before Eutyches’ letter, although the pontiff testifies in Letter 8 that the matter occurred otherwise. It may nevertheless be said that Flavian, immediately after the council had been held, sent the acts to Rome, but that they were preceded by Eutyches’ letters. This is gathered from two letters of Flavian to Leo, one of which contains a report of the proceedings, while the other is a reply to Leo’s complaint that Flavian had not reported the proceedings.

### “Formal protest petitions.”

Saint Leo calls them petitions of protest:

“He claims that he presented his petition of appeal but that it was not accepted, and that for this reason he was compelled to post petitions of protest in the city of Constantinople.”

Letter 8.

### “That a council be convened again.”

This second council was summoned in the greater portico of the holy church in the year 449. Its first session was held on the Ides of April and its later session on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.

## CHAPTER XII [Col. 1003D]

### Concerning the second Synod of Ephesus and the death of Flavian

*(From the acts of the Second Council of Ephesus, which are inserted into the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, and from the letter of Saint Leo.)*
After, then, nothing had been established to the notaries’ satisfaction concerning the falsity of the acts, Eutyches asked Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, to investigate what had been done against him and to examine the case. He therefore sought from the emperor that a universal synod be convened, so that Flavian’s judgment might be reviewed. Accordingly, Dioscorus wrote to the emperor Theodosius [Col. 1004A] that another general synod ought to be held, and Eutyches persuaded him that it should be held.

The emperor agreed and, sending a sacred letter to Dioscorus in Alexandria, ordered him to select ten metropolitan bishops and whatever other bishops he himself wished, to come to Ephesus, and, after convening a universal council, to investigate Eutyches’ case. He also ordered Barsumas the archimandrite to attend the council and to act on behalf of all the monks who were accusing the Eastern bishops.

He forbade Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, to attend the council and ordered him to remain in his own city. For Eutyches had already banished Ibas, bishop of Edessa, to many places of exile [Col. 1004B], through his son Chrysaphius, whom I mentioned above, so that he could not attend the synod.

A general council was therefore held at Ephesus. Flavian and Eutyches attended as men whose cases were to be judged; Juvenal and Thalassius attended, together with all those metropolitan bishops and their councils, as did the judges of the Council of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1003D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “and the judges of the Council of Constantinople”], who had judged Eutyches. Dioscorus, however, had with him the most powerful soldiers of the state, together with Barsumas’s monks.

When those bishops were seated in the basilica of Mary, Mother of God, the legates of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 1004D] The same codex reads: “the deacons of the Roman Church”], acting in Pope Leo’s place, were not allowed to sit [Note: [Col. 1004D] The same codex reads: “were not allowed to attend”], because the place of precedence had not been granted to their holy see. Moreover, the letter that Pope Leo had written to Flavian in condemning Eutyches had not been read, and his letter, which had been sent to that synod by the above-mentioned [Col. 1004C] legates, had been concealed. Its opening is: “The religious faith of the most clement prince,” and so forth.

When Flavian was being judged by the synod because of his condemnation of Eutyches, Dioscorus ordered the petition that Eutyches was carrying in his own hand to be received and read aloud. As it was being read, Dioscorus rose and, standing on the platform of his seat, said to the council: “Eutyches’ excellent faith agrees with the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, and Eutyches believes rightly, brothers.”

Then, at Dioscorus’s command, the synod condemned Ibas of Edessa in his absence, while many of the bishops did not know what had been done against him. Having summoned him for a third time as a contemptuous man who had failed to appear before the [Col. 1004D] holy council, it condemned him in his absence.

It was shouted, however, that testimony against him had been given by his opponents, as though he had said: “I do not envy Christ for having been made God, since, if I wish, I too become [God],” and as though he had said: “Today Christ was made God”; along with other statements of this kind, and also because of the letter that Ibas had sent to Maris.

Again, at Dioscorus’s instigation, the synod condemned Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, in his absence. He had not even left his city, because of what he had written against Cyril’s twelve anathemas and because of the letter [Col. 1005A] he had sent to clergy, monks, and laypeople against the First Council of Ephesus, before peace had been restored to the Church.

The aforementioned synod also condemned Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, because he had said that Christ was “of two perfect natures.”

Together with him it likewise condemned Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, as though he had wrongly condemned Eutyches and because he had said that “Christ is recognized in two natures.” At this, certain venerable bishops rose, grasped Dioscorus’s knees, and begged that the innocent Flavian not be condemned. But they could not continue their pleas for long, because they feared the soldiers and monks who stood there with swords and clubs.

He also deposed Sabinian, bishop of Perre [Col. 1005B]. Finally, he deposed Domnus of Antioch, who remained after the deposition of the orthodox, because he had joined Dioscorus in deposing the orthodox and absolving Eutyches.

Domnus was deposed through Dioscorus’s deceit as follows. After he had agreed with Dioscorus on everything, letters were produced in the assembly which Domnus, bishop of Antioch, had written to Dioscorus against Cyril’s twelve chapters, on the ground that they were obscure. Dioscorus condemned the sick man in his absence on that day.

When the synod had therefore decreed these things and restored to Eutyches the dignity of the presbyterate and the office of the episcopate, Flavian and Eusebius are handed over to custody [Note: [Col. 1005D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “were being handed over to custody”].

The men representing Pope Leo’s see, for their part, contradicted everything that had been done. Flavian, in response to the sentence pronounced against him, appealed through Leo’s legates to the apostolic see in a written petition, and the synod then came to an end.

After all these evils had been perpetrated by Dioscorus, Flavian was beaten and subjected to many injuries; he died of the pain of his wounds and departed to the Lord. In his place Anatolius was ordained, a deacon who had been Dioscorus’s representative at Constantinople. Maximus was ordained in place of Domnus of Antioch, Nonnus in place of Ibas, and Athanasius in place of Sabinian. No one was ordained in place of Theodoret or Eusebius.

When that council had been dissolved and the bishops had returned to their sees, a division arose among them such as had never before occurred. The Egyptian, Thracian, and Palestinian bishops followed Dioscorus; the Eastern, Pontic [Col. 1005D], and Asian bishops followed Flavian of blessed memory. This schism continued until the death of the emperor Theodosius.

If anyone wishes to know more fully about the outrages perpetrated by Dioscorus at that synod, everything becomes completely clear to the reader in the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, in which the acts of the Second Council of Ephesus—though they are not even worthy of being called a council—were read aloud and incorporated into the proceedings. We recently received these acts translated from Greek into Latin at Alexandria.

The legates of the apostolic see, fleeing from the council itself [Col. 1006A], reported to Pope Leo the iniquities of Dioscorus: how Dioscorus had conducted that synod more by force than by justice; how, after fear had been instilled [Note: [Col. 1005D] The same codex reads: “in whose proceedings fear had been instilled”], the bishops had subscribed to Eutyches’ absolution and to the deposition of the orthodox bishops who refused to accept the heresy; and how they had contradicted all his proceedings.

Following them, Bishop Theodoret informed the pope of the many evils he had suffered through Dioscorus’s plots, asking that such a cause be helped without delay by another gathering of bishops, lest Eutyches’ heretical doctrines remain confirmed by Dioscorus.

But the most steadfast Leo, after hearing the report of his legates and receiving Theodoret’s complaints, asked in letters to the emperor Theodosius and the empress Pulcheria [Col. 1006B] that a general council be held within Italy and that the error in the faith, produced through Dioscorus’s violence, be abolished.

The Roman pontiff, prostrating himself on his knees before the memory of blessed Peter, together with many bishops, also entreated the emperor Valentinian and his wife Eudoxia [Note: [Col. 1006D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “Eudoxia, his wife”] to urge the emperor Theodosius that another synod be held, in order to reconsider what Dioscorus had wrongly done and perpetrated in condemning Bishop Flavian and deposing the orthodox.

When they had written and made their request, the emperor Theodosius replied that Flavian, guilty of a harmful novelty, had received the death he deserved, so that peace and concord might reign throughout the Church, since the author of the dispute had been removed from human affairs by sacred judgment. Those who had been deposed, he said, had been unworthy of the priesthood, while those judged worthy had been received by the synod.

This is what Theodosius said about Flavian—the son of the emperor Arcadius and grandson of the elder emperor Theodosius, during whose reign all these scandals are known to have occurred.

[Note: [Col. 1006C]

On the Second Council of Ephesus.]

It was held in the year 449, at Theodosius’s command, through Chrysaphius’s influence, Eutyches’ intrigues, and Dioscorus’s ambition. Chrysaphius had almost bewitched Theodosius; Chrysaphius, Eutyches; Eutyches, Dioscorus. Chrysaphius had blinded the emperor’s mind with hatred of Flavian and jealousy of Pulcheria. By accepting Eutyches as his protégé, Chrysaphius had given him an opportunity to exercise his enmity under the appearance of defending piety. Dioscorus, relying on such great resources, hoped to recover the primacy of the Eastern Church, which he had lost. Eudoxia’s womanly jealousy against Pulcheria also assisted this scheme. For if any trust is to be placed in Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 47, Chrysaphius, in order to stir up Eudoxia to play her part in this tragedy, “aroused the empress Eudoxia, saying many things, but especially those which had grievously affected her through Pulcheria.”

Three hundred and sixty bishops attended this synod together with the legates of the apostolic see, if we believe the Brief History of the Eutychianists published by P. Sirmond. It was ecumenical, since the Eastern Church was present through its four patriarchs and the Western Church through the legates of the apostolic see. It began on the sixth day before the Ides of August, which was a Monday. [Col. 1007A] It had three sessions, whose acts were reread at the Council of Chalcedon. It was subsequently rejected by the whole Church and branded with the infamous name “the Robber Council.”

“Judgment might be reviewed.” That is, “it might be called for examination.”

“Dioscorus therefore wrote.” Nicephorus, in the passage cited shortly afterward, clarifies Liberatus’s obscure account, whether by his own conjecture or through another tradition:

“The beginning of its celebration was as follows. This Chrysaphius wielded great influence with the emperor. Since he considered Flavian’s consecration less acceptable and approved because of a prior prejudice, he suggested to the emperor that he should tell the patriarch to send him the gift of a blessing on the occasion of his election and consecration. The holy Flavian sent pure loaves. Chrysaphius, on the other hand, said that a golden gift of blessing ought to be sent. The patriarch replied that he possessed no such thing, unless perhaps he should use the sacred treasures of the temple for this purpose; but Chrysaphius himself knew very well that the Church’s sacred vessels were consecrated to God and to the poor. From this the offense arose, since the empress Pulcheria had paid no attention to the matter. Chrysaphius, inflamed with jealousy on this account, moved every possible device to drive the patriarch from his see.” [Col. 1007B]

“With ten metropolitan bishops.” The imperial sacred letter to Dioscorus says:

“Therefore, let Your Holiness take with you ten most reverend metropolitan bishops who live within your diocese, and likewise ten other holy bishops distinguished in speech and life.”

Yet since this same sacred letter was sent in identical terms to the other patriarchs and even to the autocephalous bishops, a question arises: how can these words be reconciled with the facts, since at that time there were only six provinces in the Egyptian diocese, and no properly so-called metropolitan bishops? The bishop of Jerusalem at that time had no metropolitans under his authority; the bishops of Antioch and Constantinople each had more than ten.

The difficulty is increased by the fact that the Brief History cited shortly afterward says that three hundred and sixty bishops assembled, whereas the acts count only one hundred and thirty-three, including those who attended through representatives. For however the words may be strained, how can either of those numbers be assembled from the bishops named in the sacred letter? The knot will be untied in the Life of Theodoret.

“Ordering Barsumas.” Leontius mentions a certain Barsumas in book III Against the Eutychians:

“That Barsumas was your disciple, who wickedly governed Persia according to your impious doctrines. Having removed the distinction in the conduct of life, he enacted a law that no one from the clergy, and certainly no layperson, should abstain from an unlawful bed or from polygamy—that is, from multiple marriages. For he considered drunkenness and banquets to be gifts of God.”

Although age does not prevent our supposing that the Barsumas mentioned by Liberatus and the one mentioned by Leontius were the same person, their sect seems to make this unlikely. The Barsumas mentioned by Liberatus adhered to Eutyches, whereas the one mentioned by Leontius adhered to Theodore of Mopsuestia, that is, to the defender of the opposite heresy. Yet that wicked man—whoever he was—could have changed his faith for a time; or he could have agreed with Eutyches in doctrine and with Theodore in morals.

Moreover, three charges were brought against Barsumas in the fourth session of the Council of Chalcedon. First, that he had entered the assembly with other monks, although his name had not been included in the petition submitted to the emperor by the monks. Second, that he had killed Flavian at the Robber Council, shouting that he should be killed. Finally, that he had led a force of a thousand monks against the bishops of the East. For these reasons all cried out together: “Send the murderer Barsumas outside! The murderer into the arena! Anathema to Barsumas! Barsumas into exile!”

“To act on behalf of all the monks.” The agitation of the monks against the bishops of the East had arisen already, from the time when peace was first established between the Churches. These men, ardent in their zeal for the faith, considered that peace fictitious. Hence Cyril had to admonish Maximus [Col. 1008A] not to continue abstaining from communion with his bishop John, but rather to make prudent use of a temporary accommodation. On this matter, see Cyril’s letter to Maximus, Acacius of Melitene, and Lampon. It should be observed that Cyril was not averse to the monks’ suspicion concerning John himself and the other bishops of the East. Hence these words of his:

“I wrote to him [John], but the worse things prevail”; and afterward, “As the teacher wishes, so he thinks,” and so forth.

“But Theodoret.” This was not the first time that the emperor had ordered him to remain confined to his own city; he had issued that command several years earlier.

“For Eutyches had already banished Ibas to exile.” Through Chrysaphius he had dared to do this, although Ibas seemed to have been acquitted at Tyre and Berytus. Only Liberatus explicitly mentions this exile, although certain words of Ibas in session 9 of the Council of Chalcedon might be understood in this sense. Yet the entire account of this exile—which, if it occurred at all, took place toward the end of 448 or the beginning of the following year—is highly suspect to me.

[Col. 1008B] “Together with Barsumas’s monks.” The Fathers at the Council of Chalcedon complain that a thousand were brought; only zeal for evil could have prompted such a thing.

“In the basilica of the Mother of God.” This was where the Fathers of the Catholic Council had assembled eighteen years earlier.

“The legates of the Roman Church.” In the common editions they are called deacons, but this is plainly an error, both because of the words that follow, “through the above-mentioned legates,” and because only one of the legates, Hilary, was a deacon. Julian was a bishop and Renatus a presbyter.

“They were not allowed to sit.” This is a difficult passage. Whether it means that the legates did not attend the council or that they did attend but did not sit after Dioscorus, it conflicts with the acts. It is therefore credible that they did sit after Dioscorus, but that they had first protested against the wrong done to the apostolic see by Theodosius, against the presidency that Dioscorus had accepted contrary to the canons and that the emperor had assigned to him, and against the violence inflicted upon them by both men.

Hence, in session 1 of the Council of Chalcedon, when the legates of the apostolic see [Col. 1008C] refused to sit with the Fathers alongside Dioscorus, they accused him of arrogating to himself the authority to preside “and to conduct a synod without the authority of the apostolic see—something that has never been permitted and has never been done.” Note that “authority” is used for “presidency.”

“I do not envy Christ for having been made God.” This impious statement was discussed at length in the second part of Marius Mercator’s works, where it was shown to be a saying of Paul of Samosata and the first source of Pelagianism concerning the powers of free choice. There is also Theodoret’s consolatory Letter 133 to Ibas, written amid the common disaster of their deposition.

“Because of the letter.” From it were excerpted the passages that we received from Marius Mercator and that are found in session 5, discussion 5—unless, however, Theodoret had sent several letters to Constantinople on the same subject. The chief reason why Theodoret was condemned, both here and in session 5, was nevertheless the two works: one against Cyril’s chapters, the other [Col. 1008D] against the Council of Ephesus, entitled the *Pentalogion* (*Πενταλόγιον*, “Fivefold Treatise”). It is mentioned in session 5; fragments are found partly in Mercator, which we have published, and partly scattered here and there, which we have collected.

“He also deposed Sabinian.” The common editions spell the name *Savinianus*; we restore *Sabinianus* from Theodoret’s Letter 126, addressed *To Sabinian, Bishop* (*Σαβινιανῷ ἐπισκόπῳ*). It is a consolatory letter concerning the common misfortune of the two men.

“Who remained after the deposition of the orthodox.” The passage is obscure, whether the reading should be emended or retained. If it is to be emended, one might substitute *remeantem* (“returning”), so that the expression would be a North African usage similar to the French expression *il est revenu de cela*—“he has come to regret that.” Yet this emendation does not agree very well with what follows, where Domnus is said to have been condemned while sick.

I therefore think the reading should be retained as Liberatus’s genuine text, though it was misunderstood by some unlearned [Col. 1009A] or careless translator. Finding in the Greek text *ἀμενηνούμενον* (“being weakened” or “being ill”), he translated it as though it were *ἀναμενόμενον*, “remaining.” This view is supported both by the history itself and by the following statement: “He condemned the sick man in his absence on that day.”

“Against Cyril’s twelve chapters.” Unless my conjecture deceives me, Domnus wrote to Dioscorus about Cyril’s chapters after receiving Theodoret’s Letter 112. In his letter Domnus tried to persuade Dioscorus that the chapters should not be established as a rule of faith, because they were obscure. The basis for my conjecture is that Theodoret says something similar, together with several other things, about the chapters. We have discussed the chapters at length in the notes to the second part of Marius Mercator’s works.

“Flavian departed to the Lord.” He was not beaten at the synod itself, since after his deposition he was placed in custody; rather, he was beaten on the road along which he was being taken into exile. Thus the frequently cited Brief History says:

“Flavian was led into exile and died at Epipa, a city [Col. 1009B] of Lydia, either because death overtook him or because it was brought upon him.”

Marcellinus Comes agrees about the place of exile in his *Chronicle*. See Baronius in his later notes on the *Martyrology*.

“A division arose.” The reason why the Egyptians and Palestinians adhered to Dioscorus, and why Juvenal followed Dioscorus, is clear. Anatolius, who had been Dioscorus’s representative at Constantinople and thus became the chief bishop of Thrace, led the Thracians into the same party. The Pontic and Asian bishops supported Flavian because of Flavian himself; the Eastern bishops supported him because their own head, Domnus, had been deposed, together with the distinguished bishops Theodoret, Ibas, and Sabinian, but above all because of the issue of the twelve chapters.

“The legates of the apostolic see, fleeing.” The deacon Hilary says that he fled in a letter to Pulcheria, and Leo the Great also relates this. Theodoret is a witness concerning the presbyter Renatus in Letter 116. It is strange, however, that the Brief History of the Eutychianists reports that Renatus [Col. 1009C] did not reach Ephesus but died on the island of Delos. How, then, did Theodoret write to him after the council had been dissolved? What happened to Julian the bishop is unknown. Some interpret the silence of Leo the Great, Theodoret, and others in the more favorable sense.

“Following them, Theodoret.” Not physically, but in judgment and in his writings, as is clear from Letters 113, 116, and others. He sent two rural bishops and an archimandrite of monks to carry his letters to the supreme pontiff and to advance his case at Rome.

“Valentinian and Eudoxia.” He omitted Galla Placidia, Valentinian’s mother, who, together with her son and daughter-in-law, visited Saint Peter, heard Leo’s prayers, wrote to Theodosius, and received his reply. See part 1 of the Council of Chalcedon, chapters 26 and 30.

“Prostrating himself on his knees.” The source from which Liberatus drew this detail is concealed. It is not found either in the earlier writers or in the letters of Valentinian, Galla Placidia, and Eudoxia to Theodosius. Those letters do mention prayers poured out by Leo almost with tears, but they do not mention the somewhat undignified act of kneeling.

“Theodosius replied.” Liberatus interpolated this entire response of Theodosius, for Theodosius’s letters contain no mention of Flavian’s death.

“This is what Theodosius said about Flavian, and so forth.” Why does he mention the elder Theodosius when he is speaking of the younger Theodosius? Perhaps he wished to remind the learned reader of what John of Antioch wrote to the younger Theodosius about the elder Theodosius’s esteem for Theodore of Mopsuestia:

“For Theodore—for when we say ‘Theodore,’ we mean a man distinguished in the episcopate, a man who for nearly fifty years vigorously resisted all heresies, and whose expositions, delivered in all the Churches of the East and highly approved in the imperial city, show him to have been regarded with great honor—was never judged a heretic by anyone, whether among his predecessors or his contemporaries. On the contrary, all the priests, because of the grace of doctrine that was in him, always held him in admiration, and he possessed the higher honor of glory—not only among the priests, but also with your most sacred grandfather, whom we call thrice blessed, who received the scepter of the empire from God and transmitted it to us: Theodosius. Desiring to see the man, that great emperor became a hearer in the Church of his teaching. He did not think that he had found another teacher like him; he greatly admired his doctrine, delighted in his conversation, and was amazed by him—this man whom some now despise, as though they were undertaking the task of testing and rejecting deceased teachers according to their own will.” [Facundus, book II, chapter 2.]

CHAPTER XIII. On the Council of Chalcedon and the condemnation of Dioscorus. [Col. 1010B]

(From the acts of the Council of Chalcedon and the Brief History of the Eutychianists.)

After Theodosius had died and Marcian had attained the summit of imperial power, he ordered a universal council to be assembled at Nicaea in response to the request of the pope and the Roman rulers. When six hundred and thirty bishops had arrived and were seated, Pope Leo’s legates asked Marcian to present himself to the council; otherwise, if he were absent, they themselves would not attend the council. The emperor therefore ordered the synod to be transferred to Chalcedon, so that, by coming to the council nearby, he might fulfill their request.

Some bishops feared that a disturbance might arise nearby at Constantinople, stirred up by the Eutychians. But the emperor promised that no one would dare attempt such a thing [Col. 1010C], and the synod therefore met at Chalcedon.

Accordingly, before the sacred senate, Constantine and Beronicianus, imperial secretaries, and the entire universal council, the proceedings of the Second Council of Ephesus were examined. Paschasinus and Lucentius, bishops, and Boniface, a presbyter, represented Leo, pope of Rome; Anatolius of Constantinople was present, as were Dioscorus and all the metropolitan bishops. The purpose was to investigate the deposition and death of Flavian and the deposition of the orthodox bishops who had been deposed for the faith.

In the first session, Beronicianus read the proceedings of the wicked Second Council of Ephesus, including the acts concerning Eutyches at Constantinople. The proceedings of the First Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius had been condemned by Cyril, were also read and incorporated into the acts. After everything had been properly examined, the bishops cried out:

“Anathema to Nestorius! Anathema to Eutyches! Anathema to him who divides! Anathema to him who confuses!”

Dioscorus’s iniquity was exposed and made evident concerning Flavian’s death [Note: [Col. 1009D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “His iniquity concerning Flavian’s death was exposed”] and the deposition of the orthodox bishops.

When the first assembly had thus been dissolved, during the second session, while the judges were delivering their opinions so that the faith might be discussed and confirmed with the deliberation of all the bishops, Cyril’s two letters were read—the letters contained, as we said, in the proceedings of Flavian’s council at Constantinople.

Pope Leo’s *Tome*, directed to the aforementioned Flavian against Eutyches’ doctrine, was also read. When the holy bishops of Illyricum and Palestine expressed doubts about certain passages, Theodoret and Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, demonstrated from Leo’s statements and letters that Cyril had written similar things. When the Egyptian and Illyrian bishops cried out, “We have all sinned; we all ask forgiveness,” a delay of five days was granted, so that the faith might be discussed and confirmed with full deliberation.

When the second assembly had thus been dissolved, during the third session Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, presented a petition against Dioscorus. He complained to the synod about his own deposition and that of Flavian of blessed memory, about Dioscorus’s agreement with Eutyches’ doctrine, and asked that Dioscorus be summoned and convicted by them of these charges.

The council inquired whether Dioscorus had arrived, but he was not found. Bishops Constantine of Bostra, Atticus of Zela [Note: [Col. 1011D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “Atticus of Talla”], and Acacius of Ariarathia [Note: [Col. 1011D] The same codex reads: “Acacius of Aria”], together with Himerius, a reader and notary, were sent to summon him in writing and require him to attend the council.

Dioscorus replied: “I am being guarded. If they permit me to come down, let the magistrates say so. I am ready to come, but I am being prevented.” Dioscorus committed this response to writing for the council. But when the assistant of the master of offices arrived, he gave Dioscorus permission to attend the council freely.

They again sent Pergamius Cecropius [Col. 1011C] and Rufinus [Note: [Col. 1011D] The same codex reads: “Cecropius and Rufinus were sent”], bishops, to summon him again in writing, so that he would not disdain to come to the council but would rather give an account to the council concerning the charges brought by Eusebius.

He replied to them: “Let the judges and senators judge these matters. I am weighed down by illness and cannot come to the council.”

He was summoned to the council a third time through the bishops Francio, Julian, and John, together with Palladius the notary, so that they might report in writing to the council what Dioscorus had answered. But at this third summons Dioscorus delayed coming by giving an absurd reply, and the council pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him, which was sent to the devout emperor and subscribed by the bishops.

Dioscorus was deposed from the episcopate in the seventh year of his ordination. The council instructed the Alexandrian clergy no longer to regard him as a bishop but to recognize fully that he had been cast down from his rank. Since some nevertheless thought that Dioscorus might recover his episcopate, an edict was produced, and it was made clear to everyone that Dioscorus had been irreversibly stripped of his honor.

During the fourth session, while the judges were delivering their opinions, it was determined that the following bishops should be subject to a sentence like that by which Dioscorus had been judged: Juvenal of Jerusalem, Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Eusebius [Col. 1012A] of Ancyra in Galatia, Eustathius of Berytus, and Basil of Seleucia in Isauria. They had held authority and had been the leading figures of the Robber Council of Ephesus; they were therefore to be treated as removed from the episcopate.

After this, a delay of five days was granted so that each bishop might set forth in writing what he believed, and so that Bishop Anatolius might select certain suitable and competent bishops to discuss the matter, while the rule of faith was deliberated and confirmed.

The faith of the Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople and of the First Council of Ephesus was confirmed, as was the letter of Pope Leo, which is known to have been subscribed by everyone.

Again, when the judges expressed their opinion concerning the bishops Juvenal and Thalassius, Eusebius, Basil, and Eustathius, asking what the council thought [Note: [Col. 1011D] The same codex reads: “what the synod thought”], the entire council cried out:

“God has deposed Dioscorus; God has deposed the murderer.” [Col. 1012B]

Since the council interceded for them because they had agreed to subscribe the aforementioned letter of the pope, and lest a still greater schism arise, they were ordered to remain in the council.

After this, twelve Egyptian bishops presented petitions concerning the faith with derision [Note: [Col. 1011D] The same codex reads: “with an allusion”]. The council judged that they should anathematize Eutyches and subscribe Pope Leo’s *Tome*. They replied that they could not do this until an Alexandrian bishop had been appointed, so that, with his command, they could fulfill the requirement without danger to themselves. They also said that they could not act alone on behalf of the multitude of Egyptian bishops.

It was therefore decreed that, after providing sureties and taking an oath, they should await the appointment of the Alexandrian bishop and then consent and subscribe to all the synodal decrees. [Col. 1012C] A similar arrangement was made at the council for certain archimandrites and monks who offered the same excuse, so that they might receive a delay.

When the fourth session had thus been completed, the fifth session dealt with the following matter. The bishops and judges discussed the confirmation of the faith, and, after the discussion led by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, together with all the metropolitan bishops, a symbol of faith with its definition was drafted and confirmed by everyone.

When Aetius the archdeacon read it aloud, the entire synod acclaimed:

“This is the faith of the Fathers, of Cyril and Leo” [Note: [Col. 1012D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of Cyril and Leo”]. “Many years to the emperors!”

They again requested by acclamation that all the metropolitan bishops and the entire council subscribe it at once, without delay. But the judges postponed this, so that it might first be read to the emperor [Col. 1012D]. When this had been done, the synod was dissolved.

During the sixth session, the emperor Marcian came to the council [Note: [Col. 1012D] The same codex reads: “The emperor came to the session”] together with the judges and the sacred senate. He addressed the council and, among other things, said that he had entered the synod to confirm the faith, not to display power, following the example of Constantine [Note: [Col. 1012D] The same codex reads: “following the example of the emperor Constantine.”] He added:

“Therefore, with every depravity and greed cast aside and the errors of certain persons cut away, let whatever has been established by you be observed forever.”

After the definition of the faith was read [Col. 1013A], it was subscribed without any hesitation by the entire council and by everyone.

During the seventh session, three cases were dealt with, which is why it is counted as comprising three actions.

The first concerned the confirmation of the agreement reached between Maximus, bishop of Antioch, and Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem: the two Phoenician provinces and Arabia were to belong to the see of Antioch, while the three provinces of Palestine were to belong to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1013D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “what had been agreed”].

Another action was also held, in which Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, whom Dioscorus had expelled, was judged orthodox and worthy of his see.

The third action concerned the case of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, who had likewise been violently deposed from the episcopate by Dioscorus. His case was examined, but the final sentence was deferred to another day [Col. 1013B].

During the eighth session—the tenth action—the same case was concluded. The proceedings held before Photianus, Eustathius, and Uranius at Tyre and Berytus were reread; they included the matters concerning his case that had previously been dealt with before the emperor Theodosius.

The proceedings held earlier before Domnus, bishop of Antioch, were also reread, as was Ibas’s letter to Maris the Persian. In the same action this letter was declared orthodox, and from its contents Ibas was judged worthy to recover the episcopate and his Church.

In this action it was also decreed [Note: [Col. 1013D] The same codex reads: “it was also decreed”] that what had been assembled at Ephesus under Dioscorus should not be called a council, and that the emperor should be asked [Col. 1013C] to establish this by law.

During the ninth session, an action was held concerning Bassianus, who had been ordained bishop for the city of the Evazans and had taken possession of the Ephesian Church, and Stephen, who, having himself also been wrongly ordained, had expelled the aforementioned Bassianus from Ephesus. Both were judged to have to be removed, and another person was to be ordained for that Church. But because some held a different opinion, the conclusion of the case was deferred to the following action.

During the tenth session the same case was concluded, and by the unanimous judgment of all, both men were declared subject to removal. Another case [Note: [Col. 1013D] The same codex reads: “another case was conducted”] concerned a dispute between Eunomius of Nicomedia and Anastasius of Nicaea over the city of Basilinopolis: which of them should ordain its bishop. The bishop of Nicaea was forbidden ever to presume to do this [Col. 1013D].

During the eleventh session two actions were held. The first restored Sabinian [Note: [Col. 1014D] The Tellerian Codex reads: “the Church of the Perreans”] to the Church of the Perrhaeans [Note: [Col. 1014D] The same codex reads: “Bassianus”], as bishop. Dioscorus had expelled him and had Athanasius installed in his place. Because of the charges brought against him, and because he repeatedly failed to appear when summoned to judgment and renounced the episcopate, he had previously been condemned by Domnus of Antioch.

The other action took place after the judges, senators, and legates of the apostolic see had withdrawn. Ecclesiastical regulations were established [Col. 1014A], and certain privileges were assigned to the Church of Constantinople, which Anatolius, bishop of that city, arrogated to himself, taking advantage of the condemnation of Dioscorus.

Having learned this on the following day, the legates of Pope Leo—for this was the final, twelfth day of the council—requested that they should again meet with the judges at the council. When they asked what had been decreed on the previous day, the acts were read, and they learned what Anatolius, with the council’s consent, had done and obtained. When they opposed his presumption, that opposition was accepted neither by the judges nor by all the bishops; and although the apostolic see continues to oppose it to this day, what was confirmed by the synod remains, in some fashion, through the emperor’s support.

**[Note: [Col. 1014B] Synod of Chalcedon.]** When Theodosius had died in the year 450, on 29 July, Marcian assumed the imperial power on 23 August. After approximately nine months, in the following year, on 17 May, he ordered a council to be held at Nicaea on the Kalends of September; but afterward he transferred it from Nicaea to Chalcedon, by letters issued on 22 September. The council was therefore begun, and its first session was held on 8 October, which was a Monday; the second on the 10th; the third on the 13th; the fourth on the 17th; the fifth on the 22nd; the sixth on the 25th; the seventh on the 26th; the eighth on the 27th; the ninth on the 29th; the tenth on the 30th; the eleventh on the 31st; and the twelfth on 1 November, on which day the council was concluded.

**“To assemble at Nicaea.”** When Dioscorus arrived at Nicaea with his Egyptians and saw that his affairs were almost hopeless—partly as conscience revealed this to him, and partly as the inclination of people’s minds showed it—he dared to do something by which, if he could not thereby help himself, he might at least perish more notoriously amid the upheaval of the whole Church: he pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the president of the apostolic see [Col. 1014C]. For, in his madness, he hoped that Leo would not preside through his legates, since he was hindered by ecclesiastical bonds, and that thus either Anatolius of Constantinople or Maximus of Antioch would preside; both of them, he thought, would repay the author of their dignity with gratitude.

**“Six hundred and thirty bishops being present.”** There is no single common agreement about the number of the Fathers. It was certainly enormous, which is why Epiphanius of Tyre rightly called it a great synod in the Acts of the Fifth Council of Constantinople under Mennas; and Facundus called it the most numerous, in Book II, chapter 6. Cecropius of Sebastopolis asserted that there were 1,200; Nicephorus, Book XV, chapter 26, 636; Seleucus of Amasia, 630; Lucentius, Leo’s legate, 600; the synodal report to the pope, and the sanction of the emperor Marcian to Palladius the pope, 520; the Brief Account of the Eutychianists, more than 500.

I would prefer to follow this last opinion, since it rests on greater authority—namely, the synodal report—if popular opinion had not followed Liberatus’s view. Evagrius of Epiphaneia, Book II, chapter 2, reports something astonishing about the rhetorician Zachariah: that, moved by a certain emotional inclination, he stated that Nestorius too had been summoned to the council. He himself refutes this account in the following words:

“Yet that the matter was by no means so may be demonstrated by the fact that Nestorius was completely excluded from the council by an anathema. This is also clearly shown by Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, in the letters which he sent both to John the bishop and to another John the presbyter concerning the events discussed in that council. For he writes as follows:

‘Those who diligently seek the remains of Nestorius arrived here [Col. 1015A] and began to cry out against the council in this manner: “Why is an anathema pronounced against holy men?” The emperor, taking this very seriously and bitterly, ordered his attendants to drive them far away from there.’

How, then, Nestorius, who had departed from that place, could have been summoned, I certainly cannot say.”

**“And while they were seated.”** Liberatus seems to imply that the transfer of the synod took place after the legates had taken their seats with the Fathers. From the actual decree of the transfer, however, it is clear that the matter occurred otherwise: see Part I of the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 42.

**“Before the sacred senate.”** By the name “senate,” Liberatus includes precisely eighteen judges; Eulogius must be removed, for his name slipped into the first session. Of those eighteen, ten favored Theodoretus, from whom we know that they had received letters—and some of them more than one. It is therefore no wonder that Theodoretus was admitted so readily to the assembly before his case had been examined, whereas Eusebius, Ibas, and Sabinianus, who belonged to the same party, were not treated in the same way. Nor does it help to argue that he had been restored by the apostolic see [Col. 1015B]. Ibas himself had also been present and acquitted at the Roman council, as had Eusebius; yet Eusebius did not take his seat during the first three sessions.

**“And Lucentius.”** He was bishop of Asculum and, as may be gathered from chapter 2 of this Brief Account, the author of the Chronicle commonly attributed to Prosper. I have demonstrated this in the notes to M. Mercator.

**“The acts of the First Synod of Ephesus were also read.”** Liberatus either speaks obscurely or is mistaken. The acts of the First Synod of Ephesus were not read, except insofar as they had been inserted into the acts of the Second Synod of Ephesus. Hence Aetius requested in the second session that two synodical letters of Cyril be read, since they had not been read at Ephesus during the Second Synod.

**“Session.”** This word is used for an assembly or sitting, since in the manuscript *secretarium* means the place in which the judges sit. From the place, therefore, the word was transferred to the assembly itself.

**“Two letters of Cyril were read.”** Whoever you are who pursue ecclesiastical exactness, see what extensive clarification we have provided concerning these letters of Cyril in Dissertation 2, attached to the second part of the works of M. Mercator [Col. 1015C].

**“From his statements and letters.”** Concerning the testimonies of the Fathers appended to Leo’s letter, it is worthwhile to read what we noted in the preface to Cyril’s scholia in the second part of the works of M. Mercator. They shed extraordinary light on matters otherwise extremely obscure.

**“The third session.”** In it the case of Dioscorus was heard. Since it concerned the bishops exclusively, the judges did not participate, although Dioscorus had requested this.

**“The bishops were sent.”** Observe the custom of summoning patriarchs through three bishops.

**“The sixth session.”** In it the synod reached its conclusion insofar as it concerned the faith.

**“He is shown to have been pronounced orthodox.”** All the defenders of the Three Chapters maintained this on the basis of Paschasinus’s words: “For when his letter had been read, we recognized that he was orthodox” [Greek: *Ἀναγνωσθείσης γὰρ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς αὐτοῦ, ἐπέγνωμεν αὐτὸν ὑπάρχειν ὀρθόδοξον*]; and those of Maximinus of Antioch: “And from the copy of the letter that had been read, his statement was seen to be orthodox” [Greek: *καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἀναγνωσθέντος δὲ ἀντιγράφου τῆς ἐπιστολῆς ὀρθόδοξος ὤφθη αὐτοῦ ἡ ὑπαγορία*] [Col. 1015D]. On this matter, Facundus of Hermiane should be consulted, Books VI and VII. One should also consult the letter to the bishops of Istria written in the name of Pope Pelagius II by Gregory the Great, who was then a deacon.

**“And certain privileges were assigned, and so forth.”** He correctly adds: “Anatolius, bishop of that same city, usurping this for himself, having seized the opportunity provided by the condemnation of Dioscorus.” For he usurped an unlawful presidency when no one protested—for who would have dared to do so in that state of affairs? Certainly not the legates of the apostolic see, who were absent; nor the Alexandrian bishop, since there was none; nor the Egyptians, who scarcely dared to speak because of the synod’s hostility toward them; nor Maximus of Antioch, whose affairs had not yet been firmly settled; nor the court or the senate, which desired to make the New Rome either equal to the Old or at least nearly equal [Col. 1016A].

Nor is there any reason for anyone to claim that the authority of Constantinople had been introduced by custom or sanctioned by the decree of the Second Synod. The Roman Church had not yet received the decree composed at Constantinople, and it is clear from what happened that Constantinople’s claims to jurisdiction were resisted: first, in the case of Chrysostom against the bishops of Asia; and then in the case of Sisinnius, who ordained Proclus, whom the people of Cyzicus rejected after installing Dalmatius in his see.]

## CHAPTER XIV. The Exile of Dioscorus and the Ordination of Proterius as Bishop of Alexandria

*(From the same Brief Account, Priscus the rhetorician, and the pamphlet of the Egyptian bishops to the emperor.)*

When the great and venerable Council of Chalcedon had been completed in twelve sessions and sixteen proceedings [Col. 1016B], Dioscorus was ordered to go into exile in the city of Gangra. The bishops and clerics who had come with him returned to Alexandria: Athanasius, bishop of Busiris; Nestorius, of Phlagon; Auxonius, of Sebennytus; and Macarius, of Chabasa. They had taken their seats at Chalcedon and had anathematized Eutyches and his doctrine, together with the condemnation of Dioscorus, signing Pope Leo’s letter, so that, with the consent of all the citizens, they might elect the bishop who was to be ordained; sacred letters to this effect had first been sent to Theodorus, then Augustal prefect.

The prominent men of the city therefore assembled in order to choose one who was worthy of the episcopate in life and speech. For this was also commanded by the imperial enactments. When considerable uncertainty had arisen over this matter, the citizens wishing to ordain no one at all lest they appear adulterers—for Dioscorus was still alive—the unanimous decision finally inclined toward Proterius. Dioscorus himself had commended the Church to him and had made him archpresbyter. Proterius was therefore ordained [Note: [Col. 1015D] The Tellerius Codex: “Therefore Proterius was ordained.”] and, in the presence of the bishops mentioned above, who, as stated, had subscribed at the synod, was enthroned.

**[Note: [Col. 1016C] Athanasius of Busiris.]** I do not know precisely when those four bishops expressly subscribed either to the condemnation of Dioscorus and Eutyches or to the letter of Saint Leo. For none of their names appears either in the second session, in which Leo’s letter was read; or in the third, in which Dioscorus was condemned together with Eutyches; or in the fourth, in which the subscription to Leo’s letter is recorded. Nevertheless, all are said in the first session to have approved Flavian’s faith, which Dioscorus had proscribed as heretical at the Ephesian Robber Council [Col. 1016D]. This amounted in part to a condemnation of Dioscorus and to assent to Leo’s letter. Moreover, Athanasius himself had consented at that same Robber Council to Flavian’s condemnation, though reluctantly and with groaning. Nestorius was the first to inscribe his name in the pamphlet which, six years ago, after the murder of Proterius, the Egyptian bishops and priests—defenders of the Council of Chalcedon—presented to Emperor Leo against Aelurus. Observe that no Egyptian was present at the second, third, or fourth sessions, when the case of Dioscorus was being heard.

**“With sacred letters issued for this purpose.”** In these letters, I suppose, it was decreed that the bishop should be ordained by no one other than the defenders of the council. Hence the four bishops mentioned above are later named as those who enthroned Proterius. This was the first reason why the Alexandrian Church was divided.

**[Col. 1017A] “He had made him archpresbyter.”** I interpret this term not merely as referring to one who presided over other presbyters, as archpresbyters or vicars of bishops commonly do today, but as referring to a true bishop who exercised all the pontifical functions in the city of Alexandria—like the chorepiscopi of old, the present suffragan bishops, and perhaps coadjutors. This opinion would be supported by Liberatus himself in Baronius under the year 452, no. 19, if the reading were not corrupt; for there *archbishop* is read instead of *archpresbyter*.

**“Lest they appear adulterers.”** Adultery occurs when, while the bridegroom is alive, the bride—the Church—is joined to another. Those guilty of this adultery are both the woman who is joined to another, the man to whom she is joined, and those who either arrange or approve the adulterous marriage, as it were.

**“Therefore Proterius was ordained.”** We placed his ordination at the beginning of the year 452. Victor of Tunnuna postpones it to the following year, when Vincomalus and Opilio held the consulship. This is disproved, however, by the fact that Proterius was killed after he had occupied the see for six years, if we believe Nicephorus of Constantinople [Col. 1017B]. He was killed after the news had been received in Alexandria of the death of the emperor Marcian, which occurred in the year 457, on 26 January. He was therefore killed on 28 March, almost two months after Marcian’s death, since in that year Easter fell on 31 March, and the slaughter occurred three days before Easter, as will be said later.

**“With the consent of all the citizens.”** Evagrius disagrees and states that “Proterius was elected to govern the Alexandrian episcopate by the common votes of the Council of Chalcedon.” Liberatus, however, is more credible than Evagrius.]

## CHAPTER XV. The Ordination of Timothy Aelurus and the Death of Proterius

*(From the Brief Account of the Eutychianists, and from the rhetoricians Zachariah and Priscus. In Evagrius, Book II, chapter 10.)*

After he had been enthroned, division and withdrawal of the people arose [Col. 1017C] [Note: [Col. 1017D] The Tellerius Codex: “The withdrawal of the people took place.”], because Dioscorus was alive and was in exile. Proterius therefore suffered many dangers, so that for much of his episcopate he required military assistance for his protection; nevertheless, until the death of the emperor Marcian he was able to escape the hands of his enemies.

But a certain Timothy, surnamed Aelurus, and the deacon Peter Mog(g)us [Note: [Col. 1017D] The same codex: “Mongus.”], who had been ordained by Dioscorus, separated themselves from the Alexandrian Church, refusing to communicate with Proterius. When Bishop Proterius was unable to recall them both to their proper ministry, he condemned them both.

They, however, taking advantage of the death of the emperor Marcian, gathered mobs of heretics who followed Dioscorus, ordained Timothy Aelurus as bishop, and came to Alexandria. Three days before Easter, on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated [Col. 1017D], the mobs themselves shut Proterius, of holy memory, inside the church to which he had withdrawn out of fear. On that same day he was killed in the baptistery, torn to pieces, thrown out, and his corpse was burned; his ashes were scattered to the winds.

From this Timothy onward, therefore, there began to be two bishops of Alexandria. While they held the churches, they dissolved the unity they had possessed, expelling many orthodox bishops who were under the see of the blessed Mark the Evangelist.

Meanwhile Leo assumed the imperial power, and the complaint of the Catholics concerning so great a crime reached him. Several bishops of the Alexandrian Church, who had been expelled from their sees by Timothy, went up to the imperial city accompanied by some clerics. They presented petitions to the emperor Leo, asking that the death of Proterius be avenged and that Timothy Aelurus be expelled from the episcopal see as one who had not been lawfully appointed.

The bishops and clerics who defended the Council of Chalcedon took these actions. But some bishops and clerics from Timothy’s side also went up, acting as Timothy Aelurus’s delegation, and they too presented petitions to the emperor. They repeatedly acted against the synod, asking that the Council of Chalcedon be abolished; while those on Proterius’s side, by contrast, demanded vengeance for the crime [Note: [Col. 1018D] The Tellerius Codex: “They demanded vengeance.”].

[Col. 1018B] When the emperor read the petitions of both parties and considered it excessively burdensome for priests to be troubled by so long a journey—since age, illness, or poverty prevented some of them from undertaking the labor—he judged it impossible to assemble them. Instead, he wrote to the bishops of the individual cities concerning both matters, asking what ought to be done regarding Timothy’s ordination and the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. He sent *magistriani* throughout the East, and Bishop Anatolius also sent his deacon Asclepiades. Through these messengers all the bishops who had assembled at Chalcedon were to learn what had happened at Alexandria.

They replied that the Council of Chalcedon must be defended even to the shedding of blood, because it held no other faith than that established by the Council of Nicaea [Col. 1018C]. Timothy, moreover, was not merely to be excluded from the number of bishops but also deprived of the Christian name. These letters, or reports, of all the bishops are called *Encyclica* in a single codex.

Having done this, the emperor Leo wrote to Stila, the duke of Alexandria, instructing him to expel Timothy from the episcopate by every means and to enthrone another bishop, chosen by the decision of the people, who would defend the synod.

**[Note: [Col. 1018C] “Proterius therefore suffered many dangers.”]** Concerning the riots stirred up in Alexandria by the people, who passionately loved Dioscorus and were hostile to Proterius, read Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 5, and also Theophanes in his *Chronographia*.

**“Until the death of Marcian.”** The most pious emperor died on 26 January, in the sixty-fourth year of his age, the seventh year of his reign, in the year of Christ 457. Proterius therefore occupied the see for five years and a few months; because of those months, Nicephorus of Constantinople said six years [Col. 1018D].

**“But a certain Timothy.”** This entire section has been taken from the frequently cited Brief Account, with a few words interpolated.

**“Three days before Easter.”** Since this section too was taken from the Brief Account, it may be seen from that source how the statement of Liberatus should be emended: he says that Proterius took refuge in the church out of fear, whereas the Brief Account has the customary reading. That reading might be considered preferable, since the time was one when the solemn baptism was soon to be celebrated, if the pamphlet presented to the emperor Leo by the Catholic bishops of Egypt, and Evagrius in Book II, chapter 8, following the historian Zachariah, did not agree with Liberatus in similar terms. They likewise report what Liberatus omitted, together with the author of the Brief Account: that Proterius was killed by a soldier and that his entrails were devoured by the raging crowd [Col. 1019A].

The Zachariah I mentioned is remembered by Evagrius in the passage just cited, by Nicephorus Callistus, and by Antonius Verderius in the supplement to Gesner’s *Bibliotheca*, and finally by Vossius in his *Greek Histories*. Verderius testifies that Zachariah’s history exists in manuscript, but, as far as I know, it has not yet been published.

Contrary to what Liberatus writes—that Proterius was shut up by the mobs in the church three days before Easter, on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated, and was killed there in the baptistery on that same day—stands Victor of Tunnuna, who places his death on “the sixth day before the Kalends of April, the sixth day of the week, on which our Savior and Lord was crucified by the Jews.” The frequently cited Brief Account supports Liberatus; against both stands the petition of the Egyptians to the emperor Leo. For they report that this slaughter took place when the solemn feast of saving Easter was being celebrated.

The dispute over four days is of little importance. More significant is that Tunnunensis reports that the Lord’s Easter was celebrated then on the fourth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 1019B], whereas in the year 457 the dominical letter was F, and thus Easter Sunday fell on the day before the Kalends of April. Perhaps an error entered the dates expressed in larger letters, so that IV was written for II, since the ancients used II Kalends for the day before, as Cicero does in Book XV, Letter 28: “The day before I wrote this, that is, the second day before the Nones.”

**“And while they held the churches.”** Either some inappropriate parenthesis must be recognized, or it must be admitted that something is missing for the sentence to be clear. But what can one do with an author careless both of Latin and of ornament?

**“Petitions were presented by them.”** They are found in Part III of the Council of Chalcedon, chapters 21 and 22. Aelurus also wrote to the emperor, but the letter has perished.

**[Col. 1019C] “Because it held no other faith.”** This was the common complaint, whether of the monks or of others who opposed the Council of Chalcedon: that the confession of faith issued at Chalcedon was different from that of Nicaea.

**“And these letters.”** Evagrius, drawing on the two authors Priscus and Zachariah, reports that all the letters were collected into one volume called *τὰ Ἐγκύκλια* (“the Encyclical Letters”). They are found in Part III of the Council of Chalcedon. All are synodical letters except the one written by the monk Varadatus, or Baradatus; for the names of the metropolitans and the bishops of the provinces are appended to all the others.

There is no settled agreement about how many bishops responded to the emperor. Eulogius of Alexandria counts 1,600, in Photius, codices 230 and 229. Ephraemius of Antioch counts only 570. I have observed that no synodical letter from the province of Euphratesia, of which Theodoretus was a bishop, is included among the others, nor any from Second Cilicia, where Mopsuestia is located.]

## CHAPTER XVI. The Ordination of Timothy the Catholic and Peter the Heretic

*(From the Brief Account of the Eutychianists, and from the rhetoricians Priscus and Zachariah.)*

Having received the order, Duke Stila did what had been commanded. Timothy Aelurus was sent into exile at Cherson under strict guard, and Timothy, surnamed Salophaciolus, or Asbus, was appointed in place of Proterius [Note: [Col. 1019D] The Tellerius Codex: “or Asbus; and Peter the heretic fled.”].

This Timothy, the bishop of the Catholics, lived peacefully in the Alexandrian Church without sedition throughout the entire reign of Leo and the entire reign of Zeno, until Basiliscus seized the tyranny and Zeno fled into Isauria.

When Basiliscus had obtained the imperial power, he wrote his decree to the whole world, which he called an encyclical against the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 1020A]. At that time, when Basiliscus restored the episcopate to Timothy Aelurus and the heretics to their sees, Timothy the Catholic fled to the fortress of Canopus and hid in a monastery. Peter the heretic again joined himself to Timothy, with whom he had previously been condemned.

After the emperor Zeno had returned to power, Timothy Aelurus, fearing the zeal that Zeno displayed concerning the Council of Chalcedon, wished for death. Persistently praying for this, he freed himself from human life by drinking poison. His followers say that he foresaw the day of his death; and in truth, since he was preparing to kill himself with poison, he knew it.

After his death, the heretics ordained for themselves a bishop, Peter, surnamed Mog(g)us, who was called Blaesus and had been archdeacon. At that time Timothy the Catholic was, as stated, staying in the fortress of Canopus.

When the emperor Zeno learned of the heretics’ cunning, he wrote to Anthemius, the Augustal prefect, ordering him to deprive Peter of the priesthood, restore Timothy to the episcopate, and punish the authors of Peter’s enthronement. Anthemius, having received the imperial order, expelled Peter from the priesthood as an adulterer and as one who had acted contrary to the laws of the Catholic Church. He restored Timothy Salophaciolus to the episcopal see. After receiving the episcopate, Timothy sent several clerics to give thanks to the emperor.

Among them was John, who had been made a presbyter from the position of steward of the Tabennesiotes and was surnamed Talaia, and Gennadius, bishop of Lower Hermopolis, a blood relative of Salophaciolus. Aelurus had expelled Gennadius from the episcopate, but Salophaciolus had restored him. When those who had been sent had given thanks to the emperor, Gennadius remained there in order to send replies from the archbishop together with the others.

John, who, after having been a steward, became a friend of the master Illus, descended with the others to Alexandria. He was again made steward, having charge of the affairs of all the churches. He sent many costly gifts to the master Illus, while scorning Gennadius, the archbishop’s relative, and Acacius, the bishop of Constantinople.

Meanwhile Timothy wrote to Pope Simplicius, asking and stating that that Peter Mog(g)us had been condemned while still a deacon and had now also been removed from Christian fellowship [Col. 1020D]. He likewise wrote to the emperor, asking that the same Peter be sent into more distant exile, since he was hiding in Alexandria and plotting against the Church. Pope Simplicius wrote to Bishop Acacius, asking him to urge the emperor to grant Timothy’s just request.

But Timothy was so gentle in his episcopate that even his own communicants accused him before the emperor of being excessively lenient and too mild toward the heretics. Thus the emperor wrote to him ordering him not to permit the heretics to celebrate either assemblies or baptisms [Note: [Col. 1020D] The Tellerius Codex: “not permit him to celebrate with the heretics.”]. Nevertheless, he continued to act gently. While he governed the episcopate in this manner, the Alexandrians loved him and shouted to him in the streets and in the churches: “Even if we do not communicate with you, nevertheless we love you.”

After a short time Timothy Salophaciolus died, in the twenty-third year of his episcopate and the sixth month. He died without trouble.

**[Note: [Col. 1021A] “Under strict guard.”]** Baronius disputes Liberatus, relying on the testimony of Saint Leo, Letters 100 and 101, where Leo writes that Aelurus was permitted to come to the royal city, since he had requested this in order to recover his see by means of a false profession of faith. He could, however, first have come to the royal city and afterward have been held under strict guard in exile at Cherson.

**“He wrote to the whole world.”** Once against the Council of Chalcedon, at the instigation of Timothy Aelurus, who was then staying in the royal city; and again in favor of the council, Acacius having compelled him together with several holy monks [Col. 1021B]. Both decrees are found in Evagrius, Book III.

Observe, reader, that the former was issued by Basiliscus at the urging of his wife Zenonis. Consider also, as you review the whole of this history, that three exceedingly impure women fought with all the resources of powerful wickedness against the council that the holy virgin Pulcheria had devoutly taken care to convene: Zenonis, the wife of Basiliscus; Antonina, the wife of Belisarius; and Theodora, the wife of Justinian.

**“So that he might send replies with the others.”** This was a custom of the Alexandrian Church, not equally adopted in other churches: to maintain representatives at court, not merely deacons or presbyters but also bishops. Cyril had Theopemptus and Daniel, although, in my opinion, one should adopt the distinction Liberatus seems to suggest, namely, that presbyters served as representatives of the Church, while bishops served as representatives of the patriarchs.

**“He who had been a steward.”** It is astonishing how many stewards of churches, throughout all the past centuries, have abused their administration and purchased friendships with the patrimony of the poor. This John certainly gave many costly gifts to his patron [Col. 1021C], and Zachariah the rhetorician, in Evagrius, Book III, chapter 12, says that he was elected bishop after money had been paid.

**“The master Illus.”** All the other writers call him Illus. He was consul in the year 478; afterward he became involved in many other affairs and was made commander of the East by Zeno in the year 480. Finally, when he was said to be aspiring to tyranny, he was beheaded. See Theophanes in his *Chronographia*.

**“Having charge of the affairs of all the churches.”** The illustrious Valesius thinks that the word should be corrected from *causas* (“affairs”) to *gazas* (“treasures”). This emendation had once occurred to me, but immediately I remembered the jurist who interprets *causa* as the money itself.

**“In the twenty-third year of his episcopate.”** Victor may appear to contradict this by placing Salophaciolus’s accession during the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius, which occurred in the year 460, and his departure after the third consulship of Zeno, which marks the year 480. The letters of Simplicius to Acacius, however, dated to the year 482, support Liberatus; they mention that Salophaciolus had recently died [Col. 1021D]. Victor must therefore be corrected, as must Baronius, who places Salophaciolus’s accession in the year 460. For how could it be true that in the year 482 Salophaciolus had occupied the see for twenty-three years and six months? His accession must therefore be moved back to the year 459.

Nicephorus of Constantinople must also be corrected in his *Chronicle*, where he assigns Salophaciolus only fifteen years, unless one says that he omitted the period during which Salophaciolus was in hiding, while Aelurus held the Alexandrian Church under tyranny. Yet even this remedy does not cure the difficulty; rather, a greater problem arises from the year in which Zeno’s *Henoticon* was written. For if it was issued, as is commonly reported, in the year 482, and John Talaia was expelled after the *Henoticon* was written, as Liberatus relates, and John occupied the see for three years, as Nicephorus states, how could Salophaciolus, whose successor he was, have died in the year 482?]

## CHAPTER XVII. The Ordination of John the Catholic and the Condemnation of Acacius

*(From the Brief Account of the History of the Eutychianists, from the two rhetoricians mentioned above, and also from Eustathius the Syrian.)*

John, formerly a steward and surnamed Talaia, was ordained by the bishops, clerics, and monks who communicated with him and knew his faith and administration.

At the same time, while Zeno was emperor, Simplicius presided over the Roman Church, and Acacius over the Constantinopolitan Church.

As has already been said, the heretics had secretly appointed Peter, whom the emperor Zeno ordered to be expelled as a heretic and adulterer. Concerning him Acacius also sent a synodical letter to the Roman pope, asking that he not receive an adulterer and heretic into episcopal dignity [Col. 1022B].

John Talaia, however, neglected to send his synodical letter concerning his ordination to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople. For, having the aforementioned master Illus as a friend, he wrote to him concerning his ordination. He also wrote to the emperor, asking that his entire case be arranged through the master Illus [Note: [Col. 1021D] The Tellerius Codex: “through the master Illus.”], thinking that Illus would remain in Constantinople. He therefore entrusted a magistrianus with the synodical letter, delegating everything to him to do according to Illus’s wishes.

At that time, however, the master Illus was sent by the emperor Zeno to Antioch to apprehend Leontius, who had been ordained there by the army with the approval of the empress Verina. When the magistrianus sent by John did not find the master Illus, he did not deliver the letter to Acacius, but proceeded to Antioch.

After this Acacius heard about John’s ordination and was distressed because John had not sent the synodical letters. He joined forces with Bishop Gennadius, a relative of the blessed Timothy, and, wishing to harm John, they disparaged him before Zeno. They accused him with the assistance of Peter Mog(g)us’s patrons, as though John were unfit for the episcopate: while Timothy the Catholic was alive, he had supposedly attempted to leave the Church; Timothy himself had been persuaded by him to receive Dioscorus into the diptychs after Dioscorus’s death; Peter, moreover, was dear to the people and could gather them into communion.

Some people from Peter’s side arrived, wishing, as it were, to establish unity. Acacius received them with great pleasure, presented them to the emperor, and persuaded him to write to Apollonius, the Augustal prefect, and to Duke Pergamius, ordering them to expel John from the Alexandrian see, on the pretext that he had seized it contrary to his oath, which he had sworn in the imperial city. They were also to cooperate with Peter Mog(g)us so that he might return to his see, but were not to do this until he had accepted the emperor’s *Henoticon* and sent synodical letters to Acacius of Constantinople, to Simplicius of Rome, and to the other archbishops.

Acacius, however, when Peter promised to establish unity but had not yet lawfully fulfilled his promise, permitted his name to be recited in the diptychs as though he were already installed as bishop of Alexandria [Col. 1023A] [Note: [Col. 1023D] The Tellerius Codex: “as though he were already installed as bishop in the apostolic see.”]. John Talaia was judged by Zeno to be expelled from the episcopate.

With the assistance of Peter’s patrons, Acacius persuaded Zeno to issue the *Henoticon*.
