At its promulgation or profession, he received into communion with himself Peter’s heretical clerics and the laypeople found in Constantinople. Peter Mog(g)us too entered into communion with those who descended with the *Henoticon*, wrote a synodical letter to Acacius, and received one from him.

Zeno’s *Henoticon*, which we may render in Latin as “the Instrument of Unity,” is as follows:

> **“The emperor Caesar Zeno, pious, victorious, triumphant, greatest, ever august, to all the holy bishops and to the peoples throughout Alexandria, Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis.**
>
> **[Col. 1023B]** Knowing that the beginning, stability, power, and invincible shield of our empire is the one true and orthodox faith—which the 318 holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea expounded under divine inspiration, and which the 150 equally holy Fathers who assembled at Constantinople confirmed—we strive night and day, through prayer, diligence, and laws, to see that it is multiplied throughout the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, incorruptible and undying, the mother of our scepters. In the peace and harmony that exists with God, we desire the pious peoples, persevering in these things, to offer acceptable supplications for our empire, together with the most holy archbishops, God-fearing clerics, and archimandrites.
>
> **[Col. 1023C]** For when the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ was incarnate and born from the holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and glorification and worship are praised and received together in harmony, the generations of enemies will indeed be crushed, and all will bow, after God, their necks to our authority. Peace and the good things that come from it, temperate weather, and abundance of fruits will be granted, as well as other things useful to human beings.
>
> Since, therefore, the undefiled faith preserves both us and the Roman state, supplications have been presented to us by God-loving archimandrites, hermits, and other venerable men. They plead for unity in the most holy Church, so that members may be joined to members—members which the enemy of Goodness has attempted to separate from long ages past [Col. 1023D], knowing that he is defeated when he wages war against the united body of the Church. From this it has happened that countless generations, throughout so many years, have been deprived of life: some have died defrauded of the bath of regeneration; others, never receiving holy communion, have been led to the unavoidable departure of human beings; murders have been perpetrated ten thousand times; and through the overflowing of blood not only the earth but even the air itself has been polluted.”

How could anyone not wish to transform these things into blessings? For this reason we have taken pains to ascertain that neither we, nor anywhere the most holy orthodox Churches, have had, have, or shall have—and that we know of no one who has—any other creed, teaching, definition of faith, or confession apart from the aforementioned holy symbol of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, which the aforesaid one hundred and fifty holy Fathers also confirmed. If anyone has such a thing, we regard him as alien. For we confidently believe that this alone preserves our empire. Moreover, all peoples who receive saving baptism are baptized by receiving this alone. This is what all the holy Fathers followed who assembled at Ephesus and deposed the impious Nestorius together with Eutyches.

We anathematize those who think otherwise, and we accept the twelve chapters said to have been composed by Cyril, of blessed and God-loving memory, who was archbishop of the Catholic Church of Alexandria.

[Col. 1024B] We confess the only-begotten Son and God, who in truth became human: our Lord Jesus Christ, consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and consubstantial with us according to his humanity; the same one who descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin, Mother of God, to be one Son and not two. For we say that both the miracles and the sufferings which he willingly endured in the flesh belong to the one only-begotten Son of God.

But those who divide, confuse, or introduce an appearance we altogether reject, because the incarnation in truth, accomplished without sin from the Mother of God, did not produce an increase in the Son. The Trinity remained the Trinity even when one of the Trinity, God the Word, became incarnate.

[Col. 1024C] Knowing, therefore, that neither the most holy orthodox Churches everywhere, nor their most God-loving priests, nor our empire have received or receive any creed or definition of faith apart from the aforesaid holy teaching, unite yourselves without hesitation. We have written these things not to innovate in the faith but to satisfy you. We anathematize everyone who has thought, thinks, or shall at any time think anything else—whether at Chalcedon or in any other synod—and especially the aforementioned Nestorius and Eutyches and those who hold their opinions.

Unite yourselves, therefore, to the spiritual mother, the Church, thinking as we do and remaining in the same communion according to the aforesaid one and only definition of faith of those same holy Fathers. For our most holy mother, the Church, who gave birth to you, awaits the embrace of her children after so long a time and longs to hear your sweet voice. Consider your own interests: by doing these things you will draw toward yourselves the propitiation of our Savior and Lord, and you will be praised by our empire.” 

[Note: [Col. 1024D]]

“Letter.” A fragment is preserved in Letter 14 of Gelasius.

“Synodical letters.” Note the origin of the great schism. It was customary for the bishops of every major see, including the apostolic see, as soon as they had been ordained, to send letters from the synod of their ordination to the other patriarchs; these letters were a token of communion. John sent such letters to Simplicius of Rome through the presbyter Isidore and the deacon Peter. He likewise sent them to Calendion of Antioch through Ello, a *magistrianus* who had been dispatched for that purpose. No letters were sent to Acacius, either through negligence or deliberately. Acacius, treating this as an insult, stirred up disturbances that grievously afflicted the whole Church.

Bernardinus Ferrarius, *On the Antiquity of the Church*, book II, letter, chapter 6, seems cautiously to agree with Baronius, who writes that letters of this kind were sent by the supreme pontiffs and were therefore called “synodical,” because they were issued from the synods in which the pontiffs were ordained. Ferrarius inclines rather to the view that they derived their name either because they contained the faith established in preceding synods or because, once received, they had to be read aloud in the synods.

But whether this should lessen his hesitation or overturn his opinion, it ought to have been settled by the constant custom—one which I am surprised did not return to the learned man’s memory, since it is recorded in all histories and writings of the period. For the supreme pontiffs were ordained only in synods, from which letters were sent to the other bishops. Moreover, one more often reads “synodical letters” in the plural than in the singular, not because the name of the letters is understood in the plural, but because two letters were written: one by the pontiff and the other by the synod. The pontiff thereby gave an account of his faith and granted and received mutual communion; the synod added authority to the pontiff’s letter and testified to the agreement of the Church.

“As though he were not suitable for the episcopate.” He seems to offer two reasons why John was unfit to become a bishop, but the first is difficult to understand if it differs from the second. For what does “he attempted to leave the Church” mean, unless perhaps it was because he could have appeared at that time to wish to pass over to the heretics, when he urged Timothy to enter Dioscorus’s name in the sacred diptychs? Such communion with a heretic is in some measure a defection from the Church. Or perhaps he planned, while serving as Timothy’s envoy, to leave the Alexandrian Church in which he was serving and transfer to another, such as the Church of Constantinople? A cleric who had shown contempt for a Church in preference to another would formerly have been regarded as unworthy to govern it.

[Col. 1025C] Liberatus shortly afterward touches on a much more probable explanation, which Evagrius, book III, chapter 12, sets out from Zacharias the rhetorician in these words:

“John the presbyter, to whom the administration of the august temple of the holy John the Baptist and Forerunner of the Lord had been entrusted, came to Constantinople at the urging of certain persons, to ask the emperor that, if the bishop of Alexandria should happen to die, he might be permitted to name as bishop whichever citizen of that city he wished. As Zacharias records, he was discovered to be seeking the episcopate for himself from the emperor. After binding himself by an oath that he would never seek the Alexandrian episcopal see, he returned home. Therefore Zeno decreed that after Timothy’s death he should be made bishop, provided that the clergy and the multitude of the laity chose him. Not long afterward, when Timothy had died, John was elected bishop of Alexandria after paying a sum of money—as the same Zacharias relates—and disregarding the oath he had given the emperor. When the emperor learned of this, he ordered him to be expelled from Alexandria.”

“To receive Dioscorus.” Timothy committed this offense at John’s urging, so that he might enjoy peace with the people, who were extraordinarily devoted to Dioscorus. But afterward he repented of the deed and asked Pope Simplicius for pardon, as is clear from Simplicius’s Letter 11 to Acacius of Constantinople.

“He presented him to the emperor.” It had become customary for the bishop of the imperial city to bring visiting bishops from elsewhere, including legates of the apostolic see, into the presence of the emperor. This is shown by Pope Hormisdas in the instructions he gave to his envoys to Anastasius.

“Henoticon was produced.” Concerning the *henoticon*, that is, the decree of union, take the following points briefly.

1. It is preserved in Greek in Evagrius, book III, chapter 12.

2. The translation used by Liberatus is the work of someone ignorant of Latin, who everywhere and repeatedly distorts the sense.

3. It was composed by the emperor, who usurped the pontiff’s authority—or rather by Acacius, who inscribed the emperor’s name—and by the very ministers of Peter.

4. It was directed specifically to the Alexandrians, and therefore contains nothing—not even the name of Dioscorus—that could offend them even slightly.

5. The Alexandrians received it with a favorable disposition because it approved Cyril’s twelve chapters, which they boasted contained their own faith.

6. It is composed in such ambiguous terms that none of the contending parties could fail to twist it, in some fashion, to its own interpretation.

7. It decrees that no other creed is to be admitted except the Nicene Creed, which had been confirmed at Constantinople and Ephesus.

8. It is silent about Chalcedon; by this silence, the Chalcedonian exposition of the faith may be understood to have been rejected.

“Everyone, however, etc.” This entire *pericope*—without naming them—refers to Theodoret and Ibas, whom the Council of Chalcedon received, although their adversaries claimed that they favored Nestorius and had pronounced an anathema against him only fictitiously. See the account of the conference between the Catholics and the Severians of Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Alexandrian Bishops

*(From the Brief Account, Zacharias, and Basil the Cilician.)*

After these events, the bishop of Antioch received John Talaia’s synodical letter, which John had sent through the *magistriani* of Ello the master. But the emperor, believing that John was not sound in his views concerning the Council of Chalcedon and was acting deceitfully in everything, wrote, at Acacius’s counsel, to Pergamius the *dux* and Apollonius the *augustalis*, instructing them to expel John Talaia and enthrone Peter, who accepted the *henoticon* and the clergy of Timothy the Catholic, and who had sent his synodical letter to Acacius and to Simplicius of Rome.

[Col. 1026C] Abbot Ammon and those who were with him therefore went down to Alexandria, carrying imperial documents on Peter’s behalf. Peter was enthroned by everyone, and the emperor’s written order was carried out: he was to receive those who agreed with the party of Timothy the Catholic.

John Talaia, expelled from the Alexandrian see because of Peter Moggus, went to Antioch to see Ello the *magistrianus*. After relating to him what had happened, he entered, on Ello’s advice, to see Calendion, patriarch of Antioch. Having received from him synodical letters of intercession, he appealed to the Roman pontiff Simplicius, as blessed Athanasius had done.

He also persuaded him to write on his behalf to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople; and Simplicius was indeed already favorably disposed and willing to do so.

But when Acacius received Simplicius’s letters, he replied that he did not recognize John as bishop of Alexandria, whereas he had received Peter Moggus into communion through the unifying decree of the emperor Zeno. He added that he had done this contrary to the judgment of the apostolic see and of Acacius himself, for the sake of the unity of the Churches and by order of the emperor.

When Simplicius received such a letter, he was grieved and wrote back to Acacius that he had acted wrongly by receiving a heretical man into communion contrary to the judgment of the apostolic see. A man condemned by a common decree as an adulterer ought to have been released from condemnation by a common council. Moreover, it was not enough for Peter to confess that he was a member of the Catholic Church according to the edict; he had to embrace the communion of the Church according to the definition of the Council of Chalcedon and according to the letter of Pope Leo. He therefore had to do one of two things: either persuade Peter to accept the definition of the synod purely and without qualification, or withdraw from communion with him.

But when this letter reached Acacius and he was considering what reply he ought to make, Pope Simplicius died, and Felix was ordained bishop of the Roman Church.

John Talaia, retaining the dignity of a bishop, remained at Rome. The pope gave him the Church of Nola in the region of Campania. He lived there for many years and died in peace.

Peter Moggus, however, having suffered attacks from Abbot Ammon, John the bishop of Magidos, and the abbots of the monks of Lower Egypt, and after a riot had supposedly been raised against him in the Caesarean basilica, anathematized the Council of Chalcedon and the tome of Pope Leo. He did this even though he had already written to Acacius and Simplicius that he was in communion with them and with the holy synod.

After these events, some withdrew from communion with Peter and came to Rome to report to the pope. A reply was therefore sent to Acacius, but he refused to obey.

Acacius added that, concerning another Peter, a heretic of Antioch, he had written that Peter had governed a monastery at Constantinople but, because of crimes, had abandoned it and fled to Antioch. There, after the Catholic bishop Martyrius had been expelled, he had occupied his see through a most contemptible and heretical populace. He was immediately condemned by the bishops and, by order of the emperor Leo, deported to the Oasian region. It is said that, after escaping, he returned to Constantinople and gave a pledge that he would dare nothing by means of the most contemptible mobs; but, as stated above, in the time of Basiliscus he was sent to Antioch by that condemned Timothy, who had come to Constantinople, to hold the episcopate there.

After this, the same Peter ordained John bishop of Apamea. Since the people there did not receive him, he returned to Antioch, expelled Peter, the author of his episcopate, from his see, and invaded his Church; Peter and John were condemned together.

Acacius again sent letters to Rome, asking the apostolic see that, if these men should happen to flee there, they not even be considered worthy of being seen; and that, if they had already obtained some pardon, it should be regarded as invalid.

[Col. 1027D] Why say more? Acacius sent John himself—the man whom he had condemned together with Peter—to preside over the Church of Tyre.

As for Peter of Alexandria, who anathematized the Council of Chalcedon and the tome of Pope Leo, removed the names of Proterius and Timothy the Catholic from the diptychs, and wrote in the names of Dioscorus and Timothy Aelurus; who lifted the body of that same Timothy the Catholic from the ground and threw it outside, although he had been buried among the Catholic bishops—Acacius pursued him with extraordinary praises, despite remembering that he had previously reported such serious crimes about him.

Although Acacius had repeatedly been admonished for five years to relieve the concern of the holy pope regarding the condition of the Alexandrian Church, he never deigned to give any reply. Since so many letters sent either by the pope to Acacius or to the emperor accomplished absolutely nothing, Vitalis and Misenus were sent as envoys, by deliberation of the Roman synod, to present the matters described above and to have Peter expelled from the Alexandrian Church as before.

They went to Constantinople, and the aforementioned bishops were placed under guard. Their documents were taken away so that they could not be delivered to the Catholics to whom they had been written. Afterward Acacius released them from custody and made them proceed with him, so that they might be dismissed as though Peter’s priesthood had been confirmed.

The envoys eventually returned, but monks had gone ahead of them and accused them vigorously of treachery.

[Note: [Col. 1027D] The Tellerius Codex reads: “pressed them hard concerning treachery.”]

They were heard face to face and convicted from the very letters they had brought, and were removed from their respective positions.

Felix, the defender of the Church, had been sent with the envoys but, prevented by illness, could not travel with them. After Vitalis and Misenus had left custody at Constantinople, however, he went there with the ecclesiastical documents. He too suffered the gravest imprisonment after the documents had been taken away.

When Acacius was thus fully exposed as a heretic, Pope Felix wrote to him in his synodical letters: “You have sinned; do not add to it, and implore pardon for your former offenses.”

After receiving this letter, Acacius persisted. He neither withdrew from communion with Peter nor openly urged him to accept the Council of Chalcedon and the tome of Pope Leo.

When Pope Felix learned this, he sent Acacius a document of condemnation through the defender Tutus, beginning: “You are found guilty of many transgressions.” After Acacius received such a letter, he refused to accept it, relying on the emperor’s protection. The bearers of the letter were therefore forced, through a certain monk,

[Note: [Col. 1028D] The Tellerius Codex reads: “through a certain unknown monk.”]

to hang the very document of condemnation on his cloak as he entered to celebrate the sacred rites, and then depart. Nevertheless, with the emperor’s protection, he continued to celebrate until his death.

After these events, while Acacius remained in communion with Peter, the apostolic see separated itself from the see of Constantinople.

[Col. 1028D] At the same time, Ello, together with Leontius, was defeated in Antioch by the Valamerians and those allied with them. Leontius was killed, while Ello fled to the fortress of Papyrius.

Meanwhile Calendion, archbishop of Antioch, was deposed. He was publicly accused of being disloyal to the emperor and of inciting the people to rebellion together with Ello; secretly, however, the charge was that he had not suspended communion with either Pope Felix or John.

Peter expelled the Catholic priests from their own cities. Some of them endured a most severe persecution at Constantinople. The emperor also scandalized those who belonged to the party of Abbot Nephalius and those associated with John the bishop and hegumen of the monastery of Diolchos. Acting against John himself, he deprived him of his office and handed it over to the monastery of Abbot Ammon.

Peter nevertheless remained in the episcopate, writing to Acacius that he was in communion with the synod, while deceiving the Alexandrians by claiming that he was not in communion with the synod. Consequently, some of his communicants—clergy, monks, and laypeople—recognized his deception and separated themselves from his communion. Holding assemblies apart, they refused to communicate in his name or in the name of those who later held the Alexandrian episcopate, because they had Peter’s name in the diptychs.

A certain deacon named Esaias was ordained bishop for this people in Palestine and sent to Alexandria, but he was received by no one. His followers in Egypt were therefore called Esaians.

[Col. 1029B] While the Church remained in this condition, Acacius died. After him the presbyter Flavitas was ordained. He had been connected with Saint Thecla and refused to be enthroned without the Roman bishop; instead, he sent a synodical letter to Pope Felix of Rome. Felix lived only a short time and died without receiving Flavitas’s letter. Euphemius, an Alexandrian by birth, then became bishop. He received letters from the Roman pope; after Zeno’s death, however, he was expelled by Anastasius. These events took place at Constantinople.

Not long afterward Peter Moggus also died at Alexandria, and Athanasius was ordained to that see after him. He too, through the unifying edict, entered into communion with the Churches of Constantinople, Antioch, and Jerusalem.

When the people were scandalized by him as well, because he had Peter’s name in the diptychs, some of both the opposing party and those in communion with him went up to the emperor Anastasius. While they were disputing before the emperor, some proposed that the synod should be anathematized and that they should commune on that basis; others were prepared for the unifying edict to have additions made that would satisfy those who had been in communion with Peter.

The emperor considered that, if he added anything to the edict, he would provoke a disturbance in the Church, while anathematizing the synod was impossible. He persuaded them that the unifying edict was sufficient for them to commune with one another, just as the other bishops of the Churches did. When they refused to do this, he dismissed them without granting anything.

Thus, when Athanasius the heretic had completed the term of his episcopate, John, an Alexandrian surnamed Mela, was ordained bishop of Alexandria after him. He too followed Peter and Athanasius, his predecessors,

[Note: [Col. 1029D] The Tellerius Codex reads: “followed Athanasius.”]

and through the unifying edict entered into communion with the other sees, namely Constantinople, Antioch, and Jerusalem. During his episcopate, while the Alexandrian Church was divided on account of the Dioscorites because of Peter Moggus—as though he had entered into communion with the synod—he also died, in the time of Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople.

After him John Machiota was ordained at Alexandria.

[Col. 1030A] He too followed his predecessors, accepting Zeno’s unifying edict but not the Council of Chalcedon or the letter of Pope Leo, although he did not commune with Flavian of Antioch, Elias of Jerusalem, or Timothy of Constantinople. For he said that the edict was defective and insufficient for unity because it had not anathematized the synod.

When the emperor Anastasius later wrote to him that he should unite himself with the bishop of Constantinople, he replied: “It would not be sufficient for perfect unity, since it does not anathematize the synod.”

Yet even while holding this position, he kept the Dioscorites separate because they did not receive Peter Moggus.

After John’s death at Alexandria, Dioscorus the Younger was ordained.

[Col. 1030B] During his episcopate, Theodosius, son of Calliopas the *augustalis*, was killed by the people.

This Dioscorus, when the scholasticus Socrates proposed to him, before the defender, that he accept the *henoticon* in the expulsion of the synod, accepted the unifying edict for the condemnation of the synod. The proceedings drawn up before him in the presence of the city’s defender themselves demonstrate this: in the expulsion of the synod he testified that he accepted the edict. Consequently, when those who had been communicating outside that Church because of Peter Moggus had been satisfied, they united themselves to him. For until this Dioscorus, the Alexandrian Church had remained divided.

[Note: [Col. 1030B]]

“On the Alexandrian Bishops.” The title should have been expanded, had the established reading custom not stood in the way. In printed books it is wrongly placed before the *henoticon*; it has been restored to its proper place.

[Col. 1030C] For the subject of the chapter does not fit very well, since it concerns not only the Alexandrians but also the Antiochenes and Constantinopolitans, especially Acacius. I suspect, however, that formerly several chapters were carelessly joined into one by scribes.

“Was not sound in his views.” The negative particle ought to be deleted. Otherwise, what reason could the emperor have had for expelling the man from the Alexandrian see? The emperor had tacitly rejected the Council of Chalcedon in the *henoticon*, the Alexandrian Church openly rejected it, and Moggus, who was to be preferred to Talaia, would also have condemned it by anathema. Nevertheless, the particle may be retained because of what Baronius ingeniously conjectures concerning the cunning of Zeno and Acacius, who accommodated themselves to the times, under the year 482, no. 35 and following.

“To Calendion.” He succeeded Stephen in the year 481, as I believe. For in Letter 16, sent to Acacius on the Ides of July in the year 482, Simplicius complains that the beginning of the Antiochene priesthood had been reported to him too late.

[Col. 1030D] Observe that in this letter, near the end, “the Alexandrian Church” should be read in place of “the Antiochene Church,” as is clear from the following letter.

“He appealed to Simplicius.” Namely, the bishop of the second see appealed to the bishop of the first, without whose authority no synod could depose him.

“As blessed Athanasius had done.” The words of the author of the *Brief Account of the Eutychianists* deserve attention: “For his predecessors likewise sought refuge with the Roman Church during the time of persecution.”

“To write on his behalf to Acacius.” This is the fifth among Simplicius’s letters, and the sixth agrees with it completely.

“Did not recognize him as bishop.” Although Acacius knew this perfectly well both from the report of reliable men and from common rumor, he did not know by what means John’s legitimacy was established—namely, by synodical letters, which also contained the faith of the newly ordained bishop.

“Had done this contrary to his judgment.” The printed editions read *citra* (“apart from”), but the text ought to be emended from the following *pericope*. Since Moggus had been condemned by the judgment of the apostolic see and of Acacius himself, “a man condemned by a common decree as an adulterer ought to have been released from condemnation by common deliberation.” But what force does the word “common” have here?

“Definition.” That is, *horos* (ὅρος).

“Pope Simplicius died.” In the year 483, on 2 March, after he had held the apostolic see for fifteen years, five months, and ten days. Marcellinus thinks that Simplicius died one year earlier.

“Felix.” Some call him Felix II, others Felix III.

“Suffered attacks.” That is, he was harassed and pressed by armed demands to fulfill the agreements made with the Eutychianist monks by whom he had been elevated to the throne; he had obtained the throne by promising the condemnation of the synod and of the letter of Saint Leo.

“Acacius added.” Dense darkness extends through many lines. There is no sequence of events, no coherent connection of the discourse, and indeed no suitable syntax among the words. Some light may nevertheless be expected from the source: either Liberatus received incorrectly what he wrote, or others copied it incompletely. The entire passage should therefore be restored—or rather understood—from the *Brief Account of the Eutychianists* as follows:

“The arrival of this John Talaia brought everything more fully to light. When we read Acacius’s letters, which he had sent concerning Peter and John of Antioch, we discovered that Acacius had committed very serious excesses in this matter as well. At the time when he had reported concerning Peter of Alexandria, after that and not much later he had also written concerning Peter and John: that Peter had governed a monastery at Constantinople but, abandoning it because of crimes, had fled to Antioch; that there, after the Catholic bishop Martyrius had been expelled, he had occupied his see through heretics; that he had immediately been condemned by Leo, then emperor, and sent into exile at Oasi; that after falling away he had returned to Constantinople and given a pledge that he would dare to cause no further disturbances; but, as stated above, in the time of Basiliscus he had been sent back by that condemned Timothy, who had come to Constantinople, to Antioch, so that he might again hold the episcopate there.

“After this, the same Peter ordained a certain John, the presbyter whom we said Acacius had reported, as bishop of Apamea. Since the people did not receive him, he came to Antioch, expelled Peter, the author of his episcopate, and invaded his Church. Acacius says that both men were again condemned, asking the apostolic see that, if they should happen to flee there, it not consider them worthy even of being seen; and that, if they had perhaps already obtained some pardon, it should be invalid and their repentance should not be accepted.

“When the aforementioned John, bishop of Alexandria, read this again, he could not remain silent about the fact that Acacius had sent the John whom he had condemned together with Peter—and whom he had caused to be condemned by the apostolic see without any remedy of repentance—to preside over the Church of Tyre after so many condemnations.”

Pay attention to the expression “when we read.” Either it has been corruptly placed for “when they were read”—which I do not believe—or it indicates the author of the *Brief Account*, as will become clear later.

“And after five years.” Simplicius, namely, first wrote to Acacius about Moggus in the year 477, while Felix’s synodical letter, which Vitalis and Misenus carried, was sent in the year 483.

“By deliberation, Vitalis and Misenus.” He uses “deliberation” for the synod held by Felix at Rome in the year 483, from which Vitalis of the Church of Truentum in Picenum and Misenus of the Church of Cumae in Campania were sent to Constantinople to the emperor Zeno and the bishop Acacius. See Letter 1 of Felix III, entitled “Synodical.”

“That they might not be returned to the Catholics to whom they had been written.” Especially to the archimandrites, both those residing at Constantinople and those presiding over monasteries scattered throughout Bithynia.

“The monks had gone ahead.” If we believe Nicephorus, book XVI, chapter 16, these monks were sent by Cyril, prefect of the Acaemetes, and Simeon was their leader, accompanied or assisted by the presbyter Silvanus. It is nevertheless not an implausible conjecture that the monks were sent by the Constantinopolitan presbyters and archimandrites Rufinus and Thalassius, to whom Letter 11 of Pope Felix concerns the condemnation of the defender Tutus, who had failed in his office after being corrupted by money.

“And convicted from the very letters they had brought.” In the second synod, namely the Roman synod, of which three more widely known proceedings are commonly reported: in the first, Vitalis and Misenus were convicted and deposed, although they complained of force having been used against them; in the second, Acacius was deprived of office; in the third, Peter the Fuller was likewise deprived of office.

But if we believe Liberatus, three Roman synods must be established in this matter: from the first the envoys were sent to Constantinople; in the second those same envoys were deposed and Acacius admonished; in the last Acacius was deposed. Indeed, a fourth must be added, in which the defender Tutus was condemned.

“Separated itself.” This separation lasted approximately thirty-five years, from the year 484, when Acacius was condemned, to the year 519, when his name and those of his other schismatic successors were erased from the sacred registers, in the time of the emperor Justin and John, bishop of Constantinople.

“By the Valamerians.” Namely, by the troops of Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, who was called Valamer.

“But Ello fled to a fortress.” Others report that he was killed together with Leontius and Pamprepius.

“Furthermore, Peter.” That is, Moggus, not Peter the Fuller. This abrupt manner of narration casts considerable darkness over the account if it has found readers whose attention was distracted.

“Abbot Nephalius.” He was a rival of Ammon but stood for the Catholic faith; Ammon stood for the Eutychian heresy.

“John the bishop and hegumen.” Observe that he was simultaneously bishop and hegumen. A hegumen was something quite different from an archimandrite, for he presided over several archimandrites, much as generals or provincials are now said to do.

“Esaians.” No one clearly reports who they were. I think they were named after the bishop Esaias, who is said in the *Brief Account of the History of the Eutychianists* to have served as envoy to the apostolic see on behalf of Timothy Salophaciolus.

“In this condition.” Baronius reads “in these disturbances.”

“Flavitas the presbyter.” If we believe Suidas and Nicephorus, he obtained the see of Constantinople by wicked arts and retained it by no better means.

“From Saint Thecla.” Zeno built a temple to the holy virgin as the result of a vow to which he had bound himself when he led an army against Basiliscus. He attributed his victory to the prayers of the holy virgin.

“Received letters from the Roman pope.” They were not letters of communion but letters of admonition concerning the removal of the names of Acacius and Flavitas from the sacred diptychs. See Baronius, under the year 489, no. 1.

“Not long afterward Peter Moggus also died.” Baronius assigns the death of the impious heretic to the year 490, Petavius to the following year.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Severus, Julian, and Macedonius

*(From John the rhetorician and the author of Severus’s Life.)*

At this time Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, is said to have been expelled by the emperor Anastasius on the charge that he had falsified the Gospels, especially the Apostle’s statement: “For he was manifested in the flesh and justified in the Spirit.” He is said to have altered the passage where it has ὅς, that is, “who”—a Greek monosyllable—by changing the letter ο into ω and making it ὡς, that is, “so that God was manifested through the flesh.” He was therefore accused as a Nestorian and expelled through the monk Severus.

When Severus was previously living in a monastery, he did not accept Zeno’s edict or Peter Moggus. Later, while living in the monastery of the abbot Romanus and of Mama, who succeeded him, he was sent from there to remain at Constantinople and became an *apocrisiarius* among the party of Peter Moggus. When the objection was made to him, “How is it that you formerly anathematized Peter?” he replied, “Because I anathematized Peter of Apamea.”

At Constantinople this Severus disparaged the synod and maintained that, once it had been anathematized, everyone would enter into communion. For this reason he also wrote to Flavian himself, as is indicated by his letters, and to Maronas the reader, and to the bishops Eleusinius and Eutychius,

[Note: [Col. 1033D] The Tellerius Codex reads: “Eleusinius and Eutrechius.”]

and to Oecumenius, the scholasticus of Isauria.

A statement of his is also reported, delivered by him at his enthronement, in which he accepted Zeno’s unifying edict, anathematized the Council of Chalcedon, and confessed that he was in communion with the Alexandrian and Constantinopolitan bishops. At that time Timothy was bishop at Constantinople and John Machiota at Alexandria.

Yet although he held such views, he was able to condemn Macedonius and expel Flavian from the see of Antioch. Nor did he himself possess that episcopate for more than five years. He was also harassed in his episcopate because he anathematized the synod while naming as bishops men of the synod. The manner of his expulsion is known to have been as follows.

After the emperor Anastasius died and Justin became emperor, Severus was accused by Vitalian, the master of the soldiers, a religious and orthodox man, of despising the emperor’s command and refusing to accept the synod. The emperor Justin sent a *magistrianus* to bring Severus to Constantinople so that he might give an account of his dealings against the synod. For Julian of Halicarnassus had already been expelled from his see by that same pious emperor because he did not accept the holy synod.

When Severus learned this and foresaw what threatened him, he secretly went down by night to Seleucia, boarded a ship, and fled to Alexandria, to which city Julian had also fled.

[Col. 1033D] Paul, an orthodox man who accepted the Council of Chalcedon, was ordained archbishop of Antioch in his place.

At that time, after Dioscorus the Younger had died at Alexandria, Timothy had assumed the episcopate of that Church. He received Severus and Julian most warmly, and they stayed at Labron.

[Note: [Col. 1034D] The Tellerius Codex reads: “at Labranon.”]

Under this Timothy, a controversy arose in that Church itself concerning the corruptible and incorruptible, as follows. A certain monk asked Severus how one ought to describe the body of our Lord Jesus Christ: as corruptible or incorruptible. He replied that the holy Fathers had called it corruptible. When certain Alexandrians heard this, they asked Julian, who was sitting elsewhere, what he himself said about the same question. He replied that the holy Fathers said the opposite. Each of them therefore wished to establish his own answer and wrote books against the other. These books, gaining circulation among the citizens, divided that Church and caused some to be called Corrupticolae, while others, namely the defenders of incorruptibility, were called Phantasiastae. Timothy, however, followed Severus’s opinion more closely.

When Themistius, his deacon, said to him, “If Christ’s body is corruptible, we must also say that he was ignorant of certain things, as in the case of Lazarus,” Timothy denied that this should be said. Themistius consequently withdrew from his communion and created a schism; and in Egypt his followers were called Themistians.

[Note: [Col. 1034B]

**“At this time Macedonius.”** That is, in the year 511, the twenty-first year of the emperor Anastasius, on which the ancient writers agree. Since he is said to have held office for six years, it is necessary to acknowledge that he was ordained in 504, either toward its end or at the beginning of 505.

**“As though he had falsified the Gospels.”** The passage of the Apostle, 1 Timothy 3:16, reads as follows in Greek:

> Καὶ ὁμολογουμένως μέγα ἐστὶ τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον. Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ, ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι, ὤφθη ἀγγέλοις, ἐκηρύχθη ἐν ἔθνεσιν, ἐπιστεύθη ἐν κόσμῳ, ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ.

And in Latin:

> “And plainly great is the mystery of piety: which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory.”

The Latin translator used a Greek manuscript in which Θεός (“God”) was not read, but ὅ; therefore, if Liberatus is to be believed, in Macedonius’s time Θεός was not read, but ὃς, which little word he himself changed into ὡς (“as”). Yet Liberatus’s reliability may rightly be suspected, since among much earlier Fathers—Chrysostom, Theodoret, and other commentators on Paul—Θεός is written. Moreover, no other writer remembers this little story; indeed, all give different reasons for the deposition.

**“Through the monk Severus.”** No plague was more harmful than this man. By nature he possessed a monstrous disposition, formed by savagery and calculation. He first softened his innate ferocity through the arts of love; then, when he returned to his natural character, he applied himself to legal business and even pleaded cases. Later, weary of a laborious life, he concealed himself in the solitude of a monastery, where he wished to appear, through leisure, to be pursuing true piety. For he preached the Council of Chalcedon and condemned the Henoticon, but in reality he was devising disturbances by which he would one day agitate the whole Church of the East.

He therefore returned from the monastery to Alexandria and, being experienced in affairs, was immediately sent to Constantinople to conduct in court the business of the Egyptian diocese. Soon he investigated by what means he might accomplish the crime he had conceived; and no instrument seemed more powerful to him than a woman, the emperor’s wife and consort, who was extravagantly devoted to heresy. He impiously surrendered himself to her, attacked the great council which he had previously praised and formerly called the teacher of the faith when circumstances required it, but now called it a factional gathering because that was how the Augusta spoke of it. By these arts, when he saw that the court had been deceived, he dared to seek the patriarchal see; but when his hope of obtaining Constantinople was dashed, he turned his mind toward Antioch and invaded it after expelling Flavian.

**“And Eleusinius.”** A fragment of Severus’s letter to Eleusinius, bishop, is read in the Lateran Council under Martin I, session 5:

> “We anathematize those who defined one Christ in two natures and professed the proper operations of each nature.”

**“To Oecumenius.”** He wrote several letters to the same man. From the first of them, the following passages are cited in the council just mentioned:

> “The distinction in operations, of which Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, said, ‘Each form performs what is proper to it in communion with the other,’ shall in no way be called distinction among the orthodox.”

And afterward:

> “We anathematize those who, after the union, say that there are two natures—that is, the operations of two natures—or two properties.”

Observe this manner of interpretation—that is, observe what the true opinion of the Monothelites concerning two wills was. We have treated this elsewhere at greater length, and the narrow limits of the place in which we are now working do not permit a dissertation on it.

**“His exposition is said to have been …”** The Fathers of the council held in the royal city in 518, when they were reporting the petitions of the monks against Severus to John of Constantinople, quoted the words with which Severus anathematized the holy council:

> “We anathematize what was formulated and established by the council assembled at that time in Chalcedon, and those who fight on its behalf.”

**“But named the bishops.”** That is, he recited their names in the sacred diptychs.

**“When Justin had become emperor.”** The piety of Justin and his exceptional zeal for the Catholic faith are praised in many places by the ancient writers, but especially in the acts of the council mentioned shortly afterward.

**“Julian of Halicarnassus.”** He wrote a discourse against the Manichaeans, from which those passages were excerpted that were produced in the Lateran Council under Martin I, session 5.

**“Timothy of that Church, etc.”** He succeeded the younger Dioscorus in 519, when the latter was already advanced in age. It seems to me that he is the same man who in the Acts of Saint Arethas is called Asterius, and to whom the emperor Justin is said to have written after the city of Nagran had been conquered by the leader of the Homerites and persecution had been stirred up against the Christians; for at that time he was holding the episcopate.

Why do I conjecture that he had two names? The reason is the custom of the Alexandrians, which became established after the time of Cyril. They used to distinguish bishops bearing the same name by additional names: thus they called one John “Melas,” another “Machiotas,” and a third “Eleemon”; likewise they distinguished the elder and younger Dioscorus, and Timothy Aelurus and Salophaciolus. To distinguish a third Timothy from these, I have no doubt that they called him Asterius.

If this is asserted, the solution to a question recently raised by a certain disputant against both Baronius and Riccioli will become evident—namely, the question concerning Asterius of Alexandria. Although neither of them spoke with complete accuracy on the subject, there was nevertheless no reason for the disputant, who was not well versed in the matter, to attack them as though they had thrust a man into the list of Alexandrian bishops contrary to manifest evidence. Both relied on the authority of an ancient writer, and Riccioli’s error concerning Justinian rather than Justin can be attributed to the carelessness of copyists. The disputant should, however, be forgiven this fault, as well as many others, because of his censorious disposition.

**“At Labron.”** Elsewhere *ad Labronum*, perhaps *ad Labronium*. Leontius, act 5, says:

> “They sat at the ninth.”

The Greeks call this *λαβρώνιον*, which means “voracious.” Hence it may be understood that *λαβρωνίῳ* and *ἐννάτῳ* have the noun *στόμα* (“mouth” or “opening”) supplied, as though they sat at the ninth, voracious mouth of the Nile, rather than in some district of the city of Alexandria.

**“Concerning the corruptible and incorruptible.”** This question concerned neither mortality and immortality nor dissolution into the elements and the contrary permanence. For it was always admitted—even among the Eutychians themselves—that Christ’s body lay dead in the tomb, yet had not undergone corruption.

The question was therefore whether Christ’s body suffered, just as ours does, the impairments that would make it hungry in order to repair them, require food, become weary, and need rest to restore its strength; or whether it only appeared outwardly to suffer such things and did so solely by *οἰκονομία* (“economy” or divine dispensation), as after the resurrection.

The occasion—or rather the source—of the dispute was that, since the Eutychians were being reproached as though they asserted that Christ’s body was not *ὁμοούσιον* (“consubstantial”) with ours, some denied that incorruptibility could coexist with consubstantiality, while others affirmed it. Hence the former were called Corrupticolae and the latter Phantasiastae—not because the Phantasiasts denied that Christ’s body was real, as the Manichaeans did, but because they said that such natural affections in Christ existed not in reality but in appearance and semblance.

**“The deacon Themistius.”** He is mentioned in the Lateran Council under Martin I and in the Sixth Ecumenical Council. In both places excerpts from his books are produced in support of one will and one operation. From the passages produced, however, he is revealed as an enemy of the party of Theodosius, who was expelled from the Alexandrian see. For his second discourse was also submitted “to Theodora, from the heresiarch of the Theodosians,” and he wrote against Colluthus, the defender of Theodosius.

**“Themistians.”** They were also called Agnoetae and counted among the heretics—not because they denied that Christ, as man, knew the final day, for many Fathers denied that; but because they thought this followed from Christ’s consubstantiality with us, in which they were mistaken. Perhaps, however, they were called heretics not because they held this opinion, but because that opinion produced a schism among the heretics.]

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning Gaianus and Theodosius

While these events were taking place at Alexandria, Pope Boniface of Rome died, and John, surnamed Mercury, assumed the episcopate of the apostolic see.

[Col. 1036C] The emperor Justinian sent to him Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, and Demetrius of Philippi, to consult the apostolic see against the legates of the Acephalites, Cyrus and Eulogius. The latter denied that the blessed Mary should be confessed truly and properly as Mother of God, and denied that one of the Trinity had become incarnate and suffered in the flesh. But Pope John, while we were present there, confirmed in his letter that this must be confessed and sent the letter to the emperor. [Note: The Teller manuscript reads: “against those denying that it must be confessed, he confirmed it by his letter.”]

Some monks in Rome, departing from his communion, followed the legates of the Acephalites and to this day do not accept this confession concerning Christ.

At that time, when Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople, died, the Augusta Theodora transferred Anthimus to the same see. He had been bishop of Trapezus, a city in the Pontic region, and secretly did not accept the Council of Chalcedon.

But when Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, died, Theodosius was ordained through the initiative and permission of Calotychius, chamberlain and partisan of the Augusta Theodora. Although he possessed the decree of the clergy, he did not permit the people to contend with those who wished to oppose him. The monks, whom he did not possess, supported Gaianus.

It is indeed the custom at Alexandria for the successor of the deceased to keep vigil over the body of the dead, place the dead man’s right hand upon his own head, bury him with his own hands, receive the pallium of blessed Mark around his neck, and then take his seat legitimately. While Theodosius was attempting these things at night, the people and the monasteries learned what had been done in the evening at the episcopal residence through the efforts of Calotychius and the judges—that is, Aristomachus the duke and Dioscorus the augustalis. They immediately pursued and expelled Theodosius, so that he could not gather Timothy’s funeral procession.

They enthroned Gaianus, who at that time was archbishop on the side of those who asserted incorruptibility. Having a considerable number of sympathizers among the clergy, the city’s landowners, the guilds, the soldiers, the nobles, and the entire province, Gaianus remained in the episcopate for 103 days. After this he was expelled by the judges and departed.

Two months later, the chamberlain Narses, sent by the Augusta Theodora, enthroned Theodosius and sent Gaianus into exile. He was brought to Carthage the Great and from there sent, as it were, to Sardinia; what happened to him is unknown.

Theodosius remained in the see for one year and four months, with few communicating with him; most communicated in the name of Gaianus.

The people fought for Gaianus for many days, and when they were slaughtered by the soldiers, they lost the greater part of their number. A greater number of the soldiers also fell. Narses was defeated not by weapons but by the unity of the city: women from the upper stories of the houses threw at the soldiers whatever came to hand; but he conquered by fire what he could not conquer by the sword.

That city has remained divided by this schism to the present day, so that its factions are called Gaianites and Theodosians—that is, Phantasiasts and Corrupticolae.

At last Theodosius left the see, unable to endure the riots and wars that the people were carrying on against him. He was sent to Constantinople with honor, because the Augusta’s written instructions ordered this. When he arrived there, the Augusta promised the emperor that Theodosius would be able to accept the Council of Chalcedon. But when he persisted and refused, he was sent, with her consent, into exile outside the royal city at the sixth milestone, beside the basilica of Arisphoca, on the road leading to Stomapontus. He is still alive.

[Note: [Col. 1037C]

**“Hypatius of Ephesus.”** After returning from the Roman embassy, in the year 533 he held a disputation at Constantinople, by order of the emperor Justinian, with the Severians. It is found in volume 4 of the more recent edition of CC. GG. It contains certain passages concerning Cyril’s third letter to Nestorius, Cyril’s books against Diodore and Theodore, the works of Dionysius the Areopagite, and Theodoret, all of which may rightly be subjected to examination.

**“Demetrius of Philippi.”** Baronius calls him Caesarean, and Binius follows him in the notes to the Roman council held by Pope John concerning these questions. Both could be reconciled with Liberatus, who makes him Philippian, unless Baronius made him a metropolitan. He was bishop of Caesarea Philippi in Palestine, a city subject to the bishop of Tyre; he was not bishop of Philippi in Macedonia, which was a metropolis.

**“Against the legates of the Acephalites.”** Some think that the Acephalites were infected with the error of Eutyches by Peter the Fuller, when Peter, having been deposed by the emperor Zeno, hid among them—if we believe Nicephorus—until he was restored to his see by the tyrant Basiliscus, book 16, chapter 12.

This opinion, however, cannot stand in view of Justinian’s accusation, as everyone can see. It is therefore more credible that the Acephalites, who formerly and at that time strongly resisted both Eutyches and the Eutychians, were swept away by the heat of the struggle and came almost to the opposite side, that of Nestorius.

For when they understood that the principal support of the Eutychian heresy was the claim that the blessed Virgin was properly *Deipara* (“God-bearer”) and that one of the Trinity was said to have become incarnate and been crucified; and when, through the wretched credulity of the age, they persuaded themselves, as Facundus reports, that there was nothing intermediate between Eutyches and Nestorius, they acknowledged that these two propositions were true, as the Catholic faith required, but denied that they were properly true—that is, true in exactly the same way in which any woman is called the mother of her own son or any human being is said to have suffered when he was killed. See Facundus, book 1, chapter 4.

Hence they aroused against themselves the anger of the emperor Justinian and of Epiphanius, bishop of New Rome. It must be admitted, however, that at that time the matter was debated with little learning, or at least without precision.

**“While we were present there.”** Either these things are false, which I scarcely believe, or Liberatus must have come to Rome twice: once while John was alive and again after Agapetus’s ordination. For the Roman council from which John replied to Justinian was held on the eighth day before the Kalends of April in 534.

The Carthaginian council, however, from which Liberatus the Deacon was sent to Rome with the two bishops Gaius and Peter, was indeed assembled in the same year, but toward the end of autumn, as we shall later show. Yet the legates did not leave Africa until after John’s death, which occurred on April 26, 535, and after Agapetus’s ordination had been reported. For the synodical letter addressed to John was received by Agapetus, who also gave the reply and at the same time sent a private letter to Reparatus, from which we learn the whole matter.

It reads as follows:

> “You indicated in the letter of your fraternity that, after a letter had been sent to my predecessor, and amid the delays in undertaking the voyage caused by the severity of the continuing winter, you had been informed, by the grace of almighty God, of our ordination, and that you had offered congratulations with fraternal affection because the dignity of the pontificate had granted me an office whose bestowal upon my sincerity we did not find surprising. Moreover, concerning the matters which the brothers Gaius and Peter, our fellow bishops, and Liberatus the Deacon, our son, had been sent by your fraternity to bring before us orally, we thought it appropriate to give an oral response. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September, after the consulship of Paulinus, a man of clarissima rank.”

Liberatus therefore first came to John to report the ordination of Reparatus; then he came to Agapetus to offer congratulations on his accession and to conduct the affairs of the African council.

**“Theodosius.”** He is mentioned in the Lateran Council under Martin I. The writings sent by Theodosius to the Augusta Theodora are cited there, including the following:

> “It remains that there be one deifying operation from both, since we say that all things worthy of God and all irreproachable sufferings belong to one and the same.”

And afterward:

> “The holy and wise Fathers proclaimed that the composite Christ has one operation worthy of God according to divinity and humanity.”

**“He is still alive.”** Liberatus therefore wrote under the emperor Justinian. For the Theodosius of whom he speaks died in the first year of the younger Justin, if we believe Victor of Tunnuna.]

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning Pope Agapetus and Anthimus, Bishop of Constantinople

When John Mercury died, Agapetus, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was ordained pope, being exceptionally well versed in the ecclesiastical rules. [Note: The Teller manuscript reads: “a man exceptionally well versed in ecclesiastical rules is ordained.”]

At that time Theodahad, king of the Goths, wrote to the pope and the Roman Senate, threatening that he would kill by the sword not only the senators but also their wives, sons, and daughters unless they acted with the emperor to have his army, which had been sent against Italy, withdrawn. The pope therefore undertook an embassy for this cause and departed for Constantinople.

At first, although he received honorably the persons sent to him by the emperor, he rejected Anthimus’s presence and refused to receive him for the customary greeting. Then, after seeing the emperor, he pleaded the cause of the embassy he had undertaken. The emperor, unwilling to withdraw the army sent from Italy because of the great expense to the treasury, refused to hear the pope’s petitions. But the pope, for his part, performed the mission entrusted to him by Christ.

Finally, when the emperor and the Augusta asked that the pope receive Anthimus in greeting and communion, he said that this could happen if Anthimus proved himself orthodox by a written statement and returned to his own chair. He declared that it was impossible for a transferred man to remain in that see. Although the Augusta secretly promised many gifts and again threatened the pope, the pope persisted in this position and would not hear her request.

When Anthimus saw that he had been expelled from his see, he returned the pallium he had received to the emperors and withdrew to a place where the Augusta might protect him under her patronage.

Then, with the emperor’s favor, the pope ordained Mennas in his place, consecrating him with his own hand in the basilica of Saint Mary. This Mennas had been superintendent of the larger hospice called Samson. He was Alexandrian by birth and accepted the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 1039C]

**“His army which had been sent.”** This was the army which, under the command of Belisarius, had captured the island of Sicily and was to be transported to Italy after the winter. See Procopius, book 1, *Gothic War*.

**“The pallium.”** This was the insignia of patriarchal dignity. The same is later reported of Paul of Alexandria: namely, that he was stripped of the pallium when he was deposed.

**“Then the pope, etc.”** See Evagrius, book 4, chapter 35. There he is silent about Anthimus’s deposition by Agapetus and inserts Anthimus between Mennas and Epiphanius. This is an error rejected by everyone: Anthimus did not precede Epiphanius but followed him.]

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning Silverius and Vigilius

After these events, while the pope was preparing to return to Italy, he appointed Pelagius, his deacon, as the apocrisiarius of his Church at the imperial court and died at Constantinople. When the city of Rome heard of his death, it chose Silverius, a subdeacon and the son of the former pope Hormisdas, to be ordained.

The Augusta, however, summoned Vigilius, Agapetus’s deacon, and secretly demanded that he promise her that, if he became pope, he would abolish the council and write to Theodosius, Anthimus, and Severus, confirming their faith by his letter. She promised to give him a directive to Belisarius so that he might be ordained pope, as well as seven hundredweight of gold.

Vigilius therefore readily accepted her promise, out of love for the episcopate and gold. After making his undertaking, he set out for Rome, where he arrived and found that Silverius had been ordained pope.

He also found Belisarius at Ravenna, seated in that city and occupying it. Handing him the Augusta’s directive, he promised him two hundredweight of gold if, after Silverius had been removed, he himself were ordained in Silverius’s place.

Belisarius returned to Rome and summoned Silverius to the palace. There he brought an accusation against him, as though Silverius had written to the Goths asking them to enter Rome.

It is reported that a certain scholasticus named Marcus and a certain praetorian named Julian composed forged letters in Silverius’s name, written to the king of the Goths, from which Silverius would be convicted of wishing to betray the city of Rome.

Belisarius and his wife secretly urged Silverius to fulfill the Augusta’s directive: that the Council of Chalcedon should be abolished and that he should confirm the faith of the heretics in a letter of his own.

Silverius immediately left the palace and discussed with his advisers what should be done with him. He went to the basilica of the blessed martyr Sabina and remained there. Photius, the son of the patrician Antonina, was sent to him and, after taking an oath, invited him to come to the palace. Those who stood by Silverius persuaded him not to trust the oaths of the Greeks; nevertheless, he went out and came to the palace.

That day he was permitted, on account of his oath, to return to the church. Belisarius again sent word to him that he should come to the palace, but Silverius did not wish to leave the church, recognizing the plots prepared for him. Later, however, he prayed and commended his cause to the Lord, then left and came to the palace. Once he had entered alone, his own people did not see him again.

On another day Belisarius summoned all the presbyters, deacons, and clergy and ordered them to choose another pope for him. While they hesitated and some resisted, Vigilius was ordained through Belisarius’s favor. Silverius was sent into exile to a city in the province of Lycia called Patara.

After his ordination, Vigilius was compelled by Belisarius to fulfill the promise he had made to the Augusta and to return to him the two hundredweight of gold he had promised. But Vigilius, out of fear of the Romans and with greed as his ally, did not wish to fulfill his undertakings.

When Silverius arrived at Patara, however, the venerable bishop of that city went to the emperor and invoked the judgment of God concerning the expulsion of the bishop of so great a see. He said that there were many kings in this world, whereas there was only one pope over the Church of the whole world, and that this pope had been expelled from his see.

When the emperor heard him, he ordered Silverius to be recalled to Rome and ordered an investigation of the letters: if it were proved that Silverius himself had written them, he was to remain a bishop in whatever city he lived; but if they were proved false, he was to be restored to his see.

Pelagius, however, hastening with the Augusta’s approval, wished to invalidate the emperor’s order so that Silverius would not return to Rome. But the emperor’s command prevailed, and Silverius was brought back to Italy.

Terrified by his arrival, Vigilius, fearing that he would be expelled from the see, sent word to Belisarius: “Hand Silverius over to me; otherwise I cannot do what you demand of me.”

Silverius was therefore handed over to two of Vigilius’s defenders and servants. They brought him to the island of Palmaria, where under their custody he died of starvation.

Through Antonina, the wife of Belisarius, Vigilius fulfilled the undertaking he had made to the Augusta and wrote the following letter:

> “To the lords and brothers united in the love of Christ God, our Savior, Theodosius, Anthimus, and Severus, bishops: Vigilius, bishop.
>
> “I know that the confidence in my faith has already reached your holiness, with God’s help. But because my glorious daughter, the most Christian patrician Antonina, has now caused my desires to be fulfilled, I am sending this written communication to your fraternity.
>
> “I greet you with the grace by which we are united to our God, Christ our Savior, and I declare that, with God’s help, I have held and do hold the faith which you hold. For I know that we proclaim and read among you that there may be one soul and one heart in God.
>
> “I have hastened to announce to you, from my heart, the joys of my advancement—which is yours also—with God’s help, knowing that your fraternity, which desired this, would gladly embrace it.
>
> “Therefore, no one must learn what I am writing to you. Rather, let your wisdom regard me as suspect before others, so that I may more easily accomplish and complete what I have begun to undertake.””

The subscription reads:

> “Pray to God for us, my brothers united in love in Christ our Lord.”

Under this letter Vigilius wrote his profession of faith, in which he condemned two natures in Christ. Rejecting Pope Leo’s tome, he said:

> “We do not confess two natures in Christ, but one Son, one Christ, one Lord composed from two natures.”

And again:

> “Whoever says that Christ has two forms, each acting in communion with the other, and does not confess one person and one essence, let him be anathema.
>
> “Whoever says that one of these performed miracles while the other succumbed to sufferings, and does not confess that the miracles and sufferings belonged to one and the same person, which he willingly endured in flesh consubstantial with ours, let him be anathema.
>
> “Whoever says that Christ, as man, was moved by mercy, and does not say that God the Word himself was also crucified so that he might have mercy on us, let him be anathema.
>
> “We therefore anathematize Paul of Samosata, Dioscorus, Theodore, Theodoret, and all who have observed or observe their decrees.”

Vigilius wrote these things secretly to the heretics and remained in office. In him was fulfilled the testimony which Solomon gives in Proverbs: “They shall eat the fruit of their way and be filled with their own counsels” (Prov. 1:31).

Afflicted by that very heresy and not crowned, what manner of end Vigilius met is known to everyone. But let us return to the affair of the Alexandrians.

[Note: [Col. 1042A]

**“Concerning Silverius and Vigilius.”** He likes to recount this sorrowful history in a separate chapter in order to make Vigilius, the condemner of the Three Chapters, more hated by showing how unjust his first ordination was.

**“Pelagius, his deacon.”** He was the apocrisiarius of three pontiffs—Agapetus, Silverius, and Vigilius. For this reason, in the Council of Constantinople held under Mennas in 536, he is often called “deacon of the apostolic see and of the Roman Church,” just as Theophanes is. Both are also called Vigilius’s deacons there, but by anticipation, since they were left behind by Vigilius when he hastened to Rome, confident that he would obtain the apostolic see.

Pelagius first came to Constantinople in 535 as Agapetus’s legate to Justinian. Justinian sent him back to Rome in 540. He then served as Totila’s legate to Justinian and returned to Rome to give an account of his embassy. From there he again returned to Vigilius, who was at Constantinople. It is believed that he kept Vigilius in the position of not condemning the Three Chapters for as long as this was permitted by the peace of the Church. At last he succeeded Vigilius in the apostolic see in 555.

**“He died at Constantinople.”** Victor of Tunnuna says the same. Some, however, write that he died on the journey. Perhaps they used “journey” in place of “on the road while preparing to depart.”

**“Silverius.”** Anastasius writes that he was ordained through the agency—or even by force—of Theodahad, king of the Goths; hence the appearance of the later accusation that he favored the Goths. Some have tried to stain the holy man with the taint of simony, as though he had purchased Theodahad’s favor with gold. Anastasius made this reckless statement, which some have maliciously defended.

**“Vigilius.”** At that time he was not merely Agapetus’s deacon but also his apocrisiarius, together with Pelagius and Theophanes. This ambitious man had insinuated himself into the favor of the acephalous Augusta, working upon her so that he might be able to seize the apostolic see. Indeed, it is credible that, in order to flatter her more openly, he pretended to be more favorable to the Acephalites, especially to Anthimus, and criticized Agapetus’s judgment concerning Anthimus as excessively harsh.

**“And by a letter.”** Clearly a letter of communion, of the kind reported later.

**“Seven hundredweight.”** That is, seven times one hundred Roman pounds of gold. Converted to the value of French currency, these would amount to more than six hundred thousand French livres.

**“After making his undertaking.”** The word “undertaking” may have been used by Liberatus in place of “promise,” or it may have been introduced by the copyists, which I consider more likely. For in Cicero *profiteri* means “to promise.” Vigilius’s promise, however, was made not merely orally but by a written instrument.

**“He found Belisarius at Ravenna.”** Memory has failed him: he wrote Ravenna instead of Naples, which Belisarius had recently captured. For Belisarius did not possess Ravenna until three years later. See Procopius, book 1, *Gothic War*.

**“He returned to Rome.”** This was at the time when Vitiges was pressing the siege of Rome, begun in March 538. See Procopius, book 1, *Gothic War*, and Anastasius’s Life of Silverius.

**“Written to the king of the Goths.”** To Vitiges, who, having been summoned by the Goths to the kingship, had killed Theodahad, who favored Silverius. Some use this to reject the accusation of treason brought against Silverius: how could Silverius, being of generous character, have negotiated such a matter with the murderer of his friend? But perhaps he suffered a human weakness when he saw Belisarius, to whom the city had surrendered on December 10, promoting the interests of Vigilius, who was seeking the pontificate.

**“But Belisarius secretly.”** See this entire tragedy in Anastasius’s Life of Silverius, and marvel that two women—Theodora, Justinian’s wife, and Antonina, the wife of Belisarius—could disturb the whole Church and overturn religion. What will a woman’s spirit not dare when it is deranged by the impulse either of religion or of ambition?

**“Who entered alone.”** Anastasius makes Vigilius his companion. He explains more fully what Liberatus briefly touches upon:

> “Thus Silverius and Vigilius entered the mausoleum alone. The patrician Antonina was lying on a bed, and Belisarius was sitting at her feet. When the patrician Antonina saw him, she said to him: ‘Tell us, Lord Pope Silverius, what have we done to you and to the Romans, that you wish to hand us over to the Goths?’ While she was still speaking, John, a subdeacon and regional officer of the first region, entered, took the pallium from his neck, led him into a chamber, stripped him, clothed him in a monk’s garment, and concealed him. Then Sixtus, a subdeacon and regional officer of the sixth region, seeing that he had already become a monk, went outside and announced to the clergy, saying: ‘The lord pope has been deposed and has become a monk.’ When they heard this, they all fled.”

But Anastasius confuses the two encounters Silverius had with Belisarius and the two events which Liberatus distinguishes. He adds:

> “Vigilius the archdeacon received him as though in his own faith and sent him into exile in the Pontian Islands, sustaining him with the bread of affliction and the water of distress.”

These events occurred much later, namely after Silverius’s return from exile at Patara.

**“He was sent into exile.”** Anastasius is silent about Silverius’s exile in Lycia, but Procopius speaks of it in these words, book 1 of the *Gothic War*, chapter 25:

> “Then, when suspicion arose that Silverius, bishop of the city of Rome, would defect to the Goths, he immediately sent him to Greece and supplied another in his place, a certain man named Vigilius, along with certain others who were senators.”

**“The venerable bishop.”** In my opinion, this was Licinius or Lucianus, who is recorded as having signed the acts of the Council of Constantinople under Mennas two years earlier.

**“In whatever city.”** That is, in any one city in which he might live as bishop—no longer, of course, as bishop of Rome but as bishop of that city. Baronius interprets it differently, though I fear not plausibly, as though the emperor ordered Silverius, if he were proved guilty, not to return to Rome but nevertheless to retain the supreme pontificate wherever else he might exercise it.

**“But Pelagius, hastening forward.”** This makes clear Pelagius’s conspiracy with Vigilius and the Augusta. It also shows how Pelagius was already then managing Vigilius’s affairs and performing the office of apocrisiarius.

**“To the island of Palmaria.”** He wrote Palmaria instead of the neighboring island of Pontia, which is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology.

**“He died of starvation.”** The Martyrology reports Silverius’s martyrdom somewhat differently from Liberatus. In order to spare Vigilius’s reputation, it says under June 20:

> “The feast of Saint Silverius, pope and martyr, who, because he refused to restore Anthimus, the heretical bishop deposed by his predecessor Agapetus, was driven into exile on the island of Pontia by Belisarius at the instigation of the impious Augusta Theodora, and there, exhausted by many sufferings for the Catholic faith, died.”

**Through Antonina.** Concerning this woman—utterly impure, audacious, and cruel—see Procopius’s *Secret History*.

**“To the lords,” etc.** In the published books one reads *Dominis et christis*; we restore the title from Victor of Tunnuna, who reports the letter as having this address: “To the lords and brothers joined in the love of Christ God our Savior, Theodosius, Anthimius, and Severus, bishops: Vigilius, bishop.” From this inscription the force of the arguments by which Baronius proves the letter spurious is weakened; for it was not addressed to Justinian and Theodora, as Baronius believed. What is also reported from the Sixth Synod—that an anathema had been pronounced against the libelli said to have been composed by Vigilius [Col. 1044A] to Justinian and Theodora—likewise disappears. The argument drawn from the insolence of the inscription also vanishes, since the inscription is very different from the corrupt form commonly read in Liberatus.

**Under this letter.** A profession of faith was appended to the letter, together with five anathemas. Liberatus reports nothing of the faith except one passage, which contained the poison. The first four anathemas are directed against four sentences of Leo the Great received by the Council of Chalcedon, but misunderstood. The fifth is corruptly read: *Dioscorus* must be restored as *Nestorius*. I have said that Leo’s sentences were misunderstood, as though the confession of two natures excluded one person. Therefore the first four anathemas seem to have been craftily composed to deceive the heretics to whom they were written, so that, while laboring under prejudice, they might be drawn over to the writer’s position, although what was actually being said was Catholic. Yet this cannot excuse Vigilius, any more than it later excused Honorius, who, through an unworthy policy of the Apostolic See [Col. 1044B], did not openly teach the truth, although he sat in the chair of a teacher of the Church.

It should be noted that from these earliest times thought was already being given to condemning the Three Chapters, and that Vigilius had agreed to this if Theodora’s power should occupy the Apostolic See. Victor of Tunnuna is the witness:

“After the consulship”—not of Basilius, as it is read, but “of Belisarius, in the second year,” that is, in 537—“through the faction of the Augusta Theodora,” who “never ceased to be a secret enemy of the Synod of Chalcedon from the time she began to reign, plots of persecution are prepared. Silverius, Roman bishop, is sent into exile, and Vigilius is ordained in his place. Before his ordination, the aforementioned Augusta Theodora secretly extracted from him a written promise that, once he had become pope, he would condemn, in the persecution of the Synod of Chalcedon, the Three Chapters: namely, the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, to Maris the Persian, which had been approved and judged orthodox by the judgment of the Synod of Chalcedon and included among its synodal acts; then Theodore [Col. 1044C], bishop of Mopsuestia, likewise recorded synodally in the acts at Antioch under John, bishop of that Church, and praised at Chalcedon; and the writings of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, praised together with Theodoret himself in the words of the Synod of Chalcedon.”

If this is true, the condemnation of Origen was not the reason why condemnation of the Three Chapters was first contemplated, but rather the reason why that condemnation was pressed. Yet the testimony of these two schismatics on this point may reasonably be suspected.

**Vigilius was afflicted.** What he suffered at Constantinople and Chalcedon at the hands of the emperor is narrated by Vigilius himself and lamented miserably by the Italian clergy in their letters to the envoys of the king of the Gauls. Whether he was actually sent into exile and remained there for several years is disputed by ecclesiastical historians; in my judgment, however, they are disputing over the word alone. His absence from the City was called exile, and not without reason, since it was violent.

**What sort of end he met in life.** From this we know that this *Breviarium* was written after the death of Vigilius [Col. 1044D]—that is, after the year 555, in which year Vigilius died.

# CHAPTER XXIII  
## On Paul, archbishop of Alexandria, and the monks of Jerusalem
