After Theodosius of Alexandria had therefore been sent into exile, a certain Paul, one of the abbots of the Tabennesiote monks, was ordained bishop of the Alexandrian See. Pelagius, the Roman apocrisiarius, intervened on his behalf. He was entirely orthodox and accepted the Council of Chalcedon. He was ordained at Constantinople by Menas, in the presence of that same Pelagius, Vigilius’s representative, and of the representatives of Euphræmius of Antioch and of Peter of Jerusalem.

[Col. 1045A] Severus of Antioch had already been condemned, and Anthimus of Constantinople by Agapetus, pope of Rome, and Menas of Constantinople, on the basis of libelli presented against them to the emperor Justinian by the superiors of the monasteries and by the superiors of First and Second Syria, as well as by the superiors of the monasteries of Jerusalem and of the Desert. In this way, therefore, unity was achieved among the Churches, in the tenth year of the reign of the glorious Emperor Justinian. (See the notes.)

This Paul, it is said, had been accused at Constantinople by some of his own monks and had come to Constantinople to plead his case before the emperor. Finding the vacant chair by divine providence, he deserved, through the deacon Pelagius, to receive the episcopate of Alexandria. The emperor also gave him authority over the appointment of dukes and [Col. 1045B] tribunes, so that he might remove heretics and ordain orthodox men in their place; for through those officials the people were growing powerful.

When he went down to Alexandria, through fear of him and by his own resourcefulness he had brought the whole city and all the monasteries to accept the Council of Chalcedon, unless a matter of the following kind had arisen through the intervention of the devil.

When Bishop Paul was considering removing Elias, the master of the soldiers, a certain deacon named Psoius, treasurer of the Church and a friend of Elias, wrote to Elias about all Paul’s schemes through very swift letter-carriers on foot, whom the Egyptians call *Symmachoi*.

It happened, however, that Paul discovered letters written by him in Egyptian and read them. Fearing what had happened in the case of Proterius, he became concerned about him and [Col. 1045C] began compelling Psoius to render an account of the Church’s affairs. He handed him over to the judge and reported the matter to the emperor.

At that time Rhodo was *augustalis* at Alexandria. He took Psoius into custody until the emperor’s orders should arrive. Acting on the advice of a certain former civic official named Arsenius, and having received bribes, he secretly killed him at night with all his strength and with great torment, without the bishop’s knowledge, as is reported.

Psoius’s sons and relatives appealed to the emperor and informed him by what violence their kinsman had paid the debt of death. When the emperor heard this, he summoned Liberius, made him *augustalis*, and sent him to Alexandria to investigate the matter. When Liberius arrived in that city, he ordered Rhodo to come to him and asked him how he had killed the deacon. Rhodo replied that it had been done at the bishop’s command: he claimed to possess a delegation from the emperor authorizing him to carry out by every means whatever the bishop ordered.

But Bishop Paul denied this and loudly declared that he knew nothing of it. The former civic official Arsenius, however, was found to have been the instigator of the murder and was punished with death.

After Bishop Paul had been sent into exile at Gaza, Rhodo was sent to Constantinople together with the record of the proceedings against him. When the proceedings were being read before the emperor in the palace, he ordered Rhodo to be led away by a clown [Note: [Col. 1045D] Tellerius’s codex: “to be led away by the clown”] and killed outside the imperial city.

[Col. 1046A] After this the emperor sent the deacon Pelagius, apocrisiarius of the first see of Rome, to Antioch with his sacred letters. He ordered him that Euphræmius, bishop of that city, Peter of Jerusalem, and Hypatius of Ephesus should come to Gaza, and to remove Paul’s pallium and depose him.

Pelagius therefore went to Antioch and from there to Jerusalem. With the patriarchs mentioned and several bishops, he came to Gaza. They removed Paul’s pallium, deposed him, and ordained Zoilus in his place. The emperor later deposed Zoilus at Constantinople and ordained Apollinaris, who is now head of that Alexandrian Church.

When Pelagius was returning to Constantinople, certain monks from Jerusalem—through whom Pelagius had obtained passage to Gaza—came with him to the imperial court, carrying chapters excerpted from the books of Origen. They wished to petition the emperor for the condemnation of Origen together with those chapters.

Pelagius, therefore, being a rival of Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and wishing to harm him because he was a defender of Origen, together with Menas, archbishop of Constantinople, urged the emperor to order the request of those monks to be carried out: that Origen and the chapters teaching such things be condemned. The emperor readily agreed, rejoicing that he could pronounce judgment on such matters. At his command, a condemnation by anathema was drawn up against Origen and those chapters, and the bishops found at Constantinople subscribed it together with Menas, archbishop.

The document was then sent to Vigilius, bishop of Rome; Zoilus, bishop of Alexandria; Euphræmius, bishop of Antioch; and Peter, bishop of Jerusalem. When they had received and subscribed it, Origen was condemned after death, although he had once already been condemned while alive.

[Note: [Col. 1046C]

**The superiors of the monasteries.** See all the petitions in the Council of Constantinople under Menas.

**In the tenth year of the reign.** Peace was made, with all the patriarchs joining in the one faith of the Council of Chalcedon. But how did this occur in Justinian’s tenth year, when one of the patriarchs, Paul, was ordained in the presence of Pelagius, Vigilius’s representative, whereas Vigilius is said not to have been ordained until the following year, on 22 November? Did Vigilius, when departing from Constantinople and confident that he would obtain the Apostolic See, leave Pelagius there as his own representative, just as he had been Agapetus’s representative? For Agapetus had ordered him to perform the same office there; indeed, [Col. 1046D] in 535 he had sent him to Constantinople with Theophanes, another deacon of the Apostolic See, as is clear from the Council of Constantinople under Menas, where they are called archdeacons. Or was Vigilius ordained not in the following year but in this one, when Silverius had been substituted on 17 May in place of Agapetus, who had died on 22 April?

**He had been accused.** That is, he had been accused as being less fit to govern—not because of simplicity, which was the view of some, but partly because he defended the Council and attacked Origen against the Tabennesiotes, who favored Dioscorus and Origen; and partly because of his imperious manner of governing and his extreme desire for the chief chair. Hence, as a despiser of monks, he was in turn despised by monks.

[Col. 1047A] **By divine providence.** It may indeed have happened by divine providence that he was first made bishop on account of the merit of his faith. But when he had later been deposed because of his complicity in the murder, he tried to buy back his restoration from Justinian with a large sum of money, as Procopius reports in *Secret History*, chapter 27. Paul would therefore have been restored, unless Pope Vigilius, who was then at Constantinople, had opposed it.

**The people were growing powerful.** The reading is doubtful, if not corrupt. The sense would be more probable if one read, “the heretics were growing powerful.”

**Pelagius therefore.** Victor reports that a council was held: “While celebrating the deposition of Dioscorus, his heretical predecessor, he is deposed by the Palestinian council, and Zoilus is ordained in his place.” It is not easy to determine the year in which this occurred, both because the writers contradict one another and because each speaks obscurely. Even if they expressed the matter plainly, they would not deserve great confidence, since they introduce many falsehoods into the account. [Col. 1047B] Some writers assign it to 557, like Baronius; others to 543, like Panvinius; others to 539 or 540, like Victor of Tunnuna—if anything definite can be inferred from his rather confused words. For he says that in the same year Silverius succeeded Agapetus and that Paul took possession of the Alexandrian Church. Yet Paul was deposed after spending not quite two full years in the see and had Zoilus as his successor. Since Silverius was ordained in 536, on 17 May or 20 June, we must admit, if we follow Victor, that Paul took possession of the Alexandrian Church either toward the end of 536 or at the beginning of the following year, before 17 May, and was therefore deposed either in 539 or at the beginning of the following year. I discuss this question at greater length in the dissertation.

**Arsenius.** Procopius reports that he was Palestinian by birth and a Samaritan by sect. Through Theodora’s favor he was first made a senator; then, because he had fostered the Samaritan revolt, he was expelled from the palace. Soon afterward [Col. 1047C] he incurred the Augusta’s hatred because, after Theodosius had been expelled—the man whom the Augusta had appointed—he came to Alexandria with Paul, the Catholic bishop of the Alexandrian Church, and won the favor of the people for him. Finally, when he was convicted of the deacon’s murder, he was crucified by the *augustalis* Liberius at Theodora’s command. His considerable property, which he had amassed by evil means, was also confiscated. He is said to have falsely professed Christianity twice.

**The emperor deposed him.** Liberatus agrees with Victor concerning the deposition of Zoilus, whether under “the eleventh year after the consulship of Basilius”: “Apollinarius was substituted as bishop of the Alexandrian Church for Zoilus, who was unwilling to condemn the Three Chapters mentioned”; or when he writes that “Apollinaris was promoted while Zoilus was still alive.” Evagrius disagrees: “After Zoilus died, Apollinaris took possession of the Alexandrian See.” In the sentence of condemnation against Theodore of Cappadocia, Vigilius objects that Theodore had erased Zoilus’s name from the sacred diptychs without authority and had written in its place the name of Apollinaris, a perverter and adulterer. [Col. 1047D] He not only supports Liberatus—since an adulterer is one who takes possession of the Church while its spouse is alive—but also shows that Zoilus was deposed in 551, in July. For Vigilius issued the sentence against Theodore in that same year, on 14 August.

**Who is now its head.** From this no one can determine the date when Liberatus wrote. Apollinaris remained in the episcopate for several years; one can scarcely conclude more than that Liberatus wrote after 551, when Apollinaris is said to have succeeded Zoilus.

**Being a rival.** Both men were lying in wait for the emperor’s favor and courting his goodwill. Both possessed great authority at court: Pelagius on behalf of the Apostolic See, whose affairs he administered; Theodore on behalf of his autocephalous Church. Both were powerful in doctrine; both were energetic in practical affairs. Both nourished Justinian’s foolish vanity—he sought on the throne the reputation of learning—through books issued in the emperor’s name. [Col. 1048A] Both served the counsels of the Augusta; but Theodore was the bolder, while Pelagius was more cautious in maintaining what was right.

**Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.** Concerning him, the monk Cyril writes in the *Life of Saint Sabas*, no. 105:

“After the Church had recently been freed from heresies and had recovered its breath from those long disturbances and disorders, and after peace and tranquillity had arisen in it, the evil one once again cast upon it an envious eye and stirred up against it certain followers of Nonus—namely Domitian and Theodore. Since they had long shared Origen’s views, when they also found the advantage of the times, and one of them was appointed bishop of Galatia and Theodore bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, they displayed their great power.”

I believe he became bishop toward the end of 536. He had not yet become bishop when Menas held his council at Constantinople, since he is recorded as having subscribed there: “Stephen, deacon and legate of Sotericus, most holy bishop of Caesarea, metropolitan of the first province of Cappadocia.” [Col. 1048B] Menas held his council in 536, in May, on the second day. Nor had Theodore held the Caesarean Church for long, as can be gathered from Vigilius’s letters. Before assuming the episcopate, he had spent several years at court. I believe he went there after the death of Sabas, when disturbances arose in Syria and he traveled to Constantinople to occupy the emperor’s mind.

**A condemnation was drawn up against Origen.** The writers do not agree about the time when it was drawn up. Baronius assigns it to 537; others place it almost a decade later. The question depends on the date of Zoilus’s ordination; on this see the dissertation, which is placed at the end.

**Had once already been condemned.** It is clear from the beginning of the following chapter that this was maliciously inserted so that Origen’s condemnation after death would not prejudice the case of the men of the Three Chapters, who were likewise condemned after their deaths—something which the defenders of the Chapters declared impious. Liberatus is speaking of the Alexandrian council which Demetrius convened against Origen around 231. [Col. 1048C] No one, so far as I know, mentions it before Jerome, who himself gives differing and contradictory accounts according to the different dispositions he adopted at different times. In his book *On Illustrious Men*, written before his disagreement with Rufinus, he says that Demetrius raged against Origen in great madness; after the disagreement, he says that Demetrius had been torn apart by Origen. Before the disagreement he reports that Origen was not condemned because of the “novelty of his doctrines or heresy, as rabid dogs now pretend against him, but because they could not endure the glory of his eloquence and knowledge, and, when he spoke, everyone seemed mute.” After the disagreement, he presents Origen as writing to Pope Fabian a petition of repentance because he had committed to writing things that were rightly condemned.

**Certain monks from Jerusalem.** They are mentioned in Justinian’s letter to Menas. Evagrius names four: Eulogius, Conon, [Col. 1048D] Cyriacus, and Pancratius. See the dissertation, col. 1051.

**It was then sent.** Liberatus seems to imply that Justinian wrote to Menas before writing to Vigilius and the other patriarchs; indeed, that Menas convened a council at Constantinople and that the bishops there subscribed Origen’s condemnation before the letters were sent to the other bishops. Yet Justinian himself contradicts this in his letter to Menas: “These same things, moreover, we send not only to Your Holiness but also to the most holy and most blessed pope of senior Rome and patriarch Vigilius, and to all the others,” etc.

**To Euphræmius of Antioch and Peter of Jerusalem.** This does not agree with what Theophanes writes. For he connects Peter’s first year with Justinian’s nineteenth year, which falls in the year 545, and with Zoilus’s fourth year. The entire history plainly shows that this is far from the truth, [Col. 1049A] although Theophanes, when writing this, did not depart far from the truth in joining the years of Justinian and Zoilus; for Justinian’s nineteenth year was approximately Zoilus’s fourth.]

# CHAPTER XXIV  
## On Pelagius and Theodore

When the way had thus been opened to the adversaries of the Church so that a dead man might be condemned, Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, beloved by and familiar with the rulers, an Acephalan by sect, a most determined defender of Origen, and a rival of Pelagius, learned that Origen had been condemned. Grieved by his condemnation and seeking to disturb the Church, he contrived the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia, because Theodore had published many short works against Origen and was hated and liable to accusation among the Origenists; and especially because, as is proved, the Council of Chalcedon had received his praises [Col. 1049B] in three letters. The aforementioned Theodore accomplished his condemnation by the following scheme.

While the emperor was writing against the Acephalans in defense of the Council of Chalcedon, Theodore of Cappadocia approached him together with his satellites, who, under the Catholic name, were favorable to the Acephalans [Note: [Col. 1049D] Tellerius’s codex: “were zealous for”]. With the support of the Augusta Theodora, he suggested to the emperor that he ought not to endure the labor of writing, since he could bring all the Acephalans into communion with himself by a shorter route:

“They are offended in the Council of Chalcedon,” he said, “because it received the praises of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, and because the Council itself declared by its judgment that the letter of Ibas, which is recognized as wholly Nestorian, was orthodox. But if Theodore, together with his writings and this letter, is anathematized, [Col. 1049C] the Council, as though retracted and cleansed, will be accepted by them in every way and in all respects. Once they have been joined to the Catholic Church without any labor on the part of Your Piety, with the universal Church rejoicing, the praise of Your Clemency will be everlasting.”

When the emperor heard this, and failed entirely to perceive the trick of the tricksters, he gladly accepted their suggestion and readily promised to do what they proposed.

But then, with cunning deceit, they asked him to compose a book condemning the Three Chapters. Once the book had been published and made known to the whole world, “since the emperor would be ashamed to correct it, the matter would become irrevocable. For they knew that, according to his customary fickleness, when scandal arose the emperor could correct his judgment and that they themselves would be exposed to danger.”

[Col. 1049D] The emperor agreed to their request and happily promised to carry it out. Abandoning his other literary project, he composed one book against the Three Chapters, to our misfortune, a book known to us all.

As for the other things subsequently done by that emperor among the bishops and the Catholic Church—how the bishops who consented to the condemnation of the Three Chapters were enriched with gifts, while those who did not consent were deposed and sent into exile, and some, hiding in flight, met a happy end in their afflictions—I think I must now pass over them, since they are known to everyone.

I believe it is clear to all that through the deacon Pelagius [Col. 1050A] and Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, this scandal entered the Church. Theodore himself also publicly cried out that he and Pelagius ought to be burned alive, since through them this scandal had entered the world.

[Note: [Col. 1050A]

**Beloved by the emperors.** By Justinian, because he lent his lying labor to the composition of books; by Theodora, because, although he was an Acephalan, he attacked the Council of Chalcedon. By both together, because of his flattery, servility at court, and almost idolatry. Woe to the court-loving bishops, to shepherds who desert their sheep, and so forth.

**He contrived the condemnation.** If Facundus is to be trusted, book I, chapter 2, Domitian of Ancyra confessed this:

“Domitian, bishop of Ancyra, a city of the first province of Galatia, who was an open supporter of the Origenist heresy, confessed in a petition which he wrote to the most blessed Pope Vigilius—[Col. 1050B] God forcing the confession from him—that his accomplices, the Origenists, when they saw that they could not defend their own doctrine and that no hope remained for them in the conflict, had stirred up these scandals in the Church as revenge for the actions taken against Origen.”

It is remarkable that Theodore and Domitian, men devoted to Origen, came under suspicion of association with the Acephalans. But given the circumstances of the time, the Acephalans were called such—at least by the Africans—whomever each defender of the two natures believed to be his opponent. Domitian, moreover, did not survive to the period of the Fifth Synod as Theodore did; for when the Fathers of the Synod are listed, Anastasius, bishop of Tabia, is named in the thirteenth place as deputy for Dorotheus, bishop of Ancyra.

**Because Theodore had.** It is sufficiently clear that Theodore of Mopsuestia had no shortage of opportunities to criticize Origen repeatedly, since Origen corrupted almost all the passages of Scripture through his allegories. Theodore followed [Col. 1050C] the literal sense so closely that for this reason perhaps he sometimes interpreted the Song of Songs more profanely than the ancients could endure. But no one, so far as I know, has explained what works he wrote against Origen. The matter would still be obscure if Hebediesu had not mentioned in his *Catalogue* five volumes written by Theodore against the Allegorists, which he says are preserved among the Syrians, in the Syriac language into which they were translated from Greek. Everyone can see that Origen and Origen’s followers are meant by the name “Allegorists.”

**That the Council had received his praise in three letters.** These were the letters written by John of Antioch when the question of condemning Theodore’s books was being considered and which were reread at the Council of Chalcedon. Add to them the letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian, which was likewise read there and not rejected.

**While the emperor was writing against the Acephalans.** The following words of Pope Agatho in his letter to the emperors seem to refer to a document of this kind, when he was discussing Justinian’s edicts for the rectitude of the faith disseminated throughout the world:

“Among these, one document, sent to Zoilus, bishop of Alexandria, against the heresy of the Acephalans, sufficient to satisfy the rectitude of the Apostolic faith, we offer to Your Most Tranquil Christian Majesty through the bearers of this letter, together with this suggestion of our humility.”

[Col. 1050D] There is also the following statement of Victor of Tunnuna:

“After the consulship of Belisarius, in the second year, the Emperor Justinian published books on the Lord’s Incarnation and compelled the Illyrian bishops to subscribe.”

The chronicle is in error, for *Basilius* must be read instead of *Belisarius*. If the number is not likewise corrupt, Victor’s authority refutes Panvinius, who places Zoilus’s ordination in 543, and also the dissertation-writer, who assigns it to 544. For in Victor’s usage, the second year after the consulship is the year immediately following the consulship, *ἀμέσως*—“immediately.” Since the consulship of Basilius fell in 541, the second year after the consulship of Basilius was 542. [Col. 1051A] If Justinian wrote his book on the Incarnation against the Acephalans in that year, Zoilus must have been ordained in 540. For Justinian wrote after Origen had been condemned by decree; but Origen was condemned only after Pelagius had returned to the imperial city from Zoilus’s ordination at Gaza, after the petitions of the Palestinian monks had been read and carefully examined, and after delays had been introduced into Theodore’s affair by various contrivances—events that could not have occurred without a suitable interval of time.

**“For they knew,” etc.** The passage was obscure in the published codices, where *pietas* (“piety”) was read instead of *levitas* (“fickleness”). It had to be restored so that it read:

“For they knew that, according to his customary fickleness, when scandal arose, the emperor could correct his judgment and that they themselves would be exposed to danger.”

Liberatus means, as it were: They knew that the emperor had to be held to his judgment by a written book that had been published, lest, according to his customary fickleness, he should change his judgment when scandal arose, and lest the Acephalans themselves should be placed in danger.

[Col. 1051B] **He composed a book.** Facundus speaks at length of this book, which he knew well, since he refuted it in twelve books, often with sharp and impassioned argument. To make this attack more freely, he stated beforehand that the work was not Justinian’s—whose faith he praises highly—but that of others falsely using the emperor’s name:

“They acted craftily through their accomplices, as adversaries of the truth usually do, so that the writings which they had caused to be composed would also be marked beforehand with the title of your name, thinking that by attributing their error to your person they would escape condemnation or even conviction for their rashness and falsehood. But we do not wish to call those writings yours which we know to be contrary to your faith, of which we are well aware.”

He says the same thing more fully later, in book IV, chapter 4.

**They were enriched with gifts.** He is speaking of his fellow Africans: Reparatus of Carthage, Firmus of Numidia, Primasius, primate of the council of Byzacena, Verecundus of Junca, and [Col. 1052A] Victor, bishop of Tunnuna. The first of these was deposed and sent into exile at Euchaita. The third was sent back to his own see with gifts after subscribing to the condemnation of the Three Chapters. Firmus died in exile after ten years, stubbornly refusing to assent to the Fifth Synod. Verecundus and Victor were transferred from one prison to another and finally confined in monasteries.

**Some, hiding in flight.** Facundus remained in hiding, as he himself writes in the preface of his book addressed to Mocianus.

**I think I must now pass over them.** And rightly so. For what did the Africans not dare? Or what punishments, equal to their daring, did they not deserve? Let one of them be heard:

“In the eleventh year after the consulship of Basilius, the African bishops synodally exclude Vigilius, Roman bishop and condemner of the Three Chapters, from Catholic communion, while reserving for him the opportunity of repentance. For the defense of the Three Chapters mentioned above, they send sufficiently suitable letters to the Emperor Justinian through Olympius, a *magistrianus*. At that time the seven books [Col. 1052B] of Facundus, bishop of the Church of Hermiana, shone forth, in which he demonstrated most clearly that the oft-mentioned Three Chapters had been condemned in the rule of faith of the Catholic and Apostolic Council of Chalcedon.”

**Theodore cried out.** Let the author bear responsibility for this angry writing. Yet Theodore is sufficiently deserving on other grounds, and especially on this one, of having his name infamous: abusing the power of the court, he brought evils upon the Church scarcely smaller than the remedies. And although this affair was undertaken through the insane zeal of factions and with minds incredibly hostile, nevertheless, as Evagrius observes, the admirable wisdom of God—which itself turns even evils toward good—brought it about that such great hatreds served the good of the Church, and that the errors of Origen and Theodore of Mopsuestia were condemned, all the more harmful because they were advanced under greater names.]

[Col. 1051]

# DISSERTATION FOR LIBERATUS ON THE FIFTH SYNOD AND THE EVENTS THAT PRECEDED IT

[Col. 1051C] It is worthwhile to gather in a dissertation those matters which could not conveniently be treated in the notes because of their brevity, but which nevertheless must not be omitted because of their importance. It is of interest to the learned reader that the matters which Liberatus touched upon briefly in the last four chapters of his *Breviarium* should be set out more fully. In my judgment, he did this not without reason, and for an honorable purpose. For when he had almost reached the point toward which he was heading—namely, the Fifth Synod—he seems deliberately to have halted and to have passed over many matters of importance relating to it, fearing, as it is reasonable to believe, that by indulging his feelings he might suffer what his fellow Africans Facundus and Victor suffered: their inability to restrain themselves drove them to rail calumniously against the supreme pontiff and the Catholic Church.

The matters which I think ought to be explained can readily be reduced to seven headings. This is clear from the fact that, after Justinian had first proscribed by edict the famous Three Chapters, which gave the Fifth Synod its cause, and had then wished them to be condemned by all the patriarchs, but had not obtained what he most ardently desired from Vigilius, the supreme pontiff, just as he had obtained it from his Eastern patriarchs, he decided that an ecumenical synod must be convened. [Col. 1051D] It would serve his wishes and, even against Vigilius’s will, accomplish by ecclesiastical authority what he himself had first attempted by imperial power.

The emperor had been led to proscribe the Three Chapters by the schemes of those who were grieved that Origen had previously been condemned by edict and wished to repay the authors of that condemnation in kind, so that their rivals and the defenders of the Three Chapters might in turn be grieved at their favor with the emperor. Thus they created trouble for one another: Theodore was the defender of Origen, Pelagius of the Three Chapters. Justinian had condemned Origen at Pelagius’s instigation, and Pelagius had drawn [Col. 1052C] Menas, bishop of the imperial city, over to his side. But when Pelagius was returning from Gaza to Constantinople, after Paul had been deposed from the Alexandrian See and Zoilus substituted in his place, he brought with him from Palestine monks hostile to Theodore, who presented petitions against Origen that would be very welcome to Justinian. For Justinian was burning to handle ecclesiastical affairs while leaving political matters to his wife.

Neither imperial edict—whether the one condemning Origen or the one condemning the Three Chapters—bears an inscribed date. Hence, since the writers disagree, it is not sufficiently clear when either was issued. Yet determining this is of considerable importance for ecclesiastical history.

I therefore think it necessary to investigate first when the emperor condemned Origen and then when he condemned the Three Chapters. At the same time, three closely connected matters must be examined: Menas’s council against the Origenists; the council of that same Menas against the Three Chapters; and Origen himself—whether he really was condemned at the Fifth Synod. [Col. 1052D] This is the controversy that recently occupied the learned Halloix and another recent writer. To these five chapters two more seem necessary: one containing observations on the individual sessions of the synod, and another concerning the approval of that synod by the supreme pontiffs.

# CHAPTER I  
## On the time when the Emperor Justinian issued his decree against Origen

Liberatus, chapter 23, reports that Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church [Col. 1053A] and apocrisiarius of the Apostolic See, when returning to Constantinople after Zoilus’s ordination, brought with him monks who presented the emperor with propositions excerpted from Origen’s books and petitions asking that the propositions and their author be condemned. He likewise reports that Justinian willingly accepted these petitions, with Pelagius and Menas supporting them out of envy against Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and that, following the monks’ request, a decree of condemnation was issued, sent to the patriarchs, and accepted by the subscription of all.

From this account it is clear that the date of the edict against Origen cannot be discovered more reliably than from the year in which Zoilus was substituted for Paul. Baronius thinks this occurred before 537; Panvinius places it six years later. Distinguished scholars support Baronius, while a recent dissertation-writer supports Panvinius. Arguments are advanced on both sides, and each author regards the considerations supporting his position as substantial. [Col. 1053B] To weigh them individually is neither a small labor nor entirely necessary.

Nor do I think Baronius should be followed, nor Panvinius. The former places Zoilus’s ordination earlier than is proper; the latter later. I therefore think that a middle course must be followed, and that Zoilus should be said to have been appointed to the Alexandrian Church not in 537, as Baronius wishes; not in 543, as Panvinius holds; and not in 544, as a recent dissertation-writer states in one place, but in 540, or perhaps 539. I demonstrate this in the following three arguments.

And first, against Baronius. Zoilus was appointed in the place of Paul the Tabennesiote, who held office for two years; Paul had received the see after Theodosius was expelled, when he had governed the Alexandrian Church for one year and four months. Theodosius began to sit alone after Gaianus was expelled; Gaianus had been bishop of Alexandria for three months and a few days. Theodosius and Gaianus succeeded Timothy Asterius, who is said to have held office for seventeen years; he succeeded the younger Dioscorus in the latter part of 519, as can be gathered from Letter 54 of Pope Hormisdas. If, therefore, Timothy held office for seventeen years from 519, he must have died in 536. Add to this the periods of Theodosius and Paul, nearly four years, and it is necessarily the case that Zoilus was not ordained before 539 or 540.

Against Panvinius and the recent dissertation-writer the same argument may be used. For Zoilus’s ordination cannot be postponed beyond 540 unless either the number of years during which each of the bishops mentioned above held office is increased, or Timothy’s ordination is postponed far beyond 521, or the Alexandrian see is said to have been vacant for some time. But the number of years during which each bishop held office cannot be increased without openly contradicting the authority confessed even by those with whom we are dealing; nor can the Alexandrian see be said to have been vacant. For when could that have occurred? Certainly not before Zoilus’s ordination, since Paul was deposed by the same judges, at the same Council of Gaza, and Zoilus was substituted in his place. Not before Paul’s ordination: for at Constantinople Paul was appointed in the place of Theodosius, who had arrived at the imperial city and stubbornly refused to receive the Council of Chalcedon. Not after Timothy’s death: Gaianus and Theodosius were elected by their respective parties before Timothy’s body had yet been carried out. Nor after the death of the younger Dioscorus and before Timothy’s ordination: the custom of the Alexandrian Church does not permit this to be said, since, unless something unusual occurred, the elected bishop kept vigil beside the body of his deceased predecessor, as Liberatus reports in chapter 20. If anything unusual had happened at that time, no historian would certainly have passed over it in silence.

Nor can Timothy’s ordination be postponed beyond 521—or even to 521, as the dissertation-writer attempted in order not to abandon Panvinius’s case. Severus fled from Antioch to Alexandria in 519, as Evagrius reports; but he was received at Alexandria by Timothy, who, at the time when Severus fled, “had assumed the pontificate of the Alexandrian Church after the death of the younger Dioscorus.” These are the words of Liberatus.

The dissertation-writer adduces this passage from Theophanes in his defense:

> “When Severus received that report, he fled, and likewise Julian, bishop of Halicarnassus; and while Dioscorus was still administering the Alexandrian episcopate, they went to Egypt,” etc.

But anyone may rightly wonder that an evidently defective testimony is adduced by a man who seeks to be heard as learned. First, Liberatus, who is much more trustworthy because he writes about events of his own time, contradicts Theophanes, who writes about events two centuries earlier. Second, the dissertation-writer allowed himself to be deceived by an interpreter who interpolated Theophanes’ text—not only by adding the word *adhuc* (“still”), to which nothing corresponds in the Greek, but also by adding the words “while Dioscorus was administering the Alexandrian episcopate,” attaching them to a different word rather than to the one to which they belong.

For after Theophanes had said that Vitalianus possessed such authority that he “ordered Severus to be expelled and killed,” he continues in Greek:

> Ὁ δὲ Σεύηρος ἀκούσας ἔφυγεν καὶ Ἰουλιανὸς Ἁλικαρνασσοῦ ἐπίσκοπος, καὶ εἰς Αἵγυπτον ἀπελθόντες ταύτην ἐτάραξαν, τὸν περὶ φθαρτοῦ καὶ ἀφθάρτου λόγον κινήσαντες, Διοσκόρου ἐπισκοπεύοντος Ἀλεξανδρείας.

That is:

> “When Severus heard this, he fled, and Julian, bishop of Halicarnassus, likewise; and after they reached Egypt, they disturbed it by stirring up the controversy concerning the corruptible and incorruptible, while Dioscorus was serving as bishop of Alexandria.”

From this, anyone but an ignoramus can detect three errors in Theophanes, on account of which his credibility is rightly diminished. First, he joins the flight of the two bishops together, although Julian preceded Severus. Second, he says that questions concerning the corruptible and incorruptible were raised in the time of Dioscorus, although Liberatus expressly reports that this occurred under Timothy, and all other writers agree with Liberatus. Third, he places Dioscorus’s third year in the same chronological entry as Justin’s second year. In this way he indicates that Dioscorus’s third and final year fell in the year 519 of Christ, although that was Justin’s second year.

Accordingly, someone might suppose that something has been omitted from the Greek, and that the reading should be:

> Διοσκόρου οὐκ ἔτι ἐπισκοποιοῦντος

—that is, “Dioscorus no longer serving as bishop.” But how, while retaining the existing reading, a somewhat charitable interpretation may nevertheless be applied to Theophanes’ words will be shown later; at the same time, the dissertation-writer’s futile effort will be refuted.

Now, when the same dissertation-writer asserts that Theophanes “relates the beginning of Timothy’s tenure in Justin’s third year, namely 521, after Dioscorus’s death,” this does not help his case. What he asserts must be understood either of Theophanes’ text or of the chronological table. If of Theophanes’ text, it is altogether false: the text does not mention, even in a single word, either Dioscorus’s death or Timothy’s beginning of his episcopate. If of the chronological table or register, it is indeed true that the assertion concerns Timothy; but I am surprised that a man whom the dissertation-writer himself calls active and diligent should overlook the learned interpreter’s note concerning the defects of chronological tables—defects obvious to everyone and because of which they possess scarcely any credibility unless supported from elsewhere. Such tables lose all authority for themselves when they contradict the text.

They plainly contradict it here. For since Theophanes assigns Dioscorus’s first year to the last year of Anastasius and attributes to him no more than three years in office, how could the period of his episcopate have been extended to 521? The dissertation-writer saw this difficulty and, to extricate himself, invented the addition of several months to Dioscorus’s years, supposedly enabling them to reach 521. But while using this escape to help himself, he failed to notice that by this fiction he undermined the credibility of the chronological tables, in which only the third year of Dioscorus is mentioned. If his tenure had extended into other years, the fourth or at least the fifth year should have been recorded.

But it is useful for the dissertation-writer to be compared for a little while with Theophanes, so that either the credibility granted to Theophanes may be preserved, or the dissertation-writer may be convicted of falsehood by the very witness whom he adduces. The dissertation-writer says that Zoilus was ordained in 544. It follows that Zoilus’s first year coincided with Justinian’s eighteenth year and that Zoilus’s deposition occurred in 551. Theophanes plainly contradicts this. He joins Zoilus’s first year with Justinian’s sixteenth year and his deposition with the twenty-third year, which was 549 in the Christian era; in that year Theophanes places the accession of Apollinaris, who succeeded Zoilus.

Once these opinions have been overturned, it is clear that Zoilus was ordained around the year 540. The younger Dioscorus died at the end of 519. Timothy Asterius, Dioscorus’s successor, died in 536. Theodosius, who succeeded Timothy, was deposed around 538; his successor Paul was also deposed after holding the see for two years. Zoilus, therefore, was ordained around 540.

Victor of Tunnuna is not far from this view. He appears to refer Zoilus’s ordination to the consulship of Basil, which occurred in 541. He writes:

> “In the consulship of Basil, a man of senatorial rank, when Agapetus, archbishop of Rome, died at Constantinople, Silverius was ordained bishop in his place. In the Alexandrian Church, after Theodosius and Gaianus had been exiled, Paul was ordained in their place by the defenders of the Council of Chalcedon, from among the monks of the Tabennesiotes. While celebrating the deposition of his predecessor Dioscorus, the heretic, he was deposed by the Palestinian council, and Zoilus was ordained bishop in his place.”

But, to speak frankly, Victor’s testimony is not of great importance, since nothing is more confused than this Chronicle, especially concerning these times. First, under Basil’s consulship—that is, in 541—he places the ordination of Zoilus and Silverius, although it is absolutely certain that Silverius was ordained in 536. Next, he places Silverius’s exile in the following year, 542; yet Silverius unquestionably died on June 20, 538. Furthermore, although he joins the ordination of Pope Agapetus and the death of Timothy Asterius in the same year—a conjunction not far from the truth—he nevertheless refers both to the consulship of John, that is, to 538. This is utterly absurd, both because Agapetus succeeded John II on May 3, 535, and because Timothy died in 536. Finally, by an intolerable *ἀντιχρονισμός* (“anachronism”), he places Agapetus’s arrival in Constantinople, the deposition of Anthimus, and the ordination of Menas under the consulship of Justin, which was the year 540. For after Agapetus’s death, Menas—who had been substituted in the place of the deposed Anthimus—held a council against Anthimus in the imperial city in 536. This is established with complete certainty by the acts.

Theophanes is likewise not far from this view. He assigns Zoilus seven years of episcopate and joins his first year with the fifth year of Vigilius; in this way he appears to show that Zoilus was ordained in 541. The fifth year of Vigilius did indeed fall in that year. Yet I do not think this testimony, considered by itself, deserves more weight than Victor’s statement. Nevertheless, neither testimony should be passed over, since both are highly valuable against those who abusively exploit the authority of the two chroniclers.

One objection may be raised. If Theophanes’ credibility concerning the years during which Zoilus held office is not diminished, the matter becomes troublesome. For not only Victor of Tunnuna indicates that Zoilus was deposed in 551; Pope Vigilius also shows this in the sentence of condemnation issued against Theodore of Cappadocia. If this is so, Zoilus must have been ordained in 544, provided that he held the Alexandrian see for seven years, as Theophanes and Nicephorus of Constantinople report.

But Theophanes and Nicephorus have the same authority in this matter, as was demonstrated in the preface; and no credibility is owed to Nicephorus here, since his calculation contains an obvious error. Therefore this objection should not deter us from the truth. That Nicephorus’s calculation is defective is clearly shown by the following. Between the death of John Machiotes, which occurred at the beginning of 517, and Zoilus’s deposition, which occurred in July 551, near the end of the month, there are approximately thirty-five years, counting both endpoints because one period begins and the other ends within the respective years. Of these years, by the constant agreement of all writers, three are assigned to the younger Dioscorus, seventeen to Timothy Asterius, at most two jointly to Gaianus and Theodosius, and likewise two to Paul, together with several months—namely, the months between his expulsion from Alexandria to Gaza and his deposition at Gaza.

There therefore remain approximately eleven years, which can be assigned to no one but Zoilus. Nicephorus, however, assigns him only seven. It is therefore evident that Nicephorus has made an error in calculating Zoilus’s years.

What I said concerning the several months that intervened between Paul’s expulsion from the city of Alexandria and his deposition at the Council of Gaza is confirmed by the fact that a report of his expulsion was sent from Egypt to Constantinople, and that Pelagius was then sent by imperial command. On his way he met the bishop of Antioch and the bishop of Jerusalem and brought them with him to Gaza for the trial. Such events certainly cannot take place without an adequate interval of time, whether because of the distance between the places or because of the status of the persons involved.

This, moreover, confirms our opinion concerning the date of Zoilus’s ordination. If he governed the Alexandrian Church for eleven years, he was certainly ordained in July 540; for he was deposed in July 551. Nor is it credible that Vigilius’s sentence against Theodore was delayed long after Zoilus’s deposition and the perpetration of the other offenses at the same time, since passions were everywhere raging, and it would not have been fitting to apply slow remedies to evils so great and so exasperated.

Since Theodore’s condemnation was issued on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September [August 14], and since it mentions an excommunication imposed upon Theodore thirty days earlier, it is probable, if not certain, that this was perpetrated at the beginning of July by Theodore—the act of which Vigilius complains in these words:

> “In the house of Placidia, you assembled with the bishops of the Greek and Latin parties who were present in the imperial city, and with the priests and deacons of the Church of Constantinople. There, amid loud protest, both we and our brother, the bishop of Milan, forbade all of you to give assent to the violation of the common decree, despising the bond of brotherhood. But you disregarded the authority of the apostolic see, which through us had issued the prohibition, and proceeded to the Church where those very decrees were displayed, drawing the others along with you. There, adding further violations, you celebrated the solemnities of the Mass. And as though it were not enough for you to have despised the bishop of the first see, who was present and objected, you also removed from the diptychs our brother Zoilus, bishop and priest of the Alexandrian Church, whose name had been in communion with you up to that very day, and joined to yourselves a certain Apollinaris, a perverse man and adulterer of that Church. Thus your wickedness might be revealed not only in removing a most simple priest but also in receiving a perverse man. For the present we pass over the other acts which you are proved to have committed on that same day against the apostolic see and the canons, lest, detained by an enumeration of the offenses whose author you have shown yourself to be, we delay longer than is fitting. And although thirty days earlier, on account of the excesses mentioned above, we had removed you from participation in the communion of the apostolic see,” etc.

From what has so far been established concerning Zoilus’s ordination, it is easy to conclude in what year Justinian wrote his edict against Origen. When Pelagius was returning from Palestine after Zoilus’s ordination, he encountered the monks who were bringing excerpts from Origen’s books to the imperial city, together with petitions and complaints. If we allow approximately one year for the return journey and for the preparation and completion of the entire affair—which is close to the truth—then Justinian may be said to have completed and published his book around 541, so that he might be heard as a theologian.

At that time the world could well have been astonished—or rather indignant—that an emperor, having turned the sword into a pen, should discuss matters of faith with monks and priests and place books before them, while his wife Theodora ruled the world and he waged wars almost everywhere through his generals.

It is worthwhile to observe something concerning the author of the edict and the monks who brought the petitions. Some think that the edict was written by the deacon Pelagius; others, by the monks themselves, who were its accusers; and others attribute it to both—its form to Pelagius, its substance to the monks, who had been trained by their long controversies with Origen’s party. I would add that the style was borrowed from Menas. For it does not differ greatly from the style in which the proceedings conducted by Menas against Anthimus were written.

The monks whom I have mentioned appear to be those whom Evagrius names when he recounts what was done at the Fifth Council, although, to the detriment of history, he confuses those events with the acts of the council that Menas convened in the imperial city against Origen at the emperor’s command, as will soon be explained.

But first, two questions concerning Zoilus must be resolved. The first is whether he was truly deposed or whether he yielded the see to Apollinaris through death; the second is, if he was deposed, what the cause of his deposition was.

The two Africans, Liberatus and Victor of Tunnuna, and the supreme pontiff Vigilius report that he was deposed. The former do so plainly, the latter somewhat more obscurely. In his sentence against Theodore of Cappadocia, Vigilius writes:

> “You joined to yourselves a certain Apollinaris, a perverse man and adulterer of that Church, so that your wickedness might be revealed not only in removing a most simple priest but also in receiving a perverse man.”

Someone might quibble here and say that this proves only that Zoilus’s name was erased from the sacred records at that time and Apollinaris’s name entered, not that Zoilus himself was deposed. Yet the word “adulterer” leaves no room for such a quibble: an adulterer is one who takes possession of the Church of a living bishop.

Evagrius, who completed his history forty years after the Fifth Council, may appear, in Book IV, chapter 36, to contradict the African writers and to write that Zoilus yielded the Alexandrian see to Apollinaris not by deposition but by death. For when he lists the bishops who held the greater thrones during the time of Eutychius of Constantinople, he writes:

> Μετὰ δὲ τὴν ἐκβολὴν Θεοδοσίου, ὡς προδεδιήγηται, ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Ἀλεξανδρέων Ζώιλος ἀναδείκνυται, καὶ τοῖς αὐτὸν ἡγησαμένοις προστεθέντος, Ἀπολλινάριος τὴν καθέδραν ἐγχειρίζεται.

“After the expulsion of Theodosius, as has been related above, Zoilus was appointed bishop of the Alexandrians; and when he had been added to those who had preceded him, Apollinaris took possession of the see.”

Nicephorus amended Evagrius by adding the words οὗ μετὰ μικρὸν τοῖς αὐτὸν (“after a short time, he having…”), or something similar. The learned Valesius thought that both passages required correction, reading οὗ καὶ τοῖς αὐτῶν (Ἀλεξανδρείων) ἡγησαμένοις—“after he too had been added to those who had preceded them [the Alexandrians]”—believing that αὐτὸν ἡγησαμένοις could not be said in Greek, although lexicographers, citing Homer and others, give the accusative with the verb ἡγέομαι (“to lead,” “to precede”).

Christophorsonus translated Evagrius’s words as follows:

> “After Theodosius, as was shown above, had been expelled, Zoilus was declared bishop of Alexandria; and when he had died, Apollinaris took possession of that see.”

Valesius translated them:

> “After Theodosius had been expelled from Alexandria, as was related above, Zoilus was promoted to the episcopate; and when he had been added to his predecessors, Apollinaris undertook the government of that see.”

We translate them somewhat differently:

> “After the deposition of Theodosius, as was said earlier, Zoilus was created bishop of the Alexandrian Church; and when he had been added or joined to his predecessors, Apollinaris occupied the Alexandrian see.”

These words, καὶ τοῖς αὐτὸν ἡγησαμένοις and what follows, may be understood both in accordance with scriptural usage and appropriately in relation to the history. If understood according to scriptural usage, they signify death; if understood in accordance with the historical context, they may indicate something more subtle—namely, that Zoilus, like his predecessors Theodosius, Gaianus, and Paul, had been expelled from the see. Christophorsonus and Valesius interpreted the words according to scriptural usage, and reasonably so. Whoever understands them in the second sense can easily reconcile Evagrius with the other writers. That is preferable and also more probable.

Since, therefore, the unanimous testimony of the ancients establishes that Zoilus was deposed, someone may think that this fact alone is sufficient for understanding the events of the Fifth Council, and that it is an instance of excessive curiosity to inquire into the reason for his deposition. In my judgment, however, this inquiry is entirely legitimate. Knowing the reason belongs to ecclesiastical history and may also contribute something to establishing the chronology.

Victor of Tunnuna writes under Basil’s eleventh post-consulship, though others count it as his tenth:

> “Reparatus, archbishop of the Church of Carthage; Firmus, first among the bishops of Numidia; Primasius and Verecundus, bishops of the Byzacene council, were summoned to the imperial city by command of the emperor on account of the faith. Apollinaris was substituted for Zoilus as bishop of the Alexandrian Church because Zoilus refused to condemn the three chapters mentioned above.”

He therefore thinks that Zoilus was deposed because he refused to obey the emperor’s command that the Three Chapters be condemned. If this is so, then after being rebuked by Pope Vigilius because he had subscribed to Justinian’s edict, Zoilus must have acted as a penitent and retracted the deed by a public confession. For as soon as Justinian’s edict was sent out, Zoilus himself, together with Menas, bishop of the imperial city, had subscribed in writing to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, although both added this qualification: that the condemnation should be approved by the pontiff of the first see. They knew that, in a matter of faith, it was religiously proper not to anticipate the judgment of the supreme pontiff.

If this was the cause, and Zoilus steadfastly adhered to the head of the Church, he could rightly have been counted among the confessors. Yet I wonder why he is not later said to have suffered either with Vigilius or with the Africans. Why, when Vigilius complains that Zoilus’s name was erased from the diptychs and that he himself was expelled from the see, does he not mention a cause that at the time could have appeared so honorable? Why does no ancient writer except Victor report anything of the kind? Why did Victor himself not count among the confessors the bishop of so great a Church, and one so hostile to the Acephali, whom the Africans hated with mortal hatred?

Procopius certainly reports in his *Secret History*, chapter 27, that Paul, some time after his expulsion, came to Constantinople and offered the emperor an enormous sum of money as the price of recovering the see he had lost. The emperor accepted the seven hundred *centenaria* that were offered—for such was the size of the payment—and gave Paul hope of obtaining his wish, evidently by rescinding the judgment at Gaza. But Pope Vigilius opposed the rescission of the sentence issued in his name by Pelagius, the *apocrisiarius*.

From Procopius’s account, together with Vigilius’s words in condemning Theodore of Cappadocia, one may infer the following:

1. Zoilus yielded the see to Apollinaris not through death but through deposition; otherwise the pontiff would not have called Apollinaris an adulterer.

2. Zoilus was deposed not because he defended the Three Chapters—for which pontiff would not have complained of that?—but because Zoilus himself was said to have been unlawfully substituted in the place of Paul, who had been unjustly deposed.

3. The emperor used this as a pretext in order to make good the promise purchased with gold.

4. Vigilius intervened and wished the judgment at Gaza to remain valid.

5. When the emperor could not obtain from the pontiff the restoration of Paul, he wanted Apollinaris to be bishop of Alexandria in place of Zoilus, so that it would not appear that the whole case had fallen from his hands and that the pontiff had prevailed in everything.

6. Vigilius said nothing about the gold, lest he provoke the emperor; instead, to soothe him, he conceded something. For he soon recognized Apollinaris as one of the patriarchs.

7. The pontiff was not particularly concerned to retain Zoilus, since he did not think highly of him because of his adaptable character, capable of assuming every form; and for that reason he called him an utterly simple priest, as though he were inept at conducting affairs.

## CHAPTER II. On the Council of Constantinople convened by Menas at Justinian’s command concerning Origen and the Origenists

Concerning the monks mentioned in the preceding chapter, Evagrius writes in Book X, chapter 38, in Christophorsonus’s translation:

> “After petitions had been presented to the council by the monks Eulogius, Conon, Cyriacus, and Pancratius against the doctrines of Origen Adamantius and those who followed his impiety and error, Justinian asked the assembled council what it decided concerning them. He also appended a copy of one of the petitions, as well as a letter written by Vigilius concerning the same matters. From these documents one may observe how Origen labored to stuff the simple teaching of the apostolic doctrines with the tares of the pagans and Manichaeans.”

It is useful to examine carefully the four things mentioned here. First, what council was it to which the monks’ petitions were presented? Second, what was the petition whose copy was presented together with the monks’ petitions? Third, what did Justinian ask the synod? Finally, what letter did Vigilius write concerning the same matters? Each point deserves clarification.

As for the first, the council in question is the very council that Menas convened at the emperor’s command from among the bishops present in the imperial city. The emperor writes:

> “Since we wish to drive every scandal from the most holy Church, so that no stain may remain in it, and since we obey the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, who overthrew Origen himself and his criminal and impious doctrine of this kind and rightly subjected it to anathema, we have sent this letter to Your Beatitude. We exhort you to convene an assembly of all the most holy bishops who now dwell in this imperial city, and of the most God-loving superiors of the holy monasteries that are here; and to ensure that all of them, in writing, anathematize in every way the aforesaid impious and God-opposing Origen, also called Adamantius, who was a presbyter of the most holy Church of Alexandria, together with his wicked and impious doctrines and all the chapters set out below. Send copies of what Your Beatitude has done for this purpose to all the other most holy bishops and superiors of the venerable monasteries, so that they too may, by their own subscriptions, anathematize Origen and his criminal doctrines, together with all those who will be shown to be heretics.”

Next, the one book whose copy is said to have been presented to the synod does not appear to differ from the emperor’s edict against the Origenists. For the edict has the weight and form of a book, and contains the matters that Justinian wanted the bishops to examine—or rather, to approve by a servile subscription without examination. The emperor calls his edict a “letter,” following the custom of the ancients. As we noted in Dissertation 3 on the first part of the works of Marius Mercator, imperial enactments, when addressed to bishops, were inscribed as letters out of reverence for the priesthood, rather than under any other name that would display the power of the ruler.

As for the third point, the inquiry that Justinian made of the synod, which Evagrius mentions, is no different from Justinian’s letter to the holy Council of Constantinople concerning Origen and his followers. These letters have been transferred from the history of Cedrenus into the appendix to the Fifth Council. After a brief preface, the emperor writes:

> “Since we have learned that there are in Jerusalem certain monks who follow and teach the impious errors of Pythagoras, Plato, and Origen Adamantius, we have judged that care and investigation must be directed toward them, lest they finally destroy many people with their pagan and Manichaean impostures. For they say,” etc.

And near the end:

> “Because of these wicked and destructive opinions—or rather, these absurdities—we exhort you, most holy Fathers, to gather together, carefully read the exposition set forth below, condemn each of its chapters, and anathematize, together with Origen, all who think or will think the same things until the end.”

Finally, the letter concerning these matters that Vigilius wrote and that was brought to the synod was nothing other than the pontiff’s response to the emperor’s petition or letter concerning Origen and his followers. For Justinian wrote first to Vigilius, before writing to Menas, or certainly to both at the same time. This is clear from the following words of the sacred letter to Menas:

> “We have sent these same matters not only to Your Holiness but also to the most holy and most blessed Pope of Elder Rome and Patriarch Vigilius, and to all the other most holy bishops and patriarchs—namely, those of Alexandria, Theopolis, and Jerusalem—so that they too may attend to this matter and bring it to completion.”

That the pontiff replied, and indeed in accordance with the emperor’s wishes, seems beyond doubt. Pelagius, Vigilius’s *apocrisiarius*, was responsible for securing the response and was the architect of the entire affair. This synodical response of Vigilius has perished, to the great detriment of ecclesiastical history, and, so far as I know, no record of it survives anywhere except in the passages that I shall shortly cite.

I called it “synodical.” For who could reasonably doubt that Vigilius held a council at Rome from which he could reply to the emperor, when the question concerned an important matter of faith? In the earliest periods, pontiffs did not reply to questions of this kind except on the authority of synods. Lucas Holstenius learnedly observed this in his notes on the Roman Council of Boniface, and we explained it in Dissertation 2 on the first part of the works of Marius Mercator.

That synod of Vigilius was an *ἐνδημοῦσα* synod—that is, a local or resident synod—although it may have been convened from among the bishops who gathered for the pope’s birthday on June 28. It is credible that Justinian’s enactment concerning Origen was written, or at least published, around Easter in 541 and sent quickly to Rome, so that, after synodical responses had been received from there, it might more easily be subscribed at Constantinople by a larger gathering of bishops and be strengthened by greater authority.

When I asserted that the letters brought to the synod were not the emperor’s letters to Vigilius but Vigilius’s letters to the emperor, I believe I have grasped Evagrius’s meaning as expressed by Christophorsonus. Christophorsonus read in Evagrius:

> Ἀτὰρ καὶ τὰ πρὸς Βιγιλίου περὶ τούτων ἐπεσταλμένα

—that is, “and also the letters sent by Vigilius concerning these matters.”

The newer interpreter reads:

> Ἀτὰρ καὶ τὰ πρὸς Βιγίλιον ἐπεσταλμένα

—that is, “and also the letters sent to Vigilius.”

It is more consistent with the reasoning to understand these as the letters that had been sent back by Vigilius to the emperor rather than those sent by the emperor to Vigilius. There was no reason for the former to be reported, but there was every reason for the latter. The emperor had written the same things to Vigilius and Menas. The letter written to Menas, according to custom, had to be read aloud in the council, since it contained the mandate for holding it. But since the matter concerned the faith—the chief concern among the highest authorities—it was necessary to report the response of the apostolic see, since from that see, as from a fountain, there ought to be drawn “the pure streams of doctrine that water the Church for its salvation.”

When Justinian understood this, and at the same time knew that although God had established a twofold authority by which the Church is governed—the priestly and the royal—the duties of each had nevertheless been divided in such a way that one was to teach the faithful and condemn heretics, while the other was to add authority to those who taught and pursue heretics by laws, the emperor understood that the apostolic see must be consulted whenever a matter of faith, especially an important one, was under discussion. He therefore thought that the book he had composed against Origen and the anathemas he had formulated against Origen’s doctrines should be strengthened by the authority appropriate to the matter. For this reason he decided to seek both a definition from the apostolic see and approval from the councils of the dioceses.

He therefore sent the book to Pope Vigilius at Rome. After receiving a synodical response from him, he arranged for the council that he had long before ordered to be held at Constantinople—and which, in my opinion, Menas had postponed until he knew the judgment of the first see on a matter of such importance—to begin. This seems to have occurred toward the end of 541.

The memory of this council is obscure because, from the time of Evagrius—that is, from around 593—it was confused with the Fifth Council. Four councils were collected into a single codex: three particular councils presided over by Menas and one ecumenical council presided over by Eutychius. The entire collection was given the name “the Fifth Council.”

This is not a vain or reckless conjecture but a probable opinion, supported by three considerations:

1. Until our own time, or at least until the time of our parents, the council held by Menas five years earlier against Anthimus, Severus, Peter, and Zoaras was itself inscribed in the collections of councils by Merlin, Crabbe, and Surius under the name of the Fifth Council.

2. Justinian’s *faith*—that is, the three edicts of Justinian concerning the faith, collected into one body and corresponding individually to the three councils—appears to have furnished the occasion for combining the three councils into a single volume as well, as though they were three foundations of Justinian’s faith.

3. Once this hypothesis is admitted, everything reported by the ancients concerning the Fifth Council is easily reconciled and understood. Otherwise the reports conflict with one another, or at least are so confused that learned men have been unable to disentangle them without asserting that the acts of the Fifth Council were mutilated and corrupted by the Origenists. But more will be said about this later.

The location of the council was the imperial city, Constantinople; its president was Menas. The number of bishops is unknown, but it was not small. For when, especially in the court of Justinian, was there a shortage of crowds of bishops? Pelagius, a deacon of the Roman Church, was certainly present, as can be gathered from Liberatus; indeed, he vigorously advanced the matter, both for his own sake and for the sake of the faith.

Theodore of Cappadocia was not present, although he was at court. For with what face could a bishop, first after the patriarchs, tolerate in his presence the blasphemies brought against him by the monks? Domitian, bishop of Ancyra, was likewise absent, in my opinion, although he was staying in Constantinople, because he shared Theodore’s cause. Nevertheless, since both humbly served the emperor, they subscribed to the edict and condemned Origen outwardly.

Theodore, more skilled in courtly arts, concealed his grief in his heart while condemning Origen. Domitian, as we learn from Facundus, Book IV, chapter 4, complained to Vigilius that under Origen’s name the Fathers—or those who had preceded Origen as well as those who had followed him—had been struck with anathema by the synod.

It is reasonable to believe that the proceedings began, according to custom, with a reading from the sacred text. George Cedrenus incorporated this reading into his history from ancient records. He was mistaken, however, in believing that it was addressed to the Fathers of the universal Fifth Council. The cause of his mistake is remarkable, since from the conclusion itself he could have understood that the letter was sent to Menas’s council, the council under discussion; he could also have unlearned an error popularly transmitted for four centuries, down to his own time. The passage reads:

> “Because of these wicked and destructive opinions—or rather, these absurdities—we exhort you, most holy Fathers gathered together, carefully to read the exposition set forth below (*ἐπιμελῶς ἐντυχεῖν τῇ ὑποτεταγμένη ἐκθέσει*) and to condemn each of its chapters, and, together with Origen, to anathematize all who think or will think the same things until the end.”

Who could doubt, if one trusts the judgment of one’s own eyes alone, that these words were written to those to whom the letter addressed to Menas, together with the excerpted selection from Origen’s *ἐκθέσεις* (“expositions”), properly belonged?

The subject that, according to the writers, was treated as the sole matter at the council is contained in the imperial decree: namely, Origen’s opinion concerning the preexistence of souls and the eventual restoration even of the demons. Yet the extract submitted by the monks and appended to the emperor’s treatise contains twenty-four chapters, some of which concerned other matters; but the two I have mentioned [Col. 1062A] were the most notorious, because of the disturbances that arose from them.

Nothing of this council survives except fragments: partly from the synodal letter to Justinian, partly from excerpts taken from the books of the Origenists. It is now useful to present them from Evagrius, since they in a sense take the place of the acts and reveal Evagrius’s error in assigning the event to the wrong time. He writes as follows, book IV, chapter 38:

“Accordingly, a report was sent from the aforementioned synod to Justinian, after the acclamations that they had uttered against Origen and those who followed the same error as he did. Part of it runs as follows: ‘Since you possess a soul that shares in heavenly nobility, most Christian emperor—’”

And a little later:

“Therefore we flee, we flee this doctrine; for we do not recognize the voice of strangers, and we have cast him out far from the sacred enclosures, bound as though he were a thief and robber in the bonds of anathema.”

And after a little more:

“You will learn the force and efficacy of what we have done from reading the same.”

They also appended all the chapters that the followers of Origen claimed to have learned from their teachers. From these, both their agreement and their disagreement, together with their manifold and multifaceted error, can be detected. Among them was chapter five, containing the blasphemies uttered by certain private individuals from the New Laura. It reads as follows:

“Theodore Ascidas the Cappadocian said: ‘Since the apostles and martyrs now perform miracles and are held in such great honor, unless they are equal to Christ in the resurrection, what sort of resurrection will theirs ultimately be?’ The same Fathers also reported many other blasphemies of Didymus, Evagrius, and Theodore, which they had very diligently excerpted from their books.”

These excerpts had been brought from Palestine by the four monks whom I mentioned earlier. In that province they were fiercely contending among themselves, even within the very Lauras, as can be learned from the history of this period left by the writers of the saints’ lives.

From the fragments just cited and from other indisputable [Col. 1062C] testimonies, it is clear that the council under discussion differs from the one now usually called the Fifth. For this council dealt with Origen alone and with two Origenists, Didymus and Evagrius; at the Fifth, Origen is scarcely mentioned once, and the other two never. In this council the imperial decree commands judgment to be passed on Origen alone. At the Fifth, it commands judgment to be passed only on the Three Chapters. In this council proceedings concerning Origen were completed, and they were extensive. At the Fifth, this same matter was not touched upon even in a word. Theodore the Cappadocian did not attend this council—for with what patience could he have heard the things reported about him? At the Fifth, the first of the autocephalous bishops sat after the patriarchs. This council was held while Domitian was still alive, for, on account of the council’s decision, he wrote a book of complaints to Pope Vigilius; at the Fifth, Dorotheus, prefect of the Church of Ancyra, attended in Domitian’s place.

I know what some will object in opposition to so obvious a truth. They say that, through the arts of the Origenists, part of the acts of the Fifth Synod perished—the part in which proceedings against Origen once appeared. They claim that Evagrius of Epiphania, the Fathers, the Lateran Council under Martin I, and the Sixth and Seventh Ecumenical Synods saw this part, and therefore transmitted the account that Origen had been condemned at the Fifth Synod. But apart from the fact that such conjecture and objection are the final refuge of a desperate cause, I make this one unconquerable counterargument. How could Theodore the Cappadocian have sat at the Fifth Synod and given his vote when a horrible blasphemy had openly been charged against him and had not been rejected by adequate acts? How could he have been struck with anathema in that very assembly in which he held the most honorable place?

## CHAPTER III. The time when Justinian composed the edict against the Three Chapters

Liberatus explains in his *Breviarium* how one edict arose from the other and by what arts of Theodore the Cappadocian the emperor was induced to write against the Three Chapters. He relates that Theodore, distressed that Origen had been condemned at Pelagius’s instigation, in turn induced Justinian, so that he might return like for like against his rival, to proscribe the Three Chapters. For just as Theodore seemed to defend Origen, and in Origen the Fathers, so Pelagius seemed to defend the Three Chapters, and in the Three Chapters the Council of Chalcedon.

Since the time of Origen’s condemnation has been discussed thus far, it follows that we must now investigate the date when the edict against the Three Chapters was composed. Writers do not agree on this matter: some assert that it occurred earlier than it should have, in the year 543; others place it later, in 546. I believe it happened in 545, toward autumn. I am led to this conclusion because this kind of “confession of faith” (*ὁμολογία τῆς πίστεως*), for that is how the edict is entitled in Greek, was issued, on the one hand, before Vigilius departed from Rome, and, on the other, after Pelagius’s departure from Constantinople [Col. 1063B]. For Vigilius was compelled by Belisarius to go to the imperial city only after he had long and consistently refused to agree with Justinian; and Pelagius, who enjoyed such influence with the emperor, would not, while present, have allowed himself to be so insultingly mocked by rivals eager for vengeance.

Since Vigilius left Rome on 22 November 546, while Pelagius returned to Rome in 545, and since a considerable period elapsed between the edict’s arrival in Rome and Vigilius’s departure—during which Pelagius consulted Ferrandus, who was in Africa, about the questions at issue, and received a reply from Ferrandus after a long silence—it is necessary to admit that Justinian published the edict in 545, around autumn.

To make this argument clearer, however, two points must be established separately: first, that Vigilius left Rome in 546, toward the end of November; and second, that a considerable period—approximately fifteen months—intervened between the edict’s arrival in Rome and Vigilius’s departure [Col. 1063C].

I establish the first point because this is the view concerning Vigilius’s departure from Rome held by the distinguished writers of both earlier and later times. It is recorded in the *Continuation of Marcellinus* as follows:

“In the ninth indiction, after the consulship of Basil, in the fifth year, Pope Vigilius, the fifty-ninth after the Apostle Peter, summoned by the emperor, departed from Rome and came to Sicily.”

The notation “after the consulship” designates the year of Christ 546, as is clear from the consular lists.

Anastasius agrees with the writer of the *Continuation* and adds the month and day: the tenth day before the Kalends of December, that is, 22 November.

The leading authorities generally follow both of them—Baronius, Sirmond, Holstenius, and many others—so that this opinion may rightly be regarded as the consensus of the learned.

Yet a recent dissertation-writer denies that he approves this view and offers two reasons for opposing so many men, together with two witnesses in his own support.

His first argument runs as follows. Vigilius, as everyone consistently agrees, entered Constantinople in 547, on 25 January. “It appears,” says the dissertation-writer, “that he remained in Sicily for a long time, since there he both performed ordinations, received embassies, and collected grain with which he might relieve the distress at Rome. Since a period of only one month and a few days, which is all he would have spent in Sicily if he is said to have departed from Rome at that time, was insufficient for these tasks, he must be considered to have departed long before the date assigned by all the writers—long enough, that is, to carry out conveniently the things that were accomplished.”

His second argument is this.
