The clergy of Italy sent a letter in the year 551—as the dissertation-writer himself believes—to the envoys of the king of the Gauls who were departing for Constantinople. In it they wrote that Vigilius had left Rome six years earlier [Col. 1064A]. Vigilius himself also wrote in the encyclical that he sent to the universal Church in 552 that he had left his own city seven years earlier. Neither statement, however, can stand if the pontiff is said to have left Rome in 546; both can stand if he left in 545, since from 545 to 551 six years would be counted, and from 545 to 552 seven.

The two witnesses he adduces are Sigonius and Victor of Tunnuna. The former says that the pontiff departed in the year 545; the latter says that he was summoned by Justinian in the fourth year after the consulship of Basil.

These arguments are not equal in authority—not merely to all the writers I have cited against them, but not even to a single one, such as Holstenius. They are so slight and almost futile.

Beginning with the witnesses, I cannot see how the passage from Victor could be produced by a sensible man as evidence. It reads:

“After the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus, in the fourth year, the emperor Justinian, incited by the intrigues of the Acephali, subtly compelled Vigilius, bishop of Rome, to hasten to the imperial city and, under the pretext of assembling those who were separated from the communion of the Church, to condemn the Three Chapters.”

The passage is plainly corrupt. For it implies that Vigilius left Rome in 544: if the years are counted, as Victor counts them, after the consulship of Basil, the fourth year after that consulship is 544 in the Christian era. Moreover, the words quoted do not signify a mere summons by letter, as the dissertation-writer pretends, but Vigilius’s actual expulsion by Belisarius, about which the clergy of Italy complain.

Yet it is impossible, as will soon become clear, to place Vigilius’s departure in that year; nor has the dissertation-writer himself supplied such a date, if only he would at some point speak consistently. For if he did supply it, he would immediately be forced to place in the latter part of the year 543 three events which no prudent person can fail to see are impossible (*ἀσύστατα*): namely, the ordination of Zoilus, and both of Justinian’s edicts—the one condemning the Origenists and the other the Three Chapters.

He would then have to compress into six months the ordination of Zoilus at Gaza, which took place during Pelagius’s lengthy journey from Gaza in Palestine back to Constantinople; the journey itself; the presentation to the emperor of the excerpts brought by Pelagius’s monastic companions; the presentation of those excerpts; the emperor’s careful examination of them, of which he boasts; that examination; the composition of the edict against the Origenists after Theodore’s long resistance; and its dispatch to the patriarchs; the dispatch; Vigilius’s written reply from Rome; the reply; Pope Vigilius’s council with Menna, at which the bishops found in the imperial city subscribed the edict; the subscription; the book composed by Justinian against the Acephali; the courtly arts by which Theodore deceived the good emperor’s simplicity and turned it in the opposite direction; the deception; and the edict against the Three Chapters. Whoever dares say that all these things could have happened within six months—I confidently declare that he is more than audacious.

There is therefore no valid testimony from Victor of Tunnuna, either because the dissertation-writer does not cite it in good faith but in a perverse sense, or because Victor himself spoke through error.

What objections, moreover, does the other witness, Sigonius, face? First, he is a modern writer who, when dealing with events far removed in time, deserves no more credit than he can either borrow from the testimony of the ancients or obtain by reasoning. Yet he cites no testimony, not even in the margin; he uses no reasoning, but merely dictates. Furthermore, it is difficult to see how his testimony assists the dissertation-writer. In that passage he says nothing specifically or expressly about the time when Vigilius left Rome; rather, he throws this departure, along with many other events that clearly occurred at different times, into the year 545 in a confused miscellany.

He relates, namely, under that same year the embassy of Eustochius of Jerusalem to the emperor, undertaken by the abbots Rufus and Conon; the condemnation of Origen, issued by the emperor and subscribed by all the patriarchs; Justinian’s book against the Acephali; the publication of the edict against the Three Chapters; the proceedings in Constantinople with the Africans concerning the case of the Three Chapters; the complaints of the Romans against Vigilius before the emperor; Vigilius’s forcible removal from Italy; the ordinations he celebrated at Catana; and the pontiff’s entry into the imperial city on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. After relating these events, he adds something by which he shows that he assigns them all to the year 545:

“In the following year, however, being again summoned by the Augusti to restore Anthimus,” and so forth.

The dissertation-writer himself will readily agree, and clear reasoning demonstrates, that all these things, which Sigonius recklessly heaps into one and the same year, are far removed from the truth. First, the time of the Fifth Synod is confused with the time of Origen’s first condemnation by Justinian—an intolerable chronological displacement (*ἀντιχρονισμός*) of several years.

Second, Eustochius is said to have advanced Origen’s condemnation with Pelagius’s assistance. Yet everyone knows that, when Pelagius secured Origen’s condemnation, Eustochius was not bishop of Jerusalem. Peter was bishop, and he was succeeded by Martyrius; after Martyrius had been deposed several years later, Eustochius assumed the government of the Church of Jerusalem only a very short time before the Fifth Synod.

Third, the abbots Rufus and Conon are said to have been sent from Palestine to Constantinople to ask Justinian, with Pelagius’s assistance, to proscribe the chapters excerpted from Origen’s books. Yet, according to Evagrius, the monks who came from Palestine with Pelagius to the imperial court were Eulogius, Conon, Cyriacus, and Pancratius.

Next, it is said that in the same year Origen was condemned by the emperor and Vigilius was received at Constantinople—nothing more absurd than this could be invented, as even the dissertation-writer himself must admit.

Why should I produce anything further to enhance Sigonius’s credibility [Col. 1065C], when no writer would have relied on him in this matter if he knew even the elementary facts of history, or wished to write for those who did?

No more assistance can be expected from the letter of the Italian clergy than from Sigonius’s testimony—not because the letter does not possess far greater authority than Sigonius, or even than Victor, but because it is not cited in good faith. When the Italian clergy speak of Vigilius’s arrival in the imperial city, they are represented as though they were speaking of his departure from Rome, as if one differed hardly at all from the other; yet the dissertation-writer himself places one year, or even two, between them. Consider more carefully, learned reader, the words of the clergy who wrote, and from them judge what kind of evidence it is to cite them in one’s own support:

“Having heard that Your Glory had been sent to the imperial city on an embassy, and having also learned from certain persons who said that they possessed knowledge of you of your reputation and wisdom, we have sent you, for your instruction and to be conveyed on whatever occasion may arise, a few of the many things that have occurred. Through these you may learn the persecutions and acts of violence that the Catholic priests there, and all who wish to observe the ecclesiastical rules, are suffering. For when the most blessed Pope Vigilius came there six years ago—or rather, to speak more accurately, was brought there almost by force—they began to await him there,” and so forth.

Vigilius’s words are cited with greater fidelity, but they do not carry greater weight. For when, in 552, the pontiff, wearied by his hardships, instructed that the following be referred to Justinian, who was exercising tyranny:

“We hastened to Your Piety seven years ago and departed from our city in such a way that we had no private business”—

this amounts to saying: “It is the seventh year since we departed from our city in this manner,” and so forth. Those who complain that their sufferings have lasted a long time commonly count the years during which they have been afflicted even when only a small part of the year has elapsed—as schoolboys themselves know.

But even if this interpretive explanation were lacking, Vigilius’s own manner of speaking would explain the passage. For six lines later he speaks of months in the same way as of years. Not quite six full months had elapsed from Theodore’s condemnation to the Nones of February, on which he wrote the encyclical; nevertheless he says:

“Six months ago Theodore was deprived by us, along with others, of sacred communion and was deposed from the episcopate for his wickedness.”

Earlier he had explained how the time of Theodore’s condemnation could be known:

“For what we had publicly declared by word concerning the aforementioned excommunication to all bishops, presbyters, deacons, and other clergy, we later confirmed in writing on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September just past, in the basilica of blessed Peter at Hormisdas. In that document we also condemned and deposed from the episcopal order the one who, under episcopal garb, like a ravening wolf, laid snares for the Lord’s flock and, assuming leadership of the entire scandal, disturbed and continues to disturb the universal Church of God.”

As for what the dissertation-writer alleges—that Vigilius remained in Sicily so that he might have time to perform ordinations, receive embassies, deliberate about the location of the synod, gather grain, and send it to Rome, as though there had not been enough time for these things if he left Rome on 22 November 546 and entered Constantinople on 25 January of the following year—I do not see what force this has.

Italy is separated from Sicily by a narrow strait; ordinations are customarily performed in December; and, I think, one month is sufficient to transport grain from a nearby place to those suffering from famine. Since the report of the pontiff’s future departure had long been spreading, and some delay in Sicily had to be arranged, Datius of Milan and the envoys of Zoilus who were in his company could easily have come from Constantinople to Sicily at the appointed time. Bishops could also have visited him in Sicily from nearby parts of Africa and Sardinia. Finally, letters could have been sent from Sicily to Constantinople once or twice, and replies received from there.

Now, if Vigilius departed from Rome in 546, on 22 November, as has been established on the authority of the ancients; and if a full year and several additional months passed while the supreme pontiff refused to approve Justinian’s edict; while the emperor and the pontiff almost quarreled through their mutual letters over the calling of a synod; while Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, was consulted through Anatolius and Pelagius, deacons of the Roman Church, about his opinion of the matter; while Ferrandus himself replied after a long silence; while Justinian, angered by the pontiff’s steadfast resistance, summoned a council from the whole world to Constantinople; while agreement could not be reached in Constantinople and Rome concerning the council’s location; while letters filled with opposing arguments passed back and forth; while the Roman clergy created delays so that the head of the Church would not be compelled, contrary to custom, to go where he would serve rather than preside with the dignity due to him—in short, if a full year and several additional months passed while these things were taking place, then it must absolutely be admitted that the edict against the Three Chapters was issued in 545, around autumn.

At about that time Pelagius, who enjoyed the greatest favor with the emperor, yielded the office of apocrisarius of the Apostolic See to the deacon Stephen and returned to Rome rich in Eastern gifts. With these he assisted the Romans and encouraged them to resist Totila. That distinguished deacon returned before Totila approached the City, so that he might do whatever he could to restore Justinian’s declining fortunes in Italy; and, as is reasonable to believe, he returned before the edict was published, so that the plans of the Augusta and Theodore might not be disrupted by his influence with the prince.

The first edict against the Three Chapters was therefore published toward the end of 545. Facundus relates that the four patriarchs of the Eastern Empire approved it, but reluctantly, struggling as though with fear because of their reverence for the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 1067A]. Nevertheless, the sense of official duty was overcome by the desire to retain their rank, the loss of which timid bishops humbly feared at the threats of the emperor. Justinian’s threats were all the more terrifying because in that period even bishops of the principal sees were more easily deposed by rulers. A recent example pressed upon them sharply: Menna had been substituted in the place of Anthimus, and Zoilus in the see of Paul, both of whom had been deposed.

It is useful to hear Facundus speak on this matter in his own words:

“That is unusual, that is extraordinary, and it shows the great power of truth: even the usurpers themselves were compelled by the inner goads of conscience to confess that these things had been composed for the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon. For Menna, bishop of Constantinople, the first to confirm them, while still hesitating to give them his written assent as he had been ordered, protested that this was being done against the Council of Chalcedon. But after he had consented, when he was summoned by Stephen, of venerable memory, deacon and apocrisarius of the Roman Church, and was asked why he had yielded to what contradicted his earlier judgment, to the things he had previously condemned, and about which he had promised to do nothing without the Apostolic See, he replied that he had yielded on the condition, and that it had been sworn to him, that he would receive back his signed document if the Roman bishop did not approve these things.”

And later:

“Zoilus too, bishop of the city of Alexandria, when he learned that the Roman bishop was coming, sent to meet him in Sicily, complaining that he had been compelled by necessity to affirm that decree. When he arrived, the same Roman bishop openly reproached him to his face for this, with us among others present. Ephraemius of Antioch likewise, when he was first commanded to decree this also by a written reply, refused to consent. But after he was told that he would be excluded unless he did so, he proved to be a lover of his own honor rather than of the truth. And what of Peter of Jerusalem? Does not public report state that, when a multitude of monks gathered around him, he declared under oath that anyone who consented to that novel decree would act against the Council of Chalcedon? Yet he did not refrain from consenting to it.”

The edict I first mentioned, which was sent toward the end of 545 to the bishops throughout the world, differs from the one that Theodore the Cappadocian proposed in 551 in the Church of Constantinople and elsewhere. For what Facundus says was contained in the former cannot be found in the latter.

The emperor himself testifies in the imperial decree addressed to the Fathers of the Fifth Synod that each primate consented to the edict in his own see and, as is reasonable to believe given the importance of the matter, in his own synod:

“First, while you were residing in your own Churches, we questioned you about the impious Three Chapters mentioned above, and you made your will clear to us. For this we approved you, because without hesitation and with complete eagerness you confessed the true faith and condemned the impious,” and so forth.

At that time, however, Zoilus was not in his own Church but in Constantinople. Certainly he was there shortly after this consent, at the time when Vigilius came to the imperial city; but Facundus implies that Peter was in Jerusalem when he gave his consent.

## CHAPTER IV. The Council held at Constantinople by Menna concerning the Three Chapters

I think no one doubts that Menna held a council after receiving Justinian’s edict. Four considerations persuade us of this: the example of the Origenian case, Facundus’s testimony, the authority of Pope Vigilius himself, and Justinian’s imperial decree addressed to the Fathers of this council.

First, since Menna did not approve Origen’s condemnation privately but publicly in a council, it is reasonable to believe that the Augusta and Theodore the Cappadocian, mindful of the injury done to them, indulged their anger so far that they did not think what had been done sufficient for them, but compelled Menna, with the same gathering and, as it were, public display with which he had condemned Origen, to strike Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret, and Ibas with anathema.

Next, when Facundus discusses the council of seventy bishops held by Vigilius at Constantinople, he mentions “those who had subscribed earlier”—that is, at the council of Menna. Vigilius had written to Menna and the bishops assembled with him while still on his journey, threatening them that, unless they withdrew their judgment, they would suffer the punishment of excommunication with which, upon entering Constantinople, he struck those who persisted in their purpose.

The matter is fully established by the emperor’s imperial decree to the assembled bishops, which will be discussed shortly. For this council Menna undoubtedly summoned his own clergy, as well as the bishops found in the imperial city, since the emperor had ordered men of the same kind to be assembled for the council against Origen, which was its counterpart.

The number of bishops is uncertain. That it was not small is shown partly by the circumstances of the time, when many frequented the court after abandoning their flocks; partly by the importance of the case, which stirred the whole world; and finally by Justinian’s—or rather the Augusta’s—insane passion, which seemed to be served more by necessity than by desire.

It is not unreasonable to infer the time from the remaining circumstances. If the emperor issued the edict in 545, around autumn, it will not seem incredible to anyone that Menna and the other bishops—whether those who had customarily come from the provinces for the autumn synod or those who were staying in the imperial city for private reasons—obeyed Justinian at that time when he ordered them to subscribe the edict.

Yet someone may perhaps think it more credible that this happened at the synod preceding Lent, after news had reached Constantinople of the difficulty that the supreme pontiff was raising by alleging injury to the Council of Chalcedon. For that reason, when the synod subscribed, it may have added the proviso that its consent was conditional upon the approval of the supreme pontiff and that the Council of Chalcedon suffer no harm.

But I judge it far more probable—though perhaps another writer has been bolder in declaring it certain—that this council was held toward the end of autumn in the year 546. Menna delayed for a long time and prolonged the matter, certainly devising the longest delays that a mind unwilling to serve the wishes of Theodore, who was abusing the Augusta’s power to satisfy his desire for revenge, could devise. His delays were not without reason. He said that, in a matter of faith, he was awaiting the judgment of the first see, and that it was not yet sufficiently clear to him—or to the rest of the world—how the Three Chapters could be condemned “without prejudice to the Council of Chalcedon.”

By these and other devices implied by Facundus, he evaded for a long time the zeal of Theodore, who was abusing the Augusta’s power to satisfy his desire for vengeance. He was able to avoid compliance until news arrived in Constantinople that Vigilius would shortly depart. Then he was compelled to obey the prince’s will, since the danger of deposition threatened him—and that danger was all the more certain because the Augusta, having found an opportunity in the emperor’s anger, was working passionately to restore Anthimus to his see.

Menna, therefore, together with his synod, finally yielded to the imperial threats and subscribed the edict, adding this proviso nonetheless: if the supreme pontiff disapproved what had been done, the document would be returned and the matter restored to its former state. Yet this proviso did not prevent the apocrisarius of the Apostolic See from ecclesiastically avenging the injury inflicted upon the Apostolic See by the bishops who had acted in advance.

Stephen, a deacon of the Roman Church, had succeeded Pelagius in the office of apocrisarius. When he could no longer keep the bishop of Constantinople and the others to their duty, he, as Facundus puts it, suspended himself from communion with Menna and, by his example, encouraged many others to do the same. Certainly the bishops assembled in the synod—if not all, at least a large part of them—“when they were compelled to write,” in Facundus’s words, “openly protested that this was being done against the great synod. After the aforementioned subscription, they gave petitions to Stephen, the Roman deacon, to be transmitted to the Apostolic See, confessing in them that they had subscribed under compulsion from the bishop of Constantinople.”

The pontiff learned in Sicily, partly from Datius of Milan, who had arrived to meet him, and partly from Stephen’s letters, what Menna had done. He bore it all the more bitterly because it was especially disgraceful and degrading that the threats of the emperor should have been preferred to the reverence due to the supreme pontiff by a bishop who had once obtained his throne through the favor of the Apostolic See. Therefore, disregarding the proviso entirely, he judged that vengeance should be taken. He first sent a warning by letter from the road and dispatched envoys to the emperor who were to attempt to arrange matters so that the bishop, by repentance, and the emperor, by rescinding the act, might forestall the pontiff’s retaliation.

Facundus relates the matter while addressing the emperor, book IV, chapter 3:

“But this is extraordinary: after they condemned these men, they said that they would consult the Roman Church and await the judgment of Vigilius, its bishop. Yet, as far as they were concerned, they did not permit him to judge according to his own convictions, since they had already decreed that whoever did not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his doctrines, and the letter of the venerable Ibas, should be anathema. But now, as he was coming from his journey, he issued the decree that seemed proper to him and ordered the author of this disorderly transgression to correct it. He declared that, unless what had been wrongly done were promptly removed, he would also exact vengeance, protesting and saying with the Apostle: ‘Lest, when I come, I find you not as I wish, and I be found by you such as you do not wish me to be.’ For this reason he earnestly and insistently asked Your Clemency through his envoys—as the provinces that he passed through while coming also testified—not to allow what had been done to stand.”

Vigilius himself likewise relates the matter in a letter to Menna written during his journey, which can be read in Facundus’s book *Against Mocianus*:

“When it is not unknown to us,” says the pontiff, “that the deacon Stephen, formerly our representative in the Church over which by God’s grace we preside, suspended himself from your communion, together with many Christians, for as long as he lived, and when, as we were staying on the island of Sicily, we learned from our brother and fellow bishop Datius that he himself, as well as other fellow priests of ours and many sons of the Christian Church, had likewise withdrawn from your communion—and when we asked about the causes of the scandal that had arisen, our aforementioned brother and fellow bishop replied that your fraternity had done this, something that had never been committed by any of your predecessors or during the time of our predecessors,” and so forth.

That is, either the matter of faith was being agitated or the judgment of the general synod was being retracted without awaiting the judgment of the Apostolic See.

What the pontiff had threatened on the journey, Facundus relates in the book just cited that he carried out immediately upon arriving at Constantinople, against Menna and the other bishops who refused to repent: “For when he came to the imperial city, he suspended from communion those who had communicated with such men.” This suspension lasted for three months, until it was lifted at the entreaty of the court.

From the passages reported from Facundus, it is entirely clear that the council held by Menna occurred at the time I have stated. For how could the pontiff otherwise have retained such a just anger for so long? How could he have expressed his judgment only while on the road? If, while still in Rome, he had learned of the violence inflicted upon the bishops by the emperor and of the cowardly servitude of the timid bishops, how could a prudent man, fearing the same violence, have remained within the borders of Italy?

Someone might object that Vigilius did not come to the emperor but was transported there by force. This has no force, since the account received from Anastasius—according to which Vigilius was seized from the church of Saint Cecilia by Belisarius’s agents and thrown onto a ship—seems to many learned men to be a mere fable. In any event, it must be rejected by anyone who assigns a full year, or even—if God wills—a two-year stay to Vigilius in Sicily.

As far as I know, only three documents survive from the acts of the council: the emperor’s imperial decree to the Fathers, the Fathers’ concise response to the decree, and the anathema against Theodore and Ibas. The anathema is read in Facundus, book IV, final chapter. The imperial decree and the response are appended in Greek and Latin to the acts of the Fifth Synod, as they are now preserved.

I am surprised that some men have thought that both documents—the imperial decree and the response—belong to the Fifth Synod. For although this imperial decree has some relationship to another decree that is known to have been read at the first session of the Fifth Synod, it differs from it in many respects to an astonishing degree; no one who reads them can fail to notice this.

It should also be observed that the imperial decree under discussion contains a fragment from Cyril’s apologetic book addressed to the emperor Theodosius. This fragment fills the middle portion of the decree and is inserted so awkwardly that it is astonishing that curious readers did not reject it. I have thought it should be removed when the decree is presented here with the synodal response, as certain remnants of the acts to which it will later be worthwhile to add some observations.

## LETTER OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN TO THE HOLY SYNOD CONCERNING THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA AND THE OTHERS

“Orthodox and pious emperors, our fathers, have always made it their concern, whenever heresies arose, to cut them off through the assembly of deeply religious priests, and, after sincerely proclaiming the true faith, to preserve the holy Church of God in peace.

Therefore Constantine the Great, when Arius was blaspheming and saying that the Son was not consubstantial with God the Father but a creature, made from things that did not exist, assembled three hundred and eighteen Fathers at Nicaea. When he himself had attended the council, Arius was condemned and anathematized, and Constantine endeavored to confirm the true faith. Through that faith those divine Fathers confessed that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father, not a creature, and not made from things that did not exist; and this confession is sung to the present day.”

Theodosius the Elder, when Macedonius denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit and Apollinarius, his disciple, blasphemously misrepresented the dispensation of the incarnate Word of God and said that the Word of God had not assumed a human mind but had been united to flesh possessing an irrational soul, assembled one hundred and fifty Fathers in the city of Constantinople. Having himself taken part in the council, he condemned and anathematized the aforesaid heretics, together with their impious doctrines and followers, and took care that the [Col. 1070D] orthodox faith should be proclaimed.

Theodosius the Younger, when the impious Nestorius wickedly introduced the notion that the Word of God was one being and Christ another; that the Word was by nature the Son of God and the Father, but Christ was a Son only by grace; and when he denied that holy Mary was the Mother of God, summoned the First Synod of Ephesus, consisting of two hundred holy Fathers. He sent instructions to the officials who were to attend the council, ordered Nestorius himself to be present, and commanded that judgment be passed upon him. After a careful examination had been conducted, they condemned and anathematized Nestorius together with his followers.

After these events had taken place, when the impious followers of Nestorius rose up against the most holy Cyril, they attempted, insofar as they could, to rescind the sentence pronounced against Nestorius. But the emperor Theodosius, defending the judgments that had rightly been made against Nestorius and his impious doctrines, took care that the sentence of condemnation [Col. 1071A] pronounced against him should remain valid.

After this, when Cyril had died, a certain monk and archimandrite named Eutyches arose. He attached to himself no small part of the people, approving the sect of Nestorius and his impious doctrine, and saying that the Lord’s flesh was not consubstantial with us. Then again, not long afterward, when the devil’s power prevailed, another council was forcibly convened at Ephesus—a council of robbers and by no means a holy one. Flavian of Constantinople was also sent to it, while supreme authority there lay with Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. The divine Flavian, defending the orthodox faith, was killed; the authority of the First Synod of Ephesus, however, was abolished, when certain bishops were compelled by deadly force to sign, among them Basil, bishop of Seleucia.

From this point, when the destructive doctrines of Nestorius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches were being publicly taught and especially great disturbances were arising in the East, Proterius, [Col. 1071B] the high priest, and many others were killed. In this state of affairs Marcian was divinely raised up as emperor. He summoned at Chalcedon a council of six hundred and thirty Fathers, and, with Dioscorus and Eutyches present, took part in it together with them. There Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned, and Nestorius was anathematized once again. Theodoret, Ibas, and Basil, bishop of Seleucia, were received, although they had subscribed to the earlier council; and thus, after the acts of the predatory synod had been annulled and condemned, harmony was established among all by the holy Fathers.

When these four councils had thus been conducted and confirmed, and possessed authority in the Church of God, the followers of Nestorius again endeavored to establish their heresy, through the agency of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who blasphemed things far worse than Nestorius, his disciple.

We therefore, following our holy Fathers and wishing to preserve the orthodox faith without any stain, exhort you, after examining this man’s blasphemies also, [Col. 1071C] to pronounce judgment upon him and his followers. For, besides the countless other curses that he impiously vomited against Christ our God, he also asserted that the Word of God was one being and Christ another; that Christ, troubled by disturbances of mind and desires of the flesh that caused him distress, gradually abandoned what was worse, advanced toward what was better through progress in his actions, and lived according to an unblemished and excellent way of life. He said that Christ, as a mere man, had been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, had obtained the grace of the Holy Spirit through baptism, and had been deemed worthy of adoption; that, in imitation of royal majesty, he had been worshiped as Christ in the person of the Word of God; and that after the resurrection he had possessed a steadfast mind, free from sins. Moreover, he declared that the union of the Word with Christ was the union that the Apostle describes as that of a man with a woman: “And the two shall be one flesh” (1 Cor. VI).

I further exhort you to examine what Theodoret and Ibas wrote improperly against the holy First [Col. 1071D] Council of Ephesus, and to pronounce judgment against them in the same manner.”

First observe what is said: “Eutyches approved the sect of Nestorius and his impious doctrine, since he said that the flesh was not consubstantial with us.” This is true only insofar as the two heresies agreed in denying that the blessed Virgin was properly Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “Mother of God”) and in denying that any true incarnation of the Word had taken place. Yet each offered a different reason for its denial: the former rejected the ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (*henōsis kath’ hypostasin*, “union according to hypostasis”) of the natures, while the latter rejected the consubstantiality of Christ’s flesh.

Next observe these words: “When the destructive doctrines of Nestorius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches were being publicly taught, and especially great disturbances were arising in the East, Proterius, the high priest, and many others were killed. In this state of affairs Marcian was divinely raised up as emperor,” and so forth. For they contain an intolerable ἀνιστορησία (*anistoresia*, “historical falsehood”), since Proterius was killed by the [Col. 1072A] Dioscorites of Alexandria after the death of Marcian. See Liberatus, *Breviarium*, chapter 14.

Likewise observe the following: “Marcian, having summoned at Chalcedon a council of six hundred and thirty Fathers, with Dioscorus and Eutyches present, took part in it.” The theological emperor is gravely mistaken: Eutyches was not present at the council, but had previously been sent into exile. See the acts of the council.

Fourth, observe where it is said that “Theodoret, Ibas, and Basil, bishop of Seleucia, were received, although they had subscribed to the earlier council.” The translator was mistaken. For the Greek—“Θεοδώριτον δὲ καὶ Ἴβαν καὶ Βασίλειον Σελευκείας ἐδέξαντο καθυπογράψαντας”—ought to have been rendered: “They received Theodoret, Ibas, and Basil of Seleucia after they had subscribed,” namely, to the definition of the Council of Chalcedon and to Leo’s *Tome*. See the acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

Finally, observe the fifteen-year παραχρονισμός (*parachronismos*, “chronological anachronism”): “When these four councils had thus been conducted and confirmed, and possessed authority in the Church of God, the followers of Nestorius again endeavored to establish their heresy [Col. 1072B] through the agency of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who raved things far worse than Nestorius, his disciple.” Justinian’s memory failed him. For at least fifteen years before the Council of Chalcedon was held, excerpts from Theodore’s books, circulated as books of Nestorius and burned by imperial command, had been disseminated among the people. This is plainly established by the letters of Cyril, Proclus, and John of Antioch.

Who would suppose that such absurd and unlearned σφάλματα (*sphalmata*, “errors”) belonged to a man who is rightly proclaimed an eminent and most wise writer? Who would not rather believe them to belong to someone who, if he composed the work by his own efforts, was no less ἀναλφάβητος (*analphabētos*, “illiterate”) than Justin? If he used another’s work and allowed such foul offspring to be foisted upon him, Halloixius rightly called him crude and uneducated, since through sheer ignorance he could not distinguish what he should adopt with credit.

To this letter the synod replied, after [Col. 1072C] again carefully examining the excerpts sent to it from Theodore’s books:

“The holy Council of Chalcedon received Theodoret and Ibas back into communion, after having severely attacked them in words, on no other condition than that they first condemn their own evil writings, as well as Theodore and Nestorius.

“We, in addition to all the other heretics condemned by the aforesaid four holy councils and excluded from the Church, also condemn and proscribe Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, together with his impious books. We likewise condemn what Theodoret wrote improperly against the true faith, the twelve chapters of the holy Cyril, and the holy First Synod of Ephesus, as well as in defense of Theodore and Nestorius.

“Moreover, we also condemn the letter that Ibas is said to have written to Maris the Persian. It denies that the Word of God, incarnate from the holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, became man; it brands the divine Cyril as a heretic; it criticizes the holy First Synod of Ephesus as having condemned Nestorius without knowing the [Col. 1072D] case; it spits upon the twelve chapters of the holy Cyril; and it supports Nestorius and Theodore, together with their impious writings and opinions.

“Therefore, assigning the unbridled tongues of these heretics, their most impious writings, and finally the heretics themselves, persisting in their false opinions and wickedness, to their father, the devil, the father of lies, with perfect justice, we shall say: ‘Go into the light of your fire, and into the flame that you have kindled’ (Isa. L).”

The Cappadocian is mistaken—for he was the author both of Justinian’s document and of the synodical reply—when, I say, he maliciously writes that Theodoret and Ibas were received at Chalcedon on no other condition than that they first condemn their own evil writings, as well as Theodore and Nestorius. For neither in the eighth session, in which Theodoret’s case was debated, nor in the ninth and tenth, in which Ibas’s case was dealt with, was a single word said either about Theodoret’s writings [Col. 1073A] or about Theodore. Ibas’s letter was read, at least without disapproval, if not with approval, by either the synod or Ibas himself. Yet the Cappadocian needed this falsehood in order more easily to induce the bishops to condemn what Theodoret and Ibas themselves had previously condemned at the Council of Chalcedon.

Nor was this the only fiction he devised; he invented many others, so that persistent lying may appear to be his characteristic. Halloixius therefore wrote more cleverly than accurately that Justinian’s letter concerning the Three Chapters was indeed fabricated by Theodore, but, insofar as it concerns history, dictated by the father of lies.

There is nevertheless something worth noting as true in both Justinian’s letter and this synodical reply: namely, that Theodoret “wrote improperly against the true faith, the twelve chapters of the holy Cyril, and the holy First Synod of Ephesus, and in defense of Theodore and Nestorius.” These words indicate three writings, of which only the first is generally known; the other two—if there are in fact two—have until now been unknown. [Col. 1073B] We shall publish a small portion of both in the appendix to Theodoret, which will shortly be committed to the press.

## CHAPTER V. Whether Origen was in reality condemned at the Fifth Synod

There is no single, uniform opinion among all writers concerning Origen’s condemnation at the Fifth Synod. Some, such as Halloixius, deny altogether that he was condemned. Others admit that he was condemned; but among those who admit it, some say that he was judged without the case being known, while others say that the case was known. Those who hold the latter view are again divided into two groups, according as they maintain that the case was heard either before the Three Chapters were dealt with, as the dissertation-writer holds, or afterward, as the most illustrious Marca holds.

From this conflict of opinions three questions arise: whether Origen was truly condemned at the Fifth Synod; whether judgment concerning his case was instituted at that synod; and at what time it was instituted. The last question is not difficult to settle if the other two have been properly debated; and although the first two can scarcely be solved separately, they can easily be solved together.

### § I. What Halloixius recently thought about the question

[Col. 1073C] Not long ago Halloixius wrote a work entitled *Origen Defended*, in four books. He prefaced it with testimonies of the Fathers in which Origen is praised so highly that nearly all voice is taken away from those who would accuse him, if they have any shame. For who would dare to bring a charge boldly against a man whom Alexander, bishop and martyr of Jerusalem, calls “his lord and the father of his faith”; whom Gregory Thaumaturgus calls “so skilled an interpreter of the divine utterances that he both understood the words of God as though God were speaking and explained them to men”; whom Pamphilus—or whoever was the author of the *Apology*—calls “a teacher of the Church who fought so bravely against heretics that he overturned all the foundations of the devil’s machinations”; whom Athanasius the Great calls “a man of great learning and diligence”; Gregory the Theologian, “the whetstone of all theologians”; Gregory of Nyssa, “the father of Christian philosophy”; Ambrose, “a diligent investigator of interpretations”; and Jerome, “a man whom no one but an ignorant person would deny to be, after the Apostles, a second teacher of the Churches”; and so forth.

After developing these and other testimonies, he composed in the first book an altogether remarkable life of Origen. He relates how, born of a martyred father, Origen in turn spiritually fathered many martyrs for Christ; how, although eager to pour out his blood for the faith, he was preserved by God’s singular providence for other purposes; what astonishing numbers of pagans and heretics he brought into the Church; with what reputation for learning he taught the learned men of the entire world; how much he suffered, and how grievous were his sufferings, both from rivals of his glory and from men otherwise pious but deceived in other respects; and with what great devotion he finally died, [Col. 1074A] after composing six thousand books through incredible labor.

In the second book he sets forth the virtues of so great a man, especially four: devotion to God and Christ Jesus, singular humility and modesty, charity eager for martyrdom, and tireless zeal for promoting the divine glory. These four virtues shine in his writings like four splendid lights.

After praising his virtues, in the third book he explains Origen’s mind and introduces him speaking in his own words, saying what he truly thought about the principal questions of faith and by what force of doctrine he triumphed over all the heretics of his time.

Finally, in the fourth book he turns to examine the various charges brought against Origen by various people, especially the charge that obscures all his praises [Col. 1073D]: namely, that although Jerome praised him so highly as a second teacher of the Church after the Apostles, he was nevertheless condemned by bishops who were teachers of the Church, and indeed by bishops assembled in council, as an impious man and the hydra of all heresies. [Col. 1074B] This did not happen once or in one place, but in various Churches and at various times. First, in Alexandria, his homeland, while he was alive, by Demetrius the bishop; again there, nearly two centuries later, by Theophilus; third, at Constantia in Cyprus, at the same time, by Epiphanius; fourth, at Rome by Anastasius, at Milan by Venerius, and at Aquileia by Chromatius; finally, in the year of Christ 553, at the Fifth General Synod, by all the patriarchs of the entire world. For the eleventh canon reads:

“If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Origen, together with their impious writings, and all the other heretics who have been condemned and anathematized by the holy Catholic and apostolic Church and by the aforesaid four holy councils; and those who have held or hold opinions like those of the aforesaid heretics, and have persevered in their impiety until death—let him be anathema.”

The councils that followed the Fifth imitated it, or rather copied it.

[Col. 1074C] Halloixius easily diminishes the authority of three particular councils. He relates the history of each and shows, first, that what is reported about the first Alexandrian council is doubtful, since Jerome, who is the only person to mention it, wrote one thing about the matter before his quarrel with Rufinus and another after the quarrel. Second, he shows that Theophilus, the author of the second council, was accused by the holiest men of his own age of having indulged human feeling beyond the bounds of reason in condemning the Origenists and Origen himself. Third, he shows that Epiphanius was moved against Origen by the same methods used by Theophilus against Origen as against Chrysostom, and that this agitation impelled the Cypriots to pronounce sentence against Origen.

[Col. 1074D] He understands that the objection based on canon 11 of the Fifth Synod cannot be defended so easily. Therefore, having examined more attentively the individual circumstances—the council itself, whose authority is questioned; the canon that may be defective; and Origen, between whose person and doctrine, or books, a distinction can be made—he proposes three ways of making an exception, any one of which, if established, would benefit Origen. He says that one may argue, first, that the canon is genuine but the council illegitimate; second, that the council is legitimate but the canon has been corrupted; third, that even if neither is defective, Origen’s person can nevertheless be excused, while his doctrine is condemned, just as Augustine defended Cyprian after rejecting his error concerning the baptism of heretics.

He establishes the first point with many arguments. Since no synod can lawfully convene against the will of the supreme pontiff, and since no synod possesses sufficient authority before confirmation by the Apostolic See, he argues that Vigilius initially resisted for a long time being compelled to convene a council in the East, and finally permitted it only on conditions rejected by the Greeks. He then argues that the same pontiff denied his consent to the canons that had been enacted, insofar as they concerned persons, and that this is clear from his *Constitutum*. For this reason he was driven into exile; and when, broken by hardships, he returned, he died piously in Sicily. Third, he argues [Col. 1075A] that the supreme pontiffs who knew the affairs of Vigilius well, or had even witnessed them with their own eyes, likewise denied their consent: Pelagius, who succeeded Vigilius; John, who succeeded Pelagius; and Benedict, who succeeded John. Finally, he argues that the later pontiffs did give their consent, but through an error of fact, since they had either not read Vigilius’s *Constitutum* or had too easily believed the Greeks, who claimed that Vigilius had consented immediately after the council had ended.

But, to mention in passing what the facts are, this method of defense, although it may once have had some appearance of truth, now seems entirely without foundation, provided that the decree of Vigilius in favor of confirming the Fifth Synod, which the most illustrious Marca found in the Royal Library, is genuine. It is said to have been issued before the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the twenty-seventh year of Justinian’s reign, in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, *vir clarissimus*. This may show that in that same year in which the synod was held—six months, namely, after it had ended—Vigilius revoked his *Constitutum* and confirmed the synod, and thus that the Greeks did not lie when they said that Vigilius had confirmed the Fifth Synod.

[Col. 1075B] Halloixius explains the third method of defense by comparing the case of Origen with that of Cyprian and adducing Augustine’s exceptions on behalf of Cyprian, which he demonstrates would apply to Origen with far greater force, or certainly no less force. He accomplishes this with greater effectiveness than learning. Yet, with such resources of learning and such diligence, he achieves only this: that, like Augustine, Origen’s person is defended after the defense of his doctrine has been abandoned.

[Col. 1075C] He explains the second method in such a way that he simultaneously proves something that is indisputably true: that the ancients called something other than what is now contained in the eight sessions by the name “Fifth Council.” His reasoning is as follows:

“Nowhere in the Fifth Council was Origen’s case debated; nowhere were any of his errors censured; nowhere was his name mentioned except in canon 11. Therefore either that canon is corrupt insofar as Origen’s name has been inserted into it, or the synod committed a grave offense. For who would condemn someone without a hearing, contrary to the rules of the Church?”

Moreover, everyone understands from the words of the canon that only those heretics are being counted who were condemned in the aforesaid four councils: Arius in the First, Eunomius, Macedonius, and Apollinarius in the Second, Nestorius in the Third, and Eutyches and Dioscorus in the Fourth. Since Origen was condemned in none of the four councils, it may be supposed that his name was substituted by some Acephalian for Dioscorus. Yet that Acephalian must have committed the fraud foolishly and imprudently, since the very words of the canon expose it: they show that the canon must be understood of heretics previously condemned by the Church in ecumenical councils.

Third, if Origen had been treated by name in the Fifth Council just as Theodore was, he would certainly have been identified not merely by a general anathema and in name only, but by a specific and special designation, as were Theodore and the other two, Theodoret and Ibas, who were less culpable. Yet he was not so identified, although he ought to have been above all if he really was the hydra of heresies, the father of Arius, the introducer of paganism into the Church, and so forth, as his adversaries portray him.

[Col. 1075D] Halloixius adds that Gregory the Great asserts that one person was condemned at the Fifth Synod, whereas he should have said two if Origen, besides Theodore, had been condemned.

He also adds that Eutyches had a close association with Dioscorus, so that they would naturally be joined together, whereas he had virtually no association with Origen, so that they would be joined together in the same way.

He further adds that, on account of his antiquity, Origen ought to have been placed before all the others proscribed in the canon if he was to be counted among them, since they are listed according to chronological order.

Finally, he adds [Col. 1076A] that in Justinian’s confession of faith and in the anathematizations attached to it, from which canon 11 of the Fifth Synod was taken almost word for word, there is no mention of Origen. For the text reads:

“If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and those who hold or have at any time held similar opinions—let him be anathema.”

The learned Halloixius brought forward these and other arguments, and he could have produced something still more powerful, as we shall later demonstrate. From them, however, he concludes that nothing prejudices his case—not the Fathers of the three subsequent councils, the Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth, nor even certain supreme pontiffs, since they acted in Origen’s case as the Seventh Synod did in the case of Honorius: they copied what they found in the manuscripts of the Fifth Synod, without being especially concerned about a question that was no more debated at that time than the matters concerning Arius, Eunomius, and the others.

He cites Bellarmine as the author of this exception in a similar case. When Bellarmine, in Book IV, chapter 10, *On the Supreme Pontiff*, undertook the defense of Honorius against the objections, he said:

“To the third objection I answer that the Fathers of the Seventh Synod followed the Sixth Synod and merely repeated what they had read in it; and therefore they were deceived by the Sixth Synod, which was either corrupt or had condemned Honorius through error.”

[Col. 1076B] He also cites the Seventh Synod, which appears to supply this very exception in its seventh session, precisely because it pronounces concerning Origen and Honorius in the same manner. For, after anathematizing the heretics condemned by the first four councils and by the particular council held at Constantinople under Menas, it says:

“With them we also anathematize the fables of Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus, just as the council assembled at Constantinople is known to have done, namely, the Fifth Council. We further proclaim in Christ two wills and operations according to the properties of the natures, just as the Sixth Synod at Constantinople also declared, rejecting Sergius, Honorius, Cyrus, Pyrrhus, Macarius, and those who are without a will in matters of piety, as well as those who hold opinions similar to theirs.”

### § II. What a recent dissertation-writer objected to Halloixius, and what he first thought concerning the time at which he believed Origen to have been condemned at the Fifth Synod

[Col. 1076C] The dissertation-writer attempted to refute what Halloixius advances on behalf of Origen and gathered together many points from various sources, more to heap discredit upon the learned Halloixius than to advance his own case. For he is extraordinarily hostile to the name in which Halloixius chiefly takes pride; and although he wished to appear to defend a case that was intrinsically sound, he actually betrayed it. In order to prove that Origen was truly condemned by the Fifth Synod, he brought forward arguments that were either false, doubtful, or already weakened by previous replies.

To establish, then, that Origen was condemned at the Fifth Synod, he first states when he thinks the condemnation occurred and immediately declares it certain that it happened before May of the year 553—that is, before the synod began—when the patriarchs and bishops had already arrived long before for the celebration of the synod and were examining Origen’s case, “and approving Justinian’s decree against him, issued ten years earlier.” This would mean one year before the deposition of Zoilus, if any credence is given to the dissertation-writer, who places that deposition in the year 554.

[Col. 1076D] He confirms this extraordinary chronology by the authority of George Cedrenus. Cedrenus, under the twenty-sixth year of Justinian, which corresponds to the Christian year 552, reports an imperial letter to the Fathers whom the dissertation-writer believes had come to the Fifth Synod. He thinks that, according to the testimony of Eustathius, the author of the *Life of Saint Eutychius*, they had often assembled to discuss ecclesiastical matters and had held at least one session that was not inserted into the official acts, such as those found in any manuscripts hitherto seen, since that session may have been neglected and recorded in only a few copies, none of which reached posterity:

“It was not copied into many exemplars,” he says, “because the matter did not require more serious consideration. For Origen had long before been condemned throughout the universal Church by an encyclical letter, and patriarchs, before they were consecrated, customarily pronounced an anathema against Origen. Thus Justinian’s edict commanded.”

Finally, he declares that the controversy concerning Origen was discussed shortly before the beginning of the year 553.

[Col. 1077A] Having said this, he proceeds to refute the most illustrious Marca, whose opinion in the dissertation is “that the examination of Origen’s case followed the examination of the Three Chapters, and that this is clearly shown by the sequence of the acts of the Fifth Synod.” Against a man of such learning he brings forward two arguments.

The first is that “the opposite is gathered beyond doubt from the acts of the synod. For canon 11,” in which Origen’s name is inserted, “was issued in the eighth session, held on the fourth day before the Nones of June. Since that session was the last in the case of the Three Chapters, it follows that Origen’s case had already been examined; otherwise the Fathers would have condemned Origen before examining his errors, and consequently Adamantius would have been condemned with the greatest injustice and without a hearing.”

The second argument is drawn from the fifth session, in which Theodore spoke concerning the condemnation of the dead in these words:

“We have also found many others anathematized after death, including Origen; and if anyone goes back to the time of Theophilus of holy memory, or even earlier, he will find that Origen was anathematized after death—[Col. 1077B] something that your holiness has now also done in his case, as has Vigilius, the most religious pope of elder Rome.”

After adducing this testimony, he concludes:

“Here, with the leader of the Origenists admitting it, we see that Origen was condemned by the Fifth Synod and by Pope Vigilius, and indeed before the examination of the Three Chapters had been completed. This testimony is so clear that it places the matter beyond doubt.”

These are the dissertation-writer’s words. This is the reasoning of a man investigating when an event occurred although he has not yet established whether it occurred at all, even though that is precisely what is κυρίως (*kyriōs*, “principally”) at issue, as the teachers of dialectic will judge concerning his method. Let us call each point κατὰ μέρος (*kata meros*, “in detail”) to examination.

First, he asserts that the Fathers who had arrived for the Fifth Synod assembled repeatedly before holding the synod itself in order to discuss ecclesiastical matters, and that this can be inferred from Eustathius. But that writer of the *Life of Saint Eutychius* reports nothing except what all the others relate: while Eutychius was still a monk and [Col. 1077C] apocrisiarius of the bishop of Amasea, when the question of condemning the dead was being debated before the emperor, he persuaded him, on the example of King Josiah, that it was lawful to condemn people even after their death. But how this proves that synodical assemblies were held by the Fathers, no one will clearly see. Indeed, everyone can conclusively establish that the gathering mentioned by Eustathius, which Eutychius attended while still a monk and at which he earned the episcopate by his reply, took place several months before the synod began; for Menas, Eutychius’s predecessor, died in the year 552.

He next asserts that at that time the Fathers held a session—clearly a synodical session—in which Origen was condemned and Justinian’s decree approved. There were therefore nine sessions of the Fifth Synod, a notion no one has previously entertained. Would it not be appropriate and deserved to say to the dissertation-writer what he himself elsewhere said unjustly to Halloixius: “Alas, blind hatred has driven the man headlong!” If you insist that a new session must be added to the council, [Col. 1077D] “it was your responsibility to name some worm-eaten codex somewhere in the learned or even barbarian world” in which that session was counted among the sessions of the Fifth Synod. What scruple there must be in foisting an entire session upon an ecumenical council!

I remember reading in Nicephorus Callistus that in the second session of the Fifth Synod there was a public outcry against Origen after the libelli of the Palestinian monks had been read. But this does not assist the dissertation-writer, nor am I unaware that Nicephorus confused the ecumenical synod with a particular one and was led into that error by Evagrius.

Third, he asserts that his session was not copied into many exemplars because Justinian’s edict was sufficient for everyone. I ask the man how he knows that this session of his was copied even into a single exemplar, when no codex contains it. Does not the dissertation-writer also deserve to hear what he unjustly reproaches Halloixius for saying: “Just as these things are produced without a witness against the ancient tablets, whose reliability no one has hitherto doubted, so they vanish like dreams into smoke”?

[Col. 1078A] Fourth, he asserts that Justinian’s decree against Origen, issued ten years earlier, was approved in his session. Here he plainly conflicts both with the truth, as was shown in chapter 2, and with himself. For if that session took place in the year 552, as the dissertation-writer himself will soon assert, and if the decree preceded the session by ten years, it must have been issued in the year 542. But everyone knows that it was issued after the appointment of Zoilus, which the dissertation-writer, inconsistently assigning it now to one year and now to another, nevertheless always places after the year 542, namely in 543 or 544.

Fifth, he asserts that such a session is confirmed by the authority of Cedrenus, who refers Justinian’s letter concerning Origen to the Fathers assembled in synod under the twenty-sixth year of Justinian, and therefore to the Christian year 552.

[Col. 1078B] But in this matter good faith may rightly be lacking, since three facts capable of misleading the reader’s mind are concealed.

First, in the printed royal manuscripts of Cedrenus, which are the most carefully corrected of all, it does not say “the twenty-sixth year of Justinian,” but “the twenty-fifth.” The reading is established both by the evidence of the eyes and by the explicitly marked sequence of the preceding years.

Second, in that very year in which Cedrenus writes that Justinian’s sacred letter was sent to the Fathers, he also says that the Fifth Synod was celebrated. That year, therefore, is 553. No one will remain uncertain about this who notices that Cedrenus writes that the Fifth Synod was separated from the Fourth by one hundred and two years. For who does not know that the Fourth Synod, the Council of Chalcedon, was held in the year 451 and extended from 8 October to 1 November?

[Col. 1078C] Finally, since Cedrenus confuses not only the dates but also the two Councils of Constantinople, the ecumenical and the particular, it was not the part of a learned man to fail to detect the error, nor the part of an honest man, having detected it, to cite as a witness someone guilty of falsehood.

Sixth, he asserts that “patriarchs, before they were consecrated, customarily pronounced an anathema against Origen, that this had been commanded by Justinian’s edict, and that the same is also clear concerning all the other bishops.” Whether this is mere conjecture or bad faith, I do not know. For nothing of the kind is contained in the edict, nor could it have been. Even if it were contained there, how could anyone prove that it was carried out?

These are the emperor’s words:

[Col. 1078D] “In the future, no bishops or superiors of monasteries are to be ordained in any other way unless, together with all the other heretics who are customarily anathematized in published libelli—that is, Sabellius, Arius, and so forth—they also anathematize the aforesaid Origen, together with his execrable and impious doctrines.”

Where is the name of the patriarchs? But how could it have been present, when a copy of the edict was sent to one particular patriarch? And how could the Church have obeyed secular authority in so important a matter as the profession of faith? Finally, what example exists of the edict having been observed? And with what good faith is the phrase “customarily,” which was spoken of heretics proscribed before the edict, extended to Origen after the edict?

Seventh, he asserts that “the controversy concerning Origen was discussed before the beginning of the year 553, while Menas was still alive.” This is indeed correct as far as the truth is concerned: for Origen’s case was debated several years earlier, at the council of Menas, and even before that at the council of Vigilius in Rome. But how can these facts be reconciled with the assertion that this controversy was discussed at the Fifth Synod? How could Theodore the Cappadocian have truly said—as he in fact did—that Origen was condemned by the Fathers of this synod and by Vigilius? Did the supreme pontiff attend that first session of the dissertation-writer? Why, then, did he refuse to attend the subsequent sessions? Why, during the dispute that occupied the first two sessions, was it not even once objected that he had already met with the Easterners, without any condition, only a few months earlier?

[Col. 1079A] Furthermore, the argument with which he attacks the most illustrious Marca—namely, that from the sequence of the acts it is evident that the inquiry into Origen preceded the inquiry into the Three Chapters—turns against its author and is in itself weak. For he says:

“Since the eighth session was the last in the case of the Three Chapters, it follows that the case of Origen had previously been examined, lest he be said to have been condemned unjustly.”

This argument, I say, turns against its author, provided that it greatly assists Halloix; for if no examination of Origen’s case is recorded in any session of the kind now extant, then either some new session, absent from the acts, must be invented, or Origen must be said to have been condemned with the utmost injustice and without a hearing, or the name Origen in canon 11 must be supposed to have been substituted for Dioscorus. The first alternative is nothing other than a miserable refuge for a man audaciously driven to despair. The other two establish Halloix’s case.

Certainly the most illustrious Marca, being a man of the highest intelligence, since he could not suspect anything about the session of the disputant held in the preceding year, carefully examining the acts of the synod, [Col. 1079B] perceived not only that the examination of the Three Chapters was concluded in the seventh session—for he did not confuse the examination of the case, as the disputant did, with the sentence—but also that six days intervened between the seventh session and the following one. The former was held on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, the latter on the fourth day before the Nones of June. For this reason he thought that nothing more prudent could be said in his own defense than that Origen’s case had been examined after an interval of so many days, and that in the eighth session a common sentence had finally been pronounced against Origen and the Three Chapters.

He was not, however, especially troubled by the statement of the Cappadocian, for he saw that it could easily be referred to the condemnation of Origen carried out several years earlier, when Vigilius and the other patriarchs had subscribed the imperial edict.

After the disputant had attempted in this way to say something about the time when Origen’s case was examined, he then undertakes to prove that some examination had in fact taken place. He employs four arguments, contained [Col. 1079C] partly in the authority of the synods—the Lateran Synod under Martin I, and the Sixth and Seventh Synods—which testify that Origen, together with Evagrius and Didymus, was proscribed as a heretic by the Fifth Synod; partly in the testimony of Cyril the monk, who wrote about the lives of Saints Sabas and Euthymius; of Cosmas the deacon, who recited in the Seventh Synod a passage from the Life of Saint Sabas; of Sophronius of Jerusalem, whom the disputant thinks flourished shortly after the Fifth Synod; and of the historian Evagrius, all of whom teach the same thing as the three synods; partly in bitter abuse directed against Halloix, whose defense of Origen is said to be almost equivalent to folly; in the opinion that the name Origen was substituted for Dioscorus, which is called a ridiculous conjecture; and in the declaration that those who maintain that Origen’s case was examined in the Fifth Synod acted with shamelessness; and finally, partly in certain answers that have the appearance of responses to what Halloix brought forward in support of his position.

As to the first point, by which Halloix argued that something had been added to canon 11, the disputant replies that the name Origen was found in the canons of the Fifth Synod in the form in which they existed in the codices—whether those preserved at Rome and read nearly a hundred years later in the Lateran Synod, or those extracted from the archive of the Constantinopolitan patriarchate which the Sixth Synod ordered to be read aloud before it and described as ancient and unmutilated, that is, as having had nothing removed from them.

As to the second point, although he did not dare to deny that the Fathers ordinarily associated Eutyches and Dioscorus and pursued them with a common execration, he nevertheless asserts that they were not associated in the canon because Dioscorus was delirious in the same way as Eutyches, indeed even in the same way as Origen. Hence, he says that in canon 18 of the Lateran Council Dioscorus is joined to Eutyches, but that Origen is numbered with them as well, as also in the Seventh Synod.

At this point he seemed to strengthen his response by an elaborate declamation and vehement expression of astonishment, because “not one of so great a number of Fathers, whether of the Lateran Council or of the Sixth and Seventh Synods, moved by compassion toward Adamantius or by love toward his colleagues, showed that the name Origen had been intruded into canon 11, so as to rescue him from disgrace and them from error.”

Then he attempts to dissolve the argument drawn from the authority of Gregory the Great. He says that the single person whom Gregory writes was condemned in the synod must be understood not simply and absolutely, but as one of the three whose writings were proscribed. For of those three, only Theodore was struck with an anathema, while the writings of Theodoret and Ibas alone were proscribed.

To prove this, he adduces Gregory’s own passage, but at the same time he brings forward a passage from a letter written by Nicholas I to the emperor Michael, in order to confirm his response and establish that two persons, Origen and Theodore, were condemned.

Next, against the argument drawn by Halloix from the fact that Origen’s name is not found in Justinian’s edict, he replies, with Baronius, that this occurred through the fraud of Theodore of Cappadocia, who, being as devoted to Origen as he hated the Three Chapters, composed the edict according to his own inclination. [Col. 1080A]

As for Halloix’s objection that Origen had not been condemned by any earlier synods, although he certainly should have been if he had appeared guilty of as many crimes formerly as he did later, the disputant rebuts it with an astonishing response. He does not explain the reason for the fact; rather, he maintains that Origen was condemned by all the synods, though not in his own name but in the names of others: Arius by the Council of Nicaea, Macedonius by the First Council of Constantinople—he meant the First, not the Second—Nestorius by the Council of Ephesus, and Eutyches and Dioscorus by the Council of Chalcedon.

He offers no other reason for this response than that Origen was accused by Theophilus as a sort of hydra of all heresies, although Athanasius defended him as free from the error of Arius. The disputant declares that Theophilus was right to accuse him, but that Athanasius was wrong to defend him.

Finally, he invokes certain most holy monks and bishops who lived in the time of Justinian and detested Origen’s books: Sabas, who served as envoy to the emperor on behalf of Peter, bishop of Jerusalem; John, who received the title Silentiarius; and Cyriacus, who fought most vehemently against the Origenists.

On this occasion he attacks Halloix as though Halloix had called Sabas, Theodosius, Cyriacus, and John uneducated monks. I would not have wished this charge to be made, since it is not made in good faith. Halloix spoke reverently, as was proper, of the holy men; he called no others uneducated monks except those who had presented the emperor with petitions against Origen through the agency of the deacon Pelagius.

Nor could he have thought so badly of the holy men, since he knew well that some of them had already departed to heaven, such as Sabas and Theodosius, while others were serving God in their own monasteries when this tragedy was taking place.

Halloix could easily have refuted all these objections or replies, owing to his exceptional learning, had he read them. But he has passed to heaven, where he looks down upon the insults—or rather pities and even loves the man who utters them. [Col. 1080D]

For he would have said, first, that the issue is not the time when the case was examined, about which enough has been said, but the very condemnation of Origen.

The authority of the synods concerning the name Origen, just as the Seventh Synod’s authority concerns the name Honorius, cannot properly be brought forward to establish that Origen really was condemned in the Fifth Synod. With equal right one could bring forward the authority of the Seventh Synod to demonstrate that Honorius was struck with an anathema among the Monothelites at the Sixth Synod—something which I do not know whether the disputant would dare to say.

For this reason he has cunningly concealed the argument which Halloix treated at length and pressed vigorously, recognizing the slippery ground on which he stood. If he denied that Honorius had been condemned at the Sixth Synod, either altogether or justly, and employed the exceptions of Bellarmine and Baronius, he would himself overthrow the whole structure of his arguments. For if the Seventh Synod can rightly be said to have been led into error by the Sixth, then the Sixth Synod can equally rightly be said to have been led into error by the Fifth. And others too—Cyril, Sophronius, and Evagrius—could, without doubt, be judged less prudent than the entire synod.

But if he admitted that Honorius had been justly condemned, he would rightly fear for himself before the tribunal in which, as the learned defense of Vincent of Lérins against the disputant teaches us, he was shown to be in danger—a defense composed by the distinguished Father Macedo, eminent for piety and learning.

He would have said, second, that he was astonished that Sophronius could be described by the disputant as having flourished shortly after the Fifth Synod—Sophronius, I mean, who died in the eighty-fourth year after the synod had been celebrated, that is, in the year 637, as the eminent Labbe reports, “at whose death learning was forced to grieve,” as the disputant was compelled to admit.

He would have said, third, that it seemed astonishing to him, first, that the disputant should infer from this that nothing had been added to canon 11, because nothing had been removed from the acts. For this is what he says: that the acts are contained in un mutilated codices. Yet it is not altogether astonishing that, for a man who thinks that making an objection is the same as preceding someone, adding and removing should be the same thing.

Indeed, who could easily understand with what ἀκολουθία—logical consistency—in favor of the integrity of the codices from which the Fathers of the Sixth Council ordered the acts of the Fifth Synod to be read aloud, that man labors so strenuously, when he asserts that the acts of the Fifth Synod have reached us mutilated and incomplete? Yet he cannot show when East and West agreed to corrupt the acts that were read with such care, or when they first came to exist everywhere in a corrupted form.

And I say “corrupted” not merely through variations of wording, of which many entered through the fault of copyists, but through the removal of two entire sessions—sessions of great importance for suppressing the Origenists by the authority of an ecumenical synod.

He would have said, fourth, that to the disputant’s declamation he could repeat that familiar retort, “Say it to yourself”; and, changing the name Origen to that of Honorius, he could apply what the theatrical declaimer had said against himself:

“Was the Seventh Synod, then, led into error by a corrupt copy of the Sixth? Could none of the Fathers obtain the genuine and legitimate acts of the Sixth Synod, so as to rescue Honorius from such disgrace and warn his colleagues that the name of Honorius had been intruded into the definition and other sections of the synod? Did no advocate for Honorius rise from so numerous a synod, presided over by three legates of the Apostolic See? Was no one moved by any compassion toward the bishop of the first see, the vicar of Christ, the head of the Church, the successor of Peter, the father of the Fathers?”

He would have said, fifth, that the exception brought against the argument drawn from the authority of Gregory the Great was wholly empty. For there is no reason why Gregory’s general statement concerning persons and the synod in which the Three Chapters were dealt with should be restricted to only three persons and only part of the synod.

For if the case of Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus was examined in the Fifth Synod, then without doubt six persons were involved. Moreover, since Gregory spoke indefinitely of “the synod,” and spoke there as a teacher, why, contrary to the rules of dialectic, is a proposition—as they say, a doctrinal proposition—taken in part rather than, as is customary, καθ᾽ ὅλου, “as a whole”?

Certainly what is brought from the letter of Nicholas I to Michael is irrelevant:

“Moreover, the Fifth Synod also struck with anathema those already dead, having found that Origen and Theodore, through writings deserving condemnation, did not hold right opinions.”

For Nicholas did not understand “the Fifth Synod” to mean the matter over which Halloix is disputing, but the matter that we are about to explain.

He would have said, sixth, that the following exception, which the disputant borrowed from Baronius, was no more substantial. For who would believe that, at the very time when it was most necessary to establish by example that the dead could be condemned, Origen’s name could have been omitted from Justinian’s anathema?

Who would dare to assert that this happened through the fraud of the Cappadocian, unless, against the disputant’s protest, he admitted that the following words had been falsely attributed to that same bishop?
