“We also find many others anathematized after death; likewise Origen, even if someone should go back to the time of Theophilus of holy memory, or earlier, will find him anathematized after death, as your Holiness and Pope Vigilius, the most devout bishop of elder Rome, have now done in his case.”

Are these the words of a man who refuses “to place his Origen among the condemned heads”?

He would have said, seventh, that the fiction that Origen was condemned in the first four ecumenical synods—not in his own name but in the names of those who were claimed as his disciples—is so paradoxical that no one even slightly imbued with ecclesiastical teaching could believe it or hear it without laughter.

For who would not have equal right to maintain that Origen was received and praised by the four synods, which, as Gregory says, were equal to the Gospel—not in his own name, but in the names of others who, although they were teachers of the faithful, gloried in Origen as their teacher?

Certainly the three Gregorys gloried in him: Gregory Thaumaturgus in his panegyric oration, Gregory of Nazianzus in the account preserved by Suidas and in the Philocalia, and Gregory of Nyssa in his encomium of the Thaumaturgus.

Athanasius too gloried in him, rescuing so great a man from the slander of association with Arius. Indeed, Jerome himself gloried in him. In the preface to his book On Hebrew Names, Jerome wrote that Origen could be denied to be “a teacher of the Churches after the apostles” by no one except an ignorant person. In the prologue to Book II of his Commentary on Micah, he professed that he wished to imitate one whom he would not hesitate to say was pleasing to all believers.

Finally, in Letter 65 he gave a judgment by which the entire dispute could be settled among people who do not love contention:

“Who among us,” he says, “can read as much as he wrote? Who would not admire his ardent spirit in the Scriptures? But if some Judas Zelotes should set his errors before us, let him hear plainly:

‘Sometimes great Homer nods;

Yet in a long work it is permissible for sleep to creep in.’

Let us not imitate the faults of one whose virtues we cannot follow. Others, both Greeks and Latins, have erred in the faith; it is not necessary to name them, lest we seem to defend him not on account of his own merits, but because of the error of others.”

Finally, he would have said that those most holy monks who are mentioned first did not speak of Origen’s condemnation by the Fifth Synod; second, that they more often dealt with the Origenists than with Origen himself; and that teachers are commonly burdened with the odium of their disciples, even when they do not deserve it.

Thus Augustine himself once suffered from the hostility directed against the Predestinarians of Hadrumetum and more recently against others. Moreover, the holiest men have sometimes been slandered through error.

What was not said about the admirable Cyril of Alexandria himself by men of astonishing holiness? Isidore of Pelusium certainly said to him things altogether unspeakable; and Gennadius of Constantinople wrote about Cyril’s Twelve Chapters and his person things that would fill anyone who read them with horror:

“Woe is me,” he says, “because of evils—alas, alas! For from what other point could anyone now begin? What and how many blasphemies have I encountered from Cyril of Egypt, and how many blasphemies have I heard? Who will truly give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, and so forth? The prophets prophesy wickedness, the priests clap their hands, and my people have loved it so. For what is minor or moderate in them? He has hurled every height of blasphemy against the holy Fathers, against their earlier apostles, against the Savior himself, and so forth. God will anathematize you, whitewashed wall; for it is altogether just that a similar indignation be expressed against you by those disciples, since, like Ananias, the chief priest of the Jews, you have moved your tongue against the disciples of Christ.”

§ III. Judgment is pronounced on the dispute between Halloix and the disputant.

We have so far seen two men, known through their writings, contending over the condemnation of Origen; yet it has not been clear in whose direction victory inclines—perhaps it will belong to neither.

Nevertheless, from the conflict of the opposing opinions some light emerges, in which the truth can be seen with considerable clarity. Although Halloix and the disputant came to the contest under unequal conditions—Halloix equipped with eloquence, a methodical style of writing, careful reading of the Fathers, knowledge of both learned languages, and elegance of expression, while the other was unprepared in these respects, whether because he despised them or for some other reason—each nevertheless gained part of the case and lost part; neither attained everything he was pursuing.

Halloix won the point that Origen’s case was not examined in the synod now called the Fifth; the disputant won the point that Origen was condemned in what was once called the Fifth Synod. Both, when they came near the truth, were able to see it; in both cases, emotions prevented them from seeing it. Halloix was hindered by grief over Origen’s condemnation; the disputant by envy.

Yet let us attribute to human weakness what both suffered as human beings. Let us set out what can be gathered as true after the battle, distinguishing it in five propositions.

[Col. 1083B] PROPOSITION I.—An examination was once held concerning Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus.

To pronounce judgment without examining the case against any person, especially against someone as a heretic, is permitted neither by reason, nor by evangelical law, nor by humanity itself. This is clearer and more certain to everyone than to require proof by argument.

If this equity was ever owed toward anyone, or at any time, or in any case, it was certainly owed toward Origen in the time of the Fifth Synod, when the question concerned branding him with the most disgraceful of all charges of heresy.

For hardly anyone ever had a more celebrated reputation in both directions than Origen. Some, such as Vincent of Lérins, called him “a teacher of the Church, from whose bosom countless teachers, countless priests, confessors, and martyrs have emerged.” Others, such as Theophilus of Alexandria and Sophronius of Jerusalem, called him “a many-headed hydra, from which nearly the whole plague of heresies had spread into the Church.” [Col. 1083C]

Indeed, Origen’s fate and appearance were so ambiguous that the same writer, Jerome, according to the different ways in which he viewed him, called him at one time “the second teacher of the Churches after the apostles,” and at another “the source of Arius.”

How much equity, and how much prudence and caution, ought to have been exercised when judgment was being passed upon such a man, and upon two men comparable to him, Didymus and Evagrius—comparable, I mean, not only in doctrine but also in the reputation of their moral holiness and admirable lives.

If it was never lawful by any right to pass judgment without examination upon three such men, of such fame and authority, it was certainly not lawful in those times, when the Church was divided into factions over the question; when the matter was being pursued with heightened contentiousness even among the holy inhabitants of the laurae; when an ambitious emperor, skilled in hearing legal arguments and tenacious of equity, held sway; when the very acts of the Council of Chalcedon were exposed to calumny because of some neglect of legal forms; when the lovers of Origen and patrons of the Origenists possessed great influence at court; when obstinate leaders of the factions eagerly seized upon every means of weakening the force even of the most exact canons; and when the dispute concerned not only doctrines, in which human beings may err, but the persons themselves and the charge of heresy, than which no mark can be more shameful, infamous, or disgraceful.

Add that the books of men renowned throughout the entire East were to be struck with anathema—books, I mean, that dealt extensively with divine matters, that were worn smooth in everyone’s hands, that were valued as storehouses of faith, schools of holiness, and sanctuaries of religion. From these books even the accusers themselves would have been compelled to draw what they were praised for possessing in the Church and for defending the faith.

Their authors appeared, even to the wonder-workers themselves, “to have received this greatest gift from God, and this most excellent lot from heaven: that they should become interpreters of the divine oracles for human beings, understand God’s words as though God himself were speaking, and explain them to people in such a way that they could grasp them.”

From all this it is clear that a lawful judgment was at some time carried out concerning Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius in a legitimate assembly. For it is not permissible to suppose that a sentence of condemnation was pronounced unless the case had been lawfully examined. Nor does the unanimous testimony and tradition of all the ancients permit us to deny that they were condemned, since some have written that the Fifth Synod was convened πρωτοτύπως, “primarily,” on account of Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius, so that they might be condemned.

PROPOSITION II.—In what is now called the Fifth Synod, the cases of neither Origen, Didymus, nor Evagrius were examined.

For nowhere in it is the name of Evagrius or Didymus read; nor is Origen mentioned except in a single word—once in the fifth session, where Theodore of Cappadocia mentions him as already condemned, and once in the eighth session, where canon 11 numbers Origen among the heretics.

To invent two other sessions besides the eight that are extant—one preceding all the others by more than half a year, and the other following even the promulgation of the canons—and to invent, I say, two additional sessions in which Origen’s case was examined in the first and Evagrius’s and Didymus’s in the second, as the disputant did when pressed by difficulty, is not to defend the case but to abandon it. For to posit documents is not the act of a man conducting a case, but of one driven to despair.

Yet this entire fiction concerning the two sessions, at least insofar as it concerns Origen, had already been sufficiently rejected by the very adversaries who were fighting one another, Halloix and the disputant. Halloix demonstrated that Origen had not been dealt with before the eighth session; the disputant clearly showed that he had not been dealt with after the fifth.

PROPOSITION III.—In what is now called the Fifth Synod, Origen was truly condemned by name, and it cannot be said that his name was fraudulently inserted into canon 11.

There are innumerable codices, both in the East and in the West, containing the acts of the Fifth Synod; in every one, canon 11 is found as it appears in the printed editions. It is incredible that the same error could have entered all of them, unless perhaps it already existed in the primary exemplar from which the other codices were copied.

Yet it is astonishing—indeed plainly ἀδύνατον, “impossible”—that the notaries of the council should have corrupted an instrument of such importance, and that none of the Fathers, not even Theodore of Cappadocia himself, should at that time have complained of the notaries’ bad faith and dishonesty, when each received a copy of the canons to be taken back to his province and saw it to be entirely different from what had been enacted.

This consideration, supported especially by the innumerable testimonies of synods, popes, and writers, compels me easily to dismiss Halloix’s arguments, ingenious though their invention and learned though their research, since nearly all of them rest upon falsehood.

For if the name Origen was placed in canon 11 of the Fifth Synod, it does not immediately follow that so great a man was condemned without a hearing. Rather, it follows that an examination had preceded it, and indeed a solemn one. Such an examination truly preceded it in all the patriarchal synods, and especially in the Roman synod, from which we showed in chapter 2 that Vigilius responded.

Nor does it follow that, in the synod of which Gregory the Great spoke, several persons whose cases had been examined were condemned. Only one was condemned, namely Theodore of Mopsuestia. At that time nothing had been examined concerning Origen, but only concerning Theodore, Theodoret, and Ibas.

Nor does it follow that, because Origen preceded in age the other heretics who were proscribed, he should also have preceded them in the proscription. The order of age was not observed in the canon, but the order of the time at which each person was condemned; in this order, others preceded Origen.

[Col. 1085A] Conversely, it follows that an easy answer can be given to the two questions Halloix raises: first, why Origen’s name does not appear in Justinian’s anathema but does appear in canon 11 of the synod, which was taken verbatim from the anathema; second, why Origen, if he deserved to suffer a sentence of condemnation, did not suffer it in the earlier synods.

The answer to the first question is straightforward. In another part of his confession of faith, the part that properly concerned Origen, the emperor, after the nine anathemas with which he struck his doctrines, had written against the person himself, as the tenth:

“Anathema also to Origen, who is also Adamantius, who expounded these things,” and so forth.

What need was there, after so solemn a condemnation, to curse that devoted head again with so many and such great imprecations in another part of the confession of faith, the part concerned with the Three Chapters?

The Fathers, however, listed Origen’s name among heretics already long since proscribed because he too had been proscribed by their synods approximately ten years earlier.

The answer to the second question is that heresies are customarily condemned by the Church not when they arise, but when they stir up disturbances and become, as it were, universal.

The Origenists had indeed caused disturbances long before. For that reason synods had been held by Theophilus at Alexandria, by Epiphanius on the island of Cyprus, and by Anastasius at Rome. But those synods can be regarded as having been convened either chiefly or at least especially because of the books On First Principles, Περὶ ἀρχῶν, and in order to calm disturbances that were, as it were, particular.

But now, when the Acephali and the Apollinarists were raging through almost the entire world and defending their heresies by the doctrines of Origen—the former, as Leo the Great testifies, alleging the pre-existence of souls in order to defend the claim that Christ’s flesh had not fallen from heaven and was not ὁμοούσιον, “consubstantial,” with ours; the latter alleging the restoration, even of demons, to their original state in order to establish their ἀνακυκλήσεις, “cycles” or “recurrences,” as Theodoret mentions—when, I say, those turbulent groups were raging throughout the world, they had to be restrained by utterly overturning the defense behind which they sheltered.

Thus Origen had to be subjected to anathema at that time, although earlier centuries, because of the celebrity of his reputation, had spared him patiently.

PROPOSITION IV.—An examination of Origen was held in each of the patriarchal synods; and an examination of Evagrius and Didymus was held in the Constantinopolitan synod of Menna, and perhaps also in the Jerusalem synod of Peter.

We stated in chapter 2 that the emperor had ordered the five patriarchs to hold synods in which they should submit the edict sent concerning Origen and his doctrines to examination, and should arrange for the judgment of the synods to be subscribed not only by those bishops who had conducted the judgment but also by any others in the respective dioceses.

We likewise stated that what the emperor desired was also carried out by the supreme pontiff, whose authority is primary in matters of faith. After the decree of the supreme pontiff’s synod and the responses of the other bishops had been received, a council met at Constantinople. With Menna presiding, it denounced Origen and approved the imperial edict by subscription.

From this it is clear what Liberatus wrote in the final chapter:

“The condemnation of Origen and of his principal doctrines, expressed in the form of an anathema, was directed not only to Menna, archbishop of Constantinople, but also to Vigilius, bishop of Rome, Zoilus of Alexandria, Ephraemius of Antioch, and Peter of Jerusalem. When they received and subscribed it, Origen was condemned.”

It is also clear that the examination preceded the condemnation, and that it was of the kind prescribed by the emperor’s decree—namely, careful and canonical.

An examination of Origen was therefore held in all the patriarchal synods, but in Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch it concerned Origen alone, since the edict dealt with him alone.

Menna, however, instituted a judgment concerning Evagrius and Didymus because monks presented their written petitions against both of them only to the Constantinopolitan synod as followers of Origen.

All this is plainly shown partly by the emperor’s edict and partly by the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod under discussion, which Evagrius inserted into his history.

Nevertheless, it may reasonably and not implausibly be conjectured that the same petitions of the monks were read in the Jerusalem synod. For just as those monks came from Palestine, sent from monasteries—especially those near the holy city—so it is credible that the superiors of the monasteries, whom the emperor’s edict ordered to be summoned to the synod, presented the same petitions to their primate and to the bishops assembled with him, petitions which they had given to the legates to carry to the imperial city.

Those petitions were useful for debating the case, and the emperor had mentioned them as the initial documents of the case.

PROPOSITION V.—In what the ancients called the Fifth Synod, the case of Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius was both examined and judged.

The ancients—if not all, at least many of them—embraced under the name “Fifth Synod” everything contained in Justinian’s book of faith.

That book was divided into three distinct parts. The first, as we already noted in chapter 2, was the synod of Menna against Anthimus, Severus, Peter, and Zoaras. The second was another synod of the same Menna against Origen and his two followers. The third was the very synod now commonly called the Fifth, which consisted of the eight sessions ordinarily known by that name.

Appended to these was, if it is genuine, Vigilius’s letter to Eutychius concerning the confirmation of the Fifth Synod; and, I think, Justinian’s confession of faith concerning the Three Chapters.

If matters stand thus, the truth of the proposition is evident, since in the third part the judgment carried out in the second part against Origen and his followers is confirmed in a single word.

That matters did in fact stand thus is demonstrated by the agreement of everything the ancients transmitted concerning the Fifth Synod and by the concordance of opinions that appear to conflict. No argument could be more effective on this point.

Photius writes the following about the Fifth Council in Letter 1 to Michael, prince of Bulgaria:

“The holy and ecumenical Fifth Council consecrated to itself a sacred temple in the great city of Constantine. It was confirmed by the presence and assembly of one hundred and sixty-five bishops. First Menna presided over them, and afterward Eutychius, who, in succession to him, governed the keys of the archiepiscopal church of the imperial city; and Vigilius, bishop of Rome, who was indeed in the city but was not present at the council. Although he was not ready to attend the assembly of the sacred gathering, he nevertheless approved the common faith of the Fathers in a written statement.

“There were also Apollinaris, archbishop of Alexandria, and Domnus, archbishop of Antioch; and Didymus and Evagrius, acting in the place of Eustochius, bishop of Jerusalem.

“At that time Justinian, the best of emperors, also held the Roman Empire and favored ecclesiastical decrees.

“This holy and ecumenical council completely uprooted the impious doctrines of Nestorius, which were sprouting again, together with the sower of the tares, Theodore and Dioscorus—the former bishop of Mopsuestia, the latter bishop of Tarsus. Having first conceived the heresy of Nestorius, they eventually published it in writings and left it behind as the adulterous and horrible offspring of their minds.

“Moreover, they condemned and overwhelmed with anathema Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius, ancient diseases of the faithful, who had indeed attempted to bring the fables of the Greeks into the Church of God.

“Not only these condemned doctrines, but also the heresy that had arisen shortly before—that of Anthimus of Trebizond, who supported the opinion of Eutyches, and of Severus, Peter of Apamea, and Zoaras, its authors—the sacred chorus of the Fathers overthrew, together with the rest of their wicked and manifold work, and condemned it with anathema.

“The chief leader of this holy work was Agapetus, pontiff of Rome, assisted and supported by distinguished bishops, among whom was the renowned bishop of Antioch, Ephraemius, and Peter, bishop of Jerusalem.

“Thus that divine assembly of bishops, after condemning and rejecting all these things, enacted and confirmed the true and divine decrees of the catholic and apostolic Church; and the Fifth Council consists of these matters.”

From this testimony we learn that the Photian book of the Fifth Synod contained the matters we have described. For this reason Photius wrote the following eight points about the Fifth Synod:

1. That Menna and Eutychius presided over it, but Menna first and Eutychius afterward.

2. That Justinian held the same opinion as the Fathers—that is, that his edicts corresponded to their decrees.

3. That the impious doctrines of Nestorius, which were sprouting again, were completely uprooted together with their sower, Theodore and Diodore.

4. That Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius, ancient diseases of the faithful, were struck with anathema.

5. That the sacred gathering of the Fathers overthrew and condemned with anathema not only these two older heresies but also the other heresy that had arisen shortly before: that of Anthimus of Trebizond, who supported the opinion of Eutyches, and of Severus, Peter of Apamea, and Zoaras, its authors, together with the rest of their wicked and manifold work.

6. That the chief leader of this holy work was Agapetus, pontiff of Rome, with the distinguished bishops Ephraemius of Antioch, Peter of Jerusalem, and others assisting him.

7. That all these men, τούτους ἅπαντας, “all these,” were condemned by the divine assembly of bishops, and that the doctrines of the Church were confirmed at the same time.

8. That the Fifth Council consists of these matters: καὶ τὰ μὲν τῆς οἰκουμενικῆς πέμπτης συνόδου ἐν τούτοις, “and the matters of the Fifth Ecumenical Synod are contained in these things.”

Nothing clearer can be brought forward in support of our position. For Mennas presided over the first two synods, and Eutychius over the third. Agapetus the pope gave the first its beginning; Mennas, Ephraemius, and Peter collaborated. Vigilius, Mennas, Zoilus, Ephraemius, and Peter advanced the second. Eutychius, Apollinaris, Domnus, and Elias held the third; Vigilius confirmed it by his decrees; Justinian held the same opinion as each of the synods, ἀνεφρώνησεν—“came to his senses.” Their sanctions are found to accord with their definitions. In the first, Anthimus, Severus, Peter, and Zoaras were condemned; in the second, Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius; in the third, Theodore and others. All these things agree with the historical truth.

[Col. 1087C] But when Photius wrote that Didymus and Evagrius had been Elias’s legates, he suffered a lapse of memory. They were Damianus, bishop of Sozusa; Georgius, bishop of Tiberias; and Stephanus, bishop of Raphia.

An even stronger testimony than this clear one is furnished by another, since it was pronounced by a long succession of supreme pontiffs with the greatest possible public solemnity and sanctity. For approximately two hundred years before Photius—that is, toward the end of the seventh century, shortly after the convocation of the Sixth Synod—a confession of faith was issued, either by Leo II or by Sergius I, which subsequent supreme pontiffs were to recite at their ordination. In it, when the Fifth Synod is discussed, there are many statements not merely similar to those of Photius, but possessing far greater authority on account of the sanctity of their source.

Accordingly, when the presbyter elected as supreme pontiff was professing the faith, after speaking of the four earlier synods, he spoke of the Fifth Synod as follows:

> “Thus these four holy and universal councils were followed by the venerable holy Fifth Council, which was convened in the imperial city of Constantinople under the emperor Justinian of pious memory. By its salutary deliberation our Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity, was truly proclaimed; and those who confused and divided the mystery of his sacred incarnation were struck down by the spiritual sword of this declaration.
>
> “In this council Origen, together with his impious disciples and followers Didymus and Evagrius, and those who treated God, the Creator of all things, and every rational creature of his in accordance with pagan fables, were subjected to eternal condemnation. In it Theodore of Mopsuestia, the author of Nestorius’s teaching, and likewise Diodore, together with all the disciples of the execrable division—who were also called semi-Nestorians—were cast out of the Church of God under the eternal sentence of anathema. In it Severus the Acephalite, together with Peter and Zoaras and the rest of their partners and followers in impious confusion, was struck down by perpetual condemnation.”

[Col. 1088A] Although the order is somewhat reversed, mention is made, as it were, of the three divisions of a single synod; for each is distinguished by its own condemnations of the heretics. This is especially noteworthy: it is expressly said that three, almost troop-like groups of heretics were condemned in this council.

Although these two testimonies possess great force in themselves and, in my judgment, settle the matter, it is nevertheless worthwhile to produce lesser testimonies, which, if they do not provide light, may at least receive it.

Cyril of Scythopolis, in the *Life of Saint Sabas*, chapter 109:

> “When the Fifth holy and ecumenical synod had been convened at Byzantium, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Origen, and, together with them, the impious doctrines concerning pre-existence and restoration were collectively subjected to anathema.”

An ecclesiastical judgment concerning pre-existence and restoration was exercised only in the synod of Mennas.

What Evagrius transmitted, and how far what he transmitted contributes to illuminating this passage, was demonstrated in chapter 2. Nevertheless, it is useful to note his words again:

[Col. 1088B]

> “The Fifth Synod was convened by Justinian for this reason: when Eustochius saw the supporters of Origen’s doctrines gaining strength in the monasteries of Palestine, and especially in the one called the New Laura,”

and so forth.

These words show that the judgment concerning Origen’s doctrines—and therefore the council of Mennas—belongs, together with Vigilius’s decree, to the Fifth Synod; for no other judgment was exercised on that issue.

Sergius, in the *Ecthesis* attributed to Heraclius, after mentioning the five general councils, says:

> “Following these things in every respect, and receiving their divine doctrines, we receive all whom they received, we expel all whom they expelled, and we anathematize them—especially Novatian, Sabellius, Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinaris, Origen, Evagrius, Didymus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Severus, and the impious writings of Theodoret,”

and so forth.

If he expels those whom the five synods expelled, then by the name of the Fifth Synod he must understand those three in which Severus, Origen, and Theodore were condemned. For in no other synod possessing the force of an ecumenical council, and worthy of approval by the apostolic see, were the three persons just mentioned struck by anathema. But if he does understand them in this way, everything is plain and clear.

Sophronius, in his synodical letter to Sergius, writes:

> “I accept another council, universally constituted, which was also celebrated in the imperial city while Justinian was administering the scepter of the Roman Empire, together with all its illustrious definitions. It was convened, indeed, for the confirmation of the celebrated Council of Chalcedon. But it destroys and casts into perdition, first of all, the mad Origen and all his pompous, somnolent ravings, as well as his inventions full of great impiety; likewise, with him, all the doctrines of Evagrius and Didymus, together with their pagan and monstrous fables and their legendary deliriums. After these it uproots Theodore of Mopsuestia, the teacher of Nestorius, who was rebellious against God, and, as filthy darnel, casts him and his blasphemous little works out of the apostolic Church.”

[Col. 1088D] The Sixth Synod has the same material in its definition of faith, and the synodical letter of Theodore of Jerusalem likewise contains the same. If what we have said concerning the ancient tripartite Fifth Synod is sound, these testimonies possess manifest truth; if not, manifest falsehood.

The Seventh Synod, in its definition of faith, reports what the Photius mentioned above appears to have followed. For after the Fathers had professed that they rejected those whom the four earlier synods had rejected, they continued in these words:

> “Together with them we also condemn Severus, Peter, and their manifoldly blasphemous composition, woven like a rope through reciprocal entanglements, and with them the fables of Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus, just as the Fifth Council convened at Constantinople is known to have done.”

That testimony is the more valuable because it speaks more clearly about those matters that might create doubt, while omitting what concerns Theodore as though it were beyond doubt. It is also the more emphatic in teaching that everyone recognizes Severus and Origen, each together with his associates, as having been proscribed in the Fifth Synod.

From the evidence we have brought forward, I believe that some light now arises by which what is precious may be distinguished from what is worthless in the histories of the Fifth Synod by Theophanes, Cedrenus, and Nicephorus. Although they mingled everything together in the confusion of those times, Theophanes nevertheless truly wrote that the Fifth Synod was convened *κατὰ τοῦ Ὁριγενοῦς παράφρονος, καὶ Διδύμου τοῦ ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων, καὶ Εὐαγρίου, καὶ κατὰ τῶν ἀκεφάλων κεφαλαίων*—“against the mad Origen, Didymus the Blind, and Evagrius, and against the Acephalous heads.” Cedrenus truly reported Justinian’s sacred decree concerning the investigation of Origen’s case at the Fifth Synod, as the matter was understood in those times. Nicephorus truly narrates that judgment was passed concerning Origen in the second session—by which he means a portion of the synod.

I believe that what had to be demonstrated has been established: namely, that under the name of the Fifth Synod the three ancient councils that we now distinguish were included, and that the case of Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius was examined and adjudicated in the Fifth Synod. But so that the truth may shine forth still more clearly, several related questions must be resolved.

The first is when the tripartite Fifth Synod began to be regarded in such a way that the individual synods were considered to be as many separate sessions—or, as Nicephorus calls them, συνελεύσεις, that is, assemblies. I think this happened during Justinian’s reign. For whatever was determined concerning the faith in his time, he wished to have regarded as equivalent to a single council, so that, just as his illustrious predecessors had each convened a council of his own—Constantine the Council of Nicaea, Theodosius the Great the First Council of Constantinople, Theodosius the Younger the Council of Ephesus, and Marcian the Council of Chalcedon—he too might have one by which he would appear to have completed the work of defining the faith whose foundations they had laid.

The second question is why only three are said to have been συνελεύσεις, when several synods existed during Justinian’s reign, and indeed synods convened by imperial command—for example, the one held by Mennas concerning the Three Chapters before Vigilius came to Constantinople. That synod might seem to deserve to be counted in the same way as the one concerned with Origen’s case.

Nevertheless, the three under discussion possessed an exceptional feature beyond the others, even those summoned by imperial order: they concerned the faith, were approved by the agreement of the patriarchs and by the synodical authority of the apostolic see, and therefore were approved by the judgment of both Churches, Western and Eastern. That they were convened on a matter of faith is perfectly clear, since the first proscribed the Acephali, the second the Origenists, and the third the Nestorians—the three heresies that flourished at that time.

It is equally clear that they were approved by the agreement of both Churches. Hormisdas and Agapetus added force and authority to the first. Indeed, it was nothing other than the execution of the judgment issued by those pontiffs, as is evident from the decisions of Mennas, the subscriptions of the Western bishops and the legates of the apostolic see, and many other sources. Vigilius gave strength to the second, since in his own letters he called the definition of Mennas a definition. Vigilius likewise confirmed the third by his letter to Eutychius, as it is reported.

Many prelates of both Churches participated in the first, together with legates of the principal sees—Rome, Antioch, and Jerusalem—but not of Alexandria, which was divided by the factions of the Acephali and by the schism of Gaianus and Theodosius. All the patriarchs agreed to the second, and Pelagius, the apocrisarius of the apostolic see, was present. The third was presided over in person by Eutychius of Constantinople, Apollinaris of Alexandria, and Domninus of Antioch; Eustochius of Jerusalem was present through a legate.

The emperor compelled all of them through the letters known as *tractoriae*. He confirmed them all not only by decrees but also by entire books. What he had not done when the first was held, he did approximately six years later, sending a book against the Acephali to Zoilus of Alexandria, as Pope Agatho bears witness.

The third question is whether any explicit traces still exist of a Fifth Synod composed of three parts. They certainly do. For in ancient Greek and Latin manuscripts alike, the acts against Anthimus are entitled in the name of the Fifth Synod.

As a Greek witness I cite Severinus Binius, who, in his notes on the council against Anthimus, states that he found the acts of this council in an old Greek manuscript of the Palatine Library. On its frontispiece, he says, the following inscription appears: “Acts of the holy Fifth Council of Constantinople, faithfully received.” He thinks the inscription erroneous, but he does so through ignorance—or rather lack of consideration—of the matters we have explained above.

The Latin evidence is supplied by the collection of councils of Merlin, Surius, and Crabbe. In these, not only the synod of Mennas against Anthimus but also other earlier synods are entitled by the name of the Fifth Synod. Hence this very Fifth Synod is said in such collections to have been held under Agapetus, Silverius, and Vigilius.

I have no doubt that many more manuscript codices preserve precisely what was seen either by Binius or by the other three editors of the councils. But very few Greek manuscripts were brought to the West, because of the ancient Latins’ ignorance of the Greek language. The Latin manuscripts that have survived to our times contain, for the most part, what I have just reported.

Moreover, I do not recall ever having read anywhere in the Latin manuscripts about the judgment concerning Origen. Perhaps, since the errors of the Origenists were less known in the West, the synodical judgment against them was sought with less diligence. Similarly, in the East, since the Pelagian heresy concerning grace was less well known, the Greeks were less concerned to seek out synodical decisions against the Pelagians. Thus such canons are scarcely found—if indeed they are found—in these Greek books before the eleventh or twelfth century, when John Zonaras and Theodore Balsamon lived.

The fourth question is whether it should not rightly be regarded as unheard-of and unusual to combine three synods into one ecumenical council when two of them were particular. Whoever thinks so will easily lay aside his astonishment if he remembers, first, that the synods he calls particular may rightly be called ecumenical. For, as was shown earlier, they followed the definition of the apostolic see; they may properly be said to have been equivalent to the pure execution of the decrees of the supreme pontiffs Agapetus and Vigilius; and they had the agreement of all the patriarchs, as we have stated.

Then, if the matter is to be judged by example, did not several African councils in Augustine’s time coalesce into that single council which is called the council of 418? Certainly Augustine names several councils that others count as one, as we showed in Dissertation 2 of the first part of the works of Marius Mercator.

Again, in the age of our fathers, were not the episcopal assemblies held over a period of twenty-four years—partly at Ferrara and partly at Trent—called by the single name of the Council of Trent, although they were held in different places, under three pontiffs and two emperors, to abolish various heresies and abuses?

If several and highly diverse assemblies are called by the one name of the Council of Trent because they were all directed toward one end, namely, the reformation of the Church, why should not three assemblies, likewise directed toward one end—namely, the peace of the Church—convened to suppress the disturbances of the Eutychians and Nestorians, confirmed by the decrees of the one emperor Justinian, held approximately during the time of the one Pope Vigilius, in the one imperial city, under the presidency of the bishop of the one see of Constantinople, likewise be called by one name?

What is surprising about three assemblies being counted under one name and contained in one codex when they were held over a shorter period than the Council of Trent? The latter was completed over a period of seventeen years; the former lasted twenty-four years. Yet the three were convened for one purpose, by one emperor, in the time of one pope, in one city, by the bishop of one see.

## CHAPTER VI. Some Observations on the Acts of the Fifth Synod

There is scarcely any synod whose acts require an attentive student of ecclesiastical criticism to make more observations, if he wishes to draw the truth out of the darkness in which it has been enveloped partly by the perplexing manner in which the whole affair was conducted on both sides, and partly by the devices of Theodore of Cappadocia, who produced many instruments in accordance with his own ingenuity.

I have subjected each item to a more careful examination. Since these matters would enlarge the dissertation beyond due measure, I have decided to defer them to another small work, while bringing forward three as specimens, so that the promised number of chapters might be maintained and certain popular opinions might be removed.

### § I. On the Day on Which the Synod Began

In the published codices the beginning of the synod is said to have taken place on the fourth day before the Nones of May, that is, 4 May. In the Beauvais manuscript it is the third day before the Nones, that is, 5 May. The latter reading is preferable, since in the year 553 the dominical letter was E, and consequently the fourth day before the Nones was a Sunday, while the third was Monday. According to ancient custom, synods began on the Monday after the divine service had properly been celebrated on Sunday.

The same pattern is found with the Council of Chalcedon on 8 October, when the dominical letter was G; with the Council of Ephesus on 22 June 431, when the dominical letter was D; with the First Council of Constantinople on 24 May 381, when the dominical letter was C; and with the Council of Nicaea on 14 June 325, when the dominical letter was C.

The acts of the first and second sessions of the conference demonstrate this reading of the Beauvais codex. On the day when the synod began, the patriarchs approached Vigilius with the other bishops, asking him to meet with them. Vigilius promised that he would respond on the following day. On that following day—which was the second after the synod had begun—the patriarchs returned to Vigilius. Yet they say that they returned to him two days before the second conference was held. Since the latter took place on the eighth day before the Ides of May, the first must necessarily have taken place on the third day before the Nones. This agrees completely with the reading of the Beauvais codex and not at all with the common reading.

### § II. On the List of Bishops in the First Conference

When the names of the bishops who were present are listed at the beginning of the first conference, they are arranged in a different order [Col. 1091C] from that in which they are subscribed at the end of the eighth conference. For example, Thalelaeus, bishop of Isindus, is entered after Macarius of Prymnessus and Megalius of Myra, although in the subscriptions he appears long before them. Valerianus of Obba in Africa precedes Cresconius, likewise bishop of Cuicul in Africa, by several names in the heading, but follows him in the subscription, and so on.

The argument, therefore, that some people derive from the order in which the bishops are listed in the acts of councils as they now exist, in order to estimate the years of earlier or later episcopal ordination, is weak and indeed so deceptive that it recently led a certain critic into intolerable errors. This will be demonstrated with incontestable evidence from the African Church’s own codex in a small work soon to be published, and in another that will follow concerning the bishops of Africa.

The necessity of undertaking that work reluctantly compels me to reply, in accordance with Solomon’s prescription, to a detractor who

> “not only slandered words”—I use Jerome’s expression concerning an importunate monk, in the prefaces to books 1 and 3 of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*—“but even the syllables of words, thinking that he knew something if he disparaged the works of others, and interpreting our patience, which comes from the humility of Christ, as a sign of a bad conscience.”

### § III. On the Synod of Mopsuestia Inserted into the Acts of the Fifth Synod

The synod of Mopsuestia was convened in the year 550, and therefore 123 years after Theodore’s death. He died his natural death in the year 427, while the two sacred letters by which the synod was summoned are recorded as having been issued in the ninth year after the consulship of Basil.

All the prelates of the Second Cilicia were present, as was the entire clergy of the Church of Mopsuestia, together with the leading citizens, at least those advanced in age. John, bishop of Anazarbus and metropolitan of the province, presided.

The entire business was completed in a single session, on 17 June. The diptychs of the Church of Mopsuestia were examined, and the elders were questioned so that it might be discovered when and for what reason Theodore’s name had been erased from the sacred registers.

The emperor was interested in learning this so that he might answer Vigilius, who refused to condemn Theodore on the grounds that he had died in the peace of the Church and had not been condemned by any synod. Justinian therefore wanted the matter reported both to himself and to Vigilius, and the acts of the council sent to them. This was done through the two synodical letters.

All these facts are established both by Justinian’s summons and by the acts of the council. They testify that the name was no longer present in the diptychs, but that the time and reason for its erasure were nevertheless unknown.

The synodical booklet mentions a synod of Mopsuestia in which, unless it is a different synod, everything was carried out very differently from the account given in the acts inserted into the Fifth Synod. For the prelates are said to have assembled at Mopsuestia voluntarily and out of zeal for the faith; to have questioned each of the elders judicially whether Theodore’s name had ever been inscribed in the sacred registers; and, when the elders had answered affirmatively, to have reported the matter to Vigilius, the Roman pontiff.

What if there were two synods of Mopsuestia, one remembered by the synodical book and the other by the acts of the Fifth Synod? What if Vigilius ordered one to be held and Justinian the other: Vigilius, to discover whether Theodore had ever been entered in the sacred diptychs; Justinian, to determine whether he had been erased? What if Vigilius wished the first to be convened in order to establish from it his own judgment that Theodore’s person should not be condemned, while Justinian ordered the second in order to weaken the authority of the first? In an obscure matter, one can only conjecture.

In any case, whether there was one synod of Mopsuestia or two, it was held after Facundus had completed his twelve books defending the Three Chapters, indeed after his separate work against Mocianus. For he would certainly not have remained silent about a matter that would have brought so much prejudice to his case in either direction. Facundus therefore completed his books around the year 548, or even before Justinian’s tyrannical ferocity against Vigilius burst into the open.

The name of Theodore remained for some time in the diptychs; otherwise Cyril would not have written the things found in his letter to John of Antioch concerning Theodore’s reputation in the minds of the Easterners. It was retained until Theodoret’s death, which occurred in the year 457. For how could Theodoret have allowed his Cilician friends to commit such an act against a man whom he everywhere regarded as divine?

Nevertheless, it did not remain until the year 490. For when Martyrius, the most senior of the presbyters of the Church of Mopsuestia, was questioned in the synod of 550, he swore under oath that, although he had served in the clergy of the Church of Mopsuestia for sixty years, he had never heard Theodore’s name mentioned among the bishops in the diptychs. Indeed, it does not seem to have remained even until the year 484. Otherwise that old man would have heard something about so great an affair if, when he was enrolled in the clergy, the memory of it had still been recent.

It must therefore have happened during the interval between the year 457 and the year 480 or 484.

Certain members of the clergy, moreover, such as Theodore and Parenorius—one of whom had spent fifty-five years and the other twenty-eight years in the clergy—stated that they had learned from their elders that Cyril’s name had been substituted for Theodore’s. This can reasonably be said to have occurred during the period just mentioned.

I cannot determine with certainty the time when Cyril, after Theodore’s name had been erased, was entered in the diptychs. It nevertheless seems probable that this happened when the Eutychians were at the height of their power. They were powerful when Basiliscus seized the tyranny and restored the Cnaphaeus to the Church of Antioch in the year 475; when the emperor Zeno issued the *Henotikon* in the year 482; and when, after Calendio had been expelled from Antioch, the Cnaphaeus was again restored to the see from which he had been removed, around the year 484.

At the time when the Eutychians were powerful, I say, and when disturbances were raging in Cilicia and the Acephalous heresy was gaining strength, I seem not to conjecture rashly that Theodore’s name was erased from the diptychs when, after Calendio’s expulsion, the Cnaphaeus invaded the Church of Antioch.

For what was not permitted in turbulent times? What would the Eutychian Cnaphaeus, the most celebrated adversary of his own heresy, not dare to do against Theodore? What would the clergy of Mopsuestia not endure amid arms and under their most powerful exarch, whose name would more readily have been substituted for Theodore’s than Cyril’s, by whom the Eutychians falsely claimed to be authorized?

At what time could the memory of so daring an act have been more easily erased than when everything, both imperial and ecclesiastical, was in confusion throughout the Eastern diocese, and when the people of Mopsuestia could readily agree with the Antiochenes, who had long been ruled by followers of Eutyches?

At that time, it seems, the old diptychs were removed and replaced with new ones. For those produced at the council were certainly not the old diptychs. Otherwise the Cilicians would have discovered either on the erased parchment or beneath the coating of the sheets some trace of Theodore’s name, and they would not have omitted to report it with the great ἀκρίβεια—“exactness”—of which they boast.

Perhaps this is why the bishops repeatedly asked the *cimiliarch* whether he had diptychs older than those produced, and, when he denied it, forced him to confirm his answer “by producing the divine Scriptures.”

Among the bishops listed in the diptychs of Mopsuestia, it would be pointless to look for Macedonius, who was attached to the Arian heresy. Only those who had died “from the time when the immaculate and orthodox faith was proclaimed in the Church of Mopsuestia” are listed. By “the faith,” I mean the Nicene faith, which among the ancients is understood simply by the name “faith,” ἁπλῶς.

That Macedonius, after participating in the Council of Nicaea, prolonged his life until approximately the year 350 is shown by the fact that he is said to have subscribed to the council at Sardica in the year 345. Consequently, Protogenes and Zosimus, who succeeded Macedonius and preceded Olympius, do not appear to have held the episcopal see for more than thirty years, since Olympius, who succeeded Zosimus, participated in the Second General Council in the year 381.

Olympius governed the Church of Mopsuestia until the year 391, when he died. Theodore succeeded Olympius and held the episcopate for thirty-six years. Thomas succeeded Theodore after twenty-two or twenty-three years, for Bassianus is recorded as having had a vicar at the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451.

Bassianus himself, and those who follow him in the diptychs—John, Auxentius, Palatinus, Jacobus, Zosimus, and the younger Theodore—presided over the Church of Mopsuestia until the year 547. For that Theodore is said in the records to have died three years earlier. Simeon, the last of all, died in the very thirteenth indiction in which the synod convened, after holding the episcopate for three years.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Confirmation of the Fifth Synod by the Bishops of the Apostolic See

In this matter too I have completed my work, not without care, in a small book soon to be published. For I investigated more exactly each of the pontiffs down to the time of the Sixth Synod. After that, nothing remains to be dealt with, since there exist professions of faith made by the supreme pontiffs at their ordination, in which they receive the Fifth Synod and honor it with the same reverence as the earlier councils. We shall publish these professions shortly.

For the present I shall discuss only Vigilius’s letter confirming the synod, which the distinguished archbishop of Paris, Peter de Marca, brought to light from the Royal Library in 1642.

This letter is said to have been given before the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the twenty-seventh year of Justinian’s reign and after the twelfth consulship of Basil—that is, on 8 December 553, six months after the synod had been completed.

The distinguished editor proves by several substantial arguments that it is not a forgery. First, he says, it was copied from a volume [Col. 1094A] written by hand and preserved in the old library of the Roman Church from the year 753 onward. It was copied, he adds, in the year of Christ 1276 by a man of distinguished learning, Leo Cinnomus, and at the same time commended, together with several other works and especially the acts of the Fifth Synod, to the imperial Greek library. The letter had been appended to those acts.

Second, Evagrius, in Book IV of his *History*, chapter 34, wrote that Vigilius agreed with the Fifth Synod ἐγγράφως—“in writing.” What other written document could this be? Evagrius’s authority is all the weightier because he composed his history closer to the time of the synod, namely thirty years afterward.

Third, Photius, Zonaras, Cedrenus, Euthymius, and Nicephorus Callistus report that Vigilius agreed with the Fifth Synod. They could have obtained this information nowhere else than from the acts of the Fifth Synod, which contained the decretal appended to them.

Fourth, the Sixth Synod, in its *Prosphoneticus* addressed to Pogonatus, says that Vigilius agreed with Justinian, just as it says that Leo I agreed with Marcian.

Finally, Pelagius II, in his letter to the bishops of Istria, says that the apostolic see, after long struggles for the Three Chapters and after enduring many things, finally yielded “when the truth made itself manifest.” These are the very grounds Vigilius gives for rescinding his decree: a light had shone upon him, “every confusion of mind having been removed.”

Nevertheless, those who regard the letter as suspect bring forward serious arguments on their own behalf and weaken the arguments of the distinguished editor considerably by turning them to their own side.

First, they say that this decretal contains many things that are not merely contrary to the dignity of the apostolic see but false and foolish.

For what could be more disgraceful than for the Vicar of Christ to confess that, in the matter he had debated in his council, he had been “impelled by the devil to compose many things both in speech and in writing”; that through the devil’s deceit he had been separated from his brothers; that, “having disregarded charity, he had gone into discord”; that he had previously had “confusion in his mind,” and so forth?

What could be more false than the claim that, at the time when the decretal was issued—that is, six months after the synod had been completed—“the whole world and the Church had been recalled to peace,” and that Vigilius had then, for the first time, recognized Theodore’s blasphemies in the full light that had been shed upon them?

For it is certain that, after the synod had been completed, the whole of the West was in turmoil, and that in his *Constitutum* he had marked each individual chapter of Theodore with a note.

How inappropriately is Augustine’s example introduced to excuse a change of opinion! Augustine’s case and Vigilius’s scarcely possess any resemblance. Augustine was merely one bishop; Vigilius was the head of the Church. Augustine was the teacher of one Church in his own person; Vigilius was the teacher of the entire world. Augustine retracted works written by a private individual; Vigilius retracted a decretal sent from a synod to all the faithful of the world.

Augustine specifically corrected only what he had written as a layman, or at least before becoming a bishop; he merely revised the rest. Vigilius is said to have corrected what he had published after almost seventeen years in the pontificate. Augustine corrected what he had composed on various subjects; Vigilius corrected what he had defined after mature consultation and judgment with his brothers.

Second, they say it is surprising that Leo Cinnomus, when he testifies that he found the letter in question in a paper volume preserved in the old library of the Roman Church, reported only this and omitted the remaining circumstances.

Why did he not say whether he had found and copied a Greek letter there? Or whether he had translated it from Greek into Latin? If he found a Greek letter but not a Latin one, the narrator’s credibility is rightly suspect. For why should it not be thought to have been composed either by Cinnomus himself or by some other little Greek? Why is the Roman pontiff’s letter nowhere found in Latin, and why is it certainly mentioned by no Latin author?

If he translated it from Latin into Greek, another basis for a very reasonable suspicion arises: did he translate it in good faith or otherwise? Did he add from himself things that are inappropriate, or did he find them in the original?

Certainly, if the Latin decretal still existed in the library of the Roman Church in the year 753—that is, two hundred years after the synod had ended—how did it escape the notice of Vigilius’s successors? If it did not escape their notice, why did they not mention it, when they especially ought to have done so at the time when Pelagius II and Gregory the Great were arguing more vigorously against the schismatics? This is the third argument advanced by those who reject the letter.

They add a fourth: the signs of forgery appear unmistakable. For, besides what has already been explained, Vigilius is introduced in an unlearned manner as adducing the example of his Fathers, who had retracted and corrected their own statements. By “Fathers,” I think, he means his predecessors, as can be gathered from the *Constitutum*. But which of his predecessors retracted and corrected his own statements? Hormisdas? He alone seems capable of being cited. Yet his reasoning differs astonishingly from Vigilius’s, as every learned person knows.

Moreover, when Augustine is set forth as an example for the pontiff to imitate, the master of Roman eloquence is proclaimed—imprudently, not to say ineptly. This is not, however, of very great importance, since perhaps the text should be read not as εὐγλωττίας διδάσκαλος, “teacher of eloquence,” but as εὐδοξίας διδάσκαλος, “teacher of distinction” or “good repute.” In this sense Hormisdas wrote to Possessor that from Augustine one could learn what the Roman Church believed “concerning free will and the grace of God.”

What presses more heavily is that, contrary to public report and known truth, the letter says that Theodore’s speeches had been refuted everywhere at the time when Vigilius wrote. At that time, not only Africa but also many of the Easterners were fighting in defense of Theodore’s books.

Moreover, the three later canons concerning Theodore, Theodoret, and Ibas are copied almost word for word from the decree and the synod, so that the pontiff appears to swear by the very words of those whom he opposed when exercising judgment against them. By doing so, he seems to confess that his former mind had been either blind or obstinate.

Certainly, if the pontiff really wrote the letter, he either acted with extreme imprudence, since he did not safeguard the dignity of his see despite having a circle of the most learned men assisting him, or he suffered the harshest necessity of writing from the tyranny of Justinian, who himself obeyed his own teachers. If the letter was extorted by force and fear, it possesses no authority.

Finally, they add that the arguments brought forward on the other side have no greater weight than what they borrow from the authority of the distinguished de Marca.

First, what the Greeks report—that Vigilius agreed with the Fifth Synod ἐγγράφως—may, or even should, be understood either of his first letters to Eutychius, by which the pontiff agreed to the celebration of the synod; or of the *Constitutum*, in which all the matters condemned in the Fifth Synod are condemned, except the person of Theodore; or even of a judgment issued long before, which was the cause of the disturbances in the West, and which the little Greeks seized upon in order to furnish abundant witnesses for their own fiction.

Nor is such an exception rash. It is supported by what the distinguished de Marca adduces from the *Prosphoneticus* of the Sixth Synod. For that passage concerns the agreement of Vigilius and Justinian by which the synod was convened: συνέστη συνέδριον—“the assembly was constituted.”

Next, the same most illustrious scholar adds, under number 3, that “to his preceding arguments may be added the outstanding testimony of Pelagius II, from his letter to the bishops of Istria. Its words are so clear that one may wonder how men otherwise exceptionally perceptive could have missed so explicit a statement concerning Vigilius. For there it is reported at length that the Apostolic See, through Vigilius, at first approved the Three Chapters and labored for their defense for a long time, even contending for them over an extended period and to the point of suffering insults—something that can be understood only of Vigilius [Col. 1096A]. Then it yielded, WHEN THE TRUTH REVEALED ITSELF; these words refer to Vigilius’s letter, in which he writes that, after the matter had been examined more carefully, the truth had shone upon him and that he had condemned the Three Chapters.” This whole argument, I say, does not press very forcefully. For those exceptionally perceptive men may perhaps object that Pelagius II’s words, since they are not reported κατὰ λέξιν—that is, literally—are not being fully explained. The passage under number 3 reads as follows:

“For Latin men, indeed, who were ignorant of Greek, because they did not know the language, recognized the error only slowly; and the more quickly they ought to have been believed, the more their steadfastness did not cease from the struggle until they learned the truth. Your Fraternity would certainly have despised their agreement if, with reckless haste, they had agreed before learning the truth. But after they had labored for a long time and had contended for an extended period, even to the point of suffering insults, let your Fraternity therefore consider that they would not suddenly have abandoned so many labors unless they had recognized what was true.”

And shortly afterward:

“Your Belovedness must therefore consider that the agreement of our predecessors in this matter was not afterward empty, inasmuch as previously it had labored under the harsh burdens of contradiction.”

And later:

“If, in the matter of the Three Chapters, one thing was said while the truth was being sought, but another after the truth had been discovered, why is a change of opinion charged as a crime against this See, which the whole Church humbly venerates in its author? For it is not a change of opinion, but the disposition of inconstancy, that is at fault. When, therefore, the intention remains unchangeable in seeking knowledge of what is right, what objection is there if, abandoning its ignorance, it changes its words?”

The discussion concerns, in fact, both the truth “which Pope Vigilius and the leaders of the Latin provinces did not know,” and the error recognized only slowly because of ignorance of the Greek language. Such hidden truth or unknown error undoubtedly concerned Theodore’s blasphemies and the opinions of Theodoret and Ibas. When the former became apparent and the latter was recognized, Vigilius changed the judgment which he had issued on the road by which he was traveling from Rome to Constantinople in favor of the Three Chapters: he changed it in the *Judicatum*, issued after one year, and in the *Constitutum*, issued after seven years, condemning everything contained in the Three Chapters except the persons.

For what the most learned prelate argues concerning a twofold truth previously unknown to Vigilius and later disclosed—namely, that the first truth made it possible to retract everything done in the councils, apart from the faith, while the second made it possible to condemn deceased persons who had professed heresy—will scarcely, I think, persuade anyone who either remembers the history of the matter or has read Pelagius II’s letter. Neither truth was hidden because of ignorance of the Greek language. The latter had been approved before the publication of the *Constitutum*, in Conference 5, by the testimony of sacred Scripture and Augustine; the former is established by the explicit words of Leo the Great. Therefore the change of opinion mentioned by Pelagius refers altogether to the *Judicatum*, or rather to the *Constitutum*. This is confirmed even by the witnesses produced by the most illustrious prelate himself.

For Photius, writing about Vigilius, says:

“He was present in the City, but did not take part in the synod. Although he was not altogether favorably disposed toward the assembly of the sacred council, nevertheless he confirmed the common faith of the Fathers in a written statement.”

And the following passage from the Arabic manuscript of the canons:

“The synod excommunicated both the living and the dead—something not previously done except against those alone—and this was done with the knowledge of the Roman patriarch, who also confirmed it and, in a written document delivered to the emperor, professed his faith.”

These statements must be understood of the *Constitutum* sent to the emperor, whose censure confirms the faith contained in the canons of the Fathers, not of the decretal letter sent to Eutychius.

These are, in general, the arguments of both sides. Anyone who examines them more carefully, even if he does not reject—as certainly he ought not—the very serious judgment of the most illustrious Marca concerning Vigilius’s letter, will nevertheless not approve it in such a way—as the recent dissertationist did—as to suppose that from it an invincible argument may be drawn by which the “rashness of Halloix,” who denied that the synod had immediately been approved by Vigilius, might be exposed.

## ADDENDUM

[Col. 1097]

## FRAGMENT OF VICTOR OF CAPUA ON THE PASCHAL CYCLE

*(From Book 49 of the Venerable Bede, on the Reckoning of Time.) (C,S)*

After criticizing Victor’s paschal cycle, Bede continues in the passage cited:

“But lest those who favor Victor tear us apart for having attacked him rashly, let them read the book of the most learned and holy man, namely Victor, bishop of Capua, concerning Easter—which he thought ought to be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, when Basil was proconsul for the ninth time—and they will discover how highly his teacher was esteemed by prudent and Catholic doctors of the Church. The beginning of his book is as follows:

‘When we were diligently seeking to determine on what day in particular the revered solemnity of Easter would occur during the present year’s thirteenth indiction, and, in accordance with the constitutions of the venerable Fathers, were saying that the Lord’s resurrection ought beyond doubt to be celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May [Col. 1098], our answer seemed wholly unreasonable to certain people, because a certain Victor, in the paschal cycle which he published, had assigned another day for the Lord’s resurrection, although he also designated the day which we likewise profess ought to be celebrated.’

And later in the work:

‘But now, I say, the order of the discussion requires that I clearly disclose the errors of the cycles which Victor published, since he does not know how to determine the lawful day of Easter. Thus, once it has been shown that he erred in this way in the past, he may lack authority in the present and future and lose the opportunity for false persuasion.’”

Prosody.—*A*: if lengthened, it indicates gravity; if shortened, sweetness, 123.—*Abraham*: middle syllable lengthened, sometimes the first two shortened, 188.—*Adam*: first syllable both long and short, 162.—*Advenis*: final syllable short, 20.—*Ariete*: trisyllabic, 28.—*Calceamenta*: antepenultimate syllable short, 162.—*Corrigia*: antepenultimate syllable long, 174.—*Davidis*: second syllable short; also in *Davidicus*, 173.—*Desero*: final syllable shortened, 23.—*Desino*: final syllable shortened, 23.—*Dii*: first syllable long; *Dei*: first syllable short, 181.—*Disco*: final syllable shortened, 23.—*E*: from ε it is lengthened; from η it is shortened, 27.—*Ecclesia*: antepenultimate syllable shortened, and sometimes also trisyllabic, 21, 22.—*Ergo*: final syllable short, 13, 25.—*Eremus*: penultimate syllable short, 27.—*Esuris*: final syllable short, 20.—[Col. 1109] *Fame*: final syllable lengthened, 103.—*Fio*: first syllable short, 255.—*Florianus*: first syllable short, 1.—*H*: lengthens the preceding short syllable, 88.—*Idolum*: middle syllable short, 85, 265.—*Is* in *pervenis*, *advenis*, *nescis*, *esuris*: shortened, 20, 81.—*Israel*: middle syllable lengthened, or also trisyllabic, 84.—*Jordanes*: middle syllable long, 67.—*Macedo*, *Macedonius*: second syllable long, 191.—*Maria*: middle syllable lengthened, 50.—*Melite*: middle syllable long, 256.—*Nescis*: final syllable short, 20, 81.—*O*: shortened in *ergo*, 13, 25; shortened from ω, 27; short in *desero*, *disco*, *desino*, 23; short in the final syllable of first-conjugation futures, 26.—*Obex*: first syllable short; *objex*: first syllable long, 274.—*Pariete*: trisyllabic, 28.—*Pervenis*: final syllable short, 20.—*Petiturus*: antepenultimate syllable short, 40.—*Pharao*: middle syllable long, 258, 265.—*Pilatus*: first syllable both long and short, 96.—*Psalterium*: antepenultimate syllable short, 27.—*Quomodo*: first two syllables short, 262.—*Refert*: lengthens the first syllable, 252.—*Sabellius*: first syllable both long and short, 155.—*Sacrificium*: second syllable lengthened, 236.—*Siloa*: has three possible quantities, 143.—*Simon*: first syllable both long and short, 126.—*Simonis*: middle syllable both long and short, 126.—*Solvo*: final syllable shortened, 23.—*Spado*: first syllable both long and short, 130.—*Thema*: first syllable long, 27, 205.—*Triduana*: first syllable long, 136.

**Chapter XXVIII.**—Concerning adulterous desire. Ibid.

**Chapter XXIX.**—Concerning divorce. Ibid.

**Chapter XXXVI.**—Concerning not storing up treasures on earth. Ibid.
